Madison Square Garden’s James Dolan Is Spending Big on New York’s Governor Race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee for New York governor, promised last November to erect a wall of spy gear, license plate readers, and biometric surveillance between the city and the suburbs. He has since received millions of dollars in donations from the family and businesses of James Dolan, the owner of Madison Square Garden, where a network of cameras capture the faces of (nearly) every patron who walks in the arena and corporate security forces hunt for critics of the boss.
Dolan’s support of Blakeman, the executive of suburban Nassau County, could be seen as something of a counterintuitive move in a state long run by Democrats, and in a year when political surveys are picking up indications of a blue wave. He’s down by nine points or more in most polls.
Blakeman, however, backs data centers, AI deepfakes, Flock surveillance, ICE, private militias, and president Donald Trump. All of which makes him at least somewhat simpatico with Dolan, the Trump-allied magnate operating the sports world’s best-known surveillance state. Dolan has long been a mercurial presence in the political game, and in fact, as Politico notes, he supported Blakeman’s opponent, Governor Kathy Hochul, during the last election. Dolan’s sheer amount of spending in the race could also benefit him, even if his preferred candidate loses.
Long an outsized force in sports and entertainment, Dolan now has a chance at a major political role, too.
“Dolan can step into the breach and become the biggest player in [New York’s] Republican politics, donor-wise, and I'm sure his people are smart enough to know that,” one veteran strategist tells WIRED.
James Dolan has given heavily before, including nearly a million dollars to Trump’s reelection campaign and the Republican National Committee in the 2020 election cycle. But the New York governor’s race represents another level, a review of city, state, and federal databases shows.
The Dolan family has given $108,000 to Blakeman’s campaign directly and another $970,000 to the local Nassau County Republican party, which in turn has become Blakeman’s single-largest contributor. But that’s just for starters. MSG entities have contributed another $2 million to a political action committee supporting Blakeman’s run. That super PAC, Strong and Safe New York Inc., which lists Madison Square Garden’s top government relations executive as an officer, has raised $5.3 million overall. That helped make up for a 9-to-1 cash advantage that the governor’s campaign reported over her challenger’s at the last filing deadline in July.
Dolan and MSG’s bankrolling of Blakeman could come with risks, however. Opposition to Dolan’s use of facial recognition has hit a new peak locally, where a majority of the City Council are now in favor of a bill to rein in biometric surveillance. State lawmakers introduced a bill to end the property tax break that has been worth over a billion dollars to Madison Square Garden. The federal government has agreed to take over the $8 billion renovation of the train station below Madison Square Garden—a project that could pay Dolan’s company $500 million or more. But multiple sources note that state and local authorities will likely continue to have a say.
Meanwhile, the New York attorney general’s investigation into MSG’s deployment of facial recognition continues to progress, a source familiar with the matter tells WIRED. And while mayor Zohran Mamdani’s critiques of Dolan’s security practices have been muted, so far, there are signs that may be changing. One of his commissioners said last month that “this kind of mass surveillance opens the door to abuse and discrimination.”
(Madison Square Garden, which did not respond to a request to comment for this story, filed a defamation suit in July against WIRED and this reporter over our coverage of its operations.)
Dolan’s friction with state and local officials is coming at what should be a peak moment for the mogul: the long-suffering basketball team he owns, the New York Knicks, recently won their first title in 53 years. And yet, during the Knicks’ run in the NBA Finals, his organization fought with the mayor and the police commissioner over security procedures around the Garden. In the days leading up to the championship parade down Broadway, a source with knowledge of the preparations tells WIRED, Dolan’s team tussled with the governor’s and the mayor’s for control over the event, particularly over who got to be on stage and in the audience as the players were presented with keys to the city at City Hall.
“Dolan micromanaged the Knicks parade like it was his own sweet sixteen,” the source tells WIRED.
Dolan and Blakeman, on the other hand, have in recent years demonstrated a host of common interests, common enemies, and one extremely prominent mutual friend. In June, Trump came to the Garden for game three of the Finals; Blakeman joined the president of the United States and the team’s owner in the luxury box. Two months later, in mid-August, Strong and Safe New York released an ad calling on Hochul to stop blaming the state’s problems on Trump. (Strong and Safe, which is also supporting James’ opponent in the attorney general’s race this year, recently sent $83,400 to her former employers, the Republican law firm behind Kanye West’s presidential bid in 2020.)
Blakeman has been one of the state’s most enthusiastic implementers of Trump’s mass deportation machine, ordering local detectives to work with ICE and opening up the county’s jails for those caught up in the crackdown. (Less than 5 percent of the immigrants jailed had violent criminal records, a Newsday investigation found.) He recruited dozens of armed “special deputies,” which looked a whole lot like a personal militia to critics. And when Mamdani won his New York mayoral election last November, Blakeman promised to erect a wall of surveillance along the city line to keep suburban residents safe. “We are installing technology along the border of New York City that will read license plates, that will have facial recognition, that will have video cameras,” he told Fox News. Since then, drivers in Nassau County have become some of the most surveilled in the nation, with a Flock Safety camera for every 9.5 miles of road, according to the DeFlock activist group.
Dolan has been aggressive in his deployment of surveillance at his venues, which include the Sphere in Las Vegas and Radio City Music Hall in Manhattan. Arrays of surveillance security cameras tied to a video management system running a facial recognition program are a major reason why MSG “is the most secure venue in the country,” Dolan has previously said.
“They’re in the same mindset that surveillance is good for business,” Brad Hoylman-Sigal, the Manhattan borough president, says of Blakeman and Dolan. “And I don’t know how that's a winning political issue.”
For the majority of more than three decades in politics, Blakeman presented himself as a moderate as he launched unsuccessful bids for state comptroller, US House and Senate seats, and even New York City mayor. Then in 2021, Blakeman went full MAGA, and won his Nassau County Executive race by 2,000 votes. He’s been tied to Trump and the Trumpists ever since, starting with an all-out push behind MAGA megadonor Miriam Adelson’s multibillion plan to build a casino on the site of the Nassau Coliseum. The bid was ultimately withdrawn.
Hochul’s recent political journey has gone in something like the opposite direction. Once considered a conservative Democrat, she’s become a vocal Trump critic; passed a law banning local cops from cooperating with ICE (a move Blakeman said was “written with the blood of the victims of illegal migrants,” before reluctantly complying with it; and put in place the country’s first statewide data center moratorium (Blakeman called that “crazy,” while using AI to lampoon Hochul in his TV spots).
Dolan largely stayed out of last year’s mayor’s race. But an MSG political action committee, the Coalition to Restore New York, dumped more than $400,000 into 11 local City Council races. Seven of them won, and all but one lined up to support Julie Menin as City Council president, who was seen as a check on Mamdani’s power.
Menin now holds the power to bring the Council’s bill curbing facial recognition to a vote—or to let it die without one. Menin, who returned a Dolan donation in 2023, is currently undecided on how to proceed, the veteran strategist tells me. “She doesn't want to ban facial recognition”—and to be clear, the bill in the Council doesn’t aim to do that. “She thinks that it should be reformed, and that there should be guardrails and parameters,” the strategist says. (A Menin spokesperson did not reply to a request for comment.)
One longtime outside counsel for MSG has filed a flurry of lawsuits against the Mamdani administration, while a second former outside attorney has raised a million dollars for a political organization to counter the mayor’s agenda. John Catsimatidis, a billionaire Republican donor, indicated to Politico that Dolan’s backing of Blakeman could be seen as a move against Mamdani, of sorts. “Everybody believes the governor has oversight of the mayor,” he said. (Representatives for both the Hochul and Blakeman campaigns did not respond to requests to comment for this story. Neither did a City Hall spokesperson. But Mamdani did say on Monday that a candidate "who embraces ICE and has gone so far as to create, effectively, a private militia in Nassau County” is “in many ways the antithesis” of what New Yorkers want.)
The governor is not without her own well-funded allies, however. That includes Blakeman’s ex-wife Nancy Shevell, who’s now married to Paul McCartney. She donated $18,000 to Hochul. The Pegula family, which owns the NFL’s Buffalo Bills, has given her and the state Democratic Party nearly $175,000. (A small sum to pay, considering Hochul helped steer $600 million in state money into her hometown team’s new stadium.) Uber spent more than $12 million in a six-month period to a PAC supporting Hochul, who has proposed auto insurance reforms that the ride-share giant likes.
That’s way more than Dolan has devoted to his candidate so far. But what he has given appears to be the most money a Dolan-backed business has devoted to a political cause since it spent an estimated $30 million in 2004 to stop a football stadium from being built on Manhattan’s west side, a signature project by the mayor at the time, Michael Bloomberg. Dolan’s push was so effective, it caused the mayor to sputter in public. “You’d think,” the mayor fumed on his radio program, that “a company on corporate welfare would be less selfish to the city that has been so good to it.”
For that campaign, Dolan’s firm funded an outfit called the “New York Association for Better Choices,” which took out full-page ads in every city newspaper, ran anti-stadium commercials on local TV, and counted the lobbying firm of a former US senator as one of its many advocates. For this election, Dolan’s chosen candidate is relying heavily on AI. Blakeman’s ads featuring ersatz Hochuls hiding behind dumpsters, getting clowned by Mamdani, and producing BS. One recent anti-Hochul spot lifted footage from a comedian’s bit—shot in 2011 and criticizing the Republican leader of Wisconsin at the time. “Bruce Blakeman,” the progressive local news outlet Hell Gate proclaimed, “is the governor of slop.”

LONDON, October 1. /TASS/. The United Kingdom has expanded its anti-Russian sanctions regime, adding 23 individuals and legal entities, alongside eight vessels, according to the updated blacklist published by the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office.
The new designations target Alan Gagloev, President of South Ossetia; Marat Kambolov, Advisor to the Russian President; and Sergey Tolmachev, former Deputy Governor of the Zaporozhye Region. Sanctions were also imposed on the regional heads of the Movement of the First (Dvizheniye Pervykh) councils in the DPR, LPR, Kherson, and Zaporozhye regions, as well as Crimea.

The list also sweeps in officials and military personnel from the Zaporozhye and Kherson regions, Russian FSB officers, and the company Novatek Gas and Power Asia.
Under the restrictions, any assets or bank accounts belonging to the sanctioned individuals and entities in the UK will be frozen, and the listed individuals are subject to a travel ban.

Falling numbers: Thymaina's plunging population shows Greece's demographic decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:25:41 UTC
19:25:41 KST

Desertification in rural areas and on the islands is forcing schools to shut. On a small eastern Aegean island, locals speak of soaring costs, isolation and a future without children.
"Let's go to war!" shouted six-year-old Giorgos at his older cousin, Minas, as the two chased each other with claw-like geranium stalks around the schoolyard on the tiny Greek island of Thymaina.
The two boys are the last primary school children on the far-flung eastern Aegean island, 40 kilometres from the Turkish coast.
"When I was a boy, the school had nearly 70 children," 77-year-old Manolis Mitikas, owner of Thymaina's portside cantina, mused over a game of backgammon.
Like the rest of Greece, the former pirate hideout is facing the effects of an ageing population.
The education ministry said it was shuttering 43 nurseries and 32 primary schools this year "due to very low to non-existent" student numbers.
Another 70 nurseries were merged.
The challenge is even greater in small Aegean islands far from the Greek mainland.
"If we have no more children, the school will close...and unfortunately, we have no more children in Thymaina," Marigo Kottara, deputy mayor of the Fournoi archipelago of which the island is part, told the AFP news agency.
Greece last year recorded fewer than 66,000 births compared to more than 107,000 in 2005, with the population estimated to fall by more than a million to 9.2 million by 2050.
Thymaina no longer has a nursery and its high school closed years ago.
Six teenagers still living on the island take a boat to neighbouring Fournoi every morning.
Thymaina's sole teacher, Konstantinos Fantelas, has to teach the boys everything from Greek to maths, history, religion and music.
Thymaina is only served by two ferries a week linking it to the capital Athens, a journey that takes at least eight hours, with a final hop from Fournoi. The connection can frequently be disrupted by poor weather, leaving islanders stranded for days.
Pirate lore
Fournoi's cluster of islands off Samos have many secluded coves that for centuries were perfect for piracy.
The Mitikas family claims descent from the area's last known pirate, Emmanouil Mitikas, who was executed in the 1860s.
"The pirate Mitikas was my father-in-law's grandfather," said Maria Markaki, a restaurant owner in Fournoi.
"My husband is still a pirate, he can't get enough of the sea," she joked.
The waters around the island have over 60 known shipwrecks dating back to the 6th century BCE.
Municipal officials now hope that a decade-long culture ministry initiative to open underwater archaeology parks in the area will draw more visitors.
The first of three is to open next year, Kottara said.
Cash incentives
Greece's downsizing of schools has drawn complaints from neighbouring Turkey, which criticised Athens in July for closing down eight schools catering to the country's Turkish-speaking minority.
Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has described Greece's demographic problem as a "national danger."
His government, which faces elections next year, promised tax breaks this month to parents with three children and extra cash for parents who have more than three.
But with many Greek families making do with salaries of under €1,000 amid skyrocketing energy prices, some local officials are taking matters into their own hands.
Earlier this month Nisyros, a small Dodecanese island with a population of just over 1,000, said it would offer €3,000 for each child born to permanent residents.
"It is the message that Nisyros believes in its future and that future is our children," island mayor Christofis Koronaios said.
In Thymaina locals have waited for years for works to improve the island's harbour and dirt road network.
"What are we supposed to do, raise the Turkish flag?" asked one angry islander.

As rents rise, Berlin's underground scene feels the pinch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:23:39 UTC
19:23:39 KST

As rents rise, Berlin's underground scene feels the pinch
BERLIN, Oct 1 - Max Mohr, director of Zirkus Mond, an alternative circus troupe in Berlin, got his start putting on shows in abandoned buildings before finding a home on a piece of vacant ground in the northeast of the city.
Now after eight years, the developer who had let them use the land, near the hipster neighbourhood of Prenzlauer Berg, wants it back. So he is striking his tent and moving on with his troupe of jugglers, dancers and acrobats.
"It's sad but we knew it was going to come, and we found another place," Mohr said.
Over the past decade, Zirkus Mond, and a group of other associations with names like Kollage Kollektiv, Jonny Knueppel and Mucha gradually turned the stretch of no-man's-land called "die Greife" into a jumble of bars, open air discos and performance spaces.
"Here is where the magic happens, where you interact, where you can talk and where you can make plans and feel at home, feel seen," Mohr said.
In recent decades, as Berlin has grown into its role as the capital of a reunited Germany, prices have shot up and once relatively plentiful open spaces like die Greife have slowly disappeared.
Berlin's underground culture scene has always reflected economic upheaval and the dynamics of the local property market, ever since the days of the Weimar Republic, when hyperinflation wiped out savings, or during the Cold War, when students, punks and hippies moved into the enclosed Western half of the city.
In the years following the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, old warehouses and industrial sites provided artists with plenty of space for not much money, reinforcing the city's image of rough-edged cool.
BERLIN'S IDENTITY: 'RAW AND DIY'
Now the page has turned again. Last month, a far-left party won a Berlin state election, campaigning on a pledge to take over housing from corporate landlords and cap rents, which have soared as residential property prices have more than tripled in the past 15 years.
"This type of space used to be common in Berlin," said Elva Lebrun from the Mucha association. "It's also part of the essence and identity of Berlin, raw and also DIY – everything you see here is done by us."
Juan Migama, Zirkus Mond's Spanish-born artistic director, said the cost of housing was driving away many previously drawn to the city but he said Berlin remained "a very tolerant city, really open-minded."
Berliners' long familiarity with unusually dressed people engaged in not-easy-to-define artistic pursuits has bred a live-and-let-live attitude even among those with little interest in the alternative scene.
Ironically, even the city's sometimes cumbersome administration has worked in favour of alternative groups.
"Germans have a lot of rules, it's true. And because they have so many rules, they have rules that make these things possible," Migama said. "You can be in a kind of grey area, but as soon as you follow those rules, they let you be."
City interim usage rules allowed diskoBabel, the association which runs "die Greife", to set up on the land in the first place, although electricity is supplied by generators and there is no running water.
It is not a recipe for getting rich but people living outside the mainstream have always needed to overcome obstacles, Mohr said.
"If you want this lifestyle, you have to be very driven," he said. "It's maybe a lot of work, but it is possible to do this." REUTERS

Rogue AI agents tried and failed to hack US and Canadian government websites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:22:53 UTC
19:22:53 KST

Researchers cannot confidently say who was responsible, but evidence points to rogue Google and OpenAI agents carrying out a range of aggressive tactics to collect datasets and test their vulnerabilities.
Rogue AI agents attempted to hack US and Canadian government websites, according to non-profit research lab Transluce, with evidence suggesting that Google and OpenAI’s agents were responsible.
Two incidents in particular demonstrated aggressive techniques being used to access publicly available data from the US Department of Education’s Civil Rights Data Collection, and Library and Archives Canada, a Canadian federal agency, with both ultimately failing to compromise any data.
Transluce reports that the incidents are part of a “broader pattern of automated workflows” attributed to AI agents. “These workflows use aggressive or grey-area techniques to retrieve information from government websites, sometimes using sites in unintended ways or violating explicit usage policies,” the organisation’s researchers said.
Among the additional targets were the White House, Departments of War, Justice and Commerce, as well as the Centers for Disease Control and the Securities and Exchange Commission, and state agencies in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas, and New York.
In none of these cases, however, did agents gain access to information that was not already publicly available.
The latest findings come amid a growing number of reports of unexpected or unauthorised behaviour by AI agents.
In September alone, there have been two major incidents involving rogue OpenAI agents — the first involved agents leaking private user images to public websites, and the second with agents attempting to win access to government data in the US and Australia.
The company has since decided to delay the rollout of its next-generation Astra model after safety researchers flagged “critical” cybersecurity capabilities and unpredictable, unauthorised behaviour.
US and Canadian attempts
Agents attacked the US Department of Education on 17 June while looking up school statistics.
Transluce reports that the agents made more than 200,000 requests to the website, including a failed attempt to send deliberately flawed data to test the site’s database vulnerability and consequently bypass the site’s normal filters.
The researchers found that data stored on the website appeared to match a web search task in Google’s DeepSearchQA benchmark, which they say suggests the agents were not told to carry out hacking attacks but were “graded on their ability to successfully retrieve specific niche information from the internet”.
Transluce disclosed the attempted hack to the US Department of Education in September, with the department responding they had not seen any impact on their services.
AI agents made similar attempts on Library and Archives Canada in two separate incidents, on 28 May and later on 9 June.
The agents issued 899 “collection-search” requests for data relating to divorce records from 1905-1911, according to data picked up by the official Portuguese web archive Arquivo.pt.
Of the 899 requests, 13 carried attack payloads to test the website’s vulnerability. Again, none of the attempts on either occasion were successful.
Transluce says it cannot “confidently attribute” the attempts to Open AI, but the tactics were consistent with activity it had previously attributed to the company.
The organisation reported these incidents to the Canadian government earlier this week.
The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security issued a statement in response, saying “there is no indication that government systems have been compromised at this time.”
Transluce published its findings yesterday, after carrying out research using information from Arquivo.pt and urlquery.net, the free web-based security service for URL and domain scanning.

Corn, soybean prices surge amid fertilizer supply concerns, Middle East tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:21:23 UTC
19:21:23 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu, Ali Canberk Ozbugutu, and Emir Yildirim
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and resulting supply chain disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz have triggered a severe supply crunch in the global fertilizer market, driving up corn and soybean prices.
Diammonium phosphate, a key fertilizer for staple agricultural crops, surged 28.4% in the first nine months of the year to $802.5 per metric ton.
The rise from $625 per ton at the end of 2025 pushed up costs for major agricultural commodities, with corn prices rising 13.3% and soybeans 22.6%.
The de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz to maritime shipping constrained access to agricultural inputs, as around one-third of global fertilizer trade passes through the vital waterway under normal circumstances.
Conflicts in the Middle East threatening oil supplies and risks at critical chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz pushed up risk premiums in crude oil prices, driving up the cost of diesel fuel, one of the most basic inputs for agricultural production.
The fertilizer market has felt the strongest impact through rising natural gas and ammonia prices.
Farmers have been forced to use less fertilizer due to higher costs, in turn weighing on global yield expectations.
Kutay Guzgor, investment research director at Participation Bank Kuveyt Turk, told Anadolu that these supply shocks have extended well beyond urea-based nitrogen fertilizers.
“Diammonium phosphate fertilizer is affected by logistical bottlenecks, and that a significant portion of the sulfur and ammonia supplies vital for its production pass through the Strait of Hormuz creates persistent rigidity in phosphate fertilizer prices,” he said.
Guzgor said the logistical bottleneck risks cementing a structural decline in agricultural yield expectations as farmers are forced to compromise on their targeted fertilizer applications in the 2026-2027 planting season.
Despite a brief recovery in shipments amid a temporary US-Iran agreement, the subsequent collapse of the ceasefire and resurgence of hostilities in mid-July kept export volumes well below pre-war levels.
He noted that alternative global suppliers helped reduce the immediate supply gap by rerouting supply chains across longer distances, which continues to increase baseline freight costs.
He warned that a renewed spike in regional energy prices could lead to another surge in natural gas and nitrogen-based fertilizer prices.
Guzgor said he expects the impact of high fertilizer and energy costs on planting areas and productivity to be decisive next year.
“While fertilizer costs increase farmers’ production costs and squeeze profit margins, the prolonged persistence of high costs could lead to reduced fertilizer use, shifts in allocation, or a shift towards crops needing less fertilizer – a decrease in the use of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium may limit producer costs in the short term but ultimately pressure yields in the coming period,” he added.

Two Israelis arrested in Cyprus after over 27 kg. of ketamine, other drugs found in apartment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:19:40 UTC
19:19:40 KST

Two young Israelis, aged 23 and 24, were arrested in Limassol, Cyprus, after more than 27 kg. of ketamine and quantities of cocaine, MDMA, mephedrone, and cannabis were found in the apartment where they were staying, Cypriot media reported on Thursday.
A court on Thursday morning ordered that the two be remanded for eight days for investigative purposes. Their defense attorneys did not object to the police request. The two are exercising their right to remain silent and are not cooperating with investigators, according to local reports.
Police told the court that the two entered Cyprus on September 20 as tourists, with permission to remain in the country until December 19. On September 24, they rented an Airbnb apartment in the Amathus area of Limassol and were due to leave on September 29.
On Wednesday, the apartment's owner arrived at the property and found a suitcase, four sacks allegedly used for protein powder, and a vacuum-sealing device. When she opened the suitcase, she saw plant material and white powder, prompting her to call the police.
During the police operation, however, the two young men returned to the building and headed toward the apartment. When officers stopped them for questioning and identified themselves as police, the two allegedly resisted arrest.
Israeli suspect struck Cyprus officer, police say
According to police, one of the suspects struck an officer in the face, while the other pushed an officer and tried to flee. A member of YKAN, Cyprus's anti-narcotics unit, was lightly injured, suffering swelling to the lips and redness around one eye. He received medical treatment and was released.
The investigation is being handled by YKAN's Limassol district unit. Investigators are examining whether the case is connected to the seizure of approximately 390 kg. of ketamine in Limassol earlier in September.
During a search of the apartment, YKAN officers found 27 kg. and 507 gr. of ketamine, 377 gr. of cannabis, 776 gr. of mephedrone, 269 gr. of MDMA, and 172 gr. of cocaine. Police also seized approximately €10,000 in cash.
Cyprus Police confirmed the seizure and the ages of the two suspects, while Cypriot media identified them as Israelis.
The case has attracted particular interest in Cyprus because of the major drug seizure uncovered in the city earlier in September. According to Cyprus News, although the intelligence that led to the current operation was obtained independently, investigators are examining whether the new case is linked to the approximately 390-kg. ketamine case.
No connection between the two cases has been established so far.
Rental cars with money, drugs leads police to second apartment
A further development emerged on Thursday afternoon, when investigators found money and drugs in two rental cars during the course of the investigation. Keys that were discovered led police to a second apartment, where additional drugs were found.
According to the same report, police had already received prior intelligence indicating that the second apartment was being used for drug trafficking, further strengthening suspicions of a possible connection to the previous major case.
In the earlier case, Walla reported that those arrested included a 53-year-old Israeli man and his 51-year-old wife, as well as a Palestinian couple.
Information presented to the court at the time indicated suspicions that a network had been smuggling drugs from Israel to Cyprus using luxury vessels that arrived at marinas and ports in Larnaca and Limassol. The drugs were concealed, among other methods, as construction materials and sanitary products.
The investigation is ongoing.

Will Israel's Arab parties be banned from the election? The legal fight explained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:19:40 UTC
19:19:40 KST

With fewer than 30 days until Israelis go to the polls, the most consequential campaign battle may not be happening at rallies or on social media, but in a legal process most voters barely understand. On this week's episode of The Deep Dive, host Jacob Laznik sits down with legal affairs correspondent Sarah Ben-Nun to unpack a remarkable week at the Central Elections Committee, which voted to disqualify Ra'am, the Joint List and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh from the October 27 election, while rejecting petitions against Religious Zionism and Otzma Yehudit.
If those decisions survive Supreme Court review, a fifth of Israel's population could head into the election without a party of its own. Ben-Nun walks through the three grounds for disqualification set out in Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset, explaining in plain terms why the "armed struggle" clause has become the center of the fight, and why the Supreme Court has historically read the law so narrowly that disqualifications are rare.
The heart of the conversation is the case against Abu Shehadeh, built on an Arabic-language article he published on October 8, 2023, one day after the massacre committed by Hamas. Ben-Nun explains why this case stands apart from the others: Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara opposed disqualifying Ra'am, the Joint List, and MK Ofer Cassif, but after criticism of her initially noncommittal stance, her office came out on Tuesday in favor of barring Abu Shehadeh, though only under the armed struggle clause.
Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg also cast an unusual vote of his own. Yet Abu Shehadeh's legal team has raised a pointed question about timing: if the article was criminal, why did police never act on it, and why has it resurfaced only now, nearly three years later? The episode also reveals that the Attorney General's office found Otzma Yehudit came close to crossing the incitement-to-racism threshold, which raises the obvious and unresolved question of how anyone measures "close."
Legal measures behind the politics
What makes this episode essential viewing is that Laznik doesn't let the legal mechanics obscure the politics. He presses on whether a committee made up of sitting Knesset members can fairly judge their own rivals and coalition partners, and whether the mere filing of a petition brands a candidate in voters' minds long before any court rules.
Ben-Nun brings firsthand reporting from a meeting with Arab party leaders, who fear Election Day intimidation and voter suppression at a moment when polls point to unusually high Arab turnout. The two also consider what a ruling against Abu Shehadeh could mean for future elections and for free speech on Palestinian issues during wartime.
Whatever the High Court decides, this conversation offers the context every voter needs before reading the next headline.

Syria, Hezbollah hold secret security talks in Turkey, reportedly to ease border tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:18:55 UTC
19:18:55 KST

Representatives of the Syrian government and Lebanese terror group Hezbollah have held face-to-face talks in Turkey to try to calm tensions between them, according to six sources briefed on the first known meeting between the longtime foes.
The Syrian officials and the Iran-aligned group met secretly at least once last month, the sources - who include two Syrian officials, a US official and a senior Lebanese security source close to Hezbollah - told Reuters.
Hezbollah for years dispatched fighters to Syria to defend former President Bashar al-Assad's government during the country's civil war.
After Assad was ousted in late 2024 in a lightning rebel offensive, tensions rose between Syria's new government and Hezbollah - with Damascus accusing the group of transferring arms through Syria, and the United States encouraging Syria's military to send forces into Lebanon to fight Hezbollah.
Last month's meeting involved Hezbollah representatives and Syrian intelligence and foreign ministry officials, and took place at the invitation of Turkish security and intelligence agencies in an effort to de-escalate, the six sources said.
Officials discussed mutual security concerns, sources say
All the sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive meeting, which has not been previously reported.
Syria's foreign ministry, Turkey's foreign and defense ministries and the US State Department did not immediately respond to Reuters' questions about the meeting. Hezbollah's media office declined to comment.
The meeting focused on resolving points of tension between the two parties and went well, according to the US official, the Syrian officials and the Lebanese source.
One of the Syrian officials said both sides agreed they held no hostility towards one another, and that Syria assured Hezbollah that it would not intervene militarily in Lebanon to disarm the group.
In turn, Syrian officials asked Hezbollah to help stop cross-border smuggling attempts and dismantle its remaining sleeper cells, particularly in southern Syria, the official said.
Syria said on Tuesday it had captured a Hezbollah cell preparing to launch rockets in southern Syria. Hezbollah denied on Wednesday that it was involved and said it "has no presence whatsoever on Syrian territory and has no involvement in any security or military activity there."
The Syrian official said Hezbollah's representatives had not given a direct answer on the request to halt arms smuggling and dismantle its Syria-based cells, but did pledge not to interfere in Syria's affairs.
The Lebanese source, who has direct knowledge of the meeting and its outcomes, said the two sides "made a lot of progress on security issues."
"Hezbollah wants to protect its flank," the source said, referring to concerns about a Syrian attack on the group within Lebanon.
Both the Syrian official and the Lebanese source said no final agreement had been reached and that no announcement had been planned.
The Lebanese source told Reuters that contact between the two parties via Turkey had begun about two months ago.
Reuters could not confirm where in Turkey the September meeting was held, how long it lasted and whether other meetings had been held before or since.
Turkey pushed for meeting, Iran absent
Both Hezbollah and Syria's government had signaled they would be open to speaking to one another.
In July, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Damascus was open to meeting the group. A month later, Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said in a televised address that the group had no objection to meeting Syria's leadership.
Ankara portrays itself as a key regional stakeholder in rebuilding and stabilizing Syria. Under President Tayyip Erdogan, it has also sought to position itself as a facilitator of regional dialogue and is keen to boost stability in the region.
Three of the sources said it was Turkey, a key ally of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, that pushed for the meeting as it was keen to be directly involved in those efforts.
Absent from the meetings, however, was Hezbollah's main sponsor, Iran.
The Lebanese security source said Hezbollah attended the meeting with Iran's knowledge, but that Tehran was disappointed that it was not a direct participant and that Sharaa had rebuffed any notion of direct ties to Iran for now.
That disappointment was the main reason that no final agreement was reached and no announcement about the meeting was made, the source said.
There was no immediate comment from Iran's permanent mission in Geneva.

Archeologists unearth a ‘major’ early Christian monastery in Scotland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:14:34 UTC
19:14:34 KST

The earliest days of Christianity are hazy—relatively few written records survive from this era, and religious artifacts are rare archeological finds. Still, a newly discovered early Christian monastery, dating to just six centuries after the religion got its start, could offer clues to how the faith spread across the world.
In a new study published this week in the journal Antiquity, researchers describe how a group of historians helped discover the early medieval monastery in a stroke of good luck.
The site is situated on the island of Lismore and is believed to have been founded by Saint Mo Luóc, an early Christian saint also known as Moluag. Researchers had long suspected Mo Luóc’s monastery was there but hadn’t been able to prove it until the local Lismore Historical Society led an excavation in the area, which also holds the ruins of a 13th-century cathedral.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
With the help of professional archeologists, the historians uncovered ancient grave sites, buildings, pieces of sculpture and extensive evidence of craft workshops at the site.
Gordon Noble, the paper’s senior author and an archeologist at the University of Aberdeen in Scotland, says that the evidence of craftworking is particularly exciting. The team found hundreds of clay molds and crucibles used for working bronze, silver and gold—a somewhat “unusual” find for a monastery, Noble says.
“It’s one of the largest metalworking assemblages we have from any site, secular or sacred, in this time period,” he says.
Overall, the size of the monastery suggests Lismore, which lies on Loch Linnhe on Scotland’s west coast, was likely more important to medieval Christian society than previously realized, he says.
Other sites are known to have played a major role. For example, the island of Iona, to the southwest of Lismore in Scotland, is known for being the “Cradle of Christianity.” But the new findings suggest Lismore was “a very significant mover and shaker” in the spread of the early religion, Noble says.
Noble and his colleagues plan to keep investigating the site, including an analysis of the monastery’s “vallum,” or outer boundary, often indicated by a wall or bank.
The entire monastery appears to have been “huge,” Noble says. “It’ll be really exciting to see what shows up in the coming years.”

TEKNOFEST Southeast bridges 12,000 years of history with Türkiye’s technological future
Children encounter advanced aircraft for a first as Gobeklitepe experience, aerial displays and defense technologies draw visitors in Sanliurfa
Dilara Hamit
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
ANKARA
From the 12,000-year-old story of Gobeklitepe to Türkiye’s latest unmanned aircraft, TEKNOFEST Southeast continued Thursday in Sanliurfa, offering visitors a journey through the past, present and future of technology.
The world’s largest aviation, space and technology festival entered its second day at Sanliurfa GAP Airport with aerial demonstrations, scientific workshops, immersive exhibitions and activities designed especially to inspire young visitors.
Anadolu is serving as the event’s global communications partner. The festival is organized under the leadership of Türkiye’s Industry and Technology Ministry and the Turkish Technology Team Foundation, or T3 Foundation, with the involvement of defense company STM.
Among the most distinctive attractions is the Gobeklitepe Experience Area, where visitors get to travel across roughly 12 millennia in just three minutes.
Using 360-degree screens and a replica standing stone, the installation explores the question “Where did everything begin?” while connecting technologies developed by ancient civilizations with Türkiye’s contemporary advancement.
The experience presents Gobeklitepe, often described as the “zero point of history,” not merely as an archaeological site but as the starting point of a continuing story of human invention.
“We have a screen extending from the past into the future, with one of the TEKNOFEST aircraft at its center,” coordinator Alper Aslan said. “We begin in the past and explain the development of defense technologies up to the present.”
Visitor Elanur Yasar said the presentation allowed her to see the ancient site from a different perspective.
“At Gobeklitepe itself, we experience history in its original setting. Here, we saw Gobeklitepe combined with technology and civilization,” she said.
Beyond the installation, children from Sanliurfa and surrounding provinces crowded around domestically produced aircraft, including the KIZILELMA unmanned fighter jet, KAAN combat aircraft and AKINCI drone.
For some, it was their first opportunity to see such aircraft at close range.
“I was very excited. This is my first time coming to a place like this, and I was very happy to see an aircraft up close,” said young visitor Amine Abdulvahab. “Hopefully, when I grow up, I can work in something like this.”
Ebubekir Selale said seeing aircraft both on the ground and in the sky deepened his interest in aviation, while Elif Yıldırım thanked those who brought the festival to the city.
Japanese Ambassador to Türkiye Masami Tamura, who toured the festival grounds, praised both Türkiye’s defense technology drive and TEKNOFEST’s educational role.
“I find Türkiye’s advances in defense technologies very impressive. I am also greatly surprised by such an excellent event,” Tamura told Anadolu, adding that Japan does not host a comparable event on the same scale.
He said introducing children to science and defense technology through entertaining activities was particularly valuable and predicted deeper Turkish-Japanese cooperation.
“Türkiye and Japan’s cooperation is also important for world peace,” he said. “Japanese people love Türkiye, and I particularly want to emphasize that here.”
Thursday’s program also includes another performance by the Turkish Stars aerobatic team, alongside displays featuring ATAK helicopters, HURKUS, CEZERI, ANKA, Bayraktar TB2 and TB3 drones and AKINCI.
Visitors can also explore simulators, a planetarium, science shows, educational workshops and national air, land and maritime vehicles. The day will conclude with a concert by Turkish singer Semicenk.
TEKNOFEST Southeast will remain open through Oct. 4.

House prices in the European Union rose 4.7% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, Eurostat reported Thursday.
Prices increased 1.2% compared with the previous quarter. In the euro area, house prices rose 4% annually and 1.1% quarterly.
Annual growth slowed from 5.1% in the EU and 4.6% in the euro area in the first quarter.

Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'Digger' – Tom Cruise stuck in postmodernist misfire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:11:11 UTC
19:11:11 KST

Oscar-winning director Alejandro González Iñárritu teams up with Tom Cruise for 'Digger', one of the boldest and wildest films of 2026. It may also be one of this year's biggest misfires.
NB: Spoiler-free review.
A billionaire narcissist’s hunger for power and proclivity for manipulating public narrative for personal gain threatens to unleash a worldwide disaster.
If you’re looking for escapism, Digger may not be the way to go. But that’s not the only reason you’ll want to stay away.
Digger Rockwell (Tom Cruise) is an aging oil tycoon whose 38-year-old cat is circling the drain. But poor Maggie, who has somewhere between “two weeks and five minutes” left to live, will have to wait as her master's reckless drilling in Greenland has unleashed methane chaos. This results in a massive explosion and a renegade chunk of Arctic glacier to break free. They quickly name the glacier Judy. She’s five times the size of Washington D.C., and she’s headed straight for Europe.
“Let’s blow that frozen cunt up!” suggests one general to President Compton (John Goodman). But the typical US reaction – launch first ask questions later – won't work with Judy.
“We’re up against the reality of nature,” explains Digger’s top environmental scientist Dr. Ganesh (Riz Ahmed, Digger 's MVP and looking like he just wandered off a Wes Anderson set).
Refusing to accept that the fate of the world (naturally, measured more in terms of infrastructure devastation and monetary loss rather than loss of life) could be in the hands of the wind and ocean currents, President Compton decides that the “great big dildo of a pickle” is down to Digger, who needs to avert Armageddon. And hopefully save Maggie.
Alejandro González Iñárritu (Birdman, The Revenant, Bardo), a polarising filmmaker to begin with, has made both the boldest film of 2026 and this year’s wildest misfire. Digger is certainly his most pretentious film to date and sees him employing his inarguably impressive knack for staging to tell an eco-satire with Dr. Strangelove on the mind.
It kicks off promisingly enough as a heightened farce that pokes fun at bullish American geopolitics and crisis management, the Trump administration (business above all – and the fact the threat comes from American meddling in Greenland couldn’t be timelier), and how arrogant Americans see Europe (“those little boys piss sitting down”). It’s very broad, but it’s never not entertaining... And just when it all seems too exhaustingly cartoonish for comfort comes the metatextual twist to end all metatextual twists.
You can’t fault its boldness and the promise it carries, as the reveal – which shan’t be disclosed here – not only explains the caricatured and largely one-note performances from Cruise, Goodman and Sandra Hüller (reduced to playing Digger’s half-sister Emma as someone who enters rooms and shouts), but harks back to Iñárritu’s Oscar-winning Birdman. The director goes full postmodernist once more and sets the stage for Digger to become a satire about the very concept of satire. More specifically, about the importance of lampooning past calamity, in a sort of Twain-esque “tragedy plus time equals comedy”.
While initially promising, it sadly goes nowhere, with Iñárritu, Alexander Dinelaris, Nicolás Giacobone and Sabina Berman’s screenplay never getting to the heart of the social criticism, distraction, catharsis and yes, possible narrative rewriting, the genre can offer. The script also lacks the laughs to bolster its mordant aspirations and never - excuse us – digs deep enough to engross, relying instead on Cruise’s OTT efforts to entertain.
To his credit, Cruise does pull out all the stops here, dialling it up with his prosthetic belly, terrible comb-over and Foghorn Leghorn delivery. However, this won’t be the vehicle that gets the Best Actor Oscar that has eluded him for so long, as his performances in Digger are both larger-than-life and unrewarding. It’s a shame, as Cruise has proven time and time again that he’s more than Mission: Impossible’s Ethan Hunt; however, he mistakes pantomimic and jowly excess for "serious” acting, and the divisive (by design?) film itself may dissuade Academy voters to give him his fourth acting nomination, following Born on the Fourth of July, Jerry Maguire and Magnolia. As for Iñárritu, it doesn’t look like he’ll be adding a third Best Director Oscar to his shelf, after winning two consecutive awards in a row - Birdman (2015) and The Revenant (2016) - as Digger comes off as far too sanctimonious for its own good.
Then again, when has that stopped the Academy?
Still, should reason prevail, Digger ’s award chances hang on Emmanuel Lubezki’s impressive cinematography and Dennis Gassner’s flawless production design. Both save the day.
It’s hard to write more about Digger without spoiling Iñárritu’s brave but misguided gambit, but safe to say that once he does pull the rug from under the audience, he leaves viewers with a boated folly that’s both hollow and heavy-handed in the way it loudly announces everything via didactic speeches.
It’s still uniquely fascinating in the way it means well as a commentary on complicity, knows where it wants to go while breaking every fourth wall in its way, and understands what it’s trying to say as a cautionary tale; it simply can’t get out of its own finger wagging way. One character (again, no spoilers), played by Jesse Plemons, delivers a monologue towards the end of Digger that may as well have been delivered straight-to-camera, essentially telling the audience that if this all feels too on-the-nose, it’s by design, and that if we’re not in awe at what we’ve just witnessed, it’s because we’re not getting it.
The only thing to get is that high concepts are always to be applauded. But when they end up as empty theatrics that make Adam McKay's Don’t Look Up feel like a masterclass in allegorical subtlety, conceptual bravado just comes off as self-indulgent. Chances are you won’t dig it.
Digger is out in cinemas now.

Trump launches midterm campaign push in Texas and Oklahoma as Republicans face tough races

Trump launches midterm campaign push in Texas and Oklahoma as Republicans face tough races
WASHINGTON, Oct 1 - President Donald Trump travels to Texas and Oklahoma on Thursday to begin a 32-day campaign blitz aimed at bolstering Republican candidates as his party fights to hold onto its slim congressional majorities in November's midterm elections.
Trump wants to be the face of the party's midterm campaign at a moment when some Republican candidates are unsure whether the president will help or hurt them. While a number of Republicans in competitive US House of Representatives and US Senate races have welcomed Trump's decision to hit the campaign trail, others have become increasingly willing to break with him on issues that are riling voters, including the war with Iran and the spread of electricity-guzzling data centers.
Trump told supporters at a White House event on Wednesday that he had done a bad job so far in selling his economic record since returning to the White House in January 2025. Voter discontent over his handling of the economy has fueled a shift in the electoral map, with some safe Republican seats now viewed as competitive in November by political analysts.
Texas is among eight US Senate races rated competitive. Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, the state's attorney general, is expected to appear with Trump at a stop north of Dallas, Paxton's campaign said.
Political observers will be watching for any awkward interactions between the two men following the leaking of a recording of Paxton telling a group of donors that Trump's midterm convention in September hurt him and other Republican candidates.
The Paxton campaign dismissed the recording as "manipulated nonsense." Trump on Wednesday told reporters he had not heard about the recording. "I can tell you that the convention was amazing," he said in the Oval Office.
Trump backed the scandal-plagued Paxton over incumbent US Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary, forcing the party to spend heavily to defend a traditionally safe Republican seat from Democratic challenger James Talarico.
The president is expected to tout his tariff and trade agenda in Denton during a visit to Peterbilt Motors, where the White House says Trump-era truck tariffs helped spur job growth.
The administration said Trump's truck tariffs had enabled companies like PACCAR, owner of Peterbilt, to add more than 2,000 jobs nationwide, including some 1,000 at the Texas plant.
But the costs to power these diesel and gas trucks recently reached record levels in Texas, stemming from the economic fallout of the Iran war. Diesel in Texas hit a record high of $5.97 per gallon two weeks ago and average gas costs are up almost 44% at $3.92 per gallon compared to this time last year, according to travel analyst AAA.
After his Texas stop, the president will rally in Durant in southern Oklahoma, a state he won with more than 66% of the vote in the 2024 presidential election.
The Republican National Committee, which is organizing the rally, said the location near the Texas border was chosen in part to attract supporters from neighboring Texas, where Paxton and Talarico are fighting for the US Senate seat.
On Friday, Trump will continue his campaign rallies in Alabama, a similarly reliable conservative state in the South that also does not feature marquee competitive races. REUTERS

Spanish king to visit disputed enclaves, testing Morocco ties after border crisis

Unknown Publisher

Spanish king to visit disputed enclaves, testing Morocco ties after border crisis
MADRID, Oct 1 - Spain's King Felipe will visit the disputed North African enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla this month, sources in the royal household said on Thursday, a move that could further strain tense relations between Madrid and Rabat following a border crisis this summer.
The trip by Felipe and Queen Letizia on October 13 and 14 will be his first to the enclaves during his 12-year reign. It comes just over two months after more than 72,000 migrants surged into Ceuta from Morocco in late July.
The Moroccan government has historically opposed Spanish royal visits to the two cities, over which it claims sovereignty and which it regards as occupied by Spain.
Madrid considers the strategic outposts an integral part of its territory. Ceuta and Melilla have been part of Spain since the 17th and 15th centuries, respectively.
Felipe, Spain's ceremonial head of state, has mostly refrained from commenting publicly on the Ceuta crisis since it began, first mentioning the enclave two weeks ago to praise civil protection workers there.
But at an official dinner for French President Emmanuel Macron on Tuesday during his state visit to Spain, Felipe said European countries should have shown more solidarity with Madrid, calling the situation in Ceuta "unacceptable.".
Morocco's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on the planned visit.
Political debate in Spain since the border surge has largely centred around Morocco's precise role in the crisis. Opposition parties have accused Moroccan officials of complicity or inaction and accused Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of being too soft on Rabat.
After initially praising Morocco for its cooperation in repatriating the migrants and repeatedly denying that Rabat had orchestrated the crisis, Sanchez told CNN in an interview last week that Morocco's border controls had failed during the rush.
Morocco has denied any laxness, blaming the crossing on social media disinformation, human traffickers, and the misinterpretation of a Spanish court ruling that appeared to open a legal loophole for arrivals by sea. REUTERS

Bosnia votes as foreign powers jostle for influence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:08:21 UTC
19:08:21 KST

Bosnia votes as foreign powers jostle for influence
SARAJEVO, Oct 1 - Bosnia holds national elections on Sunday which could impact its bid to join the European Union but also the influence that the United States and Russia hold over the small Balkan nation.
Voter frustration has grown over an economic slowdown, the pedestrian pace of EU entry talks and a political crisis threatening to split the nation of 3 million people.
Bosnia, the former Yugoslavia's most ethnically mixed republic, has struggled to heal since its 1992-95 war which divided the country along ethnic lines.
The population has been in decline for 25 years, according to World Bank data, as international investment stalls, corruption persists and the young seek opportunities elsewhere.
Voters say they want to move beyond the divided rhetoric of the war years, but the politics appears stuck. Candidates rarely campaign beyond their core geographical base.
Damir, 47, from Sarajevo, said he hopes the elections will bring foreign investment, judicial reforms and an end to ethnic segregation. "I expect a bit more engagement from Europe ... I hope they will realise that we are already a part of Europe and that we will remain so," he said, declining to give his full name.
COMPLEX VOTING STRUCTURE
Bosnia is divided into two regions — the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska and the Bosniak-Croat Federation — linked by a weak central government.
The US-brokered peace accords that ended the war and created the country's structure have helped maintain peace, but have been criticised for prolonging ethnic divides.
"Voters care more about issues that stretch beyond the ethnic divide, things like corruption, slow EU accession," said Mario Bikarski, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.
Voters on Sunday will cast ballots for the country's central tripartite presidency and national parliament, alongside regional legislative races in its two federal entities.
Preliminary results are expected to start being released from Monday.
The vote pits rival ethnic nationalist parties — the Bosniak SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH — against multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party (SDP).
According to tracking platform Poliwave, the pro-European SDA holds a narrow national lead with 21.4%, followed by SDP at 16.7%. In Republika Srpska, SNSD, the party run by secessionist leader Milorad Dodik, who wants to maintain close ties with Serbia and Russia, is ahead with 34.2%.
POLITICAL CRISIS AND POWER STRUGGLES
Major powers have long sought influence over Bosnia, which is sandwiched between the EU’s eastern frontier and Russian ally Serbia. The EU is seeking to expand its membership across the Balkans, although progress has been slow.
The rivalry came into sharp relief last year when a Bosnian court sentenced Serb leader Dodik to a year in prison for defying the order of an international peace envoy. The sentence was later commuted to a fine.
Russia defended Dodik, in part because state police declined to go into his Serb stronghold to arrest him, although he is banned from running for office. Meanwhile, the US has sought to gain influence and last year lifted sanctions on Dodik to soften relations.
The Bosniak-Croat Federation is advancing a $1.5 billion pipeline project to import US natural gas run by a company with links to the Trump administration. The initiative sparked concerns from European Union officials, who warned that the selection of the company lacked the competitive transparency required for Bosnia’s EU accession.
Washington has also clashed with Brussels over the role of the High Representative — an international overseer who enforces the law of the Dayton accords. Christian Schmidt, a former German government minister, resigned in May under pressure from the US. The vacancy has triggered a diplomatic standoff between the United States and Brussels. REUTERS

Legislation for departure centers outside the EU is now in place, says Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:07:57 UTC
19:07:57 KST

King Frederik picked up the brush himself to help create his first official portrait as monarch – but Danish critics are divided over the finished result.
The portrait, created by visual artist Cathrine Raben Davidsen over the past two years, was unveiled Friday evening in the Great Hall at Frederiksborg Castle.
It shows King Frederik in full uniform, standing in an abstract green landscape on a ground covered with marguerite flowers.
Some of those flowers were painted by the king himself.
Raben Davidsen asked King Frederik whether he would like to paint some of the marguerites, something he “really wanted to” do, according to the artist.
“He cared very much about painting these flowers. I thought it was nice in one way or another to allow him to also be a part of the work,” she says.
The marguerites are not there by chance. They are one of Denmark’s national flowers and also serve as a reference to Queen Margrethe, whose nickname is Daisy.
Getting to know the man behind the king
Raben Davidsen met King Frederik privately several times during the two-year process because she wanted the painting to reflect both the monarch and the person behind the title.
“It was important for me to get to know him as a human being before having to think of him as king as well,” she says.
Their first meeting took place in her studio. For their second meeting, the king invited her to Kongsøre Forest by the Isefjord.
The area has personal significance for Frederik, who spent considerable time there while training to become a frogman.
Raben Davidsen later researched the history of the area and discovered another royal connection. A royal oak once stood there, under which Frederik VII reportedly liked to stand during hunts.
“That brought yet another historical layer to it. That it was not just a special place for King Frederik, but it also had a reference to his family,” she says.
The landscape behind the king in the finished portrait is based on Kongsøre Forest and the royal oak.
Despite discussing the portrait with the king throughout the process, Raben Davidsen says she was given “completely free hands”.
She also admits that showing him the nearly finished painting for the first time was nerve-racking.
“It is certainly boundary-pushing, and you certainly hope that he can recognize himself in it,” she says.
She does not reveal how the king reacted.
But does he look like himself?
That question has also occupied Danish critics since the portrait was unveiled.
Politiken art critic Mathias Kryger sees a “slightly disarmed and worried expression” around the king’s mouth and eyes.
“Doesn’t he look more like Joachim than himself?” he asks, referring to the king’s younger brother, Prince Joachim.
Berlingske royal reviewer Jakob Steen Olsen also questions the resemblance, writing that the portrait “resembles without quite resembling”.
“You can easily see who it is supposed to depict, but the sum of the parts has not quite fallen into place,” he writes.
Steen Olsen also sees a different Frederik from the sporty and cheerful king Danes encounter at events such as Royal Run.
He compares the uniform to a “paper doll”, saying it creates the impression of a king “wearing a costume for the role he is to fill”.
Despite those reservations, Steen Olsen considers the portrait a successful effort.
Weekendavisen commentator Anne Sophia Hermansen takes a very different view.
She calls the portrait “alluring” and says Raben Davidsen has handled the task “exemplarily”.
“It can go completely wrong when a ruler is to be portrayed. (…) And it can go well, and that is the case with the first official royal portrait of King Frederik,” she writes.
Hermansen particularly highlights the king’s expression. While previous monarchs have been portrayed with “fine moustaches and magnificent sideburns”, she sees something different in Frederik.
His expression is “open and curious”, she writes, while his carefully painted stubble makes him look “like a human being more than a person of power”.
Kryger is considerably less enthusiastic.
He ends his Politiken review with a pointed question:
“How would it look if the painting of the king had been real art?”
On display at Frederiksborg Castle
The portrait was unveiled as part of celebrations marking the 150th anniversary of the Carlsberg Foundation, with King Frederik and Queen Mary attending.
From Monday, the public can see the painting at Frederiksborg Castle, home to Denmark’s national portrait collection, which includes thousands of portraits of monarchs, politicians, scientists and artists.
Raben Davidsen is the first female artist to paint an official portrait of a monarch for the Great Hall at Frederiksborg Castle.
She hopes visitors will look beyond individual details and experience the painting as a whole.
“I really hope that people will take the time to see it as a complete painting and notice the painterly qualities. That one can sense the human Frederik and King Frederik in this work,” she says.
RITZAU/Copenhagen Post

'Exhausted' Afghan Refugees Get Extension At Camp In Qatar As US Congressmen Urge Action On Their Case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:06:10 UTC
19:06:10 KST

Afghan refugees being held at a camp in Qatar have been told it will be kept open for another nine months after a deadline for its closure passed, but they face continuing uncertainty over their fate amid an ongoing bar on entry to the United States.
The As-Sayliyah camp, a former US Army base, houses some 1,100 Afghans who have been stuck in limbo since immigration requests relating to Afghanistan were halted by a presidential executive order in November 2025. It was due to close on September 30.
“We had a meeting with the camp authorities. In that meeting, the camp officials said that the camp has only been extended for nine months. It will remain open until around June. That is all they said, they did not say anything else,” a man who did not wish to be identified told RFE/RL’s Radio Azadi on October 1.
Earlier, some US media reported that the State Department had decided on a nine-month extension, but officials have not confirmed this timeline publicly.
“The State Department continues to work toward a positive resolution that provides safety for these remaining people to start a new life outside of Afghanistan while upholding the safety and security of the American people,” a spokesman told RFE/RL.
The spokesman added that work was continuing on voluntary resettlement arrangements for the camp inmates, many of whom worked for American forces during the US-led international military presence in Afghanistan between 2001 and 2021. The others are primarily their family members.
“Psychologically, it is very difficult. Waiting is very hard. I myself am very exhausted,” another inmate, who also wished to remain anonymous, told RFE/RL. “When a person is forced into a situation and has no choice, he just has to endure it and live through it. Our fate is still unknown. But still, we keep struggling and hoping that eventually a proper place and a solution will be found for us.”
Physical conditions at the camp are not said to be an issue. But many people there have told RFE/RL of the frustration and emotional strain of lives put on hold indefinitely. Many residents at the camp have also been alarmed by talk of relocating them to third countries such as Rwanda or the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
Bipartisan Letter
The situation of the people at the camp has been repeatedly raised by US lawmakers from both the Republican and Democrat parties -- most recently in an open letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed by a bipartisan group of 22 representatives from both chambers of Congress on September 29.
Noting that two Afghan nationals were admitted to the United States on September 22 under an exception to current US immigration policy, it says some “3,000 immediate family members of US service members and veterans remain stranded overseas” including some 150 at As-Sayliyah “alongside more than 1,000 Afghan allies and family members who were vetted by the US government and flown there on US government aircraft.”
The letter urges Rubio to “prioritize the immediate family members of US service members and veterans for exemption determinations and refugee processing, beginning with those at Camp As-Sayliyah.”

HANOI, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam's Law on Urban Development took effect Thursday, introducing mechanisms and policies to promote the development of special-class cities and special economic zones, local media outlet Voice of Vietnam reported.
Under the law, the southern hub of Ho Chi Minh City and other special-class cities may pilot new mechanisms and policies that differ from existing laws or National Assembly resolutions, as well as measures addressing issues not yet covered by legislation.
Those cities are authorized to pilot new models for local government organization, economic models based on science, technology and innovation, and solutions to issues that have a serious and direct impact on residents' quality of life or the city's socio-economic development.
The law also contains a dedicated chapter on mechanisms and policies for developing special economic zones.
Communes, wards and special administrative units may be recognized as special economic zones if they meet criteria including a strategic location and the presence of an international airport or a first-class or special-class seaport, the report said. ■

The U.K. unveiled a new package of 31 sanctions against Russia on Oct. 1, but also prolonged liquefied natural gas (LNG) licenses that facilitate Japan and South Korea's continued import of Russian fossil fuels.
"We are targeting both the revenues that help sustain Russia's aggression and perpetrators of horrendous crimes against Ukrainian civilians, including children," said British Europe minister Lord Wood of Anfield, in a press statement.
The listings include 22 individuals who carry out unlawful detentions, torture Ukrainian civilians, and run Russian detention centers on occupied Ukrainian territory, known for inhumane conditions.
The U.K. also targeted individuals helping Russia in its disinformation narratives, including several Georgian politicians who tried to legitimize Russia's propaganda narrative of a breakaway movement in Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast.
The listings also include the Russian energy company Novatek Gas and Power Asia, which produces gas in the western Siberian Yamal region, and eight ships identified as belonging to Russia's shadow fleet.
Ukraine's sanctions chief Vladyslav Vlasiuk welcomed the new sanctions, especially those against two Arctic LNG tankers.
"Russia's Arctic gas is one of the Kremlin's key future revenue streams, and it must stay frozen," Vlasiuk said.
However, the U.K also granted exemptions allowing LNG from the Sakhalin-2 facility in Russia's Far East to continue exporting to Japan and South Korea unhindered.
The press statement describes the decision to facilitate Tokyo and Seoul's continued import of fossil fuels as "part of the U.K.'s work with international partners to support their transition away from Russian energy," without elaborating how.
In July, the EU granted similar exemptions to Japan and South Korea, which they said at the time was requested by the two governments.

UAE launches flydubai hijacking and terrorism investigation
October 1, 2026
The United Arab Emirates' chief prosecutor's office said on Thursday that it had ordered an investigation into the apparent attempt to hijack and possibly crash a flydubai flight to Israel a day earlier.
The state news agency WAM said that "the investigation team has launched its work into the incident already" and that the probe would seek to determine "the degree to which [the incident] was linked to any terrorist activity or intent."
The case will also seek to establish whether it was a pre-meditated and planned incident involving other actors or the work of a lone perpetrator.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz had called the emergency on the flight to Tel Aviv "an attempted jihadist terror attack" that was thwarted.
Passengers described rushing the cockpit to assist the pilot after he was stabbed by his copilot, who then put the plane into a steep dive in an apparent attempt to crash the airliner.
Aside from minor curts and bruises among those who intervened in the cockpit, the passengers — the vast majority of whom were Israeli — were all unhurt.
Why does the UAE have jurisdiction in the case?
Judicial authorities in the UAE have jurisdiction over the incident.
This is because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag, the statement said, adding that UAE law applied to crimes committed on board "even if they occur outside the country's territory."
The plane was over northern Saudi Arabia for the majority of the early-morning security incident, with tracking data suggesting it briefly crossed into Jordan before turning around to make an emergency landing at the nearby Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had also indicated the likelihood of the UAE leading any investigation in a TV interview with Fox News.
"The attacking pilot is ... now being investigated in Saudi Arabia. I think he'll be taken to the Emirates, where he comes from, or at least where he left, where he flew off from, and we'll be following and possibly also participating in this investigation," Netanyahu said.
The Omani copilot's identity has not been made public as yet and his motive is not clear. US President Donald Trump said that based on a discussion with Netanyahu, he understood that the suspect was "perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job."
Asked about the possibility of Iranian involvement amid the conflict in the Gulf, Netanyahu said "it's too early to say."
Israel's Herzog nominates 4 passengers for presidential medal
Israeli President Isaac Herzog plans to nominate four passengers who helped overpower the attacker for the Presidential Medal for Civil Courage.
Herzog and Netanyahu spoke with the passengers when they arrived at Ben Gurion Airport on a replacement flight late on Wednesday.
Herzog named the passengers as Yaniv Hayoun, Shota Musayev, Zvika Manes and Asaf Rajuan.
"You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disater," Herzog said. "Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society."
The medal is Israel's highest civilian award for heroism. Herzog confers the medal but typically nominees are formally chosen by a committee.
Musayev, a dentist who administered first aid to the severely wounded Indian pilot, told Herzog everyone on board had acted courageously.
"We supported one another on the plane and also when we arrived in Saudi Arabia, and we took care of each other as we should," he said.
The Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, has also received staunch praise from Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and from India's Narendra Modi. Passengers described how the pilot fought off his attacker despite his wounds and was able to open the cockpit door to let them in to aid him. He was in a stable condition in a Saudi hospital, India's Embassy in Riyadh said on Wednesday.
"In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others," Modi said online. "His valor helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy."
