China's high-speed rail network expansion to facilitate cross-city collaboration
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
18:05:59 CST
19:05:59 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- China's newly opened high-speed railway sections will help promote cross-city collaboration and closer regional economic ties, boosting the flow of talent, technology and capital across regions, experts said.
On Monday, China opened four major high-speed railway sections spanning northern, northwestern, central and northeastern regions. This move further expands the world's largest high-speed rail network, enhancing connections between major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country.
"The opening of the four lines will promote industrial transformation and upgrading and cross-regional industrial transfer, boost the development of resources along the routes, and inject new momentum into coordinated regional economic and social development," said Yuan Baohua, deputy director of the construction department of China State Railway Group Co., Ltd.
Each of the four new sections helps bind regions closer together. The Xiong'an-Shangqiu section, for instance, tightens ties between Xiong'an New Area and central-southern Hebei, southwestern Shandong and eastern Henan, while the Harbin-Yichun line extends the two-hour transportation circle centered on Harbin in northeast China, Yuan said.
As the rail network turns from isolated lines into an interconnected web, regional cooperation is deepening, according to Ma Botao with the China Railway Economic Planning and Research Institute.
Ma said the expanding network is bringing cities and city clusters much closer together. Commuting within metropolitan areas now takes about one hour, living and working across city clusters about two hours, and business travel between neighboring city clusters and provincial capitals around three hours.
"The railway network closely binds large and small cities, making industrial division of labor and cross-city employment the norm," he said.
The benefits of the network extend beyond the areas directly along the new lines. For instance, the Yichang-Xingshan section narrows the time-space distance not just between the two cities, but between the Chengdu-Chongqing region and the city cluster in the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, Ma said.
The new lines also provide direct support for key national strategies. Noting that the Xiong'an-Shangqiu section fills the gap in Xiong'an New Area's southbound high-speed rail corridor, Liu Yanhong, deputy general manager of Xiong'an high-speed railway corporation, said that the line facilitates commuting and business exchanges for relocated enterprises and institutions, and supports stronger industrial cooperation along the route.
For cities newly connected to the network, seizing the opportunity depends on how well they position themselves. "Generally, large cities focus on research and development, finance and headquarters economy, while small cities should leverage their local agriculture, ecology, tourism and distinctive industrial strengths to undertake supporting manufacturing, agricultural product processing, and wellness and cultural tourism, serving as both industrial supporting bases and leisure backyards for central cities," Ma said.
To turn transport advantages into real development gains, Ma advised cities to strengthen connections between high-speed rail stations and industrial parks as well as major population clusters, and improve housing and public services for talent.
China is home to the world's largest high-speed rail network, with more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail in operation by the end of 2025. Under national plans, the network is projected to expand to 70,000 km by 2035, connecting major cities, city clusters and key economic zones throughout the country. ■

EXPLAINER - What to know about Brazil's 2026 presidential election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:05:58 UTC
19:05:58 KST

Brazil heads to the polls on Sunday to choose its next president.
The election is dominated by a closely fought contest between President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
A total of 12 presidential tickets are registered for the election, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.
More than 158 million people are registered to vote in the general elections, including over 918,000 Brazilians living abroad.
The election comes amid deep political polarization, with Lula representing the left-wing Workers' Party (PT) and Flavio Bolsonaro the right-wing Liberal Party (PL).
The first round will take place on Oct. 4.
If no presidential candidate receives more than half of the valid votes, a second round between the two leading candidates will be held on Oct. 25, according to the Superior Electoral Court.
Voting will take place using Brazil's electronic voting system. Polls will open at 8 a.m. and close at 5 p.m. local time.
The presidential election is part of a broader general election. Voters will also elect 27 governors, 54 senators, all 513 federal deputies and state or district deputies.
Each voter will cast six votes: one for president, one for governor, two for senators, one for federal deputy and one for state or district deputy.
Voting is compulsory for Brazilians aged 18 to 70, while citizens aged 16 and 17 can vote voluntarily.
Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive presidential term. He returned to the presidency in 2023 after previously serving from 2003 to 2010.
He is running for reelection with Vice President Geraldo Alckmin as his running mate. His campaign emphasizes social programs, reducing inequality, economic growth and combating organized crime.
His main opponent is Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, a senator and the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
The junior Bolsonaro is running for president for the first time and has received the backing of his father, who is serving a prison sentence after being convicted over a coup attempt.
His campaign has emphasized public security, conservative social values, a smaller state and market-oriented economic policies.
Beyond Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro, the other candidates have different political profiles.
Augusto Cury, a writer and psychiatrist, is running for Avante party. Ronaldo Caiado, governor of Goias, is the candidate of the Social Democratic Party (PSD), while former Sao Paulo Gov. Romeu Zema is running for Novo.
Renan Santos is running for the Missao party. The remaining candidates are Hertz Dias of PSTU, Edmilson Costa of PCB, Clariana Barao of Democracia Crista, Rui Costa Pimenta of PCO, Wilson Grassi of Democrata and Samara Martins of Unidade Popular.
Recent polls show Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro leading the first-round race, although surveys differ on the size of the gap.
A Datafolha poll conducted Sept. 22-24 gave Lula 40% and Flavio Bolsonaro 36% in the first round. Augusto Cury had 5%, Caiado 4% and Renan Santos 3%.
Another poll by Quaest conducted from Sept. 24-28 showed Lula at 39% and Flavio at 34% in the first round. Cury and Caiado had 4% each, followed by Renan Santos with 3% and Zema with 1%.
A poll by AtlasIntel, a Brazilian polling and data intelligence firm, released on Sept. 29 showed Lula at 45.3% and Flavio Bolsonaro at 42.2%. Renan Santos followed with 5.2%, while Cury had 2%, Caiado 1.8% and Zema 0.9%.
Another Palver poll released on Sept. 29 put Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro at 44% each in the first round, with Renan Santos at 8%.
The differences reflect variations in methodology, sample size and fieldwork dates, meaning individual polls should not be treated as directly interchangeable.
Several polls predict a tie between Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro.
Datafolha's latest poll showed Lula with 47% and Flavio with 45%, with the difference within the poll's two-point margin of error.
An AtlasIntel poll showed Flavio at 47.7% and Lula at 47.6%, with a one-point margin of error.
A Quaest poll also showed the two candidates tied at 42% in a hypothetical second round.
The close numbers make the distribution of votes among candidates outside the two main camps an important factor in potential runoff scenarios.
Datafolha found that 80% of voters who have already chosen a first-round candidate said they were certain about their decision.
The poll also showed that Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro had the highest rejection rates, with 45% of respondents saying they would not vote for either candidate under any circumstances.
Public security, the economy, corruption, health, social issues and education are among the main concerns of Brazilian voters.
Public security is a central issue for Flavio Bolsonaro. His campaign has proposed creating 500,000 prison places, building five maximum-security prisons and taking tougher measures against organized crime.
Lula's campaign has focused on reducing inequality, maintaining social programs and combating organized crime. His 84-page program also emphasizes national sovereignty and economic growth.
Fiscal policy is another major point of difference. Lula has proposed a gradual fiscal adjustment while seeking to preserve social spending.
Flavio Bolsonaro's platform calls for a faster adjustment of public finances, changes to spending rules, privatization and measures to reduce bureaucracy.
Environmental policy is also significant. Brazil is a major agricultural producer and holds vast natural resources, including the Amazon rainforest, water resources, oil and rare earth minerals.
Lula's program calls for an end to deforestation by 2030 and greater environmental monitoring and conservation measures.
The election is also taking place amid continued political polarization between supporters of Bolsonaro's movement and Lula's Workers' Party.
Brazil is South America's largest country and one of the world's major agricultural and commodity producers. It is also rich in natural resources, including oil, water and rare earth minerals, giving the election significance beyond domestic politics.
The election is being watched across Latin America as Lula remains one of the region's most prominent left-wing leaders, while Flavio Bolsonaro represents the political movement associated with his father.
The result could affect Brazil's relations with the US, China and European countries, as well as its role in regional politics.
The election is also being watched in neighboring Argentina, where President Javier Milei has publicly supported Flavio Bolsonaro, adding a regional dimension to the contest.
The final days of the campaign have been marked by efforts by the leading candidates to consolidate support before the Oct. 4 vote.
Flavio Bolsonaro has challenged Lula to participate in a televised debate on Globo scheduled for Oct. 1, three days before the election.
The debate comes during the final stretch of campaigning, as candidates seek to reach undecided voters and consolidate support among their political bases.
The election will determine who leads Brazil for the next presidential term and could shape the country's economic, social, environmental and foreign policies.
The result will also influence the composition of Congress and state governments, which will affect the next administration's ability to implement its agenda.
Brazil's position as South America's largest economy and a major agricultural and commodity producer gives the election broader regional and international significance.
The next government will also determine Brazil's approach to relations with the US, China, Europe and neighboring countries, as well as policies involving the Amazon, energy, trade and strategic minerals.

Russian gas exports to Europe via TurkStream up 1.4% in 9M
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:05:55 KST

MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. Russian gas exports to Europe via the TurkStream pipeline increased by 1.4% in January-September 2026 to 13.2 bln cubic meters (bcm), according to TASS calculations based on data from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG).
In September, Russian gas exports to Europe via this route fell by 17% month-on-month, and by 13% year-on-year to 1.34 bln cubic meters. The decline was partly driven by maintenance works at the Bulgarian section of the pipeline’s extension.
The average capacity utilization of TurkStream toward Europe stood at 45 mln cubic meters per day in September, down 13% year-on-year, and 14% month-on-month. Consequently, the pipeline operated at 79% of its total capacity last month.
The TurkStream gas pipeline, running from Russia to Turkey across the Black Sea with an annual capacity of 31.5 bcm, is designed to supply gas to Turkey as well as Southern and Southeastern Europe. It remains the sole operational route for Russian pipeline gas deliveries to Europe following the halt of transit via Ukraine. The pipeline originates at the Russkaya compressor station near Anapa.
TASS reported earlier, citing ENTSOG data, that TurkStream gas supplies to Europe rose by 8.3% in 2025 to a record 18.1 bcm. Russia also slightly increased its pipeline gas exports to Turkey in 2025 to 21.2 bcm. Moscow supplies gas to Turkey via two Black Sea pipelines: Blue Stream and TurkStream.

Next year, travellers will be taking more frequent, but shorter, trips, booking onto 'growth getaways' and prioritising spending time in nature for wellness purposes.
While we’re barely in October, the travel industry has already begun to turn its head towards 2027 and beyond. And Euronews Travel is not excluded from that statement, having shared our own trends and predictions for next year earlier this week.
The latest company to look into the crystal ball is Hilton, with the release of its 2027 Trends Report.
Based on a survey of nearly 15,000 travellers from the UK, Germany, Türkiye, the US, Australia and more, the hotel brand has identified five key trends that are set to hit the big time as part of a wider shift dubbed “the great rebalance”.
“We're seeing that travellers are less interested in someone else’s definition of perfection and more focused on planning travel on their own terms,” Chris Nassetta, president and chief executive officer for Hilton, said.
“This year’s report reinforces that people are looking for experiences that fit their lives, help them recharge, and create meaning that lasts long after they’ve returned home.”
What are the big trends for 2027?
One of the major trends identified by Hilton is “the micro-travel mindset”, whereby people are prioritising shorter, more frequent escapes “that are easier to plan, easier to execute and easier to fit into everyday life”.
One in four are doing so because shorter trips mean they can fit travel around their work schedule, while 29% are opting to travel this way so they can be more spontaneous.
There are two types of micro-trippers: Selectors, and stackers.
The former build a trip around one experience, like a concert, a sporting event, or a restaurant reservation, while the latter want to pack in as much as possible, with 57% of people polled saying they enjoy visiting multiple cities in a single trip.
Another trend we’re certainly looking to embrace is “the rise of ‘ish’”, aka embracing the fact that your vacation won’t be perfect, nor does it need to be.
Tourists are being “healthy-ish”, picking and choosing which habits to keep up while away; “adventure-ish”, with 28% of people figuring things out as they go compared to 18% who want a fixed itinerary; and “solo-ish”, with three in 10 travelling solo but meeting up with someone they know on arrival, and 20% joining a group excursion or day trip with others they don’t know.
Folks are now also booking “growth getaways”, with skillcations, where you expand your knowledge through language, cooking or art classes, on the rise.
Travellers are also looking to change their perspective, with 34% saying they want their travel experiences to give them a new mindset.
Wellness escapes have become much more popular in recent years, and 2027 will be no different. What is changing, however, is the importance of nature in these experiences.
Part of the trend dubbed “wellness, rewired”, 79% of those surveyed said fresh air and the outdoors are essential to relaxation, and more than half spend more time immersed in nature on holiday than at home.
Last but not least, “the travel trust equation” shows that while AI is becoming increasingly useful for planning, tourists still have more faith in personal, human recommendations.
Of those polled, 70% said they trusted hotel staff for tips, while 87% have turned to family members for advice.
Outside of family members, some 50% of people said they are more likely to trust recommendations from someone with loyalty status.

Trains to Sumy and Lozova will not be canceled amid Russian attacks, but there will be changes

Passenger trains will run despite the threats. If rail traffic is halted, Ukrzaliznytsia will arrange coordinated transportation by bus to Sumy and Lozova.
Passenger train services in Sumy and Kharkiv regions will continue despite the dynamic security situation. However, changes are being introduced: combined "train + bus" connections to Sumy and Lozova. Minister for Reconstruction, Infrastructure and Transport Mykola Kalashnyk reported this on social media on October 1, UNN writes.
"UZ will get you there" — we are maintaining passenger connections in Sumy and Kharkiv regions, where the security situation can change every day. Starting October 1, together with Ukrzaliznytsia and the regional military administrations, we are launching a pilot project for combined "train + bus" connections on designated frontline sections to Sumy and Lozova
What is planned if the train cannot reach its destination
"If, due to threats, the train cannot reach these destinations or depart from them, Ukrzaliznytsia will arrange for passengers to be transported by bus. Train and bus schedules will be coordinated: in the event of a delay, they will wait for one another," the minister explained.
According to him, Ukrzaliznytsia's monitoring centers will track threats.
Are tickets available?
"Transfer tickets for the nearest dates on the designated trains are already available in the Ukrzaliznytsia app. The availability and cost of the full ticket will not change," Kalashnyk noted.
"For residents of frontline communities, transport connections are an opportunity to get home, reach their loved ones, or leave for safer regions. We are working to preserve these opportunities while taking the security situation into account," the minister concluded.

Water wars come to the ballot box in Arizona
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:03:07 UTC
19:03:07 KST

Water wars come to the ballot box in Arizona
PHOENIX, Oct 1 - On Phoenix campaign signs, Arizona-wide TV ads and in debates for key US House races, one issue has bubbled to the top of politics in this drought-hit state: Water.
Governor Katie Hobbs, a Democrat seeking reelection in the November 3 midterm polls, says, “Arizona’s water is for Arizonans” in a TV commercial claiming she fought the federal government this year for the state's fair share of the drought-stricken Colorado River.
Right-wing group Turning Point USA hit back with street placards across the state's largest city, Phoenix, claiming Hobbs "LOST AZ BILLIONS OF GALLONS OF WATER."
That water has surpassed issues such as affordability, immigration and the Iran war as the most important campaign concern underscores how deeply worried Arizona residents have become by the drought crisis.
A survey released in September by the Center for the Future of Arizona found long-term water supplies were, for the first time, the top concern of Arizona voters. Water had previously ranked second or third in the survey, now in its fifth year.
The change followed deep federal cuts in Colorado River supplies to Arizona in August. Now, water is a central campaign issue and the focus of election ads.
Politicians have long left water issues to water managers or framed them as shared policy challenges requiring long-term solutions, like the Central Arizona Project. The concrete canal, completed in the early 1990s, provides Colorado River water to millions of people in Phoenix and Tucson.
For some observers, the prominence of water in campaign messaging is unprecedented. "This is very new. I don't think I've seen candidates running for governor talking about water issues in the past," said Sybil Francis, head of the CFA, an independent research organization.
ONCE TABOO TOPIC
For decades, the state relied on an abundant supply of Colorado River water, its population nearly tripling since 1980 to 7.6 million.
Additionally, Phoenix and other cities banked billions of gallons of Colorado River water underground as an emergency backup. As a condition for federal funding for the CAP canal, Arizona agreed to take cuts in Colorado River water before California, should supplies ever fall.
That day of reckoning arrived with this year's 27% federal cut in Arizona's water supply from the Colorado River. Under a multistate compact, reductions might nearly double after 2028 if the drought worsens, an action that could drain the CAP dry, Arizona water managers warn.
That has pushed water to the forefront of Arizona politics with the issue discussed everywhere from kids' soccer practices in Phoenix to farms in neighboring Pinal County.
"We can't continue business as usual, and the state has to figure out, particularly ways to make investments in new water supplies," said Sarah Porter, director of the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University. Consumers should expect water rate hikes and restrictions as communities invest in alternative water sources and ramp up conservation, she said.
The Center for the Future of Arizona study found around 71% of Arizonans do not believe the state's water systems can reliably support future growth and extreme heat. Such scarcity could hammer the state's economy and housing market.
"The outlook for the desert climate over the next 20 years, according to science, is not promising," said Matt Beidler, 41, a Phoenix resident who works in IT sales and is a registered Democrat. He plans to visit Chicago to check out moving there.
Others fear that one day their taps will run dry.
METRO PHOENIX CONCERNS
"We are slowly losing our water from the Colorado River," said healthcare worker Elizabeth Ramirez, 36, a Scottsdale resident who supports US Congressman Andy Biggs, the Republican gubernatorial candidate. She cited his $19 billion plan to build water infrastructure and complete a Yuma desalination plant.
Biggs said Hobbs has stoked fears that Arizona has run out of water, costing the state tens of thousands of jobs and hundreds of millions of dollars in investment.
"It is this panic narrative out there that this governor engenders," Biggs said in an interview. "We're not out of water. This is a matter of bringing it under control, managing it."
Hobbs, who did not respond to a Reuters request for an interview, said in a statement that she had stopped outsiders from stealing Arizona's groundwater, won a rightful share of the Colorado River and was converting agricultural water rights to lower-water-use urban development.
"After years of doing nothing, Biggs has suddenly decided in an election year that Arizona’s water is worth his attention," Hobbs' spokesperson Michael Beyer said in the statement.
Water security is also a big issue for US House candidates in northeast metropolitan Phoenix. The largely affluent suburban district is one of a handful that will decide who controls the US House of Representatives in November.
Republican candidate Jay Feely said Hobbs failed to negotiate a fair Colorado River deal for Arizona. The state took the majority of cuts, while states like Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and New Mexico took none.
"You have to create leverage, and you have to do a good job of advocating for your state," said the former NFL kicker and ally of President Donald Trump, pledging to be a water champion for Arizona in Colorado River talks that resume in a year.
Democratic opponent Amish Shah said the district needs to conserve water and find new sources like desalination plants in Mexico and California. He too vowed to battle for Arizona's rightful allotment of the Colorado. Unlike Feely, he opposes data centers in the arid area, which is dotted with golf courses.
"We live in a desert and we're running out of water, so obviously our voters are really scared and upset about this," said Shah, an emergency room doctor and former state legislator in his second run for the seat. REUTERS

Green tree ants (Oecophylla smaragdina) are plentiful in tropical forests from India to northern Australia. And, as this short from the science documentary series Deep Look details, their dominance has spawned quite a few imitators. With close-up looks at four of these copycats – one insect and three spiders – the video explores how each has evolved to resemble the ants in appearance, behaviour and even smell. Some leverage the ants’ reputation as fierce fighters to avoid being eaten themselves; others use their disguise to get close enough to make a meal of the ants and their young. While some disguises are more convincing than others, each is good enough to provide an evolutionary advantage that allows these creatures to reap the benefits of the green tree ant’s success.

Trump officials abandon effort to investigate election threats, experts warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:35 UTC
19:00:35 KST

The Trump administration has abandoned key security bodies meant to investigate direct threats to US elections by foreign actors and domestic terrorists, according to former officials and a recent report.
While administration officials have been actively focused on unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud by noncitizens, other credible election threats appear to have been overlooked, the officials say.
Between 2021 and 2024, the justice department’s election threats taskforce prosecuted 21 cases, like that of Solomon Peña, a failed candidate for the New Mexico house of representatives who organized shootings at the houses of election officials, or Quintez Brown, who shot up a campaign meeting of Louisville’s mayor.
Democrats and Republicans faced prosecution for harassing, intimidating and threatening elections workers, noted Nikki Fisher, former chief election security officer for the Oregon secretary of state, now the executive director of the Oregon District Attorneys Association.
Since then, the taskforce seems to have gone quiet.
“While officials are being trained to handle threats, the federal deterrent meant to punish the people making them appears to have gone quiet,” Fisher said. “To date, no new cases have been prosecuted, and the DoJ’s election threats taskforce appears to be defunct in practice.”
Contacted for comment on the status of the election threats taskforce, the justice department referred to a series of nine DoJ media releases over the past five weeks describing indictments of foreign nationals on charges of election fraud and stolen identities.
In an academic paper published in June, while she was studying at the Naval Postgraduate School, Fisher noted that the taskforce received more than 2,000 reports of election threats between 2021 and 2024. It opened more than 100 investigations into those threats.
Trump administration officials began disbanding election investigative groups within the justice department, the office of the director of national intelligence, and other agencies almost immediately after the president started his second term.
The first day after Pam Bondi won Senate confirmation as attorney general, she eliminated the FBI’s foreign influence taskforce, which had been investigating influence campaigns waged by China, Russia and other adversaries.
Administration leaders fired or reassigned personnel working on foreign election interference at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (Cisa). They also defunded Cisa’s training program for local officials to monitor and coordinate threats through the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center.
Pleas from Democratic lawmakers during budget negotiations in 2025 to retain the task force and other election integrity assets went unheeded.
“I’m less worried about jurisdictions’ ability to defend themselves in particular,” said Geoff Hale, a visiting fellow for election security at the Center for Democracy & Technology and former director at Cisa. “I’m more worried about the lack of an information-sharing environment across the community.”
Federal cuts to these agencies’ monitoring and investigative apparatus leaves local agencies blind to broader patterns, he said. “The relationships and trust that Cisa had built up over 10 years, that was how the tapestry of security professionals that support elections across the country stayed in close contact and were able to close vulnerabilities to keep events and incidents from occurring in multiple locations.”
Agencies working together with state and local election leaders offered regular warnings about suspicious activity, said Caitlin Durkovich, a former deputy homeland security adviser for resilience and response on the national security council, said at a briefing staged by the Brennan Center for Justice last week.
“This administration … has dismantled the entire apparatus that is responsible for detecting and holding these bad actors accountable,” she said. “That has all gone away at a moment when this administration is again claiming that the spectre of foreign operations is … in play.”
Meanwhile, Trump officials have been focused on some of the president’s longstanding personal grievances when it comes to election integrity.
FBI agents swooped into Fulton county in January to seize ballots from the 2020 election, ostensibly as part of a continuing investigation into foreign election interference. Tulsi Gabbard, then the director of national intelligence, was present at the FBI raid. Similarly, the ODNI and the FBI seized elections apparatus in Puerto Rico, again while investigating foreign interference.
Nothing has yet come of either event.
But both cases led up to a primetime address by Trump on 16 July, where he claimed China had acquired extensive voter information during the 2020 election cycle, characterizing it as an effort to influence and undermine legitimacy in the 2018 midterm and 2020 presidential elections.
Trump argued that US election databases and hardware had vulnerabilities to foreign adversaries, and that Venezuela had digitally manipulated its election results in ways that might be replicated in an American election.
Trump’s claims could not be substantiated from the evidence presented.
Since that address – and the public’s tepid response to the claims – the administration has pivoted to a dogged pursuit of noncitizen voters in American elections.
The DoJ has charged more than 90 people with voter-related fraud offenses, 50 noncitizens in the last five weeks, attorney general Todd Blanche said on Wednesday, contrasting it with 13 cases brought under the Biden administration.
“What we do at Department of Homeland Security is not controversial; we’re enforcing our nation’s laws,” said homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin, who was also at the event. “Underneath the Trump administration, we will always protect the integrity of our election system and enforce our nation’s laws.”

Britain’s scaffolding should be a source of national pride - instead we’re struggling to recruit workers | Adrian Chiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:34 UTC
19:00:34 KST

There’s a shortage of scaffolders. I can’t think why. It’s incredibly hard physical work, doubtless doesn’t pay enough and requires real skill to get right. Scaffolding was part of my dad’s and grandad’s business, so I did it for a while, rather badly. After a torrid few months, I slowly got strong enough to make a contribution. The first time I lifted a 21ft scaffold pole on my own was a proud day indeed. Now, I can’t even pull one off the back of a truck – this I know, because I’ve tried, being in the habit of talking to any scaffolders who can spare the time for a chat and enjoy scoffing at my weakness.
They’re a breed of their own and, alarmingly, a dying one. In March, the National Access and Scaffolding Confederation said the UK needed as many as 40,000 more scaffolders. Unless this shortfall is filled, we’re going to be putting up a lot of low-rise buildings.
As someone who went off to do something else with his life and has just pointed out what a tough line of work it is, I’m hardly well placed to speak up for the profession, but I’ll give it a bash. For starters, it has the considerable merit in this day and age of being a job that AI can’t do. The technogarchs may claim they can do everything from curing cancer to destroying humanity, but I’ve yet to hear one of them say their clever-dickery extends to erecting a massive Meccano set around a 10-storey housing development.
Also, it’s a chance to be part of a British success story, in that I reckon we do it better than anyone else. Wherever I go on my travels, I always think the scaffolding isn’t a patch on ours. In some places, you can barely see a decent right angle on the whole rig.
I was just about to say that if there were an international scaffolding championship, the UK would win hands down. However, it turns out that there is such a thing, called ScaffChamp, and we didn’t win it this year. A Lithuanian firm did, but they had home advantage, as it was held in Vilnius. Props, though, to AK Scaffolding, from Manchester, and the A-Team, an all-apprentice squad from Northern Ireland and Scotland, for flying Britain’s flag. I’m confident glory will be ours before long. Scaffolding’s coming home.
Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

AI chatbots remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when prompted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:34 UTC
19:00:34 KST

When prompted, AI chat bots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith.
The Guardian asked ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini and Claude to take the veil off an AI-generated image of a woman wearing a hijab. Both OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok bots complied with the prompt. Anthropic’s Claude responded that it does not have an image-editing or generating feature but that it would not alter a photo to remove someone’s hijab.
Gemini initially said that it could not remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people because it could not digitally alter someone’s appearance without their consent. But when asked to make the woman look more “western”, the bot created an image of her without her hijab.
The Guardian US tested the chatbots after a French far-right politician stripped a real Muslim woman of her hijab and long-sleeved dress in a picture he made clear was modified. Julien Odoul, a member of parliament and of the National Rally party, posted the altered image of the woman on X with her hair visible and arms exposed alongside the caption “LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE”, meaning French Liberty. He quote-tweeted the original image, posted by someone else, which showed the woman crossing a street wearing a hijab and full-length dress.
It was unclear which software or AI model Odoul used or even whether he modified the image himself, but experts say the MP’s actions were part of a growing pattern of tech-enabled anti-Muslim hatred around the world.
In India, where anti-Muslim sentiment is rampant, generative AI is playing an increasingly significant role in producing images that, among other things, sexualize Muslim women or dehumanize Muslims generally, according to a study by non-profit US thinktank the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH). The CSOH also found that there are similar types of AI-enabled hatred being directed at prominent female Muslim politicians in the US like Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib.
“This is just part of an ongoing trend of how we see Muslim communities, and particularly Muslim women, being targeted and abused,” said Eviane Leidig, the director of research and outreach at CSOH.
While Grok promptly complied with a request to edit an image of a woman wearing a hijab, the chatbot declined to take the dress off of an AI-generated image of a woman. When asked what the difference was, the chatbot replied, “Removing the hijab was treated as a relatively straightforward clothing/hair change (replacing a head covering with natural hair while keeping However, the chatbot said it would be willing to do a “less explicit version” of the edit and “change the dress to underwear, a different outfit, or a partial reveal”.
In May, xAI announced it had implemented technological measures that would not allow its AI image generator to comply with requests to digitally undress “images of real people in revealing clothing such as bikinis”.
ChatGPT similarly declined to remove a dress off the AI-generated woman, saying that the “distinction is that removing a hijab changes a head covering, while removing a dress would expose the person’s body.” However, ChatGPT eventually conceded that for someone who wears hijab, exposing their hair “can be a meaningful violation of privacy or religious practice.”
“The fact that an edit doesn’t create nudity doesn’t mean it can’t violate someone’s privacy, dignity, or religious boundaries,” ChatGPT responded.
These distinctions show the gaps in community guidelines that dictate how AI chatbots can behave, said Leidig, and as platforms like X soften its enforcement of existing rules, emboldening far-right figures. The de-veiling of Muslim women “may not be distinctly violative [of platform rules] but it’s still harmful,” she said.
OpenAI, Google, xAI and Anthropic declined to comment.
The Guardian conducted similar tests for other religious head coverings like a turban traditionally worn by Sikh men and a Catholic nun wearing a habit. ChatGPT readily created new images removing both the habit and turban off the AI-generated people.
Gemini initially declined to create a new image of the man without a turban. However, just as in the case of the image of the woman wearing hijab, when asked to make the AI-generated image of the man wearing a turban more western, Gemini created a new image of the man without a turban.
Despite initially claiming that it couldn’t remove a hijab from an image of a woman because “attempting to remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people relies entirely on artificial generation to guess what lies underneath”, Gemini removed the habit off of the AI-generated image.
Claude, for its part, said that if it could edit images, it would not edit an image of a real woman to remove her hijab regardless of the requester’s intent.
“That kind of edit changes how a real person is depicted in a way tied to their religious dress and identity, and it could be used to embarrass, harass, or misrepresent them – that’s true whether the woman is a public figure or someone private,” the chatbot responded.
Publicly available AI chatbots and third-party “nudify” apps have been used broadly to disrobe women, and in some cases, minors. In January, sexualized images of women proliferated across X as users realized they could ask the Grok chatbot, developed by Elon Musk-owned xAI, to undress images of women posted on the social media platform. The spread of these images prompted countries like France to investigate X. Malaysia temporarily restricted the use of Grok in the country.

The German town where the right has banned new ‘stumbling stones’ for Nazi victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:34 UTC
19:00:34 KST

The town hall of Heidenau, Germany has a freshly restored cream-coloured facade, tidy flower boxes on the windowsills and a charming shingled clocktower.
At the entrance, closer inspection reveals a single brass plaque embedded in the pavement honouring the former mayor Paul Gröger, whom the Nazis hounded into killing himself.
The plaque is one of 128,000 Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) across Europe, a donor-funded project keeping alive the memory of individual victims of the Nazi era.
It is by some measure considered the world’s biggest grassroots memorial project, and has become an integral part of Germany’s “remembrance culture” for the atrocities committed under Adolf Hitler.
But last week at the same town hall, the council of Heidenau voted to halt the laying of future stumbling stones.
In a decision that drew a national outcry, the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party joined forces with the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, to help form the majority.
“They want to drive the victims’ memory out of the city centre, just like the victims themselves were driven out,” said Anne Nitschke of AKuBiZ, a citizens’ group coupling history education with pro-democracy work in Saxony state, a hotbed of rightwing extremism.
“The point of the Stolpersteine is that you stumble across them every day and then think about who lived here and who was forced to leave,” said Nitschke, 40.
Her organisation had filed for permission to lay another 12 plaques for Holocaust victims, until the Heidenau council stopped them.
The vote came in a month in which the anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin AfD widened a lead at the top of the national polls, won two state elections and performed strongly in a third, in the capital, Berlin.
Like the other mainstream parties, Merz’s CDU has ruled out cooperation with the far right in a stance known as the “firewall”. But political realities have often made the AfD an unavoidable partner in municipal policymaking, particularly in the former communist east.
Supporters of the stumbling stones ban criticised that their placement on the ground meant they were walked on and exposed to the elements. They called for a “memorial space” in a Christian cemetery north of town “for the victims of war, terrorism, dictators and forced displacement”.
Nitschke noted that the council had not made any plans or committed funding for such an endeavour, and said the broad spectrum cited served to deny the “singularity of the Holocaust”.
Merz’s national CDU referred queries to the Heidenau chapter, which did not respond to a request for comment.
The AfD began as a Eurosceptic party 13 years ago and has morphed into an increasingly nationalist force. It has long targeted memory culture as detrimental to patriotism.
One of its founders, Alexander Gauland, compared the Nazi period to a “speck of bird shit in over 1,000 years of successful German history”.
The Saxony-Anhalt chapter, which won a record 44% of the vote in September, pledged to “liberate” Germans from shame over the Holocaust while offering “more Bismarck, less Hitler” in schools.
And the part’s co-leader, Alice Weidel, falsely called the Nazi leader “a communist, socialist guy” in a campaign appearance with Elon Musk last year. (The tech billionaire told AfD supporters at the event there was “frankly too much of a focus on past guilt” in Germany.)
Many residents of the town said they supported the Stolpersteine and were sceptical of the councillors’ motives.
“Why would they have anything against the Stolpersteine? It’s easy enough to walk around them if you don’t want to step on them,” said Christine Bauer, 85, who uses a rolling walker to move about town.
“I’m a child of the war and remember its awful aftermath,” said Bauer, who worked on Elbe river ships until she retired. “It’s not as if the town council didn’t have bigger problems to worry about now,” she added, mentioning affordability.
But Silke Schutz, 63, a baker who called herself a “staunch AfD voter”, described the Stolpersteine as “a waste of money, regardless of who pays for them”.
“There are so many victims no one cares about,” she said, citing people killed in traffic accidents. “We had nothing to do with the war and at some point it [remembrance] has got to come to an end. But when I express my opinion, I’m insulted as a Nazi.”
Started by the artist Gunter Demnig in the 1990s, the Stolpersteine are laid before a Nazi victim’s last home or workplace and inscribed with stark biographical details: date of birth and the date and circumstances of their death.
Heidenau has five, all laid personally by Demnig. He reacted angrily to the town council’s decision, calling it a “unprecedented” and wrong.
Four plaques are laid just a few minutes’ walk from the Heidenau railway station in honour of the Reiner family. Its Jewish patriarch, Maximilian, ran a local department store until he was deported to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in 1943.
He survived and, after liberation two years later, emigrated to the US and died soon after, in 1949.
Gröger, the Social Democratic mayor until 1933, refused to run up the swastika flag at the town hall and was removed from office. In June, Nazi officers spirited him away to the Hohnstein concentration camp, where they beat and tortured him. In August, he took his own life.
School pupils raised the funds for his plaque, while AKuBiZ sponsored the remaining four Stolpersteine.
Descendants often travel from abroad to attend their installation, as most Holocaust victims lack a gravesite. Local residents support the project by regularly polishing the Stolpersteine, and digital apps provide detailed information about the victims’ fates.
Nitschke said no plans had been announced to remove any of the existing Stolpersteine, but for now the 12 planned plaques were on hold, including for Fritz Goldstein, a Jew whom the Nazis stripped of his property and deported to the Soviet Union with his wife, Martha.
He died a broken man aged 50, five years after his return to Heidenau.
Juliane, 29, a music teacher who declined to give her last name, said she found it moving to learn about the victims through the Stolpersteine. “It is so important we don’t forget, so we don’t make the same mistakes again.”
But 28-year-old Philipp, a cook, said he supported the town council’s ban. “It’s not relevant to me – it’s in the past. So there’s no point in dwelling on it now. At some point, you’ve got to put it behind you.”
He said Germany’s memory culture had been imposed from abroad. “Other countries just want Germany to constantly have to justify what it did.”
Nitschke said her team planned a legal challenge to the ban.
This weekend they will lead a march through town to the sites of the planned new Stolpersteine, recounting the stories of each of the victims.

Lower cognitive ability is linked to stronger Christian nationalist views, even after accounting for education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:31 UTC
19:00:31 KST

A new study indicates that Americans with lower scores on a vocabulary test commonly used to measure cognitive ability are more likely to endorse Christian nationalist beliefs, even when accounting for their overall level of education. The findings suggest that the appeal of this political and religious ideology relates to underlying cognitive resources rather than just differences in schooling. The research was published in Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion.
The research, conducted by Samuel L. Perry, the Sam K. Viersen Presidential Professor of Sociology at the University of Oklahoma and currently a visiting scholar at the Russell Sage Foundation, explores the individual characteristics associated with Christian nationalism. Christian nationalism is a set of beliefs asserting that the United States has conservative Christian foundations. The ideology promotes the idea that the government should institutionalize Christian dominance in American society, often merging religious identity with civic belonging.
“One of the most consistent predictors that Americans adhere to Christian nationalism is that they have lower education,” Perry told PsyPost. “But there have also been a number of studies that find that persons who subscribe to Christian nationalist views (even after accounting for level of education) exhibit significant knowledge gaps across a variety of different domains.”
For example, people who strongly endorse the ideology tend to score poorly on tests about “American history or scientific knowledge,” Perry noted. “They are also more likely to hold factually incorrect beliefs about vaccines,” he said, referencing a 2021 study he co-authored, which was covered by PsyPost. “And related to that last point, they are also more likely to affirm ridiculous conspiracy theories related to COVID-19, January 6th, or QAnon.”
“The dominant explanations for these substantial knowledge deficits and the apparent credulity of Christian nationalist adults have been motivated reasoning and siloed information sources,” Perry explained. “Both of those theories are no doubt true. But we have yet to consider whether there may be evidence of a gap in cognitive resources, one that can’t be explained solely by educational background or other relevant factors.”
Perry sought to see if general cognitive ability also plays a role in explaining these patterns. Cognitive ability refers to a person’s capacity to learn, apply new information, and engage in the complex reasoning required for critical thinking. A study covered by PsyPost in 2017 provides evidence that an intuitive thinking style tends to predict higher religious belief, while lower cognitive ability predicts higher social conservatism.
“A large number of studies have already documented an association between lower cognitive ability and greater religious fundamentalism, political authoritarianism, or otherwise right-wing views,” Perry said. Based on this prior research, he anticipated that cognitive ability might similarly predict support for Christian nationalism, viewing the study as a “necessary next step to empirically connect all the dots.”
To test this, Perry analyzed data from the General Social Survey, a long-running and nationally representative survey of American adults. The researcher measured cognitive ability using a vocabulary exercise where respondents identify the closest synonym for ten different words. This test is a common proxy for crystallized intelligence, which reflects the knowledge and reasoning skills a person has accumulated over time.
The study examined two specific measures of Christian nationalist ideology. The first asked respondents how important it is to be a Christian to be “truly American,” using data from survey waves in 1996, 2014, and 2024 with a sample of 1,659 adults. The second measure asked if respondents disapproved of the Supreme Court’s decision to ban mandatory Christian prayers and Bible reading in public schools. This second question included data from 17 survey waves between 1989 and 2024, creating a sample of 18,700 adults.
The researcher accounted for a wide range of variables to ensure the vocabulary scores were not just standing in for other demographic factors. These included educational attainment, such as whether a person completed high school or earned a college degree. The models also adjusted for religious affiliation, fundamentalist beliefs (such as viewing the Bible as the literal word of God), worship attendance, and political ideology. Additional demographic controls included age, race, sex, household income, and geographic region. The results remained consistent even when further controlling for parents’ education and family income at age 16.
For both outcomes, higher vocabulary scores were consistently and negatively associated with Christian nationalist views. As vocabulary scores increased, people were less likely to say being Christian was highly important for being truly American. They were also less likely to disapprove of the Supreme Court ban on school prayer. These negative associations persisted even when comparing people with the same level of education and similar religious habits.
The negative association between cognitive ability and Christian nationalism held steady across different demographic subgroups and was consistent across all survey years for the “truly American” question. For the school-prayer question, the link was always negative but reached statistical significance in only 11 of 17 survey years (and 7 of the 8 years since 2008).
The only exception was among the least educated Americans, specifically those who did not finish high school. For this specific group, vocabulary scores did not change their likelihood of supporting Christian nationalism. Notably, the effect was just as strong for high school graduates as for those with college degrees, indicating the pattern is not simply a result of college education. Perry suggests there may be a basic level of schooling, reached sometime during middle or high school, below which cognitive ability does not incline people to reject Christian nationalist views.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2022, also authored by Perry, which found that higher support for Christian nationalism was linked to lower factual knowledge about the role of religion in American political history. Both studies link the ideology to lower test performance, though factual knowledge and general cognitive ability are different things.
“To the extent that belief systems like Christian nationalism appeal to those Americans who for whatever reason tend to be less adept at thinking carefully and effectively, it suggests Christian nationalism (like religious fundamentalism or right-wing authoritarianism) is not the result of more sophisticated and complex ruminations on politics, religious ethics, and pluralism,” Perry said. Instead, he argued, it “appeals to more basic impulses for control and binary distinctions.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding these findings. “Readers shouldn’t read further into this finding than what the evidence warrants,” Perry cautioned. “I cannot make any claims about where cognitive ability comes from here.”
The data is cross-sectional, meaning all the information was collected at a single point in time for each respondent. “I actually show in one of my appendix tables that Christian nationalist views also predict wordsum scores,” Perry said. “So the correlation could theoretically go either way.”
“While I think the causal arrow almost certainly goes in the direction of cognitive ability shaping adherence to Christian nationalism, the cross-sectional nature of the data prevents me from making that definitive claim.”
It is possible that adopting a fundamentalist religious and political worldview alters the way people engage with educational material and language. In addition, despite robust statistical controls, “I cannot demonstrate definitively that lower scores on the wordsum vocabulary exercise are not the result of some childhood exposure or socialization that might also help explain the Christian nationalism connection,” he noted.
Another detail to note is the measurement of cognitive ability. The vocabulary test is a brief exercise, not a comprehensive intelligence test. However, Perry found that two other measures available in the General Social Survey, an abstract reasoning test and a numeracy item, also correlated with Christian nationalism in the same direction. Future studies could use more robust, multi-part intelligence tests that assess mathematical ability and problem-solving. Tracking individuals over time would also help clarify whether cognitive ability shapes political ideologies, or if the ideologies influence intellectual development.
In this study, the link between cognitive ability and Christian nationalism did not depend on people’s political ideology or party. But Perry has several other studies under peer review suggesting that ideology does shape how cognitive ability relates to other social attitudes. “There is a sense in which cognitive ability inclines us toward particular social or political views,” he said. “But there is also evidence that cognitive ability simply helps us discern and defend the ideological commitments of our in-groups.”
“This would be consistent with the theory that our higher reasoning abilities help us solve social problems of status rather than guide us toward certain ‘enlightened’ moral views,” Perry concluded. “And sure enough, I find in several of these studies that more cognitively sophisticated liberals hold liberal views more strongly, while cognitively sophisticated conservatives hold conservative views more strongly.”
The study, “Cognitive Ability and Christian Nationalism,” was authored by Samuel L. Perry, author or co-author of Taking America Back for God, The Flag and the Cross, and Religion for Realists.

future-proof design relies on a chain of sustainable decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:09 UTC
19:00:09 KST

future-proof design relies on a chain of sustainable decisions
the iF design award 2026 highlights how intentional design decisions drive circular systems, material innovation, and resilient communities.
iF DESIGN EMBEDS SUSTAINABILITY INTO GLOBAL DESIGN STANDARDS
The term sustainable design has too often been reduced to a marketing label, diluted by superficial claims of recycled content or carbon offsets that mask short product lifespans. But true sustainability cannot be stamped onto a surface, it is woven into the entire process. A design is genuinely sustainable only when its creators can offer clear, responsible answers to fundamental questions across its entire lifecycle: Does this product solve a genuine problem, or does its quick path to replacement expose a design failure? Are materials selected for enduring quality and minimal extraction impact, or only to satisfy eco-branding trends? What is the object’s path after its primary function ends? Can it be repaired, remanufactured, or cleanly returned to the natural cycle? Addressing these questions requires designers to combine creative vision with rigorous, long-term strategic foresight.
This holistic approach is precisely what the iF DESIGN Award prioritizes during evaluation. Across 93 categories, environmental impact carries equal weight alongside traditional factors like function and style, setting a global benchmark. See how winning projects from the iF Design Award 2026 demonstrate how designers resolve fundamental challenges by identifying true functional needs, selecting responsible materials, and planning for post-use recycling.
INTENTIONAL DESIGN FOSTERS REGENERATIVE ECONOMY
Since 1953, the institution’s Design Award has made sustainability central to its judging framework. Covering diverse categories, environmental and social impact stands as one of five fundamental criteria evaluated by the jury. This system highlights how intentional design decisions, from micro-level material selections to macro-level architectural strategies, actively foster a circular economy and lasting environmental care.
CIRCULAR SYSTEMS, MATERIAL INNOVATION AND RESILIENT COMMUNITIES
While materials determine how a product looks, feels, and performs, they also define its environmental impact, from raw extraction and labor practices to transport, energy use, and eventual disassembly. Because industrially produced products and packaging compound their environmental impact through volume, the iF Design Award emphasizes that sustainable design must move beyond high-minded ideals to deliver intuitive, everyday utility.
Illustrating this principle, the Taiwan Textile Research Institute developed its Gold Ratio Fibrous Resin Material, a circular thermoplastic composite crafted entirely from recycled carbon fibers and plastics. Engineered for infinite repairability, the material can be reshaped repeatedly, extending product lifespans without sacrificing durability.
Grounding material innovation in local ecosystems, DesertBoard® PSB® upcycles palm fronds into a formaldehyde-free and termite-resistant building material. Converting a regional waste stream into a durable, deforestation-free resource, it establishes a circular baseline for healthier construction.
As winning projects from the iF Design Award demonstrate, circular design works at a systems level, managing what happens to materials before and after a product is used. In the UK, Geopak replaces throwaway lighting boxes with reusable, trackable containers designed for specific building sites.
Beyond individual products, circular design operates as a broader system for managing material lifecycles. In Taiwan, TRASH+ LAB collects leftover event materials in Taitung to create an online rental system for designers.
Nearby in Taichung, CyclePath Lab’s HomeWork Circular Living Project integrates zero-waste retail, material transparency, workshops, consulting, and local pilot projects under one roof. This hybrid retail and community network renders circularity accessible, actionable, and collectively practiced.
When applied to technology and infrastructure, these circular decisions transform broader urban and rural grids. PHL Reduction in Kenya deploys solar-powered cold rooms across supply chains to reduce agricultural loss and stabilize farmer incomes, while Portugal’s Galp Energy retrofits existing municipal streetlights with electric vehicle chargers to expand EV infrastructure without adding to the urban footprint.
At an architectural scale, design sets long-term physical conditions for land use and coastal resilience. Takenaka Corporation scaled circular material principles into temporary architecture for Expo 2025 Osaka-Kansai, utilizing 3D-printed biodegradable wood and handmade seed paper designed to return cleanly to nature post-event.
Demonstrating this large scale urban strategy in New York, the Financial District and Seaport Climate Resilience Master Plan for Lower Manhattan, engineered by ONE Architecture, SCAPE, NYC EDC, and Arcadis, integrates flood protection, waterfront design, and traffic systems along one mile of vulnerable shoreline. The plan connects resilience with urban planning, balancing storm protection with future public space. In South Korea, BIG and SAMOO developed OCEANIX Busan, a floating urban prototype powered by solar energy, circular water systems, and local food production. Meanwhile, Row House Zurich in Switzerland demonstrates circularity by renovating an 1890 structural frame rather than tearing it down.
Design reaches its fullest purpose when it empowers communities and protects the future. The iF Design Student Award shines a light on forward-thinking concepts, like LiliPur’s water-regenerating lagoon systems in Italy and TextileRefuge’s Limetex bricks in Ghana, which turn discarded clothing into building materials and jobs. Concurrently, the iF Social Impact Prize recognizes tangible community solutions: Malaysia’s EPIC Bamboo Home and MaxLife’s three-dollar pump part, which keeps clean water flowing for 15 million people in Malawi by making pumps last six times longer.

Chinese hair embroidery uses human hair instead of silk thread to create ultra-fine portraits

Fran Luin Beijing
While China’s iconic silk embroidery is world-renowned for its exquisite detail and painterly effects, an even more meticulous traditional technique surpasses it.
Originating in Dongtai, located in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, during the Tang dynasty (618–907), hair embroidery relies on the incredibly fragile medium of human hair. With a rich history spanning over 1,000 years, a single intricate piece can take skilled artisans anywhere from several months to multiple years to complete.
It is said that young women in Dongtai first used their own hair to weave images of Buddha as a demonstration of their piety.

The Next Generation of Weight-Loss Drugs Is Almost Here
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

The field of weight-loss drugs is moving more quickly than ever since medications that mimic GLP-1, a type of peptide hormone in the gut, hit the market to treat weight issues and diabetes. But while there has been huge interest in the drugs, their side effects—which predominantly affect the GI system—cause roughly 40% of people who start them to stop taking them within a year.
At the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, researchers from the pharmaceutical companies behind the most popular weight-loss medications reported encouraging results from studies of a new group of injectable medications that may come with fewer side effects.
Amylins are a group of peptide hormones that work in similar ways to GLP-1s by curbing appetite signals in the brain and encouraging the stomach to empty. They target different receptors on cells, so their effect can be complementary to that of GLP-1s and other drugs in their hormone group (called incretins). But unlike incretins, amylins don’t seem to cause as many severe side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and stomach cramping.
Scientists from Novo, which makes Wegovy and Ozempic, reported this week that their experimental amylin-based compound CagriSema, taken as a weekly injection, helped people who were overweight or obese lose 22.4% of their starting body weight after a year compared to those taking a placebo. The company also reported on fMRI studies of the brain that showed CagriSema changed brain responses to food, potentially making food fixations less intense. And in people with Type 2 diabetes, the drug reduced the amount of harmful fat in the liver and pancreas, an early but encouraging sign that the medication may contribute to health benefits beyond those associated with weight loss. CagriSema is a combination of the semaglutide—the active ingredient in Wegovy and Ozempic—with cagrilintide, an amylin analogue that mimics a hormone made in the pancreas that regulates feelings of being full.
Martin Holst Lange, executive vice president and chief scientific officer at Novo, says that the company also has an earlier stage study in people with Type 2 diabetes showing that CagriSema can reduce neuropathic pain, which affects about half of people with the disease. “It’s super exciting because we are showing that beyond weight loss and glycemic control, CagriSema can do more to help people in their everyday life,” says Lange. “So we are quite enthusiastic about what we are seeing.”
Researchers from Eli Lilly, which makes Zepbound (tirzepatide), reported that EloraTZP, its experimental combination drug of the amylin analogue eloralintide and tirzepatide, helped people who were overweight or had obesity and also had Type 2 diabetes to lose 23% of their starting body weight compared to 14.8% among those using tirzepatide alone after nearly a year. The weekly injectable also helped people to lower A1C, a measure of diabetes, by more than either tirzepatide or the amylin compound alone. The company has been studying the amylin part of the combination on its own, but plans to study the combination in additional studies beginning this year.
Zealand Pharmaceuticals, a Danish biotech company, also shared results from its study published Sept. 29 in the Lancet of its amylin-based compound petrelintide, an experimental weekly injectable. It helped people who were overweight or obese—but who didn't have diabetes—lose on average 10% of their body weight. (People who took a placebo lost only 1.7% of their body weight on average.) In the study, those even on the highest doses of the experimental drug reported similar rates of side effects as those who took a placebo shot.
Because of their efficacy and favorable side-effect profile, at least in experiments, amylin-based medications may one day be an attractive first-line therapy for many people who are looking to lose a moderate amount of weight without the unpleasant side effects associated with the GLP-1 group of weight-loss drugs. “The amylins still cause some nausea, but it’s at less than half the rate of what we generally see in GLP-1 trials,” says Dr. Timothy Garvey, professor in nutrition sciences and senior scientist in the nutrition obesity research center at University of Alabama who led the petrelintide trial. Not everyone needs drastic weight loss, he says, so amylin drugs could be a welcome option for them. “As more of these tools become available, we can individualize care better,” he says. “Primary care physicians may have an easier time prescribing these since they are better tolerated. So I am personally very sanguine about amylins.”
Novo has submitted a request to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for approval of CagriSema to treat overweight and obesity in people without diabetes, and the agency is expected to make a decision by the end of the year. The other products are in earlier human testing stages, but the results suggest that amylins may someday join GLP-1s in the burgeoning category of weight-loss drugs.

Can Venture Capital Help Unlock Wealth and Equality for All?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

My interest in venture capital (VC) began long before I ever imagined building an actual venture capital fund. In college, I opened a women’s clothing store and quickly learned that having a great idea was only part of what it took to build a business. I needed capital to grow, and finding that money wasn’t easy. That experience stayed with me.
Years later, when I began looking more closely at who gets funded in America—and who doesn’t—I realized that the entrepreneurial challenges I had encountered were part of a much larger story. So I started digging into the numbers.
When I first started researching the racial disparities in venture capital, what I learned shocked me. Women of color make up nearly 20% of the U.S. population, yet our best estimates indicate that only 0.39% of venture capital funding is invested in women-of-color-owned businesses. These numbers weren’t just disappointing; they infuriated me. And though Black women comprise approximately 7% of the U.S. population and start more companies than any other demographic, our research reveals that they obtain less than 0.35% of VC funding across all sectors. While we comprise over 50% of the U.S. population, women of all races combined obtain less than 2% of all VC funding. The rest is awarded to male founders.
The more I dug, the more infuriating the story became.
I learned that the vast majority of dollars venture capitalists invest come from sources like public employees’ retirement funds—their pension funds. Public employees are very diverse. In the federal workforce alone, 44% of workers are women; 18% are Black; 10% are Latino; 7% are Asian American; 2% are Native American; less than 2% are Alaska Natives; and Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islanders make up less than 1%.
Hold up!
That means, in general, white men are investing the money of women and Black and brown people, yet they direct just a pittance of those funds back to Black people, brown people, or women of any race. In other words, the money flows from the pension funds of diverse people to Private Equity (PE) and VC industries comprised almost entirely of white men. Not surprisingly then, most VC money is invested in white-owned start-up businesses. Very rarely does that money get invested into people serving the communities where the money was made.
The injustice made me sick. So not only were Black people not paid for their labor beginning in 1619, when enslavement began, and continuing until the 1860s, they were also underpaid and economically exploited for another hundred years after Jim Crow laws began to be imposed upon Black people. Yet even today their savings fund the descendants of many wealthy white landowners.
More than 150 years after Emancipation, Black people are still underwriting the accumulation of white wealth. My head spun with this reality, though another part of me wasn’t the least bit surprised to discover yet another dimension of racial economic injustice and inequity. Right then and there, I knew I had to help ensure that retirement fund investments reflect the diversity of the people contributing to them. The challenge was huge, yet I felt undaunted. If I wanted to see change, I had to be a part of making it happen.
As a Black woman, I was not only uniquely aware of the issue at hand; I was also uniquely aware of the upside possibilities that came with shifting these assets to Black and brown women more than almost any white man working in the VC space. Having grown up in and moved professionally within racially diverse contexts, I knew that the spaces wealthy white people inhabit are overwhelmingly monochrome. Their narrow lens not only leaves them with a colossal blind spot and it also makes our national and global economy incredibly vulnerable to various cognitive biases and distortions, denial, groupthink, unexamined assumptions, and the homogeneity that results when diverse perspectives are lacking—not to mention the reality that we miss out on billions of people’s God-given gifts, talents, and skill sets.
We can see the cost of inaction and the opportunity of change. Now, we need to roll up our sleeves.
Adapted with permission from Fearless Freedom: A Manifesto for Unlocking Wealth and Equality for All by Arian Simone.

Press review: Flydubai incident raises Mid East escalation risks and US ends Iraq mission
