Among the actions KKL-JNF listed as forbidden at the site were camping, setting up speaker systems, and lighting fires (including barbecues).
Celebration at Nova site akin to 'holding party at Auschwitz'
"Just as no one would dare contemplate holding a party at the Auschwitz extermination camp, it is equally unthinkable to hold any celebration at the Nova site in Re'im Forest, where 378 civilians and members of the security forces were murdered," said KKL-JNF Chairman Eyal Ostrinsky.
"We are guided by one single objective: preserving the sanctity of the memory of those murdered," Ostrinsky added.

This is how KKL acted at the Nova site in Re'im Forest, and likewise in the North, the Jordan Valley, and the South - regions where we at KKL have invested billions of shekels."

Bones of medieval tsar, 48 religious relics to be exchanged under new Greece-Bulgaria heritage MoU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:08:09 UTC
18:08:09 KST

The remains of a medieval Bulgarian tsar and nearly 50 religious Greek relics will be handed over to their respective nations under a newly signed Memorandum of Understanding between Greece and Bulgaria on Tuesday.
The MoU was signed between Greek Culture Minister Lina Mendoni and Bulgarian Culture Minister Evtim Miloshev.
As part of the agreement, Bulgaria will return 48 religious relics from the Holy Monastery of Panagia Eikosiphoinissa, the Holy Monastery of Timios Prodromos of Serres and the Holy Metropolis of Serres and Nigritis to Greece.
The relics were transferred to Sofia during WWI and have since been kept at the National History Museum of Bulgaria.
Following their return, the 48 relics will displayed at the Museum of Byzantine Culture until November 5. Afterwards, they will be returned to their place of origin.
In turn, Greece will hand over the remains of the medieval Bulgarian tsar, Samuel (997-1014), found in the Basilica of Saint Achillios in 1965.
Samuel, or Samuil, reigned from 997 to 1014 during the First Bulgarian Empire and is deemed a national hero by Bulgarians for struggling to preserve his country's independence from the neighboring, Greek-speaking Byzantine Empire.
Alongside Samuel's remains, those found in two other sarcophagi within the basilica will also be returned.
The additional remains are believed to belong to Tsar Gabriel-Radomir, Samuel's son who ruled the First Empire of Bulgaria between October 1014 to August or September 1015, and other members of the Bulgarian royal family.
The remains have recently been kept at the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki.
A 'historic' agreement between Greece, Bulgaria
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev described the accord as a "historic agreement" and said the handover of Samuel's remains ended six decades of efforts by Sofia to bring them home after their discovery in Greece.
"We have had the historic honor of achieving this," Radev said in a statement shared by the Bulgarian Culture Ministry. "I would like to express my deepest gratitude to the Prime Minister of friendly Greece, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, for his statesmanlike vision, for his political courage and for the friendship that binds Bulgaria and Greece even more strongly."
Radev emphasized that the memory of the tsar "unites, not divides," the two countries today.
"The joint membership of Bulgaria and Greece in the European Union helps each of the two countries to better understand the sensitivity of the other," he added. “On Saturday, October 3, at 12:30 p.m., I invite all Bulgarians to Battenberg Square in front of the Prince's Palace in Sofia to welcome the mortal remains together and pay homage to the great Bulgarian ruler."
The two sides agreed to continue negotiations regarding the identification and inclusion of historical artifacts of mutual interest that were not covered by the current agreement.
The official handover ceremony will take place on October 3, at the the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki. It will be hosted by Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and attended by Radev.
Reuters contributed to this report.

The FlyDubai cockpit attack is over. The hardest questions remain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:04:18 UTC
18:04:18 KST

The FlyDubai cockpit attack is over. The hardest questions remain
The incident aboard FlyDubai flight FZ1073 has yielded some confirmed facts, but it is still too early to draw firm conclusions. The passenger jet was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday when a confrontation broke out in the cockpit. The aircraft then transmitted a distress signal and made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. All 174 passengers and crew members survived. According to media reports, the plane lost altitude rapidly, while passengers and airline employees aboard helped subdue the attacker and restore control to the crew. Early wire reports offered conflicting accounts, including claims of a hijacking, because the aircraft had transmitted the corresponding emergency signal.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the copilot had attacked the captain and apparently tried to crash the plane. Defense Minister Israel Katz described the incident as an attempted jihadist terrorist attack. Israeli authorities have already characterized it as an attempted act of terrorism, drawing comparisons with the September 11, 2001 attacks. But the investigation is ongoing, and no final findings have been released. FlyDubai confirmed that an altercation had occurred in the cockpit and said investigators were working to establish its cause and the motives involved. Authorities in the United Arab Emirates also announced an investigation and urged the public not to spread unverified information. Saudi officials confirmed the emergency landing and said both pilots had been hospitalized.
The central question – what exactly happened – therefore remains unresolved. Israel has already said it views the incident as an act of terrorism. Yet the publicly available evidence is still insufficient to establish an ideological motive, an intention to kill Israelis specifically, or any connection between the attacker and an organization. Investigators are examining his motives, the circumstances of the attack, and whether it involved advance planning.
Media reports identified the suspect as the copilot and an Omani citizen, but those details came from Israeli sources and have not been confirmed by all parties. No information has been released about whether he made any statements, had contact with radical groups, or acted on someone else’s instructions. FlyDubai has explicitly warned against jumping to conclusions.
Two separate questions need to be distinguished here. The first is whether the attacker acted alone aboard the aircraft. Reports suggest that only one person carried out the attack in the cockpit. The second is whether he was a lone extremist in the political sense: someone acting on his own initiative, without outside connections, support, or a prearranged plan. That remains unknown. A single perpetrator does not necessarily mean there was no organization behind him. Equally, an attack on a plane bound for Israel does not, by itself, prove that such an organization existed.
If investigators establish that the copilot deliberately tried to destroy the aircraft because it was headed to Tel Aviv or because Israelis were aboard, the incident could be classified as a terrorist attack carried out through access granted by his job. That would distinguish it from the more familiar scenario of an attacker trying to board a plane with a weapon. In that case, the security challenge would extend beyond passenger screening to the possibility of someone exploiting a trusted position within the aviation system.
Radicalization as the political backdrop
Still, it is also too early to dismiss the incident as a personal dispute between two crew members. The flight was bound for Israel, and the confrontation occurred in a region where protracted conflict is a fact of daily life. This week, the Israel Defense Forces again struck Gaza, killing Palestinian civilians. Under those circumstances, there can hardly be any meaningful talk of a ceasefire. In September, further attacks took place in the West Bank, where no Hamas fighters were involved: an armed assailant attacked an Israeli, while settlers attacked a Palestinian family.
Radicalization in this context is not simply a matter of new armed groups emerging. It also means a growing number of people coming to see violence as an acceptable political response, assigning collective responsibility for a government’s actions to entire populations, and treating any compromise as betrayal. The longer military operations, civilian deaths, and mutual recriminations continue, the easier it becomes for extremists to portray violence as “retribution” or “resistance” instead of a crime. Different forces employ this rhetoric, but it does not absolve individual perpetrators of responsibility for attacking civilians.
Israel’s military operations in Gaza, conditions in the West Bank, settlement expansion, and inflammatory statements by Israeli officials deepen the region’s sense of injustice, particularly among those who identify with their “Palestinian brothers and sisters.” This helps radical movements emerge and readily recruit supporters who believe they have a moral right to seek revenge by any means available. In their view, all’s fair in war. This is already a significant political factor that cannot be ignored. Across the Middle East, Israel’s policies are almost universally seen as a cause of rising terrorism.
There is another side to this dynamic. Attacks on Israeli civilians and threats to Israel’s security strengthen public support within Israel for the use of force. Retaliatory measures then give fresh ammunition to those calling for radical resistance. The result is a vicious cycle in which each side invokes the other’s violence to justify its own course. The FlyDubai incident may prove to be part of that pattern, and revenge cannot be ruled out as the attacker’s motive.
Could it happen again?
There is no guarantee that similar attempts will not occur, especially if investigators confirm that the attack was ideologically motivated and deliberately targeted a flight to Israel. Such a finding would likely lead to tighter security for flights serving Israel, including more rigorous personnel vetting, revised cockpit access procedures, and closer monitoring of crew behavior. Israeli authorities have already announced stronger aviation security measures, while FlyDubai has suspended flights to Israel pending the investigation.
But a single incident is not enough to predict a “wave” of similar attacks. That would require evidence of preparations, organizers, connected perpetrators, or at least statements from groups claiming responsibility. None of that has been made public so far. What we have is an incident that was averted almost miraculously, a possible terrorist motive, and a persistently unstable regional backdrop.
Nor would the threat necessarily take the form of repeated attacks on aircraft. With security tightened, terrorist cells could turn to less protected targets and simpler methods. If the attacker is found to have gained access to the aircraft through his professional position, the most important lesson would concern more than the safety of flights to Israel. It would expose the aviation industry’s vulnerability to a new kind of insider threat.
It bears repeating that it is too early to state conclusively that this was a terrorist attack. Investigators have yet to establish a motive or reconstruct the full sequence of events. But there is also no basis for explaining it away as an ordinary quarrel between pilots. The aircraft was headed to Tel Aviv; one pilot attacked the other, and the plane subsequently lost altitude rapidly. Investigators are closely examining the possibility of terrorism alongside other explanations. For now, all that is known is that the attacker acted alone aboard the aircraft – if this was indeed a terrorist attack. Whether he had ties to a group, and what drove him, remain to be determined.
Radicalization is intensifying across the region. That does not mean every new incident is part of a wider conspiracy, or that attacks on Israeli targets will inevitably become more frequent. But the possibility of further violence will remain as long as wars, repression, mutual dehumanization, and political mobilization fueled by hatred continue – a process at which Israel’s far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich have proved all too “successful.”

German municipal budget deficit remains at record $22.7B in 1st half
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:03:55 UTC
18:03:55 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Germany’s municipalities recorded a €20.1 billion ($22.7 billion) budget deficit in the first half of 2026, matching the highest first-half shortfall since German reunification in 1990, official figures showed Thursday.
The deficit remained at the record level registered in the same period last year, according to preliminary data released by the Federal Statistical Office, Destatis.
The figures cover the core and extra budgets of municipalities and municipal associations, excluding Germany’s city states.
Core municipal budgets accounted for €20 billion of the shortfall, while extra budgets recorded a deficit of €100 million.
Expenditure rose 2.7% from a year earlier to €204.1 billion, while revenue increased 3% to €184 billion. Both grew more slowly than in the first half of 2025, when spending rose 6.9% and revenue increased 6%.
Personnel expenditure climbed 5.2% to €54.7 billion, while social benefit spending increased 3.9% to €46.3 billion. Interest costs rose more sharply, jumping 13.1% to €2.4 billion.
Meanwhile, capital investment fell 4.5% to €21.7 billion, with construction expenditure declining 2.4% to €15.5 billion.
Net municipal tax revenue increased just 0.9% to €57.3 billion. Net trade tax receipts fell 2% to €30.8 billion, with gains in other tax categories offsetting the decline.
Municipal revenue from administrative and user fees rose 5.7% to €26.5 billion.

If successful, it would mark the return of the Canadian branch of the Weston family to the UK high street, having previously owned Selfridges.
The family later sold the department store chain for £4bn in 2022. The Westons are widely known throughout Canada for owning the grocery store Loblaws and the pharmacy chain Shoppers Drug Mart.

Sycamore has been widely expected to spin off and sell Boots – alongside other parts of the group – after its takeover of the Walgreen Boots Alliance last year. It as has already split the group into five stand-alone companies.
Boots, which was founded in Nottingham in 1849 by John Boot, has changed hands several times in the past 20 years. After a merger with Alliance Unichem in 2006, the combined company was taken over by the private equity firm KKR in 2007, before Walgreens first took a 45% stake in 2012 and then completed a takeover at the end of 2014.
Boots – which has 1,800 stores across the UK – employs about 51,000 people, including about 6,000 at its headquarters in Beeston, three miles south-west of Nottingham.

Chinese hackers impersonated ex-US official to steal e-mails from AI experts

Unknown Publisher

Chinese hackers impersonated ex-US official to steal e-mails from AI experts
WASHINGTON – Chinese hackers have been impersonating US artificial intelligence experts, including a former government official, to try to steal e-mails from experts in AI at think-tanks, universities and other organisations, the cybersecurity company Proofpoint said on Oct 1.
In a report, Proofpoint said it had watched the hackers – which it dubs TA419 – regularly try to steal passwords from people working for US or Japanese think-tanks, defence contractors, universities and law firms since as far back as 2025.
Proofpoint attributed the hacking efforts to the Chinese group based on the types of malware the group used, the internet infrastructure used to carry out the attacks, and the targets it observed the group focusing on, which align with Chinese intelligence collection priorities.
It said the hackers’ recent campaign involved writing e-mails purporting to come from experts in AI or statecraft, including Lynne Parker, who previously worked as the principal deputy director of the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy.
Proofpoint said the e-mails would typically propose AI-themed collaborations or initiatives before steering targets towards password-stealing websites.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately return a message seeking comment. Beijing has long denied carrying out cyberespionage operations.
Proofpoint declined to name the hackers’ targets, saying only that they included “experts working on AI regulation, export controls and national AI strategy”.
Reuters was independently able to identify one of them: Alex Engler, a former White House official who now heads the Penn Center on Media, Technology and Democracy.
Engler told Reuters on Sept 30 that he had received an e-mail appearing to come from Parker, inviting him “to join a new AI policy project”. But he said the e-mail “felt slightly, nebulously off” and, after he checked with others in the field, he realised he was dealing with an impostor.
He said he could not speculate about why someone would try to hack him, but Proofpoint said that its view of the targeting – which involved fewer than 10 individuals working for a handful of organisations – suggested “an intelligence interest in US policymaking rather than technology theft alone”.
Parker told Reuters that Engler was one of two people who received suspicious messages purporting to come from her in early July. She added that the allegation of Chinese involvement made sense.
“The United States and China are in a competition around AI,” Parker said. “Trying to get people in the AI policy space to reveal information about their AI policy plans – if that indeed was what the objective was – it’s not surprising.” REUTERS

Lithuania Moves to Block Russian Property Deals Near High-Risk Strategic Sites
The Lithuanian government approved a draft law prohibiting citizens of Russia and Belarus from purchasing real estate in areas located near strategically important assets.
This restriction applies to individuals from both nations even if they hold valid residence permits in the country, according to LRT on September 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The proposed legislation also bars Belarusian citizens without a residence permit from purchasing real estate anywhere in Lithuania. A similar ban for Russian citizens without residence permits was already included in a previous legislative draft.
Under the provisions of the bill, the restrictions will not apply if the property ownership is transferred through inheritance. If approved by the Lithuanian Parliament, the amendments are set to take effect on January 1, 2027.
Other regional neighbors, including Latvia and Finland, have previously introduced bans on property acquisition by Russian and Belarusian nationals, with exceptions made for those holding residence permits in those countries. Estonia is currently preparing to implement a similar prohibition.
Previously, Lithuania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs submitted amendments to the country's sanctions legislation aimed at blocking pro-war Russian and Belarusian public figures from entering the country and preventing real estate purchases near critical infrastructure.
Under the proposed measures, individuals and corporate entities supporting Moscow’s war effort were to be prohibited from conducting public activities in education, culture, sports, and entertainment.
To enter Lithuania, visiting figures were required to sign a public declaration condemning Russian military aggression and supporting Ukrainian sovereignty, with refusal resulting in an automatic denial of entry. Furthermore, the draft legislation introduced real estate restrictions that prevented Russian and Belarusian citizens with residence permits from acquiring property near military grounds or key national security facilities.

Different arrangements and programmed patterns allowed each dress to switch between colors and designs, creating a changing visual effect as models moved down the runway. Unlike a screen that produces its own light, the E Ink elements reflect surrounding light, allowing the pieces to display different colors and patterns across their surfaces.
E Ink Prism is a material technology that allows programmable colors and patterns to be displayed on electronic-paper surfaces in different shapes and sizes. The technology can be used in applications ranging from color-changing vehicles and car interiors to fashion accessories.
E Ink’s electronic paper does not need to continuously consume power to maintain an image. The display retains its color or pattern after it changes, with power required mainly when the color or pattern is switched.
The collaboration reflects Anrealage’s approach to exploring unconventional materials and the relationship between clothing and perception. E Ink Japan General Manager Sumita Naoki said the brand’s approach aligns with E Ink’s goal of turning traditionally static surfaces into dynamic and expressive experiences.
Paris Fashion Week for Spring/Summer 2027 is taking place from Sept. 28 to Oct. 6, with 68 runway shows and 33 presentations scheduled throughout the event. The lineup includes established names such as Hermes, Givenchy, and Miu Miu, according to Vogue Adria.

‘Thrilling’: Dutch cattle farmers switch to rice as solution to warmer climate and sinking peatlands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:58 UTC
18:00:58 KST

Dutch cattle farming dries out peatland and releases CO2. Is switching to Japanese rice-growing a solution?
The warming climate is allowing Dutch farmers to grow a grain never before harvested in the Netherlands: rice.
For centuries, cows were the country's agricultural staple. But now farmers are experimenting with produce previously unthinkable in such a wet, temperate country.
And researchers behind the scheme hope rice cultivation could help address one of the country's most pressing environmental challenges: peat soils that are sinking as they dry out, pushing parts of the low-lying Netherlands ever lower.
"It's extraordinary," says Philippe Terheggen, chairman of the Land van Ons association that has provided the fields for the rice harvest.
"We would never have thought maybe 20 years ago that we would be able to grow rice in the Netherlands," says the 68-year-old.
"But it's also scary because it tells you what is possible... now the climate has changed," he says.
For now, the project is a pilot scheme, consisting of just 0.6 hectares, with organisers hoping to produce around three tonnes of short-grain rice suitable for sushi or risotto.
The team is working with around 30 different rice cultivars from as far afield as Russia, China, Japan and Uzbekistan, to see which grows best in the Dutch climate.
'I just want to show that things can be changed for the benefit of the future'
In a soggy field between Amsterdam and The Hague, farmer Sander Roeleveld ploughs his rice crops with a combine harvester, backdropped by windmills and canals.
Roeleveld, who describes himself as a "pioneer", says he wants to show other farmers that rice could grow in boggy Dutch soil.
"My goal is to show that more things are possible on wetland than just grass," the 53-year-old says.
"Of course, when you have had cows for 600 years, it's really hard to imagine that you want to do something else than having milk from your cow," he laughs.
"I just want to show that things can be changed for the benefit of the future."
How rice farming could cure dried out peatlands
But the project is about much more than crop diversification. Researchers believe it could help tackle one of the Netherlands' most persistent environmental problems.
Roughly one-tenth of the country is peatland, which farmers drain for grass to feed their cattle.
As the peat dries out, it releases millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide while causing the land to subside by up to several centimetres a year in the worst-affected areas.
According to Wageningen University, greenhouse gas emissions from Dutch peat soils account for around two to three per cent of the country's total emissions.
The only way to resolve this vicious cycle is to keep the fields wet – but then farmers would have nothing to grow there... until now.
"Basically it started with just a crazy idea," explains Julian Helfenstein, a researcher from Wageningen University and Research, who is piloting the project along with colleagues from nearby Leiden University.
It is a rare combination of both adapting to climate change and mitigating its effects, says the 36-year-old.
"Rice is an opportunity for this part of the world to adapt to climate change, so to grow something that previously wasn't possible," he says.
"But also to mitigate climate change because it stops this peat from degrading and emitting all the CO2 because you can keep it wet."
The peat issue affects not just the Netherlands, but much of northern Europe, including Germany, Belgium, even the Baltic states, he says.
Helfenstein and his team are closely monitoring the CO2 and methane emissions from cultivating rice compared to maintaining grassland – to ensure the cure is not worse than the illness.
"So far the results are promising," he says.
"As an environmental scientist, you're always pointing to the problems. And it can be a bit depressing, like, 'Oh, here's more climate change, here's more pollution'," says Helfenstein.
"And then here's an opportunity for science to work also towards a solution. So I find that thrilling."
'Chewy, but great': Dutch rice could be used to make sushi and sake
Local restaurants have already voiced an interest in offering premium Dutch-sourced rice, says Guusje van der Vossen from the Wij Land association which helps farmers transition to more sustainable production.
She says the rice being harvested now was a grain from northern Japan, which seems the best adapted to Dutch conditions.
The 27-year-old is one of the few people ever to have eaten Dutch-grown rice – from an experimental batch grown last year.
"It tasted delicious, to be honest," she laughs, saying the aim was to make sushi with it – and maybe sake.
"It was a bit chewy, but also great."

Would I want my child to study for a social media influencer degree? No, but it’s the way of the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:36 UTC
18:00:36 KST

Sometimes you read a story in the news that seems designed to wind up as many people as possible. This week, that story involves a degree in content creation from Nottingham Trent University. Otherwise known as the “influencer degree”, this three-year course comes with BA (Hons) status and a top-tier price tag of almost £10,000 a year, for which students will learn “hands-on technical production”, “analytics, branding and commercial strategy” and collaboration with brands and “industry partners”. Course leaders are at pains to point out it won’t turn them into overnight social media stars, but of course, while reading, I felt the cold drag of undertow forces pulling me towards world-gone-mad outrage.
We’ve been here before, obviously: media studies, women’s studies, anything that hasn’t been on the syllabus of the ancient universities for at least 500 years is vulnerable to accusations of dumbing down – and this is no different. The course was launched in 2022, meaning its first cohort of graduates are out there looking for jobs right now, while giving interviews about whether or not it was worth it. One very sensible-sounding graduate, talking to the BBC this week in what one assumes is an application of the all-publicity-is-good-publicity principle learned from her course, said that the £30,000 spend was worth it for the networking opportunities alone – an absolutely valid point and half the reason why people strive towards Oxbridge.
Still, there will be eyebrows twitching. That price tag seems punchy for a course that is currently in clearing. But the bigger issue is the triggering effect the words “social media” and “influencer” will have on parents mired in data supporting the view that their children’s lives are in constant peril from the forces unleashed by online platforms and the jobs that go with them. What next? A degree course in dropshipping?! How about an MPhil in manosphere studies? And so on and so on: all modern versions of the sinking spirits that have traditionally attended a child announcing they want to go to drama school.
In general, we’ve always been quite sniffy about vocational degrees in this country. Look at the prestige that comes, for example, from attending Columbia Journalism School in the US, despite much laughter from journalists in this country who think the best way to study journalism is to get a job in journalism. British friends with jobs in marketing hold similar views about degrees in that subject: “Get a job, it’s stupid to pay to study it.” If degree courses are supposed to teach critical thinking, so the argument goes, then these courses don’t qualify as suitably academic – not a concern anyone ever raises about medicine or law.
It’s snobbery, then, and in this case also conditioning. Influencing is empty, pointless, evil and grifty, underscored by narcissism and fulfilling no useful human or social need – an assessment that might just as easily be applied to the careers in banking that so many top graduates head towards. If anything, it seems to me that influencing is a clever spin from Nottingham Trent (and Brighton University, which also offers the course) in response to the terrible state of traditional media careers. Going forward, it’s fair to assume that for those going into the media, the smart move is to be an independent contractor rather than hold a traditional job without bonus structures or opportunities for profit-sharing.
In case you haven’t noticed, I’m trying hard here to argue against the gravitational pull exerted by my own experience of doing a traditional degree. I guess the real test would be what any of us parents would say if our kids came to us with an intention to apply for one of these courses.
In my own household, we’d have to go through a whole rigmarole in which I would definitely infuriate my children by suggesting their time might be better spent reading The Wife of Bath’s Tale or, like, the structure and function of proteins. I’d be forced to lecture them on the hollow interior life of anyone chasing fame and say the words, “Do we think the Kardashians are actually happy?” Then I’d look at the job market, at all the listings for social media managers, podcast producers and video editors and, if I could get over myself, might work my way to the conclusion that they could do a lot worse. (I’m kidding, I’d be devastated.)
- 
  Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

An organisation pushing the Green party to equate Zionism with racism has encouraged people to join the party specifically to support that agenda, and has links to activists who say that pro-Israel “infiltrators” must be rooted out of the UK, the Guardian has learned.
Some Green members are increasingly concerned that the party risks being manipulated by extremist outsiders over a motion to be voted on at the party’s annual conference this weekend, which states that “Zionism is racism”.
Some Jewish members have said privately they fear it will be difficult for them to remain in the party if the policy passes.
Zack Polanski, who leads the Green party in England and Wales, has come under pressure to take a definitive stance on the motion amid worries the controversy will harm the party in next week’s key Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Polanski is seeking to win Keir Starmer’s former seat.
The motion came top of a members’ ballot of policy issues to be debated at the event in Brighton. It calls for a single Palestinian state and, if passed, it would mean members who support Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – could be disciplined for racism.
The controversy reflects a longstanding debate about the definition of Zionism, the political movement whose supporters see it as the necessary struggle for a Jewish homeland, and whose critics see it as a colonial project that has inevitably led to the dispossession of Palestinians. The term Zionist is, meanwhile, sometimes used as a synonym for Jew by antisemites.
Efforts to push the policy have been led by Greens for Palestine (GfP), a group not formally affiliated with the party. In repeated social media posts over recent months, GfP has urged backers of the idea to sign up as Green members specifically to get the motion debated at the conference and then adopted.
Polanski last week declared he was anti-Zionist, adding that Zionism was a form of racism because it involved the displacement and genocide of Palestinians. But he has supported amendments to tone down the motion. Lubna Speitan, a leading member of GfP who co-authored the motion, has rejected the amendments.
“It doesn’t matter what the leadership thinks,” Speitan said in a recent video, adding: “We are certainly not here to negotiate the terms of our liberation or oppression with any of our oppressors.”
GfP and Speitan have links to a group called the Anti-Zionist Movement (AZM), a more militant campaign group that argues that the “so-called Jewish state” should be dismantled, along with “Zionist organisations” in the UK and elsewhere.
A key member of AZM is David Miller, a former academic who was sacked by Bristol University over his criticisms of Israel, and subsequently won a tribunal case after it ruled he had been discriminated against because of his anti-Zionist views. He now presents a show for Press TV, the Iranian state channel.
In social media posts, Miller has argued that Zionists have, as “infiltrators and subversives”, gained access to not just all UK political parties but also “the media, entertainment industries, the law, financial institutions, sports and all sorts of apparently obscure parts of the UK”.
GfP and AZM have collaborated on a series of social media posts, and Speitan attended an AZM meeting in London this year. In a video posted by AZM about the meeting, Speitan said it was important for anti-Zionist groups to collaborate.
Speaking in the same video, Miller said his aim was to “dismantle Zionist organisations wherever they are in the world, including the 3,000 or 4,000 Zionist organisations in this country”.
Some senior Greens say they are deeply worried about the links. One said: “I just don’t understand why Zack hasn’t provided any leadership on this, especially when we have such a crucial byelection just days later.”
A spokesperson for the Greens said: “The Green party is a democratic party and membership has grown as more people join to support our full policy platform. The vast majority of members joined prior to a specific attempt at mobilisation.”
They added: “The Green party does not support the views of the AZM.”
A spokesperson for GfP cited Miller’s employment tribunal, saying it “concluded that anti-Zionist beliefs constitute a protected belief”, adding: “We reject all conflations of anti-Zionism with antisemitism, just as we reject the settler colonial project in occupied Palestine.”
Asked about the links to AZM, they added: “We welcome the adoption of our motion by all anti-racist organisations, political parties and unions.”
GfP, the statement added, “affirms the Palestinian people’s inalienable right to self-determination, including the right of the Palestinian people to resistance and liberation from Israeli occupation, domination and subjugation” via any means under international law.

UK bookmakers that warned over illicit market had deal with offshore casinos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:35 UTC
18:00:35 KST

Three UK bookmakers that have repeatedly warned of the dangers of the illicit market have also benefited from a lucrative deal with one of the world’s largest offshore casinos, the Guardian can reveal.
Details of the arrangement emerged as a result of last week’s Casino Secrets leak, which saw the release of thousands of confidential files held by the gambling regulator on the Caribbean island of Curaçao, a haven for offshore betting sites.
One leaked file concerns the Santeda online casino network, which has been accused of illegally targeting vulnerable gamblers in the UK and has been fined in Spain for operating without a licence.
The file shows that Santeda signed a deal in 2022 with Sports Information Services (SIS) – a UK-based gambling content provider part-owned by Ladbrokes, William Hill and Fred Done, the billionaire owner of Betfred.
The three bookmakers have repeatedly warned the government that excessive regulation or taxation could drive their customers into the arms of rogue offshore casinos with no licence to operate in Britain.
According to the leak, all three have also benefited from a share of tens of millions of pounds in dividends paid out by SIS after it signed the contract with Santeda.
The companies are understood to have been unaware of the deal at the time it was signed. Matt Zarb-Cousin, a prominent gambling reform campaigner, advised them to get their “house in order”.
The bookmakers collectively own more than 50% of SIS, which supplies gambling sites with live horse racing, greyhound and esports content, as well as data used to settle bets with customers.
The use of such data is critical to online betting companies, helping them serve customers and process their bets.
The leaked contract shows that SIS also agreed to provide Santeda websites with these services for two years, under a contract that auto-renewed unless either side opted to terminate it.
Under the terms of the deal, SIS received a percentage of revenues from losing bets placed via Santeda’s brands.
It is not clear whether the contract is still active, or how much SIS earned from it. SIS declined to say whether the deal had been terminated.
Industry sources said that Ladbrokes, William Hill and Fred Done could not have known about the deal with Santeda, owing to controls designed to prevent them accessing commercially-sensitive information about industry rivals.
One source said the companies were “furious” with SIS for doing business with Santeda, at a time when licensed operators were stepping up their warnings about the illicit market.
Entain said it was “not a party to the commercial or customer arrangements SIS decides to strike. Now that this relationship has come to light, we take it very seriously and have raised our concerns to SIS”.
The contract with Santeda does not permit the use of SIS data in the UK.
But it appears to show that SIS supplied information to multiple Santeda websites that a previous Guardian investigation found was illegally targeting UK customers, including via promotional material apparently aimed at people trying to quit.
Santeda’s Curaçao licence does not permit it to operate in most leading jurisdictions that regulate gambling, such as the UK and US.
Companies House filings suggest that SIS’s shareholders – including Ladbrokes, William Hill and Done – have received at least £37m in dividends since the deal with Santeda was signed, including £30m in 2023.
Ladbrokes owns 23% of SIS, suggesting it has received £8.5m in payouts over the period.
Stella David, the chief executive of the Ladbrokes owner Entain, has criticised Premier League football clubs for “complicity” in fuelling illicit operators and warned that such firms could be boosted by any rise in taxes on licensed operators such as Ladbrokes.
William Hill appears to have received more than £7m from its near-20% stake in SIS.
Earlier this year, the bookmaker’s owner, Evoke, blamed the illicit market for weak online revenues.
Fred Done, who is also a director of SIS, holds an 8% stake, indicating his share of shareholder payouts was nearly £3m.
Done warned the chancellor this month that higher taxes on slot machines – under consideration as part of the upcoming budget – would drive punters to illicit market sites that don’t pay tax, contribute to horse racing or exercise regulatory controls.
Zarb-Cousin, the director of the gambling-blocking company Gamban and a longtime campaigner for tougher laws, said: “While the UK’s biggest gambling firms have been warning about the risks of growing the illicit market if the government increases tax and regulation, the very same firms are profiting from it.
“If the gambling industry is concerned about the black market, it needs to get its own house in order by cutting all ties with it.”
A spokesperson for SIS said all of its customers agreed to “only offer SIS products where it is legal to do so and where they have the necessary regulatory licences”.
They added: “Customers commit that they will comply with all such laws and licences at all times.
“Where SIS becomes aware that these terms are not being adhered to it takes corrective action to enforce the position, up to and including suspension or termination of contracts.”
The Guardian approached Evoke and Fred Done for comment.

‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of Trump

He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian revolution: a feisty leftist TV personality who spent more than two decades singing the movement’s praises on his state-funded show, The Razorblade.
Mario Silva’s devotion was such that he often hosted his programme with Chávez’s portrait behind him and he had El Comandante’s curly signature tattooed on to his left wrist.
But nine months after Venezuela’s political landscape was scrambled by Donald Trump’s abduction of Chávez’s heir, Nicolás Maduro, Silva’s show has been cancelled, and its host is livid about the revolution’s direction under Maduro’s former deputy, Delcy Rodríguez.
“[I feel] a lot of disappointment – depressed … and sometimes I wake up and feel like the world is collapsing around me,” the 66-year-old said during a rare interview at his home studio in the mountains outside the capital, Caracas.
Silva has spent recent weeks railing against Rodríguez’s interim administration on YouTube, his home since his programme on state TV was axed, berating those he blames for Venezuela’s “shameful and utterly illegitimate surrender” to the US.
Since January, a parade of high-ranking US officials – including the head of the CIA, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff and the energy secretary, Chris Wright – have visited Caracas, while Trump recently trumpeted striking “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Rodríguez’s regime. Last week, Rodríguez and Trump met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, posing for a smiley photograph that left diehard Chavistas such as Silva aghast.
“I thought it [the photo] was artificial intelligence or something like that. But it’s surrealism, utter surrealism … It’s impossible to understand,” Silva fumed on YouTube as a red flag emblazoned with the faces of Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels and Vladimir Lenin hung behind him.
“They have surrendered this country and surrendered it the most vile and despicable way,” Silva went on. “Honestly, they are dragging the country’s name through the mud. They are dragging Chávez’s name through the mud.”
In another broadcast, Silva seethed about the cosy post-Maduro relationship that has developed between one-time anti-imperialist flagbearers in Caracas and Trump officials: “Traitors and lackeys, you will have to answer for this!”
Silva is not the only Chavista loyalist struggling to comprehend the ideological U-turn being executed by Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president but has engineered a historic rapprochement with the US since his rendition on 3 January.
Elías Jaua, a vice-president and foreign minister under Chávez, is also up in arms, and claims the feeling is widely shared. “What I hear from comrades across the country is bewilderment, disagreement and indignation,” said Jaua, who believes Trump’s oil deal “amounts to an act of pillage against an entire nation”.
Juan Barreto, a former member of the ruling Socialist party (PSUV) and mayor of Caracas, said such an agreement would have been unimaginable when the Bolivarian revolution began after Chávez’s 1998 election. He said Chavistas, who had once vowed “Not a drop of oil to the empire if Venezuela is attacked!”, were now in effect saying: “All of the oil reserves [for the US], for as long as you want!”
“The current situation is one of tutelage,” Barreto said.
Rodríguez has defended the deal, claiming it will create more than $209bn (£158bn) in revenues that will help improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said in a recent TV broadcast.
Héctor Rodríguez, another prominent Chavista politician, has sought to deflect criticism of Venezuela’s interim government by recalling how Chávez was forced to make a tactical retreat after his failed coup attempt in 1992. “No one can tell me Chávez was a coward. He understood that the balance of power had shifted … and decided to take a step backwards,” Rodríguez said recently.
Last week as Delcy Rodríguez met Trump in New York, thousands of people joined a pro-government rally in Caracas, where supporters parroted the slogan “Delcy avanza, tú tienes mi confianza!” (“Move forward, Delcy. I trust in you!”).
“No matter how much they kick and scream, there’s nothing they can do to try to cover up the success of President Delcy Rodríguez’s visit to New York,” her interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, told the crowd. Unlike at previous marches, there was scant mention of Maduro and few calls for him to be released.
The depth and potential consequences of Chavista anger over Rodríguez’s embrace of Venezuela’s longtime foes in Washington remain unclear.
Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, recognised there was indignation at what some considered a sellout of their anti-imperialist ideals. “There are Chavistas that are pissed off, there’s no question about it,” he said. “There are Chavistas who see this as a betrayal of Hugo Chávez and the betrayal of the movement.”
But Pérez believed that for many Chavistas who had remained in power after Trump’s invasion, the “pragmatic reality” was that working with Washington was “a necessary evil” if it meant keeping Venezuela’s opposition out of power.
“If that means negotiating with Trump, if that means dealing with the CIA etc, it’s fine,” he said. “Beyond whatever ideological position they might have … I suspect most of them are gritting their teeth and just going along with this process as long as they can stay in power and keep their jobs. I think for most it’s as simple as that: it’s about their material wellbeing.”
However, Pérez believed Rodríguez’s government would need to demonstrate to supporters “tangible benefits to the cooperation” with the US in order to avoid a backlash. “They’re going to have to show that these things have a material consequence to the lives of their social base … if you don’t deliver, then it is going to get very volatile,” he warned.
So far there has been no sign of significant resistance from outraged supporters of Chavismo. But Silva claimed the government’s new direction and economic policies could eventually trigger a social uprising and protests.
“Worsening economic conditions will degrade [people’s] quality of life, and that pressure is bound to explode. It has to explode – it’s not just wishful thinking. This isn’t a prediction born of desire, it’s an inevitability,” said the broadcaster, who has claimed he is facing investigation for alleged acts of “aggravated defamation and slander against the interim government”.
Silva lit one cigarette after another as he recalled the early hours of 3 January 2026 when, as US troops swept into Venezuela’s capital, he realised the revolution he had spent more than 20 years defending was not going to defend itself.
The Chavista broadcaster said he moved from one strategic point to another across Caracas before finally calling the commander at his assigned post. “I said: ‘Hey, what happened? Where are the weapons?’” Silva recalled, his face settling into a sad grin as he remembered the answer. “Go to sleep, Mario,” he was told.
Silva pauses. “You have no idea how disappointed I was.”

‘They showed no mercy’: mapping the Rohingya villages being erased by rebel forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:33 UTC
18:00:33 KST

There are at least 10 camps like the one on the paddy fields at Hnget Thay, built after the insurgent Arakan Army (AA) took control of most of northern Rakhine state in 2024. These are where many Rohingya people in the state now have to live. Others hide in the mountains, or flee abroad to the refugee camps of Bangladesh or make deadly boat journeys to Malaysia.
The arrival of more than 155,000 Rohingya in Bangladesh since 2024, which amounts to 25% of the 600,000 estimated to still be in Myanmar, has raised concerns about the very survival of a people who now mostly live abroad as refugees.
The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim minority group from western Myanmar who have faced decades of persecution and clashes with Buddhist nationalists. The word translates as from Rohang – the district that is now Rakhine State. Speaking a language similar to the Bengali dialect of Chattogram (formerly Chittagong) in Bangladesh, they are reviled by many in Myanmar as a foreign people and are denied citizenship by the regime.
In a military crackdown from 2016 to 2017 that led to Myanmar being accused of orchestrating ethnic cleansing, most of the Rohingya population, about 700,000 people, sought refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh. The campaign of massacres unleashed against the Rohingya then is being investigated as possible genocide at the international court of justice (ICJ).
There are now 1.2 million Rohingya in Bangladeshi refugee camps. Since Myanmar’s civil war erupted in 2021, Rohingya remaining in the country have been caught in violence, forced displacement and oppression from both sides – the insurgent AA and government forces, which are fighting each other for control of Rakhine state.
Testimony received by the Guardian and reflected in recent UN reporting provides an insight into the “catastrophic” conditions that the UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, says Rohingya are facing, including torture, gender-based violence, arbitrary arrests, confiscation of land, displacement, forced labour and conscription.
Many of the Rohingya are confined to a makeshift camp, Hnget Thay, to which the AA forced some survivors to relocate after a massacre at Hoyyar Siri. Human Rights Watch documented hundreds of unarmed Rohingya being killed at the village by AA forces.
“This is the end of the Rohingya in northern Rakhine, there is no question about that. It might take time, but the Arakan Army is working quietly to ensure the community has no future there,” says a UN specialist on Myanmar, who requested anonymity as they were not authorised to speak.
“The Rohingya can stay in prison-like camps in appalling conditions for as long as they can bear it, but they will not be permitted to return home,” they say.
An internal UN report has identified at least 800 hectares (2,000 acres) in 23 Rohingya villages that have been seized and repurposed as camps, settlements for other communities or for military infrastructure since 2024, describing this dynamic as linked to the AA’s consolidation of territory under its control.
Muhammad Ares, 18, a Rohingya who now lives in Bangladesh, says: “They used bulldozers to clear out entire residential areas, turning our villages into completely flat, empty fields.
“They cut down all the trees and cleared away every trace of our community, leaving nothing but barren ground. In the areas where they demolished our houses, they cleared the debris and set up their own military camps and outposts.”
The changes in the Buthidaung area of Rakhine happened after the AA took control of much of the region and active fighting abated. Data from the independent conflict monitor Acled shows 12 battles in Buthidaung in 2025, compared with 103 in 2024.
Mohammed Sadik, 26, from Ywet Nyo Taung, says: “They ordered us to stop farming and declared that the land no longer belonged to us; they confiscated the agricultural fields entirely.”
“They forced us to clear roads, dig trenches, and perform heavy labour inside their camps,” he says. “They forced us to work continuously. If anyone collapsed from exhaustion, they were left in the sun.”
All of their farm tools and land were confiscated and the AA authorities refused to return them, Sadik says, even when they explained they needed to grow food to survive.
Video shared with the Guardian by people from Ywet Nyo Taung appears to show the destruction wreaked on the area during this period. The footage was filmed by two locals riding on a motorbike southwards from the main school to the village of U Hla Hpay, which was completely destroyed.
In the footage, they point out landmarks such as schools, mosques, ferry docks, shops and homes. Towards the end of the footage, the person filming points out his own home. Scorched earth is visible and the structures are almost entirely demolished apart from a former bathroom that is partially intact.
Throughout the footage, bricks are seen lined up, often in neat piles, along the side of the road.
In multiple testimonies from Rohingya who were made to work by the AA, they said the forced labour included dismantling Rohingya property to use the materials to build new buildings for the insurgents, including the construction of military barracks, locally known as the AP Battalion, in Ywet Nyo Taung, for housing forcibly recruited Rohingya.
The AA claims to fight in the interests of all Rakhine state’s ethnic groups, and since 2024 has seized control of most of the region. Outwardly, it has proclaimed sympathy for the Rohingya’s suffering but conversely stands accused of emulating the policies of the Myanmar military when it destroyed and confiscated Rohingya land and subjected people to forced labour and conscription, including in the fight against the AA.
Last year, the UN-backed Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) released a report listing seven villages the Myanmar military had destroyed in 2017 and then built bases on. The ICJ, which is expected to deliver a decision in October on whether Rohingya were subjected to genocide in 2017, has previously considered the “systematic expulsion from and destruction of homes” to be an element of genocide.
The report highlighted that land in Myanmar is owned through a leasehold system and that the military exploited laws designed for natural disasters that allowed burned land to revert to the state, stripping away Rohingya ownership. Another law passed in 2018, after the Rohingya exodus, allowed uncultivated land to be taken by the state.
It was under these conditions that 250,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh in the early 1990s, first creating the refugee camps that became the world’s largest in 2017.
The IIMM’s head, Nicholas Koumjian, says: “Clearly, those that orchestrated the attacks on the Rohingya had the objective to create ‘facts on the ground’.” However, he adds that they have not confirmed the AA is responsible for the destruction of Rohingya land. “The Rohingya still inside Myanmar seem to be targeted by all sides of the ongoing conflict and caught in the middle of that conflict.”
Aung Kyaw Moe, who was until recently the only Rohingya member of Myanmar’s “national unity government”, a pro-democracy body in opposition to the 2021 military coup leaders that operates in exile, says the Rohingya are facing a “dangerous new phase” for those inside the country and for refugees hoping to return.
“The central issue is no longer whether Rohingya can survive in Myanmar,” he says. “It is whether conditions are being created that will make their permanent displacement and the erasure of their physical, political and historical presence irreversible.
“If villages are erased and land is being transformed while refugees remain outside of the country, then return becomes progressively more difficult.”
The UN report and testimony shared with the Guardian describe how Rohingya were not only displaced from their land but forced to provide men and women to work for, and to train for, the AA.
“I was forced to undergo military training against my will. I never volunteered to join any armed group,” says a 32-year-old Rohingya man conscripted by the insurgents. He described being initially held for a month, during which time he was repeatedly beaten.
“Throughout my detention, I endured constant physical abuse, psychological intimidation and forced labour.”
Another man said his 22-year-old daughter was taken by AA militia, who subjected her to physical and sexual abuse and made her carry out housekeeping duties for them. She also had to undergo military training.
As well as being forced to provide labour and conscripts, testimony from Rohingya who escaped to Bangladesh from Rakhine describe coercion to make regular payments of “taxes” to the AA, confiscation of land and livestock, and restrictions on their free movement. All of these were tactics enforced previously by the Myanmar military.
Tom Dannenbaum, a professor of international law at Stanford University in the US, says a combination of coercion and the dislocation of Rohingya, either internally or abroad, could amount to the war crime of population transfer.
“It’s devastating for any group to be socially dislocated, inflicted with destructive conditions of life, have their property destroyed and seized,” he says. “All of that is part of making the viability of that group socially, as well as physically, ultimately [impossible]. It clearly creates conditions for that group that make it very difficult to sustain.”
Salamat Khan fled from Rakhine state to Bangladesh in 2024. He feels it is impossible to return to Myanmar, as AA fighters ordered him to leave after attacking his village: “The fighters said to us: ‘go to Bangladesh, your homes are gone, go to the [refugee] camps’.”
This independent journalism was supported by theguardian.org
Methodology
UN research identified land and property confiscation sites and camps created to confine displaced Rohingya. Interviews and additional testimony also provided information on where Rohingya villages were destroyed. Satellite imagery was used to analyse changes in these areas from before the Arakan Army’s takeover of these areas in April 2024 and after.
The photo and video of Ywet Nyo Taung were verified through the use of landmarks, notably the large school near the Mayu River, and the shape of the mountains behind the village. Nasa Fire Information for Resource Management (Firms) data was used to confirm the timing of fires in the area.

Forget ‘superintelligence’: error-prone AI nearly sparked world war three this month | Timnit Gebru and Emily M Bender
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:33 UTC
18:00:33 KST

Amid a barrage of news stories warning about superintelligent machines rendering humanity extinct, a CNN story describing the opposite scenario – one in which the US military’s reliance on brittle chatbots almost brought the US into war with China – went mostly unnoticed by the public.
The biggest international AI news of the past three weeks was Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon’s resignation. According to him, OpenAI and Anthropic are “racing straight towards self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”. Coxon’s description of a “terminator” scenario, a machine becoming much smarter than humanity and deciding to wipe us out, captured the public, journalists’ and politicians’ attention, stirring waves of fear-inducing, credulous reporting, and policy actions.
California governor Gavin Newsom issued a mandate to create an “AI kill-switch”; New York governor Kathy Hochul is similarly exploring the possibility of having “AI kill-switches”; and Senator Bernie Sanders and Congressman Greg Casar introduced legislation to “ban artificial superintelligence”.
While so many of us were focused on fictional superintelligent machines that we were told could hypothetically cause human extinction, however, there was a more serious story being reported.
A series of events almost got us to armageddon, not caused by “rogue, superintelligent AI”, but by government reliance on error-prone systems that are marketed by their manufacturers as being close to superintelligent.
A CNN report published on 18 September, which hasn’t been verified by other major outlets, describes how the US “almost started a war” with China, based on an intelligence report that claimed a Chinese ship was transporting components of nuclear weapons. Military personnel made plans to intercept the Chinese vessel, complete with aircraft and soldiers ready to board the ship. A military skirmish of this kind between China and the US could quickly escalate and spiral into world war three.
It was only moments before executing on the plan that American officials further investigated the intelligence report and found that it had been generated with the use of a chatbot and contained erroneous information about the vessel’s contents.
Unlike the terminator, “rogue AI”, scenario, this incident didn’t galvanize lawmakers into announcing calls for regulation so as to avoid potential human extinction. Media outlet after media outlet didn’t warn the public that we almost triggered a war against a nuclear superpower because of our military’s reliance on error-prone chatbots.
We describe the large language models (LLMs) powering these chatbots as stochastic parrots, that is, models that are designed to regurgitate the patterns of the data they are trained on. News coverage describing them as “powerful” “rogue” models that could render humanity extinct all on their own, bolsters perceptions of tools based on these models being infallible enough to merit usage in stakes as high as warfare.
Even CNN’s more critical coverage describes the chatbot used by the US military as presenting “profound risks” because it is “powerful, new and relatively poorly understood technology”.
In fact, today’s LLMs and the chatbots they power are not poorly understood, nor are they powerful in the sense of being effective tools for this use case. They are systems for generating plausible looking text, built out of enormous, haphazardly collected datasets and then “fine-tuned” (that is, further trained) to be especially appealing to their intended users.
CNN wasn’t able to learn which chatbot product was used in this case, but the LLM powering the product was likely fine-tuned to output text with the stylistic hallmarks of intelligence reports. Both the basic functionality and the risks of such a model have been well-understood and well-documented for years, including in our 2021 paper On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?
Claims that system behavior is mysterious arise from deliberate mystification on the part of those selling those systems, and a misapprehension of what their output is by those procuring and using it.
Unlike the unscientific and fantastical claims of OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs and those who uncritically repeat their talking points, the harmful, and well-documented, impacts of these companies’ products have arisen because people believe that the products are superintelligent, not because they actually are.
From “AI” scribes used by hospitals erroneously classifying patients as illicit drug users, to governments killing children after relying on “intelligence analysis” systems which mistake schools for military facilities, we are seeing the predictable harms that come from misplaced faith in unreliable automated software.
Meanwhile, the marketing campaigns from the companies selling this software warn of impending superintelligence, directing our attention away from the real risk to their fantasies of doom.
It is high time for us to regulate usage of systems sold as “AI”, not because they are magical machines, but because they are error-prone products that shouldn’t be used in high stakes scenarios. Any automation used in military, medical or other life-and-death situations must be thoroughly evaluated within its use case and paired with usage norms that keep accountability with people who have actual power to make decisions.
As former FTC chair Lina Khan has repeatedly reminded us, there is no exemption to the law when it comes to AI: there are existing laws that federal agencies and other regulators can enforce to protect the public against the AI industry’s unsafe and unscientific practices of pushing unsound products while marketing them as “magic intelligence in the sky”.
Going along with company executives and describing their products as beings with agency allows these executives to evade accountability while deceiving the public. We call on journalists and lawmakers to hold companies accountable rather than parrot their marketing talking points.
- 
  Timnit Gebru is executive director of Dair and author of the forthcoming book Deep Unlearning: The Radicalization of a Tech Idealist, which is available for preorders now and set to publish on 16 February.
- 
  Emily M Bender is professor of linguistics at the University of Washington and co-author of The AI Con.

Beansprouts, nonya paste and kefir – whose fridge is this?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:32 UTC
18:00:32 KST

Curry leaves
I used to freeze fresh curry leaves, but then [the chef] Romy Gill said you lose all the aroma when you do this. So now I fry them and you get curry leaf oil, which keeps them fresh. You can then crumble them into things like dal.
Tofu
I’m addicted to tofu – I have firm, medium, soft, and puffy. But this is my breakfast tofu in ginger syrup; it’s like junket but made with soya beans. Someone taught me how to make this, but the secret ingredient was plaster of paris, so I get it from the Asian grocers. I’m not a big breakfast person, but I could easily eat a whole tub of this.
Chilli
This is my chilli box, which is on wheels – I’m short and need to get to the back of the fridge! I love Poon’s Everything Everywhere sauce: it’s all I need with poached prawns or chicken, or I might do a splodge on ramen with veggies and tofu. My ethos is: “always have two so you always have one,” although I do forget which one is open.
Lamb, mince, Chinese sausage.
My meat drawer has marinated lamb for the week, mince for mapo tofu, Chinese sausage, but also white anchovies and dried scallops. I also collect parmesan rinds [in a bag] in here, which I always think I’m going to make something with, but they sometimes just sit here.
Kiwi
I’m a two-kiwi-a-day person: one in the morning and one in the evening. It’s something sharp, sweet and puckery to freshen me up.
Black sesame paste
I have this from testing various recipes, but if I’m craving something chilled and sweet, then I make tang yuan [glutinous rice balls] filled with this paste.
Shawarma marinade
I used to make shawarma marinade from scratch, but it was such a pain. We do Friday night dinner instead of Sunday lunch, and last week I smothered a leg of lamb with this marinade from Ottolenghi.
Garlic shoots
When I’ve been away, I just want a load of greens, and quickly. I’m addicted to garlic shoots, which I blanch quickly and stir-fry with Chinese sausage, then I add rice and an egg and I’m so happy.
Kefir
I don’t drink kefir – I just couldn’t – but I use it like buttermilk, which is so good in cakes, but not easy to find here – plus, buttermilk is not always consistent. Kefir is so much better.
Salmon
My son is protein maxxing, so I’ve always got salmon. I squeeze in mayonnaise to oil and protect it, then I toss the fish in soy sauce, shoaxing wine, lemon juice or rice wine vinegar, sometimes wasabi paste, and grill for two minutes per side. That goes into poke bowls, to which I can also add some edamame.
Homemade elderflower cordial
I’ve been experimenting with how little sugar I can put in this. It has come out quite sharp, but it’s very refreshing.
Vanilla essence
Every time I use a vanilla bean, I pop it in here: my seven-year-old vanilla essence. Homemade vanilla essence, cheap vanilla essence, and a good vanilla paste are all different products to me. Sometimes I want that cheap, childish flavour, but this is somewhere in between.
Tamarind
I have both Thai and Indian tamarind. I love using tamarind in baking, if I’m caramelising something, otherwise I’ll add a squeeze to dal (instead of lemon) and curries.
Beansprouts
A friend from Malaysia sent me her World of Nyonya all-purpose spice paste, which if you add coconut milk turns into laksa. I then add beansprouts, fresh egg noodles, and my puffy tofu.

Lost in translation: Montenegro's EU accession faces a language barrier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:23 UTC
18:00:23 KST

Montenegro may not be able to accurately translate all EU laws in time for accession, so the European Commission is currently weighing options for a derogation, including allowing Podgorica to use an existing EU language to fill the gaps. Croatian would be the most obvious choice.
Montenegro may fall short of translating all EU laws accurately before it joins the bloc. The European Commission is weighing several options for a temporary derogation, including letting the country use an existing EU language in the meantime.
Montenegro aims to become the EU's 28th member by 2028. But first it must adopt and translate the so-called acquis, the tens of thousands of EU laws that form the bloc's legal framework. Brussels is growing wary that it will not finish in time.
"Montenegro will need to produce translations of the acquis into its official language in good time before accession and will need to train a sufficient number of translators and interpreters required for the proper functioning of the EU institutions upon its accession," reads the country's negotiating framework with the EU.
Podgorica has invested significantly in its administrative capacity and assures that the work will be completed on time. But the EU executive has started looking at contingency plans, EU officials told Euronews.
The reason is that Croatia has been raising concerns about the quality of some translated legal texts. Zagreb is locked in a bilateral dispute with Montenegro that could delay the whole accession process.
Since Croatia, the bloc's most recent entrant, joined in 2013, the body of EU legislation has almost doubled.
Candidate countries must translate all relevant EU legislation into their future official language. The EU institutions are only responsible for a final check before publication in the Official Journal at the time of accession.
Translation is also only part of the linguistic preparation. Some laws need adapting to the candidate's institutional context, for instance by designating which authorities will be in charge of supervision.
"The Commission services are in regular contact with Montenegro and reviewing the pace of work in this regard," a Commission spokesperson told Euronews.
The Commission is assessing several options for a potential derogation, including allowing Montenegro to use another official EU language until it has time to fill the gaps and accurately translate the remaining legislation.
It would be up to Podgorica to choose, but Croatian is the obvious candidate. It is the only official EU language that shares the same core features and is understandable to a Montenegrin speaker.
"The Montenegrin standard language belongs to the same dialect continuum as the Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian standard languages, and that all are mutually intelligible," reads a recent study on the Montenegrin language.
Still, this is only one option among several, and it may not sit well with Montenegro. Identity politics runs deep in the Western Balkans, and Podgorica fought for years to have the Montenegrin language officially recognised internationally.
Derogations are not new. Malta set a precedent: short of qualified translators, it secured an exceptional, transitional derogation from the obligation to translate all EU acts into Maltese for three years after joining in 2004, with any backlog due by the end of 2008.
Ireland is another, with a key difference. Its derogation came decades after it joined, when Irish became a full official language, and it temporarily suspended the obligation to translate all EU acts into Irish.
In other words, Brussels has shown flexibility, not treating full translation of the acquis as an absolute condition for accession. Still, in this case, the most obvious fix may also be the hardest to sell politically.

Kremlin critic and chess legend Garry Kasparov said Thursday that US and Lithuanian security services had told him and his ally that their lives were in danger and urged them to take security precautions.
“News that I, along with my longtime associate and co-founder of the Free Russia Forum, Ivan Tyutrin, are on a list of assassination targets did not come as a surprise to me, but it is nevertheless a shock,” the 63-year-old said on social media.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Lithuanian and US security services informed us that our lives were in danger and that we should take precautionary measures,” said Kasparov, who lives in exile in the United States. “I did exactly that, and I will continue to do so in the future.”
His Vilnius-based ally Tyutrin, 45, told AFP the Lithuanian authorities had warned him two weeks ago to “leave my home urgently and get rid of my car.”
The warnings came after the US Department of Justice in mid-September announced charges against five alleged agents of Russian intelligence accused of conspiring to carry out attacks and murders around the world, including in the United States.
The group attempted to have a “prominent Russian dissident” living in the United States murdered this summer in exchange for an estimated $40,000, the department said. US authorities did not name the Kremlin critic, identifying him only as “Victim-1”.
One of the defendants is an officer of Russia’s FSB security service.
Lockheed Martin in ‘Deep’ Overseas Patriot Production Talks as Ukraine Eyes Domestic Output
‘Assassination plot’
Spanish newspaper El Mundo said Wednesday, citing sources close to Kasparov, that Russian agents had plotted to murder him as well as former Russian lawmaker-turned-critic Ilya Ponomaryov.
“Neither Ivan nor I were explicitly told that we were the individuals whose names are concealed in the indictment against those accused of carrying out the assassination plot,” Kasparov said.
Kasparov -- who has called Russia “fascist” -- retired from chess in 2005 to focus on political activism and has lived in exile in New York for more than a decade.
After Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, Kasparov and Tyutrin founded the Free Russia Forum in 2016, which advocates support for the Ukrainian military and organizes anti-war conferences.
Three years into the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, Russia put the forum on a list of “terrorist” organizations in 2025.
The alleged plot revealed by Washington appears to mark an escalation both in the targeting of dissidents and the reach of Russian operations on Western soil.
While Russian security services have repeatedly targeted Kremlin opponents across Europe, the US has remained off-limits for decades.
‘Bottle of gasoline’
The US Department of Justice also said the Russian agents last year were trying to have murdered a target in Lithuania, identified only as “Victim-2.”
One of the Russian agents offered a US citizen $25,000 to kill “Victim-2,” suggesting the US citizen could murder him by “throwing a bottle of gasoline” at him or “sticking a knife” in him.
The plot fell apart because the US citizen refused to carry out the murder.
Tyutrin said he did not know if he was “Victim-2.”
He said details remained scarce, but he had no doubt Russian security services were seeking to punish him for his support of Ukraine.
“It is clear that Moscow is behind this and it’s clear that there is a list of people to be eliminated,” he said.
“I believe those at the top of the list are the people who have taken the hardest line against the regime and the strongest stance in support of Ukraine.”
Followed by FBI
Both Kasparov and Tyutrin pointed to a recent spike in the Kremlin’s shadow activities against the West, with Moscow’s war against Ukraine in its fifth year and diplomacy stalled.
“This may be part of a broader plan to destabilize the situation, intimidate people, and demonstrate the West’s inability to protect those it has committed itself to protecting,” Tyutrin said.
He said he was first warned by Lithuania that he was in danger after he helped raise money for Russians fighting alongside Ukrainian forces in 2023 and then visited the Ukrainian front the following year.
Then, during a visit to the United States in April 2024, FBI agents approached him at JFK airport in New York.
They said he would be protected for the duration of his trip because they deemed him vulnerable to an attack.
“They said, ‘We don’t want this to happen on the territory of the United States,” he said. “I was followed by FBI agents for two weeks.”
After returning to Lithuania, Tyutrin was placed under state protection. The security detail was withdrawn several months later.
He said Lithuania did not provide the same level of protection following the most recent warning. Nonetheless, he said he remained grateful to his host country.
“I am grateful to them for informing me,” he said. “Forewarned is forearmed.”
