Businesses downgrade their assessments for the second month amid Russian strikes and expect prices to rise
Kyiv • UNN
The BIAI fell to 48.2 in September due to attacks, expensive resources, and a labor shortage. Businesses expect goods and services to become more expensive.
For the second consecutive month, businesses slightly worsened their performance results. This is happening against the backdrop of russia’s ongoing attacks on production facilities, logistics and warehouses, expensive fuel, and a labor shortage. Businesses forecast rising prices. UNN writes about this, citing a National Bank of Ukraine survey dated October 1.
In September, businesses gave restrained assessments of their own economic performance. In September 2026, the Business Activity Expectations Index stood at 48.2, compared with 48.3 in August 2026 (50.4 in September 2025)
Economic activity was constrained by:
-  further deterioration of the security situation; 
-  the destruction of logistics facilities, production facilities, and warehouses; 
-  higher business expenses due to rising fuel prices; 
-  limited domestic supply of goods and services; 
-  a shortage of qualified personnel; 
-  a slight strengthening of exchange-rate expectations. 
At the same time, positive factors included:
-  a stable electricity supply situation; 
-  a high harvest; 
-  the development of new logistics routes.  
What businesses expect across sectors
Industrial enterprises restored positive assessments of their activity, thanks to an improvement in the situation in the processing industry and stable conditions in the energy sector.
At the same time, construction companies, after six months of positive sentiment, gave restrained assessments, citing the suspension of state funding for the restoration of roads and infrastructure, the seasonal nature of construction work, and rising costs.
Trade and service-sector companies were also restrained in their assessments of their performance. Factors included further destruction of warehouse infrastructure, costly and complex logistics, rising fuel prices, and a shortage of qualified personnel. Trading companies expected a further decline in turnover and purchases of goods for sale, as well as in inventories / stocks of goods for sale. Respondents anticipated a further decline in their trading margins.
The majority of respondents in all sectors expected an acceleration in the growth rates of both purchase prices / prices for raw materials and supplies, and prices / tariffs for their own products / services, as well as the cost of goods purchased for sale.
The situation on the labor market remains ambiguous. Companies in most sectors were inclined to reduce staff, most notably in the services sector. Only construction companies expected an increase in the number of employees.

EU cuts aid to Sierra Leone over its help to convicted cocaine kingpin, Netherlands says

• The decision to suspend €18 million ($20 million) in payments promised for this year is intended to pressure Sierra Leone to take action against Leijdekkers, who has found refuge and high-level protection in the West African country since at least 2023
• Dutch national Leijdekkers is a convicted cocaine smuggler and one of Europe's most-wanted fugitives
• The Netherlands has demanded his extradition, but so far Sierra Leone has refused to cooperate
• Another €22.5 million promised for next year might also be suspended if the country continues its refusal to cooperate, Van Weel said
• The European Commission and the government of Sierra Leone did not immediately reply to requests for comment
• Leijdekkers was sentenced in absentia to 24 years in prison in the Netherlands for smuggling more than 7 metric tons of cocaine
• In Belgium he has been sentenced to a total of around 100 years in prison in various cases REUTERS

PM Netanyahu says Israel warned UK of suspected Iran attack plot on RAF airbase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:58:01 UTC
17:58:01 KST

After three days of investigations, including using a bomb disposal team, police said on Tuesday they had found no explosives in the vehicles, but they had retrieved a "quantity of petrol."
Israel had warned Britain that Iran was planning an attack on an airbase, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said, as he denounced the UK government for still pressuring his administration over treatment of the Palestinians.
Speaking to Fox News late on Wednesday, Netanyahu said Israel tipped off Britain about a plot shortly before Burnham's government announced sanctions on products from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank on 8 September.
"You want to hear how absurd things are there and how far the anti-Israel propaganda has gone?" Netanyahu told the US network's conservative host Sean Hannity.
"We gave the Brits the intel that there was going to be an attack and it's an Iranian-sponsored attack. And pretty much the next day, they slapped sanctions on us," he said.
Netanyahu has spent decades warning of threats from Iran's cleric-run state, sometimes meeting scepticism elsewhere.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran was involved in suspicious activity near the RAF Fairford airbase, which is used by US forces in their war on Iran.
Iran's embassy in London earlier said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation it was involved in the incident, while Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X that Burnham was "barking up the wrong tree."
US President Donald Trump also spoke of a possible Iranian role in the incident, in which a resident reported masked men near vans heading to the Fairford air base.
Since taking office in late July, Burnham has taken a tougher stance on Israel, saying his predecessor did not do enough.
He imposed the sanctions after a spate of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank against Palestinians, with nearly daily physical attacks and vandalism.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described the violence, which come as Netanyahu promotes new settlements, as ethnic cleansing.
Growing confusion
The case was plunged into confusion when UK police released on bail five British men it had arrested on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences.
After three days of investigations, including using a bomb disposal team, police said on Tuesday they had found no explosives in the vehicles, but they had retrieved a "quantity of petrol."
Then on Wednesday, The Times newspaper reported that the incident had been foiled after one of the five suspects tipped off the police himself before the group was apprehended.
US President Donald Trump and his Secretary of State Marco Rubio had previously indicated that intelligence bodies were aware of the suspects and that a foreign state could be involved, but UK officials had not weighed in.
Speculation was rife that Iran or another hostile state could have been involved, after Tehran previously warned London against allowing its military bases to be used by Washington.
Britain didn't join the US and Israel in the Iran war, which began on 28 February, and initially denied Trump’s request to use bases in the UK to strike the country.
But then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer agreed in March to let the US use bases in Britain for what he called “defensive” operations against Iran’s missiles and their launch sites following Iranian attacks on UK interests and Britain’s allies in the Gulf.
American B-1 and B-52 bombers have taken off from Fairford, 160 kilometres west of London, for operations during the Iran conflict, the only base on Britain’s mainland used for this purpose.
Iran has said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

At the time of writing, Brent crude, the international benchmark, was up 2.6% at just above $100 a barrel, while the US benchmark West Texas Intermediate was also up 2.6% at roughly $92.80.
Crude exports from the Gulf have climbed back close to pre-war levels, while Saudi Arabia has partly restored its East-West pipeline, which bypasses the Strait of Hormuz.

"We will make every effort to bring the agreement to fruition," Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian stated.
However, US President Donald Trump struck a blunter tone.
"We blow them up or make a deal," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office late on Wednesday, adding that the war would end "very soon" one way or another.
OPEC+ is expected to keep November output targets unchanged when it meets on Sunday, according to delegates cited by Bloomberg.
This comes as shipping risks remain elevated, three vessels were struck in the strait on Tuesday, according to British maritime authorities.
European markets fall, chip stocks lift Asia and US bonds teeter
In Europe, stocks fell at the open on Thursday.
The Euro Stoxx 50 was roughly 1% lower in early trading, while the broader pan-European Stoxx 600 dropped 1.5%.
The UK's FTSE 100, France's CAC 40, Germany's DAX, Italy's FTSE MIB, Spain's IBEX 35 and the Netherlands' AEX all traded between 1% and 2% lower.
Investors are weighing faster-than-expected September inflation in Germany, France and Italy, driven by the energy shock.
Over in Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 jumped almost 2% as chipmakers rallied after US memory maker Micron forecast stronger-than-expected results.
South Korea's Kospi also rose over 2% after September exports jumped 83.5% from a year earlier to a monthly record, driven by chip sales. Markets in mainland China and Hong Kong were closed for National Day holidays.
On Wall Street, the S&P 500 fell 0.3%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 0.9% and the Nasdaq composite edged up 0.2% on Wednesday as the S&P 500 ended September with a monthly loss.
Softer-than-expected US inflation data initially cut the odds of an October rate hike to around 38% from about 50%, according to CME's FedWatch tool, but stronger growth figures later weighed on stocks.
The 10-year US Treasury yield touched 5.3%, its highest since 2007, capping its biggest quarterly rise since 1994. At the time of writing, US futures were trading flat.
Investors will now turn to Friday's US jobs report for September.

Air quality has deteriorated in three cities in the Kyiv region due to fine particulate matter
Kyiv • UNN
Elevated levels of fine particulate matter have been detected in Vyshhorod, Vasylkiv and Obukhiv. Residents are advised to close their windows and avoid going outside.
A deterioration in air quality has been recorded in the cities of Vyshhorod, Vasylkiv and Obukhiv. This is evidenced by the results of observations from monitoring stations, the Kyiv Regional Military Administration reports, according to UNN.
The main pollutant at present is fine particulate matter. With prolonged exposure, it may cause breathing discomfort in older people, people sensitive to irritants, and children
Until the situation improves, experts advise keeping windows closed, avoiding spending extended periods outdoors, and drinking enough water. If you have an air purifier at home, it is recommended that you turn it on to the maximum setting.
In other settlements in the Kyiv region, no exceedances of the permissible levels of chemical and biological substances in the ambient air were observed.
The level of gamma radiation in the Kyiv region corresponds to the natural background level.
Ambient air monitoring is carried out at 15 observation stations in the cities of Brovary, Boryspil, Pereiaslav, Vyshhorod, Boyarka, Obukhiv, Kaharlyk, Bohuslav, Uzyn, Vasylkiv, Irpin, Vyshneve; the towns of Ivankiv and Velyka Dymerka; and the village of Pidhirtsi in Obukhiv district. The observation station in the city of Bila Tserkva is temporarily out of operation.

France's borrowing rate keeps rising, hitting its highest level since 2002
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:56:47 UTC
17:56:47 KST

The new rise in France's ten-year borrowing rate, now close to 5%, shows investors' mounting distrust of a public debt that keeps climbing.
Bad news keeps piling up for the government. France's ten-year borrowing rate climbed to 4.94% at 10 a.m. on Thursday 1 October, up from 4.85% at Wednesday's close. French government bonds on the secondary market last yielded a similar rate in 2002, when they reached 4.91%.
More importantly, the borrowing rate has just seen its largest quarterly increase in almost four decades, as well as its sharpest monthly rise since 2022.
This latest rise is a sign of investors' growing mistrust of French debt, just as the government presents on Thursday the outline of what could become the state budget for 2027. The task looks especially daunting for Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, all the more so as France has not had a balanced budget since 1973.
Yet this record surge hardly comes as a surprise. The day before, the prime minister had expressed regret that the warning had gone "almost unnoticed" in the public debate. "Energy tensions are pushing rates up in many countries. In France, political uncertainty ahead of the presidential election is adding to that pressure," he wrote on X.
"Let us not pile instability on top of these difficulties," he added.
"More interest to pay means fewer resources for the country's priorities. This reality applies to everyone: government, parliament, presidential candidates. Reality is catching up with us," said Lecornu, who had already announced his intention to deliver €54 billion in savings.
Beyond this rise, the seriousness of the situation can also be seen in the gap with Germany, whose borrowing rate serves as a benchmark in Europe. On Thursday, Germany's borrowing rate stood at 3.61%, around 1.30 percentage points lower than the French rate. This gap, known as the Franco-German spread, keeps widening and has now reached its highest level in 14 years.
European stock markets also opened lower on Thursday morning, with the CAC 40 stock index in Paris falling more than 1.4% by 11am, the FTSE 100 in London losing 1.8% and the DAX in Frankfurt trading 1.1% lower at the same time.
€3.596 trillion in debt
The government is under particular pressure, as public debt has reached record levels over President Emmanuel Macron's two terms, worrying investors and becoming one of the main issues ahead of next year's presidential election.
Debt now stands at €3.596 trillion, equivalent to 119% of gross domestic product (GDP), suggesting that the country's weakened public finances are likely to dominate the campaign.
One proposal to tackle the debt issue is proving particularly divisive. The La France insoumise candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has suggested cancelling French government bonds held by the European Central Bank in order to free up money for public spending, arguing that this would release resources for investment.
The idea was swiftly rejected by Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, who argues that it would be a "clear and simple violation" of the EU treaties, which forbid a central bank from financing states. She stressed that if France were to freeze its debt today, then when it returned to the markets its creditors could demand onerous terms or even flatly refuse to lend to it.
According to France's finance ministry, the country's debt is held by a wide range of investors. A quarter is owned by French investors, a quarter by investors from the eurozone and another quarter by investors based outside the currency bloc. The remaining 25% is held by the Banque de France, as part of purchases made under the European Central Bank's monetary policy.

Chita Andolan is back: Why are Madhya Pradesh's Panna villagers protesting against Ken-Betwa project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:56:35 UTC
17:56:35 KST

MP dam project: Protesters brave rain and waterlogging for 20th day
Remember the unnerving visuals from Chita Andolan in Madhya Pradesh? Displaced Tribals sleeping on pyres, standing in water for their compensation. The unique protest is back and in its 20th day with agitators battling rain, waterlogging, lathicharge and general apathy by the authorities.Activist Amit Bhatnagar, Jai Kisan Sangathan leader, who has been on a hunger strike for the past four days, was arrested on Wednesday as protesters demonstrated chita, jal, sooli, mitti, bhook (pyre, water, gallows, soil, hunger) other forms of satyagraha.
What is happening in Madhya Pradesh's Panna?Bhatnagar accused the Panna administration of suppressing the agitation by lathicharging protesters, including women.Speaking to TOI before his arrest, Bhatnagar said, "For the past three days, the police have been bringing along people dressed in plain clothes, who misbehaved with women, entered their homes and even took away people’s phones which have still not been returned. When we approach the police, they ask who took the phones. How are people supposed to identify every face and find out who took them?""There is an atmosphere of fear in the villages. If we say anything, they start resorting to lathi-charge and filing false cases against the protesters," he added.
“I am courting arrest because democracy is being murdered. Are we not even allowed to protest peacefully? We are putting ourselves through hardship to raise our concerns, but instead of listening to us, they have cut off the electricity and water. Even the British never did this.”
Several women and other protesters had fallen ill after staying in water and rain for several days, with some suffering from wounds on their feet and other skin-related problems. (ANI photo)
So why are the protesters back?The latest protest follows a 15-day agitation in July, led largely by tribal women, after which the administration had assured protesters that eligible and genuinely displaced families would be transparently included in compensation and rehabilitation lists.However, the protesters claimed that they did not get the promised compensation. Also, their houses were now inundated, with two to three feet of water entering homes in several villages which now stand waterlogged including Mandalia, Tapariya and Kuwarpur."The families whose houses have been submerged are so poor that they have been forced to continue living there, or put up one makeshift shelter next to another, and then another. Earlier, the water would rise by half a foot at a time. But this time there was heavy rain on the 26th and 27th of September, followed by a 24-hour red alert, leaving them with no time to move. The villages turned into islands,” said Bhatnagar.
For thousands of tribal families living in the path of the project, it has become a battle over land, forests, livelihoods and identity.
The protesters claim that the compensation process remains incomplete, with several families receiving only Rs 5 lakh despite the government announcing a Rs 12.5-lakh package.They are also opposing the compensation conditions, which makes several tribals ineligible for relief.“The cut-off date under Section 11 has been set as 2018, which means people who are now 25-26 years old have received nothing. Those who are older are getting only Rs 5 lakh. What are families with eight or 10 children supposed to do?" asked Bhatnagar, adding that they were not against development projects, but that this development should not come at the cost of the rights of tribals.
Affected families have staged some of the country's most striking demonstrations, standing waist-deep in river water, laying beside symbolic funeral pyres and even climbed symbolic gallows.
Bhatnagar pointed to Section 38 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, which he said raised concerns about any displacement or submergence taking place before compensation and rehabilitation obligations had been fulfilled.“Villages and homes are now submerged. Houses have started collapsing and water has entered them. Yet, Section 38 of the 2013 law says that compensation for an irrigation project should be paid six months before submergence. If the houses were submerged two months ago, compensation should have been paid eight months earlier,” he said.The authorities, on the other hand, claim that they have been conducting fresh surveys and distributing compensation to affected families. TOI reached out to Chhatarpur district magistrate and is still awaiting a response from the administration.
'Ken-Betwa River Linking Project' is India's first river-linking initiative aimed to transform the drought-prone Bundelkhand region through irrigation, drinking water supply and power generation.
What is the project aiming to accomplish?The Majhgawan dam project aims to transfer surplus water from Ken river to Betwa through the Daudhan Dam, a network of tunnels and a 221-km canal. It is supposed to address water shortages in drought-prone Bundelkhand region that spans across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.The project traces back to a plan introduced in 1980 and cleared in 2021 to connect the rivers. Prime Minister Narendra Modi laid its foundation stone in December 2024.The project is expected to improve agricultural output, curb migration and strengthen groundwater recharge through the revival of traditional Chandela-era ponds.

Swiss House backs easier access to labour market by third-country nationals
People with protection status S and third-country nationals who have been educated in Switzerland are to be granted easier access to the labour market. The House of Representatives approved a corresponding bill from the federal government on Wednesday.
The bill was passed by 128 votes to 65. It will now go to the Senate.
In future, people in employment with S protection status will be entitled to move to another canton if they are not dependent on social assistance and have been in employment for at least twelve months, or if remaining in their canton of residence is unreasonable due to their commute or working hours.
+ Switzerland extends Ukraine S status until March 2028
The process for granting residence permits to people trained in Switzerland is also to be simplified. This applies to third-country nationals who have completed higher vocational training or a postdoctoral programme in Switzerland under an employment contract and whose work is of significant scientific or economic interest.

OSINT analysts identify production facilities for the Russian Garpiya-A1 attack drone
OSINT analysts have identified the location of the production facilities for the Russian Garpiya-A1 attack drone, which was created based on the Shahed-136 concept.
Source: OSINT analyst Dnipro Osint ⟨ Harbuz ⟩ on Telegram
Details: Harbuz recalled how Almaz-Antey, a Russian state-owned company in the arms industry, recently posted a promotional video featuring the export version of the Garpiya-A1(E) and the UAV-D.
Promotional video featuring the export version of the Garpiya-A1(E) and the UAV-D
The analyst noted that externally, the Garpiya-A1 resembles the Russian Geran (Shahed-136), but it is manufactured by a different company within the Russian military-industrial complex – the Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol.
Quote: "Coordinates: 56.852355° 53.276128°. Production facilities are located on the territory of the former 300th production site of the Izhevsk Mechanical Plant. In 2019, this site was acquired by the Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol."
Details: Harbuz emphasised that the video shows building No. 12. It is used as the final assembly shop for the UAVs.
The analyst also shared that in 2023, the Russian Ministry of Defence signed a contract with Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol worth over RUB 1 billion (about US$12 million) to begin production of the Garpiya-A1. On 13 September 2024, debris of this UAV type was recorded on the territory of Ukraine for the first time.
Harbuz also highlighted that these drones have already been repeatedly used for strikes against Ukraine. In particular, on 25 September, one of them struck a railway infrastructure facility in Poltava Oblast.
According to the OSINT analyst, the production site was geolocated through joint efforts with GEOINT analysts from project CyberBoroshno.
Background: Ukrainska Pravda along with the GEOINT project CyberBoroshno recently investigated Russian "droneports" (specialised drone launch facilities) and strikes against them.

Britain’s retired Hercules head to Türkiye in December
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:52:12 UTC
17:52:12 KST

- Türkiye's Defense Ministry said the first two of 12 former Royal Air Force C-130J transports will arrive in December after maintenance in the UK.
- Six pilots and six technicians are training in the United States, and 29 maintenance personnel are training in the UK.
Türkiye will receive the first two of 12 C-130J Super Hercules transport aircraft it is buying from the UK in December, once maintenance on them is finished in Britain, the Turkish Defense Ministry said on Oct. 1, with the rest of the former Royal Air Force aircraft to follow in stages.
The ministry also said crews are already training to fly and maintain them. Six pilots and six technicians are training in the United States, and 29 maintenance personnel are training in the UK. It did not give a schedule for the remaining 10 aircraft or say where the first two will be based.
The aircraft are stretched C-130J-30 models that the Royal Air Force retired in June 2023, when the UK decided to rely on the larger Airbus A400M for its tactical airlift. Türkiye confirmed the purchase in October 2025, and the 12 aircraft were handed over to Marshall Aerospace in Cambridge, England, for overhaul and modernization before delivery. Turkish officials have said Türkiye plans to take over routine maintenance of the fleet itself once its personnel complete type training.
The UK government said in December 2025 that the sale and related work were worth more than £550 million ($727 million) to the British defense sector and Marshall Aerospace and would support about 1,400 skilled jobs in Cambridge, Turkish Minute reported.
The C-130Js will fill a gap in Türkiye’s airlift fleet. The Turkish Air Force operates about 10 A400Ms and a fleet of older C-130B and C-130E Hercules, many of them decades old. Those older C-130s were grounded after an accident in November 2025 near the border between Georgia and Azerbaijan, leaving the air force dependent on its A400Ms for heavy airlift, Aviation Week reported.
The C-130J is the latest version of Lockheed Martin’s long-serving four-engine turboprop transport, with a two-pilot glass cockpit, digital flight controls and more efficient Rolls-Royce engines than earlier Hercules models. The stretched -30 version has a longer cargo hold, letting it carry more troops, pallets or vehicles than the standard aircraft.
Türkiye is not the only buyer of the RAF’s surplus Super Hercules fleet. The UK has previously sold former RAF C-130Js to Bangladesh and Bahrain.

"Droneports": inside Russian UAV bases and why they are so difficult to destroy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:52:00 EEST
17:52:00 KST

"Droneports": inside Russian UAV bases and why they are so difficult to destroy
When the Russian forces began stepping up their use of jet-powered drones, perhaps the most common question among Ukrainians was: "Why haven't we destroyed the launch sites yet?"
Although Ukraine's defence forces regularly attack Russian drone launch sites, the strikes have not produced an effect on the scale of Operation Spider's Web, in which a dozen Tu-95MS and Tu-22M3 bombers were destroyed.
The reason is that, over the past two years, Russia has built an extensive network of specialised drone launch facilities, capable of handling dozens of jet-powered and conventional drones every hour. In Ukrainian and Russian discourse, these facilities are dubbed "droneports" – a catch-all term for dedicated sites used to operate drones.
Ukrainska Pravda and CyberBoroshno, a Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) community, have looked into Russian drone launch sites and attacks on them. Read on to find out where Russian forces launch their UAVs from and why it is highly unlikely that these droneports will ever be destroyed.
Where does Russia launch its Shaheds from?
When the first Iranian-made Shahed loitering munitions arrived in Russia in autumn 2022, little preparation was needed before they could be put to use. The drones could be launched straight out of the box.
The only thing they needed was a site from which they could be launched.
Military airfields were among the first – and perhaps the most obvious – choices for launching the drones. They already had everything needed: secure perimeters, security personnel, ground staff, air defence systems and established logistics for receiving new drones. The airfields were also located away from civilian infrastructure and prying eyes.
Long runways also made it possible to use pick-ups and lorries as mobile launch platforms for Shaheds. Lightweight launchers were also deployed at the airfields. The UAVs took off from these launchers with the help of solid-fuel rocket boosters before switching to their piston engines for the rest of the flight. For the Russians, the existing airfield infrastructure was more than enough.
The first airfields used by Russian forces to launch Shaheds were in occupied Crimea and the border regions of Bryansk and Kursk oblasts. As the number of drones Russia received grew, so did the geographical scope of their deployment. Known launch sites included Cape Chauda, Yeysk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Kursk and Seshcha.
The Russians later began using sites other than airfields to launch Shahed drones, including positions around Balaklava on Crimea's southern coast.
This enabled Russian forces to launch dozens of drones every week. The locations were also far enough from the combat zone to keep the launch sites relatively safe, yet close enough to Ukraine for the drones to reach Ukrainian territory within a few hours.
The droneports
When Russia acquired the technology to produce Shahed loitering munitions, another problem emerged: there was a shortage of existing airfield infrastructure.
Unlike the Shaheds supplied by Iran, Russia's domestically produced versions, known as Geran drones, had to be not only launched but also maintained. They had to be assembled, stored, inspected and prepared for launch somewhere. Although the existing infrastructure could support an increase in the number of launch sites, it was still not enough.
Therefore, as Geran production got underway, the Russians began preparing new launch sites in parallel.
Garages for assembling and storing drones began appearing at airfields already used as launch sites. Russia also built underground storage facilities large enough to accommodate both the drones and their warheads. Launchers were also being installed in revetments – protected bays surrounded by earth banks or blast walls.
Alongside the expansion of existing sites, new ones have begun to appear across Russia. In just a few months, large drone bases capable of launching hundreds of drones a day have sprung up on land that was previously covered by fields or forests.
Perhaps the best-known of these is Tsimbulova in Oryol Oblast, about 180 km from the Ukrainian border. Russian sources describe it as "the world's largest droneport". And with good reason: the site covers 5 sq km.
OSINT analyst Dnipro Osint ⟨Harbuz⟩ told Ukrainska Pravda: "The Alabuga began building the site in August 2024, and by February 2025, the main facilities had been completed. Its construction was directly linked to the expansion of drone production at Alabuga. This droneport has, in essence, become the first facility whose infrastructure was designed entirely for storing, maintaining and launching drones."
Tsimbulova has been equipped with runways and fixed catapult launchers for drones. The site also includes hundreds of garages and dozens of underground shelters.
The base's facilities are spread out across the site, with each one separated from the others and surrounded by earthworks. The droneports were built on the assumption that they would eventually be attacked. The Russians therefore sought to ensure that only a direct bombardment could destroy them.
The drones themselves can be stored not only inside buildings but also outdoors. Satellite imagery shows both Shahed attack drones and Gerbera decoy drones, which are also launched from these droneports.
The sites are supported by the infrastructure needed for day-to-day operations: solar panels, diesel generators, fuel depots and radio and navigation equipment for drone control. Each facility has its own access roads, parking areas and additional exit routes. It is also protected by air defence and electronic warfare systems intended to counter Ukrainian attacks.
Harbuz says: "The droneports were initially built much larger than 'necessary'. By the end of 2024, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine estimated the production rate of Shaheds at 2,000 units per month – roughly 64 UAVs a day – yet the droneport infrastructure at Tsimbulova could store up to 3,000 combat drones and 100 UAVs simultaneously. It was clearly built with capacity to spare."
In 2026, the infrastructure at Tsimbulova has continued to expand. New hangars and warehouses were built at the droneport, alongside larger specialised launchers for Geran-4/5 jet-powered drones. These drones can also be launched from mobile platforms mounted on vehicles.
An analysis of satellite images by Ukrainska Pravda estimates that Tsimbulova has 23 launchers for different types of drones, 387 garages and 26 underground storage facilities. The site is still expanding: the Russians are preparing to build four more launchers for jet-powered drones, plus 83 garages and underground shelters.
Another well-known droneport has been established at the site of the destroyed Donetsk airport (DAP). Despite being 50 km from the front line, the site now has hangars and drone launch pads used to launch drones towards frontline areas and targets in the rear.
Up to 95% of drone launches take place from bases in Russia's Bryansk, Rostov, Smolensk and Oryol oblasts, as well as in Krasnodar Krai and occupied Crimea. There are also research droneports where Russia tests UAVs in flight.
Although these sites are smaller than Tsimbulova, they have much the same basic infrastructure.
Ukrainska Pravda has identified at least 63 launchers at the main droneports, but the total could be higher. The sites can accommodate hundreds of drones and tens of thousands of combat components for them.
Can droneports be destroyed?
Ukraine's defence forces could not ignore the fact that Russians were launching Shaheds across Ukraine. Therefore, they gradually began targeting the drone launch sites, choosing their targets according to the capabilities and resources available to them.
Some of the first known strikes on Shahed launch sites were carried out in 2024. Ukrainian forces hit a Shahed depot near Balaklava and a storage facility for the drones near Yeysk.
After the strike, the area near Balaklava ceased to be used for Shahed launches. Yeysk was the first – and so far the only – case in which the impact of a strike could be seen in the launch figures. For the first time, Russia then went 48 days without launching Shaheds on Ukraine.
Russia's droneports have also been struck whilst under construction. On 26 December 2024, at least three Storm Shadow cruise missiles hit a facility between Tsimbulova and Rudnevo. Russian media outlet Astra said two Russian service members were killed and seven others were taken to hospital as a result of the strike.
A month later, the same complex was once again targeted by Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles. Ukraine's General Staff reported that more than 200 Shaheds had been destroyed. The images show damage to one of the warehouses.
Donetsk airport is another well-known target that has come under repeated attacks by Ukraine's defence forces. In a separate article, Ukrainska Pravda details how Ukraine's drone forces have been destroying Shahed launchers at the airport.
Because the airport is so close to the front line, Ukraine's 1st Separate Centre of the Unmanned Systems Forces has been able to regularly destroy Russian weapons, mobile fire groups defending the airfield and infrastructure. Ukrainian forces have repeatedly used mid-range drones and even FPV drones to strike targets at the airfield.
(12) FP-2 drone strikes on the DAP. Video: Special Operations Forces
DAP itself is a good example of just how difficult droneports are to strike.
Harbuz says: "The Russians have built drone launch sites to make them as costly as possible for Ukraine's defence forces to destroy. Ammunition and fuel depots are concealed beneath concrete and earth. Conventional UAVs cannot penetrate these structures, and even if they do, the explosion is contained inside, preventing debris from reaching other depots and triggering a chain reaction.
If any facilities are destroyed, they can be rebuilt relatively quickly and cheaply. As the example of Donetsk airport shows, the Russians are adapting and expanding the drone launch site even there, despite constant Ukrainian strikes."
Therefore, the main objective of Ukraine's defence forces when striking drone launch sites is to disrupt Russia's ability to launch drones.
Falco, an officer with Ukraine's 1st Separate Drone Centre, tells Ukrainska Pravda: "The primary objective is to disrupt their ability to launch drones, so that they are unable to launch them for an extended period. This also affects the overall coordination of their actions and the cohesion of their units. It also makes it easier for our air defence units to engage aerial assets, because there are generally fewer of them."
There are several ways to disrupt drone launches: striking launchers and storage facilities, or creating an aerial threat over the droneport. The attacks can force launches to be postponed indefinitely, while the destruction of infrastructure can reduce the overall number of drones launched.
According to Falco, launch pads and storage garages are among the easiest targets to strike: they are stationary, and there may not always be personnel nearby. But the value of hitting static targets depends on the circumstances and the overall strategy. If a garage or warehouse is packed with explosives or drones, then it makes sense to strike it.
Over the past two years, Ukraine's defence forces have stepped up attacks on Russian droneports. Alongside DAP and Tsimbulova, they have repeatedly targeted sites at Navlya, Hvardiiske, Primorsko-Akhtarsk and elsewhere. The strikes have hit warehouses, launchers, garages and drones left out in the open.
In the latest attack on Tsimbulova, on 21 September, Ukrainian strikes hit a bunker used to store combat drones. One strike penetrated the bunker, and another caused an explosion on the surface. Separate strikes also hit drones near the launch sites.
The strategy behind the strikes has also evolved. Ukraine is no longer targeting only storage, preparation and launch sites, but has also begun striking relay stations used to control Geran and Gerbera drones. UAV ground control stations have reportedly been destroyed in Trubchevsk, Russia, and in the temporarily occupied settlements of Zaliznyi Port, Skadovsk, Chornomorsk and Olenivka.
These facilities are important too, but Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces have another target in their sights: the drone operators themselves.
"The most difficult target there is also the most valuable one: the operator," Falco says. "They don't stay near the launch sites for very long. So when you take out the people launching the drones, you're taking away a scarce resource. There aren't many operators to begin with, and the enemy then has to spend even more money training new crews."
Military personnel are not the only people involved in launching Russian drones. Staff from Alabuga take part in the process on a daily basis too. In its study of Russian drone launch sites, the Molfar Intelligence Institute released several classified Alabuga documents.
According to the documents, Alabuga employees complained about "unjustified risk" after a Ukrainian attack on a major droneport in Oryol Oblast in December 2024. They said they were expected to continue working even though Russian air defence systems could not prevent strikes on the launch sites. Many employees said they wanted to leave the sites – and Alabuga itself.
Employees were threatened that they would be shot in the knees if they did not come to work, and were forced to turn up. Apart from Alabuga staff, local residents are also enlisted to assemble drones. Staff at droneports, however, complain about the low efficiency of their work.
Meanwhile, keeping droneports out of operation requires constant pressure on Russian positions.
Falco concludes: "If we want to keep the pressure on, we need to increase the scale of our strikes. The more we can hit, the better. As a country, we are constantly moving towards the level we need. But it's not just about strikes. We also have to think about how the enemy may respond and plan our operations accordingly."
Another factor that could significantly disrupt the operation of Russian droneports would be the use of Ukraine's own ballistic missiles. Their speed and penetrating power could allow them to target drone operators during launches – as has already happened at Donetsk airport – and destroy underground depots.

Is the EU planning to freeze funds to German states that voted for the AfD?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:51:51 UTC
17:51:51 KST

Claims circulating online allege that the EU is threatening to block funds intended for the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, after the far-right AfD party won a recent election there. However, there's no evidence that this is the case.
Is Brussels trying to freeze EU funds to a German state that voted for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in an election in early September?
According to several social media posts amassing thousands of views, likes and shares, and often with a picture of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen attached, it is.
They allege that millions, or even billions, of euros could be withheld from the state of Saxony-Anhalt, located in east-central Germany, after voters handed the AfD a landslide victory on 6 September.
However, the 39 seats it won were not enough to command a majority, even though the party secured more than twice as many seats as any other party.
The AfD has since struggled to establish a coalition, however, as the other parties have refused to collaborate with it.
Von der Leyen herself has repeatedly criticised the AfD in the past, and her own centre-right CDU party suffered a crushing defeat, winning just 17.2% of the vote and falling to 15 seats. This possibly fuelled the suggestions online that she is behind the scheme to freeze the EU funds.
However, there's no evidence that that's the case. Instead, the narrative seems to stem from a statement by German Green MEP Daniel Freund, who said after the state election that he would push to freeze EU money flowing to an AfD-led government if it violated any European values or misused funds.
Saxony-Anhalt is set to receive €2.95 billion in EU funding as part of the current 2021-2027 budget. This includes €1.3 billion from the European Regional Development Fund, €571 million from the European Social Fund, and €594 million from the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development.
On a per capita basis, Saxony-Anhalt benefits more from EU funding than any other German state, according to Freund, averaging over €650 per citizen over the full EU budget cycle.
He also highlighted that the EU had used similar freezing measures in the past in Poland and Hungary.
Brussels did indeed block money intended for those countries a few years ago, over rule-of-law and democratic backsliding concerns under previous governments.
Some of these funds have since been released following reforms. In Poland, for example, the European Commission formally unlocked €137 billion in cohesion and post-pandemic funds in 2024, after Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government brought in guarantees for judicial independence and the rule of law.
For Hungary, meanwhile, it has proposed unlocking a first tranche of €4.2 billion in cohesion funds and restoring access to programmes like Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.
Billions of euros had been frozen over rule-of-law and corruption concerns under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, but recent legislative actions by Péter Magyar's administration have paved the way for the money to be unfrozen.
Nevertheless, for now, the idea that this could happen to Saxony-Anhalt appears to be the opinion of a few MEPs, rather than a concerted effort by Brussels.
Under the EU's rule-of-law conditionality mechanism, funding cannot be suspended simply because a particular party takes office. The European Commission says measures can only be proposed where breaches of the rule of law directly affect, or seriously risk affecting, the sound management of the EU budget or the EU's financial interests.
Such a measure would have to be proposed by the European Commission, with the Council of the European Union ultimately deciding whether to adopt it.
A spokesperson for the government of Saxony-Anhalt also told The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, that it was not aware of any plans to freeze the EU funds heading its way.
"In the current situation, there would be no legal basis for such a course of action," the spokesperson added, noting that a new state government has not yet been formed following the election on 6 September.
The European Commission meanwhile confirmed to us that it is not considering blocking EU funds for Saxony-Anhalt.
"As a matter of general practice, the Commission monitors the situation in all Member States and regions and takes action where necessary, in accordance with the legal frameworks governing EU funding," it said. "The election result itself does not constitute a legal basis for suspending EU funding."
In addition to that vote, the AfD also saw success in another election in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in the north a couple of weeks later. The Left meanwhile won in the Berlin state election.
- This article was updated to include a comment from the European Commission.

EU halts aid funds to Sierra Leone over Bolle Jos extradition
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The European Commission has stopped payments to Sierra Leone with immediate effect because the country will not extradite fugitive drugs baron Jos Leijdekkers, known as Bolle Jos, justice minister David van Weel has confirmed.
Van Weel told De Telegraaf: “I am very happy with this step. It is galling that EU money goes to a country that does not want to cooperate with the extradition of someone like Bolle Jos.”
Jos reportedly has a child with the daughter of Sierra Leone’s president, Julius Maada Bio, and maintains close ties with the government there. Drugs shipments passing through the West African coast are an increasing concern, for which Van Weel wants to establish a permanent secretariat.
Sierra Leone was expected to receive €18 million euros in budget support from Europe this year, most of it intended to bolster education, food programs and infrastructure projects. The Netherlands is also hoping to stop a planned payment of €22.5 million to the country next year.
Van Weel travelled to West Africa recently to garner support from surrounding nations like Ghana and Liberia.
Van Weel is in Luxembourg on Thursday for a meeting with EU justice ministers, where tougher sanctions on criminals hiding outside Europe, such as entry bans and asset freezes, will be discussed.
Pressure to tackle the cocaine trade has grown since an armed attack on a farm in Overasselt, Gelderland, last month, in which a security guard was killed. The attack is thought to be linked to the drugs trade.

Zabaikalsky Region Offers Bounties for Bears as Human Encounters Rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:50:23 UTC
17:50:23 KST

Authorities in Russia’s Far East Zabaikalsky region have introduced a bounty for bear culling in the region to curb the sharp rise in dangerous encounters with humans.
The regional ministry of natural resources on Thursday offered a reward of 15,000 rubles ($180) for every bear hunted.
More than 100 bear sightings have been recorded in the Zabaikalsky region so far, with 35 taking place directly inside human settlements. Hunters have culled 70 bears across the region as part of its campaign to regulate the animal’s population.
The Zabaikalsky region introduced a high-alert status on Tuesday, with officials urging residents to avoid forests for foraging, fishing or recreation.
“The main goal of these measures is to protect human life and health and reduce the risk of dangerous encounters with wild animals,” the ministry said in a statement.
At least 22 people have been killed in bear attacks across Russia in 2026. Experts attribute the spate of killings to climate change, with a lack of berries forcing bears to look for food elsewhere, as well as people leaving food waste out in the open where it attracts bears.
Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev said Wednesday the government was drafting measures to manage the brown bear population, which has doubled over the last three decades to 308,000.
Lifting hunting quotas and setting regional population limits, as well as giving local authorities extra powers to control bear numbers, were among the proposals.

Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) has called off plans to attend the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) defence ministers meeting in Reykjavík on Thursday and Friday, due to his facing a confidence vote in Parliament.
The defence ministry announced the development in a press release on Thursday morning. Parliament is likely to take up the no-confidence motions against Häkkänen and the government on Friday.
Earlier this week, the opposition Greens' MP Atte Harjanne tabled a no confidence motion against the defence minister, with Left Alliance chair Minja Koskela seconding the proposal.
The parties have criticised Häkkänen's recent visit to Israel, where he met with his Israeli counterpart in mid September.
Deal with Israel
At the end of August, it was reported that Finland and Israel had quietly renewed a memorandum of understanding on defence materiel development and procurement cooperation.
The memorandum itself is not new. It was originally drawn up in 2013, and its previous period of validity was approaching its end. In early 2024, Finland proposed extending the agreement with Israel.
Meanwhile, the SDP has called for a vote of no confidence in the entire government. Parliamentary group chair Tytti Tuppurainen announced the move. According to the SDP, divisions within the government over Middle East policy are creating uncertainty about Finland's position.
Led by the UK, the Joint Expeditionary Force is a defence cooperation group made up of ten countries: Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and the UK.
According to the Finnish defence ministry, JEF member countries aim to build military capabilities, prevent crises, and respond together when needed. The group mainly operates in Northern Europe and the Baltic Sea region.

Gunvor publicly condemned Russia’s war but continued to do business with Russian energy firms, records show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:48:52 UTC
17:48:52 KST

CHINA CAPITAL
Gunvor publicly condemned Russia’s war but continued to do business with Russian energy firms, records show
Even as the trading giant publicly claimed to be winding down its Russia business, Gunvor privately acknowledged the deals to its bank, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, saying they complied with sanctions laws.
Shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, several major trading firms pledged to stop or reduce new dealings with Russian businesses, joining global efforts to weaken Vladimir Putin’s military machine.
One of them was Gunvor Group, a company co-founded by a Swedish businessman and a Russian oligarch close to the Kremlin. In 2014, a U.S. Treasury Department report said that Putin himself had investments in the energy trading firm and may have had access to its funds. Since then, Gunvor’s co-founders have exited, and the company, now valued at about $5 billion, has over the last decade sought to shake its image as a Putin investment tool.
Gunvor has publicly condemned Russia’s war in Ukraine, and in 2023 corporate filings stated that it had “largely wound-down the trade of Russian oil and products.”
Now, confidential records reviewed by Swedish daily Göteborgs-Posten and the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists show how, despite its public pledges, the trader, using some of its subsidiaries, continued doing business with sanctioned Russian oil and gas producers.
The records come from the archives of the U.K. operations of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, the world’s largest bank by asset size and one of Gunvor’s lenders.
While likely not violating sanction laws, the deals found in the ICBC records are at odds with the trading giant’s public posturing following the start of the war. The dealings also go against a private reassurance Gunvor made in a 2022 email to ICBC saying that it had stopped new sales to Russian entities, the investigation found.
ICBC’s records were examined as part of China Capital, an ICIJ-led investigation that exposed the inner workings of the Chinese state-owned bank and its maneuvers to advance Beijing’s geopolitical goals. The project showed how ICBC’s London units routinely financed companies with opaque financial flows and murky corporate ownership, justifying the deals as part of its support for the Chinese government’s top priorities.
China Capital found, for example, that ICBC London provided loans to Norilsk Nickel, a Russian mining company partly owned by sanctioned oligarchs close to Putin, in breach of an internal branch policy forbidding dealings with clients linked to sanctioned people or entities. ICBC’s other branches also provided foreign exchange, deposits and cash management services to Norilsk Nickel, a key supplier to China’s booming electric vehicle and battery industries.
Justin Ko, a researcher at the University of Macau who studied China’s state banks, described China’s relationship to Russia as “opportunistic.” As mounting war sanctions have forced Western traders to stop dealing with Russian counterparts, Beijing has emerged as Moscow’s steadiest ally. “In that sense,” Ko told ICIJ, “there is going to be more business, more trade, and it’s only natural that ICBC and Bank of China, as [China’s] two leading international banks, will be leading the way for that.”
To be sure, ICBC London officers made an effort to ensure the bank complied with sanctions restrictions imposed following Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, the records show.
But the bank’s continued dealings with Gunvor shows how ICBC chose to serve clients considered strategic by Beijing even when they did business with sanctioned Russian entities.
For ICBC, Gunvor was a special client. An internal memo dated 2016 said that a “China rationale” for financing the company was its ongoing expansion within China: “Gunvor is expanding its reach into the Chinese domestic market : by sealing supply contracts with new independent (teapot) refineries and supplying [specialty] ores.”
Confidential records provided by Gunvor to ICBC show that between 2022 and 2024 the company based in Geneva continued to deal with sanctioned Russian parties, using licenses and other forms of authorization.
In 2024, during an ICBC “client review” as part of a prospective $594 million credit line to support Gunvor’s “trade finance needs,” some bank officers raised concerns about the trader’s Russia dealings.
In a report marked “strictly confidential,” Gunvor had acknowledged to ICBC London that, through its subsidiaries, the “Group had dealings with Russian counterparties target of Sanctions,” including buying and selling oil, gas and other products to and from “entities part of Gazprom, Rosneft, Lukoil and Novatek groups.” But those transactions, the Gunvor report said, represented only 0.69% of the group’s revenue in the first quarter of 2024 — or about $234 million, according to Göteborgs-Posten’s estimates.
In an internal meeting, an analyst from ICBC’s Zurich office told his London colleagues that the Swiss branch found “Gunvor trading a bit more aggressive than other traders” and had chosen not to do business with the trader.
Still, ICBC London ultimately decided to keep serving its long-time client, classifying it as “high risk.” “The group remains vital part of ICBC London relationship,” a bank officer noted in an internal memo.
In response to reporters’ questions, Gunvor’s corporate affairs director, Seth Pietras, acknowledged that in 2024 the company “did undertake some limited sanctions-compliant trading of Russian commodities” and said that those activities are “disclosed transparently to our financial institutions and to relevant national competent authorities.” In his emailed statement to Göteborgs-Posten, Pietras added that all of Gunvor’s trading activity is performed in strict compliance with U.S., U.K., the European Union and other countries’ sanctions laws.
“Gunvor fully stands by its public statements relating to its decrease in trading and activities in Russia,” he said.
ICBC did not respond to ICIJ’s requests for comment.
Göteborgs-Posten’s Tobias Andersson Åkerblom and ICIJ’s Denise Ajiri contributed reporting for this article.

UAE considers terrorist attack among possible causes of Flydubai plane incident — WAM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:48:15 UTC

On December 4, 2026, Italians residing in Japan will be called to the polls to elect new members of the Committee of Italians Abroad (Comites) in the constituency of the Italian Embassy in Tokyo. However, to vote, it is not enough to meet the legal requirements and have been registered with AIRE for at least six months prior to the election date. Unlike general elections and referendums, in fact, the voting packet is not sent automatically. The form can be submitted in person, without an appointment, along with a valid ID. This role, the ambassador emphasized, “takes on particular significance in a country that is geographically distant and profoundly different in terms of history, language, and culture.” Hence the hope for a community that is “increasingly present, cohesive, and capable of engaging in dialogue with Japan.”

Swiss Senate approves Erasmus+ funding and sends EU treaty to House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:45:43 UTC
17:45:43 KST

Swiss Senate approves Erasmus+ funding and sends EU treaty to House
After around 22 hours of debate, the Senate approved the stabilisation part of the European Union treaty package on Thursday morning. The so-called Bilateral Agreements III will now go to the House of Representatives.
On Thursday morning, the Senate voted on the final federal resolution in the stabilisation package – the commitment appropriation for Switzerland’s participation in the EU’s Erasmus+ education programme in 2027. This contribution of CHF193 million ($230 million) had been the subject of controversy in the run-up to the vote. The relevant Education Committee (WBK-S) had recommended a “yes” vote on the resolution, albeit by a very narrow margin.
The final vote in the committee was cast by Chairman Matthias Michel. He argued in favour of a “yes” vote in the Senate, arguing “a ‘no’ vote would mean we could not take part in the programme, which would be detrimental to Swiss students”. Participation would strengthen the skills of trainees and students, particularly in the field of vocational training. Ultimately, this would also benefit the economy.
Some centre-right members of the Senate expressed dissatisfaction at the size of the loan required. They were reluctant to approve additional expenditure given the strained federal finances and the austerity measures. The Senate Finance Committee (FK-S) had, due to the strained federal budget, recommended a “no” vote on the Erasmus+ loan by a narrow majority.
+ Swiss Senate gives clear backing to EU treaty package
Swiss President and Minister for Research and Education Guy Parmelin pointed out during the debate that the benefits of the programme far outweighed the costs. Furthermore, a parliamentary rejection of the appropriation could be viewed negatively by the EU in its overall assessment of the discussions.
The Senate ultimately approved the commitment credit by 23 votes to 19, with 2 abstentions. Like all other resolutions in the stabilisation package, the matter will now be referred to the House of Representatives.
Food safety and health
Attention now turns to the “further development” section of the treaty package. A new agreement is to be concluded in the area of food safety. The agreement is intended to create a common food safety area. According to the Federal Council, the aim is to identify foodstuffs that pose a health risk at an early stage. Any harmonisation of Swiss and EU agricultural policy remains ruled out.
The health agreement is also part of the expansion of relations. The agreement is intended to strengthen cross-border coordination and cooperation with the EU in the event of a health crisis, such as a pandemic. Specifically, Switzerland is to gain access to the EU’s health security mechanisms and to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.
Interior Minister Elisabeth Baume-Schneider will oversee the provisional conclusion of the EU negotiations in the Senate. The dossier will then be referred to the House. The electricity agreement will be dealt with at a later date, as the relevant Senate committee has not yet completed its work on it.

Stablecoins could hinder monetary policy: Swiss central bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:45:41 UTC
17:45:41 KST

Stablecoins could hinder monetary policy: Swiss central bank
        
Stablecoins could complicate the transmission of monetary policy, one of the Swiss National Bank’s (SNB) three interest rate-setters said, calling for a regulation that safeguards the influence of policymakers.    
“Modernising the payment system is sensible,” governing board member Petra Tschudin said Wednesday at an event in Zurich.
But large stablecoins that are not integrated in the existing two-tier financial system, frame “a situation where it’s harder for central banks to fulfill their mandate,” she added.
The remarks build on the SNB’s pronounced scepticism on stablecoins and crypto assets, even as it’s at the forefront of experimenting with digital forms of central-bank money.
The institution started three years ago to issue a blockchain-based digital currency for banks – a so-called wholesale CBDC – and said that the project will continue until at least 2028.
More
Why bitcoin is inspiring a digital Swiss franc makeover
On stablecoins, the institution has warned that the assets potentially can’t deliver on promised at-par convertibility. Still, it said that local financial stability risks from the assets are small due to low volumes and low adoption.
Tschudin stressed on Wednesday that stablecoins can also improve the current financial system, for example by allowing international companies to send money around the world at lower costs.
“There’s a competition between commercial banks and stablecoins,” she said. “And in itself, competition, rivalry is a good thing, it brings innovation.”
The policymaker, who manages the SNB’s large foreign-exchange portfolio and its digital projects, spoke to an audience of professional forecasters at ETH Zurich’s KOF economic research institute.
The SNB’s tokenized currency can’t be held by consumers. That makes it different from other CBDC pilots such as those in China or the euro area, which focus on retail applications.
Tschudin reiterated the bank’s view that the benefits of such retail CBDCs don’t outweigh the risks. She added that the SNB’s CBDC isn’t used much.
“It’s not extremely big volumes that are traded there,” she said. “We believe things go in that direction, but the big lift-off hasn’t happened yet.”

The Trump administration has excluded several major NATO allies, including the UK, France and the Baltic states, from an October meeting in Poland intended to discuss the alliance’s future.
The Pentagon-led gathering is being organized by US Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby and will involve a select group of NATO countries, Politico reported on Wednesday, Sept. 30, citing six diplomats familiar with the planning.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The countries invited to participate are Norway, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Germany and the Netherlands. Colby has already held two similar meetings with representatives of those countries under a format known as the Bergen Group.
The exclusion of Britain, France and Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania has caused confusion because the countries are among NATO’s most active defense contributors and play important roles in deterring Russian aggression in Europe.
“We’re doing everything that is being asked of us,” an official from one excluded country told Politico. “We’re trying to understand what the criteria is and what the purpose of these meetings are. Not much has been passed on to us yet.”
The White House did not respond to Politico’s request for comment, while the Pentagon declined to comment.
Pentagon creates select NATO group
Colby previously described the participants as NATO members that were quickly fulfilling their defense-spending commitments, possessed sufficient military scale and were prepared to focus on practical decisions.
Trump Again Blames Ukraine for Rising US Diesel Prices, Dismissing Middle East War Impact
A diplomat from one participating country said the Bergen Group was not intended to undermine NATO. Instead, members are expected to develop proposals that can later be tested and discussed by the full alliance.
“This can be an engine for transformation” for NATO, the diplomat said.
Denmark could become the next country invited to join following an agreement allowing the US to expand its military presence in Greenland, according to a person familiar with the planning.
However, even some invited countries have questioned why Washington selected particular participants while excluding major European military powers.
“If they try splitting NATO into the good ones and the bad ones, it is dangerous for the US,” another diplomat said. “But for Europe, this is existential.”
Trump increases pressure on allies
The initiative follows repeated threats by President Donald Trump and senior administration officials to reward what they describe as “model allies” while penalizing countries that resist US priorities.
Trump has criticized NATO members over defense spending and their refusal to support the US war against Iran. His administration previously considered creating what officials described as a “naughty and nice list” of allies based on their compliance with Washington’s demands, Politico reported.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has similarly said countries supporting US interests would be treated as model partners, while those that do not could face consequences.
The latest move comes despite NATO leaders’ public efforts to demonstrate unity at their July summit in Ankara. Previously, allies pledged €70 billion ($79 billion) in military assistance for Ukraine in 2026 and promised to maintain comparable support in 2027.
The summit also reaffirmed NATO’s collective-defense commitment and its target for members to allocate 5% of gross domestic product to defense and security-related spending by 2035.

Ukraine spots “whiskered” Shahed aimed at power lines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:42:35 UTC
17:42:35 KST

- Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko published video of a jet-powered Shahed fitted with whisker-like contacts, likely to detonate on power lines.
- Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Russia appears to have used a jet drone carrying a 40-kg cutting warhead built for pylons and bridges.
A previously unseen version of Russia’s jet-powered Shahed attack drone has appeared in Ukraine fitted with whisker-like rods on its nose, a modification that Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko says is designed to detonate the warhead on contact with high-voltage power lines.
Sternenko, a Ukrainian volunteer and activist who runs one of the country’s largest drone fundraising efforts, published video of the drone on X, saying the “whiskers” are most likely there to close an electrical contact and set off the charge when the drone strikes something as thin as a power cable. A similar modification has been seen at another location, though Sternenko did not say where either drone was found or whether it was intact.
“And this is a whiskered Shahed with a specialized warhead for attacks on high-voltage power lines. Most likely the whiskers were added to close a contact and initiate the warhead when hitting small targets such as power lines,” Sternenko wrote.
A standard impact fuse needs a solid surface to trigger, so a drone that clips a cable or the open lattice of a transmission tower may fly through or fall without exploding. Rods sticking out ahead of the airframe would let the drone detonate as soon as they touch a wire.
A second development points in the same direction. Serhii Beskrestnov, known as “Flash,” a specialist in drones and electronic warfare who serves as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s adviser on defense technology, said Russia appeared to use a special warhead on a jet-powered drone for the first time on Sept. 30. He identified it as a shaped-charge cutting payload, known by its Russian initials KRSN, designed specifically to destroy high-voltage transmission towers and steel bridge structures.
According to Beskrestnov, the KRSN consists of a 40-kg (88-pound) main charge and four additional strike modules. A cutting charge focuses its blast along a line to slice through metal, which makes it suited to severing the legs of a steel pylon or the girders of a bridge rather than causing broad blast damage. Beskrestnov did not say where the drone carrying it struck or what damage it caused.
Russia has attacked Ukraine’s power system throughout the war, mainly with missiles and Iranian-designed Shahed drones aimed at power plants and substations. Ukraine’s long transmission lines, which run across open country and are hard to defend, have been less frequent targets because individual towers and cables are small and difficult for a drone to hit and destroy. The jet-powered Shahed variants, which fly much faster than the original propeller-driven model, also give Ukrainian air defenses less time to react.

Could US sanction Netanyahu? Democrats push anti-settlement bill in House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:41:57 UTC
17:41:57 KST

Six Democratic members of the U.S. House are introducing legislation Thursday that would impose sanctions on foreign individuals and entities involved in building or expanding Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank and Gaza, a proposal that could potentially apply to senior Israeli government officials.
The Stop the Settlements Act is being introduced by Reps. Joaquin Castro of Texas, Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania, Don Beyer of Virginia, Greg Casar of Texas, Sara Jacobs of California and Veronica Escobar of Texas. More than 30 other House Democrats have signed on as original co-sponsors, including several longtime members of the party.
The bill would require sanctions against foreign individuals or entities involved in establishing new Israeli settlements or outposts in the West Bank or Gaza, including through infrastructure development, construction in the area known as E1 or facilitating the movement of Israeli civilians into settlements. It would also authorize measures targeting those involved in maintaining or expanding certain existing settlements and outposts.
E1 is a strategically sensitive tract of land east of Jerusalem between the city and the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim. Settlement construction there has long drawn international opposition because critics say it would make a contiguous Palestinian state more difficult to establish.
Potential penalties under the legislation include blocking assets and denying or revoking U.S. visas. The measure would also prohibit imports into the United States of goods produced wholly or partly in Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank and Gaza, moving beyond product-labeling requirements to an import ban.
Because the legislation applies broadly to foreign individuals and entities involved in settlement activity, Israeli government officials could potentially fall within its scope. U.S. citizens would be exempt from the sanctions provisions, including Israeli settlers who also hold American citizenship.
The proposal does not itself provide a comprehensive list of locations considered settlements, leaving implementation and sanctions designations to the executive branch.
The bill represents a broader approach than previous U.S. sanctions targeting individuals accused of violence or destabilizing activity in the West Bank. Its sponsors say they are seeking to use economic pressure against settlement construction and expansion itself.
Castro said the legislation was intended to give individuals and companies a choice between participating in settlement activity and maintaining access to the U.S. economy. He said he plans to continue pressing the issue “in the coming months and in the next Congress.”
Supporters of the legislation argue that settlement expansion displaces Palestinians and undermines the prospects for a negotiated Israeli-Palestinian settlement. Several sponsors also characterize Israeli settlements as violations of international law. Israel disputes some international legal characterizations of the settlements and has historically argued that the status of the territories should be resolved through negotiations.
The proposal comes amid growing criticism among congressional Democrats of Israeli settlement policy. J Street, a U.S. organization that describes itself as pro-Israel and pro-peace, endorsed the legislation, saying economic consequences were needed after decades of international opposition to settlement expansion.
The legislation faces significant obstacles in the current Republican-controlled House and under President Donald Trump, making enactment in the current Congress unlikely. Its sponsors, however, are framing it partly as groundwork for a future Congress.
A senior Democratic official said the prospects for such legislation would also be affected by the outcome of Israel’s elections and whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current governing coalition remains in power. The official said senior Democrats’ ability to block such measures “depends entirely on whether the current coalition continues. If it does, these laws will pass.” That assessment represents the official’s political judgment rather than a certainty about future congressional action.

Photos: Kashmir’s Dal Lake faces environmental and climate challenges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:41:57 UTC
17:41:57 KST

In Pictures
Photos: Kashmir’s Dal Lake faces environmental and climate challenges
Dal Lake’s fragile ecosystem is deteriorating amid pollution, unregulated construction and climate change in Kashmir.
Dal Lake in Srinagar, the heart of tourism and cultural life in Indian-administered Kashmir, is slowly giving way under mounting population and environmental pressures.
Once renowned for its clear waters, floating gardens and houseboats, the lake is now clogged with untreated sewage, plastic waste and rampant weed growth, even as thousands of residents and businesses rely on it for transport and their livelihoods.
Unregulated construction along its shores, land encroachment and the expansion of nearby neighbourhoods have reduced its surface area and further damaged its fragile ecosystem.
The impact of climate change, including erratic rainfall and rising temperatures, is accelerating the lake’s decline.
Despite periodic clean-up campaigns and official conservation schemes, the future of Dal Lake remains uncertain, reflecting a wider environmental crisis across the Kashmir Valley.

Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said the 12-year campaign “defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region.”
Baghdad and Washington agreed in September 2024 to end the coalition’s military mission in Iraq under a timetable extending through the end of September 2026, with a transition to bilateral security relations between Iraq and member states.
The coalition was formed under US leadership in 2014 after ISIS (Daesh) seized large areas of Iraq and Syria, providing Iraqi forces with air, intelligence and training support during operations against the group.
Iraq announced in December 2017 that it had regained full control of territory seized by ISIS.
American forces first invaded Iraq in 2003 to remove Saddam Hussein, and withdrew at the end of 2011.

“But I will not stop and I will not hide... I will continue to do everything I can to rally the free world against Putin’s murderous dictatorship,” added Kasparov, whom Russia has placed on its lists of “foreign agents” and “terrorists and extremists”.
The Kremlin said in September it saw no reason to comment on the US allegations in the absence of what it called credible evidence and facts. Russia has previously denied conducting such plots on foreign soil, including in the US. REUTERS

Chinese tech giant Tencent has signed a $7 billion lease deal with US cloud provider Oracle that has enabled the company to access around 100,000 advanced AI chips, which were not available in China, the Financial Times reported on Thursday.
The world-leading internet and technology company this year agreed to a five-year lease across multiple Oracle data centers in south-east Asia amid an escalating AI race.

Tencent's largest overseas deal empowered the company to access around 100,000 advanced AI chips, which were not available in China.
