Estonia bans grain transit from Russia and Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

Estonia bans grain transit from Russia and Belarus
The government decided to prohibit, by national sanction, the transit through Estonia of grain originating from Russia and Belarus. Although until now Russia and Belarus have not used Estonia for exporting their grain, establishing the restriction excludes this also in the future.
Due to Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine, both Russian and Ukrainian grain exports through the ports on the Black Sea have essentially stopped. Russia is now seeking new export routes for its grain, and grain transit through Latvia has sharply increased in recent months.
"Russia attacks Ukraine's ports and prevents Ukrainian grain from reaching the world market. It would be cynical to let it export its own grain through our ports at the same time. Estonia will not allow this," said Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna in a press release.
According to Tsahkna, Estonia's position has been known. "We already said in September that it is not worth making plans to transport Russian grain through Estonia. Now we are putting a full stop to this with a national sanction. We will not help Russia ease the consequences of the war it itself initiated," the foreign minister emphasized.
According to the ministry, transit of Russian grain through Estonia has so far been essentially nonexistent. The ban ensures that Estonia will not become a new transit route for Russian grain.
Representatives of Latvia and Lithuania have also spoken about the plan to stop Russian grain transit through their territories.
"We are acting together with Latvia and Lithuania so that Russian grain transit does not take place through the ports of the Baltic states. The Baltic states cannot allow our ports to support Russia's war economy," Tsahkna added.
The European Union imposed customs duties on grain products from Russia and Belarus in 2024, with the aim of stopping their import into the EU. However, customs duties do not fully prevent grain transit through the EU to third countries.
The ban will be established by amending Regulation No. 93 of 29 September 2022, "Establishing a sanction of the Government of the Republic for prohibiting the purchase of goods in connection with the aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine, supported by the Republic of Belarus." The sanction prohibits the transit through Estonia of grain belonging to CN group 10 (EU Combined Nomenclature Chapter 10) originating from Russia and Belarus.
The regulation enters into force on the day following its publication in Riigi Teataja (State Gazette).

U.S. Air Force taps BAE for pulsed laser research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:33:42 UTC
17:33:42 KST

- The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory awarded BAE Systems a contract worth up to $19.7 million for pulsed and solid-state laser research.
- Work will take place at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, through September 2031, with $1 million obligated at award.
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory has hired BAE Systems to work out how pulsed lasers could be used for military missions and how to pair solid-state lasers with beam control systems the U.S. Air Force already has, under a contract worth up to $19.7 million.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee contract, for a program called Laser Utilization for Military Innovation and Novel Applications, went to BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in Broomfield, Colorado. The laboratory obligated $1 million in fiscal 2026 research funds at the time of award, and the work runs through Sept. 29, 2031. Six companies bid for it.
The contract notice describes two goals: finding ways to use the advantages of pulsed lasers, and integrating solid-state laser technology with existing beam control systems. A pulsed laser releases its energy in very short, intense bursts, while a continuous-wave laser, the type used in most laser weapons fielded so far, delivers a steady beam. Beam control is the set of optics, sensors and tracking equipment that points a laser, keeps it locked on a moving target and corrects for distortion in the air, and it is often the hardest part of making a laser weapon work.
The notice does not say what military applications the U.S. Air Force has in mind, whether the work is aimed at weapons, sensing, communications or something else, or what kind of targets or platforms are involved.
All of the work will take place at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, home to the Air Force Research Laboratory’s Directed Energy Directorate, which leads the service’s research on high-energy lasers and high-power microwaves.
BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems is the former Ball Aerospace, which BAE Systems bought in 2024. The Colorado unit builds spacecraft, satellite instruments and optical and sensor systems for the U.S. military and NASA.
As a cost-plus contract with a maximum ceiling, the deal reimburses BAE Systems for its costs plus a fixed fee, and the U.S. Air Force is not obligated to spend the full $19.7 million.

Baltic Sea shipper Tallink and sailors want state passenger ferry support to continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:33:00 UTC
17:33:00 KST

Baltic Sea shipper Tallink and sailors want state passenger ferry support to continue
Tallink and seafarers continue to warn that the government's decision to discontinue support for passenger shipping could lead to some vessels, along with their crews, leaving the Estonian flag.
A year and a half ago, the Reform Party and Eesti 200 signed a coalition agreement in which they pledged, among other things, to reinstate the passenger shipping support measure to ensure Estonia's competitiveness with neighboring countries and protect thousands of jobs on Estonian ships.
"Without a similar measure, Estonian ships and jobs could sooner or later move to neighboring countries, which would mean a loss of nearly €54 million a year in tax revenue for our country. The support helps keep costs under control, preserve jobs and keep tax revenue in Estonia," Minister of Infrastructure Kuldar Leis said a few months later in a Ministry of Climate press release.
In the end, however, the Riigikogu decided last year not to reinstate the support measure. This was largely because Reform MP Mart Võrklaev said he would support lowering the remote gambling tax in a Riigikogu vote only if the government dropped the passenger shipping support measure.
The support measure nevertheless remained in the state budget strategy at the time, meaning the government had still factored an annual expenditure of €10 million to support passenger shipping into its future plans.
The passenger shipping support measure was officially removed from those future plans only at the beginning of this week when the government agreed on a new state budget strategy.
For example, documents accompanying next year's state budget bill state that not continuing the passenger shipping support measure will save nearly €10 million a year from 2027 through 2030.
Tallink: Jobs in jeopardy
Tallink CEO Peep Jalakas said the government's decision not to continue the passenger shipping support measure in the coming years is not good for either Tallink's sustainability or the Estonian maritime sector more broadly.
Jalakas said Tallink is constantly considering whether to move any of its vessels away from the Estonian flag and the decision not to continue the measure makes that more likely.
"This could put both jobs and the long-term future of Estonia's maritime sector at risk," Jalakas said.
The Seamen's Independent Union of Estonia said a year ago, for example, that Tallink could move its ferry Victoria away from the Estonian flag, along with 300 jobs.
Jalakas declined to say how likely Tallink is to move any of its vessels away from the Estonian flag.
"We certainly won't rush into making any hasty decisions. We still hope that, ultimately, the final decisions will ensure that Estonia's maritime policy is long-term and sustainable," he said.
Both Jalakas and Jüri Lember, head of the Seamen's Independent Union of Estonia, acknowledged that the situation in the maritime sector has become more difficult.
"Fuel costs, particularly for marine fuels, have nearly doubled compared with the beginning of the year. On the other hand, since the beginning of this year, the entire passenger shipping sector has also been subject to carbon taxes, which adds millions of euros to our costs. This combination, in which costs that we cannot influence are rising, puts us under increasing pressure to consider different ways of optimizing costs," Jalakas explained.
"Very simple calculations have shown that just one vessel would already take away around €10 million in tax revenue. Those people probably wouldn't change their place of residence, but these are large sums that should be known and taken into account when entering numbers into an Excel spreadsheet," Lember said.
Minister: We want to put together a new maritime support measure
Infrastructure Minister Kuldar Leis said that ultimately, it is up to Tallink itself to decide how to proceed.
"We are in constant contact with maritime companies and the goal is for us as a country to remain competitive. On the other hand, we know the state of our national budget and what we need to do to reduce the deficit. In every area, we have to cut back on the one hand while looking at how to remain competitive on the other," he said.
Leis said the ministry still wants to support the maritime sector, but in a somewhat different way. Specifically, Estonia is seeking state aid approval from the European Commission so that companies using more environmentally friendly fuels could receive financial support from the state budget in the coming years.
"If we receive that approval, the plan is to once again seek funding from the state budget for the following years," Leis said.
Leis said the Ministry of Climate currently expects the support for environmentally friendly fuels to be roughly the same amount as was planned for the passenger shipping support measure last year, or about €10 million a year.
"The entire transport sector is becoming more environmentally friendly and Estonia is moving in that direction in every sector. This is most evident in the car market where electric vehicles are becoming increasingly common. Similarly, the Tartu and Narva rail lines are being electrified. Just as other areas of transport are moving toward more environmentally friendly fuels, so is the maritime sector," Leis explained.

The Design Museum Gent , in the East Flanders' capital, is set to reopen this coming weekend after four years of renovations. The museum has been completely renovated and expanded to include an additional building. The façade features 82,000 bricks made in Ghent from construction waste. The refurbished Design Museum Gent will showcase 500 objects, nearly half of which the museum has never exhibited before.
The refurbished Design Museum Gent now covers an area of approximately 6,500 square metres and has a total of around 3,700 square metres of exhibition space.
A new building has been added to the museum. This connects the existing buildings and provides space for lectures, workshops and events. On the 4th floor, there is an events space with a panoramic view over the fair city of Ghent.
The museum has a collection totalling 24,000 design pieces. 500 objects will be on display. Almost half of these have never been exhibited by the museum before.
10 unique loos
“I began a feasibility study in 2015,” explains director Katrien Laporte. “To identify what our needs were. And now, 11 years later, here we are in the new Design Museum Gent.”
“A great deal has changed. The building now fulfils a number of functions it didn’t have before. We didn’t have proper toilets, we didn’t have a lift, and we didn’t have a space for lectures, debates and events.”
“The new building is a very warm, accessible building, constructed entirely of timber. We also want it to make a statement. Design used to have an elitist image. This building will help to bring it down from its pedestal.”
‘You really do have to revisit the museum several times if only for the toilets. We have 10 different toilet cubicles, each with different tiles. It’s very tongue-in-cheek. And when you’re sitting on the loo, you can scan a QR code to find out how the tile was made.’
Opening festival
This coming weekend, the Design Museum Gent will reopen with a major opening festival lasting nine days.
There are more than 120 activities, including performances, music and workshops. Thirty-three shops and hotels in Ghent are transforming their shop windows into temporary exhibitions.
The festivities kick off on Friday evening with a performance by the Ghent-based brothers of 2manydjs. They will be playing from the balcony of the new building. On Sunday, between 10.00 and 16.00, local designers will be showcasing their work at 60 stalls at the Design Makers Market.
Admission to the museum and the exhibitions is free during the opening weekend.

Switch to cleaner fuel: Study calls for tech-neutral stance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:31:01 UTC
17:31:01 KST

NEW DELHI: Delhi has the strongest CNG infrastructure among the cities assessed in a TERI study and, along with Bengaluru, also has relatively strong EV infrastructure.The study, supported by the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB), found that effective charging capacity was considerably lower in Lucknow, Guwahati, Dhanbad and Chamba. It said infrastructure readiness was a key determinant of the timing of the transition and that national transition pathways needed regionally differentiated implementation strategies.The “Study on Comparative Assessment of Vehicular Fuels in India’s Energy Transition” examined petrol, diesel, CNG, electricity and LNG across two-wheelers, three-wheelers, private and commercial four-wheelers, light commercial vehicles (LCVs) and heavy-duty vehicles. It covered Delhi, Mumbai, Mumbai Port, Surat, Ahmedabad, Guwahati, Lucknow, Bengaluru, Dhanbad and Chamba.The study found that India should not adopt one fuel or technology as a universal replacement, with different technologies performing different roles across vehicle fleets, applications and stages of the transition.It found that EVs currently provide the lowest ownership costs for two-wheelers and three-wheelers, while CNG offers a relatively balanced and deployment-ready mobility solution across a wide range of personal and commercial applications.
The study said CNG has a strong position in passenger cars, taxis, buses and LCVs, while LNG remains particularly relevant for long-haul freight.The study was based partly on a primary survey of 2,315 vehicle owners and drivers across 10 locations, using stratified random sampling. The survey covered vehicle usage, travel distance, mileage, infrastructure access, fuel and maintenance expenditure, technology preferences and willingness to retrofit.Economic considerations emerged as the strongest factor in the assessment, accounting for 31.49% of the overall weighting, followed by environmental considerations at 22.34% and technical factors at 21.25%. The report said the weights reflected the importance of affordability, ownership cost and operating economics in technology selection.The study said CNG-powered vehicles have the lowest overall life-cycle emissions among the fuel options assessed for several passenger and commercial vehicle segments. It also said environmental performance cannot be judged solely through tailpipe emissions, with EV performance influenced by electricity generation, battery manufacturing and material requirements.The findings come amid a continuing debate over the role of vehicles and fuels in Delhi-NCR’s air pollution and the effectiveness of past interventions. Tarun Kapoor, advisor to PM, said better data was needed to guide policy. “Good authentic data is very urgently needed. Whatever interventions we’ve done in the past, it’s been like hitting in the dark and the results have not really been the way it was thought,” he said.The study also said electrification changes rather than eliminates energy-security risks by shifting some dependence from petroleum towards electricity infrastructure, critical minerals, imported automobile components and battery supply chains.
“The real policy question is not which fuel should replace all others, but rather which fuel is best suited for which application, under what operating conditions and at what stage of India’s transition journey,” said AK Tiwari, member, PNGRB.The study recommended a technology-neutral framework at the national level, with differentiated approaches based on vehicle segment, region and application. It also called for accelerated CNG infrastructure development, greater use of CBG and differentiated CNG and LNG strategies, with LNG focused on long-haul mobility.
Atul Mathur is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India with over 27 years of experience in journalism. Based in Delhi, he has spent much of his career reporting on governance, public policy and politics, churning out researched, data-driven stories that impact daily lives. Atul is known for investigative depth and strong human-interest narratives as he strives to bring clarity and context to complex issues. He currently tracks the energy sector, writing on power, renewable energy, coal and mines.

Corruption and EU reluctance: Ukrainians name key obstacles to EU membership – KIIS
A total of 32% of Ukrainians believe corruption in the central government is the biggest obstacle to the country's EU membership, while 29% point to the reluctance of the European Union or some of its member states to admit Ukraine.
Source: a survey conducted by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) on 12-21 September
Details: Survey participants were asked to choose one of six answers to the question of what most hinders Ukraine's progress towards EU membership.
A total of 32% cited corruption in the central government, while 29% pointed to the reluctance of the EU or some of its member states to admit Ukraine.
Another 15% cited the war, while 10% pointed to the inadequate performance of the government and parliament.
Resistance to reforms by certain influential groups was selected by 5% of respondents, while 3% cited insufficient independence of the judiciary and law enforcement agencies.
For reference: The Kyiv International Institute of Sociology conducted its nationwide Omnibus public opinion survey, which included questions commissioned by the NGO Forum on attitudes towards holding an independent competitive selection process involving foreign experts to appoint the prosecutor general, as well as Ukraine's progress towards EU membership.
KIIS interviewed 1,002 Ukrainian citizens over 18 by telephone who were living in government-controlled territory. Respondents were selected using a random sample of mobile phone numbers.
The sample did not include residents of Russian-occupied territories or Ukrainian citizens who left the country after 24 February 2022. However, internally displaced people from occupied territories were included among the respondents.
The formal statistical margin of error, taking the design effect into account, does not exceed 4.1 percentage points. KIIS notes that additional systematic deviations may occur under wartime conditions.
Background:
- The European Commission has postponed until 6 October the presentation of its assessment of how future EU enlargement will affect the bloc's key policies and what changes the EU itself may need in order to admit new member states.
- Earlier, EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos presented four areas for changes to the EU enlargement process: internal reforms of the bloc, stronger democratic safeguards, gradual integration and transitional measures.

Estonia bans transit of Russian and Belarusian grain in response to blockade of Ukrainian ports

Source: Tsahkna on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Tsahkna said Russia is attacking Ukrainian ports, blocking Ukrainian grain exports and seeking new routes for transporting its own grain, but Estonia will not provide such a route.
Quote: "I warned already in September: do not make plans to transport Russian grain through Estonia. Today, we turned that warning into law."
Details: Tsahkna added that the Baltic states are working together to ensure their ports do not become transit routes for Russia.
"Russia cannot wage a war of aggression and expect us to help keep its trade flowing. We will not help finance its war or make its aggression easier to sustain," Estonia's foreign minister stressed.
Background:
- Russian exporters have begun redirecting grain shipments from the Black and Azov seas to the Baltic Sea amid Ukrainian attacks on Russian vessels and port infrastructure.
- The Baltic states have strongly opposed the growing volumes of Russian grain being transported in transit through their territories.
- Latvia introduced border controls on grain to prevent the transit of goods stolen from Ukraine and also announced 300% tariffs on grain shipments from Russia and Belarus and their processing.
- Meanwhile, Lithuania is stepping up checks on Russian grain transported through the port of Klaipėda to determine whether it was stolen from Ukraine.

30% boost to UK military transport aircraft availability under new deal
MoD extends £190 million contract with Airbus to maintain the RAF's A400M Atlas fleet, boosting aircraft availability while sustaining over 350 UK jobs.
- £190 million contract extension with Airbus to support RAF’s A400 Atlas fleet, retaining more than 350 UK jobs.
- Agreement set to increase the number of mission-capable A400M aircraft available each day from 10 to 13 by the end of 2027.
- Britain’s air defence will be boosted under new deal.
A 30% improvement in availability for the RAF’s tactical and strategic airlift fleet will be delivered under a £190 million contract extension between the Ministry of Defence and Airbus.
The extension will see Airbus continue its maintenance, repair and support services for the RAF’s A400M Atlas fleet from its UK Support Centre at RAF Brize Norton.
As well as sustaining more than 350 UK jobs, the extended contract is set to deliver a significant boost to operational capability and will increase the number of fully mission-capable aircraft available each day from 10 to 13 by the end of 2027.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:
  This contract extension is a vote of confidence in British engineering, and the workforce at Brize Norton and Carterton who keep our A400M fleet flying.
By boosting availability of these aircraft, we’re strengthening the RAF’s ability to conduct global operations and deliver on NATO commitments when it matters most, while backing UK jobs and delivering value for money for taxpayers.
The A400M Atlas is a cornerstone of the UK’s air mobility capability, supporting operations ranging from humanitarian relief to rapid troop deployment.
Continued support at RAF Brize Norton ensures the fleet remains ready to meet these demands without interruption, forming part of the government’s wider commitment to strengthening the UK’s defence industrial base and value for money in defence contracts.
Air Cdre Si Young, Head Air Mobility in National Armaments Materiel, said:
  This contract will deliver continued improvements in A400M fleet availability, building on the growth that we have delivered over recent years and giving our Armed Forces the capability they need while offering excellent value for money to taxpayers, supporting a platform that is at the heart of the RAF’s operations now and into the future.
It reflects the strength of our partnership with Airbus and our shared commitment to supporting the continued growth and success of the A400M fleet, both now and in the years ahead.
The 31-month extension to the Medium-Term Contract means support services will continue until April 2029, sustaining more than 240 Airbus staff and 110 primary sub-contract staff.
Kata Escott, Managing Director of Airbus Defence and Space UK, said:
  Alongside the financial savings, the extended contract is set to deliver a significant boost to operational capability, with plans to increase the number of fully mission-capable aircraft available each day from 10 to 13 by the end of 2027, a 30% improvement in availability for the RAF’s tactical and strategic airlift fleet.
This will support the RAF’s ability to deliver global air mobility operations, including humanitarian relief, troop transport and NATO commitments.
The contract builds on the work of the Defence Investment Plan, which commits £298 billion to UK defence over the next four years. The plan will drive sustained investment across British industry ensuring the UK’s defence sector remains a cornerstone of the country’s economic renewal.

MOD trade, industry and contracts: 2026
Information on Ministry of Defence spending with industry and commerce.
Documents
Details
This bulletin provides figures on the composition and scope of the department’s expenditure, information on the impact of defence spending on the wider economy, and compares the MOD’s spending to that of other departments and other countries.
Section removal
The 2026 edition of the Trade, Industry and Contracts bulletin will permanently exclude the section on Major Equipment Projects when published. The underlying data on equipment spending plans had historically been included within the Project Performance Summary Table of the Defence Equipment Plan. However, this data has not been produced since 2024 and the section will now be removed since comparable figures remain unavailable. Note that broadly similar information is provided by the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority (NISTA) in the Major Projects Annual Report.
From 2026, details on defence export orders will be contained solely in the separate UK Defence Export Statistics. Before 2026 this statistical release was published by the Department for Business and Trade (DBT). However, after a Machinery of Government change effective 31 July 2025, responsibility for defence exports promotion moved from DBT to the MOD. Since MOD now takes full ownership for the production of these statistics, figures will be released in UK Defence Export Statistics only so as to avoid duplication of reporting as well as improve timeliness. The next edition of the export statistics is expected late 2026. Historic data in this time series can still be found in MOD Trade, Industry and Contracts 2025.
Future revisions
A planned revision of 2026’s Trade, Industry and Contracts bulletin is expected by early 2027. In this revision, the competition and SME status of newly placed contracts in 2025/26 will be reassessed. This is to account for the delayed reporting of new contracts which has historically resulted in a 1% adjustment to the number of contracts reported.
Should you have any comments regarding any of these changes or proposed revisions then please email Analysis-Expenditure-PQ-FOI@mod.gov.uk.

design museum gent reopens with new wing built from locally made waste bricks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:30:02 UTC
17:30:02 KST

design museum gent reopens with new wing built from locally made waste bricks
carmody groarke and ATAMA lead the new extension, while RE-ST restores the historic buildings as part of a wider transformation that rethinks the museum’s collection, exhibitions and public spaces.
Design Museum Gent opens its collection to new perspectives
Design Museum Gent in Ghent, Belgium, reopens on October 3rd, 2026, following a four-year renovation and expansion led by Carmody Groarke and ATAMA, with the historic buildings restored by RE-ST. The project repositions the museum as an open civic space where design is used to examine how objects, cities and social systems are shaped. The new 2,200-square-meter wing completes the fragmented museum complex around its historic courtyard and introduces freely accessible spaces for exhibitions, workshops, lectures, events and community activity. The extension uses timber and white brick, with a facade made from Gent Waste Brick (find designboom’s previous coverage here), a lime-cured brick produced from locally sourced municipal waste. More than 82,000 bricks were produced locally at Het Arsenaal in Ghent, hardened through a low-energy lime-curing process.
Its new exhibition, Collection. Models from the Past for the Future, places around 500 objects from the museum’s 24,000-piece collection into contemporary themes including copy, comfort, migration, folds and connections, asking what earlier design ideas can still offer and what now needs to be reconsidered. Meanwhile, Public Matter(s): Design and Democracy treats democratic systems themselves as designed structures, while projects such as the AI-powered Searcher and the collaborative CO-LAB extend the role of the institution from displaying design to testing how it can operate as a tool for participation, debate and change.
completing a fragmented museum in ghent, belgium
The architectural project brings together a complex collection of buildings dating from the 16th to the 20th century, working to connect the existing parts into a more coherent whole. The new wing occupies a previously underused southern passage and an unused plot at the center of the site. Its addition allows the historic courtyard of Hotel de Coninck to become a garden and a central point of orientation, with views toward it running through the building and helping visitors understand the relationship between the different parts of the museum.
The building is organized around six zones: the basement art-handling area, the Stadskamer reception and shop, the Forum lecture space, the Atelier workshops, the Vitrine for temporary exhibitions, and the Loft, an event space on the fourth floor with views over Ghent. The Stadskamer, conceived as a freely accessible ‘city room,’ is intended as a place where local communities and neighborhoods can meet and present their own creations.
The white color of the new wing relates to the historic houses along Drabstraat, while the scale and rhythm of the facade draw from Ghent’s guild and merchant houses. Deep window reveals and pronounced copings give the contemporary building a civic presence without attempting to imitate its historic neighbors. Historic interiors have been restored, while later additions have been adapted to create additional space and improve climatic conditions. Materials are reused where possible, positioning the renovation as an exercise in working with what already exists.
looking at the collection differently
The renewed architectural framework of the Design Museum Gent is matched by a change in how its collection is presented. Collection. Models from the Past for the Future, curated by Evelien Bracke, returns to the institution’s origins as a ‘model museum.’ Founded in 1903, Design Museum Gent originally collected exemplary objects intended to inform and inspire craftspeople and visitors. The new display takes that premise and turns it into a contemporary question. Around 500 objects are organized around five themes, copy, comfort, migration, folds and connections, rather than being presented primarily through individual designers or chronological development. The curatorial goal is to make historical design less about established canon and more about changing interpretation. Objects once regarded as exemplary can now be reconsidered through contemporary concerns, while historical techniques and approaches can offer unexpected models for the future. Contemporary designers including Kana Arioka, OpenStructures and Victor Verhelst respond to objects and themes from the collection, bringing them into conversation with new work and showing how the archive can continue to inform contemporary practice.
The scenography of the exhibition by Nord + Laura Muyldermans also stages a conversation between different forms of making. Traditional clay-plastered walls are combined with the Belgian circular steel construction system Skellet, placing artisanal and industrial approaches alongside one another.
from objects to democratic systems
The museum’s most direct expansion of its design remit comes through Public Matter(s): Design and Democracy, the opening exhibition curated by Amelie Klein and Vera Sacchetti. The premise is straightforward but consequential: democratic systems are designed. Ballot papers, parliamentary buildings and voting procedures are visible manifestations of that design, but so are the less tangible structures that determine who participates, who is represented and who is heard.
The exhibition considers questions of accessibility, including how people experiencing homelessness or visual impairments interact with electoral systems, alongside histories of women’s suffrage, civil rights and protest. Its Democracy Fitness Trail extends the exhibition into an interactive format. Visitors are invited to practice skills such as active listening, compromise and constructive conflict, treating democratic participation as something that can be exercised.
The approach grew partly from DE40, a citizens’ panel in which 40 residents of Ghent discussed how the museum could make design more accessible and relevant to people regardless of their background or prior knowledge. Their input was used as a framework for the museum’s transformation.
an institution that experiments with its own tools
 Technology becomes another way for Design Museum Gent to question how collections are accessed.
 Searcher, developed by Jon Stam, Valentin Vogelman and Boris Smeenk, uses AI to allow visitors to explore the collection of the museum through similarities in form, color and text. A museum archive can easily become a fixed narrative, organized around established classifications and historical hierarchies. Searcher presents it as a network that can be navigated through association and discovery.
The museum is also using its physical spaces as a platform for collaborative production. CO-LAB, curated by Siegrid Demyttenaere, brings Belgian and international designers, researchers and local communities together across eight historic period rooms in Hotel de Coninck. The projects address subjects including sustainable energy, queer archives, designing with nature and open-source tools.
project info:

architects: Carmody Groarke | @carmodygroarke, ATAMA | @atama_architects, RE-ST
 location: Ghent, Belgium
 opening: October 3rd, 2026
 new wing area: 2,200 sqm
 historic buildings: 6,400 sqm
 structural engineer: Ney & Partners
 building services: Boydens Engineering
 acoustics: Daidalos Peutz

'The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts,' IDF lambasts 'NAZA' documentary in detailed response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:29:32 UTC
17:29:32 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel-Hamas war
- 'The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts,' IDF lambasts 'NAZA' film in detailed response
'The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts,' IDF lambasts 'NAZA' film in detailed response
In a detailed rebuttal to the documentary "NAZA," the IDF said the film relies on anonymous, uncorroborated testimony from junior intelligence personnel to mischaracterize the IDF's strike process
The IDF published a formal response to the documentary "NAZA," saying it presents "a distorted, misleading, and disingenuous picture" of the military's target planning and strike process. The IDF said the film's narrative relies on testimony from anonymous individuals who generally describe only the initial, intelligence-gathering stages of a much longer targeting process, resulting in what it called "an incorrect and highly misleading description of reality."
The military noted that "NAZA" is the Hebrew acronym for "collateral damage," a standard term used by law-abiding militaries worldwide. It points out that the film paradoxically presents the IDF's detailed civilian harm estimation process as evidence of indifference to civilian life, when such assessments are in fact required under international law.
The IDF said the filmmakers did not submit their allegations for examination before publication and declined to provide the IDF a copy of the film after a public screening, despite the military's request. As a result, the IDF said it based its response on an account from a representative who attended a public screening, along with other public reporting and statements from the filmmakers themselves.
The IDF argued that the anonymous interviewees spoke about matters beyond their knowledge and competence, and testimony confined to preliminary stages does not establish the final assessments on which commanders relied. For example, an interviewee may recall a general, preliminary estimate of civilians present in an area around a military objective, but did not account for precautions decided later in the process.
Suggested articles
Additionally, the IDF claimed that besides the anonymous accounts, the film did not cite any military directives, contemporaneous records, or other corroborating evidence. The film's accounts of alleged strikes include no specific targets, dates, locations, or casualty figures, making the claims "general and unverifiable," the IDF claims.
Among the specific claims addressed, the IDF denied that artificial intelligence autonomously generated tens of thousands of human targets that were then struck, stating flatly that "in the IDF, artificial intelligence does not determine whether an object or a person is designated as a target, nor whether a target is struck." The military said human analysts identify targets under defined procedures, with decisions ultimately made by operational commanders.
Regarding allegations that soldiers fired on civilians near humanitarian aid distribution sites, the IDF said rules of engagement permitted fire only against armed operatives or suspects posing an immediate threat.
The IDF strongly rejected the film's suggestion that an interviewee's personal view constituted evidence of genocide, calling the allegation "outrageous and unfounded." It noted that genocide under international law requires specific intent to destroy a group, which it said, "never existed."
The military said its objectives in Gaza were to dismantle Hamas's military and governing capabilities and secure the return of hostages, not to harm Palestinian civilians. The IDF pointed to its warnings, strike cancellations, and facilitation of humanitarian aid, including more than 3.9 million metric tons of food delivered into Gaza since October 2023, as evidence against the claim.
The IDF said the film omits essential context necessary to understand its conduct during the war, including the October 7 massacre and Hamas's systematic embedding of military infrastructure within civilian areas such as hospitals, schools and mosques. It said the film's narrative is reinforced through "manipulative editing of interviews" and omits the professionals, including legal advisers and commanders, responsible for mitigating civilian harm throughout the targeting process.
"The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts," the IDF said, adding that "the IDF has acted and continues to act humanely, even if the filmmakers have done everything they can to conceal that fact."

Hegseth announces new AI and drone command
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01

Hegseth announces new AI and drone command
The Pentagon will set up a new Autonomous Warfare Command to design, produce and field robotic systems across the military, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has said in his ‘State of the Force’ address.
The announcement comes as experts sound the alarm about the threat posed by military AI, saying that over-reliance on it could lead to the erosion of human critical thinking, increase the risk of accidental escalation due to the unpredictability of the decision-making by the algorithms and make warfare even more dangerous for civilians.
During his speech at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia on Wednesday, Hegseth said that the AutoWarCom would be granted “service-like authorities built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force in the fastest peacetime shift in modern military history.”
“Drone warfare supercharged by SI-enabled targeting is the biggest battlefield revolution in generations,” he stressed.
A day earlier, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order replacing the term “Artificial Intelligence” (“AI”) with “Super Intelligence” (“SI”) in the US government’s vocabulary.
The lessons of the Ukraine conflict, in which both sides actively rely on drones, have been one of the main motivations for launching the new command, according to the secretary of war.
In a memo published the same day, Hegseth noted that the Pentagon’s long-time strategy “of buying fewer, increasingly sophisticated weapons” has lost its effectiveness.
“Warfare… has changed dramatically and suddenly. Advanced computing now enables precise, low-cost weapons to be produced at massive scale. These systems increasingly threaten our costly legacy platforms and disrupt our force projection. Urgent change is required,” he wrote.
The Autonomous Warfare Command, which will be led by a four-star general, should become operational by October 1, 2027, the secretary of war said.
Bloomberg reported last month that heavy reliance on AI, staff cuts and rushed targeting procedures contributed to a US missile strike on an Iranian girls’ school in Minab on February 28, in which at least 157 people, including 123 children, were killed.
Officials involved in the Pentagon investigation told the agency that some US Central Command (CENTCOM) personnel expected Palantir’s Maven Smart System to flag stale or inconsistent intelligence when selecting potential targets, but it failed to do so. The US hasn’t publicly acknowledged responsibility for the Minab strike.
Last week, CNN reported that AI almost caused a serious incident between US and China in spring. The American forces were about to intercept a Chinese vessel, which, according to an intelligence report, was carrying components for a nuclear weapon to Iran. The mission was called off at the last moment when it became clear that a chatbot used by the analyst misidentified the cargo, according to the broadcaster.
During a defense conference in Beijing in mid-September, Thailand’s Defense Minister Adul Boonthumjaroen warned that the world was at “a critical turning point” due to the emergence of the military AI. “The most pressing is not who will be the most powerful, but rather, how can we build an international order,” he said.

UAE attorney general orders investigation into Flydubai flight incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01

Ikram Kouachi
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi on Thursday ordered the formation of a team to investigate an incident involving a Flydubai flight traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv a day earlier.
The UAE’s official WAM news agency said Al Shamsi ordered the formation of an investigation team comprising specialized public prosecutors.
The team will investigate the incident involving Flydubai flight FZ1073, which was traveling from Dubai International Airport to Tel Aviv before being diverted and landing safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, WAM reported.
Al Shamsi directed the team to gather information and evidence and establish the facts, circumstances and motives surrounding the incident, including determining whether it was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose or involved prior planning or direction, according to WAM.
UAE judicial authorities have jurisdiction to investigate the incident under applicable legislation because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag, WAM reported.
Accordingly, UAE law applies to crimes committed aboard the aircraft even when they occur outside the country’s territory, it added.
On Wednesday, FZ1073, carrying 174 passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv, made an emergency landing at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in the northwestern Saudi city of Tabuk after an altercation was reported in the cockpit.
Flydubai said “an altercation occurred in the flight deck,” adding that crew members aboard the aircraft secured the plane and diverted it safely to Saudi Arabia.
Airport officials said both the captain and first officer were injured and taken to a hospital following the incident. All passengers and crew were reported safe and accounted for.
Saudi Arabia’s National Transport Safety Center later said its safety investigation team had begun work on the incident and was coordinating with relevant authorities to determine the circumstances, examine aviation safety aspects and collect related information and evidence.
The airport said the passengers later departed Tabuk aboard an alternative aircraft provided by Flydubai.

Global bond sell-off intensifies, as UK long-term borrowing costs pass 6%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:27:36 UTC
17:27:36 KST

The turmoil in global bond markets has intensified amid fears the US deficit is reaching unsustainable levels, helping drive UK long-term borrowing costs to a 28-year high.
The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors, who believe central banks will be forced to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.
In a morning of hectic trading on Thursday, the yield, which is a proxy for the interest rate, hit 6% on Britain’s 30-year bonds for the first time since 1998.
The yield on five- and 10-year UK bonds also rose, driving up the government’s borrowing costs and adding to the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before the budget later this month.
Stock market investors also sold heavily, knocking 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London during early trading. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s Dax and France’s CAC 40 falling by 1.1%.
“There is carnage in the bond market which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”
The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.
On Wednesday, US 10-year Treasury yields hit their highest level since 2002, while Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.
US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.
Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.
“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.
“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money, potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”
Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.
“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”

Twenty-four people were injured overnight in a fire at a nursing home in Bnei Brak, an ultra-Orthodox city near Tel Aviv, emergency services said Thursday. About 40 residents were evacuated from the eight-story building.
Two men, ages 65 and about 80, were seriously injured with second-degree burns, according to the Magen David Adom emergency medical service. Both were sedated and placed on ventilators before being taken to hospitals.
Four other people were moderately injured: a 75-year-old woman, two men ages about 50 and 80 and a 73-year-old woman. Another 18 people sustained minor injuries, including from smoke inhalation.
The injured were taken to Sheba Medical Center, Rabin Medical Center, Sourasky Medical Center and Mayanei Hayeshua Medical Center.
“This was a very difficult scene,” Magen David Adom paramedics Yissachar Weiss and Tal Sagi and emergency medical technician Yaakov Schechter said in a joint statement.
They said MDA deployed large numbers of emergency personnel, including rapid-response vehicles, ambulances and mobile intensive care units.
“We provided medical treatment to a large number of injured people, including two men in serious and unstable condition who were sedated and ventilated with burns to their upper bodies, four people in moderate condition and 18 in mild condition, and evacuated them to hospitals,” they said.
Fire and Rescue Services said the blaze broke out in an apartment on the first floor of the Mishkenot Vatikim nursing center on Amram Gaon Street in Bnei Brak.
Fire and rescue crews from Bnei Brak and neighboring Ramat Gan were dispatched to the scene, where they worked to extinguish the blaze and searched the building for people who might be trapped.
Firefighters found several residents trapped inside the burning apartment and rescued them before turning them over to medical teams, according to Fire and Rescue Services. Dozens of other residents were evacuated from the building as the operation continued.
After extinguishing the main fire, crews continued searching the building to ensure no one else remained trapped.
A fire investigator was called to the scene to determine what caused the blaze.

Sri Lanka customs launches paperless declaration process

Unknown Publisher

16:26:26 CST
17:26:26 KST

COLOMBO, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka Customs on Thursday began implementing a new paperless customs declaration process, requiring importers and declarants to submit digitally signed declarations and supporting documents.
An official launch ceremony was held at the Sri Lanka Customs Auditorium at 10 a.m. local time on Thursday under the patronage of Deputy Minister of Economic Development Nishantha Jayaweera and Secretary to the President Nandika Sanath Kumanayake.
Customs declarations submitted under the previous system are no longer accepted from Oct. 1, 2026, as the new requirements take effect across the customs clearance process.
The system is capable of detecting changes made to documents after a digital signature has been applied. Authorities expect the feature to strengthen the integrity of customs clearance and reduce opportunities for fraud and corruption.
The Paperless Customs Declaration Process was jointly introduced by Sri Lanka Customs and the Revenue Administration Reforms and Modernization Bureau of the Presidential Secretariat. The initiative is aimed at improving the speed, efficiency and transparency of customs services under the government's economic reform and public service modernization agenda. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: Chinese motor tricycles glide into international markets with innovation, customized services
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:26:26 CST
17:26:26 KST

ZHENGZHOU, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- Sturdy, agile and capable of hauling almost anything -- this is the familiar image of Chinese motor tricycles that overseas consumers have come to recognize, riding the viral "Chinamaxxing" wave on social media.
Now, an expanding set of customizable options is further boosting the vehicle's international market appeal.
With customer-oriented services and innovative modifications, Chinese motor tricycle makers are moving beyond product exports to build deeper ties with overseas markets, creating new momentum for local industries while adapting to the needs of consumers abroad.
At a motor tricycle factory in Yanshi District of Luoyang, central China's Henan Province, a new vehicle rolls off the automated assembly line every 15 minutes. The tricycles can be customized to deliver parking warnings in both Chinese and English.
Zhang Jiwei, an employee at the factory, said the vehicles can be further tailored to meet different customers' needs.
"For Egyptian and UAE customers in the tourism industry, we offer passenger and sightseeing models with attractive designs and greater comfort. In Central Asia and Africa, tricycles are more commonly used to haul goods, so we often adjust cargo compartments and fuel-tank capacity of our products," Zhang said.
Such demand has helped drive the growth of Yanshi's motor tricycle industry. The district is home to 15 complete-vehicle manufacturers and more than 270 supporting parts companies, employing about 12,000 people and accounting for more than one-third of China's motor tricycle production capacity, according to local authorities.
Behind the customized service is a "half-hour parts supply circle," with most components -- except engines, tires, carburetors and lighting equipment -- sourced locally, said Ji Xianghui, head of the district's industry, information technology and commerce bureau.
In 2025, Yanshi produced and sold about 300,000 motor tricycles, including 98,000 exported vehicles, Ji said. In the first half of 2026, another 55,000 complete vehicles were exported, with the annual figure expected to reach 110,000, he added.
Customized products, however, are only part of the story behind the growing popularity of Chinese-made three-wheelers overseas.
In Fengxian County in east China's Jiangsu Province, another major production hub with about 1,400 related manufacturers, electric tricycles are winning over African consumers with a different combination of strengths: lower operating costs and greater versatility.
Meizida, an electric tricycle maker based in Fengxian, began selling its products in Cape Verde through distributors in 2020. Annual shipments have since grown from one or two containers to about five, with annual sales exceeding 200 vehicles, according to the company.
Compared with fuel-powered vehicles, the tricycles offer lower energy costs, more stable performance and easier maintenance, said Yu Baishun, the company's general manager. Compared with ordinary motorcycles, they also offer greater carrying capacity, he added.
The products have proved particularly suitable for small and micro businesses in Africa, where a single vehicle can be used to haul goods, commute or even serve as a mobile stall, Yu said.
In the first five months of 2026, electric tricycle exports from Fengxian reached 390 million yuan (about 57.9 million U.S. dollars), up 99.3 percent year on year, according to local statistics.
Together, the experiences of Yanshi and Fengxian show how different strengths of Chinese manufacturing are finding their way into overseas markets -- from flexible customization and efficient supply chains, to versatile electric models.
For these manufacturers, however, exporting vehicles is only the first step in their overseas expansion.
In Yanshi, manufacturers are partnering with overseas companies to establish warehouses and after-sales service outlets, developing a model that combines order-based exports with joint after-sales support.
Other tricycle producers are establishing production bases and direct-sales stores in several countries, building localized production and sales networks across Africa and South America.
Such moves reflect a broader shift in China's manufacturing exports. China's well-coordinated and large-scale supply chains allow companies to shorten the cycle from design and production to restocking and logistics, enabling faster and more flexible product development and iteration, said Li Kai, an associate professor at Xiamen University's School of Economics.
"For overseas consumers, that means access to more up-to-date, reliable products and services at competitive prices," he said.
The shift is in line with China's efforts to promote higher-quality foreign trade and support sustainable economic growth. The outline of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for promoting trade innovation, improving the quality and efficiency of foreign trade, and expanding market diversification.
Yet the story of Chinese motor tricycles overseas goes beyond trade figures.
In the comment sections of buyer review videos on YouTube and other social media platforms, tricycle users from different parts of the world are sharing their experiences and memories of the vehicles.
"These small vehicles are everywhere where we live... When I was a little boy, my grandfather often rode one to take me to school," one viewer using a Chinese-language username commented.
"That's great for a large property and gardening, and for your kids learning how to drive too. Safer to learn on that than a tractor," another viewer replied.
"By choosing our products, customers are also finding connections with our everyday lives," Ji said.
In that sense, these humble three-wheelers offer a more down-to-earth glimpse of the country, beyond the image of the "world's factory" or technology giants' hub -- a place where innovation takes root in ordinary people's daily lives. ■

An Istanbul court ordered the closure of the website and social media accounts of T24, a leading independent digital news website, citing its “LGBT propaganda,” authorities announced on Sept. 30.
The prosecution cited the publication of “118 reports deemed to constitute LGBT propaganda” over the past year as the grounds for the decision.
The decision was made as part of the “My Family is Safe” operation, it said.
The operation launched on Sept. 13 and targeted LGBT community, activists and some venues.
Access to the social media accounts of organizations, think tanks and university student clubs active in the field of LGBT rights was also blocked, with warrants issued for 162 people.
In its ruling, the court justified the move on grounds T24 published “content aimed at weakening the Turkish family structure.”
In a report published on its website, T24 said the shutdown order, imposed through an access-blocking measure, was formally notified to the outlet by the Cyber Security Directorate via email in the evening on Sept. 30.
The outlet, which is headquartered in Istanbul with another office in the capital Ankara and a staff of 40, also said that a social media campaign had been launched against it.
The closure drew condemnation from a dozen Turkish journalists’ associations and the main opposition New Party.
İts leader Özgür Özel denounced the move as “repression.”
The 12 Turkish journalists’ associations called for reversion of the decision.
Justice Minister Akın Gürlek earlier said the “My Family is Safe” operation was launched as part of the government’s “Decade of the Family” initiative which is aimed at “protecting our children, the institution of the family and social order.”

Swiss glaciers lose over 5 pct of ice in "devastating" year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:26:17 CST
17:26:17 KST

GENEVA, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- Glaciers in the Swiss Alps suffered a "devastating" year due to intense heat and low snowfall, with their volume shrinking by more than 5 percent, experts said Thursday.
The decline was the second-biggest annual loss since 1950, according to Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland. "Intense heatwaves from May to September, combined with a winter with little snow, led to another devastating year for the glaciers."
It added that the freezing level rose above 4,000 meters on a record 76 days during these months, more than twice the average, and that by September, no snow remained even at 3,500 meters above sea level.
"Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions," the organization said.
Switzerland's glacier ice volume has fallen by almost 20 percent over the past five years, it said.
Between July and September, the glaciers lost around 2,200 billion liters of water in total, more than four times the annual drinking water consumption of all Swiss households. ■

====================================================================================================

Casio’s Crystal G-Shock Is the Most Expensive Ever Made
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:25:59 UTC
17:25:59 KST

At Madison Square Garden in New York City on November 9, 2017, at the G-Shock 35th Anniversary Celebration, G-Shock creator Kikuo Ibe showed off three sapphire-crystal prototype watches: one clear, one ruby, and one sapphire blue. Because machining sapphire was so difficult at the time, each watch took over a month to produce.
These were built with, for the time, high-end Casio features such as Tough Solar power and Multiband 6 radio-controlled timekeeping—but as they didn’t meet the G-Shock shock-resistance standards, the trio was never intended for sale. They were primarily a symbol of innovation for the Japanese brand, which started in 1983 specializing in super-tough performance timepieces.
Now, nine years later, in what Casio is calling the culmination of an “eight-year project” (so presumably the ball started rolling soon after the excited reception Ibe’s crystal concepts got on stage at MSG), G-Shock is launching a three-watch collection using blue sapphire as an expression of what happens when G-Shock toughness meets Japanese engineering. The flagship model, and by far the most expensive, is the $80,000 MRG-D5000, the first-ever retail G-Shock with an outer case and bezel hewn entirely from blue sapphire crystal.
The collection is called the “Blue Rose Project” because the blue rose is viewed as a symbol of making the impossible possible since it doesn’t exist in nature. It sees the super-expensive MRG-D5000 released alongside the $9,500 MRG-B5000SA-2, and the GMW-B5000SB-1A for $850.
Only 20 of the $80,000 MRG-D5000 full-sapphire G-Shocks will be made, putting these rugged “luxury” timepieces somewhat implausibly in the same price bracket as a Patek Philippe or Porsche Macan. This is quite the flex from a company that also sells its watches for less than $90.
The 2017 concept watches required metal bracing to hold the crystal sections together, which is partly why they couldn’t pass G-Shock’s rigorous toughness tests. The new MRG-D5000, however, is a fully functional G-Shock, taking construction lessons from the MR-G engineering team who found that dividing the outer case into multiple interacting components could disperse impact more effectively than a conventional single-piece construction.
G-Shock fans will have already seen this technique employed in the titanium MRG-B5000 from 2022, but this “Multi-Guard Structure” has now been reengineered specifically for sapphire crystal, with Casio claiming the construction takes inspiration from traditional Japanese timber-frame techniques, using interlocking pieces rather than placing stress around screw holes or other details that could result in cracking.
While the MRG-D5000’s bezel and outer case are entirely machined from blue sapphire crystal ingots grown over several months, sadly—unlike the 2017 concepts—the strap isn’t matching sapphire but instead a rubber strap that repeats the brick pattern seen on the watch face in raised detail. To round off the luxe makeover, the MRG-D5000’s MR-G mark, “Shock Resist,” and other lettering on the face are in 24-carat gold.
The G-Shock development team responsible for the new collection tells WIRED the fundamental challenge was building a “near-unbreakable” watch using an inherently brittle material. Making watch cases from sapphire is not new in the high-end watch world, and many distinguished makers, including Richard Mille and Hublot, have released pieces made of the crystal.
To make the sapphire case work for a G-Shock, however, Casio had to develop a brand-new, dedicated shock-resistant structure, with the Multi-Guard construction using virtually invisible seams, alongside a completely screwless assembly method to hit the required shock performance. To do this, the outer case assembly required the development of completely new, dedicated jigs and fixtures, a process apparently so demanding that only one person at Yamagata Casio (the primary “mother factory” for Casio) can currently perform it.
All three new watches, along with the proper G-Shock resistance to knocks and drops, are water-resistant to 200 meters, solar-powered, and feature radio-controlled timekeeping, world time, stopwatch, countdown timer, five daily alarms, and a full-auto LED backlight.
If the $80K G-Shock is too steep an investment, the MRG-B5000SA-2 with two two-carat facet-cut blue sapphires and a grade-5 titanium exterior is limited to 500 pieces. The cheapest GMW-B5000SB-1A2 marries a full-metal black exterior with four round brilliant-cut blue sapphires.

U.S. Navy buys more 30mm guns to shoot down drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:25:56 UTC
17:25:56 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded MSI Defence Systems US a $197 million sole-source contract for MK88 MOD4 30 mm gun mounts and MK48 MOD2 sights.
- Most of the work will be done in Norfolk, England, with deliveries due by January 2031.
The U.S. Navy has awarded British-owned MSI Defence Systems a $197 million contract for 30mm deck gun mounts and the electro-optical sights that aim them, the weapons the service is fitting to its warships to shoot down small drones and fast attack boats.
The firm-fixed-price contract, issued by Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division in Maryland, covers MK88 MOD4 gun mounts, MK48 MOD2 electro-optical sights, related hardware and spares. The Department of War did not say how many systems it buys. Deliveries are due to finish by January 2031.
Together with an operator console, the gun mount and sight make up the MK 38 MOD 4 gun weapon system, which replaces the 25 mm MK 38 MOD 3 on U.S. Navy ships. The U.S. Navy has said the older system fell short of its requirements for countering drones, and the new version adds a larger 30 mm MK44 Bushmaster II cannon, with an optional coaxial .50-caliber machine gun. The mount holds 400 rounds in two separate ammunition bins, letting the crew switch between ammunition types.
Unlike earlier versions, the MOD 4 places its camera sight away from the gun rather than on the mount itself, so the system can track a target independently and pass aiming data to the gun. The design is based on MSI’s Seahawk DS30M A2 mount, a family of guns already used by the Royal Navy and other fleets.
The destroyer USS Mustin (DDG 89) became the first U.S. Navy warship to receive the system, with two mounts installed during a maintenance period in San Diego, Naval News reported in April 2024. The U.S. Navy plans to replace the 25 mm guns on its Arleigh Burke-class destroyers with the new system, and the U.S. Coast Guard also uses it.
The new contract is far larger than earlier orders. MSI received about $23.5 million in September 2023 for 15 gun mounts in low-rate production and about $34.5 million in late 2025 for 18 more, along with separate deals for the sight system. The company first delivered eight prototype systems for testing.
The U.S. Navy awarded the contract without competition under a legal exception for production that follows prototypes successfully completed under an other transaction agreement, a faster contracting route used for experimental work.
Most of the work, 73%, will take place at MSI’s facilities in Norfolk, England, with 19% at its U.S. subsidiary in Rock Hill, South Carolina, and the rest in Bozeman, Montana, and Eagleville, Pennsylvania. MSI Defence Systems is part of British company MS International.
The U.S. Navy obligated about $61.3 million at the time of award, drawing on weapons procurement and shipbuilding funds from fiscal 2023 through 2026, including money from accounts used to build new ships.

Immigration judge rules US can deport activist Salah Sarsour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:25:23 UTC
17:25:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Immigration judge rules US can deport activist and community leader Salah Sarsour
An immigration judge ruled that the US government can deport Palestinian American Salah Sarsour, who is the president of Wisconsin's largest mosque and a US permanent resident, under a Cold War-era law.
Sarsour, who grew up in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was taken by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency in late March and released in mid-June after a federal judge said he had raised a substantial free speech retaliation claim that would render his detention unlawful.
Chicago Immigration Court Judge Jayme Salinardi sided late on Tuesday with the government's argument that Sarsour posed a security and foreign policy threat under the Cold War-era Immigration and Nationality Act, while rejecting the government's allegation that he lied on his green card application.
The US Department of Homeland Security welcomed the ruling, saying the judge "sustained multiple grounds of removability" in the case.
Sarsour said his legal team will appeal the ruling, which he called "deeply disappointing."
"I will not stop standing up for what's right and for justice in Palestine," he said in a statement. Sarsour cannot be deported until all legal avenues available to him are exhausted. He says his life will be at risk if deported to the occupied West Bank.
Islamic Society of Milwaukee, Wisconsin's largest mosque, says Sarsour has lived in the US for over three decades.
The mosque has said Sarsour was "being targeted on the basis of his Palestinian and Muslim background, and his advocacy for Palestinian rights."
He has type 2 diabetes and lost more than 30 pounds in ICE detention, his legal team said.
Sarsour has no criminal record in the US and was convicted as a teenager in Israeli military court before he came to the United States, which the Trump administration noted to cast him as a threat. Sarsour says the government has known that information for decades.
Israeli rights group B'Tselem says military courts in the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians are tried for alleged crimes, have a 96% conviction rate and a history of extracting confessions through torture.
Sarsour denies committing crimes and says he was tortured and coerced into past confessions.
"This immigration proceeding has made it clear that I am being unfairly targeted by this administration for my advocacy on Palestinian human rights," he said in a public statement last month about the situation..
"I put my trust in God and my legal team to navigate this attack on me and the life I have built in America, and that I can continue to be with my family in Wisconsin as I have for the past three decades," he added.
Trump has attempted to deport foreign pro-Palestinian protesters, threatened funding freezes for universities where protests were held, enforced a social media screening of immigrants and sanctioned critics of Israel's genocide of the Palestinian people.

October 1, 2026
The 41-year-old forward left the Portugal camp on Wednesday after coach Jorge Jesus had told reporters at the Matchday-1 press conference that Cristiano Ronaldo would not feature in the starting lineup against Denmark in the Nations League.
The move comes amid reports of a rift between the Al-Nassr player and coach, something that Jesus denied.
The 72-year-old coach conceded that his captain had been disappointed to remain on the bench in Portugal's win over Norway on Sunday, but he insisted that there had been "no incident whatsoever."
Ronaldo didn't explain why he had taken the decision, but in an Instagram post he said that "in time" he would "tell the Portuguese people the truth about the reasons" behind his departure.
"Following the national team coach's news conference, and after a conversation with the president of the Portuguese football federation, I decided to leave the national team's training camp," he said, adding that he had always "dedicated" himself to the national team.
"Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates, without exception."
For its part, the Portuguese federation (FPF) confirmed that the five-time Ballon d'Or winner had left the camp and that the team's preparations for Thursday's match in Copenhagen would continue without him.
"The entire delegation remains fully focused on the national team's upcoming fixtures and on achieving our goals," it said.
It wasn't immediately clear whether Ronaldo's departure would extend beyond the current international break.
In Wednesday's press conference, Jesus had said that Ronaldo would start on the bench and may be brought on as a sub.
"I don't know what's going to happen in the game," the coach said.
"If we need him to play, he'll play. If not, he won't."
Limited action
Ronaldo started Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales last Thursday but was substituted in the 67th minute. He was on the bench but saw no action in Sunday's 2-1 win over Norway in Oslo. Portugal face Norway again at home this coming Sunday.
Portugal leads Group A4 of the Nations League with six points from two matches, three points more than Denmark and Norway.
Wednesday's news comes with Ronaldo's long-time rival Lionel Messi set to play his last match for Argentina next week. Earlier this year, Ronaldo, who is the all-time top goal scorer in men's competitive matches (979), had said recently that this Saudi Pro League season is likely to be the last of his professional career.
Earlier this year, he had said the 2026 World Cup would be his last but did not say exactly when he would retire from international football.

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike survives 2 lethal doses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:25:00 UTC
17:25:00 KST

A Tennessee woman convicted of murder survived two lethal injection doses and was hospitalized Thursday, prompting state officials to halt all executions this year after a second botched procedure in months.
Hours earlier Wednesday, the Supreme Court cleared the way for Christa Pike, 50, to become the first woman executed in the southern U.S. state of Tennessee in 200 years, but the attempt failed.
"This event is the worst we've seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said. "There is no precedent."
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol," adding Pike was taken to an "off-site medical facility."
Her attorneys said she was transported to a nearby hospital, adding they had not been informed of her condition.
"Tonight the state of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution," the attorneys said in a statement.
Tennessee halted the execution by lethal injection of Tony Carruthers in May after medical staff could not tap a vein.
Gov. Bill Lee called for a "comprehensive, third-party review" after Pike's failed execution.
"The remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year," Lee said, apparently referencing the execution of convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton scheduled for Dec. 3.
Pike was scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. (3 p.m. GMT) at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, where witnesses including journalists were present for the injections.
Kim Chandler, a media witness for The Associated Press, told CBS News, "Pike appeared notably awake as the execution began."
After the blinds of the execution chamber closed for the final time, Pike "could be heard loudly snoring, clearly very alive in the chamber until media witnesses were told to leave the area," Chandler said.
During a livestream, an ambulance with its lights flashing left the site of the execution. It was unclear whether it was transporting Pike.
The execution procedure went ahead hours after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled it could proceed, with liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissenting.
"The Court's decision ... unnecessarily prevents that lower court from giving Pike's claim due consideration," the dissenting justices wrote.
"Worse, the Court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the state to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts."
The case has sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer's body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Pike's lawyers argued she should be granted clemency because of her young age and mental health issues at the time of the killing.
"She was 18 when she committed her crime and she was deeply mentally ill," they wrote in a clemency petition to Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee, who said he would not intervene.
The U.S. Supreme Court rejected Tuesday an application for a stay of execution, which argued Pike's history as a victim of sexual assault, post-traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant a lethal injection would cause "needless suffering."
Independent United Nations human rights experts have urged the U.S. government and Tennessee authorities to "immediately halt" the execution and commute her death sentence.
In the U.S., only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
