Explosions heard in Ethiopia's capital as war waged in north
Oct 1 - Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital Addis Ababa, three diplomatic sources said on Thursday, adding to anxiety about the possible spread of renewed conflict in the country's north.
A source linked to the opposition alliance fighting government forces in northern Ethiopia since last week said the alliance had carried out several drone strikes in Addis Ababa, including some targeting the military's headquarters.
Reuters could not independently verify the claim and there was no damage visible near the military base, witnesses said.
The sources, who gave scant details of the blasts, spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter.
If confirmed, it would be the first known drone attack by anti-government forces on the Ethiopian capital, which is hundreds of kilometres from the front lines in the northern regions of Tigray, Amhara and Afar.
Spokespeople for Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's office, the federal government and the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
INTELLIGENCE SERVICE BANS DRONE FLIGHTS OVER CAPITAL
Last week's clashes were the biggest escalation in Ethiopia since the end of a 2020-2022 civil war.
The national intelligence service had announced on Wednesday that it was banning drones over Addis Ababa and its surroundings for security reasons.
Opposition forces had not previously been known to use armed drones but there is growing evidence they may possess some capability.
On Tuesday, a pro-government militia said it had captured drone frames and batteries from forces linked to the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), one of the alliance's main members.
Reuters could not independently verify that.
Edward Bach, Senior Africa Analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said the opposition's ability to strike Addis Ababa would be "a political game-changer," undermining any government narrative that the capital is unaffected by the war and narrowing a key tactical advantage for federal forces, their aerial superiority.
TENS OF THOUSANDS DISPLACED BY FIGHTING
Last week's outbreak of fighting shattered a four-year-old peace deal between the TPLF and the federal government, whose previous two-year civil war killed hundreds of thousands.
This time, the TPLF has formed an alliance with six other armed groups aiming to overthrow Abiy's government.
Federal forces have been advancing in southern Tigray, edging closer to the regional capital Mekelle, while the opposition alliance has captured towns in neighbouring Afar.
The pro-government Tigray Peace Forces militia said on Wednesday that it had captured the Tigrayan town of Korem, about 100 km (62 miles) south of Mekelle, alongside the Ethiopian military.
In Afar, where the TPLF captured several towns in the early days of the new conflict, fighting has forced tens of thousands of people to flee their homes, Valerie Browning, a founder of the Afar Pastoralist Development Association, told Reuters.
An Afari government official told Reuters on Thursday that federal and regional forces had recaptured the towns of Erebti and Abaala, near the border with Tigray.
Reuters could not independently confirm battlefield reports.
FEARS OF REGIONAL DESTABILIZATION
The conflict could further destabilize the wider Horn of Africa region, already unsettled by Sudan's civil war, frictions over Red Sea access between Ethiopia and neighbouring Eritrea, and spillover from Middle East conflicts.
Ethiopia's government has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting the opposition alliance. All three deny that.
Afar's chief administrator Haji Awol Arba went a step further earlier this week, telling Al Jazeera that Eritrean soldiers had crossed into Afar to join the alliance's offensive.
Eritrea's information minister did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In the previous civil war, Eritrea fought in support of Ethiopia's federal government against the TPLF. But relations between the two historical rivals soured after the war, with Asmara viewing Abiy's repeated assertions that landlocked Ethiopia has a right to sea access as an implicit threat.
Abiy has said Ethiopia intends to secure sea access through peaceful means. REUTERS

Gimmick or recipe for success? Japan's convenience stores test AI flavours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01

17:07:13 KST

Japanese convenience store chains are turning to AI for dessert ideas. Some are unexpected mashups.
A pickle-flavoured lemon tart might seem an unlikely dessert, but Japanese convenience store chains are betting that artificial intelligence (AI) can help them find combinations customers never knew they wanted.
Popular convenience store chains FamilyMart and Lawson are using the technology to develop new food products, looking for ideas that go beyond familiar flavours.
The experiments come amid wider concerns about AI replacing workers and increasingly powerful systems slipping beyond human control.
Here, the technology’s role is more modest — suggesting what might go into your next snack.
AI supplied the ideas, but humans still had to turn them into something worth eating. Companies used the technology mainly for brainstorming, with human specialists involved in developing the final products.
FamilyMart fed sales data into AI to help develop a French-style canelé made with dough containing sweet potato purée and topped with caramel sauce. The chain said it wanted to create something new but likely to sell.
In July, the chain test-launched its first AI experiment with a biscuit sandwich filled with thick milk cream.
Rival chain Lawson took a different approach, asking AI for unexpected combinations without feeding it past sales figures or market data to generate ideas “unconstrained by existing ways of thinking or market trends," according to a statement from the company.
One suggestion was to pair lemon tart with pickles.
For Shingo Shiina, a 64-year-old who works in architecture, the combination came as a surprise.
“I was like ‘huh’ at first, but it actually goes pretty well, doesn’t it? The pickles. I’m surprised,” he said after tasting the tart.
“It’s a strange flavour, but it’s tasty. It really is delicious.”
Shiina was also impressed by the idea itself.
“You’d probably never come up with this, right? Pickles and this. I don’t think a human would ever think of that. That’s AI for you,” he said.
Lawson’s other AI-inspired products include a bread roll filled with red bean paste, margarine and yoghurt cream, and a Japanese-style salad presented like a parfait.
The pickle-flavoured lemon tart is being launched in Tokyo and surrounding regions in September, according to Lawson.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Ukraine Appeals to OSCE as Civilians Face Starvation in Temporarily Russian-Occupied Oleshky
Ukraine has initiated urgent consideration of the humanitarian crisis in temporarily Russian-occupied Oleshky at the OSCE Permanent Council, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X on September 30.
The issue, titled “On the catastrophic humanitarian situation in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky, temporarily occupied by the Russian Federation,” is expected to be addressed on October 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Oleshky, a city on the left bank of the Dnipro in Ukraine’s Kherson region, has been under Russian occupation since February 2022
The humanitarian situation in Oleshky has deteriorated sharply in recent weeks. Ukrainian officials have reported severe shortages of food, medicine, clean water, electricity, and medical care, while evacuation remains extremely dangerous because of mines and Russian military activity.
Sybiha stated that Ukraine’s delegation would brief participating states on conditions created by Russian occupation authorities.
“The delegation of Ukraine will inform participating States about the appalling situation created by the Russian occupation authorities, who are holding civilians, including children, hostage,” Sybiha wrote. “This is nothing less than a man-made humanitarian disaster.”
He added that Ukraine would continue challenging Russian narratives and informing international partners about conditions in the city.
“The situation in Oleshky is critical and requires urgent action by the international community,” Sybiha wrote. “I call on the Swiss OSCE Chairmanship and all participating States to condemn the aggressor and exert the strongest possible pressure on Russia.”
Sybiha also called for immediate humanitarian access to the occupied city.
“Oleshky needs urgent humanitarian relief. Russia must be compelled to allow it immediately,” he wrote.
Days earlier, the UN reported that Russia had still not guaranteed safe humanitarian access to Oleshky and nearby Hola Prystan, despite requests from Ukrainian authorities.
UN Humanitarian Coordinator Matthias Schmale noted that civilians were facing food and medicine shortages and that occupying forces are required under international law to facilitate humanitarian assistance.

Taiwan ranks 5th in net financial assets per capita
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:06:11 UTC
17:06:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan ranked fifth globally in net financial assets per capita in 2025 at NT$5.94 million (US$180,000), unchanged from a year earlier, according to a report by Allianz Research.
The report, which covers household balance sheets in nearly 60 countries, said global financial assets rose 8.6% to a record NT$9.7 quadrillion last year, per CNA. It said asset ownership is becoming important in determining who benefits from wealth creation amid market gains and the rise of AI.
Global financial assets are expected to grow another 9% this year, although slower economic growth, persistent inflation, geopolitical fragmentation, and high government debt could put pressure on asset returns over the medium term, according to the report.
Total household financial assets rose 8.7% to NT$162.69 trillion at the end of 2025, down from 9.3% growth in 2024 but above the global average of 8.6%, per UDN. The increase was below the 9.8% average for other Asian markets covered by the report, excluding Japan and China.
Securities recorded the strongest growth in 2025, rising 17.7% from a year earlier, compared with increases of 4.9% for deposits and 2.4% for insurance and pension funds. Securities accounted for 34.9% of household asset allocation, above the Asian average of 30.8% but below the global average of 46.9%.
After adjusting for inflation, financial assets grew 6.9% in real terms in 2025, roughly matching 7% growth in 2024. Since 2019, they have risen 41.5% in real terms, above the Asian average of 39.6% and the global average of 22.9%.

ASE increases influence of AI in factory operations through university partnerships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:05:52 UTC
17:05:52 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — ASE Technology Holding Co. is increasing the influence of AI in its factories through academic partnerships, turning research into tools for its advanced semiconductor packaging and testing lines.
The company has worked with six universities: National Central University, National Cheng Kung University, National Sun Yat-sen University, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, National Tsing Hua University, and National Taiwan University of Science and Technology. Twelve projects cover applications such as generative AI, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and cybersecurity, according to CTEE.
The work is aimed at improving production efficiency and process quality while making operations more resilient to disruptions and climate-related risks. ASE said the broader goal is to shift from addressing problems after they occur to preventing them in advance on its chip packaging lines.
Some of the research has already been turned into AI assistants for factory workers. One tool gathers video, image, and text content from different platforms and automatically produces daily summaries, making it easier to find and review information.
Another helps workers troubleshoot equipment by drawing on a dedicated knowledge base. The assistant is designed to speed up fault identification and reduce repair time.
A third tool checks program code and automatically corrects parts that do not meet required standards. ASE said the rate of code returned for revisions has fallen below 10% since the tool was introduced.
The technology is also changing how ASE manages production. Smart scheduling tools can simulate changes in capacity as orders shift, while real-time equipment monitoring can identify abnormalities within milliseconds and allow workers to make adjustments before they lead to unexpected downtime.
Digital twin technology gives ASE a way to test operations in a virtual environment. The company is using it for production scheduling and automated guided vehicles, helping shorten the time needed to plan and test changes.
AI is also being applied beyond production. AI-powered cameras can issue warnings about potential hazards and track people and vehicles, while AI agents can automate cybersecurity checks for industrial control systems and support recovery when problems are detected.
It is also being used to assess the physical environment of ASE's facilities. The company is analyzing climate-related risks and vulnerabilities at its sites, while airflow simulations in cleanrooms are being used to identify potential ways to reduce energy consumption.
Virtual modeling is another way ASE is working to anticipate problems. The company is combining a 3D simulation platform with AI to build digital models of its facilities. The systems can help detect equipment problems before they occur, monitor product yields in real time, and automate quality inspections.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan deserves a space in the international community, Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) said on Tuesday.

Beijing is linking the resolution with its “one China” principle to block Taiwan’s participation in international organizations, Lin said. “If allowed to stand unchallenged, this distortion will set a dangerous legal precedent and thus a pretext for future military action.”

The world is at a crossroads, Lin said. “Either we act together to defend the rule of law and maintain security, or we stand by while authoritarian states fight the free world, self-determination, and take democracy with them in their downfall.”
“The free world needs Taiwan. And a stronger UN needs Taiwan's real participation,” Lin added.

Taiwan ranks 2nd in global digital hardware manufacturing capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:05:24 UTC
17:05:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan ranked second globally in digital hardware manufacturing capacity in 2024-2025, accounting for 10.2% of the total, according to Visual Capitalist.
The Canadian data visualization media outlet cited an analysis by energy think tank Ember based on data from industry research organizations, including SEMI, TrendForce, the IEA, BloombergNEF, and other research firms. The ranking covers manufacturing capacity for semiconductors, displays, printed circuit boards, smartphones, computers, and other related electronic products.
China ranked first, accounting for 58.8% of the global digital hardware manufacturing capacity, nearly six times Taiwan’s share and more than all other economies in the analysis combined. South Korea ranked third with 6.7% of global capacity, followed by Japan at 4.8%, meaning the four East Asian economies together accounted for 80.5% of the total.
Taiwan, South Korea, and Japan together accounted for 21.7% of global digital hardware manufacturing capacity. Two of the five major companies Visual Capitalist highlighted as operating in the region are TSMC and Foxconn.
Visual Capitalist said, “Taiwan is particularly important in semiconductor fabrication and electronics assembly,” while South Korea has substantial chip and display production capacity. Japan is a major producer of electronic products, components, and technologies that support the broader hardware supply chain.
Outside the top four, India ranked fifth with 3.8% of global capacity, narrowly ahead of Vietnam at 3.6%. The US ranked seventh at 2.9%, followed by Thailand at 1.3% and Mexico at 1.2%, while Germany and Singapore tied at 0.7% each.
The figures highlight the distinction between where technology companies are headquartered and where their products are manufactured, according to Visual Capitalist. Although the US is home to many leading technology companies and chip-design firms, the manufacturing capacity behind global electronics supply chains remains concentrated in Asia.

Burnham rejects Tory/Reform UK claims his call for debate on all options for closer EU relations betrays byelection pledge
Andrew Sparrow
Yesterday Andy Burnham did a round of sit-down interviews with broadcast political editors. They were all embargoed until 5pm, which is when most Westminster journalists were on their way home after the Labour conference in Liverpool, and that meant they did not get as much pick-up as they might have done normally.
Here are some of the most interesting news lines worth recording.
Burnham rejected claims that taxes would have to go up to fund his plan for a National Care Service. On Sunday, in his interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Burnham strongly implied tax rises would be needed. But when Sky’s Beth Rigby asked Burnham if he would have to raise taxes to implement this, Burnham replied:
No, because there’s a different way of doing it. If you delay the date of introduction and you introduce a National Care Service progressively, but you could do it in a different way … You could do it earlier. So Louise Casey, Baroness Casey is looking at all of these issues.
Burnham also said that in the long run the savings from his changes to the pensions triple lock – £15bn by 2040 – would be enough to fund his plans. But he accepted that money would not be released soon.
Burnham claimed Brexit had led to more immigrants to the UK wanting to settle permanently. Speaking to GB News, he said:
One thing that I want to convey here is Brexit has changed the nature of immigration to this country because in the past, when we were in the European Union … what we had was a more revolving door form of migration, where people would come here in their younger years. Many people did from Eastern Europe … They’d maybe spend you know a few years here in their mid to late 20s, and then go home and start a family, and that was a very common form of immigration.
Now, immigration is more likely to be a permanent settlement, where people are coming on a visa to work here. And then we saw obviously the Boris wave and the changes that came through in that in that period. So it’s changed the nature of immigration.
Burnham rejected claims that having a debate on electoral reform was divisive. He told Sky News: “That isn’t divisive because most of the political parties have indicated support for that policy.”
Burnham rejected claims that, by opening a debate on how to change the UK’s relationship with the EU, he was going back on a promise he made during the Makerfield byelection that he would not propose rejoining. This is a claim made by the Tories and by Nigel Farage. (See 11.02am.) On Channel 4 News, Burnham insisted that he was not proposing to reverse Brexit; he was just opening a debate. And on ITV News he said it would not be credible to publish a 10-year plan for Britain, as he plans to do later this year, without considering the UK’s relationship with the EU.
Burnham suggested the UK could rejoin the EU without having to hold another referendum. When Gary Gibbon from Channel 4 News asked if another referendum would be needed for Britain to join, or if a government would have the authority to do that just based on a manifesto promise, Burnham told him he was “jumping the gun”. But when Gibbon asked if he was ruling out the idea that a manifesto promise might be enough, making a referendum unnecessary, Burnham replied:
I wouldn’t rule anything out at this moment in time because whatever happens has to have the full authority of the country and a majority support for it.
Speaking to the BBC, Burnham said that he wanted to have a “calm discussion about what broadly are our options here” and then see if there is” a centre of gravity or a consensus around one of them”.
Burnham hinted that he might not wait until 2029 before holding the next election. At the end of last week, to quash speculation about an early election, Burnham explicitly told an interviewer it would be in 2029. But when Sky’s Beth Rigby asked him to confirm that he would not hold an election until 2029, he replied:
I’m not going to call an early general election, no. I’m not. I’m happy to make that absolutely clear.
An election in 2028 would not count as an early election. Arguably, one in 2027 would not count as early either.
My colleague Taz Ali is taking over the blog now. I will be back in the afternoon.

Foreign Office announces fresh sanctions against Russian 'propagandists and torturers'
The Foreign Office has announced new sanctions against Russia. It says the 31 measures include “sanctioning LNG shadow fleet vessels, Kremlin disinformation networks and perpetrators of civilian torture and child indoctrination”.
In the news release about the announcement, the Foreign Office says:
Following sham elections in temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine earlier this month, the UK is now taking firm action against people and entities found to have undermined Ukraine’s territorial integrity through human rights abuses.
They include eight people involved in the arbitrary detention, torture and ill-treatment of Ukrainian civilians. These abuses are part of a wider system of repression in Russia’s occupied territories, where enforced disappearance and denial of justice have also been used against Ukrainian civilians.
A further seven individuals are being targeted for their role in the indoctrination and militarisation of Ukrainian children, including those deported by the Russian authorities. To date, an estimated 6,000 Ukrainian children have been forcibly relocated to a network of heinous so-called “re-education” camps.
Annual homelessness deaths in England and Wales have almost doubled over past decade, ONS says
The Office for National Statistics has published a report today saying there were an estimated 974 deaths of people experiencing homelessness in England and Wales last year. That is almost exactly the same as the estimated figure for last year, but 77% higher than the figure for 2013.
Prisoners freed early in England and Wales risk living on the streets, say probation officers
Hundreds of prisoners are due to be released early from jail on Thursday amid warnings that many will have nowhere to live and the probation system will struggle to monitor them, Rajeev Syal reports.
Tories suggest they would cut benefits for young people if they're living at home and parents can support them
The Conservatives have also hinted that they might cut the benefits available to young people if they are living at home and their parents can support them. They are not giving many details, but this is potentially quite a big change to the way the benefits system works. At the moment young people’s eligibility for benefits depends on their own earnings and assets; if their parents can afford to subsidise them, that is not taken into account.
The Conservative party says:
The Get to Work Allowance will also put greater emphasis on family responsibility. We will review the role of family support for young adults living at home. A university student’s access to financial support can depend on their parents’ circumstances, yet the rules for young adults claiming benefits work differently. So we will look again at how parents’ earnings and savings are treated, including where parents themselves claim universal credit. Young people without parental support, including those who are estranged, will continue to have a safety net.
What Tories say about conditions that would apply to people getting their proposed Get to Work Allowance
Here are more details from the Conservative party’s news release about the conditions that would apply to their proposed Get to Work Allowance. It says:
For the first time ever, work requirements and support will kick in immediately, as soon as a young person makes a benefits claim. Each young person will also be assigned an individual Get to Work Manager whose job it will be to make sure they get into work.
Each young person will need to complete assigned work activities to get their Get to Work Allowance each week. Activities will depend on the young person’s qualifications, experience and motivation. For instance:
-Daily attendance at a local job centre, on work experience placements, training/work readiness courses or community work schemes set up with local councils;
-Participation in job search and application workshops, and interview preparation sessions;
-Group sessions to develop the communication skills, teamwork and behaviours that employers tell us are so often missing in young job applicants.
Those who complete the Get to Work programme successfully will receive a ‘Ready for Work’ Award recording the skills they have demonstrated. After six months on Get to Work, young people still seeking to claim universal credit but not working will drop down to the Subsistence Allowance, worth 70% of their previous claim, in line with the policies announced by the Conservatives last week. This will incentivise young people to take work when they are offered it.
The party’s news release does not say what the Get to Work Allowance would be worth, or anything about the potential costs or savings from the scheme.
Badenoch proposes welfare reform that would stop many jobless under-25s getting universal credit
Good morning. The Conservatives start their conference at the weekend and Kemi Badenoch is kicking off proceedings by announcing a significant plan for welfare reform – stopping many under-25s from being able to claim universal credit, the main unemployment benefit.
Instead, they would get a new Get to Work Allowance – which would be subject to conditions from day one intended to help people find work. If after six months they are still out of work, they would go on to a new benefit, a Subsistence Allowance, worth just 70% of their previous claims.
The plans don’t relate to disability benefits, because they would only apply to people able to work.
It’s unfair to the people who get up and go to work, having others earn more than them for not working. Even families on benefits know that the system is out of control. But no one wants to be the one to get off the treadmill first. We need to force that. Government has to do that.
The Tories are describing this as a “tough love” approach designed to deal with the problem of around one million young people being Neets (not in employment, education or training). Tim Shipman, who interviewed Badenoch for the Spectator, has a more colourful description. “This is the nanny state with menaces; Mary Poppins with an umbrella gun,” he says.
And here is the Conservative party’s explanation of its plans from its news release.
The Conservatives will require all 18-24 year olds who attempt to claim universal credit and who have not previously worked for a continuous period of 6 months to participate in a Get to Work scheme in exchange for welfare.Participants will receive a new ‘Get to Work Allowance’ which is contingent on their participation in the scheme. To be exempt from these requirements 18-24 year olds will have to demonstrate that they have previously been in continuous employment for a period of 6 months or more, for a minimum of 16 hours a week. Young people on UC who are not subject to work-related requirements, such as for health reasons or due to caring responsibilities, will be exempt.
The programme would last up to six months. Participants could leave earlier if they secure a job, apprenticeship or qualifying education or training place.
For participants in the Get to Work Scheme, the new Get to Work Allowance will replace the universal credit standard allowance.After 6 months, if participants on the scheme have not entered work they will automatically move down to the new Subsistence Allowance announced last week by the Conservatives. This is paid at 70% of the current Standard Allowance and will be pre-loaded onto a Back to Work card that prevents claimants spending on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling. After six months they would continue to be subject to demanding conditions.
We have not heard from Labour yet, and that may be because the party is not sure yet how to respond. Alan Milburn, the former cabinet minister, has finished the final report from his inquiry into Neets and it is due to be published before the budget. He is also expected to propose measures that would impose more conditions on young people getting out-of-work benefits because he also wants to stop people being consigned to a life on benefits. And ministers are expected to adopt his plans. We don’t know the details of the Milburn/government scheme, and it will probably involve more carrot than stick than the Tory one. But there may well be quite a lot of overlap too.
I will post more on the plans, and the Badenoch interview, soon.
Parliament is not sitting, and there is not much in the Westminster diary. But Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, does have a rally at 2pm this afternoon where he will respond to Andy Burnham’s conference speech..

Turkish intelligence captures suspect in 2013 Reyhanli terror attack

Merve Berker
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Türkiye's National Intelligence Organization (MIT) captured Omer al-Khatib, one of the Syrian suspects in the 2013 terror attack in Reyhanli that killed 53 people, as he was preparing to flee to Europe by sea, security sources said on Thursday.
According to the sources, al-Khatib, who was wanted under an Interpol Red Notice, was involved in planning and organizing the attack in the Turkish town and coordinated between the perpetrators and intelligence officials affiliated with Bashar al-Assad.
Al-Khatib brought Yusuf Nazik, who was planning operations targeting Türkiye, together with Kifah Melhem in 2013, with details of the attack determined during the meetings.
Al-Khatib and Nazik first entered Türkiye through Hatay in February 2013 before the attack and identified the locations to be targeted. They received approval from Melhem, who was in Latakia, according to the sources.
Before the attack in May 2013, al-Khatib went with Temir Dukanci to the Latakia branch of military intelligence and received materials to be used in the explosive device.
The bomb-laden vehicle was taken to Reyhanli by Dukanci and Nazik and detonated using a remote-controlled explosive device.
Immediately after the attack, al-Khatib took Dukanci and Nazik, who had fled to Syria, to the Latakia branch of military intelligence.
Al-Khatib and others who carried out the attack were financially rewarded by the Bashar al-Assad regime, the sources said.
MIT tracks suspect step by step
MIT began efforts to capture those responsible immediately after the Reyhanli attack and closely monitored al-Khatib's activities in Syria, as it did with other suspects.
MIT captured al-Khatib as he was preparing to flee to Europe by sea and subsequently brought him to Türkiye.
Nazik, one of the perpetrators and planners of the attack, was captured in 2018; Cengiz Sertel in 2024, and Muhammed Dib Korali and Dukanci were captured in 2025.
Maj. Gen. Kifah Melhem in Syria, who gave the order for the Reyhanli attack, was appointed by Bashar al-Assad as head of the National Security Bureau in February 2024.
Melhem is known to have fled abroad following the fall of the Assad regime.

In search of a common voice for Bulgarian culture around the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:02:14 UTC
17:02:14 KST

Author
Krasimir Martinov
News
In search of a common voice for Bulgarian culture around the world
The Association of Bulgarian Cultural Organisations Abroad starts active operation
Thursday 1 October 2026 10:13
Thursday, 1 October 2026, 10:13
Vesela Raytchinova views the exhibition "Around the World with the Glagolitic Alphabet" at the Bulgarian National Radio (BNR) building.
PHOTO Krasimir Martinov
Font size
Bulgarian culture has long transcended geographical borders. It travels with people, carried in language, song, books, dance and celebrations. But when people are scattered across different parts of the world, a question arises: how can individual artists meet and communicate with one another, exchange experience and gain greater visibility, including in their homeland?
The Association of Bulgarian Cultural Organisations Abroad (ABCOA) will seek to provide an answer. The foundations of the association were laid on 29 July 2025 at a constituent assembly held at the Library and Information Centre of the Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad in Sofia. A year later, the association has obtained official legal registration, enabling it to operate as a representative umbrella organisation for Bulgarian cultural organisations abroad. Now the nine-member Management Board faces the task at the heart of its mission: attracting like-minded people from among the vast number of Bulgarian artists and cultural organisations around the world. How will it do so?
To answer this and other questions concerning the organisation's future work, we spoke to the association's chairperson Vesela Raytchinova, herself deeply committed to culture and the creator of the international festival "Bulgarian Soul of the Holy Land" in Israel, which has developed into a meeting place for Bulgarians living in different parts of the world. It was precisely her communication with them that convinced Raychinova of the need for a more lasting creative alliance.
Vesela Raytchinova: We Bulgarians enjoy a very good name in Israel
In an interview with Radio Bulgaria, Vesela Raytchinova says the idea behind the new association is to become a broader platform than the traditional cultural associations.
Vesela Raytchinova
PHOTO Krasimir Martinov
"Besides organisations, we want to attract artists who are not affiliated with any organisation. These are artists who create, but for one reason or another do not have opportunities to perform or exhibit, or who are active but are not sufficiently represented," explains Vesela Raytchinova. "In other words, we want the association to bring together a broad spectrum of organisations and individuals working to preserve Bulgarian spirituality, language and traditions abroad. Thus, creative and cultural associations, as well as various artistic groups and individual artists, writers, visual artists and public figures engaged with Bulgarian culture, can join us. Members of the association may also belong to other organisations, such as the Association of Bulgarian Schools Abroad or the association of folklore ensembles. Around the world there are also literary and writers' societies, poets' clubs, art salons and galleries. All of them can become our members."
The Management Board of the Association of Bulgarian Cultural Organisations Abroad comprises representatives from different countries. The idea is for each member of the leadership to serve, in a sense, as a link to a particular region, making it easier to build a network of contacts with Bulgarian cultural organisations and artists. Vesela Raytchinova describes the process metaphorically as a "beautiful, colourful chain", with each person adding their own bead. Behind the metaphor, however, lies a very practical task: identifying the people, organisations and initiatives that can work together.
Vesela Raytchinova in the studio of Radio Bulgaria
PHOTO Krasimir Martinov
Another objective of the association is to make the cultural activities of Bulgarians living abroad far more visible in Bulgaria itself.
"We will have very frequent gatherings in Bulgaria. In other words, we will work to present the creative work and cultural activities of Bulgarians abroad to people in Bulgaria. Our aim is also to help improve interaction between our artists and organisations working outside the country and the institutions here."
Once the organisational stage in establishing the new association is complete, including the development of an online platform, the creation of a logo and the sending of membership invitations to Bulgarian cultural organisations and individual artists around the world, the expectation is that the organisation will begin actively recruiting members in early November this year.

FlyDubai cockpit incident turns focus to crew-related hijackings
The pilot of the FlyDubai flight is suspected of having stabbed his copilot midflight in an apparent attempt to crash the plane. The incident has turned focus to similar incidents in the past, where deliberate crashes or near crashes have been instigated by on or off-duty crew.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
A pilot on a plane travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv stabbed the other pilot and then apparently tried to crash the aircraft Wednesday before being subdued by passengers and crew.
The Boeing 737 made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, where the unnamed pilot was detained, but not before an abrupt descent prompted Israel to scramble warplanes over concerns of a possible hijacking.
Here are some past examples of plane hijackings and attempted hijackings potentially involving pilots or crew members:
An off-duty Alaska Airlines pilot tried to cut the engines of a Horizon Air jet travelling from Everett, Washington, to San Francisco while riding in an extra seat in the cockpit. The plane was diverted and landed in Portland with more than 80 people. Joseph Emerson told police he was despondent over a friend’s recent death, had taken psychedelic mushrooms and hadn’t slept in days.
A China Eastern Airlines flight from Kunming in southwest China to Guangzhou, near Hong Kong, slammed into a mountain, killing all 132 people aboard. Chinese authorities have yet to release their final investigative report, but data released by American investigators earlier this year suggests the jet’s engines were deliberately shut off and there was a cockpit struggle before the plane nose-dived.
The co-pilot on a Germanwings jet traveling from Barcelona, Spain, to Duesseldorf, Germany, locked the captain out of the cockpit and deliberately crashed the plane into the French Alps, killing all 150 people on board. Andreas Lubitz had struggled with depression and suffered from sleeplessness and fear of losing his vision.
Read moreCo-pilot contacted dozens of doctors ahead of Germanwings crash
The co-pilot on an Ethiopian Airlines flight from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to Milan, Italy, hijacked the jet and rerouted it to Geneva, Switzerland. Hailemedhin Abera Tegegn, the co-pilot, surrendered to local police and sought political asylum. None of the 193 passengers were harmed.
The pilot of a Mozambique Airlines plane traveling from the southern African nation to Angola deliberately downed the jet in a national park in Namibia, killing all 33 people on board. Authorities said at the time that Herminio dos Santos Fernandes, the pilot, locked the cockpit door and set the plane on course to crash when the co-pilot went to the bathroom.
An EgyptAir flight from Los Angeles to Cairo plunged into the Atlantic Ocean off Nantucket, Massachusetts, killing all 217 passengers and crew on board. American investigators concluded the copilot, Gameel Al-Batouti, set the plane on course to crash while the captain was in the bathroom. He then shut off the engines as the captain returned and struggled to right the plane. Egyptian authorities, however, disputed the findings, concluding in their own investigation that mechanical failure was to blame.
A SilkAir flight from Jakarta to Singapore crashed near the Indonesian town of Palembang, killing all 104 people on board. Indonesian investigators concluded that “unlawful interference” likely caused the crash of the new model Boeing jet in good weather. Their report found the pilot, Tsu Way Ming, “was in the process of, or intending to, leave the cockpit” before the cockpit voice recorder cut out. Authorities also said the pilot was “facing financial problems, and had experienced several company disciplinary actions”, including a demotion.
A pilot crashed a Royal Air Maroc flight from Agadir, Morocco, to Casablanca into the Atlas Mountains just 10 minutes after takeoff, killing all 44 people on board. Investigators determined Younes Khayati switched off the autopilot and sent the plane hurtling to the ground as the co-pilot tried in vain to intervene. The Associated Press reported at the time that it was “the deliberate wish of the pilot to end his life”. A union representing pilots disputed the findings.
An off-duty FedEx flight engineer attempted to hijack a company cargo plane traveling from Memphis, Tennessee, to San Jose, California, while riding as a jump seat passenger. Auburn Calloway attacked the flight crew armed with a hammer and a spear gun. The crew subdued him and safely landed the plane, despite those who confronted Calloway suffering extensive injuries. Investigators said Calloway had intended to crash the plane after facing possible disciplinary measures.
A Japan Airlines flight from Fukuoka to Tokyo crashed in Tokyo Bay just as it was landing, killing 24 of the 174 people on board. Investigators said there was a fight in the cockpit as the pilot, Seiji Katagiri, put the engines into reverse thrust. They also later determined Katagiri, who survived the crash, had been deemed fit to fly even after having a history of mental illness, including paranoid schizophrenia.

Europe injects only 70% of gas needed for winter into storage by end-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:00:34 UTC
17:00:34 KST

MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. Europe managed to inject only 70% of the gas volumes needed for the coming winter into its underground gas storage facilities by the end of the first month of autumn, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Net gas injections - the difference between injection and withdrawal volumes - into underground storage facilities in EU countries have exceeded 47.5 bln cubic meters since the start of the summer season in April 2026. Thus, Europe has so far managed to inject only 70% of the volumes needed for the coming winter.
Under European Commission requirements, EU countries must ensure that their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% flexibility margin is allowed in the event of difficult storage-filling conditions. Thus, net injections into European storage facilities must total at least 68 bln cubic meters by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter season to meet the storage target.
Average gas injection rates into EU storage facilities in September remain the highest in the past four years amid warm weather. At the same time, gas prices at European hubs are at their highest since late 2022, indicating the European Union’s urgent efforts to fill its storage facilities for the winter even at very high prices. However, Europe has already missed the summer months that offered the most favorable conditions for injections.
As of September 29, European storage facilities were 71.54% full, 15.53 percentage points below the five-year average for that date, compared with 82.6% a year earlier. This is the lowest level for that date since records began in 2011. EU storage facilities hold around 78.3 bln cubic meters of gas, 12.7 bln cubic meters less than a year earlier and the lowest level since 2013. Gazprom has forecast that gas inventories in European storage facilities may not even reach 75% by the next heating season.
TASS reported earlier that Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas inventories. EU countries may have their storage facilities only 70-75% full by the traditional start of the autumn-winter season, which would be the lowest level ever recorded at the start of the heating season.

Russian attacks
"The enemy continues to attack Ukraine’s energy infrastructure," Ukrenergo said.

What is happening with the schedules

Please limit the use of high-powered electrical appliances from 17:00 to 22:00. This will reduce the load on the power system and the likelihood of forced restrictions due to overloading of equipment damaged by enemy shelling

Russia’s state arms giant claims a new drone-missile class
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:59:51 UTC
16:59:51 KST

- Russian state conglomerate Rostec said its S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T jet-powered strike drones perform the role of cruise missiles at lower cost.
- Rostec said the weapons are already used in Ukraine and should become standard weapons for Russian frontline aviation.
Russia’s state defense conglomerate Rostec says three of its newest jet-powered strike drones, the S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, can now do the job of cruise missiles at a fraction of the cost, and that all three are already being used against Ukraine.
Rostec made the claims in comments to the Russian Defense Ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda published on Sept. 30, describing the weapons as a new category that sits between attack drones and missiles. The company did not give prices, production numbers or performance figures for any of the three, and its claims about accuracy and combat results could not be independently verified.
“In fact, a classic cruise missile is already a fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle. However, not every UAV of this type is a cruise missile. Nevertheless, in the new S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, this line is being erased,” Rostec said in its statement.
The company said the drones have the accuracy, maneuverability and range of cruise missiles while being significantly cheaper than conventional missiles, and that the gap between the two kinds of weapon will keep shrinking as drone production matures. Rostec said it expects the new jet-powered drones to become a standard weapon for Russian frontline aviation in the near future, alongside the glide-bomb kits that Russian jets have dropped on Ukrainian front lines in large numbers since 2023.
The S-71M and S-71K are designed to be launched from fifth-generation fighters, including the Su-57, Rostec told the state news agency TASS. Both are sized to fit inside the Su-57’s internal weapons bay, which lets the jet carry them without spoiling its radar-evading shape, and Russia’s arms exporter Rosoboronexport displayed them next to a Su-57E at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt in September.
Ukraine’s military intelligence has examined debris from both. It says the S-71K, known as Kovyor, carries a 250-kg (550-pound) OFAB-250-270 high-explosive bomb as its warhead and lacks terminal guidance, and that the S-71M, called Monokhrom, contains an NVIDIA Jetson Orin computing module, a small U.S.-made computer built to run artificial intelligence software on board, Militarnyi reported. Some published reports have swapped the two designations, so details tied to each name should be treated with caution.
Rostec told TASS that the smaller Dan-T has been confirmed in hundreds of launches against Ukrainian targets and can be fired from aircraft and helicopters, including foreign-made ones, which suggests the company is aiming it at export buyers. Accounts of where the Dan-T comes from differ: some analysts describe it as the export name for the S8000 Banderol, a small jet-powered cruise missile built by Russian drone maker Kronshtadt, while Ukrainian experts have described it as a strike version of the Dan-M jet target drone that Russia used for air defense training.
Ukrainian estimates put the Dan-T’s range at roughly 500 km (310 miles) with a 135-kg (298-pound) warhead, The New Voice of Ukraine reported, citing Ukrainian intelligence officials who said Moscow wants the weapon built entirely from Russian components.
That goal follows Ukrainian findings about the Banderol, which first appeared over Ukraine in spring 2025 and is launched mainly from Su-30/34 combat aircraft, Orion drones and Mi-28 attack helicopters, often from occupied Crimea toward the Odesa region. Ukraine’s military intelligence says the Banderol contains a Chinese-made jet engine, a Japanese battery and mostly U.S.-made electronics, Euronews reported.
Cheap jet-powered weapons that fly like missiles force Ukraine to spend scarce and expensive air defense interceptors on targets that cost Russia far less to build, the same logic behind Russia’s mass use of Shahed-type drones.
Rostec placed the new drones in a wider family of guided weapons that includes the Iskander ballistic missile system, Tornado-S rocket launchers with guided rockets, Krasnopol guided artillery shells and the Kalashnikov Group’s KUB loitering munitions.

KU Leuven warns of invoice fraud with tuition fee payments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:59:18 UTC
16:59:18 KST

Leuven University is warning students and parents about fraud relating to tuition fee payments. A number of parents received an invoice that looked genuine, but the account number had been altered to that of fraudsters. The university is now urging everyone always to check payment details before transferring any money.
At present, only a few cases are known. Nevertheless, KU Leuven is warning all students and parents, as many students have yet to pay their tuition fees.
In cases of invoice fraud, fraudsters intercept a genuine invoice or bank statement and alter the account number. The document itself therefore appears legitimate, but anyone making the payment transfers the money to the fraudsters’ account.
It is possible that fraudsters have gained access to the recipient’s email inbox. KU Leuven’s own systems have not been tampered with by the fraudsters.
Check the account number
KU Leuven is asking students and parents to check the details on the bank transfer before making any payment. You can do this using the personal verification code shown on the document. On the university’s verification page, students can compare the amount, the account number and the reference number.
The official account number is also listed on KU Leuven’s website. Anyone paying via a banking app should enter ‘KU Leuven’ or ‘Katholieke Universiteit Leuven’ as the beneficiary’s name.
If the banking app displays a warning alerting you to the fact that the name does not match the account number, the university advises you to stop the payment immediately.
Paid already? No need to panic
Anyone who has already paid their tuition fees and has not received a warning email from KU Leuven may, according to the university, assume that the payment has gone through correctly.
KU Leuven is currently investigating whether it can take further legal action. The university also says it will remain vigilant against other forms of online fraud and abuse.
The UCLL University of Applied Sciences is also warning about emails containing fake invoices. So far, one person has fallen victim to that scam.

Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization (MIT) has captured Omar al-Khatib, a Syrian suspect accused of helping plan the 2013 Reyhanli bombings near the Turkish-Syrian border that killed 53 people.
Al-Khatib, who was wanted under an Interpol Red Notice, was intercepted while attempting to flee to Europe by sea and brought to Türkiye, security sources said on Thursday.
The sources said he helped plan and organise the attack and coordinated contacts between its perpetrators and intelligence officers loyal to ousted regime leader Bashar al Assad.
MIT had been monitoring his activities in Syria as part of efforts to track down those responsible for the bombings in Türkiye’s southern Hatay province.
Planning and preparation

Al-Khatib and Nazik entered Türkiye through Hatay in February that year to identify targets, subsequently obtaining approval from Melhem, who was based in Latakia, the sources said.
In May, before the attack, al-Khatib accompanied Temir Dukanci to the Latakia branch of Syrian military intelligence to collect materials for the explosive device, they added.
The sources said Dukanci and Nazik transported the bomb-laden vehicle to Reyhanli, where it was detonated remotely.
After the attack, the pair fled to Syria, where al-Khatib took them to the same military intelligence branch in Latakia. The sources alleged that the ousted Assad regime rewarded al-Khatib and the other perpetrators with money.
Efforts to track down suspects
MIT began tracking those responsible immediately after the bombings and closely monitored al-Khatib’s activities in Syria, the sources said.
His capture follows the arrests of Nazik in 2018, Cengiz Sertel in 2024, and Muhammed Dib Korali and Temir Dukanci in 2025.
Melhem, whom the sources identified as the major general who ordered the attack, was appointed head of the National Security Bureau by Assad in February 2024.
He fled abroad after the fall of the Assad regime, according to the sources.

'Inversion of reality': IDF issues rejection of 'baseless' claims made in 'NAZA' film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:57:05 UTC
16:57:05 KST

The IDF on Thursday gave its first comprehensive and detailed response and rejection of the NAZA film's claims that Israel committed genocide during the Gaza war.
According to the IDF, its delayed response was due to the NAZA filmmakers neither providing it with advance notice of the claims nor permitting it to see the movie until recent days.
Only after viewing the movie did the IDF feel it could provide a more comprehensive, point-by-point response.
The core of the IDF's response is to reject three powerful elements of the NAZA film: specific rejections of all of the movie's claims about combatant-civilian ratios for targeting, rejecting claims that the IDF used Artificial Intelligence abusively to kill more civilians, and categorizing the IDF intelligence interviewees as being experts in a middle step of the targeting process, who know much less about the final step.
Regarding the combatant-civilian targeting ratio, the IDF rejected the film's claims that there was an attack with a 500-to-1 civilian-combatant kill ratio and claims that there were frequent attacks with 200-to-1 ratios against senior Hamas officials and frequent attacks of 20-to-1 ratios against junior Hamas officials.
Humans always make final call, not AI, IDF says
Moving on to the question of whether the IDF's use of AI in its targeting led to more significant abuse and killing of civilians because the system focuses on the efficiency of killing Hamas officials and deemphasizes saving civilians, the military said that human IDF officers always make the final calls, not the AI.
The most serious problem the film presents about the IDF is that its evidence is brought by 24 mostly IDF intelligence officials involved in targeting.
If they claim the IDF is committing war crimes – either explicitly or by implication (sometimes without realizing what their words imply) – how can the military deny the claims?
To this, the IDF said that the NAZA film is problematic because it does not reveal who is making the claims (the IDF officers' identities are obscured) or even which specific attacks they are referring to.
But more importantly, the IDF said that, now that it has reviewed the film, it is clear that the IDF intelligence officials handled targeting data midstream.
In contrast, the IDF said that only the targeting cells, which include lawyers and officials with a specialty in reducing civilian harm factors, know how the final decisions are made, and not the intelligence officials who find the targets and label them as targetable.
Ratios on documents do not represent actual ratios used in strikes, IDF claims
Already early in the war, The Jerusalem Post had multiple exclusive discussions with IDF legal officials who explained that if there are documents which mention 100 to 1 or 20 to 1 as ratios, they are basically never used, but meant as maximums that cannot even be considered, the same way that the Israeli justice system has maximum punishments which courts almost never use, preferring to hand down punishments often that are half as long or even two-thirds shorter.
So a document with a 20 to 1 ratio cutoff could lead to an actual attack with a 5 to 1 or 7 to 1 ratio.
A document with a 100-to-1 ratio cutoff against a top Hamas official like Hamas military chief Mohammed Deif or Gaza Brigade Chief Ahmad Randur could lead to an attack with a 70-to-1 or 30-to-1 ratio, depending on the circumstances.
The IDF statement said, "The film NAZA presents a distorted, misleading, and unrealistic picture of the IDF’s target planning and strike processes. The film’s narrative is based on fundamental factual errors stemming from a skewed and manipulative portrayal."
Next, the IDF stated, "Binding IDF directives explicitly, comprehensively, and clearly distinguish between terrorists and uninvolved civilians in Gaza. IDF strike processes are entirely based on this distinction; they prohibit targeting civilians and mandate minimizing the risk of harm to them to the greatest extent possible.
"The IDF has never planned, authorized, or carried out any strike in Gaza where the expected outcome was the death of 500 civilians or a number approaching that figure. Nor has there ever been a serious allegation that an IDF strike caused a death toll of that magnitude or anything close to it," stated the IDF.
Further, the IDF noted, "Artificial intelligence has never independently selected targets for IDF strikes. Target identification is performed solely by qualified intelligence officers, strike planning is carried out by relevant professionals, and the decision to strike targets is made by operational commanders."
"Binding IDF directives have never granted automatic authorization for strikes on targets that endanger a predetermined number of civilians (such as 20 civilians when striking a low-ranking operative or 200 civilians when striking a senior commander, as claimed by the individual in the film)," asserted the IDF.
In addition, the IDF said regarding its Lavender AI targeting program that, "'Lavender' is not a list of targets pre-approved for attack, but rather a database designed to assist intelligence analysts.
"Binding IDF directives do not permit treating an evacuation warning issued for a specific area as authorization to conduct strikes there while disregarding the presence of civilians who have remained in the area," continued the IDF.
Moreover, the IDF stated, "The IDF does not ignore the consequences of its strikes; rather, it acts to examine them -including instances of unintended harm to civilians - contrary to the film's claims. This examination process drives the investigation of hundreds of combat incidents and serves as a basis for deriving lessons learned."
To date, the IDF has said that it has opened over 150 criminal probes into its soldiers' conduct of the war in Gaza, and over 3,000 disciplinary probes.
Interviewees only address preliminary stages of Gaza strikes, IDF says
Next, the IDF said, "The numerous errors stem, in part, from the fact that the interviewees - presented as former IDF Intelligence Corps personnel - typically address only limited, preliminary intelligence-related stages."
"They do not address the far broader process of strike planning and authorization, which falls outside the Intelligence Corps' purview and is instead the responsibility of the operational bodies that manage and execute strike operations. Consequently, it is evident that in certain instances, the interviewees offer speculations and impressions entirely devoid of factual basis," noted the IDF.
The IDF asserted, "The filmmakers chose not to show many other parties involved in the full target-planning process - such as the professionals tasked with planning operations to minimize civilian harm, legal advisors who review planned strikes, and the commanders responsible for approving or rejecting them."
In addition, the military claimed, "The result is a highly inaccurate and misleading portrayal of reality. Furthermore, to align the presentation with the narrative the film seeks to promote, the creators omit contextual details essential to understanding the war in Gaza and the IDF’s conduct during it."
Regarding October 7, the IDF said, "The film fails to give due weight to the security reasons behind Israel’s actions in Gaza and the October 7 attack; to Hamas’s strategy of deliberately embedding itself within the civilian population - the root cause of civilian casualties; and to the myriad measures and methods the IDF employed to minimize harm to civilians - including pre-strike warnings, the selection of appropriate munitions and strike planning, support for the delivery of humanitarian aid, and more."
"The processes and decisions the film omits illustrate the practical implications of the IDF’s efforts to protect civilians - demands for additional intelligence, plan modifications, the cancellation of strikes, and the foregoing of military opportunities. These decisions restricted the use of force solely based on assessments of the risk to civilians," said the IDF.
IDF accuses film of distorting reality through editing, comparisons to atrocities
Next, the IDF claimed, "Outrageously, the film distorts reality further through the manipulative editing of interviews and comparisons to historical atrocities, while falsely and baselessly attributing malicious intent to the IDF. Even the film’s title represents an inversion of reality.
For example, the IDF explained that, "'Collateral damage' is a professional term used by law-abiding militaries worldwide; it describes the assessment of potential civilian harm resulting from a strike, serving as a basis for commanders to evaluate the operation's legality and to take measures to minimize civilian casualties as much as possible."
"Absurdly, the film portrays the extraordinary effort and level of detail the IDF invests in assessing potential harm to the population during an attack as indifference to civilian lives. In reality, assessing expected harm is a requirement under international law; the IDF conducts these assessments so that commanders can determine the legality of an attack, order additional precautions, modify the strike plan, or call off the operation - all with the aim of minimizing harm to uninvolved civilians as much as possible, just as IDF commanders have done many times throughout the war," continued the IDF.
Finally, the IDF stated, "The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts. A serious discussion regarding harm to civilians requires a faithful depiction of how decisions were actually made. The film fails to provide this; instead, it presents a simplistic manifesto driven by a clear agenda. It seeks to create the impression that the IDF operates inhumanely. In reality, however, the filmmakers can only create such an impression by distorting facts, omitting necessary context, ignoring previous IDF statements and explanations, and employing emotional manipulation and dramatic effects."
Despite all of the IDF's responses, it has still failed to give an on-record discussion of its actual combatant-civilian casualty ratios.
Further, the IDF has not truly addressed the vast cumulative number of civilian casualties from the Gaza war.
While around 25,000 of those killed in Gaza were Hamas according to IDF estimates, and anecdotally 3,000-5,000 more were Palestinians killed by Hamas rocket misfires or crackdowns on opposition, that still leaves likely 40,000 or more killed Gazan civilians.
The Post has requested a response from the NAZA filmmakers.

Tallinn Defence EXPO: Counter-drone systems and robot soldiers steal the show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:57:05 UTC
16:57:05 KST

Drones have changed the face of war in Ukraine. At the Tallinn Defence EXPO, Estonian companies showed the counter-drone systems and battlefield robots they say Europe now needs.
Unmanned systems are both a growing threat and an increasingly vital part of the defence arsenal.
That theme ran through the Tallinn Defence EXPO, where more than 100 companies showed their latest products.
The stakes are high for Estonia, which borders Russia. According to an industry briefing, its defence spending rose from 1.9% of GDP in 2013 to an average of 5.4% through 2029.
The EXPO was one of six events in Estonian Defence Week, held in Tallinn over five days in late September.
The week drew around 4,500 visitors from 56 countries and featured 133 speakers across 68 sessions, including a NATO innovation conference and a Baltic defence conference.
Seeing and stopping drones
Estonian firm Marduk Technologies presented a detection system that uses powerful optics and AI to find and identify flying objects.
"It's a camera-based drone detection system. It's fully passive, and with this we can see whatever is flying. We can differentiate automatically whether it is a bird, drone, helicopter or any flying object," Leet Rauno Lember, CEO of Marduk Technologies, told Euronews Next.
"Passive" means this optical system sends out no radio signal, remaining hard to spot — unlike radars.
Lember said their optical detection system is not "better" than other technologies but complements them.
Acoustic sensors reach only a few hundred metres, he explained, while electric drones can be very quiet. Radar covers long distances but may miss drones made of lightweight foam.
"All of the layers are complementing each other, and end users are able to make better decisions," he said.
Marduk Technologies has been developing the drone-detection devices for more than a decade.
The war in Ukraine confirmed the company's early warnings, Lember said. "Back in 2016, everybody said that drones will not be a problem, at least in the near future."
Another Estonian company, DefSecIntel, combines optical, radar, acoustic and radio-frequency sensors in one mobile, highly autonomous system called Eirshield.
"This is a turnkey counter-drone system," Jaanus Tamm, CEO and founder of DefSecIntel Solutions, told Euronews Next.
It helps users detect hostile drones, track them, then decide how to intercept them. Its effectors range from jammers to interceptor drones and, if needed, lasers.
"Eirshield detection sensors will detect the drones, then the operator will select which one to go after, and then they launch the interceptor drone," Tamm said. "Then the hostile drones will be destroyed and they will not hit any infrastructure elements or do any harm for the civilians."
Tamm called Eirshield "one of the few" TRL 9 counter-drone systems in Europe that can be bought now, in large numbers. TRL 9 is the top of the technology readiness scale.
The design is open, so it can evolve. "If there are new threats coming, we can just add new effectors, or new sensors to detect better," he said.
One of those effectors is Blaze, an interceptor drone from Latvia's Origin Robotics. According to the industry briefing, France's defence procurement agency selected it at Eurosatory 2026.
Robots instead of soldiers
Unmanned vehicles can support, or even replace, soldiers on dangerous missions. Milrem Robotics presented its THeMIS unmanned ground vehicle.
The company says the technology enables "an unmanned kill zone," where robotic vehicles would detect and push back invading troops. That would minimise human casualties among the defenders.
The vehicles are remotely controlled and partly autonomous. "Instead of sending troops on the battlefield, we can send in these machines and save lives," Raul Rikk, Capability Development Director at Milrem Robotics, told Euronews Next at the company's Tallinn factory.
The modular platform can carry a machine gun, an anti-tank system or other weapons. It can also handle reconnaissance, mine clearing, logistics and casualty evacuation.
Rikk said the concept is already proven. "Nothing is theoretical anymore. Ukrainians are using them on the battlefield," he said.
Rikk said the company's current production capacity is not public. "We are talking about hundreds of vehicles, and different sizes," he said. "We can take the production everywhere, so it's not complicated to set up the production, and we can scale up quite rapidly."
For Rikk, the direction is clear. "Tomorrow's war is already in Ukraine," he said.

The AI giant said on Wednesday that it was reviewing the alleged cyberattack against Canada’s national archives agency and had provided an initial briefing to Canadian officials.

“Our priority is to provide affected organisations with accurate, useful information, and we’ll keep refining our approach as we learn more,” a spokesperson for the San Francisco-based company said in a statement to Al Jazeera.
The spokesperson added that much of the misaligned activity under review by the company involved “routine research tasks, including accessing public web content”.
The attempted hacking, if confirmed, would be the first publicly known case of an AI-led cyberattack against Canada’s government, following a series of incidents of rogue agents targeting agencies in the United States and Australia.

Transluce, a nonprofit research lab in San Francisco, said in a report released on Wednesday that it had discovered two “rudimentary” attempted attacks against Library and Archives Canada and Civil Rights Data Collection, a statistics agency of the US Department of Education.

Ukraine marks the Day of Defenders of Ukraine on Oct. 1, honoring the men and women who have defended the country amid Russia’s ongoing war.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Day of Defenders was established by presidential decree in 2014 and initially observed on Oct. 14 under the name “Day of the Defender of Ukraine.”
In 2021, its official Ukrainian name was changed to “Day of Defenders and Women Defenders of Ukraine” to explicitly recognize both men and women serving and defending the country.
The observance was moved to Oct. 1 in 2023.
President Volodymyr Zelensky marked the day from the front line in the Lyman sector, where he had met with Ukrainian troops and commanders ahead of the holiday.
Rather than recording his address at one of Kyiv’s historic landmarks, Zelensky said he chose a frontline command post because these less visible locations are where Ukraine’s history is being written.
“Here, the fate of Ukraine is being decided, without exaggeration... The fate of Europe and the free world,” Zelensky said, describing the frontline as a place where the country’s independence is defended and where the path toward peace runs.
He said Ukraine’s resilience begins at the front, where soldiers continue to hold their positions and defend the country.
Russia Strikes Odesa Infrastructure Again After Days of Deadly Attacks
“It has been 1,681 days of full-scale war – a daily struggle and hard work amid attacks, strikes and pain. Yet Ukraine stands firm, destroying the occupier and achieving what it needs. All of this is possible because our defenders – men and women alike – stand strong.”
Zelensky also paid tribute to Ukrainian service members who have been killed during the war, saying their names remain part of the country’s collective memory.
“In every Ukrainian family – for each of us – there are names we truly want to remember,” he said, honoring those who gave their lives so that Ukraine could continue to exist.
The president thanked soldiers serving across Ukraine’s defense and security forces, including infantry, airborne troops, reconnaissance, air defense, combat aviation, naval forces, artillery, engineers, and special operations units, as well as members of the National Guard, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and police.
He also singled out drone operators and other personnel whose work supports operations from behind screens and on the battlefield.
“Soldiers and sergeants, master sergeants and sailors, our Ukrainian officers; everyone currently at their positions, on missions or on combat duty; everyone serving Ukraine and giving their all so that Ukraine is never surrendered.”
The president’s address came as Ukraine entered another day of its full-scale war with Russia. On Wednesday, Zelensky had visited the Lyman sector, where he awarded 16 service members the Orders “For Courage” and praised Ukrainian forces involved in Operation Vivaldi.
According to the presidential office, Ukrainian units have returned more than 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) to Ukrainian control in the area.

US removes Syria from arms export ban

Breadcrumb
US removes Syria from arms export ban as Trump draws closer to Sharaa government
The Trump administration is removing Syria from a list of countries that are not allowed to purchase or import US weaponry, a step that is part of a monthslong process of easing sanctions on the new government in Damascus and its leaders.
In a notice published Wednesday in the Federal Register, the State Department said it was amending its International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or ITAR, so that Syria no longer was among the nations subject to a policy of denial for licenses and other approvals needed for the sale of US weapons and munitions.
The change effective Thursday means that arms sales requests from Syria will now be considered on a case-by-case basis.
President Donald Trump acted last year to ease economic sanctions on Syria that had been in place for decades during now-ousted President Bashar Assad’s totalitarian rule. In August, Secretary of State Marco Rubio rescinded Syria’s designation as "a state sponsor of terrorism", helping paving the way for the latest step in drawing closer to the current government.
The State Department has also announced plans to reopen the US Embassy in Damascus, after it has been closed for 14 years.
With Syria’s removal from the ITAR blacklist, only seven countries remain subject to the policy of denial for licenses for US arms exports: Belarus, China, Cuba, Iran, Myanmar, North Korea and Venezuela.
Syria’s interim president, former rebel leader Ahmed al-Sharaa, was part of a coalition of rebels that overthrew the Assad government nearly two years ago and has embarked on a policy of change that has impressed the Trump administration. His moves have led to hopes of eventual stability in a country that was wracked by civil war and the Islamic State insurgency that engulfed northeast and western Iraq for years.
Wednesday’s withdrawal of US forces from Iraq may mean that the Syrian government plays a greater role in preventing an IS resurgence.
