In August 2021, Meymankulyyev was lured into a car by men presumed to be working for Turkmenistan security services. He ended up inside the consulate building, where he was beaten before being released.
Then, in May 2023, Meymankulyyev was arrested at a friend’s house by Turkish police and immediately deported. Witnesses saw him later at the airport in the Turkmenistan capital of Ashgabat. He was sentenced to 18 to 22 years in prison on unknown charges, and has not been seen or heard from since.
The list obtained by reporters shows that Turkmenistan’s Ministry for National Security issued arrest warrants for both Meymankulyyev and Annayev in 2022. 
The previous year, Annayev had been beaten up on the streets of Istanbul. It was just days before he was scheduled to travel to Warsaw and speak at an event organized by the human rights office of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). He said he was convinced the attackers were working for the Turkmenistan security services. 
“I returned to Istanbul after the conference. I started to receive various phone calls, SMS messages, and death threats,” he told Turkmen.news in 2022. 
He then attended another OSCE event, and decided to seek asylum in Poland. His claim failed there, and he has tried also in Sweden and the Netherlands. 
Annayev was the victim of a knife attack a year ago in Amsterdam, which left him lightly injured. The assailants are unknown, but Annayev is suspicious they may have been working for Turkmenistan’s security services.
So far unsuccessful in his bid for political asylum, Annayev continues his bureaucratic battles in Europe, all the while unleashing a torrent of YouTube videos criticising the Turkmenistan regime.
Turkmenistan prevents internet users inside the country from accessing platforms like YouTube and TikTok, although some people use VPN technology to get around the ban. 
But the government has come up with new tactics to block his broadcasts, Annayev alleges. He says bots are being used to file complaints to TikTok and YouTube about his account, or content. 
Given enough complaints, TikTok may automatically remove an account or content. YouTube may remove content upon receiving a complaint about it displaying a person’s image. As the platform’s guidelines state, third-party complaints are accepted when “the individual whose privacy is being violated does not have access to a computer or the internet.”  
Neither TikTok nor YouTube responded to requests for comment.
Annayev said the Turkmenistan regime wants to stop diaspora activists like him from getting their messages to people inside the country.
“They are afraid, and our livestreams are very important in Turkmenistan. Why? Because there is no one else who can do that like us,” he said.

Its latest projections put average annual inflation at 0.7% in 2026 and 0.8% in both 2027 and 2028, assuming the policy rate remains at zero throughout the forecast period.
The bank warned that uncertainty surrounding the Middle East could push energy prices significantly higher than expected, further increasing inflation and curbing economic growth.

Vocational schools say extra €14 million not enough for meaningful reform

Vocational schools say extra €14 million not enough for meaningful reform
Vocational schools will receive nearly €14 million in additional government funding next year to support vocational education reform, though the sector says a new long-term funding model is also needed.
The Ministry of Education and Research aims to have at least 40 percent of basic school graduates choose applied secondary education by 2035. As part of efforts to reach that target, new four-year curricula aimed specifically at basic school graduates were introduced in vocational education this academic year. The changes have also required vocational schools to review their operating models.
Against this backdrop, the ministry has decided to allocate nearly €14 million in additional funding to vocational schools next year to support the implementation of vocational education reform, said Ülle Matsin, head of the ministry's general and vocational secondary education department.
"When the academic year began, vocational schools' budgets for the current academic year were already planned with the implementation of the reform in mind. Now, for some vocational schools that, for example, had more adult learners, their funding needs are changing. For instance, now that we have more basic school graduates at the vocational secondary education level, funding needs to be available for teaching materials and other needs as well," Matsin said.
Kuno Rooba, chairman of the board of the Estonian Association for the Advancement of Vocational Education, said the additional funding was welcome news and showed that concerns about funding for vocational education had been heard. In the longer term, however, the entire vocational education funding model needs to be reviewed, as its current form does not provide the resources needed to achieve the reform's objectives.
"The vocational education that was provided before and what is now being provided under the name of applied secondary education are very different in substance. Because there are more activities involved, more funding is also needed — for teachers, support staff and the material resources needed to carry out those activities," Rooba said.
New negotiations between the parties over the various components of the funding model will begin this Friday. The ministry also believes that the amount of funding directed toward vocational education must reflect the new situation and that the principles for funding vocational and general secondary education could be more closely aligned.
"This is something we are currently discussing with vocational school leaders, identifying where we need to change funding principles and whether we also need to change, for example, how responsibility is divided among vocational schools when it comes to leading cooperation on teacher development or professional development," Matsin said.
Looking ahead, updating the funding model could also increase the amount of money that needs to be directed toward vocational education, Matsin added.
"Our goal is for more basic school graduates to enter vocational schools than before. Since our funding is based on the cost of providing education to each student, it is clear that this alone will begin to shift a greater share of funding toward vocational education."

Russian drones over Ukraine have prompted Poland to update its rules for shooting them down - here’s what will change
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:43 EEST
16:00:43 KST

Russian drones over Ukraine have prompted Poland to update its rules for shooting them down - here’s what will change
Kyiv • UNN
Starting October 1, Poland will introduce simplified procedures for shooting down unidentified objects in its airspace. Decisions may also be made based on radar data.
Poland is changing its air defense procedures due to the ongoing Russian airstrikes on Ukraine. Poland’s Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced the full readiness of new, simplified procedures for detecting and shooting down foreign objects in Polish airspace, which will enter into force on October 1. UNN reports this, citing Gazeta Prawna.
New procedures from October 1
Poland’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced on Wednesday that new military procedures to simplify the detection and shooting down of foreign objects in Polish airspace are ready. "October 1 is always a good time to introduce procedures," he added.
On Monday, Deputy Minister of National Defense Cezary Tomczyk spoke about planned changes to the rules for Polish pilots taking part in missions to protect Polish airspace during Russian airstrikes in Ukraine. He explained that this primarily concerns changing the rules for detecting foreign flying objects. Peacetime procedures, which require visual identification of an object before it is shot down, will be replaced by so-called positive identification.
What is positive identification?
After the procedure is changed, a pilot or their commander will be able to decide to shoot down a foreign object based on information collected by radars and other systems, or information provided by the Ukrainian side, which regularly faces attacks by Russian drones and missiles.
At a press conference on Wednesday, when Poland’s Minister of National Defense was asked when the new procedures would enter into force, he announced that he had received a report from Operational Commander General Ireneusz Nowak, who is responsible, among other things, for Polish Air Force missions along the eastern border, stating that the new procedures were fully ready and were currently being implemented. "October 1 is always a good time not only to begin the school year, but also to introduce new procedures," Kosiniak-Kamysz added.
Implementation at the military level without legislative changes
When asked whether the changes to the procedures required legislative amendments, Poland’s Minister of National Defense stressed that they did not; they are being implemented at the military level. He emphasized that these are clear, "strictly programmed" procedures established by the command, which will be followed by pilots and other soldiers involved in air defense.
Under the current rules, including Poland’s law on the protection of the state border, the Operational Commander of the Armed Forces is responsible for protecting Polish airspace. He oversees the protection of Polish skies through the Air Operations Center. As a rule, the Operational Commander may decide to shoot down a foreign object that has entered Polish airspace; he may also authorize fighter pilots to make such a decision.
Abandoning the requirement for visual identification
The announced procedural change concerns the method of identifying a foreign object and the cancellation of the requirement for visual identification — that is, a fighter pilot must approach the "intruder" closely enough to determine what type of object they are dealing with. This peacetime procedure is primarily aimed at minimizing the risk of shooting down, for example, a civilian aircraft whose malfunction prevents identification and proper communication with the military.
According to representatives of Poland’s Ministry of National Defense, the current situation, in which there is a regular risk of violations of the Polish border, requires procedures to be adapted to the new reality. "Until now, we have not used such capabilities because they are usually reserved for conditions of war or martial law. However, because of the threat — since Poland today faces the possibility of drones entering our territory every day — we must implement these changes for the benefit of both pilots and the security of the state," Tomczyk stressed on Monday.

War, power games and impunity. I watched the farce that is the UN general assembly: what a tragedy, what a mess | Nesrine Malik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:00:31 UTC
16:00:31 KST

UN general assembly meetings are not usually riveting occasions. But this year’s encapsulated a world in flux and crisis, an international law and organisation structure that is falling apart, and a humanitarian order machine running hot. What unfolded was less a gathering for resolution and resolve than a display of showboating, frustration and fractiousness.
It was a snapshot for the history books of four huge destabilising conflicts for which there seems to be no means of, or interest in, resolution – Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan. Volodymyr Zelenskyy delivered an account of five years of Russian aggression: the staggering loss of life – hundreds of thousands killed on both sides – the porousness of the sanctions on Russia, the “madness” of it all. Donald Trump once again threatened to “annihilate” Iran if it did not make a deal, a promise that has now been made so many times its restating only reveals its hollowness. Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, responded in his own speech by saying that Iran has been the victim of US terrorism and aggression, and would defend itself with the “utmost strength”. The sole US delegation representative in the room walked out.
In the middle of this unbridled, unseemly pugnaciousness, pleas to restate facts were trampled over by power-lust. The Israeli government’s sense of impunity “has reached terrifying levels”, said Jordan’s King Abdullah II. “It no longer feels compelled to ask, ‘Can we get away with this?’ It already knows the answer.”
“If international law can be ignored for decades,” he added, “then what exactly is that law worth?” As if to answer that question, Benjamin Netanyahu became the only ICC indicted leader to address the UN general assembly, with a characteristically belligerent speech. Nothing – that law is worth nothing.
And on international law meaning nothing, the assembly was subjected to the farce of the United Arab Emirates, the key player in Sudan’s war, piously preaching about how Sudanese people deserve peace and civilian rule, while the UAE’s leaders are accused of arming and funding the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), itself accused of genocide and ethnic cleansing. A close ally of the US and the UK, the UAE has managed to extend Sudan’s war into a calamitous conflict, without even a breath of censure, or even acknowledgment from its friends. A $500m investment in the Trump family’s cryptocurrency scheme, and multibillion-pound partnerships with the UK, have seemingly captured the two states. Indeed, the silence it has bought is so compliantly observed that the US’s senior adviser on African and Arab affairs (Tiffany Trump’s father-in-law) acknowledged foreign interests but refused to name any of the countries.
Even procedurally, the ground was tilted by those who have the power and shamelessness to do so. The Trump administration invoked its sovereign ability to decide who could attend and who could not, wielding a sort of weaponisation of the visa system that rendered the UN not a neutral body with its own rules and protocols, but a tool to be leveraged for the interests of the US and its allies because it sits in US territory. Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas (not ICC-indicted) and 80 other Palestinian officials were denied visas to attend for the second time under Trump’s watch. The head of the Sudanese government and Sudanese armed forces, the antagonists to the UAE-backed RSF, was denied a visa, seemingly an indication of successful Emirati manoeuvrings in Washington. The dynamics were an expression of how foreign policy and conflict are managed today, with constant gaming of the system to amplify one side over the other and produce outcomes friendly to regional and global powers.
Amid the collapse there was Tom Fletcher, the UN undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs, darting energetically from meeting to meeting, with a grittily sunny disposition. He posted a hectic flurry of social media clips talking about what could be done in the middle of the fire, a sort of diplomatic “this is fine” meme. And God bless him. In one, he is on a walk with Alexander De Croo, administrator of the UN development programme, who talks about the problem being “crises piling up on one another”. “The answer,” Fletcher says, “to a lot of what we do is actually diplomacy. Getting those chokepoints open, Bab al-Mandab, the Black Sea, the strait of Hormuz, because otherwise we both have a much bigger development caseload and humanitarian caseload.”
He represents an emerging new model of international and humanitarian worker – navigating funding cuts, a lack of interest in peace and politicised drawdown of international aid to at least maintain some traffic of funds. To make sure some support gets to the millions labouring under war, the climate crisis, disease, poverty, hunger and predation. The wars will carry on, and now the strategy is to negotiate with powers to un-choke and unblock what can be opened to get supplies and relief in, from winter aid in Gaza to containing the Ebola outbreak.
But where we are now isn’t just a matter of earnest diplomats and cynical, irresponsible warring powers. A far more complex problem is upon us: the rapidly changing nature of military conflict itself. Wars are becoming vastly less containable through the spread, sophistication and low cost of AI and drones. They are now conducted remotely, veering between high-intensity and low-grade assaults that render their beginnings and ends less decisive. They are more likely to just suspend normal life with dispensable drones, the sort that have held the Gulf hostage to Iran’s response to US attacks, Sudan’s war without a clear frontline, and the “ceasefire” in Gaza essentially just a lower-grade assault.
The UN general assembly meeting of 2026 was a study in so many things – the degradation of international law, the rickety system it has bequeathed, the acceleration of the demise of international community, and the importance of resolve to somehow attend to the victims. But we are also entering an era in which belligerents themselves are coming to grips with asymmetrical warfare and an elusive status quo. There is much talk of “what comes next”: an equilibrium of middle powers in compact, a rupture with the US and within Nato, a nihilistic free for all? We as humans tend to think in clear-cut scenarios. What is more likely is what was demonstrated last week in New York – a messy prolonged state of constant stress under careless leaders giddy with what they realise they can get away with, no exit plan, and the rest of the system given no option but to work with and around them to somehow alleviate the consequences of their actions. The new world order is one of active resignation.
- 
  Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

A fifth of Swiss Alpine ice has vanished in five years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

A fifth of Swiss Alpine ice has vanished in five years
Swiss glaciers faced another "catastrophic year" in 2026, according to the Swiss Academy of Sciences. Summer heatwaves and low winter snowfall led to the disappearance of dozens of Alpine glaciers.
In 2026, Swiss glaciers lost 5.5% of their total volume, according to the latest assessmentExternal link by GLAMOS and the Swiss Academy of Sciences (SCNAT). In some areas, average ice thickness decreased by between 2.5 and 4 metres, continuing a pattern of melting and recession that experts say will have devastating effects.
“It’s staggering to see the enormous amount of ice that has melted. But what is even more striking is that events of this magnitude are now recurring year after year,” Matthias Huss, director of the Glacier monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS), told Swissinfo. “What used to be extreme events, by definition rare and very intense, now occur almost every summer.”
Over the past five years alone, the volume of ice in the Swiss Alps has fallen by almost 20%.
“These exceptional losses show that the climate is warming too rapidly for glaciers to adapt,” Huss adds.
    
        External Content    
    
            
The giant of the Alps loses 13 metres of ice
The year 2026 ranks second only to 2022 for the greatest glacier losses since measurements began. Although temperatures were higher this year, melting was slightly less severe than four years ago due to more abundant snow cover on many glaciers.
In addition, less Saharan dust settled on the snow in 2026. As a result, more sunlight was reflected back into the atmosphere.
There were, however, notable exceptions. Some glaciers, including the Rhône Glacier and the Aletsch Glacier (the largest glacier in the Alps) experienced the most intense melting ever recorded in 2026. At the lowest monitoring point on the Aletsch Glacier tongue, ice thickness decreased by 13 metres.
Too little snow to shield glaciers from the heat
Exceptionally high temperatures and repeated heatwaves between May and September were not the only reason for this year’s major glacier losses in Switzerland. Winter snowfall was well below the long-term average at all elevations, meaning the snow layer that normally protects glaciers from summer heat was simply too thin.
One indicator of these unfavourable conditions is the so-called “glacier loss day”, which marks the date when glaciers have exhausted the snow and ice reserves accumulated during winter and begin losing mass. This year, that threshold was reached as early as June 29. Apart from 2022, when it fell on June 26, that date had always been declared in July, August or even September since 2000.
Another significant indicator is the 0°C isotherm, the altitude at which air temperature reaches freezing point. Between May and September, the 0°C level remained above 4,000 metres for 76 days. “This is more than double the average and a record,” SCNAT wrote, adding that under such conditions, “Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term”.
    
        External Content    
    
            
Around 30 Swiss glaciers vanished this summer
Over the past 50 years, Switzerland has lost more than 1,000 glaciersExternal link, roughly 40% of the national total, as a result of human-induced climate change. Between 2016 and 2023, 160 glaciers disappeared, and according to Huss, this summer may have marked the end of at least 30 additional small glaciers.
The Plattalva Glacier in canton Glarus was declared extinct after disappearing completely in September. It was no ordinary glacier: in the 1950s, it hosted what was probably the world’s most detailed glacier monitoring programme, Huss notes. Measurements of seasonal glacier mass changes carried out between 1947 and 1985 constitute an exceptional data record from a period when glacier observations were still very limited.
    
        External Content    
    
        
     
Like switching off the lights: The ultimate disappearance of Plattalva #GlacierExternal link in the extreme summer of 2026.
Another glacier has gone. It may seem unremarkable but in the 1950s it hosted the maybe most detailed glacier monitoring programme worldwide@glamos_chExternal link @VAW_glaciologyExternal link pic.twitter.com/V9iwJwXV1tExternal link
Without a drastic reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, half of all Alpine glaciers could disappear within the next 20 years, according to a studyExternal link published in 2025. By the end of the century, only the largest glaciers, such as the Aletsch and Rhône glaciers, may survive.
Less water from glaciers to cope with drought
Glacier melt currently releases vast quantities of water into lowland regions and major European rivers, including the Rhine, Rhône and Danube. For now, this helps to partially alleviate water shortages during summer.
Between July and September, glaciers lost roughly 2,200 billion litres of water, according to SCNAT. This volume is equivalent to more than four times the annual drinking-water consumption of all households in Switzerland. Without this contribution, river levels would have been even lower this summer.
However, this glacier-fed water supply is expected to decline. Alpine glaciers have already reached, or will soon reach, “peak water”, the point at which meltwater runoff begins to decrease progressively.
In the future, glacier melt will no longer be sufficient to offset water deficits caused by more frequent and prolonged droughts. This will mean less water in Alpine valleys and European rivers, with implications for navigation, agriculture, ecosystems, drinking-water resources and energy production.
“The problem isn’t just that there will be less water,” saysExternal link Giovanni De Cesare, operational head of the Hydraulic Constructions Platform at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL). “Today, glaciers melt all summer long, providing a steady stream of runoff. When they’re gone, we’ll have to rely directly on precipitation – rain and snowfall – which is much less predictable.”
Long regarded as a symbol of the Swiss Alps, glaciers are disappearing at an unprecedented pace. Their rapid decline is not only transforming the Alpine landscape, but also one of Europe’s most important freshwater reserves.

UK house price growth halves amid rising mortgage interest rates

Unknown Publisher

Annual house price growth halved in the UK last month, as economic uncertainty caused by conflict in the Middle East continued to deter homebuyers.
The average price of a British home rose 0.8% in the year to September to £274,251, according to Nationwide. That was half the rate recorded in August, when house prices grew 1.6% year on year. It also marked the slowest pace of home price growth since December last year.
House prices across the UK fell 0.2% month on month, after taking account of seasonal effects.
The housing market has been subdued in recent months, as the US-Israel war with Iran and resulting disruption to Gulf oil and gas flows drive up energy costs and inflation fears. That has fed through to higher interest rates on mortgages, making it more expensive for people to buy new homes.
“Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict in the Middle East exerting upward pressure on energy prices, fanning inflation concerns,” the Nationwide chief economist, Robert Gardner, said.
“This in turn has led to mounting financial market expectations of Bank [of England] rate increases, which has maintained upward pressure on the market interest rates which underpin mortgage pricing.”
Moneyfacts reported earlier this week that the average interest rate on a two-year fixed mortgage in the UK had risen to its highest level since July 2024, while the average rate on a five-year fixed rate mortgage hit its highest level since October 2023. Both were sitting above 5.9%.
That could rise further, given that investors are pricing in a 92% chance that the Bank of England will raise interest rates, from 3.75% to 4%, at its next meeting on 5 November. Markets expect the Bank to institute at least three further rises in 2027, taking the base rate to 4.75% by the end of next year.
Threadneedle Street is trying to bring inflation, now at 3.1%, back down to its 2% target. However, it predicted last month that the consumer price index of inflation could rise above 4% in the first quarter of 2027.
Nationwide said that across the regions East Anglia posted the biggest hit to house prices, logging an annual decline of 0.7%. Northern Ireland was an exception, experiencing the strongest house price growth at an annual rate of 5.9%.
The house price slowdown has improved affordability for some homebuyers, Gardner said.
“Underlying affordability is improving, as house price growth has been well below earnings growth for some time,” he said. “These gains have been only partially offset by higher mortgage rates. This suggests that activity should regain momentum in the quarters ahead, providing the energy shock fades and confidence returns – especially if market interest rates fall back to pre-conflict levels.”
Meanwhile, prospective homeowners are preparing for the launch of the government’s Your First Home scheme, which aims to give a helping hand to first-time buyers who do not have the luxury of being able to call on the “bank of mum and dad”.
The scheme involves a government-backed equity loan worth 20% of the purchase price, with the buyer having to put down a minimum deposit of only 2.5%, which meanings taking out a standard mortgage for just 77.5% of the property’s value.
The scheme applies only to England and new-build flats or houses. News of its launch has already increased the share price of housebuilders including Persimmon, Barratt Redrow, Taylor Wimpey, Crest Nicholson and Vistry.

Russia’s Supercam S180 UAV upgraded based on special op experience — company
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:57:16 UTC
15:57:16 KST

BAKU, October 1. /TASS/. Russia’s latest high-speed Supercam S180 reconnaissance unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is continuously upgraded based on experience gained in the special military operation in Ukraine, Spokeswoman for the Unmanned Systems Group Yekaterina Zgirovskaya told TASS.
"The special military operation realities require continuous modernization. In such rapidly evolving circumstances, it’s impossible to build a drone once and fly it for four years: the situation changes at an incredible pace, requiring ever-new solutions and the implementation of new ideas. We constantly receive requests from unmanned systems troops and other units regarding what they would like to add or improve in the drones. The software requires constant updates as a minimum," Zgirovskaya stated during the ADEX 2026 International Defense Exhibition in Baku.
According to her, this is due to the constantly changing situation in the special military operation zone. "This doesn’t mean that the equipment we’ve developed is not efficient, it means that the enemy is always on the alert and quickly finds ways to counter it. That’s why we need to vary and adapt our approaches to solving the same task, as new ‘unknowns’ keep emerging." This is how the Supercam S350 was developed, until it became clear that there were missions that could no longer be carried out with maximum efficiency using it and its versions. We found a solution - we created the Supercam S180, while the S350 is being repurposed for other functions, such as data relay," said Zgirovskaya.
She emphasized that the S180, not the S350, is now being used in high risk areas. "But its development didn’t stop at creation, and it is getting upgraded, because on the front lines, new scenarios arise almost every day, and this provides an excellent opportunity to verify the correctness of various solutions and receive direct recommendations ‘from the field’ on what to improve and what to add - the main thing is to listen," the Unmanned Systems Group representative stressed.
The ADEX 2026 exhibition is taking place from September 30 to October 2.

Unia draws up complaint against Ghent University researcher Nathan Cofnas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:54:30 UTC
15:54:30 KST

Unia is preparing legal action against Nathan Cofnas, the controversial researcher at Ghent University. Unia is an independent Belgian public body that combats discrimination and promotes equal opportunities. According to the organisation, Cofnas ranks people on the basis of their origin or skin colour and uses scientific arguments to justify this. The organisation claims that as a result he may be in breach of Belgian anti-racism legislation and the UN convention against racial discrimination. Unia intends to take the matter to court.
Unia draws up complaint against Ghent University researcher Nathan Cofnas
Nathan Cofnas is an American philosopher who works as a researcher at Ghent University. He describes himself as a ‘racial realist’. His statements and research have been a source of controversy for some time.
In August, Ghent University suspended Cofnas as a precautionary measure. The university also initiated disciplinary proceedings. This followed an online article in which Cofnas accused Jason Arday (pictured below), one of Britain’s few black professors, of plagiarism. Arday subsequently resigned from Cambridge University. Shortly afterwards, he was found dead.
Debate on academic freedom
The case has also sparked a debate about the freedom of academics to conduct research and express their opinions. Around 800 academics signed an open letter, arguing that Ghent University should not have punished Cofnas for his statements.
Ghent University’s rector, Petra De Sutter, defended the university’s approach stating academic freedom remains important to Ghent University.
Ghent University’s disciplinary proceedings are still ongoing. The legal action being taken by Unia is separate from this.

Herzog recommends the Presidential Medal of Civilian Valor to the four Israelis who helped save Flydubai flight FZ1073 and its captain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:51:23 UTC
15:51:23 KST

Herzog recommends Presidential Medal of Civilian Valor for five Israelis who helped save Flydubai flight FZ1073
Herzog said, "At a time when the lives of so many people were in danger, you acted without hesitation, with courage, resourcefulness, and extraordinary mutual responsibility"
President Isaac Herzog spoke with five Israelis, Yaniv Hayun, Dr. Shota Musayev, Zvika Manes, Tali Manes, and Asaf Rajuan, who acted with what his office called extraordinary heroism during a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Israel. The incident occurred after one pilot stabbed the other and the aircraft began losing altitude.
According to the President's statement, after Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar fought the attacker and opened the cockpit door, Tali Manes, Zvika's wife, raised the alarm about the incident. Hayun, Manes and Rajuan rushed into the cockpit and 'put themselves at risk' to subdue the attacker, with Hayun helping stabilize the aircraft's controls.
After the assailant was subdued, Dr. Musayev provided life-saving medical treatment to the critically injured pilot, helping stabilize him until the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Herzog told the four men, "At a time when the lives of so many people were in danger, you acted without hesitation, with courage, resourcefulness, and extraordinary mutual responsibility. You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disaster. Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society. I am proud of you, and I thank you on behalf of the State of Israel."
The president said he intends to bring their story before the advisory committee for the President's Medal for Civilian Bravery and recommend that all four receive the award. Herzog also extended gratitude to Captain Machchhar, saying his "determination and actions enabled the neutralization of the threat and saved many lives."
Dr. Shota Musayev described the incident to the president, saying, "It was a very difficult incident, and we truly were saved." He added, It wasn't only my heroism. Everyone who was there and came near the cockpit was part of it. We were all heroes. All the passengers were heroes. We supported one another on the plane and also when we arrived in Saudi Arabia, and we took care of each other as we should. It shows our strength as a people."
Yaniv Hayun told the president, "Everyone was so moved and welcomed me with great emotion. I'm glad we're here, glad it's all behind us, and very grateful for the call and the warm embrace. It's truly moving."
Asaf Rajuan recalled the moment, saying, "It was an extraordinary incident. We felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didn't know who to turn to. But it was all instinct: to survive, to save the family, the people, and the children."
The President's Medal for Civilian Bravery was established by Herzog during the war to honor citizens who acted with extraordinary heroism, risking their own lives out of a sense of mutual responsibility to save others. The award is granted following a case review and recommendation by a presidential advisory committee and has previously been given to Israelis who distinguished themselves, including several who acted heroically on October 7 in the Gaza Envelope area.

‘You are isolated and alone’: European diplomat warns Israel of ‘tsunami of sanctions’ after elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:50:20 UTC
15:50:20 KST

A senior European diplomat, who asked to remain anonymous, warned that anger in Europe toward Israel has reached unprecedented levels.
“There has never been a government anywhere in the world that has caused such serious damage to its country in such a short time. It is simply a destruction of value,” the diplomat said.
He criticized what he described as a failure to act against settler violence.
“After three years of us talking about settler violence, nothing is happening. And not only is nothing happening, the situation is only getting worse — and settlement construction is also intensifying,” he said.
“It is unclear why Israel is not acting against the violence, which is causing it so much damage,” he added. “It is already obvious. Your prime minister says it is only a handful of people, but everyone knows it is not really just a handful. And if it is a handful, why not arrest them? The great IDF cannot arrest a handful of people? Thousands of Palestinians are being displaced from their homes. Terrible things are happening in the West Bank with the consent of, or a blind eye from, your government. What did you think, that your friends would sit quietly and allow this to happen?”
The senior diplomat continued: “Israel is more isolated than ever. You are alone. You saw it in the steps taken by Britain and 12 other countries against the settlements. The United States did not condemn them. Settler violence is causing you enormous damage. You are losing legitimacy.
“Countries in the European Union did not want to impose sanctions because of the elections in Israel, but the day after the elections they will rush to do so. Expect a tsunami of sanctions. If the current situation continues, Israel is on a sure path to becoming an apartheid state like South Africa.”
The diplomat also warned that what he called Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar’s extreme retaliatory measures against Britain and the Netherlands were provoking anger and would be met with a strong response.
“You do not understand your situation. Our ability to harm you is far greater than your ability to harm us,” he said. “You need us for your security much more than we need you for ours. There are many steps we can take in response. You are isolated, you are small, you are alone.”
He also accused Israel of ingratitude toward Britain, which he said has paid a heavy price for helping defend Israel physically. British pilots shot down about 100 drones during the war, he said, yet Israel did not even consult Britain before announcing sanctions against it.
The diplomat noted that Israel gave one month’s notice that it would close the British Consulate in Jerusalem, which employs about 30 diplomats, a move he said was inconsistent with accepted diplomatic practice.
“Russia, when it closed the British Consulate in St. Petersburg, gave the British four months to prepare,” he said. “Closing a diplomatic mission within a month is an unacceptable step and it will not pass without a response.”
That one-month period is due to end Oct. 8, after which Britain could respond to the move. So far, it has not announced what its response will be. Behind the scenes, the two countries are holding contacts aimed at lowering tensions.
The senior diplomat expressed concern that Israel was taking harsh punitive measures against European countries for domestic political reasons, in an effort to appeal to its political base rather than out of concern for its own security.
He concluded: “Israelis must wake up and understand how much damage the current government is causing you. [National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich are running wild and Netanyahu is not in control of the situation.”

Life in exile: Russian singer Monetochka thought Vilnius would be a stopover. Four years later, she says she may stay forever.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:50:12 UTC
15:50:12 KST

Life in exile: Russian singer Monetochka thought Vilnius would be a stopover. Four years later, she says she may stay forever.
First things first: We love those questionnaires kids fill out at school. Second: despite today’s grim circumstances in Europe, we’re curious about how emigrants from Russia are settling into their new homes. We put the two together and concocted a series in which people who interest us at Meduza will talk about their lives since leaving Russia. We hope these stories will offer you some support. Singer Monetochka, who has lived in Vilnius since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, filled out our first questionnaire. She also wrote an anthem for this wave of emigration, so she gets to go first. (Thanks, Liza!)
What’s your name?
Liza.
Where do you live, and how long have you lived there?
I’ve lived in Vilnius since the start of the war. It just so happened that I moved here. I thought Vilnius would be a stopover, but I ended up loving the city so much that I decided to stay — maybe forever.
Four years in, I’ve come to feel comfortable here. Maybe even more comfortable than I felt in Moscow, where I didn’t live as long. I’m quite the food expert — I can recommend restaurants, cafés, shops, and markets in Vilnius for whatever you’re in the mood for. I know where to see a children’s play in Russian and which playgrounds and concert venues are the best in town.
I often ride my bike during the day, with the kids in the trailer, taking them around the city. Vilnius is a very green, bike-friendly city. I love that, even though it’s small, there’s always some new corner to discover.
Still, I can’t say I feel like I “belong” in Vilnius. I think I’ll never feel like I “belong” anywhere again, except in my own home or with my friends, family, and listeners. Home, for me, is the world I can now take with me.
What do you love most about your new country?
Every year, Vilnius hosts a big fair called “Kaziukas.” I always look forward to it and wait until the fair to buy the things on my wish list. Shopping there is much more fun than ordering things online or going to a regular store. They sell everything: food, clothes, dishes, health supplements, and children’s toys. Everything is tied to the traditional crafts and customs of Lithuania and nearby countries — craftspeople come from Latvia, for example. You can buy an unusual folk instrument or traditional clothing there.
I’ve bought lots of things I love there: wonderful dried fruit and berries that I eat all year, mustard oil, and ceramic plates. At every “Kaziukas,” I make sure to buy at least one little plate. Whenever I see it throughout the year, it reminds me of the market. Actually, I count my years in Lithuania by how many “Kaziukas” fairs I’ve been to. I moved to the city right when one of the fairs was happening.
I don’t think my kids know what they like about Lithuania. They’ve never been to Russia, so they have nothing to compare it to — they were born in Lithuania and have spent their whole lives here. And my husband is happy wherever I’m happy.
What was hardest to adjust to in your new country?
Getting used to a new language and making new friends wasn’t easy. Life in Vilnius also moves at a completely different pace than in Moscow. Lithuania is a very calm country, with an unhurried way of life. I adjusted to the pace in Vilnius pretty quickly, and now I have lots of good friends here. It turns out that such a peaceful place makes it easier to be creative and balance work and life. After a busy tour, it’s the perfect place.
What’s your favorite place in your new city?
Kalvarijos Market. It’s an ordinary market where you can chat with everyone, haggle, find out about seasonal fruit and vegetables, or ask a local chef for a recipe or cooking advice while he’s shopping for his restaurant. It’s one of the places where people recognize me now just as a regular customer, without knowing my music.
I’ve made friends with the people at the butcher’s shop and the women at the vegetable and berry stalls. Kalvarijos Market also has the best pirozhki in the world. I don’t know who makes them, but right next to my favorite butcher’s shop, there’s a little shop that sells nothing but cheese pirozhki, meat pirozhki, and broth. I usually get a little cup of that broth with a cheese pirozhok — I enjoy that combination so much that I’d go to the market just for it.
I go to the market once a week, sometimes even more often. My friends and I go together, so it’s also a way to catch up and spend time with them. I often go with my neighbor, or with other friends after Pilates or hanging out at a café. Sometimes we just decide on the spur of the moment that we need to go.
My friends and I feel like real hunters when we go to the market. I love that — it’s exciting. You can’t just buy whatever you need there. If you want the tastiest produce, for example, you have to wait until it’s in season or a new delivery comes in. And if you want eggplant or unusual, delicious tomatoes at a good price, you have to get to the market early.
What’s your favorite local food?
My favorite food in Lithuania is šaltibarščiai — Lithuanian cold borscht. It’s a really beautiful, delicious, healthy dish. I love how that ice-cold pink kefir goes with the hot potatoes that usually come with the soup. It’s incredibly good.
My kids love šaltibarščiai too. It’s one of the few healthy dishes they like. Lots of places make good šaltibarščiai. I think the best thing to do is come to Lithuania for the cold borscht festival, pick up a map there, and try a few places.
My personal favorite is the šaltibarščiai at “Neringa.” It’s a famous restaurant in Vilnius that Joseph Brodsky loved too. He even dedicated a poem to the restaurant, titled simply “Café Neringa.” He didn’t mention my favorite soup in it, though. I’ve tried making soups at home too, but mine don’t taste very good.
Time departs in Vilnius through a café door accompanied by sounds of clinking forks and spoons, while space screws up its eyes from booze the night before and stares at Time’s retreating spine.
A crimson circle, its interior vanished, now hangs moored in utter stillness over roof-tiles and the Adam’s apple sharpens, quite as if the whole face had been transformed into a profile.
Obeying commands like Aladdin’s lamp, a waitress decked out in a cambric halter saunters about with legs so lately clamped around the neck of a local footballer.
Translation by Tomas Ventslova, The New York Review, 1978
Besides cold borscht, I love all the dairy products in Lithuania. The sour cream, tvorog [fresh curd cheese], milk, eggs, and cream here are so good. Their quality and taste just blew me away. I love going to markets, but I mostly buy meat, fruit, and vegetables there. I think the best dairy products are in regular grocery stores.
Have you taken up any new hobbies since emigrating?
I got into Pilates. I like it because I go with my friends. And I’ve gotten a little older — my body needs regular workouts and stretching. Pilates is a great way to get all of that.
I have a favorite studio and a favorite instructor. If he’s on vacation, I just skip classes. He’s Lithuanian, he tells funny jokes, and he really looks after us: he knows whose back hurts, whose arm hurts, and how to adjust the springs for each of us. He works around our needs so we don’t push ourselves too hard.
At first, I tried going to Pilates alone. Then I brought a couple of friends, and then it turned out some of my other friends were going to a different instructor. So little by little, we all got together and settled on the days and times we’d go. And we decided that after every class, we’d have coffee and a delicious breakfast at a café.
The café is an essential part of the ritual, and breakfast often lasts longer than Pilates itself. We go to the same place every time — my hobbies in Lithuania are about feeling grounded and calm, so I like going back to the same places.
Besides Pilates, I’ve started making a big deal of my birthdays. I never used to, but now I start organizing them six months in advance, planning how the day will go and what we’ll do. Guests come from different countries. This year, I got everyone together at a café, we had appetizers, and they gave me presents.
After that, we took a bus to a stable — the guests didn’t know we were going there. All I’d told them was to wear comfortable athletic clothes in the style of British aristocrats going hunting. We rode horses, brushed them, and relaxed. The kids rode ponies and brushed them. Then we went to an outdoor space by the water, where we finished with dinner and a competition. I always come up with a big quiz that the guests enjoy taking part in, and they really try hard. I come up with different categories, with questions worth 300, 500, and 800 points. For example, I did ballet for 10 years, so I include a category about that.
I try to make sure the questions aren’t all about me. Sometimes I make categories about my guests — someone might get lucky and get a question about themselves or a friend. It ends up being something like the TV show “Svoya igra” (“Your Own Game”). Making quizzes is a hobby of mine now. Friends sometimes even ask me to make them for other people’s birthdays, New Year’s, and other celebrations.
Have you managed to make new friends? How?
I’ve grown closer to friends I already had. They were already close friends, and now they’re almost like family. I can’t live without them. I mean the Alekseyev family: Vanya Noize, his wife, and their kids. I adore all of them, and I’m rooting for them in everything they do. Now it’s hard when they leave town for a month — I don’t feel right without them.
I also have friends who live in Russia and friends who moved to other countries. I keep in touch with everyone, and now when I plan trips, I try to arrange them so I can see my friends too. I’ve adjusted and realized that you can stay friends even if you live in different countries. You work around each other’s schedules and remember to keep in touch — that’s a new skill for me. We also spend time with couples who have children here in Vilnius. I’ve noticed that kids and pets help you meet people. We’ve met lots of people through preschool.
I’ve also become really good friends with my neighbor across the hall, who moved here from Belarus. We like playing backgammon in the evenings. I’m great at making friends with neighbors — and I always get lucky with them. With neighbors, you can take your rugs to the dry cleaner together, go to the hardware store for flowerpots, go swimming in a lake in the morning, or get to an urgent care clinic when someone breaks a bone. My neighbor and I do all of that together. For me, it’s a new kind of friendship, built around doing things together and sharing everyday experiences rather than special occasions.
I’m working on getting my driver’s license. Recently, I went to sign up for driving school and asked my neighbor to come with me because I was scared to go alone. I kept thinking: what if they don’t understand me, what if I don’t know the language well enough, what if something goes wrong? So I recommend taking friends along on outings like that.
Do you have enough money to live in your new country? How do you deal with financial problems?
We considered moving to other countries, and one of the things that stopped us was the cost of living elsewhere. We’re used to Moscow prices, so we’re comfortable financially in Vilnius.
Our new home also gives me a sense of calm and security. When we first got here, we rented a place before we really knew Lithuania. We didn’t pick the best location, so later we were much more careful about choosing a neighborhood. What matters most to me is that our neighborhood is very safe. We have a safe courtyard and a safe entrance to our building.
What are you doing to learn the new language?
I took language classes for a long time after moving here. I learned enough Lithuanian to get by: I can pay for things at a store and tell a taxi driver where to go. Then I stopped taking classes because work got really busy and I had my second child. But I hope to get back to learning Lithuanian soon. I’m really looking forward to it, because sometimes I don’t know enough. At the hospital, for example — I don’t have the vocabulary to explain things to the doctors.
I speak Lithuanian every day, but usually it’s just short conversations. A couple of times, people have complimented me — they said I spoke really well. I really do try hard, and even if I’m not sure exactly what some words mean, I try to use them so I can learn through practice. But I probably don’t know enough to pass a language exam right now.
Sometimes we have funny conversations. Once, a Lithuanian plumber we’d worked with tried to ask me about the connection between the Russian words “golub” [pigeon] and “golubets” [stuffed cabbage roll], which made me laugh. His Russian isn’t perfect — and I really enjoy learning about Lithuanian from him, while he enjoys learning about Russian from us.
If you have children, would you like them to make this country their home?
It doesn’t matter to me. I want my kids to build their lives however they like. Maybe they’ll want to settle in some other city or country.
My kids are already starting to ask interesting questions, like “What’s this place called Russia?” and “When will I go there?” My mom still lives there, and sometimes she comes to Lithuania to look after her grandchildren. She brings us souvenirs and treats, and Nina [Monetochka’s daughter] asks when she’ll finally get to visit her grandma.
I tell her that soon Grandma and Grandpa will be able to take her with them — she’ll visit and see what this place called Russia is like. Nina gets mad and says, “I don’t want to go with Grandma, I want to go to Russia with you.”
Of course, I can’t explain to her yet that I can’t go there. Especially given how much she and Petya [Monetochka’s son] love “playing cops.” In their game, there are the police and someone they call the “bad guy.” The police catch the “bad guy” every time and put him in jail. I don’t think Nina is ready for a conversation about how her mom is also, in a way, a “bad guy.”
In Lithuania, the kids go to an English-speaking preschool, where they also learn Lithuanian. But we speak Russian at home. For now, they’re more comfortable speaking it, although they speak English fluently.
How do you cope with intense homesickness?
First, I don’t hold my feelings in — I let them out. I might tear up when I think about my grandma or sing lines about her at a concert. I don’t push the sadness away or try to be the most successful, independent emigrant who’s got everything figured out. I don’t want to bottle up my feelings and have them come back to bite me later.
But I’ve realized that my path is to create meaning on my own. Rather than waiting for the meaning in my life to come from somewhere, I make it myself. I have children, make friends, stay grounded, live this life, and love it. I try to spend more time living in the present than remembering the past, dreaming, or comparing myself to others, including my past self.
Of course, I still miss people. My grandma did come to visit recently, though. She’s elderly and can’t travel much anymore, but we managed to bring her here — she saw the grandchildren, and it was great. But I miss being able to spend the night at her house, on her perfectly clean, ironed, beautiful old sheets, the kind you can’t buy in stores anymore. She’s had them since Soviet times, and they’re always so perfectly crisp. I miss being able to have tea at her place from the Soviet crystal cups I remember from childhood.
I often feel nostalgic and miss the past. When I moved from Yekaterinburg to Moscow, I missed home a lot then too. I’m getting older, and I miss what it was like to be a carefree teenager. I don’t think it’s a bad feeling — it’s just there, that’s all.
Do you feel like you’re losing your connection to your homeland? Is it possible to keep it?
I haven’t felt like I’m losing my connection to my homeland. I think Russia is a very big, complicated country. I know for sure that my people are there — people who listen to my music and fly to my concerts in Belgrade or Chișinău. They send me greetings from a bootleg premiere of “Spider-Man” in Russia, where the film doesn’t include my music. But they reassure me and post photos from the theater along with my song to show their support.
Of course, there’s a part of Russia I’ve deliberately distanced myself from. Everything connected to war, shows of force, and imperialism. But there are things no one could ever take out of me — things I love dearly and keep safe inside me. I don’t do anything special to keep that connection. I just keep being myself.
I was born in Yekaterinburg, and first and foremost, I’m a girl from the Urals, much more than I’m a Moscow girl or a Vilnius girl. I felt like I was losing touch with my roots back when I moved to Moscow. That move was hard for me, and I wrote a lot of songs about it. But I found my own Ural backbone somewhere inside me — and now it’s with me forever. It was always there, but I didn’t know it before. Then people started telling me I had a strong Ural accent. I immediately felt proud of it and didn’t try to get rid of it.
Then I watched other people from my region and noticed that we have similar personalities. We make decisions in similar ways. And that’s when I realized that no one can ever take my homeland out of me, even if I leave it for a while.
There are also tangible things that remind me of home, like the crunchy bread snacks “Tri Korochki” and “Kirieshki.” I get hold of them any way I can. I track them down and ask friends to bring them from Russia. Now I can have a bag of horseradish-flavored “Kirieshki” or caviar-flavored “Tri Korochki” whenever I want.
Are you happy living abroad?
Yes. Almost always, except for unpleasant moments — like today’s staff meeting, which was really stressful. Or when I didn’t plan my day well and ended up somewhere inconvenient with crying kids and no spare diapers. The rest of the time, I’m happy. I have a perfect husband, really awesome kids, and work I’ve devoted my life to. That’s what makes me happiest.
How do you imagine coming home?
For some reason, I sometimes picture myself leaving the airport, crossing the border. I try to imagine what I’d feel at that moment. Would I cry? Would I kiss the airport floor? Fall to my knees? Who would be there to meet me? I don’t know why I have these fantasies, but they’re there in my head.
If I’m ever able to return, I want my listeners to be there to meet me. I want to hug and kiss them. I’m sure I’ll cry.

KABUL, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- At least 18 fuel tankers were fully engulfed in flames and three others partially damaged when a major fire erupted at the Islam Qala border crossing in western Afghanistan's Herat province on Wednesday evening, the National Disaster Management Authority announced on Thursday.

Latvia’s State Security Service (VDD), in cooperation with the Defence Intelligence and Security Service (MIDD), detained a couple on the 28th of June on suspicion of illegally gathering information about Latvia’s defence sector on behalf of Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU, the VDD reports.
Based on information provided by MIDD, criminal proceedings against the detained Latvian citizens were launched on the 27th of June under Section 85, Paragraph One of the Criminal Law for collecting and transferring classified and other information to a foreign intelligence service on its instructions.
Such offences are punishable by imprisonment for a term of one to ten years.
The investigation established that the individuals obtained and passed information to the GRU about Latvia’s defence system, the activities of NATO allied forces and various forms of support provided to Ukraine.
Among other things, 
the individuals allegedly obtained intelligence about a National Armed Forces aviation base,
radar systems and the movement of military air transport.
At the GRU’s request, one of the suspects carried out “reconnaissance and aerial photography of the Ādaži military base using a small private aircraft”.
In the military context, reconnaissance is defined as the visual observation of terrain and enemy defences ahead of combat operations.
In addition, the suspects allegedly carried out activities intended to support potential reconnaissance and sabotage groups operating in Latvia.
On the day the suspects were detained, 
the VDD, in cooperation with MIDD, carried out criminal procedural measures at three locations linked to them
 in Riga and Ādaži Municipality.
During the searches, investigators seized a large quantity of various data storage devices, as well as documents and notes. The contents of the items seized during the searches are currently undergoing detailed examination.
Both suspects have been remanded in custody as a preventive measure.
The VDD, in cooperation with MIDD, is continuing the investigation.

Ahead of October's EU-Canada summit, both sides are considering a partnership beyond CETA and €130 billion in annual trade. Nothing is agreed on financial services, and the new "associate member" tier has no legal definition.
With tariffs, export controls and politics turning trade into a geopolitical lever, the EU seems to be shopping for partners it can count on. Canada, a like-minded economy already tied to the bloc by a free-trade agreement, is pitching itself as one.
Ahead of the EU-Canada summit at the end of October, the two sides are discussing a partnership beyond the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).
Prime Minister Mark Carney proposed exploring an integrated market for financial services, alongside cooperation on payments, strategic minerals, energy, AI, and defence production. Nothing has been agreed on financial passports, mutual recognition of licences, or bank access.
Fabian Zuleeg, Chief Executive and Chief Economist at the European Policy Centre, says the summit must deliver more than words. "So by the time we get to the summit, we should really be concrete," he says.
A trade order under strain
The EU's problem is dependence. It relies on the US for technology and security, on Chinese supply chains for critical inputs, and on outside suppliers for energy, at a time when trade access is increasingly used as leverage.
Canada offers economic gains, Zuleeg says, in areas like financial markets and technologies CETA does not fully cover. "The more important argument is political, and it's geopolitical."
The existing EU-Canada partnership is CETA, provisionally applied since 2017. It removed 98% of tariff lines immediately, rising to 99% by 2024. Trade in goods and services reached €130 billion in 2025, up 80% from €72.1 billion in 2016, according to Commission figures.
But that model has run its course. Erik van de Merel, chief economist at the European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) and associate professor at the Université Libre de Bruxelles, notes that "tariffs among developed countries and between Canada and the European Union are fairly low."
The next gains lie elsewhere, "in the area of services, technology collaboration, all these sort of intangible activities that are important for future growth," he says. Negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement began in March 2026.
What each side wants
For the EU, the appeal is security of supply. Canada says it holds deposits of more than 34 critical minerals and is a leading producer of 10 considered essential to the energy transition. Europe needs them for batteries, grids and defence.
"We are very dependent, in particular on China, at the moment," Zuleeg says. Reducing that reliance, he argues, matters less for prices than for keeping European industry running during a dispute. Cheaper energy is possible too, he adds, but not overnight.
For Ottawa, the logic is diversification. The US takes roughly seven in ten Canadian exports, while the EU was Canada's second-largest goods-trade partner in 2024 with 7.9% of its global goods trade. Canada also wants easier access to European customers and investors for its clean-energy, mining, AI, and defence firms. Canadian pension funds could co-finance mineral-processing and infrastructure projects.
Defence is already a test case. In June 2026, Canada became the first non-European country included in the EU's €150 billion SAFE defence instrument, a possible template for sector-by-sector integration.
The rule-taker question
The hardest issue is regulation. Canada wants better access to European banking, insurance, and professional services such as law, accountancy, and architecture.
Van de Merel expects the EU to ask for something in return. "The new rules that we are going to develop, to some extent, you would have to take them over," he says. If Canada wanted to set its own banking and professional rules without European oversight or harmonisation, he argues, it would have to think again because deeper market integration is a core EU goal.
Alignment, he says, is the test of whether the project works. He adds that "one has to have regulatory alignment and I think that's going to be really key and a challenge whether this is going to be a success or not." It will not be quick. The EU's single market in services remains unfinished after decades, so a newcomer seeking the same benefits faces a long catch-up.
Zuleeg is less worried about Canada becoming a mere rule-taker. Iceland follows single-market rules because it sits in the European Economic Area, he notes, but Canada would not be joining the single market. In his view, it would keep a distinct voice, for example on foreign policy. He doubts the deal would require treaty change and considers "associate membership" a misnomer. A tailored association agreement under Article 217 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU looks the more likely legal route.
Practical steps are already under way. In March 2026, a joint EU-Canada committee agreed to pursue regulatory alignment on motor vehicles and conformity assessment and to widen mutual recognition in pharmaceuticals.
The politics could still bite. In Ottawa, the question is how much EU regulation Canada can accept without a vote in EU institutions. In Brussels, candidate countries undergoing lengthy reforms may ask why Canada should get privileged access. Van de Merel is also watching the UK, which could object if Canada obtains terms it never had after Brexit.
Limits and risks
The idea should not be oversold. Canada cannot replace China's role in manufacturing and mineral processing or the scale of the US economy. Mines, refineries, and ports take years to build, and the Atlantic is a logistical hurdle. Canada's exposure to Washington means a US–Canada crisis could spill into its production and investment.
Then there is CETA itself. As of mid-September 2026, ten member states, including France, Italy, Poland, Belgium and Ireland, had still not ratified it, so its investment-protection provisions are not in force. The EU is discussing an unprecedented new tier while its flagship trade deal with Canada remains only partly ratified.
Van de Merel warns that without institutions behind it, the initiative could fizzle. "Otherwise it's just an idea that is very symbolic and without any sort of political institutional consequences," he says.

India approves $19 billion green-grid expansion plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:43:01 UTC
15:43:01 KST

India approves $19 billion green-grid expansion plan
India has approved a $19 billion expansion of its green-energy grid to remove the transmission constraints that are holding back the country from fully utilizing its fast-growing solar and wind power generation capacity, especially during peak hours.
The Green Energy Corridor Phase III (GEC-III) will enable the country’s green grid to carry up to 135 gigawatts (GW) of renewable power, and deploy 50 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage. It is targeted for completion by fiscal 2032-33.
GW is a measure of generation capacity, while GWh measures the total amount of energy produced or consumed over time.
Nearly 21GW, or about 9% of India’s installed renewable capacity, is currently connected through temporary grid arrangements while awaiting dedicated transmission infrastructure. This infrastructure gap restrains the transmission of around 12GW of power to users during periods of peak solar generation.
Grid operators had to restrict 8,133GWh of solar electricity during the April-June period, when peak power demand reached a record 270GW, because of these transmission constraints and the need to maintain grid stability, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy told India’s parliament.
GEC-III will pair the additional transmission capacity with Battery Energy Storage Systems, enabling the stored renewable electricity to be released during periods of higher demand. This will help to reduce peak-hour power restrictions and meet demand outside solar-generation hours.
New Delhi currently has about 8.66GWh of installed large-scale battery storage, against a projected requirement of 236GWh by 2031-32, according to Power Ministry data.
India crossed 300GW of installed non-fossil power capacity in July, with these now accounting for more than 54% of the country’s installed generation capacity. New Delhi is targeting 500GW of non-fossil power by 2030.

Tartu plans new pedestrian and cycling bridge

Unknown Publisher

Tartu plans new pedestrian and cycling bridge
The Tartu city government plans by the year 2030 to build the Tuglase light‑traffic bridge and the bicycle paths of the extension of Ujula tänav, which would form a bicycle‑path network connecting city districts.
The budget for the Tuglase bridge is calculated as €12 million and for the construction of new bicycle paths on Ujula tänav €1 million.
For financing the construction, support is requested to the extent of 70 percent from the climate ministry's measure for promoting a sustainable mobility environment. The construction of the light‑traffic bridge depends on receiving external funding and on its amount. For building the bridge and the bicycle path, the city wants also use money that was intended for bicycle paths on Lai and Tähe tänav.
The Tuglase light‑traffic bridge is planned on the extension of Tuglase tänav, and on the other side of the Emajõgi river it will be connected with the Ujula light‑traffic paths. The bridge is intended only for pedestrians and for bicycle and scooter riders. According to the initial plan, the new bridge is about 100 meters long and has a footpath and a bicycle path, which continues on the Supilinn side through the alley of Tuglase tänav and is connected with the recently completed main network of bicycle paths. The planned bridge would not disturb movement on the riverbanks nor interrupt the functioning of green and blue corridors.
Ujula tänav will be extended from the sandstone outcrop for 800 meters toward Kvissentali as a two‑way roadway, with footpaths and bicycle paths built at its edge.
Building the new bridge is necessary, considering both the continued growth of Kvissentali and the planning of the Uus‑Tähtvere residential area, said Tartu city government. After the development is completed, 1600–2000 new residents will live in the Uus‑Tähtvere area, and 22 new apartment buildings are being added to the growing Kvissentali area. When the new buildings are completed, the number of Kvissentali residents will increase to an estimated 3000–3500 people.
Without an additional river crossing, traffic load would increasingly concentrate in the city center, creating extra burden for the already car‑heavy bridges and streets.
The project for extending Ujula tänav improves the currently insufficient and indirect connection of the Kvissentali district with other districts of Tartu and creates better opportunities for using different modes of movement.

UK house prices post sharpest fall since May as borrowing costs rise

Unknown Publisher

15:39:48 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
UK house prices recorded their sharpest monthly decline since May in September, as rising mortgage costs and pressure on household budgets weighed on the housing market.
Average home prices fell 0.2% to £274,251 ($363,523), according to Nationwide Building Society figures. Economists had expected prices to remain unchanged.
The decline was the fourth in five months and the second-largest monthly fall this year, following a 0.6% decrease in May as prospective buyers began feeling the effects of the Middle East conflict.
The latest figures followed a modest recovery in August, when Nationwide reported a 0.2% monthly increase and annual price growth of 1.6%. The average property price that month stood at £275,465.
Mortgage rates approaching 6% are putting renewed pressure on demand, Bloomberg reported. Households also face higher energy bills from Thursday, with a further increase expected in January, potentially reducing the money available for deposits and mortgage repayments.
Savings accumulated by households and the government’s summer cost-of-living measures had helped support the market earlier in the year, according to the report.
In its August assessment, Nationwide said geopolitical uncertainty and the Middle East conflict were pushing up energy prices and market interest rates, contributing to subdued housing activity.
The lender said affordability had been improving because earnings were growing faster than house prices, although higher mortgage rates had offset some of those gains.
Nationwide’s chief economist, Robert Gardner, said a recovery in activity would depend on the energy shock easing and confidence returning, particularly if market interest rates moved back toward their levels before the conflict.

Finland rolls out new yellow-green car sticker — but do drivers know what it means?
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:37:48 EEST
15:37:48 KST

As of 1 October, 17-year-old drivers in Finland must display a yellow-green, hexagonal sticker on the rear of their vehicle.
The sticker indicates to other road users that the driver of the vehicle is under 18 years old, and its use is intended to improve road safety as well as to help police enforce new laws affecting younger drivers.
Since May this year, 17-year-olds have been prohibited from driving between midnight and 5am — but enforcement of that regulation has been difficult up to this point.
The introduction of the sticker stems from reforms to the Driving Licence Act, aimed at reducing traffic accidents involving young drivers.
The standard minimum age for obtaining a car driver's license in Finland is 18, but 17-year-olds can get a license under certain circumstances if they have an apporved reason — such as commuting to school or work.
A steadily increasing number of 17-year-olds have applied for and received their licenses in recent years after a law change introduced in 2018 loosened the terminology around the granting of the special permits.
This in turn led to a dramatic increase in the number of road accidents and fatalities involving younger drivers, with the Finnish Road Safety Council noting at the end of last year that the number of young people killed in traffic accidents in 2025 was three times higher than in 2024.
Sticker's meaning not yet widely known
Despite the fact that displaying the new sticker becomes mandatory from 1 October, many people in Finland may be unaware of what it signifies.
An informal poll taken by Yle on the streets of Seinäjoki this week found that a majority of people could not accurately say what the new sticker means.
Younger drivers interviewed by Yle also expressed concern that the requirement to display the new sticker could make them the targets of "bullying" in road traffic.
Failure to display the sticker during the day and evening could lead to a fine of 100 euros, while 17-year-olds caught driving between midnight and 5am could face a ban.

NEW DELHI: SpiceJet, the Gurugram-based budget carrier and former employer of Captain Smit Machchhar, on Thursday praised the pilot after he was stabbed by his co-pilot aboard an Israel-bound flight but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and overpower the attacker.Chairman and Managing Director Ajay Singh said that "all of India and SpiceJet" is "incredibly proud of him.""I was incredibly proud to know of this, but this is the job of a pilot. His job is to protect the lives that have been entrusted to him. And in this case, 180 lives were entrusted to Captain Smit Machchhar, and he did a tremendous job saving and preserving those lives. So really incredibly proud of him. All of SpiceJet is proud of him, and of course, all of India is proud of him," Singh told ANI.
"The first thing that will go through a pilot's mind is preserving lives, saving lives. And remember that in this case, what really saved lives was the fact that he was able to open the door of that cockpit, and let me tell you that the handle which allows that door to be opened is actually on the co-pilot's side. So, it would have needed real courage, after being stabbed, to reach out to the co-pilot side and somehow find a way to unlatch that door.
So the fact that he was able to do it essentially saved those lives because then passengers and other pilots were able to come into the cockpit and help him overpower the co-pilot and fly the plane back," he added.The captain was also able to activate the cockpit door emergency release mechanism, communicate with the crew on board and send an emergency communication signal."The mechanics are that the cabin crew or anybody on the outside can punch a code in that door. But the door still doesn't open. It needs the captain to physically unlock the door. And that unlocking mechanism is actually on the side of the co-pilot. In this case, the co-pilot was actually attacking the captain, and he still managed to reach out and find a way to unlock that door. And that is possibly what saved lives," the SpiceJet chairman and managing director said.
Machchhar, who spent 11 years with SpiceJet, has more than 13 years of commercial aviation experience and has logged 9,750 flying hours, primarily operating Boeing 737 aircraft. He later joined UAE-based airline flydubai, where he currently serves.On Wednesday, the flight was en route from Dubai to Israel's Tel Aviv when Machchhar was stabbed by the co-pilot, reportedly an Omani national. The flight was later diverted to Saudi Arabia's Tabluk, where it made an emergency landing. Around 180 passengers, mostly Israelis, were on board.Machchhar is currently recovering at a hospital in the kingdom and is in stable condition, according to the Indian Embassy in Riyadh.
