Real estate disputes over hidden faults increasingly common and aided by AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:15:00 UTC
15:15:00 KST

Real estate disputes over hidden faults increasingly common and aided by AI
Homebuyers are increasingly filing claims against sellers after closing a deal, a process that has become easier as buyers turn to artificial intelligence rather than lawyers for help.
Real estate experts say claims over hidden defects have become more common. Karlis Kolk, a lawyer and board member at real estate agency Uus Maa, told ERR that people have become more aware of their rights, but that the trend is also linked to the use of artificial intelligence.
"People don't have to turn to a lawyer right away. AI is also being used to draft claims," Kolk explained.
He said some of the most common problems involve neighbors, such as poor sound insulation between walls and excessive noise. Various construction defects, subsidence and inadequate waterproofing also occur.
"Dry rot is another issue and is a common problem in older wooden buildings," Kolk added. "Mold as well, but that is more complicated when it comes to hidden defects because you can't prove exactly when it developed or that it was already there before."
Marko Sults, head of Ehituskaitse Büroo, told ERR's "Vikerhommik" radio show that mold makes people anxious, but even in apartments in newly built developments, ventilation systems or electric underfloor heating are sometimes switched off to save electricity.
If the warranty period, which is typically two years, is then nearing its end and mold has already developed at the joints between walls and floors during that time, the cause is not improper construction methods or mistakes by the developer. Instead, it is purely a problem caused by how the property has been used, something Sults said is very common in Estonia.
"Even though the owner of an apartment or a new house hires us to provide a service, unfortunately, in these cases we have to tell them that this is not the responsibility of the developer or builder," Sults said.
Tidy apartments in unrenovated buildings especially prone to nasty surprises
Sults said the most complicated type of property is a renovated apartment in an unrenovated apartment building. In such cases, the technical solutions may be inappropriate — for example, ventilation may be connected to the wrong shaft or piping may have been installed incorrectly.
The second most common category involves residential buildings that have been renovated in stages over several decades without any documentation being drawn up. In such a building, it is impossible to determine what technical solutions have been used without opening up the structures.
According to Sults, the most expensive problems discovered after a property purchase are related to bathrooms and other wet rooms. A bathroom, shower room or sauna may look aesthetically pleasing during a visual inspection, but the structures cannot be opened up before the transaction to see what is inside.
"In wet rooms, the most common problems we have seen in recent years are inadequate waterproofing and heating and ventilation systems that are not properly balanced," Sults said, adding that mold or moisture damage can develop within a short period of time as a result.
Karlis Kolk noted that when mold has developed due to a buyer's negligence, he has told clients there is no point in settling such a claim because it has no merit.
"Then it is up to the buyer to decide whether to go to court," the lawyer said.
Good idea to mention noisy neighbors in the contract
According to Kolk, sellers are also liable for defects they are unaware of. However, a purchase agreement can include a specific provision stating that the seller is not liable for defects they did not know about, although buyers may not agree to such a provision.
Disputes often arise because sellers may not consider something a defect even though the buyer does. For example, noise that one person finds excessive may not bother someone else at all. Notaries, however, recommend documenting everything that is known in the contract.
"All known defects must be disclosed. If you're in doubt, it's always safer to disclose them because the seller is not liable for anything that has been disclosed. As an extreme example, a contract might state that a property is uninhabitable even though it is actually perfectly habitable, just to avoid claims," Kolk said.
The lawyer added that if he were selling a property himself, he would disclose even the smallest inconveniences, from relations among members of the apartment association to noise from trains, to avoid a later dispute over whether the buyer could really have failed to notice a nearby railroad.
"The more that is documented in the contract, the safer it is for the seller," Kolk said.
Buyers can also commission a pre-purchase inspection to document the condition of the building.
Claims may exceed the purchase price
Claims filed by buyers against sellers over hidden defects can reach or even exceed the property's purchase price. Kolk said such claims can arise, for example, when dry rot is discovered in a wooden house and the building has to be demolished and replaced.
"The court also considers the principle of reasonableness. If a claim is that large, the court can use its discretion to reduce it to a certain amount and grant it in part," Kolk said, adding that the law does not set a limit on the size of such claims.
According to both experts, it is relatively rare for homebuyers to deliberately look for hidden defects in an attempt to recover part of the purchase price.
Sults said people generally do not act in bad faith. Instead, defects in a new home are more likely to go unnoticed at first because buying a home is an emotional process.
"Buying a home is a happy occasion. Imagine I've picked out an apartment or house for myself. I like the location, aesthetically everything is great and beautiful and I'm already planning where to put the furniture, choosing the color of the curtains and measuring where my wardrobe will go. Maybe the property's technical condition simply gets overlooked," he said.
The Uus Maa lawyer recalled one case in which a certified civil engineer inspected an apartment, made notes about subsidence and discussed the need for further assessments. He then bought the apartment, had the assessments carried out and filed a claim against the seller. While that might suggest bad faith, Kolk said it is generally very difficult to make such a determination.
"When a claim is justified, I've always tried to find an out-of-court solution for my clients. Either an agreement is reached for the seller to fix certain defects or the seller pays financial compensation to the buyer who then decides how to remedy the defects," Kolk said.
He said he generally does not recommend going to court because it costs both sides time and money and a dispute can drag on for years, meaning legal costs may ultimately exceed the value of the matter in dispute.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Germany news: Berlin leftists seek to pave way for coalition

Germany news: Berlin leftists seek to pave way for coalition
Published October 1, 2026last updated October 1, 2026
What you need to know
- The Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats (SPD) in Berlin are to test the ground for a possible coalition
- Talks will center on accusations that the Left Party is antisemitic and has links to organized criminality, which it denies
- A fuel tax cut aiming to reduce costs for motorists goes into effect for the second time this year
Here is a rundown of the stories from and about Germany that are hitting the headlines on Thursday, October 1, 2026:
f you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your preferred source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.
Afghans denied entry despite Constitutional Court ruling
The German government has so far not granted entry to any Afghan nationals on a humanitarian list drawn up by the previous government, despite examining more than two dozen individual cases in keeping with a ruling by the Constitutional Court.
In response to a parliamentary question by Left Party politician Clara Bünger, the Interior Ministry said 25 cases had been examined since the court ruling on July 22, but all had been rejected.
After the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan in August 2021, the previous coalition government of Social Democrats (SPD), Greens and Free Democrats (FDP) had promised to grant entry to Afghan nationals who had worked for German institutions there or who were seen as endangered.
The current conservative-led government paused that program in May 2025 and in December 2025, the Interior Ministry rescinded all entry permissions that had been given under the scheme, saying there was "no political interest" in taking the people in.
The Federal Constitutional Court however ruled in July that Germany could not revoke the scheme en masse and that admission requests had to be considered on a case-to-case basis.
Bünger called on the government "to take in the some 500 people still in question immediately and in an uncomplicated manner."
She said the fact that these Afghan nationals had been forced to live for years in fear and uncertainty was unjustifiable.
Poland to extend controls on German border
Poland says it will extend controls along its border with Germany by six months until March 30 next year.
The Polish Interior Ministry said it would also be extending the measure, introduced in July 2025, on the border to Lithuania.
"Border controls are an effective tool for curbing illegal migration. Extending them will make it possible to manage migration pressure and strengthen border security," the ministry said in a statement.
Since the reintroduction of border controls, nearly 1,300 people have been denied entry into the country at the Lithuanian border and nearly 1,200 at the German border, the statement said.
Germany has also had additional border controls in place at all its entry points since September 2024.
The border controls have been imposed even though Poland and Germany are members of the EU's Schengen Area, in which borders are theoretically meant to be open to allow seamless travel between EU members.
Under the Schengen Borders Code (SBC), member states are allowed to only temporarily reintroduce border controls in the case of security threats.
Both Poland and Germany have cited the threat of illegal immigration as having prompted the reinstatement of the controls.
Fuel tax cut goes into force
A three-month fuel tax cut went into effect in Germany at midnight on Wednesday, with motorists now likely to pay prices for gas and diesel that are lower by 16.7 cents (18.9 US cents) per liter in the coming weeks.
Prices before the cut went into effect were well over €2 per liter in most places, with September the most expensive month on record at the pump.
The same measure was introduced in Germany in May and June to give relief to motorists as fuel prices spiral largely as a result of the war in the Middle East.
The tax cut technically applies only to fuel leaving storage facilities or refineries, with gas stations not directly required to lower their prices.
However, prices at most filling stations are expected to fall quickly, as happened in May and June.
Critic of the measure say it reduces incentives to save fuel and will potentially not be passed on in full to all consumers.
Supporters say it is currently the best way to relieve the burden on motorists.
NATO to receive German peace prize
NATO is to be awarded with international Westphalian Peace Prize, worth €100,000 ($113,350), on Thursday afternoon, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz set to give the laudatory address.
The prize, which is expected to be received by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at the ceremony in Münster, honors the military alliance for its contribution to the European peace order.
The award is being presented to NATO at a time when its role as guarantor of Europe's security has been cast into some uncertainty by US ambivalence under the Trump administration.
The Westphalian Peace Price, which commemorates the Peace of Westphalia of 1648, is awarded every two years by the Economic Society for Westphalia and Lippe.
The 1648 peace agreement, concluded in the city halls of Münster and Osnabrück, ended the Thirty Years' War and is considered by many as a milestone in establishing the principle of national sovereignty.
Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance changes its name
The populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) has officially dropped its founder's name from its title to become the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason.
However, it will retain the abbreviation BSW.
Secretary general Oliver Ruhnert said Wagenknecht's name had initially been used because of her popularity but that the party had now succeeded in establishing itself as a brand in its own right.
Wagenknecht, a former parliamentary leader of the Left Party, founded the BSW in 2024, stepping down as its leader in November 2025.
Although the BSW advocates economic policies that are left-wing, it also has a nationalist and anti-migration stance that are more typical of the right-wing political spectrum, making it hard to classify in conventional terms.
It also favors closer ties with Russia.
Suspected IS member arrested
Federal police arrested a suspected member of the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist group in central Germany on Wednesday morning.
Prosecutors allege that the man joined the group in Iraq at the latest by early 2016, fighting in its ranks until early 2017.
He was detained in the Waldeck-Frankenberg district, north of Frankfurt, and is now being held in pre-trial detention after appearing at the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe.
Berlin Left Party, Greens and SPD meet for clarifying talks
Politicians from the socialist Left Party, the environmentalist Greens and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) in Berlin are set to meet on Thursday to talk through several contentious issues before embarking on possible coalition negotiations.
Among other things, the talks will focus on accusations of antisemitism leveled at the Left Party, which won recent elections.
The party has also been accused of cultivating links to organized crime.
The accusations were fueled by the attendance by the head of an Arab clan with alleged criminal ties and a controversial pro-Palestinian activists at an election night event held by the Left Party in the Neukölln district of the city on September 20.
The Greens and the Left Party have said reaching agreement on these contentious issues is a "basic prerequisite" if formal exploratory talks on a coalition are to begin.
If the Left Party were to end up leading a coalition in the German capital, its lead candidate and parliamentary group co-leader, Elif Eralp, could become the first female governing mayor of Berlin.
Welcome to our coverage
A hearty guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn as the new month gets underway!
We will be looking at the pre-preliminary talks between the Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats (SPD) on possibly forming a coalition in the capital, Berlin.

This comes as another party, the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), changes its name to the catchy "Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason", while retaining the BSW abbreviation.

On Thursday night, air defense forces shot down and suppressed with electronic warfare (EW) equipment 87 out of 107 drones of various types used by Russian occupation forces to attack Ukraine, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on its Telegram channel.

Lithuanian refrigerator maker Snaigė files for bankruptcy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

06:04:00 UTC
15:04:00 KST

Snaigė, the only refrigerator manufacturer in the Baltic states, is seeking bankruptcy after abandoning its restructuring process amid unfavourable market conditions, uncertain prospects for continuing operations and persistent losses.
Snaigė CEO Darius Varnas applied to the Kaunas Regional Court on September 30 to terminate the company’s restructuring proceedings and initiate bankruptcy proceedings, the company said Thursday.
“Efforts to optimise and restructure operations did not produce the expected result,” Varnas said in a statement.
The company had shifted away from producing household refrigerators toward more specialised medical refrigerators and refrigeration monoblocks, a strategy Varnas said was the right direction for the business.
However, he said Snaigė continued to be weighed down by obligations accumulated by previous owners, a persistent shortage of working capital and limited access to credit.
“Too slowly and too little – that is probably how the efforts of recent years to restructure Snaigė and find a place for its products in a dramatically changed global market could be described,” Varnas said.
Snaigė said it has more than 12 million euros in financial liabilities to creditors.
The company reported a loss of 670,000 euros last year.
Snaigė is based in Alytus, southern Lithuania, and has been producing refrigeration equipment for decades.

The bikers assisted in the 2014 annexation of Crimea and fought alongside Russia-backed separatists in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region.
‘Message from the heavens’

Independent Russian investigative news site Agentstvo cited Prokhanov as saying they had decided to baptize the Moon to “make it Orthodox and connect it with Russia.”
The ritual involved consecrating “fragments” of the Shcheglets stone, a granite boulder located in Russia’s Novgorod region that bears Bronze Age petroglyphs.
Night Wolves leader Alexander Zaldastanov described the stone in a blog post as being of “celestial origin.” Prokhanov referred to the boulder as a “moonstone” and claimed that it “landed several millennia before our era.”
“It was a message from the heavens to this land, which later became Russia,” he said in an interview with prominent Russian tabloid Komsomolskaya Pravda.
Prokhanov’s comments came after he was asked by the paper about Donald Trump’s “appropriation” of the “Soviet Moon,” according to Agentstvo.
A piece of soil taken from the boulder was placed at the base of a ceremonial cross, after which a prayer service and procession were held and what Prokhanov referred to as the moonstone was blessed, Agentstvo reported.

Charity threatens legal action over two-year NHS wait for ADHD and autism assessments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:00:31 UTC
15:00:31 KST

ADHD UK has threatened legal action against an NHS organisation over its decision to impose a minimum two-year wait for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism assessments.
In a legal letter to West Yorkshire NHS integrated care board (ICB), seen by the Guardian, the charity alleges that the decision to force patients to wait at least two years for such assessments was unlawful and says it will seek a judicial review if the board fails to reverse the policy.
West Yorkshire ICB introduced the two-year minimum wait this year, affecting thousands of people with possible ADHD or autism in Leeds, Bradford, Kirklees, Calderdale and Wakefield.
West Yorkshire is not the only ICB to ration access to assessment for neurodiversity. The Guardian revealed last week that it was one of four – alongside Devon, Somerset, and North East and North Cumbria – to have imposed minimum waits amid spiralling costs due to the volume of assessments being sought. A further 11 have introduced other mechanisms to ration the number of assessments.
ADHD UK claims West Yorkshire failed to follow correct procedures, alleging the ICB breached equalities legislation, denied patients their legal right to choose non-NHS care, failed to involve patients, carers or the public in the decision, and that the decision ran counter to NHS contract regulations.
Henry Shelford, the chief executive of ADHD UK, said: “We have sent formal notice warning West Yorkshire that we are prepared to go to court unless it scraps that rule. We believe locking patients out of NHS choice is illegal because it breaches patients’ legal right to choose where they receive NHS care.
“We believe the processes they’ve strung together to push this through have been used incorrectly and, in some cases, improperly.”
The charity’s legal “letter before claim” to West Yorkshire ICB states: “There is no published decision record, equality impact assessment, public involvement, demand and capacity analysis, clinical safety assessment or statement of reasons specific to the two-year minimum.”
It says that unless West Yorkshire withdraws or suspends the two-year minimum, to retake any decision lawfully and to provide the information and documents that will allow the issues to be narrowed or resolved without proceedings, ADHD UK will seek a judicial review.
The disclosure comes ahead of a government-commissioned review of mental health, ADHD and autism prevalence led by Prof Peter Fonagy. The review is expected to recommend a “needs-based” system whereby patients with ADHD symptoms should not automatically be formally diagnosed but should be “triaged” and offered support without requiring a formal diagnosis. It is also expected to propose greater regulation of private psychiatry clinics.
Corinne Hunter, the chief executive of Stripes, a charity supporting children and adults with ADHD in West Yorkshire, said the ICB’s decision was devastating for patients and that the board had not let the charity know it planned to impose a minimum wait.
She said: “We weren’t consulted or told in advance about the decision – we initially heard about it through word of mouth from our own service users. There are ‘right to choose’ providers that are able to offer assessments much sooner, so for people in West Yorkshire to now face a minimum two-year wait is devastating.
“People often put off seeking an ADHD assessment for years, until they reach the point where they are really struggling to cope. Getting referred can finally feel like there is some light at the end of the tunnel, only to then be told that light could be another two years away.”
A spokesperson for NHS West Yorkshire ICB said: “We have received correspondence from ADHD UK. As this matter may be subject to legal proceedings, it would not be appropriate to comment further at this stage.”

Stepping back in time: a historic walk along Dorset’s Jurassic Coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:00:30 UTC
15:00:30 KST

Many favour a circular walk, but you can give a linear one new shape with the addition of a novel form of transport. My wife Helen, our friend Tom Cox and I take the water taxi – a rigid inflatable boat (Rib) – from West Bay on Dorset’s coast to Lyme Regis, with a plan to walk back to our starting point.
The rain stops as the boat leaves the harbour, the views open along Chesil Beach to low-lying Portland to the east, and west to Lyme Regis; on the far horizon, we can see Start Point on the Devon coast. Our skipper, Nick, is highly knowledgable and takes time to stop and point out the history of the shoreline and the treacherous waters of Lyme Bay. The seabed is studded with wrecks – fishing boats and smugglers’ ships, but some are from the two world wars.
On New Year’s Day 1915, the battleship HMS Formidable was torpedoed by a German submarine. Of its crew of 750, no more than 200 survived. In the second world war, the Dorset coast was a huge mustering station for the allied forces in preparation for D-day. During Exercise Tiger, a large-scale rehearsal for the Normandy landings, hundreds of American service personnel were killed in an attack by German boats later known as the Battle of Lyme Bay – the wreck sites are now designated war graves.
At Lyme Regis, we disembark on to the Cobb, the harbour wall that snakes unsteadily into the bay and was made famous by Jane Austen, who had Louisa jump from it in Persuasion, and by John Fowles, who lived in Lyme. The movie adaptation of his novel The French Lieutenant’s Woman starred Meryl Streep as Sarah Woodruff. Its famous trailer begins with the actor sweeping across the Cobb, the hood of her cloak covering her face. For the filming, many buildings in the town were given a 19th-century facade. For a film that plays with time, it seems appropriate that the town’s bookshop kept its temporary fascia for many years.
Our walk back to West Bay is 10 miles long and begins not along the coast but by heading inland. The west Dorset coast is friable – the cliffs keep falling on to the beaches, and the path to Charmouth takes a diversion through a golf course. It wasn’t always like this: once there was a coastal road, Long Entry, between the two settlements. In 1725, Henry Fielding, then aged 17, attempted to abduct his cousin Sarah, with whom he was infatuated, from Lyme. The future novelist made his escape along Long Entry before being stopped by her guardian.
Our walk back to the coast is interrupted by a sculpture on the path. The shape of a woman, angular and determined, a hammer in her outstretched right hand, the other holding above her head the skeleton of a prehistoric animal. There’s another recent sculpture of the same subject, Mary Anning, in Lyme Regis, recording her importance to palaeontology and to the town, but this upland creature, made by Greta Berlin, is wilder, perfectly suited to its woodland setting. The representation of the fossil held aloft is Anning’s discovery: Ichthyosaurus anningae. One cannot walk this section of Dorset’s coast without being aware of its ancient past and the fragile geology close to the surface. Our boat trip began on crumbly sandstone, which gave way to fossil-rich clay as we travelled west.
Charmouth is a pretty village with no harbour; its shallow waters make it popular with those learning to swim or paddleboard. This next section of the South West Coast Path, to West Bay, coincides with the Monarch’s Way, the route that Charles II took to flee to mainland Europe after the civil war. Our day is more peaceful but the path is steep. We’re grateful for Tom’s company – his latest novel, Everything Will Swallow You, is infused with the history and landscape of the Dorset coast and his knowledge enlivens our walk, as do the pasties he brings, baked by his wife, Ellie.
We pass the remains of St Gabriel’s Church, which fell into disuse in the 18th century, although smugglers found within its walls useful shelter for their contraband. Soon we’re on Golden Cap, the highest point on the south coast – 191 metres (627ft) above sea level, with extraordinary views over Lyme Bay. At Seatown, we stop at the Anchor Inn for refreshments, meeting friends who have opted for a shorter walk. From Thorncombe Beacon, we descend to Eype Mouth – in Old English Eype is “Steep Place”; the church in this secluded village was chosen by PJ Harvey to record Let England Shake, a Mercury prize-winning album rich with the echoes of war.
There are further reminders of the coast’s fragility on the final stretch to West Bay – one sign references a cliff fall in 2020, and the path is frequently redirected to safer routes. West Bay, a small stone town, was once the harbour from where Bridport exported its rope and was originally called Bridport Harbour, but had its name changed by the railway company hoping to attract tourists. The railway is long gone – its station now hosts a restaurant in railway carriages – but West Bay, with its stalls for chips and views back towards Lyme, is a fitting place to end, a town out of time.
OS Explorer 116 (Lyme Regis & Bridport) covers the entire walk from Lyme Regis to West Bay. The Lyme Bay Water Taxi operates during the summer months; there is a year-round bus service between West Bay and Lyme Regis. Jon Woolcott is the author of Real Dorset and The Tattooed Hills, Journeys to Chalk Figures

‘Hitler was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon’: why most of what we think we know about the rise of the Nazis is wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
06:00:30 UTC
15:00:30 KST

With your art collective Centre for Political Beauty you famously built a replica of the Holocaust memorial on a property next to the home of an AfD politician. Now you’ve written a history book about the Nazis’ rise to power. Don’t we already know everything there is to know about the 1932 elections, the Reichstag fire and the Enabling Act of 1933?
About three years ago I became interested in how Hitler’s National Socialist German Workers’ party (NSDAP) rose to prominence when Germany was still a democracy, because I hoped it could tell us something about the success of rightwing extremist movements today. From looking at historical sources, I realised that the Reichstag elections of 14 September 1930 were in many ways more important than what happened in 1932 and 1933. And I expected it to be an open-and-shut case. But the more I looked into it, the more I realised that most of the theories we have to explain the rise of the Nazis don’t make sense – the data tells a completely different, far darker story.
Why were the 1930 elections so important?
The numbers behind the vote were astonishing. In 1928, the NSDAP got 800,000 votes and 12 seats in the Reichstag. A few weeks before the 1930 election, Hitler’s propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels, history’s grand master of exaggeration, still thought they had a chance of going up to 50 to 60 seats at best. Yet on the night, the Nazis got 6.4 million votes and 107 seats. That’s a ninefold increase over the space of two years. In one night, a small splinter party from the political fringes overtook the three established parties of the right – the Centre Party, the DVP and the DNVP – coming in second place behind the Social Democrats. It was an enormous shock. It was the moment at which a racist sect of loudmouths and club-wielders, a party of absolute cranks, came to be politically legitimised.
You call the NSDAP a “party of cranks”. Didn’t Hitler have a certain dark charisma?
Among German historians, this has long been the dominant theory to explain the Nazi party’s success: that Hitler had an irresistible inner aura that captured the masses. There’s a second theory that is very similar, the führerkult idea. It argues that the NSDAP was so irresistible because it had a leader that spoke to Germans’ yearning for authoritarianism. The problem is: I couldn’t find any evidence before the 1930 vote to support those theories. Because in 1930, every party was practising a star cult around their own political leader, even the Social Democrats. The Nazi party didn’t have a USP in that respect. And the Nazis didn’t even seem to be wholly on board with the führer principle themselves at this stage. Several people in the party complained about the “Byzantine” star cult around Hitler, which is also why the campaign wasn’t really tailored around him as a personality. Let’s remember that in 1930 Hitler wasn’t even on the ballot, because he wasn’t a German citizen: he was a foreigner who had a criminal record for trying to mount a coup and was at risk of being deported.
I had grown up seeing Hitler as a monster, but one with a certain political talent. And after 1930, that’s not entirely untrue. But when you focus on 1928 to 1930, even his biographer Ian Kershaw concludes that the NSDAP’s success had very little to do with Hitler. He was going through an absolute dip in form. He only held 29 speeches in 1929, half of what was customary, and 21 of them were all in Bavaria. In 1930 Goebbels spent half the year complaining about Hitler’s prevaricating: when he travelled to Munich to track down the NSDAP leader, he didn’t even bother looking at the party headquarters. “The Reich leadership is at [Hitler’s favourite coffeehouse] Café Heck or the cinema,” Goebbels wrote sarcastically. In 1930, Hitler wasn’t a political genius. He was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon.
If not Hitler, was propaganda chief Goebbels the key figure behind the rise of the Nazis? One explanation being revisited these days is that political crises tend to go hand-in-hand with media crises: that the Nazis pounced expertly on new forms of media like illustrated news, radio and film.
When we talk about the Nazis, everyone has these images in their head that point to this slick propaganda machine: the Nuremberg rally, the cathedral of light, all these awe-inspiring spectacles. And it’s true that pre-1930 Goebbels invested a lot of effort into building up propaganda newspapers inspired by American formats, such as Der Angriff, Völkischer Beobachter and Illustrierter Beobachter. But early Nazi propaganda was an embarrassing, amateurish joke. I’ve looked through every edition of Illustrierter Beobachter, and the images they presented to the reader were laughable, such as SA men dressed as advertising pillars. It just wasn’t professional. The sales figures were pathetic: nobody was reading these newspapers. Compare it to the means that the other parties had at their disposal: they put up neon signs on street corners and hired planes for aerial advertising. Propaganda just doesn’t explain the NSDAP’s success.
What about the economy? The stock market on Wall Street had crashed a year beforehand, German exports were collapsing and unemployment was on the rise.
It’s always tempting to fall back on economic factors when explaining the rise of fascist movements. We are hearing it again in Germany now: the economy is crumbling, the trains aren’t running on time, so people are going to fall for the fascists again. But if I look at historical sources from the run-up to 1930, I come away thinking that voters weren’t that stupid. Take the unemployed. Over the last 30 years, historians have established a pretty good picture of who voted for the NSDAP. And we can say with certainty that in regions where unemployment was high, the Nazi party performed relatively poorly. If anything, unemployment was a factor contributing to anti-fascist resilience. And as to the idea that the Nazis managed to attract young first-time voters, the same applies: the NSDAP also performed badly in areas with high rates of first-time voters. The young were also running away from this party.
The global economic crisis may explain why the NSDAP managed to double its support in 1932 and attain 37.3% of the vote. But as an explanation for the ninefold boost in 1930, it falls short. Wall Street’s Black Thursday didn’t fully arrive in Germany until July 1931, when several major banks collapsed – 10 months after the Nazis got 107 seats in the Reichstag. The Weimar Republic’s GDP went into a tailspin, with a 36.6% collapse, only over the course of the two years that followed – by the end of 1930, it had merely shrunk by 7.1%, and we don’t know how much of that was as a result of the election outcome. There’s a risk here of confusing cause and effect.
What if we look at the democratic parties instead?
One of the central tenets of the Nazi party’s campaign was the alleged corruption of the established parties, but there is very little evidence that this was actually the case. The most striking – and also the most puzzling – thing I learned was that all of the three big rightwing parties of the Weimar Republic had put political hardliners in charge between 1928 and 1929. If voters had really been desperate for tough rightwing policies, they could have voted for the Catholic Centre party, the nationalist liberal DVP or the monarchist DNVP – all parties in a pole position to turn their promises into practice.
Didn’t they just experience what many conservative parties are finding out now: that when they copy the positions of the far right, voters tend to prefer the original?
I think that’s a platitude that simply isn’t true. Because in 1930 Hitler wasn’t the original, he was a washed-out copy of what was offered by the DVP or the DNVP. The DNVP ran a more antisemitic campaign than Hitler, and yet it was the biggest loser of the election, shedding 7.3% of the vote. What strikes me as much more important is credibility. In 1930, the nationalist-liberal DVP was attacked by its own party newspapers for betraying the legacy of its former leader Gustav Stresemann, who had died a year earlier. It’s not unlike the situation we now have with Germany’s Christian Democrats: a party that under Merkel was absolutely centrist and managed to retain loyal voters but then picked a figure from its right wing as their new leader in Friedrich Merz. And voters are switching to the AfD. The central lesson to me is that conservative parties can only win from the centre.
You say credibility is key. Then why do corruption scandals barely seem to hurt the modern far-right parties railing loudest against ‘the system’?
It’s true that the NSDAP in 1930 was absolutely riddled with scandals: back-stabbing, power struggles, corruption, the whole spectrum. And many German journalists at the time believed they were just one more scandal away from complete collapse. There were some excellent and brave journalists leading some really good investigations. But it didn’t work.
I look at far-right parties across Europe now, and I see undercover reporters revealing the AfD’s remigration plans, leading to the biggest protests in postwar German history. And these kinds of investigations are extremely important. But fascist or rightwing extremist parties seem to be immune to this kind of stuff. They are like lightning rods: the scandal is a flash of energy that passes straight through them into the ground and then it’s gone. A corruption scandal might temporarily damage a party, like the “Ibiza affair” did to the Austrian Freedom party, but five years later they are back at double their strength.
So why did the Nazis perform so strongly in 1930?
As paradoxical as it sounds, it might be for the same reason that voters turned away from the Nazis in 1928: its propensity to violence. Ever since Hitler had been in the NSDAP, he had talked about one thing: executing his political opponents. And the Nazi party remained absolutely consistent in that respect. In the run-up to the 1930 vote, it didn’t talk about social policy, it didn’t talk about building the autobahn. It just had murder plots.
How does that help us understand the rise of fascist or rightwing extremist movements today?
It’s hard to admit this from a modern perspective, but historical fascism’s lust for violence didn’t make it repulsive but extremely attractive to a lot of German voters. And we are seeing similar things with the AfD today, where fantasies of violent retribution seem to be integral to campaign events on market squares. We are witnessing the poisoning of an entire society, and as a democracy we should ask ourselves whether criminal law shouldn’t apply when political parties communicate that way. Communication is one thing, political plans are another. The NSDAP had both. But we know that the AfD is a radical party that seems to want to ethnically cleanse Germany. If the AfD is voted into power, one of the most highly advanced economies in the world could experience something similar to what happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
- 
  Philipp Ruch’s Der Rückfall (The Relapse) is published by Penguin

Long-time civil servant: MoD permanent secretary dismissed without due process
The government disregarded the spirit of the law when it dismissed Defense Ministry Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk, said former state secretary Taimar Peterkop.
The government removed Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kuusk on September 10 at outgoing Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur's request following controversy over military accounting and defense procurement. Although a minister may dismiss a secretary general when cooperation fails, the Civil Service Act requires them to work together for at least six months first.
Peterkop said he understood the practical reasoning but warned that ignoring legal norms damages trust and creates a precedent for quickly removing officials in the future. He called for better governance and serious action on problems repeatedly identified by journalists and the National Audit Office.
Discussing his new role on President-elect Ülle Madise's National Defense Council, Peterkop said Madise wants the council to meet regularly as the security environment worsens. The council brings together the president and representatives of the executive and legislative branches, helping political leaders develop a shared understanding of security issues. Peterkop said using it more actively would also give substance to the president's constitutional role in national defense, including time-critical powers related to war, mobilization and the domestic deployment of the Defense Forces.

FlyDubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while an investigation into the incident takes place.
What to know about the September 30 FlyDubai flight
A FlyDubai flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel was on Wednesday derouted to Dubai for an emergency landing after the pilot allegedly stabbed his copilot in an apparent bid to crash the plane.
The distress call came at 8:44am local time, about two and a half hours into the flight. It had some 170, mainly Israeli, passengers onboard.
The aircraft then swiftly lost altitude – dropping around 10,000 metres to 5,100 metres in the span of about a minute. It then circled close to the Jordanian border before landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, about an hour later.
Aviation experts said they were surprised that the plane did not crash after a descent so extreme that most of the rudder was ripped off the tail.
According to Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a passenger and a crew member managed to enter the cockpit, enabling other crew members to fly the plane to a safe landing.
Both pilots suffered injuries that required hospital treatment. Netanyahu said one of the pilots has been arrested by Saudi Arabia.
Good morning and welcome to our liveblog on the Israel-bound FlyDubai flight that was derouted to Saudi Arabia yesterday after the pilot is thought to have stabbed his copilot mid-flight.

====================================================================================================

Feature: Inside Audi's long-term plan to become an F1 contender
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:58:02 CST
14:58:02 KST

by F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
BEIJING, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- Mattia Binotto does not know where Audi sits in the Formula 1 constructors' championship.
Nor, apparently, does the man in charge of the German manufacturer's F1 project spend much time keeping track of how many points his team has scored.
"If you would have asked me where we are in the standings, I would not know," Binotto tells Xinhua during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend. "And how much are we scoring? I'm not sure."
The answer is that Audi lies eighth in the constructors' standings in its first season as a works F1 team, with an improving run of results having brought seventh-placed Haas within reach.
But while Binotto welcomes the progress, he insists neither Audi's final championship position nor its points total will determine whether its first year has been a success.
"The objective for us was more becoming competitive, which is not tangible," he says. "It's not the number of points at the end of the season in the championship. It's not about a standing position.
"It's more an attitude. It's more about creating solid foundations, giving a clear perception to the media, the fans in general, our partners, that we are building a solid and credible team for the future."
For Binotto, the more meaningful verdict will come from whether those elsewhere in the paddock believe Audi is developing into a genuine force.
"I would be very happy if, by the end of the season, everyone would share our view that Audi is here to become a strong competitor in the future."
CLOSING THE GAP
There remains plenty of work to do. Audi entered Formula 1 this year with its own power unit, developed at Neuburg in Germany, and Binotto acknowledges that the engine remains the biggest contributor to the team's performance deficit.
The FIA has assessed the relative performance of the new power units, he says, leaving Audi with a clear picture of where it stands.
"I can confirm that the biggest gap in performance is down to the power unit," Binotto says.
Audi has made only a relatively minor change to its turbo during the season, which Binotto says was aimed more at improving drivability than outright performance.
More significantly, he does not expect the deficit to disappear quickly.
"It's clear that it will take several months, or maybe a couple of seasons, before recovering completely," he says.
Binotto hopes Audi will have closed most of that gap by 2028, underlining the long-term nature of a project whose stated ambition is to be challenging for the Formula 1 world championship by 2030.
That does not mean Audi can simply wait for its engine department to find more performance. Binotto stresses that the power unit is only one area in which the team must improve, with development of the chassis continuing in parallel.
BUILDING A TEAM ACROSS BORDERS
Audi's power units are developed in Neuburg, Germany, while its chassis is built in Hinwil, Switzerland. Most of its F1 rivals, meanwhile, draw heavily from a concentrated pool of experienced personnel clustered around southern England, in so-called Motorsport Valley.
Binotto does not regard either issue as the structural disadvantage it might appear.
He points to other F1 teams whose chassis and engine operations have been separated by considerably greater distances. The physical gap matters less, he argues, in an era when engineers in different countries and regions can work together continuously through digital communication.
"What counts the most, especially today with the virtual world where you are connecting with video calls, is making sure the processes are properly in place," he says.
"It's not the proximity of a person which counts, but it's more clarifying where the responsibilities are, where the processes and priorities are.
"I don't think that's location-related. It's organizational."
The same applies to recruitment. Many of the obvious candidates with existing F1 experience are based in England, where switching teams might not even require them to move house. Convincing them to uproot their lives for Switzerland is a different proposition.
Audi has already had some experience of that challenge. Its previous team principal, Jonathan Wheatley, left in April after little more than a year in the role, with the team citing personal reasons for his departure.
Binotto, however, argues that Audi should look beyond the traditional F1 talent pool.
"Worldwide, the talents are everywhere," he says.
Switzerland, in his view, can be an attraction rather than an impediment. He points to its universities and says the team's recent recruitment has encompassed 19 different nationalities.
"Is it a problem for us to attract in Switzerland? No," he says. "I think it's a competitive advantage."
LEARNING TO LET GO OF THE DETAILS
For someone who spent much of his career in engineering, including at Ferrari when Michael Schumacher won five championships in a row, his description of his own technical abilities is surprisingly modest.
"I've never been a good engineer," he says.
Rather than involving himself deeply in individual technical details, Binotto says his task is to ensure the specialists beneath him have what they need to perform.
"My role is more, instead, supporting the team, making sure that everyone has got what's required to deliver to the best. Orchestrating, maybe, an organization.
"I don't like to play the single song. I'd rather prefer to orchestrate the overall team."
Such an approach perhaps explains his apparent lack of interest in Audi's precise championship position. Overtaking Haas would be another sign that the team is moving in the right direction, but Binotto is looking beyond where Audi finishes in 2026.
Whether the foundations being laid this year are strong enough to turn the team into a genuine championship contender will only become clear when the results he currently regards as secondary start to matter rather more. ■

SEOUL, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's elderly population reached 21.6 percent of the total population amid rapid population aging, statistical ministry data showed Thursday.
The number of people aged 65 and older totaled 11.125 million in 2026, accounting for 21.6 percent of the country's total population, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
After officially becoming a super-aged society last year when the proportion crossed 20 percent to hit 20.3 percent, the graying of the nation continued to intensify.
The ministry estimated that the elderly population will top 30 percent of the total by 2036 and 40 percent by 2050.
The old-age dependency ratio, or the proportion of the elderly population to the working-age population aged 15-64, was projected to surge from 31.3 in 2026 to 50.1 in 2036 and 100.8 in 2066.
The number of households, headed by those aged 60 and older, was 6.507 million in 2026, taking up 28.8 percent of all households in the country.
Among the elderly-led households, single-person households were the most common at 38.0 percent, followed by couple-only households at 35.1 percent.
The number of elderly households was forecast to exceed 10 million by 2038, with their share expected to surpass 50 percent of all households by 2052. ■

US President Donald Trump has again blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising diesel prices in the United States, arguing that the disruptions to Russia’s fuel production are a bigger factor than the war in the Middle East.
Speaking from the Oval Office on Wednesday, Sept. 30, Trump said a potential US ban on diesel exports could reduce domestic diesel prices, although he warned it would also have a negative impact on gasoline prices.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Trump said the war in Ukraine, including attacks by both sides that have disrupted energy production and exports, was the main factor behind rising diesel prices.
“It’s going to start to come in. You know, diesel is really hurt much more, not by the Middle East, but by what’s going on in Russia, because those diesel refineries are being knocked out at a pretty alarming rate,” he said.
“And if that didn’t happen, we wouldn’t have a diesel problem. What’s happened in Russia with Ukraine has been really the biggest problem for diesel,” Trump added.
US energy secretary points to broader disruptions
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright offered a broader explanation for the tightening diesel supply, pointing to disruptions in several major exporting regions.
“We’ve lost some diesel exports from the Middle East, although we’re restoring those, and we’ve lost diesel exports from China,” Wright said. “So that’s a lot of interruptions.”
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 30, 2026
He added that the administration expected European countries to announce additional diesel supplies soon.
According to Reuters, gasoline prices in the US have risen by more than 40% over the past year, while diesel prices reached a record $6.53 per gallon a week ago, according to AAA data.
The price surge has been driven largely by a combination of tighter supplies linked to the war with Iran and refining disruptions, including those caused by Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities, Reuters reported.
The issue also carries political significance in the US, where the Trump administration and Republican candidates face pressure to bring down fuel costs ahead of the November midterm elections, while Trump’s economic approval ratings remain under strain.
Ukraine’s refinery strikes
In mid-September, Trump called on his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, to stop targeting Russia’s energy industry, arguing that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were driving up diesel prices in the US.
Trump said Ukraine’s long-range drone strikes against Russian refineries were the main reason global diesel prices had spiked and urged Zelensky to halt the attacks.
“Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia. Let him go after targets – but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel,” he said.
“This isn’t done by the Middle East. This is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine... There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel because that’s hurting the world,” Trump told a gaggle of Irish and international reporters.
Trump’s remarks came after a record month of Ukrainian strikes against Russia’s energy sector. In August 2026, Ukrainian drone forces hit 21 Russian oil refineries – a wartime record, according to data from Ukraine’s national long-range strike database, DeepStrike UA, and strike statistics published by the Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces (USF).
The targeted refineries were located in Omsk, Saratov, Syzran, Perm, Yaroslavl, Krasnodar, Samara, Tatarstan, Tyumen and Orsk. Strikes hit some facilities repeatedly, while others – including refineries in Omsk, Perm and Tyumen – were targeted for the first time during the war, according to Kyiv Post records.
The August figure was 50% higher than July’s 14 refinery strikes and twice the monthly strike pace recorded by USF units in October 2025, when seven refineries were hit.
Trump’s criticism echoed earlier remarks by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who in early September blamed Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia for a global “energy shock” that he said was driving up energy costs.
However, energy industry analysts have pointed to other factors as the main drivers of the global surge in crude and refined-fuel prices. A US-Israeli war with Iran has brought tanker exports through the Strait of Hormuz close to a halt, while worsening Red Sea disruptions following the Houthi capture of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait have further constrained tanker traffic.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has also downplayed the impact of Ukraine’s strikes on Russia’s energy infrastructure. In comments aired by Russian state-controlled media on Aug. 22, he said the attacks had failed to produce the battlefield effect Kyiv intended.
“How effective are they – are they effective at all? And do they have any impact on the situation along the line of contact as a whole? The ultimate result for the adversary turned out to be the exact opposite of what was expected. No turning point occurred,” Putin said.
At the same time, Ukraine’s strikes have significantly disrupted Russia’s fuel production. A Bloomberg estimate published on Aug. 28 and widely cited by Ukrainian media said the attacks had reduced Russia’s production of gasoline, aviation fuel, diesel and other petroleum products by more than 30%.
Russian industry analysts have similarly estimated that fuel-processing capacity has fallen by roughly one-third, saying that restoring the damaged capacity could prove difficult as Russian air defenses struggle to intercept Ukrainian drones.

First Tennessee woman set to be executed in 200 years survives first lethal injection attempt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:54:08 UTC
14:54:08 KST

Death row inmate Christa Pike, who is set to be the first Tennessee woman executed by the state in over 200 years, survived the first attempt at her execution, Tennessee's Department of Corrections confirmed on Thursday.
The US Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that Tennessee could proceed with Pike's execution by lethal injection for murdering a schoolmate as an 18-year-old three decades ago.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement to Reuters afterwards that it planned "to move forward with the execution today."
Pike, 50, whose clemency petition highlighting childhood trauma and sexual abuse was denied by Governor Bill Lee on Monday, would also be the only person in the modern era of US capital punishment to be executed in Tennessee for a crime committed as a teenager.
In an order decided by its 6-3 conservative majority, the Supreme Court lifted a stay of execution that was granted by a three-judge panel of the 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals one hour before Pike had been scheduled to be put to death.
Death warrant due to expire, requiring new Supreme Court warrant
The appellate panel voted 2-1 to order a "short stay" to allow time to weigh Pike's claim that evidence of her childhood sexual abuse was not adequately considered during her sentencing.
But the Tennessee attorney general's office immediately asked the US Supreme Court to vacate the stay. And the high court's decision siding with Tennessee marked the final word on whether the execution was permitted to go forward before her death warrant expires at midnight.
If the state were to run out of time to conduct the execution, it would need to obtain a new warrant from the Tennessee Supreme Court, according to Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike was 18 in January 1995 when she, a 17-year-old boyfriend, and a third companion lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at their Knoxville Job Corps vocational center, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her.
The grisly nature of the slaying, which involved the perpetrators carving the shape of a pentagram in the victim's chest and taking a chunk of her skull as a souvenir of the carnage, drew intense media coverage at the time.
Trial testimony indicated that Pike viewed Slemmer as a rival for the affections of her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.
Pike and Shipp both were convicted of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the time of the murder and acted as a lookout for the other two, testified for the prosecution and received probation.
Pike's lawyers cite bipolar disorder, PTSD in request for life sentence
Currently the only woman on Tennessee's death row, Pike was also convicted in August 2001 of attempted first-degree murder in an assault on another inmate, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction.
In the 226-page petition asking the governor to commute her death penalty to a life sentence without the possibility of parole, Pike's lawyers documented her history as the childhood victim of violence, neglect, and sexual abuse, including two rapes at ages 11 and 17. They also cited the diagnoses she received in prison for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Moreover, they pointed to evidence that Pike's mother drank heavily during pregnancy, contributing to faulty brain development that made it difficult for their client to control her impulses as a young person.
"The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists," her lawyers wrote in response to Lee's denial of clemency. "Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women."
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, has spoken out in support of the execution.
Executions of female prison inmates are exceedingly rare in the US, with women accounting for just 18 of the 1,683 people put to death since the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to resume in 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Before Wednesday, Tennessee had executed 17 people.

Flydubai attempted hijacking showcased Israeli aviation security system procedures - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:53:35 UTC
14:53:35 KST

The stabbing of a pilot aboard a flydubai flight from Dubai to Israel on Wednesday, which prompted the activation of a distress signal, set Israel's aviation and security systems in motion and illustrated the chain of procedures designed to deal with a suspicious aircraft approaching Israeli airspace.
Every pilot entering Israeli airspace encounters two designated points at set distances from Israel's borders that serve as stages for clearance and monitoring. The first, farther point allows a pilot to approach Israeli airspace, while the second permits the aircraft to continue toward a landing inside Israeli airspace.
At these points, the pilot must identify the aircraft to Israeli air traffic control using a known, agreed-upon code, allowing authorities to verify that the plane has valid authorization and the necessary permits.
The first point an aircraft reaches is sufficiently far from Israel and, from the IDF's perspective, at a safe enough distance to allow fighter jets to be scrambled in the event that the pilot fails to identify the aircraft or does so but is experiencing an unusual incident for any number of reasons. Scrambling fighter jets does not necessarily mean they are being sent to shoot the aircraft down. In some cases, an aircraft's communications system may malfunction, and the crew may be unable to establish contact.
In such an extreme scenario, fighter pilots try to establish contact through procedures familiar to both sides, with particular emphasis on visual contact.
Pilots may communicate visually with fighter jets in emergencies
For example, there is a procedure under which, before a flight, the captain asks passengers to open their window shades. This allows fighter pilots flying alongside both sides of a passenger aircraft, if necessary, to see what is happening throughout the plane, including inside the cockpit. Unusual activity visible from outside can provide the fighter pilots with indications about what is taking place on board.
Pilots aboard the passenger aircraft also know how to communicate what is happening using agreed-upon visual signals, in addition to radio communications and distress buttons.
It is important to emphasize that these procedures take place over a period of time and at a distance that allows the Israel Air Force to scramble aircraft and carry out several stages of checks, providing flexibility in the decision-making process. That process ranges from monitoring, identification, examination, verification, and interception to, in the most exceptional case, shooting the aircraft down.
In the case of the flydubai aircraft, the distress signal was activated while the plane was still well outside Israeli airspace. Nevertheless, such an alert automatically activates Israel's aviation and security systems, enabling authorities to prepare an appropriate response.
"All the organizations, bodies, and officials involved are drilled for a scenario of this kind down to a matter of minutes, in order to carry out a precise process in response to an airborne terrorism scenario," a former senior Israel Air Force officer said.
Prime minister sole authority in question of shooting down civilian plane
The former senior officer further explained that in such a scenario, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the defense minister, the IDF chief of staff, and the Israel Air Force commander are brought onto a conference call within a very short period.
The available information is presented briefly during the call, and the prime minister is the sole authority empowered to decide whether the aircraft should be shot down.
The former senior officer stressed that the call is not conducted through aides or intermediaries. "The prime minister has to be on the line. He makes the decision..."
In an extreme scenario in which a civilian aircraft reaches the first designated point, continues toward Israeli airspace, and does not respond to signals from the fighter pilots, a stage is reached at which the prime minister must make a decision, potentially including an order to shoot the aircraft down.
"There is a difference between shooting down a passenger aircraft with 175 passengers and a civilian aircraft with 175 civilians crashing into the Azrieli Towers with a thousand people killed. That is why, from the moment the planes are scrambled, the prime minister is on the line, along with the defense minister, the chief of staff, and the Air Force commander," the former senior officer explained.

Expert calls for cross-party 'unemployment brake'
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:50:09 EEST
14:50:09 KST

Finland needs a cross-party agreement on an "unemployment brake" to replace the so-called 'debt brake', according to Elina Pylkkänen, an economist and former under-secretary of state at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment.
The debt brake involves political parties setting agreed targets for reducing state debt at the beginning of each parliamentary term — regardless of who is in government.
As an alternative, Pylkkänen said deploying an unemployment brake "would be a good start." She made the comments on Yle's politics programme Politiikkaradio on Wednesday.
The economist compared the debt brake's €8-11bn savings target to the real costs of unemployment to the state.
"A single unrealised career of around 40 years costs the state approximately two million euros, regardless. If we have even just a hundred thousand people whose entire working life goes unfulfilled, that amounts to €200 billion. Can we really afford this?" Pylkkänen asked.
Structural unemployment
She said unemployment is a far more serious problem in Finland than most people think. According to the former under-secretary of state, as much as 80 percent of joblessness in Finland is structural, long-term unemployment that economic cycles are unable to remedy.
Significant setbacks have occurred during PM Petteri Orpo's (NCP) coalition government. Unemployment has risen for three consecutive years, and the number of long-term unemployed has climbed to 140,000.
Long-term unemployment in particular has become an entrenched, seemingly permanent problem in Finland that policy has failed to solve.
According to Pylkkänen, Finland's decades-long policies of increasing labour supply and lowering taxation on work aren't producing results in Finland.
She said that compared to Finland, the labour market situation in other Nordic countries is in considerably better shape.
According to the economist, discussing state debt is pointless without considering the full scale of unemployment. Public finances will not be balanced without solving structural unemployment.
As a solution, Pylkkänen is calling on decision makers to adopt a new, comprehensive approach that crosses ministerial boundaries to fix serious labour market problems before it's too late.
"Do we really want to exclude these people? Can we afford to do that?"

Türkiye to create digital archive of centuries-old Turkish music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:49:27 UTC
14:49:27 KST

Belviranlı says the archive will cover the programs of the directorate’s 29 units and include tens of thousands of works. (AA Photo)
Türkiye is preparing a digital archive of centuries-old musical works, historical scores and performance recordings that will be made freely accessible to the public in 2027.
The project, led by the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s General Directorate of Fine Arts, will bring together scores from the Seljuk and Ottoman periods, along with religious hymns, gazels, concert recordings and stage performances.
The archive aims to give musicians, researchers and the wider public access to Türkiye’s musical heritage through a single online platform.
Ömer Faruk Belviranlı, director general of Fine Arts, told said that the directorate oversees 29 orchestras, choirs and musical ensembles, including six state symphony orchestras and the State Polyphonic Choir. Other ensembles specialize in traditional Turkish music, folk music, folk dances and music from different regions.
A separate project is also underway to digitally record artistic productions by the directorate’s ensembles.
He said 15 of the directorate’s 29 units have professional recording studios and that an existing archive of performances will be transferred to an online platform.
“We currently have an archive. All that remains is to bring this archive to life and transfer it to the YouTube channel, or whichever channel we will publish it on, in accordance with our minister’s instructions,” he said.
The digital archive will also include historical musical notation reflecting centuries of Turkish musical tradition.
“Turkish music is a sea,” Belviranli said. “We have in our possession, in the form of an archive, very special scores inherited from the 700-800-year-old Seljuk and Ottoman tradition to the present day, Hamparsum notation, scores written in Ottoman Turkish and many more.”
Hamparsum notation is a historical system developed during the Ottoman period to record Turkish music.
Belviranlı said an exact number of works could not yet be given, but the archive would cover the programs of the directorate’s 29 units and eventually include tens of thousands of works.
He said the recordings would allow people to study individual pieces and performances, while stressing that digital access would not replace the experience of attending a live concert.
The directorate also plans to continue sending musical ensembles abroad. Belviranlı said it had received requests from at least 42 countries for performances marking Oct. 29, Türkiye’s Republic Day.
He said foreign audiences accounted for nearly 80 percent of spectators at some overseas programs, particularly those featuring traditional music, whirling dervish performances, Turkish World music and folk dances.

Historic church aims to join Cappadocia tourism route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:49:17 UTC
14:49:17 KST

The restoration of the church, which will serve as the İncesu City Museum, was completed last year in line with its original form. (AA Photo)
The 190-year-old Aziz Eustathios Greek Church in the central province of Kayseri’s İncesu district, whose restoration was completed last year, is drawing attention with its wall paintings as works continue to include the historic building in the Cappadocia tourism destination.
Built in 1836, the Aziz Eustathios Greek Church features numerous paintings and remains on its interior walls and stands out as one of İncesu’s important historic and cultural heritage sites.
The three-aisled historic building with a vaulted roof was taken under restoration by the Kayseri Metropolitan Municipality in 2021. Its load-bearing walls and structural fabric were strengthened using materials and techniques compatible with the original construction.
The stonework and frescoes, or wall paintings, inside the building were preserved, while scenes depicted in Karamanlıca, Turkish written in the Greek alphabet, as well as charitable foundation inscriptions, reliefs and carvings on the walls were conserved and brought to light.
The building, whose restoration was completed last year in line with its original form using archival photographs and documents, will serve as the İncesu City Museum.
More than 80 percent of the exhibition and arrangement work at the church has been completed. The building is planned to be included in the tourism destinations of the Cappadocia region, such as Avanos, Ürgüp and Göreme, located 45 to 50 kilometers from the district.
Tayfun Talaslı, head of the Historical Buildings and Museums Department at the Kayseri Metropolitan Municipality’s Department of City History, Promotion and Tourism, told Anadolu Agency that the three-aisled, vaulted and rectangular-plan church is an example of classical Greek Orthodox architecture in Anatolia.
Talaslı said the building was used as a place of worship until the 1923 population exchange between Türkiye and Greece, after which it served different functions, including a military warehouse, archive, theater hall and vocational school.
Talaslı said restoration work, which began at the end of 2021 under a protocol signed between the Kayseri Metropolitan Municipality and İncesu Municipality, was completed last year.
He stressed that the fundamental principle in the largely completed exhibition and arrangement work was not to damage the historic building. He said the walking platforms installed to allow visitors to examine the frescoes comfortably, as well as lighting fixtures and display units, were designed as an independent system standing on their own supports without making any contact with the building.
Planned to open soon
Talaslı stressed that great importance was attached to preserving the building’s original character and said: “When carrying out the restoration of the church, we used old photographs as a source. In particular, we proceeded with the project and implementation in line with art history reports prepared by taking into account the oral histories of people who lived here.”
Talaslı said they planned to complete the remaining work and open the museum to visitors soon.
“As the İncesu City Museum, we will create a museum on the ground floor of the building where we will present the town’s tangible and intangible cultural heritage. Visitors will be able to see the chronology of İncesu’s history, valuable people who grew up here, figures who left their mark on its history and its architectural structures,” Talaslı said .
“We will convey many of the town’s values to visitors, from the Kara Mustafa Pasha Complex to the Roman-era milestone that is one of its symbols. They will also be able to see examples of ceramics and other archaeological finds unearthed in Örenşehir. We will create a museum where visitors can learn about everything from the local gastronomy and population to the population exchange the town experienced in the past, its chronological development, whom the building was dedicated to, its flora and fauna, geological structure, agriculture and grapes.”

Cigarettes caused 1,803 fires across Istanbul in the first eight months of the year, accounting for 9.8 percent of 18,321 cases, municipal fire department data shows.

Taner Kaboğlu, deputy chairman of the Turkish Fire Protection and Education Foundation, urged self-extinguishing cigarettes. “Cigarettes cause severe damage,” he said.

100,000 turtle hatchlings reach sea in southern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:48:45 UTC
14:48:45 KST

Sea turtles crawl across the sandy beach toward the water. (AA Photo)
Nearly 100,000 endangered sea turtle hatchlings reached the Mediterranean from nesting sites across Türkiye’s southern province of Mersin as the 2026 breeding season concluded.
The province is among the world’s top reproduction grounds for loggerhead turtles (Caretta caretta) and green sea turtles (Chelonia mydas).
With a 321-kilometer Mediterranean coastline, Mersin shelters five major nesting spots: Anamur, Göksu Delta, Erdemli Alata, Davultepe and Kazanlı. Davultepe recorded 138 nests this season, guiding around 10,000 young turtles to sea while provincial estimates indicated roughly 100,000 reached water overall.
Mersin University (MEÜ) Sea Turtle Application and Research Center Lecturer Dr. Mahmut Ergene evaluated the 2026 results. “Taking Davultepe as a baseline, we identified 138 nests where around 10,000 hatchlings reached the sea,” Ergene said. “Across Mersin, approximately 100,000 young turtles met the water.”
Davultepe saw a decline this season compared to past averages of 180 nests along its 1.8-kilometer stretch, yielding 100 nests per kilometer. Ergene said the lower tally forms part of an expected natural rhythm rather than a negative development. “Our 20-year data shows fluctuating patterns, and this year represents one of those downturns,” Ergene said.
Türkiye’s southern coast serves as an essential Mediterranean breeding habitat where conservation teams monitor nesting activity through autumn. Seasonal patrols protect emerging hatchlings from predators and artificial lights.
