'Women don't cry any more, they cash in': Shakira turns Madrid into a festival of empowerment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:14:12 UTC
14:14:12 KST

The Colombian pop star returns to Spain after eight years with a 12-show residency in Madrid, celebrating Latin culture and turning a chapter of her life into a spectacle of music, freedom and empowerment.
There are little girls barely a metre off the ground. Women who could be their mothers and others old enough to be their grandmothers. There are Colombians, Venezuelans, Peruvians and Spaniards, but also Germans, Dutch and Danes. Some wear purple wigs. Others, coin skirts. Many, glitter. And when the howling starts, for a few hours they are all the same: she-wolves.
Shakira did not want to come back to Spain with just a simple concert. No, she wanted to come back in style.
Eight years after her last tour in the country, the Colombian star has chosen Madrid for the only European residency of 'Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour' (Women No Longer Cry): 12 shows, more than 600,000 tickets and a temporary stadium built for her and her fans in the south of the capital, that can welcome around 55,000 people a night.
Shakiraworld
And around the stage she has practically built a city. It is called Macondo Park, in tribute to the universe of Gabriel García Márquez, and it offers food, music, literature, children’s areas, exhibitions and a second stage.
The gates open hours before Shakira appears. This is not meant to be just a concert: it is a festival celebrating Latin culture, built around an artist who has spent more than three decades exporting it around the world.
And the choice of Madrid is no accident either.
Shakira has explained that she chose the capital because here she found something she wanted to celebrate: a city with a huge Latin American community, where Latin culture is already part of everyday identity and openly celebrated.
But it is hard to ignore another layer to this comeback.
Madrid and Barcelona live out a historic rivalry that goes far beyond football. And Barcelona is not just any city in Shakira’s biography: it was her home for more than a decade, the city where she lived with her ex-partner, football star Gerard Piqué, where her children grew up and which she eventually left for Miami after a painful break-up.
Now her only major European landing is in Madrid.
The symbolic weight is impossible to avoid. The woman who walked away from Barcelona after one of the toughest periods of her life returns to Spain, taking over the rival city for four weekends.
And she herself seems to relish that storyline.
"Good evening, Madrid. I can’t believe I’m here," she says to tens of thousands of people. Then she recalls something someone told her before she came back: "With the face you left with, just look at the face you’ve come back with."
She-wolves support
The concert opened with 'La fuerte'. Then come 'Girl Like Me', 'Las de la intuición' and 'Estoy aquí'. In just a few minutes, the Shakira of the 90s, the global Latin pop star and the woman who in recent years turned a break-up into music all share the same space.
A digital Shakira appears at the beginning, rebuilding her own body out of sand. Then the real one, flesh and blood, makes her way through the crowd with her pack before reaching the stage. "There is nothing like when a she-wolf is reunited with her pack," she says.
And the pack answers back. They dance to 'La tortura'. They scream 'Te felicito'. They know every word of 'TQG'. They go back 20 years with 'Hips Don’t Lie'. They sing 'Waka Waka'. Song by song, an idea emerges that runs through the whole show: falling does not mean staying on the floor.
In Madrid, Shakira acknowledged that the last few years "have not been easy" and described her return to Spain as "a gift". And then she starts dancing again.
Women no longer cry
There is something profoundly feminine about the night. Not because it is a party only for women, but because of the feeling that here they can take up all the space. Be loud. Sensual. Silly. Angry. Vulnerable. Strong. Put on a violet wig, shake their hips for two hours and dance with a stranger.
During the show a line by the Chilean writer Isabel Allende appears on the screens that almost works as a manifesto: "Women on their own are vulnerable, but together we are invincible". And you only have to look around to understand why it is there.
Mothers dancing with their daughters. Groups of friends hugging. Women of different ages, countries and languages singing the same songs. For Latin women, there is something especially familiar in a show that does not tone down or hide its identity: pop, reggaeton, salsa, batucada, percussion and hips. Barranquilla is present even though we are in Madrid.
The line that ended up defining this era was not trying to be subtle either: "Women no longer cry, women cash in". And cash in she does.
600,000 tickets: women cash in too
The residency is also a huge business operation. Twelve nights over four consecutive weekends. More than 600,000 tickets. A venue built specifically for the occasion and an estimate of between €150 and 200 million in direct associated spending for Madrid.
Instead of touring Europe, Shakira has managed to convince Europeans and others to travel to her.
Madrid has becomes a destination for fans from dozens of countries and generations. And the line born as a response to a break-up takes on here a much more literal meaning.
The 10 commandments of a she-wolf
Towards the end of the concert, the ten commandments of the she-wolves appear on the screens. They are the code of this new Shakira: independence, freedom, sisterhood and a few nods to her past that the audience picks up instantly.
One of them especially teases Madrid: A she-wolf shall not covet another’s goods.
('Clara-ly').
The stadium erupts.
What a few years ago filled headlines about her private life has ended up as humour, music and spectacle. Shakira no longer tries to separate her personal story from her songs: she plays with it.
Then comes 'Loba'.
But there is still one last song, and it is hard to imagine her choosing any other.
After more than two hours spanning three decades of career, Shakira saves for the finale the session with Bizarrap in which she turned her break-up with Piqué into one of the biggest hits of her career.
Then tens of thousands of people once again shout with her: "Women no longer cry, women cash in".
The circle closes right here and the last song feels written for this very moment. Shakira left Spain in tears. She has come back to Madrid cashing in.

- Journalists witnessed Pike moving, singing, and complaining of pain before being escorted out; an ambulance left the site, though Pike's condition remains unclear.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Tennessee woman Christa Pike was in a hospital on Oct 1 after the authorities “failed” to carry out her execution, her lawyers said, with witnesses reporting the convicted murderer was breathing despite being given injections that were meant to kill her.
Just hours earlier, the US Supreme Court cleared the way for her to be the first woman to die by lethal injection in the US southern state in 200 years.
Tennessee corrections officials did not publicly confirm the outcome of the execution, which included two injections of pentobarbital, or respond to an AFP query seeking information.
“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” Pike’s attorneys said in a statement. “Christa is being treated at a nearby hospital. We have not been informed as to her condition.”
Pike was scheduled for execution at 10am local time on Sept 30 at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, where witnesses, including journalists, were present for the administration of the injections.
“It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go,” said investigative journalist John North of WBIR, who was a witness at the execution site, adding “when we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive”.
During a live-stream, an ambulance with its lights flashing could be seen leaving the site of the execution. It is unclear if it was transporting Pike.
The execution procedure went ahead hours after the US Supreme Court ruled that it could proceed, with liberal justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson all dissenting.
“The court’s decision... unnecessarily prevents that (lower) court from giving due consideration to Pike’s claim,” the dissenting justices wrote.
“Worse, the court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the state to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts.”
Mental health considerations
The case has sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer’s body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Pike’s lawyers argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of the killing.
“She was 18 when she committed her crime, and she was deeply mentally ill,” they wrote in a clemency petition to Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, who said he would not intervene.
The US Supreme Court had rejected on Sept 29 an application for a stay of execution, which argued that Pike’s history as a victim of sexual assault, post-traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant a lethal injection would cause “needless suffering”.
Independent UN rights experts have urged the US government and the Tennessee authorities to “immediately halt” the execution and commute her death sentence.
“Pike’s execution would mark the culmination of a trajectory of severe physical and psychological suffering marked by childhood abuse and nearly three decades of solitary confinement on death row,” they said.
In the US, 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. AFP

Since last week, students have staged protests outside schools over grievances ranging from timetables, class sizes and a shortage of teachers to overheated classrooms during this year's heatwaves.

Where does body fat go when we lose weight? The answer is stranger than you expect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:06:00 UTC
14:06:00 KST

Researchers estimate that around 84% of lost body fat is exhaled as carbon dioxide, while the remaining 16% is lost as water.
When body weight falls, some of the fat stored by the body disappears – but where does that mass actually go?
Two researchers from the University of Birmingham explain in an article published in The Conversation that fat loss is linked to a process that begins when the body needs more energy than it gets from food, so it turns to its fat reserves to meet that need.
The fat we eat reaches the digestive system, where it is broken down into fatty acids.
The body uses part of these fatty acids for essential functions such as building cells, regulating hormones and protecting organs, while the surplus is converted into triglycerides that are stored inside fat cells to be used later as an energy source.
The body mainly stores fat in two ways: subcutaneous fat found just under the skin, and visceral fat that builds up deeper inside the body around the organs.
When the body enters a state of calorie deficit, hormonal and neural signals start to stimulate fat cells to break down stored fat, in a process known as lipolysis.
Fat is converted into energy
After triglycerides are broken down, fatty acids travel to the mitochondria inside cells, known as the body's "power stations", where they undergo beta-oxidation.
During this process, fatty acids are broken down into compounds the body uses to produce energy, and these reactions generate carbon dioxide and water as the final by-products of metabolism.
And here lies the surprise, according to the article: most of the fat the body loses does not leave through sweat, but through the lungs while we breathe.
Based on the researchers' calculations, around 84% of lost fat is turned into carbon dioxide and leaves the body when we exhale, while about 16% becomes water that is eliminated through sweat and other bodily fluids.
The researchers note that these percentages remain estimates, as it is difficult to measure all of the body's outputs precisely during fat loss.
What does this mean for exercise?
When people exercise or cut their calorie intake, the body's need for energy rises.
If the energy supplied by food is not enough to cover this demand, the body starts using its fat stores.
But this does not mean that breathing rapidly causes fat loss. Exhaling is the route through which the products of fat burning leave the body, not the process that triggers fat burning itself. Maintaining a calorie deficit, through diet and physical activity, remains the key factor that pushes the body to tap into its stored energy.

Bushfire season begins in Australian Capital Territory
China
Unknown Publisher

14:04:24 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- The 2026-27 bushfire season began on Thursday in Australia's Australian Capital Territory (ACT), with authorities warning residents to prepare for heightened fire risks amid forecasts of a hot summer.
From Oct. 1, fire danger ratings will be published daily across the territory, permits will be required for open-air burning and total fire bans may be declared when conditions warrant, according to the ACT government.
The bushfire season will run until March 31, 2027. The ACT government said the territory experienced some of its earliest bushfires in recent years during the previous season, as well as multiple total fire ban days.
Authorities on Thursday also launched a new community preparedness campaign, dubbed CHAT. PLAN. ACT., encouraging residents to discuss emergency risks, make plans and take practical steps before an emergency occurs.
ACT Minister for Police, Fire and Emergency Services Marisa Paterson said warmer weather had already been felt in Canberra during September and households should be prepared for the possibility of bushfires and other emergencies over the coming months.
The ACT has also deployed two new heavy tanker fire trucks to strengthen its bushfire response capability. The vehicles are the first of their kind to enter service in Australia and will be operated by volunteer firefighters from the ACT Rural Fire Service.
Authorities urged residents to clear dry vegetation and leaves from around their homes, keep flammable materials away from properties, stay informed about warnings and ensure they understand the fire danger rating system. ■

China Focus: China's durian trial crop eyes market entry amid strong consumer appetite
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:04:01 CST
14:04:01 KST

This photo taken on Sept. 11, 2026 shows ripe durians at a durian planting base in Jinping County, Honghe Hani and Yi Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Yunnan Province. (Photo by Ao Pingxing/Xinhua)
KUNMING, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- This autumn, tree-ripened durians have been harvested in southwest China's Yunnan Province, as durian trees in experimental orchards have steadily come into bearing after years of trial cultivation.
Once seen as a luxury treat, the spiky, pungent "king of fruits" has triggered a shopping frenzy in China.
China's durian appetite has driven robust imports of the fruit from Southeast Asian countries. According to the General Administration of Customs, since 2022, China has approved durian imports from five countries, including Vietnam, Malaysia and Laos. China's durian imports reached 1.87 million tonnes in 2025, twice as much as in 2022.
In addition to expanding imports of the tropical fruit, China has introduced durian planting in southern provinces of Hainan and Yunnan to meet strong market demand.
"It takes at least four years for a durian tree to grow from planting to fruiting. Stable maturation and yield are extremely hard to achieve amid multiple natural challenges in Yunnan," said Ao Pingxing, director of the durian industry research center at Yunnan Agricultural University.
He said this year marks the first large-scale fruit-bearing for several pilot durian plantation trials in Yunnan, a key step in moving durian farming from sporadic trials to standardized, large-scale demonstration cultivation.
Compared to Hainan, a fully tropical province, Yunnan features diverse landforms with varying temperatures, which poses challenges to the cultivation of durian varieties.
In Honghe of Yunnan, researchers have focused on screening cold-resistant varieties and developing flower and fruit technologies for adapting the plants to the local climate. This year, 33 durian trees in the area have successfully retained fruits, yielding 123 high-quality fruits weighing over 2 kilograms each, with the highest single-tree fruit count reaching 18.
At the trial durian planting base in Jinghong City, Xishuangbanna, a mature tree can bear up to 34 fruits, with an average single-fruit weight of 3.7 kilograms and a record weight of 8 kilograms. The sugar content of the harvested durians exceeds 36.9 degrees, a premium level for commercial durian varieties.
"Comprehensive assessments on flesh color, fragrance and flavor prove that the locally-grown durians have reached a high-quality standard," said Yang Dejun, vice president of Yunnan Academy of Forestry and Grassland, adding that this round of durian harvesting has accumulated solid field data for future large-scale demonstration cultivation and industrial promotion.
Researchers and planters are still testing harvested durian fruits collected from various locations.
Data from the Yunnan Academy of Forestry and Grassland show the province's durian planting area has surpassed 17,000 mu (about 1,133 hectares), mostly in Xishuangbanna.
Currently, four durian varieties have been selected for their strong adaptability to Yunnan's climatic conditions, including premium varieties known as Musang King and Red Prawn.
In addition to Yunnan, Hainan achieved its first commercial durian harvest in 2023, marking the official entry of domestically-grown durian into the market. However, durian cultivation on the island province is confined to its tropical southern areas. The province's total durian planting area has now reached approximately 50,000 mu, yet most trees have not reached full production age. China's homegrown durian output remains far smaller than that of imported durian. ■

S. Korea's exports hit record high in September on record-breaking AI chip demand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:03:56 CST
14:03:56 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's exports hit a record high in September, topping 120 billion U.S. dollars for the first time thanks to a record-breaking global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductors, government data showed Thursday.
The outbound shipments, which account for about half of the export-led economy, soared 83.5 percent from a year earlier to 120.94 billion dollars in September, according to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources.
For the first nine months of this year, cumulative exports reached 814.5 billion dollars, overtaking last year's record-setting annual performance of 709.3 billion dollars.
The daily average exports spiked 105 percent to 5.63 billion dollars, surpassing 5 billion dollars for the first time.
Imports grew 26.0 percent to 71.09 billion dollars last month, sending the trade surplus to an all-time high of 49.85 billion dollars.
Of the country's 20 major export items, 11 products saw growth in outbound shipments.
Semiconductor exports skyrocketed 262.8 percent to 60.30 billion dollars, crossing 60 billion dollars for the first time.
The milestone was attributed to the continuous expansion of AI infrastructure investments that led to price hikes in memory chips.
Computer exports surged 435.3 percent to 7.00 billion dollars, boosted by solid demand for solid-state drives (SSDs) used in AI infrastructure.
Mobile phone shipments mounted 23.4 percent to 2.14 billion dollars, extending its growth streak to 11 months due to strong demand for premium smartphones, while display panel exports retreated in single digits.
Automotive exports declined 5.5 percent to 6.05 billion dollars, impacted by the shift of Chuseok holidays, the South Korean version of Thanksgiving Day, while auto parts shipments fell in single figures.
Exports for ships jumped 29.9 percent to 3.76 billion dollars, driven by higher deliveries of high-value ships including liquefied natural gas (LNG) tankers and very large gas carriers (VLGCs).
Shipments of oil products soared 72.0 percent to 7.22 billion dollars, and petrochemicals exports rose 5.1 percent to 3.95 billion dollars as geopolitical risks in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz pushed up global oil prices despite a drop in shipment volumes.
Dubai crude, South Korea's benchmark, averaged 113.7 dollars per barrel in September, up 62.4 percent from a year earlier.
Rechargeable battery exports advanced 14.0 percent to 720 million dollars, marking five straight months of gains on the back of higher mineral prices and a booming energy storage system (ESS) market.
Steel products shipments swelled 3.3 percent to 2.24 billion dollars on strong U.S. demand for steel sheets used for AI data center construction, but general machinery exports shrank 3.2 percent to 4.07 billion dollars owing to fewer working days and rising logistics costs.
Cosmetics shipments spiked 31.4 percent to 1.51 billion dollars, but farm goods exports retreated 4.7 percent to 1.11 billion dollars.
Exports to the United States shot up 137.0 percent to 24.33 billion dollars as a result of robust demand for chips, oil products, machinery and new vehicle models.
Shipments to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) jumped 92.6 percent to 21.29 billion dollars, while exports to the European Union (EU) picked up 20.9 percent to 8.65 billion dollars.
Regarding import items, the import of three major energy sources, including crude oil, natural gas and coal, gained 38.0 percent to 12.96 billion dollars last month.
Non-energy imports mounted 23.6 percent to 58.13 billion dollars on strong demand for semiconductor equipment and mobile devices. ■

Methane is responsible for 30% of global warming – so why is the EU trying to delay rules to cut it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:02:11 UTC
14:02:11 KST

“Methane is the quickest brake we have on warming this decade. Before ministers agree to ease off it, I'd ask them to look very carefully at what it actually costs.”
The EU has proposed to delay new rules to cut planet-warming emissions from methane, saying a delay would “relax” pressure on energy markets and therefore cut oil and gas prices.
EU energy chief Dan Jorgensen, under pressure from France and industry lobbyists, suggested the rules be pushed back by one year. He held talks with energy ministers from the bloc’s 27 nations earlier this week
Methane is responsible for about 30 per cent of the rise in global temperatures since the Industrial Revolution, meaning it made a significant contribution to the record-breaking heatwaves which gripped Europe this summer and led to at least 35,000 excess deaths.
What is the new methane regulation, will it really push up oil and gas prices and how harmful are methane emissions?
How is the EU trying to cut methane emissions and why is industry opposing it?
Since 2024, EU member states have been required to measure, report and check methane emissions and ensure mitigation efforts, such as detecting and repairing methane leaks.
The new regulation, which is at threat of being delayed, will require energy importers to ensure that imported fossil energy meets the same standards. “The rule industry wants postponed is aimed at gas that leaks, is vented, or is burned off, all of which is saleable gas being lost,” according to the Climate Crisis Advisory Group (CCAG) which argues that the regulation would make more, rather than less, gas available. “The International Energy Agency puts the volume that could be captured and sold at around 200 billion cubic metres a year. A requirement on producers to find and stop those losses adds gas to the market over time. Postponing the rule postpones that.”
The regulation had been due to apply from 1 January 2027. Some industry groups and member states are calling for it to be delayed by three years, but the EU has suggested a one-year delay.
Critics argue that if exporters are unable to comply with the new rules, they could stay away from Europe, narrowing the bloc’s sources of gas at a critical time and pushing up prices. Eurogas, and 20 other companies and organisations, argue that it should be delayed because “key accreditation, verification and certification frameworks are still not fully in place, compliance solutions remain under development, and significant uncertainty [remains]”.
Will the new methane regulation push up gas bills?
“The argument for [the delay] is that these rules will push up the price of gas. They won’t. Showing how the gas you import is measured costs a tiny fraction of what that gas sells for, and even if every penny of it were passed on, households would barely notice,” says Sir David King, Chair of CCAG and former UK Chief Scientific Adviser.
CCAG puts the cost of meeting the new methane regulation at about €0.07 per MMBtu, or 0.3 per cent of the current gas price, based on modelling by Rystad Energy for the Clean Air Task Force.
CCAG analysis shows: “Across the 76 billion cubic metres of American gas the EU bought last year that comes to roughly €190 million. If every cent were passed through to consumers it would add around €3 a year to a typical household gas bill. Sending a US cargo to Asia rather than Europe costs $3.50 (€3) per MMBtu more in shipping alone.”
“The rules also bring gas back onto the market that is at present simply leaking into the air.”
Are gas supplies in Europe really running low?
Data shows that Europe has enough gas to last through the winter, and this would be the case even with the methane regulation in place.
New analysis by Data Desk found: “While Central and Eastern European countries face minor immediate issues with Russian gas reliance, no identified supply constraints are severe enough to undermine the Methane Regulation in its current form.”
According to AFP news agency, gas storage levels average at around 70 per cent across the EU, albeit with significant differences between countries. In France for example tanks are 82 per cent full, while the rate is only 57 per cent in Germany.
Where in Europe is responsible for the most methane emissions?
According to the IEA’s Global Methane Tracker, around 55 per cent of the fossil fuel methane emissions that occur within Europe come from the oil and gas sector, mostly from downstream operations. 45 per cent come from coal mines, mainly in Poland and Ukraine.
Upstream oil and gas operations are responsible for the majority of emissions in Romania and the UK. Norway and the Netherlands have the lowest upstream intensities in the world, it says, while most other countries in the region perform near the global average.
Abandoned underground coal mines constitute a significant and overlooked source of methane emissions.
Methane gas is generated when organic matter turns to coal and is buried underground in these coal seams. When mining creates a route to the surface, much of the methane escapes. If it is not plugged, these emissions can continue for decades after a mine is abandoned.
Globally, the IEA estimates that abandoned coal mines emitted nearly 5 Mt of methane in 2024, and abandoned oil and gas wells released just over 3 Mt. Combined, these sources would be the world’s fourth-largest emitter of fossil fuel methane –- after China, the US and Russia, and ahead of Iran, Turkmenistan and India.
Since most emissions result from mines and wells that have recently been abandoned, timely action is critical, the IEA urges. Options include plugging and monitoring wells that are no longer in use, sealing abandoned coal mines, and directing methane flows for energy use.
In total, the energy sector – including oil, natural gas, coal and bioenergy – accounts for more than 35 per cent of methane emissions from human activity.
The agriculture and waste sectors are also major sources of methane emissions, but fossil fuel supply offers the greatest potential for immediate reductions in methane emissions, the IEA notes.

Explained: How the EU’s new cabin baggage rules will work – and when they start
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:00:39 UTC
14:00:39 KST

EU travellers could soon get a larger cabin allowance at no extra cost – but UK passengers flying out of UK airports are unlikely to benefit from the new rules.
European air passengers travelling within the EU could soon be entitled to more hand luggage without paying extra, under a major overhaul of passenger rights.
The European Parliament and EU member states reached a provisional agreement in June on new air passenger rules – the first major revision of the legislation since 2004.
Under the new rules, passengers buying a standard ticket would be entitled to two pieces of hand luggage free of charge.
This would include one small personal item, such as a handbag or backpack, which must fit under the seat in front. They would also be allowed one larger cabin bag weighing up to 7kg, with combined dimensions of up to 100cm.
The changes are expected to come into force from late 2027 at the earliest, with October 2027 currently thought to be the earliest possible start date. However, the rules still need to complete the remaining EU legislative process before they can take effect.
The European Parliament says the new provisions give passengers the right to carry a personal item on board “without additional fee”, potentially putting an end to some of the extra charges currently levied by airlines for cabin baggage.
The Parliament also decided that airlines will still be able to offer cheaper fares to passengers who choose to travel without hand luggage, although it remains unclear exactly how this pricing system will work once the new rules come into force.
The changes are part of a broader overhaul of EU air passenger rights, covering issues including delays, cancellations and compensation.
For travellers, the key change is that a standard fare would have to include both an under-seat personal item and a small cabin bag, rather than passengers having to pay extra for the latter.
It’s not good news for British passengers, who have not been considered European citizens since Brexit came into force.
One of the country’s largest operators, easyJet UK, says passengers on outbound journeys won’t be able to take advantage of the incoming rules, according to a report by Which?.
That will apply to all UK-based airlines, including British Airways and Jet2.
Passengers flying out of the UK will not benefit from a free item of hand luggage despite new rules in Europe, easyJet has said.
The airline said the rules will apply to UK passengers “only on return flights from EU countries”.
However, EasyJet says that alongside all other British airlines, it is reviewing its own baggage rules, in preparation for when the EU legislation comes into effect.

Unknown

Prisoners freed early in England and Wales risk living on the streets, say probation officers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:00:29 UTC
14:00:29 KST

Hundreds of prisoners are due to be released early from jail on Thursday amid warnings that many will have nowhere to live and the probation system will struggle to monitor them.
About 2,000 criminals including domestic abusers and violent offenders are to be freed over the next month, with another 3,000 in stages over the next year to ease overcrowding. The number was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by the prime minister, Andy Burnham.
Prisoners are supposed to be found appropriate accommodation before their release, significantly reducing reoffending rates.
But a probation source told the Guardian that their colleagues in some towns and cities were struggling to find hostel places.
“We have a handful of places for ex-offenders and they are full. We are now looking at releasing some people straight on to the street,” the source said.
Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said: “We know that leaving prison homeless can put people on a path back into custody. It is vital that the whole system from prisons and probation to councils and community providers work together to give people a roof over their heads.”
Napo, the probation officers’ union, has raised the issue of the accommodation shortage with prison bosses. The task of finding beds for prisoners is expected to reach critical levels from 13 October, when a second tranche of prisoners is due for release.
Ben Cockburn, the union’s national chair, said HM Prison Service seemed to be in “absolute denial” about the state of the Probation Service.
“We have massive staff shortages, unsustainable and dangerously high workloads and electronic monitoring is failing to deliver,” he said.
Ministers say the expanded early release scheme is needed to prevent the collapse of the criminal justice system. They say the Conservatives in their time in power added too few prison places while increasing the length of sentences.
Criminals will be excluded from the scheme if they have been jailed in child grooming gang cases or convicted of indecent assault. Those guilty of manslaughter will also be excluded, meaning the killers of Andrew Harper, a police officer who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible.
The releases will take place across dozens of prisons across England and Wales from Thursday.
The expansion of the scheme is happening as a result of the 2026 Sentencing Act, which allows ministers to reduce the point at which certain prisoners can be freed from 40% of a fixed-term sentence to a third.
Several hundred people are likely to be released on 1 October as part of the first phase of the expanded scheme, with more to follow in subsequent months.
The Ministry of Justice says it is launching the biggest ever expansion of electronic monitoring, with a new presumption that offenders will be electronically tagged and monitored when they leave prison.
But a report released this week by probation and police watchdogs warned that some criminals were waiting up to five months to be fitted with a tag, leading to repeated breaches of court and prison orders.
Only 55% of GPS and radio frequency tags were fitted on time, according to the report’s findings. The figure was 60% for alcohol monitoring tags.
Keir Starmer’s government launched an early release scheme in September 2024, months after the general election. Images of prisoners swigging champagne, being driven away in sports cars and thanking the then prime minister were seized upon by the government’s critics.
Figures show the number of people behind bars has jumped by more than 1,700 in the past three months. The prison population of England and Wales stood at 87,499 on Monday, according to weekly government data.
A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “This government inherited prisons on the brink of collapse and a homelessness crisis, with rough sleeping more than doubling since 2010.
“We’re pulling every lever to fix this, building 14,000 new prison places and working with councils and charities to halve prison leaver homelessness by 2029, supported by a record £700m investment in probation and community services.”

Healey urged to offer energy support in budget as bills rise 4%

John Healey is under growing pressure to offer fresh energy support for households in next month’s budget as millions face a 4% rise in charges from Thursday to an average of £1,723 a year for a typical home.
In his speech at Labour’s conference in Liverpool this week, the chancellor warned that the government had limited resources to cushion the worldwide economic shocks hitting Britain, while arguing his budget would have fiscal discipline at its core.
The quarterly energy price cap, set by the regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, will rise to its highest level in three years despite Andy Burnham’s decision to cut VAT from electricity bills to save the average household £45 a year from 1 October.
Households also face rising road fuel costs after diesel prices reached a record high of almost £2 a litre this week, which is expected to accelerate the rising cost of goods across the economy.
Treasury sources insist the 28 October budget will be tightly focused amid the challenging global backdrop, as bond market jitters add to the pressure on the public finances.
Insiders said tax devolution was likely to be centre stage to meet Andy Burnham’s promise to shake up Whitehall, while several big decisions could be pushed back to a spending review next year.
Some MPs are privately concerned that Healey and his team have failed to grasp the severity of the energy crunch ahead. “Without it [fresh energy support], the vibes will end,” said one Labour MP. “The problem is the Treasury are just not understanding where the country are.”
Healey warned in his speech that the money New Labour had in the 1990s was “simply not there now”, although he also vowed to offer “a bit of breathing space” for households and businesses.
As energy bills rise for millions of households from Thursday, a group of leading campaigners, charities, trade unions and thinktanks warned that failure to take action would risk deepening the cost of living crisis.
Writing in an open letter to the chancellor and the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, the group – including the New Economics Foundation, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation and Generation Rent – called for a package of universal energy support as well as targeted measures to help those most in need.
Coordinated by the Cost of Living Action campaign group, other signatories included Neal Lawson of Compass and Mathew Lawrence of Common Wealth – both of whose ideas have fed into Burnham’s policymaking.
With the war in the Middle East pushing up global oil and gas prices, the leading energy forecaster Cornwall Insight predicts the cap will increase by a further 16% from January to £1,999 for the average annual dual-fuel bill.
Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the TUC, said this “energy bill emergency” meant the government should “go further and faster” at the budget to protect households.
On Wednesday, Burnham said Labour “will do our best” but warned that the government faced tough financial constraints, telling the BBC there was not “huge room for manoeuvre” to take further action.
In his first weeks in office, the prime minister announced the six-month VAT holiday on electricity bills and a £2 cap on bus fares in England.
The Treasury is under pressure to extend the six-month VAT holiday, and shift the levies used to support new clean energy projects and grid upgrades from energy bills into general taxation.
The changes are understood to already be under consideration by Fahnbulleh, who is reportedly hoping to save customers an average of £120 a year on their energy bills – but this could involve putting up taxes by as much as £3bn.
However, the campaigners warned that further cost of living support was needed. “It is clear that this does not go far enough and that what is coming down the track this winter requires a much more substantial response,” they wrote.
Highlighting the risks from soaring energy bills, new polling carried out by More in Common on behalf of the Joseph Rowntree Foundation shows 28% of households are extremely worried about the prospect of the Iran war pushing up bills this winter, while 43% are quite concerned.
It found 66% of British adults think the government needs to do more to tackle the cost of energy.
Calling for bolder action, NEF urged the government to introduce a new “national energy guarantee” giving all households a basic amount of energy at a fixed low cost, with higher levels of consumption charged at market prices.
Responding to the letter, Fahnbulleh said:“I know energy price rises weigh heavily on homes across the UK this winter.
“From today, our VAT cut will give households some much-needed breathing space, making the energy price cap £45 a year less than it would have been. This follows the £150 of costs we removed from bills earlier this year.
“Alongside this, we continue to look at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills, as we drive down bills for good through clean power.”
Burnham said: “For many families, the energy bill is the one they dread the most. I don’t accept that it has to be this way, and I am determined to bring down costs for good.”

The zero-bills home: how one family is beating the energy price hikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:00:29 UTC
14:00:29 KST

Clare Naylor paid close attention to how much energy she and her family were using last winter, filling hot-water bottles and bringing out extra blankets to ensure they didn’t go over budget. This year, she won’t have to worry as she is guaranteed not to receive a bill.
While millions of British households face the highest energy charges in three years from today after a 4% rise in the price cap, and predictions of a 16% increase in January, upgrades to Naylor’s home mean she will not have to pay anything.
The four-bedroom detached home in Milton Keynes was recently fitted with a heat pump and 17 solar panels, and a large battery was installed in the garage to manage the energy generated.
The new technology, as well as four new radiators, means the house can use an energy tariff which guarantees she will not pay any bills for five years. In effect, the house behaves like a mini-power station that feeds excess energy back to the grid.
As long as the Naylor family stay within a “fair usage” limit, Octopus Energy guarantees they will not be billed for heating, lighting or any of the devices that a family with three children under 10 use.
“We were always fairly careful,” says Naylor. “Our heating was only ever set to 18C [although] we might boost it if the family were coming around. “Otherwise [it was] slippers, hot-water bottle, jumpers – that’s how you get through the winter.”
This year, she says she will heat the house before the children come home from school, which is something that did not used to happen.
The family’s energy bills were relatively low – she says they were about £130 a month, a sum they now plan to spend on holidays.
The house, which was built in the 1980s, was retrofitted for free by Santander as part of a project to examine how to fund homes towards better energy efficiency. If Naylor had to pay for the works, the solar panels, heat pump and battery would have come to just under £20,000 after a government grant was applied.
The Octopus “Zero Bills” tariff is operating in hundreds of new-build homes around the country since it was launched five years ago. The company is now testing how it works in houses, such as the Naylors’, that are older and need to be retrofitted.
Properties need to have good insulation, solar panels, a heat pump and a battery so that they can generate more energy than is being used. “Typically the homes generate slightly more energy over a year than we’d expect them to use,” said Nigel Banks, the technical director of Zero Bills at Octopus Energy. “One of the fundamental requirements is we need to make enough revenues from selling power back to the grid.”
To qualify for the tariff, homes must have no gas, even for cooking, so the Naylors had to have their gas boiler removed. The zero-bill promise does not cover charging electric vehicles (EVs).
Typically, the best candidates for the retrofitting work are homes built in the last 10 years with good insulation levels, said Banks. The usage cap will be different for each house and is set depending on how much energy they would normally use, with a margin on top.
Santander is working on how to offer financing for households who need to borrow money to fund retrofitting projects. In the meantime, using its home improvement loan, at a 6.4% interest rate over five years, would mean repaying £389 a month for a £20,000 project.
Mick Taylor from Santander said: “We’ve got a big challenge. We’ve got 1.5m mortgage accounts and the vast majority of those are paying monthly energy bills. Consumers are concerned that energy bills are only going one way – they’re probably the second- or third-biggest outgoing for most households,” he said.
“What can we do to help the country move towards net zero with such a big mortgage portfolio? We’ve obviously got a role to play.”
Naylor says that she will try to keep the home at a constant warm temperature during the coming winter. “And then train my children to keep the door shut, which will be fun,” she adds.

Rightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to Keynes | Larry Elliott
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:00:28 UTC
14:00:28 KST

Andy Burnham does a nice line in nostalgia. His first party conference speech as prime minister was full of fond memories for the Britain of the 1950s and 1960s, when working-class families could sense their lives steadily getting better. The underlying message of his address was that, given time, he could rekindle that optimism and return the country to how it was before Margaret Thatcher wrecked everything.
Much of what Burnham says is true. The 1980s was a decade of deindustrialisation, asset-stripping and financial deregulation that has shaped modern Britain – and not in a good way.
But listen a bit more closely to the speech and it becomes clear that Burnham is struggling to find a way to turn back the clock. For a start, he might not be given time. Energy bills are forecast to rise sharply this winter. John Healey’s first budget, in less than a month’s time, is expected to raise taxes or cut spending – taking money out of an economy that is already struggling.
There’s no question that Burnham and Healey would prefer not to be taking these actions but feel they have no choice. Burnham may well rail against 40 years of neoliberalism. He may think neoliberalism was a dud. But his government is constrained by neoliberal ideas and the language used to express them. Burnham and Healey would never use this language themselves, but that’s irrelevant. To make a real difference, they need to tackle head-on the nostrums of the past four decades. Otherwise they will be for ever in thrall to them.
Top of the list is the idea that the UK government is no different from a household. That means it should match its spending to its income as closely as possible, borrowing prudently and within tightly defined limits. Otherwise it will “max out the nation’s credit card” and risk spiralling into unsustainable debt.
This analogy has the benefit of sounding like a statement of the obvious to many voters, but is actually entirely false. There is no such thing as the nation’s credit card, and a country that prints its own currency can never “max out” or face bankruptcy in the way an individual can.
The notion that the government is living well beyond its means is convenient for those on the political right who have an aversion to public spending. The reality is that, as John Maynard Keynes once said: “Anything we can actually do we can afford.” It was that mentality that allowed the Attlee government to create the welfare state when debt was running at more than 250% of national income – more than double today’s level. I don’t know whether Burnham has seen the new play about Keynes in London’s West End, but it seems as if he ought to.
By the same token, it makes no sense to talk about “black holes” in the public finances every time the government looks on course to miss its targets for borrowing as set out in its fiscal rules. These rules are treated as totemic when in reality they can be changed at any time – and are ditched altogether when there is a crisis.
Again, the idea of a black hole is a convenient fiction for those with an interest in shrinking the size of the state. As with “maxing out the credit card”, it forms part of the inquisition every time a minister goes on the TV or radio with a new spending measure: “That’s all very well but how are you going to pay for it?”
Burnham is committed to re-industrialising Britain, but to do so he will have to break with the neoliberal convention that it is not the job of the government to pick winners. As the prime minister should point out, China, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea have all built up their manufacturing strength by picking winners, and Britain could do the same. Indeed, the one sector that Thatcher picked out for special care and attention – financial services – has gone from strength to strength. Breaking the taboo on picking winners is central to a successful industrial strategy.
Last but not least, Burnham has to address Thatcher’s famous dictum: you can’t buck the market. A cursory glance back at recent economic history shows that governments buck the market all the time. In 2009, the Bank of England responded to the risk of a second Great Depression posed by the global financial crisis by buying government bonds. This provided money to the banking system while cutting the interest rate – or yield – on bonds. This was bucking the market. In 2020, the then Conservative government spent hundreds of billions on a furlough scheme that paid up to 80% of the wages of workers at risk of losing their jobs during the pandemic. This, too, was bucking the market.
So when Burnham, in his conference speech, harked back to the Britain in the immediate decades after the second world war, he missed out a key part of the reason working people felt things were getting better. Rather than being constrained by fiscal rules, governments were committed to full employment. Capital controls meant that financial markets were tightly controlled.
Before we get too nostalgic, it’s worth remembering that things were far from perfect in the so-called postwar golden age. By today’s standards, growth rates were spectacular, but they lagged well behind those of Germany and France. Even so, managed capitalism certainly delivered more for working people than has been the case in the unmanaged capitalism that has followed.
The postwar status quo has been turned on its head. Then, financial markets were caged to ensure that governments could pursue domestic economic goals. Now, governments are caged and the markets are free. It is a classic case of the tail wagging the dog.
Shifting back to a world where finance is fettered is not going to be easy – but until it happens, governments will remain boxed in. Burnham and Healey will be forced to do things they know will harm the economy because they know any deviation from what is acceptable to the received wisdom risks a backlash from the financial markets.
Some new economic thinking is required, and if ever there were a time for an iconoclast like Keynes, it is surely now. He would certainly have no truck with the wrong-headed economic policies of the past half-century and the seemingly commonsense phrases – such as maxing out the credit card – that have been used to disguise just how nonsensical they are.
All credit to Burnham. His analysis of what has gone wrong has clearly rattled his political enemies. Even so, he risks becoming the nearly man of British politics: the prime minister who asked the right questions but failed to come up with the right answers.
- 
  Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

Rachel Roddy’s recipe for lasagne with three cheeses, tomato and tiny meatballs | A kitchen in Rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:00:28 UTC
14:00:28 KST

Bearing in mind that lasagne is a construction, it pays to start with some easygoing geometry. That is, think about the size of the dish you want to fill in relation to the size of the sheets you are using and the number of layers you want the lasagne to have. For four to six servings, I use a particular ceramic dish, because its 20cm x 29cm proportions mean that, broadly speaking, two fresh sheets of shop-bought egg pasta or four dried ones make a single layer (homemade pasta can be rolled and cut with scissors to whatever size you like, so is less relevant here).
Having calculated how many sheets are needed for each layer, the next question is: how high do you want your lasagne building to be? Height depends on the density of the filling, which, in the case of this week’s recipe, includes sausagemeat rolled (using wet hands and speed) into small, grape-sized meatballs that act like height-boosters in shoes. This elevation, along with tomato sauce and three cheeses, means that, even with just four layers, this lasagne has depth and cuts into satisfying squares. All this emphasis on the dish is also fitting because the word lasagne seems to derive from the Latin lasanum (cooking vessel), which in turn derives from the ancient Greek λάσανον, which signified either a cooking vessel or a tripod set over a fire.
Back to 2026, though, and this busy, joyful lasagne borrows from both the Neapolitan lasagne di carnevale, with the inclusion of very small meatballs, tomato sauce and mozzarella, and a Sicilian lasagne in the use of ricotta loosened with a little milk (so it has a soft, spreadable texture) in place of bechamel. A four-layer lasagne is also convenient in that all the other components are split into quarters, then spread, splattered or arranged on each of the layers. I suggest using fresh pasta, but dried works, too, although that will need a more liquid tomato sauce to cook through. I also recommend a 30-second pre-boil, which starts to cook and firm the sheets, although please disagree and do otherwise.
Leave the lasagne to rest for at least 30 minutes, so the flavours can settle and the whole thing firms up, before serving in geometric squares.
Lasagne with three cheeses, tomato and tiny meatballs
Serves 4-6
4 tbsp olive oil
1 small garlic clove, peeled and gently bashed so it’s broken but still intact
250g sweet cherry tomatoes, chopped
1 400g tin plum tomatoes, crushed or passed through a food mill
1 pinch red chilli flakes
  Salt
1 small handful basil
  4 pork or vegetarian sausages
  250g ricotta
  Milk, as required
300g mozzarella, drained for at least 12 hours
75-100g parmesan
  8-12 sheets fresh lasagne, depending on the size of the sheets and your dish
Working in a deep frying pan or saucepan on a low heat, warm the olive oil and garlic for a minute or two. Add the fresh and tinned tomatoes and the chilli, stir, then raise the heat so the tomatoes simmer in a lively way for about 20 minutes, mashing them with the back of a spoon to break up any lumps. Once the sauce has lost any wateriness, add salt and a few basil leaves, then set aside.
Squeeze the sausage meat from its casings, then, working with wet hands, form the meat into grape-sized balls. In another frying pan, heat two tablespoons of oil and fry the balls lightly, so they’re almost, but not quite, cooked through.
Beat the ricotta with the milk and some salt to form a soft paste, thinly slice the drained mozzarella and grate the parmesan.
If you are doing the pre-boil, bring a large pan of salted water to a boil; have a bowl of cold water ready and spread a tea towel alongside it. Working in batches, drop the pasta sheets into the boiling water for 30 seconds, lift into the cold water to cool, then lay them out on the tea towel.
Construct the lasagne in a 20cm x 29cm (or similar sized) dish, bearing in mind that it has four layers, so divide all of the components by four, but the meatballs only by three, because they don’t go on top. Rub the dish with oil, then make a base layer of two (or more) pasta sheets. Spread with a quarter of the ricotta and the tomato sauce, dot with meatballs and mozzarella, some basil, and scatter over parmesan. Cover with a second layer of pasta and repeat until everything is used up. Finish with a scattering of parmesan.
Bake at 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 for 25 minutes, until the top is golden and the sides are bubbling. Leave to rest for 30 minutes, then cut into squares and serve.

Spain’s warning on drug pricing deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Want to receive this newsletter straight to your inbox? Sign up here to receive the reporting and intel from the Gastein Health Forum.
— Europe must band together to tackle drug pricing pressures rather than being picked off one by one, Spain’s Health Secretary Javier Padilla Bernáldez tells Morning Health Care.
— Parliament’s environment committee will vote on its opinion for the Biotech Act.
— EU health ministers meet in Dublin.
Welcome to Thursday’s Morning Health Care! Kudos to all those who made it to the 6am hike ahead of another jam-packed day at the European Health Forum in Gastein. I won’t throw Claudia under the bus, but I, for one, proudly took the lie-in. For those who opted for the walk, at least their stride shouldn’t have been impacted by this news that air pollution can impact marathon times — thanks to the clear air of the Austrian Alps.
Get in touch: [email protected], [email protected]. Follow us on X: @chiappa_claudia, @domgiannini_
LET’S COME TOGETHER: Spain’s Health Secretary Javier Padilla Bernáldez has called for Europe to band together in the face of U.S. drug pricing pressures rather than seeking bilateral agreements. As pressure mounts on Germany to strike a deal with the Trump administration, Padilla Bernáldez argues any such deal risks weakening the European market.
Right now: “When [most favored nation] emerged, there was a consensus that the main strength of the European Union was being more people with a higher degree of universal health coverage, and the weakness was having a fragmented market,” Padilla Bernáldez told Morning Health Care at the European Health Forum in Gastein, Austria. “If you go bilateral, you are losing this main strength.”
The context: Europe is grappling with how to respond to the Trump administration’s most-favored-nation drug pricing policy, which risks delaying the launch of new medicines in Europe. Companies fear launching in Europe will risk a lower matched price in the U.S., limiting profits in that lucrative market.
Is the breakfast club no more? Countries initially seemed to be on the same page about the best way to respond to the pressure — as a team. Back in June, 11 countries, led by Sweden, first met to debate how to protect EU prices and agreed they were stronger when working together rather than pursuing individual deals. The Beneluxa group — a health care alliance uniting Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Austria and Ireland — also urged Europe to protect its solidarity-based health systems and warned against “uncoordinated, individual national responses.”
Sweden continues to lead discussions on drug pricing and reimbursement amid geopolitical pressure, within an EU alliance of authorities that carry out this work known as NCAPR. (The next meeting is Oct. 9.) But some may be breaking ranks.
Art of the deal: U.S. diplomats and pharma companies are eyeing deals with EU countries similar to the one Washington struck with the U.K., which will see the National Health Service pay more for medicines.
Germany has been in talks with U.S. officials over the price of its medicines, following the Section 301 investigation. It has not announced an agreement but is considering rewarding drugmakers with higher prices if they invest locally.
France this week announced a new deal with the pharmaceutical sector on drug pricing, to provide “more clarity and predictability to pharmaceutical companies.” “France is making a clear choice to invest in the future,” the government said Tuesday. Health Minister Stéphanie Rist said access to medicines was at the heart of the policy, while Public Accounts Minister David Amiel said "the resources released throughout the life cycle of medicines must make it possible to finance innovation and the treatments of tomorrow."
Bad idea? Padilla Bernáldez warned that countries are giving up Europe’s main strength, its potentially large market, by thinking that they will be treated “in a positive way by the bully government of the United States” — but “I don't think it's going to happen.”
No comment, but: The U.S. government didn’t respond to a request for comment, but when it announced its trade probe into Germany’s drug pricing policies, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the U.S. was “calling on Germany to pay its fair share for the innovative treatments its people use.”
We’ve seen this film before: “When we talk about procurement in Europe, there are always countries with big economies that think — and maybe that’s true — that they are … going to get a better price if they are going on their own,” Padilla Bernáldez said. “Maybe France and Germany think they are going to calm the United States by going on their own. It doesn't work like that.”
Muddy deals: Yannis Natsis, head of the European Social Insurance Platform, representing payers, agreed that “going it alone is no solution.” “It remains unclear what French patients and taxpayers will get in return for accepting higher prices,” he said. “Even less clear is what pharmaceutical companies are committing to in return, beyond benefiting from those higher prices.”
Yes, but: Renew MEP Stine Bosse said the new French deal has “the right instinct.” But she warned that Europe should act as one in rewarding innovation and manufacturing. Her fear is that multiple sets of rules or bilateral deals will make the EU “more vulnerable” — “we become an even less predictable place for the companies we want to invest here.” Patients will pay the price, she said, and Europe’s competitiveness will suffer. "Europe must act as one, or we will be picked off, one by one."
It’s a common sentiment in Gastein: Valentina Strammiello from the European Patients’ Forum supported the European Commission coordinating a discussion that included patients’ voices, saying it was important that stakeholders were brought together to find a solution. “Otherwise, keeping working in isolation doesn't lead to any solution,” she said.
Also pro-EU: Nathalie Moll, head of pharma lobby EFPIA, said that Europe risks losing out “as a whole” if countries put policies in place to attract manufacturing to their country. “The problem in Europe is … that there isn't enough Europe. And here we need to be smart as a region in how we consider competitiveness and what tools we put in place to attract the investment, and not fragment ourselves even further than we are today.”
What now? Ministers had asked the Commission to conduct an impact assessment of Trump’s policies at their last meeting, which Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi handed back to member states in August — although it found it was too early to assess the impact on Europe. The ball is now in the Council’s court.
Rolling coverage: EFPIA’s Moll said it was “really important” the impact of MFN on Europe is "monitored very closely, so that we can respond to it in the right way," adding there needs to be “continuous assessment.” Europe also had to look at solutions it could implement quickly, and this should include scrapping clawbacks and cost containment measures, she added.
TIME TO VOTE: The environment committee is set to vote on its opinion on the Biotech Act today. Socialists and Democrats MEP Nicolás González Casares, who wrote the draft opinion, has called to scrap or limit the proposal to extend some biotech patents. This is only an opinion since the health and industry committees lead on the proposal.
Talking about the Biotech Act: Padilla Bernáldez has used his appearance at Gastein to defend Spain’s proposal to create a “European Coordinated Market Access Toolbox” to help drugs reach the market earlier. Countries could work together to estimate demand and coordinate negotiations with companies or launch collaborative procurement.
But: Companies could have commitments such as ensuring supply continuity, maintaining European manufacturing capacity, submitting national pricing and reimbursement applications on time, and ensuring equitable launch and access.
Reciprocal commitments: Moll at EFPIA said there also needed to be reciprocal commitments on the part of states. “One of the commitments has to be to increase the value that is given to innovative medicines, so there needs to be a recognition that these products bring value beyond the value to the patient, but also to the economy and in the socio-economic context,” she told Morning Health Care.
Speed up access: Moll has another proposal — an agreement to make medicines available on the market while national pricing and reimbursement negotiations are ongoing, meaning patients would have faster access to drugs. Companies would set an initial price before discussions would start, and if negotiations stalled, patients would be able to keep using the medicine through a non-reimbursed route. Moll admitted the idea was in its early phases and hadn’t been brought to governments.
WELCOME: Ireland’s Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill will chair an informal meeting of EU health ministers in Dublin today, which will also include the EU health commissioner, the World Health Organization’s Europe director and the head of the European Medicines Agency.
Smile: Ministers were shown around Dublin’s National Institute for Bioprocessing Research and Training on Wednesday afternoon, and today’s meeting will kick off with a family photo.
On the agenda: They’ll hold closed-door discussions on innovation and improving patient outcomes; integrating care across the EU and strengthening medical ecosystems; and, of course, discuss global pressures and collective action.
Sneak peek: The Irish Council of the EU presidency wants to lean into Europe’s commitment to universal access to health for the whole population, rather than people’s ability to pay. “There's huge strength in that,” Muiris O’Connor, assistant secretary at the Department of Health, told Gastein via videolink. “We retain a core belief in science, and we purchase medicines and medical products at national scale right across the European Union. So I really think we have to remember just what is really strong about us and shore up the vulnerabilities.” A press conference is scheduled for 3.30 p.m.
SANT, ENVI VOTE ON UCPM PROPOSAL: Lawmakers in the public health and environment committees will vote today on an EU proposal for a union civil protection mechanism, or UCPM, for health emergency preparedness and response.
What’s this about? In the next multiannual financial framework proposal, the Commission wants to expand the civil protection mechanism — created to strengthen cooperation for disasters — to include health emergency preparedness and response. The proposed budget for this was €11 billion, though it’s unspecified how much will go to the civil protection department DG ECHO versus the health preparedness authority DG HERA.
Behind the report: The health and environment committees are leading on this file. Their compromise proposes increasing the budget to over €12 billion and allocating funds across sectors: 40% for civil protection, 40% for health emergencies, and 20% for flexibility.
Some of the changes: The committee draft proposes a new focus on climate-risk assessment, scenario planning and stress testing; emphasizes a One Health approach and measures to build public risk awareness and community preparedness; calls for action to fight disinformation; and expands support for resilient health care systems and workforces, cross-border medical teams, patient evacuation and stockpiling of medical countermeasures.
Smooth sailing: Lawmakers are expecting a “straightforward” vote, after reaching a “balanced agreement” supported by EPP, S&D, ECR, Renew, Greens and The Left, said S&D's Leire Pajín, a co-author with ECR's Aurelijus Veryga.
The FT looks at how Australia is battling a black market for cigarettes after a decade of tax rises.
Patients switching to Novo's Wegovy pill from shots lose more weight, Reuters reports.

American troops are coming back to Lithuania. Will they stay?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

After a six-month break, US troops are set to return to Lithuania, with about 1,000 soldiers expected to deploy under a new rotation. Lithuanian officials and defence experts say the return sends a strong deterrence message to Russia, while Vilnius is also seeking a permanent US military presence.
The Americans are familiar with the forests around Pabradė, where their presence in Lithuania grew steadily over the past decade – from several hundred troops to more than 1,000 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
But the continuous US mission ended in June as Washington reassessed its military role in Europe. A newly built facility in Lithuania stood empty for six months. Within a month, however, it is expected to house American troops again.
The new rotation will include a heavy battalion equipped with Abrams tanks, as before, while an artillery battalion will be replaced by an engineering unit, President Gitanas Nausėda said.
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said the deployment would contribute significantly to the development of Lithuania’s national division and strengthen the protection of defensive lines along the border.
The engineering capability is particularly important because Lithuania’s own engineering regiment in Kaunas is still being developed and lacks much of the equipment needed for heavy units, said retired Col. Gintaras Ažubalis.
Former military commanders said Lithuania is developing its own artillery capabilities, making the US engineering deployment a useful complement to the country’s existing forces.
“The artillery unit means fire support; now we have an engineering unit, which means logistical support, so that the tank battalion can operate effectively,” said Lt. Gen. Jonas Vytautas Žukas, who served as Lithuania’s military chief from 2014 to 2019.
The Americans will also bring specialised equipment and machinery that Lithuania does not have, said Lt. Gen. Arvydas Pocius, who served as military chief from 2009 to 2014.
The number of US troops is expected to remain around 1,000, although it is not yet clear whether the rotation will continue without another break after nine months.
“I doubt this nine-month rotation would have happened if there were no plan to continue the rotation afterward,” Žukas said.
Pocius agreed, saying there had been no indication that the deployment would be a one-time arrangement.
A regional deterrence message
Estonia has also secured the temporary return of US troops.
“That is good news, because American troops on the eastern flank are very important for our security, and it is a very clear message to President Putin: There is no point even thinking about aggression against NATO’s eastern flank,” Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.
It is not yet clear where the US troops returning to Lithuania will come from.
They could be drawn from US units already stationed in Poland, Ažubalis said, arguing that the source of the troops would not change the strategic significance of the deployment.
Former MP, security and defence expert Giedrimas Jeglinskas said the deployment was linked to US forces in Poland and Washington’s plans for a permanent base there.
US President Donald Trump has said progress has been made toward establishing a permanent American base in Poland, where negotiations have been underway for about six months.
Experts say such a move would fit into a broader strengthening of NATO’s eastern flank.
The precise form of the US presence in Poland remains unclear. It could involve a permanent deployment sought by Warsaw, potentially involving about 5,000 additional troops, or strengthened rotational forces numbering around 10,000, said Gerlinde Niehus, a former deputy director of NATO’s defence policy and planning division.
“Whatever form it takes, the overall direction is clear – strengthening the eastern flank,” she said.
Lithuania is also seeking a permanent US base.
“Since we are compensating for the presence of US troops in Lithuania, I proposed establishing a permanent US military base,” Kaunas said.
Whether Lithuania’s existing military infrastructure will be enough to persuade Washington to establish permanent bases in both Poland and Lithuania remains uncertain.
Retired officers say NATO and the United States view Poland and the Baltic states as part of a single strategic region.
“All of this is part of the security of our common region. I have no doubt that these groups will not be separated,” Žukas said.
He nevertheless argued that Lithuania should first focus on completing the establishment of the German brigade.
Germany’s brigade remains Lithuania’s priority
By the end of next year, Lithuania expects the German brigade to number about 5,000 troops – roughly five times the planned US deployment.
But Germany has faced difficulties recruiting enough personnel, particularly specialists.
“Our commitment to transfer a full-capability brigade to Lithuania no later than the end of 2027 is carved in stone,” German Ambassador to Lithuania Cornelius Zimmermann said. “We are particularly looking for specialists in information technology and other fields, and they are not so easy to find.”
Fausta Šimaitytė, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Lithuania, said the brigade should be viewed as a military commitment rather than a voluntary project.
Germany’s domestic politics could also affect the broader environment in which the brigade is established, with the Alternative for Germany party continuing to gain support.
“Germans keep their word, especially the military. Of course, much will depend on political decisions and who comes to power,” Pocius said.
Nausėda sought to reassure those concerned about the German commitment.
“I see that various messages are being spread again. Rest assured, the German brigade will be in Lithuania at full strength,” he said.
While Germany is building up its presence in Lithuania, Canada plays the leading role in NATO’s forward presence in Latvia, with France also increasing its contribution.
French President Emmanuel Macron has committed to strengthening French forces in Latvia, particularly in air defence, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said.
NATO is also moving toward transforming its Baltic air-policing mission into an air-defence mission, although for now that remains a political decision rather than a fully implemented capability.
“Of course, we would always like to have more, but what we have is a sufficient basis for deterrence,” Žukas said. “The message being sent to a potential adversary is that NATO countries will act together, and perhaps the Americans will act together with NATO.”
Pocius said the presence of US forces itself carries particular weight.
“It is sufficient deterrence. For Russia, the American flag is the main bogeyman,” he said.
The United States is expected to present its plans for its military forces in Europe in December. US forces are widely expected to decline in western Europe as Washington urges European allies to take greater responsibility for their own security.
At the same time, Lithuania and other countries on NATO’s eastern flank hope that any reduction in the US presence in Western Europe will be accompanied by a stronger American role farther east, stretching from Romania to Finland.
