From hijacking alert to false-flag claims: How Arab and Iranian outlets framed the Flydubai incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:56:08 UTC
13:56:08 KST

Arabic- and Farsi-language news outlets began Wednesday with the same basic facts: a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv suddenly lost thousands of feet, transmitted emergency codes and diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
After that, the accounts began to diverge.
Al-Bayan, a Dubai-based Arabic-language daily published by Dubai Media Incorporated, and Akhbaar24, a Saudi digital news outlet owned by the Riyadh-based Saudi Research and Media Group, stayed close to airline and airport statements. Doha-based Al Jazeera, the Qatar-funded international news network, reconstructed the aircraft’s movements from flight-tracking data. The London-based pan-Arab newspaper and news site Al-Araby Al-Jadeed gave considerable prominence to Israel’s security response. Tehran-based Mehr News Agency and the Iranian news website Tabnak leaned heavily on Israeli and regional reporting, while Iran’s semiofficial Fars News Agency introduced a far more serious allegation involving a supposed Israeli false-flag operation.
Within hours, the same flight was being presented as an aviation emergency, an Israeli security crisis, a suspected terror attack and, in some Iranian coverage, part of the confrontation between Israel and Iran.
What is known about flight FZ1073?
Flight FZ1073, a Boeing 737 MAX 8 with registration A6-FKF, was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv when it transmitted squawk code 7700, the international signal for a general emergency, and later 7500, which indicates unlawful interference. The aircraft diverted to Tabuk and landed safely.
In a Reuters report headlined “Passengers overcame co-pilot who tried to crash Flydubai flight, Netanyahu says,” correspondents Alexander Cornwell and Rami Amichay reported that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the co-pilot stabbed the pilot and tried to crash the aircraft before passengers and a crew member subdued him.
An Israeli official identified the alleged attacker to Reuters as an Omani national. Netanyahu said Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot. Israeli officials told Reuters their assessment was that the incident was an attempted terror attack rather than a mental-health episode. Saudi authorities and Flydubai had not publicly issued findings establishing a motive.
Reuters also reported that data from the Swedish flight-tracking service Flightradar24 showed the aircraft dropping nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds before the first emergency signal.
Much of the Arab and Iranian coverage appeared before Netanyahu gave his later account of what happened aboard the aircraft, helping explain some of the contradictions in early reports.
Al Jazeera reconstructs the flight
Al Jazeera reporter Mohammed al-Za'anin concentrated on the aircraft’s movements in a report headlined, in English translation, “Sharp Descent, Hijacking Code and Alert: What Happened Aboard the Flydubai Flight?”
Al-Za'anin wrote that data verified by Al Jazeera’s open-source unit showed the aircraft dropping from about 34,000 feet to 16,000 feet shortly before the emergency declaration. His report described the descent as “sharp and sudden” and cited calculated vertical speeds of roughly 14,000 to 18,000 feet per minute, far outside those normally recorded in commercial flight.
The report laid out the sequence minute by minute. According to al-Za'anin, the abnormal descent began around 8:22 a.m. Saudi time. At about 8:32, near the Saudi-Jordanian border, the aircraft transmitted 7700. Minutes later, it switched to 7500 before returning to the general-emergency code. The aircraft briefly entered Jordanian airspace before turning south toward Tabuk.
Al-Za'anin also addressed a detail that initially fueled speculation: the aircraft’s disappearance from civilian tracking screens. He reported that it had moved beyond ground-based tracking coverage and later reappeared through satellite tracking. Its disappearance from the public tracking service did not necessarily mean air traffic controllers had lost contact with it.
His report then turned to Israeli accounts of a violent confrontation between the pilots, while noting that Flydubai had not confirmed those details at the time.
An earlier Al Jazeera breaking-news report, headlined “Report of Security Incident Aboard Plane That Took Off From Dubai for Tel Aviv and Changed Course,” showed how quickly the story was changing. It initially cited Israeli media reports of a possible hijacking and military alerts, then added Israeli reports that the episode involved a confrontation in the cockpit.
How did two Gulf outlets approach it?
In Dubai, aviation reporter Louay Abdullah of Al-Bayan, an Arabic-language daily newspaper, stayed closely with the airline’s official account.
His report, headlined in translation, “Flydubai: Tel Aviv-Bound Flight Lands Safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia After In-Flight Incident,” quoted Flydubai describing an unspecified “incident during the flight” that required a precautionary diversion to Tabuk.
“The safety of our passengers and crews remains our highest priority,” a Flydubai spokesman told Al-Bayan.
Abdullah reported that everyone aboard was safe and that the airline was cooperating with the relevant authorities. He did not assign a motive or characterize the episode as terrorism.
Akhbaar24, a Saudi digital news outlet, also focused on what happened after the diversion. Its Tabuk report, headlined in translation, “Emergency Landing of Flydubai Aircraft in Tabuk and Pilot and Co-Pilot Taken to Hospital,” concentrated on the pilots’ hospitalization, care for the passengers and arrangements for a replacement aircraft.
By then, reports of a stabbing, terrorism and conflicting accounts of the pilots’ nationalities were already circulating elsewhere.
Al-Araby Al-Jadeed puts Israel’s response near the center
Al-Araby Al-Jadeed’s initial breaking report, filed from its Haifa desk, ran under a headline that translates as “Plane Carrying 150 Israelis Lands in Saudi Arabia After Changing Course.”
Rather than reconstructing the flight in the detail Al Jazeera did, the report led with an account from Channel 12, an Israeli commercial television broadcaster, that approximately 150 Israelis were aboard and that the Israeli Air Force had put fighter aircraft on alert. It also cited Israeli Army Radio, the military-run national radio station, reporting that a fight between the pilots had led to the distress call.
The report devoted considerable space to emergency consultations involving Netanyahu and senior Israeli security officials.
The emphasis was different from Al-Bayan’s. The Dubai paper centered the airline and the safe landing; Al-Araby Al-Jadeed centered Israel’s response.
Mehr follows the conflicting versions
Mehr News Agency, a Tehran-based Iranian news agency, initially relied heavily on reports from other media.
One report, whose headline translates as “Incident on Dubai-Tel Aviv Flight With 150 Israeli Passengers; Hijacking Code Activated,” cited Russia Today, the Russian state-funded international broadcaster, and Israeli Army Radio. It reported the emergency signal, the estimated number of Israeli passengers and Israeli fears that the 7500 code could indicate a hijacking. It also noted that other Israeli reports were already suggesting the event might instead have resulted from a confrontation aboard the aircraft.
A later Mehr report, “Contradictory Claims About Security Incident Involving Israeli Aircraft,” made those competing versions the focus.
Citing Al Mayadeen, a Beirut-based pan-Arab satellite news channel, and Israeli television reports, Mehr laid out several accounts: that there had been no hijacking; that a dispute had occurred between the pilots; that reports differed over the pilots’ nationalities; and that one pilot may have intentionally put the aircraft into a rapid descent before the other intervened.
The report did not settle on one version, instead presenting the uncertainty as part of the story.
Tabnak turns to the political consequences
Tabnak, an Iranian news website, subsequently focused on the repercussions for Flydubai’s operations in Israel.
A report headlined, in translation, “Request to Suspend All Flydubai Flights to Israel” said Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev had called for the carrier’s Israel service to be suspended while the incident was investigated.
Citing Channel 12, Tabnak also reported that another Flydubai flight, FZ1081, had turned back toward Dubai.
Its attention had moved from the events aboard FZ1073 to what they might mean for Israeli-Emirati air links.
The false-flag claim
The most consequential Iranian allegation came through Fars News Agency.
Shafaq News, an Iraqi news agency covering Iraq, the Kurdistan Region and the wider Middle East, reported from Tehran under the headline “Israel Planning Aviation Attack to Blame Iran: Fars” that Fars had cited Iranian security agencies claiming Iran obtained intelligence suggesting Israel was considering an attack on an aircraft or airport in the region that could then be blamed on Tehran.
According to the account, Iranian intelligence alleged that such an operation could cause civilian casualties and create grounds for increased international pressure on Iran.
A false-flag operation is an act carried out by one party but designed to make another party appear responsible.
Shafaq News reported that Fars placed the allegation alongside the diversion of Flight FZ1073. It also added a key caveat: “Fars presented no evidence linking the Flydubai incident to its allegations.”
No independently verifiable evidence has emerged showing Israeli responsibility for the Flydubai incident. Netanyahu’s later account pointed instead to the co-pilot, whom he accused of stabbing the pilot and attempting to crash the aircraft.
The Fars claim remains an allegation attributed to Iranian security bodies, not an established explanation of what happened aboard Flight FZ1073.
What the different reports emphasized
Placed side by side, the reports differed as much in emphasis as in timing.
Louay Abdullah’s Al-Bayan report stayed almost entirely with Flydubai’s limited public statement. Mohammed al-Za'anin at Al Jazeera worked from open-source flight data before bringing in reports about events inside the cockpit. Al-Araby Al-Jadeed’s Haifa desk concentrated more heavily on Israel’s military and political response. Mehr documented the competing versions circulating during the first hours of the incident. Tabnak followed the possible consequences for Flydubai’s Israel operations. Fars went furthest, placing the flight alongside an allegation of an Israeli false-flag operation.
Some of that divergence reflects when the reports appeared. The first accounts were published while the aircraft was still airborne or shortly after it landed, when Israeli officials themselves were still trying to determine what had happened. Later coverage had Netanyahu’s public description of an alleged attempt to crash the plane.
The outlets also chose different frames. For Al-Bayan, the story was largely an airline emergency. Al Jazeera treated it first as a flight-tracking and security puzzle. Al-Araby Al-Jadeed focused more closely on the Israeli response. Mehr documented the confusion surrounding the early accounts. Tabnak followed the political fallout. Fars placed the incident within the much larger Israel-Iran confrontation.
The evidence behind those versions varies considerably. The aircraft’s descent and emergency codes can be checked against flight-tracking data. Flydubai’s statements and Netanyahu’s comments are on the record. Claims about motive or covert intelligence operations depend on the sources making them and whatever evidence they can produce.
Fars has presented no evidence connecting Israel to Flight FZ1073, and no independent evidence supporting that allegation has emerged. For now, it remains one of the competing claims that grew around the flight as the story moved from an aviation emergency into the region’s political and information battles.

Netanyahu says too early to tell who was behind plane incident as flydubai halts all flights to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

04:55:41 UTC
13:55:41 KST

Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the apparent attempt to crash a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight, even as Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations called the incident a “terror attack”, without apportioning blame.
Danny Danon told Fox News on Wednesday night that Israel had “no doubt that it was a terror attack from a radical individual. We still cannot link it to a terror state or terror organisation, but for sure we know there was an intention to bring that plane down.”
Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation takes place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”.
The incident – which began when one pilot stabbed another on the flight deck in an apparent attempt to take control of the aircraft – is under investigation. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had more than 170 people on board, most of them from Israel.
In what have been hailed as acts of tremendous bravery, several passenger rushed the cockpit of the flight and wrestled the controls from the alleged attacker even as the plane descended sharply, managing to eventually taking control and stabilising the plane before making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, told Fox News host Sean Hannity: “We’ll get to the root of this attacker, whether he had accomplices” but cautioned that it was “too early to say” when asked whether there was any indication of Iranian involvement.
The pilot accused of carrying out the stabbing was being questioned by Saudi authorities, the Israeli prime minister said, adding that he expected he would soon be taken to the UAE, where the flight took off from. Netanyahu said earlier that he had spoken with the UAE’s president, who agreed that Israel would join the interrogation of the suspect.
Israeli officials, speaking on condition of anonymity to reporters, said the attacker was an Omani national, but there was no comment from Oman or the UAE.
Israel’s foreign ministry later briefed its diplomats around the world that the incident was an “attempted terrorist attack against Israelis, the United Arab Emirates, and the Abraham Accords,” referring to the deal that normalised relations between the two countries in 2020.
But on Wednesday evening Donald Trump told reporters the incident remained unclear, after he had spoken to Netanyahu. “It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job, and he stabbed the pilot,” the US president told reporters in the Oval Office.
Netanyahu was among the world leaders celebrating the bravery of the passengers and crew of the flydubai flight on Wednesday.
A video shared by the prime minister’s office showed passenger Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events on board played out.
Hayoun told the prime minister how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel.
“I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.
As others wrestled with the attacker, Hayoun said he grabbed the controls and pulled them the way he had seen on television. Then other crew members took over.
The stabbed pilot was identified as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, who was said to have made the emergency call and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing others to rush in and subdue the attacker.
In a post on X early on Thursday, Indian prime minister Narendra Modi lauded Machchhar a “hero”. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy,” Modi said.
Machchhar, an Indian citizen from Mumbai, is being treated in a hospital in Saudi Arabia’s north-western city of Tabuk, where the plane landed safely.

Danilo Taino warns China gradually eroding Taiwan Strait status quo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:43:05 UTC
13:43:05 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Italian journalist Danilo Taino warned that China is gradually eroding the cross-strait status quo as it seeks greater control over Taiwan without launching a full-scale invasion, CNA reported Wednesday.
In an op-ed for Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, Taino said US President Donald Trump made no concessions on Taiwan during his meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and maintained Washington’s position that the US does not support Taiwan independence. This led many observers to conclude that the status quo in the Taiwan Strait remained unchanged.
Taino argued that focusing only on the meeting overlooks broader developments surrounding Taiwan. He said Beijing has steadily reshaped the situation in the Taiwan Strait since Xi came to power in 2012.
Chinese military activity near Taiwan has become almost constant, Taino said. Beijing no longer respects the Taiwan Strait median line and has conducted drills that could quickly transition into an attack, he added.
Taino also cited suspicions of Chinese involvement in damage to undersea cables around Taiwan. He said Beijing has expanded disinformation campaigns aimed at convincing Taiwanese that resisting China would be futile.
Together, these measures allow Beijing to gradually alter the cross-strait balance without launching a direct invasion, Taino said. He said China combines military pressure with diplomatic efforts while continuing to call on other countries to maintain stability in the Taiwan Strait.
The Trump-Xi meeting therefore did not restore an earlier balance, Taino said. Chinese pressure on Taiwan has continued despite no major public change in Washington’s policy toward the country.
Taino also highlighted Taiwan’s global economic importance because of its central role in advanced chip production. He said the country produces more than 90% of the world’s most advanced semiconductors used in technologies such as artificial intelligence, giving developments in the Taiwan Strait broader global significance.

Scholar Yang Ming-min says Pax Silica needs Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:42:59 UTC
13:42:59 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s semiconductor and manufacturing capabilities are essential to the US-led Pax Silica initiative, Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research scholar Yang Ming-min (楊明敏) said Monday.
Yang, speaking on the sidelines of a Global Taiwan Institute seminar, said Pax Silica offers a rare opportunity for cooperation, per CNA. He said Taiwan can contribute advanced manufacturing expertise, workforce training, and experience in reducing risks in AI supply chains.
The US began promoting Pax Silica last year to strengthen economic and technology ties among countries seeking to reduce reliance on China. More than 20 countries have joined the initiative, while Panama and the Philippines have also launched measures to attract AI-related trade and high-tech investment.
A key global chip hub, Taiwan supports the initiative as a non-signatory participant through the Economic Prosperity Partnership Dialogue. Taipei endorsed Pax Silica’s principles through a joint statement in January.
Yang said the country faces challenges in supplying high-tech workers because of its declining birthrate and labor shortages. He said international cooperation will be necessary, adding that neither side can rely entirely on its own workforce.
The country also plays an important role in AI infrastructure through its server and manufacturing industries, Yang said. However, he noted that building data centers requires more than servers, with areas such as power infrastructure needing further development.

Taiwan tightens exemptions for military-age men
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:42:47 UTC
13:42:47 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of National Defense said Wednesday that amendments to physical evaluations will take effect starting Oct.31, CNA reported.
The MND recently announced amendments to physical status standards and evaluation criteria for conscripts due to illness or injury. Defense Ministry Medical Affairs Bureau Healthcare Director Colonel Tsai Shih-hung (蔡適鴻) said the bill was announced on Sept. 21 and is undergoing final review. He confirmed that the changes will take effect starting Oct. 31.
For physical status standards, the defense ministry amended 180 of 193 items. The new active-duty personnel height exemption is for people shorter than 150 cm, while the current qualifying range is 158 to 195 cm.
For evaluation criteria due to illness or injury, the defense ministry amended 160 of 176 items. It noted that reservists may then be exempt if diagnosed with cancer or gout. The defense ministry said exemption also applies to those with medium or severe hypertension-induced organ damage, provided that they have been hospitalized for up to three days with 24-hour blood pressure monitoring.
Auxiliary service personnel criteria will be split into two categories. Type A personnel qualify at 145 to 149 cm, but this does not apply to Type B personnel.
A general exemption applies to those shorter than 144 cm. The exemption also applies to those who have a body mass index of 45 or greater.

Taiwan Army phases in 86,114 new T112 rifles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:42:46 UTC
13:42:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s Army is gradually replacing its aging T91 rifles with domestically developed T112 assault rifles under an NT$8.11 billion (US$257.5 million) procurement program that includes training combat units to use the new weapons.
The Army plans to acquire 86,114 of the new rifles, along with laser modules and other accessories, through 2029, per Liberty Times. Combat units will receive the new rifles first, while reserve forces will receive refurbished T91 rifles withdrawn from service.
The 1st Battalion of the 564th Combined Arms Brigade began transitioning to the T112 in June and conducted live-fire training in Kaohsiung on Wednesday. According to Youth Daily News, the exercise involved zeroing the rifles’ iron sights at 25 meters to familiarize soldiers with the new weapons’ handling characteristics.
During the exercise, soldiers fired at targets, examined bullet-hole patterns, adjusted their sights, and fired again to verify the results. The process was intended to improve shooting accuracy.
Senior Sergeant Hung Chen-yi (洪振益), a T112 instructor, told the Liberty Times that the new rifle has design features intended to improve handling. He said its longer barrel helps reduce recoil, while a quick-deploy foregrip and other design features help shooters maintain stable positions when aiming and firing.
Sergeant Major Yang Chi-wei (楊紀濰) of the battalion’s combat support company told the Liberty Times that the transition involves coordinating training plans and sending personnel for instruction. He described zeroing as both a basic shooting exercise and an important step in establishing individual shooting parameters.
Yang said the transition also requires logistical and administrative adjustments. Units must arrange storage space, check accessories and spare parts, establish inventory records, and ensure that recorded equipment quantities match physical stock as the Army manages old and new rifles simultaneously.

Gastronomy helps convey important messages about Ukraine to the world – Gastro United founder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:42:00 UTC
13:42:00 KST

Gastronomy helps convey important messages about Ukraine to the world – Gastro United founder
Restaurateur and chef Andriy Magaletskiy, President of the Association of Culinary Professionals of Ukraine and founder of Gastro United, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"Gastronomy is a very effective tool of public diplomacy. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has a public diplomacy department, and we cooperate effectively with it," Magaletskiy said.
According to him, gastronomy and the emotions it evokes can sometimes make it much easier to convey messages important to Ukraine to foreign audiences, including explaining why the country needs assistance and why it must stand strong.
He noted that Ukrainian chefs are seeking to change the established perception of Ukrainian cuisine abroad by presenting it as modern, diverse and refined.
"It is important for us to convey to people that Ukrainian cuisine is not about sharovarshchyna. And it is not just salo, borshch and varenyky. We try to show that Ukrainian cuisine is refined, modern and very delicious," Magaletskiy said.
According to him, promoting Ukrainian cuisine in this way also helps strengthen Ukraine's position in the European gastronomic space. In the long term, it is important for foreigners to travel to Ukraine not only for its historical and cultural landmarks but also for gastronomic experiences, just as they travel to other European countries and cities where cuisine is an important part of their tourist appeal.
"I want Ukraine to be seen as part of Europe's cultural family and its gastronomic family. We have this hospitality gene: welcoming guests, offering them food, treating them, entertaining them, celebrating. It is part of our culture, and it is very interesting and vibrant," the chef said.

Pakistani airstrikes on Afghanistan kill nine, Taliban government says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:41:37 UTC
13:41:37 KST

Pakistani airstrikes on Afghanistan killed 9 people and injured 11 more on Thursday, the Afghan Taliban government said, amid an escalation in fighting between the South Asian neighbors after three months of relative calm.
The strikes destroyed three houses in Kunar and Helmand provinces, Afghan Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid said on social media website X/Twitter.
At least nine people were killed, including women and children. "We condemn this act as an aggression and crime in violation of all accepted principles," he said.
A Pakistani government spokesperson said they killed 22 "terrorists" 22 in the airstrike, as well as weapons and ammunition.
Reuters could not independently verify the information.
Former allies turned foes
Pakistan and Afghanistan have increasingly been at odds over militancy, with Islamabad accusing Kabul of harboring militants who stage cross-border attacks.
The Taliban government denies the charge and says militancy is Pakistan's internal problem.

====================================================================================================

Italy extends border checks on travelers from Spain – again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:41:24 UTC
13:41:24 KST

Travelers flying or sailing between Italy and Spain will continue to face border controls after Italy extended its temporary suspension of Schengen rules with Spain.
Italy’s Interior Ministry announced that the controls will remain in place for another 15 days, according to Reuters. The suspension has already been extended several times.
The Schengen system normally allows people to travel between participating European countries without routine checks at their internal borders.
Italy initially suspended the arrangement with Spain on July 31 after more than 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa, from neighboring Morocco.
The two countries do not share a land border, meaning Italy’s measures primarily affect passengers traveling between them by plane or ship. Those travelers must pass through border controls that would not normally apply to travel within the Schengen area.
Spain responded to Italy’s decision by introducing its own border controls for travelers arriving from Italy.

Elon Musk joins U.S. government project examining future military technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:41:18 UTC
13:41:18 KST

Elon Musk will work alongside defense technology executive Palmer Luckey and former U.S. House Speaker Newt Gingrich on a government project examining what the military will need on future battlefields.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Musk’s involvement Wednesday, according to The Guardian.
The initiative, called “Project Meridian,” will run for 120 days and is expected to produce a public, unclassified report, according to the U.S. Department of Defense.
The department said the project aims to “identify the capabilities necessary to achieve absolute technological dominance on the future battlefield.”
Hegseth discussed the initiative during a speech to soldiers at a military base in Quantico, Virginia.
“We need to look forward to achieve technological and military dominance on the battlefield in the coming decades,” he said, according to news agency dpa.
Musk previously headed the Department of Government Efficiency, known as Doge. U.S. President Donald Trump appointed him to lead the initiative in January 2025 as part of efforts to reduce the size and cost of the federal government.
Musk left Doge in May last year, and the department was shut down about six months later.
His involvement in Project Meridian comes after a public dispute with Trump last year. The two exchanged accusations and claims on their respective social media platforms.
Musk owns the social media platform X, while Trump has his own platform, Truth Social.
According to The Guardian, Musk’s new role indicates that his relationship with the Trump administration has improved since that dispute.

Flydubai pilot arrested after midair incident forces emergency landing in Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:41:12 UTC
13:41:12 KST

A Flydubai flight from Dubai to Israel made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after an incident involving the plane’s two pilots.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one pilot stabbed the other and apparently attempted to crash the aircraft. The arrested pilot is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu.
There are still unanswered questions about what happened during the flight, with conflicting accounts emerging throughout Wednesday.
Flight data showed the aircraft suddenly lost 5.2 kilometers of altitude about two hours after leaving Dubai. It then climbed before dropping another 2.1 kilometers.
The aircraft transmitted an emergency signal and later another signal indicating a possible hijacking or other interference. It landed at Tabuk airport in Saudi Arabia at 07:44 Danish time.
Both pilots were taken to hospital after landing. No information has been provided about the condition of the pilot who was stabbed. Flydubai said all passengers were unharmed.
Netanyahu identified the injured pilot as Indian captain Smit Machchhar.
“My tribute to the Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar for his extraordinary courage,” Netanyahu wrote on X.
Netanyahu said Machchhar fought back despite being stabbed and opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the other pilot.
He also said a pilot traveling as a passenger entered the cockpit and helped stabilize the aircraft before the emergency landing.
Several media outlets, including Sky News, reported that passenger accounts consistently described some form of fight between the two pilots.
Netanyahu called those who intervened “heroes,” saying they “saved many lives and prevented a major catastrophe.”

New rules guarantee young Danes mental health treatment within 30 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:41:02 UTC
13:41:02 KST

King Frederik picked up the brush himself to help create his first official portrait as monarch – but Danish critics are divided over the finished result.
The portrait, created by visual artist Cathrine Raben Davidsen over the past two years, was unveiled Friday evening in the Great Hall at Frederiksborg Castle.
It shows King Frederik in full uniform, standing in an abstract green landscape on a ground covered with marguerite flowers.
Some of those flowers were painted by the king himself.
Raben Davidsen asked King Frederik whether he would like to paint some of the marguerites, something he “really wanted to” do, according to the artist.
“He cared very much about painting these flowers. I thought it was nice in one way or another to allow him to also be a part of the work,” she says.
The marguerites are not there by chance. They are one of Denmark’s national flowers and also serve as a reference to Queen Margrethe, whose nickname is Daisy.
Getting to know the man behind the king
Raben Davidsen met King Frederik privately several times during the two-year process because she wanted the painting to reflect both the monarch and the person behind the title.
“It was important for me to get to know him as a human being before having to think of him as king as well,” she says.
Their first meeting took place in her studio. For their second meeting, the king invited her to Kongsøre Forest by the Isefjord.
The area has personal significance for Frederik, who spent considerable time there while training to become a frogman.
Raben Davidsen later researched the history of the area and discovered another royal connection. A royal oak once stood there, under which Frederik VII reportedly liked to stand during hunts.
“That brought yet another historical layer to it. That it was not just a special place for King Frederik, but it also had a reference to his family,” she says.
The landscape behind the king in the finished portrait is based on Kongsøre Forest and the royal oak.
Despite discussing the portrait with the king throughout the process, Raben Davidsen says she was given “completely free hands”.
She also admits that showing him the nearly finished painting for the first time was nerve-racking.
“It is certainly boundary-pushing, and you certainly hope that he can recognize himself in it,” she says.
She does not reveal how the king reacted.
But does he look like himself?
That question has also occupied Danish critics since the portrait was unveiled.
Politiken art critic Mathias Kryger sees a “slightly disarmed and worried expression” around the king’s mouth and eyes.
“Doesn’t he look more like Joachim than himself?” he asks, referring to the king’s younger brother, Prince Joachim.
Berlingske royal reviewer Jakob Steen Olsen also questions the resemblance, writing that the portrait “resembles without quite resembling”.
“You can easily see who it is supposed to depict, but the sum of the parts has not quite fallen into place,” he writes.
Steen Olsen also sees a different Frederik from the sporty and cheerful king Danes encounter at events such as Royal Run.
He compares the uniform to a “paper doll”, saying it creates the impression of a king “wearing a costume for the role he is to fill”.
Despite those reservations, Steen Olsen considers the portrait a successful effort.
Weekendavisen commentator Anne Sophia Hermansen takes a very different view.
She calls the portrait “alluring” and says Raben Davidsen has handled the task “exemplarily”.
“It can go completely wrong when a ruler is to be portrayed. (…) And it can go well, and that is the case with the first official royal portrait of King Frederik,” she writes.
Hermansen particularly highlights the king’s expression. While previous monarchs have been portrayed with “fine moustaches and magnificent sideburns”, she sees something different in Frederik.
His expression is “open and curious”, she writes, while his carefully painted stubble makes him look “like a human being more than a person of power”.
Kryger is considerably less enthusiastic.
He ends his Politiken review with a pointed question:
“How would it look if the painting of the king had been real art?”
On display at Frederiksborg Castle
The portrait was unveiled as part of celebrations marking the 150th anniversary of the Carlsberg Foundation, with King Frederik and Queen Mary attending.
From Monday, the public can see the painting at Frederiksborg Castle, home to Denmark’s national portrait collection, which includes thousands of portraits of monarchs, politicians, scientists and artists.
Raben Davidsen is the first female artist to paint an official portrait of a monarch for the Great Hall at Frederiksborg Castle.
She hopes visitors will look beyond individual details and experience the painting as a whole.
“I really hope that people will take the time to see it as a complete painting and notice the painterly qualities. That one can sense the human Frederik and King Frederik in this work,” she says.
RITZAU/Copenhagen Post

“I really hope that people will take the time to see it as a complete painting and notice the painterly qualities. That one can sense the human Frederik and King Frederik in this work,” she says.
RITZAU/Copenhagen Post

UN Refugee Agency Expresses Concerns About Malaysia’s Deportation of Asylum Seekers to Myanmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:35:00 UTC
13:35:00 KST

The United Nations refugee agency yesterday expressed its concerns over Malaysia’s return this week of nearly 1,500 asylum seekers to Myanmar, in spite of the ongoing conflict and dire humanitarian situation inside the country.
The 1,476 people were returned to Myanmar via ship on Tuesday, the first phase in the agreed “voluntary” repatriation of some 5,000 asylum seekers currently held in Malaysian immigration detention centers.
While Malaysia insists that the returns are strictly voluntary, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said yesterday that it was concerned about the fate of the 1,476 people, given the country’s continuing conflict and dire human rights and humanitarian situation.
Since those returned had been held in detention centers, it had “serious questions about whether decisions to return were genuinely free and informed,” UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Protection Edem Wosornu said in a statement. The U.N. agency has been blocked from accessing Malaysian immigration detention centers since 2019.
“We are concerned by these returns at a time when people sent back to Myanmar may face serious risks, and some within the group may be in need of international protection,” Wosornu said.
While recognizing Malaysia’s “sovereign responsibility” to manage asylum and migration issues, UNHCR urged the government “to ensure that all returns are subject to robust safeguards, including individual assessments and access to protection procedures.”
UNHCR’s statement came as Malaysia’s government confirmed that 3,524 refugees had been approved for the second phase of the “voluntary repatriation program.” Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil said yesterday that the individuals had been identified by the Myanmar authorities, and that their names were submitted to Malaysia in a diplomatic note dated August 13. He added that Kuala Lumpur was awaiting notification from Myanmar on the date for the repatriation.
The ethnic make-up of the two groups is unclear, but Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has justified the repatriations with reference to the recent wave of public hostility towards the large population of Rohingya Muslims in Malaysia.
Thousands of Rohingya have arrived in Malaysia since 2017, when the Myanmar military launched an ethnic cleansing campaign that pushed more than 740,000 from their homes in Rakhine State into Bangladesh. As of February, Rohingya made up 126,000 of the 193,800 asylum seekers from Myanmar registered with UNHCR in Kuala Lumpur.
A coalition of civil society groups last week raised grave concerns about the possible deportation of Rohingya Muslims to Myanmar, given the continuing conflict in Rakhine State and the likelihood that they would be subjected to mistreatment and abuse.
Among ASEAN governments, Malaysia has been among the most critical of the Myanmar military’s seizure of power in 2021, and its ruthless attempts to put down the armed uprising that followed. But the growing domestic pressure over refugees has forced Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim to adopt a more accommodating position toward Naypyidaw.
In a bid to expedite the return of refugees, Anwar is set to welcome coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing to Malaysia for an official visit later this month. Confirming the Myanmar leader’s visit yesterday, Communications Minister Fahmi said that Anwar would “hold discussions with Myanmar in the near future to facilitate the return of more Myanmar refugees to their country,” Bernama reported.
Given Malaysia’s previously principled position on Myanmar – to say nothing of its vocal advocacy for the Palestinian cause – rights groups have accused it of double standards.
“Malaysia has spoken forcefully about accountability, finding durable solutions, and the need to address the root causes of displacement in Myanmar,” Amnesty International Malaysia and Asylum Access Malaysia said in a statement yesterday. At the same time, it “is prepared to roll out the red carpet and host Min Aung Hlaing in Malaysia to facilitate the accelerated return of refugees.”
In response to these criticisms, Anwar has cited the need to prioritize the security and interests of Malaysia. “The issue of Myanmar refugees is not a new problem, but rather a legacy spanning decades that has placed pressure on the country in terms of security, social affairs and management,” he wrote in a Facebook post earlier this week.

Japan's Sanae Takaichi announces new tightened measures for foreigners seeking permanent residency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:31:15 UTC
13:31:15 KST

The measures come as the country’s conservative leader Sanae Takaichi looks to deliver on election promises, which were spearheaded by vast immigration reforms, in her historic supermajority election victory in February.
Japan toughened requirements for foreigners wanting to obtain permanent residency on Thursday, as part of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's push to tighten immigration controls.
Under new rules that will come into effect in stages, foreign residents wishing to stay in Japan permanently will have to prove their annual income is above average and they can carry casual conversations in Japanese.
Application fees will also rise 20-fold from Thursday. At one immigration office in central Tokyo, hundreds of people queued, hoping to wrap up procedures before the price spike.
"I understand that over-accepting foreigners might dilute Japan's unique culture. But at the same time, given its low birth rate and aging population, Japan has to accept foreigners," said US-born university student Yujie Chono, who was among those waiting.
The 22-year-old told the AFP news agency, in fluent Japanese, that he had been waiting for five hours to file his paperwork. Previous guidelines did not lay out specific thresholds for income, pension or language skills.
Even though Japan has a rapidly ageing population and is suffering labour shortages in many sectors, opposition to immigration is growing, prompting a push by Takaichi for tighter regulations on foreign nationals.
"As the number of foreign residents in Japan increases, the government is facing the fact that some citizens feel anxiety and a sense of unfairness," Takaichi said in an extended post on X on Sunday, adding that she was pushing for "orderly coexistence" with foreign nationals.
Programmes to attract international workers have fuelled public worry, anti-immigration sentiment has spread across social media and false claims have circulated widely, including that a significant portion of welfare payments in Japan goes to foreigners, and that they are making Japanese streets less safe.
Experts and many business leaders warn however that Japan must welcome more foreign workers to sustain itself.
"Japan should stop viewing foreigners merely as a temporary labour force and instead promote their long-term settlement by expanding Japanese-language education and improving their treatment," the Nikkei business daily said in a recent editorial.
Foreigners were a major issue in last year's upper house election which saw the sharp rise of the "Japanese-first" Sanseito party, which describes immigration as a "silent invasion".
The new rules for permanent residency come after the ruling Liberal Democratic Party last year pushed to tighten regulations for business manager visas, meaning entrepreneurs will be forced to leave Japan if they don't meet the new conditions.
Thursday's changes may prevent some people from applying for permanent residency but should not immediately push anyone out of the country.
Under the regulations, the application fee for permanent residency will soar to 200,000 yen (€1,116) from the current 10,000 yen (€56).
Candidates must also show "understanding" of social rules and demonstrate expected pension benefits equivalent to someone who has paid pension insurance for 30 years.

====================================================================================================

Country diary: Which tree sounds the best in the wind? Take a bough, the poplar | Derek Niemann
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:30:27 UTC
13:30:27 KST

The wind-catchers along the bottom of the valley miss nothing. Even the lightest breath has them whispering. And when the wind strengthens, they do a good imitation of the river streaming over boulders below their feet. Truly, when it blows, it pours.
Pass a poplar and you are enjoying the best example of psithurism, the sound of wind in trees. All this growing season, I have listened politely to oaks, alders and willows, but if I rocked up in a pub looking for chatty company, I’d want a poplar on the bar stool next to me.
The name psithurism seems to have been conjured up from Greek roots as recently as the 19th century, yet the practice is as old as humanity. It exposes a curious and inescapable fact – wind itself has no voice. The explorer‑conservationist John Muir tramped many a mile through America’s wild lands, observing that “winds are advertisements of what they touch”.
He may well have been thinking of talkative, animated aspens, but all members of the poplar clan are physiologically equipped to shoot the breeze with a wide range of sound and movement. Every broad leaf, shaped like an ace of spades, is well separated from its neighbour on a long stem. Every leaf is therefore washing on a line. Blow, wind, blow.
Right now, conditions are what meteorologists call a fresh breeze, enough to bring out a sway and a swoosh, the noise a tide over fine pebbles, the sight upper trunks tilting back and forth to the rhythm.
The top boughs are visible evidence of wind as wave, for each sprig springs to life in turn, hundreds of leaves twirling at once. The overall effect is something akin to a host of green glitterballs. Close up, each leaf appears to be spinning in agony or ecstasy, desperate to break free or stay attached. Photosynthesis must be quite a giddy wonder, for how do rotating cells catch the sun?
Over the coming weeks, these wind chimes will break, their leaves raining down. And up above, in the so-tall trees, there will be a new percussion, the click-clack creak of branch on branch, the incoming drumbeat of winter.

The United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan said last week it had documented more than 1,100 civilian casualties in the country in cross-border violence so far this year.

COLOMBO, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- The World Bank on Wednesday approved 110 million U.S. dollars to help Sri Lanka repair and reconstruct 600 km of roads severely damaged by Cyclone Ditwah.
Issuing a press release, the World Bank said the financing will prioritize roads that restore access to markets, schools and health facilities in communities most severely affected by the cyclone.

Cyclone Ditwah struck Sri Lanka in November 2025, causing an estimated 4.1 billion dollars in damage and affecting nearly 2 million people across all 25 districts.
The transport sector sustained severe damage, including nearly 2,000 km of provincial roads, more than 3,500 km of rural roads and close to 700 bridges. Recovery needs in the sector are estimated at 1.31 billion dollars. ■

Huawei unveils Mate 90 phones, leans on homegrown chip design to offset US curbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:15:00 UTC
13:15:00 KST

Huawei unveils Mate 90 phones, leans on home-grown chip design to offset US curbs
- Huawei launched the Mate 90 series featuring in-house Kirin 9050 Pro chips using "LogicFolding" technology to improve performance despite US semiconductor restrictions.
- The Mate 90 phones run on Huawei's HarmonyOS 7 and have higher prices due to rising memory and component costs.
- Huawei leads China's foldable phone market with 75% share, seeing sales rise after Apple's foldable iPhone Duo announcement in September.
AI generated
BEIJING – Huawei Technologies unveiled its Mate 90 smartphone series on Oct 1, betting on its in-house operating system and redesigned chip architecture to boost its performance in the face of US curbs on shipments of advanced semiconductors.
Speaking to reporters on Sept 29 ahead of the launch, Huawei consumer business chief Richard Yu said the company still faces constraints in the supply of advanced chips.
“Advanced semiconductor capacity remains very limited in China, and Huawei’s Ascend AI chips also draw on that same capacity,” Yu said.
“The capacity for smartphone chips remains tight, even though rising smartphone prices have curbed shipment volumes (for handsets).”
The launch will test whether Huawei can keep advancing its smartphone line-up despite US restrictions that have limited its access to cutting-edge chipmaking tools, forcing the company to develop alternative ways to boost processor performance.
The Mate 90 series succeeds the Mate 80 line launched in November 2025. Premium models, including the Mate 90 Pro Max, are powered by Huawei’s Kirin 9050 Pro, a system-on-chip built with a technique Huawei calls LogicFolding.
The method restructures a chip’s internal wiring in three dimensions rather than the conventional flat, two-dimensional layout, allowing for denser, faster processing – though it requires more wafers to produce.
Eric Xu, Huawei’s rotating chairman, said at a media event in Shanghai in September that supply of the company’s Ascend 950 artificial intelligence chips could not meet domestic demand due to capacity constraints.
Yu said China’s advanced chipmaking still relies on deep ultraviolet lithography machines, and that while extreme ultraviolet technology is “valuable”, Chinese manufacturers are still working towards it.
Huawei would use more chips built with the LogicFolding technique in future smartphones, Yu said.
Huawei did not disclose who manufactures the Kirin 9050 Pro. Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (SMIC), China’s top logic foundry, is widely believed to produce the Kirin chips used in Huawei’s Mate series as well as its Ascend AI processors.
SMIC did not respond to a request for comment.
Huawei’s latest phones run on its home-grown, Android-free HarmonyOS 7 operating system, which Huawei says supports more than 450,000 apps and services.
The Mate 90 Pro Max with 16GB of memory and 512GB of storage will be priced at 9,999 yuan (S$1,900), 2,000 yuan more than the same version of its predecessor at launch. The standard and Pro models start at 5,999 yuan and 6,999 yuan respectively.
Huawei said the top-end Mate 90 models deliver a 31% increase in overall performance over the previous flagship generation.
Higher prices for handsets
Chinese smartphone-makers are grappling with rising memory and component costs, leading them to raise prices and shift more shipments towards premium models.
Yu said rising memory prices had added an average of US$200 (S$256) to the cost of each handset, weighing on Huawei’s profit margins.
“We have to increase prices as well, yet at a slower pace,” Yu said.
China’s domestic smartphone shipments fell 7% year on year between January and August, even as Huawei’s shipments in the country rose 13%, according to research firm International Data Corp (IDC).
The average selling price of smartphones in China climbed 11.3% year on year in the second quarter to US$543, while the average price of Huawei smartphones declined 14.7% to US$628, IDC data showed.
Apple vs Huawei foldable
Apple announced its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, in September, entering a category long dominated by Samsung Electronics and Chinese rivals such as Huawei.
Yu said he welcomed Apple’s entry to the market.
“I am very pleased to see the launch of a similar product by our peers,” Yu said.
Huawei now holds about a 75% share in China’s foldable phone market, he said.
“Between Sept 10 and 13, our Pura X Max foldable phone sales shot up 76% week on week right after Apple’s iPhone Duo launch,” Yu said, adding that shipments of the Pura X Max, which is similar in size to the iPhone Duo, had topped 1.2 million units in China since its April release.
Apple is expected to ship six million iPhone Duo units in 2026, with China – the world’s largest market for foldable phones – accounting for nearly a quarter of that, according to data from Counterpoint Research. REUTERS

US-led coalition ends anti-Islamic State mission in Iraq amid heightened regional tensions and security fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:08:24 UTC
13:08:24 KST

The US-led force has been operating in Iraq for 12 years to dismantle IS terrorist group networks which had threatened to take over the region and plunge it into instability.
A US-led coalition deployed in Iraq more than a decade ago to fight extremists concluded its mission on Wednesday, a move celebrated by the country's leaders and US President Donald Trump despite fears of emboldened pro-Iran armed factions.
Coalition troops deployed to Iraq and Syria in 2014 to fight the so-called Islamic State group in Iraq and Syria, which had seized large swathes of territory, committed massacres, and forced thousands of women and children into slavery.
The group was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle its remnants.
Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind down the mission, and US troops withdrew gradually from bases across the country, restricting their presence to the autonomous northern Kurdistan region.
"This day is a victory for the United States, a victory for Iraq, and a decisive victory over ISIS," wrote Trump in a post on social media.
"I had a choice to stay or to leave, and felt, without question, that it was time for America to go home," he added.
The US-led coalition did not defeat IS alone, as it was heavily aided by Kurdish Peshmerga fighters, who played an important role, as did powerful Iraqi factions, including pro-Iran groups that have yet to disarm.
The Iraqi government believes it will deprive Tehran-backed factions of the excuse they have used to retain their arsenal. But many fear the pullout might boost the pro-Iran factions and draw the country deeper into the Middle East war.
Hours after the US announced the completion of the pullout, supporters of those groups gathered in a flag-lined public space to celebrate, with speeches delivered from a stage decorated with model drones.
Speaking at the event, a military spokesperson for Kataeb Hezbollah said the factions had been in talks on "regulating" their weapons but "have not yet received a response from the Iraqi government".
As such, they were "not bound by any timeline or agreement" to surrender their weapons, he added, and retained "the right to directly respond to any American or Zionist violation of Iraq's sovereignty".
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said "a new phase has begun, defined by Iraq's sovereignty, the strength of its institutions (and) the readiness of its forces."
Al-Zaidi, elected this year, has vowed to ensure armed factions hand over their weapons. His government set Thursday as the deadline for factions to disarm, but later said the deadline was meant to mark the start of "regulating" the armed groups.
With several Iran-backed groups refusing to disarm, senior politicians are now hoping to work out a compromise. Factions have put forward conditions that include not only the withdrawal of foreign troops but also an end to American political and economic interference.
Tehran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah has said the withdrawal of "the occupation forces ... is a start towards achieving full sovereignty”, but the group also threatened Zaidi's government.
"A government that doesn't work for the good of its people will be brought down by all possible means," it said.
Pro-Iran groups have long demanded the withdrawal of US troops, targeting them with drones and missiles, and triggering US retaliatory strikes that killed several faction commanders over the years.
During the ongoing Iran war, Tehran and allied factions intensified their attacks in Iraq, targeting US-led troops in the Kurdistan region.

South Korea’s exports hit record high on AI boom
Exports jump 83.5 percent to top $120bn for the first time amid ferocious semiconductor demand.
South Korea’s exports have surged to a monthly record amid explosive demand for chips used to power artificial intelligence.
Exports jumped 83.5 percent year-on-year to $120.9bn in September, eclipsing the previous monthly record of $102.25bn set in June, preliminary customs figures showed on Thursday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump amazed that an ‘Israeli plumber’ helped land Flydubai flight
- list 2 of 4Iran parades Shahed drones through capital
- list 3 of 4Passengers tell of ‘nightmare’ onboard diverted Flydubai flight
- list 4 of 4Iraq celebrates Sovereignty Day as US troops complete withdrawal
Chip shipments accounted for nearly half of exports, soaring more than 260 percent to $60.3bn, according to data from the Korea Customs Service.
Total exports from January through September hit $814.5bn, exceeding those for all of 2025, when exports reached a record $709.7bn.
During the first nine months of the year, the country recorded a trade surplus of $49.85bn.
“This is a valuable achievement that once again demonstrates the strength of our industries and companies, and is thanks to the sweat and efforts of our entrepreneurs who have competed fiercely in the global market,” said Kim Jeong-kwan, South Korea’s minister for trade and industry, in a statement.
“While we expect to achieve $1 trillion in annual exports, the strengthening of global protectionism and tensions in the Middle East remain major variables affecting our exports,” Kim said.
South Korea’s economy has been running red-hot this year amid a global shortage of memory chips used in AI.
Asia’s fourth-largest economy is home to one of the world’s largest semiconductor industries, led by top memory chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics.
SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics together control roughly 80 percent of the global market for high-bandwidth memory and 60 percent of the market for dynamic random-access memory, according to Counterpoint Research.
South Korea’s nominal gross domestic product (GDP) growth hit a five-decade high in the April-June quarter, skyrocketing 26.4 percent year-on-year.
South Korea’s Ministry of Finance and Economy has forecast real GDP to grow 3 percent in 2026, which would be the strongest performance since 2017, excluding the outlier years of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The AI boom has also propelled the country’s stock market into the ranks of the best-performing bourses this year, with the benchmark Kospi rising nearly 60 percent.

Israelis divided as vote that could oust Netanyahu only weeks away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
04:00:30 UTC
13:00:30 KST

On the streets of Jerusalem, crowded with secular and ultra-Orthodox Jews, religious nationalists, settlers, Palestinians, and soldiers returning from deployments, uncertainty hangs over an election less than a month away that could mark a turning point for a country profoundly changed after the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023 and nearly three years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The political battle remains on a knife-edge.
For over two years most polls have predicted that the coalition of parties led by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu will collectively slip below the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government.
But there is no clear path to power for his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, even if he maintains current levels of support, because he has ruled out going into coalition with any of the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, who are projected to claim a critical 12 seats.
For Netanyahu to stay in power, he would have to either put together a different coalition or pull off an unprecedented election night surprise. Another deeply fragmented Knesset seems likely, in which neither side is close to securing a majority.
The latest Channel 13 poll, published last week, captured that deadlock: Jewish Israeli parties opposed to Netanyahu were projected to win 52 seats, against 51 for the prime minister’s bloc, with both falling short of the 61 required for a majority.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party topped the poll with 22 seats, while Netanyahu’s Likud was projected to take 18. The lack of clarity over the next government – with both main blocs on the right – is fuelling unease among Israelis, some of whom believe little will change whoever becomes prime minister.
“I’m not going to vote because I don’t trust anyone,” said Rachel, 42, an Israeli citizen living in West Jerusalem. “I used to vote for Yair Lapid,” she added, referring to the leader of the centrist Yesh Atid party. “The party’s name means ‘there is a future’. But today, I don’t see any future for this country.”
Average public trust across the eight Israeli institutions measured consistently by the Israel Democracy Institute, a statistics body, stood at 34% in 2025, compared with 61% in 2012.
An atmosphere of pessimism and indecision is palpable in Jerusalem, where tensions between Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem – the majority of whom cannot vote in Israeli national elections – and rightwing Jewish Israelis have deepened since 7 October. The Hamas attack is likely to weigh heavily on the ballot: a recent poll by the Israel Democracy Institute found that 68% of Jewish respondents said 7 October would be a central factor in deciding how they voted.
“After 7 October, everyone in this government has to take the blame,” said Ilda, who owns a clothing shop on Jaffa Street, one of Jerusalem’s oldest and busiest thoroughfares. Referring to a Haaretz investigation claiming Netanyahu had been warned about the possibility of a major Hamas attack, which he denies, she said: “After journalists exposed what happened, look what they did: they attacked the journalists instead of taking responsibility.”
West Jerusalem has long been considered fertile ground for Netanyahu and the Israeli right. Yet Israel’s growing diplomatic isolation and the prospect of seemingly endless conflict on multiple fronts are beginning to worry voters even here, a few steps from the bustling Mahane Yehuda market, where giant election posters for Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister known for his anti-Palestinian rhetoric and championing a racist death penalty law that in practice applies only to Palestinians, loom over the streets.
“This country needs radical change. I think I’ll vote for Naftali Bennett,” said Yosef, 26, a religious Israeli, referring to the rightwing former prime minister who now leads the B’Yachad alliance and is one of Netanyahu’s main political rivals.
On one side are tens of thousands of Netanyahu supporters – called “Bibi-ists” in reference to the prime minister’s nickname – as well as backers of the far-right ministers Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who want to return the current coalition to power to “finish the job” in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon and the West Bank.
On the other are tens of thousands of voters who believe Israel is losing its standing in the world and needs a change of direction – something many see as embodied by the centre-right Eisenkot. His supporters argue that he would place greater emphasis on education, social policy and the economy, areas they say have been neglected by the current government.
“I’ll vote for anyone but the prime minister of 7 October,” said Turgeman as he enjoyed a coffee with his wife at a cafe in Jaffa during the Jewish high holiday season. “I’ve never voted Likud in my life, and I’m certainly not going to start now. I’ll vote for Eisenkot. We need a normal prime minister – someone who also cares about the economy and about prices, which have soared because of the war.”
Food prices in Israel have reached record highs amid the regional conflict and supply chain disruption, with food inflation outpacing the broader consumer price index. The cost of food, including fresh fruit and vegetables, has risen by 9.5% over the past two years.
“They think about wars, while nobody is dealing with the economic crisis,” Turgeman said. “And what has Netanyahu done? He has continued to provide financial support that benefits the Haredi [ultra-Orthodox] community.”
Since 7 October, Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community has been at the centre of a bitter dispute over military conscription. While most Jewish Israelis serve, Haredi men studying in religious seminaries have long been largely exempt.
In 2024, amid war and growing pressure on reservists, the supreme court ruled there was no legal basis to continue the exemption, fuelling anti-draft protests, roadblocks and clashes with police. Haredi parties have blamed Netanyahu for failing to pass legislation to protect the exemption.
Ultra-Orthodox Jews, who make up about 14% of Israel’s population, have traditionally voted for parties backed by their rabbis, including the two main Haredi parties in Netanyahu’s coalition. But anger among younger Haredim over conscription and the policing of protests could lead some to defy their religious leaders this time.
“All the options in this election are junk, but I think I will vote for Eisenkot,” said Pinchas, 24, an ultra-Orthodox student who recently completed his military service. “I have the impression that this time people my age won’t vote according to what the rabbis tell them. Many are angry about the way Netanyahu handled the conscription law, and especially about the crackdown on those who protested against it.”
As the Guardian conducted interviews near Jerusalem’s central bus station, an elderly passerby called out: “There is only one prime minister – Bibi!” It was a reminder that, despite the uncertainty and the opposition’s narrow lead in the polls, the Israeli leader retains a loyal base.
“I’m sure Netanyahu will win,” said Avraham Levy, 76, a Likud supporter and fruit seller at Mahane Yehuda market. “We’ll have the majority. We need to support Netanyahu because he has to finish the job. If he doesn’t, who will?” he said, referring to Israel’s wars on several fronts.
Among those still backing Netanyahu’s coalition partners are supporters of the far right, including Jakub, 23, who was due to begin his military service soon. “I’ll vote for Moshe Feiglin,” he said, referring to an extreme far-right former Israeli Knesset member who declared in 2025 that the conflict in Gaza was not against Hamas but against every child and baby in the territory, and is now running jointly with the far-right Religious Zionist party. “Because he represents my values, and he has never changed his principles,” Jakub said.
The field is wide open and the divide is also generational: by 2019, support for a Palestinian state stood at about 20%-30% among the youngest Jewish Israeli cohorts, compared with roughly 40%-55% among older generations, reflecting a longer-term shift towards more hawkish attitudes. No more recent comparable data was available.
The difficulty for the anti-Netanyahu camp is that it remains fragmented and has struggled to agree on a coherent political platform or a common strategy capable of uniting its different factions.
Parties representing Palestinian citizens, known as Arab parties inside Israel, could push Eisenkot’s coalition over the 61-seat threshold, but amid a campaign of racism and Islamophobia, he has ruled out going into government with them.
They could potentially support a minority government.
But last week, the Central Elections Committee voted to bar Ra’am and the Joint List, the country’s two main Palestinian parties, from the election, after the far-right Otzma Yehudit party filed a petition arguing that they support terrorism and deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state.
The opposition Democrats party filed a similar petition arguing for Otzma Yehudit to be banned for incitement to racism and negating the existence of Israel as a democratic state, because of racist policies pursued in power under its leader Itamar Ben Gvir. That was not upheld.
The decision is being challenged in the supreme court, which has overturned similar bans in past elections.
If allowed to run in the elections, the Arab parties will be crucial to the opposition’s prospects of forming a government and to Eisenkot’s chances of replacing Netanyahu.
Tensions between Palestinian citizens of Israel and the state have deepened since 7 October amid arrests, interrogations and other legal action against Arab citizens, often over protests or social media posts.
For these reasons, Palestinian citizens of Israel are often reluctant to express their voting preferences. In the 2025 Israeli Democracy Index survey, 70% said they preferred to remain silent about their political views in the presence of strangers, up from 45% in 2016 and compared with 53% of Jewish respondents.
But Palestinian citizens of Israel remain divided over how best to respond, with many pessimistic that any future government will defend rights they say have too often been denied. The Joint List has maintained a more oppositional stance, signalling it could support an anti-Netanyahu minority government from outside while stopping short of joining a coalition, although it has done so in the past.
“These elections are about our strength as an Arab community and our ability to have an influential political voice,” said Amir, 34, from Mashhad in northern Israel, who plans to vote for the Joint List. “We need strong, united Arab representation on equality, discrimination and the Palestinian cause, while cooperating when it benefits our community.”
Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, has instead made political pragmatism its defining strategy. In 2021 it became the first independent Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition, seeking budgets, services and greater influence for Palestinian citizens of Israel.
“Arab society is being torn apart by crime and violence, while relations with Jewish Israelis are becoming more hostile,” said Abu Mahmoud, 33, from Kafr Kanna, also in the north of the country. “That’s why I’ll vote for Ra’am: negotiate, secure budgets and work with Jewish Israelis where possible.”
He added: “I want politics that can actually improve people’s lives.”
