Owing to the paired assistance initiative, a pulu workshop was also established in the county to help transform this traditional craft from small household businesses into a larger-scale and more organized operation.

02:34:38 UTC
11:34:38 KST

Hundreds of people affected by the October 7 massacre, including former hostage Omri Miran, will share their stories as part of the "Salon Otef" initiative at 450 locations across Israel.
Salon Otef, led by 255, the Hostages and Families Organization, consists of gatherings where returned hostages, family members of living and deceased hostages, survivors of the massacre, bereaved families whose loved ones were murdered, and members of the security and rescue forces share their stories.
The gatherings take place in homes and communities across Israel, with 450 planned in early October. Thousands of people are expected to attend.
Salon Otef is being launched with the support of Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF, which views it as a strategic component of the commemoration process, and in partnership with the Konrad Adenauer Foundation. Additionally, the Atid LaOtef movement, the Nova Tribe Community Association, Edut 710, the Kumu movement, the Kibbutz Movement, and other organizations are participating in the initiative.
This year, the gatherings will also address the challenges that have continued ever since October 7: coping with loss, rehabilitation, returning home, and the effort to rebuild.
Miran calls telling the story a life mission
Miran, who was released from Gaza after 738 days in captivity, said that he views telling the stories of what happened as "an immensely important national mission, a life mission."
"To understand what happened to us on October 7 and what the hostages and their families have endured since then, we need to hear the stories firsthand from those who lived through them," Miran said.
Salon Otef gatherings all center around a direct personal testimony followed by an open conversation with participants. Some gatherings also incorporate singing and live music.
In addition to gatherings in private homes, many survivors will share their stories at companies, organizations, community spaces, and other venues.
In order to facilitate these personal, face-to-face encounters, preserve the testimonies, and enable dialogue, Salon Otef provides speakers and hosts with support and guidance ahead of the gatherings.
"The story of October 7 should first and foremost be told by those who were there and experienced it firsthand. They are the ones who should make their voices heard, describe what they saw and endured, and ensure that the story is written through their testimony," said Mor Peretz, Ceo of 255, the Hostages and Families Organization.
Salon Otef was first launched in 2024, one year after October 7, and has since taken place annually around the anniversary.

El Salvador will hold presidential elections on February 28, 2027, the electoral tribunal said Wednesday, paving the way for President Nayib Bukele to seek a third term.
El Salvador last year amended its constitution to abolish presidential term limits and allow Bukele, who has been in power since 2019, to seek re-election indefinitely.
The 45-year-old is a hero to many in his homeland and across Latin America for cracking down hard on gangs.
Under a state of exception he declared in 2022, and which is still in effect, around 92,000 people, mostly young men, have been arrested and held, many without charge.
To clear the legal backlog, the courts have begun holding mass trials.

Pentagon chief Hegseth orders US military to cut generals and admirals by 20 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
02:30:25 UTC
11:30:25 KST

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has confirmed that the military will eliminate 20 percent of its generals and admirals by January 1, 2027, announcing the measure during his annual "State of the Force" address.
Speaking to junior officers and enlisted personnel at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, Hegseth directed all armed services to double the 10 percent reduction originally ordered last spring across roughly 800 flag and general officer posts.
"I call it accountability and long overdue," Hegseth said, arguing the cuts will remove "redundant force structure to optimise and streamline leadership" and eliminate unnecessary bureaucratic layers.
The announcement comes amidst a broader cultural overhaul directed by the Pentagon chief, including rolling back diversity programmes, reviewing ground combat units with female service personnel, introducing testosterone screening for male troops, and enforcing a ban on transgender service members alongside male-level physical fitness criteria.
Congressional backlash
The aggressive restructuring drew immediate condemnation from Capitol Hill, where several senators described the move as an institutional purge.
"He's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military," said Democratic Senator Mark Kelly, a former Navy combat pilot.
"He's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it."
Republican Senator Mike Rounds of the Armed Services Committee voiced caution, noting: "If it's simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first."
The administration has already dismissed or forced the retirement of more than two dozen high-ranking commanders, including Army Chief of Staff General Randy George, Joint Chiefs Chairman General CQ Brown, Chief of Naval Operations Lisa Franchetti, and NATO representative Vice Admiral Shoshana Chatfield.
While no formal rationale was given, most dismissals were linked to previous endorsements of diversity and inclusion initiatives.
Under statutory rules, general officer quotas are established by law, though posts can be left vacant simply by withholding nominee submissions from Congress.

WASHINGTON – A Tennessee woman was expected to be put to death on Sept 30 for the murder of a high-school friend in what would be the first execution of a woman in that state in two centuries.
A decision by the US Supreme Court late on Sept 30 cleared the way for Christa Pike – the only woman on the state’s death row – to be given a lethal injection after hours of dramatic legal wrangling up and down the judicial system.
A lawyer for Pike, Luke Ihnen, told AFP that there are no plans to file for further reprieve and that the execution “should start any minute if it hasn’t already”.
“We do not plan to file anything else,” Ihnen said.
When Pike is given a lethal injection, she will become the first woman executed in the US since 2023.
Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10am (11pm Singapore time) at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, but it was halted barely an hour before by a lower court.
That court was set to review whether allegations that Pike was sexually abused as a child were fully considered in her original prosecution.
“The interests of justice and the finality of Pike’s impending execution compel the entry of a short stay of execution in order to properly analyse the parties’ fully briefed arguments,” the lower court order said.
But the Supreme Court later said it could go ahead.
“The Sept 30, 2026 order of the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit... granting a stay of execution is vacated,” the Supreme Court order said.
Liberal Supreme Court Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson all dissented.
“The Court’s decision... unnecessarily prevents that [lower] court from giving due consideration to Pike’s claim,” the dissenting justices wrote.
“Worse, the Court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the State to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts.”
Mental health considerations
The case has sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer’s body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Pike’s lawyers argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of the killing.
“She was 18 when she committed her crime, and she was deeply mentally ill,” they wrote in a clemency petition to Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, who said he would not intervene.
The US Supreme Court had rejected on Sept 29 an application for a stay of execution, which argued that Pike’s history as a victim of sexual assault, post-traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant a lethal injection would cause “needless suffering”.
Independent UN rights experts have urged the US government and Tennessee authorities to “immediately halt” the execution and commute her death sentence.
“Pike’s execution would mark the culmination of a trajectory of severe physical and psychological suffering marked by childhood abuse and nearly three decades of solitary confinement on death row,” they said.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. AFP

Switzerland’s glaciers, which are disproportionately impacted by climate change, have lost nearly 20 per cent of their mass in five years, experts said on Thursday, with 2026 registering the second biggest melt on record.

FlyDubai suspends Israel flights after apparent hijacking attempt
Dubai-based airline FlyDubai has suspended flights to and from Israel after a Tel Aviv-bound passenger jet was diverted and made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia following an apparent hijacking attempt.
Direct air travel has been one of the most visible signs of normalized relations between Israel and the UAE since the countries signed the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020.
“Following the incident involving flight FZ 1073 on 30 September, and in coordination with the relevant authorities, Flydubai flights to and from Israel will be suspended while the investigation continues,” the airline said in a statement on Wednesday.
“The safety and wellbeing of our passengers, crew and operations remain our highest priority. This temporary suspension will allow the relevant authorities to continue their work and establish all the facts surrounding the incident,” Flydubai added.

According to Israeli officials and passengers, most of whom were Israeli nationals, a fight broke out in the cockpit during which the co-pilot stabbed the captain, causing the plane to plunge. Passengers and crew members eventually subdued the assailant, after which the aircraft landed safely, with no fatalities among the 174 people on board. The captain was reportedly seriously injured during the altercation.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the attacker had apparently planned to crash the plane and that the actions of the captain and passengers prevented “a 9/11 disaster.”
US President Donald Trump, who discussed the incident with Netanyahu by phone, suggested that the co-pilot was “perhaps a terrorist, or perhaps a whack-job.”
Emirati-Israeli relations have faced growing strains since the start of the Gaza war in 2023, despite the two countries maintaining diplomatic, commercial and security ties.

Netanyahu visited the UAE on Sunday for talks with President Mohamed bin Zayed on bilateral ties and the war with Iran. Tehran condemned the visit and warned of “highly dangerous consequences,” arguing that Netanyahu’s presence threatened regional peace and security.

stone-built meadows boutique hotel takes shape around gardens in rural UK
at the meadows, an existing building and contemporary extension connect through local materials and garden spaces, placing landscape at the center of the experience.
Material-led refurbishment connects the hotel to the Cotswolds
The Meadows, an exclusive hotel in the Cotswolds, UK, transforms an existing property into an intimate retreat, high-end restaurant, and small boutique hotel. The proposal by Pardini Hall Architecture is rooted in material sensitivity, with sustainability integral from the outset. The scheme involves the sensitive refurbishment of the existing building, complemented by a contemporary extension.
Local materials are selected to reduce carbon impact while maintaining a strong connection to place. Each element is carefully considered to provide a sense of tranquillity, comfort, and connection to the landscape. This is informed by material choices and shaped by a rustic-chic approach.
garden extends Meadows Hotel into the surrounding landscape
The garden plays a central role within the overall scheme, whether through views from the interior across the meadows, or in extending the restaurant into the garden with outdoor dining and a garden-to-table experience. The landscape is not treated as a backdrop, but as an active component of the architecture, shaping the experience for guests and creating spaces for relaxation and enjoyment.
Large, glazed bifold doors open onto an external courtyard, dissolving the boundary between inside and outside and allowing the spaces to flow seamlessly into one another. Sustainability and environmental responsibility are guiding principles for the hotel’s refurbishment and extension. Alongside solar panels, strategies for water management include rainwater harvesting and greywater reuse for irrigation.
The project was commissioned to Pardini Hall Architecture Studio by a small group of clients with a shared ambition to create a rural retreat that sits in harmony with its surroundings. A boutique hotel that is defined by its relationship to place, material, and the experience of inhabiting it.

How a breast cancer trial changed the lives of survivors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
02:09:32 UTC
11:09:32 KST

How a breast cancer treatment trial changed the lives of Australian women
Donna Rullo wasn't going down without a fight.
It was early 2001, and then-40-year-old Ms Rullo had just been diagnosed with HER2-positive breast cancer.
Up to one in five cases of breast cancer are HER2-positive, which means the cancer cells have higher than normal levels of human epidermal growth factor 2 (HER2) protein, promoting growth of the cancer itself.
It's an aggressive and fast-growing cancer, but typically responds well to targeted treatments.
When Ms Rullo was diagnosed, targeted treatments weren't an option in Australia.
But 25 years ago, she took a leap of faith and joined a drug trial that changed the course of her life, and that of countless women after her.
When Ms Rullo heard about now-retired oncologist Richard Bell's involvement with a trial for a new drug called trastuzumab, she drove five hours from her regional fruit farm to Melbourne for one of his lectures.
Ms Rullo says she rang him once a week before securing a position on the HERA (HERceptin Adjuvant) trial, which went on to enrol more than 5,000 patients from 39 countries.
She recalls being motivated to watch her son, now 37, grow up.
"I went through 10 years of IVF to have him, my son's 12 and he needs me and I want to be here," she says.
She still remembers getting the call.
"He said: 'It's Richard, I just wanted to tell you, you're patient number one of the HERA trial,'" she says.
"I just cried and cried. I couldn't stop. I was so emotional."
The trial went on to show that taking the drug trastuzumab for a year "significantly improves long-term disease-free survival" for patients with HER2-positive early breast cancer.
"It was the first drug that really showed promise and women were just thinking: 'Oh my God, finally we have something we can all hold onto,'" Ms Rullo says.
The drug with a $50K price tag
Twenty years ago today, trastuzumab was added to the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) for the treatment of patients with HER-2 positive early-stage breast cancer.
It's a move which Breast Cancer Network Australia founder and then-chief executive Lyn Swinburne says has been "life-changing" for thousands of Australian women since.
Trastuzumab is now the most common HER2-targeted therapy offered to patients in Australia and New Zealand.
It may be given alongside surgery, chemotherapy, radiation or other HER2-targeted treatments, and works by attaching itself to the cancer cell HER2 receptor.
Before its inclusion on the PBS, women not on trials like Ms Rullo were paying between $50,000 and $70,000 a year for treatment, or went without.
It was an accessibility gap that Ms Swinburne and then-Breast Cancer Network Australia board member, breast cancer survivor and former Olympian Raelene Boyle wanted to address.
"I was hearing from women who were selling their houses, selling their holiday houses, selling their farms to try and get this drug," Ms Swinburne says.
"Probably knowing it wasn't going to save their lives necessarily, but it was going to extend their lives, and especially when you've got young children, that's really, really important."
In June 2001, they invited prime minister John Howard to Ms Boyle's 50th birthday, sitting him between them as they lobbied for the drug to be subsidised.
"We basically talked to him all night about this drug and the difference it made," Ms Boyle recalls.
In late 2001, the government announced a special program which allowed women with HER-2 positive metastatic breast cancer to access the drug for free.
Then, on October 1, 2006, it was added to the PBS for the treatment of patients with HER-2 positive early-stage breast cancer.
Breast cancer outcomes improving
Breast cancer is very common in Australia, with one in seven women diagnosed with the disease over their lifetime.
Although more people in Australia are being diagnosed with breast cancer each year, Breast Cancer Network Australia chief executive Kirsten Pilatti says survivors are also living longer than ever before.
"Survival has certainly improved because we know more about the specifics of different breast cancers," she says.
In 2017–2021, the chance of surviving at least five years post-diagnosis was 93 per cent, up from 75 per cent in 1987–1991.
Rachel Dear, a medical oncologist at St Vincent's Hospital in Sydney, says improved survival rates have been driven by earlier detection and diagnosis, improved awareness and "more personalised and targeted" treatments.
Understanding more about how different types of cancer behave and respond to treatment allows specialists to tailor treatments to each patient, Dr Dear says.
"Treatment has changed depending on which subtype of breast cancer we're looking at," she says.
"There are three main types of breast cancer, and within each of those three types, there are more drug treatment options that have improved survival rates.
"In 2026, we have a number of new drug treatments to offer patients."
Breast cancer's huge public profile means there is greater awareness of the disease, Dr Dear says, but has also led to greater investment in research and clinical trials, resulting in more treatment options for patients.
Ms Rullo considers herself lucky to have seen her son grow into a "remarkable" man, marry and have two kids of his own.
She encourages people facing an uncertain health diagnosis to learn as much as they can and to advocate for themselves, if needed.
"Life could have completely gone a different way, who knows what could have happened if I didn't fight to be on that trial," she says.

Putting off your tax return? You have a month to file
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
02:09:12 UTC
11:09:12 KST

A big tax deadline is looming, with the start of October kicking the countdown into gear.
Here's what you need to know if you haven't filed your tax return for the 2025–26 financial year yet.
When are tax returns due?
The due date this year is Monday, November 2.
Usually, people who do their own tax returns must lodge them by October 31.
But this year, that falls on a Saturday.
And the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) says that if October 31 falls on a weekend, the due date is the next business day.
So, this year, the due date is actually on Monday, November 2.
If you're having a tax agent file your return, they'll generally have a special lodgement schedule, which means they may be able to lodge returns for clients later than November 2.
However, the ATO says you need to engage a tax agent before October 31 if you're going down this path, so make sure you book your appointment before the end of the month.
Is there a fine for filing late?
There can be.
But the ATO says it considers a person's individual circumstances before deciding what action to take and whether they'll be sent a failure to lodge (FTL) notice.
"We recognise that sometimes people don't meet their lodgement obligations on time, even with the best intentions," the ATO says.
"Generally, we don't apply penalties in isolated cases of late lodgement."
You can expect to hear from the ATO before getting a penalty notice.
"If you fail to lodge on time, we'll warn you by phone or in writing before we apply a failure to lodge penalty and issue you a notice to lodge," the ATO says.
"This will give you the opportunity to lodge or give you the opportunity to engage with us if you're experiencing circumstances preventing you from lodging."
Will I get a tax refund?
"Some workers genuinely are owed a refund due to over-withholding or legitimate deductions," said Jenny Wong, the tax lead at accounting body CPA Australia.
"But a significant group overestimates what they'll receive."
Part of the expectation for a tax refund comes from the days of the low and middle income tax offset (LMITO).
For Australians earning up to $126,000, LMITO delivered a tax break ranging from $255 to $1,080 in 2018–19, 2019–20 and 2020–21.
There was a one-off increase to ease cost-of-living pressures in 2021–22, lifting the base amount to $675 and the full amount to $1,500.
"LMITO created an expectation of a tax refund in prior years," Ms Wong said.
And even though that offset ended years ago, its impact on the Australian mindset about tax returns has lingered.
The LMITO hangover
The hangover from the LMITO years may have led some to assume this year's budget announcements would result in a $1,250 cash payment in their tax returns, when that's not the case.
But it's more than that.
Our tax returns can have complications we didn't anticipate (more on that below), and we may have overestimated how much deductions will benefit us.
For example, it's easy to assume a few thousand dollars in work expenses and charity donations will all come back to us as a refund.
But the way deductions are calculated often means taxpayers receive only a small fraction of that money back.
"Australia has a clear culture around deductions," said Elizabeth Morton, a senior lecturer at Curtin University and chartered accountant.
"A lot of errors taxpayers make relate to problems with deductions."
Dr Morton said that included:
- claiming things that aren't deductible
- not being able to substantiate an expense
- not apportioning how much of their deduction is used outside of work
- not claiming in line with prescribed methods
- claiming capital expenditure outright
"All of these will likely result in over-claiming of deductions, therefore underpayment of tax," Dr Morton said.
How much should we be getting back?
Obviously there's no one answer to this question. It really depends on your own personal circumstances.
However, let's assume you have only one job and no income from other sources, no work-related deductions, and no donations to charities in the past financial year.
"If the employer calculates Pay As You Go salary withholding tax correctly, it should generally cover an employee's final tax bill," Ms Wong said.
"The employee should not expect a tax refund."
It's a good idea to approach filing your tax return with low expectations.
"We need to be careful of assuming that we will get a refund each year," Dr Morton said.
But aren't we entitled to claim?
There's a balance to strike here, because there are plenty of legitimate reasons to claim deductions on your tax return.
And Dr Morton said the onus was on taxpayers to get it right.
"It is important that taxpayers understand that they are permitted by law to claim deductions that are allowable," she said.
"So taxpayers can miss out on deductions if they are not aware of the rules, or if they don't keep proper records."
The taxation system can seem daunting, so many people turn to accountants to help them navigate the process.
While the cost of using professionals to prepare your tax return is tax deductible, the up-front cost for an accountant can be prohibitive.
There are, however, a series of free tax clinics around the country that offer eligible people help to file their tax returns.
Many of those clinics are in major cities, but some do offer virtual sessions for people in regional and rural areas.
You can check if you're eligible for free tax assistance here and check out the nearest tax clinic to you here.
The ATO also has a comprehensive guide to deductions according to a range of industries.
So why is my tax return so low this year?
"There could be multiple reasons why people are caught off guard by minimal refunds or tax bills," Ms Wong said.
"A worker working multiple jobs but then ticks the box on their Tax File Number (TFN) declaration form telling all their employers to stop taxing the first $18,200 from their pay — meaning each employer withholds less tax than they should.
"Or the worker may have student HELP/HECS debts but did not tick the box to withhold extra from their pay."
The Medicare levy surcharge may also catch higher earners out if they don't have what the Australian Taxation Office defines as appropriate private health insurance.
"Whether they have private health insurance can lead to some issues, particularly if their income is above the threshold, or the rebate rate they are claiming is not aligned to their income," Dr Morton said.
The threshold for paying the Medicare levy surcharge is more than $101,000 for singles and $202,000 (plus $1,500 for each dependent child after the first one) for families.

Trump’s AI lunch included every major tech company. Except Apple
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
02:07:06 UTC
11:07:06 KST

When President Donald Trump gathered execs from the world's most powerful tech companies in the White House on Tuesday to discuss the future of artificial intelligence, one company was conspicuously absent: Apple.
Neither Chairman Tim Cook nor his successor as CEO, John Ternus, were present, while leaders from every other tech megacap – and many other companies – lunched with Trump.
Apple didn't respond to CNBC's questions about the meeting, nor did the White House.
Social media buzzed with conjecture that Apple wasn't invited because the company is behind on AI.
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, a powerhouse investor in Silicon Valley and a Trump ally in the second term, called Apple's absence a "nothing burger" int an interview with CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday.
"I can assure you, they're very much read in on all of this, and I suspect they agree with all of it," Gerstner said.
Cook, as Apple's public face with government officials around the world, was at the White House less than a week ago, when he attended Trump's state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Gerstner pointed out.
Cook stepped down as Apple CEO in September, handing the baton to hardware specialist Ternus.
As part of the transition, Apple noted that Cook would still handle "engaging with policymakers around the world" as the company's executive chairman. His new role was underscored last week at the state dinner with Xi.
Over the years, Cook has put in the time to maintain a good relationship with Trump. He's made over 10 public appearances at events in the president's second term, including Trump's inauguration, in the oval office, at Davos, and at state dinners on multiple continents. He attended the "Melania" screening at the White House.
Throughout his dealings with Trump over the past two years, Cook has stayed on message, focused on Apple's manufacturing interests and trade issues, at a time where its products could be subject to tariffs. The company has given the Trump administration wins on issues like American investment and jobs while trying to ward off Trump's longstanding desire for the company to make iPhones in the U.S.
More recently, Apple has reportedly sought to use Chinese-made memory chips as prices skyrocket around the world, but doing so requires a license. Commerce Secretary Lutnick said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal that "the Trump administration is not in favor of that."
A different approach
Gerstner, in his CNBC interview, said that the participants at the lunch were the companies that were "really pushing the frontier on model development."
That's not Apple.
The iPhone makers' in-house models are smaller and more efficient than the so-called "frontier" models developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, which were both represented. Apple Foundation Models are mostly designed to run on Apple's own silicon inside iPhones and Mac computers. They run parts of Siri, while OpenAI and Anthropic's models use massive Nvidia-based clusters of chips.
Apple is a consumer company, whereas most of the frontier lab AI competition happens in the enterprise. Apple partners with Google to develop its models. Its capital expenditures are tiny compared to the sums Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon are investing.
While some investors fret that Apple is falling behind in AI, the market has increasingly seen it as a hedge to other capex-heavy tech names. And the company just launched a new AI-powered Siri earlier to mostly positive reviews.
Apple's stock is up 22.5% so far in 2026, outpacing the Nasdaq and almost all of its megacap peers other than Nvidia, which is up about the same amount.
Though Apple is very much touting the power of AI and its role in the technology's future, company executives have been mostly absent from the public debate around AI safety or alignment, which were primary topics at Trump's luncheon.
Nobody at Apple has penned the long manifestos like the ones coming from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft and others.
As part of Tuesday's meeting with Trump, the White House and the leading AI companies signed an accord, committing the industry players to various safety measures. After the meeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI COO Greg Brockman, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei all signed the document.
Cook has said several times over the years that Apple is more likely to weigh in publicly on policy that "intersects with our company in some way." Apple's not dealing with alignment issues on the frontier.
"If it doesn't intersect — if it's something where we would just be another voice out there and not have a unique perspective to bring — then we don't say anything," Cook said in a 2021 DealBook interview.

Tunisia replaces jail terms with fines for ‘false news’ under cybercrime law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
02:06:27 UTC
11:06:27 KST

Adel Elthabti, Tarek Chouiref
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Tunisia has replaced prison sentences with financial penalties for spreading "false news" under its cybercrime law, according to an amendment published Wednesday in the country's Official Gazette.
Before the amendment, Decree 54 provided for prison terms of up to five years for spreading false information deemed harmful to public security or the rights of others.
Under the amended provision, such offenses are punishable by fines ranging from 10,000 to 20,000 Tunisian dinars ($3,300-$6,600).
The same penalties apply to spreading fabricated or falsified material, personal data or false claims intended to defame others, damage their reputation, cause material or moral harm, incite attacks or promote hate speech.
Repeat offenses can still carry a six-month prison sentence and a fine of 50,000 dinars (more than $16,000), while penalties are doubled when the targeted person is a public official or equivalent.
The amendment came after a Cabinet meeting chaired Tuesday by President Kais Saied to consider changes to Decree 54 and other legislation.
Decree 54 has faced criticism from rights groups over concerns about its impact on freedom of expression.

Trolling Trump: Why Macron and Carney became ‘leaders of the resistance’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Earlier this year, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent offered some avuncular counsel to Western allies at Davos, weary of being belittled and trolled by President Donald Trump and his advisers: “Sit back, take a deep breath, do not retaliate,” he urged. “Let things play out.”
His remarks focused primarily on tariffs, but at the Swiss Alpine gabfest, Bessent and other Trump aides repeated the same advice on almost everything concerning the U.S. president. And on the whole, the leaders of Washington’s allies heeded their warning, even as they struggled to contain their outrage over Trump’s threats to invade Greenland.
For Gavin Newsom, the Trump-bashing California governor who was also at Davos, it was all too much. The world leaders in attendance were “pathetic,” he said. “I can’t take this complicity of people rolling over. I should have brought a bunch of knee pads for all the world leaders.”
Advertisement
Since then, however, things have moved on — especially for Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron, who have both been giving as good as they get in recent weeks. Amid rising trade tensions and differences with the White House over Russia, they haven’t hesitated to escalate when attacked, sometimes even taunting Trump without immediate provocation.
Carney and Macron have become the “leaders of the resistance,” said Rohinton Medhora, the Canadian economist and professor at McGill University who has dubbed Carney’s evolving political vision as “value-based realism.” Medhora, who sits on various international and Canadian commissions, said: “They’ve tried flattery. They’ve tried ignoring him. Nothing’s worked, and they are not losing out now with their retaliatory trolling.”
Carney may have lectured the Trump administration “to stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough,” but that hasn’t stopped him from offering public mockery of his own.
The Canadian prime minister’s freewheeling swipes have included teasing Trump for claiming “sabotage” after his teleprompter malfunctioned during an address to the United Nations last year. Experiencing a similar technical hiccup in Toronto, Carney deadpanned: “I would now like to inform you that the teleprompter has ceased to function. Unlike a certain world leader, I do not view this as a conspiracy.”
So, what’s going on? And are there any risks to poking the bear?
Advertisement
According to former White House strategist and current MAGA influencer and podcaster Steve Bannon, there is. “They’re playing with fire,” he told POLITICO. “They’re totally dependent on us for trade.” He also added a dark warning about “the Alberta secession movement picking up momentum” — Bannon and other MAGA luminaries have been encouraging the oil-rich Canadian province to break away.
Bannon also cited the deal Trump recently struck with Denmark and Greenland as an example of U.S. power and Washington’s ability to get what it wants. “Our Greenland deal shows the reality of Canada’s inability to defend itself from being the next Ukraine — this time in the Arctic,” he said.
But Ivo Daalder, a former U.S. ambassador to NATO, draws a different lesson from the Greenland deal, which extends an earlier agreement dating from 1951 and does not give Trump control of the island, as he said he wanted. For Daalder, this deal shows that when allies stand their ground, the U.S. president backs down. “With that deal Trump literally got nothing,” he told POLITICO.
Donald Trump, Macron and Carney attend a working lunch during the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France on June 16, 2026. | Pool photo by Evelyn Hockstein via Getty Images
“I think what’s happening is the allies are starting to understand how to play him,” said Daalder. “Now they’re ignoring his bluster, and do and say what they think is important for their own good. By doing so, they have as good a chance as any in getting what they want.”
It’s also not surprising that Macron was quicker to taunt Trump than other Western leaders, said Daalder. “He’s French, after all.” Even during the first Trump presidency, Macron was willing to go mano a mano with the U.S. president, squeezing his counterpart’s hand in a handshake until their knuckles turned white and refusing to let go even when Trump tried to pull away.
But the French president’s tone seems sharper now, his actions even more pointed. Fort his, Daalder points to Macron’s maneuvering of Trump this June into inking an interim deal with Iran at Versailles — a palace infamous for a treaty that ended one world war but led to another. Macron, Trump’s critics trumpeted, had pulled off an epic diplomatic “troll.”
Advertisement
What audiences are these two leaders trying to reach and influence? “That’s a good question,” said Medhora. “It is clearly not Americans.” And there’s certainly a domestic component, as both men are scoring political points by standing up to a man they portray as a bully.
But Medhora believes there is likely a broader, more strategic, aspect to their posturing. “By doing these things very publicly, they’re encouraging other leaders to overcome their hesitation and join them,” he said. “And if others come along, then everyone is stronger in the anti-Trump camp.”
But that’ll only work if they can do it with serious consequence — and there’s always a chance that it could all backfire.
Perhaps with Trump facing a likely setback in the U.S. midterm elections, Carney and Macron would be better off taking Bessent’s advice and letting things play out, as the U.S. leader may emerge from the vote facing new constraints from emboldened Democrats. But, for now, both seem to be having far too much fun poking the bear to do that.

“There were lot of mistakes that President Trump committed in the last months. The war in Iran is affecting the world economy,” Chega President André Ventura. | Marion Solletty/POLITICO
ERICEIRA, Portugal — Donald Trump is bleeding support on the European far right.
The leader of populist Portuguese party Chega has joined a chorus of nationalist politicians criticizing the U.S. president — their ideological ally — over the war in Iran and its ripple effect on fuel prices.
“There were lots of mistakes that President Trump committed in the last months. The war in Iran is affecting the world economy,” Chega President André Ventura said on the sidelines of an event organized by the populist, pan-continental Patriots’ foundation in the beach city of Ericeira, near Lisbon.
Advertisement
Ventura, whose party has surged in recent election cycles, is often described as a Portuguese Trump for his confrontational tactics and heated campaign rhetoric targeting Portugal’s ruling elite. The Chega leader traveled to Washington, D.C. for Trump’s inauguration and borrowed the MAGA slogan during last year’s parliamentary election campaign, saying he wanted to “make Portugal great again.”
But with Portugal now among many European countries hit by increasing fuel prices caused by war in the Middle East, Ventura appears to be turning on his American role model — like other populist chiefs across Europe who have jabbed the U.S. president’s “erratic” war goals or walked back support in the face of a snowballing cost-of-living crisis.
“I wish this war didn’t exist, especially for Portugal, Spain, France, Italy. We are paying more than the United States the price for this war,” he said during the interview. “It’s not very fair that one country starts the war and the others pay for the costs.”
Residents and antifascist activists protest outside the Patriots’ event venue. | Marion Solletty/POLITICO
The former sports commentator turned leading politician — whose early steps in politics were marred by controversies over comments widely criticized as racist — has elevated his party from barely registering in the polls to becoming the largest opposition group in the Portuguese parliament. He secured a third of the votes in February’s presidential election.
His recent electoral gains place Ventura among several far-right leaders and parties currently surging across the continent. Representatives from several of his European allies, including France’s National Rally, Spain’s Vox, Hungary’s Fidesz and Italy’s League, traveled to the Ericeira event where they shared views closely aligned with the MAGA-boosted narrative that Europe is suffering civilizational decline because of uncontrolled immigration and crippling regulation.
Ventura urged like-minded European politicians to unite, including by working with parties currently not part of the continental Patriots alliance, such as the Alternative for Germany. The AfD was kicked out of the ID Group, one of the precursors to the Patriots, in 2024 over downplaying Germany’s Nazi past. Its stellar performance in this month’s regional elections in eastern Germany has highlighted a schism in Europe between far-right parties eager to soften their image and those, like the AfD, who are doubling down on their radical positioning.
Advertisement
“I think we have to cooperate and collaborate within our values and principles,” Ventura said, despite having “different positions” on some subjects, chief among them Russia and Ukraine.
Asked whether the AfD’s pro-Russian positions were an obstacle to deeper cooperation, Ventura said they shouldn’t be. “We stand with Ukraine in the war, we will keep standing with Ukraine,” he said, adding that “we don’t have to be thinking the same on all issues … The AfD is fighting against illegal immigration, against crime and to give more authority for police services so we have a lot of things in common.”
Chega’s growth is not without backlash in Portugal. As Ventura was talking to reporters in Ericeira over the weekend, some 150 residents and antifascist activists protested outside the Patriots’ event venue, forcing attendees and speakers from sister European parties to enter and exit to the sound of loud shouting and under tight security watch.

This 00s video game is Genesis Owusu's biggest influence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Genesis Owusu on video game music, winning ARIAs and Prince
The first time seven-time ARIA award winner Genesis Owusu heard The Rolling Stones was as a kid playing popular video game Guitar Hero III.
"It's how music transports itself through the generations," Owusu explains on Take 5 with Zan Rowe.
Now 28, Owusu has covered the Stones' Paint It Black on triple j Like A Version.
The born performer's genre-defying music has cemented him among Australia's most exciting boundary pushers with an explosive collision of rap, post-punk, soul, funk, pop and R&B.
"So much of my life and artistry comes from fusion," he says. "My biggest experience of that … was this video game I played when I was five years old called Jet Set Radio Future."
Released in 2000, the Sega title puts you in control of a gang of rollerblading graffiti artists combating a mega-corporation who rules futuristic Tokyo as a police state.
"Freedom of expression is outlawed, and you guys are the last bastion of resistance," Owusu explains. Hitting play was "like a gust of wind that blew all my hair back".
"It was the music, the visuals, the themes, all mixed together in this Pandora's box."
To generations of young gamers, franchises like Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, Grand Theft Auto, FIFA and NBA2K are vehicles for musical discovery.
For Owusu and Jet Set Radio Future, "it's all sound-tracked by this pirate radio station hosted by DJ Professor K", introducing him to cult acts like Bis, Bran Van 3000, and Cibo Matto.
"It's super abrasive [and] taught me ugly was also to be appreciated. I think of food: sour and bitter … can be used to create complex emotions and flavours.
"I feel the same way in music, ugly and abrasive can be used just as powerfully as sweet and lovely.
"This game is the biggest creative influence in my life."
Jet Set Radio Future's lingering influence extends to Owusu's latest album, Red Star Wu & The Worldwide Scourge, which opens with a track titled Pirate Radio that skewers Donald Trump, Elon Musk and the degrading effects of "blue check mania".
Elsewhere, he takes aim at the manosphere, bible-bashing politicians and a paranoid, fragmented world growing apathetic to global atrocities in favour of absurdities served up in algorithms.
The political bent sharpens Owusu's lyrics, bolder and more urgent than the metaphors of his first two albums, where black dogs symbolised racism and depression, or an indestructible roach represented resilience.
"My music has been political from the jump," Owusu says. "A lot of my early music, there was still the veil of creative writing, make everything a metaphor and dress it up.
"But in this day and age … we don't have time for the dress-ups. This is what it is: I don't want you to be able to hide from it or misunderstand in any way."
The Genesis of Genesis Owusu
At age two, the artist born Kofi Owusu-Ansah emigrated with his Ghanaian family to Canberra.
"There was always an overarching layer of Ghanaian high life music, sizzling jollof on the stove."
His home was filled with gospel music, via his choir leader mother, and the eclectic tastes of his father.
"[He] liked anything with an interesting album cover."
Each Saturday, "our cleaning day", the chores were soundtracked by recent CD acquisitions.
"I've always said it was Missy Elliott one weekend, Missy Higgins the next."
When his older brother, Kojo, began making music, as Citizen Kay, from a makeshift home studio, "everyone assumed I would follow in [his] footsteps", says Owusu.
"For a while, I pushed back."
Turning his focus to short stories and poetry only encouraged his older brother, who was "basically begging me to start rapping because he saw how the poetry would transition".
"For my birthday one year he gave me a shitty little mp3 player [with] a few of his beats on there."
Clicking with one track that came up on shuffle, Owusu Jnr "started writing [his] first verse".
It became the debut from the Ansah Brothers, with a music video filmed at the local golf course in Narrabundah.
At first, Owusu's parents had a "very typical immigrant parent reaction" to their sons pursuing music: "You're supposed to be a doctor, lawyer or engineer.
"Luckily for me, my older brother took the brunt of it."
It wasn't until TV and festival bookers came knocking, with a pay cheque, that their parents changed their tune. That's when Owusu said "by the way … I'm gonna be a rapper, too", he laughs.
They've been "extremely supportive" ever since.
"My dad, to this day, is probably still my biggest fan."
When Owusu appeared on one of Barack Obama's internet-famous playlists, "he saw it before I did".
Busting racial stereotypes
The Ansah Brothers were the only black kids in a "very white school [and] city", says Owusu.
"There was a cultural idea of who black people were supposed to be.
"I had two choices at the time. I could be the Eddie Murphy funny-man or the 50 Cent gangster. Basically, the novelty or the threat."
Thankfully, he discovered alternatives: The swagger of hit-maker Pharrell Williams; the political hip hop of Lupe Fiasco; the outsider artistry of Outkast's Andre 3000.
And the big one: Prince.
"I'm in a lineage of black weirdo boundary-breakers, and Prince is one of the godfathers of that family.
"He breaks so many rules that I had been taught as to what a song should be."
Whenever Owusu got stuck making his debut album, he'd think: "What would Prince do if he was a rapper from Canberra in the 2020s?"
The resulting record, Smiling With No Teeth, won Album of the Year, Best Hip Hop Release and Best Independent Release at the 2021 ARIA Awards.
Its follow-up, Struggler, swept the same categories in 2023. He's nominated for eight categories this year.
"I'd never really seen people like me represented in the Australian music landscape," reflects Owusu, likening the accolades to winning a war.
"Because so much of my life at that point was battling against the obstacles that came from not being accepted. It was like 'our community is changing …'
"It fulfils the mission I gave to myself at 10 years old to be a lifelong student and fierce boundary breaker."
It's an artistic duty he plans on sticking to.
"A person that continues to strive for new experiences in every avenue. That is who I have to be until I'm in the dirt."

RBA relaxed about housing downturn, deeply worried by AI and bonds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

RBA relaxed about housing downturn but deeply worried by AI and bonds
In short:
The RBA estimates less than 2 per cent of owner-occupier mortgage borrowers have a cash flow shortfall, while most have large offset or redraw buffers.
It is concerned about "circular financing" and increasing borrowing to fund the AI boom, as well as a spike in government bond yields.
What's next?
The RBA Monetary Policy Board will announce its next interest rate decision on November 3.
Despite Australia's rapid housing downturn, which threatens to be the worst in decades, the Reserve Bank believes the main threats to the nation's financial stability come from overseas.
That is the key takeaway from its latest half-yearly Financial Stability Review (FSR), released two days after the bank increased its cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent on Tuesday.
While Australian households remain among the world's most indebted, a rise in real household disposable income per capita since a recent low point in 2023 and 2024 means most borrowers are better placed to cope with their mortgage repayments, even though rates have passed the peak of 4.35 per cent in that period.
As at the end of June, the RBA estimated that less than 2 per cent of variable-rate owner-occupier mortgage borrowers had a "cash flow shortfall" — that is, where their income was insufficient to cover scheduled mortgage repayments and essential expenses.
The RBA forecast that this might rise to 2 per cent, or slightly above, in coming months as the cash rate has risen once since then to 4.6 per cent and is expected by financial markets to potentially rise further.
However, this is well below peaks close to 5 per cent in 2023 and 2024 during the post-COVID inflation spike, when the cash rate rose rapidly to 4.35 per cent.
The bank also noted that the median, or middle of the range, borrower has offset and/or redraw buffers that would cover more than a year of scheduled mortgage repayments at current interest rates.
Even if borrowers find themselves unable to make their mortgage repayments, the bank said most would be able to sell their home in order to pay off their loan in full.
It estimated that less than 1 per cent of borrowers were in negative equity and owing more on their loan than the market value of their home.
The RBA noted that even a 20 per cent plunge in house prices would only see around 5 per cent of mortgages falling into negative equity, due to the substantial run-up in property values ahead of the latest downturn.
The central bank also modelled a "very adverse downturn", where unemployment increases to 6.3 per cent (from 4.6 per cent currently), inflation nearly doubles to 7 per cent and the cash rate climbs a further percentage point to 5.6 per cent.
Even under this scenario, it estimated that just 5 per cent of mortgage borrowers would be "at a higher risk of defaulting on their loans", similar to levels seen in 2023.
Global threats 'continue to mount', Australia 'unlikely to be immune'
While the Reserve Bank is relatively relaxed about the domestic situation, it warned ominously that "threats to international financial stability continue to mount".
It cautioned that the interaction of intractable global conflicts disrupting key supply chains, the pace of technological development and the disruptions it causes, and the increase of severe weather events due to climate change, are key threats which "could be making a system-wide shock more likely and its potential consequences more severe".
Loading...
Reflecting recent comments from the RBA governor and other senior officials, the bank warned that a bursting of the potential AI bubble could trigger broader financial fallout.
"Low risk premia in major equity and credit markets have contributed to buoyant financial conditions for businesses, but these risk premia could move sharply higher in response to an adverse shock potentially in a disorderly manner," the review noted.
"One possible trigger could be a shift in sentiment towards the AI investment boom, which is increasingly fuelled by expectations of sustained rapid earnings growth and a debt-financing cycle that is becoming more opaque and circular."
While the RBA noted that hyperscalers and hardware producers were generally viewed as lower risk due to alternative revenue streams and generally solid financial positions, there are "pockets of higher risk firms in the AI value chain", including data centre construction, utility and neocloud providers.
It also noted the rising risks even for the large hyperscalers and hardware producers at the centre of the AI boom.
"The AI industry has been increasingly using off-balance sheet arrangements to finance large projects, such as data centres," the FSR observed.
These "opaque" arrangements sit outside of the hyperscalers' balance sheets for now, but the RBA warned "their financial obligations to these projects are becoming significant, with estimates ranging from $US1 trillion to $US1.5 trillion", or $1.4 trillion to $2 trillion.
The RBA also highlighted concerns about "circular financing" within the AI sector, for example where chipmakers provided financial support to neocloud firms who then purchased their products.
While there are financial risks posed by a collapse of the AI boom, the RBA also noted increasing risks if that boom continued.
A key concern is increasing vulnerabilities to AI-driven cyber attacks, especially the reliance of financial institutions on a small number of critical technology service providers.
In addition, it warned of financial market risks around "herd behaviour and market correlation" as AI agents played a greater role in investment decisions.
Loading
RBA concerned about risks of 'disruptive sell-off' in bond market
Another key global risk that is concerning the Reserve Bank is the recent jump in key advanced economy government bond yields, including the increased participation of investors, such as hedge funds, loading up on debt to play the market.
The RBA noted that hedge fund "repo" debt was near record highs, at more than $US3 trillion for US hedge funds alone, which was equivalent to about 10 per cent of that nation's annual GDP.
"This raises the prospect of increased volatility — and potentially a disruptive sell-off — in core bond markets that are central to the operation of the global financial system," the bank warned in the FSR.
"Australia is unlikely to be immune should international funding conditions abruptly tighten."

How AI could ‘supercharge’ election risks across south-east Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
01:58:40 UTC
10:58:40 KST

Years ago it would have been an elaborate operation involving an army of cyber troops creating fake news websites, social media accounts and forged dossiers, all deployed to spread disinformation en masse.
Now, all you need is AI.
In a worrying sign of how AI could “supercharge” fake news, Anthropic recently revealed how Claude AI was used in a political influence operation in Malaysia. It created a commercial election manipulation platform, utilising a network of about 1,000 X accounts, a fake news outlet called “Malaysia Pulse” and a series of fabricated documents.
The operation appeared designed to target voters in recent state elections, pulling in census and electoral data to exploit sensitive political and social fractures, including race, religion, and royalty across all 222 Malaysian parliamentary constituencies.
The experiment was ultimately ineffective once Anthropic stepped in but has sparked alarm about how AI could be weaponised in future elections in south-east Asia, a region already deeply vulnerable to fake news.
Katie Harbath, who formerly worked on public policy for global elections at Meta, says the case is an example of how AI brings a new level of sophistication and ease to the disinformation landscape.
“AI can supercharge it in terms of you can make a lot more content that’s more personalised, quicker and cheaper,” says Harbath, who now heads the tech consultancy company Anchor Change. “But you still need a distribution mechanism, and at the moment, that’s still your more social media type platforms.”
Anthropic detailed the Malaysia election operation in its latest threat assessment, released in September. The report revealed how actors used Claude to build networks of fake social media profiles and news websites that targeted audiences on six continents. Anthropic said the actors included “governments, state-aligned propaganda institutions and state media, as well as private firms selling influence”.
‘Flood the zone’
South-east Asia is no stranger to disinformation. In recent years Nobel laureate and Filipino journalist Maria Ressa has likened the Philippines to a “petri dish” for the weaponisation of disinformation and fake news, with techniques tried and tested in the south-east Asian nation later successfully replicated in the west.
But AI makes it all much easier.
“Basically AI is just mimicking what we would have, I guess, termed a few years ago, a troll factory,” says Rossine Fallorina of Sigla, a Philippine thinktank that researches AI. “Mostly because it speeds up the production process. So you don’t need 10 people to create a narrative or a story. You can just prompt it and then have it propagated.”
Last year OpenAI banned accounts using AI to generate comments about Philippine politics and public officials across social platforms, with many fictitious comments generated in support of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr.
Across south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper connected populations, some fear the divisive potential of AI on social media.
“It feeds political polarisation and it feeds on divisions,” says Bridget Welsh, from the University of Nottingham Asia Research Institute Malaysia. “That’s really what’s concerning about the fragmented nature of what’s happening in Malaysia.”
Malaysia’s general election could be called for late 2027, while the Philippines and Cambodia have polls in 2028, and Indonesia the following year.
Already in the region, AI has been effective. In Indonesia, an AI-generated cartoon image of now-president Prabowo Subianto that helped soften his strongman image became wildly popular in the 2024 election.
It has also been used to inflame tensions, such as inciting hatred toward ethnic Rohingya refugees who fled to Malaysia from Myanmar during the civil war, says Dr Ben Loh, a media lecturer at Monash University Malaysia.
“It’s come to the point where people already have this deep-seated hate in their minds and when they see the content like this, even though it’s AI-generated to them, it’s merely reinforcing what they believe is already true,” says Loh.
The Anthropic report notes that the fake news outlet scraped legitimate Malaysian reporting and had the model rewrite it several times before republishing it under fabricated bylines. It also republished articles from Russian and Chinese state-aligned foreign outlets, including TV BRICS, Xinhua, Sputnik/RIA, and CGTN, stripping them of attribution.
Anthropic said in its threat assessment that in each case of identified political influence the company “disrupted the activity, used what we learned to strengthen our safeguards, and shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners, where appropriate”.
In future, Harbath says AI could be used to “flood the zone” in an attempt to influence the large language models (LLMs) from which AI models draw their information.
“If there’s any sort of news drought, or if you have a place where there’s mostly government-sponsored media,” she says, “It wouldn’t take very much money to kind of flood the zone.”

Gaza documentary NAZA tops Italian box office in breakout debut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
01:45:34 UTC
10:45:34 KST

Tarek Chouiref
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
The Gaza war documentary NAZA topped the Italian box office on its first two days in theaters, with total ticket sales reaching nearly €1.1 million ($1.24 million) by Tuesday, the Italian box office tracker Cinetel said Wednesday.
The film opened at No. 1 on Monday with €451,872 in ticket sales and 60,467 admissions, more than twice the €179,612 earned by the “Avengers: Endgame” re-release that day, Cinetel figures showed.
It remained in first place Tuesday, taking another €623,164 and drawing more than 83,000 viewers. The film has grossed €1,096,816 cumulatively, drawing 146,720 admissions.
NAZA was initially released as a three-day cinema event from Sept. 28-30 in 515 theaters across Italy, many of them sold out. Screenings are continuing beyond the initial run following strong demand.
Directed by Oscar-winning Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the documentary examines the killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza through testimony from Israeli military and intelligence personnel.
Secretly filmed over three years on rooftops in Tel Aviv, it features testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence insiders whose identities, voices and appearances were digitally altered for protection.
Israeli military personnel featured in the film describe systems used to identify, track and strike targets despite expected civilian casualties. Some said they witnessed residential areas used as shelters being set ablaze and Palestinians being killed during food distribution in Gaza.
The film takes its name from NAZA, an abbreviation used by Israel’s military intelligence agency Aman to denote the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike.
NAZA recently won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice International Film Festival after receiving a standing ovation lasting about 25 minutes at its premiere.
The documentary has also drawn backlash from Israeli officials. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said earlier this month that he would push legislation targeting those who “defame” Israeli soldiers following the film’s screening.

US military cuts generals, admirals by 20%, Hegseth says

US military cuts generals, admirals by 20%, Hegseth says
October 1, 2026
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that the United States military has slashed the number of its generals and admirals by 20%.
He made the announcement while addressing junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia during what he called his "State of the Force" address.
"The number-crunchers say we fired 10% of the generals and admirals across the force," Hegseth said, adding: "We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10%."
"So yes, 20% reduction across the board," he noted. "The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue."
Cutting the fat or a purge?
The address came a year after a similar speech to top officers in which Hegseth said the US military was too fat, too focused on leftist "woke" ideas, and in need of major shake-up.
Since the start of Donald Trump's second term as president early last year, a number of top military personnel have been forced out of their positions.
Trump, for instance, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Charles "CQ" Brown, without explanation in February 2025.
Other senior officers pushed out include the heads of the US Army, Navy and Coast Guard, the general who headed the National Security Agency, the vice chief of staff of the US Air Force, and a Navy admiral assigned to NATO.
Hegseth has insisted the president is simply choosing the military leaders he wants.
But Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about the potential politicization of the US military.
Some members of Congress have called the latest cuts to the general ranks a "purge" that will take years to rebuild.
"He's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” Democratic Senator Mark Kelly told the Associated Press. Kelly is a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth. "He's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it."
Republican Senator Mike Rounds, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand Hegseth's reasoning.
"If it's simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first," Rounds said.
What Hegseth said about the new command
On Wednesday, Hegseth also announced his intention to create a new drone-focused warfare command, which would oversee the rollout of autonomous and robotic capabilities.
He said that "the pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it."
The defense secretary pointed to Ukraine's use of drones to combat Russian forces to underscore how warfare and battlefield tactics are changing.
"Ukraine's lesson is not that one type of drone wins wars, but rather the need for a purpose-built system that maximizes the ability to adapt," Hegseth said.
To study the future of warfare, the secretary unveiled a task force led by tech billionaire Elon Musk, former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Anduril Industries.
He said the work "will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes." The Pentagon chief pointed to the need to dominate "any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon."

Lockheed Martin in ‘Deep’ Overseas Patriot Production Talks as Ukraine Eyes Domestic Output

ARLINGTON, Virginia – Lockheed Martin is in advanced talks with allied countries about producing PAC-3 air-defense interceptors outside the United States as global demand for the missiles triples, Dan Tenney, the company’s Senior Vice President for Global Business Development and Strategy, told Kyiv Post on Wednesday.
The US defense giant is investing up to $9 billion through 2030 to expand missile production, strengthen supply chains and bring new factories online as governments race to replenish stocks and reinforce air defenses.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We have historic demand for the PAC-3 around the world,” Tenney said. “We have seen a tripling of the demand.”
He said the company is investing in at least 20 US facilities over the next five years while simultaneously exploring production beyond American territory.
Where does Ukraine fit?
Kyiv Post asked directly where Ukraine fits into potential PAC-3 production and how quickly such cooperation could begin.
According to Tenney, Lockheed Martin is already in advanced negotiations with several countries over future production sites and participating suppliers.
“We already have dialogues with a number of nations,” he said.
“I don’t want to comment on particulars because negotiations are continuing about where we will produce these capabilities [and] which suppliers” will be involved.
“We are in pretty deep discussions on this.”
US Extends Waiver for Russian-Controlled Serbian Oil Firm as Exit Talks Drag On
Lockheed Martin and the US government have already agreed to expand annual PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement, or MSE, production capacity from roughly 600 to 2,000 interceptors by the end of 2030.
The company is also preparing PAC-3 ACE, a lower-cost interceptor within the same missile family, as it seeks to increase capacity across multiple variants.
“We’re going to increase capacity for both of these missiles around the world,” the executive said.
PAC-3 demand triples
Pointing to its advanced seeker technology and hit-to-kill precision, the vice president underscored the interceptor’s battlefield performance.
“The PAC-3 missile is the most advanced capability in the world for interception,” he said. “The capability for it to hit on target is unprecedented.”
PAC-3 MSE is designed to intercept ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, advanced aircraft and other airborne threats – capabilities that have become increasingly critical as Russia continues using ballistic missiles and other high-speed weapons against Ukrainian cities.
Asked what was preventing Lockheed Martin from expanding production even faster, the executive gave a simple answer.
“Really, it’s just time,” he said. “It’s time for us to build new factories to bring the global demand that we’re seeing at scale.”
Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky said US President Donald Trump had made the final political decision allowing Ukraine to pursue domestic production of Patriot missile interceptors.
Trump first floated the idea in July, calling Ukrainian production of Patriot missiles a “cool idea.” The proposal later reportedly ran into concerns over the transfer of sensitive US military technology.
According to Zelensky, Trump has now given the political approval needed for Kyiv to move forward with plans for domestic production.
Lockheed expands across Europe
Speaking to a roundtable of journalists, the senior executive elaborated on Lockheed Martin’s broader plans to expand production, maintenance and logistics partnerships across Europe.
“We are expanding our work across Europe,” he said. “We think it’s healthy.”
The company is also exploring locations for a missile maintenance facility in Europe, though no country has yet been announced.
Microwave ‘drone killer’ targets swarms
The company is also investing heavily in cheaper ways to defeat mass drone attacks – a challenge that has become central to Ukraine’s defense.
The executive highlighted MORFIUS X-Rotor, an autonomous counter-drone aircraft using high-power microwaves instead of conventional missile interceptors.
He said MORFIUS can neutralize more than 50 drones before returning to recharge.
“It can take down 50-plus drones before it has to come back [and] get a recharge,” he said.
The system takes off vertically, transitions to horizontal flight and uses onboard targeting capability to hunt drones before attacking them with high-power microwave energy.
AI battle management
Lockheed Martin is also developing an AI-driven counter-drone battle-management architecture capable of integrating different sensors and weapons.
The executive said the system can learn from detected threats and share that information across the network, helping determine which defensive weapon should be used against each target.
That could mean choosing between electronic warfare, lasers, microwave weapons or kinetic interceptors rather than automatically assigning an expensive missile to every incoming drone.
“It has the ability to put the right effector on that particular drone,” he said.
Black Hawk without a pilot
Autonomy is also moving into some of Lockheed Martin’s best-known aircraft.
Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company, has developed U-Hawk, an autonomous aircraft derived from the Black Hawk helicopter.
“What we did with U-Hawk is take the entire cockpit out of the Black Hawk,” the executive said.
The aircraft uses Lockheed Martin’s MATRIX autonomy system and can transport up to 10,000 pounds into contested environments without putting an aircrew at risk.
“You’re not risking the life of a pilot,” he said.
Unlike a remotely piloted aircraft following only predetermined waypoints, the system is designed to interpret its surroundings, use information from other platforms – including space-based assets – and adjust its route autonomously.
U-Hawk was developed in about 10 months and is expected to fly this year, according to the executive.
F-35 sales remain government decisions
Asked whether Lockheed Martin decides which countries receive F-35 fighters, the executive stressed that such decisions remain with governments.
“Any kind of military sale is a government-to-government transaction,” he said.
Lockheed Martin works with Washington and partner governments to provide production capacity and capabilities, but approval for individual countries remains a US government decision.
The company is nevertheless looking to expand the F-35 industrial supply chain internationally.
“We’re always open to new partners,” Tenney said, noting that any expansion requires close coordination with the US government.

Can Myanmar’s New Government Revive the Stalled Dawei SEZ Project?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

Myanmar’s military-backed administration is again trying to put the long-stalled Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) project on the agenda. This time, Russia has emerged as a potential partner for some of its port and energy plans, but it remains unclear whether it can turn the area into a functioning economic zone.
The Dawei SEZ, with its proposed deep-sea port, sits on Myanmar’s Andaman coast. It faces the Indian Ocean and has an overland connection to Thailand and the wider Mekong region. The 138-kilometer-long Dawei-Htee Khee road, opened in 2013 but still requiring major upgrades, could connect the SEZ to the Southern Economic Corridor through Bangkok, Phnom Penh, and Ho Chi Minh City. For Thailand and the wider Mekong, Dawei could offer a westward route to the Indian Ocean that bypasses the Strait of Malacca. This position has long underpinned the project’s strategic and economic significance.
Dawei was an ambitious project from the beginning. Launched in 2008 under Myanmar’s military regime, it combined a deep-sea port, an industrial estate, power generation and utilities, and a road link across the border to Thailand. The early estimates for the entire project exceeded $50 billion. However, financial and development problems led to major restructuring in 2015–16, during Myanmar’s democratic transition. The challenge was raising enough capital and moving different parts of the project forward together.
The industrial zone needed power, water, transport, and access to a seaport. The port, in turn, relied on cargo and industrial activity. Investors also needed confidence that the wider infrastructure would be built. Much of Dawei’s regional potential also rested on having a reliable connection to Thailand. Yet the Dawei-Htee Khee road on the Myanmar side was poorly suited to serve as a major industrial corridor. Limited border facilities and cargo transfer capacity created additional bottlenecks.
Successive governments tried to address these constraints during Myanmar’s decade of political and economic opening. Myanmar and Thailand created a joint development vehicle in 2013, and Japan joined in 2015. Later, the government recast the Dawei project into initial and full phases. The first, smaller phase was estimated to cost about $1.7 billion. Financing remained difficult. In January 2020, under Myanmar’s elected civilian government, the Dawei SEZ Management Committee revised the concession terms to allow staged financing and reduce extra government risk.
By December 2020, it had terminated all nine initial-phase contracts with Italian-Thai Development after repeated delays and unmet financial obligations. The committee said the termination would allow it to rethink the project and seek new partners. The decision came just weeks before the February 2021 coup.
Dawei was hard to manage even when Myanmar had more access to international investors and development partners. Its problems with coordination and financing now exist in a much tougher economic, political, and security environment.
An ISP-Myanmar report based on official investment data shows recorded FDI falling from more than $28.7 billion in 2016-2020 to $7.4 billion in 2021-2025. Targeted post-coup sanctions remain in place, but the fall in investment reflects a wider deterioration that also includes armed conflict, policy uncertainty, difficult business conditions, and major corporate exits. Inflation and foreign-exchange pressure further complicate long-term investment.
The SEZ now effectively sits in a conflict zone. The fighting between military forces and local resistance groups has reportedly intensified around the project area, with reports of violence against civilians by military forces. The road toward Thailand crosses conflict-affected parts of Tanintharyi Region. The Htee Khee border trade area has also been controlled by the Karen National Union and its allied resistance forces since May 2025. For a cross-border SEZ, reliable access and security will remain central to long-term investment and development.
In this tougher setting, the Myanmar military-backed administration began making efforts to revive the project last year. Closer post-coup ties with Russia have brought Dawei back into active investment talks on power plants, oil refineries, and seaports. In June 2026, the Russian state-owned firm Inter RAO and the Myanmar military-controlled Launglon Economic Development Company signed an agreement for a 660-megawatt coal-fired power plant. Russia is seeking majority stakes during the project payback period to meet its banks’ lending conditions. The broader project plan is under discussion. Financing remains unsettled and undisclosed.
Beyond Russia, Dawei is reappearing in regional economic diplomacy. In August, Thailand also held bilateral talks on the Htee Khee-Dawei corridor under its policy of “calibrated re-engagement” with Myanmar. A month later, when coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing visited Vietnam, Myanmar’s military-backed administration promoted Dawei to Vietnamese investors at a business forum in Hanoi. Dawei appears to be part of the new administration’s regional re-engagement talks, despite unresolved issues around financing, security, and implementation.
Alongside these challenges, the project’s revival raises concerns about its impact on local communities. A 2014 survey of more than 1,500 households reported concerns about land loss, limited consultation, and incomplete compensation. These concerns are now compounded by questions about ownership, transparency, environmental safeguards, and local benefits.
Dawei’s viability depends on more than building individual assets, but even that will be difficult under current conditions. The seaport, power plant, and transport links must support industry while also creating economic opportunities and benefits for communities. Without that wider ecosystem, Dawei could remain a scattered collection of infrastructure rather than a functioning and sustainable economic zone.
