Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
00:10:06 BST
08:10:06 KST

Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine
- Published
When Vladimir Putin arrived to address Russia's parliament on Wednesday, a warm welcome was guaranteed.
"The Special Election Operation", as one Russian newspaper dubbed last month's legislative vote, has produced a State Duma even more pro-Putin than anything before it.
The ruling party, United Russia, now has more MPs than ever.
It allows the Kremlin to claim it has been handed a huge mandate from the Russian people.
But for what? How will Putin use it?
Are there any signs he is prepared to halt what he calls the special military operation? Or should we brace for further escalation in Ukraine and in tensions with Europe?
On Thursday I'll be watching to see whether Russia's leader sheds light on his plans during an appearance at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow. Traditionally the president's speech at this annual foreign policy forum provides insight into Putin's world view.
Right now, everything points to Putin continuing Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine: despite his country's huge battlefield losses to date and the damage being done to Russia's economy.
Putin's speeches and statements suggest he remains confident that Russia can secure a military victory.
Judging by what is being reported in Russian media, Moscow is encouraged by the shortage of air defence missiles in Ukraine, as well as the expectation that Russian strikes this winter will increase pressure on Ukrainians. Kyiv has spoken of its difficulty in shooting down Russia's ballistic missiles and new jet-powered drones, which have been targeting Ukraine every day.
And further afield?
The Kremlin has made no secret of the fact it wants European states to slash their military and financial backing for Ukraine: the kind of support Moscow says is prolonging the war - or, rather, getting in the way of a Russian victory.
To achieve this, Western officials believe Russia has been sending not so subtle signals.
They accuse Moscow of waging an escalating hybrid war on European countries through cyber-attacks, acts of sabotage, and Russian drones violating European airspace. In Germany, a drone carrying an explosive device was found close to Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig airport.
A covert campaign in the "grey zone", that space between peace and war.
This week I asked Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, does he admit that his country is waging a hybrid war against European countries?
"Do you mean when we destroy drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe are supplying Ukraine with, and which are used to attack us?" Lavrov replied.
"If you admit your weapons are being used to strike us and we destroy them, call it whatever you want. But I have no doubt this is a war Europe is waging against us. We've been saying so for a long time."
That, indeed, has been the official Russian stance for some time: that what is happening in Ukraine amounts to a European war on Russia. It is a narrative that skips over the fact that in 2022 it was the Kremlin that launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and that Russia continues to wage war there.
How far would Russia go to sever European support for Kyiv?
Is Moscow, for example, actively preparing to initiate military conflict in Europe with a Nato member state? That seems unlikely. After more than four-and-a-half years of war Russia's army has not yet managed to occupy the whole of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, right next door to Russia.
Fighting Europe may not be the plan, but freaking it out, to reduce support for Kyiv, could well be the intention.
Listen to the messaging.
"If they continue this war, a European war with American help, against Russia, on Ukrainian territory, sooner or later we'll feel the need to escalate," warns prominent foreign policy strategist Sergei Karaganov, honorary chairman of Russia's Council for Foreign and Defence Policy.
"According to my scenarios, the first series of blows will be conventional," he told me. "But if Europe does not surrender, unfortunately, we will have to go nuclear. There will be little left of some European countries."
But if Russia went nuclear there would be a response from Europe, and nothing would be left of Russia, I suggest.
"No, there will be no response from Europe," said Karaganov. "What, Britain will attack Russia with nuclear weapons? I hope you're not that crazy. I'm sure the Americans are not that crazy."
I asked him if he agreed the last four-and-a-half years had been disastrous for Russia, in terms of casualties and the worsening security and economic situation.
"We've lost a lot of people, yes," he admitted, "and I criticise my government for not being rough enough. But now we are getting rough enough in Ukraine. We're doing away with Ukraine as a viable state."
If "doing away with Ukraine as a viable state" is Moscow's goal, it is hard to imagine the war ending soon.
Meanwhile, Russia continues to rail against what it sees as the double standards of the West. In his recent address at the UN General Assembly, Sergei Lavrov accused the West of resorting to "brute force" around the world.
"What they did in Venezuela, was that soft power or brute force?" Russia's foreign minister asked me this week. He was referring to America's military operation in Caracas to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro back in January.
"The fact that [the US] bombed and destroyed Iran's leadership, along with their families, including children, is that not brute force?"
But was Russia not resorting to brute force every day in Ukraine, I replied.
"If you mean the destruction of infrastructure used by a Nazi regime backed by the West to wage war on the Russian Federation, then we are resorting to brute force to eliminate this direct threat to us."
Not only is this another element of Russia's official narrative: painting Ukraine as a neo-Nazi state, creating a false pretext to justify Russia's actions.
With the admission of Russia's use of "brute force" in Ukraine, it is also further evidence that Moscow is in no mood to stop fighting.

Measuring the Skills That Travel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:07:15 UTC
08:07:15 KST

Ratnesh Jha discusses English proficiency and workforce mobility
Adaptability has become one of the most valued qualities in today’s workforce. Employers want people who can adjust to new technologies, move between roles, work across cultures, and respond to challenges that may not have existed when they were first trained.
Workers feel that pressure too. In the 2026 ETS Human Progress Report, 77% of employees globally said job security no longer exists without continuous adaptation. The challenge is that adaptability is difficult to define and even harder to measure well. We talk about it constantly, but it is not a quality that lends itself easily to a single score.
For those of us in assessment, that should give us pause. The answer is not necessarily to create a new measure for every quality employers say they value, whether that is adaptability, resilience, or agility. Some human capabilities are simply too complex to reduce in that way. A more useful question is what adaptability looks like when someone actually has to perform. Language offers an interesting way to think about that.
A language assessment cannot tell us whether someone is an adaptable person, and it should not try to. What it can help us understand is whether someone can take what they know and apply it as the situation changes. That is something we do constantly when we communicate. We listen, interpret meaning, read the context, choose language that fits the audience, and adjust when a conversation moves in an unexpected direction or when we are misunderstood.
“Competence is not only about what someone knows. It is also about what they can do with that knowledge when the context changes.”
For multilingual people, there may be another layer of complexity. They often move between languages, cultural expectations, levels of formality, and different ways of expressing the same idea. That does not mean multilingualism automatically makes someone more adaptable in every aspect of life or work. It does, however, illustrate an important principle. Competence is not only about what someone knows. It is also about what they can do with that knowledge when the context changes.
That distinction matters more as the world of work becomes less predictable. We cannot prepare people for every task they will encounter over the course of a career. We cannot know exactly which technologies they will use, what industries they may enter, or what responsibilities they may eventually take on. What we can do is help people build capabilities that transfer across situations and become better at recognizing when those capabilities are genuinely there.
Language assessment has been grappling with this question for years. A meaningful assessment of communication should do more than determine whether someone recognizes vocabulary or understands a grammatical rule. It should also show whether that person can understand information, interpret meaning, and communicate effectively for a particular purpose.
The question is not simply whether someone knows something, but whether they can use what they know. That distinction has implications well beyond language.
If the skills employers increasingly need involve judgment, communication, and the ability to respond to unfamiliar situations, assessments that primarily reward the reproduction of familiar answers can only tell us so much. We need to understand how knowledge holds up when circumstances shift.
Workplace language assessment provides one example of how that role is already expanding. Research conducted for the TOEIC Global English Skills Report found that employers are using English assessments at several points in an employee’s journey. They may use them during recruitment, before training, or when considering employees for advancement.
These are very different moments. During hiring, an assessment may help determine whether someone is prepared for a particular role. Before training, it can help identify where development is needed. Later in a career, it can help make progress and newly acquired capability more visible.
In each case, the assessment does not predict the person’s future. It provides a clearer picture of what that individual can do now and where further development may create additional opportunities. That is an important shift in how we think about the role of assessment.
Assessment has often been viewed primarily as a gateway. A person reaches a certain score and gains access to a program, role, or opportunity. That function will always matter, but assessment can also help guide development. It can give learners a clearer understanding of where they stand, help employers identify areas for growth, and provide individuals with a way to demonstrate progress over time.
As the role of assessment changes, assessment itself also has to become more responsive to how skills are actually used. A single, uniform approach makes less sense when organizations are hiring and developing people for very different roles, industries, and communication needs.
We have seen this firsthand in the development of TOEIC Link, which allows organizations to assess listening, reading, speaking, and writing skills individually or in combination depending on their needs. The point is not that every assessment should become modular. It is that the way we measure skills should continue to evolve alongside the environments in which those skills are used.
As work becomes more dynamic, assessment should become more flexible too, while preserving the rigor, reliability, and comparability that make the results meaningful.
The same principle applies after an assessment is complete. A score is most useful when it helps someone understand what to do next. Measurement can identify a strength or a gap, but its value grows when learners can act on that information through targeted practice, feedback, and continued development.
That creates a more useful relationship between assessment and learning. Instead of measurement being the end of the process, it can become part of an ongoing cycle of understanding, development, and progress.
Language is particularly relevant because proficiency can expand the number of environments in which someone is able to participate. An engineer may be able to contribute to an international project. A frontline employee may become eligible for a regional role. A researcher may gain access to a wider professional community. A manager may be better equipped to lead colleagues across countries. In that sense, language proficiency can create greater optionality.
Learning English does not guarantee career mobility, and no language score should ever be treated as a proxy for intelligence, talent, or potential. It can, however, expand the range of settings in which someone is able to communicate effectively and contribute with confidence.
In an unpredictable labor market, having more options matters. The career someone begins in their 20s may look very different from the work they are doing in their 40s. Industries change. Technology changes. People retrain, relocate, and take on responsibilities they never anticipated.
Do our assessments require people to apply knowledge rather than simply recall it? Do the tasks reflect the situations in which those skills will actually be used? Do the results help people develop as well as demonstrate what they can already do? Can those results remain meaningful as people move between institutions, jobs, and countries?
Most importantly, we should ask whether we are only measuring what a person knows or whether we are getting closer to understanding what that person can actually do. Language assessment has been wrestling with these questions for decades. As education and work become more dynamic, they are becoming relevant far beyond language.
The future of assessment should not be about pretending we can predict exactly who will thrive in an uncertain world. It should be about giving people better ways to demonstrate capabilities that remain useful even as the world around them changes.
Language is one of those capabilities. Its value is not merely that it helps someone communicate today. It can also expand where they can contribute, how they can grow, and the opportunities they may be able to pursue next.
If adaptability is what we increasingly expect of workers, then assessment should be willing to adapt as well.
Ratnesh Jha is Global General Manager, Institutional Products, at ETS.

aston martin DBX GT wraps 717 horsepower in a quieter, softer-riding SUV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:05:45 UTC
08:05:45 KST

aston martin DBX GT wraps 717 horsepower in a quieter, softer-riding SUV
aston martin retunes its fastest SUV around comfort, with memory foam seats, revised dampers, and a quieter V8.
aston martin gives its 717-hp DBX a softer side with new GT
Aston Martin has added a second personality to its fastest SUV. The new DBX GT arrives alongside the more overtly performance-focused DBX S, using essentially the same mechanical package while tuning the experience around comfort, reduced cabin noise, and a more restrained exterior. Under the hood is the familiar 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 producing 717 bhp, enough to send the large SUV from 0 to 60 mph in 3.1 seconds and on to 193 mph.
The interesting part is what Aston Martin has done around that engine. The GT keeps the speed, carbon-ceramic brakes, and quicker steering ratio of the DBX S, then changes how much of all that activity reaches the people inside.
Suspension calibration has been revised, including new internal damper valves designed to absorb the small, rapid movements produced by coarse pavement and rumble strips before they travel through the cabin. The standard wheels are 22 inches rather than the available 23-inch setup, paired with all-season tires chosen partly for ride quality and road noise.
the DBX turns down its visual aggression
The difference begins at the front, as the team at Aston Martin has replaced some of the DBX’s harder-edged detailing with a double-vaned metal grille that stretches visually toward the outer vents and daytime running lights. Lower sections of the front bumper, side sills, and rear diffuser come painted in the body color, while a two-piece metal side strake mixes polished and satin surfaces. A new set of horizontal quad exhaust tips finishes the rear.
It is a subtle shift in emphasis for a car that still has the proportions of a high-performance SUV. The standard 22-inch forged wheels leave a little more tire visible around the rim, and the body-colored lower sections reduce some of the contrast usually used to make performance cars appear lower and sharper.
Marek Reichman, Aston Martin’s chief creative officer, describes the GT as a more discreet interpretation of the DBX, with its outright performance receding visually even as the underlying hardware remains close to the DBX S.
more attention goes to the people inside
A larger part of the GT treatment happens where the changes are easiest to feel. Aston Martin has redesigned the front and rear seats with additional cushioning and reshaped bolsters, adding a 10 mm layer of memory foam to the seat base. The rear bench also gains two more deeply sculpted outer seating positions with taller headrests, while retaining space for a fifth passenger in the center. A panoramic glass roof comes standard.
There is plenty of labor buried in the upholstery. Aston Martin says each front seat uses 691 meters of thread and 3,297 perforations, requiring more than four and a half hours of work. Semi-aniline leather and deep-pile carpeting are joined by additional sound-deadening in the doors, wheel arches, and cargo area, along with acoustic laminated rear side glass.
The company reports a 13% improvement in its Articulation Index, a measurement concerned with how easily occupants can understand conversation while the vehicle is moving.
717 horsepower stays in the background until you ask for it
The 4.0-liter V8 uses turbocharger technology shared with Aston Martin’s mid-engine Valhalla and produces 664 lb-ft of torque. The nine-speed automatic has received revised calibration for smoother gear changes, while the throttle mapping has been adjusted to make smaller pedal inputs easier to control.
Engineers also added a stiffer transmission mount and dampers between the body and rear subframe, aimed at reducing movement through larger bumps and compressions.
Even the exhaust has been retuned around that idea. Gas flow is mixed twice inside the rear muffler to remove some harsher metallic frequencies, with GT mode keeping the sound subdued and Sport modes opening things up when the driver wants the V8 to come forward. First deliveries of the Aston Martin DBX GT are scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2026.

 power: 717 bhp
 transmission: nine-speed automatic
 0–60 mph: 3.1 seconds
 top speed: 193 mph / 310 km/h

Tennessee execution of Christa Pike can go ahead, US supreme court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:03:13 UTC
08:03:13 KST

A Tennessee woman convicted of murdering a schoolmate 30 years ago has been taken to hospital after surviving two attempts to execute her with lethal injections.
Witnesses reported that Christa Pike was still breathing despite the injections intended to kill her late on Wednesday. It was the second botched execution in Tennessee this year.
Her attorneys told a local news station: “This has turned into agony and a violation of Pike’s right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.”
The Tennessee Department of Correction later confirmed in a statement that Pike had survived the state’s effort to execute her: “The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening.”
Pike had been transported to an “off-site medical facility”, they said.
In a press conference, media witnesses described hearing Pike snore 40 minutes after she was administered two doses of pentobarbital.
The failed execution is the second in Tennessee this year, after prison officials in May aborted attempts to execute a man convicted of murders after failing to find a suitable vein for his lethal injection.
Tennessee governor Bill Lee, who denied Pike’s clemency petition on Monday, issued a statement after the botched execution, suspending all executions this year and calling for a “comprehensive, third-party review” of Pike’s execution attempt, according to Nashville’s the Tennessean.
Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution at 10am local time on Wednesday for a killing she committed when she was 18, and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, but hours later the US supreme court overturned that stay.
Pike’s attorneys have filed an emergency motion to the US supreme court asking to halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and the state is violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.
Seven journalists who were in the room to witness the execution said afterward, on a livestream hosted by WVLT television station, that after the injection Pike was clearly alive and snoring before corrections officials escorted journalists out.
“It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go,” said investigative journalist John North of WBIR, who was a witness at the execution site. “When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive,” he said.
Earlier Pike, who was convicted of murder 30 years ago, had her execution halted by an appeals court in a 2-1 ruling, that said the delay was necessary to assess whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing. The state governor and the supreme court had earlier refused calls for clemency.
Tennessee’s attorney general immediately appealed against the ruling to the supreme court, writing that the 11th-hour stay rewarded “abusive delay tactics by Pike’s attorneys”, according to the Associated Press.
The US supreme court sided with Tennessee in an order signed by justice Brett Kavanaugh.
Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by fellow liberal justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, dissented from the court’s order “because its decision clears the way for the state to execute Pike before her still-pending legal challenges to her conviction can be properly considered”.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps in 1995.
The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder.
According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area behind the agriculture campus steam plant at the University of Tennessee on 12 January 1995. Pike cut Slemmer’s stomach and throat with a box cutter before smashing her head with a rock.
Shipp carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of Slemmer’s skull.
Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing and was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement that was included in her clemency petition.
On Saturday, May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, said she was waiting for Pike’s execution.
“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” Martinez told the Associated Press, adding: “Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst.”
The Associated Press contributed reporting

Swiss glaciers lose more than 5% of ice after record heatwave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:03:04 UTC

Swiss glaciers lose more than 5% of ice after record heatwave
- Swiss glaciers lost over 5% of their ice in 2026 due to a record heatwave and low winter snowfall, marking one of the worst years for glacier melting.
- In the past five years, nearly 20% of Swiss glacier ice has disappeared, threatening future water supplies and raising concerns about Europe's ice fields.
- The largest glacier, Aletsch, had its biggest melt ever, with scientists estimating a loss of 2.2 trillion litres of water between July and September, causing visible landscape changes and sadness among experts.
AI generated
LES DIABLERETS, Switzerland – Swiss glaciers are shrinking rapidly after suffering one of their worst years of ice loss during a record-breaking European heatwave.
Switzerland’s glaciers lost more than 5% of their ice in 2026, a report by the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network (GLAMOS) and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation of the Swiss Academy of Sciences showed on Oct 1.
The findings underscore the accelerating pace of glacier retreat as extreme melt years become routine.
Over the past five years, Swiss glaciers have shed almost a fifth of their ice, the report showed, threatening future water supplies and raising questions about the long-term survival of Europe’s ice fields.
“Now we are in this new world, in this future, where glaciers are just melting away,” Matthias Huss, director of GLAMOS, said.
A combination of a winter with too little snow and record temperatures in the summer led to what Huss called “enormous” melting in 2026.
‘A really worrying situation’
“We are seeing extreme years almost every year now and this is really a worrying situation,” Huss said.
Still, the rate of ice loss has not yet quite reached the record highs of 2022, when dust clouds from North Africa settled on the snow and accelerated melting, Huss said.
Switzerland’s largest glacier, Aletsch Glacier, suffered its biggest-ever melt in 2026, while Glacier de Tsanfleuron lost more than 4m of average thickness. Huss said this would have been unthinkable a few years ago.
In total, the scientists estimate Swiss glaciers lost around 2.2 trillion litres of water between July and September alone, equivalent to more than four times the annual drinking water consumption of Swiss households.
That has one positive side effect: glacier melt contributes to easing summer water shortages.
But, as ice-covered areas shrink and glaciers become smaller, this benefit is decreasing, Huss said.
“It’s not that we’re surprised because we know how fast the glaciers are melting, but to see the colours of the mountains where there is no snow left, there are just these rocks,” Huss said. “It makes me sad.” REUTERS

France: Hundreds arrested as student protests escalate
October 1, 2026
Security forces in France on Wednesday detained over 600 people as protests at high schools in parts of the country have intensified.
Authorities said violent clashes and arson attacks have also left dozens of security personnel wounded.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez condemned what he called an "escalation of violence" outside certain schools.
The violence left 83 police officers and gendarmes wounded on Wednesday, he said, adding that 32 teachers and pupils were also injured. The protests affected 356 schools, the minister noted.
He slammed the "targeting of law enforcement officers, the throwing of projectiles, acts of violence, verbal abuse, attempted arson, and what amounts... to urban violence."
Why are students protesting?
Teenagers at French lycées (equivalent to US high schools) have been blockading their schools since last week.
They are protesting overcrowded classes, heavy workloads, poor-quality learning materials and teacher shortages.
"There are cockroaches and rats everywhere in the school," Fadila, a 17-year-old student, told the Reuters news agency. She said temperatures in classrooms could swing from sweltering to below freezing, depending on the weather.
The movement began in the Ile-de-France region around the capital, Paris, but has since spread to other regions.
The cities worst affected Wednesday include Paris, Bordeaux in the southwest and Lyon in the southeast, and the northern city of Lille, where police again used tear gas in clashes, the AFP news agency reported.
What did the government say?
President Emmanuel Macron said the young people's concerns were legitimate but could in no way justify violence and attacks on police officers and teachers, among others.
"High schools are meant to be open and to share knowledge. They are not meant to be blockaded or to have trash cans set on fire," he told reporters in Madrid.
Both Macron and Nunez accused far-left groups of inciting violence during the protests.
"We observed that, in certain places, there were individuals acting as agitators — people who, moreover, moved from one school to another to stir up high school and other students and incite them to commit acts of violence," Nunez said.
Over the past few days, officials and politicians have denounced the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed or LFI) party and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon for rhetoric they said was stoking students' anger.
On Monday, Melenchon had accused the government of implementing a "crackdown" with "obvious racist undertones."
"Hands off our youth!" he wrote on social media, while encouraging LFI activists and officials to support the protests wherever they could.

Floating scarecrows: how Cornish fishers are stopping seabirds drowning in their nets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:01:21 UTC
08:01:21 KST

Bird-shaped kites and a floating scarecrow are being tested to try to stop endangered seabirds drowning in fishing nets.
Every year an estimated 95,000 diving birds, including razorbills and guillemots, are accidentally caught in nets off European coasts.
But simple deterrents tested by Cornish fishers and devised by scientists and the RSPB have been shown to reduce the toll by about two-thirds.
The scarecrow – or more properly a looming-eyes buoy – has a spinning head with two large eyes that scare diving birds away from gillnets, walls of netting which hang vertically beneath the surface.
The LEB was tested alongside a commercially available scarybird kite.
Ten Cornish fishers and Fishtek Marine, which created the LEB, fitted cameras to boats to monitor the effect of the devices on seabird behaviour.
The results of the two-year trial, which was analysed by scientists from the University of Exeter and published in the journal Conservation Letters, showed that the chance of seabirds being caught in gillnets fell by 59% using LEBs and by 71% using kites.
The research revealed that in Cornwall most seabirds were caught in winter, which will help target the use of the devices by season.
Tom Horton, lead author of the University of Exeter research, said: “This study provides some of the strongest evidence to date that simple, practical deterrents can substantially reduce seabird bycatch in gillnet fisheries.
“By also identifying when and where bycatch risk is highest, we now have a clear opportunity to target mitigation measures where they can deliver the greatest conservation benefit for vulnerable seabird populations and encourage sustainable fishing practices.”
Yann Rouxel, bycatch programme manager at the RSPB, said: “After over a decade of research into gillnet bycatch and its solutions, it’s great to see this work moving towards real-world implementation.
“The performance of the LEB and kite, as evidenced in this study, is a major milestone in the effort to reduce seabird bycatch without impeding gillnet fishers while at sea.”

US Senate rejects bill targeting AI data centre electricity costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:58:21 UTC
07:58:21 KST

US Senate rejects bill targeting AI data centre electricity costs
Democrats criticise bill as lacking ‘teeth’ and push for mandatory measures to address soaring electricity bills.
The United States Senate has thwarted a bill that would have required state regulators to consider forcing data centres and other major electricity users to bear the costs of the infrastructure built to serve them.
The measure failed by a vote of 57 to 43 on Wednesday. The proposal needed to pass by at least 60 votes to prevent a filibuster, a procedural hurdle in the Senate that can stymie a bill indefinitely.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3What’s the US–China AI ‘hotline’ that Trump plans to pitch to Xi Jinping?
- list 2 of 3China vs US: Who is winning the AI race, in four charts
- list 3 of 3How an OpenAI ‘agent’ hacked Australia’s Medicare and what that means
Only four Democrats — Maggie Hassan, Amy Klobuchar, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock — joined Republicans to support the bill, which proponents argue would have eased the burden of rising energy costs on individual households.
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has led to increasing demand for data centres, which provide computing power for the new technology.
There are as many as 5,400 data centres currently in the US, according to some estimates. Critics argue the facilities require substantial amounts of energy to operate, contributing to higher electricity costs.
The Ratepayer Protection Act, a first-of-its-kind bipartisan bill, was aimed at addressing the economic concerns linked to the expansion of data centres.
It passed the House of Representatives earlier this month in a landslide vote of 417 to three.
But Democrats in the Senate argued the bill does not go far enough to protect consumers from high electricity bills. Rather than requiring states to “consider” a federal utility rate standard, some senators advocated instead for mandatory enforcement to guarantee consumer relief.
Other critics described the bill as a last-ditch Republican effort to secure a legislative victory ahead of the November midterm elections.
Senate Democratic Party leader Chuck Schumer, for instance, dismissed the legislation as “toothless”. He noted that the bill failed to require data centres to cover the costs they incur in upgrades to electricity infrastructure.
“We need real action on data centres, and what do Republicans decide all of a sudden to push forward? A bill that is totally optional,” said Schumer.
He challenged Republicans to prove their commitment to the issue by passing a Democratic alternative that “has teeth”.
Despite widespread pushback, thousands of data centres already span the US, with construction underway for dozens more. While the states of Virginia and Texas lead the nation in operating facilities, California, Ohio and New York follow behind closely as top digital infrastructure hubs.
According to a September poll, 53 percent of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centres on electricity prices or water supplies in the communities where they are built.

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who has pleaded for EU spending rules to be relaxed, speaks during a press conference with Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš in Prague on Sept. 29, 2026. | Milan Kammermayer/AFP via Getty Images
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wants the European Commission to relax its fiscal rules to allow countries to better help firms and families deal with rising prices, driven by a crunch in energy supply.
Speaking at a media event on Wednesday, Meloni said she is writing to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen about the issue and wants it discussed at upcoming Ecofin and European Council meetings.
“We believe that, in the face of rising inflation caused by high global energy prices, it is necessary to grant member states additional flexibility to support households and businesses,” she said.
Advertisement
European countries are struggling with higher energy costs driven by the war in Iran, and fear that increased costs will put delicate growth at risk and stoke inflation.
“I am writing to President von der Leyen to ensure that the issue is addressed at the Ecofin meeting to be held next week in Luxembourg, and then, of course, at the next European Council, which is in two weeks,” Meloni said.
Gasoline prices have been the biggest political issue in Italy for weeks, putting the government in trouble. Political parties are already getting on a campaign footing ahead of a national election next year.
Italy’s government overspends its income by the equivalent of more than 3% of its GDP, breaching EU fiscal targets. Meloni’s government plans to meet the 3% target next year, after failing to do so this year.
Several other countries also run above or close to the 3% threshold and Meloni may find she has allies in the European Council in her fight for more flexibility.

Greece’s Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis also wrote to von der Leyen, Council President António Costa and Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis on Wednesday, slamming a request for countries to use less energy and instead calling for more fiscal space.
“We have already raised the issue at the Ecofin meeting regarding the need to take into account the higher inflation recorded during this period when calculating the European targets that must be met and the permitted deficit,” Meloni said.

The waiver allows NIS to continue operating the Pančevo refinery, importing crude oil and conducting transactions necessary to maintain Serbia’s fuel supplies despite US sanctions imposed over the company’s Russian ownership.
Russian stake still on the table
Russian companies Gazprom Neft and Gazprom together control about 56% of NIS, while the Serbian government owns 29.9%. The remaining shares are held by minority shareholders and employees.
Washington has been pressing for the Russian stake to be divested, with Hungarian energy group MOL negotiating a potential takeover.
Serbian Energy Minister Dubravka Đedović Handanović said talks between OFAC and MOL over the transaction were continuing and needed additional time.
“We have completed our part of the work when it comes to the agreement between the shareholders, if MOL takes over NIS and the US approves it,” she said.
Until a deal is completed, Belgrade will continue taking measures to maintain fuel supplies and limit potential market disruptions, she added.
Sybiha Meets Japanese Lawmakers in Kyiv to Discuss Further Security Cooperation
NIS is particularly important to Serbia because its Pančevo refinery is the country’s only oil refinery and supplies a large share of the domestic fuel market.
The company has repeatedly received temporary US sanctions waivers while negotiations over its ownership continue.
The latest extension follows a previous waiver granted in August that allowed NIS to operate through Sept. 30.
Serbia has also released 5,000 metric tons of diesel from state reserves amid high fuel prices, logistical problems and low water levels on the Danube that have complicated imports.
Đedović Handanović said keeping the Pančevo refinery running at maximum capacity was particularly important ahead of the winter heating season.
Serbia still reliant on Russian gas
While Washington is pushing Russian ownership out of Serbia’s oil sector, Belgrade remains heavily dependent on Moscow for natural gas.
Serbia and Russia separately agreed Wednesday to extend their existing gas arrangement for another three months, through the end of 2026, AFP reported.
The head of state-owned Srbijagas, Dušan Bajatović, said Gazprom would continue supplying Serbia under the same favorable conditions.

"And I think we're in a good place because oil prices are going to start to come down," Trump added.

But his latest comments appeared to show him cooling to the idea of an export ban, even as he declined to rule it out entirely.
"We're in a very good place," Trump said, highlighting a recent resurgence in crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz.
The strait is a major throughway for the global oil trade that saw ship traffic stifled after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. But this week it saw daily exports return to prewar levels.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright, standing next to Trump at the Resolute Desk, said, "You've seen diesel prices come down the last week. I think you'll see them move meaningfully down in the coming weeks and days."
But Wright acknowledged that diesel supplies are "tight" because of export loss related to conflicts in Russia and the Middle East, as well as from China.
"So that's a lot of interruptions. But American refiners are running at record highs," Wright said, "and you will hear announcements from our our friends in Europe about new diesel supplies that'll come to the market. That'll meaningfully push diesel prices down."
When a reporter asked if Wright has advised against a diesel export ban, Trump interjected, saying, "No, I think it's something that we think about and we talk about every day."
"But it just seems that it would have a negative impact on gasoline," he said. "That would go up a little bit and diesel would come down a little bit."
Trump also repeated his claim that Russia's war against Ukraine was "really the biggest problem for diesel."
Diesel prices have soared to record highs amid the continuing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, which have caused major disruptions to global energy flows. Oil prices rose on Wednesday as the prospect of U.S. talks with Iran appeared to stall out once again.

International Criminal Court (ICC) Registrar Osvaldo Zavala Giler called Wednesday for political support from EU states to ensure the court can continue its work "undeterred."
Speaking in a video message from Brussels, where he addressed EU states at the Working Party on Public International Law - International Criminal Court subgroup (COJUR-ICC), Giler said ensuring resilient justice requires efforts both from the court itself and its member states.
"Ensuring that justice is resilient and that the ICC continues to do its work undeterred requires work," he said in the video, which was shared by the court in a post on the US social media platform X.
Giler said the court must ensure that mechanisms and processes are in place to make its operations sustainable but stressed that it also needs "political support from states parties."
"That's why I'm here in Brussels today at the EU, discussing with EU member states ways in which they can provide political support to the ICC," he said.
Such support, he added, is needed "to make sure that our joint efforts guarantee the resilience of our operations and that justice can be undeterred."
The ICC said Giler, during the COJUR-ICC meeting, called for support for the court "in its mission to bring justice to victims of the gravest crimes."
The call came amid increasing pressure from the US against the court, as Washington has already sanctioned 13 ICC officials, including nine of the court’s 18 judges.
US President Donald Trump renewed criticism of the ICC last week during his UN General Assembly address, calling on member states to leave the court.
Washington’s criticism intensified after the ICC issued arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes in Gaza. The US and Israel are not ICC members.

Watchdog finds no Fed misconduct in renovation; Trump calls for Powell’s resignation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:37:00 UTC
07:37:00 KST

Watchdog finds no Fed misconduct in renovation; Trump calls for Powell’s resignation
- The Federal Reserve’s Inspector General found no criminal or administrative misconduct in the US central bank renovation, despite a nearly US$1 billion cost overrun due to poor project oversight.
- President Trump called for Jerome Powell’s resignation, blaming him for mismanagement and pushing for legal action amid ongoing conflicts over monetary policy.
- Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh plans to follow recommendations for better project management and independent auditing, while lawmakers remain divided on the report’s implications for Fed accountability.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Federal Reserve’s Inspector General on Sept 30 said it found no grounds for a criminal referral or evidence of administrative misconduct tied to cost overruns in a US central bank renovation project.
However, its conclusion there was lax oversight drew a fresh call from President Donald Trump for former Federal Reserve chief Jerome Powell’s resignation.
The Fed watchdog’s report highlighted extensive problems with project oversight that contributed to a roughly US$1 billion (S$1.28 billion) cost overrun for the renovation of the central bank’s two historic buildings on the National Mall in Washington.
Trump had latched onto the cost overrun on the project, which now has a price tag of about US$2.4 billion, in his effort to engineer Powell’s ouster and gain influence over the direction of monetary policy. Trump is also trying to sack Fed Governor Lisa Cook over alleged wrongdoing in an unrelated matter.
The IG’s report noted that “at no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the US attorney general”.
“Further, while our report outlines deficiencies in the management of the renovation project, resulting in our recommendation of corrective actions in accordance with the Inspector General Act, we did not identify administrative misconduct during our evaluation,” it added.
Powell declined to comment on the report, the latest chapter in an ongoing feud with Trump that goes back to 2018, when the president first criticized the Fed chief for not cutting interest rates. Trump had nominated Powell for the top Fed job in late 2017.
“At a minimum, ‘Too Late’ Powell should be forced to resign from the Board. He can’t manage a Building, and he certainly shouldn’t be allowed to manage his High Interest Rate Policy (only on “TRUMP!”),” the president wrote on Truth Social.
“If he doesn’t resign, he should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government, for either corruption or incompetence, both of which are completely unacceptable.”
Trump said he had directed Attorney General Todd Blanche “to study the report, and make a determination as to what to do”.
Besides Powell, who led the Fed through most of the project, Fed Vice-Chair Philip Jefferson heads the central bank’s Committee on Board Affairs and serves as the “administrative governor” most directly involved in project oversight.
Jefferson did not have any immediate comment on the report.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who took over from Powell in May, said he would follow the report’s recommendations on project management and hire an independent auditor to “verify accuracy and compliance” of all awarded costs to date.
Cost overruns on government projects are common. Trump’s own budget for White House ballroom renovations, now underway, doubled from initial estimates to at least $400 million.
Reaction from US lawmakers split along party lines.
“Inflation does not change the Fed’s responsibility to manage its resources prudently and be accountable to Congress,” said Republican Senator Tim Scott, who chairs the Senate Banking Committee, calling the cost overruns “egregious” and promising “rigorous oversight” of the Fed.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, the committee’s top Democrat, said the report’s findings showed “no basis to restart the president’s witch hunt” against Powell.
Congress oversees the Fed, though the central bank sets its own budget and is not subject to the political appropriations process.
White House pressure campaign
Trump had for years chafed at Powell’s leadership of the Fed, publicly and incessantly berating him for not lowering interest rates. The spiralling cost of the Fed renovation project arose early in the president’s second term as a fresh focal point for the White House’s attacks on Powell.
Key members of the Trump administration and their allies in Congress suggested wasteful spending on luxury upgrades had ballooned the project’s budget to hundreds of millions of dollars more than earlier estimated.
Powell countered that the extra costs reflected unexpected challenges, such as asbestos abatement and higher-than-estimated prices for materials and labour as the construction went deep underground.
He also asked the Fed’s IG to take a fresh look at the project and its costs. The report on Wednesday said design elements like marble, water features and a garden terrace cited by critics in the White House “did not materially contribute” to the cost overruns.
The 120-page document did, however, outline extensive management shortfalls, including a failure by the Fed to follow through on what it intended to be a “guaranteed maximum price” contract that would make the contractor responsible for cost overruns. The maximum price, in effect, was never actually established, with Fed project managers awarding subcontracts that continued to escalate the price and timeline of the project.
The central bank, for example, ultimately paid US$346 million for plumbing and air conditioning on the project, triple the initial estimate.
As controversy over the renovations escalated, Trump, accompanied by Scott, visited the renovation site in July 2025 to press his criticisms. The visit led to a memorable on-camera incident in which Powell appeared to fact-check the president’s stated cost-overrun number.
Tensions rose sharply in January 2026, when US Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro issued subpoenas to the Fed Board seeking information about the cost overruns and Powell’s testimony to Congress about them.
Powell disclosed the Department of Justice’s threat to criminally indict him in an unusual Sunday night video statement, calling it an attempt to intimidate an institution that sets interest rates based on what is best for the country rather than according to the president’s preferences.
The revelation of the DOJ probe prompted an outcry against political interference in the central bank, not only from Powell’s global peers and economists but also, closer to home, from lawmakers, including some of Trump’s fellow Republicans.
A federal judge quashed the DOJ’s subpoenas in March, agreeing with Powell that they were a pretext for pressuring the Fed chief into lowering rates, as Trump wished, or resigning. Pirro’s subsequent decision to close her investigation and refer the matter to the Fed IG convinced Republican Senator Thom Tillis to allow Trump’s nomination of Warsh as Powell’s successor to proceed.
Powell, however, has stayed on at the Fed as a governor.
“I have said that I will not leave the Board until this investigation is well and truly over, with transparency and finality, and I stand by that,” Powell said at his final press conference as Fed chief in April.
Pirro’s office said on Sept 30 that it had received the report and was reviewing it. REUTERS

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday that Albania's goal of joining the European Union is "in sight," describing the country as one of the front-runners in the bloc's accession process.
"You in Albania have been working hard to turn Albania's European dream into reality," von der Leyen told Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama at a joint news conference in Tirana.
"I think the goal is in sight. Albania is among the front-runners in our accession process," she said, pointing to "remarkable progress" over the past year.
Von der Leyen noted that Albania had opened the final clusters of negotiating chapters and in July closed its first three chapters, including external relations.
She said Albania is now "100%" aligned with the EU's common foreign and security policy, adding that the two sides "see the world with the same eyes."
She stressed, however, that further reforms are required across open chapters, particularly in the areas of justice, the electoral framework and environmental protection.
"Adopting the reforms is important, but it is, of course, also equally important to implement those reforms thoroughly to make sure that they deliver real change for the people of Albania," she said.
Rama, for his part, reaffirmed Albania's "ironclad will" to move ahead with everything required in the accession process, saying the country is preparing to begin closing further negotiating chapters before the end of this year.
He also highlighted Albania's efforts against organized crime and corruption, saying it was now clear that "if up until a while back corruption was the system, now the system is fighting corruption."
Von der Leyen said Albania has completed more than 80% of reform steps under the EU's Growth Plan and has already received €213 million ($241 million) in EU funding, with further payments expected in the coming weeks.
She also announced that the commission will present its pre-enlargement policy reviews next week, examining the EU’s institutions, policies and budget to prepare the bloc for future members.
"Accession will always remain merit-based, but merit-based does not mean slow," she said.

Russia sends nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:31:00 UTC
07:31:00 KST

Russia has warned NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave that borders the Baltic Sea.
In a document sent to NATO and seen by Reuters, Moscow accused the alliance of a "dangerous and reckless course" that entailed "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict."
The document said this included the possibility of "Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance's member states right from the outset."
"Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country," the diplomatic note said.
The warning highlighted Moscow's urgent concern at what it has presented as a growing NATO threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized Russian territory that is wedged between Poland and Lithuania and is slightly bigger than the US state of Connecticut.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova, in a commentary on the ministry's website, cited statements by dignitaries from NATO states which she said demonstrated "Russophobia" and a readiness to wage war with Moscow.
These figures, Zakharova wrote, "need to be brought back down to earth. We hope that our warnings will be heard by those to whom they are addressed."
"If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different sort of war – a very short war."
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance had responded to Russia's message by declaring: "We are a defensive alliance. And stop the nuclear threats. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful."
In its response to the Russian document, seen by Reuters, NATO also said that none of its "exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation."
"We call upon the Russian Federation to end its unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine. We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behavior towards the Allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric," it said.
Asked if the risk of nuclear weapons being used against the Baltics was now real, Rutte told a defense conference in Brussels hosted by broadcaster Euronews: "No, it's not. Putin knows that he can never win (against) NATO, so I don't take this that seriously."
Risk of miscalculation
Nikolai Sokov, a Vienna-based nuclear analyst and former Russian diplomat, said it was becoming increasingly hard for Western countries to keep stepping up their support for Ukraine without tipping into direct confrontation with Moscow.
He said the Russian warning may indicate that hardliners are gaining influence in a debate over how to respond to Western actions that include arms supplies to Kyiv, new sanctions on Moscow, interceptions of Russian ships, frequent military exercises and intelligence flights near Kaliningrad.
"They (Russia) expect more action, including a blockade of the Baltic Sea - just below the level of war in European calculation, but for them this will be open war. I see a risk of mutual miscalculation," Sokov said.
In an online interview, he said Russia and Europe were on a collision course. Both sides needed caution and calculation.
Instead of this, the Europeans were applying "full-court pressure," and Russia was delivering a serious warning that this was highly risky, Sokov added.
Europe says it faces 'hybrid war', Russia denies it
In addition to the private warning, Russian embassies in at least three European countries have issued statements in the past three days accusing NATO of escalating tensions through military exercises and planning scenarios involving Kaliningrad.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described these as diplomatic reminders to "hotheads in Europe."
Relations, already dire since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, have sharply worsened this year, with European governments accusing Moscow of stepping up a "hybrid war" on the continent through acts including sabotage and arson.
Russia denies that, and rejects repeated statements by Western politicians that it is gearing up for a possible military attack on a NATO country.
A NATO diplomat said: "I would say that the Russian letter is only another Russian attempt to intimidate Europeans, and that the response by NATO is firm and responsible. (It) reaffirms that we will not be dissuaded from supporting Ukraine."
A senior European defense official said: "(This is the) first time since (the) Cold War that Russia is threatening us like this. So this is serious."

There is currently no direct threat to NATO from Russia, while the Kremlin’s nuclear threats are a diversionary tactic to distract from its failures in Ukraine. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said this, reports UNN, citing Euronews.
Details
According to Rutte, he does not take Russia’s nuclear threats seriously, as Moscow cannot defeat NATO.
We are ready for this, we anticipated it, and this applies to all of NATO. We will defend every inch of NATO territory. There is no such threat at present, and if something happens, we are ready to confront it
He called on Moscow to stop its nuclear blackmail, as "there is absolutely no need for it; it helps in no way."
"If necessary, of course, we will defend ourselves. But the main point is that all of this is happening because the war in Ukraine is going badly for him (Russian dictator Putin — ed.). He wants to divide us and divert our attention from Ukraine," the NATO chief added.

Eastern Libya forces deputy commander meets Bahraini delegation on UN-led efforts to unify Libyan institutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:29:32 UTC
07:29:32 KST

Muetaz Wannes, Serdar Dincel
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
The deputy commander of eastern Libya’s forces met with a Bahraini delegation Wednesday to discuss their support for international and UN efforts to unify the country’s institutions ahead of elections.
Saddam Haftar received the delegation headed by Sheikh Ahmed bin Abdulaziz Al Khalifa, the chairman of Bahrain’s Strategic Security Bureau, in the eastern city of Benghazi, according to a statement by the eastern Libyan forces.
The two sides discussed several “issues of mutual interest” and affirmed support for UN-led international efforts to unify the country’s institutions ahead of elections, the statement said.
Libya has faced years of political and institutional division between rival centers of power in the country’s west and east, along with the proliferation of armed groups and recurring security tensions.
Presidential and parliamentary elections originally scheduled for December 2021 have remained stalled because of political and legal disputes.
On Aug. 30 this year, Libyan parties reached a UN-facilitated agreement on reconstituting the board of the High National Elections Commission and addressing outstanding issues in the legal framework governing presidential and parliamentary elections. The agreement commits the parties to work toward holding elections within no more than 24 months.

NEW DELHI: A curative plea has been filed in Supreme Court against a verdict on the law on appointment of Chief Election Commissioner and ECs, citing "reasonable apprehension of bias and propriety" on the part of Justice Satish Chandra Sharma.DELHIThe plea, filed by Jaya Thakur, said Justice Sharma's son Siddharth Sharma was standing counsel of the EC before Madhya Pradesh HC. It alleged that the judge's presence on the bench raised an apprehension of bias.A two-judge bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sharma gave a split verdict on whether validity of the law should be referred to a constitution bench, but agreed to refer the case to a larger bench for the sake of early adjudication of the issue.
Validity of several provisions of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, has been challenged on the ground that the law gave the executive "overwhelming" power to appoint its nominee. The selection panel, comprising the PM, a cabinet minister and the LoP, gave the govt a 2:1 majority.While Justice Datta pointed out flaws in the law and said its validity could be examined by a division bench, Justice Sharma held that the issue had to be decided by a constitution bench.The petition said "a mere ground of appearance of bias and not actual bias is enough to vitiate the order" and argued that the judgment dated Sept 23 was vitiated due to Justice Sharma's presence.

Pentagon creates 'Autowarcom' to expand AI and drone capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:23:02 UTC
07:23:02 KST

Pentagon creates ‘Autowarcom’ to expand AI and drone capabilities
- The US Pentagon announced the creation of the Autonomous Warfare Command to expand AI and drone capabilities, led by a four-star officer, reflecting a shift to cheaper, autonomous military systems.
- Experts warn of risks from unchecked AI development and international rivalries, urging guardrails and consensus on military AI use, including nuclear weapons.
- The war in Ukraine shows drone warfare's impact, with drones causing about 70% of Russian casualties, highlighting the need for advanced autonomous systems in modern conflicts.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Sept 30 announced the creation of a new military command that would be dedicated to building and providing autonomous and robotic capabilities across the US military.
The command, which Hegseth said would be called “Autonomous Warfare Command,” highlights the rapidly changing nature of warfare and the need to make progress on systems like drones and the use of artificial intelligence.
Creating a new command is not common – the last one was US Space Command in 2019 – and the move reflects the Pentagon’s push to shift from costly conventional weapons platforms to cheaper, AI-driven autonomous systems that have proved decisive in recent conflicts.
Speaking in front of hundreds of junior officers and enlisted personnel at Quantico, Virginia, in a speech peppered with attacks on the media, Hegseth said the command would be led by a four-star officer.
“The pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it,” Hegseth said in a speech called the State of the Force,” in which he announced other changes, including the creation of the office of religious affairs.
“Cheap compute, superintelligence, and advanced commercial manufacturing have enabled the proliferation of low-cost, high-precision strike,” Hegseth added.
The US military currently has 11 combatant commands, which are responsible for different parts of the world and specific tasks.
Experts warn of AI risks
Experts have expressed fears over the potential for unchecked AI development and technology rivalries that could further heighten risks across the global security environment.
Both China and the US — the two major drivers of cutting-edge AI development and its global adoption — have been at loggerheads over AI policies and industry practices. Security experts from both countries have called for guardrails and consensus-building regarding AI in military systems, including nuclear weapons.
The United States has long relied on its vast military budget to field some of the world's most expensive weapons systems. But there is an increasing realization within the Pentagon that this is not sustainable.
"Today we need both quality and quantity," Hegseth said.
War in Ukraine illustrates drone warfare
The technology of war has evolved rapidly in recent years, a shift starkly illustrated by Russia’s war in Ukraine.
What began as a conflict dominated by tanks and artillery has increasingly become a drone war.
Outgunned in conventional armour and aircraft, Ukraine turned to inexpensive unmanned systems for reconnaissance and attack. Drones are estimated to account for about 70% of Russian casualties, enabling strikes to be carried out remotely and reducing the risk to pilots and aircrews.
The Pentagon has in recent years made some progress, including the creation of a task force — Joint Interagency Task Force 401 – that is focused on countering drones. REUTERS

Google on Wednesday unveiled Gemini 4 Argon, a new frontier artificial intelligence (AI) model, beginning its rollout to trusted cybersecurity defenders ahead of wider availability.
The model is designed to sustain deep reasoning across complex tasks in software engineering, legal and financial work, and cybersecurity, it said.
“Today, we’re announcing our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon,” Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google DeepMind’s senior vice president and Google’s chief AI architect, wrote.
Initial access is being provided through Google’s Fairwind Program. The company is also participating in the US government’s voluntary process for pre-release model access.

The company said Argon can autonomously identify, validate and patch critical software vulnerabilities.
Google is expanding the model’s output limit to 1 million tokens from 64,000, allowing it to sustain longer reasoning and generation.
Thousands of Google employees are already using Argon for specialized coding, research and writing, the company said.

A buyer's market without buyers: Housing downturn deepens with nationwide falls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:21:13 UTC
07:21:13 KST

in brief
- House prices have fallen 1.1 per cent in September, marking their sixth monthly decline.
- The latest data from Cotality suggests widespread national downturn, rather than isolated declining regional markets.
Australian property values fell 1.1 per cent in September, dropping for the sixth consecutive month as the national housing downturn continues to pick up speed.
Cotality's latest home value index report shows overall property values are now 5.2 per cent lower than their March peak, with clearance rates faltering. Houses are sitting on the market for an average of 39 days across capital cities, up from 23 days a year ago.
The property market analysis firm's executive research director, Tim Lawless, said the downturn reflects a "combination of affordability constraints," including higher interest rates, elevated living costs, and weaker consumer sentiment. All of these have "reduced purchasing capacity and dampened buyer demand", Lawless said.
On Tuesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates to their highest level in 15 years, bringing the cash rate to 4.6 per cent, in a bid to tackle persistent inflation. Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows that borrowers are now spending an average of roughly $4,500 per month to service a standard 30-year loan.
"Borrowers are not only facing higher mortgage costs, but also an extended period of elevated living expenses and negative real income growth," Lawless said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Together, these pressures are narrowing the pool of buyers able to qualify for a mortgage and reducing the amount they can afford to pay."
Total advertised housing stock increased 23.1 per cent year-on-year, despite fresh listings entering the market, which dropped 9.2 per cent, as sales velocity declined.
"The lift in available stock is improving choice for buyers, but ironically, many prospective buyers don't have the confidence or financial capacity to buy at the moment," Lawless said.
A national downturn
While the market first showed signs of a downturn in the capital cities of Melbourne and Sydney, the scope and scale of the shift has widened to include virtually every market in the country.
In capital city suburbs, 97 per cent recorded a drop in dwelling values over the three months to the end of September. Every capital city recorded a monthly value fall in September, except Darwin, which rose 0.4 per cent.
In Sydney, housing values fell 1.4 per cent last month, and have dropped 8.6 per cent from their peak in February. The current pace of the decline is slightly faster than what was seen during the equivalent phase of the 2022-23 downturn.
"Sydney continues to lead the housing correction ... highlighting how rapid demand has weakened across the nation's largest housing market," Lawless said.
Melbourne property values dropped 0.7 per cent in September and are down 7.2 per cent below their November 2025 peak.
In regional areas, 71 per cent of local sub-markets dropped over the last month, falling 0.7 per cent. However, regional values remain 5.6 per cent higher annually.
Conditions shift in Brisbane
Brisbane saw the sharpest fall of all capital cities in September, dropping 1.5 per cent, outpacing Sydney's decline.
"The result highlights how sharply conditions have shifted in what had previously been one of the strongest performing housing markets," Lawless said.
Sales volumes have fallen the fastest in major cities which were previously growth leaders in the market. Brisbane is down 27.2 per cent, with Sydney just behind on 26.5 per cent and Perth at 24.2 per cent.
In mid-sized cities, the decline was less pronounced. Perth's home values have dropped 1.2 per cent over the past month while Adelaide fell 1.3 per cent.
Decline still has further to go
While the market is largely being driven by economic conditions, the Cotality report identifies changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax arrangements as having added "another layer of downside risk".
However, high construction costs, driven by inflationary pressures and labour force tightness, continue to suppress new housing supply, stabilising the market. Low unemployment rates are also preventing widespread selling, the report finds.
Speaking to ABC News on Thursday morning, Lawless said the property market is a buyer's market without buyers.
"Seller numbers are right down and I think that this really reflects the confidence in the housing market and the broader economy and cost of living pressures and high interest rates," he said. "So for now, even though it is a buyer's market, the missing piece of the puzzle is actually buyers."
Lawless pointed to the federal budget as having sent "a shudder" through the housing market, something Labor has frequently denied, and said that even bargain-hunters are staying away out of expectation that the market will continue to decline until interest rates drop.
The country's four largest trading banks all predict that interest rates will remain at their current level, if not higher, with the cycle starting to come down well into next year.
"It's pretty clear that headwinds facing demand are outweighing those supply-side challenges," Lawless said.
"That will be the case, I think, for at least going into 2027 — probably around the middle of next year."

Paramount takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery clears legal hurdle
A federal judge on Wednesday approved a settlement clearing Paramount’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery after 12 US states challenged the deal on antitrust grounds. The agreement includes safeguards for CNN’s editorial independence and requires the merged studio to release at least 30 films a year for its first two years.
A federal judge on Wednesday approved a settlement between Paramount and a group of US states that clears the way for its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, creating a Hollywood empire spanning television, news and cinema.
Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin of California signed the consent decree, binding the concessions that Paramount offered to end an antitrust challenge brought by 12 states. The commitments run for five years, and the court will have the power to enforce them.
Paramount, which is run by David Ellison, whose ultra-wealthy family has ties to US President Donald Trump, won a bidding war against Netflix in February for control of a stable of assets that includes Warner Bros. Pictures, CNN and the HBO Max streaming service.
The same day, Ellison named Mattel Chief Executive Ynon Kreiz as co-CEO of the combined company once the merger closes.
Ellison will stay on as chairman and CEO, focusing on strategy, creative direction and technology, while Kreiz will handle day-to-day operations and the integration of the two businesses, the company said.
Read moreParamount settles with US states, clearing path for Warner Bros. merger
"Bringing together Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery to create a next-generation global media company is a transformational moment for our industry," Ellison said in a statement.
"In Ynon, I'm adding a partner with strong leadership and the operating firepower this integration demands," he added.
Kreiz, who has led Mattel since 2018 and oversaw its move into film with the 2023 blockbuster "Barbie", will join Paramount on October 5 and take a seat on the board at closing.
The Trump administration approved the deal, one of the largest-ever media mergers, in June without demanding a change to its business, before 12 US states sued to block the transaction.
Financing for the deal reportedly includes about $24 billion in equity from the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.
David Ellison's father, billionaire Oracle founder Larry Ellison, provided major funding and a guarantee to lenders backing the deal.

Tunisia's Saied eases penalties under cybercrime law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:17:10 UTC
07:17:10 KST

Breadcrumb
Tunisian president eases cybercrime penalties after rights groups' criticism
Tunisian President Kais Saied on Wednesday eased penalties under a cybercrime decree that human rights groups had said was designed to muzzle dissent.
The move marks a rare retreat by Saied since he consolidated control over much of Tunisia's political system in 2021 and came hours after civil society groups, led by the UGTT union, announced plans for a large national march in protest against what they see as curbs on rights and freedoms.
Under the decree amendment, prison terms of up to 10 years in some cases will be replaced by financial penalties ranging from 10,000 to 20,000 Tunisian dinars ($3,370 to $6,740) for first-time offences. Repeat offenders will face six months in prison and a fine of 50,000 dinars.
Under the previous decree, offenders could face up to 10 years in jail when their target was a public official or equivalent, and could be fined up to 100,000 dinars.
The decree, which came into force in 2022, drew widespread criticism from Tunisian and international rights and press freedom organizations, which described it as repressive and used against journalists, activists and political opponents of Saied.
Several journalists and activists have been jailed in cases involving the decree.
The authorities have defended the legislation as necessary for combatting cybercrime, false information and attacks on individuals and public order.
Saied has repeatedly said that freedoms are guaranteed in Tunisia and that he will not become a dictator.
Saied seized additional powers after suspending parliament in July 2021 and dissolved it in 2022, moves that his opponents have described as a coup.
(Reuters)

Eiffel Tower boss to resign after female staff ‘sidelined’ during Hindu visit
Patrick Branco Ruivo, the director general of the company operating the Eiffel Tower, has said he will step down amid controversy over female employees being replaced by men during a visit by Hindu dignitaries.
According to French media, Branco Ruivo told staff and the board of directors of the Societe d’Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel (SETE) on Tuesday that he would leave by the end of the year. However, he denied issuing “any instruction aimed at sidelining or replacing women” during a September 5 tour of the monument by members of the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a global conservative Hindu religious organization.
“Nevertheless, women were indeed sidelined, and I regret that,” Branco Ruivo said, as cited by Le Figaro.
His decision followed an internal investigation that uncovered “a series of dysfunctions and failures” in the organization of protocol visits, which SETE said had led to the “unacceptable” sidelining of female employees.
A separate investigation launched by the City of Paris is still underway, according to French media.
The scandal broke after Eiffel Tower employees said management had issued instructions that led to female staff “being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the BAPS delegation’s visit in early September.
“Some [women] were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts they were replaced by men. And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present,” staff at the iconic landmark said.
The CGT trade union representing Eiffel Tower employees held a strike on September 7 to protest the treatment of female staff, forcing the landmark to remain closed for the day.
SETE said at the time that the Hindu delegation had requested arrangements limiting “interactions with women,” adding that “these conditions should not have been accepted.”
BAPS, however, denied asking for “female employees to be hidden, removed or excluded from the visit,” insisting that its monks observe their “personal spiritual commitments” without seeking to impose them on others. The organization nevertheless apologized for “any pain or inconvenience caused” by the incident.
BAPS is known for building large Hindu temples and cultural complexes around the world, including in London, Abu Dhabi and Robbinsville, New Jersey. The delegation’s Eiffel Tower visit coincided with celebrations surrounding the inauguration of a new BAPS temple in the Paris suburb of Bussy-Saint-Georges.
