Ukraine urges US to sanction entities supporting Russia’s Starlink rival
- Ukraine urges the US to sanction Russian entities aiding the development of the Rassvet satellite network, a domestic rival to SpaceX’s Starlink, to prevent real-time targeting of Ukrainian territory.
- Russia aims to operate Rassvet by 2027, posing a significant threat, while Starlink remains banned in Russia and Ukraine seeks expanded satellite coverage to counter missile attacks.
- Ukraine highlights Russia's attacks on US businesses in Ukraine and calls for stronger sanctions and better air defence to protect both civilians and American investments amid ongoing conflict.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Ukraine is urging the United States to impose sanctions on several Russian entities that it says are helping develop Moscow’s Rassvet satellite network as a domestic alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink, its acting ambassador said on Sept 30.
Denys Sienik, deputy chief of mission at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, told reporters that Russia was rapidly expanding the Rassvet satellite network, saying its goal to start operations in 2027 would pose grave risks to Ukraine.
“If they launch Rassvet by the end of 2026, they will be able to target to hit Ukrainian targets real time on our territory,” Sienik said, adding that he would share details with the US government and Congress about the firms and individuals that Kyiv accuses of aiding Rassvet.
“If these entities are not sanctioned, it will actually make this programme possible for Russia and that will be a game-changer,” Sienik said.
He also stressed Ukraine’s urgent need for some 300 additional Patriot interceptors by winter, saying that Russia was producing more than 100 ballistic missiles per month.
The US Treasury Department had no immediate comment on Ukraine’s push for new sanctions.
Russia plans to start operating Rassvet, a smaller version of Elon Musk’s Starlink system, in 2027, Alexei Shelobkov, chief executive of Iks Holding, the company developing the service, said in June. The company launched its first 16 low-orbit satellites in March and plans to reach 900 over several years.
SpaceX currently has over 10,000 satellites in orbit. Starlink is banned in Russia, and the use of its equipment is subject to fines.
Western nations have targeted the infrastructure behind Russia’s space-based communications efforts, but gaps remain. Kyiv has been pressing Washington to expand sanctions against a broader group of Russian companies and individuals.
Ukraine has been clamouring for access to expanded Starlink satellite internet coverage so it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located inside Russian territory, a message backed by Finnish President Alexander Stubb last week.
Shortage of air defence
With winter looming, Ukraine has an acute shortage of air defences to repel Russian ballistic missiles, and Kyiv officials believe that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target the Russian launchers that fire the missiles.
Sienik also expressed frustration about the lack of US response when American firms were hit in Ukraine, noting that US officials had complained loudly when Ukraine had targeted US assets in the Caspian Sea, resulting in closer cooperation and more precise targeting.
But Washington remained silent in terms of messaging to Moscow when US firms in Ukraine were struck, and officials were even reluctant to name the companies affected, he said.
Sienik last week posted details of US firms being hit by Russia missiles in Ukraine, including offices of Boeing, Flex and Bunge.
A Coca-Cola facility in the Kyiv region was also hit in September, along with a logistics facility serving McDonald’s, he said in his message on X.
“It is not a coincidence, Russia knows what it is doing by attacking regular businesses operating in Ukraine, supported by American investment and serving civilian needs,” he wrote.
“While Russia must be deprived of the possibility to cause more deaths and destruction by strong sanctions, Ukraine must have enough air defence capabilities to protect itself but also to ensure the security of the American businesses operating and investing in Ukraine.” REUTERS

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has praised the profound solidarity between Türkiye and Palestine following an emotive friendly football match hosted in the central Turkish province of Konya.
"Tonight in Konya, the friendly match between Konyaspor and the Palestine national football team was an exceptional example of the brotherhood, solidarity and unity of hearts between our countries," Erdogan stated in a message shared on the X platform.
The Turkish leader conveyed his "most heartfelt greetings and affection" to the visiting Palestinian squad members who travelled to Türkiye for the encounter, as well as to the wider Palestinian population enduring ongoing conflict.
Erdogan thanked local supporters in Konya who packed the 42,000-capacity stadium to welcome the Palestinian national squad and openly show collective backing for the Palestinian cause.
Tributes to Palestinian children
The president noted that the fixture served as an urgent reminder to the international community regarding the ongoing "tragedy and genocide" unfolding in Palestine and Gaza.
"As Türkiye, we will continue to stand united and in solidarity with our Palestinian and Gazan brothers and sisters, defend their rights on the international stage, and demonstrate our solidarity with them in the strongest possible way," Erdogan added.
The fixture took place on Wednesday evening as the centrepiece of dedicated "Palestine Day" commemorations in Konya, featuring emotional tributes and ceremonies designed to draw global attention to the thousands of children who have lost their lives in Palestine.
On the pitch, the match delivered competitive drama.
Konyaspor opened the scoring inside two minutes courtesy of Melih Ibrahimoglu, before the Palestine national team responded with two clinical goals from Mohammed Sandouqa in the 12th and 25th minutes to seize a 2–1 advantage.
Konyaspor striker Mostafa Mohamed found an equaliser in the 28th minute to level the scoreline before the break.
Despite persistent attacking opportunities created by both sides throughout an energetic second half, neither team could break the deadlock, concluding the historic friendly in a 2–2 draw.

2026 Global South Modernization Forum calls for effective use of AI
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:23:18 CST
06:23:18 KST

Guests attend the 2026 Global South Modernization Forum in Cairo, Egypt, Sept. 30, 2026. The 2026 Global South Modernization Forum was held in Cairo on Wednesday under the theme "The Rise of Artificial Intelligence: Opportunities and Challenges for Modernization in the Global South." (Xinhua/Ahmed Gomaa)
CAIRO, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 Global South Modernization Forum was held in Cairo on Wednesday under the theme "The Rise of Artificial Intelligence: Opportunities and Challenges for Modernization in the Global South."
More than 100 experts and scholars from nearly 30 countries and regions attended the forum.
Participants said innovation in artificial intelligence (AI) technology presents enormous opportunities while also posing governance challenges.
At the 18th BRICS Summit earlier this month, Chinese President Xi Jinping put forward important initiatives to empower new industrialization with AI and promote open-source and inclusive AI development, outlining a direction for AI development that serves the common good, they said.
Modernization in the Global South is at a crucial stage of overcoming development constraints, addressing capacity gaps and transforming growth drivers, they said, calling for effective use of AI to continually strengthen the internal drivers of development.
Participants said AI is a shared asset of all humanity and urged Global South countries to seize this historic opportunity to use AI to empower a wide range of industries and improve people's well-being.
They called for improving global AI governance, practicing genuine multilateralism, bridging the AI divide and ensuring that development and security reinforce each other.
They also urged greater exchanges and mutual learning in AI, a commitment to open-source development, openness, cooperation and sharing, and deeper theoretical and practical research to ensure that AI better benefits humanity.
The forum was jointly hosted by the State Council Information Office of China, the Party School of the Communist Party of China Central Committee (National Academy of Governance), the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, Peking University, Renmin University of China and Cairo University.
The event featured four parallel forums. "The Rise of the Global South: An Atlas of Academic Research on Modernization in the Global South" and "Top 10 Buzzwords in Global South Modernization Research of 2026" were released at the forum.
Academic exhibitions, youth exchanges and think tank seminars were also held before and after the forum. ■

Seven people were killed and four others wounded on Wednesday when unidentified assailants attacked a vehicle in Syria's central Homs province, state news agency SANA reported. (Str/Xinhua)
DAMASCUS, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Seven people were killed and four others wounded on Wednesday when unidentified assailants attacked a vehicle in Syria's central Homs province, state news agency SANA reported.
The attack targeted the vehicle while it was crossing the Masyaf Bridge in the Homs countryside, SANA said, without immediately providing details about the attackers' identities or motives.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a Britain-based war monitor, said the vehicle belonged to the Al-Matin company and was carrying engineers and workers when it came under attack on the bridge near the Houla area.

The incident comes amid continuing security challenges in parts of central Syria, where sporadic killings, armed attacks, and other security incidents have been reported in recent months. ■

German inflation rises to 3-year high in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:23:08 CST
06:23:08 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- German inflation accelerated to 3.3 percent in September, its highest level since late 2023, as a sharp rise in energy prices continued to push up consumer costs, preliminary data showed Wednesday.
The rate rose from 2.9 percent in August after hovering at elevated levels in recent months, according to the Federal Statistical Office.
Energy prices jumped 14.9 percent year-on-year in September, accelerating sharply from a 10.5-percent increase in August, the data showed.
Inflationary pressures in Europe's largest economy have intensified in recent months as the conflict in the Middle East has driven up energy prices.
To ease the impact of high fuel prices and rising inflation, the German government has announced a temporary fuel tax cut from Oct. 1 through the end of the year, at an estimated total cost of 2.5 billion euros (2.8 billion U.S. dollars).
"The fuel tax cut is likely to dampen inflation again by around 0.3 percentage points in October," said Holger Schmieding, chief economist at Hamburg-based Berenberg.
The measure, however, is expected to provide only temporary relief as broader energy-related price pressures remain elevated.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING Research, noted that gas storage levels were below 60 percent at the end of September, historically low for this time of year.
"Low gas storage levels are likely to lead to higher gas prices over the coming weeks, translating into higher retail prices at the start of next year," he said, adding headline inflation could remain above 2 percent until the end of 2027.
Persistent inflation pressures are also reflected in a joint forecast released last week by Germany's five leading economic institutes, which projected inflation to rise from 2.2 percent in 2025 to 2.8 percent this year and further to 3.2 percent in 2027, before easing to 2 percent in 2028. ■

DAMASCUS, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Three power plants in Syria went out of service on Wednesday after an explosion in a gas pipeline supplying the Tishreen thermal power plant in the eastern countryside of Damascus, Syrian state media reported.
The Syrian Electricity Company said the Deir Ali, Nasiriyah and Tishreen power plants were taken offline after the explosion disrupted gas supplies needed for their operation.
A fire sparked by the explosion was still burning Wednesday evening as specialized teams worked at the site, according to the company.
The company warned that the shutdown would reduce nationwide electricity output and temporarily extend power-rationing periods due to the drop in generation capacity.
It added that further updates would be released as the situation develops.
Earlier, the official Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) reported that the explosion occurred on a gas pipeline feeding the Tishreen thermal power plant near the town of al-Otaiba, with civil defense teams reaching the scene.
Syrian state-run Al-Ikhbariya television said no damage had been reported in surrounding areas.
A Xinhua correspondent who happened to be in the nearby city of Jaramana at the time of the blast saw large orange flames rising into the night sky from the direction of the explosion.
The Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said the blast occurred in the Wadi al-Rabie area adjacent to the Tishreen plant, between the villages of Harran al-Awamid and al-Otaiba.
Large flames could be seen from towns across the Eastern Ghouta region and areas surrounding the capital, it added.
The cause of the explosion remained unclear as of Wednesday night, and authorities had not announced whether it resulted from a technical failure or other causes.
The incident came just two days after a separate explosion and fire hit a gas pipeline between al-Shoula and Deir al-Zour in eastern Syria.
The Syrian Petroleum Company said that the earlier blast was caused by a "sabotage act" targeting a sectional valve on the pipeline, disrupting gas supplies from the Jbessa gas plant to power-generation facilities.
Civil defense and petroleum company teams extinguished the fire on Tuesday, with no injuries reported, SANA said.
The two incidents come as Syria's electricity sector continues to face constraints in fuel supplies and generation capacity. Energy affairs chief Mohammad al-Bashir said earlier in September that the country requires about 24 million cubic meters of gas per day, compared with domestic production of around 8.5 million cubic meters per day, according to media reports. ■

Roundup: Dutch food industry looks to innovation ecosystem for transition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:22:58 CST
06:22:58 KST

THE HAGUE, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Dutch food industry is seeking to transform by building an innovation ecosystem that links research institutions, companies, private investors and government to turn emerging technologies into commercially viable solutions for a more sustainable food system.
For Cosun, a Dutch agricultural cooperative with more than 8,000 sugar beet growers, innovation is closely tied to making greater use of plant-based raw materials and reducing waste.
"We really try to make sure that we valorize our co-products to the maximum," said Fanny Weinbreck, chief R&D officer at the Cosun Innovation Center in Dinteloord, in the Dutch province of North Brabant, on Tuesday.
Rather than using co-products simply for energy or animal feed, Cosun seeks higher-value applications, including food ingredients, plant-based proteins and fibers.
The cooperative works with universities, research institutes, startups, incubators and corporate partners through an open-innovation network.
According to Weinbreck, the model helps established food companies provide a pathway for emerging technologies to move beyond the laboratory and toward commercial applications.
For startups, the challenge is likewise to move technologies from the laboratory into commercial production.
GOA Ventures, a Dutch startup focused on seaweed processing based in Yerseke in the Dutch province of Zeeland, is working with research institutions to scale up its technology toward commercial production.
"The Netherlands has provided an ecosystem in which startups like ours can develop these technologies, work with research institutes such as NIOZ (Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research) and move from an initial idea toward commercial-scale production," said Theo M. Verleun, CEO and co-founder of the company, on Tuesday.
The company's current demonstration facility processes about 15 kilograms of seaweed a day and is being used to test the technology and work with research and investment partners.
"The next challenge is to demonstrate that the technology can work economically and at industrial scale," Verleun said.
But financing remains a challenge in the transition of the food industry in the Netherlands.
The Protein Brewery, a Dutch company developing protein and fiber ingredients through fermentation, has progressed from laboratory research to pilot production and commercial manufacturing.
"The first investment was based on the fact that the technology was very robust," said Thijs Bosch, CEO of The Protein Brewery in Breda, in the Dutch province of North Brabant, on Monday.
The company raised its first investment around 2020, when interest rates were low and investors were actively backing sustainable food technologies. Fundraising has since become more difficult as interest rates have risen and investors have become more cautious, Bosch said.
"Now it's extremely difficult because interest rates are high. Many funds themselves are having trouble raising money," he said.
Peter Wennink, former CEO of Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML, also highlighted the funding challenge for startups and early-stage technologies in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, on Monday.
"We have to acknowledge that lack of funding for startups and early-stage development is a critical issue," Wennink told hundreds of founders and entrepreneurs looking to scale up, connect and innovate at LEVEL UP 2026 event.
The Dutch government's 2026-2030 coalition agreement explicitly identifies biotechnology, genetics, cultured meat and innovative fermentation as technologies that will play a role in future food production. Feature: Across borders, Chinese pianists find a voice in Chopin
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:22:50 CST
06:22:50 KST

WARSAW, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Piano melodies flowed through a concert hall in Warsaw, gathering strength before softening into delicate phrases. As the final notes faded, the audience rose to its feet in applause.
For Chinese pianist Wang Zitong, returning to Poland for this performance in September meant renewing a connection forged through Chopin's music a year earlier.
It was here, at the 19th International Chopin Piano Competition in October 2025, that she won third prize and the prestigious best sonata performance award. Invitations from around the world soon followed, opening doors to a wider international stage.
Born into a musical family in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Wang grew up surrounded by piano music.
At 13, she left for the United States to pursue her musical ambitions, studying at the Curtis Institute of Music and later the New England Conservatory.
Over more than a decade of study, the piano became woven into her daily life. "Music is both a way for me to express my feelings and my profession. I feel very fortunate that the two can be one and the same," she said.
Long before the Chopin competition, music had become an indispensable part of Wang's life. As her professional career has developed, so too has her understanding of Chopin.
Through reading Chopin's biographies and letters, studying his musical manuscripts and visiting places associated with his life across Europe, Wang has come to see a connection between the emotional expression in his music and the subtlety and restraint she finds in Chinese culture.
For the young pianist, this cultural experience has offered a personal perspective on Chopin, allowing performers and listeners from different backgrounds to find common ground through music.
Wang's feelings about Chopin's music are shared by fellow Chinese pianist Lyu Tianyao, whose life far from home has deepened her understanding of his works.
Lyu began learning the piano at five. On the day she jointly won fourth prize and the award for best concerto performance at the 2025 competition, she had just turned 17.
Her decision to move to Chopin's homeland was inspired by Polish pianist Katarzyna Popowa-Zydron. Deeply moved by Popowa-Zydron's playing at a masterclass in China, Lyu resolved to study with her, a decision that took her to Poznan in November 2024.
After spending two years away from her family during the Spring Festival because of concert commitments, Lyu knows what it means to miss home. That homesickness, she said, has helped her connect with what she describes as the apparent simplicity of Chopin's music.
She brought that personal understanding to the stage for Warsaw audiences in September, playing Chopin with an orchestra. Later that month, she also performed at a Chinese National Day reception in the city at the invitation of the Chinese Embassy.
As invitations to perform multiply, Lyu is discovering an increasingly personal connection with her audience. When listeners approach her in tears, she recognizes something of her younger self in them.
She hopes her performances can give them strength, she said, while their support, in turn, enriches her music.
"I am grateful to every one of them," she said. "It brings me such joy that we can connect through music, and that what I play can reach their hearts." ■

Tunisia amends cybercrime law to replace prison terms with fines for first offenses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:22:48 CST
06:22:48 KST

TUNIS, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Tunisia has amended Article 24 of Decree-Law No. 54 of 2022 on combating offenses related to information and communication systems and networks, replacing prison sentences for certain offenses involving false information with financial penalties for first-time offenses, according to the Tunisian official gazette, Journal of the Republic of Tunisia, published Wednesday.
Under the amendment, the previous penalty of five years in prison and a fine of 50,000 Tunisian dinars (about 16,786 U.S. dollars) has been replaced by a fine of 10,000 to 20,000 dinars.
The provision applies to anyone who deliberately uses information and communication systems or networks to produce, promote, publish, transmit, or prepare false news, data or rumors, or fabricated, forged or falsely attributed documents, with the aim of violating the rights of others, harming public security or national defense, or spreading terror among the population.
The same fine applies to the deliberate use of information systems to disseminate false information or fabricated or forged documents, or data containing personal information or falsely attributing acts to others, with the intent to defame, damage reputation, cause material or moral harm, incite attacks, or promote hate speech.
For repeat offenses, the amended provision stipulates six months in prison and a fine of 50,000 dinars. Penalties are doubled when the target is a public official.
The amendment was reviewed Tuesday at a Council of Ministers meeting chaired by Tunisian President Kais Saied at the Carthage Palace. ■

Denmark unveils annual climate plan as margin for 2030 target narrows
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
05:22:44 CST
06:22:44 KST

OSLO, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Denmark's government released its annual climate program on Wednesday, warning that the projected margin for meeting its 2030 emissions reduction target had narrowed sharply.
The country is still expected to meet its target of cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 70 percent from 1990 levels by 2030. The projected margin has fallen to 0.4 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, down from 1.5 million metric tons in last year's assessment, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Utilities said.
Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa warned that even a few delays could wipe out the remaining margin, making closer monitoring of implementation essential.
"We have come a long way, but we are not there yet," she said in the ministry's statement.
The program introduces an assessment of uncertainties surrounding the main expected contributions to emissions reductions through 2030 and 2035. It examines risks sector by sector to identify where closer monitoring and timely policy decisions are needed.
Agriculture remains a particular concern. The program projects that emissions covered by the target for agriculture, forestry and land use will fall by about 52 percent by 2030 compared with 1990, below the binding reduction target of 55 to 65 percent.
The government plans to review progress toward the agricultural target in 2027 and is prepared to take further action if the sector remains off track, according to the program.
Denmark's Climate Act, adopted in 2020, requires the government to publish an annual climate program assessing progress toward national targets and whether they can be achieved. ■

Lithuania’s government has approved a proposal to bar Russian and Belarusian artists and other cultural figures from performing in the country if they had previously worked in occupied or annexed Ukrainian territories.
The government backed the measure on Wednesday, Sept. 30, Lithuanian media LRT reported. The ban would also cover anyone who has directly or indirectly supported Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Exemptions would apply to those who have “clearly acted against aggression, occupation or annexation, publicly demonstrated their opposition to these actions and whose activities objectively did not contribute to the implementation of the interests of the occupying authorities,” according to the proposal.
Awaiting parliament’s approval
The amendment must still pass Lithuania’s parliament, the Seimas. If approved, it would take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. The government has not yet set out the specific criteria for determining who would fall under the ban.
Until now, Lithuania has handled such cases individually, barring several performers who support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s regime and have performed in Russia or in occupied Crimea from entering the country.
Around the same time on Wednesday, the Lithuanian government also backed a separate measure to ban Russian and Belarusian nationals from owning property near strategic sites.
The restrictions, however, would not apply to ownership acquired through inheritance.
Russian Attacks on Kyiv Continue Into Thursday as Drone Crashes Near Playground and Fires Erupt
The move follows similar steps by both Finland and Latvia, who had already restricted property purchases by Russian and Belarusian citizens, exempting those who hold residence permits.
Meanwhile, Estonia is working on comparable legislation.
Possible risks for anti-war artists
Under the proposal put forward by Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry, artists and cultural figures would be required to sign a publicly available declaration condemning Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and supporting its territorial integrity.
Those who refuse would be barred from working in Lithuania completely.
However, signing such a declaration poses significant risks for Russian citizens. Since the full-scale invasion, Russia has prosecuted numerous civilians for anti-war statements and has also moved against Yabloko – its only registered liberal party – whose ban was upheld by the Supreme Court in August along with an 11-year prison sentence for its deputy chairman.
In July, Turkey deported a 24-year-old anti-war activist Ariadna Litvinova to Russia, where she faces up to seven years in prison for writing slogans such as “Peace to Ukraine” on banners at a pro-war exhibition in St. Petersburg.
Rights advocates said the case was part of a wider pattern of transnational repression targeting Russian anti-war exiles.
Moscow courts have also ordered the arrest in absentia of anti-war pop singer Monetochka, who now lives and performs in Europe, and sentenced novelist Boris Akunin to 14 years in prison in absentia after he voiced support for Ukraine, The Moscow Times reported.
Such sentences would take effect if the exiled artist returned to Russia or were extradited.
Rising tensions with Moscow
The measures come amid heightened tensions between NATO members, particularly the Baltic states, and Moscow.
On Sept. 11, Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said Lithuania would “disappear from the map of the world” if it lifted its long-standing ban on nuclear weapons.
Russia’s embassy in Belgium warned on Sept. 28 that Moscow was ready to use its entire arsenal if NATO countries tried to isolate Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave bordering Lithuania.
NATO dismissed the warning, condemning Russia’s irresponsible nuclear rhetoric while reiterating that it is a defensive alliance. Vilnius rejected the threat by framing the warnings as a form of psychological pressure.
The warning came days after Putin claimed on Sept. 25 that the rights of Russian speakers were being violated in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, while insisting that Russia had no plans for military action against Europe.
The Kremlin used similar unfounded claims to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Trump demands Powell resign from Fed board over headquarters renovation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:17:01 UTC
06:17:01 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday demanded that Jerome Powell immediately resign from the Federal Reserve's Board of Governors over cost overruns in the central bank's headquarters renovation.
Trump said he had asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to review an inspector general's report on the project.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump cited findings of deficiencies in the management of the Washington, DC, renovation project and accused Powell of failing to control its costs.
"This is Jerome Powell's fault, and he should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY!" Trump wrote.
He said he had instructed Blanche to study the report and determine what action to take over a project that, according to his post, would cost at least $2.5 billion.
Trump threatened legal action if Powell refused to step down, saying the US government should sue him "for either corruption or incompetence."
The inspector general's review, however, found no grounds for a criminal referral and no administrative misconduct, while identifying significant shortcomings in the Fed's oversight of the renovation.
Powell remains a Fed governor after his term as chair ended in May.
Trump highlighted passages stating that the Fed board did not obtain a project cost estimate from its construction manager until January 2026, three-and-a-half years after construction began and after more than $2 billion in construction costs had been awarded.
According to the passages quoted in his post, the board had also failed to establish a guaranteed maximum price by July 2026, leaving it without cost certainty and without transferring material risk to the construction manager.
Trump predicted that the final bill could reach $3.5 billion or $4 billion and claimed he could have completed the renovation for $25 million while preserving the buildings’ historic appearance. 
Dispute over interest rates
The renovation has become a focal point of Trump's broader dispute with Powell over interest rates and the central bank's independence.
In January, Powell disclosed that the Justice Department had served the Fed with grand jury subpoenas threatening a criminal indictment related to his June 2025 Senate testimony about the renovation.
Powell said the threat stemmed from the Fed setting interest rates according to its assessment of economic conditions rather than the president's preferences.
He described the renovation and his congressional testimony as pretexts for the pressure.
In April, Powell said the Justice Department had provided assurances that it would not reopen the investigation without a criminal referral from the Fed's inspector general. 
Renovation of 2 historic buildings
The project covers the Marriner S. Eccles Building, the Fed board's headquarters, and the neighboring 1951 Constitution Avenue Building.
The Fed has listed the board-approved renovation budget at $2.46 billion.
It said the work aims to modernize building systems, remove asbestos and lead contamination, improve safety and accommodate modern workplace technology.
Construction costs alone rose from an estimated $921 million in February 2020 to $2.018 billion by December 2024, according to the watchdog's findings.
The Fed has attributed overruns to inflation, unexpected remediation expenses and additional requirements from agencies reviewing the project.

Details: The Russian attack damaged the roof and facades of two buildings. The blast wave shattered windows and partially destroyed walls on the fourth floor. Firefighters quickly extinguished the fire.
Lysak said that infrastructure had been damaged.
He added that no information about casualties had been received as of the time of publication.

ACCI says small business will carry burden for end of credit, debit card surcharges
The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) says the end of credit and debit card surcharges will create a significant burden for millions of small businesses.
As of today, Australian businesses are banned from charging customers credit, debit and prepaid card surcharges.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has welcomed the change, saying the "annoying" charges would ease pressure on people in a tough economic environment.
But ACCI chief Andrew Mackellar says it could cause some businesses to reprice their services to meet the provider payments.
"These surcharges are not going away. Somebody still has to pay this. The payment service providers, the credit card issuers, they're not working for free. They're continuing to charge the same fees through whatever means they can to their business customers," Mackellar says.
"It's just now much more difficult for those small businesses to work out how they wear that expense."

On the morning after last year's landslide Labor election win, Jim Chalmers declared a shift in priorities for the government's second term.

At the midway point of this term, the scorecard on both is grim.

As for productivity, Bullock was even more blunt: "Productivity is doing nothing."

The Master Builders Association says construction forecasts have deteriorated following May's federal budget.

Phase one of Thriving Kids, the new NDIS alternative for children under nine with developmental delay or autism who have "low to moderate" support needs, begins today with the launch of a phone line and online resource hub for families.
More intensive supports such as group therapies and playgroups will be rolled out by states and territories over the next 15 months.
The changes are happening alongside cuts to the NDIS passed by the parliament in August, which are expected to remove 240,000 participants over the next four years, saving about $38 billion.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers acknowledged this morning that, while families still have many questions and concerns, the government believes it will be able to "take care of" those who need disability support while also making sure the NDIS is financially sustainable.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers is being asked about the government's housing tax changes amid falling house prices.
ICYMI, house prices fell for a sixth straight month in September, bringing cumulative declines to 5.2 per cent below March's peak.
Experts say house prices could drop about 15 per cent in the coming months amid rising inflation and interest rate hikes.
Chalmers has been asked if the government's reforms are working as intended.
He said house prices were at a similar level to November last year — suggesting prices had flattened — and added that multiple factors contributed to lower prices, including interest rates and broader economic conditions.

Google announces Gemini 4 flagship AI model after months of delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:06:14 UTC
06:06:14 KST

Google restricts access to new AI model Gemini 4 Argon over safety concerns
- Google is limiting access to its new AI model, Gemini 4 Argon, to cybersecurity experts due to safety concerns and potential misuse by hackers.
- The model excels in software engineering, legal, financial tasks, and cyber defence, detecting flaws missed by other AI systems.
- Google and other AI firms are implementing safeguards and working with the US government to ensure safe, phased AI deployment amid rising cybersecurity risks.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Google on Sept 30 said it would withhold its most powerful AI model from the public for now, releasing Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers.
“Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach,” wrote Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google’s chief AI architect, in a blog post announcing the model.
Google said it is voluntarily giving the US government early access to the model and will gather feedback from testers before making it widely available.
The cautious rollout mirrors the approach of rival Anthropic, which has kept its most advanced model, Claude Mythos Preview, restricted to a few trusted organisations.
Washington briefly forced Anthropic to suspend access to its publicly released Claude Mythos and Claude Fable models in June, and has since set up a voluntary process for vetting the most powerful AI models before release.
The announcement came a day after President Donald Trump hosted top tech executives, including Google chief Sundar Pichai and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, at the White House, where they signed a voluntary accord pledging to police the risks of their own artificial intelligence systems.
Cybersecurity experts fear the state-of-the-art technology could be used to hack banks, hospitals and government systems.
Google said Argon excels at complex tasks in software engineering, legal and financial work and cyber defence, with a leading ability to find and fix critical software flaws.
Early testers used Argon to uncover a flaw in software used by hospitals around the world that exposed sensitive personal information – something other advanced models had missed, Google said.
Google said Argon is designed to refuse requests that could help carry out cyberattacks or develop chemical, biological or nuclear weapons.
OpenAI – the maker of ChatGPT – and Anthropic have built similar safeguards into their most advanced models.
Google said it is monitoring the model’s reasoning to stop it from straying beyond what users intended, a risk researchers call misalignment.
The issue has taken on new urgency since OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its models, including one not yet released, broke out of a sealed test environment during a cybersecurity evaluation and hacked into the servers of AI company Hugging Face. AFP

Why the closure of Russian publisher Individuum is such a loss for Russian-language literature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:02:59 UTC
06:02:59 KST

Why the closure of Russian publisher Individuum is such a loss for Russian-language literature
Individuum is closing. In its 11 years, the publisher’s team showed that there was another way to publish literature in Russian: with energy, flair (just look at their covers), and speed. Founded by people with media backgrounds, the publisher always understood what interested readers at any given moment. Literary critic Alex Mesropov explains why its closure cannot be ignored.
Many people have a favorite Individuum book.
In 2020, I picked up Brian Raftery’s “Best. Movie. Year. Ever.” and realized I was no longer surprised to see nonfiction published in Russia in paperback, with original cover designs — just like in the West. It’s the kind of book you want to display prominently on your shelf.
And that’s before you get to what’s inside: Raftery’s book explores the landmark films of 1999 that many millennials remember from childhood. The publisher had thought of everything: owning such a beautiful book made you feel special, while its subject connected you with other readers — fans of “The Blair Witch Project” or “The Sixth Sense,” for instance.
Perhaps that was Individuum’s greatest achievement: choosing its books made you feel both unique and part of something shared and important.
The people at Individuum were true publishing nonconformists: they wanted to publish radically different books in Russian — and that led to a genre they called “adventure nonfiction.”
They also made sure their books were professionally produced. I think many, if not all, of those who worked with them would confirm how different their approach was from that of other Russian publishers. Original design, thorough editing, their own research and fact-checking, decent pay, attention to authors’ views — everything reflected their professionalism.
Individuum reminded us that independent publishing involves more than selfless devotion to culture. Everyone involved deserves respect, and that should be normal.
Perhaps they managed all this because they had worked outside the book industry. Alexey Dokuchaev and Mikhail Vrubel, who founded Individuum in 2015, came from media and film. Felix Sandalov, who became editor-in-chief in 2018, had worked in the media for more than a decade, including at Afisha in its heyday. Maxim Balabin, who later became the publisher’s art director, had also worked there. Their books were available as ebooks through the easy-to-use Bookmate service. In other words, they all understood modern media, how it changes reading habits, and what interests young readers.
So what was new about their “adventure nonfiction”? Individuum knew that many people in Russia had unique professional experiences that could interest others — all that remained was to turn those experiences into gripping books. Publishers had previously overlooked these experiences: Russian nonfiction was very conservative.
But in the Russian media of the late 2000s and the first half of the 2010s, people with unusual experiences had already begun sharing them. You could find excellent long-form writing that connected personal stories with issues of public importance. Individuum approached the writers with a proposal: let’s turn your long-form pieces into great books. Whether you were an anthropologist or a reporter, a young mother or a stage actor made no difference. Everyone had a right to tell their story, especially if their experience was unlike anyone else’s.
This approach produced books that became hits in 2019–2021 and cemented Individuum’s reputation as one of Russia’s leading publishers: Olga Allenova’s “Forpost” (“Outpost”), Daniil Turovsky’s “Vtorzheniye” (“Invasion”), Robert Garayev’s “Slovo patsana” (“A Boy’s Word”), Maxim Semelyak’s “Znachit, uragan” (“That Means a Hurricane”), and others. These books explored different — often ugly — sides of contemporary Russia. They brought readers stories that had been pushed out of public view: uncomfortable testimony about the terrorist attack in Beslan, the story of Russian hackers working for the Kremlin, a chronology of the rise of criminal culture in Tatarstan in the 1990s, and the rightward turn of Russia’s cultural elite in the 2000s.
The writers’ personal perspectives made these stories emotionally engaging and, surprisingly, even universal (good editing probably had a lot to do with that). Writers and readers found a sense of solidarity: it turned out that professional anthropologists, doctors, and reporters with international experience worried about the same things as ordinary young city dwellers. You could even talk about those problems with the authors in terms you both understood: the editors had made sure the books were clearly written. Readers would then go to book launches and fairs, where they met these authors, sometimes also running into them at vodka bars or rallies. And all of this was thanks to one independent publisher.
Individuum did more than publish the latest Russian-language nonfiction — it also released a wide range of translations. These included internationally acclaimed classics of journalism that had long been unavailable in Russian, such as John Hersey’s “Hiroshima,” as well as unusual books about women’s place in society, from Stoya’s “Philosophy, Pussycats, & Porn” to Christine de Pizan’s “The Book of the City of Ladies,” written in the 15th century.
Its fiction was distinctive, too: think of the novels and short stories of Roman Mikhailov, who quickly attracted a community of fans, or Charlie Kaufman’s “Antkind” — a brilliant, challenging novel by a director whose work is equally brilliant and challenging.
The publisher had an excellent instinct for what to release. Producing a timely book quickly, without sacrificing quality, became routine. Have all your friends taken up birdwatching? Here’s a classic on the subject. Or become technology skeptics? Here’s a book for you. Is everyone arguing about gender? Here’s the big new book from the United States.
That remained true throughout, including the last two years, when Alexey Kiselyov was editor-in-chief. Bold new bestsellers kept coming out during that period, too — under very different, very difficult conditions.
Since 2022, the publisher has done more than stay relevant — it has become even more relevant. As everyone watched the state destroy documentary theater in Russia, Individuum published a book by the founder of Teatr.doc. As years of debate continued over mass killings and who bore responsibility for them, it published a book about genocide and retribution.
When books in Russia began appearing with passages removed because of censorship, it released an edition of “Yevgeny Onegin” with cuts. And when the state began persecuting publishers, it released a scholarly study of literary policy in the Third Reich.
The publisher’s team had faced pressure from law enforcement even before the war, but the first truly devastating blow hit its imprint, Popcorn Books, in 2025. It was Popcorn Books that had published the young adult hit “Leto v pionerskom galstuke” (“Pioneer Summer”).
A call by one “well-wisher” to set fire to the publisher’s office was followed by a sequence of events familiar from the news of recent years. The Justice Ministry added employees and authors of Popcorn Books and Individuum to its register of “foreign agents.” Online booksellers — including Labirint — began withdrawing their books from sale. Novels and nonfiction with queer themes disappeared from stores after the “international LGBT public movement” was declared extremist.
The forced sale of Individuum to businessman Denis Kotov in 2022 and the transfer of control to the publisher Eksmo in 2023–2024 did not change the situation. The criminal prosecution known as the “publishers’ case” began in May 2025, when three Individuum employees were charged under a law concerning an “extremist organization.” In 2026, they received suspended sentences.
In this appalling situation, public support from the frightened book industry was barely visible. Only the publisher’s readers offered real help. But there were obstacles even here: Moscow’s Non/fiction and several other book fairs repeatedly refused to let Individuum participate — often at the last moment, when staff were already setting out books at their booths. In 2026, the publisher said it was closing.
Still, Individuum will not disappear without a trace. And its legacy goes beyond books. A community formed around the publisher in which young writers, editors, translators, and other professionals learned a great deal from one another. Some have left the country and others have stayed, but there is no doubt that these young publishing professionals will, in one way or another, carry on the work Individuum began. The Syrian Electricity Company meanwhile warned that the shutdown of the three power plants would increase power rationing hours due to dwindling electricity supplies.
Wednesday’s blast was the third to hit Syria’s gas network in six weeks. The Syrian Petroleum Company said the two earlier incidents were sabotage.
No one has claimed responsibility for any of the explosions.
Syrians have complained about rising energy costs in recent months, with protests breaking out across the country two weeks ago after the government increased diesel prices by as much as 40 percent and petrol prices by 28 percent.

The White House Is Starting to Panic Over the Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

President Donald Trump has told aides that he thinks Republicans could still outperform expectations in the midterm elections this November, seemingly unwilling to confront the worsening political climate for the GOP.
But aides acknowledge privately that the national polling for Trump is shockingly bad, and the White House, in recent weeks, has begun to contemplate for the first time losing both the House and Senate majorities.
One longtime Trumpworld operative, who correctly predicted weeks before the 2024 presidential election that Trump was on course to win every battleground state, summed it up for Inner Loop: “Oh, yeah, we're going to get creamed.”
Trump's approval rating recently dropped to 37 percent in a Wall Street Journal poll, the lowest of any president heading into a midterm election dating back to 1990, when these polls first began. Trump’s more positive outlook has been informed in part by internal polling that shows Republicans down by less in individual House races, the sources say.
“No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle tells WIRED. “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”
To counter the deeply negative political environment for Republicans this cycle, Trump's team started looking for foreign policy wins last month that he would be able to tout to voters in order to encourage turnout from his MAGA base, sources say.
That led Trump to quickly sign an agreement between the US and Denmark that allows more American forces on Greenland, even though it stopped short of a US takeover that the president has long desired.
Trump also proclaimed an oil deal with Venezuela. However, that deal is likely to need renegotiating because it asserts a 100-year concession on oil production that contravenes Venezuela's national hydrocarbons law barring such practices.
But while Trump sees foreign policy as a legacy-defining issue, voters have been far more focused on domestic issues like high grocery and gas prices.
Diesel prices hit a record high this month and regular gasoline reached a national average of $4.43 a gallon, according to the AAA, while Trump has been on the opposite side of public opinion on tech issues like AI regulation and data centers.
Now, with their election chances that much slimmer, Trumpworld is much more concerned about planning a response to what will likely be an immediate crush of subpoenas from Democrats in Congress, the sources say.
Broadly speaking, the White House expects a dual track of Trump asserting executive privilege and attorney-client protections, the bedrock legal principle designed to protect confidential discussions with lawyers, to shield senior aides from oversight probes.
Attorney-client privilege is set to be supercharged when it involves government lawyers, after the US Supreme Court ruled in the so-called Trump immunity decision in 2024 that not even federal courts could “peel back the curtain” to examine discussions that involve deliberations central to the presidency.
One unique aspect of Trump's second term has been the conversion of his personal lawyers into government lawyers, producing a consistent network of overlapping legal protections around himself and his top aides.
Trump's former personal lawyer Todd Blanche, for example, has become the attorney general. Many of Trump's aides were previously represented by the current number three at DOJ, Stanley Woodward, who also was a Trump 2024 campaign lawyer. Trump's former appellate lawyer, Will Scharf, recently moved from White House staff secretary to White House counsel, replacing former Trump lawyer David Warrington.
Trump's aides are hoping that the double protections will stymie Democrats for years. And they have some precedent: Trump's White House counsel from his first term, Don McGahn, only testified to Congress about the Mueller investigation after Trump had already left office.
After November 3, the midterms will end in the minds of most Americans. But for Trump’s White House, it’s all just beginning.
This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Rachel was located 365 kilometers (227 miles) south-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, a coastal area in the western state of Jalisco, and 495 kilometers west of Lazaro Cardenas, a port city on the Pacific coast of southwestern Michoacan.

The National Civil Protection Coordination urged authorities and residents to remain attentive to updates on Rachel's development and movement.
The storm's strengthening comes during Mexico's Pacific hurricane season, which runs from May through November and regularly brings tropical storms and hurricanes to the western coastline.
Authorities have continued to monitor Rachel's location, intensity and projected trajectory to assess any potential effects on coastal areas.
Based on its current trajectory, Rachel was not expected to make landfall in Mexico, according to information released by the National Civil Protection Coordination.
The agency advised residents in potentially affected areas to follow weather updates, as the conditions and trajectory of tropical systems can change as they develop.
Rachel's development will continue to be monitored as the hurricane moves northwest over the Pacific, with authorities expected to issue updates on its strength and trajectory.

Russian troops practice tactical assault in high Arctic (MOD VIDEO)
The Russian Defense Ministry has shared footage of troops practicing an amphibious assault against a simulated enemy deep in the Arctic.
The tactical exercise was held by a unit with the Russian Northern Fleet at an island in the Sedov Archipelago in the Kara Sea. According to the scenario of the drills, an armed group was entrenched on the island, and the troops had to conduct a search and destroy operation.
The drills involved a recon group brought in by a Ka-29 deployed to the island to watch the simulated enemy and coordinate naval artillery fire support provided by a patrol vessel. The recon team was backed up by an amphibious assault group, which disembarked onto the island from a landing ship while riding DT-10PN ‘Vityaz’ all-terrain vehicles, designed specifically for harsh Arctic conditions.
The force successfully captured the bridgehead and rapidly advanced into the designated area, finding and dismantling all the mines and improvised explosive devices along the way, the ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
Russia possesses the largest coastline in the Arctic, measuring over 24,000 km. Moscow has repeatedly outlined defending its interests in the region as a major priority and has expanded its military presence there in response to hostile moves of the US-led NATO bloc, while developing the Northern Sea Route.
The route is the shortest maritime passage between the Asia-Pacific region and northern Europe. While use of the corridor remains limited due to harsh conditions and accessibility constraints, its potential significance has been growing due to the prolonged crises along multiple key global routes.
Moscow has been expanding its fleet of nuclear and conventional icebreakers to facilitate passage of cargo vessels, while climate change in the coming years is expected to make the route more appealing for international freight.

Global steel forum agrees joint action to tackle rising excess capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:51:46 UTC
05:51:46 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Members of the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity agreed Wednesday on a comprehensive framework for joint action to tackle rising excess capacity and its impact on steel producers and workers.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer chaired the ministerial meeting in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, where participants reached consensus on the "Milwaukee Framework," according to a statement from his office.
The framework outlines measures countries intend to implement under their national laws, reflecting domestic circumstances and international commitments.
These include reducing market-distorting subsidies, strengthening monitoring of steel imports and coordinating efforts to detect and address circumvention of trade restrictions.
Members also intend to pursue antidumping, countervailing duty and safeguard investigations where appropriate, alongside other trade measures targeting steel and steel-containing products from sources of global excess capacity.
The framework calls for greater transparency on where steel is first melted and poured to help identify suspicious trade patterns and prevent imports displaced from one member's market from entering through another.
Greer said US tariffs, trade agreements, tax policies and energy measures were supporting a revival in the American steel industry, urging partners to adopt similar policies.
"If like-minded partners adopt similar policies, they can hold accountable those countries that are contributing to the problem of global overcapacity in steel," he said.
Excess capacity projected to hit decade high
Despite increased national action and trade remedies, global steel excess capacity continues to rise, according to the ministerial statement.
It is projected to increase from 601 million tonnes in 2024 to 745 million tonnes by 2028, reaching its highest level in a decade and exceeding the forum members’ current combined production by 319 million tonnes.
Ministers warned that their steel industries could not compete on a level playing field without further collective intervention.
They tasked the forum with reviewing implementation of the framework and reporting progress at its next ministerial meeting.
Türkiye, the US, EU, UK, Japan, Canada, Brazil and other economies participated in the meeting.

Hegseth Unveils New Autonomous Warfare Command in ‘State of the Force’ Address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:49:52 UTC
05:49:52 KST

MARINE CORPS BASE QUANTICO, Va.—Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced plans for a new four-star command to lead the military-wide drive to field autonomous systems, as the Pentagon’s takes a bullish approach towards artificial intelligence and drone warfare. He also unveiled five other initiatives during what he promised will become an annual “State of the Force” address here Sept. 30.
Hegseth plans to launch the Autonomous Warfare Command within a year as a combatant command endowed with “service-like authorities, built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force,” he said. Its portfolio will include drones, artificial intelligence, and command and control systems.
Hegseth also announced the creation of a new program office, led by a two-star officer, to ensure military installations can generate their own power to isolate themselves from attacks on public grids. Bases in the homeland are increasingly seen as possibly contested environments where the U.S. military must be able to operate while under threat in a age of increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks and so-called hybrid warfare activities by America’s adversaries.
And he confirmed plans to slash the total number of generals and admirals across the military by 20 percent, a move Air & Space Forces Magazine and other outlets had reported would be part of Hegseth’s speech.
Other initiatives include:
- A new group, dubbed “Project Meridian,” to study the future of warfare led by tech leaders Palmer Luckey and Elon Musk and former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich, who were in attendance.
- An initiative, called the “Next Great American Base,” to build a new military installation to host 15,000-25,000 service members. Hegseth said governors and adjutant generals from every state will be invited to the Pentagon to pitch locations.
- The creation of five new corps of cadets at Hillsdale College, Louisiana State University, Liberty University, Mississippi State University, and Tuskegee University, which will all be given priority in officer commissioning.
- A new “Office of Religious Affairs” reporting directly to the Secretary of Defense to give chaplains better access to senior leadership.
Exactly one year after Hegseth summoned hundreds of senior officers and enlisted from commands across the globe to Quantico for an address outlining his vision for the U.S. military, he spoke this time to an audience of around 600 E-6 enlisted members and O-3 officers, who the Pentagon said were selected by their units for their performance and leadership potential.
Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Air Force Gen. Dan Caine briefly addressed the crowd and introduced Hegseth.
Autonomy
The new Autonomous Warfare Command will drive the design, development, and fielding of autonomous and semi-autonomous capabilities and systems.
“The autonomous and robotic revolution has enormous implications for equipment, doctrine, organization, and the assumptions that have governed warfare for decades,” Hegseth said. “Civilian leaders can provide direction and urgency, but lasting change must be anchored in military command structures and operationalized by leaders across our joint force.”
The Pentagon is already leaning heavily into autonomy, and the new command is designed to significantly accelerate that effort. Lawmakers in the Senate had proposed the creation of such a combatant command during deliberations for the 2027 defense policy bill. The measure cleared the committee, but the bill is still pending. To be authorized, the House would also have to approve the measure.
It is not yet clear how the new four-star command will be structured, who will lead it, or how it will work with the autonomy efforts already underway within the different services. In a memo, Hegseth wrote the Pentagon plans to work with Congress to stand up the command by October 1, 2027, a year on from the announcement.
Hegseth said it will start with an interim step, dubbed “Project Agincourt,” named for the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. Project Agincourt will draw from existing efforts like the Defense Innovation Unit and the Drone Dominance program, Hegseth said, and pair “operators with entrepreneurs in rapid adaptation cycles while distributing decisions and dollars closer to frontline units.”
Project Agincourt will be guided by DIU director Owen West and Navy SEAL Senior Chief Max Strasiser, the first enlisted SEAL to graduate from Navy Test Pilot School. Creating Autonomous Warfare Command will take place “over the course of several months,” Hegseth said.
The Air Force and Navy are already developing Collaborative Combat Aircraft: semi-autonomous drones designed to work alongside crewed fighters. The Air Force is also pursuing a lower-cost intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance drone with autonomous capabilities under its Massed Modular Aircraft program, and the Navy is working to field an unmanned tanker drone, the MQ-25.
The growth of autonomomy and the Penatagon’s future plans to harvest technology with its new command represent the “fastest peacetime shift in modern military history,” Hegseth said.
“Drone warfare supercharged by SI-enabled targeting is the biggest battlefield revolution in generations,” he added, using an acronym for so-called super intelligence, President Donald Trump’s favored term for AI.
At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference earlier this month, Air Force leadership made it clear they see autonomous systems as central to the service’s future. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach told Air & Space Forces Magazine at the conference that while true autonomous aircraft are a “few years off,” the service is leaning heavily into autonomy in its current future Force Design model.
“The FQ-42 and the FQ-44 [Collaborative Combat Aircraft] are autonomous fighters, and then we’re going to have perhaps other platforms that are autonomous, where you don’t actually need a crew to do a fighter mission,” Wilsbach said during a session with reporters. “You just send the aircraft off, and it does its mission because it’s automated.”
The Pentagon has deployed uncrewed surface vessels operationally in the Middle East for a few years for maritime surveillance. This summer, a U.S. Navy drone boat was even able to rescue two downed Army Apache pilots near the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Southern Command, which has been conducting strikes on boats suspected of smuggling drugs for over a year, recently established an autonomous warfare branch that will employ its own uncrewed vessels and aerial intelligence-gathering platforms. On the southern border, the U.S. military is now using 10 uncrewed surface vessels to patrol the Rio Grande River, Assistant Secretary of Defense for Homeland Defense and Americas Security Affairs M. Roosevelt Ditlevson told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview.
“We’re moving into next-generation tools here that we’re going to employ to make sure that we hold these narcoterrorists at bay,” Ditlevson said, referring to the drug smugglers. “I’m very excited about what is going to happen in the autonomy space and how we’re going to employ these different systems.”
But the Pentagon is automating more than aircraft, ships, and vehicles.
The Pentagon’s Maven Smart System has become a key tool for the U.S. military, a system aggregating sensors, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, and command and control as part of the targeting process. Maven is used for operations ranging from targeting assistance in the Middle East to, more recently, counter-drone and anti-smuggling efforts on the southern border.
Ditlevson said AI, through Maven, will also feed into the Pentagon’s sweeping Golden Dome missile defense shield. “Maven Smart System is going to feed into the Golden Dome picture,” he said.
At the border, the Defense Department also uses autonomy software called Fortress, an adaptation of Anduril’s Lattice, which integrates data and sensors using AI. “All of our systems must be compatible with Maven Smart System,” Ditlevson said. “Everything that we have, that data needs to be integrated into Maven and into Lattice.”
To support all these new autonomous systems, Hegseth said, each military service will phase in new military occupational specialties for autonomy.
“We need institutional knowledge and career paths for a new generation of autonomous warfighters,” he said.
Fortress America
Hegseth also said the Pentagon is creating a new initiative called “Fortress America” to ensure military installations are able to generate their own power. The Pentagon has been working on building nuclear microreactors at key U.S. bases in the homeland and has previously said it plans to field a nuclear reactor at a military base by September 2028.
The Air Force in particular is working on a microreactor at Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, with plans to build more at other bases in the coming years. The service has also explored using alternate power sources like solar panels, geothermal plants, and more to create so-called “microgirds” for bases so they’re not entirely reliant on local civilian power grids.
The drive to give bases their own energy sources is driven by concerns that adversaries may target critical infrastructure, around 80 percent of which is currently in the commercial sector, to kneecap the military’s ability to generate forces. The Pentagon chief referred to the program as “nation’s insurance policy” in a memo directing the establishment of Fortress America.
“If an adversary takes down the grid by cyber attack, by sabotage, or by any means, our bases stay lit, our aircraft keep flying, our command centers never go dark,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth is also slashing the number of general and flag officers, cutting billets by 20 percent. That doubles down on the 10 percent cut to general and flag officers he ordered last year, which he dubbed the “less generals, more GIs” policy.
“The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force, and that number sounds about right,” Hegseth said. “And I know because I directed it that we’ve also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent. So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board.”
Generals and admirals make up less than 1 percent of the military. According to the Congressional Research Service data, there were about 850 general officer positions in 2023. Some of those positions were unfilled at the time, as is the case today.
The maximum number of general officers allowed per service is set by law, though those caps do not apply to joint positions. The law also sets a minimum number of general officers in joint jobs.
The Air Force has roughly 250 generals. The Space Force has roughly 30 generals, and has plans to continue to grow that number.
A year ago, most senior military leaders gave stoic reactions during politically charged speeches from Hegseth and Trump, keeping with the military’s apolitical tradition. The troops at this year’s addres gave Hegseth a more vocal reception, particularly during his reference to Musk, Luckey, and Gingrich, and Hegseth exited to applause from the troops, though service members appeared to avoid visual reactions to Hegseth’s more ideological comments. Attendees were separated by branch, and were given a “War Department Field Manual,” a collection speeches by Hegseth with a forward written by Trump. Earlier in the day, the service members in attendance participated in a physical training session with Hegseth on the grounds of the Pentagon.

where le corbusier’s plan voisin sought to organize paris, chtcheglov chose to drift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:45:01 UTC
05:45:01 KST

where le corbusier’s plan voisin sought to organize paris, chtcheglov chose to drift
a clash between urban order and the unpredictable experience of wandering, where efficiency gives way to mood, chance and discovery.
le corbusier’s plan voisin reorganizes paris
Le Corbusier’s Plan Voisin imagines Paris as a highly ordered urban system, replacing a large section of central Paris with cruciform office towers, residential blocks, open space and a hierarchical road network. The 1925 proposal responds to congestion and poor sanitary conditions, but it also advances a particular idea of urban life, where functions are separated, movement is organized, and the city becomes legible as a complete system. The scheme would have removed much of the existing fabric of the Marais and surrounding areas while preserving monuments including the Louvre, Palais-Royal and Place Vendôme. Eighteen cruciform office towers would rise from an open landscape, with residential buildings arranged separately from the business district. Plan Voisin was never built, but its principles became part of a wider modernist approach to urban planning. The separation of functions, concentration of buildings vertically and prioritization of circulation and open space continued to shape architectural thinking through the development of the Ville Radieuse and the Athens Charter.
then chtcheglov starts somewhere else
Almost three decades later, French philosopher Ivan Chtcheglov looks at the modern city and sees boredom as the main problem. In his Formulary for a New Urbanism, written in 1953 under the pseudonym Gilles Ivain, he calls for ‘new, changeable decors’ that can alter with the people living in them. He is not particularly diplomatic about Le Corbusier. Chtcheglov describes his architecture as suitable for ‘factories and hospitals’ and, eventually, prisons, before accusing him of destroying ‘joy’ and ‘love, passion, freedom.’
In the place of cities based on Plan Voisin, he imagines architecture that can alter moods, generate dreams and change the way people experience their surroundings. He describes houses that move with the sun, sliding walls that allow vegetation to enter, and buildings whose appearance changes according to the wishes of their inhabitants. He also proposes an entire city divided according to feeling, with a Bizarre Quarter, Happy Quarter, Noble and Tragic Quarter and even a Sinister Quarter.
a city built for getting lost
While Le Corbusier’s proposal begins with the idea that the city can be reorganized according to a rational structure, Chtcheglov is interested in what happens when the experience of moving through it is not as organized. The Situationists described this wandering through the city as the dérive, allowing streets, buildings and changing surroundings to determine where the journey goes. For Chtcheglov, a building or street did not have to serve one purpose. It could change the mood of a walk, pull someone in another direction or make a familiar part of the city feel strange. Getting somewhere was only part of the experience; the journey could be the point. Drifting runs against the logic of optimization. The shortest route gets you there faster. Chtcheglov was interested in what you might find by taking the long way. ‘The main activity of the inhabitants will be CONTINUOUS DRIFTING,’ he writes. The landscapes of the city would change from one hour to the next, producing what he calls ‘total disorientation.’ The point is not simply to arrive somewhere, but to see where the city takes you.
For Chtcheglov, even a familiar street could become something else. A building might draw you in, a change in atmosphere might send you in another direction, or an unexpected space might make an ordinary part of Paris feel unfamiliar. It is difficult to imagine anything further from Plan Voisin. Le Corbusier’s city is drawn from above, with its functions and circulation worked out in advance. Chtcheglov’s city only really comes alive once people start wandering through it.
the value of taking the long way
Plan Voisin was responding to real problems. Paris was dealing with overcrowding and poor sanitary conditions, while modernist architects were looking for ways to bring more light, air and open space into the city. But the more completely those problems are solved through planning, the more the city becomes predetermined. If every building has a function, every road has a purpose and every movement has been accounted for, there is less room for the detours and unexpected uses that make a city feel alive. This is what Chtcheglov finds troubling. He is drawn to things that are difficult to measure, such as the mood of a place, the attraction of a particular street, the feeling of discovering somewhere by accident. He takes the idea much further than simply making cities more entertaining. His imagined city is full of spaces designed around those feelings. The Sinister Quarter, for instance, would be unsettling without being dangerous. Elsewhere, there are rooms for dreaming and places intended to bring back a sense of secrecy or exoticism.
There is something almost funny about putting these two visions side by side. Le Corbusier wants to make the city more efficient; Chtcheglov wants people to wander through it and see what happens. His city does not need every space to have a clear purpose, a strange idea to put against the logic of convenience and efficiency.
The fastest route may be useful, but it is also predictable. Chtcheglov is interested in the things that happen when you take the wrong turn or come across a place you were not looking for. Plan Voisin leaves little room for that kind of accident. Chtcheglov envisions it in the city.
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Russia plans to run budget deficits for the next three years with a combined shortfall of nearly 16 trillion rubles

Reuters, which reviewed the document, reported that the 2027 budget called for record military spending of 17.1 trillion rubles.
