Telcos seek to 'rebuild trust' with mobile roaming during disasters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:32:06 UTC
05:32:06 KST

Telcos activate temporary disaster roaming agreement for mobile coverage
In short:
From October 1, telcos will activate temporary disaster roaming (TDR) when one network goes down during a severe weather event.
It will only be available outside major cities, and not if a network goes down in large parts of regional Australia where there is only one provider.
What's next?
The telcos will decide when to switch roaming on and off, but neither the industry nor government has outlined accountability measures.
After years of testing, Australia's three major telcos are ready to switch on a system that would give customers access to a rival network if their own goes down during a weather emergency.
Known as temporary disaster roaming (TDR), Telstra, Optus and TPG will work together to decide when to activate it in regional areas where a mobile service has been disrupted by severe weather.
"You'll continue to be able to make phone calls, send text messages, and you'll have limited capacity data services," the chief executive of Australian Telecommunications Alliance, Luke Coleman, said.
"You can't expect to have your full usual high-speed data, but you will still have enough data to send a WhatsApp or an iMessage, maybe even to check an emergency service website like Fires Near Me, for example."
For TDR to work, another network must be available in that area that mobile users can roam onto.
That means it will not work if a network fails in large parts of regional Australia served by only one provider.
Telstra has indicated it would also be willing to consider allowing Optus and TPG customers to roam onto its network during disasters in Telstra-only areas, if they were satisfied it would not affect network capacity.
Regional Independent MP Helen Haines has long been advocating for such a service, which she described as a "game changer".
"When disaster knocks in regional communities and pulls out a mobile network, people shouldn't have to wait for their own provider to restore that service before they can reconnect," she said.
"This is existential in times of disaster."
Telcos in charge
TDR is already available in some form, either mandated or agreed to by industry, in several countries including the United States and Japan.
In 2023, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission found TDR technically feasible, and in 2024 the Regional Telecommunications Review recommended mandating it "at the earliest possible opportunity".
Ms Haines previously tried to have this legislated through a private members' bill and amendments, but it did not have government support.
"I'll keep pushing to make sure that the telecommunications companies ensure that there's enough network capacity to facilitate temporary disaster roaming, that the telecommunication companies ensure that there's power backup to our mobile network," she said.
Mr Coleman said the telcos were best placed to be the custodians of the initiative as they "have full visibility of the network's capacity" and could make sure the "surviving network continues to operate".
He said telcos would monitor its progress but did not specify any benchmarks or framework to measure success.
"The telcos are being good corporate citizens here and this is part of rebuilding trust with Australians to show that there is no additional charge for this,"
"If you're a consumer, your phone will just automatically start using another available network where it is safe to do so."
Under the terms of the agreement, the service will be available only outside major cities and will be implemented in up to three different disaster areas at any one time.
There can only be up to 15 towers within each area, and those areas must be at least 400 kilometres apart.
When asked how a decision would be made in a situation where multiple areas in the same region might be affected, Mr Coleman said telcos were best placed to make a choice.
"Those areas do need to be spaced a certain distance apart because there is a risk otherwise of the network being overloaded," he said.
Communications Minister Anika Wells was not available for interview.
A statement quoting a ministerial spokesperson did not answer the ABC's questions, including whether there would be any accountability around the initiative.
"The government will continue to engage closely with industry to make sure TDR is working as intended to keep communities safer," the statement said.
No change to Triple Zero
Mobile roaming differs from an existing permanent provision known as "camp on," which allows mobile users to call Triple Zero (000) no matter what network they are subscribed to, as long as at least one network is available.
For TDR, Mr Coleman said "most modern smartphones" would have settings to enable VoLTE technology, which would allow them to roam when activated.
He would not confirm if there would be subsidies for anyone needing to upgrade their phone, but encouraged people to approach their telco for advice.
TDR is also different from domestic roaming, which the ACCC is currently reviewing to see if it should be mandated on a permanent and more widespread basis.

Thriving Kids launches today. Here's what parents should know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:30:24 UTC
05:30:24 KST

In brief
- The government has argued there are more people on the NDIS than originally intended.
- The $4 billion program will be co-funded by state, territory and federal governments.
On 1 October, the first stage of Thriving Kids begins to roll out. This new program, announced just over a year ago, is part of the federal government’s sweeping changes to the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS).
It means children aged eight and under, who have developmental delay or autism and low to moderate support needs, will increasingly receive support outside the NDIS, through Thriving Kids. The $4 billion program will be co-funded by state, territory and federal governments.
But this doesn’t mean children are being moved off the NDIS today. Changes to NDIS access won't begin until January 2028.
So, what will Thriving Kids provide? And — after more than a year of negotiation, consultation and controversy — what questions remain?
How did we get here?
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The government has argued there are more people on the NDIS than originally intended, and the scheme’s budget is growing too quickly.
One group the government says is particularly over-represented is children under 15. They make up just under half of all NDIS participants. One in two new entrants to the scheme is under nine — many with autism or developmental delay — and across the country one in ten six-year-olds receives NDIS support.
There is also mounting concern the scheme doesn’t serve all these young children well.
The government has argued these children would benefit more from strong, mainstream and community services, rather than an individual NDIS package.
But there wasn’t much initial detail
When Thriving Kids was announced in August 2025 there was relatively little detail. This caused considerable anxiety among families and disability advocates.
Since then — after an advisory process, a parliamentary inquiry, and lengthy negotiations between the Commonwealth and states and territories — we know more about the program.
The proposed national model will combine broad, or universal, supports with more targeted assistance for children who need additional help. Support will respond to children's needs rather than simply depend on a diagnosis, recognising that children's developmental and support needs are not static but can change over time.
So, how will Thriving Kids work?
Currently, children on the NDIS are assessed individually and receive a certain amount of funding their family can use to access services such as speech therapy or visits to a psychologist.
But Thriving Kids will provide supports where children are already going about their lives: in schools and early childhood centres, as well as community spaces (such as libraries or organised sport) and health care. These are known as foundational supports.
Some foundational supports will be universal, meaning they are available to all children and families. These include providing information about child development and linking families to services.
Some universal supports will begin on 1 October — such as supported playgroups for children aged five and under — or shortly after, such as the Medicare-funded health check for three-year-olds, done by GPs and rolling out in November.
Some supports will be targeted to kids' specific needs and provided by allied health professionals, such as occupational therapists, speech pathologists and physiotherapists. These will require some form of assessment to access.
Children with permanent and significant disability, including children with high support needs, will continue to be eligible for the NDIS.
State and territory governments will take the lead on designing and commissioning services that are appropriate to their local population. But Queensland is yet to sign up, so important questions remain about how this will work.
What have some of the sticking points been?
Important questions about Thriving Kids' implementation remain.
One of the biggest challenges has been working out who is responsible for providing and paying for supports outside the NDIS. This problem predates Thriving Kids.
In 2023, the NDIS Review argued the NDIS had blown out its estimates so much because states and territories had moved away from providing disability supports, forcing people to seek NDIS support.
Foundational supports — jointly funded by all governments — are meant to be part of the solution. Thriving Kids is the first program of this kind to be launched.
But while states and territories initially signed up to the federal government’s new model, the relationship has become more fractious as plans have developed.
And while the other states and territories have signed on to deliver Thriving Kids and are developing plans about what these will look like in their communities, Queensland is yet to sign up.
At the moment we don’t know what this will mean for younger children with low-to-moderate needs in Queensland. For example, some aspects of Thriving Kids’ first stage will be rolled out, focusing on general supports. But it’s unclear whether targeted services will be developed.
What do we still need to know?
The Queensland minister for disability services, Amanda Camm, has previously said the federal government has not sufficiently defined what it means by developmental delay or different levels of support needs. She argues the federal government simply wants to shift costs to the states and territories.
The Queensland government shares a concern with a number of disability advocates: that children and families might fall between gaps in services if they’re no longer eligible for the NDIS but can’t get the specific support they need through Thriving Kids.
NDIS eligibility is set to tighten, with the government seeking to cut 160,000 participants from the scheme over the next four years.
So what will happen for families whose children age out of Thriving Kids — at nine — but aren’t eligible for NDIS support? This is a key concern.
The kind of early intervention offered by Thriving Kids is important, but for most children their support needs won’t disappear as they age.
The government has floated the idea of a Thriving Teens scheme, but there are no solid plans yet.
What happens next?
This first stage of Thriving Kids focuses on general universal supports, such as information and advice for families who have concerns about their child’s development, and supported playgroups for children aged five and under.
From January 2027, states and territories will start to develop and roll out targeted supports. These are for children who need additional support, for example, low-cost assistive technologies or speech therapy.
The NDIS will not change its eligibility criteria until January 2028, meaning children will continue to be admitted to the scheme until these changes take place.

Trump’s AI Safety ‘Accord’ Is a Fancy Pinky-Swear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:30:09 UTC
05:30:09 KST

On Tuesday, executives for Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, and Nvidia all signed “The White House Accord on Super Intelligence,” which was announced following a luncheon held by President Donald Trump.
The effort was an act of “tremendous self-regulation,” as Trump put it, but the agreement is not the sweeping AI regulation that people inside the companies themselves have been asking for. And while failing to honor these public commitments could count as illegally lying to consumers, even that wouldn’t be enough to trigger massive reforms.
The statement says that companies “should implement” several things: First, they should ensure they have “robust internal controls” to monitor their models’ capabilities and ability to not go rogue or hack things in unintended ways. Second, they should “empower” an internal team to do that work (and remediate when things go wrong). Third, it encourages them to partner with an external monitor who is “empowered” to do independent assessments to make sure that all of that work is happening. And finally, they should make sure their board of directors has set up a committee to receive reports about all of these efforts.
The voluntary commitments are some indication that the frontier labs are making an effort to figure out how to make products that are safe for the general public. However, if there were any hopes for a blanket blessing from the US government, those were quickly dashed after news broke that the Federal Trade Commission intends to investigate several AI companies over potential consumer protection issues.
The statement is the culmination of weeks of debate over AI regulation. It also follows frontier AI labs seeking an antitrust exemption so they can coordinate on safety work without regulatory scrutiny. (Notably, antitrust experts and practitioners say such an exemption is unneeded because AI ending humanity—which researchers have warned will come about if nothing is done—is arguably anti-competitive because humans are an essential part of any given marketplace.)
There’s been a lot of build-up to this particular statement, but this is not the first time that these companies have signed a voluntary agreement about their AI safety practices with a government. In early 2025, the United Kingdom and the Republic of Korea announced a set of “Frontier AI Safety Commitments,” which included promises about doing internal and external red-teaming of AI models for “severe and novel threats” and also “to work toward information sharing” on AI safety issues.
Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment. The White House also did not immediately respond.
Neil Chilson, a former chief technologist for the FTC, posted on X of the accords that “this is the kind of pledge that the FTC could potentially enforce, if a company materially failed to follow through on any of these promises.”
But those hoping for a sweeping settlement and a dramatic reining-in of rogue “super intelligence” based on the accords alone might find themselves disappointed.
(Disclosure: This story’s author previously worked in the Office of Technology at the FTC and resigned in November 2025.)
Not following through on a public promise could be considered a deceptive business practice and a violation of the FTC Act. When the FTC alleges that a company deceived its customers, the remedy it usually prescribes is making the company promise not to lie again.
For example, the FTC recently announced it had settled with three companies after it alleged they were touting a service that could help businesses target ads based on audio recordings collected from smartphones, smart TVs, and other devices. The companies, the agency said, lied to businesses about their ability to creep on consumers. The fix? The companies are no longer allowed to misrepresent their advertising services and the collection and use of consumers’ voice data, among other things. The case does not address whether it’s OK to collect voice data from your phone, and the settlement doesn’t set out any guardrails if one of the three companies wanted to actually do that in the future (other than not lying about it.)
OpenAI has been remarkably open about the number of times its agents have broken into other people’s systems and how it needs to improve its safety practices. But, as experts have pointed out to WIRED, the US government can open investigations into companies even if they eventually decide there’s no enforcement action to bring. (The FTC, for example, reportedly sent a civil investigative demand to OpenAI in 2023, but it’s unclear what came of that.)
Following Tuesday’s AI luncheon with Trump, the New York Post reported that the FTC was planning a “sweeping probe” into Anthropic, OpenAI, other unnamed frontier labs, and a nonprofit called METR that does third-party evaluations. METR and the labs didn’t respond to a request for comment.
The Post says that the agency still hasn’t issued any civil investigative demands to its intended targets—usually one of the first steps in any sort of investigation. An FTC spokesperson confirmed that there is some sort of investigation, but they declined to provide any additional details, including what consumer protection issues were of concern.
FTC chairman Andrew Ferguson, who was included on the “super intelligence” luncheon’s seating chart, has previously explained that enforcers don’t always have a fully baked case from the get-go. “You're constantly looking for smoke to see if there's fire,” he told a crowd of antitrust enthusiasts last year.
Even if the FTC investigation moves forward and the agency does identify violations, some are skeptical that it will result in any action against the AI firms.
“It should be encouraging to Americans worried about AI that the FTC is investigating these companies,” says Douglas Farrar, who was the head of public affairs for the FTC during Lina Khan’s tenure as chair. “But let’s remember that Ferguson may chair the FTC, but Donald Trump runs it, and I doubt after yesterday's love fest with his AI CEO buddies that Trump will allow any legal action with teeth against these companies.”

Haiti: Attack in Artibonite underscores the urgent need to turn international commitments into effective protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:27:03 UTC
05:27:03 KST

In response to the attack reportedly carried out on 28 September by members of the armed gang Kokorat San Ras in Gros-Morne, Artibonite department, in which at least 11 people were killed and several others injured according to available information, Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director, said:
“Once again, a Haitian community is mourning after a brutal attack by armed gangs. The killings in Gros-Morne reveal an unbearable reality: as violence continues to spread beyond Port-au-Prince, people are paying with their lives for a deepening crisis.
The killings in Gros-Morne reveal an unbearable reality: as violence continues to spread beyond Port-au-Prince, people are paying with their lives for a deepening crisis.
Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director.
“The Haitian authorities must effectively investigate these killings and bring all those suspected of criminal responsibility to justice in fair trials. Armed gangs must immediately end killings, kidnappings and other abuses against the population.”
According to available information, the attack took place after an operation by the Gang Suppression Force (GSF), a multinational security support force authorized by the United Nations in 2025, against Kokorat San Ras positions in the area. Members of the gang subsequently reportedly attacked the population in retaliation. On 29 September, the United Nations Security Council extended the GSF mandate for six months, until 31 March 2027.
“Renewing the GSF mandate does not in itself protect the Haitian population. Commitments made by the international community must urgently be translated into an effective and sustainable response that places the protection of people’s human rights at its core, with particular attention to children.”
Commitments made by the international community must urgently be translated into an effective and sustainable response that places the protection of people’s human rights at its core, with particular attention to children.”
Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director.
“The regional response to the crisis must also include protection for Haitians who have been forced to leave the country. There is a profound inconsistency when governments such as those of the Dominican Republic and the United States call at the United Nations for a stronger international response to protect the Haitian population, while continuing to carry out collective deportations to Haiti amid this devastating human rights and security crisis.
“States must suspend forced removals to Haiti and ensure effective access to asylum procedures and international protection, fully respecting the principle of non-refoulement. Governments cannot tell the United Nations that Haiti is facing an emergency requiring extraordinary action while, at the same time, sending people back to face those very same dangers,” Ana Piquer concluded.

Ukraine’s air-raid sirens can sound for 10 hours a day. Its economy minister says every hour costs $45 million.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:25:29 UTC
05:25:29 KST

Ukraine’s air-raid sirens can sound for 10 hours a day. Its economy minister says every hour costs $45 million.
Air raid alerts warning of Russian attacks cost Ukraine about $45 million an hour, Ukrainian Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko estimated in an interview with The Guardian. He said Ukraine sometimes spends up to 10 hours a day under alerts, which regularly force most businesses in the country to suspend operations while employees take shelter.
To reduce the economic damage, Ukraine’s government introduced a new two-tier alert system: a “red” alert signals the threat of a missile strike and requires people to take shelter, while a “yellow” alert signals a drone threat and allows businesses to keep operating.
More than half of businesses keep operating during “yellow” alerts, Kravchenko said, although the danger remains. On the afternoon of September 28, during a “yellow” alert, a Russian drone struck a building in central Kyiv belonging to Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences. Two people were killed.
The Kremlin intends to paralyze Kyiv before winter, The Economist reported. Several senior Ukrainian officials told the publication that Vladimir Putin had ordered strikes on civilian sites. One of the officials said, “They want people to be afraid of going to the supermarket.”
Russia did step up its attacks on civilian infrastructure in August and September. Kravchenko sees this as an attempt to “destroy pretty much the entire economy” of Ukraine. He estimated that attacks on factories, warehouses, data centers, and other sites have caused about $10 billion in damage since the start of the year. These losses are putting increasing pressure on the budget.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky recently estimated the shortfall in the 2026 budget at about $27 billion. The figure raised concerns among EU leaders. Kravchenko said spending cuts had reduced the deficit to $20 billion. But Kyiv will need $52.6 billion in external financing next year. Less than half of that amount has been secured so far, and the authorities are discussing further spending cuts and tax increases.
But Kravchenko does not attribute the deficit to mismanagement, corruption, or excessive spending under former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. “The cost of war is simply increasing,” he said.
Ukraine now needs to strengthen its air defenses and speed up development of drones capable of intercepting Russia’s new jet-powered drones, Kravchenko said. He said Ukraine is better prepared this year for what could be the hardest winter of the war.
The war in photographs: Kyiv and Vyshhorod
Overnight on September 30, Russia attacked Kyiv and the Kyiv region with drones and various types of missiles. Two people were killed in the capital, and four others were injured. In Vyshhorod, in the Kyiv region, a child was killed, and three people were rescued from the rubble of a destroyed house.

Sybiha Meets Japanese Lawmakers in Kyiv to Discuss Further Security Cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:24:23 UTC
05:24:23 KST

Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has met a delegation of Japanese lawmakers in Kyiv to discuss deeper security cooperation, despite Russia intensifying its daily barrage on Ukraine nationwide.
The delegation, made up of members of Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and led by former Japanese Defense Minister Itsunori Onodera, arrived in Kyiv as planned, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Wednesday, Sept. 30.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Ukraine is ready to develop mutually beneficial cooperation with Japan, drawing on our experience and capabilities, and to identify areas in which our countries can strengthen each other’s security,” Sybiha said, noting that “what is happening in Europe has direct consequences for Asia, and vice versa.”
Europe and Asia’s shared security
The two sides discussed additional ways to expand bilateral cooperation, with particular focus on security.
The meeting also covered the links between security in Europe and the Indo-Pacific, including Russia’s deepening military partnership with North Korea, whose troops increasingly fight alongside Russian forces against Ukraine.
An agreement was reportedly reached on the need to step up pressure on Moscow, including cracking down on sanctions evasion and making full use of immobilized Russian assets for Ukraine’s benefit.
According to the Foreign Ministry, Sybiha and Onodera also discussed Russia’s efforts to block shipping in the Black Sea and the need to restore safe navigation, which the ministry described as critical for global food security and trade.
Ukraine Completes 17 of 42 Resolutions Needed to Unlock $29.5B in Aid
Long-standing partners
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, Japan has emerged as one of Ukraine’s most important allies in Asia, with its financial and humanitarian support exceeding $20 billion.
In April, Kyiv received a $1.3 billion grant from Tokyo, funded by profits from frozen Russian assets under the G7’s Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration initiative.
Japan also contributed $14.7 million in May to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – a mechanism intended for financing deliveries of US-made weapons to Ukraine.
A speaker of Japan’s House of Representatives, Eisuke Mori, became the first holder of the position to speak in the Ukrainian parliament’s plenary chamber on Tuesday, Sept. 15. He came to the Verkhovna Rada wearing a vyshyvanka, a traditional Ukrainian garment.
President Volodymyr Zelensky described the meeting as “particularly important” due to Japan’s possible participation in the PURL.
Tokyo has also been exploring a role in Ukraine’s Drone Deal initiative, while supplying demining tools, forensic laboratory equipment and emergency vehicles.
Kyiv has also backed Tokyo on a key territorial issue.
In 2022, Zelensky signed a decree recognizing the southern Kuril Islands, which Japan calls its Northern Territories, as Japanese territory under temporary Russian occupation.
Japan’s diplomatic ties with Moscow deteriorate
Meanwhile, as Tokyo’s partnership with Kyiv has grown, its relations with Moscow have significantly worsened.
After Japan joined Western sanctions imposed over Russia’s war in Ukraine, Moscow suspended peace treaty talks and ended programs allowing former Japanese residents to visit the disputed islands.
Tensions escalated further on Aug. 13, when Russian President Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the islands in more than 25 years in power.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the visit “absolutely unacceptable,” and Tokyo summoned Russia’s ambassador in protest.
Moscow responded by summoning Japan’s ambassador, Akira Muto, with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov accusing Japanese officials of having “crossed the line of decency.”
Around the same time, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev claimed that the islands “were, are, and will remain Russian land,” and that anyone who fails to understand this will face direct consequences.
The dispute over the islands, which the Soviet Union seized in 1945, has prevented the two countries from ever signing a formal peace treaty ending World War II.
The remarks are part of a broader pattern of threats from senior Russian officials. On Sept. 11, Medvedev said Lithuania would “disappear from the map of the world” if it lifted its long-standing ban on nuclear weapons.
Days later, Putin again raised Moscow’s long-standing complaints about the treatment of Russian minorities in the Baltic states, while insisting that Russia had no plans for a military action against Europe.
The Kremlin used similar unfounded claims that Russian speakers faced violations of their rights in Ukraine to justify its full-scale invasion of the country.
The rhetoric has fueled growing concern among NATO members, already on alert due to repeated sabotage campaigns and frequent drone incursions on their territory, as well as intelligence warnings that Russia could test the alliance by conducting a limited ground attack.
On Monday, Sept. 28, Russia’s embassy in Belgium warned that Moscow was ready to use its entire arsenal of weapons should NATO members try to isolate Kaliningrad.
NATO rejected the threat, reiterating that it is a defensive alliance. It also condemned Russia’s “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric” and threats of force.

EU aviation agency warns airlines to avoid parts of Saudi airspace amid Houthi attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:23:43 UTC
05:23:43 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency on Wednesday warned airlines to avoid flying in parts of Saudi Arabian airspace amid increased missile and drone attacks.
In an information bulletin, the agency said the regional security situation remains "highly volatile" due to the military conflict between the US and Iran, with significant military activity affecting Saudi airspace.
The agency said the Houthis significantly increased the frequency and geographic scope of attacks against Saudi maritime, energy and infrastructure targets in September, including in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.
Military and aviation-related infrastructure across Saudi Arabia has also been repeatedly targeted by missiles and drones, it said.
While southern and southwestern Saudi airspace remains particularly exposed due to its proximity to Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen, recent attacks have demonstrated the group's ability and intent to strike deeper inside the country, the agency said.
It cited the Riyadh, Tabuk and Yanbu areas among those affected.
The agency warned that recurrent missile and drone attacks, together with the activation of air-defense systems, increase the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified, as well as risks from interception activity and falling debris.
It advised operators to avoid flying at any altitude in a designated part of Saudi airspace, particularly areas exposed to heightened risks from missile and drone activity.
The restricted zone is defined by aviation navigation points within the Jeddah Flight Information Region, while operators were urged to exercise caution across the remainder of Saudi airspace.
The warning is valid until Nov. 16 unless reviewed earlier, according to the bulletin.

Netanyahu, UAE president discuss flight security after flydubai incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:23:17 UTC
05:23:17 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke with United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed on Wednesday following a serious incident aboard a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Israel and security concerns that arose in its aftermath, an Israeli source told Walla.
Netanyahu referred to the conversation, saying: "I spoke with bin Zayed and we agreed to arrange the security issues."
The conversation came after an incident aboard Flydubai Flight FZ1073, during which one of the pilots stabbed his colleague, and the aircraft began losing altitude. Passengers and crew members subdued the attacker, and the plane ultimately landed at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
Earlier, Netanyahu said that the pilot "apparently tried to crash the plane with its passengers on board," although the motive behind the act is still under investigation.
The incident raised questions regarding security arrangements on flights departing from Dubai to Israel. Earlier on Wednesday, the UAE approved allowing Shin Bet security personnel to conduct inspections at Dubai Airport in the coming days, a move that will temporarily allow Israeli airlines to continue operating flights to the country.
Netanyahu, bin Zayed met just days prior in the Abu Dhabi
The conversation between Netanyahu and bin Zayed took place only days after the two leaders met in the UAE. Netanyahu arrived in Abu Dhabi on Sunday and met with the Emirati president.
The Prime Minister's Office said afterward that the visit focused on strengthening relations between the two countries and addressing regional challenges.
The UAE's official news agency, WAM, confirmed the meeting and said that bin Zayed welcomed Netanyahu and that the two discussed bilateral relations and ways to strengthen and develop them.
The meeting lasted several hours, and Israeli officials said Iran was at the center of the discussions. Netanyahu was accompanied, among others, by senior Israeli security and policy officials.
Now, less than three days after that meeting, the unusual incident aboard the Dubai flight has returned security cooperation between the countries to the center of the agenda, as both sides work to arrange security measures surrounding flights between the UAE and Israel.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar spoke over the phone on Wednesday evening with UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Sa’ar updated his Emirati counterpart on the return of the Israeli passengers. The UAE foreign minister said he was pleased that all the Israeli passengers had returned home safely.

All flydubai flights to and from Israel's Ben-Gurion Airport were temporarily suspended on Wednesday after the attempted hijacking of FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier that day, the airline said in a statement.
"This temporary suspension will allow the relevant authorities to continue their work and establish all the facts surrounding the incident," the statement read. "We remain in close coordination with government authorities, regulators, and airport stakeholders and will review the suspension as more information becomes available."
The airline's announcement follows a recommendation by the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) earlier on Wednesday that flights between the United Arab Emirates and Israel should be suspended until the investigation progresses.
Israel is set to ramp up security checks on pilots flying into the country, a spokesperson for the prime minister's office said, after it said a co-pilot on a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv had stabbed the pilot and attempted to crash the plane.
The dramatic incident was only defused after passengers helped subdue the co-pilot before other on-duty pilots employed by the airline on the plane landed the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia. The Dubai state-owned airline warned against "premature speculation" and said much remained unclear.
Saudi authorities have arrested and interrogated the co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 from the United Arab Emirates to Israel that was carrying 174 people, almost all Israelis, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said.
In an interview with CNN, Netanyahu revealed that Israel would join the investigation into the incident and be permitted to interrogate the Omani pilot along with the UAE.
Rising scrutiny over how pilots are vetted
The incident has sharpened questions about how pilots are vetted and what sorts of security protocols they face, including but not limited to the Middle East, according to government officials and aviation analysts.
Israel's government frequently urges Israelis and Jews to remain vigilant when traveling outside Israel, amid concerns that they could be targeted. This comes as antisemitism has surged globally in recent years, including violent and sometimes deadly attacks against Jews. So far, however, no motive has been given for the flydubai incident.
"Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the pilots' identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check," Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister's office, told Reuters.
He said Netanyahu had instructed authorities to "ramp up security" on flights to Israel operated by Israeli and non-Israeli carriers.
"Anywhere that an Israeli is going to be flying into Israel. Our job right now is to do our best - even if they're not on Israeli airlines - to make sure that those security procedures are much higher," Spielman said.
The UAE civil aviation regulator, the GCAA, did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on how it vets its pilots.
Netanyahu identified the pilot who was attacked as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar. He said that, despite being "stabbed and seriously injured," Machchhar fought back and opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the attacker.
Pilot vetting post 9/11
Pilots have faced substantial security screenings, especially since the 9/11 attacks in New York 25 years ago, experts told Reuters.
"Every pilot goes through extensive background checks but also continuous medical and psychological assessments," said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in Britain.
Individual countries and airlines implement screening and security standards set out by the International Civil Aviation Organization, but experts told Reuters there is flexibility in how they are interpreted.
Two pilots working in the Middle East but not for flydubai told Reuters that pilots must go through the same security screenings as passengers, meaning they cannot bring weapons such as knives or guns on board.
"It's always the airline's responsibility," said Eric Schouten, the head of aviation intelligence consultancy Dyami.
"The airline has to do a proper vetting according to national guidelines on who is in the cockpit, and every country does it differently."
The European Aviation Safety Agency told Reuters that flydubai's certification and safety oversight rest with the GCAA. "This includes responsibility for ensuring that the operator meets the applicable requirements concerning its flight crews and their fitness to fly," EASA said.
Reuters could not determine what weapon was used by the pilot to stab the other. Passengers on board the flight have reported that a man was holding a knife while one of the pilots lay bloodied. A pilot flying in the region but not for flydubai told Reuters pilots might have access to metal knives from a meal service or a crash axe available in most cockpits.
Spielman said Israel already had some of the toughest security checks, and these would only get tighter.
"This is an opportunity for everyone to wake up. Israel has the most thorough security checks in the world, and they're there for a reason. They're there so that an incident like this doesn't take place," he said.

'We didn’t think for even a second about our own lives': Flydubai heroes adjust to new reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:31:42 UTC
19:31:42 KST

Dr. Shota Musaev, the dentist who treated the wounded Indian captain aboard the Flydubai flight targeted in an attempted hijacking, said Thursday that his medical instincts — and the example set by his late parents — guided him as passengers fought to save the aircraft.
“I come from a family of doctors. My late father was a cardiologist and my late mother was a biologist, so I knew what to do when I was faced with the injured pilot,” Musaev, 47, said at his home in Rishon Lezion, south of Tel Aviv.
Musaev was among a group of Israeli passengers who intervened during Wednesday’s dramatic flight to Tel Aviv after the Omani co-pilot allegedly tried to crash the aircraft. He said he saw three Israelis — Yaniv Hayun, Zvika Manes and Assaf Rajuan — rush the co-pilot and realized he had to help.
“My wife initially tried to stop me, but I saw there were heroes there and I joined them,” Musaev said. “At that moment, we didn’t think for even a second about our own lives or what might happen to us. We thought about how to save the entire plane.”
Musaev, who owns a dental clinic in Holon and was born in Georgia, helped restrain the suspected attacker before turning his attention to the wounded captain, Smit Machchhar.
“The captain told me he wanted to live and didn’t want to die there,” Musaev said. “There were moments when I thought we wouldn’t manage to land in time because he was bleeding heavily, but after we stopped the bleeding, his condition stabilized.”
Musaev said a series of chance events played a role in preventing a disaster, including a child going to the bathroom at a critical moment, the passengers who rushed the cockpit and additional pilots who happened to be aboard.
He said he now considers Hayun, Manes and Rajuan members of his family.
“I wrote in the WhatsApp group we created after the incident that all of us were born again yesterday,” he said. “We went through a historic event and even landed in Saudi Arabia.”
Passengers praise treatment in Saudi Arabia
The aircraft made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, where Musaev said passengers were treated well.
“There was some chaos after landing because the children were under a lot of stress,” he said. “Even very senior officials came and spoke with us, and they assigned doctors to us who made sure everything was OK.”
The Israeli passengers then faced another difficult decision: whether to board another Flydubai aircraft for the trip home to Ben Gurion Airport.
Musaev favored returning on the airline despite what had happened.
“I spoke with a very senior official and with the manager of the local airport,” he said. “I was on the side that said we should get on the flight, mainly because you can’t fly only on Israeli airlines. Despite the serious incident we experienced with Flydubai, you can’t simply rule them out.”
He said passengers ultimately made the decision together after learning that an Israeli aircraft would not be allowed to land there.
“I told everyone we needed to get on,” he said. “We told the parents with children that they would decide what we did, and in the end, when they said they wouldn’t allow an Israeli plane to land there, we made the decision together and boarded.”
Musaev said he took several girls into the cockpit to meet the pilots before the flight home.
Back with his wife and children Thursday, he said the enormity of what happened was only beginning to sink in.
“We’re emotional to be with them again and are starting to understand more deeply that we’re alive,” he said.
Musaev stressed that saving the plane had been a collective effort.
“The act of heroism was something we did together,” he said. “I tied up the terrorist pilot and then treated the other pilot. But the other three were the ones who entered the cockpit and neutralized the terrorist. Others took care of the children on the plane. We did everything together, hand in hand.”
‘I’m an upgraded plumber’
Hayun, 38, of Ness Ziona, helped stabilize the aircraft as the Omani co-pilot allegedly tried to disable the instrument panel.
On Thursday, Hayun responded to remarks by U.S. President Donald Trump, who described him as an Israeli plumber who had never flown a plane and rarely traveled by air but saw what was happening and intervened.
“I’m an upgraded plumber,” Hayun joked. “He wasn’t wrong. I don’t work at NASA and I don’t deal with space. I deal with stinking pipes, and he was right. I wasn’t offended.”
Hayun said he never imagined the U.S. president would talk about him.
“I never dreamed Trump would talk about me and what I did. I actually like his sense of humor,” he said. “It was amusing how he described it. I’m not exactly Bruce Lee. But I did manage to overpower the terrorist with a few other Israelis and pull him backward in a chokehold, and that’s the most important thing.”
Hayun said he had not slept since the ordeal.
“I just want to get back to my routine now, to work, to my truck,” he said. “I’m getting so much love and I thank everyone — everyone who was on that flight, who worked hand in hand and helped us get our lives back because they were hanging by a thread. I hope it doesn’t come back to me in my dreams.”
Herzog recommends civilian bravery awards
President Isaac Herzog spoke with the passengers who intervened and said he would recommend that Musaev, Hayun, Manes and Rajuan receive the Presidential Medal for Civilian Heroism, Israel’s highest civilian bravery award.
“At a time when the lives of so many people were in danger, you acted without hesitation, with courage, resourcefulness and extraordinary mutual responsibility,” Herzog told them. “You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disaster.”
“Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society,” he added. “I am proud of you, and I thank you on behalf of the State of Israel.”
Herzog said he would bring their actions before the advisory committee responsible for the award and recommend that they receive the honor.
The president also praised the Indian captain, who fought the co-pilot and opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers to intervene.
Herzog later recommended Tali Manes, Zvika Manes’ wife, for the same civilian bravery award after further accounts indicated she played a crucial role in alerting passengers to the danger.
According to the President’s Residence, Manes heard violence and commotion coming from the cockpit and was the first to alert other passengers and call for help, prompting those who ultimately rushed in and subdued the suspected attacker.
After he was restrained, she continued to act, calling pilots who were traveling in the rear of the aircraft to come forward and help restore control of the plane.
“Tali, the more we learn about what happened in those dramatic moments, the clearer it becomes how significant a part you played in saving the lives of the passengers,” Herzog told her.
“You heard that something terrible was happening, immediately understood the scale of the danger, raised the alarm, called for help, and did not stop acting even after the attacker had been subdued,” he said. “The resourcefulness, responsibility, and composure you showed in moments of mortal danger are civilian heroism in the fullest sense of the word. You are a hero, Tali, and I am proud of you and thank you on behalf of the State of Israel.”

The AFLW is speeding up and these numbers prove it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:21:35 UTC
05:21:35 KST

Ask a regular punter down the street what they think of AFLW and there's a good chance you'll get some version of "it's improving every year".
While this is not intended to be dismissive of those pioneers who helped lay the groundwork for the league a decade later, there is clear evidence that games are faster, more competitive, and more entertaining than ever.
And yes, there are teams still dwelling down the bottom, struggling to grow alongside the rest of the competition, but there is increasing pressure on those clubs to make adjustments in order to catch up.
The numbers are stark. Average scores are the highest they've ever been as metrics across the competition indicate increasing strategic control, and a growing desire to move the ball to attack, rather than focus wholly on defending the opposition.
Over the opening seven rounds of the 2026 season, teams are kicking an average of 45.6 points per game. This is an increase of 4.6 points compared to the previous all-time high of 41.1 points struck last year.
Of the 18 clubs, only four have failed to average a higher score in 2026 compared to 2025: Brisbane (-9.8 points per game), North Melbourne (-5.2), Port Adelaide (-18.5), and St Kilda (-7.2).
In line with this, inside 50s (avg. 35.1) and shots on goal (avg. 15.4) are at an all-time high, as are goal assists (avg. 4.2), all suggesting greater nuance in the attacking style employed by clubs.
Scoring is ultimately the end product of the way sides are moving the ball down the ground. Early days of AFLW were stoppage and tackle-heavy, keeping things caught in a rolling maul for extended periods of time.
But as we've seen fitness, skill, and strategy develop, the capacity to move the ball on the outside has become a weapon for a host of sides.
Rule changes last year — specifically, the adjudication of holding the ball — forced stoppages down from an average of 67 per game in 2024, to 44 in 2025.
That number has dropped again by 2.9 per game, which is another indicator of that desire to spread away from contest and use the ball in a more productive way.
Fewer sides are relying on resetting the ground via a stoppage in order to regain control.
Fremantle has been the clearest proponent of this shift. In 2025 it was caught out, relying heavily on a contested possession game, the late news that the holding the ball interpretation had been changed throwing the club out of sorts. No longer could heavy contest be the solution, and adjusting on the run was tough work.
This year, the Dockers have moved away from that contested game, averaging a positive uncontested possession differential for the first time in their 11-season history, and are reaping the benefits of the shift.
It is just one example of increased reliance on outside ball, with uncontested possession at an all-time high of 142.4 per game, up 10.2 on last year's record, while contested possession has marginally dropped. Disposal efficiency has also shot up to a record 63.6 per cent.
Teams are establishing far more control in game with ball in hand and enjoying a greater connection between lines.
Transition the key for improving sides
Clubs have opted to go one of two ways with their ball movement this year. The likes of Richmond, Hawthorn, and Adelaide have leaned into kick-mark football, choosing to control play with systematic build up. Whereas teams like Geelong, Gold Coast, and Carlton have taken the AFLW by storm with aggressive run and carry, moving the ball by hand and at speed.
Both methods have been beneficial in the increase in end-to-end transition throughout the season, with defensive half to inside 50 movement up to 20.6 per cent from 18.6 per cent last year, and defensive 50 to inside 50 movement also up by two per cent. This is combined with effective metres gained rising by 120 per game as well.
There has been AFLW-wide growth in handball metres gained with the average going from 160.7 last year to 224.5 this year, led by the Suns (+197) and Geelong (+130). A shift in Collingwood's game style has also seen it grow in this area (+119) and Carlton (+90) has doubled down on this after making its big move in this area last year.
It's hard to quantify the increased trust teams have in their system and willingness to attack, rather than simply rely on defence. With long kicks down the line marginally down — an indicator of the preference to build the ball up rather than opt for a bail out kick — and the aforementioned uncontested possession and stoppage metrics, there has been a clear move toward system, structure, and attack.
It requires teams to go into matches with faith that their system will do the job, rather than simply planning for how to stymie the opposition's style of play.
So, when that punter says that the AFLW is improving every year, they are correct, but this year more than ever. And the numbers back it up.

Pentagon’s Hegseth says 20 percent of US generals, admirals cut, ‘no fatties, no trannies’
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday that his department had cut 20 percent of US admirals, generals and officers who did not fit his vision. "Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors – just tough, ready, committed troops," he said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that the United States has slashed the number of its generals and admirals by 20 percent, in a move he said is aimed at "accountability."
Hegseth suggested the cuts targeted officers who failed to get on board with his efforts to ensure the military is focused on war-fighting rather than the "woke" policies of previous administrations, describing the reductions as an "accomplishment".
"The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force," Hegseth told troops at the Quantico military base, saying: "We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent."
"So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board," he said. "The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue."
Read morePentagon removes top Navy official amid military shake-up
The address to junior officers and enlisted personnel at Quantico came a year after a similar speech to top officers in which Hegseth said the US military was too fat, too focused on leftist "woke" ideas, and in need of major shake-up.
He said Wednesday that top officers who "responded positively" to the previous speech are "leading newly focused and newly empowered and disciplined formations," while those who did not "no longer work here."
"We are no longer the woke department, or the weak department," Hegseth said.
"Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors – just tough, ready, committed troops."
Cutting 'fat'
Hegseth ordered major cuts to the US military – including a 10-percent reduction to the overall number of generals and admirals, and a 20-percent decrease in the highest four-star ranks – in May 2025.
There were 831 active duty US generals and admirals as of the end of that month, but Pentagon figures from the end of July 2026 – the latest available – showed there were actually more top officers – a total of 851.
Asked to clarify if the 20 percent cuts had been completed or were still ongoing, the Pentagon said: "We have nothing further to provide beyond the secretary's comments."
During his confirmation hearing in January 2025, Hegseth argued that the Pentagon's bureaucracy was top-heavy and in need of cuts.
"It's going to be my job, working with those that we hire and those inside the administration, to identify those places where fat can be cut, so it can go toward lethality," he told lawmakers at the time.
Since returning to office early last year, Trump has overseen a purge of top military personnel, including the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, general Charles "CQ" Brown, whom he fired without explanation in February 2025.
Other senior officers pushed out include the heads of the US Army, Navy and Coast Guard, the general who headed the National Security Agency, the vice chief of staff of the US Air Force, a Navy admiral assigned to NATO, and three top military lawyers.
The chief of staff of the Air Force also announced his retirement without explanation just two years into a four-year term, while the head of US Southern Command retired a year into his tenure.
Hegseth has insisted the president is simply choosing the leaders he wants, but Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about the potential politicization of the traditionally neutral US military.

UK may reverse Brexit – Burnham
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:16:12 UTC
05:16:12 KST

UK may reverse Brexit – Burnham
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK could eventually rejoin the European Union as his government considers options for reshaping relations with the bloc a decade after the Brexit referendum. 
In an interview with the BBC on Wednesday, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good,” arguing that the current settlement was holding back economic growth and had failed to deliver the promised control over immigration. 
He said the government would examine alternatives ranging from maintaining the status quo to joining a customs union or the single market, or even potentially going “all the way” and returning to the EU. 
Talk of reversing Brexit has grown recently, with several prominent British politicians floating the idea. Burnham’s comments are the clearest indication yet that rejoining the EU could be on the table, although any such move would reopen questions over sovereignty, immigration, and regulatory control that drove much of the Leave vote.
Why did Britain leave the EU in the first place?
Britons voted 52% to 48% to leave the EU in June 2016, triggering years of negotiations over the terms of Brexit. The UK formally left the bloc in January 2020 and exited the single market and customs union at the end of that year. 
For many Leave voters, Brexit was primarily about sovereignty and immigration rather than economics. An Ashcroft poll conducted immediately after the referendum found that 49% of Leave voters said their main reason was wanting decisions about the UK to be made in Britain, while 33% pointed to regaining control over immigration and borders. Only 6% primarily cited expected benefits from leaving the EU for trade and the economy. By contrast, 43% of Remain voters said their main concern was the risk Brexit posed to the economy, jobs, and prices.
What did Brexit achieve?
Brexit ended EU free movement and gave London control over who could move to Britain from the bloc. That did not, however, translate into lower overall immigration. Net migration instead surged as arrivals from outside the EU increased, reaching a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 before falling sharply following tighter visa rules. Non-EU nationals continue to account for most immigration. 
The change also worked both ways. British citizens lost EU freedom-of-movement rights and are now subject to the entry requirements that apply to non-EU travelers in the Schengen area.
Brexit also gave Britain an independent trade policy, allowing it to negotiate agreements without the approval of EU members. The UK has since struck deals with Australia, New Zealand, and India and joined the CPTPP, a major Indo-Pacific trade bloc. However, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimates that the long-term economic gains from post-Brexit trade agreements are small compared with the impact it expects from higher trade barriers with the EU. 
The bloc nevertheless remains Britain’s largest trading partner, accounting for about 41% of UK exports and roughly half of imports in 2025.
Why is the issue being reopened now?
Critics contend that the economic costs of Brexit have overshadowed its benefits. The OBR estimates that Brexit will ultimately reduce the trade intensity of the British economy by around 15% and productivity by about 4% relative to remaining in the EU. These are long-term modeling assumptions rather than directly observed losses, while Britain’s economic performance since Brexit has also been affected by the Covid-19 pandemic, the Ukraine conflict, and wider disruptions to global trade. 
Leaving the EU single market and customs union also created new barriers to trade with Britain’s largest trading partner. Businesses face customs declarations, rules-of-origin requirements, and additional checks that did not apply when Britain was an EU member. 
While Brexit gave Britain greater control over legal migration, Burnham has argued that it weakened the country’s ability to tackle irregular migration by reducing cooperation with European countries, particularly over Channel crossings.
Is preserving the UK part of the calculation?
Burnham has not explicitly linked his EU rethink to preserving the United Kingdom. But it comes as pro-independence and Irish nationalist parties in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland push for independence or Irish reunification while presenting closer integration with the EU as part of their preferred future. 
This month, the pro-independence SNP and Plaid Cymru, together with the pro-Irish-unification Sinn Fein, jointly asserted their nations’ right to self-determination and called on London to facilitate a constitutional change, declaring that their future “belongs in the European Union.” 
Burnham, meanwhile, has made preserving the UK an explicit priority. Responding on Tuesday to Scottish First Minister John Swinney’s prediction that he would be the UK’s last prime minister, he vowed to “fight with everything I’ve got to keep it together.”
Haven’t Britain and the EU already been moving closer?
In security policy, Britain and the EU have already moved significantly closer despite Brexit. The UK remains one of NATO’s leading European military powers, while the 2025 UK-EU Security and Defense Partnership established regular strategic consultations and expanded cooperation on Ukraine, sanctions against Russia, military mobility, and arms production. It also opened the way for greater British involvement in EU defense initiatives.
Much of the alignment has centered on Russia and Ukraine. London and its European partners have coordinated weapons supplies and training for Kiev, sanctions against Moscow, and efforts to expand European arms production. 
In July, Britain secured participation in the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, allowing British defense companies to compete for procurement contracts financed through the scheme. The UK agreed to make a contribution proportionate to the value of contracts awarded to British companies.
Could Britain simply rejoin the EU?
Any return would be neither automatic nor a restoration of Britain’s previous membership terms. The UK would have to formally reapply and go through the EU accession process, requiring unanimous approval from member states and the consent of the European Parliament. Nor would Britain be guaranteed the opt-outs and special arrangements it enjoyed before Brexit; the terms of any renewed membership would have to be negotiated. 
Immediately after the 2016 referendum, EU leaders said they regretted Britain’s decision but respected the result. During the subsequent withdrawal negotiations, Brussels took a firm line, insisting that Britain could not retain the benefits of EU membership from outside the bloc and rejecting “cherry picking” from the single market. 
A decade later, however, Brussels is not ruling out London’s return. In July, EU Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said applying for membership was “entirely a prerogative” of the UK. Former EU Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier said in June that the EU’s “door is open,” while stressing that Britain could not simply choose which EU rules to follow.

The Verkhovna Rada Committee supported the bill on unified social assistance for low-income families

The Verkhovna Rada Committee supported the bill on unified social assistance for low-income families
Kyiv • UNN
The bill on Basic Social Assistance was recommended for its second reading. It will consolidate payments and provide social services and employment assistance.
The Verkhovna Rada Committee supported the bill on Basic Social Assistance (BSA) and recommended it for the second reading. The Ministry of Social Policy reports this, UNN informs.
Details
It is noted that the document lays the regulatory foundation for a fundamental reform of the state payments system and the creation of a single targeted instrument for providing financial support to Ukrainian families.
The approval of the bill by the relevant committee is an important step toward the final adoption of the changes. The Ministry also contributed to the drafting of the bill so that BSA would become an effective springboard for families: with a single payment, the necessary social services, and a chance to return to stability
What is BSA
Basic Social Assistance is the first step toward a new support model for low-income families. The new system combines disparate payments into a single, clear mechanism and strengthens financial support with comprehensive assistance:
-  social services; 
-  case management; 
-  employment assistance. 
The main goal is to help families overcome difficult life circumstances and return to economic independence.
Key changes:
-  assistance is calculated for the family, taking into account the average monthly aggregate income and the property status of its members, rather than being assigned separately to each of them; 
-  the amount of BSA is calculated individually for each family - as the difference between the base amount for the family and its average monthly aggregate income; 
-  the bill combines financial support with social services and employment promotion measures; 
-  a social manager will help assess needs and organize case management or personalized support for able-bodied family members who are not working. 
Reminder
Minister of Finance of Ukraine Serhii Marchenko called the subsistence minimum a purely calculated indicator. According to him, payments need to be decoupled from the size of the subsistence minimum.

Russian cosmetics brand Mixit’s CEO faces fraud charges amid dispute with former employee who says she co-founded the brand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:12:24 UTC
05:12:24 KST

Russian cosmetics brand Mixit’s CEO faces fraud charges amid dispute with former employee who says she co-founded the brand
Oleg Pai, CEO of Mixit, one of Russia’s most recognizable and successful cosmetics brands, was detained in Moscow on September 19. He is accused of fraud, and a court placed him under house arrest. Mixit co-founder Yelena Nazarova linked his detention to a corporate dispute. “We don’t understand how a civil dispute with our former employee could have turned into a criminal investigation. We see this as pressure on our business, as an attempt to seize control of the company,” she said. Forbes reported on the dispute with the former employee and how it might have led to Pai’s detention. Meduza summarizes the Forbes report.
Mixit makes mass-market skincare and makeup products. It promoted itself through the television show “Oryol i reshka” (“Heads and Tails”), worked with popular bloggers such as Ksenia Sobchak, and amassed more than three million Instagram followers. Today, Mixit is one of the most recognizable and best-selling affordable cosmetics brands in Russia and other post-Soviet countries. It is among the top sellers on Wildberries and Ozon, as well as at the beauty retailer Golden Apple. In 2025, Mixit’s revenue exceeded 15 billion rubles, up 140% from the previous year.
Mixit has been in business since 2014. According to the official account of its founding, Nazarova and Pai met in 2011 and decided to launch a brand of customized organic cosmetics. Nazarova, a former hairdresser, took charge of product development and marketing, while Pai handled finances and strategy. He also provided 30 million rubles in startup capital from his own savings. Before Mixit, Pai had worked in the furniture business.
Galina Ryazanova, a chemist and Mixit’s former lead product developer, gave a different account of the company’s founding. She said she met Nazarova in 2013, when Nazarova attended her workshop on making cosmetics at home. The women decided to go into business together. A few months after they began, Ryazanova noticed that Oleg Pai’s company was paying some of the new business’s expenses. She described Pai as Nazarova’s live-in partner. They agreed that he would join them as a third partner “with equal ownership stakes.”
Ryazanova said the agreement was verbal. Pai promised to formalize her 30% stake in Mixit once he had set up a suitable legal structure for the business, but he never did. Although she never officially became a shareholder, she received payments that she considered dividends, both in cash and by bank transfer. The transfers were retroactively documented as interest-free loans: Pai persuaded Ryazanova to sign loan agreements, saying this would prevent questions from the tax authorities.
By 2019, Ryazanova’s relationship with Nazarova and Pai had soured. She said that, during the dispute, Pai first offered to make her Mixit’s director and then offered to buy her stake for 100 million rubles. She rejected both offers. Pai then said she owed the company more than eight million rubles under the interest-free loan agreements she had signed. In 2021, a court ordered Ryazanova to pay the money. She responded by filing a police complaint against her former partners. Mixit’s offices were searched in 2024 and 2025. It is unclear whether the searches were connected to her complaint.
Another aspect of this dispute
In January 2019, Galina Ryazanova left Mixit and joined Shine Is, a cosmetics brand founded by another former Mixit employee, Maria Moshkova. Ryazanova took charge of production.
Shine Is entered the market in April 2019. Shortly afterward, Mixit released a product line called No Fake Shine. Bloggers and customers noticed similarities between the two brands’ product formats and packaging designs. Shine Is said Mixit had copied its packaging and formulas. Mixit said the No Fake Shine line had been in development long before its release, that the former employees had helped create it, and that they could have copied that work.
Shine Is appears to have stopped operating — the brand stopped updating its social media accounts in 2023.
A law enforcement source told Interfax that the criminal investigation into Pai involves forged documents. Nazarova effectively confirmed that it grew out of the dispute with Ryazanova. In a video statement, she said the conflict with a “former employee” had been going on since 2019. “The dispute has been resolved many times. We won those cases, and they were closed. But now the case has been reopened as a criminal investigation, which we don’t understand at all,” she said. The video is no longer available.
The alleged document forgery could “fundamentally change how the corporate dispute is viewed under the law,” Fyodor Trusov of the law firm Sokolov, Trusov and Partners told Forbes. Forging documents does not, in itself, constitute fraud: investigators would need to prove that the forged documents were used specifically to steal property.
Trusov also said investigators would need to establish the basis for Ryazanova’s claim to a stake in the company and prove that Pai intended to commit fraud. “In theory, investing money in a business and failing to receive a promised stake is not enough to bring a fraud charge. In practice, though, it happens,” Trusov said.

Burnham 'concerned' Man City's Abu Dhabi owners could sell club
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owners decided to sell the club after they were found guilty of serious breaches of financial rules.
Burnham praised the ownership group led by Sheikh Mansour for its investment in Manchester since taking over the club in 2008.
"I would be really concerned to lose them," he told the BBC. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."
The Premier League said on Tuesday that City had used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million ($1.2 billion) over nearly a decade.
City have denied wrongdoing and said they will appeal.
Burnham, who was previously the mayor of Greater Manchester, drew parallels with Everton's battle with the league's profit and sustainability rules, when he argued the club he supports had not been treated fairly.
Everton received a 10-point deduction, that was later reduced to six points, after being found to have breached the league's financial rules over a three-year period ending in 2022.
"It would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before," he said.
With sanctions yet to be determined and appeals expected, Burnham acknowledged there was "a lot at stake" for City, their supporters and Manchester, but said it would be inappropriate for him to intervene in the disciplinary process.

Meet 'America': Trump's AI chatbot changes answers after challenging his claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:08:13 UTC
05:08:13 KST

Meet 'America': Trump's AI chatbot changes answers after challenging his claims
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
Donald Trump has launched "America", an AI chatbot designed as a digital portal for US government information. But its responses appear to be changing. The chatbot initially challenged several of Trump's claims, including on the 2020 election and inflation, providing evidence and links. More recently, it has refused to answer some of the same questions. Other responses still contradict Trump, while some echo his views. Vedika Bahl tests the chatbot, and its varying answers in Truth or Fake.
Donald Trump has launched a new AI-powered government chatbot, America.gov, which he has described as a "one front door for every single question" for Americans seeking information about the government.
The platform is designed to bring information from 29,000 US government websites into a single portal. But its launch has drawn attention for another reason: because the chatbot was challenging Trump's own false claims and fact-checking them, and then changed course entirely by refusing to answer certain questions.
We tested the chatbot by asking whether there was widespread fraud in the 2020 presidential election. It responded that it only answers questions about US government services: "I help with official U.S. government services and information. I do not comment on political or legal status of individuals." We received the same response when asking whether Trump had been convicted of felony charges. We also asked about Trump's own claim that he inherited the "worst inflation in history". Again, the chatbot declined to answer.
Those responses differed from answers reported earlier in the rollout.
CNN senior correspondent and longtime Trump fact-checker Daniel Dale asked America.gov about the 2020 election and received an answer that contradicted Trump's claim that the election was stolen. The chatbot cited official information showing that there was no widespread fraud that changed the outcome. Dale also received a response rejecting Trump's claim about inheriting the worst inflation in history and providing supporting figures.
Newsweek also reported receiving an answer confirming that Trump was found guilty on 34 counts of falsifying business records in the first degree. When we asked the same question, the chatbot declined to answer.
The changes appear to extend beyond those questions. Some responses still contradict Trump. For example, when asked about climate change - which Trump has long called a "hoax" - the chatbot said US scientific agencies attribute current warming largely to human activity, and that the Earth is indeed getting warmer.
But on other issues, the chatbot follows terminology adopted by the Trump administration. Asked about the Gulf of Mexico, for example, it referred to the body of water as the "Gulf of America". It also referred to the Pentagon as the headquarters of the "Department of War", following Trump's order to use that name alongside the official Department of Defense designation.
It remains unclear how to what extent this AI will be modified. During our testing, we received different answers to some questions depending on the browser used, or different answers to the same questions in general. Responses also varied when questions were asked in different languages, with some responses more detailed.
What is clear is that America.gov's responses have changed during its rollout, and that Trump's chatbot "America" is no longer fact-checking or challenging some of Trump's claims, and refusing to answer instead.

WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump said on Sept 30 he has done “a very bad job” of explaining his economic record as his job approval rating sags under the weight of high gasoline prices ahead of the November mid-term elections.
Trump, speaking to a supportive crowd at a Hispanic Heritage Month event at the White House, made the comment as he prepares to embark on a 32-day campaign blitz for Republican candidates ahead of the Nov 3 elections that will decide whether his party retains control of the US Congress.
“I’ve done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing,” Trump said, insisting that “the country’s doing better than it has ever done”.
Trump noted that the party in power usually loses congressional seats in the first election after a presidential election and urged his supporters to get out and vote.
“We have to turn this around,” he said.
Many American voters, however, increasingly give Trump low marks in public opinion polls for his management of the economy, which has been buffeted by his global tariff policies and a war on Iran that sent energy prices soaring.
US consumer confidence plunged to a near 12-and-a-half-year low in September, the Conference Board said on Sept 29, with households expecting a deterioration in business and labour market conditions over the next six months.
Consumers have been downbeat on the labour market, despite job growth accelerating in August after hitting a speed bump through much of the summer. Home prices have increased as well, adding to the strain from rising mortgage rates.
Trump travels to Texas and Oklahoma on Oct 1 with a stop in Alabama planned for Oct 2 and one in Ohio on Oct 3.
The Republican Party is pouring millions of dollars into seats once considered safe but are now viewed as competitive as voters grow weary of the economic fallout of the Iran war.
“We’re not getting the word out,” Trump said, referring to what he considers his strong stewardship of the economy.
“I’m going out because nobody’s selling it. We’re doing an extremely poor job of promotion, and an extremely great job of running the country. But we’ll get the word out. It should not be hard.” REUTERS
