Palestine Action US founder funded radical media outlets, is tied to Iranian state TV - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:04:19 UTC
05:04:19 KST

A network established by the founder of Palestine Action US has helped fund and develop a web of media outlets used to promote its radical messaging, with the network extending into organizations connected to Iranian state media.
This was revealed exclusively to The Jerusalem Post by Honest Reporting on Wednesday.
Honest Reporting’s investigation maps a media ecosystem allegedly funded or supported by the network behind US-designated terrorist group Palestine Action, showing how its ideology and messaging spread through seemingly independent outlets.
Palestine Action is an anti-Israel protest group founded in the UK in 2020. Its work - before its proscription by the UK in 2025 - mainly involved the vandalism and destruction of defense factories, companies and Israel-linked institutions.
A US branch of Palestine Action was launched in October 2023 by multi-millionaire heir turned communist activist James Cox ‘Fergie’ Chambers. Palestine Action US describes itself as a “direct action network.” The UK branch was recently designated and sanctioned by the US Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in August 2026. The US branch has not been designated.
Founder facing extradition to the US over Hamas financing, support
Chambers is currently facing extradition from Spain to the US over alleged Hamas financing and Hamas support. The Irish Times cited Chambers’ partner Stella Schnabel as saying he is accused of providing Hamas with $7.5 million in funding. He himself received $250 million after divesting from his family’s media conglomerate, Cox Enterprises, in 2023, according to his spokesperson.
In July 2026, Chambers tweeted, “If Pal Action is terrorism, terrorism is awesome.”
The Post also found a November 2023 interview with the LA Magazine where Chambers said he uses some of this wealth to pay the legal fees for members of UK Palestine Action.
Under Chambers’ leadership, a wider network was born.
In July 2023, ahead of the creation of the US branch of Palestine Action, Chambers and a few of his “comrades” created the Babochki Collective, described as “a cadre collective focused on revolutionary funding, propaganda and political education, direct action/legal support, and the open proliferation of a steadily stronger anti-imperialist united front.”
Among the Babochki founders was Palestine Action co-founder Calla Walsh as well as Paige Belanger, both of whom participated in a November 2023 Palestine Action vandalism attack on a New Hampshire Elbit Systems facility.
According to Honest Reporting, Chambers and Babochki have financially backed and founded several news outlets and organizations, “expanding their violent radicalism across the information landscape.”
The financial records of the Babochki Collective show that it transferred $350,000 to the Atlanta Community Press Collective, “an abolitionist” nonprofit media organization, on October 9, 2023. The Atlanta outlet itself lists Babochki among its donors.
Additionally, as reported by the Free Press, Chambers’ Alford compound housed the journal Combat Liberalism and the Berkshire Communists (the former edited by Chambers and the latter founded by him).
Furthermore, according to Chambers himself, Babochki gave three financial grants to anti-Zionist news outlet Mondoweiss: two grants in the first three months of the Collective’s operation, and $20,000 in October 2023.
Radical outlets funded by communist heir of Cox Enterprises
The financial relationship was accompanied by direct publishing ties. Mondoweiss published two pieces under the byline of Palestine Action US, including the group’s May 2024 manifesto, “Flood the Gates: Escalate.” The piece called for escalation from protests and blockades to “sabotage and dismantling” of what it described as genocidal infrastructure, and called for building an infrastructure of militancy.
Additionally, Babochki is understood to have funded Sovereign Media, which describes itself as a “Nairobi-based socialist and anti-imperialist news outlet,” and as a coalition of “anti-imperialist” outlets.
Sovereign Media has published articles proclaiming that “Israel is not Africa’s friend,” and that the Jewish state was using Somaliland as a “pawn” in its war against Palestinians.
On Sovereign Media’s social media, it revealed that it has received significant funding from Chambers and the Babochki Collective.
In a February 2026 X/Twitter post, Sovereign Media said it was “funded by The Babochki Collective,” while insisting that its reporting was not influenced by Chambers. In the same post, it said Chambers and Babochki had donated $1 million to Palestinian causes.
Sovereign Media is additionally part of a media coalition with another Babochki-backed project, Vox Ummah.
Vox Ummah is an Islamic ‘anti-imperialist’ site founded in May 2025 with support from Chambers.
Its editor and political director is Shabbir Rizvi, who is also a contributor to Sovereign Media and a member of Babochki. He also maintains connections to pro-terror media networks, serving as a contributor to the pro-Hezbollah Al Mayadeen and Iranian state media outlet Press TV.
“The Palestine Action US-linked media network shows how radical groups attempt to influence populations beyond just physical acts, but also through the advancement of propaganda outlets and mouthpieces,” Honest Reporting told the Post.
“The close ties of Iranian state media with the Babochki-backed news coalition also show how these propaganda efforts are being enhanced by state actors. The extended Palestine Action US network should be scrutinized not only after its terrorism designation, but also for suspected ties to Iran."

Mayoral candidates grappled with the use of the word “genocide” to describe the Gaza war and how Israel’s foreign policy intersects with domestic issues as they vied Tuesday night for votes at an event organized by the Jewish community.
City Council member Nithya Raman told the packed audience at the Skirball Cultural Center that she understood that the word “genocide” was painful to many Jewish people.
“I understand its historical context and the weight of that historical context for the world, not just for the room but for the entire world,” said Raman, who is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, a group that has campaigned for candidates who are strongly critical of Israel.
“I used it because other experts have used it to describe what’s happening and because I felt compelled to speak out about issues that we saw, the images that are coming, the targeting of hospitals, the deaths of children.” Israel denies deliberately targeting hospitals, and rejects the charge of genocide.
With mail-in ballots headed to voters this week and the Nov. 3 runoff election approaching, the forum gave Jewish voters a chance to hear directly from Raman and her Democratic incumbent opponent Karen Bass. California has a “jungle primary” system, in which the top two candidates in the primary - whatever their party - advance to the runoff, which means Democrats frequently face off in the general election.
Candidates further discuss homelessness, disaster preparedness, social safety net
Alongside issues like Jewish safety, antisemitism, and Israel, the candidates also spoke of their views on homelessness, disaster preparedness, and the city’s strained social safety net.
Raman is vying to unseat Bass, a Democrat who has led America’s second-largest city since 2022. A recent poll showed Raman leading Bass by 11 points, though roughly a third of voters remain undecided.
The forum - organized by the Jewish Federation Los Angeles - featured back-to-back 45-minute conversations between each candidate and the local journalist Alex Cohen. About 1,000 people attended the event, which was also livestreamed.
The sharpest exchanges centered on Israel and antisemitism. Raman, as she has in the past, called the war in Gaza a genocide. Bass said she rejected that characterization.
When asked to define genocide, Raman said she was “not an expert on those issues,” but added that she had relied on genocide scholars, including Israeli scholars, who have used the term.
Raman, interviewed first, was asked about her characterization of Israel’s actions and her appearance on left-wing streamer Hasan Piker’s show. Piker has been a vocal critic of Israel and has made derogatory statements about the country, such as calling it “Jewish ISIS.”
Raman said political candidates need to reach voters wherever they are, noting that Piker’s audience includes many young Angelenos.
Raman went on to discuss her response to the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel, saying she was the first person at LA City Hall to condemn what happened. Raman said she wants Jewish and Israeli-American residents to feel safe in Los Angeles. Los Angeles is believed to have the largest Israeli-American population in the country.
“This city deserves to feel safe for every single resident,” said Raman, who represents Council District 4, which includes neighborhoods such as Silver Lake and Los Feliz as well as portions of the San Fernando Valley, one of Los Angeles’ major Jewish population centers.
Asked about Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions, a protest movement targeting Israel’s economy, Raman said, “I think boycott, divestment and sanctions, the BDS movement, is a legitimate form of peaceful protest. I support people’s ability to protest,” and she cited the First Amendment.
Bass, when asked what she would do if an Israel sanctions policy came before the City Council, said, “the pencil would hit,” an apparent reference to a veto.
Asked if she thought Israel’s actions in Gaza constituted genocide, Bass said, “No, I don’t.” But she also emphasized the limits of the mayor’s role in international affairs. “When I think of foreign affairs, especially conflicts, my focus is on how they impact the city of LA,” she said, adding that her responsibility as mayor is to keep Angelenos safe.
She also referenced her personal connections to Los Angeles’ Jewish community, noting that growing up she attended public schools alongside many Jewish peers, where she encountered her friends’ Holocaust survivor parents and grandparents with numbers tattooed on their arms.
Mayoral candidates discuss antisemitism, Jewish communal security
The candidates also addressed antisemitism and Jewish communal security.
Bass said Los Angeles does not have enough police officers and described public safety as “the No. 1 issue” she must address as mayor. She said her administration has pursued LAPD recruitment while also expanding alternative responses for situations that do not require armed officers.
Asked specifically about implementing California’s new Safe Worship Zone Act, which bars protests within 100 feet of religious institutions, Bass said she would convene the city’s working group on Jewish community safety and its interfaith council, then work with LAPD to determine how to implement it. Much of the organized Jewish community began advocating for the state law after a pro-Palestinian protest targeted Los Angeles’ Wilshire Boulevard Temple, while children were on campus.
Bass said her administration had already called for increased patrols and security around Jewish holidays and community events. Raman similarly condemned the rise in antisemitism, including in her own district, and said antisemitic hatred comes from “every side of the political spectrum.”
Raman said, “As a progressive elected representative, as someone who’s more on the leftward side of the spectrum, I never want progressive politics to be conflated with antisemitism.”
Throughout her 45-minute conversation, Raman repeatedly sought to shift the discussion toward local issues, including housing, homelessness and disaster response.
Bass devoted much of her time to those same issues, including lessons from the January 2025 Palisades wildfire and the need for better disaster prevention. She called the fire one of the worst moments she had experienced and said the city of Los Angeles and Los Angeles County had not been adequately prepared for the extreme weather event. Bass was out of town when the fire started, and her initial response to it has drawn widespread criticism.
She also acknowledged shortcomings in her administration’s handling of homelessness, saying she entered office knowing the system was dysfunctional but did not realize “how profoundly dysfunctional” it was. She said she now supports making the city more independent from the county on homeless services.
Rabbi Noah Farkas, president and CEO of Jewish Federation Los Angeles, said the forum “gave attendees a deeper understanding of where the candidates stand on key priorities facing our city and community,” and “will help them make the most informed choice at the ballot box on Nov. 3.”
Los Angeles is home to the nation’s second-largest Jewish community, with about 600,000 Jews residing in the metro area. The local Jewish federation organized Tuesday’s forum in partnership with Skirball and the local branches of the American Jewish Committee, the Anti-Defamation League, and Jewish Family Service.

Far-right figure James Fishback likens abortion to Holocaust, demands US decouple from Israel

James Fishback, a fierce critic of Israel and a far-right politician, offered scathing remarks about the Jewish state and likened abortion to the Holocaust during a Tuesday evening address hosted by the University of Mississippi’s Turning Point USA chapter.
Fishback, a former GOP gubernatorial candidate in Florida, recalled that earlier this summer the Combat Antisemitism Movement flagged as antisemitic one of his X/Twitter posts describing abortion as a holocaust.
“Abortion is a holocaust, and by every single historical metric available, it was worse than the other one,” Fishback said, claiming that “61 million children have been killed in the womb since Roe v. Wade was wrongly decided in 1973.”
He also had harsh words for the state of Israel. “It is time for President Trump to call [Prime Minister] Benjamin Netanyahu and cut him off. We must decouple from Israel to save America,” he added.
The 31-year-old investor is a newcomer to politics, entering the scene last November when he announced his candidacy in Florida’s Republican primary for governor. Fishback’s prospects in the race were seen as a long shot from the get-go, as he had no experience and was up against Byron Donalds, a congressman who had secured the backing of President Donald Trump.
'If you're really bad they'll call you an antisemite'
Throughout his campaign, Fishback espoused much of the language that has become popular among far-right activists, including antisemitic terms like “goyslop,” a slur used by neo-Nazis to blame Jews for low-quality, ultra-processed foods.
Ultimately, Fishback suffered a massive loss, placing a distant third with just 10.5% of voter support. He trailed far behind the winner, Donalds, and Jay Collins, who earned 47.8% and 25.2%, respectively.
But while Fishback lost the gubernatorial primary in a landslide, political analysts have highlighted his success in winning over far-right Gen-Zers, providing a window into the possible future of the MAGA movement if not the entire Republican Party.
A Quantus Insights poll in early August, prior to the primary, indicated that Fishback commanded 26% of voters ages 18 to 29 and 38% of voters ages 30 to 44, according to the Algemeiner. Donalds and Collins each held just 21% in the younger bracket and 28% and 14%, respectively, in the older one.
Many Republican Jews had been hoping that Fishback’s loss would end his influence, but his continued popularity among far-right youth shows he hasn’t disappeared from the scene. In addition to Tuesday’s invitation, Fishback has upcoming speeches at Mississippi State University, Auburn University, the University of South Alabama, and the University of Alabama in the coming days.
During his campaign, he repeatedly embraced the perspectives of ultra-conservative political commentators and personalities like Nick Fuentes and Tucker Carlson, while championing anti-immigration policies and conspiracy theories about the “great replacement of American workers.”
As for Israel, he repeatedly targeted the country and its supporters, declaring that “it is not antisemitic to criticize Israel.” He warned in a campaign video that calling Netanyahu a war criminal or accusing Israel of committing genocide could get the accuser “convicted of antisemitism.”
Born and raised in Florida to an immigrant mother from Colombia and a landscaper-turned-bus driver father, Fishback attended Georgetown University but dropped out after two years.
Fishback doesn’t seem daunted by his failed campaign, embracing continued opportunities to appear in public and court young voters who align with his views. At his Monday event, he not only delivered an hour-long speech, but he also stayed and continued to livestream for an equal amount of time to answer questions and take photographs with every single student who approached him.
Fishback and Turning Point USA
This particular event was a Pick Up the Mic forum arranged by members of the University of Mississippi chapter of Turning Point USA, the organization founded by the late Charlie Kirk.
Kirk had established Turning Point USA as a way of connecting to young voters, particularly college men, whom he viewed as previously overlooked by the right. During his many years overseeing Turning Point, Kirk repeatedly clashed with Fuentes, the white nationalist and Hitler admirer whom Fishback has often defended.
But after Kirk’s assassination last year, Turning Point has emerged as a central arena for shifting debate within the Republican Party surrounding Israel. At times, those arguing to cut off US support have employed antisemitic tropes.
Although Fishback’s social media links his college tour stops to Turning Point USA, they do not appear on the group’s national website. Instead, these forums appear to be organized by the local campus chapters of the organization.
The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reached out to Turning Point for clarification about this affiliation, but did not receive a response.
Turning Point’s nationally recognized “America: Love It or Leave It Tour,” which is happening across the country over the next few weeks, features speakers like Erika Kirk, the organization’s new leader and widow of Charlie Kirk, as well as Donald Trump Jr., Glenn Beck, Tulsi Gabbard and Ben Shapiro, the Jewish conservative political commentator who founded The Daily Wire.
Shapiro previously described Fishback as “a serial liar and fraud” but did not respond to a request from JTA for comment.
Turning Point events have become a hub for “America First” ideology and, since Kirk’s death, have featured several audience questions on Israel that went viral. Notably, Vice President JD Vance declared that Israel does not “control this president” in response to a question about the country’s influence on Trump.
Back at Monday’s University of Mississippi forum, Fishback slammed immigration policies on both sides of the aisle — Republicans for too few mass deportations and Democrats for an influx of foreign workers — Fishback declared, “It’s time to stand up and tell both parties that no, American jobs are for Americans only.”
He noted, however, that making such demands could result in a person being labeled a racist or misogynist, and that “if you’re really bad they’ll call you an antisemite.” Stressing that he condemns “all forms of religious hatred,” he maintained that “the most virulent” type is the hostility “against Christians in this country.”
Fishback blamed Israel and the inability of the US to “tell them no” for drawing the country into the war with Iran. That war, he argued, has pushed gas prices higher.
“Two hundred and fifty years ago, our founding fathers declared their independence from a foreign power,” Fishback said. “In 2026, our leaders must declare their independence from a foreign power called Israel.”

Indian flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar unlocked cockpit, named assailant, while wounded - report

The flydubai pilot who was stabbed on flight FZ1073, Indian national Capt. Smit Machchhar, reportedly unlocked the cockpit door before losing consciousness, passenger Yaniv Hayoun told Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu when the two spoke at Ben-Gurion Airport on Wednesday.
Hayoun told Netanyahu that the cockpit door was unlocked, but Machchhar was close enough to the door that it was difficult to open. "My conclusion is that he resourcefully managed to open the door for us before he collapsed," he explained.
Netanyahu later expanded on this in a Twitter/X statement praising Machchhar's heroism.
"Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," the prime minister wrote. "He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals."
Several passengers, including Israeli dentist Shota Musayev, administered first-aid care to Machchhar, keeping him alive until he was hospitalized in Saudi Arabia after the plane made an emergency landing at Tabuk Airport. Musayev told Walla that Machchhar was badly wounded, bleeding heavily from his head and hands. The dentist was able to stop the bleeding and told Walla that his condition did stabilize after that, but deteriorated once again as the plane was landing.
Musayev also said that Machchhar was able to verbally communicate that the other pilot stabbed him.
Machchhar is an experienced pilot, specializing in training new recruits
According to several Indian news outlets, Machchhar is a Gujarati Indian from Mumbai. According to his LinkedIn profile, he spent over a decade flying for Indian airline SpiceJet, where he also served as a training captain and mentor for new pilots, before moving to flydubai. His profile also notes that he accumulated about 9,750 flying hours on the 737-800 and the 737 MAX 8 and 9.
The LinkedIn profile also indicates that Machchhar is a father.
The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was "admitted in a hospital in Tabuk city in northwest Saudi Arabia and [is] receiving necessary medical attention."
The embassy said that while they have not received a full update on the pilot's health, he is reported to be in stable condition. Officials are also in touch with Machchhar's family, the embassy added.

‘It was the first election where I could vote — and didn’t know the result in advance.’ Meet Russian-born Berlin politician Elizaveta Kapinos.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:01:39 UTC
05:01:39 KST

‘It was the first election where I could vote — and didn’t know the result in advance.’ Meet Russian-born Berlin politician Elizaveta Kapinos.
Voting in elections for Berlin’s House of Representatives (the city parliament) and district councils ended on September 20. The vote decided who will govern Germany’s capital for the next five years. Among the winners was Elizaveta Kapinos, a Russian woman who moved to Germany in 2020. She was ninth on the Greens’ party list in Tempelhof-Schöneberg, where the party won 14 district council seats. Meduza spoke with Kapinos about her childhood in Kamchatka, her political career in Berlin, and working with Alternative for Germany (AfD).
‘Berliners aren’t as optimistic about the future anymore’
— Congratulations on winning a seat! How do you feel?
— Thank you. I’m feeling a lot of things right now. On the one hand, an intense election campaign is over, and I feel like I can relax. On the other, everything is just beginning. The joy of winning outweighs my thoughts about the work ahead, though I know it’s only beginning, but I can still take a little time to rest.
— Were you surprised by the election results and how the Greens did?
— We were following the [pre-election] polls, but the Left Party did better than we expected. Congratulations to them on their victory — and especially to their candidate for mayor, Elif [Eralp]. They ran an excellent campaign. Of course, we [the Greens] wanted a result like that, too. But I think we did really well, despite the growing popularity of AfD and similar parties. A full 15% of Berliners voted for us.
In Tempelhof-Schöneberg, where I ran for the district council, we received the most votes and won 14 seats. For the past five years, the district has been headed by someone from our party. So the Greens’ election result shows that people in our district were happy with what we were doing and want us to continue.
— You were born in Kamchatka, and now you’re about to represent residents of Berlin’s Tempelhof-Schöneberg district. That’s quite an unusual journey. What do you remember about your childhood?
— It really is a long way to Berlin. I think of myself as a Kamchatka native first, and I have very warm memories of it. I was born in a small town, then moved to Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, where I lived until I was 15. Growing up somewhere with an ocean and volcanoes had a big influence on me. Kamchatka has a special energy that gives those of us born there a boost. Of course, I have childhood memories that other children from Russia don’t. For example, my friends and I would talk about flying “to the mainland” — that’s what people in Kamchatka call the rest of Russia. I had classmates who had never left the peninsula because the only way to leave is by plane. It makes you feel like you live in a separate, magical land.
One of the things I miss in Berlin now is snow. Kamchatka isn’t as cold as many people think, but because we were close to the ocean, we got enormous amounts of snow. I remember sometimes not being able to leave for school — so much snow had fallen overnight that we had to wait for someone to clear the snow from outside the door.
— How did you end up in Berlin?
— First, I moved to Moscow to study. When I finished school, I didn’t know what I wanted to do, but I was interested in subjects that brought together society, languages, and history. I enrolled in the international relations program at the Higher School of Economics because Kamchatka didn’t have any suitable programs at the time.
I first came to Berlin on an exchange in 2018 because I was studying German at university. On that very first visit, I fell in love with the city and decided this was where I wanted to live. After graduating, I enrolled in a master’s program in political science at the Free University of Berlin, and I stayed.
— What made you fall in love with the city?
— Berlin is unlike other German cities. That’s probably why I like it. I first came here in September: people were still sitting in parks, rainbow flags hung from balconies, and there was graffiti supporting refugees on the walls. It was paradise for a student with progressive views. I also found myself in a lively student community — students at our university were constantly organizing protests, performances, fairs, and concerts, and I got swept up in it.
Hi, I’m Katya.
I’ve been running Meduza’s crowdfunding since 2021. Today, supporting Meduza is a crime in Russia. You can be sent to prison just for donating. We’re still able to do our work thanks to thousands of our Russian readers who now live abroad. But even they’re no longer safe.
Imagine you’ve left Russia, but then your mom becomes seriously ill. It could be your last chance to see her, so of course you go home. At the border, you’re interrogated. Officers hack into your phone and search for any trace that you’ve donated to Meduza.
The Kremlin is counting on that fear, and it’s working. People are afraid to donate. I’m afraid for our supporters, because any one of them could end up in prison. And I’m afraid for Meduza. Without crowdfunding, we simply can’t continue. So if you live outside Russia and don’t have to worry that donating to Meduza could keep you from going home to your family, I’m asking for your help. Please support our work.
— It’s been eight years since your first visit. How has Berlin changed in that time?
— It’s not just the city that’s changed — I have, too. I’m no longer a student who only sees the good in everything around her. Moving to another country has its phases: after the initial overwhelming joy comes a difficult period, and then things level out — your feelings about the city settle down, and you become more objective. I don’t feel the same euphoria about Berlin anymore, but I still love it very much. Berlin is still the open, progressive city it was before. But people here are more afraid of the future now than they were eight years ago.
There have been a lot of crises over those years that have changed the capital and the way people live. The cost of living in Berlin has risen noticeably, and that has a big effect on its residents. Unlike other capitals, Berlin isn’t the richest city in its country. A lot of artists, dancers, people in theater, and nonprofit workers live here. Their work doesn’t pay very well, but it shapes the city’s character.
You can see the price increases even with döner kebabs. When I first arrived, a döner cost €3–€3.50; now it’s €7–€7.50. Everything is getting more expensive, including rent. A lot of people say Berlin has gotten dirtier over the years. I don’t think so — there was always trash in the city. I don’t want to get pessimistic and say that “everything used to be better.” But Berliners aren’t as optimistic about the future anymore — people have a lot of fears and worries now.
— How do those worries affect the direction the city is taking? And who its residents vote for?
— The election results show that most Berliners vote for progressive policies, despite all the crises. A lot of parties on the right appeal to nostalgia — they talk about how bad everything has gotten and how to go back to the past. They’re always against something — curbside barriers, for example, or bike lanes — and I’m not sure what kind of future they’re actually proposing. By contrast, I like that the progressive parties that together won a majority [in the state election] offer a concrete vision of the future. And I’m glad Berliners want to move in that direction, so there’s definitely hope. We live in a world of multiple, overlapping crises. It’s easy to feel like you’re at the mercy of events. And the best way to fight that feeling is to take action yourself and see the effect of what you do. That’s why I decided to become a district council member.
— Tell me more about that. When and why did you decide to go into politics? Did you want to do it when you lived in Russia?
— For a long time when I lived in Russia, politics seemed like a closed world that you couldn’t just walk into. I didn’t grow up thinking I’d become a politician. But I did get actively involved in Russian politics as a student through women’s rights activism — that was what the first rally I ever attended, in Sokolniki Park, was about.
When I moved to Germany, I started following local politics closely. But it didn’t occur to me that I could hold elected office here. Partly because, in Russia, I simply didn’t know anyone who had become a politician or run for office. I remember very clearly the moment [in November 2024] when I decided to join a party. I was on a work trip and went for a beer with colleagues after a long event. People in the pub looked worried — [former German Chancellor Olaf] Scholz was about to give a speech. We pulled up a livestream on a phone, and Scholz announced that the coalition was breaking up.
My colleagues and I started discussing what was happening, and I realized Germany was heading in a direction I didn’t want. Something clicked: I wanted to help shape events myself through the party system, even if my contribution was small. That day, I decided to join a party.
— Why did you choose the Greens? Did you consider other parties?
— There were parties I definitely didn’t like: AfD, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), and the Christian Social Union (CSU) — I don’t share their views. Among the remaining parties, the Greens stood out for several reasons.
First, they had the clearest idea of where they wanted to go. I liked being able to work toward an inspiring vision of the future rather than just complain about how bad everything was. Second, protecting the climate matters to me. We can spend a long time discussing tax rates or whether to take housing away from companies and redistribute it to residents. But if we lose our planet, none of those conversations will matter.
The Greens also have a great approach to how climate change affects people. The party recognizes that climate change hits people with low incomes, people in poor health, and older people hardest. That matters to me, too.
Third, it was important to me that the Greens had always supported Ukraine. The Left Party [Die Linke] has historically had a complicated position on this issue because of its overall approach to international relations.
— How does joining a party work in Germany? Is it difficult?
— It turned out to be easier than I thought. First, you can attend any Greens event even if you aren’t a party member. When I found that out, I went to a party meeting to select candidates for the Bundestag [Germany’s federal parliament].
I saw the candidates, listened to their speeches, and stayed until the results were announced — it was all very interesting. There was a nice atmosphere — people were polite and relaxed. They’d set up a potluck buffet, and everyone had brought something: some people made salads, others baked pastries. The organizers had also set aside a space where you could leave your children. For example, if a mother with three children comes to vote, she can leave them with a babysitter during the event.
When I saw all that, I thought, “Great! I want to be part of this, too.” Then I just filled out an application online and paid the membership dues. With the Greens, your dues are proportional to your salary — at least 1% of your after-tax pay, and you can pay more if you want. But nobody asks you for proof of income — you enter how much you earn on the form yourself.
The main thing is that you can join the party without German citizenship. A lot of people in my district branch don’t have a German passport, and I joined before I got mine in spring 2025. By law, only German citizens can vote to select candidates within a party. But the Greens get around that restriction: first, all party members vote, including those without citizenship, and then there’s a final vote among members who are citizens — they “confirm” the results of the first vote.
— How important is the Greens’ support for migrants to you? You didn’t mention it when you listed your reasons for joining the party.
— When I joined, I didn’t yet know how important this issue was to the Greens. We should work on our public image so that people outside the party understand that.
The Greens want to give people who don’t have a voice in politics a chance to be heard. That’s why the party has one of the highest proportions of members who were born outside Germany or have at least one parent born in another country — what’s known as a Migrationshintergrund, or migration background. I feel very willkommen — welcome, in the literal sense of the word. It’s as though the party is actually saying “Welcome!” to you, even if you don’t have a German passport.
The Greens have a lot of elected representatives at different levels who aren’t native Germans, and it’s also the only party with more women than men in its Bundestag delegation. The party doesn’t just want to give underrepresented groups a voice in politics — it has real ways to make that happen. And I’m living proof.
‘It’s easier to talk to me about your problems than to your average Herr Müller’
— Why did you decide to run in this year’s election?
— During the pandemic, when I had a lot of free time, I came across a program called Diversify online. It aims to help people who are underrepresented in German politics gain political experience. I was accepted into the program and invited to choose a mentor from any party. I approached Marianne Burkert-Eulitz, a Greens member of Berlin’s city parliament, and she agreed. There was no formal structure to the “mentoring” — we just met in cafés and talked about different things. Marianne kept encouraging me to get involved in politics: she invited me to events, introduced me to people, and explained how the party worked. Thanks to her, I stopped thinking politics was only for Germans and decided to run for office. It was Marianne who helped me with the speech I gave at our district’s internal party election.
The party was very supportive, and [after the internal party election] a lot of people told me how glad they were that someone whose first language isn’t German and whose surname isn’t German wanted to represent the Greens. A lot of people in Berlin don’t have German citizenship — around 25%. And first-generation migrants — people who moved to the country themselves — are very poorly represented in Germany’s government institutions.
— You ran in Tempelhof-Schöneberg. What kind of district is it? How long have you lived there?
— I’ve lived in Tempelhof-Schöneberg since I first came to Berlin. So, given how much of my life I’ve spent here, I consider myself a local. Our district is one of Berlin’s largest, with the population of a small city. It’s very diverse and stretches south from central Berlin. The central part of the district, Schöneberg, is known for its hip bars and restaurants. Nollendorfkiez is a neighborhood famous for its queer venues and rich queer culture. There’s also Kurfürstenstraße, where there are problems with drug addiction and prostitution.
I live in Tempelhof, which strikes a nice balance: it isn’t as gentrified as many other neighborhoods, and it has architecture from every period. There are the famous older apartment buildings known as Altbau, Nazi-era architecture, and West German prefabricated apartment blocks. South of Tempelhof are houses with gardens, where [well-off] families with cars live.
All kinds of Berliners live in Tempelhof-Schöneberg. Working in politics in a district like that isn’t easy — it’s hard to appeal to everyone. But you have to look at residents’ different interests and ways of life and try to take everyone into account.
— If I understand correctly, you didn’t have a platform of your own. But the Greens have a platform for each district, which you’ll be putting into practice. Which parts of it matter most to you?
— I wouldn’t say I don’t have my own agenda. Of course, I’ll be implementing the Greens’ platform, but there are areas that interest me most.
Women’s rights and the rights of vulnerable groups — those who suffer most from rising prices in the city or from climate change — remain especially important to me. For example, I really want us to be able to increase the number of spaces in women’s shelters in our district. Those shelters previously had their funding cut.
During crises, violence against women and queer people increases. In Germany, and even in Berlin, it’s at historically high levels. Through my political work, I want to support the places and people who help survivors of violence.
I also care about buildings, because that’s the field I work in. A lot of buildings in our district aren’t energy-efficient, and that needs to change. We’ll see what we can do at the district level. It’s important to me that our district be environmentally friendly and accessible to everyone. Since we aren’t managing to slow climate change, we need to adapt. For example, we need to plant more trees, because being outside in sweltering heat without any trees is unbearable. This summer in Berlin was very hot — it was especially hard on older people and people with children. After all, women picking their children up from daycare often have to be outside in that heat.
— How did you prepare for the election?
— The main way we campaign is by talking to people on the street. We set up somewhere busy in the district, hand out flyers, tell people about the candidates, and just talk to them. Another way to reach voters is canvassing door to door. For this election, we canvassed 42,000 apartments. I can’t even imagine how many steps our party members took, considering how few elevators there are in Berlin. Personally, I canvassed 50 apartments an hour.
Another important part of the campaign is posters. If you’ve been to Berlin before any election, you’ll have noticed that every pole in the city is covered with posters from several parties. This year, I put up posters myself — it’s a real acrobatic feat: you have to climb a tall ladder and carefully thread special cords through the poster to attach it to the pole. You can only start putting up posters at noon on Sunday [August 2]. I think Berliners find it funny to see supporters of different parties pouring out from every direction at midday and competing to see who can claim a lamppost first.
As the election gets closer, the schedule gets busier. My day often went like this: I’d get up at seven in the morning, go hand out flyers, then head to work. After work, I’d canvass apartments, then go to bed and do it all again the next day. But it’s great — you meet a lot of people in the district who are really interested and want to make an informed choice.
— How did Germans feel about you essentially asking them to vote for a candidate from Russia?
— I didn’t get any negative comments about that. People are pretty neutral about it [being from Russia] these days. Some could hear from the way I spoke that German wasn’t my first language and asked me about my background. A lot of people admired my courage — they were happy to see someone from outside Germany getting involved in politics.
— You moved to Germany as an adult. How does that affect the problems you notice in the city?
— On some issues, we [migrants] have a fresh perspective because we have something to compare Germany with. Sometimes the comparison favors Germany, sometimes it doesn’t. I think migrants sometimes notice things Germans don’t see because they’re used to them. For example, public spaces here aren’t as well lit. My friends from Moscow often told me they sometimes felt unsafe at night in Berlin. But the poor lighting is often because of rules to protect birds and animals, which the Moscow authorities didn’t worry about much.
Migrants also have expertise in areas Germans have no experience with. For example, Germans don’t go to immigration offices, and a lot of people think those offices have been so bad precisely because native-born Germans don’t use them. If they did, they’d raise hell right away. Language courses, getting qualifications recognized, and so on — Germans don’t face these problems, so the perspectives of people with immigrant backgrounds matter here. People often don’t talk about problems in these areas because they don’t know how to seek help or whom to contact.
Even though I won’t be able to influence the immigration authority directly, I hope somebody will find it easier to talk to me about their problems than to your average Herr Müller.
— What powers do district council members actually have?
— Unlike the city parliament, district councils don’t pass laws. They can make demands of the district administration, propose improvements, and oversee its work. Council members can request information from the administration, oversee its work, review budgets, and help set the district’s priorities.
Berlin has a problem: a lot of things fall under both city and district authority. Take a road or a school, for example — authority over it is shared by the city and the district. That often leads to responsibility being passed back and forth [between the city parliament and the district council], because nobody knows exactly whose job it is.
Districts definitely have responsibility for local transportation policy. The simplest example is a question like “Where will the new bike lane go?” But districts also decide where roads and parking spaces go and how they’re laid out. Revenue from parking goes into the district budget, not the budget for all of Berlin. The district is also responsible for the condition of buildings and can approve or reject construction plans, and so on.
— What will you do first in your new role?
— We’ll keep working on the issues our party’s previous council group left unfinished, because politics doesn’t stop when an election is over. One issue carried over from the previous council that matters to me is the plan to build a Jugendzentrum [a center for children and young people] in our district. For a long time, the center didn’t have a permanent building. A decision was finally made to build one, but a conflict arose between the organization responsible and local residents. Residents don’t like the prospect of having a center next door that hosts rock concerts for young people in the evenings.
I can understand residents who are worried about possible noise. At the same time, I think building the center is a very important project, because there are hardly any places left in the city where young people can spend time with their peers. I want to find a compromise so the center finally gets a space, and residents don’t feel the decision was made without their say.
— Turning to another difficult issue: proposals to develop Tempelhof Field in your district have drawn attention even from people who don’t live in Berlin. Where do you stand, and how can you influence the former airfield’s future?
— Let me explain the context first. After the airport closed, the Berlin authorities held a referendum [in 2014], and residents voted to leave the field as it was. In recent years, there’s been a lot of support for building on the field, including from the CDU. If not all of it, then at least “around the edges.” The Greens oppose those plans. That’s an unpopular position, including among Russian speakers, so it’s important to me to explain in detail why I think this way.
First, there’s the democratic argument: people decided in a referendum not to build on the field. It’s a unique space that, according to studies, serves as our city’s lungs.
Second, it’s simply a wonderful place: people rollerblade and cycle, and you can barbecue and garden there. The former airport building hosts concerts, operas, and circus festivals. An ecosystem of its own has developed there, with animals, insects, and plants.
At the same time, there’s none of the infrastructure needed for housing beneath the field — things like sewers or power lines. So building housing would mean digging up the field and installing all that infrastructure from scratch. That means the apartments wouldn’t be cheap. And really, there’s no way to build cheaply on the field — imagine how good the view from the window would be.
Developing Tempelhof Field won’t solve Berlin’s affordable housing problem, because that housing won’t be ready anytime soon, and it won’t be affordable. The district council also doesn’t have much influence over this situation. Although the field is in our district, Berlin’s city government decides whether it can be developed. All we can do is try to influence Berlin’s parliament through the district leadership and persuade its members to keep respecting the referendum results.
‘My German peers don’t realize that democracy is fragile’
— What did running for office give you? How did it change your sense of yourself and your relationship with the city?
— It gave me a sense of agency. I started to feel that I could make a difference, and the feeling of helplessness eased. Climate catastrophe, economic crisis, the rise of the right — all those things worry me. As right-wing parties become more popular in Germany, there’s more and more anti-migrant and even dehumanizing rhetoric. That’s partly why I decided to go into politics. As someone from Russia, I’d seen where those attitudes lead, and I was afraid something similar could happen in my new home. Maybe if I hadn’t won a district council seat, my answer would be less positive. But even the process itself — talking to people with different opinions, working with volunteers — is very inspiring and a wonderful antidote to hopelessness.
— AfD has been getting strong results across Germany — even your district council will have seven of its members. How do you see your future work together?
— It’s hard for me to imagine a situation where we’d vote the same way. I doubt we’ll agree on anything or work on anything together — that sounds like pure fantasy. But parliamentary work doesn’t depend on everyone agreeing. It depends on coalitions of several parties.
The distribution of votes means AfD will even be able to appoint a municipal official roughly equivalent to a minister — a Stadtrat — this year. That’s another challenge for us, and it’s important for us, the progressive parties and politicians on the left, to work together. If we’re divided by conflicts, we won’t be able to achieve our goals, and even more people will say, “Let’s vote for some party at the opposite end of the spectrum as a protest — maybe they’ll shake things up.”
That’s a very dangerous trend. A lot of people don’t realize they’re playing with fire. People who grew up under authoritarian regimes understand the danger better. Historically, authoritarian forces first come to power democratically, then dismantle the system piece by piece, and after that, you can’t remove them anymore. A lot of people say, “If AfD doesn’t do anything good, we’ll just elect another party next time.” As a Russian, I tell them, “Guys, in five years, you might not have that chance anymore.”
— Russia held its State Duma elections at the same time as Berlin’s elections. Were you following them? What do you think of the result?
— Of course I follow events in Russia — I care about what’s happening in the country. I also think what’s happening in Russia holds a lot of lessons for Germany and other European countries. I often tell my German friends, “While you still have the chance, do something — through government institutions, activism, demonstrations.” I’m afraid people my age who grew up in Germany don’t realize that democracy is fragile. They think, “The sky is blue, the grass is green, democracy exists and always will.” But when you look at Russia, you realize that isn’t true. Of course, the election result in Russia didn’t surprise me. I like to tell my German friends that the Berlin elections were the first ones where I could vote and didn’t know the result in advance. That’s a new experience for me.

The surprising link between resilience and challenging ayahuasca experiences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:00:44 UTC
05:00:44 KST

A longitudinal study of people attending ayahuasca retreats found that those with higher levels of resilience before the retreat tended to report somewhat more intense challenging experiences during their ayahuasca ceremonies. More resilient participants also showed a stronger link between these difficult experiences and searching for meaning in life a month later. The paper was published in Psychedelic Medicine.
Ayahuasca is a psychoactive brew traditionally used by Indigenous communities in the Amazon for religious, spiritual, and therapeutic purposes. Its acute effects can include mystical experiences and psychological insights, but also difficult physical symptoms such as nausea and vomiting and emotional reactions such as fear, paranoia, or distressing hallucinations. These adverse experiences are referred to as challenges or challenging experiences.
People vary considerably in how they interpret these challenging experiences. Some describe them as harmful “bad trips,” while others view them as meaningful parts of healing or spiritual transformation. Individual characteristics such as age, previous psychedelic experience, motivation, mindset, and psychological state can influence both the immediate experience and its longer-term effects. The social and environmental settings in which ayahuasca is consumed can also shape its psychological impact.
In this context, resilience, a person’s capacity to adapt positively and recover when confronted with stressful or difficult experiences, might be particularly important. People with greater resilience might be better able to engage constructively with difficult emotions and experiences during ayahuasca use, potentially influencing whether challenging psychedelic effects ultimately contribute to positive psychospiritual outcomes.
Study author Yitong Xin and colleagues explored whether the acute effects of ayahuasca, and particularly its challenging effects, depend on a person’s resilience. More specifically, they examined the associations between resilience measured at the start of an ayahuasca retreat and acute challenging experiences reported at the end of the retreat, as well as whether resilience moderates the relationship between these experiences and psychospiritual outcomes reported 1 month after the retreat.
Data were collected between August 2022 and August 2023 at two Soltara Healing Center retreat locations, in Costa Rica and Peru. A representative of the Soltara Healing Center helped the researchers recruit participants. Of the 291 retreat guests who met the study criteria, 267 enrolled and completed a survey at the start of the retreat. Of these, 247 also completed the survey at the end of the retreat, and 233 completed it 1 month after the retreat. Participants’ average age was 41 years, and 56% were women. Most were White (83%), lived in North America (87%), and had a college education (95%).
In the surveys, study participants reported their demographic data and completed assessments of resilience (the Resilience Scale for Adults), challenging ayahuasca experiences (the Challenging Experience Questionnaire, the Ayahuasca Experience Inventory-Discomfort Subscale, and the Ayahuasca Purging Experience), meaning in life (the Meaning in Life Questionnaire), and personality (the Big Five Inventory-10). Study participants also reported on their previous use of psychedelic compounds and completed a questionnaire assessing the effects of the setting on them during the ayahuasca experience.
Results showed that 79% of participants had past experience with psychedelics, while 22% had used ayahuasca before. More than half of the participants reported at least moderately intense challenging experiences such as feelings that led to crying, body shaking or trembling, emotional or physical suffering, feelings of grief, and heart palpitations. In contrast, fewer than 5% of participants reported feeling that people were plotting against them. Nearly three-quarters of participants reported at least moderate exhaustion after taking ayahuasca.
Individuals with higher neuroticism (i.e., lower emotional stability) tended to report somewhat stronger acute challenging experiences. More resilient individuals also tended to report somewhat more intense acute challenging experiences.
Additionally, resilience measured at the start of the retreat moderated the link between challenging ayahuasca experiences and searching for meaning in life. More specifically, the more resilient a person was, the stronger the association between having an intense challenging experience and searching for meaning 1 month after the retreat. The same was true for uncomfortable ayahuasca-related experiences: their association with searching for meaning in life was stronger in more resilient participants. However, resilience did not moderate the links between these experiences and the presence of meaning in life, that is, the sense that one’s life already feels meaningful.
“Findings from this study contribute to our understanding of ayahuasca effects and resilience, highlighting ayahuasca’s therapeutic potential from a resilience standpoint. Evidence from this study could be used by mental health providers in support of preparation or integration therapy practices for individuals who seek out help following their ayahuasca retreat experience or those who are interested in attending retreats,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of ayahuasca experiences. However, it should be noted that the design of the study does not allow any definitive causal inferences to be drawn from the results. In addition, participants were predominantly White, college-educated, North American, and relatively affluent, and all attended retreats run by a single provider, so the findings may not generalize to other populations or settings.
The paper, “Baseline Resilience as a Predictor of Ayahuasca Acute Effects and Moderator of the Relationship between Acute Effects and Psychospiritual Outcomes,” was authored by Yitong Xin, Alan K. Davis, Susan Yoon, and Mo Yee Lee.

US judge rules Wisconsin mosque leader Salah Sarsour can be deported
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

05:00:36 KST

US judge rules Wisconsin mosque leader Salah Sarsour can be deported
Sarsour’s lawyers say the decision threatens free speech protections and plan to fight the ruling.
A United States immigration judge has ruled the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque can be deported under a controversial law that United States President Donald Trump’s administration has used against non-citizens advocating for Palestinian rights.
Judge Jayme Salinardi ruled on Wednesday that Palestinian-born Salah Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, can be removed from the US based in part on a memo by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that “his actions undermine US foreign policy to combat antisemitism around the world”, according to his lawyers.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump admin asks top US court to reverse pro-Palestinian scholar’s release
- list 2 of 4Palestinian Americans meet US lawmakers as Trump seeks $2.8bn for Israel
- list 3 of 4US judge orders release of Palestinian rights advocate detained by ICE
- list 4 of 4Rights groups, Milwaukee leaders slam ICE’s arrest of Palestinian advocate
Sarsour, who has lived in the US for more than three decades, called the ruling “deeply disappointing”.
“I will continue fighting to defend the right to free speech and to stay in the country I have called home for more than three decades,” he told The Associated Press news agency.
His lawyer, Patrick Taurel, strongly rejected the decision.
“I wish the world could see the evidence that we presented and hear the testimony that the court heard because the case we presented compels only one conclusion, which is that Salah is not deportable,” Taurel told reporters on Wednesday.
“He’s done nothing wrong. He should be given back his green card, frankly, with an apology for what’s being done to him.”
The ruling does not mean Sarsour will be immediately deported.
His lawyers have 60 days to argue that sending Sarsour back would put him at risk of torture, which could protect him from deportation under the Convention Against Torture. If they lose, they plan to appeal. Taurel said he can’t be deported while that appeal is pending and will remain in the US for the “foreseeable future”.
‘Extreme deference’
Sarsour was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Milwaukee in March, nine months after Rubio issued a memo declaring him deportable on foreign policy grounds.
The June 2025 memo invoked a rarely-used US law that allows the Secretary of State to seek the deportation of non-citizens whose presence could have “potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences.” The administration has used the same provision against pro-Palestinian activists Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi.
Sarsour’s lawyers criticised the “extreme deference” Salinardi gave to Rubio’s memo. But Taurel said the judge believed his hands were tied by an earlier ruling in Khalil’s case, which found that a letter from the Secretary of State could be enough to make someone deportable on foreign policy grounds.
That meant Salinardi could not look behind Rubio’s decision to examine the evidence supporting it, Taurel said.
“If the Secretary of State says the person is deportable, it is game over,” he told reporters Wednesday.
The government did not win on all of its arguments.
Salinardi rejected its allegation that Sarsour had lied on his green card application. Taurel said the judge also rejected an allegation that Sarsour had falsely claimed to be a US citizen in order to vote.
Al Jazeera reached out to the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security but did not receive responses by the time of publication.
Decades-old convictions
Sarsour is separately fighting the Trump administration in federal court over his detention while his deportation case is ongoing.
A federal judge ordered his release from ICE custody in June after 81 days, questioning why decades-old convictions that US authorities had long known about suddenly justified detaining him. The judge found there was a “substantial” case that the government was retaliating against him for speaking out about Palestinian rights.
The Trump administration has appealed his release, arguing that Sarsour’s convictions in Israel make him a security threat. He was imprisoned in 1988 after confessing to throwing stones and a Molotov cocktail at Israeli military personnel, and was convicted again in 1995 over an attempt to hold weapons.
Sarsour denies the offences, and his lawyers say the confessions were forced through torture. His former lawyer, Jawad Boulos, testified in August that Sarsour was coerced into signing confessions and was not convicted of an offence tying him to a “terrorist” organisation.
Taurel criticised Salinardi for giving what he called “extreme deference” to Israeli government records submitted by ICE, which Sarsour’s lawyers argue were incomplete and relied on confessions obtained through torture.
“A great deal of evidence we presented was ignored,” Taurel said.
The evidence challenged Israel’s military court system, where he said secret evidence can be used and Palestinians can be denied access to lawyers for extended periods.
Luna Droubi, an attorney representing Sarsour, said the case raises broader questions about whether immigrants can speak freely on political issues without fear of being targeted by the government.
“Why raise these arrests now?” she said. “Do I have the right to speak out about issues that matter to me? What if I draw a political cartoon? Am I going to be arrested and detained because of that?”
‘The end of my life’
Sarsour said being deported to the occupied West Bank “means the end of my life”.
His lawyers argue his prior treatment in Israeli custody shows he could face torture if sent back. Taurel said Sarsour’s former lawyer testified that his case stood out because Sarsour told him that Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, had taken him to hospital while in custody.
The judge also named Jordan as a possible destination. Sarsour travelled to the US on a Jordanian-issued document, but his lawyers say he is not a Jordanian citizen and has no right to live there. They believe he could ultimately be returned to the West Bank and Israeli custody if sent to Jordan.

'Alternative Nobel' honours women taking on authoritarian rule, patriarchy and Big Tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:00:25 UTC
05:00:25 KST

Four winners from 200 nominees are honoured for standing up to authoritarian rule, patriarchal violence and unchecked AI development.
The Right Livelihood Award, often called the alternative Nobel Prize, has this year honoured women and women-led organisations who, in the jury's words, confront some of the world's most deeply entrenched power structures: authoritarian rule, patriarchal violence and unregulated artificial intelligence development.
What they have in common is that they stand up to systems that push people to the margins.
Four laureates have been selected from 200 nominees in 72 countries. They will receive the award on 1 December in Stockholm.
One of them is Jalila Haider, a Pakistani human rights lawyer, recognised for breaking barriers as the first female lawyer from the Hazara community and for challenging ethnic, state and patriarchal persecution, guided by the conviction that "no person should be forced into illegality", as the jury puts it.
The Rural Women's Assembly is being honoured for forging a powerful movement of rural women in southern Africa, enabling them to defend their land, seeds and bodily autonomy against the tyranny of corporate interests and patriarchal exploitation, the jury said.
The Georgian Young Lawyers' Association is recognised for its work, carried out despite political repression, to build and safeguard Georgian democracy and to protect civilian control of power.
Timnit Gebru, an Ethiopian-born computer scientist, is also among this year's laureates. According to the citation, she has challenged the concentrated power in the field of artificial intelligence and played a pioneering role in developing digital technologies rooted in justice, real-life experience and an understanding of human agency.
The Right Livelihood Award was established in 1980 by German-Swedish writer and philatelist Jakob von Uexkull to honour those offering practical solutions to the planet's and humanity's most urgent problems.
The prize comes with long-term support intended to help the laureates expand and promote their work.

Kremlin Rejects US Sanctions-for-Prisoners Deal, Calls Proposal "Completely Inappropriate"
The Kremlin denied on September 30 that Russia and the US were discussing the release of Russian political prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief.
This was reported by The Moscow Times on September 30. The outlet cited Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, who rejected reports that such an arrangement had been discussed with US officials.

“In this formulation, the issue was not discussed and could not be discussed because we categorically deny the existence of any political prisoners,” Peskov stated during a briefing. He described the framing of the proposal as “completely inappropriate.”
Memorial, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning Russian human rights organization, currently recognizes 1,826 people as political prisoners in Russia. Peskov nevertheless acknowledged that Russian and US intelligence services remain in regular contact over prisoner exchanges.
Russia and the US have carried out two prisoner swaps since Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025. Earlier this week, the White House nominated John Coale to serve as its special envoy for hostage affairs.
The statement followed an earlier briefing that the Trump administration was considering sanctions relief for Russia in exchange for the release of political prisoners.
On September 29, it was reported that the proposal was developed by White House special envoy John Coale and could involve gradually easing sanctions if Moscow released prisoners. The approach reportedly mirrors a similar arrangement used with Belarus, where prisoner releases were tied to sanctions relief and potential economic agreements.

Ukraine’s war chest is running low at the worst possible moment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

The building of the private medical clinic Dobrobut burns following a second Russian drone strike on central Kyiv on September 28, 2026 in Kyiv. | Nikoletta Stoyanova/Getty Images
KYIV — Vladimir Putin is intensifying Russia’s pressure on Ukraine, smashing cities, factories, bridges and ports with constant waves of killer drones and missiles.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi warned journalists this week that Ukraine faces a $27 billion defense funding gap this year, with Kyiv hoping to cover about $7 billion domestically and looking to partners for the rest. Some EU financing remains tied to reforms Kyiv must pass to unlock the money, while other allies have yet to fill the remaining gap.
Advertisement
Overnight, Russia launched more than 190 missiles and drones in a nationwide assault that heavily targeted energy infrastructure, causing blackouts in Kyiv.
“Since the summer, there has been virtually not a single day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. But an attack of this scale and intensity has not occurred since the end of the last heating season,” Koretskyi said Wednesday.
Following the attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy renewed his call for allies to send more air defenses. “Every interceptor missile truly saves lives,” he said. “And the closer we get to winter, the more of this protection we need. We must do everything we can to ensure that Russia’s strategy of ballistic and drone terror does not succeed.”
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy walks to the dais during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 23, 2026. | Spencer Platt/Getty Images
Russia, in recent weeks, has escalated near-continuous drone and missile attacks. Air raid alerts are relentless — day and night — in Kyiv. The strikes have hit railways, energy plants, ports, factories and other critical infrastructure across the country, hammering Ukraine’s economy and adding to pressure on public finances. The government is also considering tax increases as it looks for domestic methods to close part of the defense gap.
“Of course, raising taxes is never ideal, but in wartime, we cannot afford the luxury of populism or pretend we can avoid asking anything of the public,” said Oleksandra Myronenko, an economist with the Center for Economic Strategy think tank.
Without money, Ukraine’s ability to continue resisting Russia would be undermined, Koretskyi warned. Kyiv needs cash now to place advance orders for weapons and ammunition due next year.
Advertisement
“This applies particularly to long-range drones — our ability to carry the war back to where it came from. This is a critical need that needs to be fulfilled,” he said.
Koretskyi told reporters that Kyiv will have to shift spending to keep the country fighting and basic government services functioning.
“This entails a strict regime of public finance austerity and the deferral of certain non-priority expenditures. These funds are intended to ensure payments to military personnel and support for their families,” Koretskyi said. “First and foremost, we are financing: defense, pensions and social payments, as well as salaries for teachers, doctors and other budget employees.”
Newly appointed Ukraine’s Prime Minister Sergii Koretsky delivers a speech to member of Parliament during a session of the Ukrainian parliament in Kyiv on July 16, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images
Zelenskyy underlined this week that his administration’s “clear task” is to “meet Ukraine’s current defense funding needs. Everything we can do together with our partners, using their funding — and this applies first and foremost to defense orders — must be 100% complete by the end of the year.”
Russia also feels the pain
Ukraine is not alone in feeling the financial strain. Moscow is also being forced to absorb rising fiscal costs — but its larger economy and ability to raise taxes give it more room to sustain the war.
The federal budget deficit reached 5.8 trillion rubles (€60.4 billion) in the first half of the year, which is being financed by a host of tax increases. Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion rubles (€180 billion) on defense in 2027, Reuters reported, a 27 percent increase on what it had previously budgeted for that year and accounting for more than a third of all budget spending.
Advertisement
The Kremlin has lowered its estimates for oil and gas revenue for next year; Ukraine’s ongoing bombing campaign against refineries and energy infrastructure has wrought havoc with production.
The Russian military has suffered more than 1.5 million casualties in the war, according to Ukrainian estimates. Russian President Vladimir Putin this week raised the authorized size of the armed forces to about 2.4 million personnel, the fourth expansion since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022.
A woman walks past a billboard advertising contract service in the Russian army as an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle operator for a period of 12 months, offering 5.4 million rubles per year with a two-month training period, in Tambov, on September 9, 2026. | Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images
Despite the cash crunch, Ukraine is still able to exert a painful toll on Russia.
Ukraine’s army reported last week that its ongoing Operation Vivaldi had pushed Russian forces back in part of the eastern front and captured more than 250 prisoners. Kyiv is also investing heavily in domestic long-range missiles and drones to strike targets inside Russia.
Europe under pressure to pay up
But Ukraine needs money to fund that war effort.
That’s putting pressure on European allies, which supply the bulk of Kyiv’s weapons and finances after the U.S. ended most new aid when Donald Trump returned to the White House last year.
Advertisement
The EU is currently paying out installments on its two-year €90 billion loan to Ukraine, but Kyiv is asking for the money to come faster to fill the budget gap. “The funds are needed this fall … especially given the mobilization that the enemy is planning right now,” Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara urged this week.
But before releasing more funds, Brussels wants Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, to complete crucial reforms that are part of the country’s roadmap to eventual EU membership.
“As reforms in the Rada progress, more budget support too. We have €37 billion still available in this calendar year,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote after meeting Zelenskyy at the U.N. General Assembly earlier this month.
Kyiv, for its part, is also putting pressure on Brussels to revisit the more than €200 billion in Russian central-bank assets immobilized across the EU. “We need our friends, our European politicians, to be brave enough and to make some bold actions,” said Ukrainian Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko.
Next year looks even more fraught.
Marchenko told donors in Brussels this week that Ukraine would require $52.6 billion in aid in 2027, while about $32.6 billion remains unfunded.
“Ukraine has no reserve funds to cover its entire spending. If we fail to get external financing, we’re facing a strong cut of all non-priority expenditures — and could even extend to protected expenditures,” said Myronenko, the economist.
“If we don’t have the actual cash in our accounts, we won’t have the means to pay military salaries, pensions, and so on. So, if there is no international aid, then everything will be very bad,” she added.

Saudi Arabia investigates flydubai emergency landing in Tabuk

US 10-year Treasury yield climbs to 24-year high as inflation concerns fuel bond selloff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:58:39 UTC
04:58:39 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note climbed to its highest Wednesday since May 2002, as persistent inflation concerns continued to weigh on government bonds.
The yield reached 5.306% in intraday trading, narrowly surpassing its 2002 intraday peak.
Treasury yields, which move inversely to bond prices, have risen with few interruptions since March, when the outbreak of the Iran war drove energy prices higher.
Despite recent declines in oil prices, investors remain concerned that elevated energy costs could feed into broader inflation and prompt the Federal Reserve to continue raising interest rates.
Stronger economic activity and concerns about heavy government debt burdens have also added pressure to the bond market.
The rise in long-term yields came despite softer-than-expected US inflation data released Wednesday, which led traders to reduce bets on another Fed rate increase next month.
The 10-year Treasury yield serves as a key benchmark for borrowing costs across the economy. Higher yields can increase financing costs for households and businesses while weighing on investment valuations.
