Why Gadi Eisenkot should support Palestinian elections without promising statehood - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:27:12 UTC
04:27:12 KST

I hope that Gadi Eisenkot will be Israel’s next prime minister, even if I am not voting for him. It disturbs me that he refuses to say that he will deal differently with the Israeli-Palestinian conflict than how Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has dealt with it since 2009.
I recognize that the trauma of October 7 has changed Israeli society profoundly. But we should also understand that Hamas’s massacre shattered assumptions about security, deterrence, and the possibility of simply containing the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
Rather than confronting the reality that this conflict cannot be managed and must be resolved, Israeli politics has moved sharply toward the Right and focuses solely on increased military strength as a solution and distrust of Palestinian intentions.
It is therefore understandable that politicians competing for the Israeli mainstream are cautious when talking about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Words such as “Palestinian state” and even “two-state solution” have become politically explosive for many Israelis. And political leaders all too often follow public opinion rather than shaping it.
But avoiding the need to resolve the conflict does not eliminate it.
Netanyahu’s political strategy for many years was based on determined opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside Israel. But preventing Palestinian statehood did not erase the Palestinian aspiration for freedom and self-determination. Three years of devastating war have not made that aspiration disappear. If anything, the issue of Palestinian self-determination has become even more central to the conflict.
Nor has the idea of two states disappeared internationally. Despite profound disagreements over how such an outcome could be achieved, broad international support remains for a negotiated future in which Israel and a Palestinian state exist alongside one another. In September 2026, the vast majority of countries, including Britain, France, Canada, and more than 100 other countries, again publicly reaffirmed support for a two-state solution.
Eisenkot has built much of his public identity around responsibility, sober judgment, and learning lessons from failure. That makes the question of what comes next especially important.
The lesson that Israel must learn should therefore be larger than the failure to “manage” the conflict. The Palestinian national question cannot simply be wished away. Israel cannot suppress Palestinian aspirations, resist them, or postpone dealing with them.
And there is something happening on the Palestinian side that Israelis are barely discussing. Israelis will vote for a new Knesset on October 27. Palestinian legislative elections are scheduled for November 28 – almost exactly one month later.
New Palestinian political lists are entering the process, including representatives of a generation that has never before had the opportunity to vote in a national Palestinian election. What Israel says – or does not say – during this period will inevitably form part of the environment in which Palestinians make that decision.
Why it's important for Israel to support Palestinian elections
There is a remarkably simple message that an Israeli leader could convey without promising a Palestinian state, accepting a particular negotiating formula, or prejudging the outcome of future negotiations.
It is this: If the Palestinian people elect leaders who are sincerely committed to achieving genuine peace between the Palestinian people and the people of Israel, they will find a partner for peace in Israel.
That sentence should not be controversial. It does not ask Israelis to forget October 7. It does not ask them to trust Hamas. It does not prescribe borders, Jerusalem, settlements, refugees, or security arrangements. It does not even require Eisenkot, during an Israeli election campaign, to use the words “two states.”
It simply tells Palestinians that political choices matter. That message could have significance far beyond Israeli domestic politics.
Imagine being a young Palestinian who has never voted in a national election. You have grown up watching negotiations fail, settlements expand, violence recur, and Israeli governments increasingly argue that there is no Palestinian partner. You are now being asked to choose among political movements offering very different visions of the Palestinian future.
One of the central questions confronting such a voter is obvious: Does choosing a peaceful political path actually lead anywhere?
If the answer coming from Israel is silence – if Palestinians conclude that Israel will reject them regardless of whom they elect or what policies those leaders adopt – then advocates of diplomacy have a much harder argument to make. But if a major Israeli leader says clearly that Palestinians who choose leaders committed to genuine peace will encounter an Israeli partner, the political equation changes.
It does not guarantee peace. Nothing could. But it restores the essential principle upon which diplomacy depends: Political choices can produce political consequences.
Such a statement could also resonate internationally. Israel today faces an extraordinarily difficult diplomatic environment. Criticism of Israeli policy has intensified across many countries, international institutions, and younger generations abroad. Whatever Israelis believe about the fairness or motivations of that criticism, the deterioration of Israel’s international standing is a strategic issue that cannot be dismissed.
An Israeli leader saying that Israel remains prepared to pursue genuine peace with genuinely peaceful Palestinian leadership would communicate something important to the world as well: Israel has not abandoned the search for a political future beyond permanent war.
Most importantly, however, this should not be about public relations. It should be about strategy. Israel cannot determine whom Palestinians elect. Nor should it try. But Israeli leaders should understand that what they say influences the Palestinian political debate just as Palestinian rhetoric influences Israelis.
For decades, Israelis have asked a legitimate question: Where is the Palestinian partner? Palestinians have increasingly begun asking the mirror-image question: If we choose a different path, will there be an Israeli partner?
The elections of October and November 2026 provide an unusual moment when both societies will be making political choices almost simultaneously. There is no certainty about what either electorate will decide. But there is an opportunity to establish one principle before those choices are made.
If Palestinians choose leaders genuinely committed to peace with Israel, Israel should be prepared to meet them. That is not a peace agreement. It is not a concession. It is an invitation to choose a different future. And sometimes history begins with something as simple as one sentence.

Cholera affects more than 12,700 in eastern DR Congo: UNICEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:27:07 UTC
04:27:07 KST

James Tasamba
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
By 
 (AA) - More than 12,700 cholera cases, including 175 deaths, have been recorded in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo’s South Kivu province since the beginning of the year, UNICEF said Wednesday.
UNICEF said it is working with partners and has deployed an integrated response to save lives and curb the spread of the epidemic.
"Cholera response teams intervene with affected households, ensure community surveillance, and support laboratory analysis of suspected cases," it said.
Widespread flooding, population displacement and inadequate access to safe water fuel the transmission in the country.
Since January, Congo has recorded more than 30,400 cases and nearly 700 deaths, according to UNICEF.
The eastern North Kivu and South Kivu provinces remain the epicenter of the outbreak.
Health officials said cholera continues to spread through communities because attention and resources since May have been increasingly focused on the Ebola outbreak.
Fifteen cholera deaths were recorded in South Kivu province from Sept.14 0 20 in four health zones, including Shabunda, Fizi, Ibanda and Uvira, according to the latest South Kivu provincial health report.
UNICEF wants urgent action to protect children as cholera rapidly spreads in West and Central Africa, with outbreaks affecting several countries and placing thousands of children at increasing risk.

Joy mixed with fear as US forces leave Iraq amid potential security vacuum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:26:42 UTC
04:26:42 KST

Iraqis celebrated the departure of US forces after more than two decades of war on Wednesday, though many feared that any security vacuum could increase the power of Iran-backed militias or provide an opening for the return of Islamic State (ISIS).
The withdrawal of the final troops, mainly from an airbase in Erbil in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region, ended the biggest US war of the century, which brought widespread devastation and chaos from which Iraq has yet to fully emerge.
Iran, which has entrenched its influence in Iraq through allied armed groups and is determined to drive all US forces out of the Middle East, views the US pullout as a triumph for its "axis of resistance" of allied armed groups across the region.
Iraqi troops paraded in vehicles through the streets of Baghdad and the Shi'ite holy city of Najaf to mark the pullout.
The withdrawal "fills our hearts with joy," said Baghdad resident Ahmed Salah, who said he felt reborn at the age of 70. But he also said it was now time for powerful militia groups to surrender their weapons, "and let the government be the one responsible to protect me and you on the ground, sky and water."
Pullout plans drafted under Biden, performed under Trump
The pullout was agreed in 2024 under former president Joe Biden and carried out by the Trump administration even as it waged war against Iran next door.
US forces invaded to topple Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein in 2003, triggering years of upheaval and chaos. The Americans initially left at the end of 2011 but came back less than three years later to assist Iraqi forces after Islamic State fighters seized a third of Iraq and imposed violent rule.
US President Donald Trump said that the United States leaves Iraq with "wonderful" Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi, saying in a Truth Social post that he would "hopefully be able to handle things very well."
More than 4,500 US troops died in Iraq, around twice as many as in the parallel war in Afghanistan. The Iraq Body Count project says more than 200,000 Iraqi civilians were killed.
The Pentagon said the United States and its coalition partners formally concluded "Operation Inherent Resolve" and Washington would continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi partners.
The Iraqis are expected to lead the effort to secure the country, an ally of both Washington and Tehran, and keep the remnants of Islamic State suppressed.
“The end of the international coalition’s mission does not mean the end of our battle against terrorism, but rather Iraq’s transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability," said Zaidi in a statement.
'Security vacuums can be extremely dangerous'
While the departure of US forces is broadly popular among Iraqis, some worry that security forces trained and funded by the United States still can't protect the country.
"The lesson from the past two decades is that security vacuums can be extremely dangerous," said Jassim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi analyst who advises the security forces.
Adil Salman, 45, a high school English teacher, said Iraqis "should not rush to celebrate" the withdrawal.
"Militias still operate outside the state's control and (Islamic State) still has not disappeared," he said. "I'm concerned that the US departure could lead to a new period of instability. In the end, people will judge this decision by one thing: whether security remains stable in the coming years."
Hundreds of supporters of pro-Iranian Iraqi militia groups gathered in Baghdad to celebrate the pullout, chanting "Death to America."
They carried portraits of Iran's slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, his son and current Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, and top Iranian general Qassem Soleimani, who was killed in a US airstrike on his convoy in Baghdad in 2020.
With US forces present alongside armed groups allied to Iran, Iraq has been caught up in this year's war.
Of the 18 US service members listed as killed since Trump launched Operation Epic Fury alongside Israel's Operation Roaring Lion in February, seven died in Iraq. The last was an army sergeant who died during the controlled detonation of a drone at a base near Erbil in July.
The withdrawal raises "the possibility that Iran's proxies will feel increasingly empowered in the absence of a Western military presence. These groups may attempt to expand their role in shaping state policies and consolidating their presence within key institutions," said Baghdad-based political analyst Ahmed Younis.
Some Iraqi security officials say the US pullout also risks giving new life to Islamic State fighters, who, despite the defeat of their self-proclaimed caliphate nearly a decade ago, retain a sleeper cell network.
The last time the US withdrew, the Iraqi army proved no match for Islamic State: soldiers took off their uniforms and fled when the group captured Mosul, Iraq's second-largest city, in 2014.
"The most important question now is whether Iraq's security institutions have prepared a viable Plan B for the post-coalition phase," said Iraqi Army Gen. (ret.) Mohammed al-Jubouri, who led a brigade in the war against Islamic State.

Flydubai, a state-owned company, didn’t suffer in its valuation because it isn't publicly traded.
Flydubai pilot attempts terror hijacking of flight to Tel Aviv
A flydubai flight, which was going from Dubai to Tel Aviv, was diverted to and landed in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday morning after what Israeli officials said was an attempted hijacking by one of the pilots that led to a mid-air altercation.
An Israeli official told The Jerusalem Post a “major disaster was narrowly avoided” amid growing fears that one of the pilots attempted to hijack the plane with the intention of crashing it into the ground. Additional flight crew, aided by Israelis on board the flight, managed to subdue the pilot and bring him under control, the official told the Post.

The growing assessment among the Israeli security establishment, including the IDF, Mossad, and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), is that the incident was intended as an act of terror. During the altercation, the aircraft plunged about 4,000 meters, the official noted.

Unknown

04:24:12 KST

The Pentagon has committed nearly all of the $400 million in military aid Congress approved for Ukraine, only a day before the funds were set to expire.
Senator Chris Coons, a senior member of the Senate defense appropriations subcommittee, told The Washington Sun on Tuesday, Sept. 29 that Pentagon officials had informed him during the same morning that 99.8% of the funding had been obligated.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Coons sharply criticized the Department of Defense for waiting until the final hours of the fiscal year, despite months of pressure from both Democratic and Republican lawmakers.
“The fact that they are finally doing it, like on the last possible day, tells you everything you need to know about that relationship,” Coons said. “They don’t brief us on time. They don’t follow the law, and the partnership is struggling,” he added.
A last-minute push
The funding comes from the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI), a Pentagon program through which the US procures weapons and equipment for Kyiv.
Congress approved the $400 million late last year, and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced its allocation in June, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
As of late July, the funds had still not been obligated, according to Reuters.
By early last week, the defense department had obligated $307 million and planned to lock in the remaining $93 million before the deadline, three sources familiar with the plan told Reuters on Sept. 25.
Ukraine Completes 17 of 42 Resolutions Needed to Unlock $29.5B in Aid
The funds did not have to be spent by the end of the fiscal year on Wednesday, Sept. 30, but they would have expired if not placed under contract by then.
However, signing the contracts does not mean immediate deliveries. The first shipments of weapons and equipment began in September, while the remaining items are expected to arrive by October 2029, Reuters reported.
Months of pressure from Congress
At a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on April 30, Pentagon Comptroller Jules Hurst said the funding had recently been released and would be “put to work very shortly.”
The department then missed a May 15 deadline it had set for providing Congress with a spending plan, according to The Washington Sun.
In response, Senators Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) and Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) led a bipartisan letter urging Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to obligate the funds.
The letter also called for the release of congressionally approved funding for the Baltic Security Initiative, a program supporting the defense of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
Republican Sens. Kevin Cramer and Thom Tillis, along with Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet and Catherine Cortez Masto, also signed it.
No Patriot interceptors included
The Pentagon’s plan allocated $200 million for weapons, ammunition and explosives, $99.9 million for vehicles, spare parts and equipment.
Another $100 million is intended for services such as transporting military equipment, Reuters reported in July.
The more recent contracts include offensive weapons and spare parts for armored vehicles.
However, the package does not include Patriot interceptors, one of Reuters’ sources said, despite Ukraine’s repeated appeals for more ahead of winter, when Russia is expected to step up attacks on the country’s critical infrastructure.
Currently, the Patriot systems are the only weapons in Ukraine’s arsenal that can reliably down Russian ballistic missiles.
During the 81st United Nations General Assembly held last week, US President Donald Trump told President Volodymyr Zelensky that he had made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine licenses to domestically produce Patriots.
He had previously made a similar pledge during the NATO summit in Ankara on July 7-8, but retreated from the commitment weeks later, citing concerns over sharing sensitive weapons technology with other countries.
In the meantime, Ukraine announced that it was signing contracts with partners for the supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles ahead of winter.
Around the same time, Germany announced it would urgently transfer the PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from its own Bundeswehr stocks.

AI Isn’t the Cause of Education’s Demise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:22:00 UTC
04:22:00 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Students shouldn’t “cheat themselves of the cognitive friction and productive struggle necessary for actual learning.”
This was one of many insights in MIT’s Ad Hoc Committee’s paper titled, “AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training”. In this paper, the committee explores the impact AI is having at MIT on teaching, instructional design, student health, and, most importantly, learning.
The paper argues that AI is deeply impacting learning (at MIT but arguably in general) in the way students approach learning itself, in how teachers design curricula and educational assessments, and in how students and teachers approach the learning enterprise itself.
Ironically, the paper highlights that AI is bringing to the surface what has arguably been a slow degradation in education that’s been happening for decades. AI is accelerating that degradation but is not really the cause of it.
A key thread in the paper is that education is not merely “content delivery.” Rather, it’s a robust experiential enterprise that is based on a contract between the student and the teacher. Learning is both a process and a product:
… the process of education is necessarily a productive struggle, and that the most important product of [a student’s] education is not a GPA or a diploma but themselves: their personal growth and intellectual maturity and the development of their own imagination, insight, and judgment.
This also highlights the root of the decay. Education has become a highly competitive means to getting a good job or prestige or status rather than and end in and of itself. If students don’t value learning primarily for it’s own sake, then using AI tools will only amplify behaviors that help them “get ahead” in the competitive learning landscape.
When it comes to the educational experience itself, the committee argues that learning happens when students are, “disentangling the steps of a mathematical proof with [their] study group, adjusting an experiment over and over until it works, or having a spirited argument with a peer.”
So, not unexpectedly, they see a tremendous value in on-site learning. While that has a strong self-serving odor, their bases for making these claims are not unfounded. When it comes to digital learning and the use of AI, they see both tremendous opportunities and serious risks.
For example, learning that is created using AI tools ,
. . .helps [teachers] develop customized, interactive learning tools that allow students to explore subject content with more depth and for instructors to create learning experiences for their students that are new or newly tailored to each student.
They see a lot of possibilities in what AI tools can do to augment education. Education, they argue, degrades when AI is used to automate it.
For us in the digital education space, the paper summarizes a lot of core educational philosophy that we can and should bring into the materials we’re creating. AI can and should be used. But the Ad Hoc Committee urges us to do so thoughtfully and intentionally.
While the paper is focused on AI’s impact on education at MIT, much of it is transferrable to any learning institution and it is rich with ideas for any instructional designer, teacher, and student. Definitely worth reading in full.

Slower au pair visa approvals hit Australian families
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:20:38 UTC
04:20:38 KST

Families waiting for au pairs face uncertainty as visa delays continue
Johanna Paulina Gorek postponed university for a year and turned down a job at home in Germany to become an au pair in Australia.
But a slowdown of working holiday visa processing times is threatening her plans.
"I had already found a host family in Melbourne who had basically offered me a position, but eventually they decided to cancel because they did not want to wait longer for my visa," she told the ABC.
Ms Gorek said she applied for her visa on September 3 and had spent more than $1,500 on visa application and au pair agency fees.
She wanted to become an au pair to improve her English and learn Australian culture, she said.
"It's so disappointing to still be waiting and not knowing exactly when I will be able to go," she said.
"I'm also worried that the longer I have to wait, the fewer opportunities I will have to find a suitable host family."
The Department of Home Affairs began prioritising processing of onshore visa applications in July.
A spokesperson said it slowed down processing first-year working holiday visas and prioritised second and third-year visas "to better manage demand and ensure the sustainability of the program over the long term".
"The government will now manage first-year WHMs (working holiday makers) processing to deliver an average processing time of approximately three months," the spokesperson said.
"This balanced approach will provide greater control over the impact of WHMs on NOM [net overseas migration], while supporting regional labour market needs."
The department's website recommends that visa applicants not "book flights or make travel, work or study commitments until their visa has been granted".
Au pairs are typically young overseas visitors who live with an Australian host family and help with child care and light household tasks, in exchange for accommodation, meals, weekly pocket money and a cultural exchange experience.
Cultural Au Pair Association of Australia (CAPAA) president Anna Prasad said that before July applications for the working holiday visa (subclass 417) were granted "in a matter of hours".
Ms Prasad, who is also the inbound manager for the American Institute for Foreign Study (AIFS) which facilitates au pair placements, said visas for "hundreds" of AIFS' au pairs had been delayed since July.
She said "high season" for au pairs usually started in July, with 30 to 40 arranged through AIFS arriving on working holiday visas each week, but only 10 to 12 had arrived between then and the second week of September.
"Families are waiting for their au pairs to arrive and they have no other option in some cases," she said.
The number of au pairs who come to Australia is unknown due to the informal nature of the sector, but Ms Prasad said at least 500 were connected with Australian families by the AIFS each year.
Ms Prasad said the processing delays did not put Australia in a good light.
"It's a nightmare,"
"We are starting to see au pairs pull out of placements, choosing to travel to other countries instead for their gap year experience."
Filling gaps in child care
Backpackers' contribution to child care was "overlooked", said Western Sydney University heritage and tourism studies lecturer Donna James.
"A lot of working holiday-makers are filling gaps in child care, particularly for families in remote, regional areas where child care is already very inaccessible,"
"But also for people who are working unusual hours."
Dr James added that au pairs cost less and offered more flexibility than nannies.
However, Migrant Justice Institute co-executive director Laurie Berg said a paper she co-authored in 2018 found that most au pairs worked long hours, were doing work beyond child care and did not have a genuine cultural experience in Australia.
"We need much more detailed official guidance on the rights of au pairs," she said.
"It's really important there are stronger regulations and processes in place to ensure that all parties are safe, secure, and are meeting their legal obligations."
Backpacker visa delays affect families
Some families find au pairs indispensable.
In Perth, university lecturer Renae Barker has had to take annual leave to look after her children while she waits for her family's new au pair to arrive.
"We line up our au pairs, three, four months in advance," she said.
"But at the moment because of the slowdown in processing, we've ended up with a gap between au pairs."
Dr Barker, whose husband works fly-in, fly-out in the mining industry, said au pairs helped with school pick-up and drop-off, along with after-school activities.
She said they offered flexibility, as her job could "be very demanding and often time-sensitive", while her husband was away working for eight days at a time, followed by six days at home.
"We're going to have to pull the kids out of some of their therapies or some of their after-school activities because I can't actually get there,"
She added that an au pair offered more than just help, but also the opportunity for her children to learn about European culture, language and food.
'I feel sorry for making them wait'
Shodai Kitahama, from Japan, said he was still waiting for the working holiday visa that he lodged at the end of July.
"The hardest part for me is that my host family has been waiting for me for a long time,"
"I didn't think the visa process would take this long, so I feel sorry for making them wait."
Mr Kitahama said he wanted to come to Australia to improve his English and experience its culture.
He said the lack of updates on his application had caused him anxiety and made it difficult to make plans.
"I took a break from university and quit my job because I was preparing to go to Australia," he said.
"Right now I'm not working or studying, I'm just waiting to find out when I can leave."

Russia is now wiring its attack drones into one network in flight, so a single drone can scout, strike, and relay for the rest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:20:07 UTC
04:20:07 KST

Russia is wiring its long-range attack drones together by a mesh network in flight and buying pricier, higher-resolution cameras for them, Ukraine's Air Force reported on 29 September. Its spokesperson said one drone could serve as a scout, strike drone, and relay for the rest, which is why they often fly one behind another over long distances. Chains of them keep crossing near the Belarus border, UkrInform reports.
For Ukraine, the danger in each such upgrade is arithmetic: the more Russia networks cheap, once-disposable drones and pushes its control links away from the front, the harder they become to jam or shoot down, and the more of them reach the cities they are aimed at.
Sharper, pricier eyes
Ihnat said on a national broadcast that Russia is sourcing higher-quality materials and raising the resolution of its drone cameras. The cameras it buys are increasingly expensive and higher-quality, he said, which lets its operators study the ground in fine detail and use each drone for a specific purpose.
On a mesh network, he said, the drones talk to each other and hand the control signal back toward the operator, so no single link has to carry it alone.
Russia is mapping everyday targets across Kyiv, from trolleybus depots to Zhuliany airport, top monitoring channel says, ahead of next ballistic strike
Chains along the Belarus border
Asked about relays operating out of Belarus and about Russia's guidance of jet-powered Shaheds, the exploding drones it fires in swarms, Ihnat said Moscow had already claimed its satellite network was ready. He confirmed mesh networks are in use and said their use was quite dangerous. Ukraine has no information yet on whether Russia is using towers, he said.
It often sees drones crossing long distances in chains along the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, so nothing can be ruled out, but intelligence would have to confirm whether such relays exist. Asked whether Russia is preparing a fresh ballistic strike, he said intelligence would warn when extra vigilance is needed.
Ukraine's countermeasures
Ihnat has also said Russia launched more attack drones in September than in August, counting 3,177 jet-powered drones so far this month against 2,850 in August. To knock them down, Ukraine leans mainly on tactical aviation, including F-16 fighters, and on ground-based air defense when missiles are available, he said, with shoulder-fired man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS) working well against jet drones inside their range. He said Ukraine needs more missiles for both Patriot systems and ground-based launchers, plus faster domestic solutions it can scale up.

Saudi Arabia not to compromise on security as Houthis choose ‘chaos’: MBS
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman says the kingdom ‘will not hesitate to respond firmly to any threat’.
Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) has promised not to compromise on the kingdom’s security in the face of attacks by the Houthi armed group, saying the Yemeni rebels chose “chaos and destruction, threatening the Yemeni people and the region”.
In a speech delivered Wednesday on behalf of King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud during the opening of the third year of the ninth session of Saudi Arabia’s Shura Council, Prince Mohammed said the country “will not hesitate to respond firmly to any threat or attack aimed at undermining” its security.
He pointed to the trilateral Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Turkiye and Pakistan that was formalised in August, saying the alliance shows the Saudi leadership’s intent “to strengthen regional stability, shield it from the repercussions of tensions and conflicts and coordinate efforts”.
At the same time, the crown prince said, Saudi Arabia is making “every possible effort to de-escalate tensions and support diplomatic solutions without the slightest compromise on preserving our security”.
Maritime coalition to defend Red Sea
MBS also addressed the targeting of vessels by the Houthis in the Red Sea along the Bab al-Mandeb strait, rejecting the use of international waterways as a tool for political or economic pressure.
He said a “multinational defensive maritime coalition” was set up to ensure “common interests” are protected in international waterways.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, as they fight Yemen’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government forces.
Last week, Riyadh said it intercepted six ballistic missiles aimed at Taif in western Saudi Arabia and the Yanbu port area on the Red Sea.
The Houthis also said they attacked “a sensitive target” in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
On Tuesday, Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif said Islamabad will make “whatever means” available to Saudi Arabia under the mutual defence pact if the Houthi attacks on the kingdom continue.

Police arrested five British men on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences, but later released them on bail.
On Tuesday, after three days of investigations that included deploying a bomb disposal team, police said no explosives had been found in the vehicles, although they had recovered a "quantity of petrol".
US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had previously suggested that intelligence services were aware of the suspects and that a foreign state could be involved, but UK officials had until now not commented.
Speculation had mounted that Iran or another hostile state could be responsible, after Tehran warned London against allowing its military bases to be used by Washington.

Ukraine Working on Large-Scale Purchase of 20mm Ammunition for F-16s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:18:19 UTC
04:18:19 KST

Ukraine is negotiating with several European countries and manufacturers to obtain tens of thousands of rounds of 20mm ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, sources told Bloomberg.
Ukraine is increasingly using the M61A1 Vulcan cannon on its F-16 fighters to destroy Russian drones.
According to Bloomberg’s sources, using the cannon to intercept drones is currently the most cost-effective and operationally effective solution.
Due to shortages of AIM-120 and AIM-9 air-to-air missiles, Ukrainian F-16 pilots are increasingly using the 20mm cannon against drones.
According to the news agency’s sources, about 150 rounds are required to intercept a single target, or approximately 10,000 rounds per day.
As of the end of September, Ukrainian F-16 pilots had already shot down more than 3,150 aerial targets.
The destroyed targets included 666 cruise missiles and 2,500 drones of various types.
The M61A1 Vulcan is a U.S. six-barrel 20mm aircraft cannon with a rotating barrel assembly.
It uses an electric drive to rotate the barrels and provides a very high rate of fire.
The cannon was developed by General Electric for use on various aircraft, including F-15 and F-16 fighter jets.
It has primarily been used against aerial targets, as well as to engage lightly armored and ground targets.

Five EU states plan first deportation center in Africa for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:16:00 UTC
04:16:00 KST

EU states plan first deportation center in Africa for 2027
September 30, 2026
Deportation centers are legally contentious, expensive and the subject of political controversy: For years, Brussels has been grappling with the issue of establishing such centers outside the EU for rejected asylum seekers. Previous attempts have failed due to legal objections, but now, a "group of five" consisting of Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands believes it has overcome these hurdles.
During an interview with the Greek television channel ANT1, Greece's Minister of Migration, Thanos Plevris, stated that the first of these so-called "return hubs" is scheduled to begin operations as early as the second half of 2027 — just in time for Greece to assume the EU Council Presidency.
Plevris said Greece had chosen an African country but could not reveal its name yet. Diplomatic circles and media outlets close to the EU have repeatedly cited Rwanda or Uganda, but neither country has been confirmed as the location.
No sealed detention centers
"We are not talking about centers in the sense that someone whose asylum application is rejected is sent to a closed facility in a third country," Plevris said.
The plan was rather to establish "open facilities" while the final return to the actual country of origin is being organized, he added.
The responsibility for the transferred individuals will not be transferred to the African partner country in order to prevent legal action for human rights violations, but will remain with the five participating EU member states. The EU "group of five" will also finance the project entirely on its own.
There are also plans for international organizations such as the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) or the International Organization for Migration (IOM) to monitor operations to ensure that international human rights standards and principles of international law are upheld.
Various attempts have been made in recent years to outsource asylum proceedings or deportations to countries outside the EU. None of these models worked as planned. All failed due to legal impediments, changes in government, or high costs. Below are some of the best-known precedents.
The British "Rwanda Model" (2022–2024)
The United Kingdom, under the Conservative government of Boris Johnson — and later under Rishi Sunak — sought to permanently deport migrants who had entered the country irregularly via the English Channel to Rwanda so they could undergo their asylum proceedings there.
However, the British Supreme Court ruled the plan illegal, finding that there were substantial grounds for believing that asylum seekers sent to Rwanda faced a real risk of refoulement — being returned to countries where they could face persecution or other inhumane treatment.
Prior to that, the British government had spent £715 million (€835 million/$966 million) in taxpayer funds on the Rwanda partnership and related implementation costs. In return, a total of four people had voluntarily relocated to Rwanda
Italy's Albania model (in place since 2024)
Under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Italy signed an agreement with Albania to transport migrants intercepted in the Mediterranean directly to Italian-run centers established in Albania where expedited asylum proceedings could be conducted.
However, immediately after the camps opened, Italian courts halted the relocation. Judges argued that countries of origin such as Bangladesh or Egypt should not be classified as "safe" outright if certain groups face persecution there. These first migrants had to be returned to Italy immediately.
Italy is now using one of the camps solely as a deportation center for men whose asylum applications in Italy have been definitively rejected. Since the facility was converted in March 2025, only about 500 people have been sent there. By 2028, this comes at an estimated total cost of more than €670 million ($775 million).
Denmark's stand-alone initiatives (2021–2023)
In 2021, Denmark passed a law intended to allow asylum seekers to be flown to third countries outside the EU. Copenhagen engaged in intensive negotiations with Rwanda regarding a dedicated reception center. However, the European Commission and human rights organizations sharply criticized the initiative. In early 2023, the Danish government put the negotiations with Rwanda on hold. It became clear that the Danish plan was virtually impossible to implement legally and logistically. The government subsequently moved toward pursuing third-country return arrangements in cooperation with other European countries.
Changing legal framework
According to previous EU law, deportations to third countries often failed as courts required that a migrant have a personal connection to that third country, whether through language skills, relatives living there or a previous stay. The revised European asylum law, however, now allows individuals required to leave the EU to be transferred to a safe third country without a prior personal connection in certain circumstances — provided there is a corresponding agreement or arrangement with the third country.
A further basis for this new joint effort is the EU Return Regulation, agreed upon politically on June 17, 2026 by the Council and European Parliament. However, the regulation has not yet been formally adopted by the Council. Unlike before, the new legislation is an EU regulation and no longer merely a directive. As a result, it will apply directly once it enters into force in the EU member states bound by it. The regulation thus establishes a common EU framework for such return centers.
Furthermore, according to the new plans, the entire asylum procedure will no longer be outsourced to non-EU countries. The United Kingdom and Italy rejected this proposal. Instead, these "return hubs" will serve solely as transit stations for individuals whose asylum applications have already been legally rejected while they are financed and monitored by EU member states.
Inadequate oversight and high costs?
Supporters hope that these measures will undermine the basis for human rights lawsuits regarding permanent asylum protection. Critics such as Doctors Without Borders and Amnesty International still see significant risks: They doubt that independent oversight, effective legal representation and medical care can be fully guaranteed in the hubs. They also fear that third countries could still deport people to their unsafe home countries without proper assessment.
Furthermore, experience to date shows that the construction and security of such centers, as well as the transport of those affected, often costs hundreds of millions of euro, and only a small number of people actually end up being returned.
This article was originally published in German.

Ukrainian combat simulator, used to train more than 500,000 troops, can now be ordered from NATO’s supply catalogs by single code
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:12:29 UTC
04:12:29 KST

A Ukrainian combat simulator can now be found and ordered in NATO's supply catalogs by a single code. L7 Simulators, whose trainers have prepared more than 500,000 Ukrainian troops, has had its entire lineup NATO-codified, with each device assigned a 13-digit NATO Stock Number, Defender Media reports.
L7's more than 50 trainers, from the Browning M2 to the Stinger to the NLAW, now carry those codes, and the company can codify new ones itself, opening the door to government procurement in Ukraine and across the alliance. It is another Ukrainian defense maker stepping toward NATO's standards and supply chain.
Every trainer gets a NATO number
A NATO Stock Number is a unique 13-digit code, a kind of military barcode for supplies, that lets defense logistics systems across the alliance identify, catalog, and purchase equipment. Every simulator in L7's catalog now has one, and the firm has also won the status to assign numbers to its future products directly, rather than starting the process over for each one.
The code identifies, not certifies
The company is careful about what the step does and does not mean. Codification is not a certification that the product meets NATO's technical standards, L7 stresses, but rather a mechanism for unambiguously identifying an item within the shared defense-logistics system.
The firm entered that system in December 2024, when its UNITS training platform, already cleared for use by Ukraine's Defense Ministry, received the first number.
Half a million have trained on them
L7's range runs to more than 50 types of trainers, tied together in a single ecosystem the company calls UNITS: fire-training systems, anti-tank and air-defense simulators, and trainers for unmanned aircraft, with models for the Stinger, NLAW, Carl Gustaf, RPG-7, and SPG-9 among them.
The simulators are used by the armed forces, the National Guard, and other security agencies, and more than 500,000 service members have trained on them, with over 70,000 of them free of charge at the company's own training center.

Norway launches probe into 11 senior officials over US Epstein files links
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:10:03 UTC
04:10:03 KST

Norway launches probe into 11 senior officials over US Epstein files links
Norway investigates over $13m in state grants linked to Epstein and top ministers.
Norway’s Parliament has launched an investigation into 11 current and former high-ranking ministers — including Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere — over alleged ties and grants linked to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
US President Donald Trump’s Department of Justice in January released millions of Epstein-related documents, revealing connections to politicians, royals and the ultra-rich around the world.
Norway, home of the Nobel Peace Prize and often a fulcrum of international diplomacy, has seen major fallout, triggering parliamentary inquiries and police investigations.
The public hearing, which began on Wednesday, comes in light of reports that the Foreign Ministry allocated over 130 million kroner ($13.5m) to the International Peace Institute between 1997 and 2018.
The United Nations-affiliated think-tank was led by Terje Rod-Larsen, a prominent Norwegian diplomat and chief architect of the 1993 Oslo Accords, from 2005 to 2020. Stoere, who has denied any wrongdoing, served as foreign minister from 2005 to 2012.
A central figure in the Middle East peace talks in the 1990s, Rod-Larsen was implicated in the files and Norwegian media investigations that exposed an alleged relationship involving illicit loans and visa fraud for sex-trafficked women. Epstein also left Rod-Larsen’s children millions of dollars in his will.
The government must explain what it is doing to restore trust in the foreign service, said Jonas Andersen Sayed, who chaired the hearing at Parliament’s Committee on Scrutiny and Constitutional Affairs.
“There are many people who have demonstrated very poor judgement,” Andersen Sayed told the Reuters news agency in reference to friends of Epstein.
While testifying, the prime minister maintained that he had never had any relationship with Epstein and said the “problems” were isolated lapses, not systemic to the Foreign Ministry.
“There is no reason to speak of an unhealthy culture at a large organisation just because of what one or several people may have done,” Stoere told the committee.
Stoere added that, to his knowledge, Epstein wielded no influence over Norway’s foreign policy, development aid or any other government decisions.
Erik Solheim, a former development minister who will testify on Wednesday, has said parliament’s probe is an overreaction that will throttle the foreign service as diplomats opt for needless self-restraint, harming the national interest.
Though not appearing before Parliament, a number of other prominent Norwegians with ties to Epstein — including former premier Thorbjoern Jagland, Roed-Larsen and his wife, ex-diplomat Mona Juul — are under police investigation on corruption accusations.
All three have denied any wrongdoing.
“The Epstein documents raise serious questions about abuse of office, a culture of accountability failures and poor management of development aid funds,” said Andersen Sayed.
“The issue concerns public trust in the entire system. It is essential that all the facts are brought to light, that accountability is established and that the necessary reforms are implemented,” he said.
Parliament has also set up an independent inquiry tasked with a much broader examination of the case, which is due to submit its final report by January 31, 2028.

Furry Airline Pilots Are Just Minding Their Own Business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:09:57 UTC
04:09:57 KST

The greatest threat to humanity’s survival isn’t climate change, nor is it AI. It’s airline pilots who like dressing up as hot cartoon foxes.
That seemed to be the takeaway from a bizarre speech made last week by Alabama Republican Tommy Tuberville on the Senate floor last week. During a lengthy anti-trans rant about “gender confusion,” Tuberville started pontificating on the furry fandom, a subculture consisting of people who enjoy drawing and dressing as anthropomorphized animals. “Many airline pilots, flight attendants, and air traffic controllers are part of the furry community,” Tuberville alleged. “Lord help us. It’s terrifying when you think about this.”
To bolster his point, he later posted a viral audio clip of airline pilots at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport meowing and barking at each other over the radio, though there is no evidence that the pilots in question were furries; the video was possibly a reference to a joke in the 2001 movie Super Troopers. “When you walk onto a commercial flight, it’s possible that the pilot flying your plane could have a deranged fetish of dressing up like an animal,” Tuberville said. (Interest in the furry fandom is not necessarily sexual, nor do all furries dress up as animals.)
Tuberville’s tirade went viral, with everyone from Jimmy Kimmel to The Daily Show weighing in on the absurdity of his remarks. But there was one detail largely omitted from the coverage: on at least one point, Tuberville was (kind of) correct.
“It’s definitely something we’ve talked about before, why there are so many furries in the aviation community,” says Toby, a professional flying instructor who has been running a flight school for the past eight years; he is also a prominent member of the fandom whose fursona (the fandom’s term for an animal-inspired alter ego) is a wolf.
Vulan, who works as a pilot for a major American airline, agreed. (Due to the stigma associated with the community, all of the furries I spoke with requested they be referred to by their fursonas rather than their real names.) Vulan, who uses they/them pronouns and whose fursona is of a fox, runs a group chat for furries in aviation—one of nearly a dozen that they know of. “It’s kind of a big deal in the furry fandom because it’s such an odd, out-of-left-field thing,” they say of the overrepresentation of furries within the air travel industry.
Given its taboo nature, as well as the general dearth of data surrounding the fandom, there aren’t really many reliable numbers regarding furry employment. But the aviation industry does appear to be fairly strongly represented within the fandom. Toby hosts aviation panels at furry conventions, and he says that they are among the most popular events, with recent ones attracting upwards of 400 attendees. All fursonas, he says, are represented, though airline pilots “do tend to favor birds.”
One furry who worked for four years at an airport kiosk says he knew of a number of other furry employees during his time there, including a baggage handler who had a tattoo of his fursona. “Some people are more vocal about it than others, but in my experience most don't talk about it,” he told me.
Vulan says that at their airline alone, they know of “at least 40” other self-identified furries, from pilots to baggage handlers to air traffic controllers. It’s not, however, something they discuss openly in the workplace. “I don’t feel the need to be represented at work, and I don’t know anyone who feels that way,” they say. “I think everybody understands this is something we enjoy at home, and we're not asking to bring it into work, just like we're not asking anybody else to bring their home life into work if they don't want to.”
Still, the question remains: Why does there appear to be so much crossover between the furry community and those who work in the friendly skies? Generally speaking, there is an “overlap between furries and transit nerds,” says Patch O’Furr, the editor-in-chief of the furry fandom publication Dogpatch Press. “It's a meta fandom full of roleplay so imaginative that it goes beyond species, so you get lots of people with intense special interests.”
Some furries I spoke to cited the popularity of famous anthropomorphic pilots, such as the titular character—a half-man half-pig—in the 1992 Miyazaki film Porco Rosso (Italian for red pig), or the bear Baloo from the 1990s Disney cartoon TaleSpin, as having sparked a childhood interest in aviation. Others pointed to the preponderance of neurodivergent furries within the fandom, many of whom may consider aviation among their specific obsessions—though it’s worth noting the medical requirements for becoming an FAA-licensed pilot are extremely stringent, and neurodevelopmental disorder diagnoses like autism or ADHD can present barriers.
The correlation between furries and the aviation industry may also partially stem from the fact that both involve heavy travel—many furries spend months ping-ponging across the country, going from con to con—and an intense level of interest. “For most of us in aviation, it’s not just a job, it’s a passion,” says Toby. “It’s not as plug-and-play as many other kinds of jobs, it’s a way of life. And I think the kind of mind that is attracted to aviation is the same kind of person that would be attracted to the furry fandom.”
The often misunderstood furry fandom has been subject to a slew of attacks from the right over the past few years, mostly as a proxy to culture wars about LGBTQ people. In 2024, right-wing commentator Megyn Kelly amplified a false rumor that furry students at a Utah middle school were engaging in animalistic behavior like biting and scratching; viral footage of a protest linked to the issue led to the school getting bomb threats. And in 2022, a GOP lawmaker had to publicly apologize after promoting a debunked conspiracy theory that public schools were putting litter boxes in classrooms to cater to students who had started self-identifying as furries.
With his unhinged ravings about “gender confusion”-afflicted furry pilots terrorizing the airwaves with perverse meowing, Tuberville, who did not immediately respond to a request for comment, appears to have been attempting to resurrect this type of moral panic—perhaps not coincidentally, just in time for the midterm elections. But the general public, which largely reacted to his comments with ridicule, doesn’t seem to be buying it. Nor, for that matter, are the furry pilots themselves, who shared Tuberville’s rant within their group texts with eye roll emojis.
“We’re furries at home, and we’re airline pilots at work, and these are two separate things,” says Vulan. “I would never ask somebody to dig up their personal life at work, and I don’t think anybody wants us to do that, either.” Plus, they note, it would be impossible for them to wear their fur suit in the cockpit: “mine has terrible vision.”

Fugitive opposition politician granted safe passage to return to Poland against prosecutors’ wishes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:08:37 UTC
04:08:37 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A Warsaw court has approved a request from Marcin Romanowski, a fugitive former government minister who has been on the run for almost two years, to receive safe passage back to Poland. Romanowski is believed to currently be in the pro-Russian Moldovan breakaway region of Transnistria.
Although Polish prosecutors have long been seeking Romanowski’s return, they opposed his request for safe conduct, arguing that he cannot be trusted to comply with its terms given that he has repeatedly sought to evade the law.
Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, has already announced that prosecutors will appeal the court’s decision, which he claims was issued by an illegitimately appointed judge and in violation of regulations.

Romanowski served as deputy justice minister in the former Law and Justice (PiS) government between 2019 and 2023. After PiS lost power, prosecutors sought to bring charges against him for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served in government, including participating in an organised criminal group.
However, Romanowski fled Poland in December 2024 and was granted asylum by Hungary, which was then ruled by Viktor Orbán, a conservative ally of PiS. When Orbán lost power earlier this year, Romanowski went on the run, and for months his location was unknown.
In August, it emerged that Romanowski had sent a letter to Poland requesting safe passage to return. The document indicated that he was in Tiraspol, the capital of Transnistria, a region that sought to break away from Moldova in the 1990s and is now effectively under Russian control.

At the time, the spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, Przemysław Nowak, said that there were “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland.
He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”.
However, on Wednesday, Warsaw’s district court approved Romanowski’s request. A spokeswoman for the court said that the decision had been made as “previous methods used [to secure Romanowski’s return] were ineffective” and safe passage would “allow the case to be clarified”.
The politician’s lawyer, Bartosz Lewandowski, said that safe passage meant his client could not be detained in Poland and that a European Arrest Warrant against him, which applies in other EU countries, would no longer be valid.

In a subsequent justification for the ruling, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily, judge Konrad Mielcarek wrote that Romanowski had pledged to “voluntarily return to the country”.
Conditions for his safe passage include Romanowski reporting to the court and prosecutors at designated times and places, not leaving his declared place of residence, and not seeking to obstruct the criminal proceedings against him.
The judge said that prosecutors had failed to provide adequate arguments as to why Romanowski’s request should be denied. He also found that Romanowski had not obstructed proceedings against him, but had merely exercised available legal remedies.
The fact that Romanowski had fled Poland does not count against him, argued the judge. In fact, “the very nature of safe passage is to provide a person residing abroad with a legal guarantee…in exchange for voluntarily submitting to the jurisdiction of Polish authorities”.
The judge also clarified that safe passage is neither a “reward” nor a “privilege” and that, given that evidence in the case is already secured and Romanowski no longer has influence over justice ministry officials, the risk of tampering is low.
The National Prosecutor’s Office immediately issued a statement declaring its opposition to the ruling and its intention to appeal. It noted that there had been no confirmation that Romanowski really is in Tiraspol and that the suspect had repeatedly sought to evade the law.
“These circumstances do not provide assurance that the suspect will comply with the conditions of the letter of safe conduct,” wrote the prosecutors, who also pointed to the fact that Romanowski had admitted to using travel documents issued under a false identity.
Żurek, meanwhile, noted that Mielcarek is one of the so-called “neo-judges”, appointed by a judicial body rendered illegitimate by PiS’s reforms. There are legal doubts about the status of such judges and the rulings issued by them, some of which have been overturned on that basis.
In his statement, the justice minister also argued that, under the law, safe passage cannot be issued without a prosecutor’s consent. Lewandowski, however, cited examples of case law that he said disproved this. He also noted that prosecutors had not filed any motion to recuse Mielcarek from the case.

Romanowski served in the justice ministry when it was led by Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of PiS, who is also wanted by the Polish authorities on suspicion of 26 crimes relating to his time in office.
Like his deputy, Ziobro also obtained asylum in Hungary. When Orbán lost power, Ziobro fled to the United States, reportedly with help from a senior Trump administration official. Poland has requested that Ziobro be extradited, though that process could take years.
Both Ziobro and Romanowski deny committing the crimes they are accused of and claim that they are being pursued as an act of “political revenge” by the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

US FCC head says controversial Trump ads do not raise concerns

US FCC head says controversial Trump ads do not raise concerns
Series of publicly-funded television spots have been criticised by Republicans and Democrats as self-promotion by Trump.
A series of taxpayer-funded advertisements that critics say are political campaign spots for United States President Donald Trump are not improper and do not need to be reviewed, according to the head of the country’s broadcast regulator.
“There’s nothing in there that strikes me to merit any sort of FCC review,” Brendan Carr, who Trump appointed as head of the Federal Communications Commission, said on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3ABC News says FCC is carrying out intimidation campaign to shape coverage
- list 2 of 3Trump threatens to report journalist Kristen Welker to broadcast regulator
- list 3 of 3Trump says he plans to campaign for 32 days before midterm elections
Carr likened the advertisements to public service announcements, echoing an argument the White House has made in response to criticism that Trump was using public funding to promote himself and his policies. Media freedom groups have criticised Carr for helping Trump to “weaponise” the FCC to go after news and television networks whose coverage of him he has not been happy with.
The US Constitution bars Trump from running for a third term as president, but he has nevertheless floated a third stint in the White House and has promoted merchandise bearing the words “Trump 2028”.
“The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads,” the White House said in a statement last week defending the campaign. “President Trump is not on the ballot, and there is no call to action. Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border, and abroad.”
Bipartisan condemnation of advertisement campaign
On Tuesday, Democratic senators wrote to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) asking it to stop spending funds on a series of television advertisements promoting the Trump administration’s recent actions.
“These ads need to immediately come off the air, taxpayers need to be paid back for this theft, and everyone responsible needs to be held accountable for this corrupt and illegal propaganda,” Senators Patty Murray and Chris Murphy wrote in a letter to the agency’s head. The lawmakers said DHS was planning to spend $20m on the advertisements.
But criticism of the television spots has come from prominent Democrats as well as Republican lawmakers, who have said the campaign appears to violate legal provisions meant to bar publicly funded political propaganda.
Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said the advertisements resembled something former Hungarian leader Viktor Orban would put out.
Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota said he agreed with the message in one of the advertisements, but “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars”.
Some Democrats have been more direct, saying the administration could face criminal liability for its actions. “This may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes,” Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, wrote on X, citing a Trump advertisement that aired recently.
Raskin said any government employees who worked on it could have violated the Hatch Act, a 1939 law that specifically prohibits government employees from engaging in political activities.
‘Love me’
The advertisements have aired on national television during national sports matches and other highly-watched programming.
One advertisement is a monochrome video featuring Trump walking down a hall in slow motion. In an audio clip taken from his last presidential election campaign, Trump can be heard saying Americans are now engaged in a “final battle” and that he and his supporters will “demolish the deep state, expel the warmongers from our government, we will drive out the globalists, we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists”.
In another advertisement, a montage of Trump is shown with audio of him saying, “Together, we will defeat communism, socialism, and Marxism,” before text in red capital letters notes a series of claimed accomplishments like “largest tax cuts in American history” and “reigniting American manufacturing”.
The advertisement is set to a song titled Love Me by artist JMSN, who wrote last week on X that Trump had used it without permission. Lawyers representing the artist wrote to the White House on Monday, saying they would take further action if the music was not removed from the video. JMSN, the letter said “does not want to be viewed as directly or indirectly affiliated with the President or his Administration.”

Türkiye joins global framework to address steel overcapacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:04:45 UTC
04:04:45 KST

Türkiye and fellow members of the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity (GFSEC) adopted an action framework to combat global overcapacity, Trade Minister Omer Bolat has said.
Bolat said in a statement on the Turkish social media platform NSosyal on Wednesday that members adopted the Comprehensive Framework for Joint Action and a ministerial statement during a meeting on the sidelines of the G20 trade ministers’ gathering in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
The forum assessed ways to prevent excess steel capacity from increasingly harming international steel trade, alongside coordination of members’ investment, production and foreign trade policies, he said.
Participating countries agreed to continue efforts to address the problem, Bolat added.
The minister is representing Türkiye at the two-day meeting, held under the US presidency as geopolitical tensions, mounting uncertainty and the risk of economic fragmentation weigh on global trade.
The gathering runs from Sept. 30 to Oct. 1 and is hosted by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
Bolat said Türkiye is sharing its approaches and proposed solutions on preventing food from being used as an instrument of political and economic pressure, addressing structural overcapacity, the most-favoured-nation principle and eliminating forced labour from global supply chains.
He said Türkiye would continue efforts under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s leadership to strengthen its influence and competitiveness in global trade, diversify trade relations and defend its interests on international platforms in line with its Century of Türkiye goals.

Unions want big tech to pay levy to build Australian-owned AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:02:29 UTC
04:02:29 KST

Unions and academics want big tech to pay levy to build Australian-owned AI
In short:
Big tech companies wanting to build data centres in Australia would pay a levy to fund the local AI industry under a plan from researchers and unions.
The proposal would not seek to build an Australian AI model from scratch but could include a homegrown chatbot like Claude.
What's next?
The Australian AI industry is already struggling to access the level of computing resources needed for frontier development.
Tech giants who want to build data centres in Australia would be slugged with a levy to help fund a local artificial intelligence (AI) industry under a plan being pushed by researchers and union figures.
In a joint statement, the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) and leading AI academics argue the government must force investment in domestic AI capability and infrastructure, rather than depending on foreign companies to provide access to the technology.
The ABC can reveal companies such as US monoliths Anthropic and OpenAI would be required to hand over a portion of their data centre computing capacity in return for developing AI on Australian soil under the proposal.
The siphoned "compute", or processing power, would be pooled and distributed by the federal government, while an "AI capability contribution" may also be paid by those same companies to fund the people, software and infrastructure needed to use it.
Leading AI researcher Sue Keay from UNSW said Australia did not have a shortage of talent but lacked the "confidence, investment and coordination" to back its own ability.
"The Medicare incident is a reminder that buying AI from overseas does not outsource the risks or our responsibility to manage them,"
"If AI is going to shape our health care, public services, workplaces and economy, Australians need genuine influence over how those systems are developed, governed and deployed."
The proposal, signed by the UNSW AI Institute, the Australian Institute for Machine Learning at Adelaide University and the Kingston AI Group as well as the ACTU, describes the need to "cultivate our own AI industry" instead of playing a supporting role to US-based multinationals.
"Australia has the talent, sector expertise and demand to build substantial AI capability. What it lacks is a funded national ambition and coordinated access to computing resources, skills, research support and patient capital," it reads.
Governments in several countries, including the UK, Norway, the US and Korea, have already committed billions to develop publicly owned AI computing resources and infrastructure.
Asked on Thursday about the levy proposal, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the government would "engage constructively with companies, including major ones which are internationally based".
"This is a technology that has been driven from US and china, but that's not to say there won't be Australian-based businesses and there are already involved in AI, and there is a real opportunity for Australia," he said.
"AI does have risk but it does also have potentially enormous benefits to humankind."
Custom AI for the Australian system
Under the proposal, framed as the "next logical step", Australia-specific AI would be developed to make work more productive and keep jobs in the country "that would otherwise move overseas".
It outlines how investment in a homegrown industry could both safeguard Australian access to the technology and ensure local communities get a return for hosting big tech.
The plan would not seek to build a frontier AI model, like the most powerful releases from Anthropic or OpenAI, but could include narrower models used for specific use cases or customised to work with existing Australian organisations and systems.
"We don't need to build the biggest AI models out there," ACTU assistant secretary Joseph Mitchell said.
"[Let's develop] smaller models built for Australian conditions, adapting open-weight models, and keeping critical services operating if access to US-based frontier models are disrupted again."
Mr Mitchell said requiring multinationals making money in Australia to push the local AI industry forward would set up permanent accountability.
"The hack of Medicare by OpenAI shows we can't trust our nation's future to US tech bros,"
The ACTU also floated the potential involvement of the superannuation industry as an investment solution, urging the government to include the sector in a coordinated effort to bring a sovereign AI industry online.
The concept of a tax or levy on AI is gaining ground, with tech magnate Bill Gates saying during an interview on the Ezra Klein podcast this week he believed the next policy step would be "robot tax".
"If you've let go of a worker and hired a robot to do that job, why are you so incentivising the trade-off against the human labour that you don't ask the robot to also pay into the pension fund?" Mr Gates said.
Government wants Australian ownership as part of tech deal
The government is already working on how Australia can extract value from the AI industry, given the interest from big tech companies who want to set up shop in the country.
Later this year, the prime minister hopes to introduce laws that would require developers to build renewable power infrastructure to meet the demands of their tech projects and minimise water use.
Andrew Charlton, Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy, has signalled he also wants to broker computing power from the AI companies as an additional requirement to build in Australia.
He told the Joe Walker podcast in August the government must make sure "big compute build-out delivers benefits to Australians" but admitted there were unanswered questions about the government's ability to "extract rent".
Already, Australia is struggling to meet existing local demand for AI infrastructure, with much of the GPU capacity — the heavy-hitting technology needed for AI frontier development — being found offshore.
Last month, startup accelerator Stone & Chalk chief executive Stela Solar, who runs the Buy Australian AI initiative, said securing domestic computing power was critical for growth of the sector.
"If we don't secure compute capability for homegrown technologies, we actually risk being squeezed out of the very sovereign AI foundations that we're building here," she said.
"That means while we might experience productivity gains from AI, we won't gain from the wealth growth that AI is bringing because that will land in other countries."

A drone-developing startup linked to Trump’s sons aims to bring Ukrainian technology to the United States — media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:02:15 EEST

A drone-developing startup linked to Trump’s sons aims to bring Ukrainian technology to the United States — media
Kyiv • UNN
America’s Powerus is preparing to merge with Aureus, which is backed by the younger Trumps. The company is holding talks with Ukrainian drone manufacturers.
The American drone startup Powerus, which is preparing to go public through a merger with a company backed by Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, aims to bring Ukrainian and other foreign technologies to the United States to meet growing demand from the Pentagon, company executives said, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Powerus, founded a year ago, is set to merge in early October with Aureus Greenway Holdings, a company listed on the Nasdaq. Aureus is engaged in owning and managing golf courses, while the Trump brothers hold an indirect stake in it through the American Ventures investment fund. According to regulatory filings, the fund is expected to hold a 9.9% stake (in the form of beneficial ownership) in the combined company.
The Florida-based company is part of a portfolio of drone and military technology businesses backed by the Trump brothers. The portfolio also includes XTEND AI Robotics, an Israeli drone manufacturer that went public in early September after merging with a publicly traded construction company in which American Ventures also held a stake.
Powerus executives and representatives of Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump say that the brothers are passive investors in Aureus and play no operational role in the drone-manufacturing company’s activities. However, "it never hurts when their name is associated with a project," said Powerus advisory board member Keith Kellogg, Trump’s former special envoy to Ukraine and a retired U.S. Army lieutenant general.
Companies and investors are seeking to capitalize on the rapid growth in demand for drones from the Pentagon and foreign buyers, which emerged after the war in Ukraine demonstrated the importance of autonomous systems on the battlefield.
In interviews with Reuters over recent months, company executives said they planned to grow through acquisitions, foreign partnerships and domestic manufacturing. The goal is to turn Powerus into an American partner capable of bringing in military technologies developed abroad, particularly in Ukraine, and arranging for their production in America.
Brett Velicovich, Powerus’s president and a former U.S. Army special operations intelligence analyst, said he aims to make the company a one-stop provider (a "single-window solution") for the Pentagon, offering foreign technologies with an "American face." According to him, Powerus is in talks with Ukrainian defense technology firms and would like to expand its capabilities, including by adding long-range strike drones to its product line.
The 42-year-old Velicovich has received praise from U.S. President Donald Trump. After Velicovich discussed drones on Fox News last summer, Trump wrote on the Truth Social platform that he "really knows his stuff."
In addition
Despite a number of recent deals, the company is still at an early stage of development. It was incorporated in October last year and, as of early 2026, had not yet conducted revenue-generating operations. After forming a lineup of aerial and maritime drones through the acquisition of other companies earlier this year, it reported first-quarter sales of $1.2 million.
In March, the company unveiled its Guardian interceptor drones, which Velicovich said were the result of "joint development" with Ukrainians.
Its MatrixFold strike quadcopter was not among the leaders in the recent second phase of the Pentagon’s "Drone Dominance" program— a $1 billion initiative aimed at rapidly deploying large numbers of low-cost strike drones. Velicovich said the competition’s requirements for resilience against electronic warfare were particularly challenging.
Recently, Powerus announced that it had received a contract worth up to $90 million from the U.S. Air Force, as well as a commercial agreement worth $22.3 million to protect energy infrastructure in the Middle East on behalf of an undisclosed client. The company also reported talks with Gulf countries.
During a trip to Pakistan in mid-September, Powerus received a limited order from the Ministry of Defence to supply aerial drones and provide operational support for them, and also signed a preliminary agreement with the Pakistan Army on potential cooperation. In addition, the company signed a memorandum of understanding with the Pakistan Air Force, Powerus told Reuters, declining to disclose details. Pakistan's military did not respond to a request for comment.
In Islamabad, Velikovich told Reuters that the aim was to combine American and Pakistani technologies, and that the company was holding meetings with local manufacturers. "We are exploring ways in which we could potentially even manufacture this technology here," he said.
