Russia summoned Denmark’s ambassador to Moscow on Wednesday because of an incident earlier this month in which a Russian frigate allegedly fired flares at a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea.
The Foreign Ministry said that it lodged a protest with the ambassador regarding the “unprofessional and provocative” actions of the Danish helicopter directed at the Soobrazitelny corvette of Russia’s Baltic Fleet, which it said took place earlier in neutral waters in the southwestern Baltic Sea.
The corresponding statement said the helicopter made a “dangerous” approach toward the corvette, "threatening navigational safety" among others, and that all warnings transmitted regarding the helicopter's altitude were ignored.
“To draw attention, two signal flares were fired from the corvette in a direction away from the helicopter. The aircraft subsequently ceased its provocative actions and departed the area. These facts are confirmed by objective monitoring data and are indisputable,” said the statement.
It also said the ambassador was informed that Moscow viewed the maneuvers by the helicopter as a “gross violation” of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
“Emphasis was placed on the unacceptability and absurdity of the accusations leveled against Russia by the Danish authorities regarding the incident – accusations that are entirely baseless,” it said.
The statement added that amid heightened tensions in the Baltic region “directly linked to increased anti-Russian military activity by NATO,” it was stressed that a recurrence of the “reckless” actions could lead to escalation and create the risk of a serious incident.
On Sept. 15, the Danish Defense Ministry said that a Fennec helicopter belonging to the Air Force was fired at with flares "in connection with routine photo coverage of a Russian frigate, which was in international waters off Gedser," a coastal town on the island of Falster.
The ministry said the Russian frigate fired two flares at the helicopter during the incident on Sept. 14, with one passing "within a short distance" of the aircraft.
Meanwhile, Denmark also summoned Russia's ambassador in the country over the incident, who later told Russian media that Moscow would thoroughly investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident.
In a later statement on Sept. 16, the Russian Defense Ministry said the incident occurred as the corvette operated in international waters in the southwestern Baltic Sea, and that its crew detected the helicopter as it approached the vessel and “failed to respond to calls" made via an international communication channel.
"The corvette's commander made the decision to fire two red signal flares to prevent a provocation by the Danish helicopter, after which the helicopter left the area," it added.
The incident off Denmark came amid escalating tensions across Europe over a series of alleged sabotage attacks and airspace violations that European countries have blamed on Russia.

Greens leader David Shoebridge wants to woo the same angry voters as One Nation — but from the left

He wasn't the only contender to lead the party — Sarah Hanson-Young and Mehreen Faruqi also put their hands up for the top job.
Faruqi is reportedly divisive inside the party and Hanson-Young, despite being the longest-serving Greens senator, is seen as too moderate, according to sources.
Greens leadership talks are usually done under a cloak of secrecy, driven by consensus. But yesterday's contest broke convention.
Greens whip Nick McKim read out the results of the leader and deputy leadership ballots, a sign the Greens had heard the concerns that they were too secretive.
Transparency can't be something you bang on about if you don't reveal your cards. And the cards they have revealed tell you everything about how they believe politics needs to be played.
Shoebridge moves to the left
The Greens have been frustrated at an inability to capitalise on public anger at the big end of town, and that One Nation have been the only big winners, despite a collapse in support for the two big parties.
The Greens want to replicate the success of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's progressive campaign.
Shoebridge may not have the charisma of Mamdani (let's be honest, few do), but he came straight out of the blocks with over-the-top rhetoric indicating he would focus the party's direction on the cost of living and a strident left-wing economic agenda.
After more than a decade in NSW politics, he entered federal parliament when the Albanese government was elected in 2022 and is known for his relationship with hard-left Greens MP Lee Rhiannon. He holds the Greens' defence and foreign affairs portfolios.
The Greens have long had a tension between the so-called watermelons — those who are more economically focused, old-school lefties — and those who are a product of the environmental movement.
The Greens are desperate to seize the moment rather than follow the Australian Democrats' path, a past Senate balance-of-power party that collapsed because of a deeply unpopular policy compromise on the Goods and Services Tax and ugly infighting.
This moment will test the party. Can they stay together and unite around a more radical leadership?
Loading
Path is harder for Labor
Yesterday Shoebridge vowed to take the fight to both Labor and One Nation and positioned the left-wing party as needing to become the alternative for a growing base of disaffected and raging voters.
His framing is all about Labor and One Nation.

"That is the dead politics of Labor, it's the dead politics of the Coalition, and when you really test it, it's the dead politics of One Nation," he said.
"People are desperate for material change. They don't want another meaningless message being delivered by some Labor hack that they know isn't going to change their lives. They want to take on the vested interests."
In a social media statement, Faruqi said she was disappointed by the result.
"Globally, people are struggling against genocide, wars, surging fascism and the twin crises of capitalism making working life too expensive and climate breakdown threatening our future," she said.

Under Larissa Waters, the Greens supported the government to pass nature laws, including the establishment of a federal environment watchdog, and Labor's changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. She vowed to be the leader who would get "shit done".
Shoebridge wants to hold Labor's feet to the fire. He will be a thorn in Labor's side rather than a deal maker.
The government's pathway through the Senate just got a whole lot harder.

Therefore, the military expert noted, there are currently no signs that the war will end through military means, so diplomatic efforts are needed—a combination of these two approaches is required. Even if the negotiations taking place in recent days have not made any substantial progress, it is important that they are happening, according to Hasala.

The US’s main trade regulator is conducting an industry-wide investigation into Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI labs to uncover the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers.
The investigation by the Federal Trade Commission is the first official US enforcement action that delves into rogue AI agents, following a surge in incidents first reported in July that have stoked fears among the public that uncontrolled AI could one day harm humans.
The FTC plans to issue formal demands for information and compel testimony from executives at top AI developers, including Anthropic, OpenAI and the research group Metr, according to multiple reports.
Anthropic and OpenAI have used Metr to conduct independent investigations into security incidents involving their agentic AI technology.
Anthropic, OpenAI and Metr did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The New York Post first reported the news.
Andrew Ferguson, the FTC chair, had concerns about the companies before AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked the open-source platform Hugging Face. The incident, in which OpenAI agents probed the AI coding hub for vulnerabilities before carrying out a large-scale attack, sparked global discussion of the issue.
Ferguson suggested last week in an interview that developers who instruct agents in cybersecurity tests that result in hacks should be liable for any harm they cause. The US should look to existing laws before seeking to pass new ones regulating AI, Ferguson said at an event in Austin.
The FTC has broad authority to sue companies over unfair or deceptive practices, and has used that authority in the past to take action against companies for failing to take reasonable measures to secure consumers’ data.
Donald Trump met with top AI executives on Tuesday, where the companies agreed to establish voluntary standards.
Trump has repeatedly called fears about AI a hoax as he seeks to prioritize US dominance in the technology over regulation. At the same time, he has also said the government can use existing laws against AI companies for any harm they may cause.

No 10 gathering evidence on public support for UK rejoining EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:33:20 UTC
03:33:20 KST

Senior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test public support for the UK rejoining the EU.
Aides to Andy Burnham have been talking to EU experts in a range of organisations about how the public would view a promise to rejoin, as momentum builds behind including such a pledge in the next Labour manifesto.
Some in No 10 are keen to promise that Labour would at least negotiate over re-entry to the bloc, something Burnham has previously said he wants to see happen “in his lifetime”. Others are nervous, however, that making such a promise could revive the flagging political fortunes of Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.
Burnham used his first Labour conference speech as leader to announce a review of the options for Britain’s relationship with Europe, and added on Wednesday that these options should include rejoining entirely.
The prime minister told delegates on Tuesday: “Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners.”
On Wednesday he clarified that this would include an option to rejoin – something ruled out by his predecessor Keir Starmer.
Burnham told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what [the former Conservative chancellor] George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market, or we could go all the way.”
Burnham’s comments sparked joy among pro-EU campaigners, who argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates – and outrage from political opponents.
Alex Burghart, the Conservative deputy leader, said: “Labour cannot blame a democratic vote from over a decade ago for the consequences of their own economic decisions.”
The Guardian has learned that Burnham’s comments are part of a wider effort by No 10 to test consensus over rejoining, with a view to possibly including such a promise in the next manifesto.
Officials have been in talks with several prominent thinktanks and pollsters, who have been working on projects to flesh out arguments over rejoining and test public opinion.
Last week, the Tony Blair Institute released a paper arguing that Burnham should seek talks with Brussels over becoming a member once more but should only do so if Europe relaxed its regulations in sectors including energy and technology.
On the same day, the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain released a megapoll conducted by YouGov suggesting Labour could more than double its seat total if it went into the next election promising to rejoin.
Over the coming weeks, the influential Institute for Public Policy Research will release a paper calling for the country to rejoin, while Think Labour has also been looking into how difficult it would be to do so.
Some in Downing Street are buoyed up by polling which shows that promising to re-enter the bloc does little to boost support for Reform. They also point out that Farage attacked the prime minister’s speech for the promise to change the pensions triple lock, rather than his comments about Europe.
The Guardian has been told that some at the top of government wanted the prime minister to use this week’s speech to promise to begin work on rejoining after the next election, rather than carrying out a review.
In the end, such an option was ruled out because the party was already bracing itself for a fight over pensions and did not want to give succour to Farage while he faces accusations about millions of pounds’ worth of donations to his party.
No 10 said the prime minister did not ever consider making such a promise in the speech and that it was not included in any draft of it.
Some believe it would be difficult to persuade Brussels, which has engaged in multiple rounds of talks about Britain’s relationship with the EU, to embark on negotiations over re-accession.
But in a major boost to supporters of rejoining, Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday welcomed Burnham’s comments. “Welcome back,” the French president said in English at a press conference in Madrid on Wednesday.
He continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”
An EU spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”
Burnham’s willingness to look at all options seems to have been accompanied by fresh engagement on the EU’s Made in Europe legislation, which threatens to lock UK goods out of certain supply chains on the continent.
No 10 has sought to have British manufacturers classified as European for the purposes of that legislation, with officials threatening to delay an EU-UK summit until London receives signals that there could be an accommodation.
Since Burnham’s speech, however, there is now talk of holding the summit on 20 November.
One EU diplomat said it was necessary to get Starmer’s old reset agenda concluded before talks of “a real reset” could begin, confirming support for a UK-EU summit as early as possible.
A second diplomat said there was “a good feeling” that Burnham was now looking at all options and seeking a consensus, “something Brussels has wanted to see”.

Flydubai terror attempt brings to mind the hijackings of 1970s in Israeli consciousness - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:32:43 UTC
03:32:43 KST

For a tense stretch on Wednesday morning, the news carried Israelis back to an older chapter of terror.
Not October 7. Not the bus and café bombings of the Second Intifada. Further back: to the aircraft hijackings of the 1970s, when a flight carrying Israelis could become a hostage crisis and an entire country would wait anxiously to learn where the plane had landed and what would happen to those aboard.
Dawson’s Field in Jordan. Sabena. Entebbe. Names that older Israelis need little explanation for, and that younger Israelis know from the history books.
Then came Wednesday’s alerts, in rapid succession: a flydubai plane en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv transmitted an emergency signal associated with hijacking. The plane changed course in midair. Israeli fighter jets were scrambled.
Suddenly, a routine flight home became the focus of national attention.
Israelis followed updates with bated breath, they were 'our passengers'
Where was the plane? Who was controlling it? Had someone seized it? Were the passengers safe?
Israelis followed the updates with bated breath. Those with relatives or friends aboard faced their own immediate terror. Others needed no personal connection. A plane carrying Israelis, in distress somewhere over the region, was enough.
Each update mattered. A report that contact had been lost deepened the anxiety; the first indications that the plane was not hijacked offered hope.
Then came the news everyone had been waiting for some 90 long minutes: the aircraft landed safely in Saudi Arabia. The passengers were safe.
Relief.
The first reports suggested an altercation between the pilots rather than a hijacking. That offered further reassurance: perhaps this frightening episode would turn out to have an explanation other than another attempt at the wholesale murder of Israelis.
But subsequent accounts suggested something much darker, and Israeli officials increasingly described the incident as an attempted terrorist attack, with the Omani co-pilot suspected of stabbing the Indian captain and trying to crash the aircraft with all aboard, 9/11 style.
Alongside those reports, however, came accounts of remarkable resourcefulness. Israeli passengers and other crew members had intervened and subdued the suspected attacker. They averted disaster even as the aircraft plunged.
They had refused to remain passive while their lives, and the lives of everyone around them, were in danger.
That brought pride alongside relief. “How Israeli,” many undoubtedly thought.
The older hijacking stories are remembered largely through the commandos who ultimately rescued the hostages. Wednesday’s emerging story centered on passengers and crew helping save themselves, while the emergency was still unfolding in the air.
Ordinary people rose to meet extraordinary danger
Ordinary people on an ordinary journey home had found themselves facing an extraordinary danger. They rose to meet it.
Clips circulated of passengers clapping and singing “Am Yisrael Chai” (the People of Israel live) after the plane landed in Saudi Arabia. The song expressed what many watching at home felt as well: joy that they were alive, pride that passengers had acted, and gratitude that the morning ended in celebration rather than mourning.
The relief extended well beyond the cabin.
Israel is a small country, and in moments like these it feels smaller still. People who have never met became “our passengers.” Their danger was followed on phones across the country. Their survival was a national relief.
That does not erase the country’s divisions. Indeed, by early afternoon, the incident was already being drawn into arguments about the election and the prime minister’s security warnings.
But before that came a simpler, shared response: let them be safe. And then, thank God, they are.
Crucial questions remained on Wednesday about vetting processes for pilots flying to Israel and the sequence of events in the cockpit. False reports and rumors spread quickly. The entire incident will require a thorough investigation.
But the passengers who overcame the co-pilot did not have the luxury of waiting for certainty before acting. Nor could they wait, as in the 1970s, for commandos to come to the rescue. They acted with extraordinary courage and resourcefulness.
Another striking difference from the hijacking era was the geography.
The aircraft was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, a route made possible by the Abraham Accords and normalization between Israel and the United Arab Emirates. It landed in Saudi Arabia, with which Israel still has no formal diplomatic relations.
An Israeli journey home through Dubai is now part of the region’s regular daily life. That would have been difficult to imagine during the era whose memories resurfaced on Wednesday.
Yet the limits of that regional transformation were also apparent. The Saudi authorities refused to permit an Israeli civilian aircraft to collect the passengers. Instead, another flydubai aircraft was sent, a prospect that - understandably, given the ordeal they had just endured - spooked some passengers.
The safe landing in Saudi Arabia was welcome. But the difficulty of arranging their return reminded everyone of the distance that remains between emergency cooperation and normal - even basic human - relations.
Still, the contrast was striking. Israelis experienced a hijacking fear associated with an older Middle East while traveling through a region that has changed profoundly.
That combination - new possibilities alongside enduring threats and dangers - is painfully familiar. And Wednesday abruptly exposed how fragile certain things are that we take for granted: like getting on a plane and expecting to get home safe and sound.
It also revealed how quickly anxiety, relief, and pride can once again become a shared national experience.
“Am Yisrael Chai,” the passengers sang after the plane landed in Saudi Arabia. Indeed. The passengers were alive. They had survived. They could sing.
And a country that for a terrifying hour and a half in the morning could hardly breathe was able to exhale again.

US-led delay in confronting Houthis a ‘grave mistake,’ says former Houthi spokesman - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:32:00 UTC
03:32:00 KST

The US delay in confronting the Houthis in coordination with Saudi Arabia “is a grave mistake that will cost dearly later,” Yemeni politician, writer, and former Houthi spokesperson Ali Al-Bukhaiti told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.
According to Axios, US President Donald Trump has rejected multiple requests from Riyadh to strike the Houthis, despite repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Saudi assets. Bukhaiti said the delay was a strategic error that the West could spend years paying for if it is not corrected soon.
“Defeating them after a few more years will be extremely costly for the region and the world, and may become impossible, forcing the world to recognize them as it recognized the Taliban government,” Bukhaiti said. “Worse, the Houthis control an international shipping lane, so the pain will be chronic for the West and the world, unlike the Taliban, who primarily harm their own people.”
Bukhaiti highlighted that, unlike the Taliban, the Houthis lack a large support base and remain a minority movement able to continue operating by exploiting “chaos and divisions of other political actors” and a unifying ideology.
“Washington and the West must therefore understand that the Yemen file is not like Afghanistan, and that defeating the Houthis is far easier than defeating the Taliban - especially with a capable, strong state that has powerful allies inside Yemen, namely Saudi Arabia,” he continued.
“Houthi rule is closer to Alawite rule and Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria, and it will unravel in the same way Assad’s system did…They resemble the Taliban only in that they are a cohesive religious movement; they resemble Assad in that they are a minority and most of the population is against them.”
Bukhaiti: Continued Houthi presence means 'end of American imperial era'
Bukhaiti also argued that the West needs to understand that failing to confront the Houthis and allowing their position to grow stronger at a strategic location next to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait would mean “the end of the American imperial era,” with consequences reaching far beyond the Gulf.
“If the United States cannot secure the Middle East, its presence there, and the sea lanes through it, the Chinese will not respect it over Taiwan, nor the Russians over Ukraine - or even Europe - and the world will face a grave danger,” he cautioned. “What is needed is an American strategic mind in the mold of Henry Kissinger, to grasp the extremely dangerous implications of a Houthi takeover of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.”
The Houthis claimed control of Perim Island earlier this month, which sits directly in the middle of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its narrowest point.
Now “sitting at zero distance from the shipping lane, the Houthis can now close the strait at any moment without Iranian support,” he explained.
“They can also fight Saudi Arabia and the [internationally recognized] Yemeni forces arrayed against them so long as the war stays as it is: one front active while the others sleep. But if Saudi Arabia chose a full-scale war, committed all allied forces, and forced them to fight together rather than in pieces, the recognized Yemeni government, its allied forces, and Saudi Arabia could successfully topple Houthi rule.”
Despite assessing a strong possibility of a Houthi defeat, Bukhaiti doubted Riyadh retained the “boldness it had in 2015,” suggesting Saudi decision-makers would err on the side of caution, particularly over concerns that Tehran could become more directly involved if a genuine Houthi defeat appeared likely.
He also argued that Riyadh’s confidence in its Arab and American alliances was waning, creating uncertainty that helped pave the way for the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed with Pakistan and Turkey in August.
“Once Saudi Arabia reaches a clear agreement with Pakistan and Turkey that they would confront Iran if it intervenes - and once advance warnings are sent to Tehran not to do so - I believe Saudi decision-makers would then launch a full-scale war against the Houthis aimed at bringing them down,” he predicted.
That lack of trust has also prevented the Yemeni majority opposed to the Houthis from taking action. Bukhaiti said economic collapse, unpaid salaries and growing corruption had pushed public anger in Houthi-controlled areas to a high point. However, fear of Houthi repression and a lack of confidence in the internationally recognized government and Saudi Arabia had kept people from rebelling.
If Yemenis were given a credible force they could trust to support them, he argued, the public could turn against the Houthis and their rule could collapse rapidly.
Explaining the Houthis’ motives, Bukhaiti identified two apparent aims. First, on the domestic front, he said the Houthis are seeking to ease their economic crisis by pressuring Riyadh to pick up the tab for employee salaries. Second, they aim to “squeeze Saudi Arabia by stopping its ships from passing through Bab el-Mandeb, completing a siege after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz.”
Houthis likely to be a part of eventual Saudi-Iranian peace agreement
The second aim, he argued, is tied to the Houthis’ alliance with the Islamic Republic of Iran.
Any conflict between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government of Yemen, he reasoned, would be addressed in an Iranian ceasefire agreement, protecting the Houthis from potentially having to fight alone in a full-scale war.
He said Tehran and the Houthis remain in close contact, but “the Houthis do not take orders from Iran.” Rather, the group’s leadership is almost free to decide when and to what extent it is willing to risk its own interests and survival for Iran’s benefit.
Though the Houthis are able to make some decisions on their own, Bukhaiti alleged that some members of the group’s leadership are closer to Iran than others and, as a result, the Islamic Republic of Iran “has hidden, dormant tools of influence.”
Those closer to the regime “press” Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi and persuade him that moves aligned with Iran would better serve the movement and are worth certain strategic risks.
“Abdul-Malik al-Houthi lacks a deep grasp of international and regional politics - though he is shrewd at managing the local internal struggle - so he cannot always choose the right decisions,” he claimed.
“He does not submit to Iranian diktats, but his weak regional and international political awareness leads him to accept advice from some of his own commanders who themselves have been shaped by Iranian counsel.”
With the Islamic Republic of Iran already viewed as a “good and honorable ally” by the Houthis’ religious base, accusations that the Houthis are serving Iranian interests over other Yemeni ones would not threaten domestic support, he added.
“Most civilians in areas they govern, however, believe the Houthis are gambling with their lives and interests for Iran’s sake - but those civilians have no influence and are powerless.”
Though the group is likely banking on a ceasefire agreement between Washington and Tehran including them, Bukhaiti stressed that they could not be trusted to honor those commitments.
“The assurances they sent the United States and Israel are deceptive and tactical, meant to keep Washington, Israel, and their regional allies from joining Saudi Arabia against them. They fear an international coalition like the one that brought down ISIS and al-Qaeda, and they know that once Saudi Arabia is sure the United States is with it - or at least will deter Iran from intervening - Saudi and Yemeni forces can topple their rule,” he said.
“Whenever the Houthis decide it serves them to target American ships or bar them from Bab el-Mandeb - if the war in Gaza reignites, another global crisis erupts, or even China or Russia asks, and they cooperate on other files - they will do it. They are an adventurist group and will cut shipping at any moment against America and the rest of the world.”
Bukhaiti insisted that cooperation between Riyadh and Jerusalem would be “dangerous for the Houthis,” but he doubted that such cooperation would ever be confirmed publicly or handled directly, especially as Saudi officials doubt Jerusalem would remain quiet on such dealings.
Despite the danger such a partnership could pose to the Houthis, he argued that opposition to Israel in the region could mean such a coalition risks further legitimizing the Houthis.
“The better course is for Israel to press the United States and the West to form an international coalition…,” he reasoned, adding that it wasn’t necessary to have boots on the ground to win this war.
“Some airpower, political and military support, and a clear green light for Saudi Arabia to wage the campaign against the Houthis until their authority falls in Sanaa and even in Saada would suffice. The US-led coalition must also pledge to cover Saudi Arabia’s back against any Iranian intervention. Then, once those conditions are in place, Saudi Arabia and Yemeni forces would have the ability to topple the Houthis within a few months.”

Kyiv • UNN
Papal envoy Matteo Zuppi held talks in Moscow on humanitarian issues related to the war. He also visited Ukrainian prisoners of war.
On Wednesday, Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs reported that the papal envoy, Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, discussed humanitarian issues related to the war in Ukraine during talks with Russian officials and also visited Ukrainian prisoners of war, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Zuppi’s three-day talks coincided with the Pope’s call for Russia and Ukraine to sit down at the negotiating table and discuss ways to end the war, which has been ongoing for four years. The pontiff also criticized state leaders who, he said, “are beginning to talk about nuclear weapons and wars that are becoming increasingly destructive.”
The Foreign Ministry said that Zuppi met with Russian presidential aide for foreign policy Yuri Ushakov and other Russian officials, discussing prospects for resolving the conflict and humanitarian issues, including the exchange of prisoners of war and the situation of displaced children.
According to the statement, Zuppi, who heads the Italian Bishops’ Conference, also discussed living conditions in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky (Kherson region of Ukraine); according to Ukrainian officials, over the previous weekend Ukrainian forces used drones there to deliver food and medicine to the civilian population.
The Russian Foreign Ministry statement claims that Ukraine is allegedly blocking all attempts to provide the city’s residents with essential resources. At the same time, Ukrainian officials say that Russian troops are preventing people from leaving the city.
The ministry reported that Zuppi was granted permission to visit prisoners of war and “was able to speak personally with Ukrainians and see for himself that Russia is strictly complying with all relevant humanitarian standards.”
It is noted that the visit “confirmed the constructive and regular nature of the dialogue between Russia and the Vatican, as well as the readiness of both sides to continue cooperation on humanitarian issues.”
Zuppi’s previous visit to Moscow took place in October 2024; at that time, they discussed prospects for ending the war that began as a result of Russia’s invasion of its neighboring country in 2022.
Zuppi also held talks in Kyiv with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Direct talks with Israel only way to regain Lebanese territory: Foreign minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:28:19 UTC
03:28:19 KST

Naim Berjawi and Sahin Demir
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji said Wednesday that direct negotiations with Israel under US auspices are the only way to regain Lebanese territory and allow residents to return to their villages.
Rajji made the remarks during a discussion organized by the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington, according to a Lebanese Foreign Ministry statement.
The discussion, chaired by former US diplomat Elliott Abrams, was attended by council members, journalists and representatives of research centers, the ministry said.
It addressed the situation in Lebanon, reasons for delays in implementing the framework agreement, Hezbollah's weapons, the future of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon and relations with Syria's new government, the statement said.
Rajji said Lebanon's priority is to ensure stability, adding that the Lebanese want their country to once again become a cultural, tourism and economic hub in the region.
However, he said this could not be achieved while weapons exist outside state authority.
He described the Lebanese government's decision to restrict weapons to state control as "courageous," saying Lebanon's stability and prosperity require "ending the occupation and Hezbollah handing over its weapons."
"We want peace with all our neighbors," Rajji said.
He also stressed that Iran must "stop interfering in Lebanese affairs" and said the Lebanese army is the country's "only hope."
Rajji welcomed US assistance to the Lebanese military and expressed hope that the support would continue.
He reiterated the government's commitment to direct negotiations with Israel under US auspices, describing them as "the only way to regain the territories and allow residents to return to their villages."
On Sunday, Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem called on Lebanese authorities to “freeze direct negotiations with Israel and move toward indirect negotiations” in order to halt what he described as concessions and correct the course of the talks.
Direct negotiations between Lebanon and Israel began on April 14, 2026, with a meeting in Washington under US auspices.
Subsequent rounds addressed a ceasefire, Israeli withdrawal, borders, prisoners and missing persons.
On June 26, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-sponsored "framework formula" in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army in areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Despite the agreement, Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon have continued, while Israel still occupies areas in the south, some held for decades and others seized during recent wars and military operations.
Since March 2, Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed at least 4,386 people and injured 12,413 others, while displacing more than 1 million people, according to Lebanese authorities.

P1-SUN JetKiller Destroys Geran-5 Jet-Powered Drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:26:34 UTC
03:26:34 KST

The Ukrainian P1-SUN JetKiller interceptor drone, manufactured by SkyFall, destroyed a Russian Geran-5 jet-powered UAV.
SkyFall told Militarnyi about the interception.
Operators of the Lasar’s Group unmanned systems unit of Ukraine’s National Guard intercepted the target.
During the combat mission, the crew also used a remote control system developed by SkyFall that allows operators to control the interceptor over the internet while remaining at a considerable distance from the launch site.
The company previously integrated this system into P1-SUN family interceptors. In particular, in June 2026, at Eurosatory, the company unveiled the P1-SUN Long with an integrated AI module, which also supports remote control from any location with a stable internet connection.
SkyFall presented the JetKiller in July 2026 at the Farnborough International Airshow. The interceptor can reach speeds of up to 370 km/h, has a flight range of up to 30 km, can operate at altitudes of up to 9 km, and can remain airborne for up to 15 minutes. Its warhead weighs 500 grams.
The interceptor can be equipped with day or night cameras, as well as an AI module for automatic target detection, tracking, and acquisition. The guidance system can detect a target up to one kilometer away.
In September, Russian forces began using a new modification of the Geran-5 equipped with an autonomous optical navigation system and a modified fuselage design.
According to official data from Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, the Geran-5 is about 6.5 meters long, has a 3.2-meter wingspan, and a maximum takeoff weight of up to 850 kilograms. Its warhead weighs about 90 kilograms, while its cruising speed is 450-600 km/h. Its flight range is about 950 km.
In September, the Defense Forces demonstrated several successful interceptions of similar aerial targets using various Ukrainian systems. In particular, on Sept. 28, a crew of the 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Regiment destroyed a Geran-5 that was traveling at about 425 km/h when it was intercepted.
SkyFall manufactures several Ukrainian unmanned systems, including interceptors, Vampire heavy strike drones, and Shrike FPV drones. In August 2023, more than 270 Vampire strike drones were transferred to the military as part of the Army of Drones project.
The company developed a separate line of specialized interceptor drones in the P1-SUN family. Their use against jet-powered targets was first reported in late 2025, when a P1-SUN destroyed a Russian jet-powered Shahed.
In May, P1-SUN interceptors shot down Russian Gerbera drones carrying FPV drones.

NASA directive might increase the odds of contaminating Mars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:25:22 UTC
03:25:22 KST

A new NASA directive seeks to loosen “planetary protection” rules meant to avoid the contamination other worlds with microbial life from Earth.
The policy shift arrived via a message to NASA personnel that was obtained and shared yesterday by the independent watchdog sites NASA Watch and Astrobiology.com. In it, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman writes that procedures for avoiding contamination “must reflect our current scientific knowledge” and argues that this knowledge has shifted since the current rules were established decades ago.
The directive “ensures we can use our incredible data to lower costs on our missions,” says Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate. “This process will also help increase commercial capabilities — getting more missions into space by streamlining space exploration.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In 1964 members of the International Council for Science’s Committee on Space Research (COSPAR), led by the United Nations–affiliated International Council of Scientific Unions (now the International Science Council), feared that the breakneck pace of the space race could lead to spacecraft accidentally contaminating alien worlds with microbial life from Earth. If those interplanetary hitchhikers were sufficiently resilient and numerous to form self-sustaining populations on Mars or other planets, they could forever alter those otherwise-pristine environments and sabotage all future efforts to discover true alien life there. So COSPAR issued a resolution that any mission to another potentially habitable or inhabited world must demonstrate a less than one-in-10,000 chance of exposing such places to terrestrial life capable of interplanetary colonization.
The new directive notes that COSPAR subsequently tightened those rules to account for the flurry of Mars-bound missions, some carrying human crews, that were widely expected to launch in the intervening decades. Codified in 1969, those more stringent and costly restrictions have guided—and greatly limited, some critics say—Mars exploration ever since. But “human exploration did not progress as quickly as all believed,” Isaacman’s message reads, while technology for sterilizing spacecraft has improved markedly. “Our long-standing policies were designed in a different era,” he writes.
Now, the message states, NASA’s rules will immediately be restored to the looser 1964 restriction of less than a one-in-10,000 chance of biocontamination for each Mars-bound mission. And in the meantime, NASA officials will perform a rapid-fire “modernization assessment” of the current science and technology concerning contamination risk, with a December 2026 deadline for delivering recommendations to lower that threshold even further.
A statement from NASA clarified that the new directive isn’t “weakening” existing planetary protection protocols so much as updating them. “This directive moves NASA toward a quantitative, performance-based approach that measures actual contamination risk and applies protections accordingly,” the statement said. Additionally, missions looking for past or present life on Mars—such as NASA’s Perseverance rover—will “continue to carry requirements appropriate to protecting those investigations.”
Such cautions are crucial, experts say, especially since Perseverance has uncovered tantalizing hints of possible ancient biosignatures in some of the rocks it has studied; samples from those rocks are now in limbo, awaiting an as-yet-unclear ride back to Earth for further analysis.
“We are actively seeking to learn if the organics we have found on Mars are biological in origin,” says Linday Hays, NASA’s senior scientist for Mars exploration. This policy change will not threaten that goal, she says, but “will allow us to bring decades of science from our Mars exploration to help make our processes more straightforward for robotic and, in the future, human exploration of the Red Planet.”
Editor’s Note (9/30/26): This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

DOJ accuses Minnesota federal judges of misconduct for NY Times immigration interviews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:24:35 UTC
03:24:35 KST

The Department of Justice on Wednesday filed a judicial misconduct complaint against all but one Minnesota federal judges on active status for interviews they gave to The New York Times that criticized the Trump administration's handling of immigration enforcement cases in the state.
The DOJ asked the 8th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals to force the recusal of all seven judges who spoke with The Times from any case involving the Department of Homeland Security.
The complaint also asks the 8th Circuit, which handles cases arising from the District of Minnesota, to investigate what the DOJ called "the judges' improper and unethical conduct" in speaking to the newspaper.
The complaint singles out Senior Judge Patrick Schiltz and Senior Judge John Tunheim, who were quoted by name in the article, which ran under the headline "Trump's Minnesota Surge Threatened Democracy, Judge Warns."
Schiltz until July 1 had served as chief judge in the District of Minnesota, having succeeded Tunheim in that role in 2022.
Schiltz had issued a Jan. 28 order demanding that Immigration and Customs Enforcement stop violating orders issued by Minnesota federal judges in cases related to a surge in immigration enforcement actions in the state. Schiltz told The Times that ICE's violations of the orders "created a grave threat to the rule of law."
Tunheim was quoted by The Times after a paragraph that said the judges considered that most of the detainees whose cases they handled "seemed to be ordinary people with homes and jobs," and not immigrants who DHS officials claimed were "the worst of the worst."
"They weren't arresting, in my view, people who were dangerous criminals on the street," Tunheim said, according to The Times.
The other judges spoke to the newspaper on the condition of anonymity.
"Judge Schiltz and Judge Tunheim, at least, have flagrantly violated the Code of Judicial Conduct with their improper and unethical comments to the New York Times," says the complaint by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, Jr.
Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement, said, "Seven federal judges in the District of Minnesota talked to the New York Times about cases, some of which are on-going, in a manner that the Department of Justice views as a clear violation of their ethical duties."
"Their conduct has undermined public confidence in an impartial judiciary in Minnesota," Blanche said.
A spokeswoman for U.S. District Court in Minnesota defended the judges' contact after CNBC requested comment from Schiltz and Tunheim about the complaint.
"As legal-ethics experts have confirmed, our judges were acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to the New York Times," said Rebeccah Parks, the spokeswoman.
"Indeed, in February of this year, the Committee on Codes of Conduct issued an advisory opinion to emphasize that federal judges may "speak[] and writ[e] on core judiciary matters such as advocacy for the rule of law and judicial independence,'" Parks said. "Our judges acted within this capacity."

Ukraine Completes 17 of 42 Resolutions Needed to Unlock $29.5B in Aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:20:36 UTC
03:20:36 KST

Ukraine’s government has now adopted 17 out of 42 resolutions it needs to unlock international financing, with less than three weeks left before its self-imposed deadline.
The Cabinet of Ministers approved four more decisions at its meeting on Wednesday, Sept. 30, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in a statement. The government has entered what he described as a regime of maximum austerity and postponed non-priority spending.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The remaining 25 resolutions must be completed by Oct. 15.
“Over the next two weeks, we need to accelerate the work as much as possible and ensure that every decision is fully implemented,” Koretskyi said, adding that “any delay comes at a very high cost.”
The decisions are required to secure €27 billion ($29.5 billion) in planned international financing by the end of the year, which depends exclusively on Ukraine meeting its reform commitments to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the EU.
The government originally planned to finish the work by Nov. 1 but moved the deadline forward as pressure on public finances grew.
Parliament’s share of the work
The commitments fall into two groups: government measures and legislative changes that require votes in Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada.
Koretskyi thanked lawmakers who supported several of the necessary bills in their first reading last week, calling the process “a joint effort and our shared responsibility.”
Ukraine Plans Fourth Phase of Operation Vivaldi, Zelensky Says
The cabinet has asked parliament to hold an additional plenary session on Oct. 12, a day before lawmakers are scheduled to return from recess. According to UA.News, among the funds at stake is an EU tranche of about €3.7 billion ($4 billion).
President Volodymyr Zelensky has also pressed lawmakers to act on Monday, Sept. 28, saying that if the government meets its commitments by Oct. 15, parliament must follow an equally clear schedule.
A $27 billion defense gap
The push comes as Ukraine’s defense budget faces a $27 billion shortfall.
On Monday, Ukraine’s government announced that it adopted a decision setting the priority order for state expenditures.
Koretskyi said that the government will fund mainly defense, pensions, social payments and public-sector salaries, while postponing nonessential spending.
“Under these conditions, we continue to adopt strict anti-crisis measures to ensure the most important priorities – defense needs and the welfare of our people,” he said.
The government’s budget plans to cover about $7 billion through austerity, including cutting and reallocating spending, while the remaining $20 billion is expected to come exclusively from its Western partners.
“It is time, finally, to stop spending money on non-priority items,” he said, urging local self-government bodies to set similar priorities in their own budgets and to cut spending that is not currently essential.
Throughout 2026, Kyiv has struggled to receive foreign aid on time and in full because of delayed reforms and corruption scandals.
Much of the support comes from the EU’s €90 billion ($102 billion) Ukraine Support Loan for 2026 and 2027, which is to be repaid from reparations owed by Russia, according to the European Council.
The EU has allocated up to €45 billion ($51 billion) of it for 2026, including €17 billion ($19 billion) in budget support and €28.3 billion ($32 billion) for Ukraine’s defense industrial capacities.
Ukraine’s total war costs will reach $155 billion this year, Reuters reported, citing Koretskyi on Wednesday.
It marks the first time Kyiv has published an estimate of its annual war costs, so there is no comparable figure for previous years, though officials say the cost of the war has grown as both sides rely more heavily on missiles and drones.
Funding from Western partners
On Sept. 27, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced almost €710 million ($809 million) in EU support for displaced people and crisis relief worldwide, €52 million ($59 million) of which will be allocated to Ukraine ahead of winter.
European Pravda separately reported that an EU-proposed €100 billion ($115 billion) funding package for Ukraine remains largely undisputed in negotiations on the bloc’s upcoming seven-year budget, spanning from 2027-34.
The EU disbursed €3.3 billion (roughly $3.7 billion) to Ukraine for the procurement of missiles and drones.
Separately, the EU approved a €6.1 billion ($7 billion) defense package for Ukraine on Sept. 11, allowing Kyiv to purchase the PAC-3 Patriot interceptors.
According to von der Leyen, the EU has already mobilised nearly €15 billion (approximately $17 billion) to Ukraine in 2026 alone.

Girls in Gaza forced into child marriage as Israel’s genocide fuels hunger and displacement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:20:30 UTC
03:20:30 KST

Safaa’s face bears marks of fatigue and exhaustion far beyond her 19 years. Squeezed into a torn nylon tent on the sandy coast of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza, months into a supposed ceasefire that has done little to ease the hardships of her people, she sits at the entrance with hollow eyes and brittle nails — the visible signs of malnutrition and vitamin deficiency. She is also pregnant, waiting to give birth while gripped by unrelenting fear.
In 2024, her parents married her off with the promise that she would live in better conditions. “There was no house, no walls, no celebration,” she tells Mondoweiss quietly, asking to be referred to by her first name only.
Instead of finding reprieve in her marriage, she found herself responsible for gathering firewood, cooking over an open fire, and washing clothes by hand amid a water shortage — burdens her frail body was not built to bear.
Her pre-war life in Shuja’iyya was the picture of an ordinary childhood. Then their home was struck and leveled in 2023, leaving her family of eight with no roof and no income. Her pregnant mother grew weaker by the day. Safaa herself suffered constant dizziness from malnutrition. When a young man proposed, promising food and stability, she agreed at 15 and was married at 17.
But the illusion collapsed on the first day.
Before October 2023, child marriage in Gaza had been declining. According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, the rate of girls married under 18 had fallen from 22.2 percent in 2015 to 17.9 percent in 2022. The war reversed that progress entirely. A 2024 UNFPA survey found that 71 percent of respondents reported growing pressure to marry girls under 18, driven by displacement, poverty, and the collapse of protective systems.
“Girls in Gaza are not choosing marriage. They are being driven into it by hunger, fear, and displacement,” UNFPA Country Representative Nestor Owomuhangi said in April 2025. As such, childhood marriage can put young girls in precarious conditions where they are unable to make educated decisions about their future.
“Under continuous bombardment and repeated displacement, I see parents pushed toward excruciating, zero-option scenarios,” Walaa al-Othmani, a field specialist with the al-Shafi Association for Family Development, told Mondoweiss. “Through my direct work with these families, I witness how extreme deprivation drives them to make the most painful decision: marrying off their young daughters.”
Losing everything
In a narrow, dark corner of a school run by UNRWA in Nuseirat refugee camp sits Manal, 17, wedged between piles of discarded school furniture. Before the war, she was a top student planning to study at an arts college. Today she lives in a chaotic, overcrowded environment where hundreds of displaced families share classrooms and hallways with no privacy, and diseases spread from overflowing sewage and a chronic water shortage.
In 2024, her father convinced her that marriage would protect her and ease the family’s burden. Two of her older sisters had already been married off. She had no say. Within days, she was transformed from a student carrying a school bag into a wife responsible for running a household inside a displacement corridor.
“I never once imagined that I would become a wife living in a classroom crowded with displaced people,” she said, asking to be identified by her first name only. “No protection, no stability, not even a private space to cry. I lost my school and my childhood at the same time.”
The collapse of education was a direct driver. According to UNICEF, more than 97 percent of Gaza’s schools have been damaged or destroyed since October 2023, leaving around 658,000 school-age children without access to formal education. The UN has described this destruction as deliberate and systematic. What was once a protective space for young girls has ceased to exist.
“Child and early marriage is witnessing a marked rise; amidst wartime conditions, some families have come to view it as a safe way to secure their daughters’ futures,” Maryam Zaqout, Director of the Aisha Association for the Protection of Women and Children in Gaza, told Mondoweiss. “Yet, at a time when these girls ought to be in school, we see them carrying their own children and sometimes coming to the association seeking protection from the harsh reality in which they live.”
Al-Othmani describes how the concept of protection has been distorted beyond recognition: girls are being promised security and safety in marriages in exchange for their childhood. “Fathers escape this fear by passing responsibility for the girl to a husband, believing a male presence will shield her,” Zaqout says. “But what we witness on the ground is that this protection is an illusion. The young girl moves to a new tent only to find herself completely unprotected and far more vulnerable to abuse, without her own family there to back her up.”
This is what happened with Amal, the 15-year-old wife whose frail body was subjected to sexual abuse and violence from the first day of her marriage. She lives in the southern edge of Khan Younis, in a sand-battered tent with her family, surviving on a single free meal each day from a communal charity kitchen. At 15, she was married off in a hasty agreement between her father and her aunt, despite her own mother’s objections. Amal found no room to maneuvere. “It felt as though my father simply wanted to get rid of a heavy burden in the tent and cut expenses,” she said.
Since October 2023, Israel has tightened its siege over Gaza, imposing a famine that starved its population and killed dozens. Months into a ceasefire, Gaza’s families remain trapped between hunger and soaring living costs: food prices are still about 235 percent above pre-October 2023 levels, while shortages of cash, jobs, cooking fuel, and clean water make even basic meals difficult to afford. In July, the World Food Program found that 45 percent of households surveyed reported going to bed hungry at least once in the 30 days preceding the survey, with 6 percent experiencing this more than ten times.
On her wedding night, and as a result of sexual violence, Amal’s weak body endured severe bleeding and serious health complications which were exacerbated by a complete lack of medical care or nearby hospitals capable of handling her case. “I thought moving to my husband’s tent might mean better food,” she recalled. “Instead I found myself sinking into something even harsher.”
Soon after, she got pregnant with a baby she quickly lost as a result of malnutrition and overall physicall unwellness. Grappling to navigate the emotional, mental, and physical tool the marriage has had on her, Amal feels numb. “I just wanted to go to school, finish my education, graduate, and not have to constantly worry about having enough food or calculating every bite just to make it last. I didn’t want much from this world — just to breathe freely and see the sea, not something that would choke the life out of me,” she said.
The legislative vacuum
Israel’s assault on Gaza has wiped out the judicial system’s infrastructure entirely — demolishing court buildings, destroying decades of records preserving marriage contracts, paternity records, and custody rulings, and killing or displacing judges and licensed marriage officiants. The result is the total paralysis of the official legislative system.
“Under normal circumstances, Palestinian law and sharia courts enforced strict procedures prohibiting the documentation of any marriage for those under 18, except through stringent judicial exceptions requiring a judge’s approval, medical examination, and social assessment,” al-Othmani explained. “Today, amid the absence of the court, the judge, and the registrar, marriage decisions are made individually inside camp tents — without legal oversight or statutory deterrents.”
Data from the Supreme Sharia Court, cited by the Associated Press, shows that 20.6 percent of the 35,474 marriages recorded in 2024 and 2025 involved a girl under 18, including 627 marriages of girls under 15. Rights advocates warn that even these figures undercount the reality: most child marriages now take place verbally, entirely outside any statistical record.
The collapsed healthcare system also adds to the physical toll these young wives face.
In Zeitoun, east of Gaza City, 16-year-old Fatima suffered three consecutive miscarriages within six months of her forced marriage, a direct result of grueling physical labor, including hauling water and gathering firewood while walking for long distances over rubble, severe malnutrition, and the complete collapse of healthcare in northern Gaza. Before the war, she had opened her own small food stand and had great ambitions. Air strikes destroyed it along with her family’s home in Beit Hanoun. “The war took my home, my work, my dream, my health, and my unborn children,” she told Mondoweiss, explaining that destitution and her family’s struggle to find food drove her into this marriage. “I was completely deprived of medicine or care throughout my miscarriages,” she added, lamenting the circumstances that crushed her dreams and independence.
Only 50 percent of Gaza’s hospitals are functioning even partially, according to the World Health Organization. Pregnant minors face a complete absence of prenatal care, ultrasound checkups, and essential supplements, producing a sharp rise in premature births, uterine rupture, severe hemorrhaging, and recurrent miscarriage. According to UNFPA, approximately 10 percent of all newly registered pregnancies in Gaza now involve adolescent girls.
A last line of defense
Faced with this crisis and the absence of official protection, grassroots initiatives have emerged as the only available response.
The al-Shafi Association for Family Development, working in partnership with UNFPA, operates through three strategies inside the displacement camps: expanding safe spaces and dedicated tents exclusively for adolescent girls; running direct awareness campaigns for parents using medical evidence on the dangers of early pregnancy; and offering legal guidance to families who proceed with a marriage, encouraging them to draft temporary contracts signed by the camp’s mukhtar (a respected elder tasked with mediating disputes) and recognised community figures, preserving dowry rights and proof of paternity until sharia courts reopen.
Al-Othmani describes how eagerly the girls turn up. “They are fully aware of the rights they have lost,” she says, “and are in urgent need of self-care and an outlet for their emotions.”
But the scale of what has been lost cannot be offset by tents and awareness sessions. As the genocide continues and all traces of normalcy are erased, girls continue to be forced into marriage in hopes of better living conditions, purpose, or an escape.
Field estimates place the rate of marriage among girls under 18 at above 35 percent.
Manal still carries her school notebook. Its pages are worn from being leafed through in the displacement corridor where she now lives as a wife. “Every time I remember what my life was supposed to be,” she says, “I feel like I can’t breathe.”

Ukraine war latest: Russia uses drone with warhead designed to cut power pylons for 1st time, Zelensky adviser says
Key developments on Sept. 30:

- Drone crashes in Moldova, Romania scrambles fighter jets amid Russian mass attack on Ukraine
- Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45 million for every hour businesses stop, economy minister says
- Zelensky visits Lyman sector, says Operation Vivaldi reclaimed 125 square kilometers
Russia has for the first time used a jet-powered drone equipped with a warhead designed to destroy high-voltage power pylons and steel bridge structures, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Sept. 30.
The development comes as Moscow renews its large-scale campaign against Ukraine's energy system ahead of winter, launching its heaviest combined attack on energy infrastructure in months overnight on Sept. 30.
"Bad news. Today, the enemy for the first time used a special shaped-charge cutting warhead on a jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)," Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technologies, wrote on Telegram.
According to Beskrestnov, the warhead was developed specifically to destroy high-voltage pylons and steel bridge structures. It consists of a 40-kilogram main charge and four additional destructive modules.
"I think the enemy plans to attack important high-voltage power transmission lines," he said.
Russia's overnight assault involved nearly 190 attack drones as well as ballistic missiles, Zelensky said. Energy infrastructure in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast was the primary target, while critical infrastructure was also struck in several other regions.
By the evening, emergency power outages had been introduced in the capital and surrounding region as well as in Chernihiv and Zhytomyr oblasts following repeated Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, according to the Energy Ministry.
The Sept. 30 attack marked a sharp escalation in Russia's renewed campaign against Ukraine's power system.
"Since the summer, there has been practically no day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. But such a massive and combined attack has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season," Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said following the attack.

Drone crashes in Moldova, Romania scrambles fighter jets amid Russian mass attack on Ukraine
A drone flew into Moldovan airspace, crashed outside a village, and exploded in the early hours of Sept. 30 amid a Russian mass attack on Ukraine, Moldova's Defense Ministry said.
The drone entered Moldovan airspace around 5:43 a.m. local time and fell down near the village of Hirbovat in the central Anenii Noi district, where it exploded, according to the ministry.
According to preliminary information, no injuries were reported from the explosion. Moldovan police and army teams were headed to inspect the site.
Romania's Defense Ministry said that its radars detected an aerial target east of Izmail during the night and two F-18 fighter jets of the Spanish air force stationed in the NATO country scrambled as a precaution. No object entered Romanian airspace, the ministry said.
Overnight, Russia attacked across Ukraine with 188 drones, 86 of them jet-powered, as well as with Zircon, Onyx, and Iskander missiles, according to Ukraine's air force. The air force said it shot down or suppressed 5 missiles and 155 drones.

Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45 million for every hour businesses stop, economy minister says
Missile alerts cost Ukraine an estimated $45 million for every hour they force businesses to stop operating, Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko told the Guardian in an interview published on Sept. 30.
"If people are in a bunker, business stops," Kravchenko told the Guardian.
Kravchenko said prolonged missile alerts can bring large parts of the economy to a standstill as workers move into shelters, with some alerts lasting for hours.
Ukraine introduced a two-tier air raid warning system on Sept. 2 to reduce the economic disruption caused by prolonged alerts. Red alerts are issued when there is a missile threat and require businesses to halt operations and people to seek shelter. Yellow alerts warn primarily of drone threats and allow many businesses to continue operating.
Russia has intensified its aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure. Kravchenko said more than half of businesses continue operating during yellow alerts, but those warnings do not mean there is no danger.
On Sept. 28, a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv during a yellow alert while employees were still inside. The attack killed an aide to former National Security and Defense Council Secretary Volodymyr Horbulin and injured others.
"What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything," Kravchenko said.
Russian attacks have caused an estimated $10 billion in damage to fixed assets in Ukraine this year alone, according to Kravchenko. Steel plants, warehouses, logistics hubs, and data centers have all been hit as Moscow increasingly targets infrastructure supporting the country's economy.
Russia has also stepped up attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea ports and maritime export infrastructure, adding pressure on one of the country's main trade routes.
The government is now discussing ways to allow more private companies to purchase Ukrainian air-defense systems to better protect their facilities, Kravchenko said, while acknowledging that businesses cannot fully shield themselves from Russian missiles and drones.

Zelensky visits Lyman sector, says Operation Vivaldi reclaimed 125 square kilometers
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky visited the command post of the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade in the Lyman sector running across Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts to award soldiers and meet brigade comannders on Sept. 30.
Zelensky thanked the troops for returning more than 125 square kilometers of territory from Russian occupation to Ukrainian control, in cooperation with other units of the Third Army Corps as part of Operation Vivaldi.
"Thank you for protecting our state, sovereignty, and territorial integrity," he said.
In his talks with the commanders, the President discussed issues of procurement, especially pick-up trucks for brigades, and increasing funding for drones, simplifying procurement, and expanding staffing, Zelensky said. He also highlighted the need for long-range artillery.
Ukrainian forces under the command of the 3rd Army Corps liberated three villages in northern Donetsk Oblast as part of the ongoing Operation Vivaldi, corps commander, Brigadier-General Andrii Biletskyi said on Sept 28.
The villages of Ridkodub, Nove, and Katerynivka were liberated, while full Ukrainian control was restored over Karpivka and Novomykhailivka.
This phase, described as the "third season" of Operation Vivaldi, inflicted over 2,000 Russian losses and saw over 250 Russian soldiers taken prisoner, according to Biletskyi.
The two previous "seasons" of Operation Vivaldi were each announced in similar updates, first on Sept. 15 when the offensive was given its name, and then on Sept. 20, when the liberation of the villages of Shandryholove and Derylove were announced.

Rwanda open to hosting migrants transferred from Europe, EU lawmakers say
BRUSSELS, Sept 30 - Rwanda had held preliminary discussions with some EU member states about potentially hosting facilities for migrants transferred from those countries, two European Parliament lawmakers said on Wednesday, citing discussions with Rwandan officials.
During their visit to Kigali last week, the lawmakers, Tineke Strik and Anna Strolenberg of the Greens/EFA and Volt groups, said Rwandan officials told them they are open to the idea but that discussions remained at an early stage and no agreements had been reached.
Rwandan officials were not immediately available for comment.
Earlier this month, five European countries said they aimed to strike agreements this year to send migrants without a legal right to remain in the European Union to countries outside the bloc.
Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands, known as the Group of Five, said they had agreed on concrete steps towards establishing return hubs in a non-EU country as part of a wider European push to increase deportations and curb irregular migration.
The countries have not publicly identified potential host states.
An EU official told Reuters, on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to speak publicly, that Rwanda was among the countries being considered by the Group of Five.
During their visit, the lawmakers were shown two facilities prepared under Britain's abandoned Rwanda deportation scheme that could potentially be used to house migrants transferred from Europe. One of the sites was a hotel.
The five countries are expected to meet again on Thursday on the sidelines of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council.
Rwanda has in recent years positioned itself as a destination for migrants that Western nations would like to remove, despite concerns by rights groups about human rights in the country.
Last year, Rwanda received migrants deported from the United States after the two countries reached an agreement for the transfer of up to 250 people.
In 2023, the UK Supreme Court ruled that a government plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda was unlawful. Rwanda later asked Britain for a £50 million ($63.62 million) payment after the asylum deal was cancelled.
Rights groups have criticised return hub proposals, saying they risk undermining safeguards for migrants and asylum seekers, while supporters argue they could boost returns and deter irregular migration.
"The deportation plans by these five member states are unrealistic, inhumane and costly," Strik said.
Uganda and Rwanda, which host large refugee populations, have also been hit hard by cuts in US foreign aid, forcing humanitarian agencies to scale back food assistance, healthcare and other services for displaced people.
“Uganda and Rwanda are one of the few stable countries in the region. Pressuring these countries by sending even more people is tempting fate,” said Strolenberg. REUTERS

Intl Register of Damage for Ukraine opens all 43 claim categories for compensation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:15:10 EEST
03:15:10 KST

The International Register of Damages for Ukraine has opened the last three categories out of the 43 categories of claims submitted by the State of Ukraine: "Other property losses," "Environmental Damage," and "Theft and/or Misappropriation of Natural Resources," the President's Office said.
"The International Register of Damages for Ukraine has opened all 43 categories of claims for compensation for damages, losses, or harm caused by Russia's full-scale aggression against Ukraine. The three categories of claims recently opened for the State of Ukraine are: "Other Property Losses," "Environmental Damage," and "Theft and/or Misappropriation of Natural Resources,"" according to a statement posted on the presidential website on Wednesday.
It is reported that claims in the last three categories may be submitted by the state, central, regional, and local authorities, as well as state and municipal institutions and organizations. This makes it possible to document damage to the natural environment, the value of illegally seized or appropriated natural resources, and the damage, destruction, or loss of state and municipal property that are not covered by other categories of claims.
It is noted that there are a total of 21 categories of claims for individuals, 11 categories for legal entities, and 11 categories for the State of Ukraine. These categories cover various consequences of Russia's aggression against Ukraine: the death and disappearance of loved ones, bodily injury, torture, sexual violence, forced displacement, loss of housing, jobs and private businesses, damage to property and infrastructure, economic losses to businesses, damage to cultural heritage and the environment, humanitarian expenditures by the state, and other types of losses.
The International Register of Damages was launched on April 2, 2024. Since then, it has received 195,000 claims, of which more than 65,000 have already been entered into the system, and the rest are currently being processed.
The registry is the first component of the international compensation mechanism for Ukraine. The second component is the International Compensation Commission for Ukraine, which will review the claims on their merits, determine the amount of compensation in each case, and issue decisions. The convention establishing it has been signed by 40 states and the EU, and 10 of them have already ratified it. Twenty-five ratifications are required to establish the commission. The final component of the mechanism will be the International Compensation Fund, from which payments will be made in accordance with the commission's decisions.

Global air passenger demand falls 0.8% in August as Middle East slump deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:14:28 UTC
03:14:28 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Global air passenger demand fell 0.8% year-on-year in August as a deepening downturn at Middle Eastern airlines interrupted the region’s recovery, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) said Wednesday.
Total demand, measured in revenue passenger kilometers, declined despite a 0.3% increase in capacity, IATA said.
The passenger load factor, which measures how much available capacity was filled, fell 0.9 percentage points to 85.1%.
Excluding Middle Eastern carriers, global demand increased 0.6%, half the growth rate recorded in July.
“Global demand for air transport contracted by 0.8% compared to August 2025 as the recovery trajectory for carriers in the Middle East was interrupted,” said Marie Owens Thomsen, IATA’s senior vice president for sustainability and chief economist.
Middle Eastern airlines recorded a 14.6% decline in overall passenger demand, while capacity fell 9.3%.
Owens Thomsen said forthcoming data would show whether higher energy prices, which have reduced travelers’ purchasing power, and geopolitical instability were prompting consumers to adjust their travel budgets.
 
Forward schedules for October indicate cautious optimism, with available seats projected to increase 2%, she added.
International demand weakens
International passenger demand fell 0.9% year-on-year, while capacity was unchanged, IATA said. Excluding Middle Eastern carriers, international demand rose 1.3%.
Middle Eastern airlines’ international traffic dropped 14.2%, reversing the gradual stabilization seen since the Iran war began in February, according to IATA.
The contraction on Middle East-Asia routes deepened to 11.7%, compared with an 8.6% decline in July.
European carriers recorded a 2.1% increase in international demand, while traffic on Europe-Asia routes rose 12.2%.
Transatlantic traffic fell 2.4%, with declines across several markets, including the UK and France.
International demand at North American airlines fell 1.7%, while Asia-Pacific carriers registered a 0.1% decline.
African and Latin American airlines both reported international demand growth of 6.7%.
China bucks domestic downturn
Domestic passenger demand fell 0.5% in August despite a 0.7% increase in capacity, IATA said.
The domestic load factor declined 1.1 percentage points to 85.3%.
India recorded the sharpest contraction among the domestic markets covered, with demand falling 7.5%.
US domestic traffic declined 2.9%, while Japan’s fell 2%.
China’s domestic demand rose 5.8%, supported by summer travel, while Brazil and Australia recorded increases of 4.3% and 2.3%, respectively.
