CAR: More Than Half of Identified Components in North Korean Missiles Counterfeit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:59:13 UTC
02:59:13 KST

Researchers have identified counterfeit electronic components in Russian, Iranian, and North Korean weapons seized in Ukraine.
The findings are detailed in a report by the international organization Conflict Armament Research (CAR).
The highest share of counterfeit components was found in North Korean Hwasong-11 (KN-23) ballistic missiles, with more than half of the identified components found to be counterfeit.
Since January 2024, CAR specialists have examined the debris of 11 North Korean missiles, recovering hundreds of microchips, voltage converters and memory components.
CAR sent 147 requests to manufacturers to identify components. Ten companies confirmed that markings on components were likely or definitively counterfeit.
Of the 81 North Korean missile components CAR traced, 42, or 51.9%, were identified as counterfeit or suspected counterfeits.
By comparison, counterfeit components accounted for 16% of those identified in Iranian weapons and about 20% in Russian weapons.
Among the counterfeit components were metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) from a U.S. brand, found in a Hwasong-11 missile after a strike on the Poltava region in December 2024.
The U.S. manufacturer confirmed the components were counterfeit, citing discrepancies in casing shape, marking placement, and serial numbers.
Manufacturers identify counterfeit components by errors in logos, incorrect fonts, or date codes indicating periods when the company did not yet exist at the time.
The widespread use of counterfeit components indicates the effectiveness of international sanctions, which are forcing North Korea, Iran, and Russia to procure components on the black market.
The use of uncertified components directly affects missile reliability and accuracy, which helps explain the high rate of deviations among North Korean missiles in early 2024.

How to Talk to Your Child About Body Image
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:58:54 UTC
02:58:54 KST

When your kid comes home from school and says they hate their stomach, that nobody wants to be their friend because they’re “fat,” or that everyone in their class is better-looking than they are, you’d probably do anything to help them see what you see—which means the reassurance practically flies out of your mouth. “You’re beautiful!” “You’re perfect!” How could they possibly think otherwise?
That impulse comes from a good place—but it can shut down the very conversation you want to have, says Dr. Whitney Casares, a pediatrician in Portland, Ore., and author of Raising Body-Confident Kids. “It tells a child, don’t feel what you’re feeling,” she says. Instead, start by making room for those feelings. “The goal is to help kids feel heard first and really to keep the door open.”
We asked experts exactly what to say when your child is struggling with how they look.
“Tell me more about that.”
Before you can help, you need to know what you’re responding to. Did a classmate make a rude comment? Did your child see something triggering online? Or is their body feeling unfamiliar as they go through puberty? Those possibilities call for different conversations, Casares says. A kid who says everyone is thinner than they are might be comparing bodies in dance class—or feeling left out by a best friend and assuming their appearance is the reason.
Give your child time to explain, and let them know you’re glad they trusted you with something hard to say. “It’s a really good sign if your kid’s coming to you with a question,” says Charlotte Markey, a psychology professor at Rutgers University and author of books including The Body Image Book for Girls. Even if you’re scrambling to figure out how to respond, showing that you welcome the conversation makes it more likely they’ll come to you again.
“I can see why that would have been really upsetting for you.”
It’s important to validate your kid’s feelings without agreeing with whatever harsh judgment they’re making about themselves. That’s why Markey likes this way of acknowledging the hurt without reinforcing the criticism. “It can be really difficult when we feel like someone doesn’t have a positive opinion of us,” she says.
If a classmate’s comment set this off, follow up with: “Why do you think that person said that?” Maybe Preston the fourth-grader was insulting everyone, or didn’t even understand the word he was using. Exploring what happened can help your child question how much weight to give the remark. “If the kid can get to the place of feeling like, ‘No, they’re wrong,’ on their own, it’s much more powerful,” Markey says. After all, your insistence that they’re beautiful comes with an obvious caveat: You’re their parent. Of course you think that.
“Bodies come in different shapes and sizes.”
“Why am I bigger than my friends?” can feel like a loaded question, but there’s room for a straightforward answer: Genetics help shape our bodies, just as they influence our height and eye color, Markey says. Talking about family resemblance can help make those differences feel ordinary. The message is that your child doesn’t need to look like their best friend—and their body isn’t a project they need to fix.
If they ask, “Am I fat?” resist the reflexive “No!” advises Giulia Suro, a clinical psychologist in Washington, D.C., who specializes in eating disorders. That response can reinforce the idea that being fat is something to fear. Instead, get curious about what the word means to them and where they learned to associate it with something negative. You can acknowledge differences in body size without treating one as better than another or promising your child they’ll eventually be smaller.
“What’s the scariest thing about that?”
During her first week of kindergarten, Suro’s daughter came home and announced: “I’m not the prettiest girl in the class.” Even for a psychologist who specializes in eating disorders, it was startling to hear. Instead of reassuring her daughter about her looks, Suro asked what felt scariest about that. Her daughter worried she wouldn’t make friends—that no one would like her, and she’d end up eating lunch alone.
Now Suro had something concrete to help with. They could talk about which classmates her daughter might sit with, whether she could ask a teacher for help, or whether Suro could volunteer at lunch. Asking about the fear beneath an appearance concern can reveal worries about belonging or being good enough that a compliment won’t resolve. As Suro puts it: “How can we help you address what’s really fearful or threatening about this?”
“That sounds like a mean thought.”
When your child says something cruel about their appearance—“My stomach is disgusting” or “I look terrible”—try not to immediately argue with them. Instead, Suro suggests helping them create some distance from the thought by saying: “That sounds like a mean thought.” It’s something their brain produced, not an objective fact or a verdict they have to accept.
Then ask: “How does that thought make you feel when it’s in your head?” You might also dive into what it makes them want to do: Skip school? Change into a new outfit? Quit an activity? Avoid their friends? The goal is to help them notice when a harsh thought starts making decisions for them. “We want actions to always be based on the things that are important to us, our values, our passions, excitement, motivation, and not on critical thoughts,” Suro says. “We really don’t want to give them that much power.”
“I’m actually interested in what you’re interested in.”
If your son’s Instagram or TikTok feed is full of impossibly muscular men, you might be tempted to tell him to log off. Instead, start by asking him to show you what he’s watching, suggests Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and founder of Hilltop Behavioral Health in Summit, N.J. If he seems embarrassed, try: “I’m actually interested in what you’re interested in.” Then explore the appeal: Is he hoping to play like that athlete? Look like him? “Is this meaningful to you?” Pollack suggests asking. “Is it meaningful to your friends?” Understanding what he’s drawn to gives you a way to talk about the pressure he might feel to measure up.
You can also discuss what goes into the images your child is comparing themselves with: filters, professional photographers, makeup artists, and, sometimes, an entire team devoted to someone’s appearance. “Our job is not to look like a celebrity,” Markey says.
“What did your body do today?”
Your child probably has plenty to say about how their body looks. This question gives them something else to notice, Pollack says: Did they walk the dog? Laugh with a friend? Have a great soccer practice? Build an elaborate Lego creation? Make it part of your everyday conversations, giving them room to appreciate experiences that have nothing to do with a mirror. The lesson: “My body is not for presentation,” Pollack says. “My body is for functionality.”
For children who play sports, that means being mindful of what you celebrate. Rather than admiring emerging abdominal muscles, for example, focus on how their body lets them participate in something they enjoy. And keep the conversation bigger than athletic accomplishments: helping someone, making something, and connecting with friends count, too. Pollack wants kids to experience their bodies as “a vehicle of expression and connection,” not just something to look at.
“Swimsuits can make bodies feel really exposed.”
Sometimes there will be clues that your kid is struggling with their body image. Maybe they don’t want to swim anymore, or they duck out of every family photo. Acknowledge the discomfort before jumping into solutions, Casares says. Then explain that you don’t want them missing out on something they enjoy, and ask: “What are some ways we can get around this so you can still participate?” Ask what would make joining in feel more comfortable—maybe wearing a swim shirt at the pool or taking a photo with the family dog.
If they keep sitting things out or start avoiding more activities, it’s worth getting help from a mental-health professional, Casares says. “It may be that they’re getting bullied. It might be that they’re developing an eating disorder.” Finding out what’s behind the change can help you figure out what kind of support they need.
“I love the way you creatively chose that outfit today.”
None of this means you can’t compliment your child’s appearance. Casares suggests noticing choices they’ve made: “I love your haircut,” for example, or “That color looks great on you.” “Those are things that are about choices and decisions kids are making for self-expression,” she says. That gives you something more specific to appreciate than how closely they happen to resemble a beauty ideal.
Some of the most meaningful compliments won’t be about their appearance at all. Pollack recommends pointing to specific things you’ve seen your child do: taking care of a sick sibling, helping a friend who’s having a bad day, or saving money so they can go to the amusement park that summer. “I’m talking about actionable values, things that can be behaviorally seen versus just believed,” he says. You’re showing them exactly what you appreciate about the person they are.
“You don’t have to love your body, but it’s important to treat it with respect.”
Even adults have days when they don’t like how they look. Kids shouldn’t feel like they’re doing something wrong when that happens to them, too, Suro says. The goal is to help them eat enough, get some rest, and keep doing things they enjoy, even when they’re not feeling particularly confident. “Expecting anyone, even a child, to love their body all of the time is unrealistic and can become another standard they fail to meet,” she says.
That’s something parents can practice alongside them. “Even when you’re not talking directly to your kids, your kids are watching what you say about yourself,” Casares says. They notice the criticism you mutter at the mirror and whether you’re only having a smoothie while everyone else chows down on a full meal. “No script that you can say about self-love to your kids will override what you’re doing in your own body,” she says.

Vatican envoy discusses humanitarian issues, visits POWs in Russia, Foreign Ministry says
Sept 30 - Papal envoy Cardinal Matteo Zuppi discussed humanitarian issues in the Ukraine war in talks with Russian officials and visited Ukrainian prisoners of war, Russia's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.
Zuppi's three days of talks coincided with an appeal by Pope Leo to Russia and Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end the four-year war. The pontiff also decried national leaders who he said were "beginning to speak about nuclear weapons and wars that are becoming ever more destructive".
The Foreign Ministry said Zuppi met Kremlin foreign policy officer Yuri Ushakov and other Russian officials and discussed prospects for a settlement as well as humanitarian issues, including prisoner of war exchanges and displaced children.
The statement said Zuppi, head of the Italian bishops conference, also discussed conditions in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region, where Ukrainian officials said Kyiv's military used drones last weekend to deliver food and medicine to civilians.
The Foreign Ministry statement said Ukraine was blocking all attempts to provide supplies to the town's residents. Ukrainian officials say Russian forces are preventing them from leaving the town.
The ministry statement said Zuppi was permitted to visit prisoners of war and "was personally able to talk with Ukrainians and see for himself that Russia strictly follows all the relevant humanitarian standards".
It said the visit "confirmed the constructive and regular nature of the Russian-Vatican dialogue and the willingness of both sides to continue cooperating on humanitarian issues".
Zuppi last visited Moscow in October 2024 to discuss prospects for ending the war launched by Russia's 2022 invasion of its neighbor.
Zuppi has also held talks in Kyiv with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. REUTERS

Saudi Arabia’s National Transport Safety Center (NTSC) said Wednesday that it has launched an investigation into the emergency landing of a Flydubai passenger plane at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport in the northwestern city of Tabuk.
The center said it received a report concerning Flydubai flight FZ1073, which made an emergency landing at the airport Wednesday.
An aviation safety investigation team has begun work and is coordinating with authorities to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident, verify aviation safety-related aspects and collect information and evidence, it said.
The flight was traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv when it was diverted to Saudi Arabia.

The Dubai-based carrier said all passengers and crew were safe and accounted for, adding that the reasons and motives behind the altercation remain subject to a formal investigation.
Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz International Airport earlier its Air Traffic Control Center received a distress call from flight FZ1073 at 8.44 am local time (0544GMT) requesting an emergency landing.
The airport said the captain and first officer were injured and transferred to a hospital for medical treatment.
The flight, carrying 174 passengers, reportedly transmitted the international emergency code “7700” and later “7500,” a code used to indicate unlawful interference with an aircraft, including a possible hijacking.
The airport later said all passengers departed at 5.40 pm local time aboard an alternative aircraft provided by the airline.

Defenders of Ukraine Day, the Feast of the Intercession, and Cossacks’ Day: why they are celebrated on October 1
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:57:05 EEST
02:57:05 KST

Defenders of Ukraine Day, the Feast of the Intercession, and Cossacks’ Day: why they are celebrated on October 1
Kyiv • UNN
October 1 brings together the Feast of the Intercession, Defenders of Ukraine Day, and Cossacks’ Day. The date symbolically unites faith, Cossack heritage, and remembrance.
On October 1, Ukraine marks several important dates at once: the Feast of the Protection of the Most Holy Theotokos, the Day of Defenders of Ukraine, and Ukrainian Cossacks Day. This coincidence is not accidental. It connects religious tradition, the history of the Ukrainian Cossacks, and the modern commemoration of the military personnel who defended and continue to defend the state.
UNN explains why these dates fall on October 1, how their historical connection emerged, and which traditions have survived to this day.
Why the Feast of the Protection and the Day of Defenders of Ukraine are celebrated on October 1
The Feast of the Protection of the Most Holy Theotokos is one of the most revered Christian holidays in Ukraine. According to church tradition, its origins are connected with events at the Blachernae Church in Constantinople in the 10th century. When the city was in danger, Saint Andrew the Fool-for-Christ and his disciple Epiphanius saw the Mother of God praying together with the people and extending her omophorion—a veil—over them. In Christian tradition, this image became a symbol of intercession and protection.
Until 2023, Ukraine celebrated the Feast of the Protection on October 14. After the Orthodox Church of Ukraine switched to the Revised Julian calendar, fixed church holidays shifted 13 days earlier than their dates according to the Julian calendar. The OCU introduced the Revised Julian calendar on September 1, 2023, and the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church also switched to the new style for fixed holidays.
It should be noted that parishes of the OCU that decided to continue using the Julian calendar retained the right to celebrate religious holidays "according to the old style." Therefore, in some parishes, the Feast of the Protection may continue to be celebrated on October 14.
Following the calendar reform, the date of the state holiday also changed. In July 2023, the Verkhovna Rada adopted a law moving the Day of Defenders of Ukraine from October 14 to October 1. The president also changed the date of Ukrainian Cossacks Day. Thus, the state preserved the symbolic connection between the Feast of the Protection, the Cossack tradition, and the commemoration of Ukraine’s modern defenders.
The Day of the Defender of Ukraine itself was established in 2014, after the beginning of Russian aggression. In 2021, it was renamed the Day of Defenders of Ukraine, emphasizing that both men and women participate in defending the state.
The Feast of the Protection and the Zaporozhian Cossacks: why the holiday became a "Cossack" one
The special place of the Feast of the Protection in Ukrainian culture was largely formed during the Cossack era. The Zaporozhian Cossacks considered the Mother of God their heavenly patroness, and the Feast of the Protection was one of the most important holidays on the Sich. On that day, councils were held to elect atamans and senior officers.
Churches dedicated to the Protection also held a special place in the Cossack community. A Church of the Protection stood at the center of the Cossack stronghold, and before campaigns the Zaporozhian Cossacks turned to the Mother of God in prayers for protection.
During the Cossack era, a distinctive type of icon also became widespread—the "Cossack Protection." In these icons, the Mother of God was depicted with her outspread omophorion, beneath which were Cossacks, hetmans, senior officers, clergy, and other representatives of Ukrainian society. Thus, the religious subject gradually also became an image of the protection of the community and the state.
Respect for the Cossack military tradition did not disappear after the liquidation of the Zaporozhian Sich. Its symbols, names, and images were used by Ukrainian military formations in subsequent historical periods. During the Ukrainian Revolution of 1917–1921, Cossack names, ranks, and symbols appeared in the army, while military units were named after Bohdan Khmelnytsky, Ivan Mazepa, Petro Doroshenko, and other figures of the Cossack era.
How Ukraine celebrates the Feast of the Protection and the Day of Defenders today
After the beginning of the full-scale war, October 1 acquired an even more pronounced memorial significance and also became a day of remembrance for those who died defending Ukraine. Therefore, on October 1, memorial ceremonies, flower-laying ceremonies, religious services, meetings with military personnel and veterans, exhibitions, and educational events are held in various cities. Schools, museums, and libraries organize themed events dedicated to the history of the Ukrainian military, the Cossacks, and the modern Russian-Ukrainian war.
Practical support for military personnel and veterans is becoming an increasingly important tradition as well. This may include donations to trusted units and volunteer funds, assistance to the wounded, support for the families of service members and the fallen, as well as veteran initiatives and businesses. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance also identifies support for combat units as one of the practical ways to thank the defenders.
For believers, October 1 remains first and foremost a religious holiday. Churches hold services in honor of the Intercession of the Most Holy Theotokos and pray for defenders, the wounded, prisoners of war, those missing in action, and the families of the fallen.
Greetings to Ukraine’s defenders and the traditions of the Intercession
Greetings on October 1 have a somewhat different tone today than ordinary holiday wishes. During wartime, it is more appropriate to avoid overly grandiose formulations and, above all, to thank military personnel for their service and protection.
Defenders, both men and women, are wished strength, endurance, good health, reliable brothers- and sisters-in-arms, and a safe return home. At the same time, it is worth remembering that not every service member is comfortable with loud celebrations. For some, this day is associated with the loss of friends, injuries, or painful memories, so simple personal words of thanks are often more appropriate than standard holiday cards.
Among the traditions of the Intercession are attending church services, praying for relatives and defenders, engaging in charity, and helping those in need. In folk tradition, the Intercession was also an important milestone in the autumn calendar and was associated with the completion of fieldwork and the beginning of the wedding season. This is the origin of numerous sayings and unmarried women’s customs connected with requests for a happy marriage.
Today, however, the main meaning of October 1 for Ukraine is defined by the war. A religious image of protection, the memory of the Cossack military tradition, and gratitude to the people who are defending the state now have converged on one date. Therefore, the Day of Defenders and Defender Women of Ukraine, the Intercession, and the Day of the Ukrainian Cossacks remain holidays with different origins, but they are united by a common theme - protection, service, and remembrance.

Russia may have been preparing the murders of Kasparov and other opposition figures in the United States — media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:56:28 EEST
02:56:28 KST

Russia may have been preparing the murders of Kasparov and other opposition figures in the United States — media
Kyiv • UNN
The US has charged five people linked to the preparation of assassination attempts against Russian opposition figures. There is no evidence of a personal order from Putin.
Russian intelligence services may have been preparing the assassinations of opposition figures abroad, including Garry Kasparov and former State Duma deputy Ilya Ponomarev. UNN reports this, citing materials from the U.S. Department of Justice and an investigation by El Mundo.
According to the U.S. investigation and media reports, some of the operations were planned to be carried out this summer in the United States.
Details
In mid-September, the U.S. Department of Justice announced charges against five people whom U.S. prosecutors link to a network operating in the interests of Russian intelligence services. According to investigators, the network was involved in surveilling Russian dissidents and defectors, preparing possible assassinations, as well as sabotage operations in countries supporting Ukraine.
The charging documents state that in the summer of 2026, members of the network recruited a person who was in the United States to surveil a prominent Russian opposition figure whose name is concealed in the case materials under the designation Victim-1. The person was given two addresses associated with the target and instructions for covertly recording photographs and videos. After the assignment was completed, the organizers offered approximately $40,000 to eliminate the person. When the recruit refused to carry out the murder himself, he was offered the opportunity to find another perpetrator. One of the organizers also claimed to have contacts with a group in Mexico that could carry out such an assignment.
According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, preparations for the operation had been ongoing since at least late July. In August, the recruited individual was given geolocation data, addresses, and recommendations regarding operational security, including orders to put the phone into airplane mode and delete correspondence.
Whom they may have planned to kill
The U.S. Department of Justice is not disclosing the names of the potential victims.
At the same time, El Mundo, citing sources, reports that the first victim may have been former Russian State Duma deputy Ilya Ponomarev, who has lived between Ukraine and the United States since leaving Russia. The network of Russian spies may have surveilled his home and office in Washington.
The publication separately reported a threat to former world chess champion and Russian opposition figure Garry Kasparov. This summer, U.S. law enforcement officials warned the man that he might have become a target of Russian intelligence services. He was reportedly provided with special protection afterward.
Information about the heightened threat to Kasparov was also partly confirmed by the Renew Democracy Initiative, with which he is associated. The organization said that following information from U.S. authorities, it had been forced to strengthen security measures.
Context
The U.S. investigation also refers to a separate operation that the Kremlin may have been preparing in Lithuania. According to prosecutors, a Russian handler recruited a U.S. citizen near the Estonian-Russian border and instructed him to photograph the address of another Russian émigré near Vilnius.
After conducting surveillance, the perpetrator was allegedly offered approximately $25,000 to kill the "target." Among the possible methods discussed were a knife attack and the use of an incendiary mixture. The perpetrator refused.
El Mundo assumes that the main victim in this case may have been one of the Russian opposition activists living in Lithuania, in particular Ivan Tyutrin. However, there is no official confirmation of this. The publication also mentions Vladimir Kara-Murza among the possible potential targets, although his name is likewise not given in the U.S. prosecutors’ materials.
Who is involved in the case
The U.S. Department of Justice names five suspected members of the network.
They include Yury Khrameyev, whom U.S. law enforcement describes as a former colonel in the Russian intelligence services; his son Kirill Khrameyev, whom the United States links to the FSB; as well as Cuban nationals Oemis Romagosa Durruti and Yaydel Delgado Suarez and Venezuelan national Angel Eduardo Castro.
They are accused of conspiring to finance terrorism, while some of the individuals involved are also accused of conspiring to arrange a contract killing. Under U.S. law, the defendants could face decades in prison on some of the charges.
The network is also linked to acts of sabotage in Europe
According to the U.S. investigation, the network’s activities were not limited to targeting Russian opposition figures. Its members are also linked to preparations for acts of sabotage in European countries that support Ukraine. The case materials mention operations in the Czech Republic and Lithuania, as well as potential targets in Poland.
According to the prosecution, they discussed setting fire to warehouses, railway and energy infrastructure facilities, as well as other attacks against NATO countries.
Separately, the U.S. authorities link members of the network to an attack on a Lithuanian company that manufactured mobile radio equipment for the Ukrainian military.
Is there evidence of a personal order from putin
Several media publications have put forward the theory that operations to eliminate Kasparov and other opposition figures may have been carried out on the personal orders of vladimir putin. However, the publicly available materials from the U.S. Department of Justice currently contain no evidence of such a direct order. The American prosecution points to the suspected network’s ties to Russian intelligence services and its activities in the interests of the Russian state, but does not claim that putin personally ordered a specific killing.
What they are saying in moscow
As of September 30, the Russian authorities had not publicly provided a substantive response to reports about the possible preparation of the killings of Kasparov, Ponomaryov and other Russian opposition figures abroad.

Syria removed from US arms export ban list
US has gradually loosened restrictions placed on Syria during the Assad era to aid country’s recovery from conflict.
The United States has removed Syria from a list of countries banned from buying or importing US weapons as Washington continues to strengthen ties with the government in Damascus.
The US Department of State said on Wednesday that it was changing the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or ITAR, to remove Syria from the list and allow US arms sales on a case-by-case basis.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Syrian president warns Israeli attacks endanger delicate post-war recovery
- list 2 of 3Syria arrests five former al-Assad-era officers over strikes on civilians
- list 3 of 3Pentagon says US troop withdrawal from Iraq is complete
“On August 19, 2026, the Secretary of State approved a new defence trade policy for Syria that would permit the review of defence article and defence service transfers to Syria on a case-by-case licensing basis,” the note, posted on the Federal Register Wednesday, reads.
“The Secretary directed the Department to codify this change by publishing an amendment to the ITAR removing Syria from the list of countries for which it is the policy of the United States to deny licenses and other approvals for exports and imports of defence articles and defence services destined for or originating in those countries.”
The change is the latest instance of the Trump administration easing previous restrictions placed on Syria during the decades-long rule of the al-Assad family, which ended with the ouster of former President Bashar al-Assad by rebels in December 2024.
The country’s current president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, has placed a strong focus on improving relations with the US and obtaining relief from economic sanctions that he says hinder the country’s path to recovery after years of devastating civil war. Al-Sharra is a former fighter who was aligned with Syria’s al-Nusra Front armed group.
The Trump administration, expressing optimism about its relationship with the new Syrian government, has gradually loosened a number of restrictions.
Trump eased some economic sanctions last year, and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced in August that the US was removing Syria’s designation as a “state sponsor of terrorism”.
The US also announced in February that it planned to eventually reopen its embassy in Damascus, which has been closed since 2012.

Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:54:13 BST
02:54:13 KST

Announcing her death, Dame Esther’s family paid tribute to the “most wonderful mother” and “cherished grandmother” who would be remembered for her “endless capacity for joy”.
Dame Esther’s family described her as the ‘most wonderful mother’ and ‘cherished grandmother’
Credit: Television Stills
Dame Esther was a vocal supporter of the Assisted Dying Bill, claiming in March that most people “want and need” the right to end their own lives.
When the bill was defeated in the House of Commons in September, as MPs voted 286 to 270 against the legislation, she called it a “tragic day”. The bill would have allowed those with less than six months to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives.
In 2024, she said that she had joined the Dignitas assisted-dying clinic in Switzerland.
Writing for The Telegraph at the beginning of September, Rebecca Wilcox, Dame Esther’s daughter, said her mother was “too ill now to travel to Dignitas as she had planned and paid for”.
Earlier this month, Dame Esther said in a statement that it was too late for her to “buzz off” to the clinic in Switzerland and said Britain’s current laws on assisted dying are “messy and cruel”.
In a final message shared by her family, the presenter said she had been “immensely lucky” for the support she had received from the public, which she said had enabled her “to live such a long and happy life”.
She added: “Sadly, all good things come to an end, as they say. So I particularly wanted to say goodbye and thank you so very, very much. Perhaps I will see you eventually, on the other side. I do hope so. With very good wishes, as ever, Esther.”
Rebecca Wilcox, Dame Esther’s daughter, campaigning for assisted dying
Credit: Eddie Mulholland for The Telegraph
In a statement announcing her death, Dame Esther’s family said: “Our adored mother Dame Esther Rantzen died today.
“Her legacy of compassion and understanding will live on in her charities Childline and the Silverline, and through those of us who were lucky enough to love and be loved by her.”
“We are grateful she is finally at rest with her beloved husband, Desmond Wilcox, but we will miss her immeasurably. She was our sunshine.
“We will always remember her endless capacity for joy, her ability to comfort every heartache, her beautiful way with words and her expert guidance in all things.
“She was the most wonderful mother to us three children and a cherished grandmother to her five treasured grandchildren. We have been so lucky for so long, no matter how much time we had with Mum, it could be never be enough, but we are so grateful for our lives together.”
The broadcaster was made a dame in 2015 for services to children and older people
Credit: Heathcliff O'Malley for The Telegraph
They added: “Mum’s work with charities and campaigning, particularly for children, older people, and the terminally ill, meant the world to her, so thank you to everyone who has written to her, shared their stories with her over the years and worked alongside her.
“We hope the humour, ingenuity and audacity she brought to her work may continue to inspire you as it will do us. We kindly ask that we are given privacy and time to grieve.”
Dame Esther with her husband and three children
Credit: Alpha Press
Andy Burnham led tributes to Dame Esther, saying she “changed countless lives and gave a voice to people who often went unheard”.
The Prime Minister said: “I will always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life. My thoughts are with her family and all who loved her.”
Dignity in Dying, with whom she worked closely on her campaign to legalise assisted dying, said she had used her fame to “speak truth to power”.
Meanwhile, Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the Terminally Ill (Adults) Bill, paid tribute to her as “a strong, warm and compassionate woman and a fighter to the end”.
Chris Sherwood, the chief executive of the NSPCC, said Dame Esther’s “unwavering determination and tenacity in ensuring children were safe and heard never diminished”.
“Esther was a unique and truly remarkable woman who during her life did incredible things and went to exceptional lengths to ensure children and young people across the UK had somewhere to turn when they were in need of help.
“She loved nothing more than spending time in our bases and connecting with our volunteer counsellors. Thanks to her vision, energy and courage we now have an extensive network of Childline staff and volunteers working around the country.”
Dame Esther at the launch of Childline’s helpline for the victims of bullying
Credit: Fiona Hanson/PA Archive/
Paul Farmer, the head of Age UK, said her “dedication and commitment to older people is unrivalled”.
He said: “Esther was a true inspiration and spent her life working tirelessly to help others. After founding the Silver Line helpline in 2012, now part of Age UK, she has helped to support thousands of lonely older people, making sure they have someone to talk to whenever they might need it.”
Dame Esther with the then Duchess of Cornwall during a visit to Charlestown School in 2022
Credit: Chris Jackson/Getty Images
Born in Berkhamsted, Hertfordshire, in 1940, she attended a private school in north London and Oxford University before beginning her career as a sound effects assistant at the BBC.
She rose to fame in 1973 as the presenter of That’s Life!, having been a researcher for Braden’s Week, its predecessor programme, for several years.
The magazine show featured reports on consumer affairs often blended with satire, and soon became one of Britain’s most popular programmes. It expanded the traditional role of the consumer programme to investigating life-and-death issues, such as a boarding school employing paedophiles and a shortage of organ donors.
Dame Esther rose to fame in 1973 as the presenter of That’s Life!
Credit: Chris Ridley/Radio Times/Getty Images
Dame Esther founded Childline, a helpline for children in danger or distress, after a temporary helpline open for viewers impacted by a programme about a toddler who had starved to death was swamped with callers.
The calls mainly came from children suffering sexual abuse they had never been able to disclose to anyone else, giving Dame Esther the idea for a specific helpline for children, open around the clock.
When That’s Life! came to an end in 1994, Dame Esther presented her own chat show, Esther, until 2002. She also appeared in consumer affairs show Old Dogs, New Tricks, and competed in both Strictly Come Dancing and I’m a Celebrity Get Me out of Here!
Dame Esther pictured in May 2023
Credit: Kirsty O'Connor/PA Wire
In 2010 she stood as an independent candidate in that year’s general election, winning 4.4 per cent of the vote in Luton South.
Her husband David Wilcox, a fellow television presenter and journalist, died in 2020 and she is survived by her three children Miriam, Rebecca and Joshua Wilcox.
She was made a dame in the 2015 New Year Honours for services to children and older people through Childline and the Silver Line.

Stella McCartney spotlights sea life at Paris fashion week as animal rights returns to headlines

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:51:18 UTC
02:51:18 KST

Stella McCartney has been talking about animal rights at fashion week for 30 years. She is usually a lone voice, but the issue is back in the headlines this season. Outcry over the physical restraining of a Peta protester at a catwalk show by Steven Kolb, the president of New York fashion week’s governing body, has put cruelty in wool production – previously considered niche compared to the hot button topic of fur – on the news agenda.
“There is no wool on the runway this season, and I’m proud of that,” McCartney said after her show. She has been working on wool alternatives, including Brewed Protein, a fermented alternative to cashmere and wool developed in collaboration with the Japanese biotech firm Spiber, which was first used in her collections a year ago.
The issue, she says, is “a tricky one. I’ve got alpacas at home, and I have to shear them. If you can shear a sheep in a kind, humane way, then I don’t, personally, think that’s the end of the world. When we do have wool in our collections it is responsibly sourced. But the way a lot of [wool production] is done today is deeply cruel.
“At the end of the day it’s about how kind you are, but monitoring that kindness requires real work. At Stella, we police everything from start to finish at my cost, at my time. If I use wool, I can show you exactly where it’s coming from, and I’m proud of that. But I’m alone in that, and I shouldn’t be.”
McCartney’s remarks on sustainability were interrupted by paparazzi clamouring for a portrait of the designer with the front row guest Jennifer Lopez, wearing a skirt suit with a faux-fur trim and matching stole with a dramatic black net face veil. Tension between fashion week razzmatazz and values-led gravitas is in the Stella McCartney DNA.
This season, McCartney’s spotlight is on sea life. “Sea life, not sea food. That’s the point I wanted to make,” she said, after posing with Lopez and dispatching Juliette Binoche with a promise to join her for a glass of champagne shortly. “I’ve never eaten fish, really, but my mum and dad used to point out that one minute people are watching a sea life documentary with David Attenborough and exclaiming about this magical world and the next, they are looking at a seafood menu. It is grotesque.”
The invitation to the show, held in the vast gardens of the British embassy in Paris, was delivered via a video message from 91-year-old Sylvia Earle, the legendary oceanographer who has spent more than 7,000 hours underwater. Fancy long-sleeved swimsuits walked the catwalk as evening looks; dolphins frolicked on T-shirts. The cursive hems of party dresses looked like Hokusai waves.
“We are at war with the oceans, at war with the creatures that live in there,” McCartney said. “For every fish you eat, countless are thrown back dead.”

Circumstances
- A Flydubai passenger plane en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv signaled an emergency on Wednesday morning, according to Channel 12.
- The pilots first transmitted code 7700, signaling a general emergency, before transmitting code 7500, indicating a possible hijacking.
- No further updates about the flight were available afterwards.
- There were approximately 180 passengers on board, Channel 12 said. Israeli authorities denied the plane permission to land, and it was diverted to Saudi Arabia near Jordanian airspace.
- Fighter jets were scrambled after the distress signal, the TV channel reported.
- The plane had reached the border of Jordan before it was diverted to Tabuk Airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia without actually entering Jordanian airspace, data from Flightradar24 indicated. No further updates about the flight were available afterwards.
- The plane landed at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia, a source in a Middle Eastern air traffic control service told TASS.
- Flydubai later confirmed to TASS that the flight had landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
- All passengers are safe, the airline told TASS.
- The plane’s captain and co-pilot were hospitalized with injuries, Saudi airport operator Cluster 2 said.
- Flydubai confirmed to TASS that a conflict broke out in the cockpit.
- Other crew members on board took control of the aircraft.
Versions of what happened

- The TV channel said the initial hijacking theory is now being ruled out, while the circumstances remain under investigation.

Embassy in Paris Hosts Meeting on Sardinia’s Bid for the Einstein Telescope
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
19:50:28 CEST
02:50:28 KST

The Italian Embassy in Paris hosted the conference “Listening to the Universe – Making the Invisible Visible: Gravitational Waves as the ‘Sound of the Universe’. Sardinia at the Center of the New Scientific Frontier,” dedicated to the Einstein Telescope (ET) and Italy’s bid to host the future major European infrastructure for the study of gravitational waves at the Sos Enattos site in Sardinia.
                                    
                                       
				   The Einstein Telescope represents one of the most ambitious new-generation European research infrastructures and is part of a field in which Italy and France boast a long and prestigious tradition of scientific collaboration. The Virgo project, born out of cooperation between Italy’s INFN and France’s CNRS and developed within the framework of the European Gravitational Observatory (EGO) in Cascina, stands as one of the most significant examples of the two countries’ ability to jointly build major scientific projects that have subsequently become part of Europe’s research heritage. Following opening remarks by Chargé d’Affaires Ludovico Serra, Alessandra Todde, President of the Autonomous Region of Sardinia, opened the proceedings by outlining the strategic value of Sardinia’s bid and the region’s commitment to supporting the project. “As a region, we have invested 350 million euros in its construction, in addition to the 950 million from the national government,” stated President Todde, who also emphasized the importance of collaboration with Paris: “France is a strategic partner. The VIRGO collaboration demonstrates that together we can build major scientific infrastructure. I hope there will be political support for the ‘double-L’ solution as strong as that already expressed by the scientific community, so that we can achieve a genuine sharing of expertise and responsibility among member countries.” This was followed by remarks from Panebianco, the French delegate from the Ministry of Education, Research, and Space, who provided an overview of the Franco-Italian collaboration on major research infrastructure. The scientific aspect of the meeting was led by some of the leading Italian and French researchers in the field of gravitational waves. Fulvio Ricci, from Sapienza University of Rome and former spokesperson for Virgo, traced the history of the Italian-French collaboration on Virgo; Michele Punturo, of the INFN and European coordinator of the Einstein Telescope project, presented the prospects for the future infrastructure; Marica Branchesi, of the Gran Sasso Science Institute, spoke about the scientific value of the new generation of gravitational-wave observatories. Marie Anne Bizouard, Virgo’s spokesperson, traced the common thread linking Virgo to ET, and Patrice Verdier, the French principal investigator for ET, illustrated aspects related to France’s contribution to the technological development of ET. The meeting highlighted how the Sos Enattos bid fits not only within the framework of Italian scientific excellence but also within the broader context of European cooperation. Large-scale research infrastructures are, in fact, essential tools for strengthening Europe’s scientific and technological capabilities, attracting talent, and creating international networks of knowledge and innovation. The conference is part of the Italian Embassy in Paris’s activities aimed at promoting scientific diplomacy and fostering collaboration between Italy and France in the fields of research, innovation, and major scientific infrastructures.

Indonesian authorities on Wednesday began demolishing 10 “apartment” units inside a West Java prison after their discovery triggered an investigation into preferential treatment for inmates.
Corrections Director-General Mashudi led the demolition at Cibinong Class IIA Prison in Bogor, Indonesian state news agency Antara reported.
“All 10 units. It will be finished today,” Mashudi said as heavy machinery tore down buildings inside the prison compound.
The demolition followed an agreement between the House of Representatives’ Commission XIII and the Immigration and Corrections Ministry during a visit to the prison, according to Antara.
Ministry Inspector General Rudi Setiawan said the buildings and facilities had been documented and inventoried before demolition.
A preliminary investigation found they were not financed through Indonesia’s state budget but were built independently, the news agency reported.
Indonesia’s Ombudsman uncovered the compound during a surprise inspection on Sept. 23, finding apartment-style accommodation allegedly occupied by inmates.
The units included air conditioners, large televisions, refrigerators, sofas and dining areas, according to the Ombudsman findings reported by Antara.
Investigators also found a gym and a golf simulator under construction.
The Immigration and Corrections Ministry subsequently suspended five officials, including Cibinong prison chief Wisnu Hani Putranto, while investigating the findings.
Dozens of inmates and prison employees have been questioned as authorities investigate whether prisoners received unauthorized privileges and whether payments were made in exchange for access to the facilities.

‘Whoever is hearing me, we need help’: how flight 1073 survived its 17,000ft plunge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:47:25 UTC
02:47:25 KST

As flight FZ 1073 soared west over the waters of the Gulf towards Israel, its passengers may have bemoaned a 20-minute delay at takeoff. For a low-cost airline route, flydubai’s daily service to Tel Aviv is usually convenient and reliable. The nonstop flight takes about three and a half hours and departs early enough from Dubai that it usually lands at Ben Gurion airport at about 9am local time.
That was not the case for Wednesday’s catastrophic flight. The passenger jet never made it to its scheduled destination. Instead, it dropped thousands of feet in seconds before limping down to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia – perhaps miraculously, since photos suggested a large part of the tail of the aircraft was missing.
Passengers evacuated, some covered in blood, with stories to share of a pilot-on-pilot stabbing, and footage posted online from inside the fuselage showed the aftermath of violence.
In one video, two men lie on the floor with breathing masks on their faces as passengers stand over them in the cramped gangway. One wears a white shirt soaked red with blood, and the distinctive pilot stripes on his shoulders. He appears almost unresponsive. The other man blinks slowly, with blood smeared on the wall next to him. A person off camera appears to encourage the injured man to remain conscious: “No sleep,” he says.
More footage, apparently from a seat further back, shows passengers screaming and weeping in distress as the Boeing 737 Max shakes. Israeli media reported that the plane was carrying about 150 Israeli passengers.
Accounts from the airline, passenger testimony, flight trackers and Israeli officials describe a series of horrific events starting about two and a half hours after takeoff.
The flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft abruptly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes. Investigators will look at whether such a sudden and ferocious movement was the reason for damage to the aircraft’s rudder.
Minutes later, the plane sent out a series of emergency transponder signals in the form of “squawk codes”. These four-digit codes are normally used by pilots to broadcast their position but can be used in an emergency situation, even if pilots are in radio contact with air traffic control.
Aircraft trackers at Flightradar24 said the flydubai plane transmitted emergency and hijack signals. The aircraft made an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border before turning around and heading south.
In one video, a passenger with blood dripping from an open wound on his head pleads for assistance and says the jet is descending into Saudi Arabia. “Whoever is hearing me, we need help,” the man says in Hebrew. “We are in the Tabuk area of Saudi Arabia, which we don’t know. All the passengers are OK except for the pilot. We need help.”
What was happening during these critical minutes is still being investigated, but early unconfirmed reports pointed to a cockpit fight, followed by passengers storming up the aisle, and then either one or more pilots who were travelling as passengers wresting control of the plane to avert a disaster.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz cited a passenger as saying that the plane lost control and began to dive.
Dalia Shpigel was quoted as saying that “suddenly there were terrible screams throughout the plane” before “three to five guys burst into the cockpit” and subdued the alleged assailant and began treating an injured pilot.
“We realised that the situation was stabilising and continued the flight. Gradually, information began to emerge about what had happened in the cockpit,” Shpigel told Haaretz.
Her fellow passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the “co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane”.
Speaking to reporters via speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion airport, she said the plane “was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him”.
“There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them … but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do,” she said.
The Emirati carrier, in a statement later on Wednesday, said the aircraft was “successfully secured by on-duty flydubai crew travelling on the flight”, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport. Airlines often move pilots around different airports as passengers, and it is possible it was these pilots who sent the emergency codes.
One passenger, Almog Itali, was quoted by the BBC as saying that one of the pilots onboard who stabilised the plane was British. “There were two spare pilots who were supposed to operate the next flight,” he said. “The relief pilots are European, one of them British, who entered [the cockpit] and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia.”
Stanislav Bukhman, the head of risk at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation security firm based in the UK, said investigators were likely to focus on a few key areas, including how pilots were vetted, and crew screening at the departure airport.
On how the flight deck might have been accessed, he said cabin crew could request entry to the cockpit using an emergency access code. “This exists for situations where the pilots are incapacitated. There is a safeguard built in, though. If the pilots are conscious and operating normally, they can deny that request and keep the door locked. This is designed to protect the flight deck in a hijacking or hostage situation,” he said.
“At this stage there isn’t enough information to say how the flight deck on FZ 1073 was accessed. The door may have been opened by the captain, who reportedly resisted the co-pilot’s attempt to take control, or by cabin crew using the emergency procedure.”
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, announced that one of the pilots had planned to crash and kill its mostly Israeli passengers, who stopped a “major disaster” with their actions. The alleged assailant was arrested after the plane landed, Netanyahu said.
“During the flight, as they approached the country, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone onboard,” Netanyahu said in a video message, calling the passengers “heroes”. All the passengers were accounted for and safe.
Flydubai, however, said an “altercation” occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073, and it warned against drawing conclusions about the motive.
“At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” a flydubai spokesperson said in a statement. “We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

Senate Democrats sink 'toothless' stock trading ban, data center bill in last act before election recess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:44:15 UTC
02:44:15 KST

Senate Democrats on Wednesday defeated a pair of bills that aimed to address data center-related affordability concerns and limit Congress members' ability to profit on the stock market while in office, arguing both were watered-down proposals.
The data center bill, dubbed the Ratepayer Protection Act, failed on a vote of 57-43. A second bill, known as the Stop Insider Trading Act, which also includes a controversial voter-identification provision, was defeated on a party-line, 53-47 vote. Each bill needed 60 votes to overcome the Senate filibuster.
Republicans will likely use the votes as fodder on the campaign trail this fall, as the GOP seeks to hold narrow majorities in both chambers despite President Donald Trump's falling approval ratings and persistent concerns about affordability. The Senate is due to recess as soon as Wednesday, as lawmakers seeking reelection will return to their home states to campaign ahead of the 2026 midterm election.
"EVERY Senate Democrat just joined 94% of House Democrats in voting AGAINST banning congressional stock trading.," House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., posted to X immediately following the vote. The bill, he said, provides "the accountability the American people demand. But every Democrat blocked it from becoming law."
The Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House on a 417-3 vote earlier this month, would establish a regulatory framework that states could consider adopting to require large artificial intelligence data centers to cover their own energy costs, rather than passing them down to customers.
But Democrats have railed against the measure. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called the proposal a "toothless messaging bill" in a speech in the Senate on Tuesday.
"The bill is a fraud. I can sum up the shortcomings of Republicans' data center bill with one word: optional," Schumer said.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who has called for a national moratorium on data centers until developers can demonstrate they will cover the full cost of their construction and operation, called the legislation a "silly piece of nonsense."
"Give us something of substance and we'll vote on it," Warren said ahead of the vote.
Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, cited similar concerns when he blocked the bill earlier this month after Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, requested unanimous consent for quick passage.
Husted is in a "toss up" race for reelection against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, according to The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter. Brown has accused his opponent of helping to bring data centers to the state when he was lieutenant governor.
Husted and other Republicans could use a messaging win on the data center front, which has evolved in recent months into a potent campaign issue as opponents seek stricter guardrails for developers.
Meanwhile, the congressional stock trading bill, passed the House in July on a 232-198 vote, would prohibit sitting members of Congress from buying individual stocks. But it would not force members to divest their existing portfolios, a sticking point for some Democrats who have advocated a more stringent trading ban.
Republicans tacked on to the measure a controversial voter identification provision, which Democrats largely oppose.
Schumer similarly criticized the stock-trading proposal on Tuesday, calling it a "theatrical farce" and the voter ID provision a "poison pill."
And Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said the Republican proposal was a half measure.
"It's obviously a sign that they don't take seriously the issue of insider trading. If you wanted to get a stock ban done, you would put a stock ban on the floor," Kaine said on Wednesday.
Husted, in a post to X on Tuesday, called both proposals "commonsense, bipartisan bills."
"Lowering energy costs, requiring photo ID to vote, and banning stock trading for members of Congress could be bipartisan wins," Husted wrote. "Senate Democrats are the only ones standing in the way of delivering what the American people have asked us to do."
— Irit Skulnik contributed to this story.

A deal between the United States and Iran remains possible, and the Trump administration believes it can resolve the confrontation imminently, Dr. Sebastian Gorka, the White House deputy assistant to the president and senior director for counterterrorism, told The Jerusalem Post in an interview that will run in full on Friday.
“Iran will imminently be resolved,” Gorka said in an interview with the Post. He declined to provide details of what President Donald Trump is planning, but insisted that the administration’s objectives toward Tehran have not changed.
“The decision lies with the mullah in Iran,” Gorka said.
Gorka, who will take part in the National Conservatism Conference (NatCon) in Jerusalem next week, argued that Israelis and others concerned that Trump could accept a watered-down agreement with Tehran should look at the president’s record rather than speculate about what a potential deal might look like.
“You’re talking to the man who literally wrote The Art of the Deal,” Gorka said, referring to Trump’s 1987 book.
“Nobody has ever defeated President Trump in 50 years in business, in almost six years now as president. This man is undefeated.”
Trump remains tough on Iran, WH aide tells 'Post'
“If one president brings one peace deal [during an] eight-year term, that’s deemed a success, and they may even get nominated for a Nobel Peace Prize,” he said. “The fact that he’s closed eight peace deals in less than 12 months, you wouldn’t believe it.”
Gorka said the administration’s objectives toward Iran remain consistent with the demands Trump laid out in a letter to Iran’s then-supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
“What we wish to achieve in Iran is shaped by the president’s first letter a year ago to the then Ayatollah, to Khamenei,” Gorka said.
He described the letter as “very explicit,” saying it addressed Iran’s nuclear program, its support for regional proxies and its broader activities in the Middle East.
“It was about nuclear weapons. It was about funding proxies. It was about everything they do in the region to destabilize that part of the world,” Gorka said. “So nothing has changed with regard to the president.”
Gorka pointed to Trump’s public statements as the best indication of the administration’s intentions.
“If you want to understand the president’s intent, you don’t need a top-secret clearance,” Gorka said. “All you have to do is get a Truth Social account and listen to what he puts on Truth Social. Listen to his press events.”
Asked specifically about concerns in Israel that Trump could agree to a weaker deal than the one he has demanded from Iran, Gorka dismissed the idea that such concerns should drive expectations.
“I find it so peculiar that those who are worried,” he said.
Gorka then offered a comparison that he said illustrated Trump’s negotiating approach: Greenland.
“Everybody said, ‘Oh my gosh, outrageous or impossible,’” he said. “Well, neither was it outrageous, nor was it impossible.”
He argued that the eventual arrangement showed the president’s ability to pursue what initially seemed like unlikely geopolitical outcomes.
Gorka said the agreement provides long-term strategic benefits for the United States and its allies, particularly in preventing China and Russia from undermining Western security.
“Just watch the man and see what he has done,” Gorka said.
“People need to calm down and look at the man who is behind the Resolute Desk and look at what he’s achieved.”

Satellite images reveal ethereal auroral storm raging above the North Pole
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:38:47 UTC
02:38:47 KST

Auroras swirling above the North Pole are a gorgeous sight from Earth’s surface—and from space.
A satellite named Smile has captured an auroral substorm raging above the North Pole. The footage represents the first images released from the mission’s ultraviolet (UV) camera. The satellite was launched into a highly elliptical orbit above Earth in May and is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Chinese Academy of Sciences to study solar and geomagnetic storms and space weather.
The images show the somewhat hurricanelike swirl of UV light during the auroral substorm over the North Pole. This kind of storm is caused by solar wind interacting with Earth’s magnetic field.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Taken on July 24, during a particularly large influx of solar particles into the atmosphere, the observations reveal the full extent of the northern lights in UV light.
Storms like this are best viewed in the ultraviolet range because there’s no interference from daytime sunlight. Smile will be recording auroras for 45 hours at a time, according to the ESA.
Smile’s x-ray camera also captured the bright remnants of a distant exploding star—but in the future, it, too, will be pointed at Earth in order to better understand our planet’s place in space.

The Atlantic hurricane season has been so quiet it’s unprecedented
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:38:26 UTC
02:38:26 KST

We’ve never had an Atlantic hurricane season without a single hurricane through the end of September since reliable records began—until now.
That fact underscores how remarkable this season has been, with an exceptionally strong El Niño—likely to become the biggest in living memory—keeping a lid on tropical cyclone activity in the Atlantic while supercharging it in the eastern Pacific (and giving Hawaii one of its busiest seasons on record).
“No hurricanes through September is unprecedented in the modern record, and it’s a little surreal to look at the maps every day this month and see the deep tropics basically shut off,” says meteorologist Michael Lowry.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
There isn’t a single other hurricane season in the reliable records where there wasn’t at least one hurricane from sometime between the June 1 start of the season and the end of September. The lack of any hurricanes so far this season is particularly jarring because September is usually when tropical cyclone activity peaks in the Atlantic: at that time, ocean waters have become plenty warm after summer, and the cross-cutting winds that can stymie storms tend to relax.
Though ocean waters across the Atlantic are amply warm right now, those cross-cutting winds—known as wind shear—aren’t abating. That’s thanks to El Niño. This cyclical climate phenomenon happens because of an eastward shift in warm ocean waters in the Pacific, although it has worldwide effects on the weather. The movement of warm waters, in turn, changes where heat enters the atmosphere, which alters the motions of atmospheric currents. In the Atlantic, that means there is more wind shear and air that pushes downward, both of which stymie cyclone development.
It’s possible the new record low for Atlantic hurricane activity could be overturned later. As Lowry wrote in his blog, Tropical Storm Fay, which began as a tropical depression far out in the Atlantic on September 19, came close to reaching the hurricane threshold of 74-mile-per-hour winds, and one satellite estimate measured winds of 84 mph on September 20. But that method of measuring winds tends to produce falsely high readings, Lowry notes. The National Hurricane Center will examine the data more closely after the season to see if it needs to revise Fay’s status to that of a hurricane.
If Fay is designated as a hurricane, it would still set the mark for the latest hurricane formation ever in the Atlantic in reliable records. Either way, this has been a hurricane season unlike any Lowry can recall.
“We expected a notably down year, activity-wise, across the Atlantic due primarily to the record-setting El Niño. But none of us in the hurricane space could’ve confidently predicted it’d be this dead through September,” Lowry says.
As we move away from the peak of the season, it becomes harder for hurricanes to spin up. So, assuming Fay doesn’t get the hurricane nod later, we could potentially go the rest of the season—until November 30—without a hurricane. That’s never happened before in modern history, but if it did, this would be one of the likeliest seasons for it to occur.
As disorienting as the current weather is, it’s a relief to communities that have been hard-hit in recent years. “After a decade of active to hyperactive hurricane seasons with some of our costliest and deadliest U.S. hurricanes,” Lowry says, “this is one record I’m relieved to see!”

Fourteen more Ukrainian children have crossed from Russian-occupied Kherson Oblast back onto Ukrainian-held ground, the oblast's military administration said on 29 September. They join a years-long effort to recover children from land Russia seized in 2022, with thousands more still deported or unaccounted for.
Ukrainian authorities say Russia has deported nearly 20,000 children since its 2022 full-scale invasion, and Zelenskyy insists the true figure is far higher. Those taken to Russia are placed in institutions or Russian families and pushed through Russian "re-education" aimed at erasing their Ukrainian identity.
These 14 add to roughly 2,000 children Ukraine has brought back since 2022—a recovery effort still dwarfed by the numbers Russia holds and keeps adding to.
Who made it out
The 14 are four boys and 10 girls, aged 6 to 17, said Oleksandr Prokudin, who heads the administration. Rescuers also brought back one young adult who had been deprived of parental care.
Each case shows what pushed the children toward the return. One 16-year-old boy was being forced onto Russia's military registration rolls under occupation, part of a pipeline that moves teenagers from a Russian passport toward conscription at 18. A 17-year-old girl had sought a Ukrainian education despite the risks and Russian control, Prokudin said. A 10-year-old girl, he added, had longed to come home and did all she could to reach safety.
The running tally
The children left through Bring Kids Back UA, the repatriation program President Volodymyr Zelenskyy launched in 2023, working with the Ukrainian charity Save Ukraine. That brings to 204 the number of children returned from occupied Kherson Oblast since the start of 2026, regional authorities said.
The wider deportation campaign
In 2023, the International Criminal Court in The Hague issued arrest warrants for Russian leader Vladimir Putin and his children's rights commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, over the illegal deportation of children from occupied Ukraine to Russia.

The Guardian view on Lula v the Bolsonaros: the decision of Brazilian voters will affect us all | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:37:06 UTC
02:37:06 KST

Sunday’s election in Brazil could hardly be a clearer-cut choice – nor a closer call. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, is neck and neck in the polls with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son and champion of the jailed far-right former president Jair. Mr Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup to “annihilate” democracy after losing the last election.
Brazil is Latin America’s largest democracy, but military dictatorship is in its recent past. Mr Bolsonaro wants to free his father and those who rioted in his support in 2023. The senator has campaigned as a less crass and temperamental version of his father, but he is no less extreme. For many on both sides, this is a vote against a man they detest more than an endorsement of their own candidate. Most voters disapprove of both men.
Initially, pundits predicted victory for the leftwing incumbent. Some feel that at 80 he is too old to begin a fourth term, though he remains energetic. His social programmes are extensive, but frustration at Brazil’s enduring failure to match its economic record to its potential may hobble him, especially with growth slowing. Violent crime remains a top issue.
Then came the Banco Master financial scandal, which has snowballed into a corruption case spanning Brazilian politics and the judiciary. First, Flávio Bolsonaro was caught on tape asking the failed bank’s playboy owner, Daniel Vorcaro, for almost $27m to make a film about his father. He denies wrongdoing.
Then compromising messages between Mr Vorcaro and the supreme court judge who led the prosecution of the ex-president were revealed. The allegations fed the perception that politicians are all dirty, and bolstered the unfounded far-right claim that Mr Bolsonaro Sr was stitched up. His son has also papered over a damaging public rift with his stepmother Michelle – an influential figure, key to the evangelical support he needs.
Mr Bolsonaro Jr has said he will abide by the election’s result. But the Bolsonaros have spent years working to undermine trust in internationally respected Brazil’s electronic voting system. A narrow first-round victory for Lula would probably be contested. With other candidates on the right, Mr Bolsonaro Jr would also have an advantage in a second-round vote. He has talked up the prospect of privatisation and cuts to public spending and taxes if he wins. He has pledged to pack the supreme court with anti‑abortion conservative judges, who would also be critical to future election disputes. He has vowed to introduce the kind of aggressive anti-crime drive that has trampled human rights elsewhere.
President Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, will be further emboldened in their “Donroe doctrine” of aggressive intervention in the western hemisphere if Mr Bolsonaro Jr is victorious. US meddling in this election has often backfired – high tariffs on Brazil have allowed Lula to run as the patriot defending the country against foreign interference. But it is no less disturbing.
Mr Trump’s more ruthless and reckless second term also offers an alarming vision of how another Bolsonaro presidency might look. The first showed historic levels of deforestation in the Amazon as well as a surge in illegal resource extraction and the invasion of Indigenous people’s lands. Those fell sharply once Lula returned to power. A Bolsonaro presidency would be bad for women, the poor and minorities. Democracy would probably be its first, local victim. But the climate would surely be another – with consequences for us all.

The Guardian view on falling pupil numbers: a chance to improve opportunities for young people | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:36:26 UTC
02:36:26 KST

School closures are an alarming symptom of Britain’s shrinking birthrate. Several factors have contributed to falling enrolment, but the most significant is that people are having fewer children. Declining pupil numbers could be an excuse to free up spending for an ageing population. Instead, the government should see this as an opportunity to improve the quality of provision for young people.
The fall has been most acute in inner London, where 90 schools have shut since 2021. In Southwark, where the number of children born each year has dropped by more than a third since 2010, eight primary schools have closed in the past six years. As London’s councils have observed, high living costs are pricing families out of the centre and dissuading people from having children. It is no surprise that Islington and Westminster, two of the most expensive places to live in Britain, also have among the lowest fertility rates in England and Wales.
Declining enrolment shapes the quality of education that schools can provide. They receive funding for each child they enrol, which is currently £7,000 per primary-age pupil in England. Schools with fewer pupils are forced to make their funding stretch further, cutting teachers, merging classes, and losing extracurricular activities. Official forecasts have previously overestimated the future number of young people, making it harder for local authorities to plan. They have not been helped by the promotion of free schools, which have created a surplus of school places, or the expansion of academies, which decide their own admissions and can entice pupils away to neighbouring areas. The government has recently given local authorities greater powers to object to academy expansion, which should help them plan more effectively.
The Treasury may be tempted to recycle savings from falling pupil numbers towards rising demand for health and social care. Over the past seven years, for example, as primary school pupil numbers in England fell by 5%, the number of teachers and classes shrank by 4%. But treating this development as a justification for cutting spending on education would be a mistake. Lucy Powell, the education secretary, has promised expanded enrichment activities and earlier intervention for children with special educational needs. Falling pupil numbers offer an opportunity to deliver these ambitions, provided the government retains the resources to do so. The gap between private school fees and state school spending per pupil has more than doubled over the past decade, and spending more on state school pupils would help narrow this inequality.
The closure of a school shapes an area. “Without this school it’s all just tourists, isn’t it?” one parent recently said of Soho’s last remaining primary school, which is at risk of imminent closure. Fewer schools make areas less attractive to families, particularly in rural places where alternatives may be miles away. Yet if people continue having fewer children, more schools will probably have to close. In some cases, this may be unavoidable.
Schools that have large numbers of unfilled places tend to perform worse on average, but closing them won’t necessarily improve results. Local authorities, which have excelled at selling off public assets, should be required to keep hold of shuttered schools. Empty classrooms could be repurposed as youth clubs, turned over to nurseries, or transformed into Sure Start centres. The focus should be on managing resources to improve education and opportunities for young people in an increasingly old society.
