Carol Sansour: Palestine, poetry and the power of ordinary life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:36:17 UTC
02:36:17 KST

Breadcrumb
'I want to remember the ordinary': Carol Sansour on the Palestine that exists beyond destruction
"Before Palestine was something I had to explain to anyone, it was simply the trees, the breeze and the world in which I knew myself," begins poet and cultural producer Carol Sansour.
In other words, for Carol, Palestine was rooted in the ordinary details of childhood. On snow days in Beit Jala, when the roads were covered in snow and the family was cut off, her mother would cook lentils to keep them warm. Inside, the television would be tuned to Jordan TV, one of their few options, while the family gathered around the ‘Aladdin’ gas heater, burning orange peels in it.
Those memories remain part of how Carol understands Palestine today, and they have also shaped the way she writes about it.
Born in Jerusalem in 1972, she has lived and worked between Palestine, the United States and Europe. Her first poetry collection, In the Time of the Apricots, appeared in Cairo in 2019, followed in 2022 by Jamelia and the French edition, À la saison des abricots.
Her poetry, translated into French, English, Italian, Spanish, Greek and German, moves between intimate memory, displacement, identity and the everyday.
She now lives in Athens, where she directs the Athens Palestine Film Festival and has founded Dounias, a non-profit organisation that produces and presents Arab art and culture in Greece.
Speaking in more detail, Carol shares more about her experiences with The New Arab.
The New Arab: What would you like us to notice if we could walk together through the Beit Jala of your childhood?
Carol Sansour: Just breathe in the scent of the first apricots of the season, feel the fresh breeze on your skin, and listen to the sounds around you. Before I tell you anything about Palestine, I want you to notice how the place makes you feel.
Can we go into the women who shaped your understanding of Palestine and life?
There are women everywhere in my work: Jamila, my great-grandmother, and Jalilah and Ramona, my grandmothers. They shaped not so much my understanding of Palestine as my understanding of life, while showing me that their lives could not simply be reduced to ideas of 'Palestinian womanhood'. Simply by being who they were, they guided the curious little girl I was towards the matters that really mattered.
Their hardships, and more importantly, the ways they carried themselves through them, taught me things that no political language or official history could have taught me.
I carry their experiences differently because I have the privilege and responsibility of looking back on them, placing them within a larger history and asking questions they may not have had the space to ask.
If you could remove the words 'occupation' and 'genocide', how would you describe Palestine to somebody who has never encountered it?
It is really occupying me... forgive the pun... I find it very difficult to imagine who we could have been without occupation and genocide. I don’t know what my psyche would have been like if I had been born free. I wonder: what does it feel like to be free?
But oppression has not made Palestinians jaded.
If anything, it has made us understand the essence of life in a very particular way. Maybe because we cherish it, because we long for it, we know how to find pleasure in it.
There is an insistence on living, not simply surviving, but finding ways to laugh, love, celebrate, and be together.
Palestinian women are often represented internationally either as victims of suffering or as figures of heroic resistance. What kinds of women, and what kinds of ordinary life, disappear between those two images?
What disappears between those two images is the woman herself. Mothers, daughters, lovers, difficult women, funny women, angry women, women who contradict themselves, women who desire things, women who make mistakes.
The dangerous thing about these two images, however, is that both are useful. The victim creates sympathy; the heroine creates admiration. But neither necessarily creates intimacy.
That is where I want to live. In the space between the headline and the symbol. In the ordinary life that continues alongside history.
In the expectation of representation, do you see a contradiction between European institutions celebrating Palestinian artists and deciding which Palestinian speech is acceptable?
I have seen how the expectation of representation can erase the diversity of Palestinian experience.
I experienced this directly when a poem I wrote about Palestinian political prisoners was removed from a German anthology of Arab poets writing in Europe.
I was being included as a Palestinian poet while a part of my Palestinian voice was being excluded.
Institutions and individuals can be very eager to celebrate Palestinian artists; to programme us, translate us, exhibit us, talk about our work, but sometimes that welcome comes with an invisible condition.
I believe solidarity should create space for somebody to speak in their own voice.
When those offering solidarity begin deciding what can be said or which parts of Palestinian experience are acceptable, it becomes another form of control.
What we need is not necessarily more people speaking on our behalf.
We need more spaces where Palestinians can speak for themselves, including when what they say is uncomfortable, contradictory, angry, inconvenient or simply not what is expected to hear.
An institution can create a platform for my Palestinian voice while controlling its boundaries. I call this a very sophisticated form of silencing because, from the outside, it can appear to be inclusion.
They are handing the Palestinian the script and not the microphone.
Through the Athens Palestine Film Festival, you've insisted on encountering Palestinian cinema as cinema rather than merely political testimony. What can a Palestinian comedy, love story or science-fiction film tell the audience about Palestine?
Through the Athens Palestine Film Festival, I have insisted that Palestinian cinema should be encountered as cinema.
They imagine futures. They make jokes. They fall in love. They are bored, ridiculous, tender, ambitious, angry. They are, in other words, human beings.
I can’t believe I am saying that. For a moment, the Palestinian is not a political subject, not a headline. They are simply a person whose experience is recognisable.
For me, the most powerful moments are often not the large political scenes but those in the laughter in the cinema, in an uncomfortable silence, or in the reaction to something so ordinary that it could have happened in a Greek or Palestinian home.
Those moments are incredibly powerful because they don't require us to manufacture a connection. The connection is already there.
I don't want Palestinian cinema to become acceptable only when an audience can recognise itself in it. A Palestinian comedy doesn't have to teach a Greek audience about Palestine; it can simply make them laugh.
A love story doesn't have to explain an occupation, but it can simply break their heart. When, for a moment, nobody is being asked to perform their identity, and we are just sitting in the dark watching a film together.
Palestine has been encountered internationally through an overwhelming visual archive of unprecedented destruction, occupation, famine and genocide. How do you protect your own memories of Palestine from being overwritten by those images? What are you afraid the world will remember about Palestinians and, perhaps more importantly, what are you afraid it will forget?
Is it too much to say that I no longer care very much about what the world remembers or forgets about Palestine? What is ‘the world’, anyway?
I am more concerned with my own responsibility to remember and, specifically, the silence of my grandparents and ancestors. That silence was born of human brutality, but it could also be a means of survival.
Sometimes people survive by not speaking, by putting certain memories away. I want to leave a trace of my own childhood in Beit Jala, in Jerusalem, in Haifa and in Gaza and its Mediterranean coast, of what it felt like to be there before these places became almost entirely represented through images of destruction.
I want to remember the ordinary and the complicated, because they are part of what is being erased too.
I want to be a witness, but also a thorn in the side of those who think that futures can be built on the corpses of my people without those people having futures of their own. A thorn in the side of perpetrators, and of anyone who would rather history become clean, convenient, and forgetful.
What would Palestine ask Carol Sansour?
I think Palestine would ask me, "When are you coming back to be physically with me?" I am sure ‘She’ misses me as much as I miss ‘Her’.

Tatiana Svorou is a journalist covering forced migration and humanitarian policy, with a focus on the Mediterranean

The Burnham bounce: Is Labour gaining ground against Farage’s Reform?
British opinion polls suggest the Labour Party steadily gaining favour as Reform UK dips.
Just more than two months into office, Andy Burnham was roundly praised for his first speech as prime minister at the Labour conference in Liverpool.
The Financial Times described his vision as “courageous”; the broadcaster Piers Morgan said the speech was “one of the best, and most powerfully delivered, by a British politician in a very long time”, and journalist Andrew Marr said he remembered seeing Tony Blair speak, but “Andy Burnham might be better”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Pro-Palestine Action group to rally at Labour conference led by Burnham

The new premier’s pitch focused on his plans for social welfare. And in recent months, the Labour Party has been enjoying what has been dubbed a “Burnham bounce”.
Some polling still reflects that bounce, especially in the race against the right-wing Reform UK party.
The Survation polling platform on Wednesday predicted Westminster’s voting intention for the Labour Party had risen two percentage points to 29 percent, while Reform UK fell one point to 23 percent.
“Very little” of Labour’s recovery is because of large numbers of Reform voters moving towards Labour, said Tim Bale, politics professor at Queen Mary University of London.

Since the Labour Party won the 2024 general election, it has been in constant competition with Reform UK, led by the telegenic Nigel Farage.
A YouGov poll last week found that if an election were called tomorrow, Labour would win the most seats but would face a hung parliament, with 241 seats. In contrast, the Conservatives would secure 130 and Reform UK 123.
But in reality, “voters will gather around the candidate best placed to beat Reform”, predicted Patrick Diamond, professor of public policy at Queen Mary University of London.

Burnham bounce
A YouGov poll published on Tuesday showed Reform UK slightly ahead of Labour, a sign of how fragile the Burnham bounce is.
At least 25 percent would vote for Reform UK, while 24 percent would choose Labour and 19 percent would choose the Conservatives, YouGov polling suggested. Only 12 percent would vote for the Liberal Democrats, 11 percent for the Greens, and 3 percent for the far-right Restore Britain party.

However, Prime Minister Keir Starmer proved to be an unpopular leader while Reform UK gained more interest.
In July, Starmer resigned.
“Once Starmer left, Labour’s position recovered, but Burnham has boosted that further,” said Diamond. “The Labour brand remains reasonably popular – recent difficulties were more related to the unpopularity of Keir Starmer as PM and public antipathy to his government.”
Starmer was criticised over a range of issues from his position on Israel-Palestine and his policy U-turns to his lack of leadership qualities.
As Starmer’s popularity dropped, Farage took support from the Conservatives and, for the first time in Reform’s relatively brief political life, had polls predicting it could win an election.
A year ago, a More in Common poll of nearly 20,000 Britons showed how Reform could secure a 96-seat majority in parliament, taking 373 seats. In the May 2025 local elections, Reform outperformed expectations, winning 677 of the 1,637 seats up for grabs, or 41 percent of all seats available.
But in July, a More in Common poll found Reform UK’s chances of success had shrunk, with the party projected to win 293 seats.
Burnham’s promises
Burnham on Tuesday promised to “break with the direction of the past 40 years and put Britain on a new path”.
He said he would overturn former Conservative Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher’s 1980s reforms and give the public more control over housing, water and energy.
While potentially popular with some Labour supporters, Diamond said that Burnham needs to address people in the centre.
“Centrist voters who are broadly from the middle class are ones to watch. They often live in marginal seats,” he said.
“They like some Labour policies on public services and support measures to boost economic growth, including by moving closer to Europe. But they are also very sensitive about the issue of tax, believing they already pay enough and want the government to be more efficient. That is a big test for the Burnham administration,” he added.

France's Macron, Spain's Sanchez welcome idea of UK rejoining EU after Burnham remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:34:00 UTC
02:34:00 KST

France, Spain welcome idea of UK rejoining EU
September 30, 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Wednesday welcomed the idea of the United Kingdom rejoining the European Union.
During a visit to Madrid while meeting with Sanchez, Macron reacted to the idea of a UK rejoin with two words in English: "Welcome back."
"If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news both for his country and for Europeans," Macron continued in French.
At the same time, Macron said the UK cannot take an a la carte approach to its relationship with the EU, while remaining outside the bloc.
"You cannot choose between the freedoms of the union and decide to take what suits us and not the rest," he said.
Sanchez said the UK's decision to leave the EU as a result of a referendum in 2016 is "a huge loss, both for the British population and for the whole European project."
The Spanish prime minister said if the UK indeed does try to rejoin the EU, "then of course Spain would applaud it and open its arms again to a brotherly people."
In a separate statement from the EU, European Commission spokesperson Balazs Ujvari said: "The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward."
"We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward," Ujvari said.
Burnham: UK should consider options in regards to EU ties
In an interview with the BBC earlier on Wednesday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain should look at various options when it comes to the relationship with the EU.
"We could stay as we are. That's definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay," Burnham said, while saying one option would be to "go all the way."
Other possibilities might include rejoining the EU's single market or a customs union between the two sides, he said.
During a speech at the annual Labour Party conference on Tuesday, Burnham said that "Brexit has done more harm than good." He added he would set out "different options" for the UK-EU relationship closer to a summit between the two sides in November.
Such a decision to move closer or rejoin the EU could open up a tense political debate in the UK.
Although recent public surveys suggest that the majority of Britons back rejoining, the idea of adopting the Euro currency or contributing to the EU budget would likely spark fierce backlash. Moreover, the UK is unlikely to receive the same exemptions it had when it was previously a member of the EU.
For now, Burnham is committed to the 2024 Labour Party manifesto, which ruled out rejoining the EU and other elements such as returning to the EU single market. However, Burnham could push Labour for a closer approach to the EU in the next general election, which is slated for no later than August 2029.

In pictures: A week of Russian jet drone terror in Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:33:45 UTC
02:33:45 KST

In pictures: A week of Russian jet drone terror in Kyiv
Smoke from a Russian drone strike rises over a residential area in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 23, 2026. (Roman Chop/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
Editor's note: The Kyiv residents quoted in the story asked to be identified only by their first names.
Russian drones have filled the skies over Kyiv, striking at the city around the clock, making it feel increasingly like there is nowhere safe to hide.
The attacks once came in waves, followed by periods of relative calm. Now, Russian strikes are coming almost nonstop. Using newer jet-powered versions of Shahed-type drones, the onslaught began last month, but has increased in intensity each day over the past week.
The city is filled with the constant noise of drones striking their targets and the thunder of air defenses firing back. Then there is the sound of a drone approaching — a distant roar that can swell in seconds as it tears through the sky at speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour (370 miles per hour), leaving little time to act.
"At any moment, you don't know where a strike might land," Kyiv resident Khrystyna told the Kyiv Independent after an attack on Sept. 23 set a historic market near the central railway station ablaze.
read also
The latest barrage stretched from night into day. At 12 hours and 44 minutes, the air raid alert in Kyiv on Sept. 30 was one of the longest single alerts the city has ever recorded. Several more have sounded since, and at the time of writing, another was stretching into the late evening.
Preceding the daylight drone barrage, Russian forces attacked the capital overnight with ballistic missiles.
Earlier this week, Russia struck the Ukrainian National Academy of Sciences in the center of Kyiv, forcing people trapped inside to climb out through upper-floor windows to escape the flames. About two hours later, another Russian strike hit a medical center a mere 15-minute walk away.
Kyiv's data centers and internet hubs have also been among Russia's latest targets. Strikes on this infrastructure can disrupt Ukrainian online services far beyond the capital, degrade connectivity in Kyiv, and potentially cut people off from the internet they rely on to track drone movements.
Another troubling sign came on Sept. 30, when Russia resumed strikes on the capital's energy infrastructure.
Under a seemingly endless barrage of Russian drones, and with no certainty about what the next morning will bring, Kyiv continues to push through the attacks as it braces for colder weather — and another difficult winter.
"We try to put it out of our minds and stay composed. But lately, our morale has taken a hit," Yana, a real estate agent who survived a Sept. 25 attack in the city center, told the Kyiv Independent.

Trump's latest global tariffs face trade court challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:33:45 UTC
02:33:45 KST

President Donald Trump's near-global tariff policy is being challenged in federal court — again.
A panel of three judges at the U.S. Court of International Trade in Manhattan heard arguments Wednesday from a group of small businesses and Democratic-led states who say Trump's sweeping "Section 301" tariffs overstep the law.
It's the third time in less than two years that the courts have been asked to intervene against the president's attempt to impose sweeping tariffs on the vast majority of U.S. imports.
The latest tariffs put 10% or 12.5% rates on goods from 86 countries, covering 99.4% of U.S. imports. The Trump administration said they were imposed in response to the targeted countries failing to effectively enforce bans on the trade of goods produced using forced labor practices.
But an attorney for the challengers said at the start of Wednesday's hearing that a "constellation of factors" show the government's justification was a "pretext" in pursuit of reviving Trump's worldwide tariff regime.
"We know this was not the only reason that they did this," the attorney, Pratik Shah, said.
One of the judges pushed back. "So what?" she asked, probing whether the government having additional motivations for the tariffs was enough to rule against them.
Shah replied that the administration's "unprecedented" use of Section 301 — slapping tariffs of similar size on dozens of economies in "one fell swoop" after a truncated investigation — does not satisfy the statute's requirements.
Specifically, the attorney argued that the government must show that each country's trade practices are unreasonable and impose a burden on U.S. commerce. "It's the lack of the country-specific findings" that violates the statute, Shah told the panel.
Eric Hamilton, a lawyer for the Department of Justice, countered that the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative "relied on data, economic principles, case studies, hearing testimony, and comments, as well as logic, in concluding that all 60 of the investigated economies burden U.S. commerce."
That office did perform a country-by-country analysis, rather than make a blanket determination, Hamilton told the panel.
"To be sure, there's a common basis for the determinations" that were made, he added.
The hearing began at 10 a.m. ET and ended at 12:30 p.m. The judges said before adjourning that they will issue a ruling as quickly as they can.
Trump's tariff efforts
The Trump administration started its investigations into foreign forced labor practices in March, shortly after the president's protectionist agenda suffered a major legal setback.
The Supreme Court in February struck down the "reciprocal" tariffs that Trump had unveiled in April 2025, trashing a huge piece of his trade agenda and forcing his administration to refund more than $100 billion.
The day that ruling came down, Trump announced a worldwide 10% tariff under a different statute known as Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. That authority only allowed the tariffs to last for 150 days — but in that interval, the federal trade court ruled against them. An appeals court paused that ruling, allowing them to stay in effect for their duration.
Right as those tariffs expired in July, the Trump administration imposed new duties under Section 301 of the same 1974 trade law.
The move "is the most sweeping international labor rights action the United States has ever taken — that any country has ever taken," a senior Trump administration official told reporters at the time.
The legal challenge being heard Wednesday morning contends that the administration invoked the forced labor argument as a pretext to reimpose the worldwide tariffs that were previously struck down.
"In short, Defendants have now tried to re-create materially the same global tariff regime under three disparate statutes," the plaintiffs wrote in a court filing in August in the case, which consolidates multiple legal challenges. "But there is a reason they did not begin with Section 301 and are instead turning to it now only as a last resort."
The plaintiffs comprise a number of small businesses who say they import goods that are subject to the Section 301 tariffs, as well as a coalition of 25 states
Attorneys for the Department of Justice insist the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative fully complied with the law.
"The actions that USTR has taken at the direction of the President in this case are consistent with the text, object, and purpose of the Section 301 statute, as well as with the President's firm commitment to create a level playing field for U.S. workers, producers, and exporters by conditioning access to the U.S. market on concrete action to prohibit international trade in forced labor goods," they told the court in early September.
Trump in late July told Fox News that the 301 tariffs are "doing the same thing" as the ones that the Supreme Court struck down.
Sara Albrecht, chairman and CEO of Liberty Justice Center, the legal nonprofit that brought one of the lawsuits against the new tariffs, told CNBC at the time that Trump's remarks bolstered its argument.

Inside Milei's Two-Week Ultimatum to U.K. Over Falklands Oil Exploration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:33:44 UTC
02:33:44 KST

Argentine President Javier Milei has threatened legal action against the U.K. over an oil exploration project off the coast of the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory at the center of a yearslong sovereignty dispute.
Setting a two-week deadline on Monday, Milei said if the Sea Lion offshore oil project—a venture between British and Israeli companies—has not been stopped, then he will take the matter to the “International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea,” an independent judicial body responsible for the application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Milei said Argentina’s Foreign Ministry and legal teams have been prepped to “initiate international arbitration” against the U.K. The oil companies—Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum—have said they have valid licenses for the planned extractions. TIME has reached out to the companies for further comment.
The threat from Milei comes after weeks of escalating tensions between Argentina and the U.K. The Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as “Islas Malvinas,” sit roughly 300 miles from the Argentine coast, and have been a British territory for almost two centuries, but Argentina has never accepted British sovereignty over the area. As such, Milei is adamant the oil exploration project would amount to an “illegal plundering of [Argentina’s] resources.” U.S. President Donald Trump further stoked tensions in late August when he suggested the U.S. is reviewing its neutrality on the sovereignty dispute.
In response to Milei’s deadline, a spokesperson for the U.K.’s Foreign Office told TIME: "These latest threats are another attempt to deny the Falkland Islanders the right to pursue their own economic development and decide their own future. As the Prime Minister [Andy Burnham] has made clear, our support for the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination is unwavering, and we will always defend it.”
In a 2013 referendum, Falkland residents voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining under British rule. The referendum saw 92% of all eligible voters turn out, with 99.8% of votes being “yes.” Yet the topic continues to be a rallying cry in Argentina for Milei, as it was for the Argentine Presidents that came before him.
There are vast energy reserves in the Sea Lion oilfield, with the basin estimated to contain 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
“The Argentine Republic will not stand idly by and will continue to firmly defend its sovereign rights, using all the diplomatic, administrative and legal tools recognized by national and international law,” read a presidential statement condemning the oil exploration project. The statement said that Milei’s office would seek to initiate arbitral proceedings under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)—an international treaty that sets rules for the use and governance of the world's oceans and their resources.
Marcelo Kohen, a professor emeritus of international law at the Geneva Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies, says the two-week ultimatum is tied to a procedure Argentina has to follow before seeking provisional measures from the tribunal.
“Argentina gave the U.K. two weeks to accept the provisional measures requested by Argentina, and in case the U.K. doesn't comply with this request, Argentina will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg,” he says. Once the case has been taken to the judicial body, “both parties will go to the tribunal, and there will be oral hearings, and then the tribunal will decide whether the United Kingdom must stop the exploitation of hydrocarbon resources.”
This isn’t the first time Argentina has turned to international legal mechanisms to resolve maritime disputes. In October 2012, Argentina initiated arbitration after Ghana detained an Argentine naval training ship. The tribunal unanimously ordered Ghana to release the vessel.
However, experts tell TIME that the international court has previously said it does not view it to be within its jurisdiction to rule on territorial sovereignty disputes.
Milei’s turn to international law comes amid his fierce criticism of the United Nations, which he has accused of looking "the other way" amid escalating tensions with Britain.
During his speech at the General Assembly in New York last week, Milei called the U.N. a “useless organization, whose only purpose is to sustain a cast of fatally arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats.”
“The Sea Lion project is moving towards oil extraction on the Argentine continental shelf in the North Malvinas basin under British licenses that Argentina rejects as illegal and illegitimate,” he told delegates.
The ultimatum is the latest escalation from Milei over the Falklands. Earlier in September, he announced that Argentina would sanction oil companies operating in the area and strengthen the government’s ability to respond to what it views as threats against its sovereignty.
Following through on that threat, Argentina's Foreign Ministry on Sept. 15 said it had sent approximately 180 warning and risk assessment notes to individuals and legal entities located in 30 countries and filed three criminal complaints involving 10 companies and their directors.
TIME has reached out to Argentina's Foreign Ministry for further information.
Do the Falklands belong to Britain or Argentina?
The Falklands have been administered by Britain since 1833 and remain a British overseas territory, but Argentina continues to claim them. The Falkland Islands have been on the U.N.’s list of non-self-governing territories since 1946.
In 1982, Argentina invaded the Falklands, sparking a bloody 74-day conflict that Britain ultimately won.
Matthew Benwell, a reader in human geography at Newcastle University, tells TIME that the Falklands remain a “largely self-governing British overseas territory.”
“Aside from the U.K.'s provision of defense and foreign affairs—the islanders continue to rely on that assistance—the U.K. government and political parties across the spectrum support the islanders' right to self determination,” he says, referencing the 2013 referendum.
But Argentina approaches the sovereignty question through a different legal framework.
Kohen says that Buenos Aires regards it as “a case of de-colonization” in which self-determination does not apply.
Argentina points to a 1965 U.N. Resolution, which calls for bilateral sovereignty negotiations and consideration of the islanders’ “interests,” but does not expressly apply the principle of self-determination to them.
The Argentine permanent mission to the U.N. similarly characterizes the issue as a “colonial situation” and “reiterates its willingness to resume bilateral negotiations with the United Kingdom in order to reach a peaceful resolution to this sovereignty dispute.”
Benwell, however, describes the sovereignty argument as a “persistent one-way debate between the U.K. and Argentina, that predominantly comes from Argentina.”
How Trump stoked Falklands tensions
Trump, a long-time ally of Milei’s, prompted discussion in late August when he told reporters in the Oval Office that the U.S. was reviewing its position regarding the U.K.’s administration of the islands. “I always review every position. That's just one of many,” Trump said.
Milei appeared to seize on Trump's comments during a national address on Sept. 3, insisting that the “winds of change blowing around the world” are favorable to Argentina’s long-standing sovereignty claim over the South Atlantic archipelago.
In an interview with a British broadcaster, Trump declined to offer a clear pledge of support while emphasizing the islands’ distance and tying the issue to Britain’s refusal to aid the U.S. in the Iran war. “Your country was not there to help me,” he insisted.
On Sept. 12, Trump, during a sit-down with Irish Taoiseach (Prime Minister) Micheál Martin, called the mounting tensions over the Falklands a “potential disaster” and said he would “probably be able to settle it out,” without providing details of what that would entail.
Burnham and Trump discussed the Falklands issue in New York last week on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, but the details of the conversation have yet to be made public.
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Benwell says Trump’s comments, although potentially divisive, are no indication that U.S. foreign policy is set to change.
“These are just statements so far, and there's been no substantive changes to U.S. foreign policy,” he emphasizes.

AIIB reaffirms commitment to close global infrastructure financing gap at Doha meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:33:39 UTC
02:33:39 KST

The 11th AIIB annual meeting brings policymakers, investors and business leaders from around the world to Doha to explore how technology, sustainability, connectivity and investment are reshaping the way cities and economies develop.
Financing the infrastructure of the future is a growing global challenge, as countries work to meet their development goals.
The 11th edition of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank's (AIIB) annual meeting tackles one of the most critical questions in sustainable development: how to finance the infrastructure of the future and ensure it delivers for the communities it serves.
At her first annual meeting as president of the Beijing-based bank, Zou Jiayi said AIIB aims to broadly double its annual financing to around €17.6 billion by 2030, while focusing on areas where it believes it can add the most value.
“We will focus on infrastructure that supports climate resilience, renewable energy, digital transformation, regional connectivity, nature conservation, and people-centred development. We will leverage modern technology and mobilise private capital. Innovation is how we deliver impact,” she said.
In 2025, AIIB approved €9.4 billion in financing for 57 projects, with 71% of approved financing supporting climate-positive outcomes, surpassing its target. It also mobilised €4.3 billion in private capital.
Building on multilateralism
AIIB has teamed up with other multilateral development banks as part of its efforts to invest in global infrastructure projects.
The bank has established co-financing agreements with the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the African Development Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, while also working with major banking institutions across multiple regions.
At the end of 2024, 131 of AIIB’s 303 approved projects had been co-financed with other multilateral development banks.
The model, designed to pool resources and share expertise, has gained added significance at a time when global trade is becoming more fragmented, disrupted and challenged by rising protectionism.
For AIIB, cooperation remains central to the bank’s mission.
“Cooperation is also at the heart of infrastructure. Infrastructure facilitates connections, and building it requires collaboration across borders, institutions, and markets,” Zou added.
Qatar’s role
Qatar, the host country and a founding member of AIIB, sees itself as part of that effort.
Qatari finance minister Ali bin Ahmed Al Kuwari reaffirmed the Gulf state’s commitment to advancing AIIB’s goals, even as the country faces uncertainty amid regional disruptions.
“Qatar comes to these discussions as a founding shareholder, as an investor in infrastructure across Asia and beyond, and as a country that has learned this year how much resilient infrastructure matters,” he said.
Qatar was among AIIB’s founding members in 2015, joining an institution that has since grown to 111 approved members across the world. The bank is now a $100 billion-capitalised multilateral development bank, with a mandate extending beyond Asia.
Creating impactful change
Qatar’s involvement extends beyond its position within AIIB. Through the Qatar Fund for Development (QFFD), the country has sought to combine development assistance with longer-term investment, supporting infrastructure, healthcare and education projects internationally.
QFFD believes that institutions like AIIB can help create partnerships and identify opportunities for co-investment, while increasing the capital available for sustainable development. For QFFD, the broader strategy is to help communities use grants to create a self-sustaining investment loop for themselves.
“We want to empower them to be development partners and to shift from grants to loans and investment to enable them to grow and generate income and have a more sustainable life, which eventually helps in developing others' lives,” said Noora Khalid Mohammed, the assistant manager of the investment department at QFFD.
Infrastructure in action
From Indonesia to the Maldives, Turkey to Egypt and Uzbekistan, AIIB’s strategy is being put into practice through projects spanning transport, energy, healthcare, digital connectivity and climate resilience.
In 2025 alone, the bank approved financing for projects ranging from climate-resilient roads in the Ivory Coast to a public-private partnership hospital in Kazakhstan and climate-adaptive water management in Cambodia.
The 12th edition of the bank’s annual meeting is set to be held next year in Baku, Azerbaijan. The Central Asian country is already working with AIIB on green energy and other infrastructure projects, including railway and solar initiatives.
With trillions of dollars still required every year to ensure that global development happens at the same pace, both the key and the challenge lie in unlocking the capital needed to build the infrastructure of the future.

Türkiye transfers management of 3 banks, 2 factoring firms to deposit insurance fund
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:33:38 UTC
02:33:38 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Türkiye’s banking regulator decided Wednesday to transfer the management of three investment banks and two factoring companies to the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF), following developments linked to an ongoing fund investigation.
The decisions cover Tera Investment Bank, Destek Investment Bank, Hedef Investment Bank, Destek Finance Factoring and Tera Finance Factoring, according to a statement from the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BDDK).
The regulator said its board adopted the measures following assessments of recent developments related to the process publicly known as the “fund investigation.”
TMSF will exercise shareholder rights, excluding dividend rights, attached to certain shares in the three investment banks.
The board also ordered certain shares in the two factoring companies to be transferred within six months to individuals or legal entities meeting statutory requirements.
TMSF will exercise the voting rights attached to those shares during that period.
The three banks account for 0.22% of the banking sector’s total assets, while the two factoring companies represent 1.45% of total factoring sector assets, according to the regulator.

Israeli restrictions on 65% of Gaza's land 'main obstacle' to aid, shelter: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:29:39 UTC
02:29:39 KST

Yasin Gungor
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Israeli restrictions in nearly two-thirds of the Gaza Strip represent the primary barrier to humanitarian relief and flood protection efforts, the UN said Wednesday.
"Our humanitarian partners stress that the main obstacle is restrictions on access of 65% of Gaza's land," spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters at a media briefing. "The remaining 35% is already overcrowded."
The constraints come as the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and partner groups assess emergency measures to protect families from winter downpours. Aid teams inspected three potential relocation zones for temporary shelters to assist families choosing to leave flood-prone grounds near structural ruins at risk of collapse.
In parallel, humanitarian teams are evaluating more than 450 existing displacement camps facing severe flooding hazards, which house roughly one-fifth of Gaza's population, said Dujarric.
He explained that mass voluntary movements require extensive groundwork, emphasizing that explosive ordnance contamination must be cleared at newly identified sites before relocation begins. Teams must also level sandy terrain, install water lines, drainage, and lighting, open access roads and resolve land tenure issues.
Relief organizations also face severe logistical bottlenecks due to entry restrictions. Dujarric stressed that agencies urgently require additional Israeli permits to import heavy machinery, spare parts, engine oil and critical supplies, alongside funding for emergency fuel and durable materials to repair damaged structures.
The operational hurdles have extended into healthcare delivery. While aid workers train local personnel to handle "noncommunicable diseases," medical shortages severely constrain screening and treatment. Gaps remain critical across specialized cancer care, including essential chemotherapy and radiotherapy supplies, while diagnostic systems suffer from depleted generator fuel and mechanical parts, according to Dujarric.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000, while 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed.
Israeli violations of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement have resulted in the deaths of 1,431 Palestinians and injuries to 5,026, Gaza’s Health Ministry said Wednesday.

UK ends 'one in, one out' migrant returns deal with France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:28:58 UTC
02:28:58 KST

Only about 4% of small-boat arrivals were sent back under the year-long pilot, which cost an average of €65,500 per return, as Paris pushes for an EU-wide replacement.
The UK's Home Office said on Wednesday that its year-old deal with France to return migrants crossing the Channel on small boats had ended.
"The government's pilot with France to remove asylum seekers in exchange for an equal number of legal migrants is no longer processing new cases," the Home Office said, confirming the end of the so-called "one in, one out" deal, which was launched in August last year and was due to expire on Thursday.
The scheme, known as Operation Hillmore, was part of efforts by London and Paris to tackle illegal migration across the English Channel.
Under the arrangement, Britain could return to France some migrants who arrived illegally by small boat and were judged to have no right to remain in the UK. In exchange, Britain accepted an equal number of asylum seekers from France considered likely to qualify for protection, with priority given to vulnerable nationalities and people with family or other links to the UK.
The two countries agreed in June to extend the pilot until 1 October. The most recent Home Office figures show that 1,087 people were returned to France between 4 August 2025 and 30 June 2026, while 1,117 were transferred to the UK under the scheme. Over the same period, 27,920 migrants arrived in the UK on small boats, meaning only about 4% of arrivals were sent back.
That was one of the clearest signs of the programme's limited impact, despite government claims that it would deter people-smuggling gangs.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told MPs on 15 September that it cost the UK taxpayer an average of about £56,000 (€65,500) per migrant to return them.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who succeeded Keir Starmer in July, said that Brexit had made stopping small boats harder because the UK no longer had the same level of cooperation with the EU. He declined to set a date for ending the crossings, but told the BBC he and Mahmood would not stop until they had cracked down on "every element of this criminal, illegal activity".
Burnham has said his government is "changing the whole approach" to small boats, pairing tougher enforcement with safe legal routes for asylum seekers, which he argues would take away the smuggling gangs' main selling point.
France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez told lawmakers in June that France wanted a more European approach to illegal migration. He also argued that France should not have to bear sole responsibility for policing an EU external border, blaming weak controls in countries of first entry and onward movement within the Schengen area.
Migrants trying to reach Britain pay smugglers thousands of euros for places on overcrowded inflatable boats to cross one of the world's busiest shipping lanes. Research has also shown a sharp rise this year in small boats setting off from Belgium, as smuggling networks look for new launch points.
Overall, some 197,000 people have crossed the Channel in small boats since the route emerged as a major migration pathway.

Bank of England governor calls for rigorous AI testing before regulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:28:05 UTC
02:28:05 KST

Aysu Bicer
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey on Wednesday called for rigorous testing of artificial intelligence systems to identify vulnerabilities and establish safeguards before turning to regulation.
In his first article for Substack, Bailey said the risks surrounding AI were “real and increasingly significant,” while stressing that development of the technology should not be halted or prohibited.
“On the contrary, the benefits are immense,” Bailey said, adding that there must be a system for intervention and clear boundaries within which AI operates.
Bailey said important work was already underway in the UK to test AI systems, pointing to the country’s AI Security Institute as part of efforts to develop standards.
“But the pace of progress must accelerate,” he said, adding: “We should proceed with a degree of humility.”
Bailey said testing would inevitably reveal failures and instances in which “models will behave unexpectedly.”
“That is not evidence that testing has failed, rather it is evidence of why testing is necessary,” he said.
Bailey stressed that testing should not be viewed as an alternative to future regulation, saying a more formal regulatory framework could emerge over time.
“But regulation is not, in my view, the right place to start,” he said.
The Bank of England governor specifically highlighted so-called frontier AI – highly advanced, self-learning systems.
Without effective intervention mechanisms, Bailey warned, such systems could become “a closed loop in which the model progressively governs itself.”
US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has rejected calls for a slowdown, saying the US is leading the AI race ahead of China.
“And, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said.
On Tuesday, after meeting executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google, Trump said they had signed a “morally binding” document that would serve as a “form of protection” against potential AI risks.
Trump also renamed it “Super Intelligence.”
The White House Accord on “Super Intelligence,” described as a “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities,” calls on companies developing and deploying frontier models to establish internal processes and controls.
The accord says the measures should ensure systems operate as intended and potential problems are identified and addressed quickly.
According to the accord, each participating company should implement four layers of controls and audits covering model development and deployment.

Trump's Title IX Announcement Is Cruel. But It Does Not Change The Law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:25:44 UTC
02:25:44 KST

Even though transgender people represent only an estimated 1% of the United States population, we are increasingly the target of restrictive government policies and election-year fear-mongering. This has been especially true under President Donald Trump, who, since day one of his second administration, has targeted transgender people across all areas of life—from education to employment to military service to identification to health care—and used trans people as political pawns to mobilize his perceived base.
This week’s announcement that the administration is rescinding Biden-era regulations enumerating protections for LGBTQ students is yet another example of the federal government’s unrelenting effort to bully transgender young people, particularly as elections approach. But while this latest attack is gratuitous and cruel, the rescission does not actually change the law; schools can and should continue to include transgender students equally in all educational programs.
Title IX, the landmark 1972 law prohibiting sex discrimination in schools, is often associated with efforts to even the playing field in sports, but the statute addresses all sex discrimination in education from the classroom to the teacher’s lounge to the basketball court.
In 2024, the Biden Administration took important steps to ensure that LGBTQ students were fully protected. While I would argue that the Biden Title IX rule fell short in some respects, it also included comprehensive regulations prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation and transgender status. Those regulations were blocked in court, however, and never took effect; instead, the government reverted to a 2020 rule issued under then-Education Secretary Betsy DeVos. The Trump administration’s action this week to formally reinstate the DeVos rule does not change the standards currently being enforced or reduce existing legal protections for LGBTQ students. Rather, it is a cruel and unnecessary gesture that demeans the importance of legal protections for LGBTQ students and the dignity of trans youth.
As much as President Trump may suggest that he can rewrite Title IX, that is not within the power of the executive. Title IX itself still prohibits sex discrimination in education, and the Supreme Court has held that it is impossible to discriminate against someone for being gay or transgender without discriminating on the basis of sex. Unless and until the Supreme Court says otherwise, this general proposition still stands, which means LGBTQ students retain protections under federal civil rights law.
To be sure, earlier this year the Supreme Court permitted the exclusion of transgender students in the unique, zero-sum, context of sports, where, it said, states and schools may exclude transgender women and girls from women’s and girls’ sports. But neither that decision nor the now-revived 2020 Title IX regulations says that schools must exclude transgender girls from girls’ sports. And, outside of sports, both federal and local protections for LGBTQ students remain valid and fully enforceable. With the administration's continued cruel anti-trans rhetoric, it is more important than ever that schools do not waver in their commitment to protecting LGBTQ students.
Even without these latest attacks on their rights, LGBTQ students documented elevated rates of discrimination in school. A recent survey of 2,800 LGBTQ-identified students reported that 68% experienced harassment or assault based on their transgender status and 62% experienced harassment or assault based on their sexual orientation. That same survey conducted a follow-up focus group after the 2024 election. In doing so, they documented significant increases in “hostility, bullying, and harassment” following the 2024 election.
A vulnerable group of young people is being made more vulnerable by the political conditions and rhetoric demonizing them. Now all eyes must turn to the state and local officials charged with protecting them.

Russia Sends NATO Formal Nuclear Warning Over Kaliningrad
Russia privately threatened NATO that it could use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, Russia’s heavily militarized exclave between Poland and Lithuania, Reuters reported on September 30.
In a diplomatic note sent to NATO and reviewed by Reuters, Moscow accused the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that carried “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict.”
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The warning comes amid growing concern over Russian hybrid operations across Europe, including sabotage, arson, cyberattacks, and other hostile activity that governments have linked to Moscow. UNITED24 Media recently detailed how these operations have intensified across the continent.
The document warned that such a confrontation could include “Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance’s member states right from the outset.”
“Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country,” the note stated.
Kaliningrad is a heavily militarized Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. Reuters noted that Moscow has increasingly portrayed allied military activity around the region as a direct threat.
NATO rejected the accusation in a written response also reviewed by Reuters, stating that it is a defensive alliance and that its exercises do not threaten Russian territory.
“None of NATO’s exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation,” the alliance stated. “We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behaviour towards the Allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.”
Nikolai Sokov, a Vienna-based nuclear analyst and former Russian diplomat, told Reuters that the warning could reflect growing concern in Moscow over Western arms supplies to Ukraine, sanctions, military exercises, intelligence flights, and possible restrictions on Russian shipping in the Baltic.
“They expect more action, including a blockade of the Baltic Sea — just below the level of war in European calculation, but for them this will be open war,” Sokov stated. “I see a risk of mutual miscalculation.”
Russian embassies in at least three European countries have also issued warnings in recent days accusing NATO of escalating tensions around Kaliningrad, Reuters wrote. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov described the statements as diplomatic reminders to “hotheads in Europe.”
A NATO diplomat characterized the Russian note as another attempt to intimidate European countries and emphasized that the alliance would continue supporting Ukraine. A senior European defense official told Reuters it was the first threat of this kind from Russia since the Cold War and described it as serious.
A day earlier, Russia had already threatened nuclear retaliation if NATO attempted to blockade or attack Kaliningrad, with its embassy in the UK warning that Moscow could respond using “all means available,” including nuclear weapons.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Frodo uses a 6×6 wheel configuration and can reach a top speed of 40 kilometers per hour. The developer lists its standard payload at up to 200 kilograms, rising to a maximum of 400 kilograms, while its range can extend to 150 kilometers.

“We see the future battlefield as a robotic environment where it is critically important to control not only the air but also the ground. The unveiling comes as Ukrainian forces increasingly integrate ground robots into battlefield operations. Cabinet clears Rs 1,789cr intelligent traffic system for Delhi, first planned before 2010 CWG

Cabinet approves Intelligent Traffic Management System for Delhi
NEW DELHI: Paving the way for Delhi to get a smart, technology-driven traffic management system over the next couple of years, the Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved the implementation of ITMS at an estimated cost of Rs 1,789 crore. The project to be implemented by Delhi police will feature AI-enabled signals, real-time congestion detection, automated enforcement and priority movement for ambulances across 42 key corridors.The proposal for an Intelligent Traffic Management System (ITMS) was first initiated ahead of the 2010 Commonwealth Games, though now the scale has been expanded to use the latest technology to detect nearly 20 types of violations and cover more stretches.Announcing the decision, Union I&B minister Ashwini Vaihnaw said the project will add “brain” to Delhi’s traffic management system as it will make the city’s traffic management infrastructure “intelligent” by integrating existing traffic signals, CCTVs, and AI capabilities into a unified, centralised control system.PM Narendra Modi, in a post on X, said the decision will “ensure the usage of technology to boost ‘Ease of Living’ across Delhi.”
The project will be implemented in three phases over two years, followed by five years of operation and maintenance.On the need for the project, Vaishnaw said that at present, Delhi’s 1,529 traffic signals run on fixed timings with manual interventions and these can’t adjust on their own when traffic builds up at a junction. He added that the cameras installed to detect red-light jumping and speeding work in isolation as “there is no single city-wide system that links signal control, enforcement, traffic information and diversions or that uses AI to flag wanted vehicles”.He added that the ITMS brings signal control, enforcement and live traffic information onto one technology platform. Govt said under this new regime, adaptive signals will be synced across corridors and congestion can be spotted early. The AI-enabled system will detect violations and can flag stolen or hot-listed vehicles as well.In an official statement, govt said the system will enable traffic signals to automatically adjust timings based on prevailing road conditions and coordinate signals along identified corridors to reduce stoppages and delays. It will also facilitate priority movement of ambulances and other emergency vehicles through green corridors, besides enabling quicker detection of congestion, slow-moving traffic and road incidents, allowing police to take faster operational measures.It said variable message signs and digital platforms will provide commuters with information on congestion, diversions, parking availability and traffic conditions. Such information may also be shared with navigation service providers.The system will strengthen automated enforcement against violations such as red-light and stop-line violations, speeding, wrong-way driving, non-use of helmets and seat belts, illegal parking and use of mobile phones while driving. AI-based analytics will also assist in identifying repeat violators and vehicles linked to hit-and-run incidents.Officials said the system will have multiple layers. The physical layer includes data centres, networks, controllers, sensors, and enforcement cameras that can read vehicle number plates automatically. The digital layer will integrate devices for real-time data capture and processing, while the application layer will cover traffic analytics, enforcement, parking, congestion and signal control, incident management, video systems, and adaptive traffic control.The system will also assist police in handling vehicle breakdowns, debris on roads, accident detection, monitoring VVIP movements, and managing route diversions. During emergencies, it will also help ensure smooth and priority movement of ambulances and disaster response vehicles by monitoring and clearing routes, officials added.
P K Sikdar, a former director of Central Road Research Institute (CRRI), said the decision will provide additional smartness to the city’s traffic."However, the smart city infrastructure and all these additional features need to be developed to an integrated platform with matured participation from all executive agencies of the city involved directly and indirectly in the transport system of the city," he added.Sikdar said this integrated platform should serve enforcement against all types of violations to incident detection and emergency response, and also for the alerts to the road users. "Most importantly, the public transport system is required to be highly modernised to change the preference of the public for the personalized modes. This is the opportunity to change the future direction of the city; but that is likely to demand significantly more resources," he said.

September 30, 2026
Last week, some students in Saudi Arabia were told they should stay at home and attend classes online, due to continued threats from attacks by the Houthi group in neighboring Yemen. But the very next day, they were given the all-clear and allowed to return to school in person.
The conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia in Yemen seems to have become part of everyday life in Saudi Arabia. After a period of comparative calm, the Houthis have been ramping up attacks on the country, starting July, and have fired many missiles and drones over the border.
Over recent weeks, the Houthi militia have also pushed further into Yemen, taking more control of the Yemeni coast and several islands in the Red Sea. This means they can oversee maritime traffic in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
The renewed Houthi attacks endanger Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's ambitious project to move the kingdom away from its dependence on oil revenues, which was conceived by Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. To make Vision 2030 a reality, Saudi Arabia needs stability — but right now, the outlook is moving in the opposite direction.
"The escalation in Yemen is drawing the Saudis deeper into the regional war, a war that Saudi Arabia actually wanted to prevent," said Marcus Schneider, who heads the Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Regional Peace and Security Project in the Middle East.
Impact on world's energy
Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure is particularly vulnerable to Houthi attacks, which have already disrupted the so-called East-West pipeline, which runs for over 1,200 kilometers. It was being used to transport oil after other routes, such as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, became precarious due to fighting between the United States, Israel and Iran.
Houthi attacks disabled the pipeline although reports from a week ago suggest it is being used again. And thanks to the Houthis, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — which means "gate of tears" in English — is also coming under pressure.
Andrew Leber, a nonresident scholar in the Middle East program of the US think tank, the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, calls it a "one-two punch of pipeline attacks and Red Sea seizures." In fact, it may send the Saudis back to the Strait of Hormuz to try to ship their oil, even though that route is still heavily restricted.
Who will help?
It is unlikely that Saudi ally, the US, is going to send help. Washington has said it will support the Saudis with intelligence and reconnaissance, but President Donald Trump appears reluctant to get involved in a direct military campaign against the Houthis.
According to a US-based think tank, the Center for Strategic and International Studies, this may partially be because the it is feeling the strain of its ongoing campaign against Iran.
"The US military is reportedly facing serious challenges, including shortages of some sophisticated interceptors," the CSIS wrote in a commentary last week.
The US Council on Foreign Relations, or CFR, has also written about dwindling stocks of Patriot and interceptor missiles, as well as cruise missiles.
So the risk of opening another front in its war with Iran, in Yemen, is not a welcome prospect for the US.
As it is, US airstrikes are unlikely to resolve the Houthi problem anyway. The CFR writes that to defuse the Houthi threat, a large, coordinated ground operation is needed, especially if forces want to push the Yemeni militia back out of the areas they recently took around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Saudi Arabia is not too enthusiastic about this either. Despite help from the US and neighboring United Arab Emirates, a Saudi coalition that fought against the Houthis between 2015 and 2022 failed to achieve any kind of decisive victory. It also demonstrated the limits of Saudi military power.
There's clear military asymmetry. Saudi Arabia possesses modern weapons and spends enormous sums on its armed forces. But the Houthis don't need to win a conventional war. It is enough for them to use missiles and drones to threaten infrastructure and disrupt shipping.
"The Houthis are well-established in Yemen and can withstand considerable blows," Schneider told DW. "Saudi Arabia, on the other hand, needs stability above all for its 2030 economic vision. And this is currently further away than ever."
Help from the Europeans?
Since early 2024, through what is known as Operation Aspides, Europe has been protecting international shipping in the Red Sea. Italy has recently said it intends to secure passage for its own merchant ships with its navy. And a few days ago France said it would send soldiers, radar systems and air defense to the Saudis in order to protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, the terminus of the East-West pipeline.
Still, these European initiatives are unlikely to bring about any sort of strategic shift in Yemen. And experts argue Europe is unwilling to accept the political and military cost of a protracted war there.
"The fact that France has now announced it will provide concrete military assistance has been received very positively in Riyadh," Schneider explained. "But still the question remains as to whether this can fundamentally alter the military balance."
The recently formed mutual defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey, known as the Mecca alliance, also has its limits. The military leaders of all three countries have consulted with one another over recent Houthis attacks but Turkey and Pakistan are also reluctant to be drawn into a conflict that would see them confronting Iran directly.
Diplomacy the way forward
All this means that diplomatic overtures will likely become more important again.
In a previous interview with DW, Abdulghani al-Iryani of the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies noted that the Houthis do actually have an interest in relations with Saudi Arabia.
"Yemen is completely economically dependent on Saudi Arabia, both as a source of humanitarian aid and as a labor market for Yemeni migrant workers," al-Iryani said.
In recent years, Saudi Arabia has tried to curb the Houthis' influence through diplomacy and by uniting divided Yemeni government forces. However the militia's current advance seems to demonstrate the limitations of this strategy.
This story was originally published in German.

Ukraine Plans Fourth Phase of Operation Vivaldi, Zelensky Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:21:52 UTC
02:21:52 KST

Ukraine is preparing the fourth phase of Operation Vivaldi, its counteroffensive in the Lyman area of the Donetsk region, which to date has significantly disrupted Russia’s military objective of seizing the entire Donbas.
The plan was discussed with Ukraine’s military personnel at the command post of the 3rd Army Corps, which is leading the operation, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a statement on Wednesday, Sept. 30.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Over the first three phases, Russia has suffered more than 5,000 casualties, while another 250 Russian soldiers have been captured.
Ukrainian forces have also retaken 176 square kilometers (68 square miles) of territory. The Atlantic Council’s analysis said that the offensive has reversed more than a year of Russian advances.
“Ukraine’s Defense Forces have thwarted Russia’s plans to break through the rear of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk” region, and the situation has been stabilized in that section of the front, Zelensky said.
Robots in place of soldiers
Zelensky also met the commanders of units directly involved in the operation, discussing their needs in detail, including artillery and financial support for troops.
He singled out ground robotic systems as a key lesson from the offensive.
“Replacing our soldiers with ground robotic systems whenever possible is a highly promising area at present,” Zelensky said, adding that “during Operation Vivaldi, this element made it possible to accomplish a great deal.”
Sybiha Meets Japanese Lawmakers in Kyiv to Discuss Further Security Cooperation
In April, Zelensky ordered Ukraine’s Defense Forces to dramatically increase the number of ground robotic systems used in service in 2026, aiming to drastically reduce the need for soldiers to be physically present in the most dangerous parts of the battlefield.
Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, adopted a law that exempts transactions for the supply of GRC from value-added tax (VAT) in May. The measure was intended to lower procurement costs for ground robots and to speed up their delivery to frontline units.
As of June 9, the Ukrainian military has already carried out more than 50,000 logistics and evacuation missions using GRCs (Ground Robotic Complexes), with the number expected to significantly grow by the end of the year, as preserving human lives remains a priority.
According to a follow up statement from Zelensky, the presidentalso met with soldiers from the 21st Kraken Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment, which is taking part in the operation.
Their discussion centered on scaling up the military’s unmanned capabilities, developing GRCs, equipping crews and the distribution of e-points – a system that rewards units for confirmed battlefield results with points they can exchange for drones and other equipment.
He also presented awards to troops from the 21st Regiment, the 125th Separate Heavy Mechanized Brigade and the 25th Separate Antitank Battalion for their role in the offensive.
“Thank you for defending Ukraine and for carrying out this highly successful operation – for your courage and heroism, and for achieving the right outcome, bringing our country closer to justice,” Zelensky said.
Why is the operation so important?
The operation’s stated goals include pushing back Russian forces, dismantling their infiltration tactics and cutting their supply lines, with its main focus centering on the Donetsk region.
In 2014, after illegally annexing Crimea, Moscow began backing separatist forces in the Donbas, who went on to seize parts of both regions, including their regional capitals. According to CNN, the conflict in the Donbas simmered for almost eight years, claiming around 14,000 lives, until Russia escalated it into a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
More than a decade later, the region remains at the center of Russia’s war aims.
While the Kremlin insists that Kyiv cede the remaining parts of partially occupied Donbas as a prerequisite for a peace deal, Ukraine rejects any arrangement that would require it to give up its territory and sovereignty.
Kyiv nonetheless calls on Moscow to agree to an unconditional ceasefire and is urging its allies to increase pressure on Russia to end the war.
Last week, 51 countries issued a joint statement backing Ukraine and calling on Russia to accept an unconditional ceasefire. The Kremlin has rejected every such proposal so far.
During the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) held in New York last week, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov – representing Russian President Vladimir Putin – said that the Kremlin will not pause its “special military operation” even during negotiations, adding that Ukraine would have kept its 1991 borders if the European nations had not “engaged in their shenanigans.”

Russian troops confiscate Ukrainian drone-delivered food in occupied Oleshky as civilians injured by mines while fleeing, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
17:21:19 UTC
02:21:19 KST

Russian troops confiscate Ukrainian drone-delivered food in occupied Oleshky as civilians injured by mines while fleeing, officials say
One person was killed and four others were injured by landmines in occupied Oleshky over the past day, while Russian forces confiscated food delivered by Ukrainian military drones and questioned residents found with non-Russian products, the local military administration head told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 30.
Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mines, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make it impossible to evacuate safely.
Tetiana Hasanenko, exiled head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, confirmed reports circulating on Telegram that four civilians were injured and one was killed by landmine explosions around Oleshky over the past day.
Hasanenko told the Kyiv Independent that four people were attempting to leave the town when they stepped on a mine and were injured, while a man collecting nuts was killed by another mine. The incidents occurred along routes used by civilians to leave the occupied town.
"These people left Oleshky at 6 a.m. and must have failed to spot something before stepping on a landmine. One woman suffered a back injury and injuries to her limbs. She was taken to the hospital on a bicycle. The others were transported in garden trolleys," Hasanenko said.
The local hospital, which is operating without basic medical supplies, electricity, or running water, is also struggling to function, Hasanenko said. Four doctors, all elderly former hospital staff, continue to work there, she said.
"But there are absolutely no medical supplies. The only thing they can do is stop the bleeding. There are no medicines," Hasanenko said.
Since Russia destroyed the nearby Kakhovka Dam in 2023, the hospital has had to rely on generators for electricity, but fuel supplies have also become increasingly difficult to obtain, according to Hasanenko.
Ukrainian forces had carried out food drops for residents several times this year, with the latest delivery totaling around four metric tons, Kherson Oblast Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said on Sept. 27.
Some Oleshky residents confirmed they found the packages in messages sent to Oleshky evacuation volunteer Kseniia Arkhipova.
At the same time, Hasanenko confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that some residents received packages while others did not. She added that Russian troops had taken some of the food delivered to residents.
According to Hasanenko, Russian forces also question residents found with products that were not manufactured in Russia, treating possession of such goods as possible evidence of cooperation with the Ukrainian military.
"They ask immediately: 'Where did you get this from?'" Hasanenko said. "And then they say: 'If the Armed Forces of Ukraine are dropping food to you, then you are cooperating with them.'"
Hasanenko also said residents continue to disappear in the occupied town after being detained by Russian forces.
"We have a family that disappeared without a trace. We don't know where they are. They were taken to a basement, and that was it. Whether they are alive or not is unknown," she said.
Kherson Oblast Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said Russian forces have attempted to disrupt the deliveries, including by shooting down the drones carrying food. The governor also accused Russian forces of confiscating or reselling humanitarian supplies and detaining residents who receive aid.
"The occupiers are detaining residents of Oleshky for receiving humanitarian aid parcels, throwing them 'into the cellar', beating them brutally and resorting to violence," Prokudin said.
The reports came amid a worsening humanitarian crisis in Oleshky. Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said that around 2,000 people, including nearly 50 children, remained in the occupied town with severely limited access to food, drinking water, electricity, and other basic services.
The U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said no food supplies had reached the occupied town between May 26 and June 24.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sept. 30 that Ukrainian intelligence had information that Russia was preparing to stage dozens of videos in occupied Oleshky, in which local residents would allegedly be forced to say they were "happy, well-fed, and grateful to Russian forces."
Sybiha said the planned videos were part of a weeks-long Russian propaganda campaign aimed at denying the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky. He called on international organizations to increase pressure on Moscow and demand immediate humanitarian access to the town.
On Sept. 25, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O'Flaherty raised concerns about the worsening humanitarian situation in Oleshky. O'Flaherty said civilians, including children, were struggling to access food, medicine, medical care, clean water, and electricity, warning that some could face a serious risk to their lives.
O'Flaherty said international humanitarian law requires occupying authorities to ensure civilians have access to food and medical supplies and to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid.

Netanyahu speaks with MBZ after Flydubai attack as Israel reassesses UAE flight security
