Automated optical inspection (AOI) equipment supplier Machvision Inc (牧德) yesterday raised its annual capacity expansion target by more than 60 percent, aiming for a production output of NT$10 billion (US$314 million) from the NT$6 billion it estimated in March, driven by a surge in demand for artificial intelligence (AI)-related applications.
In addition, the company’s new semiconductor automated inspection division is expected to see growth accelerate next year driven by the broadening market adoption of wafer-level inspection, optical transceiver systems and electrical testers, Machvision said.
Starting as a substrate AOI system supplier, the company expanded to the semiconductor inspection market three years ago.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
Machvision chairman Collin Wang (汪光夏) told an investor conference in Taipei yesterday that the company has longer and clearer order visibility this year, compared with three to four months ago.
Wang attributed the strong order outlook to continued demand for AOI tools used in graphics processing units and advanced substrates for AI servers, high-end substrates and advanced packaging technologies such as chip-on-wafer-on-substrate and fan-out panel-level packaging.
Machvision chief executive officer Jasper Chen (陳復生) said that among the company’s four major product lines, AOI tools for semiconductors and substrates would have the strongest growth momentum, with order visibility exceeding one year, and some substrate inspection orders even reaching three years.
The company expects AI-related products to contribute about 70 percent to its total revenue this year and make up 80 to 90 percent next year, Wang said.
Within two years, the company’s semiconductor AOI equipment is expected to surpass substrate inspection tools, underpinned by the vast scale of the broader semiconductor inspection market that is worth NT$30 billion a year, he said.
“We believe 2026 marks only the initial stage of this growth trajectory,” Wang said. “Next year, the growth will be more significant.”
The company’s growth momentum is expected to extend into next year after registering a sixth consecutive month of record revenue, Wang said.
The company has seen monthly revenue rise to all-time highs for 30 straight months, he said.
The company’s revenue grew about 14 percent to NT$2.63 billion during the first eight months of this year from NT$2.3 billion a year earlier.
Machvision semiconductor AOI systems falls under its parent company ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控).
While the company maintains high confidence regarding next year’s revenue outlook, it acknowledged that supply chain fluctuations pose a risk to dampening growth momentum.
To overcome this, Machvision said it has boosted its component inventory to 1.5 times of their lead time and added new suppliers.

Thieves swap drugs with flour under nose of Fiji police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:22 UTC
01:39:22 KST

Detectives were sifting leads yesterday after a massive drug heist in Fiji, searching for dozens of cocaine parcels swiped from an evidence vault and replaced with baking flour.
Better known for stunning beaches that draw tourists in droves, the South Pacific nation has become an unlikely stopover for cartels shipping drugs from Latin America into Australia.
Fiji police seized 39 bricks of cocaine in a 2019 raid, each weighing about 1kg and wrapped in plastic.
Photo: Reuters
Fiji Police Force Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu said investigators noticed seven bricks had gone missing earlier this year.
This prompted forensic testing of the remaining haul held inside an evidence vault at the High Court in the capital, Suva.
Tests showed that the cocaine once held inside the vault had been swiped under the nose of police and swapped with bundles of flour.
“Based on the discovery of the missing seven bars and the tampering of evidence, it was decided to test the remaining parcels — which tested negative for any trace of illicit drugs,” Tudravu told reporters.
Previous tests carried out after the bricks were confiscated in 2019 confirmed they held cocaine at the time, he said.
“Fiji police is taking seriously the concerns raised by the government, and I give my assurance we are tackling this investigation with utmost urgency,” Tudravu added.
Pacific islands such as Fiji and Tonga sit at the crossroads of ocean-trafficking routes used to shift cocaine from Latin America.
The so-called “Pacific drug highway” has in the past few years been flooded with synthetic methamphetamine.
This illicit cargo is increasingly spilling over into local hands, feeding drug addiction in communities where serious crime had been rare.
Intravenous methamphetamine use has fueled surging rates of HIV in Fiji, which was recently declared a national emergency.

Russian disinformation is a threat that relies on UK complicity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:21 UTC
01:39:21 KST

In November 2020, former US president Barack Obama warned of an “epistemological crisis” facing Western democracies. Polarization and radicalization were corroding trust in established information sources.
“If we do not have the capacity to distinguish what’s true from what’s false, then by definition the marketplace of ideas doesn’t work,” he said.
That vulnerability has grown since then. Democracy’s enemies have become more determined to exploit it. This is the threat that British Prime Minister Andy Burnham highlighted in a speech at the UN on Tuesday last week.
He accused Russia of waging an “industrial-scale assault” on the UK’s information environment using bot armies and fake Web sites to spread falsehoods, interfere in elections, foment discord and poison inter-community relations.
The prime minister announced the creation of a National Center for Information Defense to thwart campaigns of epistemological sabotage by hostile actors. It is an overdue enhancement of the UK’s civil defense capabilities.
Burnham is right to highlight the threat, but he told only part of the story. The Kremlin would be wasting its money pumping out disinformation if large US tech platforms did not provide convenient channels for the toxin to spread, if there were not a complicit audience in the UK sharing the offending material and if the market for spreading pernicious propaganda were not so lucrative. Information warfare is only effective when it exploits structural vulnerabilities in the target society. Far-right material sowing hatred against migrants is most fruitful where the terrain has been fertilized by domestic politics.
Earlier this year, an analysis by the Guardian found that more than half of accounts on X that were posting about racially aggravated riots in Belfast and civil disorder in Southampton were based outside the UK. Seven of the most-read tweets originated in the US, including one posted by X’s proprietor, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man.
Musk has been assiduous in promoting a warped, dystopian idea of the UK as a failed state whose culture is being corroded by mass migration. His platform has been invaluable to far-right activists who have mustered gangs of masked men into mobs that obstruct roads, intimidate people and threaten asylum claimants at British ports. Last year, Musk addressed a rally organized by far-right activist Tommy Robinson, where he called for the Labour government to be removed. Earlier this year, Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, traveled to Moscow on a trip funded by the Musk Foundation.
The purpose of the trip was to “see the beauty of a civilized society,” he said.
Burnham did not address that side of the anti-democracy equation in his speech, perhaps because he felt that it would be impolitic to impugn US big tech under the president’s nose. US President Donald Trump is also an originator and disseminator of falsehoods online, but the nature of transatlantic diplomacy prevents a British prime minister from confronting him with that record.
Under the circumstances, it made sense for Burnham to concentrate his remarks on the threat from the Kremlin, but that must not signal the limit of his policy focus. British democracy is indeed under attack from Russia, but an effective campaign to build resilience has to recognize also the complicity of domestic extremists and the digital privileges they enjoy thanks to US technology companies.
If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets. Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. They end wargames when missiles stop flying and submit policy papers after the fate of a beachhead is decided. This narrow focus ignores the grim reality of “the day after.” To address this blind spot, the Irregular Warfare Center (IWC) published a seminal study on March 5, 2026, titled China’s Way of Occupation: Implications for Taiwan. Authored by Jan K. Gleiman and others, the report analyzes Beijing’s actions in Tibet, Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and Hong Kong to expose a chilling playbook

Transportation minister bikes Cycling Route No. 2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:21 UTC
01:39:21 KST

Minister of Transportation and Communications Chen Shih-kai (陳世凱) yesterday inspected and biked part of the 1,019.4km around-the-nation Cycling Route No. 2 (環島二號線) along with other government officials.
Unlike the 960.8km Cycling Route No. 1 (環島一號線), the new route gives people the option of cycling at their own pace, Chen said.
“They can get to know Taiwan better by riding one section at a time,” he said.
Photo: Lin Chih-yi, Taipei Times
The ministry said it is scheduled to have a final inspection of the route and open it to the public by December.
The route combines bike lanes, local highways, riverside roads and old railway lines, with new road signs and guard rails, resurfaced pavement and refreshment stops marked along the way, Chen said.
The route is designed to address cyclists’ safety concerns, while allowing riders to enjoy the scenery along the way, Chen said.
The new route is comprised of 37 percent exclusive bike lanes, up from Route No. 1’s 11.2 percent, while only 12.3 percent of Route No. 2 contains sections in which cyclists and motorists must share the outer lanes, compared with 37.4 percent on Route No. 1, he said.
Because the new route contains road sections that have relatively lower traffic flow, more than 50 percent of the route is considered cyclist-friendly, he added.
Cyclists would also pass through several railway stations along Cycling Route No. 2, including Dongshan (冬山) in Yilan County, Ershuei (二水) in Changhua County, Chaojhou (潮州) in Pingtung County and Chihshang (池上) in Taitung County, the ministry said.
The stations have covered cycling lanes, bicycle repair and assembly areas, and public bike rental stations nearby, it said.
The route connects several destinations, including the North Coast, Ershuei Bikeway and the “canal greenway” built along the Chianan Irrigation Canal (嘉南大圳).
The Tourism Administration is planning to offer services to cyclists from overseas along the route, including a luggage transfer service.
Separately, the ministry is considering capping the availability of non-reserved seats on the high-speed rail system under certain conditions, Chen said, following overcrowding the day before the Mid-Autumn Festival and Teachers’ Day long weekend.
On Thursday last week, train cabins at Nangang, Taipei and Taoyuan were overflowing with a large number of passengers with non-reserved seats. Some people with reserved seats were unable to board trains.
The ministry might consider capping the availability of non-reserved seats when the first day of a long weekend coincides with peak commuter travel times, Chen said.
Chen said he has asked the Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp (THSRC) to study the issue, and determine the maximum number of non-reserved seat passengers each train can accommodate during peak travel hours, as well as find ways to ease congestion at stations and in train cabins.
The company must find ways to maximize passenger volume without compromising comfort, he said.
The Taiwan Railway Corp and freeway bus operators should also determine how many passengers they can absorb should THSRC cap the non-reserved seats available during peak hours of long weekends, he said.

The ‘Ocean Wave’ that is hitting Taipei now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:18 UTC
01:39:18 KST

In 40 years of watching politics, I have never seen anything quite like Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) breed of politician. He has a presence that commands attention, and a combination of qualities that appear to be the result of powerful political currents.
What is it that makes Shen different? Throughout the past decades of local elections, I have not seen anyone seriously discuss a long-term vision for urban planning, let alone with the kind of clarity and insight that Shen possesses that compels people to keep listening.
He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision for the city that brings complex policy ideas to life and offers real strategies for solving problems. Shen is able to frame his thinking on issues in terms of the everyday needs of citizens, putting people at the heart of the urban planning discussion and offering warmth in his approach to policy.
The contrast between Shen and incumbent Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) could not be clearer. Where Shen answers questions directly, Chiang skirts around them. Shen speaks clearly and persuasively on municipal planning, while Chiang is still looking for answers even after almost four years as mayor. Chiang has avoided policy debates with Shen entirely, trying instead to meticulously build his image through selective media appearances, but is now under the most intense level scrutiny he has faced in politics. The manufactured image is being torn away, and what remains is looking increasingly — almost painfully — insubstantial.
A person’s character is often revealed in the details. People online have shared encounters and heartwarming stories about Shen on social media, garnering a following of loyal supporters.
Taipei is a pan-blue stronghold, and for Shen to have brought the race neck-and-neck after only a few months of campaigning is no small achievement. Whether he can ultimately win hinges on three things:
First is to overcome the pan-blue camp’s mobilization of hatred. Having exhausted its usual tactics, Chiang’s team has one main remaining strategy: stoking the pan-blue camp’s sense of crisis. Where Shen seeks public consensus and support, Chiang seeks to mobilize hostility. If he is to win, Shen must find an effective way to counter these efforts.
Second is to secure the youth vote. Many young people in Taipei were once supporters of former Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) and are now swing voters. Shen possesses many of the qualities that appeal to young people; his campaign should work with university student organizations to hold policy forums and bring his ideas directly onto campuses.
Third is to persuade centrist voters. Beyond the campaign team, this requires effort from across his supporter base to mobilize, bringing undecided friends and relatives along to a Shen policy forum, or sharing videos of his addresses online. I think anyone who spends five minutes listening to and getting to know Shen would come away liking him.
Swing, centrist and younger voters could be the key to victory in this Taipei mayoral election, but the key to their support lies with active civic momentum: the tremendous energy that comes from the spread of people’s enthusiasm. Puma Shen is a new model of politician, one who is reigniting citizens’ political imaginations. He taps into what one imagines politics — from the national to the local level — should truly look like, and demonstrates exactly the kind of vision and action that politicians ought to embody.
Michelle Wang is the deputy secretary of the Northern Taiwan Society.

Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈柏洋) yesterday unveiled an ambitious campaign plan, as Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) doubled down on his drive for a “smoke-free city.”
Speaking at a news conference at his headquarters, Shen said his plan for the next few months is to stump in Taipei’s six electoral districts, roll out a platform for voters to air their opinions on the issues, and announce policies and timetables for every district.
The rallies, dubbed “‘ocean current’ street-sweeping” (洋流大車掃), would feature a drive-through and an evening stump in each electoral district to draw direct voter-candidate discussions on policies, he said.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
Shen wants to address concerns raised by Taipei residents during these events with substantive answers on the spot, he said.

The campaign is using the Line app to enable supporters to take part in the street-sweeping drive, follow its progress and use their phone cameras to access additional content on campaign posters using an augmented reality function, he said.
At campaign events, voters can scan a QR code to submit questions for Shen that would be displayed on a big screen, or talk with him on stage, he said.

Senator says that the US must honor Taiwan deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:16 UTC
01:39:16 KST

Washington’s security commitments to Taiwan must be upheld, US senator and Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman Roger Wicker said following a meeting on Tuesday with Representative to the US Alexander Yui (俞大?).
Four other senators from US President Donald Trump’s political party called on his administration last week to release more than US$14 billion in stalled national security assistance for Taiwan.
The US is Taiwan’s most important international backer and weapons supplier.
Photo: CNA
Washington is bound by the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself.
“As members of Congress, we have a duty to make sure this law is adhered to and that decisions about the defense needs of Taiwan are based on our joint assessment of military necessity,” Wicker said in a statement.
China has repeatedly called for arms sales to Taiwan to end, and in May, Trump said he was holding a package worth US$14 billion in abeyance after a trip to Beijing.
After meeting President Xi Jinping (習近平) in Washington last week, Trump said only that the Chinese leader understood his position on Taiwan.
Wicker said the US should uphold a precedent from the “six assurances” that the US would not consult Beijing on arms sales to Taiwan.
“In response — and in accordance with the Taiwan Relations Act — Congress has authorized and appropriated a surge in resources to provide Taiwan with enhanced training, security assistance and arms sales. These authorities must be used for the purposes that Congress intended,” Wicker said.
Taiwan is in continuous talks with Washington about arms sales and had received reassurances since the summit between Trump and Xi that US policy on Taiwan had not changed, Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said earlier on Tuesday.

We need civilian energy resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:13 UTC
01:39:13 KST

Taiwan’s energy security debate has been hyperfixated on fuel inventories, generation capacity and diversification of external supplies. While these measures are necessary, national endurance also depends on governance distribution and responsibility sharing. The rollout of the World Alliance for Disaster Management, in addition to this year’s Global Cooperation and Training Framework Energy Resilience Workshop and 921 Large-Scale Mobilization and Disaster Relief Exercise, proves Taiwan’s security narrative has expanded into civilian cooperation. The challenge Taiwan faces is one of sustainment through crisis and preservation through resilience, or how Taiwan can mobilize its communities, civil organizations and businesses to preserve essential services and distribute energy access during a prolonged disruption.
To harden domestic energy continuity, Taiwan must deepen its public-private partnerships and collaboration. The industrial sector has the largest share of electricity demand. Businesses are naturally inclined to blunt market volatility and operational risk by enhancing grid resilience. However, the challenge lies in mobilizing the private sector, where rules for participation remain vague and contested.
One such instance is in the case of solar panels. On Aug. 1, the Ministry of the Interior began implementing measures to deepen business sector involvement by updating its standards for installing solar panels. The amendment mandates that buildings with more than 1,000m2 of floor area install 1kW of solar energy generation capacity for every 20m2. Hurdles for success include disputes over ownership and maintenance responsibility for the installed solar systems, which only have a 10-year service life. Similar efforts have been made with the Energy Administration Act (能源管理法), where a partial amendment was passed on Aug. 21 mandating large energy consumers install self-use renewable energy generators or power storage systems. However, the amendment only applies to new or expanding facilities.
The problem lies in the lack of a clear framework that outlines specific responsibilities industry partners would have to take on for successful implementation of energy continuity. Current policies lack a comprehensive, holistic approach to infrastructure planning, one where construction costs, maintenance responsibility and updates must be clearly defined between government, businesses and property owners. If the top-down solutions are ineffective, Taiwan must restructure its business-to-government relationships. By closing the communication and trust gaps between the central government and the private sector — especially around national security priorities and business confidentiality — business-government partnerships could align more effectively and deliver on policy.
Second, mobilization of civil-based organizations is a developing but underutilized mechanism for establishment in energy-resilience planning. A common denominator presented during last month’s Urban Resilience Exercise during Han Kuang 42 and this month’s National Disaster Prevention Day Drills is the expansion of bottom-up social capital.
Taiwan has not only a strong force of emergency personnel in the police force and firefighters, but also specific interest groups — such as Taiwan’s Disaster Medical Development Association (DMAT) and the Tzu-Chi Foundation — that are becoming more and more active, largely with the rise of awareness in contingency planning.
During the Large Scale Earthquake Resilience exercise on Sept. 17, Phoebe Pham joined Cheng Ming-tai (鄭銘泰) from DMAT in Taitung County to observe evacuation management practices under disrupted conditions and how volunteer forces and local government organized emergency management procedures and joint-alternative command efforts.
The drills demonstrated that while backup technology and stand-alone communication devices are useful during power disruptions, Taiwan’s biggest challenge remains in improving its multilayered redundancy for supply distribution and logistical coordination.
This sentiment was echoed at the Resilient Taiwan for Sustainable Democracy Forum by DMAT honorary chairperson Hsiao Ya-wen (蕭雅文), a member of the Presidential Office’s Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Committee, who said that sustaining communications vis-a-vis energy distribution and human coordination in disaster management is often an underrated but critical element.
This is similar to Han Kuang 42’s incorporation of alternative planning for critical functions during last month’s Kaohsiung-Pingtung urban resilience exercise, where civilian and military personnel rehearsed support for emergency supply distribution. Bridging civil-military cooperation and building trust across all sectors of society is an emerging — and increasingly vital — factor.
For Taiwan, this year has been one of litmus testing concepts of integration for whole-of-society resilience and energy sustainability. There are several challenges that Taiwan must address in order to achieve “full integration” of civil society into energy resilience planning — and, by extension, disaster management.
First, the government needs to create a more comprehensive policy tool that could mobilize independent generators and grids, and improve the efficiency of energy procurement, especially during crises. While there is an inventory for national electricity generation, there is no mechanism for mobilizing civil sources.
Second, the central government needs to expand information-sharing protocols to foster trust and clarity between itself and civil society. Based on observations during the drills and high-level forums that took place this past month, local resilience actors are the first to respond in a disaster scenario and serve as a channel for cross-sector partnership. Plugging in community capacity by increasing threat literacy would serve as a key juncture in facilitating joint preparedness.
Third, businesses must engage incrementally via feedback on capacity, constraints and investment needs to better synergize joint preparedness. For industry to buy in with government needs, they must possess basic internal preparedness before they are able to be operationalized on demand.
Energy resilience is not just a planning problem but a participatory process. This past month has served as a useful first step in addressing how to deepen cooperation between all levels of society: government, industry and civil organizations.
Taiwan must leverage its social capital by conveying clearer, simpler rules of the game: who does what when the grid goes dark, and how trust turns local capacity into national endurance.
Phoebe Pham is a MOFA Taiwan 2026 Fellow and visiting researcher at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research in Taipei. She previously worked for RAND and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. The views expressed here do not reflect those of the US government or other affiliations. Lin Jun-rong is a policy analyst at the institute. Her work focuses on resource management and energy resilience from the perspective of non-traditional threats to industrial and economic security.

He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision

Apple Inc is set to sell about 6 million units of the iPhone Duo this year, Counterpoint Research said, offering the first estimate for how the company’s inaugural foldable device would fare.
The figure, more typical of the niche foldable segment than Apple’s usual smartphone sales, is contingent on how well the company ramps up production of the new hardware, Counterpoint senior analyst Ivan Lam (林科宇) said.
Priced at US$1,999 and set for a release this month, the iPhone Duo sits atop the Apple lineup and carries industry wide hopes for stoking greater interest and sales of foldables.
Photo: Bloomberg
Market researcher IDC Corp estimates that shipments of foldables would grow 13 percent to 22.9 million units this year with Apple’s help. Without the iPhone Duo, the segment would have seen a decline, it said.
Introduced alongside the Duo this month, Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro family has gotten off to a fast start in China, Counterpoint said. The company’s Pro edition smartphones were for the first time released without a corresponding base-model upgrade, steering consumers looking for an upgrade to the pricier models and helping deliver a 12 percent rise compared with the iPhone 17 Pro’s initial sales. That performance bucked a broad downtrend in the world’s largest smartphone market, with Chinese brands taking the brunt of a 17 percent year-on-year decline across this summer, the researchers said.
That helped Apple grab 33 percent of China’s highly competitive smartphone arena, an unusual feat when companies such as Huawei Technologies Co (華為), Oppo Mobile Telecommunications Corp (歐珀), Vivo Communication Technology Corp (維沃) and Xiaomi Corp (小米) usually have about equal shares with Apple.
However, elevated component costs are forcing all phone makers to raise prices and try to make up the shortfall of unit sales in higher revenue per unit. That works in Apple’s favor by narrowing the cost advantage of its rivals.
“Price hikes of over US$200 on many Chinese flagship models may have raised the price anchor, strengthening the iPhone’s relative value proposition,” Lam said.

EDITORIAL: Optimizing defense manufacturing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:12 UTC
01:39:12 KST

Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) Tuesday said that US policy toward Taiwan has not changed and that Taipei is in continuous talks with Washington about arms sales. He added that 66 F-16V fighter jets are being readied for delivery after production delays.
Koo’s comments come as a record US$14 billion arms package remains stalled following US-China talks, amid pressure from Beijing to halt arms sales to Taiwan. Analysts expect sales to continue, although they might face short-term delays as Washington and Beijing seek to manage tensions ahead of two planned summits later this year.
For Taiwan, the lesson should be broader.
Taiwan cannot control US production capacity, US foreign policy or the demands placed on the US military. However, it can control how much of its own defense requirements it can produce.
The nation has almost US$30 billion in approved but undelivered US arms. The backlog predates the war with Iran and reflects production constraints, supply-chain problems and long manufacturing schedules. US military operations in the Middle East have added pressure to munitions stockpiles, demonstrating another vulnerability for countries that depend on US weapons.
This is not an argument for abandoning US procurement. Taiwan needs US systems that it cannot readily reproduce, but it should also accelerate domestic research, development and production wherever doing so is feasible.
The National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology produced 2,577 missiles over the past five years, including Hsiung Feng II and III anti-ship missiles, Wan Chien air-to-ground missiles and Tien Kung air-defense missiles. Production capacity is growing.
The significance is not simply that Taiwan can design sophisticated missiles. It is that it is demonstrating an ability to manufacture them at scale.
That distinction matters in a war. A fighter jet or submarine might remain in service for years, but an interceptor or anti-ship missile can be expended in seconds. If Taiwan cannot replenish those weapons during a conflict, even a technologically advanced arsenal could eventually become depleted.
That makes Taiwan’s proposed T-Dome air-defense system an important test of its ambitions.
T-Dome is intended to combine US systems such as Patriot PAC-3 MSE and NASAMS with indigenous missiles, sensors and command systems. One of the planned components is the Strong Bow interceptor, designed to counter tactical ballistic missiles.
Strong Bow illustrates what Taiwan has achieved and what remains to be done. Developing an interceptor is one challenge. Producing sufficient quantities, maintaining the hardware and integrating it into a larger air-defense network are much bigger ones.
It does not need to reproduce the entire US defense industry. That would be unrealistic. Instead, it should prioritize capabilities that would be consumed rapidly in a conflict and would be particularly difficult to replenish if foreign deliveries were interrupted.
That means missiles and defensive interceptors, but also drones, counter-drone systems, artillery rounds and other ordnance. It means developing domestic supply chains for the components required to keep those weapons in production. And it means ensuring that factories and production capacity are sufficiently dispersed and resilient to survive a war.
Taiwan’s indigenous submarine program offers another example. The Hai Kun (Narwhal, 海鯤) has progressed to sea trials, demonstrating that Taiwan can undertake highly complex defense projects domestically. However, the program has shown how difficult and time-consuming it can be to develop a new industrial capability from the ground up.
Ten years is both a long and a short time.
It is long enough for Taiwan to substantially expand missile production, stockpiles and domestic supply chains, but it might be surprisingly short if the goal is to create an industrial base capable of sustaining production during a major war.
Nor can Taiwan assume that domestic production would guarantee readiness if China attacked before those capabilities matured. Factories, supply chains and production facilities would be vulnerable to attack, while critical components could still depend on foreign suppliers.
The objective should be to reach a point where an interruption in US deliveries creates a serious problem for Taiwan, but does not leave critical parts of its defense dependent on a supply line it cannot control.
Taiwan has already demonstrated that it can develop sophisticated missiles and other advanced weapons. The more urgent question is whether it can produce enough of them, quickly enough, and maintain the industrial capacity to replace them during a conflict.
That is a question Taiwan has a limited amount of time to answer.
If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets. Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. They end wargames when missiles stop flying and submit policy papers after the fate of a beachhead is decided. This narrow focus ignores the grim reality of “the day after.” To address this blind spot, the Irregular Warfare Center (IWC) published a seminal study on March 5, 2026, titled China’s Way of Occupation: Implications for Taiwan. Authored by Jan K. Gleiman and others, the report analyzes Beijing’s actions in Tibet, Xinjiang (East Turkestan), and Hong Kong to expose a chilling playbook

He said he would refuse to serve as a judge for any literary award that does not explicitly prohibit the use of AI in creative writing. The use of AI in creative and academic work has become increasingly common. My son, who attends National Chengchi University, says he is exasperated after working to complete assignments on his own, only to receive lower grades than classmates who used

Beneath that, however, it was an encounter between two distinct Taiwanese experiences, two generations and two different political vocabularies. Wang grew up in a military dependents’ village. His parents came to Taiwan with the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) government, carrying with them the legacy of war, displacement, the loss of a homeland, and an identification with Chinese culture

This year’s Pride, themed “Our Voices, Our Journey,” is to be held on Oct. 31, the parade organizer said yesterday. This year’s Pride would emphasize that by listening to others’ stories, people can overcome prejudices and misunderstandings, and move forward together. Protecting democracy and freedom means safeguarding an environment in which different voices can be heard, which is essential to protecting gender equality, it said. The association called on voters who care about equality to vote for candidates who support diverse communities and gender equality. It also partnered with 20 organizations to make a Pride Month calendar promoting LGBTQ-related events, ensuring that LGBTQ+ advocacy extends beyond just the parade and into everyday life.

Heat to top 36°C
The Central Weather Administration (CWA) yesterday issued a heat warning for Taipei, New Taipei City, Taoyuan, Yunlin County, Tainan and Pingtung County, where temperatures reached more than 36°C. Independent meteorologist Wu Der-rong (吳德榮) said a high-pressure system kept the weather sunny and stable yesterday. The weather would be mostly sunny to partly cloudy today, with afternoon showers isolated to mountainous regions. Moisture would increase from tomorrow to Sunday, bringing brief localized showers to northern and eastern Taiwan as well as mountainous areas, he said. While daytime conditions in central and southern regions would remain hot, overall temperatures would drop slightly, accompanied by cooler mornings and evenings. On Monday next week, a strengthening northeast monsoon would bring a noticeable temperature drop and distinctly cooler weather to northern Taiwan.

Wage increase garners mixed reactions: survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:11 UTC
01:39:11 KST

Taiwan’s latest minimum wage increase has drawn mixed reactions from employers and workers, with nearly three in 10 companies saying they might scale back hiring while almost half are considering raising prices to offset higher labor costs, a survey released yesterday by online job bank yes123 showed.
The minimum wage is set to rise for an 11th consecutive year next year, pushing the hourly rate above NT$200 and the monthly minimum above NT$30,000.
About 75.2 percent of employers surveyed said that they plan to raise average starting salaries for their job openings in response to the increase. However, only 33.8 percent of workers expect their own pay to rise, underscoring a gap between companies’ plans to adjust entry-level wages and employees’ expectations of broader pay gains, the survey showed.
Photo: CNA.
The increase could also affect hiring decisions, as 29.6 percent of employers said that the higher minimum wage would make them less willing to hire, while 63.6 percent of workers said it would encourage them to take on part-time jobs to supplement their income, the survey found.
At the same time, 61.7 percent of workers expect employers to reduce their reliance on hourly workers and instead increase the workload of full-time employees, potentially adding pressure on existing staff, it indicated.
Businesses are also weighing higher prices, as 46.6 percent said they are considering raising prices for products or services next year to offset higher labor costs, the survey showed.
That prospect is raising concerns among workers, with 88 percent saying that they worry the wage increase would also drive up consumer prices, it found.
Yes123 spokesman Bingo Yang (楊宗斌) said the higher minimum wage is intended to support lower-paid and economically vulnerable workers, who are also among those most exposed to rising living costs.
The increase in the hourly wage could particularly benefit women returning to the workforce, older workers and students who rely on part-time jobs, Yang said.
The monthly increase is likely to directly benefit foreign and dispatch workers, while higher starting salaries for new graduates could also put pressure on employers to raise pay for existing workers, he said.
However, higher labor costs could also prompt companies to pass costs on to consumers, reduce hiring, accelerate automation or, in some cases, close outlets or businesses, Yang said.
Cutting the use of hourly workers while increasing workloads for full-time employees could also increase the risk of burnout and staff turnover, he said.
For service businesses and small companies that rely heavily on part-time labor, the risk of higher prices could be particularly significant. If businesses pass higher labor costs on to customers through more expensive meals and other services, some of the wage gains could ultimately be eroded, Yang said.
The broader economic impact would therefore depend on whether wage gains outpace price increases. If workers’ pay rises faster than consumer prices, their purchasing power would increase, potentially supporting domestic consumption and creating a positive cycle for the economy, the job bank said.

Ministry updates pension waivers and NHI coverage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:07 UTC
01:39:07 KST

The Ministry of Health and Welfare yesterday announced a series of new policy measures taking effect today, including raising the threshold for waiving interest charges on overdue National Pension Insurance payables and expanding National Health Insurance (NHI) coverage for several medications.
Interest charges would be waived if the total interest payable for the month is less than NT$100 (US$3.14), up from NT$30, which is expected to benefit more than 100,000 citizens each year, the ministry said.
Meanwhile, the National Health Insurance (NHI) is this month expanding coverage for several major medications for rare diseases, cardiovascular conditions, blood disorders and cancers.
Photo: Taipei Times file
Aspaveli/Empaveli would be covered for people with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria who respond poorly to C5 complement inhibitors.
Clinical trials showed the medicine improved hemoglobin levels and reduced reliance on blood transfusions, the NHI Administration said (NHIA), adding that about 12 to 16 people would benefit annually from the policy change.
The anticoagulant rivaroxaban (such as Xarelto) would also be covered for people with symptomatic peripheral artery disease or coronary artery disease who face a high risk of ischemic events.
There would be significant additions to cancer care medication coverage, such as Pembrolizumab (Keytruda) for metastatic or recurrent unresectable head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, as well as Yescarta — a CAR-T cell therapy — for people with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or high-grade B-cell lymphoma.
A clinical evaluation is needed to verify qualification for Yescarta coverage, the single-treatment cost of which is about NT$8.19 million, the NHIA said.
The medication is used by about 36 to 88 people per year, it added.
Poteligeo (mogamulizumab 4 mg/mL) would be covered for people with rare conditions such as mycosis fungoides or Sezary syndrome and have undergone at least one systemic therapy, regardless of their CD30 expression levels.
The eligibility threshold for Galafold (migalastat hydrochloride) for people with Fabry disease would also be lowered from 16 years old to 12 for those with amenable mutations, offering them with an oral treatment option, the NHIA said.
People battling lung and esophageal cancers would gain expanded access to Tevimbra (tislelizumab).
The therapy covers late-stage or metastatic esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, as well as first, second and third-line non-small cell lung cancer, benefiting 726 to 1,108 people annually, it added.

White House Taps Miller to Lead US Space Command
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:05 UTC
01:39:05 KST

The White House has nominated Lt. Gen. David N. Miller Jr. to lead U.S. Space Command, succeeding Gen. Stephen Whiting, who is expected to retire by January 2027.
A notice of Miller’s nomination for promotion to general appeared in the Congressional Record on Sept. 29, but the notice did not include an assignment. U.S. Space Command and the Space Force both confirmed Sept. 30 that Miller has been tapped for the SPACECOM commander job.
“Congratulations to Lt. Gen. Miller on his nomination to serve as Commander, U.S. Space Command,” Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said in a statement. “He is an exceptional Guardian who has represented our service with distinction, and we believe he is a strong candidate for this critical joint leadership role.”
Miller, currently the Space Force’s deputy chief of space operations for strategy, plans, programs, and requirements, is a career space operator. He served as commander of Combat Forces Command—then Space Operations Command—from 2024 to 2025, and was director of operations, training, and force development at U.S. Space Command before that. Earlier in his career, he was chief of the Space Control Division within Air Force headquarters, led weapons and tactics development for the 21st Operations Group, and was an intercontinental ballistic missile operator and instructor.
His nomination would make him SPACEOM’s fourth leader since the command was reestablished in 2019, and its third to hail from the Space Force. Charles Galbreath, director of the Mitchell Institute’s Spacepower Advantage Center of Excellence praised Miller as a “straightforward leader” and said he’s glad to see another Guardian in the top SPACECOM job.
“The unique relationship between the space-focused service and combatant command is undeniable,” Galbreath said. “I look forward to seeing that partnership continue to mature under the leadership of Gens. Schiess and Miller.”
If confirmed, Miller would take the reins of the command as the U.S. military’s reliance on space capabilities both in peacetime and in combat takes center stage—and as leaders increasingly emphasize the role of offensive operations in the domain.
Top Pentagon officials have said military space assets and SPACECOM forces played a key role in operations against Iran, providing electronic warfare, navigation, missile warning, and communications capabilities. Speaking at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Sept. 14, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed that the Space Force has “space control weapons”—the Defense Department’s most direct acknowledgement to date that the U.S. operates offensive systems in orbit.
Miller will also oversee construction of SPACECOM’s first purpose-built headquarters at Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Ala., and the accompanying relocation of personnel and operations from Peterson Space Force Base, Colo. The new facility is in the midst of a phased transition slated to conclude in 2031.
Whiting, the current SPACECOM commander, has been at the helm since January 2024. During his tenure, he has been a vocal proponent of better space domain awareness capabilities, a stronger space “kill chain,” and more dynamic, maneuverable satellites. In a recent speech at the AMOS Conference in Maui, Hawaii, he advocated for improved space-based target tracking and detection capabilities, which he said are foundational to the military’s ability to effectively perform space control operations.
“To be able to negate threats in space, we must be able to find, fix, track, and target those threats,” Whiting said Sept. 16. “Targeting in the space domain is maturing, but it still has a long way to go.”

Court lifts limits on US’ third-country deportations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:04 UTC
01:39:04 KST

The US Supreme Court on Tuesday lifted restrictions on the deportations of immigrants to countries that are not their own, while agreeing to hear the issue on its merits in December.
The conservative-dominated high court granted an emergency request by US President Donald Trump’s administration to suspend a lower court ruling that restricted, but did not outright ban, so-called “third-country removals.”
The lower court had said people targeted with deportation must be given effective notice ahead of time about where they are being sent to allow them to raise concerns about potential persecution.
Photo: Reuters
The three liberal justices on the nine-member bench said they would not have granted the administration’s request.
Trump campaigned on promises to expel millions of undocumented migrants from the US and has taken several actions aimed at speeding up deportations since returning to the White House last year.
The Trump administration has defended third-country deportations as necessary since the home nations of some of those who are targeted for removal sometimes refuse to accept them.
In a brief to the Supreme Court, opponents of lifting the restrictions argued that the lower court ruling did not fully block all third-country deportations, “it simply requires them to do so lawfully.”
Meanwhile, US Solicitor General John Sauer told the court that the rapid deportation to third countries was “an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens.”
The lower court ruling “created substantial logistical problems” with removals, he said.
The US has offered multimillion-dollar deals and threatened visa restrictions to get “third countries,” especially in Africa, to take such deportees, an Agence France-Presse investigation found.
Once in these countries — and outside US jurisdiction — deportees have been subject to abuse by local guards, indefinite detention, or quickly re-deported to their home countries.
The US has deported more than 25,000 people under secretive agreements with 35 countries to take migrants with no ties to those nations, an investigation published last week showed.

Trump touts AI boss pledge to self-regulate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:01 UTC
01:39:01 KST

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the tech executives gathered at the White House to discuss regulating artificial intelligence (AI) had signed a “morally binding” commitment to build adequate safeguards on the fast-moving technology.
“They’re going to police themselves,” Trump said after the meeting that gathered the top leaders in AI, including Nvidia Corp’s Jensen Huang (黃仁勳), OpenAI’s Greg Brockman and Anthropic PBC’s Dario Amodei.
Trump said the tech bosses had signed a deal that would put on paper their commitment to self-regulate in a morally binding agreement that would not be legally enforceable.
Photo: AFP
However, the final document, dubbed the White House Accord, left the door open “to codify these steps into laws or regulations” if it made sense over time.
Speaking to reporters outside the Oval Office surrounded by the world’s tech titans, Trump also confirmed he would officially rename the technology “super intelligence” instead of artificial intelligence, “because it’s not artificial.”
Hours later he released an executive order in which he says the terms “super intelligence” and “SI” shall be used by the federal government whenever possible, because “’Super Intelligence’ more appropriately captures the promise, potential and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies.”
Meta Platforms Inc boss Mark Zuckerberg said the White House accord aims to assure customers that AI technology “works in the way that we intend.”
The commitment includes “robust internal controls” and multiple layers of auditing — from internal risk reviews to external auditors and oversight from the companies’ boards of directors, he said.
Zuckerberg called it a starting point for industry wide standards.
Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, said the executives essentially agreed to “grading each other’s homework, which is a lot better than if people just grade their own homework for obvious reasons.”
The lunch meeting also included Amazon.com Inc founder Jeff Bezos, Satya Nadella of Microsoft Corp and Sundar Pichai of Google.
Of the 31 guests, two were women: Susie Wiles, Trump’s chief of staff, and Advanced Micro Devices Inc chief executive Lisa Su (蘇姿丰).
The gathering occurred as attitudes toward AI sour in Washington, with lawmakers increasingly under pressure from voters to curb or slow its development over fears it could displace workers and upend society.
Trump, advised by Huang and his former AI czar David Sacks, has urged unfettered AI development to outpace China and fuel a US economy increasingly dependent on AI-driven growth.
The issue of data centers, the vast computing facilities the technology requires, has emerged as a flashpoint in midterm election races in both parties, with more and more communities worried about rising electricity bills and strains on water and land.
Trump has dismissed opponents of these data centers and after the meeting insisted that AI companies “will be very generous” with communities who open their doors to them.
“They’ll help with their schools, they’ll help with their teachers,” he said.

Military draft regulations to be changed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:39:00 UTC
01:39:00 KST

Defense officials yesterday announced new physical eligibility standards for conscription and a military exercise next month that would include new tanks, drones and command-and-control systems.
Tsai Shih-hung (蔡適鴻), director of the Ministry of National Defense Medical Affairs Bureau’s Department of Health Service and Medical Care, told a news conference at the ministry in Taipei that the height and weight requirements for military draft would be adjusted.
The changes were finalized following the end of the policy’s public comment period on Monday last week, he said.
Photo: Fan Wei-li, Taipei Times
The new rules stipulate that people shorter than 1.44m or those with a body mass index (BMI) higher than 45 would be exempted from mandatory military service, as part of extensive changes to the regulations governing physical requirements of active service troops, he said.
The amendments would result in fewer exemptions, as current regulations grant the status to people who are shorter than 1.45m, taller than 1.96m, or whose BMI is under 15 or over 35.
The preview of the regulations for the public comment period showed that officials plan to change 160 out of the 176 rules governing exemptions and medical discharges from active military service.
The rules would simplify the standards for exempting or discharging troops with cancer and gout.
Malignant tumors would lead to a blanket exemption or discharge after the diagnosis has been confirmed with no additional conditions, and people who experience gout-related joint inflammation, joint damage or tophus would be discharged.
Blood pressure standards would remain, but the verification and documentation process is adjusted to prevent draft dodging.
The new rules stipulate that blood pressure must be measured multiple times during one to three uninterrupted days of hospital stay, instead of over 24 hours.
People who have had pulmonary tuberculosis would be medically discharged only if they also showed moderate or severe impairments to lung function,
Separately, Major General Lin Shih-wei (林士偉) told a news conference that the second edition of the national brigade-level drills would pit the 269th Combined Arms Brigade against the 564th Combined Arms Brigade from Oct. 14 to 23.
The event, named “Lu Sheng 2” (陸勝2號), would serve as a certification test for the army’s recently acquired M1A2T Abrams main battle tanks, Taiwan Tactical Network, Eutelsat OneWeb satellite telecommunications and uncrewed aerial vehicles, he said.
The units would engage in simulated combat from the first day of the exercise through its conclusion with no scripted maneuvers or predetermined outcomes, Lin said.
The drills are centered on brigade and battalion-level command and control, fire support coordination, delaying actions, joint air-land operations, and the use of drones and special operations forces, he said.
The army increased Lu Sheng 2’s duration to 10 days from seven days to exercise the troops’ ability to conduct sustained operations without pause, Tsai said.
The exercise area is relocated to Taiwan proper’s strategically important northern region to familiarize units with key terrain features for defensive and offensive operations, he added.
The Army Corps-level headquarters would form commands tasked with coordinating and conducting joint operations, and the reserve commands would liaise between the military and local governments, Lin said.
The exercise should function as an end-of-the-year test for combat preparedness and tactical proficiency for army brigades, he said.

16:38:59 UTC
01:38:59 KST

The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) yesterday criticized the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus’ decision to list a proposed amendment allowing national referendums to overturn Constitutional Court judgments as priority legislation saying it would introduce chaos and undermine the entire democratic system.
The proposal stems partly from a dispute over amendments to the Constitutional Court Procedure Act (憲法訴訟法) passed by the Legislative Yuan in December 2024.
The amendments, proposed in January last year, required at least 10 Constitutional Court justices to participate in deliberations and at least nine to agree before the court could declare a law unconstitutional. With only eight justices then in office, the changes would have prevented the court from hearing constitutional cases.
Photo: Wang Yi-song, Taipei Times
However, the Constitutional Court on Dec. 19 last year ruled that the amendments were unconstitutional and violated the constitutional principle of separation of powers, ordering the provision to be repealed immediately.
The KMT’s amendment to the Referendum Act (公民投票法) would allow referendums to target Constitutional Court judgements except those concerning the impeachment of the president or vice president.
Under the proposal, a law, local ordinance or Constitutional Court judgement rejected by voters in a referendum would be nullified three days after the result was announced. A law declared unconstitutional because of the rejected law would be restored.
The proposal would require the president or appropriate government agency to implement an approved referendum within three months, while executive agencies would be barred from reversing a major policy approved or rejected by referendum for three years.
The KMT has argued that voters should be able to challenge Constitutional Court judgements they consider unacceptable or unlawful, saying such judgements do not have the same legal status as the Constitution itself.
It cited past cases in which Constitutional Court justices changed previous interpretations, arguing that the court’s judgements should not be beyond challenge. As constitutional amendments proposed by the Legislative Yuan must themselves be approved by voters, Constitutional Court judgments should likewise be subject to referendums, the KMT said.
DPP caucus deputy chief executive Chen Pei-yu (陳培瑜) said on Facebook that the proposal was another attempt to expand legislative power and place the legislature above the judiciary and executive branches.
Chen cited former Constitutional Court justice Huang Hung-hsia (黃虹霞), who said the referendum system allows voters to approve or reject laws, establish legislative principles or decide major public policies, but does not extend to judicial decisions.
Unless the Constitution is amended, no government institution or person, including the president, has the authority to declare a Constitutional Court judgement invalid, Huang said.
The Legislative Yuan cannot amend the Referendum Act to empower voters to overturn or invalidate a Constitutional Court judgment through a referendum, she said.
Chen said the KMT’s decision to list the proposals as priority legislation showed that it was trying to expand legislative power while undermining the authority of the judiciary and the executive branch.

New Taipei detains man for breaching protection order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:38:57 UTC
01:38:57 KST

The New Taipei District Court yesterday ordered a man to be detained incommunicado for allegedly breaching a protection order after his daughter was seen in New Taipei City’s Sanchong District (三重) wearing a sign with vulgar wording.
Prosecutors requested that the man be detained, as he was suspected of assault, coercion, endangering a juvenile’s development and breaching a protection order, the New Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office said in a statement on Tuesday.
The evidence raised concerns that the man could commit similar offenses or collude with witnesses, the office said.
Photo: CNA
The office did not specify what the man allegedly did, how his daughter came to be wearing the sign or what restrictions were in the protection order against him.
The case came to light on Monday after someone posted on Threads that a girl had been seen wearing a paper sign bearing her name and vulgar words including “thief” and “bastard” (畜生).
The girl appeared dazed and had injuries on her face and arms, and two people, believed to be family members, were seen urging her toward more crowded areas while recording the incident on their phones, the post said.
Police found that the girl’s father might have breached a protection order against him and arrested him, Ministry of Health and Welfare official Huang Jui-wen (黃瑞雯) said on Tuesday.
The girl was placed in protective care following the incident, Huang said.
The New Taipei City Social Welfare Department had already opened a case involving the girl and would take appropriate measures in response to the incident, Department of Protective Services Director-General Kuo Tsai-jung (郭彩榕) said.
The city’s Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault Prevention Center had also applied for a protection order for the girl, Kuo added.
Asked why the girl had not been placed in protective care earlier, despite the existence of a protection order, Kuo said that such orders can contain provisions that would have still allowed the father and daughter to live together.
She did not specify what was in the protection order.
Breaching a protection order is a criminal offense that requires police intervention, Kuo said.
It carries a prison sentence of up to three years, Kuo added.

US-led coalition ends mission in Iraq years after IS defeated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:38:56 UTC
01:38:56 KST

After more than a decade, the US-led coalition yesterday ended its mission in Iraq, having helped save the country from the Islamic State (IS) while causing persistent friction.
Coalition troops deployed to Iraq and Syria in 2014 to fight the IS, which had seized large swathes of both countries, and committed massacres and atrocities.
The group was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle the group’s remnants.
Photo: AFP
Baghdad and Washington agreed in 2024 to wind down the coalition’s mission, and its troops withdrew gradually from bases across the country, restricting their presence to the autonomous northern Kurdistan region. Their final withdrawal from there was yesterday.
The Iraqi government believes the coalition’s withdrawal removes the excuse powerful Tehran-backed militant factions have used to retain their weapons.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi declared that Oct. 1, the day following the coalition’s departure, should be celebrated as Sovereignty Day.
It is “a national occasion that affirms the completion of Iraq’s path toward sovereignty and consolidates the presence of the state and its institutions,” the heads of the executive, legislative and judicial branches said on Monday.
They added that “the presence of weapons outside state authority must be addressed ... in line with timelines set by the government, in a manner that strengthens state sovereignty.”
Al-Zaidi, who came to power this year with the US’ blessing, has vowed to reinforce the state’s monopoly on arms and ensure that armed factions hand over their weapons to the state.
His government initially set yesterday as the deadline for factions to disarm, but later withdrew the time limit as talks continued to “regulate” weapons — an issue that has fueled tensions and is expected to take much longer to resolve.
With several powerful groups refusing to disarm, senior politicians have intervened and are now hoping to work out a compromise deal.
Factions have put forward conditions that include not only the withdrawal of foreign troops, but also an end to US political and economic interference.
The powerful Kataeb Hezbollah group said in a statement on Monday that the withdrawal of “the occupation forces ... is a start towards achieving full sovereignty.”
However, the group also threatened al-Zaidi’s government.
“A government that doesn’t work for the good of its people will be brought down by all possible means,” it said.
During the battle against the IS, the US-led coalition and Tehran-backed factions fought the militants, their common enemy.
However, after the IS’ defeat, the presence of the coalition turned into a persistent point of contention between Iraqi authorities and the factions.
Those groups demanded the withdrawal of US troops and began targeting them with drones and missiles, triggering US retaliatory strikes that killed several faction commanders over the years.
During the Middle East regional war, Iran and its allied factions intensified their attacks, targeting US-led troops in the Kurdistan region.
Kurds in Erbil, capital of the Kurdistan region, said they are increasingly anxious about who will protect them from drones that have repeatedly targeted their autonomous canton, once the coalition interceptors leave.
The coalition left Syria earlier this year.

Fernando Tatis Jr on Tuesday night hit the first leadoff homer in Padres playoff history on the Cubs’ first pitch, Michael King took a no-hitter into the seventh inning and San Diego rolled to an 8-0 victory over Chicago in their National League Wild Card Series opener.
Manny Machado also homered in the first inning and added an RBI double in the third during an emphatic opening statement by the 91-win Padres. Xander Bogaerts also homered off Cubs starter Matthew Boyd and Jackson Merrill added a two-run single later.
San Diego provided more than enough support for King, who struck out eight over seven stellar innings while throttling the majors’ highest-scoring team. King set the tone by striking out probable National League Most Valuable Player Pete Crow-Armstrong with the first three pitches.
Photo: AP
“It gives me confidence knowing the team has confidence in me to pitch in these games,” King said. “But then when you have our superstars showing out like that in the bottom of the first, it makes it a lot easier.”
Nico Hoerner got the Cubs’ only hit off King with a one-out infield single in the seventh, but King racked up two more strikeouts to earn the last of several standing ovations from the raucous sellout crowd watching his third career playoff start.
“The crowd was awesome,” Chicago manager Craig Counsell said. “They had a lot to cheer about tonight, and we didn’t give them anything to be quiet about.”
The series winner faces the MLB-best Milwaukee Brewers in the best-of-five division series.
In New York, Cam Schlittler pitched another playoff gem against the Red Sox, while Ben Rice also burned their hometown team with a late grand slam and six RBIs as the Yankees opened their American League Wild Card Series rematch by romping to a 9-0 victory.
With the Yankees minus star slugger Aaron Judge because of a calf injury, Rice homered twice, doubled and had four hits to power the offense. Schlittler, a clear frontrunner for the American League Cy Young Award, struck out 10 in a dominant performance reminiscent of the one that ended Boston’s season last year.
Rice and Schlittler were both raised among Red Sox fans in Massachusetts and went to college in New England before getting plucked by the Yankees out of Boston’s backyard in baseball’s amateur draft.
“Pretty remarkable,” New York manager Aaron Boone said. “Obviously that’s been a storyline for a couple of years now. For them to go out and have that kind of night together to start this post-season, pretty amazing and kind of hard to grasp a little bit, frankly, but I’m certainly glad we have those two.”
Earlier in the other American League Wild Card matchup, Colson Montgomery hit a solo homer and Sam Antonacci drove in two runs to lead the visiting Chicago White Sox over the Houston Astros 6-3.
The White Sox, in the post-season for the first time since 2021, made a remarkable turnaround this year to become the only team in major league history to follow consecutive 100-loss seasons with a playoff berth. They had lost 100 games three straight seasons, including 121 defeats in 2024, setting the record for most losses since 1899.
“We came here to win the series and the first part of that is getting this first win, which is great,” manager Will Venable said.
In Atlanta, Austin Riley hit a three-run homer off All-Star closer Jhoan Duran in the eighth inning as the Braves rallied past the Philadelphia Phillies 5-3 in the opener of their best-of-three National League Wild Card Series.

A shark stranded in a canal in the South Korean port of Busan has become the country’s latest wildlife sensation, with the city saying about 600,000 people have flocked to see it over the past two weeks.
The 3.5m shark was first spotted in a narrow waterway in North Port on Sept. 18.
As the days passed without the shark finding its way back to the ocean, authorities on Tuesday launched a rescue operation to guide it out, but the effort failed.
Photo: Yonhap via AP
The South Korean Coast Guard and other agencies deployed vessels to spray jets of water behind the shark to gently propel it toward the open ocean, but it swam away from the streams, videos published by Yonhap News Television showed.
Officials plan to use a net to try to guide the shark out of the canal tomorrow, the Chosun Daily reported.
The shark, reported to be a bronze whaler, has become something of a celebrity in South Korea and has been dubbed “Bukangi,” a nickname derived from “Buk Hang,” the Korean name for Busan’s north port, and the Korean suffix “-i”.
During the four-day Chuseok holiday last weekend, about 480,000 people visited the waterfront park where the shark was stranded, compared with the park’s usual daily average of about 2,000 visitors on weekends, according to a Busan city statement and media reports.
On Tuesday, Busan declared the shark an honorary public relations ambassador for the city after a poll on the city’s official Instagram account received 91 percent approval from about 8,000 participants.
Other animal escapades have gripped South Korea in the past.
Earlier this year, a wolf that escaped from its enclosure at a South Korean zoo spawned a cryptocurrency meme coin and even prompted a message of concern from the country’s president.

The Thai Meteorological Department warned that the heavy rain would continue in most parts of the country through today, citing a strong low-pressure system over the central region and strengthening southwest monsoon conditions. In Nepal, teachers mourn students who never returned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:38:53 UTC
01:38:53 KST

Each morning at a school in flood-ravaged Nepal, teachers taking attendance are served a painful reminder of the disaster as they mark in red the names of students who never came back.
The catastrophic flood, triggered by a glacial collapse near the China-Nepal border, on Aug. 26 killed more than 1,400 people, the majority in Nepal.
More than 5,000 remain missing in the Himalayan nation one month after the tsunami-like waves swept away roads, bridges and settlements in the mountainous regions up north.
Photo: AFP
At the Neelakantha Secondary School in hard-hit Rasuwa, a teacher marked red circles beside the names of children missing since the flood.
Unlike more than a dozen schools destroyed by the floods, the Neelakantha school, sitting on relatively higher ground, remained largely intact.
However, it lost 70 of its students and four teachers.
“If you look at Rasuwa, you can’t find a family that has not lost a family member,” principal Madhav Lamichhane said. “All the students and teachers are going through the same pain.”
Most of the missing Neelakantha pupils were on their way to the school from riverside settlements when floodwaters tore through the valley.
“We have been remembering our students with every breath,” said Rama Paudel, a 36-year-old teacher. “They have lost their lives in this disaster at such a young age. It’s a great loss.”
Across Rasuwa and neighboring districts, about 500 students and 24 teachers remain missing, while 18 schools have been damaged, with recovery costs estimated at up to US$15.47 million, Nepalese government data showed.
“This is the worst situation ever the education sector has experienced,” Nepalese Ministry of Education and Sports spokesman Shree Prasad Bhattarai said.
Initial assessments by UNICEF show learning has been disrupted for more than 14,000 children at 62 schools and learning centers across the flood-affected region.
“Education is a critical part of children’s recovery after a disaster,” UNICEF representative Alice Akunga said last week. “Returning to learning provides children with a sense of stability, routine and hope at a time when many have experienced significant loss and uncertainty.”
However, for many families, sending children back to school was not yet possible.
Fewer than half of Neelakantha Secondary School’s 508 students have resumed classes since lessons restarted two weeks ago.
Lamichhane said about 150 students were still unable to reach the school, because bridges and roads had been swept away.
Some classrooms have been repurposed as relief distribution centers, underscoring the challenges of restoring normalcy.
Teachers say psychological scars might prove even harder to overcome than damaged infrastructure.
“We have many students who do not have their parents or have seen their friends being swept away,” teacher Shiva Ram Bhatta said. “It has been a month now, but it is difficult for them to focus.”
Relief supplies are reaching many survivors, he said, but the next phase of recovery would require much more than food and shelter.
“We have enough relief materials,” he said. “Now we need psychosocial therapy and a permanent way out so that they can feel normal again.”

Man City found guilty of serious financial breaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:38:52 UTC
01:38:52 KST

Manchester City face severe sanctions after being found guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules over a nine-season period, the league said on Tuesday.
Abu Dhabi-backed City were found to have arranged “sham” contracts with a number of commercial partners to artificially inflate the club’s revenues and reduce costs by more than ￡900 million (US$1.2 billion) between 2009 and 2018.
In doing so they concealed the true state of their finances and avoided breaches of Premier League and UEFA spending limits as a result.
Photo: AP
An independent commission also found the club guilty on the majority of charges in relation to their failure to co-operate with the league’s investigation.
No sanction has yet been imposed and City said they would appeal the decision.
However, the ruling would send shock waves through English soccer, with City’s place in the Premier League at risk and questions over whether titles could be stripped.
“The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade,” Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in a statement. “This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history.”
The commission found City arranged commercial deals whereby companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The remainder was funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan’s Abu Dhabi United Group Investment and Development, which owned the club.
Further arrangements, funded by the group, enabled the club to record lower operating expenses than they actually incurred.
As a result, City failed to accurately report income and expenditure for the purposes of the Premier League and UEFA’s financial sustainability rules.
The scheme was found to have inflated revenue by more than ￡830 million, while income from image rights was overstated by almost ￡74 million, with liabilities for staff contracts understated by nearly ￡17 million.
The commission found they would have breached spending limits “by a very substantial amount” if City had reported accurately.
In addition, City were found to have “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League” during a four-year investigation.
The commission found that evidence given by several important factual witnesses on behalf of City was “false in a number of key respects.”
It added that “certain of those factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest.”
“It’s incredibly serious, the Premier League report is incredibly stark,” British Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Lisa Nandy said.
Since a 2008 takeover from Sheikh Mansour, vice president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, City have become the Premier League’s dominant force.
They have won eight Premier League titles, four FA Cups and seven League Cups over the past 15 years and also won the Champions League for the first time in 2023.
That same year they were hit by the Premier League with more than 100 charges following an investigation into alleged breaches of rules.
“If the appeal fails, Manchester City cannot stay in the league, they have to suffer, and I say that as a supporter and a fan,” former City chairman David Bernstein said.

Chen made the remarks at the 100 Outstanding Young Farmers ceremony.
The ministry is drafting a budget and plan to give young farmers parental-leave benefits similar to those available to other workers, Chen said.
Photo: CNA
Taiwan’s agricultural workforce is changing, while the declining birthrate is expected to further reduce the pool of agricultural workers, he said.
Farming should be a dignified profession, and farmers should have access to welfare benefits comparable with those in other sectors, Chen said.
Most farmers do not have conventional employers and therefore cannot use the labor system’s unpaid parental-leave scheme, he said, adding that the ministry would develop a separate system for farmers.
Details such as the length of leave, subsidy amounts and payment methods are still being worked out, Chen said.
The ministry might use the minimum wage as the basis for calculating the subsidy, and be flexible over the length of leave and payment period, he said.
The scheme would require government funding, and the ministry would seek resources, Chen said.
The ministry yesterday honored 106 young farmers as agricultural role models. They have an average age of 34, while 27, or 25.5 percent, are female.
The awardees work in crop production, fisheries, livestock farming, beekeeping and specialty crops. Of the 98 winning entries, 68 were in crop production, eight in fisheries, 12 in livestock farming, four in beekeeping and six in specialty crops.
This year, the ministry added a new category recognizing young farmers who have developed local industries and contributed to their communities.
Some awardees have used technology in greenhouse farming, aquaculture, production and sales, while some have developed processed products, brands and new sales channels, the ministry said.
Others have promoted food and agricultural education, and helped develop local communities in their hometowns, it said.
Chen said the ministry would continue helping young farmers with funding, technology, marketing and welfare benefits, while working to ensure that the profession offers stable livelihoods and opportunities.
