There are “strong indications” that Iran played a role in events in which five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire as part of a terror investigation, Andy Burnham has said.
Speaking to the media at the end of the Labour party conference in Liverpool, Burnham said he could not give any more details amid a police investigation, but that Iran was believed to be involved.
On Tuesday, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said Washington believed “a foreign actor” was involved in the events on Sunday night at the airbase, which has been used by US planes for missions against Iran.
In an interview with BBC News, Burnham said: “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation.
“And of course, we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America. So it’s ongoing.”
Noting that he had held a meeting of the government’s Cobra emergency committee while in Liverpool, Burnham said: “We are on top of it in every possible way imaginable.”
He added: “We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part.”
Asked why he believed this, Burnham replied: “Well I can’t go into all of those details, but obviously I wouldn’t say it lightly.”
In a separate interview with Sky News, Burnham was asked if he needed to recall parliament, which is in recess for the party conference season. He replied: “At this stage there is not an urgent need to do that, but should that arise, of course, I wouldn’t hesitate.”
The five men, all in their 20s and from London, were arrested in the Gloucestershire countryside near the airbase after a local woman driving home saw a series of vans and men in masks, and called police.
They were first arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism. All five were released on police bail on Monday after an examination of what was found in the vans, and searches of addresses linked to them across London.
On Tuesday the Guardian reported increasing confidence of an Iranian link to the weekend’s events.
The decision to release the men has prompted criticism from the Trump administration, with Rubio saying he was “disturbed” by it.
Questioned by the BBC about US criticism of the bail decision, Burnham said this had happened only with very strict conditions.
He said: “I think people need to understand that when it says released, that isn’t as people might think. It’s obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions. We’ve been talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done. I have complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this.”
It emerged on Tuesday that one of the five men arrested called the police to report the incident.
The local woman who also phoned police subsequently told newspapers that she was alarmed the men had been allowed to get so close to the airbase without apparently being noticed.
However, UK officials and Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, have indicated that security services were aware in advance of what was happening.
A statement from Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police hinted that officers swooped on the rural location for several reasons.
Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor said: “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford.”

A new map points out U.S. rivers most worth protecting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

A new map points out U.S. rivers most worth protecting
The detailed assessment suggests what would have the biggest conservation bang for the buck
First, the bad news: Of all the rivers in the contiguous United States, only 6 percent are both in healthy condition and meaningfully safeguarded. The good news is that many more may be just one repair away from thriving.
A new map highlights where conservation money and attention would do the most good as the climate warms, researchers report September 16 in PLOS One. The effort is the most comprehensive to date, assessing the health of the lower 48 states’ rivers and streams.
“We can now point at a map for the first time and say, these are the rivers most capable of sustaining diversity of aquatic life, and this is what each one needs,” says Mary Khoury, a freshwater ecologist at The Nature Conservancy who is based in Chicago.
For decades, conservation in the United States has been organized primarily around land. Scientists know for the most part which forests are intact and who owns what. Rivers have never gotten that treatment, even as more than 150,000 dams have fragmented the country’s waterways — cutting fish off from spawning grounds and cold-water refuges — and climate change has altered the temperatures and flows these animals depend on.
The new assessment, which took four years, maps one-third of the nation’s stream distances. Each small watershed was rated on four measures: how connected its river network is, meaning whether animals including fish and mussels can freely travel along it; the condition of its floodplain and water quality; how much water it has; and how much its flows have been altered. Those ratings were laid over 91 existing assessments of where freshwater life is concentrated. Dozens of scientists and partners from 44 states adjusted the measures for river systems in regions as different as the humid East, the arid Great Plains and the deserts of the Southwest.
River resilience
A four-year assessment graded every river and stream in the lower 48 for its ability to sustain aquatic life in a warming climate. The healthiest ones cluster along the Pacific Coast, in the northern Rockies and across the Southeast. The most vulnerable sit in the Southwest deserts, the Great Plains and southern New England.
Rivers doing well on all four criteria — more than half of the mapped stream distances — came out as resilient. The rest score near average, and were classed as restorable, still functional but held back by a problem, such as runoff from a farm or an obstructing dam, that one intervention could solve.
Together the two categories form what the authors call a freshwater resilient and connected network, a shopping list of what the country would need to look after to keep its freshwater life going. “A resilient system is one that gives species options and environments in which to adapt,” Khoury says.
Dams leave the clearest mark on the country’s rivers, carving them into more than 9,000 separate pieces. The study maps where reconnecting rivers would pay off most. Among the long unbroken stretches within the resilient system are Oregon and California’s Klamath River, whose lower dams came out in the largest removal project in U.S. history, and the Delaware River, which runs free of barriers along its main stem from New York’s Catskill Mountains to the sea.
“I can see this being overlaid in the future, for example, with where dam licenses will expire, in order to find the most effective restoration opportunities,” says Rafael Schmitt, a hydrologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara who was not involved in the work.
Unlike on land, the study found, a river’s health says almost nothing about whether anyone is looking after it. On land, the healthiest places tend to be the protected ones. In water, however, 13 percent of the country’s stream distances are in good shape with no real safeguards, roughly twice the 6 percent that is both healthy and protected.
The unprotected healthy rivers are the ones most at risk of slipping, because nothing keeps them in that condition. Locking in protection is harder for a river than for a forest. A designated preserve can hold a kilometer of stream while the water arriving in it may drain 100 kilometers of farm fields, dams and subdivisions. “It matters what’s going on upstream of that protected area,” Khoury says.

Russian strikes on Ukraine are likely about to get worse, analyst says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:59:10 UTC
00:59:10 KST

Russia is stockpiling weapons to intensify attacks on Ukraine, analysts say
Kyiv — A daytime Russian attack on Ukraine Monday damaged civilian buildings and wounded more than 100 people across the country, according to local authorities.
A drone exploded into the National Academy of Sciences in the heart of Kyiv. Hours later, a second drone damaged a private medical clinic just blocks away. In Dnipro, Ukraine's fourth-largest city, emergency crews rushed to evacuate wounded civilians from a business center also hit in broad daylight.
And yet, the attack could have been much worse.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia used 124 attack drones from 6:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. on Monday — much fewer than in previous barrages this year, which have regularly included more than 500 drones and 50 missiles within the same time frame.
Analysts and Ukrainian officials told CBS News that Russia is stockpiling weapons so that it can launch intensified late-autumn and winter barrages.
During Monday's attack, Russia used primarily "jet-powered drones," a new model of long-range strike drones that fly faster and are harder to intercept. Ukraine's Air Force said that 86 of the 124 drones used in the attack were jet-powered.
Since Russia began deploying the new models in June, Ukraine's interception rate against them is 57% — a sharp drop-off from the military's 90% to 95% success in intercepting older models.
Russia has two models of jet-powered drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, and has been stockpiling both. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit, estimates that Russia will produce 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 in September, and projects those numbers to grow each month.
During his speech at the United Nations General Assembly earlier this month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia has used just 7,700 jet-powered drones in attacks so far this year.
Viktoriia Chekalina, an analyst at the Come Back Alive Initiatives Center, estimates that Russia has stockpiled 450 to 700 units of the older non-jet-powered drones, the newer jet-powered models and dummy, non-explosive drones known as "Banderols" during each Russian attack this spring and summer.
"Despite the capacity to launch 600-1,000 units in a single massive attack, only about 150-300 drones were actually used," Chekalina told CBS News, explaining that attacks this autumn and winter "could reach around 1,500 units per one raid."
Because Russia has found success striking targets with relatively small barrages of jet-powered drones, it has also managed to save up its cruise and ballistic missiles, which are vastly more expensive and difficult to manufacture.
In the early spring and summer, Russia's attacks on Kyiv included barrages of over 70 cruise and ballistic missiles multiple times per month, according to estimates released by Ukraine's Air Force. In August, Ukraine stopped publicly releasing the numbers of missiles Russia used in each attack, but military analysts told CBS News that there was a drop-off in the number of mass-missile barrages in August and September.
Over this period, Russia has also increased its production of cruise and ballistic missiles. Chekalina said Russia has surpassed its missile production targets by 110% to 120% and estimated that it had stockpiled 130 ballistic missiles by August.
Solutions to countering Russia's ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones remain elusive. Ukraine continues to run dangerously low on American-made PAC-3 ballistic interceptors. And in an address this week, Zelenskyy said that while new defenses against jet-powered drones are being tested, they are not yet ready to be scaled, raising concerns that Ukraine may remain vulnerable heading into winter.
"Russia's goal during winter campaign will be complex: they will focus on attacking electrical and heating infrastructure as they are critical for civilians," Chekalina said. "At the same time, they will use turbojet drones along with missiles on local businesses, warehouses, and other targets."

The War in the Sky: Kyiv braces for another winter of Russian attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:58:34 UTC
00:58:34 KST

A Euronews documentary goes inside Ukraine’s battle to defend its skies, from air-defence crews battling Russia’s drone threats to workers repairing the damage and families preparing for another winter of attacks.
For years, Ukrainians have lived with a war raging not only along the front line, but above their heads. In Kyiv, the battle in the sky has become part of daily life, measured in air-raid alerts, the sound of air defence and the explosions that follow.
At an air-defence position protecting the capital, the work begins before anything appears overhead. Soldiers prepare their weapons and scan for threats that can arrive at radically different speeds and from different directions.
The challenge is no longer simply the number of weapons Russia can put into the air. Its attacks increasingly combine different threats: Shahed-type attack drones arriving in large waves, ballistic missiles that leave defenders little time to react, and new, faster drones that have added another danger.
Routes change. Timing changes. Weapons approach from different directions. The aim is to find gaps and overwhelm the layers of defence protecting the city.
For the soldiers watching the sky, it has become a technological race. Whenever Ukraine finds a cheaper or more effective way of stopping Russian drones, Russia adjusts how its weapons fly, how fast they travel or how they approach their targets.
Ukraine adapts. Russia adapts. And the cycle begins again.
Pavlo Tsugunov, an anti-aircraft battery commander, has watched that evolution from the ground.
“The past few weeks have seen constant attacks on Kyiv, its suburbs, the city centre, the Kyiv region and the Chernihiv region,” he said. “In other words, on the homes where our loved ones live.”
Tsugunov believes the pressure on civilians is itself part of Russia’s strategy.
“This tactic is most likely intended to intimidate the civilian population,” he says. “As they are currently failing to make any headway in direct combat operations on the front line, they are attempting to intimidate the population so that it stops supporting the army. And, consequently, so that the army will agree to surrender.”
But the limits of air defence can be seen across Kyiv.
Outside a kindergarten damaged in an attack, a young boy points at the building and tells Euronews he watched the drone strike it.
“The drone flew right above our heads and hit it here,” he says.
When the weapons get through
When a weapon gets through, another race begins, this time on the ground.
One of Russia’s main targets remains Ukraine’s energy system. At a damaged electricity facility in the Kyiv region, repair crews are working to restore the network while the threat of another attack continues.
They work for DTEK Kyiv Regional Grids, the distribution system operator responsible for the network that carries electricity through power lines and substations into communities across the Kyiv region.
Crews can begin repairing the damage only when the security situation allows. After an attack, they must wait for clearance from the military and emergency services before entering damaged sites.
Serhii, a repair technician, said residents were waiting for electricity to return, but repeated air-raid alerts were slowing the work.
“People are asking us to turn the lights on, but we can’t do that because the alarms are going off constantly, every day, all day long,” he says.
As he speaks to Euronews, explosions can be heard nearby. Another drone is heading towards the area.
“Let’s move a bit further away from the site, because you can hear what’s going on,” Serhii says.
It is a dilemma that has become familiar to Ukraine’s energy workers: the same attacks that knock out the electricity can also prevent the crews from safely restoring it. Moreover, often they target the people fixing the damage.
DTEK Kyiv Regional Grids says its teams have restored electricity to more than700,000 homes in the region after Russian attacks. In some cases, crews have had to return power to the same households more than once.
Previous winters have also changed the way the company prepares for the next one. Protecting infrastructure is only part of the task. Being able to repair it quickly after another strike has become just as important.
Oleksii, head of high-voltage network operations at DTEK Kyiv Regional Grids, described the relationship between those trying to stop the weapons in the air and those tasked with repairing the damage when they get through.
“I very much hope that our air defence systems will help us by shooting down the vast majority of the weapons currently being used,” he says.
“And after that, it’s up to us. We will repair whatever has been damaged.”
He said the crews have already been through the most complicated case in the past years, when Moscow deliberately tried to freeze the people, leaving them without electricity, heating and even water.
Preparing for another winter
For Ukraine’s energy workers, preparations for winter never really stop.
DTEK Kyiv Regional Grids says that since the beginning of the year it has repaired more than 1,200 kilometres of power lines and upgraded more than 400 energy facilities across the Kyiv region.
It has also been building reserves of replacement equipment and materials, strengthening protection around energy facilities and preparing emergency crews to respond rapidly when something is hit.
Those crews can move in only once the security situation allows. In a winter of repeated attacks, the ability to restore power quickly can matter almost as much as the preparations made beforehand.
But there is a limit to what preparation can achieve. No electricity network can be completely protected from missiles and drones.
Behind those power lines and substations are millions of ordinary routines that depend on them.
After several winters of war, Ukrainians no longer need to imagine what prolonged power cuts can mean. Electricity can disappear. Heating can become uncertain. Communications can become harder. Ordinary life begins to depend on batteries, generators and whatever electricity is available.
And so households are preparing too.
“Everyone is getting ready for winter,” says Anna, a Kyiv resident. “Everyone is preparing very well. Even my parents, even my friends.”
Some of the preparations are strikingly domestic. With Russia now increasingly targeting food warehouses, people are coming up with new ways of stocking up food for the winter.
“My younger friends, they’d never preserved food before, but now they’ve learnt how,” she says. “You could say it’s a good habit. Some people are installing inverters and solar panels, whilst others are installing batteries and stocking up on power banks”.
There is something telling in the ordinariness of the list. Preserved food. Batteries. Solar panels. Inverters. After years of attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, measures that would once have seemed exceptional have simply become part of preparing for winter.
Anna has already fled Russia’s war once. She left Luhansk after Moscow’s first invasion in 2014.
She stayed in Ukraine when the full-scale invasion began in 2022, in part because of her elderly parents. But after the hardships of last winter, she says she is now considering leaving the country for the first time.
“If the situation gets really dire, I’ll go. I’ll go because I’m worried about my child.”
For her 10-year-old son, this is the second phase of Russia’s war he has lived through. Born in Luhansk, he was a small child when Russian-backed forces seized the city in 2014.
“I think that’s really frightening. Some people don’t speak like this even at 25, the way children do now,” Anna admits emotionally.
“When they talk about something going ‘boom’ somewhere, they say: ‘If that’s my death, then I’ll accept it.’ Children are already saying things like that. My son says that to me too.
“My son tells me that if that’s my death, I’ll accept it. And if not, then, of course, I’m a lucky one.”
Growing up under attack
For Maryna, another Kyiv resident, survival begins with the sound coming from her phone.
“I always turn up the volume on my phone so I can tell exactly what sort of alarm is going off,” she says.
If the warning is for missiles, the calculation is immediate.
“Then we have two seconds to get out into the corridor. We can’t make it down to the shelter. We don’t have that time, because within two seconds we’re out in the corridor or the bathroom, and the loud, powerful explosions have already started.”
Her daughter Emma is nine years old. She has never known school without war and doesn’t remember peaceful days.
For children of her generation, the vocabulary of air raids has been absorbed into childhood. They know the alerts. They can even differentiate the sound of explosions above their heads and recognise their nature. They know where to go. And they have their own ways of describing sounds that adults immediately recognise.
Asked what it sounds like when air defence is active near her school, Emma answers simply:
“Like popcorn.”
“Air-defence interception sounds like popcorn popping?”
“Yes.”
It is a child’s description of a sound that has become part of growing up in wartime Kyiv.
The battle for Ukraine is still being fought in trenches and towns along a front stretching hundreds of kilometres. But the same war is being fought in the skies above cities far from that front.
And as another winter approaches, what happens in that sky will help determine what happens below it: whether homes stay warm, whether the lights stay on, whether children can remain in their classrooms and whether ordinary life can continue.
Ukraine has learnt to adapt. But so has Russia.
And for millions of Ukrainians, the question is brutally simple:
When the next missile comes, will there still be something there to stop it?

French court jails six men for manslaughter over mass drowning in Channel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:58:30 UTC
00:58:30 KST

A Paris court has jailed six men for manslaughter over the deaths of at least 27 people in the worst mass drowning on record from a small-boat crossing in the Channel.
Seven other men were found guilty of lesser smuggling charges with varying degrees of seriousness, including facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised gang and criminal conspiracy.
Five years on, another four people are still missing.
The court heard that the sinking of an inflatable dinghy in November 2021 was caused by “individuals driven by greed, with utter disregard for human life”.
Prosecutors said the convicted men helped launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”.
Emmanuel Daoud, a lawyer for one victim’s family, called the proceedings a “trial of greed, cynicism and inhumanity”.
Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for.
The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers.
Sentences for the six men found guilty of manslaughter ranged from six to 10 years in prison. For others, sentences ranged from six months suspended to four years in prison. The court heard that the men were linked to Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks that organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France. One man was found innocent.
According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat, which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea.
Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived.
For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by a French fishing vessel.
A separate investigation is continuing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel. They have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations.
Zana Mahmand Mohammed travelled from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to address the court about his younger brother, Twana, 18, who drowned in the disaster but whose body has never been found.
He said: “We’ve been waiting for our brother’s body for five years. I live with the uncertainty of ever finding out what happened. We lost a member of our family. He had a project for another future to live … ”
The family had tried to dissuade Twana from leaving home, but he had wanted to find a job and develop his sporting success as a black belt in taekwondo and escape the violence and insecurity of his region.
Mohammed said every time he read in the media about other small boats in difficulty, he relived the tragedy. “Destruction is being repeated,” he said.

Rumen Radev: War in Ukraine Fuels Political Instability Across Europe

Campaign Donations for Four Bulgarian Presidential Tickets Exceed €387,000

The war in Ukraine is creating not only security and economic challenges for Europe, but also waves of political instability and growing populism across the continent, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Wednesday.
“We need to understand what the outcome will be if we do not change our approach to this war. It is important to take a realistic view and find a path to peace as soon as possible,” Radev said during the Euronews Defence & Space Summit in Brussels.
Radev described the war in Ukraine as a war of attrition, calling it a serious challenge to global peace and an increasingly significant risk.

30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
US mortgage applications fell 6% last week as borrowing rates rose for a sixth consecutive week, weighing on refinancing activity and demand from homebuyers, according to Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) data released Wednesday.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances of $832,750 or less increased to 7.30% from 7.12% in the week ending Sept. 25 to its highest since November 2023.
Points, including the origination fee, rose to 0.75 from 0.73 for loans with a 20% down payment.
Applications to refinance a home loan declined 9% from the previous week and were 56% below their level a year earlier. Refinancing accounted for 38.3% of total applications, down from 39.3%.
Mortgage applications to purchase a home fell 4% on a weekly basis and were 14% lower than a year ago, as higher borrowing costs continued to squeeze affordability.
Borrowing costs climbed further this week. A separate daily index from Mortgage News Daily showed the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate reaching 7.58% on Tuesday, up from 7.50% on Monday and its highest since Nov. 1, 2023.
Mortgage News Daily attributed the increase to bond markets adjusting expectations for Federal Reserve policy, economic growth and inflation.

‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:56:09 UTC
00:56:09 KST

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi University by three men who posed as police officers.
Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang-raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year-old were reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by a bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.
Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.
Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang-raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic under-reporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and it could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi University, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.
While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country required a deep societal shift where men no longer felt they had ownership over women’s bodies.
“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,” she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”
Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.
“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”
Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women. As one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.
Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender equality initiative, said she had experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.
She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”
The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before, but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.
“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe’.”
Many of the Delhi University students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.
Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for a master’s in English, said: “Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades. It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”
Many on the marches said it was no coincidence that they were taking place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, in which hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians took to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

3 in 4 EU employees face cyber threats at work: Survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:53:06 UTC
00:53:06 KST

Melike Pala
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Three out of four employees in the EU have encountered suspicious emails, messages or links at work, according to a Eurobarometer survey released by the European Commission on Wednesday.
Phishing was the most commonly reported workplace cyber threat, with 39% of employees saying they encountered fraudulent messages or websites aimed at stealing data or gaining unauthorized access.
Phishing is a type of cyberattack in which criminals pretend to be a trustworthy person or organization to trick someone into revealing sensitive information or clicking a malicious link.
Eighteen percent of employees reported attempts to steal personal data; passwords came in at 16%, malware attacks at 17% and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated scams at 15%.
The findings highlighted a gap between employees' awareness of cybersecurity risks and their everyday practices.
While 83% of respondents said the potential consequences of cyberattacks are serious, only 48% said they could recognize an AI-generated fake video.
Some 69% also recognized sharing work-related information on social media as a cybersecurity risk.
Most employees said they knew they should report suspicious emails and install software updates.
Only 54% said, however, that they check the sender before opening links, despite 72% saying they could identify suspicious emails.

L’UE accusée de dissimuler l’impact environnemental des datacenters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:52:33 UTC
00:52:33 KST

L’UE accusée de dissimuler l’impact environnemental des datacenters
Une ONG a déposé une plainte, affirmant que la Commission européenne dissimulerait des données sur la consommation d’énergie et d’eau des centres de données, portant ainsi atteinte au droit de savoir des citoyens.
Selon les chiffres de la Commission européenne, les centres de données européens ont consommé 20,7 térawattheures d’électricité et plus de 8 millions de mètres cubes d’eau en 2025. | Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP via Getty Images
Une plainte déposée lundi contre la Commission européenne dénonce l’opacité de l’UE sur la consommation d’énergie des centres de données.
Dans le détail, cette plainte déposée cette semaine par Lighthouse Reports, comme l’a révélé POLITICO, accuse l’exécutif européen d’avoir mis en place des règles empêchant le public de connaître la consommation d’énergie et d’eau de chaque datacenter.
Cette action en justice intervient alors que l’opposition ne cesse de croître à travers l’Europe contre ces centres de données énergivores, indispensables au fonctionnement de l’intelligence artificielle, et alors que les prix de l’énergie sont en hausse.
Advertisement
Lighthouse Reports, une ONG basée aux Pays-Bas qui mène des enquêtes dans plusieurs pays sur de potentiels méfaits commis par des gouvernements et des entreprises, accuse la Commission d’ériger un “mur du silence” autour de la question de la consommation d’énergie.
Les décideurs politiques de l’UE seraient déterminés “à refuser ou à dissuader l’accès aux informations relatives aux performances des centres de données, et à en brouiller la compréhension”, peut-on lire dans la plainte déposée au titre de la Convention d’Aarhus, un traité international juridiquement contraignant qui garantit au public le droit à l’information et à la participation aux décisions en matière d’environnement.
Cette procédure affrontera son premier test en novembre, lorsque le Comité d’examen du respect des dispositions de la Convention d’Aarhus se réunira pour statuer sur sa recevabilité. Par la suite, la Convention d’Aarhus pourrait conclure que l’UE a manqué aux obligations qui lui incombent en vertu du texte.
Contactée par POLITICO, la Commission n’a pas répondu à notre demande de commentaire.
Des gourmands en énergie
Alors que l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle entraîne une hausse de la demande énergétique, l’UE a officiellement annoncé son objectif de tripler la capacité de ses centres de données dans les années à venir, afin de rester dans la course face aux Etats-Unis et à la Chine. Parallèlement, face à la hausse des prix de l’énergie, la contestation citoyenne contre les centres de données prend de l’ampleur à travers l’Europe.
Afin de limiter l’impact environnemental, la Commission a présenté la semaine dernière un nouveau label de transparence destiné à orienter les investissements vers des installations plus respectueuses de l’environnement ; des normes minimales de performance devraient suivre.
Advertisement
“Si nous ne veillons pas à ce que ces grands consommateurs d’énergie respectent bel et bien nos objectifs généraux [...] ils risquent alors de compromettre notre capacité à atteindre nos propres objectifs”, avait alors déclaré Dan Jørgensen, le commissaire européen chargé de l’Energie, dans une interview accordée à POLITICO.
Selon les chiffres de la Commission, les centres de données européens ont consommé 20,7 térawattheures d’électricité — soit à peu près autant que la consommation totale de la Croatie — et plus de 8 millions de mètres cubes d’eau en 2025. Cela représente une augmentation de 26% de la consommation d’électricité et de 52% de la consommation d’eau par rapport à 2024.
Mais ces chiffres ne reflètent pas complètement l’utilisation réelle du secteur, car ils résultent de données incomplètes recueillies par l’exécutif européen. Ces données n’ont été publiées que sous forme agrégée, conformément à une loi de 2024 interdisant à Bruxelles et aux Etats membres de divulguer “toutes les informations et tous les indicateurs clés de performance relatifs à chaque centre de données”, après un lobbying des géants de la tech, qui invoquaient des intérêts commerciaux.
“La transparence devrait être le point de départ”, a estimé Diego Solier, qui n’a pas souhaité s’exprimer sur la plainte elle-même — elle n’avait pas encore été rendue publique. “En même temps, la transparence doit être proportionnée et ne devrait pas obliger les entreprises à divulguer des informations vraiment sensibles sur le plan commercial.”
Le droit de savoir
Selon Lighthouse Reports, la Commission “porte la responsabilité principale [d’avoir] empêché le public de prendre connaissance des effets de l’expansion massive des centres de données en Europe”, en permettant aux opérateurs de garder secrets les détails de leur consommation et d’échapper ainsi à tout droit de regard — en violation de la Convention d’Aarhus, ratifiée par l’UE en 2005.
Advertisement
Après avoir tenté en vain de contraindre la Commission et les gouvernements nationaux à divulguer les données dont ils disposent, Lighthouse Reports les accuse de se retrancher à tort derrière des clauses d’exemption.
“La Commission se trouve au sommet d’un système de non-divulgation qui englobe la grande majorité de l’UE”, écrit l’ONG. “Privilégier le secret commercial au détriment du droit de savoir des citoyens érode la légitimité et entame encore davantage la confiance.”
Les nouvelles mesures visant à renforcer la transparence, notamment un système de notation vivement critiqué par les organisations professionnelles, ne suffisent pas à redresser la barre, ajoute Lighthouse Reports.
A partir de l’été prochain, ce système imposera aux opérateurs d’évaluer leur efficacité énergétique, leur consommation d’eau et leur recours à l’énergie propre sur une échelle allant d’A à G. Cependant, l’ONG fait valoir que ces règles ne révèlent toujours pas la consommation énergétique totale ni d’autres indicateurs clés permettant d’évaluer correctement l’empreinte carbone de ces infrastructures.
“Le fait de privilégier les ratios plutôt que les chiffres réels de consommation ne repose sur aucune contrainte technique ; il s’agit d’un choix qui favorise les intérêts du secteur au détriment de l’intérêt général”, argumente Lighthouse Reports dans sa plainte.
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
German automaker Volkswagen terminated several company-level collective bargaining agreements on Wednesday as it sought further cost reductions, drawing a sharp response from the IG Metall union.
The agreements will end Dec. 31.
Volkswagen said economic challenges required changes to provisions in its labor agreements while rejecting the union’s demand for a 5% wage increase.
Arne Meiswinkel, the Volkswagen brand’s board member responsible for human resources, said the automotive industry’s economic environment had deteriorated significantly over the past 18 months.
Meiswinkel cited growing competition from Chinese manufacturers in Europe and described the market changes as structural and far-reaching.
He said Volkswagen faced an increasing need to bring costs to a competitive level.
IG Metall said Volkswagen on Wednesday handed over termination notices for 10 agreements during a meeting in Hannover intended to review commitments under the company’s 2024 restructuring deal.
The affected agreements cover pay, working conditions, additional compensation, employees with special working hours, and staff in specialist or management roles, according to the union.
Parts of the agreement governing apprentices’ employment after training were also terminated, it said.
The agreements include a framework governing working hours, 30 days of annual leave and protections for older employees and those with health limitations, according to IG Metall.
The union stressed that the employment guarantee through the end of 2030 remained unaffected.
It also said terminating the agreements would not immediately remove every provision because some continue to apply after termination.
IG Metall negotiator Thorsten Groeger accused Volkswagen of seeking to shift business costs and risks onto employees who had already accepted substantial concessions under the 2024 deal.
The union said those concessions contribute around €1.5 billion ($1.7 billion) annually from 2025 in return for commitments to invest in the future of Volkswagen’s sites.
Works council chair Daniela Cavallo said employees had already reached the limit of acceptable concessions in 2024 and warned of a fierce dispute around the turn of the year.
IG Metall said it would consult its bargaining commission and employee representatives on its next steps, with strikes possible from Jan. 1, 2027.

The far-right National Rally party's Jordan Bardella has denied being the author of antisemitic messages attributed to him by investigative outlet Mediapart, which were published on Monday.
National Rally figurehead Jordan Bardella hit back at French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday, after Macron called reports that Bardella had sent antisemitic messages in 2013 "extremely serious and unacceptable" and urged him to clarify his position.
Responding to Macron on X, Bardella stated: "After October 7, 2023, I walked the streets of Paris and travelled to Israel. He did not."
Earlier on Wednesday, during a two-day state visit to Spain, Macron said France would "never tolerate antisemitic statements", calling the remarks allegedly made by Bardella "appalling and unacceptable" and adding that they required "the most extreme condemnation". The French President urged those responsible to "provide clarifications".
Contrary to Bardella's claims, Macron did travel to Israel on 24 October 2023, in order to express France's "solidarity" with Israel following Hamas’ October 7 attack.
Bardella — who French far-right leader Marine Le Pen has said will be her prime minister if she wins the country's presidential election next spring — has vigorously denied authorship of comments about supposed Jewish banking monopolies and other antisemitic conspiracy theories, which were attributed to him in a piece published by investigative media outlet Mediapart on Monday.
Macron also criticised the National Rally's "inflammatory language" directed at Mediapart, saying such rhetoric leads to escalation. He also deemed it "unacceptable to use violent language against political opponents" and "to target those who are, in part, organisers of this debate", in an apparent reference to the media.
At a press conference on Tuesday, Bardella referred to "the beginnings of an all-out war, of attempts to destabilise the presidential campaign".
He accused Mediapart of seeking "to kill his political career" and announced he would take legal action for defamation. Sitting by his side, Le Pen said she had "absolute confidence" in him.
According to Mediapart, the messages were written more than a decade ago. At the time, Bardella, now the president of the National Rally, was a teenager and a member of its predecessor, the National Front. The party was founded by Jean-Marie Le Pen, Le Pen's father, who repeatedly made Holocaust-denying remarks and was convicted several times for hate speech before his death in 2025.
The outlet said the comments it attributed to Bardella were drawn from private written exchanges but did not specify whether they were emails or another format. It said it had independently authenticated the exchanges but did not detail how, or say how it obtained them.
In 2023, Bardella was asked during an interview whether he believed that Jean-Marie Le Pen was an antisemite, to which he replied: "I do not search people's hearts and minds, but I don't believe it."
Days after the interview, he walked back his comments, describing them as a "clumsy remark", before declaring in May 2024 that the founder of the National Front had made statements which were "eminently antisemitic".
In recent years, the National Rally has courted Jewish voters by positioning itself as a bulwark against Islamic extremism in France, as Le Pen has made huge efforts to dissociate herself from her father's legacy. Researchers and critics of the party have dubbed this the "de-demonisation" of the party, after she expelled him from the National Front in 2015 and rebranded it in 2018.
Israel's Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli defended Bardella in a statement shared on X on Tuesday, describing the National Rally figure as "one of the clearest voices in Europe against Hamas" who "spoke in Jerusalem against antisemitism", while denouncing France's left as "experts at character assassination", just like "leftists in Israel".

Ukraine Says No to Australia’s Retiring Tiger Helicopters Despite Offer to Transfer Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:50:47 UTC
00:50:47 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine Says No to Australia’s Retiring Tiger Helicopters Despite Offer to Transfer Them
Ukraine has withdrawn its request for Australia’s retiring Eurocopter Tiger attack helicopters after concluding that operating and maintaining the aircraft would create additional costs and logistical challenges for its military.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on September 29, Ukraine’s Ambassador to Australia Vasyl Myroshnychenko confirmed that Kyiv had decided not to pursue the helicopters, which Canberra is replacing with US-made AH-64E Apache Guardians.
Defense Express reported, citing its own sources, that the decision followed an assessment of several factors, including the Tiger’s flight-hour cost, availability of spare parts, technical condition, and the equipment configuration that Ukraine could expect to receive.
Although Australia had been prepared to transfer the helicopters as military assistance, Ukraine would still have needed to establish the infrastructure required to operate them, train pilots and ground crews, secure spare parts, and maintain the aircraft in combat-ready condition.
Additional details were reported by Militarnyi on September 30, also citing Myroshnychenko. According to the outlet, Ukraine originally submitted its request for the Australian Tigers in 2024 before withdrawing it in early 2026.
Militarnyi reported that another factor was US-made equipment installed aboard the Australian helicopters and subject to International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or ITAR. Transferring such components to Ukraine would require US approval, while removing some of the equipment could reduce the helicopters’ combat capabilities.
Australia operated 22 Tiger ARH aircraft, an armed reconnaissance version derived from the French Tiger HAP. The helicopters are equipped with a 30-mm cannon, 70-mm unguided rockets, AGM-114 Hellfire II anti-tank guided missiles, and electro-optical systems for detecting and tracking targets.
However, Australia’s Tiger fleet faced persistent readiness and maintenance problems during its service.
A 2016 Australian National Audit Office review found that the helicopter reached final operational capability around seven years later than originally planned. Auditors identified 76 capability deficiencies at the time, 60 of which Australia’s Defence Department classified as critical.
Aircraft availability was also below planned levels. In 2015, an average of 3.5 helicopters out of 16 operational aircraft were serviceable at a given time, compared with a target of 12, according to the audit.
Operating costs were another concern. By June 2016, the Tiger cost approximately $22,500 per flying hour, compared with a target of about $14,800, while the long-term average was roughly $29,300.
Maintenance challenges continued into the aircraft’s final years in Australian service. Australia’s Defence Department reported for 2024–2025 that availability and sustainment remained problematic, with components from aircraft already being withdrawn used to keep other helicopters operational.
Australia formally selected the AH-64E Apache Guardian as the Tiger’s replacement in January 2021. The country is acquiring 29 Apaches and received its first aircraft in October 2025. On September 23, 2026, Australia announced the end of Tiger flight operations in Darwin.
Discussions about potentially transferring the retiring Tigers to Ukraine had continued since 2024. Defense Express reported that Australia had been considering the option while determining the future of the fleet. Instead, Ukraine is examining other options for modernizing its army aviation.
Instead, Ukraine is considering other platforms to modernize its army aviation. In July 2026, Army Aviation commander Brigadier General Pavlo Bardakov named the US-made UH-60 Black Hawk as a preferred future replacement for Ukraine’s aging Soviet-designed helicopter fleet, citing its balance of capability, operating cost, and effectiveness.

EU consumer authorities launch coordinated action targeting video game companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:48:50 UTC
00:48:50 KST

Burak Bir
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
EU consumer protection authorities launched coordinated actions targeting video game companies to strengthen gamers’ rights, the European Commission said Wednesday.
In a statement, the commission said the Consumer Protection Cooperation Network action follows its Key Principles on in-game virtual currencies, guidelines aimed at promoting transparency and fairness under EU consumer law.
The measures seek to ensure clear and transparent pricing, prevent costs from being obscured and prevent unwanted currency purchases, the commission said.
They also seek to provide clear information before purchases, respect consumers’ right to withdraw and ensure fair and understandable terms, it added.
The commission said the action also aims to ensure that game companies provide appropriate safeguards to all consumers, including vulnerable users such as children.
The Consumer Protection Cooperation Network brings together national authorities responsible for protecting consumers in the EU and the European Economic Area.
Coordinated by the European Commission, the authorities act against consumer law breaches that affect people in multiple member states.
In a separate statement, the network said it seeks to foster a competitive European video game market that provides a supportive environment for businesses.
“A broad consensus among academics, consumer advocates, and gamers is that some video game business models and design practices harm consumers, especially vulnerable groups such as children,” it said.
The network said some video games “directly exhort” children to make purchases despite an explicit prohibition under EU consumer protection law.
It announced 11 coordinated actions requesting Activision Blizzard UK Limited, Crytek GmbH, InnoGames GmbH, King.com Limited, Mojang AB, Plarium Europe S.a.r.l., PLR Worldwide Sales Limited, Riot Games Limited, Supercell Oy and Ubisoft EMEA SAS to bring practices involving in-game virtual currencies into line with EU consumer protection laws.

Civic education finds its place in Bulgarian schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:48:10 UTC
00:48:10 KST

Wednesday 30 September 2026 17:12
Wednesday, 30 September 2026, 17:12
PHOTO BNR Archive
Font size
The city of Vidin on the Danube is among the places taking part in the national European Civic Education programme. The initiative was created by the Institute for Public Policy together with the Ministry of Education and Germany’s Hanns Seidel Foundation. The partners provide training for teachers of civic education in different parts of the country.
What does civic education look like in Bulgaria?
Civic education has a history of more than a century in Bulgaria, incorporating European ideas, traditions and experience into the Bulgarian context. After the Second World War, between 1944 and 1989, it was replaced by teaching the fundamentals of communism, aimed at instilling a particular ideological worldview in young people.
Following the democratic changes of the early 1990s, civic education was gradually reintroduced at the initiative of NGOs, associations and teachers, initially as an optional subject for pupils from grades 1 to 12. It was not until 2020 that it became part of the compulsory curriculum for students in grades 11 and 12.
PHOTO BNR VIDIN
A study by several NGOs, Civic Leadership and Active Cooperation, looks at the role of civic education in Bulgarian schools. It explores how the subject can be taught more effectively and how its importance can be better recognised by school heads, teachers, parents and students. Yulia Mishkova of the Teach for Bulgaria Foundation, who manages the initiative, told BNR Vidin:
“This spring, we spoke to more than 1,000 teachers through surveys, focus groups and interviews, asking them what civic education means to them, where they see its place in the education system and how they understand their own role. Most of the teachers we spoke to consider civic education important and believe it has a place in schools. But with all the other demands on their time, many have concerns about how effectively it can be taught alongside everything else they are expected to achieve and all the exams they have to prepare their students for. This naturally affects how much time they are able and willing to devote to it.”
Yulia Mishkova
PHOTO zaednovchas.bg
Do the attitudes and needs of teachers in smaller towns differ from those of their colleagues in regional centres?
“I don’t think there are any major differences. What we see is that teachers share similar concerns, as well as similar examples of good practice. Generally, when teachers have the support of their school management and are given enough room to work – and perhaps have more experience – they feel somewhat more comfortable bringing different topics into the classroom. What remains an issue everywhere is whether they have enough time for meaningful discussions with students about issues that arise in everyday life and to explore them properly from different points of view. Just as important is whether teachers themselves have enough time to prepare for such discussions.”
 
PHOTO zaednovchas.bg
Civic education is taught in the final two years of secondary school. At the Yordan Radichkov Foreign Language School in Vidin, one of the teachers of the subject is Valya Aleksandrova.
What does she see as the strengths and weaknesses of civic education as it is currently taught?
“The first major problem is that one lesson a week in both the 11th and 12th grades is simply not enough. The second is the lack of teachers specifically trained in civic education. You really need knowledge across several academic fields rather than a narrow specialisation, because teaching civic education means constantly keeping up with changes in the world around you. You need a grounding in economics, philosophy, geography and history. The teacher’s own motivation to work with young people and teach the subject is also important. You have to want to make it as useful to your students as possible.”
Valya Akeksandrova
PHOTO BTA
Emilia Emilova is a 12th-grade student at the Vidin school and believes civic education helps develop students’ critical thinking:
“I find the lessons very interesting. For example, we look at articles of the Bulgarian Constitution. We might be given 20 and asked to choose the ten we think are most important, and then we discuss our choices. As well as learning about our rights and responsibilities, we develop critical thinking because we discuss all sorts of things in class... We often talk about disinformation and fake news and how to recognise them, and I think that will be very useful in the future when we come across something like that...”
Her classmate Niya Marianova believes civic education should be introduced earlier and studied in greater depth:
“I think the textbooks give us enough information about the institutions, but what worries me is that many young people don’t know enough about politics. The time will come when they have to vote, and they won’t know who to vote for, what they are voting for, how or why.”
PHOTO facebook.com/YordanRadichkovVidin
Raisa Krumova is in the 11th grade and will study civic education for the first time this year. She already sees its importance and its relevance beyond the classroom:
“I’m beginning to understand my role as a young person and as a member of society. I take an active part in various extracurricular activities related to European values, civic participation and the school community. I’m also a member of the student council, where we have the opportunity to organise initiatives, express our views and work together for different causes. To me, that is what civic education is really about – not just knowing your rights and responsibilities, but wanting to get involved, express your views, respect different opinions and contribute to your community.”
Editor: Yoan Kolev, based on a report by Teodora Yordanova-Spasova of BNR Vidin
Supervising editor: E. Karkalanova

Iran, Russia offer solutions to accelerate economic cooperation
TEHRAN- Iranian Oil Minister announced that Iran and Russia have offered bilateral solutions to remove existing obstacles and accelerate the implementation of decisions and agreements of the Joint Committee for Economic Cooperation.
According to IRNA, citing the Oil Ministry, Mohsen Paknejad said regarding his video conference with Sergei Tsivilev, Russia's Minister of Energy: "A detailed meeting was held via video conference within the framework of the Joint Committee for Economic Cooperation between Iran and Russia."
He continued: "In this meeting, the desired topics that had previously existed and been defined in the Joint Committee for Economic Cooperation between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Russian Federation were reviewed again."
Referring to a review of the achievements and decisions previously made in this committee, the Minister of Oil announced: "The two sides offered solutions for the existing obstacles so that we can achieve better results in the shortest possible time."
The Joint Committee for Economic Cooperation between Iran and Russia is one of the main mechanisms for following up and developing cooperation between the two countries in various economic fields, and a significant portion of issues related to energy, investment, trade, and the implementation of joint projects between the two countries is pursued within the framework of this commission.
The 19th Joint Committee for Economic Cooperation between Iran and Russia was held in February 2025 at the International Conference Center of the National Iranian Oil Company (Koushk), and a wide range of issues were examined, including the completion of the International North-South Transport Corridor, gas transfer from Russia to Iran, and the development of cooperation in the fields of space industries, nuclear energy, commercial and economic affairs, finance and banking, customs, industry and mining, agriculture, health, culture and tourism, science and technology. The results of these negotiations were compiled in the form of the committee's document and signed by the ministers of the two countries.
The Iranian Minister of Oil and the Russian Minister of Energy had previously met in Tehran in Tir of this year and assessed the implementation process of the understandings reached at the 19th meeting of the Iran-Russia Joint Commission for Economic Cooperation and the implementation of the 146 agreed-upon clauses between the two countries, and examined the existing obstacles to the implementation of these understandings.

'We will defend every inch of NATO territory’: Rutte dismisses Russia’s nuclear threat

Aysu Bicer
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on Wednesday dismissed Russian nuclear warnings over Kaliningrad, saying Moscow could not win a confrontation with the alliance.
Speaking at the Euronews Defense and Space Summit in Brussels, Rutte said NATO was prepared to defend its territory.
“We will defend every inch of NATO territory. That threat is not there, and if anything happens, we are ready to counter it,” he said.
His comments followed reports that Russia, in a letter, had warned NATO against any attempt to cut off Kaliningrad, its western exclave between Poland and Lithuania, saying it was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons.
Rutte declined to confirm the contents of the reported letter but rejected the suggestion of an imminent nuclear threat to the Baltic states.
“We are a defensive alliance. Stop the nuclear threat. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful. And particularly stop the war in Ukraine, which is an unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine,” he said.
Rutte also said Russian President Vladimir Putin could not defeat NATO. “Everybody knows that he can never win against NATO. I don't take this seriously.”
 
Europe’s defense role
Rutte said Russia was suffering heavy losses in Ukraine and claimed 43,000 troops were being killed or seriously wounded each month.
He said Moscow was trying to divide NATO allies and shift attention away from the battlefield.
“If necessary, of course we will defend ourselves. But the most important thing is this is all happening because the war is not going well for him in Ukraine. He wants to divide us. He wants us to lose attention when it comes to Ukraine,” Rutte said.
The NATO secretary general also said Europe must become more capable of handling security threats without relying so heavily on Washington.
“Why are the Americans doing it, taking out the Iranian nuclear capability? Because we can't. But in the future, we have to make sure that as Europeans, we can do this ourselves,” he said.
Rutte said increased European defense spending should eventually allow the continent to assume greater responsibility while keeping the US engaged in NATO.
“Still, the US being involved not only in the nuclear sense but also in the conventional sense, but the Europeans taking much, much more responsibility for the defense of this part of NATO,” he said.

Frontline Robotics Unveils Universal Frodo UGV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:46:19 UTC
00:46:19 KST

Ukrainian defense company Frontline Robotics has unveiled the Frodo universal 6×6 unmanned ground vehicle (UGV), designed for logistics, evacuation, and strike missions.
The company told Militarnyi that the Frodo uses a 6×6 wheel configuration and can reach a maximum speed of 40 km/h.
The platform has an effective payload capacity of up to 200 kilograms, a maximum payload capacity of up to 400 kilograms, and a claimed range of up to 150 kilometers.
The chassis features independent adaptive suspension and adjustable ground clearance ranging from 170 to 330 mm, intended to enable movement over rough terrain. A low center of gravity improves the platform’s stability, while the running gear is designed to keep moving if one wheel is lost.
According to the developer, a single service member can replace the UGV’s battery packs. The Frodo also supports several communications channels, including Starlink, LTE, Silvus, ELRS, and TBS.
The Frodo UGV has already been codified and is now available for procurement by the Defense Forces.
The platform can transport cargo and evacuate personnel, as well as carry remotely operated combat modules.
In particular, the Frodo can be equipped with the Burya turret manufactured by Frontline Robotics. The first version of the system for the Mk 19 40 mm automatic grenade launcher was unveiled in 2024, and the company began its serial production in early 2025.
In late 2025, Frontline Robotics presented the upgraded Burya 2.0, which received a universal mount and can operate with Mk 19, RDS40, and AGS-53 40 mm automatic grenade launchers, as well as the Browning M2 heavy machine gun and its equivalents.
“We see the future battlefield as a robotic environment where it is critically important to control not only the air but also the ground. If drones have already changed the principles of warfare in the sky, ground robotics is now going through the same stage of development on the ground,” Frontline Robotics CEO Yevhen Tretiak said.
According to him, entering the unmanned ground vehicle sector is part of the company’s strategy to build a multidomain robotic ecosystem.
In February 2026, the Burya turret was integrated onto the Ukrainian ARDAL UGV to operate an Mk 19 automatic grenade launcher, including from concealed positions. In August 2025, it was mounted on the THeMIS tracked UGV manufactured by Estonia’s Milrem Robotics.
In addition, Frontline Robotics agreed with Danish-Ukrainian company Dropla to integrate the Burya turret with its Logist ground platform and jointly develop AI-based threat-detection solutions.
Frontline Robotics has also developed the Linza 3.0 bomber drone, which features visual-inertial navigation and can operate in electronic warfare conditions.
In April, the company presented the upgraded Z00m 3.0 reconnaissance UAV, adapted to operate under active electronic warfare conditions.

US Senate block West Bank anti-Palestinian violence report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:46:02 UTC
00:46:02 KST

Breadcrumb
US Senate block West Bank anti-Palestinian violence report
US Senate Republicans on Tuesday blocked a bid to require President Donald Trump's administration to report to Congress on increasing violence in the occupied West Bank, including the deaths of American citizens.
The procedural vote was the latest sign of friction between US Democrats and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government over Israel's treatment of Palestinians and of Republicans' continuing strong support for his coalition.
The Senate voted 47 to 51 to block the resolution. The vote was largely along party lines, with every Republican voting no except for Rand Paul of Kentucky and every Democrat except John Fetterman of Pennsylvania in favor.
The resolution would have required the State Department to report to Congress on the killing of US citizens by Israeli settlers or Israeli security forces in the West Bank and to assess the human rights situation.
Violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the territory has risen sharply this year.
While the resolution would not have cut aid to Israel, the largest cumulative recipient of US foreign assistance since World War Two, a failure by the administration to deliver the report could have triggered restrictions on aid.
Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, the measure's lead sponsor, had argued that it was "long past time" to examine human rights in the West Bank, including the deaths of nine Americans since 2022.
"It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values," he said in a statement, referring to Israel.
Republicans accused Democrats of seeking to score political points as Israel is under threat, seven months after US and Israeli forces launched airstrikes that began an ongoing conflict with Iran.
"I urge my colleagues to vote no on this resolution so we can stand with our ally Israel as they beat back the scourge of Iranian-backed terrorism," Montana Republican Senator Steve Daines said in a speech.
Elections loom
The vote took place weeks before US midterm elections on November 3, in which polls show Trump's Republicans could lose their congressional majorities, signaling a potential shift in Israel policy in the new Congress.
Polls show the war with Iran is not popular with Americans, who are frustrated with higher energy prices resulting from the conflict.
Netanyahu, who has long aligned himself with US Republicans, faces an election in Israel on October 27, which public opinion polls show his right-wing coalition could lose.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. The UN and most countries consider settlements there illegal under international law governing military occupation.
Some Democrats — and a few Republicans — also have called for curbs on military aid to Israel over its conduct of the war in Gaza, with tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and much of the enclave in ruins.

2026-09-30
15:45:23 UTC
00:45:23 KST

More than 400 people, most of them minors, were detained in France over the past day and dozens more were injured in a wave of student protests over teacher shortages, deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms.
The demonstrations, which have included blockades at school entrances, began last week and on Tuesday merged with a broader public-sector strike. They have become a focus of political tension in France at a sensitive time: A presidential election is due next year, and the government is set to present its 2027 state budget Thursday, which is expected to include spending cuts aimed at easing pressure on public finances.
Scenes of violence emerged Wednesday from several locations across France. In Saint-Denis, a large suburb north of Paris, students stood outside their school gates near a fire that had been set as police looked on, while images from Lyon and Lille showed protesters throwing objects at officers.
"There are cockroaches and rats everywhere in the school," Fadila, a 17-year-old student, told Reuters. She said classroom temperatures swing between unbearable heat and freezing cold, depending on the weather. “We can't work in those conditions,” she said.
Gamze, a 17-year-old student from Saint-Denis, said students in the suburb, historically home to a working-class population, were treated unfairly compared with pupils elsewhere.
“It's always us ... who are suffering when, in Paris or in the countryside, they're not in such a situation,” she said.
French Education Minister Édouard Geffray told RTL radio that 76 people have been injured since the protests began, including students and staff members.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told BFM that about 440 people were detained or arrested Tuesday alone in connection with the high school protests, most of them minors. Nuñez said there were seven incidents in which protesters threw hydrochloric acid at police officers.
Organizers of the student protests said disruptions or shutdowns were reported at about 400 of France’s roughly 3,700 high schools.
Access roads and entrances to high schools across the country were blocked as part of the protests, with open support from France Unbowed, or LFI, the far-left party led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Polls have shown Mélenchon reaching the decisive second round of next year’s presidential election, where he is expected to face far-right leader Marine Le Pen.
Officials and politicians have condemned Mélenchon’s party, arguing that rhetoric from its members, some of whom joined the demonstrations, has inflamed students’ anger and contributed to the unrest.
Bally Bagayoko, an LFI mayor who was quoted as saying violence can sometimes be legitimate, said his comments had been taken out of context.
Valérie Pécresse, the conservative president of the Île-de-France region and a member of The Republicans, accused LFI of acting “like firefighters who are themselves the arsonists.”
The government condemned violence that broke out during some of the demonstrations but said the problems facing high schools must be recognized and addressed.
In a statement Wednesday, President Emmanuel Macron said anger did not justify violence and that political leaders must not give it legitimacy.
The student protests have also become part of a broader wave of public-sector unrest, which included a strike Tuesday involving nearly 10% of state employees.
“Raise wages!” “Freeze prices” and “From hospitals to nonprofits — the same attacks, the same struggles!” read signs carried by demonstrators marching in Paris.
Laurence Roubière, an elementary school teacher marching in Marseille, said frustration had reached a breaking point as she called for more resources and urged the government to stop directing funds toward the war budget.
In Nantes, in western France, demonstrators carried signs reading “Fed up with low pay” and “France is burning, and your firefighters with it.”
In Paris, thousands of firefighters marched in a separate procession after being stretched to their limits during historic wildfires over the summer.
Since 2017, France’s public-sector salary index has been increased only twice: by 3.5% in 2022 and 1.5% in 2023, for a cumulative rise of just over 5%.
Over the same period, cumulative inflation since 2017 is projected to reach 24.17% by the end of 2026.
Calls for higher teacher salaries and increased education funding come as France ranks third in public debt among eurozone countries, behind only Greece and Italy.

Greeks cross borders for cheaper fuel as energy costs mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:44:35 UTC
00:44:35 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Energy poverty, poorly insulated homes and an aging vehicle fleet leave Greek households exposed to rising energy costs, the Kathimerini newspaper reported Wednesday, as residents in northern Greece cross borders for cheaper fuel.
Around 20% of Greek households experience energy poverty, double the European average, limiting their ability to reduce consumption, according to the newspaper.
The proportion unable to keep their homes adequately warm stood at 18.1% in 2025, compared with an EU average of 8.8%.
More than half of Greece’s homes were built before 1980, while around six in 10 lack adequate insulation. Three-quarters of the building stock falls into low energy-efficiency categories.
Despite approximately €2.5 billion ($2.8 billion) mobilized through renovation programs over 15 years, only 9.5% of residents reported an energy upgrade in the preceding five years, compared with a European average of 23.9%.
Transport accounts for around 43% of final energy consumption, while passenger cars average 17.8 years old, against 12.7 years in the EU, Kathimerini reported.
Residents in northern Greece, meanwhile, are traveling to Bulgaria and North Macedonia to fill their tanks at lower prices, the LiFO news outlet reported, citing Mega television.
Drivers from Serres, Drama and Kilkis regularly cross through the Promachonas checkpoint into Bulgaria, where unleaded gasoline costs around €0.56 less per liter and diesel €0.33 less than in Greece.
In North Macedonia, gasoline is about €0.60 cheaper per liter and diesel €0.54 cheaper.
Fuel market representatives estimated that new refinery pricing could bring an additional increase of nearly 2%, while the government was preparing additional support measures, LiFO reported.
