Energy bills: what to do as prices head for £2,000 a year, from switching deals to insulating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:44:17 UTC
00:44:17 KST

Household energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to reach £1,999 a year for the typical household from January. Photograph: Simon Dack/AlamyView image in fullscreenHousehold energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to reach £1,999 a year for the typical household from January. Photograph: Simon Dack/AlamyExplainerEnergy bills: what to do as prices head for £2,000 a year, from switching deals to insulatingThe price cap is to soar for about 20 million households in Great Britain from January, but there are ways to save Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from January Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical bill forecast to jump by £276 to the equivalent of nearly £2,000 year.It is a worrying outlook but there are practical steps you can take to mitigate the predicted price shock.Fixed energy deals“Switching energy tariff to a well-priced fixed deal is the biggest lever households on the price cap can pull to bring their costs down right now,” says Richard Neudegg, the director of regulation at Uswitch.About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable tariffs set by Ofgem’s price cap, which increases by 4% from Thursday, equivalent to taking the typical annual dual-fuel bill up by £60 to £1,723.The cap is due to rise 16% further to £1,999 in January, according to the latest forecast from the consultancy Cornwall Insight. “The cheapest deal on the market is currently £324 less than this,” says Neudegg.The number of cap-beating deals has been steadily declining in recent weeks but there are still 34 deals below the January forecast, with some cheaper than October’s rates. At the moment the cheapest is Fuse Energy’s 12-month fix at £1,675, beating the October price cap by £48, and potentially January’s by as much as £324.Check your boiler and hot water settingsCombi boilers work best when they heat radiators to 60C or below. But in many homes the “flow temperature” is often set much too high at 70C- 80C. It only takes a few minutes to turn it down and this alone could save you about £60 a year. With some people reluctant to fiddle with their boiler settings, the charity Nesta has a step-by-step guide on its website.Combi boilers allow users also to control the temperature of hot water supplied to taps and showers. Reducing the hot water temperature to 42C reduces the amount of fuel needed to heat the water and doing this could shave 2% off your gas bill, it suggests.Block draughts ... then turn down the thermostatView image in fullscreenTurning down the thermostat by 1C could save about £120 a year. Photograph: RossHelen editorial/AlamyInstalling inexpensive draught-proofing strips around windows and doors is a quick and easy DIY job that could shave £25 a year off your energy bill.You can buy foam, metal or plastic draught strips, or brush seals for sash windows, cut them to size and attach around opening casements. Use a thicker option for doors. Flues can be plugged easily with a chimney balloon or a draught excluder.Curtains are another easy way of reducing draughts and retaining heat. You could invest in some heavy-duty thermal-lined curtains, or alternatively buy a thermal lining for your existing ones.According to the World Health Organization, the lowest comfortable temperature for most people is between 18C and 21C so if you’re warm enough, try turning your thermostat down by 1C – this could save you about £120 a year, according to the Energy Saving Trust.Turn down radiatorsIf you have thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs), the dial that controls how much hot water enters the radiator it is attached to, you will be able to adjust the temperature separately in each room. TRVs usually have a scale from 0 to 6, where 0 is off and 6 is fully open.The Energy Saving Trust recommends putting it on the lowest setting that keeps the room at a comfortable temperature, which could be 3 or 4 for rooms you use the most and 2 or 3 for others. Managing the temperature this way can save a household about £40 a year.Insulate your hot water tank and pipesMost modern hot water tanks have plenty of insulation, but an older tank might have only a small amount. Adding an 80mm jacket to a tank with 25mm foam built-in can save homeowners in Great Britain about £45 a year, it says. The jackets cost about £20 and are widely available from DIY retailers.Insulating (or lagging) pipes helps keep in the heat and prevent damage during cold winter months. There are several different types of material used for lagging but the most popular is polyethylene foam mainly because of how affordable and easy it is to install.Insulate your loft (and walls)View image in fullscreenInsulating a loft is a job many homeowners can do themselves after watching an online tutorial. Photograph: DWImages/AlamyHomes can lose about 25% of their heat through an uninsulated roof. Many already have some loft insulation but topping it up can help retain more heat. If your current setup is about 120mm thick, increasing it to the 270mm (the minimum recommendation for new builds) could save you in the region of £20 a year.There are plenty of online tutorials showing you how to do this yourself. DIY stores sell rolls of mineral wool insulation, with a roll of standard “top-up” insulation £27 at Wickes, for example.Most homes built between 1920 and 1990 were constructed with uninsulated cavity walls, and the Energy Saving Trust estimates adding cavity wall insulation (where an installer injects insulation material from the outside) could save £200 a year.Get a heat pumpIf your boiler needs replacing it might be time to explore a green alternative. The government’s boiler upgrade scheme offers grants of £7,500 to help homeowners in England and Wales with the cost of installing an air-to-water or ground-to-water heat pump system.Households not connected to the gas grid qualify for an additional £1,500 in support, increasing the grant to £9,000. If you live in Scotland, you may be able to get an interest-free loan or a grant to make your home more energy efficient.When it comes to bills, the Energy Saving Trust says the biggest saving comes in homes that switch to a dedicated heat pump energy tariff and add other green technologies such as solar panels.The tariff is vital because heat pumps run on electricity, which is generally more expensive per unit than gas. On a standard tariff, this can lead to substantial energy bills, negating some of the efficiency benefits. Heat pump users moving on to a time-of-use tariff can save about £330 a year compared with sitting on a flat-rate tariff, the trust says. This rises to about £800 with extras such as solar, although these add to the upfront costs.Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsHousehold billsConsumer affairsEnergy industryEnergy efficiencyHeat pumpsexplainersShareReuse this content

US ceasefire plan for Sudan could lead to Libya-style partition, adviser says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:43:00 UTC
00:43:00 KST

US ceasefire plan for Sudan could lead to Libya-style partition, adviser says
Sept 30 - A US ceasefire proposal to pause Sudan's civil war could push the country towards a Libya-style partition in its current form, a top adviser to Sudan's army-led authorities told Reuters, in some of the strongest criticism by a Sudanese official of the plan so far.
The remarks come a week after Reuters reported that army leader General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's visa to attend the UN General Assembly in New York had been withheld because he had not yet accepted the proposal.
Sudan's army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, when the two fell out over issues including how to integrate their forces in a planned transition to civilian rule.
The proposal, put forward by US Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos, would impose a 90-day ceasefire, followed by negotiations to end the war and resume the move to civilian rule.
Amjad Farid, an adviser to Burhan on political and international affairs, told Reuters that the army-led government had presented its proposed changes to the deal, chief among them an internationally monitored withdrawal of the RSF from urban areas, but the US had appeared to ignore them.
"Mr Boulos seems to be putting pressure on us to accept a de facto partitioning of the country similar to Libyan model," he told Reuters, speaking from New York where he attended the General Assembly.
"Our concern is that the approach Mr Boulos continues to advance appears to accommodate the militia’s continued existence and preserve a place for it in Sudan’s political future," he added, referring to the RSF.
A Sudanese delegation had been preparing to meet Boulos to discuss the ceasefire in Washington last week, but the meeting was cancelled after Burhan's visa was withheld, two Sudanese diplomats told Reuters, asking not to be named because they were not authorised to speak.
The US State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Last week, it said neither the RSF nor the armed forces "represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan."
EFFORTS TO SET UP PARALLEL GOVERNMENT
The US has accused the RSF of committing genocide and the army of carrying out war crimes, including the use of chemical weapons.
Analysts and officials have long raised fears that the conflict could lead to a de facto division of Sudan that resembles neighbouring Libya, which has been split into rival eastern and western administrations for over a decade.
Since last year the RSF has been trying to establish its own parallel government in the city of Nyala in the western Darfur region. Ministers have been appointed and some police are active, though they have not set up public services or institutions such as schools, hospitals and courts.
Following recent battlefield defeats, the RSF has not made any recent statements on the US proposal and its leader has said its fighters intend to continue the war. REUTERS

After hours of terror, 174 Flydubai passengers finally land at Ben Gurion Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:42:26 UTC
00:42:26 KST

Nearly half a day after taking off from Dubai for Tel Aviv, all 174 passengers aboard Flydubai Flight FZ1073, including 27 children, landed at Ben Gurion Airport on Wednesday evening after surviving what Israeli officials have described as a suspected attempted terrorist attack.
Magen David Adom teams and medical staff at Ben Gurion Airport met the passengers arriving from Saudi Arabia with mobile intensive care units and ambulances on standby.
MDA paramedics examined the passengers after landing. A 51-year-old man was evacuated to hospital in mild condition with an upper-body injury.
Among those returning were passengers who helped overpower the suspected attacker during the violent confrontation in the cockpit.
Some passengers initially refused to board another Flydubai aircraft for the journey home, saying they were afraid to fly with the airline again. They eventually agreed after being told there was no alternative and after Saudi authorities refused to approve an Israeli-chartered rescue aircraft.
The rescue flight departed Tabuk after the Mossad completed background checks on the Flydubai crew and cleared the aircraft for departure.
The ordeal began at around 8:21 a.m., when, according to the emerging Israeli assessment, an Omani pilot stabbed the captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, which was carrying mostly Israeli passengers.
Passengers helped overpower the suspect, according to testimony from the flight, allowing another flight crew aboard the aircraft to regain control and eventually make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Defense Minister Israel Katz later described the incident as an “attempted jihadist terrorist attack” and said it had been thwarted by the actions of Israeli passengers. “According to the initial information in our possession, the terrorist had one intention: to crash the aircraft with all its passengers,” Katz said.
One passenger described the terrifying moments in a video recorded while the aircraft was still in the air.
“We’re on the flight from Dubai. We took control of the situation here. There was an attacker with a knife who stabbed one of the pilots,” he said.
“A few of us just jumped in and pulled him out of the cockpit. Everything is OK now. The terrorist has been neutralized.”
The passenger said one pilot was seriously wounded and another appeared to have been injured but remained able to help bring the aircraft down safely.
“There is a pilot here who is seriously wounded and apparently another pilot inside who is injured, but he is managing to land the plane,” he said. “There are two crew members inside the cockpit. We made sure they locked the door. I love you, and everything is OK.”
The original aircraft landed safely in Tabuk after issuing emergency signals and making a rapid descent. Flydubai has said the incident remains under official investigation and has cautioned against speculation over its cause or motive.
Hours later, the passengers who had begun their morning expecting a routine three-hour flight from Dubai finally arrived home at Ben Gurion Airport.

Flydubai flight drama: How Indian pilot Smit Machchhar stopped Omani co-pilot from crashing plane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:41:19 UTC
00:41:19 KST

The captain has years of experience and was a SpiceJet pilot till 2022
NEW DELHI: An Indian pilot has been identified as the captain who helped prevent a flydubai passenger plane from crashing after his co-pilot allegedly tried to take control of the aircraft during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, according to Israeli media reports and an Israeli journalist.The Indian pilot has been identified as Captain Smit Machchhar, based in Dubai, who intervened to stop his Omani co-pilot allegedly trying to take control of the aircraft and crash it.The Indian captain was stabbed repeatedly and drenched in blood, according to various witness reports and officials.Machchhar is an experienced commercial pilot with more than 13 years of flying experience on Boeing 737 aircraft. He has been a captain with flydubai since June 2022, having previously spent 11 years with SpiceJet, where he served as a senior commander and Line Training Captain.During his time at SpiceJet, Machchhar reportedly flew more than 9,500 hours, including over 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, and served as a Line Training Captain from November 2020 to June 2022. His experience includes pilot training and mentoring, crew resource management, flight standards and compliance, and B737 NG and MAX operations.
The incident unfolded aboard flydubai Flight FZ1073 on Wednesday, with the Boeing 737 sending emergency signals before making an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The flight was carrying around 180 Israeli passengers, all of whom were reported safe.Also read: Passengers recall harrowing ordeal on flight that nearly crashed
What happened inside the cockpit
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was flying over Jordan when it transmitted an emergency signal, followed by another signal indicating possible unlawful interference.Israeli officials said the emergency signals followed a physical altercation between the two pilots. Reuters reported that the co-pilot was believed to have stabbed the captain before cabin crew entered the cockpit. Both pilots were later hospitalised after the aircraft landed in Tabuk.Israeli media reports said the suspected attacker attempted to take control of the aircraft and force it into a descent. Passengers reportedly heard screaming and saw blood inside the cockpit.Flight-tracking data showed the aircraft plunging rapidly from around 34,000 feet to about 20,000 feet, with Reuters reporting a drop of nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds before the aircraft stabilised.The aircraft was initially treated as a possible hijacking, prompting Israeli fighter jets to be scrambled. The Israeli prime minister's office later said the incident was not believed to have been a hijacking.Israeli media reports have described the incident as a possible attempted suicide or deliberate crash, while Israeli officials cited by Reuters said they were assessing it as a possible attempted "terror attack". Reuters also reported that officials did not believe the incident was related to a mental-health issue.Later, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the pilots became involved in a physical altercation as the flight approached Israel. “During the flight as they approached the country one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot,” Netanyahu said in a video address.“Apparently he tried to crash the plane with its occupants.” Netanyahu added “almost all” passengers were Israelis, with some passengers and crew members breaking into the cockpit and subduing the attacker. “I spoke with one of the Israeli passengers. He told me that the plane went into a spin and began to dive. He told me that somehow he managed to break into the cockpit with one of the crew members and together they neutralized the stabbing pilot while he was trying to sabotage the aircraft’s systems,” Netanyahu said. “Another air crew that was on the plane entered the cockpit and managed to stabilize the plane,” he added. He also praised those who intervened, saying: “I salute these heroes who showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage.
Flydubai has confirmed that Flight FZ1073 experienced an incident during its journey from Dubai to Tel Aviv and diverted to Tabuk, where it landed safely."Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities. Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available," the airline said.Read more: Passenger's mother says pilot tried to kill co-pilot on Flydubai flightThe airline has not publicly confirmed the identities or nationalities of the pilots or provided details about what happened inside the cockpit.The investigation is continuing, with Israeli authorities examining the circumstances of the cockpit confrontation, the alleged attempt to take control of the aircraft and the security clearance given to the crew.

In the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors, half of the September hearings did not take place

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
18:40:56 EEST
00:40:56 KST

In the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors, half of the September hearings did not take place
Kyiv • UNN
The court scheduled 13 hearings in September in the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors. However, motions to postpone the hearings, requests for the judge’s recusal, and the non-appearance of participants in the proceedings once again delayed the proceedings.
For September, in the case involving Odrex doctors, the court scheduled 13 hearings at once—a schedule that was supposed to allow it to make progress in examining the evidence and move on to hearing the medical expert. However, nearly half of the hearings did not take place or were postponed: the reasons included motions to adjourn, motions to recuse the judge, non-appearances by participants in the proceedings, and technical circumstances. As a result, the court did not hear the key expert in September after all, UNN writes.
Details
The Kyiv District Court of Odesa continues the trial in the criminal case against Odrex doctors Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Biełotserkovska, who are accused of committing a criminal offense under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine—improper performance of professional duties by a medical worker. According to the investigation, their actions or inaction may have caused the death of businessman Adnan Kivan.
The proceedings have stalled because of motions by the defense to postpone hearings, motions for the judge’s recusal, and the defendants’ non-appearances. Of the 13 hearings scheduled for September, six took place. In seven other instances, the hearing was postponed or the court was unable to proceed to consideration of the case on its merits.
The series of disruptions has already drawn a reaction from the court itself. After Rusakov’s lawyers asked to postpone two consecutive hearings because they were participating in other proceedings, presiding Judge Viktor Chaplytskyi found the reasons for their non-appearance unjustified and said he would forward the information to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar. The commission must now assess whether the defense lawyers’ actions constitute a disciplinary offense.
Oleksandr Sytnykov, a retired judge of the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine, previously explained to UNN that if lawyers’ non-appearances or motions systematically block the progress of a case, the court cannot limit itself to recording yet another postponement. Ensuring that proceedings are considered within a reasonable time is the court’s own duty, so the presiding judge must respond to possible delays in the proceedings.
Andrii Misiats, acting head of the Higher Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar, also drew attention to the systematic nature of such non-appearances.
A combination of non-appearances may indicate not an accidental violation, but a certain pattern of behavior by the lawyer and his bad-faith attitude toward his professional duties
And this is despite the fact that, since May, the court has been unable to move on to hearing the medical expert. The expert is to analyze the medical records, expert conclusions, compliance with treatment protocols, and explain the medical component of the possible causal link between the doctors’ actions and Adnan Kivan’s death. The final assessment of the evidence and questions of guilt is made exclusively by the court.
It should be noted that this is already the court’s second attempt to reach this stage. The previous time, in May, when the expert arrived at court, Rusakov’s defense raised the issue of changing the venue.
The regular motions filed by the lawyers for the accused doctors, which may appear to be procedural maneuvers, have a potentially much broader consequence than simply delaying the proceedings. Lawyers interviewed by UNN did not rule out that the combination of such actions could be aimed at allowing the statute of limitations in the case to expire. If this scenario materializes, the accused doctors may avoid liability even if the court of first instance finds them guilty.

Sweden must apologise for harm done to Sami people, says state-backed report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:40:28 UTC
00:40:28 KST

An independent commission set up by the Swedish state has called on the country’s government to apologise for the “harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people” and to start a national process for “redress and reconciliation”.
The Truth Commission for the Sami People also called for a special apology to be issued urgently to elderly Sami people who were forced as children to attend segregated so-called “nomad school” and other boarding schools where they were “subjected to violations or abuse”.
The commission’s report, published on Wednesday, is the outcome of a four-year investigation and hundreds of interviews with Sami people across Sweden. It was due to be presented to a government representative at a ceremony featuring readings from the text, but with no government yet in place after the election earlier this month, it went instead to Parisa Liljestrand, the last government’s culture minister.
The commission’s chair, Lena Nyberg, told her: “We hand over a big responsibility.” Liljestrand thanked the members of the commission and those who were interviewed for the report, saying it had been a “historic process”.
There have been similar truth commissions into the treatment of Sami people – Europe’s only recognised Indigenous people – in Norway and Finland. Norway has issued an official apology and discussions in Finland are ongoing.
The new report accuses Sweden of failing to meet its domestic and international human rights obligations and says that as a “direct consequence” of mistreatment, the Sami people today face “major challenges” in preserving and developing their culture.
It coincides with rising anti-Sami rhetoric in Sweden, including from political leaders, amid clashes over land used for grazing by Sami reindeer herders for hundreds of years, which the state wants to mine for rare-earth minerals.
The report says issues with the handling of Sami land rights in Sweden have been “reinforced and aggravated” by an ideology that Sami people are “an inferior people and therefore neither deserving of nor capable of exercising the same rights and responsibilities as other citizens”.
It adds that the Swedish state has failed to implement the United Nations declaration on the rights of Indigenous peoples.
The commission’s 71-point call to action recommends an official apology for the harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people, as well as financial compensation and completing the process of ratifying the International Labour Organization’s convention on Indigenous and tribal peoples.
It calls for the establishment of a national centre for redress and reconciliation, and for authorities to recognise that the Swedish nation was founded on lands belonging to two peoples – the Sámi and the Swedes – and that parts of the land have Sami names and are part of Sami cultural heritage.
It also urges recognition that Sápmi, the region traditionally inhabited by the Sami people, extends across present national borders; an end to racial discrimination against Sami people; and better provision for children to learn Sami languages. It adds that the Swedish government must uphold the Sami people’s right to practise reindeer husbandry and other cultural practices on their traditional lands.
The report concludes that the state, including the Swedish parliament, government and public authorities, and in some cases the Church of Sweden, must “bear responsibility” for policies and decisions that led to the violation of Sami rights.
It says: “Accepting responsibility also requires the state to work towards providing redress for the harm inflicted on the Sami people and individual Sami, while pursuing policies that do not repeat these historical injustices.”

He added that Russian President Vladimir Putin has no interest in negotiating to end the war in Ukraine.

Trump's meeting with tech leaders leaves AI safety more unsettled than ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:36:20 UTC
00:36:20 KST

After President Donald Trump's lunch with AI leaders on Tuesday, the leading artificial intelligence companies are right where they were before: policing themselves.
Trump hosted top execs from Alphabet, Meta, SpaceX, Nvidia, Palantir, Anthropic, OpenAI and other companies following a three-week stretch during which the topic of AI safety turned into an intense nationwide debate, with leading industry researchers and executives warning of the extreme threats posed by the most powerful models.
But while the concerns voiced this month by the likes of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei have led many policymakers and industry experts to demand government regulation, Trump has steadfastly opposed any such moves, and called AI fears a "hoax."
On Tuesday, Trump brought leaders to the White House to sign a two-page document that he shared on his Truth Social account. It was titled, "White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities."
The document says that the group believes "every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public." Signatories included some of the same people who have been insisting that, in the absence of a coordinated safety effort, their technology can't be trusted.
"You saw two weeks ago almost all those same CEOs say they should be regulated," said Bradley Tusk, CEO of Tusk Ventures, in an interview on CNBC's "Closing Bell Overtime" on Tuesday. "It's not because they fundamentally believe in the power of the state. They want something that creates an equalizer for each other."
The four action items in the document call for each company to establish "robust" internal monitoring of models, have an internal team that ensures the controls are working, partner with outside auditors or evaluators, and designate an independent committee of the board to oversee the internal team.
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations," the last paragraph begins. When asked by reporters outside the White House if the rules are binding, Trump said they're "morally binding."
Though the document left the door open to further regulation, comments from House Speaker Mike Johnson made the push for AI oversight in Congress much more unlikely. Multiple bills have been proposed in both chambers to rein in AI, and while the midterms could shift power, Trump maintained his stance that the industry should be left "exactly where it is."
Trump wasn't just holding the event to promote the new accord. Separately, he said he signed a document purporting to "officially" change the name of AI to "super intelligence," trying to push through a rebrand after crowdsourcing a new name on social media last week.
'This is a start'
While tech companies aren't likely to swap out their use of the AI acronym anytime soon, their top leaders, after Tuesday's lunch, were quick to voice their support for Trump's broader effort. It's been a consistent theme during Trump's second term as corporate America, particularly the tech industry, attempts to stay out of the president's crosshairs.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg told reporters that the agreement is designed to "give the American people and our customers confidence that the technology works in the way we intend."
"The idea isn't that this is the only thing that we'll ever do," Zuckerberg said. "It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry can come to."
Compared with his peers like Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Zuckerberg has been more in the camp of self-regulation, alongside Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Days after Amodei's explosive essay earlier this month urging AI labs to "pace the frontier," Zuckerberg wrote in a post on X that "trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models."
Amodei, who's had a rocky relationship with the White House but had dinner with Trump late last week, offered a fairly innocuous comment to the group of reporters after the signing, saying, "If we do this right, if we work with the president and everyone here we can win safely."
And Alphabet's Sundar Pichai described the moment as "historic and consequential."
But with the concerns surrounding high-profile security breaches escalating, and public sentiment toward AI companies turning decidedly sour heading into the November midterm elections, calls for regulation are only likely to grow louder.
According to Verasight's September national survey, 63% of respondents said AI should slow down while only 5% said it should accelerate.
Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said Tuesday that he's introduced legislation to require "rigorous testing and evaluation" of leading AI technology and to strengthen security and reporting "before the most powerful models are deployed."
"The companies building the most powerful AI systems are warning us that the technology is advancing faster than our safeguards," Warner said in a release. "The president's response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves. But changing what we call artificial intelligence does nothing to address the very real risks that come with increasingly powerful AI systems."
— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger, Samantha Subin and Lora Kolodny contributed to this report

What Pninat Yanay’s appointment says about Israel’s new posture in Greece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:36:04 UTC
00:36:04 KST

When Pninat Yanay arrived in Athens as Israel’s ambassador to Greece on August 17, 2026, her appointment seemed routine.
But a closer look at her profile suggests otherwise.
Yanay’s resume shows she is a lawyer, strategic adviser and TV commentator – not a product of Israel’s foreign service.
Greek reporting has described her as the “first non-career diplomat” to serve as Israel’s top envoy to Athens.
She succeeds Noam Katz, a senior career envoy whose four-year term had just ended.
On December 14, 2025, the Israeli cabinet approved her nomination for three years from August 2026, with the option of a one-year extension.
When putting her name up for the appointment, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said in October 2025 that her public speaking and media skills mattered for an ambassador “in the current environment”.
The fact that he played up her media credentials while overlooking her lack of formal diplomatic training reflected Tel Aviv’s view of Greece as more than just another conventional European posting.
Bilateral ties between the two countries go beyond the traditional realm and now encompass defence procurement, military exercises, cybersecurity, energy and Eastern Mediterranean geopolitics.
In fact, the embassy frames the relationship around defence, energy, tourism, investment, and innovation.
On August 25, Yanay met General Dimitrios Choupis, chief of the Hellenic National Defence General Staff, for talks on “strategic cooperation” in defence and security.
Just a few days earlier, Choupis had been in Israel to meet Lieutenant-General Eyal Zamir, a visit described as underscoring the deepening military alignment between Israel and Greece.
The diplomat Yanay replaced
Katz was the opposite of Yanay. A career diplomat since 1994, he served in Athens from September 2022 after heading the Foreign Ministry’s Public Diplomacy Directorate.
He had been the minister for public diplomacy in Washington, director of public affairs in Israel, and ambassador to Nigeria, Ghana and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS).
His profile was purely diplomatic: spokesmanship, African postings and the ministry bureaucracy, then Athens as defence and strategic ties with Israel deepened under his watch.
In other words, Katz was deeply embedded in the foreign service, while Yanay was appointed laterally and without relevant credentials.
From law to defence deals
The embassy biography presents Yanay as a lawyer, strategic adviser and media commentator.
She holds an LLB from Bar-Ilan University and completed postgraduate work in public and international law through Tel Aviv University with Northwestern University in Chicago.
Between 2012 and 2020, she represented big Israeli companies in defence and security, as well as firms in cybersecurity, homeland security and energy “particularly in Africa”.
The official account says she developed contacts with presidents, ministers and senior officials and “worked to advance Israeli economic, defence and technological interests,” then founded a consultancy in government relations, business development and high-level negotiations.
After the October 7, 2023, cross-border blitz by Palestinian resistance group Hamas, she founded LOVE ISRAEL, a digital platform that supplies officials, diplomats and journalists with “survivor testimony” – a fact that shows she arrives in Athens not only with defence-business experience, but with an explicitly activist public-diplomacy background.
She has appeared as a political and defence analyst on Israeli TV, hosts The Main Issue with Adv Pninat Yanay, and writes for Maariv newspaper.
She is the sister of Ofer Yanay, founder of Nofar Energy and owner of Hapoel Tel Aviv basketball club – another fact that signals her proximity to political and business networks.
Defence deals
Defence deals have taken centre stage in the Israel-Greece relationship.
In April, Greece signed a contract worth about $750 million for 36 PULS multiple rocket launchers from Israel’s Elbit Systems. It was “one of the largest defence acquisitions” in recent years and deepened Greece’s integration into Israel’s defence ecosystem.
In late August, Athens and Tel Aviv signed a much larger Achilles Shield air-defence package worth $3.6 billion, further tying Greece’s air-defence infrastructure to Israeli technology. It is meant to integrate three Israeli air-defence systems, including David’s Sling, which is designed to counter ballistic and heavy missiles.
The other two systems are Spyder, which intercepts aircraft, helicopters, and unmanned aerial vehicles, and Barak MX, which intercepts aircraft and missiles. The system is being built on “Israeli architecture”, with key radars, missiles, sensors and command-and-control technology supplied by Israeli companies.
Israel’s Defence Ministry called it one of the largest export deals in the state’s history.
The agreement has also faced criticism inside Greece, with opposition groups warning that it deepens Athens’ military dependence on Israel.
These contracts follow a series of earlier defence deals.
In 2021, the two countries signed a $1.65 billion deal for Israeli defence contractor Elbit Systems to run a Hellenic Air Force training centre for 22 years.
In December 2025, Greece, Israel and Greece-administered southern Cyprus agreed to deepen military and security cooperation.
Energy deals between Tel Aviv and Athens also run in parallel.
Bilateral trade rose 41 percent in 2024, from about $920 million to $1.3 billion.
International media has described the alignment among Greece, Israel, and Greece-administered Cyprus as an effort to offset Turkish power.
Diplomacy or political deployment?
Yanay was not selected through the ordinary foreign-service ladder. The process, albeit legal, was political. She is supposed to be close to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The statement announcing her arrival in Athens made her public-diplomacy brief obvious.
“As a lawyer who has always defended the truth, I intend to fight fake news about Israel and present the beautiful side of the country,” she said.
The implied job is hybrid: manage defence and energy contracts, work the political elite, and contest the narrative in the Greek media at a time when Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza has made the partnership between the two countries more controversial in Greece.
Israel seems to have sent a media personality to Athens as top envoy whose working life has been at the junction of law, government access, defence contracts, and advocacy – instead of a dyed-in-the-wool diplomat like Noam Katz.
A wider shift in embassy’s role?
Israeli diplomacy has long mixed career envoys with political appointees to “high-value” diplomatic postings.
A decade ago, Greece was just like any other country with which Israel sought to increase trade and tourism.
But the growing relationship between Tel Aviv and Athens now looks like a defence-industrial and strategic alignment, marked by deeper military integration and growing reliance on Israeli defence systems with a public-opinion problem attached.
That’s why the profile of the new Israeli ambassador to Athens matters more than similar appointments elsewhere.
After all, a career diplomat is trained to carry out the whole set of diplomatic duties in a traditional manner. But a political operator with a defence and media background, such as Yanay, is expected to leverage her networks in ministries, defence contractors, journalists, and political circles.
The coming years will show whether Athens is a classic embassy that handles diplomatic business as usual, or a platform for deal-making and narrative management.

Ansarallah’s gains could reverberate beyond Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:36:01 UTC
00:36:01 KST

Ansarallah’s gains could reverberate beyond Saudi Arabia
TEHRAN - In a commentary published on its website, the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace said that victories by Yemen’s Ansarallah forces against Saudi-backed forces have brought them within 80 miles of Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, which houses the United States’ only permanent and largest military base on the African continent.
The article, written by Andrew Leber, a nonresident scholar in Carnegie’s Middle East Program, and Lesley Anne Warner, a visiting scholar with the Endowment’s Africa Program, argues that the fallout from Ansarallah’s advance could extend beyond Saudi Arabia.
Testifying before Congress last year, General Michael Langley, then the commander of U.S. Africa Command, warned that Ansarallah already possessed the capacity to strike the base facilities, should they decide to escalate attacks against the United States or its interests.
The article adds that military interventions by both the Biden and Trump administrations against Ansarallah forces ended in “strategic defeats”.
The following is a slightly edited version of the article:
Earlier this month, Ansarallah, an armed political movement that has controlled much of Yemen’s territory for more than a decade, took control over Yemen’s Red Sea coastline. Their rapid capture of the Port of Mokha marked the group’s first major military advance in nearly five years. It also further threatened global oil trade at a time when the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz (by Iran in response to the U.S.-Israeli war of aggression) has spiked energy prices worldwide.
Ansarallah initially stayed out of direct involvement in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. Still, their advance into Mokha reflects a steady escalation between Saudi Arabia and Ansarallah since mid-July, after the collapse of an initial U.S.-Iranian memorandum of understanding. On September 19, Ansarallah bombed a fuel depot at the main airport in Riyadh, sending a plume of black smoke over the Saudi capital.
This development reflects both the dynamics of a no-longer-frozen domestic Yemeni conflict and continued fallout from the U.S.-Iranian military and diplomatic stalemate in the Persian Gulf. It has also raised the possibility of additional U.S. intervention in the region against Ansarallah, though President Donald Trump has thus far declined to use force against the group.
Ansarallah’s advance gives them control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a crucial chokepoint at the southern end of the Red Sea. It also raises the possibility of opening a second front in the current Persian Gulf conflict—one that could target Saudi oil facilities and threaten an additional Red Sea chokepoint for global energy trade and other goods shipments. Past attacks on Red Sea traffic have already curtailed shipping through the strait while raising insurance and security costs on the remaining vessels.
Previous air campaigns by Saudi Arabia (with the support of other countries) sought to dislodge Ansarallah. However, these efforts contributed to a humanitarian catastrophe in Yemen and entrenched the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces in a fraught stalemate with Ansarallah. Later military interventions by both the Biden and Trump administrations against Ansarallah forces likewise ended in strategic defeats.
The latest advance also calls Saudi Arabia’s bluff that it could contain Ansarallah on its own, through a combination of quiet diplomacy and the unification of fragmented forces.
In the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, Ansarallah now controls the island of Perim (also known as Mayyun), which allows them to harass and disrupt maritime traffic. The advance also brings Ansarallah within 80 miles of Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, which houses Combined Joint Task Force–Horn of Africa and is the United States’ only permanent military facility on the continent. 
 
 Since the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas conflict and the resulting impact on maritime insecurity in the Red Sea, Djibouti has reportedly not allowed the United States to use its base for offensive operations against Ansarallah. The country has continued to play a balancing act between its criticism of Israel’s approach in Gaza and its utility as a relatively secure, geostrategic country that houses several foreign military bases.
When testifying before Congress last year, General Michael Langley, then the commander of U.S. Africa Command, warned that Ansarallah already possessed the capacity to strike the base facilities, should they decide to escalate attacks against the United States or U.S. interests.
How does this affect Saudi Arabia’s energy shipping?
Ansarallah’s control of Red Sea shipping corridors (at least the southern end) compounds a disastrous period for Saudi energy shipments. Around the same time as the Bab al-Mandeb takeover, the kingdom’s crucial East-West Pipeline was severely damaged. That energy corridor, combined with Red Sea ports in Jeddah and Yanbu, had allowed Saudi Arabia to offset a significant portion of the U.S.-Iran war’s direct economic costs.
The one-two punch of pipeline attacks and Red Sea seizures, however, risks forcing Saudi Arabia into relying more on fraught “dark crossings” of the Strait of Hormuz—or face a dramatic drop in oil revenues. Tellingly, the kingdom has already begun canceling key oil shipments to Europe.
Ansarallah’s gains further complicate efforts by the Arab Persian Gulf states to establish a common position for negotiating with Iran on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
There’s also a Somaliland dimension to this that doesn’t get much attention outside specialist circles.
Following Operation Al-Aqsa Flood on Oct. 7, 2023, and continuing during the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran this year, Ansarallah has targeted Saudi commercial vessels in the Red Sea—including more recently near the 18-mile-wide Bab al-Mandeb that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The Bab al-Mandeb is a maritime chokepoint through which roughly 12 percent of seaborne-traded oil travels, and the uptick in threats has forced many vessels to reroute around South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope. This has increased the strategic value of Somaliland, that declared independence from Somalia in 1991, and has added to the view in some Washington-based foreign policy circles that the United States should recognize Somaliland’s independence.
The Mogadishu-based federal government has never recognized Somaliland, treating it as an autonomous region. Tensions between Somaliland’s capital, Hargeisa, and Mogadishu escalated in 2024, when Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland, granting landlocked Ethiopia a fifty-year lease on approximately 20 kilometers of Somaliland’s coastline for a naval base and commercial port access, with the prospect that the former would extend formal diplomatic recognition to the latter in return. The memorandum provoked fierce opposition from Mogadishu, which accused Addis Ababa of violating its territorial integrity. In December 2024, Turkey brokered the Ankara Declaration between Ethiopia and Somalia, which committed both parties to respect each other’s territorial integrity and work toward “mutually advantageous” commercial arrangements for Ethiopian port access.
In defense policy circles, increased U.S. military engagement in Somaliland could be perceived as a hedge for the U.S. military presence in Djibouti, where President Ismail Omar Guelleh has been in power for almost three decades and is approaching his eighties. In addition, with the establishment of China’s first overseas military installation in Djibouti in 2017, Djibouti is the only place on the planet that has a permanent military presence from both the United States and China.
Until Israel’s unilateral recognition of the region as an independent state in December 2025, no country had ever recognized Somaliland. There has been speculation as to whether the United States would follow suit, due to Trump’s close relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his frequent disparagement of people of Somali descent as well as Somalia as a whole. In addition, Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi (also known as Irro) was in Washington recently, making the case for Somaliland recognition. As yet, there are no public indications that the executive branch has changed U.S. policy on recognition of Somaliland as an independent country.
It remains to be seen if Ansarallah forces can consolidate their hold on port cities such as Mokha and Dhubab, as well as the Red Sea island of Perim.
It also remains to be seen to see whether domestic pressure mounts on Saudi de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman to “do something” about the security dilemma facing the kingdom, as happened in the run-up to Saudi Arabia’s intervention in Yemen last winter. Currently, Saudi commentators are more focused on exhorting the international community to take action.
So far, Trump has demurred, with U.S. diplomats reaching out to Ansarallah counterparts mainly to ensure that the conflict does not directly implicate the United States. Saudi Arabia has reportedly reached out to China instead to try to restrain Ansarallah forces via Iran.
From the U.S.-Africa policy perspective, it remains to be seen whether the worsening of the security environment in the Red Sea and Horn of Africa provides additional justification for increased U.S. engagement. In fact, non-recognition of Somaliland has not inhibited high-level U.S. engagement with the region. A recent State Department report to Congress noted that the U.S. military “has regular engagements with Somaliland authorities and is exploring areas for potential cooperation.”
The United States has also been exploring a closer relationship with Eritrea, which sits north of Somaliland and Djibouti along the Red Sea. Last week, Washington allowed sanctions to expire on members of the ruling party and security forces tied to Eritrea’s conduct during the 2020–2022 conflict in northern Ethiopia, when it was on the side of the Ethiopian government. Given anticipation of renewed conflict in northern Ethiopia (and that Ethiopia and Eritrea have again fallen out and would be on opposite sides of the conflict), overlaid on rising insecurity in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb, I would not be surprised if these developments provide additional justification for U.S. engagement with Eritrea—notwithstanding the country’s human rights record.
The impact on maritime security, given the slight uptick in Somali piracy, which peaked over a decade ago also needed to be watched. Back then, a combination of industry-led measures and multinational naval patrols addressed the threat, but there are a few new variables this time around. One is that international order is more contested, meaning less coherence around military and nonmilitary means of addressing the evolving threats in the Bab al-Mandeb. The second is that the cross-strait relationships are now more evolved and strategic. The third is that the battlespace has evolved: Al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia already use drones for reconnaissance, and the latter group conducted its first confirmed drone strikes in January 2025. Given trends in commercial off-the-shelf drone technologies in the Sahel and West Africa, an expansion in use cases for these technologies seems likely.
Higher insurance costs for the shipping industry as a result of insecurity and higher freight costs associated with any need to reroute from the Bab al-Mandeb around the Cape of Good Hope is anticipated. These costs will inevitably be passed on to consumers. In particular, African economies have already weathered a succession of geopolitical shocks in recent years, with little time in between to increase their resilience, and they will have to brace for higher commodity costs.

‘We don’t need handouts’: Key takeaways from Putin’s first address to Russia’s new parliament

‘We don’t need handouts’: Key takeaways from Putin’s first address to Russia’s new parliament
Russian President Vladimir Putin has addressed the newly elected State Duma for the first time, outlining priorities from economic self-reliance and social spending to defense and long-term national security.
Speaking at the opening session of the ninth convocation of the lower house of parliament on Wednesday, Putin urged lawmakers to avoid economic missteps and “destructive populism,” stressing that Russia has the resources it needs to achieve its goals without outside assistance.
Here are the key takeaways from the president’s address.
‘We don’t need handouts’
Russia will not go around the world “begging for handouts with an outstretched hand,” Putin said while discussing the country’s finances and the new federal budget.
“Firstly, because it is humiliating. Secondly, nobody will give us anything, we know that very well. And thirdly – and most importantly – we don’t need it,” he said.
Putin described Russia’s financial system and economy as confident, but warned that mistakes are “absolutely unacceptable.”
He called for a balanced and realistic budget, while demanding that the government fully fund national projects and federal programs and meet all of its social commitments.
Putin also called for measures to boost investment and urged lawmakers to reduce administrative barriers for businesses.
Security and the Ukraine conflict
Defense and support for Russian troops and their families should remain among parliament’s top priorities, Putin said.
Lawmakers must focus on issues of “state importance,” strengthen the country’s defense capabilities and “do everything for our victory,” according to the president.
Putin also welcomed veterans of the Ukraine conflict elected to the new parliament, saying they had already demonstrated their commitment to the country “on the battlefield.”
He said national unity would allow Russia to “achieve its goals” and provide “reliable guarantees of security and sovereignty” for generations to come.
Developing the new regions
The first sitting coincided with Russia’s Day of Reunification, marking four years since Moscow incorporated the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics and the Kherson and Zaporozhye regions following referendums in September 2022.
Putin described the vote to join Russia as “clear” and “lawful,” and said the entire country is now involved in rebuilding and developing the territories.
The four regions are represented in the State Duma for the first time following this month’s election.
Putin said residents who went to the polls despite shelling and threats had demonstrated that the Russian people “cannot be broken or intimidated.”
Election shows ‘national unity’
The September 18-20 vote was accompanied by a massive Ukrainian drone raid targeting Moscow and other Russian regions.
Russian officials said more than 1,600 UAVs were repelled, including 450 on approaches to the capital, describing the unprecedented attack as an attempt to disrupt the elections. At least two civilians were reported killed in Moscow Region.
Putin said the turnout and election results had reaffirmed the strength of Russia’s multiparty political system and national unity in the face of what he called “historic challenges.”
The ruling United Russia party secured 349 of the State Duma’s 450 seats. Putin told the newly elected deputies that they bore a “particular responsibility” to voters and urged them to remain closely engaged with the people they represent.

Gulf media delays reporting on flydubai hijacking, consider Israeli sources unreliable - analysis

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:33:06 UTC
00:33:06 KST

An initial review of Gulf media reactions to the crisis aboard a flydubai flight that rapidly lost altitude and then landed in Saudi Arabia shows most media are taking a cautious approach to reporting the details.
While Israeli officials increasingly view the incident as an attempted hijacking and a disaster that was narrowly avoided by heroes on the plane, many reports in the Gulf appeared wary of reporting details at this point.
Hours after the incident unfolded, and after video showed bloodied passengers and crew, Al-Arabiya noted in the late afternoon that “a flydubai flight traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after an altercation occurred in the cockpit, the airline says.”
The report noted that “Flight FZ1073, which was traveling from Dubai International Airport to Ben Gurion International Airport, was secured by off-duty flydubai crew members who were traveling on board, according to the airline.”
Relying on the airline, the report said the crew diverted the aircraft and landed it in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. “All passengers and crew members were safe and accounted for, flydubai said…The airline said the reasons and motives behind the incident remained unknown at this early stage and would be subject to a formal investigation.”
Gulf media sources did not report the incident hours after it occurred
A further look at Gulf media revealed that some media outlets did not even report the incident, despite many hours having passed.
Other media provided only basic details. The National in the UAE, for instance, noted that “flydubai pilots taken to hospital after stabbing on Tel Aviv flight.
Saudi authorities say all passengers safe and accounted for after emergency landing in the kingdom. Video: Hijacking ruled out as flydubai flight lands safely in Saudi Arabia.” Gulf News in the UAE had not reported on the incident by 17:35 UAE time. Al-Ain media had also not covered it by the same time.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia had more coverage. Arab News noted, “Flydubai passenger jet pilots in bloody mid-air fight, Israeli media reports. Plane landed safely at Tabuk airport, all passengers are accounted for, the airline says. An Israeli official says pilots sent emergency signals after a physical altercation. Mystery surrounded the forced landing in Saudi Arabia of a flydubai flight traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, as conflicting accounts of the incident raised fears of a possible hijacking.”
Gulf media cautious, considers news from Israel unreliable
As noted above, Al-Arabiya had covered it. It also included an interview with a passenger where the passenger had said the co-pilot had stabbed the pilot. “The co-pilot stabbed the pilot and tried to bring the plane down.”
In Bahrain, the Daily Tribune had no articles on the story by 16:38 Bahrain time, which is 17:38 in the UAE. In Oman, the Muscat Daily also had no coverage at that time. Similarly, the media site Al-Jarida had no coverage by that time.
The difference in coverage between Israel and the Gulf was clear. Gulf media was more cautious. This is not entirely surprising. The Gulf prefers caution. Many media also prefer official statements. There was a statement from flydubai by the late afternoon. However, in the absence of other statements, many were reluctant to report further.
Well-known professor and author Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, who has a large following on X/Twitter, noted that “Israeli sources regarding the flydubai flight are not credible and are seeking to achieve a media scoop at the expense of reliability. Awaiting clarification from the Dubai Media Office.”

What the data really shows about ‘settler violence’ in the West Bank - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:33:04 UTC
00:33:04 KST

Fresh sanctions were recently imposed against Israel by the UK, France, and other governments, which cited – as did British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband – “ethnic cleansing perpetrated by settler terrorists.”
This argument was also front and center in the recent UN General Assembly, in a series of heated anti-Israeli speeches by world leaders. Yet newly obtained exclusive data from the Israeli Police through a freedom of information request cast serious doubt over the widely repeated “settler violence” narrative.
The “settler violence” campaign has been extremely effective in convincing European governments, and even some supporters of Israel, that hordes of Jewish terrorists attacking Palestinians are one of the top security challenges of the Middle East and pose a strategic threat to the prospects for peace.
Yet very rarely do politicians present verifiable evidence that illustrates what exactly they mean by “settler violence.” Statements often include a smoke screen of ominous warnings but provide few measurable metrics.
The data we obtained reveal a striking gap between the dire rhetoric and the unvarnished numbers.
First, nationalist violence among Israeli settlers has seen a sharp, 57% decline between 2023 and 2025. October 7 and the ensuing war have actually led to a sharp decrease in cases, amid a heightened military presence throughout the territories and the attention diverted to Gaza: 969 complaints in 2022, 1,066 in 2023, then 679 in 2024, and merely 614 incidents in 2025.
Unlike the acceptable method in the US, the data provided by the Israeli Police covers all complaints and hotline reports, without filtering out verified incidents.
But even taken at face value, this represents a crime rate of 3.07 per 10,000 people, an extremely low rate compared to Palestinian terrorism, crime in Israel’s other regions, antisemitic incidents in Europe, or crime rates in many large US cities.
Among Palestinians, abundant terrorist attacks, including murder and foiled suicide bombings, amount to 37.1 cases per 10,000 Palestinians – more than 12 times more than Israeli settlers.
Second, qualitatively – not just quantitatively – these figures represent not cases of murder, but delinquency, such as property theft, agricultural vandalism, or vehicle arson.
About 5-7% of the counted reports covered settlers confronting Israeli security forces rather than attacks on Palestinian civilians.
Vandalism and assault are doubtlessly crimes, but considering them as a state-sponsored effort of ethnic cleansing or as terrorism is absurd.
Third, openings of investigation files by the Police Interrogation Unit soared by 27% year over year, from 802 in 2024 to 1,024 in 2025, alongside dozens of criminal indictments – 40 in 2024 alone.
Most cases are prosecuted by the State Attorney’s Office, rather than the Police, and logically many more indictments are filed beyond these. This directly contradicts the widely quoted claim that Israel does little to prosecute perpetrators – even actively abetting them.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, President Issac Herzog, and even US Ambassador Mike Huckabee all personally condemned these crimes as “criminal acts of violence” that are committed by “a handful of hooligans who are violating the law, disturbing the IDF in fulfilling its missions, and harming Israel’s global reputation.”
The data follows the narrative
A larger prism tells us that vocal critics of “settler violence,” including heads of state, rely on extremely problematic figures, provided by impartial actors. The UN as well as the EU have both come under criticism for abandoning basic professional standards in their reporting on Israel.
The same goes for virtually any topic concerning Israel: Miliband cited the widely repeated and inflated figure of 70,000 fatalities in Gaza, a figure provided by the UN but has already been debunked as exclusively relying on data provided by Hamas’ “Health Ministry” – by the UN’s own admission.
The same applies to “settler violence,” where the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) cited as its sources “municipal authorities, Palestinian District Coordination Offices, UN agencies, human rights organizations, and media reports,” without naming any specific sources.
As previously revealed, a look at the OCHA database reveals that of the 6,285 alleged “settler violence” incidents it cites, 27.1% took place in Jerusalem, another 21% covered mere visits by Jews to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem (alongside Muslim worshippers and tourists), while others involve tensions between Israeli police and rioters in Jerusalem.
Testifying before the Knesset, the then-commander of the Central Intelligence Unit of the Israeli Police’s Judea and Samaria District, Avishai Mualem, confirmed the above-mentioned steep decline, as well as the false complaints phenomenon by Palestinians and far-left anarchists: “When 191 cases were opened, 90 of them were confirmed as false complaints around the South Hebron Mountain district. … In the Jordan Valley district, there were 70 incidents, of which 50% also ended up as false complaints.”
The EU, on its part, cites the far-left Israeli NGO B’tselem as the exclusive source for its figures. Unsurprisingly, its roughly $3.7 million budget originates primarily from the EU, the UN, and European governments, the same entities that later use the data to compile damning reports on Israel.
B’tselem falsely claims that “settler attacks” against Palestinians have seen a “sharp increase,” and its database includes multiple incidents such as “road blocking,” “verbal confrontations and threats,” and incidents in which “settlers stole a flock of grazing sheep.”
All of these may constitute wrongdoing but are far from fitting neatly within the customary understanding of ethnic cleansing or terrorism – nor are they uncommon in any large city in Europe or in the US.
Much lower crime rate than Baltimore
Indeed, compared with crime statistics elsewhere, 614 complaints of violent crimes attributed to a Jewish population of 462,000, or 3.07 per 10,000 people, is far below the rates in Baltimore (143.4) or New York City (70), representing over 46 and 22 times higher crime rates than Judea and Samaria, respectively.
Judea and Samaria also boast Israel’s lowest overall crime rate, by a wide margin: in 2024, the civil crime rate in Judea and Samaria reached 64 violent cases per 10,000 people, 1.4 times lower than Tel Aviv (91.7), and 2.1 times lower than the South (135.4).
Sharp increase in Palestinian terrorism
These incidents pale especially in comparison to the rate at which Israeli settlers themselves are targeted by Palestinians on a daily basis, including two different attacks last week alone, one of which resulted in the murder of Netanel Shukrun.
Rescuers Without Borders counted 6,389 attacks by Palestinians against Israelis in 2024 and 5,013 attacks in 2025. These figures include murder and shooting attacks, rather than mere vandalism or theft.
The Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) reports a 291% surge in the foiling of “substantial attacks” in Judea and Samaria between 2022 and 2025, in a coordinated effort with the IDF to arrest thousands of terrorists: 472 attacks were foiled in 2022, compared with 1,374 in 2025.
Once again, far from graffiti incidents, these were planned suicide bombings, hostage taking, and explosive cars.
Factoring in both actual and foiled Palestinian attacks, this amounts to 37.1 cases per 10,000 Palestinians – more than 12 times more than Israeli settlers.
Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria are routinely targeted by Palestinian terrorism: 71 Israelis were murdered in 2024 and 2025, while 744 were injured. Those victims include three Israelis murdered in January 2025 when a Palestinian gunman opened fire at bus line 55 en route to their settlement and two Israelis, including a 16-year-old, murdered at a gas station near their settlement. The two phenomena are simply incomparable in scale or lethality.
Palestinian state-sponsored terrorism
While the Israel Police has increased the opening of investigation files by 27%, and the Chief Prosecutor’s Office is indicting dozens of suspected offenders, the Palestinian Authority has been leading actual state-sponsored terrorism.
Not only does it fail to investigate Palestinian terrorism, but it actively rewards it by allocating over $10 billion in financial benefits to terrorists over the past decade alone.
While the top brass of Israel’s leadership condemned these delinquent attacks, Palestinian Authority chairman Mahmoud Abbas hailed the “martyrs,” a term widely used for terrorists, as the “stars in the sky of the Palestinian nation’s struggle.”
Abbas further stressed before the UN General Assembly that “even if we were left with just one penny, we would pay it to the families of the martyrs and prisoners.”
Based on evidence or a political objective?
The purpose of this analysis is not to excuse violence nor present a whataboutism argument. Anyone who commits a crime should be held accountable to the full extent of the law, as many of them eventually are.
Rather, the point is narrower: to put a widely circulated claim in proportion, and facts ahead of narratives, particularly in a region plagued by genuine terrorism and strategic security threats.
The data showed that while documented incidents of wrongdoing or criminal offenses among the Israeli settler population do occur, the “settler violence” narrative rests on shaky foundations, nor does it fit the established legal definition of ethnic cleansing.
There is no public record of Miliband referring to the genuine ethnic cleansing against Christians in Nigeria, where at least 50,000 people have been murdered, nor in Syria, where Israel ultimately intervened militarily to prevent further bloodshed.
Instead, Miliband dedicated a passionate 21-minute address to 614 cases of vehicle arson and graffiti.
The true objective of the “settler violence” campaign may be much simpler than debate over numbers: serving as a tool in the arsenal of smearing Israel’s very presence in the territories and putting political pressure to make concessions.
Israel, on its part, may do well in making these figures public and accessible, alongside the traditional defense of the overall law-abiding residents in Judea and Samaria.
We are all exposed to disinformation online, and in an online environment inundated with widely repeated claims, verifying them is becoming increasingly harder. Yet heads of state should distinguish facts from politics and take a sober, more balanced approach to an otherwise complicated conflict.
The author is an independent national security analyst and the host of the podcast Underscore. He was the founder and executive director of the David Institute for Security Policy under IDSF – the Israel Defense and Security Forum.

Russia draws up measures to control bear population after spate of deadly attacks

Russia draws up measures to control bear population after spate of deadly attacks
Sept 30 - The Russian government said on Wednesday it was drawing up urgent measures to control the population of brown bears that has spiralled out of control in some regions, with at least 22 people killed in attacks.
In the latest attack, reported by state media, a 23-year-old man out gathering berries was killed by a bear this week in Kamchatka, in Russia's far east.
Last week, a Russian woman in Siberia was fatally mauled by a bear in her garden, amid a nationwide spate of killings that experts blame on climate change and human incompetence.
"It is clear that as the population grows, so too does the number of problems. Systemic measures are needed to ensure that humans and animals can coexist safely and to maintain the necessary balance," said Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev.
"In this regard, the Russian government is currently preparing a series of priority measures," he said.
The government said it would look at lifting hunting quotas on brown bears, would establish regional population limits, give local authorities extra powers to control their numbers, and identify regions that need more financing to tackle the problem.
The population of brown bears has more than doubled in the last three decades to 308,000, in part due to shorter and milder winters. At least 22 people have been killed by bears across Russia, the world's largest country, since this spring, the RIA state news agency said.
Experts cited in Russian media have said bears have been forced to look further afield for food this year because an early and dry spring meant there was a lack of berries for them to feed on in September.
People are also guilty of leaving food waste out in the open where it attracts bears and of ignoring safety rules, experts say.
Investigators in Krasnoyarsk in Siberia — home to nearly 27,000 bears according to environment ministry data — said last week that they had opened a criminal case into the local environment ministry, accusing it of negligence that led to the deaths of seven people in September alone.
The federal environment ministry has sought to play down the spate of attacks, saying that around 20 to 30 cases of bear attacks have been recorded annually in recent years, but that social media and smartphones are making such attacks seem more widespread. REUTERS

According to a post published afterward by one of the hoaxer’s friends, the incident was a preplanned attempt to "troll media systems in Israel." The post claimed that during the interview, the hoaxer provided false details, invented names for himself and his brother, and claimed that both were on the flight. It also claimed that no one on the production team stopped the interview in time and that the hoaxer ultimately ended the conversation after feeling the prank had "already become too embarrassing."
The post’s author sharply criticized Channel 12 News’ handling of the incident, calling it "journalistic clownery." He claimed that the fact that the hoaxer managed to pass screening and remain on air for several minutes demonstrated a failure to verify the identities and credibility of interviewees during a developing event.
The incident quickly became a subject of jokes on social media, but it also raised broader questions about the process of verifying real-time testimonies, particularly during sensitive security incidents in which false information can spread within minutes. Channel 12 News declined to comment.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
US private sector employment increased by 90,000 in September, exceeding market expectations, payroll processing firm ADP said in a report Wednesday.
The figure surpassed expectations of 68,000 and accelerated from August's downwardly revised increase of 36,000.
Service providers added 59,000 jobs, while goods-producing industries created 31,000 positions, the report said.
Education and health services led employment gains with 55,000 new jobs, followed by leisure and hospitality with 22,000.
Manufacturing added 17,000 positions, while construction employment rose by 15,000.
Financial activities shed 16,000 jobs, professional and business services lost 11,000, and natural resources and mining employment declined by 1,000, ADP said.
 
The Northeast accounted for much of the increase, adding 56,000 jobs, according to the report.
By company size, businesses employing between 50 and 499 workers added 54,000 positions.
Base pay increased 3.2% from a year earlier, while gross pay rose 4.7%, ADP said.
"After a three-month slowdown, job creation rebounded and pay growth remained solid," ADP chief economist Nela Richardson said.
The report comes ahead of Friday's September employment figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which cover both private and public sector employment.
Economists expect nonfarm payrolls to increase by 84,000, following August's gain of 162,000, with the unemployment rate forecast to remain at 4.1%.

Ukraine’s intelligence reveals data on 23 Russian companies producing Pantsir missiles
Ukrinform reports this, citing HUR’s post on Facebook.
The data have been published on the War&Sanctions portal.
“Pantsir” is a family of Russian self-propelled short-range anti-aircraft gun-and-missile systems designed to provide air defense for important areas and individual military and industrial facilities.
Russia also uses these systems to strengthen air defense at low and extremely low altitudes and to protect against mass attacks involving air-launched weapons. Since 2023, the Russians have been installing Pantsir systems on rooftops in Moscow. This year, another modification of the system, the Pantsir-SMD-E, was spotted there. Unlike earlier variants, it uses smaller TKB-1055 Gvozd missiles instead of automatic cannons.
Previously, the HUR published information on more than 50 companies involved in producing the 72V6 combat vehicle used in the Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft gun-and-missile system.
Now, data on another 23 companies involved in producing 95Ya6 missiles have been disclosed. The 95Ya6 is the main medium-range missile used by various Pantsir modifications.
A key role in developing these missiles is played by the Academician Shipunov Instrument Design Bureau, the main developer and manufacturer of 95Ya6 missiles. The company is already known for its involvement in producing weapons for the Orion unmanned systems, Krasnopol guided projectiles and cannons for Su-family fighter aircraft.
At the same time, about one-third of the companies whose information was published today are not under sanctions imposed by any country in the sanctions coalition.
They include:
Komponent plant – a manufacturer of proximity target sensors for 95Ya6 missiles;
Sergo Ordzhonikidze Saratov Electrotechnical Plant – manufactures and supplies emission and power-supply units for these missiles;
Tambov Elektropribor plant – a manufacturer of steering units for 95Ya6 missiles.
The HUR emphasizes that, to effectively weaken Russia’s military potential, it is important to coordinate restrictions against companies involved in the production of the full range of Russian weapons, rather than offensive systems alone.
Air defense capabilities, including Pantsir systems, protect Russian enterprises that manufacture cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as Russian troop formations during offensive and defensive operations in Ukraine and other important facilities in Russia.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, the HUR has released data on 14 banks, financial intermediaries and payment systems that enable Russia to conduct international transactions while circumventing sanctions restrictions.
