European preference in defence is a 'luxury' debate, NATO chief tells Euronews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:30:14 UTC
00:30:14 KST

NATO chief Mark Rutte told Euronews the European preference debate is a "luxury" since neither Europe nor the US can meet the growing demand for defence products and the industry should ramp up its capacity.
A Brussels debate over a European preference in defence contracts ignores a basic problem: Europe's defence industry cannot produce enough, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte told Euronews on Wednesday.
"The problem is not: do you buy in Europe or do you buy it in the United States? The problem is: can you buy? The money is there. But the defense industrial base in Europe is underdeveloped. It is not producing enough," Rutte said at the Euronews Defence & Space Summit in Brussels on Wednesday.
In recent months, the EU has debated whether to favour European-made products in public defence contracts, deeply dividing France, which wants a strict preference, and Germany, which favours a more open approach towards NATO allies.
Rutte, who said he comes from a free-market tradition, called the debate misplaced because neither European nor American factories can meet surging demand.
"It's always better if you have these free markets functioning as open and independent as possible. But at the moment, I think it is a discussion of luxury, whether you buy European or American, because we cannot buy on both sides. There's not enough production," he said.
He urged industry to invest to meet long-term demand and to innovate to develop state-of-the-art products.
"European companies like Thales are investing in the US. US companies are investing in Europe. It is a transatlantic defence industrial base that is working as one, and that's exactly as it should be," Rutte continued.
He cited Ukraine's urgent need for anti-ballistic missile interceptors, which neither the Franco-Italian SAMP/T nor US-made Patriot systems can be produced in sufficient numbers to supply.
"There is enough money for everybody. And there will be a defence dividend coming from this, because all these investments will also lead to societal returns, not only in the defence output and the defence industrial base, but also innovation and everything else," Rutte added.

Russia ramps up disinformation attacks on French media ahead of 2027 Presidential race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:29:40 UTC
00:29:40 KST

Russia ramps up disinformation attacks on French media ahead of 2027 presidential race
Pro-Russian influence operations have caused a surge of 850% in fake news stories mimicking real media brands, according to a report published this week by disinformation specialist, NewsGuard. Out of the 15 most imitated news outlets, eight are French – including FRANCE 24.
Issued on: Modified:
The Russian disinformation operations that emerged at the start of the war in Ukraine have ramped up in the past year, with fake news articles and reports hijacking trusted media brands, to undermine public trust and deceive AI systems, a NewsGuard report released on Monday found.
Specialists from the US media watchdog found that three pro-Russian influence operations were the source of 950 fake news stories that mimicked 163 “supposedly trusted news brands” in 21 countries.
Among the 15 most imitated media brands were eight French outlets, including FRANCE 24, which saw its brand coopted by fake news stories 34 times over 12 months.
“It's no surprise that France, which is one of the biggest contributors of aid to Ukraine, is being specifically targeted,” said Chine Labbé, Europe editor at NewsGuard.
“We know that every time there is a show of diplomatic support for Ukraine – whether it's a speech by Emmanuel Macron, or a trip to Kyiv – disinformation campaigns follow within the same day.”
And ahead of the 2027 Presidential elections, France seems evermore in the crosshairs of pro-Russian actors.
Three presidential candidates who have pledged unwavering support for Ukraine – Raphaël Glucksmann, Gabriel Attal and Édouard Philippe – have all recently been the subject of fake news stories linked to pro-Russian groups.
Read moreRussia ramps up disinformation war as French presidential elections draw nearer
Europe on the front line
There are multiple objectives for Moscow’s information war according to NewsGuard, which compiled the report with the Ukrainian agency, Center for Countering Disinformation, French government agency Viginum, and anonymous research group, Antibot4Navalny.
These include discrediting support for Ukraine, undermining the reputation of Western leaders, stoking tensions within European democracies and disrupting electoral processes.
Year-on-year, the report found there had been an 850 percent increase in fake news stories mimicking known media brands – rising from 44 in the first half of 2025 to 421 in the first half of 2026.
“The explosion of this phenomenon may mean that the Russians see it as an effective tactic for eroding Western citizens' trust in the media – or at the very least, that there is significant potential to be tapped at little cost,” said Labbé.
“These days, it costs nothing to create a fake news site using AI and generate a lot of content.”
The report found pro-Kremlin influence campaigns had imitated media from global news outlets such as the BBC and CNN, to local news sites such as Ukraine’s Kyiv Independent and France’s La Montagne.
But European media outlets were the main target for this form of hybrid warfare linked to the Russian government under operations known as Matriochka, Storm-1516 and Doppelganger.
The most imitated outlet by far was Euronews, a multilingual platform based in France, which was the target for 82 fake articles between March 2023 and September 2026.
An example from 2026 was published shortly before Hungary’s parliamentary elections, which resulted in pro-Russian former prime minister Viktor Orban being removed from power.
It falsely claimed that pro-European candidate and current Prime Minister, Peter Magyar, called US President Donald Trump a “senile grandpa”, and that he wanted to end agreements between their two countries.
The other seven French news outlets among the 15 most targeted include Libération, Charlie Hebdo, BFM, FRANCE 24, Le Figaro, Le Parisien and Agence France-Presse (AFP).
“In every case, the Russian campaigns hijack the brands’ logos and layouts, sometimes creating a new site using a URL similar to the authentic one, making it difficult for the typical user to discern that it is counterfeit,” wrote NewsGuard. “The stories often include invented quotes from actual subject experts.”
“Leveraging a trusted media brand makes it possible to produce more credible fake news,” added Labbé. “But the long-term goal isn't to make you believe this or that piece of information. Their aim is to sow doubt in all our institutions.”
Read moreRussian interference in Armenia: A nation tested by disinformation
“It could damage trust, not only in our media, but in all media,” Cécile Mégie, Director of Editorial Strategies and Partnerships at France Médias Monde (FMM), which includes FRANCE 24 and RFI, told NewsGuard.
“It’s creating a climate of doubt about everything… The challenge is to navigate this climate and to show we are trustworthy media.”
Influencing AI
Disseminating disinformation on an industrial scale requires an army of fake social media accounts and pro-Kremlin media outlets that NewsGuard identifies as "the Pravda network", also known as Portal Kombat.
Made up of 280 websites that publish articles from pro-Russian outlets, Newsguard estimates that Pravda published approximately 6.3 million articles spreading 115 false claims in 2025.
One of the network’s stories published in 12 languages appeared to be from French news site Le Point. It falsely reported in 2026 that 20,000 Ukrainian soldiers had been evacuated to France for medical reasons where they had then deserted the army to join criminal gangs.
Read moreHybrid warfare: The threat of Russia looms over the Mediterranean
Official figures show that a little over 200 Ukrainians were transferred to French hospitals between February 2022 and April 2025, most of whom were war-wounded or children with serious medical conditions.
But the flood of fake news was enough to convince Google’s AI tool that the story could be real.
When questioned, the tech giant’s AI chatbot sourced fake articles supposedly from Le Point to claim that “thousands” of Ukrainian soldiers had received medical care in France.
“That's one of Matriochka's goals: to whitewash the Russian narrative by getting picked up by other media outlets or finding its way into chatbot responses,” said Labbé.
Read moreAI chatbot responses polluted by pro-Russian disinformation
Google defended its AI tool to NewsGuard, saying it had been unable to reproduce responses that referenced the fake news story.
“We have a high bar for our AI features in Search, and we invest significantly in the quality of responses,” a Google spokesperson said.
Yet another disinformation tactic aims to “overwhelm fact-checkers” themselves, using email campaigns to bombard journalists with fake reports, urging them to investigate their claims.
The goal – according to a 2025 Vigium report, is that fake stories will get picked up and gain traction.
Even if fake stories don’t go viral, they can still erode the overall quality of online news. “We need to be careful about how we address certain narratives,” said Labbé.
“We should treat fake news stories that don’t go viral differently from those that generate millions of views, but we still must continue to monitor them and document the tactics being used. If we don’t fight back, there’s a risk that AI tools will be influenced and citizens will be misinformed.”

Macron backs Spain over Ceuta migration crisis and urges firm EU action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:29:05 UTC
00:29:05 KST

Sánchez and Macron back cooperation between Spain and France and call for greater EU unity on migration, economic and geopolitical issues, despite the Spanish Senate's rejection of the bilateral Friendship Treaty.
The Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez and French president Emmanuel Macron highlighted the close relationship between their two countries and urged greater European unity to confront key migratory, economic and geopolitical challenges.
The joint press conference at the Moncloa Palace was also marked by the Spanish Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Friendship between Spain and France.
Sánchez apologised to Macron for the Upper House's no vote and promised that parliament would approve an agreement of this kind before the end of the current term. "All I can do is apologise," the Spanish premier said of Tuesday's rejection, insisting that the treaty would be adopted again to reaffirm the "sense of brotherhood" between the two countries.
The Treaty of Friendship, signed by Sánchez and Macron in Barcelona in January 2023, had already been endorsed by the lower house of parliament and ratified by France. However, the Senate voted it down on Tuesday, with 142 votes against from the PP and Vox, compared with 106 in favour and one abstention.
The rejection came six days after the Constitutional Court ruled unanimously, on 23 September, that the text was compatible with the Spanish constitution. One of the main flashpoints is a clause allowing a member of the French government to take part in meetings of the Spanish cabinet, and vice versa. Madrid and Paris exchanged letters clarifying that such participation would fall outside regular meetings of the Council of Ministers, but the PP has maintained its objections.
The parliamentary procedure still offers ways to resolve the stand-off between the two chambers. Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares accused the PP of "sabotaging" the agreement, while the conservatives insist their stance does not call into question France's strategic importance as a neighbour, ally and European partner.
Sánchez stresses cooperation between Madrid and Paris
During his remarks, Sánchez thanked Macron for France's "solidarity" with Spain during the "difficult days" of the Ceuta migration crisis and pointed to the cooperation between the two countries in various emergency situations.
"Together we have fought a thousand and one battles in a Europe that has faced multiple crises," the prime minister said, citing as examples the joint efforts to secure the EU's Next Generation recovery funds and their collaboration during last summer's wildfires.
Sánchez acknowledged that Spain and France have had their differences, but underlined that both governments have always sought to reach agreements. In this regard, he pointed to a "very strong bond" between the two countries in defending the European project.
Macron likewise stressed the historic ties between France and Spain, recalling that their peoples have "always fought side by side". The French president also highlighted the close bilateral cooperation in areas such as the economy, defence and energy interconnection.
Sánchez responds to Vivas and defends contact with Ceuta's government
Asked about the testimony given by Ceuta's president, Juan Jesús Vivas, before the National Court, Sánchez said that although he was not aware of the precise content of the questioning, there had been constant communication between the central government and the regional executive ahead of the mass arrival of migrants.
"There was constant communication with him and with his government," Sánchez said, explaining that in the days before the incident three-way meetings were held between the central government, the Autonomous City of Ceuta and the government's regional delegation. The prime minister insisted these were not isolated contacts. "There was not one or two, but many exchanges," he said.
Sánchez also argued that no one, including Ceuta's own authorities, could have foreseen the scale of the arrivals that eventually took place. "No one anticipated, neither did they, that we might see a mass influx like the one that occurred on 30 and 31 July," he said.
On a possible visit by the King and Queen of Spain to the autonomous city, Sánchez said there would be an official announcement in due course, but declined to give a date. "You will see when the time comes," he added.
By contrast, Macron stressed that Spain had been "the victim of a multiple attack" and expressed surprise at the reaction of some European countries which, he said, failed to show solidarity with Madrid despite having demanded such support themselves during similar migration episodes. His comments were a thinly veiled reference to Italy and the government of Giorgia Meloni.
Macron calls for balance between solidarity and responsibility on migration
The Ceuta crisis featured prominently in Macron's address. The French president voiced his country's solidarity with Spain and argued that the European pact on migration and asylum must strike the right balance.
"The balance between solidarity and responsibility is very important," Macron said, calling for "robust solutions" to protect the borders, but always within the framework of EU law and in full respect of the Union's values.
Spain and France urge greater ambition for Europe
The two leaders also agreed on the need to strengthen the European project. Sánchez called for a "far more ambitious" EU budget, while Macron argued that the bloc's finances will be crucial in meeting future challenges.
The French president also emphasised the need for EU member states to maintain a common line on trade relations with China. "If we are not united as Europeans, we have no chance of succeeding," he warned.
Sánchez urged deeper European cooperation on security and called for "more transparency" around algorithms and "more control" over fake accounts on social media. He also argued for new mechanisms to shield member states from possible "foreign interference in electoral processes".
Defending multilateralism and a rules-based international order
On foreign policy, Sánchez stressed that Spain and France share a "global vocation" and hold similar positions on a number of crises, including the war in Iran and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Both governments back a two-state solution.
"In the face of the law of the strongest and the fascination with authoritarianism, Spain and France will always stand up for multilateralism and a rules-based international order," Sánchez said.
The Spaniard argued that cooperation between the two countries stems both from their principles and from the interests. "A world without rules is a more insecure world for our citizens," he added.
Macron likewise underlined the need for a common European stance and praised coordination between Paris and Madrid in defending sovereignty, peace and international stability.
Macron's visit has thus served to publicly reinforce the alliance between Spain and France, despite the political strains surrounding the Treaty of Friendship. Both governments have stressed the need to maintain close cooperation and a coordinated position on the main challenges facing Spain, France and the European Union as a whole.

‘He persuaded us’: Labour ministers moved by Andy Burnham’s emotional conference speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:28:45 UTC
00:28:45 KST

The hottest ticket at Labour conference – after Andy Burnham’s speech – was an afterparty in Liverpool’s Baltic Triangle, headlined with a set by the noughties girlband Sugababes. As Labour activists and ministers belted out the lyrics under pink spotlights, it was hard not to draw some parallels with the party’s recent history.
There have been painful lineup changes and a lot of internal division, but this week onstage in Liverpool the originals are back together and they only played the hits. The fans can’t get enough.
Burnham’s own show on the main stage had the conference hall in raptures not because of Brexit or social care but because of the display of raw emotion after the tightly choreographed repression of the last six years. He may as well have walked across the stage with his feet crunching over the debris of shattered Ming vases.
The speech combined plans that had been forming inside Burnham’s head for the last decade as well as seat-of-his-pants political instinct. On the morning of the conference, the prime minister took off early for a morning jog and then returned to make final amendments. Even moments before he went on stage, he was still rewriting, aides said. About a quarter of the speech was entirely ad-libbed.
When Burnham was rehearsing the speech, aides said, he knew he was going to cry when he got to the paragraph about his late father – he never managed to get through any of the practice runs without tears.
But the long pause as he composed himself was the most emotional he had been. Several ministers said they themselves had been moved to tears, including Ed Miliband, who had recently lost his mother, as well as Louise Haigh and Anneliese Midgley, who are Burnham’s closest friends in government and the architects of his ascendancy.
After his speech, Burnham gathered all his ministers for a private pep talk. He said he knew they would not agree with everything, but – with the aura of a general sending his troops into battle – he told them to “get out there” and fight for it. He said he would not send them out with “a pea-shooter” – they needed proper weapons for the fight ahead and he promised he would provide them.
In the hallway outside the conference hall, minister after minister spoke with voices quivering with emotion. “This is all I have ever wanted,” one said.
The bar for speeches from political leaders has been low for the past decade or more. It is rare for clips to be anything more than a soundbite for social media and then a long shopping list of statistics and achievements. Burnham’s was the first time many MPs can recall a speech that was pure political argument.
And there was much in the speech that in normal times would have been a recipe for rebellion: Brexit, the triple lock, electoral reform and the lingering question marks over growth and defence.
“I found parts of the speech challenging, if I’m honest,” one cabinet minister admitted. “It contained things I had always thought we should never touch or an argument about public control which I would previously have said was too backward-looking. But in the room I agreed with every word because he persuaded us, he made an argument and made me question myself. It was a quite extraordinary thing.”
Even within the cabinet, there are those who grimace at the idea of electoral reform. “But you know, he believes in it, and I’m going to swallow it,” said one.
Burnham called his cabinet ministers in for a last-minute meeting just before the speech, where he laid out his private arguments and took their comments and feedback. “I feel almost embarrassed admitting this, but that has never happened before with any other leader,” one said.
On the sidelines of the conference, when cabinet ministers are at their most candid, they sometimes talk as if they have been through a kind of collective trauma – and the Burnham ascendancy has given them the release they need to confess how hard they have found the last two years. There are close new friendships and alliances forged in the coup, which defy previous factional lines.
“There’s the management-speak slogan: ‘Culture eats strategy for breakfast.’ Well, this is proof positive,” one cabinet minister said. “The past two years were utterly miserable, almost every single thing we achieved was poisoned by petty fighting. Every meeting was a choreographed exercise in pointlessness. Now we are discussing ideas and politics among colleagues who respect and like each other. I look back and I am so overwhelmed with relief that we did this.”
Another cabinet minister said: “I wasted so much of my own bandwidth fighting over the most puerile things, or defending my own staff who were being made miserable. Keir [Starmer] never dared to take it on.”
Even veterans of the Starmer years said they found themselves persuaded despite themselves. “Feels like there’s something quite psychologically profound about daring to take on the triple lock and finding that the planes don’t fall from the skies,” Starmer’s former strategy director Paul Ovenden posted.
Darren Jones, the ousted chief secretary who has made himself the face of the awkward squad, was also quick to lavish praise. “[The speech] told the story of his politics and the type of Britain he wants to build,” he said. “He told us we’d be in no doubt what his priorities are for the country, and he was right.”
Burnham will not welcome the comparison, but the closest recent one is how it felt at the Conservative party conference in the pre-disgrace Boris Johnson years: an electric electoral prospect who can genuinely reach across the political spectrum, hypnotising his doubters by the sheer force of his personality.
But this prime minister has no hint of the sleaze or incompetence that was always in the shadows for Johnson. If it comes, Burnham’s downfall will probably be his own voracious appetite for political risk – but that could also be the making of his premiership.

What happened on the diverted Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv?
Israel’s prime minister said one of the pilots stabbed the other and then tried to crash the plane.
A flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel was diverted to Saudi Arabia after one of the plane’s two pilots attempted to stab the other in the cockpit on Wednesday.
UAE’s Attorney General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi ordered an investigation into the incident on Thursday. According to his office, the investigation team would “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details, and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it”.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, said it was too early to declare a motive for the incident, which occurred on a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, while responding to a question on whether he thought Iran was behind the incident.
Netanyahu added that Israel would “possibly” be participating in the probe into the incident.
“It’s too early to say; the attacking pilot is … now being investigated in Saudi Arabia. I think he’ll be taken to the Emirates, where he comes from, or at least where he left, where he flew off from, and we’ll be following and possibly also participating in this investigation,” Netanyahu said in an interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity on the Hannity programme.
The Flydubai flight FZ1073 was diverted as it flew from Dubai to Tel Aviv through Jordanian airspace, prompting Israel to deploy warplanes, the Reuters news agency reported. Passengers on the flight reached Israel safely on Wednesday after the copilot’s attempt to crash the aircraft was foiled, Israeli officials said.
The struggle began when he stabbed the pilot and sent the jet plunging nearly 14,000 feet (4,267 metres) in less than 30 seconds.
Earlier, Netanyahu had noted that one of the pilots had stabbed the other and then tried to crash the plane. He added that Israel was preparing for other “potential threats” after the incident.
“At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” a Flydubai spokesperson said in a statement. “We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts.”
At Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport, where the plane landed, officials said the plane’s captain and first officer were taken to hospital after sustaining injuries, according to a statement from Tabuk airport, carried by Saudi state-run Al Ekhbariya TV.
India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia later identified the injured captain as Indian national Smit Machchhar. It said he was receiving treatment at a hospital in Tabuk and was reported to be in stable condition, adding that it was in contact with his family and Saudi authorities.
The UAE has become a popular holiday destination for Israeli tourists since the countries normalised ties in 2020. Here’s what we know about what happened.
What happened?
Footage taken on board the plane appears to show the injured pilot lying on the cabin floor with several stab wounds, and a passenger with a bloody head wound.
The leaders of Israel and India hailed pilot Machchhar as a hero for saving passengers after his colleague stabbed him.
Machchhar was covered with blood on the floor when he managed to click the release to open the cockpit door, a spokesperson for Netanyahu told Reuters.
That allowed passengers and crew to overpower the copilot and enabled a second pair of Flydubai pilots on board to land the jet in Tabuk.
“He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals,” Netanyahu said in a post on X. “All passengers are out of harm’s way,” he had earlier said in a video statement released by his office.
In a post on X early on Thursday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi lauded Machchhar, calling him a “hero”.
In another video, passengers wept and cried out in distress as the aircraft shook.
Yasmin Abukasis, the mother of one of the passengers on board, said her daughter Miriam thought she was going to die. “The plane started to lose control,” she told journalists at Israel’s Ben Gurion airport, before the aircraft was stabilised.
Flight tracking data indicated the plane descended almost 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds about two and a half hours after leaving Dubai. Flightradar24 said on X that an initial general emergency signal designated by code 7700 was issued at about 05:31 GMT and later changed to another emergency signal with code 7500 declaring “unlawful interference”.
Passenger Dalia Shpigel told Israeli newspaper Haaretz that some people seated towards the front of the plane broke into the cockpit after it began to descend and they realised something was wrong.
“An hour before landing, we felt that there was no control over the plane, that it was starting to jump,” she said. “The guys saw that the plane had begun to dive and broke into the cockpit.”
Netanyahu said he later spoke to one of the Israeli passengers who broke into the cockpit and overpowered one of the pilots who was reportedly trying to sabotage the aircraft’s systems.
“I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage,” Netanyahu said in a statement. “They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster.”
Passenger Yitzhak Lieber, reportedly one of the men who overpowered the copilot, sent a video to his family from the plane, international media reported. In it, he says: “There is a pilot who was seriously injured. They’ve evacuated him. We overpowered the terrorist, and he is tied up.”
The mostly Israeli passengers were later flown to Tel Aviv on a replacement flight, Tabuk airport confirmed.
The Times of Israel reported that Netanyahu was at Ben Gurion’s Terminal 1 building to greet passengers when the replacement flight landed shortly before 16:00 GMT. Families were waiting in a designated area at the domestic arrivals hall while security officials prepared to interview them.

What do we know about the motive for the incident?
The motive of the apparent attack was not immediately clear. Netanyahu said Saudi authorities were interrogating the pilot accused of carrying out the attack.
“We’ll get to the root of this attacker, whether he had accomplices, whether Iran was behind it. I think we’ll find out very soon,” the Israeli PM said on Wednesday.
Israel’s Defence Minister Israel Katz said preliminary information indicated the attacker intended to crash the plane and kill everyone on board, calling the incident an “attempted jihadist terror attack”.
An Israeli official who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity identified the attacker as an Omani national.
Israel does not have formal diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia or Oman, maintaining a policy of occasional dialogue through informal channels. Muscat has chosen not to join other countries in the region in normalising ties with Israel over Palestinian rights. Saudi Arabia has made normalisation of Israeli ties conditional on Israel’s acceptance of a Palestinian state.
The incident comes days before the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and which triggered Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians – mostly women and children – including about 1,400 since a United States-brokered “ceasefire” took effect in October 2025.
Was a second Flydubai flight diverted?
No. A second Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, FZ1081, was erroneously reported in Hebrew media to have turned around, according to The Times of Israel.
The news outlet added that the mistake was likely due to a glitch on flight-tracking sites.
The plane did not issue any emergency signal, and it was reported to be on course to Tel Aviv without disruptions.
What has the response been?
Reuters reported that Netanyahu has ordered authorities to “ramp up” security on Israeli carriers and non-Israeli carriers, quoting a spokesperson for the prime minister’s office.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid claimed Netanyahu’s political allies had attempted to pass off the incident as the fulfilment of warnings a day earlier about a possible attack on Israel ahead of its legislative election scheduled for October 27.
“The warning about activity abroad is specific, has been in place for more than two years, and has nothing to do with planes or anything resembling what happened this morning,” Lapid wrote on X.
Speaking of Netanyahu, Lapid said: “He’s trying to hitch a pathetic ride on heroic Israelis who prevented a disaster that he [once again] wasn’t prepared for.”

China Focus: Beijing deploys 400 mln parasitic wasps in biological control effort targeting invasive fall webworm
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:25:45 CST
00:25:45 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Beijing is fighting an invasive pest with an army of natural enemies. Since Monday, the Chinese capital has been releasing another 400 million parasitic wasps to control a surge of fall webworms.
These wasps, known scientifically as Chouioia cunea Yang, are dominant parasitic natural enemies of the pest and safe for humans and livestock. "Earlier this year alone, Beijing unleashed nearly 700 million of them," said Yang Zhongqi, chief scientist at the Chinese Academy of Forestry and also the discoverer of the wasp.
The fall webworm, a major invasive pest native to North America, produces three generations a year, each passing through four life stages, namely egg, larva, pupa and adult. Beijing is currently in the peak damage period of third-generation fall webworm larvae, with a surge of mature larvae set to descend from trees to pupate, Yang said.
The fall webworm can damage more than 300 plant species. In the capital, over 200 species of trees, fruit trees, flowers and crops are under threat, with ash, mulberry and plane trees among its favorite targets. The pest only damages plants -- neither its larvae nor adults are toxic or harmful to humans, the expert added.
In response to residents' reports that fall webworms have been noticeably more numerous in Beijing this year compared with previous years, Yang Sihan, with the Beijing municipal landscape and greenery resource protection center, attributed the increase mainly to warmer winters and frequent summer rainfall.
Warmer winters in recent years have pushed up the survival rate of the pest's overwintering pupae. "Our five-year survey of overwintering populations in some areas shows that the survival rate of overwintering pupae rose from 65.3 percent in 2023 to 84.2 percent this year," Yang noted, adding that frequent rainfall in Beijing this summer also hampered pest control operations.
Experts explained that the difficulty of controlling the fall webworm is directly tied to the pest's own characteristics and the practical challenges involved.
The fall webworm has an extremely strong reproductive capacity. A single female moth lays an average of 300 to 600 eggs, and up to 2,000 under favorable conditions. Even a small number of surviving insects can allow the population to rebound rapidly. Moreover, the fall webworm showed pronounced generation overlap this year, with multiple life stages present at the same time.
Urban operational conditions also pose challenges. Narrow spaces, tall trees with dense canopies, and the limited range of some ground sprayers can all reduce the effectiveness of pest control.
Despite these challenges, local authorities have rolled out a coordinated response combining early warning and control measures.
According to Yang Sihan, almost 3,000 monitoring sites have been set up across the city under a grid-based management system. Based on pest patterns, meteorological data and expert consultation, officials issue rolling long-, medium- and short-term warnings to guide precise action.
On the control front, beyond releasing parasitic wasps for biological control, crews manually remove larval webs and wrap corrugated paper and non-woven fabric around tree trunks to trap mature larvae descending to pupate.
Traps and insect-killing lamps are also deployed to trap and kill adult moths, thereby breaking the reproductive cycle. In addition, authorities use high-efficiency, low-toxicity, eco-friendly pesticides and carry out ground spraying at staggered times.
The Beijing Municipal Forestry and Parks Bureau is calling on residents to help control this pest.
The bureau advised residents to clear away dead branches, fallen leaves and clutter around their homes to remove places where larvae can pupate. It also suggested cutting off infested branches and leaves when larval webs are spotted, and disposing of them in sealed bags. Mature larvae on tree trunks or the ground, notably, can simply be crushed underfoot.
Meanwhile, anyone who notices chewed leaves, webs or mature larvae on trees in public areas can call the 12345 citizen hotline or report it to their local landscaping and greening department, the bureau added. ■

Ukraine Needs 20mm F-16 Ammo to Down Russian Jet Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:25:39 UTC
00:25:39 KST

Ukraine wants to purchase tens of hundreds of thousands of 20-millimeter rounds for its F-16 fighter aircraft to shoot down Russia’s increasingly deployed jet-powered attack drones.
Kyiv is negotiating with several European countries and ammunition manufacturers about potential supplies, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, Sept. 30, citing people familiar with the discussions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The ammunition would be fired from the F-16’s built-in cannon, offering Ukraine a potentially cheaper and more widely available alternative to using scarce air-to-air missiles against each Russian drone.
According to Bloomberg, destroying one drone may require approximately 150 rounds. At the current intensity of Russian attacks, Ukraine could need around 10,000 such rounds per day.
Cheaper option against Russian drones
Ukraine has used AIM-9 Sidewinder and AIM-120 AMRAAM missiles launched from F-16s to intercept Russian aerial targets. These guided missiles are considerably more expensive than cannon ammunition and are also needed by ground-based air defense systems.
Ukrainian F-16 pilots are already using their aircraft’s 20-millimeter cannons against jet-powered drones when other intercept options were unavailable.
The F-16 carries an internally mounted M61A1 Vulcan six-barrel rotary cannon that fires 6,000 rounds per minute. Using it allows pilots to preserve guided missiles for cruise missiles and other high-priority targets.
Each aircraft carries 500 usable rounds of semi-armor piercing, high-explosives, incendiary (SAPHEI) PGU-28 20mm cartridges.
Pentagon Commits Nearly All $400M in Ukraine Aid a Day Before Deadline
In employing the gun against airborne targets, pilots usually fire half-second bursts which puts out 50 exploding bullets in each brief trigger squeeze. And the trigger is positioned in the same place as it is when shooting a firearm – under your right index finger.
The tactic nevertheless requires pilots to approach drones at relatively close range. Shahed drones are approximately 1/10 the size of an average fighter, which at maximum range for the typical gunshot of 4,000 feet slant range, the target is about 2 milliradians or about the size of the smallest item in the heads-up display (HUD) which is a dot, or about the size of a decimal or period on this page.
Falling debris from destroyed drones and overspray from the natural dispersion of projectiles that don’t hit the target may also endanger people and property within the Vulcan’s ground projected elliptical footprint when intercepts take place over populated areas.
Bloomberg reported that global supplies of 20-millimeter ammunition are more plentiful than stocks of Patriot and Western air-to-air missiles, potentially allowing Kyiv to obtain the rounds more quickly.
Russia expands jet-powered drone attacks
Russia has rapidly increased its use of jet-powered drones, which fly faster and higher than conventional propeller-driven Shaheds and are more difficult for mobile fire groups and existing interceptor drones to destroy.
According to Ukrainian Air Force, Russian launches of jet-powered drones rose from around 350 in June to approximately 2,850 in August.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia launched more than 100 drones on Tuesday, including 29 jet-powered models. Ukrainian forces intercepted 18 of the faster drones, he said.
Ukraine is simultaneously developing high-speed interceptor drones and other domestic systems to counter the new threat. Zelensky said on Tuesday that officials had selected the first prototypes of a dedicated countermeasure and established deadlines, financing requirements and planned production volumes.
Kyiv has also received urgent deliveries of F-16 ammunition from Belgium, Spain and other partners. Belgium has agreed to transfer three additional F-16 fighters to Ukraine by the end of 2026.
“As Russia escalates its attacks every day, we need to add more capabilities to shoot down aerial targets and protect people,” Zelensky said.

China calls for improving global human rights governance: envoy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:25:15 CST
00:25:15 KST

Jia Guide, China's permanent representative to the UN Office at Geneva and other international organizations in Switzerland, speaks at the 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) at the Palais des Nations in Geneva, Switzerland, Sept. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Lian Yi)
GENEVA, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China called on the international community to establish a just, equitable, and inclusive global human rights governance system guided by the Global Governance Initiative on Wednesday.
Jia Guide, China's permanent representative to the UN Office at Geneva and other international organizations in Switzerland, made the remarks while delivering a joint statement entitled "Improving International Human Rights Governance," on behalf of 71 countries at the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council at the Palais des Nations.
The Global Governance Initiative, proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sept. 1, 2025, has received support and positive responses from numerous countries and international organizations.
Jia noted in this joint statement that the international landscape is undergoing profound changes amid a complex and turbulent environment, while global human rights governance is facing profound adjustments.
He said that China puts forward four proposals:
First, adopt a people-centered approach. It is up to the people of each country to assess and improve their own human rights situation, so as to stay true to the original purpose of human rights governance and meet the people's needs.
Second, uphold sovereign equality. All countries should participate, make decisions and benefit on an equal footing. Greater attention should be paid to the voices of the Global South. We advocate fairness, objectivity and non-selectivity, and call for dialogue and cooperation based on mutual respect.
Third, uphold fairness and justice. We oppose the politicization and instrumentalization of human rights, take a holistic approach to all categories of human rights, advance human rights reform in a prudent manner, and support multilateral human rights institutions and experts in discharging their mandates objectively and impartially.
Fourth, uphold the international rule of law. We champion the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, ensure the equal and consistent application of international law and international rules, and oppose double standards, interference in the internal affairs of other countries under the pretext of human rights, and imposition of one's own standards on others.
The joint statement is based on the platform of The Group of Friends of Global Governance in Geneva, officially launched on Feb. 27, 2026, at the Palais des Nations. ■

Thailand's economy broadly stable in August: central bank
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
23:25:13 CST
00:25:13 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's economy remained broadly unchanged in August on a monthly basis, as higher private investment and a slight rise in private consumption offset declines in manufacturing output and service-sector activity, the central bank said on Wednesday.
According to the Bank of Thailand, merchandise exports excluding gold held steady at a high level, dipping 0.1 percent in August from a month earlier, supported by the global technology and artificial intelligence (AI) cycle.
Electronics exports decreased, reflecting lower shipments of computer parts and electronic integrated circuits and components. Automotive exports also dropped, while exports of petroleum and agricultural products increased, the central bank said in a statement.
Inbound tourists rose 1.8 percent from the previous month, mainly driven by higher arrivals from China, partly due to stronger travel demand during the summer school holiday period, the central bank's assistant governor, Chayawadee Chai-anant, said.
Despite that, tourism receipts remained relatively stable as the average length of stay for foreign tourists shortened, reflecting the recovery of long-haul flights to levels close to those seen before the outbreak of the Middle East conflict, Chayawadee told a news conference.
On domestic demand, private investment rose 2.2 percent month-on-month, boosted by higher investment in machinery and equipment and supported by the global technology cycle and investment in data centers, Chayawadee said.
Private consumption picked up 0.4 percent from a month earlier, fueled by higher spending on services, notably hotels and restaurants, in line with increased foreign arrivals, while spending on durable goods also continued to grow, she noted.
Looking ahead, the central bank expects the Thai economy to recover, though unevenly across sectors, with key growth drivers being exports and private investment, which benefit from the global electronics and AI cycle.
Meanwhile, household consumption is supported by government stimulus measures and improving labor income prospects, consistent with the rebound in tourism and higher agricultural commodity prices, the central bank said.
It added that geopolitical conflicts and international trade protectionist policies, alongside the impact of flooding and El Nino weather conditions, were among the key factors to monitor. ■

====================================================================================================

Western F-16s promised safe skies over Kiev: Why could they all go MIA soon?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:24:18 UTC
00:24:18 KST

Western F-16s promised safe skies over Kiev: Why could they all go MIA soon?
Ukraine’s NATO-donated F-16 fleet is out of commission more often than it engages Russian drones, The Wall Street Journal has claimed.
The American-produced fighter jets were touted as the latest “gamechanger” weapon in Kiev’s conflict with Russia, a tool that will help “achieve goals outside of Ukraine,” as Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said when the first batch was set to arrive in the summer of 2024.
However, a key EU member in the European-led scheme cannot keep up with necessary maintenance of the fleet, according to the newspaper.
What is the F-16 initiative?
The plan was launched in 2023, as Ukraine’s fleet of Soviet-built military aircraft was dwindling. Pro-Kiev propaganda implied that the US-made multirole jets would help Ukrainian forces challenge Russia’s air dominance over the front line. But it was hardly a secret that they would be kept far away from Russian SAMs and fighter jets and only engage long-range drones and cruise missiles.
Donor nations announced they were prepared to spend years training Ukrainian pilots, refurbishing the aircraft they were willing to spare, and happily signing deals for modern replacements to bolster their own militaries – the F-16 initiative was effectively a NATO-backed pyramid scheme allowing everyone to spend big and upgrade their air forces.
Ukraine has since received about 40 jets, roughly half of what the donors pledged, and lost several of them during combat missions, reportedly after corners were cut for expediency during training courses. It is now facing winter with an acute shortage of air defense systems.
What’s the problem?
Belgium’s Sabena Aerospace Engineering, awarded a $235.5 million contract for maintenance of Ukraine’s F-16 fleet, is not keeping up with the demand, according to the Wall Street Journal editorial board.
An inspection that normally takes two to six weeks lasts “as long as 40 weeks in Belgium,” retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery said. Another Western source said more than half of Ukrainian jets are now in maintenance limbo, with the rest set to become grounded by the end of the year.
Was the issue unexpected?
Media reports saying that the Ukrainian F-16 fleet is being overworked surfaced as early as July, as Kiev’s shortage of ground-launched interceptor missiles became more acute. There were also indicators pointing to a bottleneck in Belgium.
In April, the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation reported that not one of the six F-16s that Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store pledged to Ukraine in 2023 had been delivered. Four of them were not airworthy to begin with, but the two others were previously used to train Ukrainian pilots in Denmark.
The six jets were stuck at a Sabena workshop in Belgium due to “significant capacity problems,” the report said.
Is Ukraine getting more jets?
There were delays in deliveries as well.
Belgium promised in 2024 to transfer 30 aircraft set to be phased out by its air force, which was expecting F-35 replacements. Then-Defense Minister Ludivine Dedonder said Ukraine would start receiving the old jets “as soon as the F-35s arrive on Belgian soil,” but no transfers have been reported since.
Most of the aircraft that Kiev did get reportedly came from the Netherlands and Denmark, the co-leaders of the F-16 initiative.
Why does Ukraine have air defense problems?
A shortage of Western weapons partially caused Ukraine’s current situation.
When this summer Vladimir Zelensky announced a 40-day “pressure campaign” of long-rage strikes on refineries, civilian ships, and commercial warehouses, his team reportedly hoped that images of smoke-plumes stretching over big Russian cities would support his bid to receive more Patriot missile interceptors from the limited US stockpile.
If true, the plan backfired. NATO nations are scrambling to provide what Kiev wants, while the economic damage caused by Russian retaliation is mounting. And Ukraine already has a $27 billion military budget hole that European donors are struggling to fill.
Ukrainian forces previously learned that Western arms gifts come with caveats. Donated NATO artillery systems lacked interoperability and were described as a “zoo” by troops. Much-hyped NATO battle tanks turned out to be mostly useless in drone-driven warfare and had to be kept away from the front line.
Can Ukraine come up with alternatives?
Zelensky puts on a brave face talking about the dire situation. Last week he claimed Ukraine had successfully tested four new interceptor drones designed to shoot down faster-moving jet UAVs – the kind of targets the WSJ claimed F-16s are well-suited to take down.
But an earlier Reuters report said trials in July “did not go to plan” as the prototypes lost control and “crashed into nearby fields and forests.”
Ukrainian opposition lawmaker Sergey Rakhmanin, who sits on the national defense committee, has said Kiev missed Russia’s rapid development of jet kamikaze drones. He said Ukrainian interceptors cost up to $100,000 apiece and that scaling up production would require too much time, even if funding becomes available.

Readings in Korean Confucian Philosophy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:23:00 UTC
00:23:00 KST

When I first held Ivanhoe and Wang’s Readings in Korean Confucian Philosophy in my hands and leafed through it, I immediately regretted retiring from teaching a couple of months earlier. I had taught Korean cultural history for decades but, since most of my students couldn’t read Korean or Classical Chinese, I couldn’t include substantial excerpts from the writings of Korean Confucian philosophers among the primary sources I asked them to read. Now that I was no longer teaching undergraduates, I had finally found a book with material I could have assigned. Moreover, the excerpts translated are short enough (with the exception of a lengthy translation at the end of Dasan’s reflections on Mencius) that undergraduates wouldn’t be frightened by them.
Making it even more useful for students, the book opens with a concise survey of the history of Neo-Confucianism on the Korean peninsula, focusing on the eight individuals who provide the material translated for this work. I am disappointed that the introduction doesn’t discuss the earlier history of Confucianism in Korea. However, I realize that this is probably because the earlier versions of Confucianism in Korea were not particularly philosophical. Instead, they were more concerned with government administration, history, and literature. Nevertheless, this book should have been called Readings in Korean Neo-Confucian Philosophy, since only that more philosophical version of Confucianism is covered in these pages.
Ivanhoe and Wang chose to translate excerpts from the writings of eight individuals important in shaping Korean Neo-Confucianism over the five-plus centuries of Joseon (1392-1910). The first two, Jeong Dojeon (1342-1398) and Gwon Geun (1352-1409), were major figures in the introduction of Neo-Confucianism to Korea in the late 14th and early 15th centuries. The next two, Seo Gyeongdeok (1489-1546) and Yi Eonjeok (1491-1553), helped solidify Neo-Confucianism’s presence on Korean soil by delving deeply into its core principles as articulated earlier in China. The third group consists of two of the most important philosophers in all of Joseon’s history, Yi Hwang (1501-1570) and Yi I (1536-1584). Both men are often given credit for Korean-izing Neo-Confucianism in the 16th century by focusing attention on issues which Chinese Confucians had not paid as much attention to, such as the role of emotions in stimulating behavior. Finally, the last group, Jeong Jedu (1649-1736) and Jeong Yakyong (1762-1836), were active in the second half of Joseon. They are known for pushing the boundaries of Neo-Confucian philosophy in Korea, promoting approaches which, though still undeniably Confucian, departed significantly from the mainstream.
The translations in this anthology are readable and, by and large, faithful to the original texts. However, I would have liked to have seen a better indication in the translations of key terms that Confucianism is more about doing than being, more about what happens or is done than about what is, and more about interactions than about solitary existence.[1] One example of a somewhat misleading translation is “sincerity”. In English, that term suggests an absence of deceit or hypocrisy. But the Chinese character translated here as “sincerity” (seong/cheng) means much more than that. It refers to acting in a selfless manner, doing what one is supposed to do according to the role one is playing in the situation one finds oneself in, without trying to gain some personal advantage or follow one’s personal predilections. Because “sincerity” is such an important term in the revered classic The Doctrine of the Mean, it appears in the writings of all eight men featured in this anthology. Gwon Geun, when explaining Neo-Confucianism to his students, told them that sincerity encompasses the different ways human beings act appropriately, saying it referred to the “actual cycle of operations” of major human virtues (55). Readers should have been reminded of that active sense of sincerity when that term reappears in this book.
“Pattern” (i/li) is another problematic translation. It does mean pattern, but it is more dynamic than that translation alone suggests. It refers to normative patterns, which both define and direct appropriate actions in interactive situations. I wish Ivanhoe and Wang had been more explicit about the normative and directive nature of “pattern” and had also signaled in the way they translated that key term that it always refers to at least potential interactions. As Gwon Geon explained, “Pattern is the public-spirited Way (i.e., not some private or personal point of view)” (8). Way is their translation of Dao, which, as Ivanhoe and Wang well know, means the proper way to behave. Unfortunately, their decision to stick to the standard way of rendering those key Neo-Confucian concepts in English means that their translations do not adequately reflect the behavioral implications of these core Neo-Confucian terms.
Those are not their only translation choices which fail to reflect the dynamism I would have liked to have seen. For example, in a poem by Yi Eonjeok, “i ryun” is translated as “the unvarying standard” (136). This is an incomplete translation. “I ryun” means “the unvarying ethical standards”, the fundamental guidelines for human interactions. Similarly, they translate Yi I as defining human nature as “humaneness, righteousness, rites, wisdom, and trustworthiness” (191). Since those five terms refers to different ways of acting appropriately, they should have been translated as verbal phrases rather than as nouns. Yi I was saying that human nature is the potential for acting in humane, righteous, polite, wise, and trustworthy manners.
Two key terms, terms which appear multiple times throughout this text, are eum and yang (C. yin and yang), which Ivanhoe and Wang wisely left untranslated. However, it would have helped readers unfamiliar with Confucian ways of thinking if they had explained the eum and yang are not things. They are instead complementary ways of interacting, with eum referring to the less active and yang to the more active. That meaning is implied in the statement by the Chinese Neo-Confucian Zhu Xi (1130-1200) cited by Yi Hwang: “The Supreme Ultimate moves and produces yang, is still and produces eum” (139).
These quibbles of mine do not mean that I disagree with their translation choices overall. In fact, I may borrow for my own work their “reverential attention” for gyeong (C. jing) and “sympathetic concern” for seo (C. shu). Nor does my preference for more action-oriented translations mean that I would be uncomfortable assigning this to undergraduates. Far from it. I like the wide range of material included, from poetry and letters to philosophical essays and civil service exam policy questions. And I was pleased to see that they even include such visual aids to understanding Neo-Confucianism as the “Chart of the Human Heart-mind and the Heart-mind of the Way” (195).
However, it would have been helpful to those more familiar with Western philosophy than with traditional East Asian philosophy if the translators had pointed out in their introduction how philosophy was done differently in East Asia. Epistemology, ontology, and formal logic were not of much concern. Instead, Confucian philosophers were more concerned with questions of ethics, of how we should behave and how we can discipline ourselves to behave the way we should behave. Even their cosmology, if we can call it that, was more about the fundamental processes, not the fundamental things, which constitute the universe. Even the Confucian description of how the universe came to be is not intended to be chronological. Instead, it is intended to show how everything is related to everything else, that everything has its roots in the stillness behind motion.
The translators could also have let their readers know that much Korean Confucian philosophizing consisted of interpretations of earlier Confucian works, primarily the ancient Chinese Classics, as well as the writings of the Song dynasty (960-1279) scholars in China who systemized Neo-Confucianism. That is implied when they identify the Chinese sources drawn upon by the writers they translate. As can be seen in the translations, Korean Neo-Confucian philosophers interacted with earlier Chinese texts when they laid out their philosophical arguments. It is important, if we want to understand why they say what they say, to know who and what they are relating to. That is why naming their sources is helpful.
That said, I would have preferred to see the names of those Chinese philosophers cited here provided in the romanization of the Chinese pronunciation of their names rather than the Korean pronunciation. Many people who will avail themselves of the translations in this anthology will be more familiar with Chinese Confucianism than with Korean Confucianism and therefore will be puzzled when they encounter the name Ju Hui, whom they would more easily recognize as Zhu Xi, or the name Jeong Ho, whom they would more easily recognize as Cheng Hao. The translators do provide the Chinese pronunciation of key names and terms in parentheses after the first use of the Korean romanization, but readers may skip around among the various translated selections and may therefore miss seeing the more familiar Chinese way of pronouncing those names and terms.
Nevertheless, the pluses of this book far outweigh any minuses. There is much readers can learn from this first-of-its-kind collection of translations of selections from the writings of Korea’s most important Neo-Confucian philosophers. One theme careful readers will notice running through these selections is tension over where li (“pattern”) can be found. Jeong Jedu insists that li operates only within the human heart-mind. Li may tell us how to interact with the external world, but it is not found in the external world. That may be because, for Jeong, li stimulates and directs moral behavior and only human beings can be moral (239-244). Yi Hwang, on the other hand, insists that li exists within everything, human or otherwise. For Yi Hwang, though li and the matter which coagulates into things need to be analytically distinguished, material objects cannot take the shape they have or operate the way they do without their own li (139-142). Yi agrees with Jeong that li is normative, but he disagrees on whether it needs consciousness to operate. Yi argued that the unconscious li in things resonates with the li in our heart-minds and tells us how to interact with them. This view that li is everywhere became the dominant position in Chosŏn, as we can see in Jeong Yakyong’s insistence that “Dogs have the pattern of dogs. Oxen have the patterns of oxen. There clearly are not in me” (327).
It is important to know where to look for li since it is only by identifying the li applicable in a particular situation that we can act appropriately. Philosophy, both in the East and the West, is the search for knowledge. But what does knowledge mean to Korean Confucians? Knowledge for them is primarily knowledge of li, of knowing how to act. This is not epistemology. It is not questioning how we know but discussing how we ensure that our knowledge is an accurate guide to appropriate behavior.
Once we know how we should act, Neo-Confucians insist we have to act that way. It is clear in the selections in this anthology that Neo-Confucianism is an ethical philosophy. It is all about learning how to act appropriately and then disciplining ourselves to act appropriately. What does acting appropriately mean to a Neo-Confucian thinker? It means acting selflessly, putting the common good ahead of any personal benefit or advantage. To ensure you do that, you have to minimize your selfish thoughts and emotions (329-330).
This practical ethical emphasis makes Korean Confucianism quite different from the way philosophy is often practiced in modern philosophy departments in the West.[2] That should be obvious to anyone who reads through the selections in this book. Despite what seem at times to be metaphysical debates, the question of how to act appropriately was always central to their discussions. The glimpses of Korean Confucian thought contained in this book reveal to those unfamiliar with traditional Korean philosophy how its issues and its approaches to solving those issues constitute a philosophical tradition which should become better known in the West. Ivanhoe and Wang have done the field a great service by making that possible.
REFERENCES
Roger T. Ames. Confucian Role Ethics: A Vocabulary. Hong Kong: Chinese University of Hong Kong, 2011.
Halla Kim, “Korean Philosophy Today: Retrospect and Prospect,” Journal of Confucian Philosophy and Culture 40 (2023): 5-29.
[1] For an analysis of Confucianism as primarily action- and interaction-oriented, see Roger T. Ames. Confucian Role Ethics: A Vocabulary. Hong Kong: Chinese University of Hong Kong, 2011.
[2] A good discussion of what makes Korean philosophy Korean can be found in Halla Kim, “Korean Philosophy Today: Retrospect and Prospect,” Journal of Confucian Philosophy and Culture 40 (2023): 5-29.

US appeals court halts Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in two centuries

- Pike was convicted for a brutal 1995 murder committed as a teenager; her clemency petition citing trauma and mental illness was denied by Governor Bill Lee.
- Her case has attracted international attention, with human rights experts and trauma specialists urging commutation due to the potential psychological harm of lethal injection.
AI generated
NASHVILLE, Tennessee – A US appeals court on Sept 30 halted the execution of death row inmate Christa Pike in Tennessee, less than two hours before she was scheduled to become the first woman that state has put to death in more than 200 years.
The 6th US Circuit Court of Appeals ordered a “short stay of execution” to give it time to weigh Pike’s claim that her allegations of childhood sexual abuse were not adequately considered during her sentencing. The court did not provide a specific timeframe.
Pike, whose clemency petition highlighting childhood trauma and sexual abuse was denied by Governor Bill Lee, would be the only person in the modern era of US capital punishment to be executed in Tennessee for a crime committed as a teenager.
The Tennessee attorney-general’s office immediately asked the US Supreme Court to vacate the stay order.
The Supreme Court on Sept 29 rejected an 11th-hour bid for a stay of execution, which is set to take place at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, the state capital.
Pike, now 50, was 18 in January 1995 when she, a 17-year-old boyfriend and a third companion lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a classmate at their Knoxville Job Corps vocational centre, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her.
The grisly nature of the slaying, which involved the perpetrators carving the shape of a pentagram on the victim’s chest and taking a chunk of her skull as a souvenir of the carnage, drew intense media coverage at the time.
Trial testimony indicated that Pike viewed Slemmer as a rival for the affections of her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.
Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing, and both were convicted the following year of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the time of the murder and had acted as a lookout for the other two, appeared as a witness for the prosecution and received probation.
Currently the only woman on Tennessee’s death row, Pike was also convicted in August 2001 of attempted first-degree murder in an assault on another inmate, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction.
In a 226-page petition asking the governor to commute her death penalty to a life sentence without the possibility of parole, her lawyers documented her history as the childhood victim of violence, neglect and sexual abuse, including two rapes at ages 11 and 17. And they cited the diagnoses she received in prison for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Teen who committed murder ‘no longer exists’
Her lawyers also pointed to evidence that Pike’s mother drank heavily during pregnancy, contributing to faulty brain development that made it difficult for their client to control her impulses as a young person.
“The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists,” her lawyers wrote in response to Lee’s denial of clemency. “Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women.”
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has spoken out in support of the execution.
Executions of female prison inmates are exceedingly rare in the US, with women accounting for just 18 of the 1,683 people put to death since the Supreme Court allowed capital punishment to resume in 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre. Before Sept 30, Tennessee had executed 17 people.
Pike’s case has drawn international attention, with a group of United Nations human rights experts issuing a recent statement calling for commutation of her death sentence.
Sexual violence and trauma experts have also spoken out on her behalf, arguing that the procedures surrounding lethal injection would likely cause Pike to experience severe, traumatic flashbacks of child sexual abuse and rape, adding to the cruelty and anguish of her death.
Tennessee prison officials in May aborted attempts to execute a man convicted of murders after failing to find a suitable vein for a lethal injection. REUTERS

Photos: Kashmir’s 600-year-old Wazwan wedding feast adapts to modern life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

In Pictures
Photos: Kashmir’s 600-year-old Wazwan wedding feast adapts to modern life
Wazwan, a multicourse mutton feast, reflects Kashmiri cultural roots with recipes dating back to the 14th century.
As autumn approaches, the rhythmic thud of wooden mallets pounding lamb echoes across courtyards and back lanes in Kashmir, where cooks prepare Wazwan – a lavish, multi-course mutton feast that remains central to traditional wedding celebrations.
Wazwan arrived in the valley from Central Asia in the 14th century, when rulers brought skilled chefs along with the carpet and shawl weavers that later defined the region’s craft heritage.
Today, the feast is both a marker of social status and a powerful symbol of Kashmiri identity.
Among its guardians is 74-year-old Ghulam Nabi Baba, a veteran Wazwan chef who traces his lineage to those early migrants. His forefathers settled in Srinagar’s old city as part of a community of cooks known as Wazpora.
“There were only seven mutton dishes at that time. Over the centuries we added more, and now there are around 20,” Baba said.
He explained how the number of dishes and the amount of meat often reflect a family’s wealth.
“Forty years ago in Delina [a village in north Kashmir] I cooked 4,500kg (9,920 pounds) of meat. That was a very big wedding. Normally, at an average marriage we cook 200kg (440 pounds),” he added.
Despite the expanding menu, the core techniques have changed little. Lightly spiced meat is still pounded by hand before being simmered slowly over wood fires – a labour-intensive process Baba has followed since joining his father as a cook at 15.
But the pressures of modern life are reshaping the tradition. Baba’s son has chosen to open a restaurant rather than work weddings, saying the round-the-clock demands are too exhausting.
He believes he is still carrying forward the family’s centuries-old culinary legacy – just in a different setting, as Wazwan adapts to contemporary tastes and lifestyles.
