DR Congo politician killed for defending Ebola measures – ruling party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:06:14 UTC
00:06:14 KST

DR Congo politician killed for defending Ebola measures – ruling party
An official from the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party has died after being attacked following a radio appearance in the Ebola-hit eastern city of Butembo, local media reported on Monday.
Marie-Celestin Karondwa, a spokesperson for the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) in Butembo, was assaulted on Sunday and later died from his injuries, the Congolese Press Agency (ACP) reported, citing a party statement. His property was also looted and his home set on fire.
As quoted by Reuters, the party said he was “an innocent victim for having defended the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease... and the threat it poses to the population.”
The motive remains unclear, although the party has linked the attack to his public support for measures against Ebola. The UDPS called for an investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.
The killing comes amid resistance to the Ebola response in eastern DR Congo. The World Health Organization (WHO) has said insecurity and attacks on health facilities are complicating efforts to contain the outbreak by restricting access for response teams, disrupting surveillance and discouraging people from seeking care.
The WHO recorded 12 attacks on health care between the declaration of a public health emergency of international concern on May 17 and mid-August, with additional incidents under verification. Similar resistance has hampered efforts to contain previous Ebola outbreaks in the region.
The Ebola response is also being complicated by insecurity and mass displacement. The WHO has said conflict is restricting access for response teams and hampering disease surveillance, contact tracing, and access to care.
The DR Congo’s mineral-rich east has been plagued by decades of violence, with dozens of armed groups, including M23, fighting Congolese forces for power and control of resources such as gold and coltan. Clashes escalated in early 2025, killing thousands and forcing large-scale displacement, according to UN agencies. The rebels seized Goma, the capital of North Kivu, in late January and later captured Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu.
Ceasefire efforts have repeatedly faltered, including Qatar-facilitated talks in Doha. Congolese authorities have long accused Rwanda of supporting the militants, allegations backed by a UN panel of experts. Kigali has denied the claims. The accusations have strained Rwanda’s relations with Western partners, including Belgium. In March, Kigali severed diplomatic ties with Brussels, accusing it of harboring “neo-colonial delusions” and interfering in the conflict.
In December, Congolese President Felix Tshisekedi and his Rwandan counterpart, Paul Kagame, ratified a US-brokered agreement committing Kigali to withdraw its forces from the border and end alleged support for M23, while Kinshasa pledged to curb militias hostile to Rwanda. US President Donald Trump has said the pact, which includes calls for a joint security mechanism, gives Washington rights to local mineral wealth. The fighting has continued despite Trump’s claims that he ended the decades-long conflict.
The outbreak has meanwhile continued to grow. As of September 27, DR Congo had recorded 8,116 confirmed cases and 3,924 deaths, according to the country’s National Institute of Public Health (INSP). The case fatality rate stood at 48.3%.
The disease is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola virus. There is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the strain, although candidate vaccines and treatments are being studied, according to the WHO.
Russia has provided assistance to countries affected by the outbreak. Rospotrebnadzor has sent specialists to Uganda and supplied Russian-developed PCR diagnostic tests to Uganda, DR Congo, and the Republic of Congo.
In July, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow was prepared to establish mass production of a vaccine adapted to the Bundibugyo strain once it obtained the necessary biological material.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:03:11 UTC
00:03:11 KST

St. Petersburg plans to raise officials’ base salaries by up to 5% annually over the next three years while proposing sharp cuts to this year’s spending on education, health care and infrastructure, the RBC news website reported Wednesday.
The pay increases are included in the city’s draft budget for 2027 and its spending plans for 2028 and 2029. The city government approved the document on Sept. 29 and submitted it to the Legislative Assembly.
The plans would increase pay for lawmakers, deputy governors, city government members and other officials as the authorities seek to curb borrowing and narrow the budget deficit. Payments to Russian troops fighting in Ukraine and their families would also rise.
The Legislative Assembly speaker’s monthly base salary would increase from about 149,100 rubles ($1,804) to 168,800 rubles ($2,042) by 2029. Base salaries for deputy speakers and deputy governors would reach 159,400 rubles ($1,929), while those for city government members would reach 154,700 rubles ($1,872).
Officials’ total pay is higher because it includes allowances, bonuses and other supplementary payments.
Separately, the city administration has proposed cutting its 2026 budget by 70.2 billion rubles ($849.4 million), from 1.651 trillion rubles ($19.98 billion) to about 1.58 trillion rubles ($19.12 billion).
The largest reduction, 36.7 billion rubles ($444.1 million), would fall on spending classified under the economy. Transport spending would be cut by 9 billion rubles ($108.9 million), with another 10.8 billion rubles ($130.7 million) removed from construction of the Shirotnaya high-speed highway.
Education spending would fall by 15.5 billion rubles ($187.6 million), while the health care committee’s budget would be reduced by 8.5 billion rubles ($102.9 million).
Housing and utilities spending would be cut by about 6.8 billion rubles ($82.3 million). Spending on improvements to public spaces would fall by 2.3 billion rubles ($27.8 million), and road repairs would lose 1.9 billion rubles ($23 million).
Meanwhile, payments to troops fighting in Ukraine and their families would increase by 6.4 billion rubles ($77.4 million).
The city administration attributed the proposed spending cuts to high borrowing costs, a planned cooling of the economy and efforts to reduce borrowing.
It said the revisions would narrow the 2026 budget deficit by about 80 billion rubles ($968 million), from 189 billion rubles ($2.29 billion) to 108.8 billion rubles ($1.32 billion).
The draft budget projects a deficit of 103.4 billion rubles ($1.25 billion) in 2027.

Starlink falls short of Russia’s Rassvet system in data transmission quality — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:02:30 UTC
00:02:30 KST

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Thanks to its laser communication channel, the Russian low-Earth orbit satellite constellation Rassvet outperforms Starlink in terms of data transmission quality, retired Colonel Yury Knutov, a military expert and director of the Museum of the Air Defense Forces, told TASS.
"The [Rassvet] system differs from Starlink in that the communication channel between the satellites is laser-based – it provides broadband Internet, and the speed and quality of data transmission are higher than those of Starlink. Although Starlink will soon be implementing something similar as well," he said.
Knutov also noted that Rassvet can operate without special satellite terminals. According to him, in the future, mobile devices will be able to connect directly to the satellites.
The Rassvet low-Earth orbit satellite system was developed by the private Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440 (founded in December 2020 in Moscow, part of X Holding). It is designed for broadband data transmission to any location on the planet. Work is being carried out as part of the Data Economy and Digital Transformation of the State national project for the period from 2025 to 2030. In late March, the company successfully launched the first 16 satellites of the Rassvet low-Earth orbit constellation into orbit.
Roscosmos CEO Dmitry Bakanov previously stated that the Rassvet project is Russia’s answer to the American Starlink.

Strange things happen in four dimensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:01:33 UTC
00:01:33 KST

This article is from Proof Positive, our friendly newsletter that explores the joys and peculiarities of math. Sign up today for a weekly math essay and puzzle in your email inbox.
“Either this is madness or it is Hell.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“‘It’s neither,’ calmly replied the voice of the Sphere, ‘it is Knowledge; it is Three Dimensions: open your eye once again and try to look steadily.’”
This dialogue is from Edwin Abbott’s 1884 novel Flatland. In it, the protagonist, A. Square, who lives in a two-dimensional world, encounters a three-dimensional sphere for the first time. Although ostensibly a satire of Victorian society, the work also contains a mathematical treatise on the fourth dimension. What if we live in a four-dimensional world, but—much like A. Square—have been trapped in a lower dimension?
Many people associate thoughts of higher dimensions with works of science fiction, such as the books of H. P. Lovecraft or blockbusters such as Christopher Nolan’s Interstellar. But the natural sciences have also been studying higher dimensions for centuries.
Mathematicians, for example, investigate which geometric objects could exist in these unimaginable environments and how they can be ordered and measured. In doing so, they have discovered that although many dimensions are relatively easy to analyze, a 4D world specifically poses surprisingly large problems. As mathematician Ciprian Manolescu of Stanford University explains in a Numberphile video, many theorems hold true for all dimensions n except when n = 4: “That’s what makes dimension four so fascinating.”
But why are four dimensions so special? To understand this, one must venture into the abstract field of topology. While topology deals with geometric figures, “details” such as distances or precise curvature play no role. Thus, a sphere with a dent is identical to an ordinary sphere, or a circle is the same as a quadrilateral. In other words, two objects are considered topologically identical if they can be deformed into one another without tearing holes in them or gluing them together at any point.
Even though it sounds complicated, we constantly use topology in our everyday lives without realizing it. For example, we imagine our planet as a sphere, even though Earth, strictly speaking, deviates from a perfectly round shape.
In topology, mathematicians try to reduce objects to their essential properties. This allows them, for example, to make statements about an entire class of objects without having to examine each one individually. One famous example is that, topologically speaking, a doughnut and a cup of coffee with a simple ring handle are the same: they each have exactly one hole.
As long as you stay in one, two or three dimensions, everything is fine. But problems begin in four dimensions. The deformations you can make to transform two shapes into one another can become more complex. If you want to mold one smooth shape into another, sharp corners and edges can suddenly appear during the process. That’s like saying that in order to transform a circle into an oval, you first need to reshape it like a star. This kind of change is unnecessary in one, two or three dimensions, but in four dimensions, it’s sometimes unavoidable.
This phenomenon has led to the existence of two types of equality in topology: First, two objects are generally topologically equal if they can be deformed into each other—regardless of how the process occurs. There is also a stricter form of equality, however: two figures are what mathematicians call “diffeomorphic” if they can be deformed into each other smoothly, without ever creating corners or edges. Thus, in higher dimensions, there are objects that are topologically equal but not diffeomorphic—that is, they cannot be transformed into each other smoothly.
This is a general characteristic of higher dimensions. But four dimensions remain a special case. If you consider a space Rnspanned by n real numbers in each dimension (that is, something like an n-dimensional coordinate system), then this space is always unique for all dimensions n except four. In other words, all spaces that are topologically equivalent to the n-dimensional space Rn are also diffeomorphic to it. This means that one will not encounter vertices and edges when transforming one space into the other. In 1981 mathematician Michael Freedman discovered that the 4D space R4 is an exception. In fact, there are infinitely many 4D figures that can be transformed into the 4D R4 in different ways without being diffeomorphic: all of them exhibit a different kind of pattern of vertices and edges during the transformation.
This makes 4D space a very strange place. But it’s not just 4D space itself that’s strange—so are 4D figures.
Imagine you lived in a five-dimensional world and wanted to sort 4D surfaces: Which ones are diffeomorphic to each other? What classes of surfaces are there?
To understand this, it’s easier to start with our familiar 3D world. There, we can examine 2D surfaces, such as spherical surfaces or a torus (a doughnut shape). As it turns out, all (closed) 2D surfaces can be divided into only three categories, as Henri Poincaré proved as early as 1907: they are either equivalent (diffeomorphic) to a spherical surface, to connected doughnuts, or to connected projective surfaces (which include, for example, the Klein bottle). No matter how complicated a 2D figure may appear, it can always be transformed into one of the three categories—and in a straightforward manner.
If one were to live in the fourth dimension and consider 3D surfaces, eight different categories would emerge: every 3D surface can be reduced to eight basic shapes. William Thurston had suggested this in 1982, but this so-called geometrization of 3-manifolds was only proved in 2003 by Grigori Perelman, who, in doing so, incidentally proved the Poincaré conjecture that every 3D surface without a hole can be deformed into a 3D spherical surface. The result shows that a classification scheme also exists for 3D surfaces.
When turning to higher dimensions and examining surfaces in five or six dimensions or more, things become more difficult. How can such complex objects be categorized?
Mathematicians often use the so-called Whitney trick: Imagine throwing a lasso around a shape and observing its behavior as it contracts to determine if the surface has holes. This method distinguishes a sphere from a torus. Although every closed loop on a sphere contracts to a point, this is not the case with a torus, which has a hole in it.
This approach also works very well for surfaces with more than four dimensions. When a lasso is contracted, a circular area, a disk, is formed. To determine the type of surface, all possible types of resulting disks must be examined separately. The lassoed areas can overlap, however—which poses a problem from a mathematical perspective. For n > 4, the additional dimensions can be used to separate two disks. This is similar to the process of separating two intersecting lines in a plane: moving left-right or up-down is ineffective. Only a third spatial dimension allows the lines to be separated by depth. The same principle applies in five dimensions to two 2D disks. In this way, the Whitney trick can be used to determine which surfaces with a dimension of five or more are diffeomorphic to each other.
So all categories of 2D, 3D, 5D and higher-dimensional surfaces have been found. And, of course, the fourth dimension causes problems once again because, as it turns out, it’s impossible to classify diffeomorphic 4D objects—this world is utter chaos!
The 4D world also holds a secret that Manolescu in his video says is perhaps the most significant problem in topology: Can every 4D surface without a hole be diffeomorphically deformed into a 4D spherical surface? This is the smooth Poincaré conjecture. The ordinary Poincaré conjecture has already been proved for all dimensions n but only in the general topological sense: this allows deformations that produce vertices and edges.
Topologists are therefore interested in how the n-dimensional Poincaré conjecture turns out when only diffeomorphic deformations are permitted. They have now found an answer for every spatial dimension—except for n = 4. The conjecture does not hold in seven dimensions, for example, in which there are 28 different versions of a spherical surface, so-called exotic spheres: that is, 28 different figures without a hole that can only be transformed into one another using vertices and edges.
The number of exotic spheres can also be calculated for all other dimensions, and this number can sometimes be very large. So far, no object has been found in four dimensions that does not have a hole and is not diffeomorphic to a sphere—but it also has not yet been proved that none exist.
Many mathematicians assume that exotic 4D spheres exist. After all, infinitely many different versions of 4D R⁴ space already exist. But perhaps the fourth dimension will surprise us in this case as well.

Yabloko Leader Demands Investigation After Political Analyst Alexander Kynev Was Reportedly Tortured During Arrest
Unknown

2026-09-30
15:01:14 UTC
00:01:14 KST

Yabloko party Chairman Nikolai Rybakov said Wednesday that he formally asked Russian law enforcement authorities to investigate reports that independent political analyst Alexander Kynev was beaten and tortured following his arrest in Moscow last week.
Rights groups have said that Kynev was hospitalized at a medical facility inside a Moscow detention center for bone fractures and other injuries after his arrest on drug charges. Officials have not commented on those allegations.
“I believe those responsible should not only be named and punished, but immediately dismissed from law enforcement agencies,” Rybakov wrote in a post on Telegram. “Regardless of how state security agencies feel about the detainee, torture and violence are categorically unacceptable.”
Exiled Russian political commentator Ekaterina Shulmman, who knows Kynev personally, claimed on Tuesday that police officers broke one of his legs and electrocuted him in what she described as an attempt to make him confess to treason charges. She did not say where she had received that information.
Kynev’s attorney later denied Shulmann’s claim, stating he was unaware of any evidence that his client was tortured or faced allegations of treason. The drug charges Kynev currently faces, and which he has denied, carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.
News of Kynev’s arrest came the same day that Russian election authorities announced the final results of this month’s parliamentary elections, which handed the ruling United Russia party an unprecedented supermajority in the lower-house State Duma.
Independent experts have described the elections as the least competitive in Russia’s modern history. Voters were left with virtually no real opposition option after Yabloko, Russia’s oldest liberal party and the only registered political force campaigning for peace, was struck from the party-list ballot by the Russian Supreme Court in August.
Kynev, who wrote regular opinion columns for The Moscow Times before it was designated an “undesirable” organization in 2024, chose to remain in Russia despite his public criticism of the government and the invasion of Ukraine.
Russia’s Justice Ministry designated Kynev a “foreign agent” in February. Over the years, he has worked for a number of independent political organizations, including the now-disbanded election observer Golos.
Separately, Rybakov was himself briefly detained on Tuesday and charged with disorderly conduct for spoiling his ballot during the Sept. 20 elections at a St. Petersburg polling station.

September 26′ Reading-Round Up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:01:08 UTC
00:01:08 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Welcome to the September 26’ Reading-Round Up! This month’s round-up experiments with a different format. Each round-up will have readings grouped into three broad tracks (1) Consciousness Attribution (2) Agency & Autonomy, and (3) AI Welfare. I’ll provide a ‘general verdict’ on the paper, my recommendation of whether to read, for who, and why. As always, please let me know in comments your feedback.
At the end, I have: My Top Pick — everyone should read this ⭐️
The AI Consciousness Attribution Track
- 
Seemingly Consciousness AI| Bariach, Schoenegger, Bhaskar, & Suleyman| June 2026| AI and Ethics| Verdict—Worth the Read
Provides an excellent overview on the literature on AI consciousness & adjacent issues; raises fantastic questions about the potential future possibilities of organising the world around the assumption that AI is conscious; includes survey data from experts on these future possibilities, which is interesting in its own right. My take away: experts do not take seriously enough the possibility that our institutions may radically change to accommodate AI consciousness, and that’s not a good thing.
- 
The Abstraction Fallacy: Why AI Can Simulate But Not Instantiate Consciousness| Lerchner | March 2026 | No Clear Publication Venue | Verdict — Worth the read if you are knee deep in AI consciousness literature
Interesting paper with a novel argument against functionalism; genuinely helpful and novel intervention in the AI consciousness literature; My take away: the core premise the paper’s main argument rests on is not defended, so functionalists may not be convinced by his position. This is the biggest weakness of the paper.
The AI Agency & Autonomy Track
- 
AI Agents Push Humans Out of the Loop |Mitchel, Ghosh, & Passi| August 2026 | arXIV| Verdict —-Worth the Read for tech folks (deployers, developers, engineers) and policy, governance, and lawyers looking to keep AI agential systems in check.
Dissects clearly how norms for human oversight of AI systems currently degrade the overseer, by de-skilling and monotonous exhaustion; offers tangible solutions for deployers and developers. My take away: a much needed paper that developers and deployers should sit up and pay attention to. It’s also a paper that names what is long overdue: the problem of requiring humans to do work that does not take into account how human condition works, while also degrading human cognitive skills.

Yabloko Leader Demands Investigation After Political Analyst Was Reportedly Tortured During Arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:01:00 UTC
00:01:00 KST

Yabloko party Chairman Nikolai Rybakov said Wednesday that he formally asked Russian law enforcement authorities to investigate reports that independent political analyst Alexander Kynev was beaten and tortured following his arrest in Moscow last week.
Rights groups have said that Kynev was hospitalized at a medical facility inside a Moscow detention center for bone fractures and other injuries after his arrest on drug charges. Officials have not commented on those allegations.
“I believe those responsible should not only be named and punished, but immediately dismissed from law enforcement agencies,” Rybakov wrote in a post on Telegram. “Regardless of how state security agencies feel about the detainee, torture and violence are categorically unacceptable.”
Exiled Russian political commentator Ekaterina Shulmman, who knows Kynev personally, claimed on Tuesday that police officers broke one of his legs and electrocuted him in what she described as an attempt to make him confess to treason charges. She did not say where she had received that information.
Kynev’s attorney later denied Shulmann’s claim, stating he was unaware of any evidence that his client was tortured or faced allegations of treason. The drug charges Kynev currently faces, and which he has denied, carry a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.
News of Kynev’s arrest came the same day that Russian election authorities announced the final results of this month’s parliamentary elections, which handed the ruling United Russia party an unprecedented supermajority in the lower-house State Duma.
Independent experts have described the elections as the least competitive in Russia’s modern history. Voters were left with virtually no real opposition option after Yabloko, Russia’s oldest liberal party and the only registered political force campaigning for peace, was struck from the party-list ballot by the Russian Supreme Court in August.
Kynev, who wrote regular opinion columns for The Moscow Times before it was designated an “undesirable” organization in 2024, chose to remain in Russia despite his public criticism of the government and the invasion of Ukraine.
Russia’s Justice Ministry designated Kynev a “foreign agent” in February. Over the years, he has worked for a number of independent political organizations, including the now-disbanded election observer Golos.
Separately, Rybakov was himself briefly detained on Tuesday and charged with disorderly conduct for spoiling his ballot during the Sept. 20 elections at a St. Petersburg polling station.
A Message from The Moscow Times:

We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.

All of a flutter: how butterflies avoid being a predator’s lunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:00:43 UTC
00:00:43 KST

Naturalists have long wondered how brightly coloured butterflies manage to evade the attention of birds that make a meal of other insects.
New research from British ecologists suggests it is not simply a matter of good luck but instead a visual illusion created by their fluttering wings.
The study by researchers from the universities of Exeter and Essex concluded that the spots and stripes found on many butterfly wings – combined with their dancing flight – scramble a predator’s sense of the insects’ speed and direction.
George Hancock, of the University of Exeter’s Centre for Ecology and Conservation in Cornwall, said very few European butterflies were toxic or unpalatable and they were relatively easy to spot in flight, so they needed something special to stay out of harm’s way.
“The illusions interfere with the predator’s most basic visual targeting system and disrupt the final ballistic attack,” Hancock said. “As a result, birds and other predators often miss.”
Jolyon Troscianko, also of the University of Exeter, said: “Butterfly wings deform as they fly, clapping together on the upstroke and peeling apart on the downstroke, so their stripes shift angle and point in different directions as they flap.
“Combined with their unpredictable flight paths, this patterning creates misleading motion illusions, causing a predator to miss entirely or to strike a less vulnerable part of the wing, such as the hindwing or tail.”
The experts compared the mechanism to the “barber pole illusion” – the red and white stripes appear to travel upwards even though the pole is only spinning in place.
The breakthrough came when Troscianko put a slow-motion video of a butterfly flying upwards through a “bird-vision” computer model. It seemed to indicate – wrongly – that the butterfly was moving downwards.
Troscianko said: “First I checked this wasn’t a coding error, that I’d swapped up and down somehow, but then it dawned on me that this would be a perfect way to confuse attacking predators.”
The team looked at hundreds of types of European butterflies and found different patterns created different effects.
Swallowtail butterflies were found to be among the best at using motion confusion. Troscianko said: “They are also thought to be closest to the ancestral butterflies, suggesting motion confusion might have been around right at the point when butterflies evolved away from night-flying moths.
“Swallowtails have little tails trailing from their hindwings that help increase their levels of motion confusion. They are frequently found with their tails missing and beak-shaped holes cut from their wing edges by failed bird attacks. This fits with our modelling that shows how the wing markings should deflect attacks sideways and behind the butterfly’s vital body and inner wing sections.”
The team used a high-speed camera to film butterflies taking off to capture how their patterns behave in flight. To test how patterns might affect attacks, 100 human volunteers acted as “predators”, trying to catch virtual butterflies on a touchscreen. They struggled.
The study found that largely white butterflies also managed to dodge predators. The researchers believe that when in flight they appear to move more quickly than they actually do because of the stark contrast they make with their background – which may put out the timing of strikes from predators.
Troscianko said the discovery could be used to begin to explain how other animals used motion confusion. “We think it is likely to be far more widespread in nature than previously realised, from the flapping wings of birds to the flicking tails of lizards and fish. It opens up an exciting new research avenue.”
The study – Butterfly wing patterns in flight create powerful illusory motion cues – is published in the journal Nature.

Israel's defense minister claims Flydubai was 'attempted terror attack'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:00:39 UTC
00:00:39 KST

Serdar Dincel
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz claimed Wednesday that an incident involving an Israel-bound Flydubai flight was an "attempted terrorist attack."
The Dubai-based carrier Flydubai said an altercation broke out in the flight deck of the Israel-bound plane, and that crew members managed to secure the plane and divert it safely to Saudi Arabia.
It "was a jihadist terrorist attack attempt, thwarted only thanks to the bravery of several Israeli passengers who broke into the cockpit," Katz alleged, according to the Ynet newspaper.
The airline, however, said the reasons and motives behind the altercation remain unknown and are subject to a formal investigation.
“We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts,” Flydubai cautioned.
In a statement released by his office on the US social media company X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that "one of the pilots stabbed the second pilot, and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone on board."
Passengers and crew members subdued the "stabbing pilot," who was arrested and is now being interrogated by Saudi officials, he said.
No further statements were issued by Flydubai or Saudi authorities to confirm the statements by Israeli officials on the motives behind the incident.

Why did Trump and Xi seal a deal on World War II soldiers’ missing remains?
Reviving the decades-long effort is one of the ‘least controversial’ ways the two nations can cooperate, observers say
3-MIN READ3-MIN
7
 Listen
Cao Jiaxuanin Beijing
A decades-long effort by Beijing and Washington to recover the remains of US servicemen missing in China since World War II has resurfaced in the wake of the summit between the nations’ leaders.
The commitment was included in an eight-point list of outcomes from Chinese President Xi Jinping’s three-day state visit last week, alongside other agreements covering issues including artificial intelligence and trade.
According to a statement issued by China’s foreign ministry after the summit, the two sides agreed that their militaries would “continue to cooperate in searching for the remains of missing US service members in China”.
Why was cooperation over the remains included in the summit outcomes?
During the summit, Xi and US President Donald Trump repeatedly invoked their countries’ alliance during World War II, contrasting with the strategic rivalry that defines much of their relationship today.
Against that backdrop, the continued search for remains provides a practical area in which the two sides can cooperate, observers say.

Ban on election observers, tariffs with China, and plummeting birth rates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Ban on election observers, tariffs with China, and plummeting birth rates
Welcome to our press review of events in the United States. Every Wednesday we look at how the Swiss media have reported and reacted to three major stories in the US – in politics, finance and science.
“It’s not the voting that’s democracy, it’s the counting,” wrote British playwright Tom Stoppard. Following the Trump administration’s exclusion of OSCE election observers from November’s midterm elections, some commentators in Switzerland are concerned that this clears the way for manipulating the result.
Help us improve the press review
As a reader of our weekly press review, your feedback is important to us. Please take two minutes to answer a short survey and help us improve our journalism. This survey is anonymous and all data is confidential.
👉 [Take the surveyExternal link]
The United States has not invited any OSCE observers to November’s mid-term elections, for the first time in almost 25 years. This is a move more commonly associated with Russia, say several Swiss media.
“In early August, the OSCE expressed its “grave concern” following Russia’s decision not to invite observers to monitor the elections to the Duma, the federal parliament. On Wednesday, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe described the US decision to do the same as ‘regrettable’,” Le Temps wrote last week.
“For the first time since 2002, Washington has chosen to do without external, ‘non-partisan’ observers of its electoral process, in breach of its commitments,” the Geneva newspaper said. “While Moscow’s stance comes as no surprise – this is the third refusal – the fact that Donald Trump is following in Vladimir Putin’s footsteps marks a new stage in the widening rift between the United States and the European continent.”
Trump’s decision comes as no surprise to the diplomatic correspondent of Swiss public broadcaster SRF. “Behind the scenes, the US spent months trying to persuade the OSCE to withdraw its report on the 2020 election, when Joe Biden was elected president,” he wrote on Thursday. “Donald Trump still claims to this day that Biden wasn’t elected at all. However, the OSCE came to the clear conclusion that the election was conducted correctly – and that doesn’t sit well with Trump and his supporters.”
So what’s the US’s game? For the time being, there has been no explanation from the US for the non-invitation.
But, according to SRF, it’s not implausible that the Trump administration wants to use the exclusion of OSCE election observers to clear the way for actually manipulating the election result. “If the Republicans lose, they could also claim that the elections were not conducted properly,” it said, adding that this would be much more difficult if the OSCE confirmed that the election had been fair. “After all, OSCE election observation is regarded as the ‘gold standard’, so to speak.”
Lower tariffs on electric razors, camels and rabbit fur: at last week’s summit between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping the two heads of state “kicked the major issues down the road”, said the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ).
Expectations for the summit in Washington had been modest from the outset, the NZZ wrote on Monday. “It’s now becoming clear that this was justified.”
“The only tangible outcome is an agreement under which the US and China intend to lower tariffs on selected, so-called non-sensitive goods. Beijing, for example, intends to significantly reduce tariffs on rabbit fur, dolphins, camels and goose liver pâté from the US. In return, the US government has promised, among other things, to lower tariffs on Chinese toys, electrical appliances such as electric razors, and fishing hooks.”
The Zurich newspaper reported that, in total, Washington was lowering tariffs on 77 Chinese products and the Chinese government was reducing duties on 1,619 products from the US. “What initially sounds like a substantial easing of market access is, on closer inspection, nothing more than a drop in the ocean,” the NZZ said.
This, it pointed out, was because the agreed tariff cuts relate to a trade volume of just $60 billion (CHF50 billion) – $30 billion on each side. Last year, however, the total trade volume between the US and China came to $415 billion.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the US would continue to advocate for “fair, balanced and reciprocal trade between the US and China”. Above all, the US is demanding that China purchase significantly more agricultural products from the US.
“All eyes are therefore now on the next meetings between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping,” the NZZ said. The leaders of the world’s two largest economies are expected to meet again for talks at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November. The G20 summit will take place in Miami in December.
“Xi and Trump could also sit down together there to discuss the outstanding contentious issues,” the NZZ said. “However, a major breakthrough in resolving their differences is hardly on the cards. This was demonstrated by the two summits last week in the US and in May in Beijing. The rapprochement between the two rivals is a painstaking, inch-by-inch process.”
Is the United States facing the same birth rate crisis as Switzerland? This week Swissinfo warned of a slump in birth rates in the US, partly because having children has become too expensive.
Since the financial crisis of 2007 and 2008, the number of children per woman in the US has fallen steadily, we reported in an exclusive detailed analysis. “In less than 20 years, the fertility rate dropped from 2.1 to 1.6 children per woman, a historic low.”
This has not escaped the attention of the Trump administration. Mehmet Oz, head of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and a former television doctor, declared in May that the US was “under-babied”.
My colleague Marc Leutenegger, who wrote the article, noted that biological infertility is on the rise in the US, but people who choose not to have children are by far the bigger demographic factor.
An analysis by the Pew Research Center, an independent thinktank in Washington, shows the scale of this phenomenon. The share of women aged 20 to 30 who do not want children rose from 7% in 2002 to 23% in 2023. Among women aged 20 to 24, this figure is even higher at 34%. Men score similarly high numbers.
There are many reasons for this development. “Demographers attribute this trend to a general shift in social values, rising costs of living, limited career prospects for parents, particularly the so-called motherhood penalty, as well as factors like the loneliness crisis and the influence of social media on lifestyle and living standards,” Leutenegger wrote.
“If the US fails to tackle the cost-of-living crisis soon, existing trends could intensify, particularly the growing reluctance to have second or third children, as has happened in Switzerland,” he concluded. “With huge numbers of young women and men already saying no to having children, the US could face the same dilemma as Switzerland: falling below 1.4 children per woman. Demographers consider this a critical threshold for a society.”

LONDON - Saudi Arabia turned down a request by Israel to allow its planes to bring back Israeli passengers from a flydubai flight that made an emergency landing in the kingdom, two security sources said on Sept 30.
The request was made to allow Israeli military planes to bring back Israelis from Saudi Arabia, which has no diplomatic relations with Israel, the sources said.

The Israeli air force was preparing to send Super Hercules planes to pick up Israeli passengers, one of the sources said.
The passengers were set to continue their journey on flydubai aircraft, the airline said.
The co-pilot of a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv tried to crash the plane after stabbing the pilot, but passengers then held him down while other pilots landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sept 30.
US President Donald Trump has been pushing for Saudi Arabia to join the US-brokered Abraham Accords under which several Arab states established ties with Israel. The kingdom has long rejected joining the accords without a pathway towards Palestinian statehood.
A senior Saudi official on Sept 30 denied reports of a meeting between Saudi and Israeli officials, after Israeli media reported that Netanyahu had met Middle Eastern officials, including a Saudi official, during his recent visit to the United Arab Emirates. REUTERS

Electoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham – but so far he’s on a winning streak| Zoe Williams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:55:28 UTC
23:55:28 KST

A number of people have admitted to tears during Andy Burnham’s Labour party conference speech, and most of them mean when he talked about his father, who died very recently. But then there were a few (not me) who welled up when he announced a commission on electoral reform. It was just the sheer shock of it: that we may finally have a prime minister who will follow through on his own long-held beliefs and remain loyal to his long-term support base, even if it makes him avoidable enemies and, medium-term, destroys Labour’s only-trodden path to victory. It felt a bit like slipping through time, and I couldn’t even tell you to when (definitely not the 1990s).
Burnham’s support for proportional representation has always been extremely unusual for a Labour politician. To this day, he ascribes that to his experience of winning an election as mayor of Greater Manchester on a supplementary votes system, where people get to choose a first- and second-preference candidate. He said that campaigning under that system “finally aligned the conversation on the door with what people want from politics, which is about problem-solving first and foremost, not about point-scoring”. He went a bit further this morning, asking Nick Robinson on the Today programme: “Can we really watch a party with less than 30% walk into Downing Street?”
Plainly, he was talking about the spectre of a Reform government, and it’s that very context that makes this already difficult constitutional conversation even more vexed. Back in May, the all-party parliamentary group for fair elections held a meeting to discuss the aftermath of the local elections. It feels like a long time ago, and furthermore, so different in atmosphere as to be irrelevant to the prime minister, but 2020s politics are defined by their switchblade turns. In the matter of constitutional reform, the overriding priority has to be to build a system that’s fair across a range of imaginable scenarios, not just the one in front of you.
The locals delivered great results for Reform, and satisfactory ones for the Liberal Democrats, which reflected the realities of a first-past-the-post (FPTP) system – first, it rewards the winner, and second, it rewards geographical concentration. Labour walked away from the 2024 general election with 63% of the seats on 34% of the votes, the largest overrepresentation ever. The Greens have spent years commanding the fervent support of a geographically diffuse but not insignificant minority, with almost nothing to show for it in parliamentary terms.
The distortions of FPTP have been well-known for years, but historically they were only ever discussed in terms of the barrier to entry they presented to insurgent parties, and the democratic deficit they constituted to any voter who didn’t live in a marginal seat, which is to say the majority of voters. So the counter-arguments were that, for all its flaws, by keeping out insurgents, the traditional voting system kept out extremists: and who wouldn’t sacrifice a little bit (or a huge amount) of democracy, for the sake of steadiness?
Stability was the first myth to fall, when it transpired, over the past 10 years, that you can keep on returning one of two main parties as reliably as you like, and they will have no problem confecting so much intra-party turmoil that you might as well have voted for the Monster Raving Loony party. The efficacy of FPTP in keeping out extremists, meanwhile, was – like a stock market bubble – true until it wasn’t. Once politics has fragmented, the system rewards short bursts of popularity with potentially very long periods of power. That has a toxic effect on the supposedly sober heads of the political centre who, once they see extreme, often bigoted, positions pay off in the polls, steer straight towards them. The best prophylactic against extremism is not a gamified voting system but some political backbone. Undoubtedly in response to all that, public attitudes to proportional representation have changed enormously, hitting an all-time high of 60% support last year. In 2011 it was 27%.
To return to that meeting in May, there was one more finding from the local elections: once you start to lose, under FPTP, you lose calamitously. So the obvious solution, to a room full of already fully committed constitutional reformer MPs, was for the next prime minister to change the system, right? Psephologists John Curtice and Prof Tim Bale sounded the warning: you can’t change the rules just because you’re losing. The point was so self-evident, from such trusted sources, that all the air seemed to leave the room. But four months on, Labour is ahead in the polls, Reform’s support is tailing off and seems to have further to fall. Far more importantly, this week Burnham showed himself prepared to have a thorny, inconvenient debate that wouldn’t necessarily even serve his political interests, and even if it did, would certainly disperse his power, because he believes in his cause and does so persuasively. So he doesn’t look like he’s losing.
- 
  Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Ukraine’s new ground robot switches from land to water in seconds. It just ran its first supply mission, 40 kilometers to positions others can’t reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

23:55:21 KST

A Ukrainian ground robot drove toward the front, reached the water in its path, and kept going, swimming across with ammunition and food aboard and no soldier at risk. It ran the first logistics mission with an amphibious ground robot, covering more than 40 kilometers over land and water to resupply positions, the Defense Ministry said.
Water is one of the front's quiet chokepoints: rivers, canals, and marshes that stop ground robots and force risky detours, and that air resupply cannot always solve. The amphibious robot drives like a normal ground vehicle, then switches to swimming in seconds, letting one machine cross terrain that halts the rest.
It is the latest of Ukraine's battlefield-robot firsts, which this year have included air-dropping robots behind Russian lines.
Water stops the others
The robot was developed through Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed defense-innovation cluster, which links developers with the military and government.
The one such robot gains additional capabilities to carry out missions across different terrains.
For this operation, the system was refined over several months in close cooperation with the military, taking into account real tasks, operational experience, and the specifics of frontline terrain. The Brave1 defense innovation cluster provided grant support for the system, helping bring the solution to practical use.
The ministry says it is "expanding the capabilities of robotic systems" so soldiers have more tools for the fight.
Robots with grenade launchers
Earlier, Ukraine employed a new tactic during its major Operation Vivaldi in Donetsk Oblast. During the 3rd Army Corps' offensive, fighters from the world's first experimental unit of unmanned ground-strike vehicles, "NC13", upgraded their kamikaze ground drones with grenade launchers.
During the operation, UGVs equipped with two Bullspike grenade launchers attacked Russian positions, then detonated directly inside their shelters. The occupiers believed they were being attacked by an entire assault group. In reality, they were being torn apart by robots from the 3rd Assault Corps.

Russia’s War Against Ukraine Runs on Credit as Moscow’s Debt Hits 24-Year Record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:55:14 UTC
23:55:14 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s War Against Ukraine Runs on Credit as Moscow’s Debt Hits 24-Year Record
Russia is preparing to drive government debt to its highest level in more than two decades as the Kremlin increasingly turns to borrowing to cover widening budget deficits and another surge in military spending.
Under the government’s draft budget, Moscow plans a sharp increase in domestic borrowing over the next several years as defense spending rises to levels unseen since the Soviet era, according to budget documents reported by The Moscow Times on September 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s Finance Ministry plans to sell trillions of rubles in government bonds annually, with borrowing continuing to rise through 2029.
The result, according to ministry projections, will be a steady increase in state debt from roughly 19.9% of GDP in 2026 to 21.7% next year and 24.1% by the end of the three-year budget period.
That would be Russia’s highest debt-to-GDP level since 2002.
While that ratio remains relatively modest compared with many large Western economies, the speed of the increase is significant for a country that spent much of the 2000s aggressively paying down its sovereign debt with revenues from high oil prices.
During the first years of Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, Moscow relied heavily on its National Wealth Fund to cover spending gaps. As those liquid reserves have diminished, borrowing has become increasingly important.
Finance Ministry estimates indicate that state debt increased by roughly $227 billion between 2024 and 2026.
The Central Bank is also playing a larger role in keeping that borrowing machine functioning.
“Without support from the Central Bank, it is impossible to finance the budget deficit even this year,” economist Sergei Aleksashenko said.
Russian banks have increasingly received central-bank liquidity through repo operations backed by government bonds. The volume of those operations has risen by roughly $30 billion since the beginning of the year, reaching about $72 billion by September 30.
The debt itself is also becoming increasingly expensive to service. Interest payments are projected to reach $55 billion next year, then climb to $64.5 billion in 2028 and more than $68 billion in 2029.
By that point, around 10.6% of Russia’s entire federal budget could be consumed simply by servicing debt, compared with roughly 4.4% before the full-scale invasion. Reuters reported that debt-service costs are already projected to account for 9.4% of spending in 2027.
The driving force behind the borrowing surge is military expenditure.
Russia plans to allocate $205 billion to national defense in 2027, roughly 35% of total federal spending and 27% more than previously planned. Total defense expenditure over the next three years is expected to reach around $600 billion.
Earlier, CIA Director John Ratcliffe warned Russian officials that Russia’s economy could collapse in a Soviet-style crisis if the war continues.
A senior diplomat familiar with the CIA’s briefing to Western partner services after Ratcliffe’s late-August visit to Moscow told FAZ that the intelligence assessment was the trip’s central purpose. “Russia is losing the war,” the diplomat said, describing the US assessment as conclusive.

Ukraine Turns Wartime Military-Tech Experience Into New High-Tech Export Drive
Ukraine plans to turn its wartime military technology and digital resilience experience into a broader high-tech export push, with the US among the prospective partners.
This was reported by Reuters on September 30, based on an interview with Ukraine's Minister for Digital Transformation, Oksana Ferchuk.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ferchuk told the agency that Kyiv aims to use its expertise in military technologies and digital innovation, including AI, to sharply increase high-tech exports in the coming years.
"We are ready to cooperate and consult other states in this experience," Ferchuk stated, according to Reuters.

Reuters noted that Ferchuk traveled to Washington this week to meet US economic, cybersecurity and telecommunications officials, as well as senior World Bank leaders. She is pitching the US, the European Union and other partners on cooperation projects in the digital sphere.

Ferchuk acknowledged the destruction of infrastructure at dozens of telecom and data center locations, yet described the country's digital services as "alive and running."
Built-in redundancies across locations and cloud providers have kept them functioning, she emphasized. The attacks had been painful, she indicated, but had not significantly disrupted services.
Ferchuk previously oversaw digital transformation at the defense ministry. Reuters described Ukraine as a test bed for the newest weaponry, already helping other countries build their drone defenses.
According to the report, cheaper products and quicker innovation have allowed Kyiv to disrupt the generally slower-moving global military technology sector.
The minister argued that the same approach could work in civilian fields, with AI incorporated along the way. She warned that companies or countries that skip investment in Ukraine risk missing the transformation of new sectors.
Ferchuk added that she had already met World Bank officials in Kyiv, who showed strong interest in Ukrainian digital tools, including platforms for education, telecommunications and social services. Further discussions with the bank were planned for this week, Reuters reported.
Earlier, on July 22, Ukraine and the US signed a bilateral statement of intent establishing a framework for the temporary export of Ukrainian unmanned systems for testing by the Pentagon.
By July 31, F-Drones had delivered the first 2,000 F10 FPV drones under the $1 billion Drone Dominance Program, making the F10 the first Ukrainian drone authorized for export to the US under the initiative.
A broader drone-defense agreement was ready for signing as of September 23, though it had not yet been finalized.

Mali has taken its case against Ukraine to the UN. What is behind it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:53:57 UTC
23:53:57 KST

Mali has taken its case against Ukraine to the UN. What is behind it?
Mali has taken its case against Ukraine to the UN again, two years after severing diplomatic ties with Kiev over a rebel ambush that killed dozens of Malian soldiers and allied Russian forces.
Malian Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop told the UN General Assembly on Monday that Ukraine was aiding armed groups in the Sahel and urged the international community to respond.
Why has Mali raised the accusation again?
Diop’s remarks follow a series of coordinated militant raids in Mali and new reports of Ukrainian assistance with drone operations. Pointing to attacks on April 25 and July 4, he said they exposed a “dangerous connection” between jihadists and separatist rebels, and accused Kiev of aiding forces that threaten his country’s territorial integrity.
“Ukraine is just the visible part of the iceberg,” he said, claiming the violence was part of a wider effort to destabilize the Sahel states and obstruct their break with former colonial influence.
The April offensive by the Al-Qaeda-linked Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) struck several cities and killed Malian Defense Minister Sadio Camara. Mali’s army said it repelled assaults on military sites and key infrastructure with support from Russia’s Africa Corps, killing more than 200 militants.
Malian Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maiga described the offensive as an attempt to seize power. The Russian Defense Ministry acknowledged the assault, saying it amounted to an attempted coup and claimed that the attackers had received training involving Ukrainian and European mercenary instructors.
How did the dispute with Ukraine begin?
In July 2024, Tuareg rebels ambushed Malian troops and Wagner Group contractors near Tinzaouaten, close to the Algerian border. Ukrainian military intelligence spokesman Andrey Yusov later said the rebels had received “necessary information” that enabled the operation, adding that “there will be a continuation.”
Yuriy Pyvovarov, then Ukraine’s ambassador to Senegal, shared Yusov’s interview on Facebook, writing, “The work will continue. There will certainly be other results.” Senegal summoned him over the post, while Mali cited the remarks as evidence of Kiev’s involvement, and severed diplomatic ties.
What has been reported about Ukrainian involvement since then?
Le Monde reported in 2024 that Ukrainian intelligence had taught Tuareg rebels to build and operate explosive drones, citing sources close to the group. This month, CNN interviewed Ukrainian personnel who said about 15 specialists were assisting the FLA with unmanned aircraft. One described remotely directing rebel drone missions.
Fousseynou Ouattara, vice president of the defense commission of Mali’s transitional council, told TASS in July that authorities had identified fighters who had received drone training in Ukraine. Malian outlet Bamada also reported that soldiers recovered a drone bearing Ukrainian writing and documents allegedly linked to Ukrainian intelligence during operations against JNIM.
What has Ukraine said?
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry has rejected the Sahel states’ terrorism allegations, describing them as “groundless and untrue” and calling Mali’s decision to sever ties “hasty.” In August 2024, it said Bamako had provided no evidence of Ukrainian involvement in the Tinzaouaten attack. Ukraine’s military intelligence agency also referred CNN to earlier official remarks when approached for comment on its September report of Ukrainian drone specialists assisting rebels in Mali.
Is Mali alone in making the accusation?
Niger and Burkina Faso have also accused Ukraine of supporting armed groups. The three Alliance of Sahel States (AES) members filed a complaint with the UN Security Council in August 2024.
During a televised interview on Sunday reviewing his four years in office, Burkina Faso’s interim President Ibrahim Traore said he had placed Ukraine on his country’s “map of enemies.” Speaking about what he described as attempts to destabilize Mali and Niger, he warned these were “only the beginning.” He cited Pyvovarov’s comment, saying the diplomat had “clearly stated that they were involved” in supporting armed groups in the Sahel.
What does Moscow say?
Russia backs the Sahel states’ accusations. Last month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov accused Kiev of “state terrorism” against countries in the region, citing reports of serving Ukrainian troops joining attacks alongside armed groups. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova previously said Kiev was opening a “second front” against Russia in Africa by supporting militants in countries friendly to Moscow.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Borisenko told TASS on July 17 that Ukrainian instructors trained in drone warfare were embedded with Islamist militants in Mali. He also alleged Ukrainian involvement in attacks on Russian interests in Libya and support for paramilitary forces in Sudan, extending Moscow’s accusations beyond the Sahel.
Why have the Sahel states turned to Russia?
Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso ended defense ties with France, accusing it of failing to contain the insurgency and interfering in their affairs. They have strengthened counterterrorism cooperation with Russia.
Nearly 49,000 people have been killed in violence linked to militant Islamist groups in the Sahel since 2022, the Africa Center for Strategic Studies said in August.
Mali and Russia signed a military cooperation agreement in June 2019. Bamako sought Russian private military assistance in 2021. Wagner was replaced by Russia’s Defense Ministry-run Africa Corps in June 2025. The corps operates at African governments’ official request, Lavrov said last month.
At the UN on Monday, Diop said the AES remained open to partnerships respecting its members’ sovereignty. “We do not accept dictates; rather, we seek sincere and healthy cooperation,” he said.

Report: Estonian e-commerce among the top in Europe  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:52:52 UTC
23:52:52 KST

TALLINN - According to the 2026 European E-commerce Report, European e-commerce is still growing, but the pace has slowed. Estonia stands out in the report on several fronts: its e-commerce turnover per capita reached 4,252 euros in 2025, the second-highest result among European countries.
European B2C e-commerce turnover was 911 billion euros in 2025, a 7 percent increase from the previous year. For 2026, turnover is projected to grow to 961 billion euros, a 5 percent increase. Adjusted for inflation, real growth last year was 4 percent. Western Europe remains the largest market, accounting for 57 percent of European e-commerce turnover. However, the markets in Southern and Eastern Europe are experiencing the fastest growth.
For Estonian companies, 97 percent of online sales came through their own websites or apps, the highest figure in Europe. "Estonia's result shows that our e-commerce sector is mature, with companies having built strong, independent sales channels. At the same time, the low use of marketplaces means many businesses have not yet capitalized on the opportunity to reach new customers outside Estonia. Cross-border sales represent the next significant growth area," Tõnu Väät, head of the Estonian E-commerce Association, said in a press release.
In 2025, 93 percent of Europeans used the internet, a figure projected to rise to 95 percent by 2026. Last year, 75 percent of Europeans aged 16-74 made purchases online, compared to 68 percent in 2021.
According to the report, efficiency and customer experience are becoming more crucial in mature markets. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in customer service, marketing, personalization, pricing, and analytics. In the future, agentive AI may start handling a larger share of the purchasing process on behalf of the consumer.
Consumers have become more price-sensitive, comparing prices more frequently, seeking cheaper alternatives, and placing greater importance on used goods and cross-border purchases. Payments and logistics are also evolving rapidly, with advancements in mobile payments, digital wallets, instant payments, buy-now-pay-later services, and the proliferation of parcel lockers and pick-up points.
"The era of rapid growth in mature markets is over, and success now hinges on efficiency. Artificial intelligence helps companies improve their service, pricing, and customer understanding. At the same time, we must ensure that regulations do not become overly burdensome for small merchants and that we compete with non-European platforms on a level playing field," Väät added.
The Estonian E-commerce Association is an umbrella organization with over 530 member companies. The association also issues the "Secure Shopping" trustmark.

RIGA - The Ministry of Health is seeking additional EUR 826 million in next year’s budget, as reported on Wednesday at a joint meeting of the Saeima’s sustainable development committee, the Latgale subcommittee of human rights and public affairs committee, and the public health subcommittee of the social and labor affairs committee, by deputy state secretary Boriss Knigins.
According to data compiled by the Ministry of Health, the ministry’s identified needs and established priorities for 2027 total EUR 826,053,948. Of this amount, 49.2 percent or EUR 406.7 million are reportedly needed to improve the accessibility and quality of healthcare services. This amount includes funds for increasing the salaries and pay components of healthcare professionals.
Additional EUR 135.39 million is planned to be allocated to improve the system for government-funded medications and medical supplies. Knigins acknowledged that, according to forecasts, the deficit for government-funded medications could reach EUR 35 million this year. This is reportedly due to budget planning that does not account for potential new patients who will require government-funded medications.
As reported, the Latvian Trade Union of Health and Social Care Employees (LVSADA) has demanded that the 2027 state budget provide for a pay raise of at least 30 percent for all healthcare workers, with the necessary funding included in the tariffs for state-funded healthcare services. A request has also been made to revise the Cabinet of Ministers’ regulations on the minimum monthly wage and special allowances for healthcare workers, as well as to introduce a mechanism for regular wage reviews.
Under the Cabinet of Ministers’ regulations on the minimum monthly wage and special allowances for healthcare workers, the minimum monthly wage set for nursing aides and medical assistants is EUR 863, which is EUR 43 higher than the minimum wage planned for 2027, while the minimum monthly wage set for nurses is EUR 1,189. LVSADA notes that without a commensurate increase in healthcare workers’ salaries, the labor shortage in the sector will worsen.
The Cabinet of Ministers’ draft response to the 2027 state budget acknowledges the need for additional funding for the healthcare sector in the amount of EUR 663 million, but only EUR 45.2 million are allocated for human resources. The draft does not specify the actual amount of funding to be allocated, notes LVSADA.
If the government does not adopt specific and financially secured decisions regarding healthcare funding and pay raises for all employees in the sector, the LVSADA Executive Board has been instructed to convene an emergency council meeting to decide on further measures to defend collective interests as provided for in regulatory acts.

If NATO collectively decides to do so and there is a need, nuclear weapons could be deployed in Latvia - Rinkevics  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:52:36 UTC
23:52:36 KST

RIGA - If NATO collectively decides and there is a need to do so, nuclear weapons could be deployed in Latvia, Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics told members of the press today.
The Lithuanian Seimas voted this month in a first reading to support the repeal of the constitutional ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons on the country’s territory. Currently, Article 137 of the Lithuanian Constitution stipulates that weapons of mass destruction or foreign military bases may not be located on Lithuanian territory.
Rinkevics emphasized that the Latvian Constitution does not contain such a ban. "We have no legally established obstacles in our laws to the deployment of nuclear weapons in Latvia," said the president.
He explained that in 2003, as Latvia was preparing to join NATO, each member state had confirmed that it would not impose any restrictions on the full implementation of NATO’s collective security mechanisms, including participation in the nuclear deterrence system. "If the need arises and if such a collective NATO decision is made, nuclear weapons will be deployed in Latvia," Rinkevics stated.
At the same time, he emphasized that no specific negotiations regarding the deployment of nuclear weapons in Latvia are currently underway.
Commenting on the United Kingdom’s offer of nuclear umbrella to the member states of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF)-the Baltic states, the Nordic countries, and the Netherlands- Rinkevics argued that without nuclear deterrence, several conventional wars would have long since broken out in Europe. The use of nuclear weapons is a last resort, but they deter aggressors from unpredictable or large-scale actions, Rinkevics noted.
The politician pointed out that the United Kingdom is already part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence system and that Latvia is currently under the NATO nuclear umbrella provided by the United States and the United Kingdom, but as a member of JEF, Latvia views all additional security measures and elements positively. "We understand that this is still part of NATO’s overall policy," the president said.
As reported, the United Kingdom has offered a "nuclear umbrella" to members of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) military partnership (the Baltic states, Nordics countries and the Netherlands) as part of a wider defence agreement.
The umbrella is a security guarantee by a nuclear-armed state to protect a non-nuclear ally.
The offer was confirmed during a visit by General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord and Chief of the UK’s Naval Staff, to Finland on Monday, where he met with MP Heikki Autto (NCP), chair of parliament’s defence committee.
It is believed that the JEF member countries will sign an agreement at a meeting in Oslo in November.
The deal would mean a separate nuclear umbrella outside of Nato’s extended deterrence strategy offered by the US, UK and France to all non-nuclear member states within the alliance.
"Finland is under the nuclear umbrella. It is guaranteed by our submarines, which are patrolling the Atlantic right now," Jenkins said.
JEF is a coalition of ten like-minded countries-Denmark, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, the United Kingdom, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Finland, and Sweden - that comprises high-readiness forces capable of responding rapidly to crises in the high north and Northern Europe.
The coalition was established in 2014 on the initiative of the United Kingdom in response to Russia’s annexation of Crimea. Finland and Sweden joined the JEF in 2017, even before these countries were admitted to NATO. The JEF is now considered a first-response force that complements NATO.

RIGA - Riga Technical University (RTU) has been ranked among the world's top 1,000 universities, according to data from the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2026.
Over the past year, RTU has risen from the 1,001st-1,200th range to the 801st-1,000th range. The university’s score has improved in all five evaluated categories.
The other Latvian universities included in the ranking are not ranked higher than 1,001st place. The University of Latvia (LU) has maintained its position in the 1,001st-1,200th range, while Riga Stradins University (RSU) has moved up to 1,201st-1,400th range. The Latvian University of Life Sciences and Technologies (LBTU) is ranked below 2,001st place.
The universities have shown improvements in several categories. RSU and LU have seen their rankings rise in four categories. Meanwhile, LBTU’s scores have improved in three categories - research environment, research quality, and international outlook - but have dropped in the categories of teaching and industry collaboration.
The universities’ performance was rated highest in the international outlook category, where the score of each university is its highest across all categories. RTU and RSU performed best in this category, scoring 71.2 and 66.8 points, respectively. All four universities saw their scores improve in this category.
A total of 2,297 universities were evaluated in this year’s ranking. Oxford University received the highest overall rating, with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in second place, while Princeton University and Stanford University tied for third.

Two men, born in 2001 and 2007, were arrested on September 23 in connection with the incident. During searches at the suspects’ residences, law enforcement officers found and seized substances believed to be narcotics. The suspected drugs have been submitted for forensic tests.
On September 24, the two suspects were remanded in custody as a security measure by a court order.
Criminal proceedings for kidnapping in an organized group have been initiated in connection with the incident. Such a crime is punishable by a prison term of three to 12 years, with or without confiscation of property, and with or without probationary supervision for up to three years.
Both suspects had previously come to the attention of law enforcement in connection with offenses committed under the influence of intoxicating substances.

RIGA - Although there is much talk in many quarters about a possible direct Russian invasion of one of the NATO member states, Latvia currently has no such indications or facts that would prove that, President Edgars Rinkevics told reporters today after a meeting with Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List).

Similar reports of sabotage carried out by Russia have also emerged in other countries, the president noted.
Rinkevics did not deny that there may come a time when someone actually loses their life in such incidents. "That, of course, is a completely different situation," the politician remarked.

Public involvement is crucial in this regard, Rinkevics noted. Rinkevics assessed that Russia currently has two objectives regarding Latvia. The president noted that, in his discussions with leaders of other countries, he has observed that understanding of Russia’s objectives is also beginning to take hold elsewhere.
Rinkevics does not consider the statement made by Egils Zviedrs, director of the Constitution Protection Bureau (SAB), in an interview with LETA, that Russia, unable to defeat Ukraine, is raising the stakes in Europe, and that civilian casualties cannot be ruled out, is anything radically new. "We have already called on people and warned them to be prepared - without excessive panic, but with great vigilance," the official said.
Kulbergs, for his part, emphasized that Latvia understands very well what to expect from Russia, and understands it much better than many countries in the West. That is why Latvia is investing in security, especially along the border, concentrating its capabilities, and spending enormous resources on defense and internal affairs, the prime minister noted, adding that Latvia does so to a much greater extent than many other European partners who are less informed about Russia.
He asserted that Russia currently lacks the conventional capabilities for another large-scale military operation, but at the same time, we must understand and be prepared for provocations. "There is no need to be alarmed, but we must be vigilant," the prime minister said.
As reported, Zviedris noted in an interview with LETA that SAB has been warning about an escalation of Russia’s unconventional military operations since early spring. Specifically, Russia is unable to achieve its stated goal - victory in the war against Ukraine, and is therefore escalating the situation in Europe, given the support Western countries are providing to Ukraine.
This escalation includes hybrid threats such as cyberattacks and acts of physical sabotage, as well as information warfare. Russia is escalating the situation because it has failed to reduce Western support for Ukraine or to secure a relaxation of sanctions, Zviedris explained.
Consequently, we are seeing incidents such as drones filled with explosives at Leipzig Airport and acts of sabotage on railway lines in European countries. "Russia is raising the stakes, and unfortunately, we cannot rule out civilian casualties either," emphasized the director of Latvia’s special services.
Zviedris pointed out that so far in Europe, Russia has not carried out only false-flag operations, as everything else has already happened. He reminded that in Latvia there have been acts of desecration of monuments and the arson attack on the Museum of the Occupation, while in Lithuania there have been attacks on Russian opposition figures living there. Meanwhile, recent warnings by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk about Russian threats were directly related to false-flag operations. Similarly, there was a recent Russian attack on a Ukrainian passenger train just two kilometers from the Polish border, Zviedris noted.
"Consequently, Tusk warned of Russian attacks near the borders of NATO countries. Such statements serve as a warning to Russia that we are monitoring its activities near our national borders and will not tolerate them," added the director of SAB.
Zviedris noted that Latvia has requested the deployment of four NATO fighter jets here during the Saeima elections, a request to which Germany has agreed. This step was taken to rule out any possible provocations, such as the appearance of an unidentified flying object in Latvian airspace, which could subsequently spark speculation about the legitimacy of the election process.
"So the Russian threat is real, and since the aggressor has been unable to achieve its goals in Ukraine, the stakes are being raised," Zviedris added.
