Kyiv • UNN
On October 1, a court in Lviv is scheduled to announce the verdict for Viacheslav Zinchenko in the case concerning the murder of Iryna Farion. He faces life imprisonment.
Today, October 1, a court hearing is due to take place at the Shevchenkivskyi District Court of Lviv, at which Vyacheslav Zinchenko, accused of murdering linguist Iryna Farion, is to be handed down the verdict in the case. Zinchenko faces life imprisonment, reports UNN.
Details
The court hearing in case No. 466/12967/24 concerning premeditated murder will begin at 10:30 a.m. at the premises of the Shevchenkivskyi District Court of Lviv. Iryna Farion’s daughter, Sofia Osoba, is appearing as the injured party. The accused is Vyacheslav Zinchenko.
Additional information
On July 19, 2024, linguist Iryna Farion was shot in Lviv. It was reported at the time that the attempted assassination took place at around 7:30 p.m. on one of Lviv’s streets. An unknown individual fired a weapon in Farion’s direction.
It later became known that Farion died in hospital after the attack.
The then Minister of Internal Affairs, Ihor Klymenko, stated that the attack on Iryna Farion had been classified as an attempted premeditated murder. Police had several theories regarding the linguist’s murder, including her public and political activities and personal animosity. Law enforcement officers found a shell casing after the shooting and did not rule out a "Russian trace" in the crime.
On July 25, it became known that an 18-year-old suspect in Iryna Farion’s murder had been detained in Dnipro. Klymenko stated that law enforcement had sufficient evidence to assert that Vyacheslav Zinchenko was the person who shot the woman. According to him, the investigation lasted 139 hours.
The first court hearing on choosing a preventive measure for Zinchenko took place on July 26, 2024, at the Halytskyi District Court of Lviv. The court then remanded him in custody without the right to bail, while in September of that year Zinchenko himself asked the court to extend his preventive measure because he feared for his life.
They want to transfer me to a pretrial detention center. Know that if something happens to me, if my preventive measure is not extended, I will... I do not want to kill myself, I am not planning to, under any circumstances. So know that if something happens to me, then someone helped. I ask the prosecutors and judges to extend my preventive measure
At the first hearing, Zinchenko did not admit his guilt and asked journalists to pose more interesting questions, calling theirs "some kind of boring stuff."
At the end of December 2024, the prosecutor’s office submitted the case concerning Iryna Farion’s murder to court.
Prosecutors from the Lviv Regional Prosecutor’s Office completed the pretrial investigation and submitted to court an indictment against an 18-year-old resident of the city of Dnipro, accused of murdering public figure and People’s Deputy of Ukraine of the VII convocation Iryna Farion
At the same time, law enforcement authorities reclassified the case concerning Farion’s murder as the murder of a person in connection with the performance of a public duty, motivated by national intolerance, as well as unlawful handling of weapons. Under the charges, Zinchenko faces life imprisonment.
On September 17, court pleadings concluded at the Shevchenkivskyi District Court of Lviv in the case concerning the murder of linguist Iryna Farion. After that, the court retired to the deliberation room to reach a decision.
At the beginning of the hearing, the defense asked for additional time to review the case materials, in particular the forensic medical examination. The female lawyer also stated that certain materials had been scanned improperly and spoke about pressure on the defense.
The court granted the defense 20 minutes to review the materials. After the break, the female lawyer asked to postpone the hearing until September 18 in order to complete preparations for her statement during the pleadings.
The prosecutors objected to this motion. They noted that the defense had already been given time to review the case materials.
According to the prosecutor, during the pretrial investigation in the case, more than 60 examinations were ordered, more than 1,500 people were questioned, and footage from surveillance cameras was processed.

LONDON, September 30. /TASS/. The average price of diesel in the UK has surpassed the psychological milestone of 2 pounds ($2.66) per liter for the first time in history, according to calculations by Sky News.
Earlier this week, diesel prices had already broken the June 2022 record, reaching 1.9918 pounds per liter. This means filling up a typical family car with a 55-liter tank now costs 110 pounds ($146) – an increase of 31 pounds ($41) compared to the period before the war in Iran began.
The RAC motoring group warned that record-breaking diesel prices will bring financial pain not only for drivers at the pumps but for all consumers, as the delivery of goods and services relies heavily on diesel-powered trucks and vans.
Petrol prices have also hit a new high since late February. On September 28, petrol was priced at 1.74 pounds ($2.31) per liter, making the average cost of a full tank 95.8 pounds ($127). This is 22.8 pounds ($30.3) higher than before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran.

More than 44,000 file legal objections to Palantir NHS platform handling their data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:51:08 UTC
23:51:08 KST

Tens of thousands of people have formally demanded NHS England blocks the Palantir-powered national medical data platform from handling their personal information.
More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the nationwide Federated Data Platform (FDP) operated using the US company’s AI technology.
The coordinated campaign utilises rights enshrined in data protection laws and means the NHS must stop using the data unless it can provide a “compelling reason” to continue.
Hundreds of thousands of people have signed petitions demanding the government cancels its £330m deal with Palantir, and Andy Burnham will be required to make a decision to back or axe Palantir within months.
Campaigners have voiced anger at Palantir’s work for the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, and two House of Commons select committees have called for Labour to exercise a break clause in the seven-year deal which comes into force in February 2027.
David Murray, a retired IBM systems engineer and one of those requesting the data block, said: “I am a believer in the NHS having really good data on their patients, but I want it to be something you can really trust to be used for the right purposes. I am not happy about Palantir’s involvement with the IDF in Gaza and ICE in America.”
On Wednesday, the human rights group Amnesty International and patient campaign group, Just Treatment, parked a van styled like a shot-up Palestinian ambulance outside Palantir’s London HQ in a stunt that asked: “Why should a company linked to Israel’s destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system have any place in ours?”
Protesters have also raised concerns, acknowledged by the NHS England chief executive, Jim Mackey, that the benefits to public health from the Palantir-powered platform may not be as significant as has been claimed.
Palantir says the FDP, which is designed to connect sprawling health service data on topics ranging from surgery schedules to discharge planning, is helping to cut waiting lists and frees up beds. Louis Mosley, the company’s executive vice-president for UK and Europe, has accused people who disagree with that assessment of suffering from “Palantir derangement syndrome”.
A spokesperson said: “Palantir software is helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days.”
Mosley has said its technology was used for locating hostages, not military targeting, in Gaza, although when challenged last year by a protester alleging “Palantir kills Palestinians” in Gaza, the company’s chief executive, Alex Karp, replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.”
The formal objections to the FDP using personal data cite article 21 of the UK General Data Protection Regulation and express concern that “the involvement of Palantir undermines my personal trust in NHS data confidentiality”. Palantir said its patient data could only be handled according to the NHS’s instructions and remained in the UK.
Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, a not-for-profit that coordinated the data objections, said: “The scale of this public backlash should be a huge wake-up call for the government.”
A spokesperson for NHS England said: “All NHS organisations remain in control of their data within the FDP, with suppliers unable to access it for their own purposes, and we will respond to the objection requests in line with data protection law.”
The 44,000 objectors have also asked that the NHS halts processing of their data through the Palantir platform while their main request is assessed.

A Palestinian imam and religious radio presenter was killed Wednesday in an Israeli drone strike while he was preparing a media report on Quran memorization in the southern Gaza Strip, according to an official.
Mohammed Abdul Aziz al-Najjar, 38, was an imam as well as a producer and presenter of religious programs at Quran Radio, affiliated with Gaza’s Ministry of Endowments and Religious Affairs.
Ikrami al-Mudallal, the ministry’s media director, told Anadolu that al-Najjar was targeted by an Israeli drone strike “while carrying out his work producing media material related to Quran memorization.”

His death brought the number of Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks Wednesday in Gaza to seven.
Five Palestinians were killed earlier in an Israeli strike on a vehicle pulling a passenger cart in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood of southern Gaza City.
A Palestinian woman, Iman Abdul Aal, was also killed and her husband critically injured in an Israeli airstrike on a home on Al-Wahda Street in Gaza City early Wednesday.
Israeli violations of a ceasefire agreement have killed 1,431 Palestinians and injured 5,026, according to figures released Wednesday by Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 in Gaza, according to Palestinian figures. Around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed.

Mounting pressure on Iran could lead to attack on Israel, ex-national security council head warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:50:19 UTC
23:50:19 KST

Former national security council head Meir Ben-Shabbat warned that mounting pressure on Iran could still push Tehran toward a direct attack on Israel, while arguing that a future agreement between Washington and Tehran could provide the Iranian regime with a strategic lifeline, he told Maariv in a Wednesday interview.
Ben-Shabbat, who was among the architects of the Abraham Accords, said the Iranian regime remained under severe pressure but had not yet reached a point of desperation.
“First, regarding Iran’s situation: despite the challenging reality it faces, the impression is that the regime in Tehran still does not have its back against the wall. In medical terms, its condition is serious but not critical.
The Iranians are probably counting on the American willingness to reach an agreement, continue to exist, and save them if they reach the edge of the abyss. In any event, Israel must always be prepared on the assumption that at a certain point in time, which will not necessarily be possible to predict, Iran will consider attacking it,” he said.
Ben-Shabbat also warned that a US agreement with Iran could have serious strategic consequences regardless of whether it formally restricted Israel’s freedom of action.
“Israel’s freedom of action to defend itself against an existential threat is a matter about which there is no dispute. The consequences of an agreement with Iran are very severe even if they do not have an effect on Israel’s freedom of action," he said.
"Any agreement with the Iranians, even if it meets the parameters set by the American administration, will ultimately be a lifeline for the regime in Tehran; it will finance its recovery and preserve the dangers from it."
"This clear and unequivocal position was voiced a few days ago by Gen. Jack Keane, who served as vice chief of staff of the US Army and received the Presidential Medal from Trump. He precisely defined the strategic trap placed before the American president and recommended making the creation of conditions that put the Iranian regime on a path to collapse a goal. Any additional word is unnecessary.”
Iran has been waging a campaign against Europe 'for some time'
Asked whether an attempted attack on RAF Fairford, if linked to Iran or one of its proxies, would indicate that Tehran was expanding its campaign against the West into Europe, Ben-Shabbat said Iran had already been waging such a campaign for some time.
“Iran has been waging a campaign against Europe for some time. I remind you that Iran has already attacked European bases: Iranian UAVs, apparently launched from Lebanon by Hezbollah, directly struck the British Air Force base at Akrotiri in Cyprus.
"The confrontation between Iran and European countries is admittedly not being conducted as a frontal conventional war, but it certainly exists as a multidimensional hybrid campaign combining warfare in the ‘gray zone,’ terrorism through proxies, cyberattacks, and economic influence. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in June 2025 that Israel ‘is doing the dirty work for all of us’ in reference to the campaign against Iran. He was right then, and his words are also correct today.”
Asked whether Israelis and Jews abroad should prepare for an increase in attempts to target them amid rising pressure on Iran, Ben-Shabbat replied: “The system and the citizens must assume so.”
Netanyahu's visit to the UAE tightens important relationship
Ben-Shabbat also addressed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s reported secret visit to the United Arab Emirates, saying coordination with Abu Dhabi was particularly important given the possibility of either military escalation with Iran or a diplomatic agreement.
“I remind you that we are in the midst of the confrontation with Iran, with on the one hand – a possibility of military escalation, and on the other hand – a possibility of a diplomatic arrangement. A common position and alignment by Israel and the Emirates are things that require discussion and coordination.”
On the possibility of expanding the Abraham Accords, including through Saudi normalization, Ben-Shabbat said the current regional uncertainty reduced the chances of a breakthrough.
“In general, the chances of this during periods of uncertainty, election campaigns or fighting, are not high. Israel’s value as a security and technological-economic partner is clear. Israeli's interest in expanding the agreements is clear, but it must come from Israeli strength. Under no circumstances should we court them or pay compensation.”
When will the Hezbollah conflict be over?
Turning to Lebanon, Ben-Shabbat said Hezbollah had suffered a strategic blow but that the campaign against the group was far from over.
“The pager operation and the Israeli attack that followed it two years ago were a turning point in the war between Israel and Hezbollah, which led to the elimination of the person who had ruled southern Lebanon and the Shi’ite terrorist organization for 40 years, cut off Iran’s strongest and most important proxy arm that it had in the region, enabled the collapse of the Assad regime and the shattering of the perception of Syria as Iran’s backyard, and created significant shock waves in the Middle East.
“Above and below the surface, the signs of the change that occurred can be seen in every field: Hezbollah lost the control it had over the territory and the line of villages along the border with Israel, it also lost commanders, fighters, infrastructure, and strategic assets; and beyond that, its status in the Lebanese arena.
"Naim Qassem is finding it difficult to step into Nasrallah’s shoes and fill the military, political, or social vacuum he left behind. Lebanese voices expressing deep frustration over the heavy price of Hezbollah’s war, which is not necessarily Lebanon’s war, are growing, and alongside all of these – the Lebanese government, despite its weakness, is trying to establish a new order.
“The Lebanese-American researcher and commentator Hussein Abd al-Hussein determined in an article he published recently that Hezbollah suffered a strategic defeat but refuses to acknowledge it. From Israel’s point of view, these are significant achievements, but the work is not complete and it is too early for summaries.
"All the players in the system understand that the way Iran emerges from the current confrontation will directly shape Hezbollah’s power, status, and future policy. Therefore, Israel must tighten its control over the areas it has defined, maintain a continuous offensive initiative, block every attempt at renewed force buildup, and not ease the pressure on the enemy’s throat for even a moment.”
Israel continues to strive to destroy Hamas
Ben-Shabbat rejected the idea that Israel had shifted from seeking to destroy Hamas to merely weakening the organization.
“I am not aware of a change in the goals of the war regarding Gaza, and in my opinion there is no room for such a change. Determination, patience, and persistence are the key to success. Israel must complete the task until the military and governing capabilities of the Hamas organization in the Strip are completely eliminated, the territory is completely demilitarized, and there is Israeli security control.
"From the perspective of the State of Israel, it is not enough to settle only for removing the security threat; it should have an interest in the area in which the cruel monster that carried out the October 7 massacre grew, becoming eternal testimony to the prices that anyone who thinks in the future about attacking Israel will pay.”
Asked about European measures targeting goods from the West Bank, east Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights, and their possible economic impact on Palestinians, Ben-Shabbat said he did not have the exact figures but accused some international actors of prioritizing pressure on Israeli settlements over Palestinian economic welfare.
“I am not familiar with the precise economic data, but among some of the players in the international system, the desire to harm the settlement enterprise in Judea and Samaria outweighs the interest in ensuring the economic well-being of the Palestinians there. This is another expression of the double standard and hypocrisy on their part.”
Turkey: A growing power in the Middle East
Ben-Shabbat also focused on Turkey, which he described as a growing regional power taking advantage of changes in Syria, Africa, and the eastern Mediterranean.
“The Greek defense minister, Nikos Dendias, said a few months ago: ‘If we ask the United States and Turkey how they see the future of the world and the region in ten years, we will receive two completely opposite answers – and that is the whole story.’ His words capture the abyss between the American vision and Erdogan’s ambitions for the Middle East and the international system.
“More than any other country, Turkey knows how to exploit global great-power competition and the changes in the Middle East in order to establish its status as a dominant regional power. It dances at every wedding and collects diplomatic brokerage fees from all the players. Following the collapse of the Assad regime and the forced withdrawal of the Iranian military presence, Turkey became the dominant player in Syria. From local territorial control in northern Syria, it moved to exercising broad influence across the entire country.
“Syria is only part of Erdogan’s broader vision of ‘neo-Ottomanism.’ He seeks to restore Turkey to the status of a regional superpower and expand its influence far beyond its official borders. The implementation of this concept was recently evident in the signing of the ‘Mecca Joint Defense Agreement’ with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, but even before that, in its efforts to open intercontinental trade corridors, in its deep involvement in Africa, and in the adoption of the ‘Blue Homeland’ doctrine (Mavi Vatan), which expresses its ambitions in the eastern Mediterranean.
“When these trends are added to Erdogan’s overt hostility toward Israel, it is difficult to ignore the potential for friction and strategic confrontation with him, and this is even without mentioning the Palestinian issue and his support for Hamas. Turkey continues today as well to host senior members of the Hamas leadership on its territory and is conducting a legal and information campaign accusing Israel of war crimes.
“And despite all this, Turkey is not Iran: it is a member of NATO, Erdogan has a close relationship with Trump, and relations with Israel, despite the deep crisis, are still not severed. Precisely in order to prevent this rivalry from turning into a military confrontation, Israel acted correctly when it clarified its red lines in Syria and in general.
“In addition, Israel is also acting correctly when it deepens and expands its security relations with Greece and Cyprus, and also when it enters Africa, into strategic areas that Turkey has its eyes on. In my opinion, beyond all these actions, Israel needs to lead an international move to declare the global Muslim Brotherhood organization an illegal organization, and it must also act systematically to push the Turks out of operating in Jerusalem or in connection with it. With determination, but not necessarily demonstratively.”

South Africa lodged a diplomatic protest with the US ambassador to Pretoria after he criticized the government in media interviews, according to local media on Wednesday.

Bozell has repeatedly accused President Cyril Ramaphosa of failing to adequately address five demands presented by the White House as conditions for easing diplomatic tensions between the two countries, according to News24.

The latest protest comes amid deteriorating relations between South Africa and the US since President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year.
Trump has criticized Pretoria’s land and Black economic empowerment policies.
The US is seeking exemptions for American companies from Black economic empowerment rules, an end to land expropriation without compensation and government condemnation of the “Kill the Boer” chant.
It also wants Pretoria to address farm killings and not oppose Trump’s program to grant refugee status to white Afrikaners who say they face racial persecution.
Bozell also warned of further escalation after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced visa restrictions targeting South African officials.

Fighting has displaced an estimated 150,000 people, drawing responses from Qatar and the UAE as Ethiopia and its neighbours trade accusations.
Qatar has condemned what it called the military escalation against Ethiopia’s federal forces, while the United Arab Emirates has voiced support for the Ethiopian government amid renewed fighting in the country’s north.
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said the fighting threatened Ethiopia’s unity and sovereignty and the stability of the wider Horn of Africa.
It called for an immediate end to the fighting, protection for civilians and respect for the Pretoria Peace Agreement between Tigray and Ethiopia.
The Qatari statement did not name the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) or the new alliance of armed groups fighting the federal government. Qatar said its “full support” was for efforts to reduce tensions and resolve disputes through dialogue.
The UAE condemned what it described as attacks by the TPLF and its armed allies on federal forces, as well as the seizure of airports in Tigray and the spread of fighting into neighbouring Afar and Amhara.
UAE Minister of State Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan said his country stood in “full solidarity with the government and people” of Ethiopia. He also rejected attempts to change the country’s constitutional order through force.
Fighting spreads beyond Tigray
The statements followed the most serious fighting in northern Ethiopia since the agreement ended the 2020–2022 war, in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed.
Tigrayan forces seized the airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire last week, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to the region.
The TPLF says it is fighting defensively after federal forces attacked Tigray using drones, artillery and ground troops. The federal government accuses the group of launching a planned offensive.
Tigrayan forces captured Erebti in Afar over the weekend. On Monday, pro-government forces said they had taken control of Alamata, an important supply town around 120 kilometres south of Tigray’s capital, Mekelle.
A drone also struck the headquarters of Tigrai TV in Mekelle on Sunday. Journalists said they had left the building after hearing an earlier explosion. No casualties were reported, and the federal government did not comment on the strike.
Médecins Sans Frontières said the number of wounded people treated at hospitals in Korem and Alamata rose to more than 420 between 22-25 September. More than 300 wounded people arrived at Suhul Hospital last week.
The Afar Pastoralist Development Association estimates that around 150,000 people have been displaced by the fighting.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “gravely concerned” by the seizure of the three airports and the spread of hostilities beyond Tigray.
He urged all sides to stop the fighting, protect civilians, allow aid groups to reach those in need and return to talks under the peace agreement.
Ethiopia and its neighbours exchange accusations
Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting armed groups fighting the government. He did not provide evidence for the accusations.
Sudan’s army rejected the allegation and accused Ethiopia of allowing its territory to be used to support Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
Egypt’s Foreign Ministry did not name Ethiopia directly but dismissed suggestions that Cairo interfered in other countries as baseless. Spokesperson Nader Zaki said Egypt respected the sovereignty and territorial integrity of other states.
Eritrea has also denied supporting Ethiopian armed groups and accused Addis Ababa of attempting to shift responsibility for the fighting.
The TPLF joined six other armed groups this month in an alliance that says it wants to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establish a transitional administration.

'No ban but also not 24x7': SC on firecrackers in Delhi-NCR ahead of Diwali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:46:23 UTC
23:46:23 KST

"We need to find a solution by which we can give a specified time," the SC bench said.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday said it would not impose a blanket ban on firecrackers in Delhi-NCR, but would also not permit fireworks throughout the day, saying a balance had to be struck between public health concerns and people’s sentiments.A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale said the court would consider allowing firecrackers only during specified hours."We will make it very clear. Neither we are going to agree for total ban, nor are we going to allow them to do it (fireworks) for 24 hours a day. Total ban will affect sentiments. And allowing them throughout the day will have huge impact on every other living being including the old, sick and children," the bench orally observed, as quoted by PTI."We need to find a solution by which we can give a specified time," it added.The observations came during a hearing in which the Centre proposed a limited relaxation for a category of next-generation joined green crackers developed with technical inputs from the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI).Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati submitted a note saying the court could consider permitting the specified green crackers subject to conditions on their manufacture, chemical composition, noise levels and emissions.
According to the note, only duly licensed manufacturers would be allowed to produce the crackers. They would also have to meet the prescribed noise limit of 125 dB(AI)/145 dB(C) peak and could not contain banned chemicals.The proposed crackers are linked or joined fireworks formulated with reduced quantities of barium salts, with the aim of lowering emissions. The proposal is based on the category recommended by CSIR-NEERI and would be subject to applicable safety, noise and emission standards.
The bench further said it would consider the issue concerning the use of barium in firecrackers on October 15.The court's latest observations come ahead of Diwali and follow its earlier orders regulating the manufacture, sale and use of firecrackers in Delhi and the National Capital Region.Last year, the Supreme Court allowed the sale and use of green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR subject to conditions, including restrictions on when they could be used.The court had said their use would be limited to specified hours on the days before Diwali and on Diwali itself, as part of measures aimed at balancing festival-related celebrations with concerns over air pollution and public health.

TEKNOFEST fuels confidence revolution to defeat 'we cannot do it' mindset: Bayraktar

Selcuk Bayraktar, chairman of the board of trustees of the Türkiye Technology Team Foundation (T3 Foundation) and chairman of the TEKNOFEST board, described the festival as “a confidence revolution” challenging the mindset that says “we cannot do it”.
“TEKNOFEST is a confidence revolution. It is a rebellion against the mentality that says, ‘We cannot do it.’ It is an objection to imitation and learned helplessness,” Bayraktar said in his opening address on Wednesday at TEKNOFEST Southeast.
Türkiye’s premier aviation, space and technology festival TEKNOFEST opened its doors to visitors on Wednesday in the southeastern province of Sanliurfa.
TEKNOFEST Southeast, a leg of the event held in southeastern Türkiye, brings together tech enthusiasts, young investors and thousands of visitors for various shows, exhibitions and the finals of technology competitions across 14 categories from Wednesday through October 4.
Describing Sanliurfa as “the zero point of history,” Bayraktar said it was among the lands where humanity transitioned to settled life, developed agriculture and laid the foundations of civilisation.
‘More than 1.6 million young people applied’
Holding its 15th festival since its launch in 2018, Bayraktar said the TEKNOFEST “seedling we planted in 2018 has today turned into a major technology movement.”
He said young people from all 81 provinces of Türkiye and 97 countries were participating in the festival, adding that more than 730,000 teams and over 1.6 million young people had applied to technology competitions in 62 categories.
“These are not just numbers. They are Türkiye’s changing story,” Bayraktar said.
He highlighted the participation of young people from southeastern Türkiye, saying children in the region were learning artificial intelligence and robotics at DENEYAP Technology Workshops.
Referring to the region’s hot climate, Bayraktar said: “When we came to Urfa, we understood something else. If a system works smoothly at noon in the Urfa heat, it will work anywhere in the world, and even in space.”
‘National Technology Initiative is not only in the sky’
Bayraktar said confidence strengthens production, production strengthens technology, and technology creates the foundation for independence.
“That is why the National Technology Initiative exists,” he said.
“The National Technology Initiative is not only in the sky. It is in the fields, factories, laboratories, hospitals, workshops and universities.”
He said the initiative aims to turn ideas into economic value, dreams into production, projects into employment and technology into prosperity for Türkiye.
“Our goal is high technology, domestic production and value-added exports,” Bayraktar said.
“We want to build an entrepreneurship ecosystem that will strengthen our country’s full independence, led by the TEKNOFEST generation.”
Agricultural technologies in focus
Bayraktar also highlighted the strategic importance of agricultural production, saying food had become a more critical issue than ever.
“We can no longer view agriculture simply as a traditional sector. Agriculture must become one of the high-technology fields of the future,” he said.
He pointed to next-generation national agricultural technologies, AI-supported solutions, genetic science, efficiency and sustainable production as areas of focus.
“As the solutions developed by young people meet these fertile lands, our future will become stronger and more prosperous,” he said.
Bringing science together with conscience
Bayraktar also addressed the rapid transformation driven by artificial intelligence, saying the technology could accelerate learning and research but should be viewed as a tool that expands human potential rather than a guide that replaces human judgment.
“Technology is a tool. It is the human who determines its direction and must make the final decision,” he said.
“Our aim is not merely to develop technology, but to determine what kind of spirit and direction we will give it,” Bayraktar said.
“We want to use technology for the benefit of humanity. We want to bring science together with conscience, intelligence with morality, and power with justice.”

How Europe’s housing crisis is fuelling a new movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:45:43 UTC
23:45:43 KST

It was billed as one of the largest real-estate events in Europe, attracting as many as 15,000 people ranging from investment firms to developers. But as the District trade show and summit got under way last week in Madrid, housing campaigners from 140 organisations across the globe turned up, intent on holding their own “counter-summit” to push back against the idea of housing as a financial asset.
Many of the campaigners arrived in the Spanish capital as Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who uses a wheelchair, was being evicted from the apartment where she had lived for seven decades. As anger over the eviction gave way to days of protests and an encampment in the heart of Madrid, the presence of campaigners from Italy to Ireland was a poignant reminder of the global dimension of the crisis.
The eviction underscored how brutal access to housing had become for so many around the world, said Teresa Mamede, a housing campaigner from Lisbon who travelled to Madrid for the counter-summit. “Nobody among us is safe from having this happen to them.”
The Guardian has long reported on the depth of the housing crisis across Europe. Within the EU, prices soared by 53% between 2010 and 2024, according to Eurostat, while rents increased 25% over the same period.
Not all countries have been hit equally; while Vienna remains a bright spot for its ample stock of public housing that has tempered rental costs, Estonia has seen rents surge 208% in the same time period, while Ireland and Hungary have seen increases of more than 100%.
Some of the soaring costs can be chalked up to the “ever-intensifying social experiment” playing out in Europe, research fellow Tim White noted last year, as officials see whether the machinations of finance capitalism can deliver on the fundamental need for housing. “The evidence now seems overwhelming: no.”
Instead, vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected by the market’s shortcomings, while others warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. “We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse,” Jaume Collboni, the mayor of Barcelona, told me last year.
Voters in Berlin, however, recently opted for another path. In a city where rents had climbed nearly 70% in the past decade, a quarter of voters backed the leftwing party Die Linke in this month’s state elections, making it Berlin’s strongest party. The strategy behind their success was far from rocket science, said Guardian Europe columnist Fatma Aydemir. “Because, more than any other party in this campaign, Die Linke made this issue [of housing] unmistakably its own: the question of who gets to live in Berlin, and at what price.”
‘This is just getting started’
Some have sought shared solutions to the shared crisis. At the Madrid counter-summit, campaigners launched a pan-European alliance to demand indefinite rental contracts and rent control across the continent.
Earlier this month, dozens of organisations launched the European Citizens’ Initiative, calling on people to sign their petition for EU-level measures to protect tenants, curb speculation and convert empty buildings into homes. “In every European country, in every major survey, and across all age groups, housing emerges as the number one concern of citizens,” the initiative notes. “We see and feel it every day: workers who can no longer afford the city they build, young people who cannot leave their parents’ home, tenants pushed out of their neighbourhoods after renovation, empty buildings while people sleep on the street.”
In Spain, where the days-long encampment in Madrid has led to similar camps in cities such as Barcelona, Seville and Palma de Mallorca, the protests have already begun to have an impact.
Maricarmen, the evicted octogenarian, will be allowed to return to her apartment, it was confirmed on Tuesday. Her rent will remain around the €500 a month she had paid for years – significantly less than the €2,650 the investment firm that owns her apartment had initially demanded.
This week the Spanish government also said it had approved two housing decrees that include reforms such as a ban on evictions until 2030, and the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room. But these measures will now have to win approval in the country’s fractured parliament.
What exactly comes next for the housing movement that has gripped Spain in recent days is anyone’s guess. With the spectre of general elections looming and the Socialist-led coalition scrambling to shore up its base of progressive voters, campaigners have spotted a singular opportunity to tackle an issue that Spaniards have long ranked as one of the country’s biggest problems.
“The coming days will be crucial,” the Madrid Tenants’ Union said on Tuesday as it called for further protests this weekend. “A historic window of opportunity has opened to reverse decades of the commodification of housing. That is why we need to step up the pressure.”
Or, as the Málaga Tenants’ Union put it in an online post: “This is just getting started.”

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. Lawmakers of the State Duma – Russia’s lower house of parliament – must recognize their enormous responsibility to those who voted for them, President Vladimir Putin said addressing the first meeting of the 9th Duma.
He stressed that, unlike some others, Russia would not run around the world begging for handouts with an outstretched hand.
Putin also said that the country must and will meet all its social obligations to citizens in full.
TASS has compiled the Russian leader’s key statements.
Work of State Duma lawmakers
Citizens’ active participation in the recent State Duma elections and the results of the campaign once again demonstrated the unity of Russian society in the face of major historical challenges: "I want to reiterate that both the high turnout and the election results once again confirmed the strength of our multiparty political system and the unity of the people in the face of historical challenges."
Key decisions for the country will be adopted in the State Duma with the consolidated support of all parties and lawmakers: "I certainly expect that in the new convocation, too, decisions that are crucial for the country and our people will be made with the united, consolidated support of all parliamentary parties and lawmakers, because we are all like-minded people and comrades-in-arms in what matters most: our desire for the success, security and prosperity of our homeland."
State Duma lawmakers must recognize their enormous responsibility to those who voted for them: "This is serious and extensive work, but it is also, of course, an enormous responsibility to the people who voted for you."
Participants and veterans of the special military operation elected to the State Duma proved their devotion to Russia on the battlefield: "Participants and veterans of the special military operation received broad voter support – these are people who proved their unconditional devotion to the Motherland on the battlefield. I see them in this hall. I am confident that, by preserving the traditions of frontline brotherhood, they will strengthen and enhance the ranks of lawmakers."
The authorities must respond to society’s demands and needs, which determines their effectiveness: "Your attention must always be focused on improving our citizens’ living standards and quality of life. This includes employment, healthcare and education, the environment and culture – everything that matters to people. After all, the authorities’ effectiveness, including at the legislative level, is determined by how they respond to society’s demands and voters’ instructions."
United Russia bears increased responsibility as the majority faction in the State Duma: "I am confident that United Russia will continue to follow democratic principles, building dialogue with colleagues from other factions."
Government bodies must cooperate actively and improve the legislative framework to bring key areas of the country’s development to leading positions: "We need to work together to strengthen the country’s legislative framework and the advantages of national jurisdiction, moving step by step toward leadership in all key areas of development. We should act more boldly to remove outdated legal and regulatory barriers to entrepreneurship, breakthrough ideas and innovative scientific research."
Social obligations
Russia must and will meet its social obligations to citizens in full: "While maintaining macroeconomic stability, we must finance all national projects and federal programs. The state’s social obligations to our citizens must and certainly will be met in full."
A support system for special military operation fighters has already been established and is operating, but "it must continue to be improved."
Budget, economy
The country’s budget for the next three years must allocate sufficient funds to address demographic challenges and support families with children: "Sufficient funds should be allocated to address exceptionally important demographic challenges and improve the housing conditions and well-being of Russian families, especially those raising children."
When drafting budgets for the coming years, the authorities must focus on ensuring steady, long-term economic growth and launching a new investment cycle: "We must support our regions, their fiscal sustainability and tax base. We must also back overall economic development, steady and long-term growth, and the launch of a new investment cycle. Specialists and experts believe that the previous cycle has ended and many programs have been completed, so we need to provide fresh impetus."
The budget "must be balanced and realistic," while "destructive populism" must be ruled out during its consideration: "Mistakes are absolutely unacceptable, especially now."
"One of the key laws of your first fall session is the federal budget for the next three years. The budget package has been prepared by the government. These are crucial documents in which resources must be carefully calculated and our capabilities balanced against current priorities and strategic goals. While maintaining macroeconomic stability, all national projects and federal programs must be financed."
Russia, unlike some others, will not run around the world begging for handouts with an outstretched hand: "Russia, unlike some others – we will not point fingers – cannot run around the world humiliating itself by begging for handouts with an outstretched hand."
"The Russian financial system and economy are in a strong position. The main thing is to avoid any mistakes and approach the tasks in these critically important areas responsibly."
In an era of rapid technological development, Russia must remain "at the forefront of these changes": "We have all the capabilities, groundwork and domestic resources needed for this."
Regional development
A unified advanced development territory in the Far East and the Russian Arctic Zone must become operational on January 1, 2027.
Russian legislation must meet the demands of the times and look to the future to provide citizens with the best possible opportunities: "This means unlocking the enormous potential of the entire country: the Far East, Siberia, the Russian North, the central regions, Crimea, Donbass, the Caucasus and the Urals – every single region."
Donbass, Novorossiya
The first meeting of the 9th State Duma was held on a special day: "Exactly four years ago, the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics and the Zaporozhye and Kherson Regions became full-fledged constituent entities of Russia. I am pleased to congratulate you and all citizens of our country on Reunification Day."
The day marking the reunification of the historical regions with Russia has come to embody the righteous struggle of Russian people across the country, including Donbass and Novorossiya, for freedom and justice: "This holiday has come to embody our people’s unstoppable drive to restore historical unity and the righteous struggle of Russian people across the country, including residents of Donbass and Novorossiya, for freedom and justice."
No one can break or intimidate the Russian people: "It is symbolic that on the day of reunification [of the Donbass and Novorossiya regions with Russia], lawmakers from our four historical regions are beginning their work in the State Duma for the first time. <...> Their voters, who came to the polling stations, were not intimidated by shelling and threats and reaffirmed their choice. Once again, they proved that no one can break or intimidate our people."
All of Russia is now involved in implementing comprehensive development programs for Donbass and Novorossiya: "Russian constituencies are providing patronage assistance selflessly, sometimes at risk to their lives. I want to emphasize this in particular: this is not a figure of speech. Construction and utility workers, drivers and railway workers, teachers and medical personnel are doing their jobs while risking their lives, and public fundraising drives are being held."
The unity of Russian society will provide "reliable guarantees of the country’s security and sovereignty for generations to come": "That is how it will be; I am absolutely certain."

Unconditional jail demanded for attacks on emergency workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:44:44 UTC
23:44:44 KST

Unconditional jail demanded for attacks on emergency workers
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
People who attack emergency workers, including police officers, paramedics and train staff, will face an unconditional prison sentence from Thursday, under new rules from the public prosecution service (OM).
Prosecutors will no longer settle such cases with a fine or community service, and every suspect will have to appear in court, the OM said on Wednesday. The rules will apply to offences committed from October 1.
It sets fixed sentencing guidelines for three offences: public violence, assault, and attempted serious assault. An attempt to seriously assault an emergency worker without a weapon and without causing injury, for example, will carry a demand of 3 months in prison.
Justice minister David van Weel told MPs that a similar attack on a member of the public would usually lead to a demand for 80 hours community service, broadcaster NOS reported.
Besides emergency workers, the rules cover security staff, sports referees, public transport workers, teachers, judges, lawyers, politicians and council staff. They also apply to attacks on journalists.
“The impact of this violence on society is huge, but unfortunately we are not seeing it decline,” Lisan Wösten, the OM’s national lead on the issue, said in a statement.
Pressure from MPs
 MPs called for tougher sentences early this year after police and firefighters were attacked at New Year, with officers in some places lured into ambushes. “I fully support that approach,” Van Weel wrote in his letter to parliament, according to NOS.
Police officers faced almost 13,000 violent incidents in 2025, and the force’s national lead on the issue, Corry van Breda, has called for heavier sentences.
Since 2006, prosecutors have been able to seek sentences 200% higher for attacks on people in public roles. However, research by the justice ministry’s research centre WODC found this was rarely applied in practice.
The new rules remain a starting point from which prosecutors and judges can still exercise discretion according to the circumstances of a case.
A separate proposal to ban community service for these attacks altogether was criticised last year by the Council of State and judges, who said it would limit their room to weigh individual circumstances.

Latvia’s International Image Policy Coordination Council resumes work to develop a unified and coordinated national image strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:43:52 UTC
23:43:52 KST

On 30 September 2026, Latvia’s International Image Policy Coordination Council (the Council) held its first meeting since 2020 at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, chaired by Foreign Minister Baiba Braže. As the Council resumed its work, participants discussed cooperation among institutions to strengthen Latvia’s international visibility and develop its national image, including preparations for Latvia’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the second half of 2028. The meeting addressed the Council’s future operating model, the development of Latvia’s national image strategy for 2027–2031, preparations for the EU Council Presidency and related public diplomacy initiatives.
Foreign Minister Baiba Braže stressed that developing Latvia’s national image is a shared responsibility of all state institutions and their partners. A unified and coordinated national image strategy is therefore needed, bringing together the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), relevant state and municipal institutions, the diaspora, non-governmental organisations and businesses. This cooperation should strengthen Latvia’s international visibility, ensure consistent and sustainable messaging internationally, and support the effective use of public resources.
“The national image strategy must incorporate, well in advance, the major events already known to offer opportunities for Latvia’s international visibility and communication. These include Latvia’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union, the Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles, the XXVIII Nationwide Latvian Song and XVIII Dance Celebration, and other national and international events,” she said. She emphasised that a strategy coordinated in advance and implemented over the long term is essential to building a lasting international image and securing benefits that continue beyond the Presidency.
Jurģis Miezainis, Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Economics, said: “For Latvian businesses, it is important that our country’s reputation helps open doors in export markets and attract investors. We must continue to build our national image on our strengths and the achievements of our companies, ensuring coordinated work among institutions. Latvia’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union will provide an opportunity to showcase our economic potential more widely and establish new partnerships.”
In discussing the Council’s future operating model and responsibilities, participants agreed that it would serve as a platform for political and interinstitutional coordination on issues requiring joint action by several institutions.
LIAA will continue to lead the development of Latvia’s national image within its remit. Institutions represented on the Council will help coordinate Latvia’s international communication and apply shared national image principles in their own work and that of their subordinate institutions.
LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere said at the meeting: “The achievements of Latvian companies, scientists and professionals in other fields form the basis of our international story. LIAA draws on these achievements in its daily work with investors, export partners and tourists. The Council’s work will help align this approach with the activities of other institutions, ensuring that Latvia’s representatives abroad complement one another’s efforts.”
LIAA proposed adding a representative of the Foreign Investors’ Council in Latvia (FICIL) to the Council, allowing discussions to draw more extensively on investors’ experience and perspectives on Latvia’s reputation and competitiveness.
The Council discussed cooperation in preparing for Liepāja’s year as European Capital of Culture in 2027, Latvia’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the second half of 2028, the next Song and Dance Celebration, and Latvia’s participation in the Los Angeles Olympic Games.
Edgars Kiukucāns, Director of the Secretariat of Latvia’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union, presented an update on preparations for the Presidency and related public diplomacy initiatives. Participants emphasised the importance of coordinated communication and representation to ensure that these events strengthen Latvia’s international visibility.
During the Presidency in the second half of 2028, Latvia will host approximately 250 events at various levels, including meetings of heads of state and government, ministers and experts, as well as sectoral conferences and seminars. Up to 20,000 representatives from across the European Union are expected to visit Latvia over the six-month period.
Laura Andrejeva, LIAA’s Nation Brand Manager, presented the approach to developing Latvia’s national image. The meeting also discussed the national image strategy for 2027–2031, which will build on previous work while adapting it to changes in the international environment.
Participants agreed that the insights shared during the Council’s discussion would inform the strategy’s development. The Council will be presented with the concept for the new strategy in early 2027 so that it can provide institutional support for its implementation.
Latvia’s International Image Policy Coordination Council is a coordinating body established by the Cabinet of Ministers to ensure cooperation among public administration bodies and other institutions in successfully developing Latvia’s international image. The Council is chaired by the Minister of Foreign Affairs, with the Minister of Economics serving as deputy chair.
Its membership also includes the Minister of Culture, the Minister of Education and Science, representatives of the Chancery of the President and the Prime Minister’s Office, the Director of the Latvian Institute, the Director of the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia, the Director of the Latvian Tourism Development Agency, a board member of the Riga Tourism Development Bureau, the Secretary General of the Latvian Association of Local and Regional Governments, the Director General of the Employers’ Confederation of Latvia, and the Chair of the Board of the Latvian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

RIYADH – As Flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv approached the Jordanian border on Sept 30, passengers knew in an instant that something was wrong when the plane began plummeting from the sky in a rapid dive.
It was like “we were having very big turbulence, but there was no turbulence”, passenger Almog Italie told AFP, describing the sensation of losing thousands of feet of altitude in seconds as similar to riding a “roller coaster”.
According to data from the Flightradar website, the aircraft suddenly dropped from nearly 10,360m at 0521 GMT to less than 5,180m a minute later.
But there was no “hysteria” among passengers, Italie noted, even as fighting erupted near the cockpit for control over the aircraft.
“The other passengers from the front took over control,” he told AFP via video call from Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk, where the plane landed safely following what passengers described as a violent attempt by one pilot to kill the other.
Still, Italie said, “people kept calm”.
In photos sent to AFP by one of the passengers, travellers – including children – are seen gathered in an airport lounge, with some sitting on the floor. One man is wearing a white T-shirt and jeans stained with blood.
Miryam Shira Ohayon, who was also on board the flight, described the aircraft as being “pretty much out of control” as the fight ensued.

“It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him,” she said.
“There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them. Other than the pilot, there were no injuries, but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do.”

Private sector jobs rose by 90,000 in September, better than expected, ADP reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:42:04 UTC
23:42:04 KST

Private job creation picked up in September after a brief slowdown, providing further indication that the U.S. labor market has stabilized, according to an ADP report Wednesday.
The payrolls processing firm said company employment rose by 90,000 for the month, higher than the downwardly revised 36,000 in August and better than the Dow Jones consensus estimate for 68,000.
There also was a fair amount of balance in the report, with service providers adding 59,000 positions while goods producers contributed 31,000.
Base pay rose 3.2% from a year ago, while gross pay accelerated by 4.7%.
"It's a strong report," said ADP's chief economist, Nela Richardson. "After a three-month slowdown, job 
creation rebounded and pay growth remained solid."
Education and health services contributed the most, with 55,000 new hires. Other areas of growth included leisure and hospitality (22,000), manufacturing (17,000), and construction (15,000).
A handful of sectors saw job losses, including financial activities (-16,000), professional and business services (-11,000), and natural resources and mining (-1,000).
Much of the employment growth came from the Northeast, which added 56,000. By size, companies with between 50 and 499 workers saw a gain of 54,000.
Broadly, the report helped confirm sentiment expressed by multiple Federal Reserve officials that the labor market is mostly sound following a growth scare in 2025. Policymakers see the greater policy risk now as the persistent inflation that pushed central bankers to raise benchmark borrowing rates by a quarter percentage point earlier in September.
The ADP count serves as a precursor to the nonfarm payrolls report that the Bureau of Labor Statistics will release Friday. The Wall Street consensus is for a gain of 84,000 jobs, down from a 162,000 increase the prior month, and the unemployment rate to hold steady at 4.1%.

U.S. levies sanctions on suppliers to Iran’s defense industry, including network tied to Shahed drone manufacturer HESA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:40:23 UTC
23:40:23 KST

The United States has imposed sanctions on 10 individuals and entities that, according to the U.S. Treasury Department, procured weapons and components for Iran’s Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics (MODAFL). Among the recipients of the components, U.S. officials said, was state-owned Iran Aircraft Manufacturing Industrial Company (HESA), which produces Shahed- and Ababil-family drones of the type that Russia has used in its war against Ukraine. HESA had also earlier worked with at least three Russian companies, according to U.S. sanctions records reviewed by The Insider.
The U.S. Treasury Department announced the new restrictions on Sept. 29. The sanctions target individuals and companies in Iran, Hong Kong, China, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey. Washington says those named were involved in procuring weapons, electronics, and components for MODAFL, which oversees enterprises involved in developing ballistic missiles and drones, among other systems.
One of those sanctioned is Seyed Asghar Alizadeh Tabatabaei, MODAFL’s representative in Beijing. According to the U.S. Treasury Department, he coordinated Iranian procurement in China of complete weapons systems and dual-use components.
Electronics for a Shahed manufacturer
A separate part of the sanctions targets Iran’s Kavoshcom Asia R&D Group. The U.S. Treasury Department says the company procured electronic components, including connectors, for HESA. Kavoshcom also supplied electronics to the Shahid Bakeri Industrial Group, or SBIG, which is responsible for Iran’s solid-fuel ballistic missile program.
Kavoshcom director Ali Fotovat Ahmadi and representative Parisa Lali were sanctioned along with the company. The restrictions also target Hong Kong-based EC Mojo Technology and its representative, Li Fen. According to the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, or OFAC, EC Mojo supplied electronic components for Kavoshcom’s procurement activities, while Li Fen sought to evade sanctions and export controls.
HESA has been under U.S. sanctions for years. In 2023, the U.S. Treasury Department said the company manufactured Iranian Ababil- and Shahed-family drones.
HESA’s ties to Russia have also been documented in official sanctions records. In January 2023, the European Union added HESA to its sanctions list, explicitly stating that drones made by the company were being used by Russia in its war against Ukraine.
In September of that year, the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned three Russian companies for cooperating with HESA: Technical Center Delta-Aero LLC supplied the Iranian manufacturer with propellers and tires for An-140 aircraft that HESA converted for military use, NPP Aerosila conducted ground and flight tests for HESA and facilitated deliveries of auxiliary power units, and NPP Zvezda had contracts to repair An-140 components.
Russia later localized production of Shahed-family drones in Tatarstan. In 2025, The Insider cited data from U.S. research group C4ADS indicating that Moscow had paid Iran for drone-production technology in part with gold bars worth about $104 million.
Pakistani arms manufacturer acted as an intermediary for Iran
A second part of the new sanctions network centers on Pakistani businessman Waseem Pasha Tajammal. He heads Cavalier Group, a private defense conglomerate that manufactures armored vehicles, ballistic protection equipment, and drones, among other products. The U.S. Treasury Department says Tajammal and Cavalier Group acted as third-party intermediaries for MODAFL and used business connections to procure and distribute weapons on behalf of Iran’s Defense Ministry.
The sanctions list includes three entities linked to Tajammal: Pakistan-based Cavalier Dynamics Private Limited, Saudi-based Cavalier Dynamics for Technologies Company, and Turkey-based Cavalier Dynamics Teknoloji Ticaret. The United States imposed the restrictions on the Saudi company in coordination with Saudi authorities.
On its website, Cavalier Group describes itself as Pakistan’s only privately owned diversified defense manufacturer. Its listed business lines include combat vehicles, small arms, armor protection, tactical equipment, and drones.
The new sanctions are part America’s “economic offensive” against Iran
All 10 targets were sanctioned under U.S. Executive Order 13382, which targets proliferators of weapons of mass destruction and the delivery systems for such weapons. The targets’ property and interests in property under U.S. jurisdiction are blocked, and U.S. individuals and entities are barred from doing business with them. Companies owned 50% or more by sanctioned persons are also automatically subject to the restrictions. The Treasury Department additionally warned that foreign financial institutions could face secondary sanctions if they conduct significant transactions on behalf of those on the list.
The new package was imposed as part of Operation Economic Outcast, a broader U.S. campaign of economic pressure on Iran that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced on Aug. 24, describing the initiative as an “economic D-Day.” The U.S. authorities say they intend to cut off channels through which Tehran earns revenue, acquires technology, and evades international sanctions. Washington has imposed restrictions on more than 60 individuals, companies, and vessels and has threatened secondary sanctions against organizations that continue helping Iran circumvent the restrictions.

Is Spain’s anti-eviction decree a fix for its housing crisis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:40:01 UTC
23:40:01 KST

Is Spain’s anti-eviction decree a fix for its housing crisis?
The government blames ‘savage speculation’ as critics say new measures leave small landlords ‘out in the cold’.
Spain’s left-wing coalition government has announced measures to ban evictions until 2030 to address the country’s housing crisis, after the forced removal of an 87-year-old woman last week triggered mass protests.
The new measures, including rolling over contracts and banning so-called vulture funds from the housing market, will be divided into two decrees to be voted on Friday in parliament, where Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority left government will face an uphill battle to secure support.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Migrants ‘are not to blame’: How the Ceuta crisis engulfed Spanish football
- list 2 of 3Spain’s Sanchez warns of far-right threat in UNGA speech
- list 3 of 3Thousands protest in Madrid against Spain’s housing crisis
Spain’s housing crisis has driven a sharp political and social split between renters and property owners, with critics saying the proposed measures risk unfairly lumping small landlords who rely on rental income together with profit-driven real estate companies.
Health Minister Monica Garcia has framed parliament’s approval as non-negotiable, after a similar decree seeking to roll over rental contracts was blocked in April by right-leaning parties.
“Right-wing parties have to choose: either they’re with the citizens, or they’re with the foreign vulture funds,” she said on X on Wednesday. “Let them prove their patriotism beyond bracelets and flags.”
“And if they don’t, may it cost them dearly,” she added.
Why did the eviction of an elderly woman cause outrage?
The eviction of wheelchair user Maricarmen Abascal, who was removed from her home of more than seven decades on a stretcher last week, drew more than 10,000 protesters to the streets.
Abascal was living in the property in Madrid’s central Retiro neighbourhood under a rent-capped lease contract signed by her father in the 1950s. The property was then bought by the real estate and investment firm Urbagestion in 2018.
Urbagestion sought to terminate Abascal’s contract and evict her after raising her rent from 500 euros ($572) to 2,650 euros ($3,010) – nearly double her pension of €1,350 ($1,533) a month – according to Spanish newspaper El Pais.
When the police carried out her eviction on their fourth attempt on September 23, hundreds of activists who had been protesting against her losing a home she had lived in her entire life were waiting outside.
The videos of Abascal’s personal struggle made the rounds on social media, turning the 87-year-old into a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis.
Spontaneous demonstrations began the same day in front of a controversial luxury penthouse that the Madrid regional government, led by Isabel Diaz Ayuso of the conservative People’s Party (PP), recently purchased for unclear purposes.
Protesters cried out: “Ayuso’s penthouse for Maricarmen!” and “Shame! Shame!”
The platform #Niundesahuciomas (Not One More Eviction) called for simultaneous protests in Avila, Barcelona, Cadiz, Oviedo, Sevilla and Valencia.
Speaking at the recently concluded United Nations General Assembly, Sanchez, of the Socialist Party, described evictions as “a social tragedy that we cannot accept as a country” and blamed the local and regional governments of Madrid led by the People’s Party (PP).
Housing Minister Isabel Rodriguez Garcia said that the eviction “evidences the consequences of savage speculation and of rolling out the red carpet to the vultures and the speculators”.
According to data collected by the Bank of Spain reported by El Pais, real estate wealth now exceeds €7.4 trillion ($9.53 trillion), but the gains are far from evenly distributed. Property wealth is highly concentrated, with the richest 10 percent of households owning about one-third of all real estate wealth, while the bottom half owns only about 15 percent.
Additionally, the number of owners with two, five or more properties was found to have risen significantly, while the share of small owners with just one property declined.
The minister said the government was seeking to broaden the definition of what constitutes a vulture fund beyond large private equity funds to any fund or company that buys housing for speculation.
The minister named investment firm Urbagestion, which owns Abascal’s apartment, as an example of a firm that might fall into that category.
Abascal’s lawyer Beatriz Duro said on Tuesday that Urbagestion had offered a preliminary agreement that would allow her return to her home, paying 30 percent of her pension over the next eight years, equivalent to about 500 euros a month.
Why is there controversy over the proposed reforms?
Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing on all measures and wanted safeguards for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain and who would be treated the same as large institutional investors.
The party’s parliamentary spokesperson Miriam Nogueras said the agreement left “small landlords out in the cold”.
“We all agreed that evictions – where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros – obviously need to be stopped,” she said on RTVE.
“Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property – putting them all in the same basket – is a mistake.”
Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the leader of the conservative PP, said “eight years adrift in housing policy aren’t fixed with an 11th-hour decree” and that his party would not support the legislation in parliament.
Feijoo had previously argued that tackling the housing crisis required dramatically increasing supply and offering major tax incentives for young buyers, opting for market expansion rather than government regulation.
Over the past decade, home prices have increased by almost 50 percent while not enough properties are available for rent. Spain’s National Statistics Institute (INE) found the national housing price index more than doubled since 2014, with prices 2.3 times higher than in Madrid.
INE data also showed that the cost of housing was absorbing a large share of household income. In 2024, 28.1 percent of people renting a home at market rates were spending more than 40 percent of their disposable income on housing, compared with an average in the European Union of 19.2 percent.
Marta Soler Gallart, head of the Department of Sociology at the University of Barcelona, said that neither of the two decrees addresses the problem in the medium and long term.
“Models such as Vienna’s, with its low rents, are cited in support of these decrees, but it is overlooked that the Vienna model and others have low rents because of their long history of creating and maintaining public social housing,” Soler Gallart told Al Jazeera. “In Spain, however, public funds are invested in social housing which, after a while, the recipients sell at market price.”
Soler Gallart also said the new measures disadvantage small landlords by extending five-year tenancy agreements by a further two years and by providing an indefinite extension of their tenancy agreements.
“However, these extensions are not compulsory if the landlord can prove that they need the property for their own use,” she said.

The flydubai hijacking exposed a flaw in Gulf security. Here's how the GCC can counter it - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
14:39:35 UTC
23:39:35 KST

Given the sensitivities surrounding the regional security environment and the limited information currently available, it is important to await the outcome of the official investigation into the flydubai FZ 1073 in-flight cockpit incident before reaching definitive conclusions about what transpired. That said, several analytical scenarios merit consideration.
If this proves to be an isolated incident, it would nevertheless underscore the extent to which Iranian influence networks and affiliated non-state actors have expanded across the region. The concern is no longer limited to organized proxy groups. Increasingly, the operational landscape appears to include sleeper cells, independent operatives, and ideologically motivated sympathizers who may act with varying degrees of coordination. Such individuals can represent valuable assets for Tehran’s broader strategic objectives while remaining sufficiently deniable and ultimately expendable.
This dynamic recalls patterns witnessed during the 1970s and 1980s, particularly with organizations such as the Abu Nidal Organization (ANO), which employed airline hijackings, assassinations, and attacks against Arab and Gulf targets as instruments of coercion and political pressure. The lesson from that period is that unconventional actors can generate significant strategic effects disproportionate to their size and capabilities.
A second and more concerning possibility is that this incident forms part of a broader evolution in Iranian strategy. Following years of reliance on conventional proxy warfare and indirect confrontation, Tehran may be exploring alternative tracks that shift the battlefield toward disruption, psychological pressure, transportation infrastructure, aviation security, and other forms of asymmetric activity. If so, such actions would represent a new phase in an already expanding regional conflict environment.
Regardless of which scenario ultimately proves correct, the incident should be viewed as a potential escalation signal. Even if the event is later determined to be isolated, it highlights the growing challenge posed by decentralized actors operating below the threshold of conventional conflict.
To mitigate these emerging risks, GCC security leadership should prioritize five immediate policy actions: enforce strict cockpit integrity protocols and expand air marshal deployments on sensitive routes; establish a real-time GCC aviation intelligence-sharing database to cross-reference watchlists and flight deck personnel data; transition to dynamic, continuous crew vetting paired with behavioral and psychological assessments; synchronize civil air traffic control hubs with military air operation centers for immediate air defense interception during transponder squawk 7500/7700 events; and harden aviation supply chains through comprehensive counter-infiltration audits of foreign recruitment and ground-handling contractors.
Until the investigation is completed, definitive attribution remains premature. However, if deliberate hostile intent is ultimately established, the incident may indicate either a troubling expansion of proxy-linked activity or the emergence of a new asymmetric pressure campaign in the Gulf. Both possibilities carry significant security implications for the region.
Policy steps the GCC leadership can take now
For Gulf states, the priority will be to strengthen intelligence cooperation, aviation security, and counter-infiltration capabilities while avoiding premature conclusions until the facts are established through the investigative process. To mitigate these emerging risks, GCC security leadership should prioritize five immediate policy actions:
- Enforce strict cockpit integrity and air marshal deployment: Mandate continuous two-person cockpit presence protocols across all GCC flag carriers and expand discreet sky marshal coverage on high-sensitivity regional and international flight routes.
- Establish real-time GCC aviation intelligence sharing: Construct a centralized, real-time threat sharing database across Gulf civil aviation authorities to cross-reference watchlists, flag suspicious background changes, and share intelligence on ground and flight crew personnel.
- Transition to dynamic crew vetting and psychological assessment: Upgrade periodic background checks to continuous, automated vetting systems paired with dynamic psychological and behavioral monitoring for all commercial flight deck personnel operating in GCC airspace.
- Synchronize civil-military emergency air defense interception: Harmonize emergency response protocols between civil air traffic control hubs and military air operation centers to ensure immediate, coordinated fighter interception during transponder squawk 7500/7700 incidents.
- Harden aviation supply chains and counter-infiltration: Conduct comprehensive counter-infiltration audits of foreign national recruitment, ground handling contractors, and third-party maintenance providers to prevent covert access to critical aviation infrastructure.
Ultimately, whether the flydubai FZ 1073 incident is formally attributed to an isolated personal crisis or a deliberate asymmetric probe, it serves as a decisive catalyst for the Gulf Cooperation Council to re-examine the perimeter of regional defense. Modern security in the Gulf can no longer be defined solely by air-defense batteries, maritime patrols, or regional troop posture, but must extend into the subtle, high-trust operational spaces that enable everyday commercial infrastructure.
Given Tehran's established operational doctrine of exploiting gray-zone ambiguity, GCC’s and Israel’s security planners cannot afford a purely reactive stance that absorbs initial tactical hits before adjusting defense perimeters; strategic prudence demands anticipating worst case Iranian intent and hardening potential targets proactively. By implementing this counter infiltration roadmap, GCC leadership can systematically close emerging vulnerabilities, deny hostile actors the leverage of grey zone disruption, and ensure that Gulf airspace remains an unassailable pillar of regional stability and economic resilience.
