China claims 100th Asian Games diving gold
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:48:06 CST
21:48:06 KST

Gold medalist Lian Junjie (L) and bronze medalist Zhao Renjie of China pose after the awarding ceremony for the men's 10m platform final of diving at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Tokyo, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Zhizun)
TOKYO, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Olympic champion Lian Junjie won the men's 10m platform gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday, delivering China's 100th Asian Games diving gold medal and completing the Chinese team's sweep of all 10 diving titles at the Games.
Lian scored 501.25 points at the Tokyo Aquatics Center to take the title. Japan's Rikuto Tamai finished second with 497.20 points, while China's 15-year-old Zhao Renjie took bronze with 427.50.
"First of all, I'm very happy," Lian said. "To win the 10th gold medal for the Chinese diving team at these Games, and the 100th Asian Games diving gold in the team's history, on the final day of the competition, was really hard-earned. I'm very happy that we managed to hold on to it."
Lian built his advantage in the fourth and fifth dives, scoring 91.80 points on both his reverse 3 1/2 somersaults and back 3 1/2 somersaults. He finished with 501.25 points. Tamai, also the Paris Olympic silver medalist, scored 93.60 points on his final dive but finished 4.05 points behind Lian.
"It was another silver medal, but more than anything, I feel a great sense of relief," Tamai said. "Of course, I was aiming for gold, but there was also a part of me that realistically thought I might finish with bronze. So I'm really happy that I was able to move up a place and win a medal here at home."
China's Zhao, making his Asian Games debut, meanwhile made an eye-catching start. He scored 86.40 and 91.80 points on his opening two dives before producing 96.90 points on his stunning third dive, a reverse 3 1/2 somersaults. The first three dives also saw judges award several perfect 10s.
"I felt pretty much the same as I did in training," Zhao said of his opening rounds. "I was able to bring out what I normally do in training."
The 15-year-old then suffered two costly mistakes on his fourth and fifth dives, earning only 27.00 and 44.40 respectively, but recovered to finish with bronze.
"There was a little fluctuation in my emotions, but I adjusted afterward," Zhao said. "My coach told me not to be nervous and not to think about the previous dive. Every dive is a new beginning."
Tamai also spoke about Zhao, "I see him as a strong rival," he said. "He's a lovely kid and is well-liked by everyone around him. But I try not to be pulled into that and instead compete with him as an equal athlete." The Japanese diver said the two were similar in some ways and described Zhao as being "like a younger brother."
For Lian, the gold also carried a deeply personal meaning. When he first arrived at the Tokyo Aquatics Center, he said he was quite emotional because the venue reminded him of the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, when he missed out on selection and could only watch his teammates compete on television.
"Being able to come here and compete individually was already very difficult for me," said Lian, now 25. "To be able to come here, win the gold medal and complete what I wanted to do, I feel it is something really worth remembering. In a way, it is also a form of closure for me."
Lian, who has already won the men's synchronized 10m platform title with Yang Hao at these Games, said the men's platform remains one of the most competitive events in diving.
"There is never such a thing as being assured of victory on the 10m platform," he said. "It is about who can withstand the pressure and who can adjust their mindset better."
Earlier in the day, Olympic champion Chen Yiwen scored 358.05 to win the women's 3m springboard title, also China's 99th diving gold in Asiad. Teammate Chen Jia finished second with 347.45 points, while Japan's Sayaka Mikami took bronze with 332.35.
The victory gave Chen her second gold medal at the Games, after she teamed up with Chen Jia to win the women's synchronized 3m springboard title on Sunday. Chen said she had arrived in Aichi-Nagoya aiming for two gold medals, but admitted the road to completing the target had not been easy.
"I was aiming for two gold medals, so the result was in line with my expectations, but the process could definitely have been better," Chen said. "I've had some ups and downs in form over the past two years, so I put some pressure on myself."
Beyond the medals, Chinese divers also pointed to the hard work and values passed down from one generation to the next as key to the team's sustained success.
"First of all, it all comes down to hard training," Lian said. "Without hard training, there would be no solid fundamentals, physical reserves or the ability to adjust mentally."
But training alone is not the whole story. Lian, who once learned from senior divers, now sees himself as part of the generation responsible for passing that experience on.
"I hope the younger athletes can see the spirit of our predecessors, never giving up and continuing to work hard," he said. "I also hope I can set a good example for them."
The younger diver Zhao has already identified Lian as someone he looks up to. "Lian Junjie is particularly strong, and he is also my idol," Zhao said. And for him, the path ahead is already clear.
"I hope to learn from the older brothers, make it to the Olympic stage and become an Olympic champion," he added. ■

Economic Watch: China's September PMIs return to expansion amid firming recovery
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:47:57 CST
21:47:57 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's manufacturing activity was back in expansion territory in September while non-manufacturing activity rebounded markedly, with both above the boom-bust line, official data showed on Wednesday, adding to signs of a firming recovery in the world's second-largest economy.
The purchasing managers' index (PMI) for China's manufacturing sector stood at 50.1 in September 2026, up 0.3 percentage points from August and returning to the expansion zone, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 signifies contraction.
The manufacturing sector's business climate improved further in September, with the PMI rising for a second consecutive month, said Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the NBS.
Among the 21 industries surveyed, 12 reported a PMI above the expansion threshold, four more than the previous month, Huo noted.
The sector saw expansion in both manufacturing output and market demand in September. The production sub-index climbed to 51.7, up 1.3 percentage points from August, while the new orders index was at 50.5, still above the threshold.
Driven by the acceleration in production, enterprises' willingness to purchase strengthened, with the procurement volume index reaching 51.0, an increase of 0.5 percentage points from the previous month, said Huo.
PMIs for the equipment manufacturing industry, the high-tech manufacturing industry and the consumer goods industry stood at 51, 52.5 and 50.7, respectively, all remaining in the expansion zone.
Affected by rising international commodity prices and growing demand in some industries, the purchasing price index for major raw materials and the ex-factory price index for manufacturing stood at 60.8 and 54, respectively, up 4.2 percentage points and 3.6 percentage points from the previous month.
PMIs for medium-sized and small manufacturing enterprises came in at 49.7 and 48.9, respectively, increases of 0.3 percentage points and 1 percentage point from the previous month, as business activity picked up.
Non-manufacturing activity also increased. The business activity index for the non-manufacturing sector reached 50.2 in September, a rise of 1.2 percentage points from August. The construction sector index rose 3.4 percentage points to 50.3, the highest level this year, while the services sector index increased by 0.9 percentage points to 50.2, with both returning to expansion.
"The traditional peak season and the upcoming National Day holiday have driven up demand in transportation, tourism and related consumer services," said Wu Wei, an analyst with the China Logistics Information Center.
The improvement came as a package of pro-growth measures was rolled out at a faster pace. The National Development and Reform Commission on Wednesday said it, together with the Ministry of Finance, had allocated the fourth and final batch of 62.5 billion yuan (around 9.28 billion U.S. dollars) in ultra-long special treasury bonds for consumer goods trade-in programs, bringing this year's total to 250 billion yuan.
Starting Oct. 1, China will implement interest subsidies for housing loans for eligible first-home buyers, offering an annualized subsidy of 1 percentage point on loans of up to 1 million yuan for up to five years, the Ministry of Finance and other departments said.
The People's Bank of China, China's central bank, announced a raft of strengthened support measures on Tuesday, including cutting the one-year interest rate of the pledged supplementary lending (PSL) facility from 1.75 percent to 1.5 percent, to better incentivize policy banks to support the real economy and serve national strategies.
It has also decided to increase the quota of the relending facility for sci-tech innovation and technological upgrades by 200 billion yuan and for agriculture and small and micro businesses by 500 billion yuan, out of which 300 billion yuan is dedicated to financial support for private firms.
"The recent policy mix is characterized by stepped-up counter-cyclical adjustments and the concentrated rollout of incremental tools," said Wen Bin, chief economist with China Minsheng Bank.
"With existing policies becoming more effective and incremental policies continuing to be introduced, economic momentum is expected to pick up further in the fourth quarter," he noted.
Looking ahead, China's manufacturing sector is expected to maintain steady and moderate expansion in the fourth quarter, said Wen Tao, an analyst with the China Logistics Information Center, citing accelerated implementation of major projects, including about 2 trillion yuan of planned investment by central state-owned enterprises in six major infrastructure networks this year. ■

Fijian minister warns of possible power rationing amid prolonged dry conditions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:47:55 CST
21:47:55 KST

SUVA, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Fiji could face electricity rationing if prolonged dry weather pushes water levels at major hydropower facilities to critical levels, Infrastructure Minister Ro Filipe Tuisawau said on Wednesday.
Tuisawau said the water level at Monasavu Dam, Fiji's largest hydroelectric facility, stood at 732.2 meters as of Monday, which was 17.2 meters above the safe operating level and 12.8 meters below the dam's spill level.
He said Fiji's Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) is conserving water at its hydropower dams and increasing thermal power generation to help safeguard electricity supplies amid concerns over below-average rainfall.
EFL currently has 295.07 megawatts of available generating capacity, according to the minister.
However, Tuisawau warned that continued declines in dam water levels could force the government to introduce power rationing, with essential services such as hospitals prioritized.
Fiji is experiencing El Nino conditions, which the minister said could bring below-average rainfall through the end of 2026 and into early 2027.
The government is also investing in renewable energy as part of efforts to reduce the country's dependence on hydropower and fossil fuels. ■

by sportswriter Xiao Shiyao and Wang Haizhou
OSAKA, Japan, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's young forward Wang Yudong said Wednesday that he hopes to take the next step in his career by playing in Europe after testing himself against South Korea's European-based players in the men's football semifinal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
China lost 2-1 to South Korea in the semifinal despite taking an early lead through Wang.
"I feel the gap between us and the top Asian teams is narrowing," the 20-year-old said after the match. "Physically, I believe we are comparable to South Korea. Tactically, we performed well in this game and did not give them many clear chances."
Wang also highlighted South Korea's Eom Ji-sung, who plays for Swansea City in the English second-tier Championship and operates in a similar position.
"South Korea's No. 7 plays in the same position as me and has a similar style," Wang said. "His movement and decision-making on the ball are really impressive. After all, he is playing in the English Championship, and there is still a lot I can learn from him."
The experience has strengthened Wang's desire to try in European football.
"I think the first thing is to take that step and give it a try," Wang said when asked about his future. "No matter what, I want to experience life and the rhythm of football outside China. Once you go abroad, you have to rely on your own."
Asked whether this year would be the right time for him to move overseas, Wang said there were many factors to consider.
"There are many things that need to be taken into consideration, so we have to look at everything as a whole," he said. "If there is an opportunity, I will definitely take that step. Once you take that step, I think things will become much better."
Reflecting on the semifinal, Wang said China had performed well and believed South Korea's high press was not as intense as expected.
"I personally think we played a very good game," he said. "We found that South Korea's high press was not that aggressive, so we were able to keep possession and move the ball around better."
"Football requires both ability and a bit of luck, and it's a shame that we couldn't win," he added.
South Korea scored the winning goal in the 82nd minute. Wang said China's late push for an equalizer was their only option.
"Their second goal came quite late, so all we could do was throw everything forward," he said. "As for Zhang Yuning's final shot, I think it should have been a penalty."
China will play the loser of the other semifinal between Japan and Uzbekistan in the bronze-medal match on Saturday. Wang remains confident that the team can finish the tournament with a medal.
"Our overall goal is definitely to take a medal home," he said. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: National Day floral displays in festive Beijing tell tough past, promising future
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:47:44 CST
21:47:44 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- A grinning "boy" in sleek VR goggles stretches out his arm, pointing a finger forward. The plant sculpture in central Beijing has become a popular photo spot, with visitors striking the same pose as the "boy" for the camera.
The sculpture is one of 10 themed floral displays installed along a roughly 6-km stretch of Chang'an Avenue, Beijing's main east-west thoroughfare, ahead of the National Day holiday, which begins on Oct. 1. It continues a tradition that has lasted more than four decades.
Remarkably, some of this year's installations have captured young visitors' attention, sparking lively discussion on social media. "It's so, so cute, especially considering he's entirely green," one Rednote user commented on the plant-sculpted "boy" wearing VR goggles and sporting a distinctly cheerful expression.
Echoing this animated and geek-chic sculpture is a running humanoid robot with a green-grass body and metallic "joints," installed at another major intersection along Chang'an Avenue. "This year's National Day plant sculptures are so funny," wrote another on Rednote. "Is it because the post-2000 generation has taken over?"
"The displays were designed to appeal to people of all ages," said Lan Hailang, chief designer of this year's National Day floral displays. However, efforts to engage younger generations are perhaps most evident in the fluffy, grass-covered "cats" installed across the capital ahead of the National Day holiday.
People have been sharing photos of them and guides to their locations. Among them, a 3.5-meter-tall kitten, outside Chang'an Avenue, stands out for its lifelike appearance. Designers used buffalo grass to recreate its long, fluffy fur, said Li Mengyu, a member of the design team.
Beyond their appeal to youngsters, the 10 floral installations along Chang'an Avenue, alongside the centerpiece of a giant flower basket at Tian'anmen Square, tell stories of the country's revolutionary history, showcase its technological progress and aspirations for the future, and offer glimpses into the everyday lives of its people.
The displays feature themes ranging from new quality productive forces and harmony between people and nature, to urban renewal and the beautiful countryside.
"In earlier years, the floral displays were mainly about creating a festive atmosphere and giving people something to enjoy," said Lan. "In recent years, they have also become a window into the country's development and people's lives."
Starting from Jianguomen, visitors first encounter a display themed "Carrying Forward the Long March Spirit." This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March.
The Long March was an epic military trek from 1934 to 1936, during which the Communist Party of China-led Red Army broke through encirclement by the Kuomintang forces. Red Army soldiers braved raging rivers, snow-covered mountains and treacherous grasslands, with some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers. The maneuver helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
Ninety years on, the spirit of the Long March remains a source of inspiration for many Chinese, reminding them to tackle difficulties head-on.
"Compared with the formidable obstacles Red Army soldiers encountered during the Long March, many of the challenges we face in everyday life seem no big deal," said Zhang Caimeng, who traveled from Tianjin to Beijing ahead of the National Day.
Standing before the display, she tried to inspire her son, who is preparing for next year's college entrance examination.
Farther west, at the bustling commercial hub of Dongdan, the displays at four corners of the intersection feature technological achievements, including the Tiangong space station, a reusable rocket, a sprinting humanoid robot and a CR450 high-speed train.
For more than 40 years, floral displays have been a prominent feature of National Day celebrations along Tian'anmen Square and Chang'an Avenue.
The first flower display appeared in Tian'anmen Square in 1984. More than four decades later, the simpler flower arrangements of the early years have evolved into large-scale three-dimensional installations. The varieties of plants used have grown tremendously.
Some of the displays are so exquisitely crafted that they too have become social media hits. One features a garland-wearing girl playing the violin, surrounded by black storks, red-crowned cranes and milu deer, creating a vivid scene of harmony between people and nature.
The hem of the girl's floor-length gown is made up of brightly colored flowers. Her posture, the position of her bow and even the placement of her fingers on the strings are rendered with striking precision. A musical staff woven into the display spells out the beloved melody of "My Motherland and I," adding an unexpected touch that has delighted visitors and social media users alike.
The display is more than a visual spectacle. At scheduled times, a recording of the violin solo "My Motherland and I" fills the air, drawing visitors to stop, film the scene and take in the experience.
Li Lifang, an executive of the Beijing urban construction, landscaping and horticulture company, has been involved in building National Day floral displays for more than two decades.
She said that while floral sculptures once depended heavily on the skill of artisans and craftsmen, technologies such as 3D modeling and simulation have made it possible to achieve greater precision and realism.
For 29-year-old resident Hou Yueru, the displays depict scenes that feel close to home. Cycling along Chang'an Avenue, she was struck by the variety of scenes, from a kitten nestled in a rural setting and people paddleboarding along a waterfront, to community gardens and digital cultural and tourism experiences.
"There are cutting-edge innovations that reach into the sky and deep underground, but there are also scenes that reflect the everyday lives of ordinary people," she said.
Future aspirations are also woven into the plant sculptures. This year marks the beginning of the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The 18-meter-tall flower basket at Tian'anmen Square contains 15 types of plant-assembled "flowers" and five types of "fruit," symbolizing hopes for abundant blossoms and fruitful results during the five years.
At Fuxingmen, the display titled "Forge Ahead" features galloping horses above the words "Strive ahead in the 15th Five-Year Plan period, work hard to open up new horizons," symbolizing a vigorous start to the new five-year period and the determination to pursue high-quality development through hard work. ■

Xi's article on people's wellbeing to be published
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:47:38 CST
21:47:38 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- An article by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, on improving the people's wellbeing will be published on Thursday.
The article by Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, will be published in this year's 19th issue of the Qiushi Journal, a flagship magazine of the CPC Central Committee.
The article is a collection of excerpts of Xi's important discourses on the issue between November 2012 and January 2026.
It says that the people's wellbeing must always come first in Chinese modernization, adding that it is important to ensure and improve the people's wellbeing in the course of development.
Highlighting a people-centered philosophy, the article urges efforts to ensure that public services are inclusive, meet essential needs and provide a cushion for those most in need.
It also calls for better, more balanced and accessible public services to make solid progress toward common prosperity.
Continued headway should be made in improving people's access to childcare, education, employment, medical services, elderly care, housing and social assistance, the article says.
Efforts should continue to promote social fairness and justice so that the people will have a more robust, solid, and sustainable sense of fulfillment, happiness and security, it adds.
At the same time, efforts to ensure and improve the people's wellbeing should be based on economic development and fiscal sustainability, the article says.
It is essential to integrate economic development with improvements in the people's wellbeing to ensure they reinforce each other, it adds. ■

Thailand's industrial output rises 4.44 pct in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:47:33 CST
21:47:33 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's industrial output picked up further in August, mainly due to rising demand for electronics amid the artificial intelligence (AI) and data center boom, official data showed on Wednesday.
The Southeast Asian country's manufacturing production index (MPI) rose 4.44 percent last month compared to a year earlier, up from a revised 3.97 percent gain in July, according to the Ministry of Industry.
The index stood at 103.43 in August, up 0.11 percent from the previous month. Capacity utilization increased to 58.28 percent from 57.55 percent in July.
The August figures are the first under a revised methodology. The ministry's Office of Industrial Economics (OIE) said the revision makes the index better reflect the current structure of Thai industry.
The agency has added products that now play a major role in the production structure, namely notebook and laptop computers, optical transceivers, and backup power units for processors, said OIE Director-General Supakit Boonsiri.
The sample also now includes newly opened factories making integrated circuits and other electronic components, Supakit told a news conference.
Communications equipment led the growth, jumping 24.41 percent year-on-year, driven by optical transceivers, as global AI and data center infrastructure spending continued to grow, he said.
Primary plastics and synthetic rubber posted the steepest decline, falling 13.37 percent. Some plants shut for maintenance, and some producers ran short of raw materials owing to the impact of tensions in the Middle East, he noted.
The ministry upgraded its MPI growth outlook to between 2.75 percent and 3.75 percent this year, from 0 percent to 0.5 percent in an earlier projection. ■

Hungary's tourism declines in August as foreign visitor numbers tumble
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:47:32 CST
21:47:32 KST

BUDAPEST, Sept. 30 (Xinhua) -- Hungary's tourism sector recorded a significant decline in August, with the number of guests falling 7.3 percent year-on-year and guest nights dropping by 5.8 percent, the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH) said Wednesday.
Nearly 2.6 million guests spent 6.9 million nights at tourism accommodation establishments in Hungary during the month, according to KSH.
The decline was particularly pronounced among international visitors. The number of foreign guests fell 13 percent year-on-year to nearly 1.2 million, while nights spent by foreign visitors decreased 9.3 percent to almost 3.1 million.
Foreign guest numbers declined in all of Hungary's tourism regions. Budapest recorded a 15-percent decrease, while the number of foreign visitors to the Lake Balaton region fell by 14 percent.
However, domestic tourism proved more resilient, with the number of domestic guests declining 2.5 percent to 1.4 million and domestic guest nights falling 2.8 percent to nearly 3.9 million.
Private and other accommodation establishments registered particularly steep declines, with foreign guest numbers down 29 percent from a year earlier.
Portfolio, a leading Hungarian business news outlet, said the stronger forint may have contributed to the decline in domestic tourism, by making foreign travel relatively more attractive for Hungarian households, particularly amid perceptions of high accommodation prices at home. ■

U.S. Army scouts armored humanoids for risky missions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:47:17 UTC
21:47:17 KST

- The U.S. Army named five xTechHumanoid winners on Sept. 11, 2026, after nine finalists demonstrated technologies at Marine Corps Base Quantico.
- The winners include IHMC's Alex humanoid robot with ballistic protection, plus power, tactile sensing and command-and-control technologies from four other companies.
The U.S. Army has picked five winners in a competition to test how commercial humanoid robots could be used by the military, including a two-legged robot called Alex that is built to take hits and carries ballistic protection.
The Army announced the xTechHumanoid winners on Sept. 11, two days after nine finalists demonstrated their technology at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia, in front of military leaders, technical experts and evaluators. The competition drew 103 white paper proposals, which were narrowed to 10 finalists.
Only one of the winners is a complete robot. Alex, developed by the Florida Institute for Human and Machine Cognition, known as IHMC Robotics, uses actuators designed to survive impacts, has ballistic protection, and runs on what the U.S. Army calls hybrid autonomy, combining artificial intelligence with human control for complex and dangerous missions.
The other four winners supply parts a working military humanoid would need. ACES Group offered an integrated power system with scalable energy storage, from individual robot batteries up to larger infrastructure. Hydroplane showed a lightweight, compact mobile generator designed to provide long-duration power where supply lines are under threat. Ras Labs won with fingertip sensors that let a robot feel force, shape and slip when it grips an object, and Velocity Explorations with software that turns commanders’ intent and trusted information into specific actions for a humanoid robot.
The U.S. Army did not say how much each winner received. The competition had a total prize pool of $490,000, with separate follow-on contracts or agreements of up to $1.25 million possible outside the prize competition, Army Recognition reported.
“xTech is our method of surveying the industry landscape and fast-tracking promising technology rather than falling victim to years-long studies,” said U.S. Army Chief Technology Officer Alex Miller.
The U.S. Army says it is looking at robotics and autonomy to keep soldiers away from dangerous and physically demanding tasks. Humanoid designs are appealing because they can, in principle, use equipment, vehicles and buildings made for people, though the service has not said which missions it has in mind for them.
The competition was run by the Army’s FUZE xTech program with the Humanoid Community of Collaboration, a joint group set up in December 2023 to work on developing humanoid robots and fitting them into military operations. The U.S. Army said the results give it and the other services a baseline on how mature commercial humanoid technology is and what problems remain.
“The xTech competition is really an interesting and unique one because it allows you to pressure test your technology in a field exercise paradigm,” said Alec Leesberg, president and co-founder of Velocity Explorations.
Power is one of the problems the U.S. Army has flagged. Two of the five winners focused on energy, and the Humanoid Community of Collaboration said its next work will address power and energy limits that could shape how humanoid and other robots are used in the field.
IHMC, based in Pensacola, Florida, has a long record in humanoid robotics, including a second-place finish at the DARPA Robotics Challenge finals in 2015.

Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:47:15 UTC
21:47:15 KST

Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under Donald Trump’s hardline immigration policy.
However, Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial details.
Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to about half a dozen African nations as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of dollars.
In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.
Mutoni said preparations were under way to arrange accommodation, living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.
“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.
Burundi aimed to both strengthen diplomatic relations and provide hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson added.
The US state department did not immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.

12:45:57 UTC
21:45:57 KST

The donors’ discussions focused on Ukraine’s budget needs for 2027. According to Undersecretary Ratnik, support for Ukraine must continue actively using all available means, including through European Union instruments.
“At a time when Russia’s extensive drone and missile attacks against Ukrainian civilians, the economy and critical infrastructure are increasing, and Russia has shown no sign whatsoever of abandoning its objectives, it is important to continue supporting Ukraine in all areas. There is no doubt that Ukraine’s international partners remain committed to doing so. We must support Ukraine’s economy and resilience, particularly in view of the coming winter,” Ratnik said.
Ratnik stressed that Estonia supports closer alignment of Ukraine’s reform commitments with the European Union accession process. “Better alignment between reform requirements and the accession process would make it possible to focus on a smaller number of more impactful reforms. This would help reduce Ukraine’s administrative burden and accelerate the successful implementation of reforms,” Ratnik said.
During her visit, Undersecretary Ratnik met with representatives of the donor platform’s member states and members of the cabinets of European Commission Commissioners to discuss preparations for the Ukraine Recovery Conference, which will take place in Tallinn in January 2027.
“Ukraine’s recovery and its accession to the European Union are inextricably linked. Strengthening resilient, democratic institutions that uphold European values directly supports Ukraine’s progress towards the European Union. That is why one of the central themes of the conference in Tallinn will be Ukraine’s closer integration with the European Union and the reforms needed to achieve this, from the rule of law to digital governance,” said Ratnik.
The Ukraine Donor Platform coordinates international support to meet Ukraine’s budgetary needs and support economic recovery and reconstruction. The platform was established at the initiative of the G7 leaders in December 2022 with the aim of improving the planning and coordination of assistance and avoiding duplication of activities and funding.

How could Great Britain look under proportional representation? See the results for your area
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:45:42 UTC
21:45:42 KST

New analysis produced exclusively for the Guardian reveals how different voting systems would return significantly different seat totals in the UK parliament, based on recent polling.
While the current first past the post (FPTP) system could leave Labour short of a majority with 250 seats, the modelling shows how proportional systems would be likely to reduce the number of seats given to the leading party – and give the UK a more finely balanced parliament that better represents the votes people cast.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has announced a new national commission on electoral reform aimed at changing the electoral system, a plan supported by more than 100 Labour MPs as well as parties such as the Liberal Democrats, the Greens, the SNP and Plaid Cymru. Electoral reform has enjoyed increased public support in recent years.
The research conducted by More in Common suggests that, under proportional systems such as single transferable vote or regional party list, the UK could end up being governed by a minority government – or a progressive alliance of parties.
How proportional systems could change the map
Proportional representation (PR) aims to produce a parliament that more closely reflects how people voted, allowing voters to back their preferred party without worrying about tactical voting. It often makes it harder for a single party to win a majority and is more likely to result in coalition governments.
Alongside the current first past the post system, More in Common modelled three different PR systems for the Guardian: regional party list, single transferable vote (STV) and additional member system (AMS).
The More in Common research shows that no single party would achieve a majority according to their projected polling, regardless of which system is used.
The current FPTP system would come the closest, giving Labour 39% of the seats off just 26% of the vote – still short of a majority. The party would most likely need the support of the Lib Dems and the SNP to form a majority government.
The proportional systems would not give Labour such a boost: regional party list is estimated to give the party 26% of seats off 26% of the vote; AMS would give it 26% of the seats off 29% of the vote; and STV would give it 27% of the seats off 28% of the vote.
Under each of these systems, either a progressive coalition of parties – a combination of Labour, the Lib Dems, the Greens, the SNP or Plaid Cymru – or a Reform-Conservative-Restore coalition would be the only paths to forming a government. Even then, several scenarios would lead to a minority government in a finely balanced parliament.
While the leading Labour party would lose the largest proportion of seats under the proportional systems, smaller parties would be the biggest winners.
The Green party would win only three seats under FPTP under current polling, but more than 50 seats in all three PR systems that we’re modelling – 9% of the seats on offer, more closely matching their vote share. Likewise, the far-right Restore Britain party would surge above 30 seats in each of the PR systems, compared with winning just one seat under FPTP.
Charlie Buckley, a senior research associate at More in Common, said: “With [Nigel] Farage’s [Reform UK] party having lost some momentum and Andy Burnham being – for now – a more popular prime minister, it’s Labour who would reap the benefits from our current electoral system.
“Despite only being four points ahead of the Tories, our model shows Labour winning double the number of seats under first past the post, while a proportional system would give us a parliament which better reflects the close three-horse race we now have between Labour, Reform and the Conservatives.”
Burnham said in his conference speech that Labour shouldn’t “open the door” to a “divisive government” that could win power on “less than 30% of the vote”.
The proportional systems were more likely to remove the regional dominance of any one party. In London, Labour is estimated to gain 69% of seats under FPTP. This number would drop dramatically under PR, to 37% in the party list system and 42% under AMS.
Reform and the Greens would be the biggest beneficiaries in the capital: while Reform would win one seat and the Greens nothing under FPTP, they’d collectively win 18 seats – nearly a quarter of London’s seats on offer – under the party list system.
The same disparity can be seen in the east of England, with the poll-leaders there, Reform, gaining 43% of the seats under FPTP but falling to 29% under both the party list and AMS systems.
How would your local representation change?
Use the postcode search below to see how your local representation would change under each system. Under systems that use regional vote counts to produce more proportional results, you would have regional representatives in place of – or in addition to – constituency ones.
What is wrong with first past the post?
The most recent polling in Britain, as well as recent elections, show an unprecedented fragmentation of the political system. Labour leads on an average of 26%, with Reform second on 23% and the Conservatives third on 20%. The Greens and the Lib Dems are each polling at 10%.
This is based on an average of the last 10 polls, with Labour enjoying a slim lead in the national polls since the party chose Burnham as its new leader and prime minister.
With three parties clustered closely together in the polls, the FPTP system means small shifts in vote share could produce highly volatile and sometimes counterintuitive seat projections, as marginal changes in local contests are amplified into large swings in parliamentary representation.
In the last general election, Labour won 411 of 650 seats with just 34% of the vote.
A report from the Electoral Reform Society modelled the 2024 vote under different voting systems. Only first past the post gave Labour a majority, with all proportional systems giving smaller parties more representation and leading to a hung parliament.
There have been renewed calls for proportional representation. In his conference speech, Burnham said: “We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone’s vote counts and everyone’s voice is heard.”
Farage has also previously called for electoral reform, calling the current system “outdated” and “not fit for purpose”, but has gone quiet on the subject since Reform went on to lead the polls – until Burnham’s Labour retook a slim lead.
Could the voting system change?
Experts say any attempt to introduce proportional representation for Westminster elections would be likely to face strong pressure for a referendum, given its significance as a constitutional change and the precedent set by the 2011 referendum on the alternative vote system (AV).
The referendum saw voters decisively reject AV, showing the difficulty of winning public support for electoral reform. Experts warn that any future move to proportional representation could face similar challenges, as voters are familiar with first past the post and may be reluctant to replace a system they already understand.
Buckley said: “The real winners with a PR system would be on the edges of the political spectrum. The Greens would go from a handful of MPs to a sizeable bloc, while Restore Britain would arrive in parliament in numbers, potentially giving these smaller parties a kingmaker role in the formation of coalitions.
“So the prospect of forming a workable majority – already a dubious one in our current electoral system – looks even more complicated under a proportional one. Regardless of the system in place, our fragmented politics would make any election in Britain a challenge for those seeking to enter and control government, and the idea of a ‘commanding majority’ is out of reach for all the major parties right now.”
When More in Common conducted similar modelling in July, Reform was leading in the polls, and they found the proportional systems would equally not give Reform the same seats boost that FPTP would. The researchers said then that it was difficult to predict how voters might adjust their own behaviour under a new system.
Darren Hughes, the chief executive of the Electoral Reform Society, told the Guardian: “The prime minister’s pledge for a new commission to look at electoral reform is an important step in the right direction. This needs to be an independent and trusted process that focuses on making sure parliament properly reflects the way the country voted.
“There is a growing problem with our democracy in that parliament is looking less and less like the way people voted. The last general election saw the biggest mismatch in British history between the votes people cast and the seats parties won.
“This is largely due to the fact that our outdated two-party voting system can’t cope with the multiparty politics we now have, and is throwing up increasingly distorted and unstable results.
“Simply put, bringing in a system of proportional representation would mean parliament better reflects how the country voted by making sure seats match votes.”
Methodology
Latest polling and seat distribution figures were provided by More In Common (MIC). Alternative electoral system modelling is based on MIC and Guardian assumptions about constituency boundaries.
Party list uses 11 regions – the nine official English regions plus Scotland and Wales – with variable seat totals. AMS uses a combination of the eleven regions and 631 existing first past the post constituencies. STV uses 52 subregional constituencies – composed of the current FPTP constituencies – of variable size depending on aggregate population.
Northern Ireland and the Commons speaker’s seat of Chorley are excluded from the modelling. This results in 631 total modelled seats for FPTP, STV and party list systems, and in 1,052 seats for AMS.
The exact details, shown as seat totals, boundaries and regional groupings, are based on assumptions on how the new proportional systems could work, and in reality, these totals and exact workings would vary should another voting system be adopted.
Where parties have separate parties in each nation, Scottish and Welsh parties have been included in one national total for the purposes of this analysis.

Saudi Arabia Flag (AA Photo)
Türkiye and Saudi Arabia have approved a reciprocal visa waiver agreement for holders of diplomatic and special passports, allowing eligible citizens to travel between the two countries without obtaining a visa.
 
The Saudi cabinet approved the agreement during a meeting in Riyadh chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Sept. 29, the Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported.
 
Türkiye had approved the deal in June, with the presidential decision published in the Official Gazette on June 13.
 
The agreement was signed on May 6 in Ankara after a meeting of the Türkiye-Saudi Arabia Coordination Council. Foreign Ministers Hakan Fidan and Prince Faisal bin Farhan signed the agreement.
 
The arrangement is intended to facilitate travel between the two countries, although it applies only to diplomatic and special passport holders and does not cover ordinary passport holders.
 
Under the agreement, eligible travelers will not need visas to enter, transit through, leave or make temporary stays in the other country. Visa-free stays will be permitted for up to 90 days within any 180-day period.

Bosnia elections: Polls overshadowed by exhaustion, exodus and geopolitics as ethnic politics eclipse real problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:45:00 UTC
21:45:00 KST

Bosnia votes as ethnic politics eclipse real problems
September 30, 2026
Picture a country that has lost nearly one in six of its citizens — roughly 600,000 people —through emigration in just ten years.
A country that has conducted only a single census since being ravaged by war in the 1990s, counting just over 3.5 million people in 2013.
A country where young people aged 20 to 29 are leaving faster than any other age group and where demographers warn of a looming population collapse because the birth rate has trailed the mortality rate every year since 2009.
This is Bosnia and Herzegovina.
But when voters here go to the polls on October 4 to elect people to the most powerful positions at both state and entity levels, the focus of the election campaign will not be on how to stop the country hemorrhaging citizens. It will — once again and for the umpteenth time — be about who is Serb, who is Bosniak, who is Croat and who supposedly threatens whom.
That fact alone says more about the state of Bosnian politics than any opinion poll could.
A complicated electoral system
After the brutal 1992-95 Bosnian War, Bosnia and Herzegovina was left divided by the Dayton Peace Agreement — a compromise that stopped the killing but built ethnicity into the state's architecture as a permanent rather than a temporary fix.
Three decades on, that architecture hasn't changed, and progress has stalled completely.
The complicated constitution drafted at Dayton produced an equally complicated electoral system.
Bosnia is divided into two entities, the Serb-majority Republika Srpska and the Bosniak-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Brcko District. It has a total of 14 governments and parliaments at state, entity and cantonal level — a lot for such a small country.
On October 4, voters will elect a new presidency at state level. The presidency in Bosnia comprises three people. Each of the three ethnic groups elects its own representative: a Serb chosen in Republika Srpska, and a Bosniak and a Croat chosen in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
On top of that, voters will be electing a new president in Republika Srpska and lawmakers for both the state-level and entity parliaments, while the Federation's president and the remaining parliamentary chambers are filled after the vote through ethnic quotas.
Voting along ethnic lines
Bosnia today operates as a patchwork of parallel, ethnically defined power structures whose chief skill is blocking one another. And that isn't a design flaw, it's the design.
"Many citizens will keep voting for parties that represent their own people, because political elites constantly manufacture a sense of threat and fear, turning elections into a referendum on national survival," political scientist Mladen Bubonjic told DW.
This is far removed from the issues affecting voters in their day-to-day lives: high prices, low wages and pensions, unaffordable housing, precarious jobs, corruption, poor public services and the steady drain of people leaving the country.
Same script, new faces
Poll after poll shows that voters don't believe campaign promises, and their answers in such polls tend to boil down to the same thing: "Nothing has changed in 30 years."
That sentence could have been spoken a decade ago, or even two decades ago. And that's precisely the problem: Bosnian politics isn't stuck by accident, it's stuck by design, because the system rewards whoever keeps the divisions alive and punishes anyone who tries to make meaningful change.
Elections in Bosnia have never simply been about getting better roads or cheaper electricity. They function as an act of tribal defense, and every side knows it and cultivates it. Research consistently shows that ethnic identity remains the single strongest predictor of how people vote, far outweighing economic self-interest.
This campaign, too, has been dominated by identity politics and institutional paralysis rather than any real debate over jobs or prices. This means voters are choosing fear, because no one is seriously offering them a real alternative.
"Unfortunately, out of a decades-old habit, ethnic tensions keep rallying citizens around ideological and identity issues. Corruption, poverty and demographic collapse have all been absorbed into political identities," political analyst Tanja Topic told DW.
What voters actually want fixed
But step off the political stage and onto the street and people's priorities sound the same as they do in any other country: They want jobs, a paycheck that covers the bills, an affordable home, healthcare that actually works and a government that doesn't steal.
People blame corruption as the reason reforms stall before they are completed, and young people choose to leave the country rather than cast a ballot.
The real fight is over identity and wartime history, not economic hardship. Emigration gets mentioned mostly as an alarming statistic, rarely as an issue anyone is racing to solve.
"The Bosnian triangle, dominated by three ethnic principles, is disastrous for all of Bosnia's citizens. But if you don't vote along those lines, you get branded a traitor to your own people. Which is disastrous for the country's progress," Vehid Sehic, a political analyst from Tuzla, told DW.
EU accession recedes further into the distance
Bosnia has been an EU candidate since 2022. In 2024, it got the green light to open accession talks. In practice, however, progress along that path has all but ground to a halt.
An independent analysis shows that, according to the EU's own progress reports, Bosnia's readiness score dropped from 4.14 to 2.91 out of ten in a single year — the steepest fall of any candidate country.
Bosnia still hasn't appointed a chief negotiator for EU accession talks, and of the 113 reforms required for EU accession, not one has been implemented.
For ordinary citizens, EU membership is no longer a burning question. It has curdled into a tired, accepted truth that when politicians speak of the "European path," it amounts to little more than ink on paper.
Geopolitical backdrop
Bosnia's elections, alongside Serbia's on October 25, are taking place at a time when the Western Balkans has once again become a stage for intense rivalry between Russia, the European Union and the United States.
Against this backdrop, political forces across Bosnia are already looking for allies abroad.
Bosnia is heading into this election as a country that has spent three decades spinning in place, at the exact moment its internal paralysis has turned it into a playing field for other people's geopolitical bets.
Meanwhile, the 600,000 people who have already left in search of a normal life have effectively answered the question of whether they think anything is about to change.
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

What Will Indonesia Do With Its New Aircraft Carrier?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:45:00 UTC
21:45:00 KST

Febry Triantama has asked difficult questions in these pages about the strategic reasoning behind Indonesia’s acquisition of KRI Sriwijaya, a small aircraft carrier formerly owned and operated as the Giuseppe Garibaldi by the Italian Navy. Much regarding the future of the carrier (and the future of the Indonesian Navy) depends on how much Indonesia invests in maintaining and optimizing the vessel and its air wing.
The acquisition of the warship puts Indonesia into a growing club of navies in the Western Pacific to operate aircraft carriers. In recent years Australia, India, China, and Japan have all built or acquired flat-decked aircraft carrying warships. Most of these are considerably larger than the new Indonesian warship and can accordingly carry more and more varied aircraft and operate at greater distances from base. Thailand joined the aircraft carrier club in the 1990s with the Spanish-designed Chakri Naruebet, similar in size to KRI Sriwijaya.
Two decades ago vessels like the Thai and Indonesian carriers might be expected to operate V/STOL (vertical or short take off and landing) fighters. But it does not appear that Indonesia will go this route. The world’s only operational V/STOL fighters are the AV-8B Harrier and the F-35B Lightning II; the former are old and expensive to operate, while the latter have yet to be offered to Jakarta, and in any case are extremely expensive. The Sriwijaya is better understood as an amphibious support ship than as an aircraft carrier, a warship with substantial aviation capabilities but without an airwing capable of offensive or defense air superiority operations. This would place the ship in the same category as Australia’s Canberra-class landing helicopter docks (LHDs).
The best model for the Indonesia Navy may be the TCG Anadolu, a Turkish amphibious warship built along the same lines as vessels operating for Spain and Australia. While Anadolu was originally expected to fly the F-35B, disputes with Washington have put those plans on ice, perhaps permanently. Instead, the Turkish Navy has used Anadolu as a platform for experimenting with a variety of uncrewed aircraft, including the Bayraktar TB3 and the Bayraktar Kimilelma, both of which have multimission capabilities. Following the Turkish lead would allow Indonesia to avoid the expense of acquiring F-35Bs and, perhaps more importantly, the difficulties of maintaining trained pilots and aircrew for a very small combat wing. Indonesia has already signed a deal with Turkiye for the transfer of a number of drones, and may be able to take advantage of Turkiye’s experience operating advanced UAVs from a maritime platform.
If Anadolu represents the best case, the Thai Chakri Naruebet represents the worst. The Thai carrier was initially expected to operate AV-8B Harriers, but the notoriously difficult fighter proved too much of a hassle and the small force was retired in the early 2000s. Since the Chakri Naruebet has become known as a “harbor queen,” barely operational beyond a few high profile humanitarian assistance/disaster relief (HADR) operations. Thailand had expected more from its carrier but serial financial crises de-emphasized the navy and the navy’s most expensive ship.
Of course, Indonesia is considerably larger than Thailand and its navy has far greater responsibilities. The Sriwijaya is an older vessel and will require considerable modification before service, but Indonesia has already engaged with Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri to modernize the warship, an arrangement that should also improve Indonesia’s capacity for keeping the ship at sea.
An aircraft carrier of any size is a huge opportunity, but also a huge responsibility. Indonesia is rolling the dice on its capacity to keep the ship in service, as well as on the durability of a very old vessel. It could pay off with a much enhanced HADR capability, as well as a platform capable of taking advantage of the latest in drone technology. Or Indonesia could end up with its own harbor queen.

Kubilius: Europe's response to Russian hybrid attacks should be 'as painful' for Moscow

The European Commissioner for Defence tells Euronews that the EU must sharpen its response to a growing spate of hybrid attacks attributed to Moscow, while rejecting those who say it's time to engage the Kremlin in diplomacy.
Russia should feel the pain of Europe's response to hybrid attacks, the European Commissioner for Defence, Andrius Kubilius, has told Euronews, warning that President Vladimir Putin is seeking to occupy "the hearts and the minds" of Europe's population.
"If we are hit by Russian hybrid attacks, our answers should be as painful as that attack," Kubilius told EU Editor Maria Tadeo during an inteview at Euronews' Defence and Space summit.
"How can that pain be created? It’s up to us," he added.
Europe has seen a recent uptick in hybrid attacks attributed to Moscow, with Estonia accusing the Kremlin of orchestrating an arson attack on a drone maker supplying Ukraine earlier this week.
Earlier this month, Germany attributed an attempted drone attack on Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport to Moscow.
Kubilius warned that Russia is seeking to sow fear by "occupying the hearts and the minds of people", and called on Europe to sharpen its response.
"If we are facing hybrid war against us, we need to have hybrid defence."
The Commissioner, who previously served as the Prime Minister of Lithuania, also rejected those who call for diplomatic engagements with the Kremlin in order to bring the war in Ukraine to an end.
Earlier on Wednesday, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told the Euronews summit that the EU should engage diplomatically with Russia to avert a devastating nuclear attack
"There is a limit to just delivering weapons and supporting, because the final peace set-up will be done by diplomacy, not by delivering weapons. So our call is to listen more to each other, to open the lines of communication," Radev said on Tuesday.
"The problem is that no one is raising the question about nuclear risk. Does it exist? Maybe not, I don't know, but this is a risk," he went on.
Commissioner Kubilius said efforts at diplomacy have not yielded outcomes and risk undermining Ukraine.
"Russians are standing with their position very clear: Ukraine needs to surrender - that is their diplomacy position," he said.
"(President Vladimir) Putin needs to understand that in the end he won't achieve anything with this war," he added, "and Putin needs to feel that war is coming to Russia itself."
He also warned that opening a diplomatic track with Russia could embolden Putin to escalate and put European security at further risk.
"So in my view, that doesn’t lead to anywhere which could make both Ukraine and the whole of Europe safe," he explained. "And that would be a victory for Putin, and we can expect what would come next."

Fire Point uses data from strikes by Russian Iskander missiles and North Korean missiles in the development of Freyja
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:44:26 EEST
21:44:26 KST

Fire Point uses data from strikes by Russian Iskander missiles and North Korean missiles in the development of Freyja
Kyiv • UNN
Fire Point is integrating data on strikes by Iskander and North Korean missiles into Freyja's algorithms. The first interception is planned by mid-2027.
The Ukrainian defense company Fire Point collects and analyzes data on Russian strikes using Iskander ballistic missiles and North Korean missiles in order to integrate the information obtained into the algorithms of the European Freyja anti-ballistic system. Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh said this during her speech at the Euronews Defence & Space Summit 2026 in Brussels, UNN reports.
When is the interception of ballistic missiles planned?
We are stockpiling interceptor missiles for the future, conducting trials and system integration, and testing it in real combat conditions in Ukraine. We are also collecting all the data from attacks against us involving Iskanders and North Korean missiles and incorporating it into Freyja’s algorithms
The company expects to receive some of the improvements to the system’s MVP (minimum viable product, or first working version) by the end of 2026.
Our goal is to conduct a "zero" test this year, and achieve an actual interception by the middle of next year—and that is an extremely ambitious goal. To achieve it, everyone must work in exceptionally close coordination. There must be no delays in supplying radars, issuing licenses, or signing individual documents
Iryna Terekh explained that the developers had compressed the process of creating an anti-ballistic program from 40 years to slightly more than two years. According to her, the project is currently undergoing an intensive phase of technical integration and testing.
But it is still shots and launches, launches and launches, until we achieve a result
What is special about Freyja?
The Fire Point CEO recalled that Freyja is being developed as an anti-ballistic system to protect Europe, and that its concept takes into account the experience of the war in Ukraine, including the scale and number of missile threats.
She noted that initially Freyja would not be able to replace the American Patriot air defense system, which remains one of the best systems in the world. However, Patriots were not designed to handle the number of threats Ukraine is facing.
That is why every element of Freyja is designed according to the design-for-manufacturing principle. In other words, from the outset, the system is intended to be scalable, relatively inexpensive, reproducible, and as independent as possible from critical external components or technologies.
In particular, Fire Point is working to create a system using European components, which will allow Freyja to be independent of U.S. ITAR export controls and Chinese components.
The company places primary emphasis on system interoperability and avoiding dependence on a single manufacturer.
An open architecture makes it possible to combine solutions from different European manufacturers into a single system. This means more alternatives, less dependence on individual suppliers, and the ability to quickly integrate new technologies
No less important is the absence of the so-called kill switch—a "switch" that could deprive the owner of an air defense system of the ability to use it. In other words, using Freyja will not require permission from partners or the manufacturer.
If you own your air defense system, you must truly own it
How many interceptors will be produced per year?
As already noted, Fire Point is currently working on stockpiling FP-7.x interceptor missiles for Freyja and scaling up their production. The company plans to apply to Freyja the approach it has already used when scaling up its other developments.
Regarding interceptor missiles, it should be understood that 600–700 interceptors per year will not change anything. We live in a world where the threat will only grow, and the count must be in the thousands and thousands of missiles
The company took this into account when developing the FP-7.x.
The FP-7X interceptor missile from Fire Point, which is currently part of Freyja, was designed for a production capacity of at least several thousand units per year. Of course, much work remains ahead to make this a reality, but it is possible because the missile was designed for future scaling from the very beginning
What is Freyja?
Freyja is a Ukraine-initiated project for a joint European antiballistic system, the first track of the Antiballistic Coalition, which includes 10 countries and more than a dozen leading European defense companies. The system is intended to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.

Malaysia’s capital topped a global pollution ranking on Wednesday and nearby Singapore came in third, with smoke from wildfires in neighbouring Indonesia blamed for the unhealthy conditions.
A milky haze has shrouded the cities for more than a month as smoke drifted from fires on Borneo and Sumatra islands.
Kuala Lumpur was the world’s most polluted major city early on Wednesday, according to Swiss monitor IQAir, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) reading of 166. Singapore ranked third at 155.
The AQI converts measurements of pollutants into a single figure indicating air quality and potential health risks. Readings above 150 are classified as unhealthy, while levels above 300 are considered hazardous.

Kiev loses 1,505 troops along engagement line in past day – latest figures
The Ukrainian army lost roughly 1,505 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.

In the Sumy direction, Battlegroup North units struck formations of three mechanized brigades of the Ukrainian army and two territorial defense brigades in areas near the settlements of Turya, Rovnoye, Boyaro-Lezhachi, Vakalovshchina and Khoten in the Sumy Region, it said.

During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup Center units liberated 164 buildings and destroyed as many as 35 Ukrainian troops in Dobropolye, the ministry reported.
Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 455 personnel, an armored combat vehicle, eight motor vehicles and an electronic warfare station in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 280 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 280 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed four enemy motor vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of an assault brigade, two air assault brigades, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Nikolskoye in the Zaporozhye Region, Chaplino, Malinovka, Demurino and Kolomiytsy in the Dnepropetrovsk Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 280 personnel and four motor vehicles in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 35 Ukrainian troops in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 35 Ukrainian troops and destroyed seven enemy motor vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Dnepr units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade and an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army in areas near the settlements of Orekhov, Preobrazhenka and Yulyevka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.

Russian forces strike Ukrainian ammo, radio-electronic equipment depots in past day

Russian air defenses intercept 768 Ukrainian UAVs, three smart bombs in past day
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 768 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and three smart bombs over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.

“We have no legal obstacles” – Rinkēvičs on deploying nuclear weapons in Latvia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:43:00 UTC
21:43:00 KST

Earlier this month, the Lithuanian parliament, the Seimas, backed in a first vote the removal of a constitutional ban on deploying nuclear weapons in the country. Article 137 of Lithuania’s Constitution currently stipulates that weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases may not be stationed on Lithuanian territory.
Rinkēvičs stressed that Latvia’s Constitution contains no such prohibition.
“We have no legally established obstacles in our laws to the deployment of nuclear weapons in Latvia,” the President said.
He explained that in 2003, as Latvia was preparing to join NATO, each member state had affirmed that it would impose no restrictions on the implementation of NATO’s full collective security mechanism, including participation in the Alliance’s nuclear deterrence system.
“If such a need arises and if NATO makes such a collective decision, nuclear weapons will be deployed in Latvia,”
Rinkēvičs said.
At the same time, he stressed that there are currently no specific discussions about deploying nuclear weapons in Latvia.
Commenting on the United Kingdom’s offer to extend nuclear protection to members of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) – the Baltic states, Nordic countries and the Netherlands – Rinkēvičs argued that without nuclear deterrence, several conventional wars would likely have spread across Europe long ago.
The use of nuclear weapons is an absolute last resort, but their existence deters an aggressor from unpredictable or large-scale actions, Rinkēvičs said.
The President noted that the United Kingdom is already part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence system and that Latvia is already protected by NATO’s nuclear umbrella, provided by the United States and the United Kingdom. As a JEF member, Latvia views all additional security measures and arrangements positively.
“We understand that this remains part of NATO’s overall policy,”
the President said.
As previously reported, the United Kingdom’s offer was confirmed by the head of the Royal Navy, General Gwyn Jenkins, during a visit to Finland on Monday, where he met Heikki Autto, chairman of the Finnish parliament’s Defence Committee.
“The [British] head of the armed forces has emphasised the United Kingdom’s strong commitment to JEF cooperation, and these new opportunities have also been created through that cooperation,” Autto told Finnish news agency STT, commenting on his meeting with Jenkins.
“Finland will be under the nuclear umbrella, and this will be guaranteed by submarines currently patrolling the Atlantic Ocean,” Jenkins confirmed.
An agreement on the creation of a new type of combat force within the JEF is expected to be signed in November.
The new group will have wartime defence plans and is expected to be capable of immediately engaging in military operations in the event of a threat from Russia.
The JEF is a coalition of ten like-minded countries – Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom – comprising high-readiness forces capable of responding rapidly to crises in the High North and Northern Europe.
The coalition was established in 2014 at the initiative of the United Kingdom in response to Russia’s annexation of Crimea. Finland and Sweden joined the JEF in 2017, before becoming NATO members.

Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
13:42:34 BST
21:42:34 KST

Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
- Published
Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukraine's Prime Minister has said.
At least five people were killed in overnight attacks across the country, including a child in the Kyiv region, Serhiy Koretskyi said.
The strikes also impacted people's power supplies, with Ukraine's biggest private energy firm DTEK saying power to 8,000 homes had been restored following "a difficult night" for the capital.
The Russian defence ministry said one of its targets was the Trypilska power station, the largest supplier of electricity to Kyiv. The operator confirmed damage to the plant.
Koretskyi wrote on Telegram: "Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day without enemy attacks on our energy infrastructure.
"However, a mass and combined attack of this scale has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season."
Ukraine has been expecting another protracted Russian assault on the country's energy grid. It has happened every winter so far since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022.
In total, 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian enterprises and railways also targeted, Koretskyi said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there had been strikes on critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions.
On Wednesday, some households in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Sumy and Kharkiv regions remained without power, Ukraine's energy ministry said.
State-owned grid operator Ukrenergo advised residents not to use powerful electrical appliances between the hours of 10:00 and 16:00 local time as electricity supplies were lower than usual.
In Kyiv, people woke to find the city blanketed by thick, acrid smoke after a night punctuated by the sound of explosions. An air raid alert was still on and the distant sound of air defence gunfire echoed through the murky atmosphere.
Residents in several districts were advised to close their windows until the smoke cleared.
Among those killed in the overnight strikes was a child whose body was found under the rubble of a house, Kyiv regional head Timur Tkachenko said.
Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klischko said three people were killed in total in the capital, including a Ukrainian utility company worker who was killed at a warehouse building.
Another person was killed in the southern Mykolaiv region, acting regional head Heorhiy Reshetilov said.
Two more people were killed in the north-eastern Sumy region on Tuesday, regional head Oleh Hryhorov said. A school was also hit there in a separate strike, he added.
Russia's defence ministry said it had launched massive overnight strikes on Ukrainian facilities.
It said targets included the Trypilska thermal power plant, located some 40km from Kyiv, and claimed the plant supplied electricity to Ukrainian defence facilities.
The operator of the plant, Centrenergo, said it was assessing the scale of the damage.
Russia's military added that it had intercepted more than 380 Ukrainian drones overnight over a number of regions, including Moscow.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said it had struck a number of Russian military targets, including a drone warehouse in the occupied Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine.
Russia currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including a large area of Donetsk.
On the battlefield, Ukraine's Third Army Corps said it had recaptured several settlements near the city of Lyman in Donetsk this week, as part of a counter-offensive called Operation Vivaldi. Zelensky visited troops in the area on Wednesday.
But elsewhere, the front line remains largely stagnant, with both sides failing to make significant gains.

U.S. Army taps five firms for 1,000 km HIMARS missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:42:25 UTC
21:42:25 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded five Other Transaction Authority agreements on Sept. 29, 2026, to develop Precision Strike Missile Increment 4 prototypes.
- Anduril, Castelion, Lockheed Martin, Mach Industries and RTX will develop HIMARS-launched missiles to hit moving ships and relocatable land targets at least 1,000 km away.
The U.S. Army has picked five companies to build competing prototypes of a new Precision Strike Missile that can be fired from a HIMARS truck and hit moving ships and relocatable land targets 1,000 km (620 miles) or more away.
Anduril, Castelion, Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control, Mach Industries and RTX each received a separate Other Transaction Authority agreement on Sept. 29 for PrSM Increment 4, the U.S. Army said. Other Transaction agreements are a faster contracting route used for prototypes outside standard procurement rules. The service did not disclose the value of any of the five awards.
The companies will now race each other in two rounds. In fiscal 2027, which begins on Oct. 1, initial prototype work will end in a competitive fly-off, after which the U.S. Army will cut the field. Vendors whose designs prove mature enough will be eligible for follow-on agreements and a final fly-off in fiscal 2028.
The requirement is demanding. The U.S. Army told industry in March that the fly-offs would focus on three things: a range of at least 1,000 km, compatibility with the M142 HIMARS launcher with room to move to other launchers later, and the ability to strike moving targets at sea as well as mobile targets on land, such as missile launchers and air defense systems.
That range would roughly double the reach of today’s PrSM. The first version of the missile, Increment 1, entered service in 2023 as a replacement for the older Army Tactical Missile System, which flies up to 300 km (186 miles). Lockheed Martin designed Increment 1 for about 500 km (310 miles), and the U.S. Army has said it has been tested against targets more than 400 km away. The missile was used in combat for the first time in March against targets in Iran.
The PrSM family is being upgraded in steps. Increment 2 adds a seeker that lets the missile hit moving ships, and the U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin a contract worth up to $1.2 billion for its production earlier this month. Increment 3 is meant to add new warhead and payload options, while Increment 4 is the long-range version.
Two of the five winners have been working on the long-range missile for years. In 2023, the U.S. Army gave Lockheed Martin and a team of Raytheon and Northrop Grumman contracts to develop new propulsion and airframe designs for what was then called the Long Range Maneuverable Fires missile, with Lockheed receiving $33.3 million and the Raytheon team nearly $100 million, Breaking Defense reported at the time.
Lockheed Martin has said its Increment 4 design pairs a rocket booster with an air-breathing ramjet engine to double the range of the current missile while keeping it the same size, so it can still fit existing HIMARS and M270 launchers. In June, the company and L3Harris completed a ground test of the handoff from booster to ramjet, which Lockheed described as the main technical hurdle before flight testing.
The other three awards bring newer defense firms into a program that Lockheed Martin has so far dominated. Castelion is developing the Blackbeard hypersonic missile, which the U.S. Navy selected earlier this year for its Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector program. Anduril and Mach Industries have not publicly described their Increment 4 designs.
