Sloped ceilings and narrow halls don’t have to waste space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:21:01 UTC
21:21:01 KST

Partner content
Sloped ceilings and narrow halls don’t have to waste space
Dutch homes are famously charming – and famously awkward to furnish – for cabinetmakers at Cabinetheroes, that is the whole point. Narrow facades, steep staircases, and rooms that seem to defy right angles: these aren’t quirks, they’re history.
Property taxes in many Dutch cities were once linked to the width of a building’s frontage, and the result can still be seen today: narrow hallways, steep staircases and rooms where standard furniture is difficult to place.
The familiar hooks above many gabled windows are another reminder of these challenging layouts – they were traditionally used to hoist furniture through the windows because getting large pieces up the stairs was often impossible.
Converted attics bring their own challenges. In a typical “zolder”, sloped ceilings and unusual angles can leave large parts of the room unused. Standard wardrobes are made for straight walls and predictable dimensions, and simply can’t use that kind of space. A made-to-measure cabinet, by contrast, can follow the exact shape of the room and turn overlooked corners into valuable storage. The result: rooms that look bigger on paper than they feel in practice, with corners and slopes often written off as wasted.
“You often have more space than you think – you just aren’t using it yet,” says Sven, managing director of the Cabinetheroes franchise network and an experienced carpenter himself.
Planning around the room, not against it
 This is where made-to-measure solutions like those from Cabinetheroes come in. With the Cabinetheroes, creating a cabinet built around a room rather than the other way around is straightforward. Instead of adapting a home to fit off-the-shelf furniture, a personal Cabinethero visits, discusses your ideas, measures the room and plans a solution around the space and the way you live.
As an experienced cabinetmaker, he understands both the design and the craftsmanship behind it, and once the cabinet has been individually manufactured, he also takes care of the professional installation. From the first measurements to the finished cabinet, you have one personal point of contact – and every important step is handled by a skilled professional. Two recent projects show us what this all means in practice.
The hallway that finally feels welcoming
 Christian’s hallway was more of a narrow passage than an inviting entrance. A conventional cabinet would have made the space feel even tighter, yet leaving it empty meant coats, shoes and everyday items had nowhere to go.
After measuring the hallway personally, Sven planned a fitted cloakroom cabinet that uses the available space down to the millimetre, with an integrated LED strip adding light and a warmer atmosphere.
“Tidy, I’d say,” is how Christian describes the practical result. But the emotional difference mattered just as much: “You feel welcome.” His verdict on the process was equally clear: “It was really professional. I’d recommend it to anyone.” Every step along the way was handled by one point of contact.
An open dressing area beneath a sloped roof
 For Jennifer, a sloped ceiling appeared to rule out a spacious dressing area. Standard wardrobes would have left gaps beneath the roof and wasted valuable space in the lowest parts of the room. The made-to-measure design follows the ceiling precisely and uses the space right into the furthest corner.
Instead of doors, the open layout keeps clothing and accessories visible and easy to reach, with socks, belts and other smaller items each getting their own place, helping the room stay organised in everyday life.
“We’d never had such a beautiful cabinet,” Jennifer says. Everything was “matched exactly to the room”, while the personal planning took place comfortably in her own home. Her conclusion: “Quality, style and something completely individual.”
Starting with the room, not the shop
 The lesson from both projects: start with the room rather than with the limited dimensions offered by a furniture shop. Slopes, alcoves and awkward corners are not necessarily wasted space – they simply require accurate measurements and thoughtful planning, with lighting, sockets and everyday routines considered from the beginning.
Features such as integrated LEDs are much easier to incorporate during planning than to add afterwards, and even a few centimetres can determine whether standard furniture fits at all.
As Sven puts it: “Your room can do more.”
For anyone facing a similar layout, the Cabinetheroes offer a free, non-binding enquiry: a personal Cabinethero will visit, discuss the possibilities, take precise measurements and guide the process through to individual planning and professional installation.

New Delhi reveals number of Indian sailors in troubled waters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30

21:20:25 KST

New Delhi reveals number of Indian sailors in troubled waters
More than 4,500 Indian seafarers are aboard commercial vessels operating in the Persian Gulf amid repeated attacks on regional shipping, New Delhi has said. The Indian government is monitoring their safety after one sailor from the country was killed and another went missing this month. 
Six India-flagged commercial ships and six foreign-flagged vessels carrying cargo to India are currently in the Gulf west of the Strait of Hormuz, with around 163 Indian seafarers aboard them. The more than 4,500 Indians are serving on other commercial vessels operating in the area, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Tuesday. 
An Indian sailor was killed when the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier MV Cape Dao was attacked in the Gulf of Oman on September 23. Ten days earlier, an Indian crew member went missing after the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia was struck while passing through the Strait of Hormuz. 
At least 85 shipping incidents had been recorded in and around the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East by September 24, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) confirmed, highlighting the growing risk to commercial vessels operating in the region. 
India has tightened precautions in response. Shipowners and managers have been advised since July to avoid deploying Indian seafarers on voyages through the Strait of Hormuz until further orders. A 24-hour control room and real-time monitoring system are also tracking vessels and crews in coordination with the Indian Navy and other agencies. 
The safety push has also moved to the diplomatic level. India and Liberia launched a new Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers at the United Nations last week, bringing together around two dozen countries with major roles in shipping, vessel registration and supplying crews.
India is now the world’s second-largest supplier of seafarers, with 311,936 maritime professionals accounting for 12.16% of the global workforce, according to the 2026 BIMCO-ICS Seafarer Workforce Report cited by the Shipping Ministry.
The targeting of commercial ships and crews in international waterways is “simply unacceptable,” Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar told the UN General Assembly on Saturday, calling for restraint, de-escalation, and uninterrupted flows of energy and commerce.
Traffic through Hormuz remains well below pre-conflict levels. Ten commodity vessels crossed the strait on September 23, compared with a ten-day average of about 17. Before the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February, around 125 large commercial vessels typically used the route each day.

Nominees for Rasoul Prize announced, awarding cemony in Dec.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:18:13 UTC
21:18:13 KST

The shortlist for the second edition of the Rasul Medal was recently released, revealing four finalists selected in Engineering Sciences, four in Mathematics, four in Computer Science, eight in Life and Medical Science and Technology, two in Chemistry, and two in Physics. The winners are to be announced in November and honored at a ceremony in December.
According to the Scientific Committee of the Rasul Medal, previously known as the Young Scientist Medal, the initial list of nominees included more than 100,000 candidates across seven categories: 55,878 candidates in Life and Medical Science and Technology; 4,675 in Physics; 7,897 in Chemistry; 1,965 in Mathematics; 5,589 in Computer Science; and 26,377 in Engineering Sciences. The special category of Nanotechnology also involved 14,000 eligible candidates in the initial list.
After holding several meetings, the Mustafa(pbuh) Prize Scientific Committee finalized the shortlist, which consists of four finalists in Engineering, four in Basic Sciences, four in Mathematics, four in Computer Science, and eight in Life and Medical Sciences and Technology.
The winners of the Medal are expected to be announced in late October, with the award ceremony scheduled to take place in November-December 2026.
Hossein Naderi-Manesh, the head of the scientific committee of the Rasul Medal, also stated that, given the international nature of the event, it would be desirable for the award ceremony to be held in various Islamic countries, emphasizing the need to harness the immense capacities available across the Islamic world to host the event.
The Medal’s secretariat released a call last December for scientists under the age of 40 residing in Islamic countries. Scientific organisations or individuals were invited to nominate candidates by January 20, 2026.
The Rasul Medal was established through the endowments of several Mustafa(pbuh) Prize laureates. Professors Ugur Sahin, Omid Farrokhzad, and Dr. VahabMirrokni dedicated their cash prize to this cause upon receiving their Mustafa(pbuh) Prize in 2019, 2023, and 2025, respectively. The first edition of the Medal was held concurrently with the 6th edition of the Mustafa (pbuh) Prize in 2025.
Rasul Medal Nomination
The Medal is awarded to impactful works in the fields of Life and Medical Science and Technology, Basic and Engineering Sciences, and Computer Science by young scientists of the Islamic countries. The candidates must be nominated by a third-party scientific or technological body, such as universities and research centers, reputable scientific and technological associations and institutions, academies of sciences, or science and technology parks.
The candidates for the Rasul Medal must be under 40 years old at the end of the year in which the medal is awarded. This means that candidates for the 2026 Young Scientist Medal must be born in 1987 or later.
The winners are bestowed a medal, a certificate, and a $10,000 cash prize in each category.
The Rasul Medal promotes scientific and technological breakthroughs by young scientists in the Islamic world and recognizes their influential achievements. Established as a symbol of excellence and scientific merit, the medal honors the contributions of the young generation of scientific talent.

Swiss commission ready to mediate disputes over looted art
Applications regarding cultural assets that are the subject of dispute may be submitted to the newly created Commission for Historically Problematic Cultural Heritage.
Former Swiss President and Commission Chair Simonetta Sommaruga, along with Vice-Chair Felix Uhlmann, briefed the media on Wednesday in Bern. The Commission has now adopted the procedural rules for dealing with such individual cases, which the legal scholar Uhlmann discussed at the conference.
It will thus act as a mediator between the parties where there is a prospect of reaching an amicable agreement. If not, proceedings will be initiated, culminating in a non-binding recommendation. This applies to objects from the Nazi and colonial contexts.
In September, the committee consulted federal institutions on their handling of cultural property with a potentially controversial history. It also intends to seek dialogue with museums outside the federal sphere. One priority is to carry out an inventory of human remains in Swiss collections that came to be held there in a context of injustice.

US Uncovers Russian Intel Plot to Assassinate Anti-Kremlin Activists on US Soil
Unknown

US Uncovers Russian Intel Plot to Assassinate Anti-Kremlin Activists on US Soil
Russian intelligence-linked operatives planned to assassinate chess grandmaster and Kremlin critic Garry Kasparov in the United States this summer, Spanish outlet El Mundo reported on September 30.
US authorities informed Kasparov that he was the target of a Kremlin-linked assassination plot and placed him under special protection. According to El Mundo, preparations to kill former Russian lawmaker Ilya Ponomarev were even further advanced.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“US authorities confirmed to him this summer that he is a target,” a source close to Kasparov told the newspaper.
US prosecutors have identified five alleged members of a network linked to Russian intelligence services that recruited people to surveil and kill Kremlin opponents.
El Mundo reported that two targets were to be killed in the United States, while another potential victim was targeted in Vilnius, Lithuania.
The network, described as the “RIS Network,” has allegedly operated since at least 2024 and previously organized sabotage attacks in Europe using recruited criminals and local operatives. Its alleged preparations for assassinations on US soil marked a significant expansion of such operations, according to El Mundo.
Kasparov has lived outside Russia since 2013 after years of threats linked to his political activity. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow designated him a “foreign agent,” added him to its list of “terrorists and extremists” in 2024, and placed him on an international wanted list in May 2026.
Ponomarev, another alleged target, was the only member of Russia’s State Duma to vote against the annexation of Crimea in 2014. He later joined Ukraine’s territorial defense and has stated that he survived five assassination attempts, El Mundo reported.
A person recruited by Moscow photographed two locations in Washington linked to an individual identified by US prosecutors as “Victim Number 1.” The planned killing carried a $40,000 payment.
The surveillance instructions required videos of at least 30 seconds from several angles, with an agreed hand gesture visible to prove the material was recent. El Mundo reported that the group used coded language, calling surveillance “measuring the land” and the planned killing “construction.”
The assassination was ultimately not carried out after the recruited individual refused to proceed beyond surveillance.
US prosecutors allege that five men formed the Russian intelligence-linked network, including former Russian intelligence colonel Yuri Jrameev and his son Kirill, an FSB officer. Two Cuban nationals and one Venezuelan were also charged, and all five remain in Russia, according to El Mundo.
All five face charges of conspiring to finance acts of terrorism, while three are additionally accused of conspiracy to commit murder for hire. The network also allegedly recruited people to carry out sabotage in countries supporting Ukraine.
El Mundo reported that Russian-linked operatives had also targeted exiled activists in Lithuania, including Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin and Bashkir activist Ruslan Gabbasov. Gabbasov discovered a tracking device on his car in 2025, after which Lithuanian prosecutors identified an alleged plot to kill him.
The alleged US plots would represent an unusual expansion of Russian intelligence operations. Moscow-linked assassinations and attempted killings have previously been concentrated in Europe, including the 2018 Novichok poisoning of Sergei Skripal in Salisbury and the 2019 killing of Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin, El Mundo wrote.
Russia has increasingly relied on recruited foreign nationals and local criminals for sabotage and covert operations abroad, allowing its intelligence services to distance themselves from those carrying out attacks.
Days earlier, Ukraine’s Security Service detained an alleged FSB operative in Kyiv who was preparing to assassinate a Russian opposition figure fighting for Ukraine.
Investigators stated that she had received weapons training from the FSB and collected a pistol from a concealed cache before being arrested near the intended target’s workplace.

Bulgaria's parliament passes law protecting journalists from abusive SLAPP lawsuits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:17:49 UTC
21:17:49 KST

Most SLAPPs are for defamation or reputational harm and tend to be used by those rich and powerful enough to afford the necessary lawyers' fees.
The Bulgarian parliament passed a law on Wednesday aiming to better protect journalists, activists and others from abusive lawsuits designed to censor or intimidate critics.
In doing so, Bulgaria has gone beyond the minimum European Union requirement in a bid to protect the media in a country where the freedom of the press has come under sustained pressure.
Known as strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPP), the use of legal action is intended to silence or financially bankrupt reporters, whistleblowers and rights groups, rather than win the case outright.
Most SLAPPs are for defamation or reputational harm and tend to be used by those rich and powerful enough to afford the necessary lawyers' fees.
While the reform implements a European directive from 2024, which requires member states to protect journalists from abusive cross-border lawsuits within the bloc, Bulgaria has also chosen to extend the safeguards to purely domestic cases.
In particular, it allows for clearly unfounded claims to be thrown out at an early stage, requires the courts to rule within short deadlines and toughens the conditions under which defendants may face interim measures such as asset seizures.
The new rules will also apply to proceedings already under way but which have not yet had their first hearing.
Lawyer Alexander Kashumov, who has been involved in various SLAPP lawsuits, called the law "a major step forward."
According to Kashumov, dozens of such cases, each involving "tens or even hundreds of thousands of euros," are currently before the courts, with a "paralysing effect on freedom of expression."
In its latest global press freedom ranking, Reporters Without Borders put Bulgaria at 71 out of 180 countries, saying press freedom in the country is "fragile and unstable."

As elections near, Israel is increasing 'assassinations' in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:16:48 UTC
21:16:48 KST

Breadcrumb
As elections near, Israel is increasing 'assassinations' in Gaza despite alleged ceasefire
Israeli raids in the Gaza Strip are no longer limited to targeting sites or areas that Israel claims are linked to Hamas. Self-declared "assassinations" of Palestinian leaders and operatives have become increasingly frequent, even as Israel claims to that the so-called ceasefire remains in effect.
On the ground, however, there is no actual ceasefire for the Palestinian community.
On Wednesday, five Palestinians were killed and 15 others injured in an Israeli strike targeting a civilian vehicle in the Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood, southwest of Gaza City, according to Palestinian medical sources.
In a separate incident, four Palestinians, including two children, were injured in an Israeli strike on a tent sheltering displaced people west of Khan Younis.
Meanwhile, three others were wounded, two of them critically, by Israeli gunfire in the Abu al-Ajeen area, southeast of Deir al-Balah.
These attacks came a day after Israel's announced the assassination of Izz al-Din al-Beik, commander of the northern Gaza brigade of the al-Qassam Brigades, Hamas's armed wing, in a raid targeting an apartment in Gaza City's al-Nasr neighbourhood.
The strike coincided with an attack on al-Quds Brigades commander Musab al-Balbisi, who Palestinian sources reported was critically wounded.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz claimed that al-Beik had been involved in planning attacks and recruiting fighters.
The al-Qassam Brigades, however, announced his death in what it described as an Israeli "assassination operation", saying he was a member of its General Military Council and commander of the northern Gaza brigade.
Ongoing assassinations
Israel claimed its operations target Hamas members accused of planning attacks or rebuilding the movement's military capabilities.
Hamas has denied attempting to rebuild its arsenal or launch attacks, instead accusing Israel of violating the ceasefire agreement.
Since the agreement came into force last October, Israel has announced the killing of several senior al-Qassam Brigades commanders, including Izz al-Din al-Haddad, Raed Saad, Nayel Abu Obeid, Mohammed al-Yazouri, Mohammed Naeem Jundiya and Shadi Abu Hasira, in addition to al-Beik, whose death was announced on Tuesday.
On Tuesday, Katz also threatened to target Hamas leaders outside the Gaza Strip, saying that they too were "within the scope of targeting".
Mustafa Ibrahim, a Gaza-based political analyst, told The New Arab that the increase of attacks is significant given the approaching elections in Israel, but cautioned against assuming an absolute and direct connection between the two developments.
"Netanyahu's statements had revived discussion about the possibility of renewed escalation on one of Israel's fronts, potentially reigniting the Gaza front, and whether this could affect the country's electoral timetable," he said. "At this stage, there is no information proving a direct connection between the two matters."
He said, however, that bringing security and war back to the forefront of public discourse could shift the Israeli political debate away from accountability for the failures surrounding the Hamas-led 7 October attack and towards external risks and perceived threats.
Ibrahim argued the Israeli election campaign could enter a phase in which security becomes central to the political battle, potentially encouraging a focus on external threats while pushing questions about the 7 October failures and political accountability into the background.
He stressed, however, that any connection between the security rhetoric, renewed military escalation and a possible postponement of elections remained a matter of analysis rather than an established fact.
'We no longer know who the target is'
These political and security calculations are far from abstract for Gaza's Palestinian residents.
The repeated deadly and horrific strikes by Israel have created a pervasive sense of uncertainty, with civilians saying they can no longer distinguish between locations considered potential military targets and those they might reasonably regard as safe.
Mohammed Abdullah, a resident of Gaza City, told TNA that civilians were living in a state of constant fear.
"We hear about a specific person being targeted, only to discover that civilians have been killed or wounded. We no longer know who is being targeted or where the next strike might land," he said.
He pointed out that the ceasefire had done little to dispel the fear among residents.
"People do not feel the war is over. The shelling continues, the gunfire continues, and the assassinations continue. Everyone fears being in the wrong place at the wrong time," he added.
Sally Abu Shawish, from central Gaza, told TNA that fear had become part of daily life, particularly for displaced people living in tents and other makeshift shelters.
"Even when we go out to buy food or water, we constantly wonder if the place is safe," she said. "No one knows what a ceasefire means anymore, because the killing hasn't stopped."
The continued targeting of vehicles and individuals in densely populated areas has heightened concerns among displaced Palestinians, many of whom have already been forced to move repeatedly during the war and have few options for finding safer locations.
The Israeli announcements that it will continue pursuing figures it identifies as Hamas leaders, both inside and outside Gaza, have added to those fears. For civilians living in crowded areas, the targeting of a particular individual can have consequences far beyond the stated target.
Gaza-based political analyst Ahed Ferwana told TNA that the recent developments reflected what he described as a renewed Israeli pattern of targeting gatherings, vehicles and individuals in Gaza, alongside increasingly explicit rhetoric about pursuing Hamas leaders.
He said the occupation has resumed targeting civilian gatherings, describing the incident as a "massacre" amid reports of the initial casualty toll.
The series of targeted killings, he added, indicated that Israel did not view the ceasefire as the conclusion of its military campaign against Hamas, but rather as a framework within which it continued operations that it considered necessary to prevent the movement from rebuilding its capabilities.

Ukraine's Constitutional Court strikes down govt's power to limit rights during epidemics
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
15:16:43 EEST
21:16:43 KST

The Grand Chamber of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine (CCU) has declared unconstitutional a provision of the law "On Protection of the Population from Infectious Diseases" that allowed the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine to independently establish temporary restrictions on the rights and freedoms of individuals and legal entities amid the spread of infectious diseases.
According to a statement by the CCU's Communications and Legal Monitoring Department posted on the court's website, on Sept. 29 the CCU issued a ruling in a case concerning a constitutional petition by the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights regarding the constitutionality of a provision in Part Four of Article 29 of the Ukrainian law "On Protection of the Population from Infectious Diseases" of April 6, 2000, No. 1645-III, as amended.
"Having considered the issues raised in the constitutional petition, the court concluded that the separate provision of Part Four of Article 29 of the law, namely: 'temporary restrictions on the rights of individuals and legal entities shall be established,' contradicts the Constitution of Ukraine," the CCU said.
According to the statement, it is precisely the challenged provision of the law that allows the Cabinet of Ministers to restrict constitutional rights and freedoms amid the spread of infectious diseases dangerous to human life and health, "because the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine did not initially regulate such a significant issue as the restriction of rights and freedoms under the specified conditions by law, but authorized the highest executive body to carry out such regulation."
"Any doubts that state authorities may have regarding their powers in matters of restricting rights and freedoms must be interpreted from the standpoint of protecting those rights and freedoms, which also includes a guarantee that they may be restricted exclusively on the basis of law," the CCU quoted from the ruling.
At the same time, the Constitutional Court emphasized that the Cabinet of Ministers may, on the basis of and in accordance with the Constitution and laws of Ukraine, regulate by normative acts matters concerning the implementation of temporary restrictions on constitutional rights and freedoms, provided that the Constitution and laws of Ukraine define the grounds, legitimate purpose, scope and manner of the relevant restrictions.
Thus, as the CCU explained, the government's powers consist of specifying the procedure for implementing restrictions on rights and freedoms established by Ukrainian laws, rather than independently establishing new restrictions.
"The provision of Part Four of Article 29 of the law declared unconstitutional ceases to have effect from the date on which the court adopted this ruling," the CCU's Communications and Legal Monitoring Department said.

US presses Europe to release more emergency oil reserves as prices surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:16:12 UTC
21:16:12 KST

Washington says European countries have yet to deliver promised oil releases, as soaring crude and diesel prices intensify pressure on governments to intervene.
The United States has urged European countries to release more emergency oil reserves to curb soaring energy prices, as Washington announced it would put another 40 million barrels onto the market.
“While the United States and Japan are delivering on their commitments, several European member countries have released only a fraction of the crude oil and petroleum products they pledged,” US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on September 29. “We urge every member country to fulfil its commitments.”
The appeal comes as the Trump administration considers a 90-day diesel export ban in an effort to contain domestic fuel prices ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Washington says its latest release from strategic reserves is part of a coordinated effort to stabilise oil markets as disruption in the Middle East sends prices sharply higher.
US diesel has surged to $7 a gallon while Brent crude oil has been trading between $97 and $102 per barrel since late September, an increase of $25 to $30 per barrel compared to pre-war levels.
Disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, escalating tensions in the Gulf of Aden and attacks on Russian refineries have put further pressure on an already tight oil market.
European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said on September 29 that the EU had spent more than €100 billion extra on energy this year without receiving any additional gas or oil in return.
Europe still has reserves to draw on
The International Energy Agency (IEA) coordinated the release of 400 million barrels of oil in March, with the EU contributing roughly 20 percent, shortly after US and Israel's attacks on Iran on 28 February.
But IEA executive director Fatih Birol played down the prospect of another coordinated emergency release when he spoke to reporters in Dublin in the margins of an energy ministerial meeting on September 29, shortly before Washington issued its call.
Birol said another release was not currently a priority and that much of the oil already pledged had yet to reach the market.
“About two-thirds [of emergency oil reserves] have been released and hit the markets, and one-third is still to come,” he said.
European countries had made significant efforts, Birol added, but still had stocks of both crude oil and refined products available.
US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, however, suggested Europe could do more, particularly on diesel.
The Trump administration was “discussing a lot of options”, Burgum told reporters in Washington on September 29, adding: “I don’t want to get ahead of anybody.”
But, he stressed, European countries “have a lot of diesel reserves”.
Any new coordinated emergency release would normally be overseen by the IEA, with the European Commission then coordinating the positions of EU member states. The IEA did not respond to a Euronews request for comment by the time of publication.
Europe has built up a substantial emergency oil cushion, although stocks vary considerably between countries.
In May 2025, EU countries collectively held 108.6 million tonnes of emergency oil stocks, including about 43.5 million tonnes of crude, 39 million tonnes of diesel and gasoil, and 10.4 million tonnes of petrol, according to the European Commission.
But the cushion is unevenly distributed. Finland had reserves equivalent to 178 days of net imports in May 2025, compared with 112 days in Greece, 108 in Belgium, 107 in Sweden, 105 in Malta and 104 in Spain.
Ireland held the equivalent of 83 days, Czechia 79 days and Bulgaria 88 days.
The Commission has not yet published comparable figures for 2026.
Between a rock and a hard place
A US diesel export ban would add to the pressure on European consumers and industry, according to Francesco Sassi, assistant professor of political science at the University of Oslo.
“The immediate consequences would be even costlier supply scenarios for European consumers and additional costs for industries and energy operators,” Sassi told Euronews.
Governments would also face higher public spending as they sought to cushion households and businesses from soaring energy prices, he said.
Sassi warned that prolonged supply disruption could also increase pressure on Europe to reconsider Russian energy supplies.
“The EU continues to ignore the severe disruptions to supply the market has been experiencing since the beginning of the war in the Persian Gulf and the blockade of Hormuz,” he said, arguing that Europe remained heavily dependent on supply routes protected by other powers or controlled by global markets.
Ireland’s Energy Minister Darragh O’Brien said on September 29 that a US diesel export ban was “unlikely” because it would damage economies on both sides of the Atlantic.
But he urged Europe to prepare for the possibility.
“We have to be guarded,” O’Brien said. “We can’t be complacent.”

Russia is preparing to make daily life in Kyiv harder before winter, aiming at the ordinary places civilians use rather than at military sites, The Economist reported. Ukrainian officials say the push blends bombing, sabotage, and disinformation, and expect it to peak in November.
Every winter of its full-scale invasion, Russia has tried to freeze Ukrainians into surrender, and each year the strikes reach deeper into ordinary life. The civilian casualties recorded in 2026 have already passed the whole of last year, the UN says.
From the power grid to the grocery store
Russia has already turned its drones on Kyiv's supermarkets, food warehouses, and data centers this year. On 28 September, a Russian jet drone struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv. The strike killed two people, the Academy said. Survivors climbed from the windows of the burning building. A senior Ukrainian official told The Economist the Kremlin now wants shoppers too afraid to enter a store. Russia is also keeping its winter routine, hitting electricity, water, and sewage systems.
Cheaper jet drones that stream live to their pilots
Most of the damage now comes from Russia's cheap jet drones, The Economist said. Pilots guide them onto targets and watch a live video feed. They are hard to stop, and Russia's ballistic missiles are deadlier still as Ukraine's supply of Patriot interceptors dwindles. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv had agreed a new Patriot interceptor package, but it remains short of interceptors of its own. A security official told The Economist that Russia has thousands of drones stockpiled and plans to use its entire ballistic missile stock within two months.
War is costing Ukraine $155 billion per year. With Western aid running late, Kyiv is freezing everything but army, pensions, and public wages
Sabotage, chaos, and a city that won't switch off
Ukraine's counter-intelligence services say they foil seven or eight Russian plots a week, and officials believe some sleeper cells remain. The campaign's third element, disinformation, targets war fatigue and corruption scandals. Russia runs the same plan every year, hoping its bot farms will push Ukrainians onto the streets to demand surrender, said Andrii Kovalenko, who heads the Center for Countering Disinformation at the National Security and Defense Council.
"It's nonsense," he told The Economist, adding that someone is feeding the idea to Putin so they can steal more money.
Kyiv is also far harder to shut down than Moscow assumes, Kovalenko said. The city's internet is too decentralized for a handful of strikes to knock out, The Economist noted. Energy expert Olha Babii said the test is how fast crews restore power, not whether it can be destroyed. The capital is emptying, its population down from about 3.7 million to 3.3 million by The Economist's count.

2025 Among Driest Years for Global Rivers in 35 Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:12:00 UTC
21:12:00 KST

Global river discharge in 2025 was among the lowest recorded in the past 35 years, according to a new World Meteorological Organization (WMO) report on the state of the world's water resources.
The data show that river discharge was below normal in 36% of the world's river basins last year. For the seventh year in a row, the share of basins with normal water levels remained well below the long-term average.
Between 1991 and 2020, an average of 46% of river basins were considered to be in a normal state, the WMO said. Over the last seven years, that proportion has fluctuated between 34% and 38%.
The report also points to an ongoing reduction in terrestrial water storage, which includes groundwater, lakes and rivers, soil moisture and vegetation, along with snow and ice. These water reserves have continued to decline since the 2014–2016 period.
"We are depleting the planet's 'savings account'," WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo warned, referring to the long-term decrease in terrestrial water storage.
Groundwater conditions are of particular concern. Almost two-thirds of monitored boreholes around the world recorded deviations from historical norms in 2025, with the overall balance moving further toward a deficit compared with 2024.
Glaciers also recorded mass losses for the fourth consecutive year across all major glaciated regions worldwide. The cumulative loss between 2023 and 2025 is estimated at about 1,400 gigatonnes of water, equivalent to roughly 560 million Olympic-sized swimming pools.
The WMO said the global water cycle is becoming increasingly unpredictable, with severe droughts alternating with extreme flooding. Asia and Africa have suffered the greatest impact over the past five years, together accounting for at least half of all reported extreme water-related events and more than 80% of the deaths linked to them.
Regions with persistently low river discharge in 2025 included parts of North America, the La Plata and São Francisco basins in South America, Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia.
The WMO report draws on observations, satellite data and modeling from 68 countries and more than 3,000 monitoring stations. The organization warned that changes in the water cycle are increasingly affecting agriculture, energy production, ecosystems and the security of water supplies.

After Flydubai incident: Should Israelis prefer flying blue-and-white?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:10:52 UTC
21:10:52 KST

The unusual incident on the Flydubai flight, which carried approximately 180 passengers including more than 100 Israelis, has reignited a question concerning many Israelis: What safety implications come with choosing to fly with a foreign carrier.
The unusual event quickly sparked a wave of concern among Israelis on social media. Alongside questions about what exactly occurred in the cockpit, many began to wonder whether choosing to fly with a foreign airline - especially on routes where Israeli carriers do not operate - involves a different level of risk.
'An insane price hike at El Al from now on'
Reactions from Israelis online reflected the anxiety. "Only El Al direct, the incident from this morning changed the picture," wrote one user. Another addressed potential financial consequences: "An insane price hike at El Al from now on."
"I've always been El Al only; whoever wants to save money should account for the risks involved," others wrote, questioning whether the incident would lead Israelis to prefer flights on Israeli airlines, even at higher prices. "The case this morning gives El Al and all Israeli companies the legitimacy to double prices; they'll take advantage of the country now," another user wrote. Others even stated their intention to cancel pre-booked flights: "We booked for August and will cancel; I hope they let us do it without a fee."
'The security aspect in Israeli companies is handled differently'
Hagay Meyer, chairman of the Pilots Association, emphasizes that at this stage it is too early to determine what exactly happened in the cockpit, and that the findings of the investigation must be awaited. However, according to him, there are differences in how airlines address security issues, and a passenger's decision to fly with a foreign carrier is a choice they must make while aware of these differences.
"I want to note to the credit of Israeli companies that we know their security rules; they are strict, and there we are more at ease," he says. "But people, by their own decision, also choose to fly with other companies." He refers to many passengers choosing to fly with airlines like Emirates and Etihad due to significant price gaps between them and Israeli airlines: "True, that's completely fine. But if the price point also comes with - I don't want to say risk levels, but different levels of service, with security being only one part of it - then everyone makes their own decision."
According to him, this does not mean every flight on a foreign carrier is dangerous. "I do not question the decision of any citizen to fly with a foreign company," he says. "I am only pointing out that the security aspect in Israeli companies is handled differently."
'They take a certain responsibility upon themselves'
The differences highlighted by the Pilots Association chairman take on particular significance regarding destinations where Israeli airlines do not operate due to security considerations.
"There are even more extreme situations where, for example - I want to mention Dubai and Abu Dhabi - Israeli companies are prevented from flying there due to security reasons, but Israelis choose to fly there with other carriers," he says.
When asked whether this means an Israeli passenger who chooses such an airline takes on a certain risk, he replies: "I won't say risk, but they take a certain responsibility upon themselves." According to him, "Anyone who takes responsibility upon themselves, whether for themselves alone or for themselves and their family, knows what stands behind that responsibility."
However, he stresses that the current incident does not allow conclusions to be drawn at this stage regarding the safety level of Flydubai or foreign carriers in general. "What happened there in the cockpit? Right now we don't know for certain. We will wait for further details."
"If there was some kind of fight there, the situation is much more problematic for the airline," he says. According to him, if it turns out that this is indeed what happened, the investigation will need to examine, among other things, the pilots' background, their hiring process, and the checks they underwent before they began flying passengers.
'We never know what we prevent'
According to him, airlines perform screening and psychological evaluations for pilots, as well as training and refresher courses on CRM topics, which deal among other things with flight crew relations and teamwork. "All companies, based on unfortunate events that happened in the past, conduct strict screening and psychological evaluations for their pilots," he says. "We never know what we prevent; that's how it is in safety."
He emphasizes that precisely because such events are extremely rare, one should not infer from them that every passenger flying on a foreign carrier is in danger. However, according to him, any unusual incident requires an in-depth investigation to check if there were early signs or failures in the recruitment and training process. "Who are these people? What is their background? Where did they come from? And after the airline understands where they came from, they will now ask who hired them and what checks they underwent before entering the job," he says. "It's a deep investigation."
Ultimately, he asks to wait for the investigation's findings before drawing conclusions about the incident or the airline. "I am glad the systems are working properly and are vigilant, whether for a minor case or a severe one, and that the plane landed safely and the passengers are safe."

Inflation accelerates again in Italy: September rate hits 4.2%, a three-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:10:25 UTC
21:10:25 KST

Consumer price index accelerates driven by energy goods and fresh food. Between historical memory and daily worries, Istat records a sharp drop in confidence among households and firms.
Inflation continues to climb on the back of rising energy prices due to the disruption cause by the Iran war. In Italy, just like in Spain, price increases are now at the highs of the recent years.
According to preliminary estimates released by Istat, in September the national consumer price index for the whole community (NIC) jumped by +0.7% month-on-month, with a year-on-year acceleration that pushes the annual rate to +4.2% (from +3.3% in August).
To find a higher level of inflation we have to go back three years, to September 2023, when the annual change reached 5.3%.
The "invisible monster": a psychological and social tax
Economists often describe inflation as the "most unjust tax", because it hits everyone and silently drains purchasing power. For Italy’s collective memory, the return of inflationary pressure recalls ghosts from the past that were never entirely laid to rest.
Those who lived through the 1970s and 1980s remember all too well what it meant to live with double-digit inflation, which even exceeded 20% at the height of the oil crises of 1974 and 1980, amid the race between wages and prices and the loss of value of a lifetime’s savings stashed away in post office passbooks.
Although today’s figures are still, fortunately, far from those dramatic peaks, the psychological impact on citizens follows the same pattern.
Every percentage increase, however limited it may look on paper, translates in human terms into forced choices: giving up a Saturday night meal out, postponing a small purchase for the home, or watching the display at the petrol pump with a touch of anxiety as the counter ticks up too fast.
The loss of peace of mind about the future is the highest price that inflation demands of households.
The energy surge and its impact on food prices
Returning to Istat’s survey, this latest spike in prices is driven almost entirely by the energy sector, which is experiencing a sharp flare-up: the overall increase in the cost of energy goods rises from +17.1% to +22.3%.
The acceleration affects both components of the sector as regulated energy jumped from +18.6% to +25.9% with a clear month-on-month increase of +5.9% in September alone), and unregulated energy: rises from +17.0% to +22.2% (+4.4% on a monthly basis).
Alongside energy, Italian households are also feeling the squeeze from unprocessed food products (such as fresh fruit and vegetables), whose annual growth rate quickens from +3.8% to +5.5% (+2.2% compared with August).
Recreational and cultural services (+2.9%) and transport-related services (+1.6%) are also rising at a faster pace, although the latter record a seasonal monthly decline (-2.5%).
Core inflation holds up and the goods-services gap widens
There is partial reassurance from so-called "core inflation", calculated net of energy goods and fresh food: the index shows a modest increase from 1.5% to 1.7%, while the measure excluding only energy goods rises from 1.7% to 2.0%.
This confirms that the current inflationary tensions are, for now, mainly concentrated on energy commodities and fresh fruit and vegetables.
By contrast, the gap between the movement in goods prices and services prices is widening significantly with goods accelerating from +4.1% to +5.4%, services grow more moderately, moving from +2.4% to +2.6%.
The gap between the two sectors also widened to -2.8% from -1.7 in August).
Looking at the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), the monthly change stands at +2.0% (an effect linked to prices returning to normal after the end-of-season summer sales), taking the annual figure to +4.1%.
Prices fall at the pump but price lists remain a sticking point
On the mobility front, the Ministry for Business and Made in Italy (Mimit) notes that data from the Fuel Observatory show a slight easing in pump prices.
Road network (self-service) is averaging €2.111/l for petrol and €2.316/l for diesel, while motorway network (self-service) has an average of €2.138/l for petrol and €2.345/l for diesel.
However, Mimit points out a "significant gap" between the various retailers around the country: the introduction of a price cap by major operators such as Eni, IP and Q8 means that their stations are offering significantly lower prices, at €1.99/l for petrol and €2.19/l for diesel.
Confidence collapses
The hard economic data are immediately reflected in the public mood, with Istat recording a simultaneous and widespread decline in the climate of confidence: the consumer confidence index drops from 94.5 to 91.2 points, while the composite indicator for businesses falls from 97.0 to 95.9.
When the perception of inflation puts the brakes on consumption, a chain reaction is almost inevitable, leading families to postpone non-essential spending and companies to freeze new hires and investment.
The fear of bills and the rising cost of living is thus turning into a collective caution that points to an uncertain autumn, reminding us that the economy depends above all on the confidence people are able to place in tomorrow.

Tanker crew death toll revealed after Somali pirate overthrow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:08:39 UTC
21:08:39 KST

Tanker crew death toll revealed after Somali pirate overthrow
Somali pirates killed five crew members of an oil tanker they held captive for more than five months before security forces retook the vessel, authorities in Somalia’s semi-autonomous Puntland region have said.
The Palau-flagged MT Honour 25 was seized on April 21 with 17 crew members on board. Puntland authorities said 16 suspected pirates were detained during the operation to regain control of the vessel, while others escaped.
“Puntland Maritime Police Force (PMPF) has concluded an operation to secure the MT Honour 25. The vessel is now safe and under Puntland Government control,” the force said on X on Tuesday.
According to the PMPF, three of the five victims were Pakistani nationals, one was from Myanmar and another from India. Four other sailors – three Pakistanis and one Indian – were wounded. The tanker was carrying around 18,500 barrels of fuel when it was seized.
From 2008 to 2018, Somali pirates disrupted critical world waterways, causing widespread chaos. The new incident comes amid a resurgence in piracy off the coast of Somalia following years of relatively low activity. At least 15 attacks have been recorded in the region this year, according to an analysis of International Maritime Organization data, with Somali pirates successfully hijacking at least six commercial vessels since April.
Puntland forces regained control of the Eritrean-flagged oil tanker Sibu 1 earlier this month after it had been held by pirates for more than a month.
In August, Somali forces working with the Turkish Navy also retook the Cameroon-flagged cargo ship MV Lutuf after it was hijacked off Puntland. Somalia’s Defense Ministry said 14 suspected pirates were killed and four of their boats destroyed during the ten-day operation.
In an analysis published last week, the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) linked the resurgence in piracy to turmoil in the Middle East, saying naval assets have been diverted from the Somali coast toward the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. It also cited higher global oil prices as a factor that may have made hijackings more attractive. The spike has come during a year of major disruption to energy shipments from the Persian Gulf.
Countries in the region have stepped up maritime security cooperation amid the renewed activity. Russia and the Seychelles, an Indian Ocean island nation roughly 1,300 km southeast of Somalia, are planning joint anti-piracy exercises in November during a Russian Navy port call, Seychelles’ defense chief said on Saturday.

Patient confidentiality in Estonia – a bone of contention between the minister and medical professionals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:08:17 UTC
21:08:17 KST

In the letter, the doctors emphasize that trust forms the foundation of the doctor-patient relationship and that maintaining patient confidentiality is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. Patients must be absolutely certain that the information they provide to a doctor will not end up in other hands.
Neeme Tõnisson, President of the Estonian Medical Association, stated that the current situation—where the police and other state institutions can access patient information—is unacceptable and undermines trust in the entire healthcare system. Patient confidentiality must remain intact even after the information has been entered into the database.
The health information system and its administrator, TEHIK, operate under the authority of the Minister of Social Affairs, who is responsible for data security. The Medical Association has called on Joller to block access to patient information via other government systems unless the patient has given their consent. However, in cases where access is required under the exceptional circumstances defined by law, it must be authorized by a court order.
Joller noted on social media that the Medical Association is pushing at an open door
- the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs is already preparing legislative amendments to be submitted to the government soon, a fact the Association is well aware of. The Minister emphasized that TEHIK has done nothing wrong and is acting in accordance with existing laws. Meanwhile, the police and the Border Guard—whose personnel have at times requested health system data without sufficient legal grounds—have reportedly already put an end to this practice.

Russia raises nuclear threat as Baltic tensions grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:07:50 UTC
21:07:50 KST

- Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russian policy documents provide for a nuclear response if NATO countries blockade Kaliningrad.
- Peskov said Russian diplomats were reminding "hotheads in Europe" of those documents after statements from Poland and other European countries.
The Kremlin said on Sept. 30 that Russia’s official policy documents provide for a nuclear response if NATO countries try to blockade Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea wedged between Poland and Lithuania.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russian diplomats were reminding “hotheads in Europe” of those documents after what he described as outrageous statements about Kaliningrad from Poland and other European countries. He did not say which statements he meant or which document he was referring to.
His remarks followed several days of similar messages from Russian diplomats. Over the preceding three days, Russia’s embassies in Belgium, the United Kingdom and Ireland warned that Moscow was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if NATO blockaded the exclave.
Kaliningrad, the former German city of Königsberg, has no land connection to the rest of Russia. Its roughly 1 million residents depend on sea links across the Baltic and on road and rail transit through Lithuania and Belarus, which leaves the region exposed to any interruption of those routes. The exclave is also home to the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet.
In June 2022, Lithuania stopped some goods covered by European Union sanctions from crossing its territory by rail to Kaliningrad. Moscow called the move a blockade and threatened retaliation, while Vilnius said it was only enforcing EU sanctions and that non-sanctioned cargo was still moving. The dispute eased after the EU clarified transit rules the following month.
Russia has also based nuclear-capable weapons in the region. Moscow said in 2018 that it had permanently deployed Iskander short-range ballistic missiles to Kaliningrad, a system that can carry conventional or nuclear warheads and reach targets across Poland and the Baltic states. Lithuanian officials have long said Russia kept nuclear weapons in the exclave well before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Peskov’s reference to policy documents points to Russia’s nuclear doctrine, which President Vladimir Putin updated in November 2024. The revised version allows a nuclear response to a conventional attack that creates a critical threat to the sovereignty or territorial integrity of Russia or Belarus. The published text does not mention Kaliningrad or a blockade by name.
Peskov did not describe any specific NATO plan to isolate Kaliningrad, and no NATO member government has announced one.

Taiwan farmers turn fields into safer habitats for endangered turtles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:07:00 UTC
21:07:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Wildlife-friendly farming practices are helping protect two endangered native turtle species in central Taiwan.
The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Nantou Branch on Wednesday recognized 50 farmers for adopting such practices and helping preserve turtle habitats. The agency’s ecological conservation program encourages farmers to avoid herbicides, rat poison, and other wildlife-unfriendly control methods.
Farmers are also encouraged to retain vegetation and fallen leaves in their fields during winter and take steps to prevent turtles from drowning. These measures help the endangered yellow-margined box turtle and yellow pond turtle — both native to Taiwan — by providing places to forage and shelter in habitats that often overlap with areas where people live and farm.
Ten communities in Nantou and Yunlin counties were also recognized for their efforts to protect habitats for the two species. Their work includes removing traps used to capture wild animals and improving local habitat conditions, helping create safer places for the turtles to live and forage.
The yellow-margined box turtle, Taiwan’s only fully terrestrial native turtle species, lives at elevations below 1,000 meters, mainly in forests, foothills, and plains. Because its habitat overlaps with areas of human activity, the species faces particular challenges from habitat loss and illegal capture, according to the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency and the Academia Sinica.
Population surveys conducted in Yilan and Hualien in 2014-2015 and 2018-2019 found that the species’ range and population had declined rapidly or disappeared entirely in some areas over the previous 15 years. Only scattered individuals were found in some locations, while many remaining populations were too small and had such low densities that natural reproduction was unlikely to sustain them over the long term.
The yellow pond turtle was first recorded in Taiwan in 1908 and is found mainly in aquatic habitats in northern, central, and eastern mountainous areas. The loss and degradation of aquatic environments and terrestrial areas, along with illegal hunting, have caused wild populations to decline rapidly, according to the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The KMT legislative caucus announced Tuesday that it would seek to amend the Referendum Act to allow referendums to overturn Constitutional Court rulings.
The KMT caucus announced 40 legislative priorities for the current session, including establishing rules governing the use of surplus tax revenue for cash handouts, increasing maximum fines for major food safety violations, and amending the Referendum Act, per Liberty Times.
The amendment, proposed by KMT Legislator Weng Hsiao-ling (翁曉玲), would allow referendums to overturn Constitutional Court decisions, except rulings involving presidential impeachment, per Newtalk. It would also bar the Central Election Commission from reviewing referendum proposals initiated by the Legislature.
The KMT caucus argued that if the public finds a Constitutional Court ruling unacceptable or believes it violates the law, a referendum could serve as a means of challenging the decision, per Liberty Times. It said Constitutional Court rulings have less legal status than constitutional amendments and can be subject to changes in subsequent rulings.
The caucus argued that because constitutional amendments require approval through referendums to take effect, Constitutional Court rulings should not be excluded from potentially being put to a public vote.
DPP Legislator Chen Pei-yu (陳培瑜) said Weng's amendment would limit the executive and judicial branches while expanding the power of the Legislature, per CNA. Chen cited Soochow University Law School Professor Chang Chia-yin (張嘉尹), who said allowing referendums to overturn Constitutional Court rulings would expand the powers of both referendums and the Legislature beyond the scope permitted by the Constitution while diminishing the core authority of the judiciary.
Asked about the legality of the proposed amendment, Lawyer Fang Yen-hui (房彥輝) said it could violate the separation of powers and the principle of checks and balances, per Business Today. Meanwhile, the Constitutional Court's ability to operate remains a point of political and legal dispute.

That view has been echoed by three of the eight Constitutional Court justices who declined to participate in the court's proceedings following a controversial ruling that restored the court's operation. They argued that the court could not function because it had failed to meet the quorum required by law.
The three justices — Tsai Tzung-jen (蔡宗珍), Yang Hui-chin (楊惠欽), and Ju Fu-mei (朱富美) — previously argued that although the Constitution grants the court the authority to interpret laws, it must also follow procedural rules enacted by the legislature. They said ending the previous paralysis would require the nomination of new justices to meet the quorum.
Retired Tunghai University professor Lin Teng-yau (林騰鷂), meanwhile, cited rulings issued by the court since it resumed operations as evidence that it is not paralyzed, per Storm Media. Judge dismisses Trump administration suit against Georgia secretary of state Brad Raffensperger seeking voter records
A federal judge on Wednesday dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit against Georgia’s Republican secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, over his refusal to hand over unredacted, sensitive voter information to the Department of Justice.
The justice department had demanded that the state’s senior election official email a copy of Georgia’s statewide voter registration list, including each voter’s driver’s license number, social security number and date of birth, arguing that the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law, entitled it to this information.
The US district court judge, Victoria Marie Calvert, ruled that the federal law does not require states to disclose sensitive voter data to the federal government, and does not take precedence over Georgia’s state law protecting the privacy of information provided to the state by registered voters.
Raffensperger was the Georgia state official Donald Trump called on 2 January 2021, in the aftermath of the 2020 presidential election, asking him to “find 11,780 votes” for Joe Biden that could be tossed out as fraudulent, which would have allowed Trump to reverse his loss and win the state by one vote.
Trump incorrectly claims pipeline to move liquefied natural gas means 'gasoline prices in Alaska are going to tumble'
In keeping with his near-constant use of his office for thinly disguised campaign events, Donald Trump had Alaska’s Republican senator Dan Sullivan by his side in the Oval Office on Wednesday when he announced that South Korea plans to spend $54bn to build a liquefied natural gas pipeline in Alaska.
Sullivan is facing a strong challenge from Democrat Mary Peltola to retain his Senate seat in the November midterm elections.
Unfortunately for Sullivan, the president wrongly suggested that an issue that is infuriating voters in his home state, the high price of gasoline and diesel, would be solved by the pipeline, which will transport an entirely different kind of petroleum, natural gas, when it is completed in three years.
The Alaska LNG project includes an 807-mile (1,299km) pipeline to carry natural gas from the North Slope to a liquefaction facility on Alaska’s southern coast, allowing the fuel to be shipped to Asian markets.
Asked by a reporter about whether there has been any discussion of building another oil pipeline in Alaska, given the high cost of gasoline for consumers, Trump appeared to confuse the liquefied natural gas, known as LNG, with gasoline, which is made from oil.
“Well, this is going to bring those prices down. One of the reasons, Alaska prices are going to come way down,” Trump said of a project that has nothing to do with gasoline used to fuel cars.
After Trump was informed that the the LNG pipeline is going to take three years to complete, which would lower the cost of LNG in Alaska, but have no impact at all on the cost of another petroleum product, gasoline, Trump turned back to reporters and said: “Gasoline prices in Alaska are going to tumble.”
Trump also said that the Korean investment was part of a $200bn package of projects that would also include a 6-gigawatt power generation facility in Texas, another state where his party is in danger of losing a Senate seat.
The announced investment follows pledges South Korea made in 2025 to invest up to $350bn in the US as part of a trade deal in exchange for lower US tariffs on South Korean cars, auto parts and other products.
Without providing those details, Trump credited his tariffs for making the announcement possible, saying “our trade agreement with South Korea, they have to invest hundreds of billions of dollars.”
“For doing that, I reduced their tariffs to 15%. But they paid to get them reduced,” Trump said. “And, part of that money is going into this project.”
Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, marking the SpaceX CEO’s first return to government since he ran the chaotic, so-called “department of government efficiency”, or Doge. Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House.
A defense department press release on the effort, called Project Meridian, described its goal as “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations.
The defense department’s project brings Musk back into government work a little more than a year after his explosive tenure as leader of Doge, which gutted federal agencies while failing to achieve its stated cost-cutting goals. It is also a sign of how Musk has re-entered the good graces of the Trump administration after a dramatic falling out with the president last year.
Trump says Netanyahu told him FlyDubai pilot was 'perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job'
Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday that he had spoken to Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, about the security incident on a FlyDubai commercial flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel on Wednesday.
“It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job,” Trump said, before giving a dramatic account of the intervention of a passenger who subdued the pilot who reportedly stabbed his co-pilot.

Now this is the story that I heard. I don’t know if it’s true, but that’s the story I got from Bibi.”

Our media’s shameful lust for political retribution blinds them to the consequences of reckless, so-called ‘reporting’. So-called journalists – juiced up on Trump derangement syndrome – think they’re fighting against our president, but they’re really undermining you – our warfighters.”

DIU Identifies 23 Companies Involved in Pantsir SAM Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:06:15 UTC
21:06:15 KST

Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence has published information on 23 Russian companies involved in producing 95Ya6 anti-aircraft guided missiles for Pantsir air defense systems.
The agency reported this on the War&Sanctions portal.
The 95Ya6 missiles are the main medium-range munitions used by various versions of the Pantsir family. They are utilized to intercept aerial targets at ranges of up to 20 km.
The JSC Design Bureau of Instrument Making Named After Academician A. G. Shipunov (Shipunov Design Bureau) plays a key role in their production; it is the main developer and manufacturer of the 95Ya6 missiles and supplies them to the Ministry of Defense of the Russian Federation under a state defense order.
The production network also includes Tulamashzavod and Tulatochmash, which assemble the missile’s sustainer stage and equipment compartment and manufacture gyroscopes, engine components, and separation mechanisms.
The Perm Powder Plant and Kamensky Combine Plant supply the solid-fuel 17A6-1 motors, while the JSC V.V. Bakhirev State Research Institute of Mechanical Engineering manufactures the warheads.
Among the other companies involved in the production network, the DIU names the JSC Plant Komponent, which manufactures proximity target sensors and electronics; the PJSC Saratov Electrical Instrument Manufacturing Plant Named After Sergo Ordzhonikidze, which supplies radiation and power units; and the PJSC Tambov Plant Elektropribor, which manufactures steering drives for the 95Ya6.
The production network also includes the JSC Izhevsk Mechanical Plant, which supplies wing sections and warhead casings; the JSC Murom Instrument-Making Plant, which manufactures pyrotechnic components; and PJSC Energiya, which produces batteries.
About one-third of the companies identified by the DIU are still not subject to sanctions by any country in the sanctions coalition.
Ukrainian intelligence had already exposed the production network behind the 72V6 combat vehicle of the Pantsir-S1 system, involving more than 50 companies.
Militarnyi previously reported that Belarusian industry is also involved in producing new Pantsir systems. Since 2024, the Minsk Wheel Tractor Plant has been supplying Russia with armored MZKT-7930 chassis for integration of the 72V6 combat module.
In 2026, Russia also stepped up the deployment of the Pantsir-SMD-E variant, primarily adapted for countering drones. It lacks 30 mm automatic cannons and can use both standard 95Ya6 missiles and smaller TKB-1055 Gvozd missiles.
Russia also deployed such systems on rooftops in Moscow to strengthen the capital’s air defenses.
