‘Economic war’: Is Iran losing its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:05:45 UTC
21:05:45 KST

Is Iran losing its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz?
Crude flows through Hormuz have recovered, but tanker insurance costs and geopolitical risks remain barriers to a return to normality.
As Iran and the United States work with mediators to end seven months of hostilities, the reality in the Strait of Hormuz is shifting in ways that could prove to be a game-changer in ongoing negotiations.
According to the latest data from tanker-tracker websites, traffic through the key waterway has been steadily increasing, with some estimates putting oil and petroleum flow through the Strait of Hormuz at nearly 80 percent of what it was before the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iran shifts trade north to Caspian Sea as war impairs Strait of Hormuz
- list 2 of 3‘Iran ready for doomsday war’, FM Araghchi says
- list 3 of 3Why has Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal?
This could dent Iran’s leverage in reaching a favourable deal for itself in its attempts to end the fighting, which has seriously hampered its already heavily sanctioned economy, amid the US blockade of Iranian ships and ports.
Despite that, experts believe it would be a mistake to think normality in the Strait of Hormuz is imminent, or that Iran will fold easily despite growing economic hardship.
“The fact that oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz is encouraging, but flows are not yet regarded as completely secure or guaranteed, particularly while the wider conflict remains unresolved,” Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, told Al Jazeera.
Moreover, oil prices remain high globally, including in the US, where President Donald Trump faces a crucial midterm election that could see his party swept away in both houses of Congress.
Tanker insurance costs also remain elevated, and energy flows through Hormuz are still far from secure, suggesting Iran’s leverage may be weakening rather than disappearing.
Oil flows through Hormuz recovering
The latest data from commodity analytics firm Kpler points to a significant recovery in oil exports from the Middle East.
Crude exports reached an estimated 16.328 million barrels per day (bpd) in September – their highest level since the war began in late February, the firm reported this week.
Flows through the Strait of Hormuz itself were expected to reach about 9.719 million bpd during the month. Saudi Arabia has driven much of the increase, with its exports rebounding from 2.446 million bpd in August to about 5.4 million bpd in September.
Kpler said Middle East crude exports have recovered to just less than 80 percent of their pre-war level. But the figures remain about 3.2 million bpd below the 19.513 million bpd exported in February.
The data also does not include ships crossing Hormuz with their tracking systems switched off, meaning actual traffic could be higher.
Prior to the war, an estimated 120-140 vessels crossed through the waterway daily, roughly half of them oil tankers moving approximately 20 million barrels per day. At the height of the fighting, traffic through the waterway collapsed to as few as two tankers a day after Iran effectively closed the strait in retaliation for US-Israeli attacks.
Is Iran losing leverage?
The rebound in oil flow presents a challenge for Tehran. Iran has sought to use its ability to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz – one of the world’s most important energy chokepoints – as leverage against Washington’s military and economic pressure.
But if large volumes of oil can continue moving through the strait while Iran itself remains under a US naval blockade, Tehran’s bargaining power could diminish.
Iran, however, rejects any assessment that its control over the strait is slipping.
Hossein Mohebbi, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson, said on Wednesday that there is an ongoing “military conflict” in the Hormuz Strait.
“We have been hitting small ships and preventing them from passing for a long time, but America does not respond,” Mohebbi said in an interview with the semi-official Fars news agency.
Separately on Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre said unknown projectiles struck three ships in the waterway on Tuesday, including a crude oil tanker.
Oil prices are another indication that Iran has not lost all of its leverage.
Brent crude fell 2.6 percent to $102.59 a barrel on Tuesday as traders focused on recovering Middle East exports. But it was still heading for a roughly 13 percent gain in September.
Chris Beauchamp, an analyst at IG, said markets were beginning to incorporate evidence of recovering flows but remained wary about how durable that recovery would be.
“It takes time for evidence to filter through to markets,” Beauchamp said. “Oil prices came off yesterday as the narrative began to take hold, and should continue to fall.”
But he said concerns persisted over whether the US protection system could withstand a renewed barrage of Iranian missiles and drones.
Streeter of Wealth Club said the market still had a geopolitical risk premium built into crude prices, despite the improving flows.
“Insurance costs for tankers also remain elevated because of the perceived risks of operating in the region, adding to the cost of transporting crude even as more ships make it through the waterway,” she said.
Moreover, Streeter warned that crude figures tell only part of the story. Flows of refined fuels, particularly diesel and petrol, remain constrained, while damage to infrastructure has placed additional pressure on energy supply chains, she added.
There is another vulnerability, the investment strategist pointed out. Countries including the US have relied heavily on strategic oil reserves to cushion the impact of the disruption and help contain prices.
“With those stockpiles now significantly depleted, there is a thinner buffer if there is another disruption, which is helping to keep a floor under crude prices,” Streeter added.
‘Economic war’ on Iran
There is little doubt that economic pressure on Iran is intensifying, potentially increasing Tehran’s incentive to reach an agreement.
Official data from the Statistical Center of Iran earlier this month showed gross domestic product (GDP) contracting 10.1 percent year on year between March 21 and June 20, while the crucial oil and gas sector shrank 26.4 percent.
Iran has also been battling high inflation and a plunging currency as the US blockade constrains oil exports and foreign currency earnings.
Twelve-month average inflation reached 69.9 percent earlier in September, while the rial had fallen beyond 2.2 million to the US dollar in early September.
In August, the US announced a new economic pressure campaign against Iran, promising to target Tehran’s financial interests across the world.
Mohammad Eslami, a research fellow at the University of Tehran, told Al Jazeera that Iran was facing an “economic war” alongside the military conflict.
“There is a US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which affects Iran’s revenues from oil exports and other products such as petrochemicals, which are important to Iran’s economy,” Eslami said. “As a result, Iran’s dollar revenues have been affected by the blockade.”
But he cautioned against judging Iran’s economy solely through the value of its currency.
“The exchange rate is a very important indicator, but it is not the only measure for explaining what is happening or the difficulties and challenges facing Iran’s economy,” Eslami said, adding that Iran has faced US economic pressure for “five decades”.
Negar Mortazavi, political analyst, and the host of The Iran Podcast, echoed Eslami’s opinion that the economic blockade is imposing “enormous pressure on Iran”, but that does not mean it will fold, she told Al Jazeera.
“Tehran has shown that it is prepared to tolerate considerable economic pain rather than negotiate entirely on Washington’s terms.”
The war is hurting the US economy too
Iran is not alone in facing economic pressure. US diesel prices hit a record $6.53 a gallon ($1.73 per litre) this month, more than 70 percent higher than the price before the US waged its war on Iran. The Trump administration is discussing restrictions on diesel exports to ease prices before November’s midterm elections.
Higher energy costs have also fuelled inflation, experts say, contributing to the Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates by 25 basis points this month – its first increase in three years.
Additionally, the cost-of-living crisis in the country is also weighing on Trump politically. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll put his approval at a career-low 32 percent, with just 17 percent approving of his handling of living costs.
From time to time, Iran has seized on this pressure, often mocking Trump for prematurely declaring victory in the war despite the apparent economic downturn in the US.
Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf this month used a math equation to suggest that Tehran’s ability to disrupt energy supplies is influencing US monetary policy. Analysts say while the claim is exaggerated, it does highlight Iran’s own economic leverage over Washington.
Can a deal be reached?
Despite the military and economic pressure, negotiations have not collapsed.
At the United Nations General Assembly last week, Tehran and Washington engaged in three hours of indirect talks, as US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
President Trump later described the encounter as “very good” and “very productive”.
Iran also proposed a seven-day roadmap under which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened and normal maritime traffic restored if Washington meets Tehran’s conditions, a plan Trump categorically rejected.
Those conditions included ending the naval blockade on Iran, easing sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian funds.
However, on Wednesday, the Reuters news agency reported that Araghchi had received US feedback on the proposal through Qatari mediators.
An official briefed on the talks said the main disagreement now centred on the sequencing of measures rather than the components of the plan.
Mortazavi said Iran’s latest proposal shows Tehran is willing to be flexible because it wants to bring the war to an end.
The proposal builds on the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US but offers a much faster timeline, including an immediate end to the war, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz within a week and a rapid return to nuclear negotiations.
“Iran is offering compromise in order to stop the war, not capitulation under pressure,” Mortazavi said.
But that flexibility is tied to reciprocal concessions from Washington, she added. “There has to be something in return from the US.”
Mortazavi said there was a “danger” if Trump misreads Iran’s willingness to compromise as weakness. “That could instead prolong the war,” she warned.

OpenAI follows Meta into the red-hot market for personal agents. But will users pay?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:04:46 UTC
21:04:46 KST

Following Meta's blockbuster release of its Muse AI agent earlier this month, OpenAI jumped into the personal agent market on Tuesday with Dots, setting the stage for what could be the next big battle in the artificial intelligence market.
At its annual DevDay developer conference, OpenAI described Dots as "always-on" agents designed to help users complete a range of tasks. Since the release of Muse three weeks ago, investors have rallied around Meta, sending the stock up 29% in September, on pace for its best month since 2013.
That level of enthusiasm underscores the power of personal agents and the promise that consumers and office workers will be able to use the technology to book travel, pay bills, respond to emails and perform many more tasks. But OpenAI's entry, arriving soon after the launch of Muse, serves as a reminder that the AI market includes a handful of large companies all converging around the same types of products with little ability to lock in users.
Google calls its Gemini Spark offering "your 24/7 personal AI agent" for help, and Apple is trying to step up its position in the AI battle with its redesigned Siri AI, which it describes as "a profoundly more capable and personal assistant."
"I think what we are watching is an inevitable evolution of the technology," said John Waldmann, CEO of HR tech startup Homebase and a user of various AI agent-related tools. "It's probably no surprise that it's all happening around the same time."
It's not just the big companies that see the opportunity.
AI assistant startup Instinct announced Monday that it raised $1 billion from venture firms including Sequoia at a $10 billion valuation. And another startup, Town, is reportedly looking at a $1 billion valuation.
Town CEO Jean-Denis Grèze told CNBC in a statement that OpenAI's debut of Dots, "continues to validate the category and the need for work assistants."
"It's been our focus at Town from the very beginning," Grèze said, adding that he welcomes the competition.
On Tuesday, all eyes were on OpenAI, as investors and AI enthusiasts anticipated what the ChatGPT creator would unveil in the wake of last week's Meta Connect developer conference. There, Meta announced forthcoming AI devices, including a pendant, and CEO Mark Zuckerberg called Muse the "centerpiece" of the company's AI strategy.
Taking the stage in San Francisco for DevDay, Altman called Dots "remarkably capable" and "built to handle really anything you can think of." Although developers could already use OpenAI's existing tools to manage scores of AI agents for various office tasks, Dots promises to be an easier way for workers to use powerful digital assistants to help with tools like Slack and Microsoft Teams.
More uplifting than AI safety
The rush of new agents hitting the market offers a more uplifting story for AI companies at a time when the leading labs are facing intensifying scrutiny due to emerging concerns that the most advanced models are at risk of spinning out of human control.
On Tuesday, as Altman was attending DevDay, his second-in-command, Greg Brockman, was in Washington for a lunch that President Donald Trump was hosting for top technology leaders. The topic was AI safety, and the event came more than two weeks after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei sent shock waves across the industry, writing an essay urging AI companies to slow the pace of frontier model development.
Nick Deveau, CEO of AI sales startup GrottoAI, is a fan of AI agent tools like Instinct and sees the vision as companies start building them for a wider audience.
"The interesting thing about all of these, which I think has become apparent really quickly and is evidenced by some of the valuations, is that people see this as the first successful proof point of true agentic work hitting consumers," Deveau said.
There's still the question of whether consumers will pay. Meta's Muse is free with a usage limit and can be purchased starting at $20 a month after that. OpenAI's Dots is only available starting at the $100 per month Pro plan and higher.
And even with Muse racking up millions of downloads across app stores, that doesn't mean people are actively using it or other AI agents, Waldmann said.
"People will try it, but is it really adding value?" Waldmann said. "Is it part of a daily habit?"
Thomas Randall, a research director at the Info-Tech Research Group, said in an email that "the race is on," as AI companies search to figure out how consumers want to use agents and what will keep them coming back.
"Once leading systems are broadly capable, the winner will likely be determined by which agent is the easiest to adopt, the most connected, and the hardest to leave," Randall said. "We'll see who's distribution will gather steam first."

Germany is buying every missile it can get. What is Berlin preparing for?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:04:33 UTC
21:04:33 KST

Germany is buying every missile it can get. What is Berlin preparing for?
Over the past few months, there’s been a noticeable surge in reports regarding Germany’s interest in missiles – ranging from ballistic and cruise missiles to land- and sea-based systems. Various partners are involved in the initiative, including the US, Ukraine, Türkiye, and Israel. It looks like Germany intends to spend its entire budget on missiles, aiming to become the leading missile power in Western Europe.
Berlin’s financial commitment to advancing military programs has reached unprecedented levels. The country is significantly ramping up defense spending. Between 2024 and 2025, approximately 200 new defense industry companies emerged in Germany, and another 100 have appeared since November 2025. A notable example is Rheinmetall, which has dramatically increased its artillery ammunition production from about 70,000 units to 1.5 million shells per year. Over the next six years, the company plans to invest around €30 billion ($34 billion) into arms and munitions manufacturing. Moreover, Germany is actively seeking to procure ready-made missile systems and is interested in establishing joint production facilities.
Aligned with these initiatives, Germany is establishing new ground forces capable of striking military targets deep within potential enemy territory, essentially creating missile troops within the Bundeswehr. On the one hand, this expansion enhances NATO’s strike capabilities and allows for flexible responses to any external threats over distances of thousands of kilometers. On the other hand, such offensive capabilities could easily inspire ideas of military dominance and hegemony. Historically, we’ve already seen this in Germany.
At the forefront of this new German strategy will be American Typhon MRC (Mid-Range Capability) missile systems, equipped with Tomahawk cruise missiles with a range of up to 1,600 km. The Bundeswehr plans to allocate nearly €3.4 billion for the procurement of these missiles. They will provide the German military with a strategic edge, enabling strikes against command centers, airbases, missile units, logistical hubs, and other critical targets far beyond the potential front lines.
Germany’s main argument in favor of this military buildup is, of course, the need to deter the “threat from the East” – a classic case of history repeating itself. The fact that Russia has no intention of attacking NATO doesn’t seem to matter; it serves as a convenient excuse and a rallying cry to ramp up militarism. Technically, from German territory, Tomahawk missiles can only reach parts of European Russia, but Berlin’s ambitions extend well beyond this missile system.
Germany’s interest in missiles has grown to such an extent that the Bundeswehr is exploring even some rather unconventional projects, such as Ukraine’s Flamingo and Bars cruise missiles, as well as the Anthem missile project. In fact, the Ukrainian Flamingo missile was considered a potential alternative to the US Tomahawk. With a range of 3,000 km, the Flamingo surpasses the Tomahawk in terms of range. Additionally, it boasts an impressive warhead weighing 1,150 kg – a record in its class. The only real question is whether the 10-meter-long missile can successfully hit targets. So far, experience has shown that most of the Flamingos launched by Ukrainian forces are intercepted by air defense systems.
Germany is also ready to produce Bars missiles on its soil, but primarily for export purposes. It remains unclear whether this initiative leans more toward a business venture or a strategic investment in domestic armaments. Bars missiles might not be of much interest to German military officials since they essentially function as a cheap and simple alternative to more costly missiles.
Another notable project is the Anthem long-range cruise missile developed by the US-Israeli startup Covenant. Recently, Reuters reported that Germany is interested in a missile with a range exceeding 1,500 km and a warhead weighing over 200 kg. What’s more, Covenant is willing to establish production of Anthem missiles in Germany. This likely piqued the interest of Bundeswehr officials, especially considering the impressive promised production output of 1,000 units per year. So many missiles can be produced by relying on a simplified design and fairly modest performance specifications. Naturally, there’s no talk of stealth technology here; it’s essentially an alternative to inexpensive long-range kamikaze drones. If this contract goes through, Germany would acquire its own surface-to-surface missile system.
But that’s not all. The Bundeswehr is considering other missile projects as well. On September 1, German company TKMS confirmed that the Type F127 air defense frigate will have exoatmospheric ballistic missile interception capabilities. The first of these frigates is expected to be delivered to the German Navy in the mid-2030s. It will be equipped with SM-2 Block IIIC and SM-6 Block I interceptors. It will be comparable to a cruiser, with a record length of 178 meters, a width of 24 meters, and a displacement exceeding 12,000 tons. Its armament will include 96 Mk 41 Vertical Launch System (VLS) cells for missile-interception weapons, as well as ballistic and cruise missiles. The construction of at least five such ships is planned. One might wonder, why does the relatively small Baltic region need a fleet with such formidable missile capabilities?
At the beginning of September, the German Navy conducted its first test launches of Israeli LORA (Long Range Attack) ballistic missiles from an F125-class frigate. These launches were primarily demonstrative, with missile containers temporarily mounted on the stern of the Sachsen-Anhalt frigate. Two missiles were fired during the tests. The sight of Israeli ballistic missiles similar to American ATACMS aboard a German frigate is quite unusual. This notable experiment illustrates that the Bundeswehr is open to exploring alternatives to US weapons systems. Furthermore, Israeli missiles are modern and highly accurate, boasting ranges from 90 to 430 km and a circular error probable (CEP) of under 10 meters. It’s also quite possible that such missiles could soon be integrated into the Bundeswehr’s land forces.
Simultaneously, Germany is preparing to begin production of ATACMS ballistic missiles in collaboration with US company Lockheed Martin. Rheinmetall expects to receive its first order by late 2026 or early 2027, with a memorandum already signed to establish production at its facility in Unterluess, Germany. This will mark the first production of ATACMS missiles outside the US. Production is anticipated to start between 2028 and 2029. European demand is estimated at 600-800 units.
Additionally, Berlin is showing interest in Türkiye’s missile programs. Reports indicate that Germany is interested in Turkish hypersonic projects and specifically the Yildirimhan long-range ballistic missile with a range of up to 6,000 km. For Türkiye, having Germany as a customer is a compelling prospect, and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Turkish companies would be eager to secure such an order.
But why is Germany showing such interest in missiles? And behind the facade of nuclear cooperation with the UK, does a part of the Berlin establishment harbor nuclear ambitions? Ideas to replace the American nuclear umbrella amid a perceived “threat from the East” are still popular; and defense companies and war hawks certainly welcome these initiatives. But what will happen if the funding runs dry? Or worse – if this ‘Chekhov’s gun’ goes off in the ‘next act’?

Russia Preparing ‘Happy, Well-Fed’ Propaganda Videos as Oleshky Civilians Face Humanitarian Crisis, Kyiv Says

Russia is preparing to stage dozens of videos featuring residents of occupied Oleshky in the Kherson region, forcing them to claim they are “well-fed and happy,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
“According to our intelligence, Russia is preparing to stage dozens of videos in occupied Oleshky, forcing local residents to say on camera that they are happy, well-fed, and grateful to the Russian occupiers,” Sybiha wrote on X, calling it another example of what he described as Russian cynicism.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Oleshky, on the left bank of the Dnipro River in southern Ukraine’s Kherson region, has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
According to earlier reports, around 2,000 residents, including nearly 50 children, are facing dire conditions in the town, with limited access to food, drinking water and electricity, while Russian forces block attempts to leave.
“First, they occupy a town, cut off civilians’ escape routes, and block humanitarian aid. Then they force local residents to act in staged propaganda videos,” Sybiha wrote.
He called the alleged recordings part of a “disgusting Russian propaganda campaign” aimed at denying the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky.
Sybiha urged the international community and humanitarian organizations to increase pressure on Moscow and demand immediate access to the town. He said Ukrainian forces were also working to save civilians, including by delivering humanitarian aid with heavy-lift drones.
Medical Center in Central Kyiv on Fire After Russian Jet-Powered Drone Attack
“Every day counts in saving people who are starving and dying there. We urge our international partners to act now and demand immediate humanitarian access to end this disaster,” he said.
Ukrainian forces have already used drones to deliver about 4,000 kilograms of food to Oleshky, according to Kherson Regional Military Administration (OVA) head Oleksandr Prokudin.
Prokudin said the deliveries have been carried out since March in cooperation with units of the Ukrainian National Guard, Marines and Border Guard Service.
“We recently managed to carry out one of the largest operations of this kind,” Prokudin said, describing a coordinated delivery of around 4,000 kilograms of food to 100 designated locations across the city.
Addditionally, Russian forces have attempted to intercept the supply drones and, according to Ukrainian officials, have stolen or resold food intended for children and elderly residents.
Ukrainian authorities also accuse Russian forces of detaining and abusing civilians who accept humanitarian aid, including holding them in basements and subjecting them to physical violence.
In mid-September, Russian authorities failed to honor previously agreed arrangements for a humanitarian mission to evacuate civilians from occupied Oleshky.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) was prepared to participate within its mandate, while Ukrainian security and defense forces had made arrangements for a ceasefire during the proposed operation.
“These people must be saved,” Ukrainian Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said on Sept. 16, warning that “the city has been turned into a death trap.”
Lubinets said his office had received 176 appeals about the humanitarian situation and verified at least 358 people who urgently need to leave.
He estimated that more than 6,000 people, including around 200 children, could remain in Oleshky and the surrounding district. The figures could not be independently verified because Russian occupation authorities severely restrict access to information.
Some residents have reportedly attempted to flee independently through mined areas, despite the risk of artillery shelling and near-daily drone attacks.
The town has also been cut off from basic supplies. Residents have reportedly gone months without food or medicine deliveries, while some have resorted to bartering.
Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, said on July 10 that no vehicles had entered or left the town since May 26.
The hospital’s only pharmacy reportedly ran out of essential medicines months ago. Power cuts and fuel shortages have further disrupted medical care.
Hasanenko also said the hospital morgue was destroyed by shelling, forcing bodies to be stored in a basement, while Russian occupation authorities allegedly prevent the burial of some drone-strike victims pending forensic examinations elsewhere.
Residents also cannot access their bank accounts because cash withdrawals require leaving the town.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said international humanitarian law requires occupying powers to ensure access to food and medical supplies and facilitate humanitarian relief when local resources are insufficient.
According to the same report, at least 29 civilians were killed and 54 wounded in Oleshky and nearby occupied Hola Prystan in 2026, with many casualties independently verified by the UN Human Rights Office.

New Lebanon-Israel talks set for 20 Oct as Golani Brigade leaves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:02:16 UTC
21:02:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon-Israel talks to resume in Florida on 20 October: sources
Lebanon and Israel are expected to hold a new round of negotiations in Tampa, Florida, later this month, according to information obtained by The New Arab, as Beirut seeks US intervention to halt Israeli attacks and secure further withdrawals from southern Lebanon.
Lebanese presidential sources told The New Arab that Beirut had been informed of the planned talks, which are expected to take place before Israel's general elections on 27 October, potentially on 20 October. However, a final date has yet to be officially confirmed.
The negotiations, which will be exclusively military in nature, are expected to focus on the situation on the ground, security arrangements and the first pilot zone, which includes the southern towns of Froun, Srifa and Zawtar al-Sharqiya.
The development comes as the Israeli military announced on Wednesday that its Golani Brigade had ended a seven-month deployment in southern Lebanon, although Israeli attacks and the occupation of Lebanese territory continue.
The last round of negotiations between Lebanon and Israel took place in Rome on 6 August. An eighth round, initially expected to take place in the Italian capital in September at a technical and political level, was postponed until October, according to the US State Department.
Tampa was subsequently selected as the venue because the upcoming round will focus on military matters and developments on the ground, according to TNA's sources.
The direct talks, which began in April, have faced repeated obstacles, with little progress on the implementation of a trilateral framework agreement amid continued Israeli attacks and its refusal to meet Lebanese demands.
The US-sponsored framework, signed between Lebanon and Israel on 26 June, calls for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from designated pilot zones, followed by the redeployment of the Lebanese army in those areas. Under the agreement, the Lebanese military is responsible for ensuring that the zones are cleared of Hezbollah weapons and infrastructure.
The first three pilot zones were announced in July, but no further areas have been designated.
Lebanon presses US to secure Israeli withdrawal
Lebanese government sources told The New Arab that Prime Minister Nawaf Salam had urged Washington to pressure Israel into complying with the framework agreement and returning to the negotiating table during his recent US visit, particularly in his meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Salam received assurances that the US would take steps in that direction, the sources said.
The upcoming negotiations in Tampa represent an important opportunity to break the diplomatic deadlock and address military developments and security arrangements, they added.
Lebanon intends to reiterate its demands for a complete halt to Israeli military operations in the south so that the Lebanese army can fulfil its responsibilities in bringing weapons under state control, alongside an Israeli withdrawal from a second pilot zone.
Salam also stressed during his meetings in Washington that the framework agreement must be implemented on the principles of reciprocity and a phased approach.
He called for a clear timetable linking Israeli withdrawals to the Lebanese army's efforts to establish exclusive state control over weapons, with both processes advancing simultaneously.
Lebanon should not be the only party complying with the agreement while Israel continues to violate it daily, the sources said, adding that Beirut was relying on US leadership to ensure that both sides fulfilled their commitments.
The sources described Salam's meetings in the US as positive, saying he had received messages praising the Lebanese government's decisions, particularly its commitment to bringing weapons under state control and engaging in direct negotiations with Israel.
However, some US officials also stressed the need for more serious and faster action.
US officials reportedly told Salam in New York this week that Israel would continue to occupy parts of southern Lebanon and expand its operations if the Lebanese government failed to bring Hezbollah's weapons under state control.
Washington nevertheless reaffirmed its support for Lebanon and maintained that the framework agreement remained the only viable path towards security and peace, according to the government sources.
Despite these assurances, no progress has been made on the ground. Israel continues to reject demands to halt its attacks, while efforts to resolve the future of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) and establish an alternative coordination mechanism remain stalled by unresolved complications.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun and Salam have repeatedly maintained that diplomacy is the only viable means of ending the conflict and have urged Washington to exert greater pressure on Israel.
Israel currently occupies large parts of southern Lebanon and has expanded its so-called security zone in recent months, with dozens of towns and villages razed or heavily damaged.
Israel has maintained that it will not withdraw until Hezbollah is fully disarmed, while the Iran-backed group has rejected disarmament as long as Israeli forces remain on Lebanese territory.
Israeli forces continued their attacks across southern Lebanon on Thursday, despite the prospect of renewed negotiations.
Israeli warplanes carried out strikes on the town of Bani Hayyan in the Marjayoun district, while artillery bombardment targeted Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Mays al-Jabal, Haris, Khiam, Beit Lif and Wadi al-Slouqi.
Israeli forces also carried out a demolition in Khiam, while Israeli military vehicles were seen moving towards the town of Mansouri.
Israeli aircraft subsequently bombed Mansouri, while Israeli forces set fire to several homes on the outskirts of Baraachit, towards the neighbouring town of Kounine.
Golani Brigade ends seven-month deployment
Separately, the Israeli military announced on Wednesday that forces from one of its elite infantry brigades had withdrawn from southern Lebanon after seven months of operations.
Israeli army spokesperson Ella Waweya posted footage on X showing troops from the Golani Brigade's combat team leaving the area.
She said the forces, operating under the army's 36th Division, had been deployed in the so-called security zone in southern Lebanon to eliminate what she described as threats to northern Israel.
In recent months, the troops operated in the Shqif Heights area around Beaufort Castle and had recently completed a "focused military operation" to destroy infrastructure near the Litani River, Waweya said.
She added that Israeli forces had destroyed more than 900 structures allegedly used by Hezbollah and discovered weapons depots containing RPG rounds, explosive devices, booby-trapped drones and Kalashnikov rifles.
Earlier this month, Israeli forces demolished an underground Hezbollah complex beneath the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge, raising fears that Israel could advance towards the nearby city of Nabatieh as it seeks to control other strategic heights in the south.
Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed close to 9,000 people since October 2023, while more than 30,000 others have been wounded, with many civilians among the casualties.

MITS Capital, Freedom Fund, Norwegian VC Gardar and an unnamed new investor have invested in Ukrainian defense tech M-Fly. This is the second round of funding the startup has received from MITS Capital, the largest US-Ukraine defense-focused investment group.
The size of the round and the company’s valuation were not disclosed. M-Fly produces combat-tested laser guidance systems and high-precision gyro-stabilized gimbals for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to a press release sent to the media, the new funding will help the company accelerate its growth and meet battlefield needs amid rising demand in Ukraine and from NATO countries.
M-Fly develops the core components – from motors and camera lenses to cameras and software – in-house. This approach has allowed the company to price its systems almost on par with Chinese offerings while keeping the share of Chinese components below 6%, M-Fly said in the press release.
“Over the past 12 months, we have doubled our team and increased revenue severalfold,” Vladyslav Myhovych, M-Fly’s founder and CEO, said in the press release. He added that demand from Ukrainian customers and NATO allies has increased significantly since the beginning of 2026, Myhovych added.
                                                                                                                                                                         
EU Approves 5 Defense Projects Worth $369M, Ukraine Takes Part in 4 of Them
The main drivers are the growing use of interceptor drones in Ukraine and the resulting need for cheaper reconnaissance UAVs equipped with high-quality imaging systems. According to Myhovych, a gimbal can account for around one-third of a reconnaissance UAV’s cost, while some imported gimbals can cost several times more than the aircraft they are mounted on.
“Amid the global crisis called RAMageddon, we became almost hardware-agnostic, which protects our supply chain and unlocks scaling,” Myhovych said, referring to the worldwise shortage of memory chips. He expects the drone camera market to exceed $100 billion over the next five to seven years. “New funding will allow us to scale our production facilities and pace of product adaptation to hold a visible share of this market.”
This is the second time American-Ukrainian investment group MITS Capital, invests in M-Fly.
“What matters even more than performance is that the company has cracked the unit economics, allowing it to price its products significantly below those of its closest competitors,” the press release quoted Denys Gurak, co-founder and COO/CIO of MITS Capital. “That’s why we decided to support the next stage of its growth with additional funding.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
What is M-Fly
M-Fly was founded in late 2023, growing out of the founders’ earlier military-focused volunteer project supporting the military. By mid 2026, the company had raised $1.4 million through a friends-and-family round, grants from the state-owned defense tech cluster Brave1, and VC funding from MITS Capital, Freedom Fund, Resist.ua, and Ukrainian entrepreneur Borys Shestopalov, co-founder of HD-group.
As of fall 2026, M-Fly’s portfolio includes laser guidance systems and high-precision gyro-stabilized gimbals for air, maritime, and ground unmanned platforms. The company has tested its core technologies on the battlefield in Ukraine, confirming the stabilization platform’s performance at speeds of up to 350 km/h.
M-Fly offers a line of cost-efficient laser-guided systems, including RB-150CW and Seeker, to improve unmanned platforms’ efficiency.
M-Fly products include:
- RB-220, a heavy-duty gimbal suitable for large UAVs, manned aviation, helicopters, and naval drones, can also be used as a ground-based station for air defense applications
- RB-150GD, a dual-sensor gimbal with thermal and daylight video channels designed specifically for medium-class drones
- Based on this platform, the company is developing the RB-150 Marine, a weather-resistant gimbal for boats and vessels.
M-Fly plans to release the RB-100, the lightest product in its lineup and designed for small drones, in the first quarter of 2027, the press release says.
                                                                                                                                                                         
In 2026, M-Fly also migrated its processing architecture from random-access memory (RAM) to a graphics processing unit (GPU)-based platform. The shift makes its systems less dependent on specific computing components and lets engineers adapt more quickly when particular chips or memory components become unavailable.
As of September 2026, MITS Capital’s portfolio includes 20 companies. MITS Accelerator has graduated two six-month cohorts of startups. A third cohort – Batch 3 – is now in acceleration, focused on critical defense components, connectivity and control systems, AI-driven software, advanced weapons, counter-drone systems, and battlefield automation.

====================================================================================================

Wildlife arrives on time at rewilded chalk grasslands built along HS2 route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:00:43 UTC
21:00:43 KST

The air is scented with the sweet tang of ladies bedstraw and made musical by skylark and blackcap song. An abundance of marbled white butterflies, small skippers and common blue damselflies dart over the flowering knapweed, yarrow and wild carrot.
That the largest chalk grassland in the Chilterns is full of wildlife may not surprise you. But the fact that it is completely artificial, only four years old and has been built by the much-maligned HS2, may do.
The Western Slopes “rewilding” project is due to open to the public next year on land beside the high-speed railway as it dives under the M25 and into a 10-mile tunnel beneath the Chilterns. The trains may be running late, but the wildlife has already arrived.
A decade ago, this area was a vast wheatfield with precious little biodiversity. Today, as the construction effort winds down, more and more of the 127-hectare site is being turned into wildlife-rich grasslands, wet meadows, ponds and small woods.
It is now one of the largest wildlife habitat creation projects in south-east England, and has already witnessed the arrival of hedgehog clover, which hasn’t been recorded in Hertfordshire since 1878, alongside water voles, lesser emperor dragonflies and pyramidal orchids.
The transformation began when Matt Hobbs, lead ecologist at Jacobs, was invited to take a look at the huge planned HS2 works around the south entrance to the Chilterns tunnel.
“I asked the engineer: ‘What’s coming out of the tunnel?’ When he said ‘chalk’, it was like a lightbulb moment. I thought, I know what I’d like to do with that chalk,” said Hobbs, who has designed and overseen the Western Slopes project for HS2.
Chalk grassland is one of the most wildlife-rich habitats in southern England because a wide range of wildflowers flourish on its thin, nutrient-poor alkaline soils, alongside an array of associated invertebrates, including rare moths and bees.
According to Hobbs, the valley slopes could have been expensively restored to arable land by HS2, as much of the land temporarily taken for the huge construction effort will be. “We saw the opportunity to do something different,” he said. “This project is unique. The whole landscape was predicated on what’s the best thing to do with the earthworks and soils. We’re not moving any soils or material off site. Any concrete waste from this site is crushed and used as aggregate under the grasslands.”
Reusing 10m cubic metres of chalk, topsoil and subsoils from the construction effort in the immediate vicinity of the tunnel mouth has also drastically reduced CO2 emissions, and the construction traffic that dumping it elsewhere would have entailed.
According to HS2’s calculations, the wildlife grasslands here could sequester 7% of the carbon impact of the whole high-speed line’s construction, because grassland is much better at storing carbon than regularly-ploughed arable land, which releases carbon every time it is ploughed.
Over the past four years, all the chalk excavated from the tunnel has been sculpted into rolling “downs” on the land above the Colne Valley, creating varying topsoils and a future mosaic of grassland, scrub, woodland and ponds and wet areas.
It took the ecologists a bit of effort to retrain the digger drivers who were spreading the chalk over the site. Groundworks teams are trained to leave everything beautifully smooth and neat, whereas the ecologists were seeking topographical variation, with dips, hollows and “untidy” rough areas.
The future vision is a “wood pasture” landscape, inspired by rewilding sites such as Knepp in West Sussex, where a mixture of scrub and wildflower glades are grazed by herbivores.
Four cattle-grids have been installed on roads – believed to be the first in Hertfordshire – to enable free-roaming cattle to graze within four separate compartments.
“They were really key to the project. We wanted to have that Knepp rewilding technique where you have cattle that can move anywhere they want within the site – it’s brilliant for soil health, soil carbon and dung beetles,” said Hobbs.
Luke Craner, a senior landscape clerk of works for the HS2 contractor Align, said: “I’m really keen to get livestock grazing sooner rather than later so we can kickstart biological processes. We’ve already got a really good grassy sward establishing. We want natural regeneration to occur, because it’s always much more beneficial for wildlife. We’ve already got loads of hawthorn and quite a few oaks coming up. It’s already going out nicely.”
Later this summer, green hay from other calcareous grassland in the local area will be spread on the Western Slopes to bring in more invertebrates. As ant populations develop, rare butterflies including the Adonis, chalkhill and small blue are likely to arrive, with these species interacting with ant colonies. There is also a mammal shelf built into a culvert beneath the railway, enabling badgers, stoats and other mammals to safely cross the high-speed line.
Some footpaths through the site are set to be opened up in the next 18 months, although the western portion of the site is likely to remain protected from public access to boost the ground-nesting birds – from skylarks to little ringed plover – that have quickly colonised the land.
While HS2 is still under construction, the forthcoming track-building and electrics phase will require a much smaller construction footprint, enabling the nature areas to be expanded.
At the bottom of the slopes, beside the River Colne, nearly five hectares of new wetlands have been established. These pretty ponds have been rapidly colonised by club-rush, water mint and sneezewort, as well as breeding reed warbler and lesser emperor dragonfly.
“We’ve definitely extended the population of kingfishers,” said Craner, who has also recorded new sightings of water vole on a tributary of the Colne. “Water voles are a massively declining species because of habitat loss – we’ve put in habitat that’s good for water voles. They’ve colonised it immediately.”
What Craner has noticed is the changing soundscape. While the roar of the M25 and the clank of ongoing construction is never far away, in certain glades the human din is now overwhelmed by birdsong and insect hum.
“We didn’t have this harmony last year and all of a sudden it’s never silent,” said Craner. “This is our hidden gem.”

From Malaysian chicken to Caribbean crab: four global curry recipes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:00:41 UTC
21:00:41 KST

Mandy Yin’s chicken and squash curry (pictured top)
Curry runs through Malaysia’s veins; it’s in every kitchen and at every food stall, whether run by Malays, Chinese or Indians. We tend to cook curries using either a wet spice paste (rempah) straight from the morning market, or a good curry powder – every household keeps a pack of Adabi or Baba’s in the cupboard as a fallback; we have no shame in this at all. Only when you’ve got time on your hands, or you’re cooking to impress, do you build a rempah from scratch.
My favourite curries come from the Mamak Tamil Muslim cooks behind Malaysia’s all-night kopitiams, who make the best roti canai going. Go for the roti and the meat curries alongside, washed down with teh tarik – strong black tea sweetened with condensed milk, pulled until it froths.
In my cookbook Simply Malaysian, I included my take on Dad’s Mamak lamb and potato curry. He starts with a whole leg, which he bones and trims himself, a heavy hand of curry powder, then the aromatics Malaysians call empat sekawan (the four friends): star anise, cassia, cloves, cardamom. Here, I’ve swapped the lamb for chicken thighs on the bone – they’re cheaper, quicker and what most of us reach for on a weeknight – and the potatoes for butternut squash. Pumpkins and gourds are a staple of Malay cooking, and are most at home in a coconut gravy, though they rarely share a pot with meat. So, squash takes the potatoes’ place and earns its keep, holding its shape and drinking up the sauce.
A word on the meat. In Malaysia we cook it in the curry it’s going to be served in – not seared or simmered separately and folded in at the end – so the two season each other the whole way. And we cook it on the bone, always: bone-in gives a richer, glossier sauce than any fillet will. Like all curries, this eats even better the next day, once the flavours have settled. If you’re not eating it straight away, reduce the cooking time in the penultimate step to 10 minutes (to allow the squash to finish cooking when reheating it). Any leftover sauce eaten with rice and a fried egg or two is one of life’s simple pleasures.
Prep 15 min
 Cook 45 min
 Serves 4-6
1 medium onion, peeled and roughly chopped
4 garlic cloves, peeled
  1 inch (2½cm) piece ginger, peeled and roughly chopped
5 tbsp vegetable or peanut oil
  ¾ tbsp table salt 
4 tbsp Adabi meat curry powder – alternatively, combine 1 tbsp chilli powder, 1 tbsp ground coriander, 1 tbsp ground turmeric, 1 tsp finely ground black pepper and 2 tsp ground cumin
½ tsp chilli powder
  1 star anise
  4 cloves
  1 stick cassia bark, or ½ cinnamon stick
2 green cardamom pods, lightly bashed with a pestle to crack the skin
1kg skinless, bone-in chicken thighs
200g tinned chopped tomatoes, or fresh tomatoes, roughly chopped
1 butternut squash, or part of a pumpkin, peeled, deseeded and cut into 3cm x 2cm chunks (approximately 800-850g)
200ml coconut milk
30g bunch coriander, finely chopped stalks and all (optional)
Finely chop the onion, garlic and ginger in a food processor. Heat the oil in a large, non-stick wok/saucepan or a deep casserole dish over a medium heat, then add the onion-garlic mix and salt, and stir-fry for five minutes, until softened.
Turn the heat down to medium-low, then add the curry powder, chilli powder, star anise, cloves, cassia and cardamom, and stir-fry for two minutes. Add a splash of water if the spices start to catch on the bottom of the pan.
Add the chicken thighs and turn them through the paste, until every piece is coated. Pour in 200ml water and the tomatoes, stir, then bring up to a boil. Lower the heat to medium-low, cover and simmer for 15 minutes, turning the thighs and stirring every five minutes.
Add the squash/pumpkin and coconut milk, then cover and bring back to a boil over a medium heat. Check in every few minutes to see whether it has come up to a boil, and give it a stir. Take your time, as the chicken and squash slowly release their juices into the sauce, so you end up with enough liquid to keep almost everything submerged.
Once boiling, lower the heat to medium-low and cook, uncovered, for 15 minutes, stirring every few minutes and nudging the squash carefully back under the sauce. Turn the heat off, stir through the coriander and serve with plenty of rice.
- 
  Simply Malaysian by Mandy Yin is published by Quadrille at £27. To order a copy for £24.30, visit guardianbookshop.com
Keshia Sakarah’s curry crab, roasted corn and cassava dumplings
When most people think of curry, they probably don’t think of the Caribbean, yet many of our dishes incorporate spices in a variety of ways. While they aren’t native or indigenous ingredients, they are now very much part of daily life. 
 They were introduced to the region by the indentured labourers from the Indian subcontinent. Their use of spices in this new part of the world transformed the cuisine in many ways, using ground spices to flavour slow-cooked meat and fish, or toasting whole ones in oil to finish vegetables, and brought about a brand-new cooking style.
I’ve eaten curry throughout my life, and thinking of my love for it unearths many fond memories: when I’m at Notting Hill carnival, I have to support my favourite food stands off Kensal Road. And then there are my many visits to the Caribbean. Experiencing curry on different islands, in a variety of ways, always piques my curiosity; it speaks to the cultural layers of the region and how the Caribbean really is a microcosm of the many communities that make up the world. In Guadeloupe, I tried colombo – a classic French Caribbean curry (usually chicken or fish), which incorporates toasted, ground rice into the spices and lots of lime juice into the sauce. Unlike the curries of the anglophone islands (Jamaica, Antigua, Grenada, for example), it is more acidic and paler in complexion, yet still served with rice and beans. In Trinidad, home to one of the largest Indo-Caribbean communities, curry is a staple, originally found mostly in homes, but now also in roti shops across the island. Some of the best are in central Trinidad, where generations of Indian communities have settled for generations.
Prep 10 min
Rest 30 min
 Cook 55 min
 Serves 4
For the cassava dumplings
125g cassava flour
  125g plain flour
  1⅛ tsp fine sea salt, plus extra for cooking the dumplings
½ tsp baking powder
1 tbsp olive pomace or rapeseed oil, plus extra for cooking the dumplings
  180ml cold water
For the green seasoning
2 spring onions
  6 garlic cloves, peeled
  5cm piece ginger
  15g flat-leaf parsley, leaves and stalks
  30g coriander, leaves and stalks
  75ml cold water
  1 lime, juiced
  2 tbsp rapeseed oil
For the curry base
2 fresh corn cobs
3 tbsp ghee or rapeseed oil
   2 tbsp curry powder
   2 tsp ground turmeric
   4 tsp garam masala or amchar masala
   1 scotch bonnet, pierced
   600ml good-quality coconut milk
   290g white crab meat
Combine all the ingredients for the cassava dumplings in a bowl, then knead to form a soft dough; set aside to rest for 30 minutes.
Blend all the green seasoning ingredients apart from the oil in a blender until almost smooth, then transfer to a jar and stir in the oil.
Roast the corn cobs over an open flame or under a hot grill, turning occasionally, until charred all over; set aside to cool. Once cool enough to handle, slice off the kernels and set aside, discarding the husks.
For the curry base, heat the ghee/oil in a pan set over a medium heat. Add the spices and toast lightly for 30 seconds to a minute. Add 200ml cold water and gently boil for three to four minutes, then add two tablespoons of the green seasoning, the scotch bonnet and half the grilled corn, and mix well.
Tip in the coconut milk, increase the heat until lightly boiling, then reduce to a simmer and cook for 10-12 minutes, until the sauce looks smooth and emulsified.
Meanwhile, divide the dumpling dough into 32 equal pieces, then roll into balls. Place them spaced out on a tray, dusting with a little extra flour if they’re sticky. Cover with a tea towel and set aside.
Bring a pan of water to the boil, then add a teaspoon of salt and a teaspoon of oil. Once boiling, cook the dumplings in batches for eight to 10 minutes, or until they float. Remove from the pan with a slotted spoon to a bowl of cold water (they will cook further in the curry later).
To finish the curry, give the pan another stir – it should have reduced and thickened slightly. Remove the scotch bonnet and discard, then pour the curry into a blender and blitz smooth. Pass through a sieve, then return the liquid to the pan.
Put over a medium-high heat, add the cooked dumplings, then reduce to a low simmer and cook foreight to 10 minutes, until the dumplings are soft and have absorbed some of the colour from the curry. Remove from the heat and gently fold in the crab meat, ensuring it doesn’t break up. Finish with the remaining grilled corn and a few more drops of the green seasoning, then serve.
- 
  Caribe by Keshia Sakarah is published by Hardie Grant at £30. To order a copy for £27, visit guardianbookshop.com
Tim Anderson’s garlic mushroom curry doria (Japanese rice gratin)
Japan’s curry doria – also known as yaki-curry, or baked curry – is one of my all-time favourite blank-slate meal formats. It is essentially a rice gratin, containing plump grains of Japanese short-grain rice smothered in smooth Japanese curry sauce, all tucked under a luxurious duvet of molten cheese. In other words, a masterclass in comfort cookery.
Because its core elements are so amenably mellow in terms of flavour, the curry doria format works with just about any veg or protein you like, or whatever’s in season. But I like to lean into its heartiness with rich, meaty ingredients, such as the mushrooms and greens I’ve used here, along with a liberal dose of garlic and butter, inspired by old-school baked mushroom starters.
Prep 10 min
 Cook 45 min
 Serves 4
Butter, as needed
4 portions cooked Japanese rice (300g uncooked)
400g mushrooms – I love oyster mushrooms, but use any you like
4 garlic cloves
  Salt and black pepper
100g mustard greens or chard, coarsely chopped
1 pack (around 90g) Japanese curry roux
50g grated mozzarella
  50g grated medium or mild cheddar
50g grated Emmental
1 small handful flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
Some kind of crunchy onion product, such as cheese and onion crisps, onion rings, or fried shallots (I highly recommend the brand Wild Rice), to garnish
Rub a medium baking dish (around 23cm square,) with butter. Pack the cooked rice into the bottom of the dish in an even layer, using a bit of force so it’s relatively dense – if it has too many air gaps, the curry sauce will flow into it, and the gratin will become more stodgy than saucy.
Then, prepare the mushrooms. Oyster mushrooms, shimeji, or ordinary white or chestnut mushrooms can simply be broken into bite-size pieces; smaller mushrooms like buttons and chanterelles can be left whole; shiitake should be de-stemmed; and if you are using any long, tough mushrooms like king oysters or enoki, they should be chopped into roughly 1-inch chunks. Remember to clean any wild mushrooms so they’re free of dirt or grit before cooking.
Peel and chop the garlic, sprinkle it with salt, then continue to mince it finely, and drag the side of your knife through it, to smash it into a coarse paste; the salt will help soften the garlic and draw out its pungent oils.
In a wide saute pan, melt a generous knob of butter over a medium-high heat, then add the garlic, mushrooms, greens, and a few grinds of pepper. Toss them through the butter, then cook without stirring for four to five minutes, so the mushrooms brown on one side. Remove from the heat, then scrape everything out of the pan and on to the rice in the baking dish. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.
In the same pan you used to saute the mushrooms, prepare the curry sauce according to packet instructions – but don’t add any additional meat or veg, if it calls for them. Once the sauce is cooked out and smooth, pour this over the mushrooms and rice.
Top with the cheeses and bake for about 20 minutes, until browned on top. Serve piping hot, garnished with a little chopped parsley and a scattering of the crunchy onion product of your choosing.
- 
  Japanese Curry by Tim Anderson is published in October by Quadrille at £14.99. To order a copy for £13.49, visit guardianbookshop.com
Maunika Gowardhan’s rajasthani papad ki sabji
Although I grew up in Mumbai, I hail from a family with roots in the Konkani and western coastal region sprawled across the Deccan Plateau in India. Dishes from this region are robust, hearty and we celebrate curries with warmth, aroma, and complex flavours.
Travelling across India, the food changes within regions and reflects the ingredients available, the seasons and changes in climate. But this is one of my favourite curries from the state of Rajasthan. Papad ki sabji is a staple in homes across the north-west of India and primarily made with turmeric, coriander and fenugreek in a rich gravy simmered with cooked papad (poppadum). This dish is often served in a Rajasthani thali, which is vibrant and delicious, but it is also served as a weekday curry with plain rice.
Yoghurt added to the curry is cooling and lends richness to the gravy. Traditionally, the papad is deep-fried but my recipe uses roast papads, which can be done in the microwave in just a few seconds (follow the packet instructions for cooking the papad). The charred edges on the papad lend a lot of flavour to the curry.
Prep 10 min
 Cook 30 min
 Serves 4
4 garlic cloves, peeled and roughly chopped
1 inch (2½cm) piece ginger, peeled and roughly chopped
1 small bird’s eye green chilli, deseeded if you prefer less heat
100g tomatoes, roughly chopped
1 tbsp tomato puree
  3 tbsp vegetable oil or ghee
  ½ tsp cumin seeds
  A pinch of asafoetida
  1 tbsp coriander powder
  1 tsp turmeric powder
1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
  250g Greek yoghurt, whisked well (make sure there are no lumps; this way it won’t split as it cooks)
  Salt
2 tbsp dried fenugreek leaves (kasoori methi)
4 roasted papads/poppadum
Fresh coriander, to garnish
Put the garlic, ginger, green chilli and a splash of water in a blender and blend to a smooth, fine paste; set aside.
In the same blender, blend the tomato and tomato puree to a paste.
Heat the oil in a heavy-based nonstick saucepan over a low heat. Add the cumin seeds and asafoetida, and fry for two seconds. Add the garlic/ginger paste and fry for 20 seconds, then add the blended tomatoes and cook for six minutes, stirring well.
As the oil leaves the sides of the pan, add the powdered spices and fry for a minute. Tip in the yoghurt a little at a time, stirring well, then cook and stir on a low heat for three to four minutes.
Add 300ml water, season to taste and simmer for six to eight minutes. Add the fenugreek leaves, along with the roasted papad and cook, covered, for two minutes. Garnish with coriander and serve with rice.
- 
  Curry by Maunika Gowardhan is published by Quadrille at £26. To order a copy for £23.40, visit guardianbookshop.com

How to turn gherkin brine into a savoury ice-cream – recipe | Waste not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:00:40 UTC
21:00:40 KST

While researching gherkins for a Food Filter column last year, I came across Kühne’s recipe for pickled cucumber ice-cream and couldn’t resist. Niche, I know, but I’ll bet there are a lot of gherkin fanatics out there who’d be willing to give it a go. If not, the cocktail I’ve used as inspiration might well suffice. The pickleback is made with pickle juice and a spirit such as whisky, tequila or, my favourite, vodka, and that same punchy, sweet-and-sour combination comes together to make possibly the quirkiest ice-cream flavour you ever come across. Delicious in a cone and topped with a gherkin, and out of this world when served with waffles, bacon and maple syrup.
Pickled cucumber and vodka ice-cream
This is one for the true gherkin fanatic, with a wild and funky flavour that tricks the mind with a rollercoaster of unexpected tastes. It’s sweet and dilly, but also tart and sour, with a lingering complexity from all the spices used to make the pickles. Fortified with a classic, creamy custard base, it’s best served with savoury waffles.
1 egg
  70g sugar 
  100ml milk 
  250ml double cream 
  10g dill, finely chopped
10ml pickle juice 
  20ml vodka (or rum, tequila or whisky)
4 ice-cream cones, to serve 
4 pickles, to serve
In a bowl, whisk the egg, sugar, milk and cream until well combined, then pour into a thick saucepan and cook, stirring continuously, over a very low heat until the custard thickens enough to coat the back of the spoon. (Take care not to let it catch on the bottom, but, if it does, don’t fret: simply pour the custard through a fine sieve without scraping the bottom of the pan.) Take off the heat, stir in the dill and pickle juice, then stir in the vodka.
Blend smooth, then churn in an ice-cream machine or transfer to an airtight container and freeze for at least five hours, stirring every 30 minutes to break up any ice crystals. Serve at once, or, if serving the next day or thereafter, pop the ice-cream in the fridge for 30-45 minutes (or leave it out at room temperature for 15 minutes) to soften. Serve in cones and topped with a gherkin.

A single dose of MDMA prevents trauma-fueled drinking in genetically prone rats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
12:00:16 UTC
21:00:16 KST

A recent experiment in rats suggests that MDMA can prevent the increase in alcohol consumption that often follows a traumatic event, particularly in subjects genetically predisposed to drink heavily. The findings indicate that the drug alters the way fear is expressed in the moment rather than permanently strengthening the brain’s ability to unlearn fear memories. The research was published in Neuropsychopharmacology.
Post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD, is a mental health condition triggered by experiencing or witnessing a terrifying event. Many individuals with PTSD also develop alcohol use disorder, drinking to cope with intrusive memories and emotional distress. This relationship is complex and mutually reinforcing, as chronic alcohol use dysregulates stress systems in the brain, often worsening trauma symptoms over time.
To treat PTSD, therapists often rely on fear extinction. This is a learning process where an individual is repeatedly exposed to trauma-related cues in a safe environment until those cues no longer trigger a fear response. A 2015 study covered by PsyPost in 2015 indicated that administering MDMA prior to this exposure process helped accelerate fear extinction in mice.
Building on such animal research, early human studies suggest that MDMA-assisted therapy might ease symptoms of both PTSD and addiction, including a small, uncontrolled 2021 pilot study that found the approach safe and promising for treating alcohol use disorder. At the same time, scientists recognize that the connection between fear and alcohol is strongly influenced by genetics. For example, a 2016 study provided evidence that rodents selectively bred to prefer alcohol also display exaggerated fear responses, pointing to an innate biological link between anxiety and drinking.
Despite this progress, it was unknown whether giving MDMA specifically to treat trauma-like symptoms would also reduce a later urge to drink in subjects actively displaying both behaviors. The research, led by Kade L. Huckstep, Billi Newton, and Leigh C. Walker of the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health and the University of Melbourne, set out to see if MDMA could curb trauma-triggered drinking in genetically prone animals.
“One of the challenges with clinical trials of MDMA-assisted therapy is determining how much of the observed benefit is attributable to MDMA itself,” Walker, deputy lead of Mental Health Research and Group Head of the Hormone and Behaviour Laboratory at the Florey Institute, told PsyPost. “Because the subjective effects of MDMA are very noticeable, effective blinding can be difficult, and factors such as expectancy and the therapeutic setting may also influence outcomes.”
To overcome this, the researchers aimed to mirror real-world research. “We wanted to develop a rodent model that, as closely as possible, reflected ongoing clinical trials investigating MDMA in people with co-occurring PTSD and alcohol use disorder (e.g., MPATHY),” Walker explained. “This allowed us to examine the effects of MDMA in a highly controlled setting, without expectancy or placebo effects, and determine whether MDMA itself alters fear-related behavior and alcohol consumption.”
“Importantly, we also wanted to identify any unintended effects, e.g., whether MDMA could worsen fear-related behavior or alcohol consumption under particular conditions, an important factor relevant to our clinical collaborators conducting the corresponding human trials,” she added.
To explore this, the team used 53 Indiana alcohol-preferring rats, a strain selectively bred to voluntarily consume high amounts of alcohol, and 64 Wistar rats, a standard outbred strain. Both male and female rats were used. The animals first underwent auditory fear conditioning, a procedure where a specific tone is repeatedly paired with a mild, one-second electrical foot shock. This teaches the animals to associate the sound with an aversive event, causing them to freeze in place whenever they hear it. A separate control group heard the tone but received no shocks.
Following this conditioning, all the rats were given intermittent access to a solution of twenty percent alcohol and water for six weeks. This allowed them to develop a voluntary drinking habit. Afterward, the researchers removed the alcohol for three weeks to simulate a period of abstinence.
At the end of the abstinence period, the animals received an injection of either MDMA or a simple saline solution. Thirty minutes later, they were placed into a fear extinction session where the tone was played repeatedly without any foot shocks. The following day, the rats underwent a drug-free test to see how well they remembered the extinction learning. Finally, they were given free access to alcohol again for eight sessions to measure their post-treatment drinking behavior.
The researchers found that the initial fear conditioning modestly increased later alcohol consumption, but only in the genetically vulnerable Indiana alcohol-preferring rats. The Wistar rats learned to fear the tone just as strongly, but this distressing experience did not drive them to drink more alcohol than their unshocked counterparts. This finding suggests that trauma-like stress drives increased drinking specifically when a genetic predisposition is present.
When the rats received MDMA before the fear extinction session, their immediate reactions to the tone changed. The drug initially reduced their freezing behavior early in the session. However, as the session went on, the two strains reacted differently. The Indiana alcohol-preferring rats ended up freezing more overall while on the drug, while the female Wistar rats froze less.
Despite these in-the-moment changes, MDMA did not improve how well the rats remembered the safety of the tone the following day. During the drug-free recall test, the MDMA-treated rats showed no better fear extinction than those given the saline solution. However, the MDMA treatment had a modest protective effect against trauma-induced drinking. In the Indiana alcohol-preferring rats that had experienced fear conditioning, those treated with MDMA did not show the trauma-related escalation in alcohol intake that was seen in the saline group.
“For us, the most important finding was not necessarily how large the effect was, but that it differed depending on the animals we studied,” Walker noted. “MDMA reduced drinking in rats that were particularly vulnerable to high alcohol use and more stress sensitive — and this effect persisted over 3 weeks. It will be interesting to see whether a similar pattern emerges in clinical trials, and whether particular groups of people may benefit more from MDMA-assisted therapy than others.”
To verify whether the drug’s effects on fear depended on the animals’ six-week history with alcohol, the team tested an additional group of 25 Indiana alcohol-preferring rats. These animals went through the same conditioning, MDMA, and extinction procedures, but went straight to extinction the day after conditioning, skipping the weeks of drinking and abstinence.
In this alcohol-naive group, MDMA still altered their immediate fear expression during the extinction session without improving their drug-free memory of it the next day. When these rats were introduced to alcohol for the first time after treatment, the MDMA-treated males showed lower initial consumption than those given saline, but this reduction was short-lived, and their overall drinking quickly matched the control group. This indicates that MDMA’s most reliable benefit in this model is blocking the long-term escalation of drinking that results from a combination of trauma and prior alcohol experience.
This decoupling of fear and drinking behavior was an unexpected outcome for the team. “We were surprised that MDMA’s effects on alcohol consumption did not seem to be directly linked to its effects on fear,” Walker said. “We initially thought that reducing fear responses might also reduce subsequent drinking, but the two effects appeared to be separate. This suggests that MDMA may influence alcohol use through other mechanisms that we still need to understand.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study measured voluntary alcohol consumption under a limited-access schedule and did not measure blood alcohol concentrations, meaning the shifts in drinking might not reflect intoxication-level binges. The team also tested a single dose of MDMA given thirty minutes before extinction. Different doses or timing schedules might yield varying effects on learning and alcohol consumption.
“The main caveat is that this was a study in rats, and our findings should not be taken to mean that MDMA will reduce alcohol use in people,” Walker cautioned. “What the study does show is that responses to MDMA can vary considerably depending on the individual, including their vulnerability to heavy drinking and their sex. Understanding these differences will be important as we learn more from ongoing clinical trials. If so, we can use this model to delve into the mechanisms that may be responsible.”
There are a few other things to keep in mind regarding how these animal behaviors translate to humans. Animal models of fear extinction only capture a narrow aspect of trauma therapy. They cannot replicate the complex relational and emotional support that defines MDMA-assisted psychotherapy in clinical settings.
Moving forward, the researchers hope to use this model to investigate the biological foundations of the treatment. “We would like to understand the brain and biological mechanisms that drive the effects of MDMA and MDMA-assisted therapy,” Walker said. “Ultimately, this could help identify who is most likely to benefit from treatment. Understanding how these treatments actually work may also help move the conversation beyond some of the stigma or fear associated with taking drugs such as MDMA during therapy, allowing their potential benefits and risks to be considered based on scientific evidence.”
“One important lesson from this study is the need to better reflect human diversity in preclinical research,” she added. “By studying co-occurring conditions such as trauma and problematic alcohol use, and considering biological factors such as sex and genetic vulnerability from the outset, we can uncover differences that might otherwise be missed. Keeping these factors at the forefront may help us better understand why treatments work for some people but not others, and ultimately improve how findings from animal studies translate to the clinic.”
The study, “MDMA alters fear extinction, and reduces alcohol consumption in inbred alcohol preferring iP rats but not outbred Wistar rats,” was authored by Kade L. Huckstep, Billi Newton, Grace Bailey, Annai Charlton, Amy J. Pearl, Xavier J. Maddern, Robyn M. Brown, Gavan P. McNally, Dan I. Lubman, Shalini Arunogiri, Kirsten C. Morley, Erin J. Campbell, Andrew J. Lawrence, and Leigh C. Walker.

Anthropic raises alarm over elite hacking ability of Chinese firm Z.ai’s GLM-5.3
The open-weight AI model almost matches Claude Mythos for cyber capabilities, but has far weaker safeguards, Anthropic says
The US artificial intelligence giant Anthropic has warned of the potential danger posed by Chinese firm Z.ai’s GLM-5.3, with the open-weight model showing a troubling mix of powerful hacking abilities but weak safety constraints.
GLM-5.3 almost matches Anthropic’s most advanced model in terms of its cyber capabilities, but has far weaker safeguards, meaning there is greater potential for the model to be co-opted by bad actors, according to the San Francisco-based firm.
In a report released on Tuesday, Anthropic said it had tested GLM-5.3’s ability to build end-to-end cyber exploits. The Chinese model successfully completed 50 out of 410 exploit attempts, compared with 56 for Claude Mythos Preview, a frontier Anthropic model that can only be used by vetted users.

House Speaker Mike Johnson stumping and fundraising for California GOP congressional candidates
-    Click here to listen to this article

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- House Speaker Mike Johnson is heading to California’s Central Valley and Inland Empire to campaign and raise money for Republicans in midterm contests.
- The California trip is part of Johnson’s plans to campaign in 22 states in an effort to help Republicans retain control of the House before the Nov. 3 election.
