Sound and vision: Creators Olivier Calvert and Jose Luis Agreda on the art of animation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:40:27 UTC
19:40:27 KST

Greece's biggest International Animation Festival, Animasyros, is now firmly ranked among the top events of its kind in Europe. With a programme richer than ever, this year's festival showcased more than 280 films by established and emerging filmmakers from 50 different countries.
Animasyros, one of Europe's major animation festivals, recently wrapped up its 19th consecutive year of celebrations in Ermoupoli, flying the flag for the Greece's biggest International Animation Festival.
Beyond the seven competition sections (International, Student, K.ID.S, AnimaPride, National Competition, TV & Commissioned Films and Feature Films), this year's edition included a special focus on Irish animation, a theme marking 200 years of Ermoupoli, educational workshops, parallel events, international collaborations and the Market, which has now become a key reference point for the entire industry in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Vassilis Karamitssanis, President of the Animasyros International Festival, spoke to Euronews about what the event has achieved so far and what lies ahead next year, when Animasyros celebrates its 20th anniversary:
"In the 18-19 years that Animasyros has been in the spotlight, or that have elapsed since its founding back in 2008, I believe it has become the most important hub for animation in the Mediterranean and in Greece. It places strong emphasis on showcasing Greek and European talent around the world and also aims to highlight new techniques and technologies in the field of animation, which I consider to be the key to a sustainable future for the audiovisual sector in general and for European animation in particular."
Listen up
One of the most prominent guests at this year's edition was the internationally recognised and multi-award-winning sound designerOlivier Calvert.
With a long track record of collaborations with leading directors and organisations, the Montreal-based Canadian creator has shaped the sonic universe of numerous acclaimed productions, including the Oscar-nominated short film The Girl Who Cried Pearls. He was also part of the Oscar-winning sound team for Denis Villeneuve's Arrival.
During the festival, Calvert presented a masterclass devoted to sound as a decisive storytelling tool. The festival paid tribute to his work and screened a selection of films:
"Sound design shapes the overall sound of a film, which means you can work with its sonic environment. It can be realistic – birds, traffic noise, the sea, the waves. But it can also operate on a subconscious level. You can really create tension in a scene by adding other sounds beneath the music or the voice, or by removing sounds," explained Calvert.
"You can build tension that way. It is important, because sound is the filter through which you look at the image. It gives you the emotion with which you perceive that image. There is a saying I like very much, which was also the subtitle of my workshop: 'The image is the body, but sound is the soul'."
"For me, it is the whole emotional landscape of the film. It is all the sound, not just the music. Every sound is music in a way, so it contributes to the emotional impact of the film. There is a big difference between fiction films and animation. In live-action films you first create sound for a normal environment. In animation everything is constructed, an entirely new world, so why should the sound be natural, real? In an animated film we do not need the sound to be realistic. So yes, we can create a completely different world, a unique world. A new universe to discover, both in terms of image and in terms of sound.
"Sometimes I get involved very early in the creative process, especially with directors I have already worked with. They now bring me in at a very early stage, because we can shape the film using sound as a storytelling device. You can tell a story purely with images and you can tell a story purely with sounds. So the challenge is to build a story through the collaboration between images and sounds. That is where I can help the director achieve this. I am something like an artistic director for sound," added Calvert.
"I dare to take on the role of adviser for them. As soon as I am hired for a film, we start to discuss ideas around it. And we work together with the composer. I am not a composer. That is why I always collaborate with someone else on the sound, who is the composer. This trio (director, composer and sound designer) is very important. For me the soundtrack of a film is a whole. There is the music on the one hand and the sound effects on the other. Everything goes together, so it is a major collaboration between director, composer and sound designer. Yes, there is great synergy between the three."
Cross-border collaborations
This year's festival opened with the Greek premiere of Decorado by Goya-winning Spanish creator Alberto Vásquez (Unicorn Wars, Birdboy: The Forgotten Children), with the support of the Embassy of Spain in Greece and the Cervantes Institute. The film, which received the Paul Grimault award at this year's Annecy animation festival, recalls The Truman Show in animated form.
It is an existential black comedy about the absurdity of modern life and the control that others seek to impose on us, featuring the director's trademark macabre visual style, which combines innocence and dark humour with a dystopian contemporary reality.
José Luis Ágreda, the film's creative director spoke to Euronews about the project: "Decorado, the film we presented here at Animasyros, is a parable, a dark parable about our society and the way in which each of us, every individual, feels within it. The film is also about how society or, more specifically, companies try to dehumanise people.
"The story is about a man without a job for whom everything seems strange. He does not perceive things as reality because they have nothing to do with him. There is humour and these funny animal characters," said Ágreda_. "But when the viewer enters the world of the film, they realise that it is a dystopia, a universe that becomes ever darker. And they understand that it concerns them, as it reflects today's world. This was our way of getting audiences to think about what is happening around us today."_
"The animation style we use has many references to classic Disney cartoons. I mean classic American animation. But we give it a different twist, so that viewers do not immediately recognise it, while at the same time realising that there is something strange. It is as if we have a very happy world, like the society they try to sell us, but inside it there is something rotten. So we try to work with these characters and this kind of environment, yet we create odd colours, unusual combinations of colours. In the end, people feel: 'OK, this is a nightmare, not a dream'."
"What happens to the hero, Arnold, is very similar to what we experience on social media. You feel that you are at the centre of attention and of everything, but you are not. Everything around you is constructed, fake, not real. That is because we live in a society that stays with appearance and not with being. This is the idea behind our film: that we are on a stage, on a set, where we play a role while ignoring what is really happening around us. We do not realise that everything around us is fabricated. This gives us the impression that everything is perfect. The result? We do not deal with the great problems of our society."
The Awards
The Grand Prize of the International Competition at the 19th Animasyros was awarded to Please by Anna Mantzaris, while the prize in the Greek Competition went to Konstantinos Demis for The Dog.
In the Student Competition, the award was won by Gauze, a film about Palestine created by a team of five students from GOBELINS Paris, Noran Fikri Alezabi, Nicholas Arujah, Xinyue Ma, Yulin YUE and Xiaonan Zhou.
In the Television and Commissioned Films category, the prize went to Saltwater by Eilidh Nicoll from the United Kingdom.
The Animapride competition section features films with LGBTQI+ content and showcases creativity, queer expression and acceptance. The jury awarded its prize to Eyeliner by Aisha Boujilouli. The first prize in the K.ID.S category was given to The Eagle and the Kinglet by Paul Jadoul from the Czech Republic.
The Audience Award at Animasyros was collected by Martin Lund's Unstoppable, a subversive and emotional, humourous adventure film.

Are Russian ‘Iva’ MANPADS Chinese Knock-Offs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:40:15 UTC
19:40:15 KST

A report on the Russian Rossiya 1 television channel on Monday, Sept. 28, was intended to show soldiers from a mobile fire group of the 51st Air Defense Division in Rostov.
It included an interview with an operator demonstrating a shoulder-launched man-portable air defense system (MANPADS) weapon. The soldier referred to it as the “Iva” – Russian for willow.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Milbloggers and other open-source analysts began to question the origin of the weapon.
They argued that the launcher didn’t share the characteristics of other Russian systems such as the Igla or Verba – other words used for willow.
Chinese, Iranian, or a hybrid?
The milblogger Dead District, posting on X on Monday, suggested the weapon was an Iranian Misagh-2, while other military analysts disagreed.
The US military issues site The War Zone (TWZ) and Ukraine’s Militarnyi compared the launcher with existing Chinese and Iranian designs and concluded that it more closely resembled the Chinese QW-18/QW-18A or QW-19 series of MANPADS, rather than Iran’s Misagh-2 or 3 – derivatives of the Chinese launchers.
The Swiss analytic site MiGFlug, citing TWZ, offered other possibilities for the weapon’s origin: a system bought directly from China, perhaps for evaluation; an Iranian-built derivative; a Russian copy of one or other design; or, unlikely but possible, a North Korean weapon.
The arguments were further complicated by another suggestion from the Defence Blog military issues site which said that Pakistan’s Anza-2 MANPADS is also thought to be based on a Chinese design.
Russia Keeps Pounding Kyiv in Daytime After Overnight Strike – Supermarket Hit, Debris Near Embassy
Previously, in July, Reuters reported that China was expected to transfer several hundred MANPADS to Iran as part of an arms deal.
China has been accused of being involved in the illegal global trade in shoulder launched surface-to-air missiles (SAM), as summarized in the 2022 report by the Small Arms Survey.
Why would Russia need foreign MANPADS?
It is logical for mobile fire groups in the Rostov region, which shares a border with Ukraine and frequently faces drone attacks, to deploy MANPADS.
The presence of an apparently foreign MANPADS system, assuming it is something more than a publicity stunt or has been simply provided for evaluation, raises the question as to why?
Russia inherited the capability to build its own MANPADS from Soviet times and has exported them all over the world. It could be that stocks of MANPADS, along with other weapons systems, have been denuded by the war in Ukraine.
Examples of Moscow addressing shortages since the 2022 full-scale invasion through expedient measures include taking 50-year-old tanks out of mothballs to replace frontline losses and cannibalizing Russia’s RM-48U training missiles, combining their components with parts from air-defense missiles and foreign electronics to supplement its ballistic missile capabilities.
In the meantime, the weapon experts will continue to investigate the origin of the “Iva” system which will then enable them to technically assess its potential in the role for which it is being used in Rostov.

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
Earlier this month six men were extradited from South Africa for allegedly conning more than 100 U.S. women out of more than $6 million. According to the FBI, the men were members of a large organized crime ring that sometimes crafted and maintained elaborate romantic relationships to defraud their targets.
The idea of someone using romance to con you isn’t new; it’s practically a tale as old as time. But the Internet made it possible to implement these schemes from the other side of the globe. Thanks to the ubiquitous nature of online socializing and dating, it no longer sounds inherently fishy to fall for someone you’ve yet to meet in person.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Fangzhou Wang is an assistant professor of criminology and criminal justice at the University of Texas at Arlington who studies online financial crimes. She says that now AI is the latest technological advance that’s making romance cons harder to spot—and easier to scale.
Thank you so much for coming on to talk with us today.
Fangzhou Wang: Thank you for inviting me.
Feltman: So how did you get interested in studying romance scams?
Wang: So initially when I get into the field of online scams, so my research actually broadly focuses on online financial crimes and how technology actually creates new opportunities for the offenders to target and exploit the victims in cyberspace. And over time, my work has somehow expanded from what I study in the Ph.D. into, you know, online scam more generally, particularly, you know, [the] human side of those scams. So how scammers actually use persuasion, trust and deception to influence people’s decisions. So this kind of, you know, progression of my research, you know, naturally lead me to online romance scam because this is very interesting scam and how people actually tricking the victims on dating apps, where in the same time financial exploitations is oftentimes built around this kind of, you know, interpersonal, loving relationships.
And more recently, I have also studied, you know, a little bit regarding to the aftermath of the scam, where you have money mules, money launderers and, you know, broader networks that actually help move those illicit funds. And in more recent years, I began to focus in on, you know, how online scam or online financial crime impacting, you know, different populations, specifically elderly population, which could be one of the most vulnerable populations in the societies.
So that is how my research actually progressed, you know, moving from online financial crime, online scam, to romance scam and, more recently to, like, money mules or scams against elderly populations and ultimately, you know, of course, leading me to understanding a more broader, you know, psycho-eco systems that may impact the victims and also the societies as general.
Feltman: Well, to take a step back, could you tell our listeners, a little bit about what kind of scams are, are out there these days that you’re studying?
Wang: Well, the current scam I’m currently studying is, of course, the first one is online romance scam, and the second one I focus most heavily on is going to be the Bitcoin scam, meaning that, how scammers actually utilizing Bitcoins or broader, you know, cryptocurrency systems to elicit, you know, fund from the victims, and how those scams can potentially impacting both the victims and societies.
And aside from the general online scams, I have been also studying, you know, a little bit regarding to cyberstalking and also cyberbullying as well, especially those against teenagers and also minors. And in addition, with regarding to a more broader, you know, abusive nature of cyberspace potentially, I also study a little bit regarding to “sextortion” and also a little bit regarding to, you know, how image-based sexual abuse can potentially be penetrated online and against, you know, different victims from different age groups.
Feltman: Could you give us some examples of common romance scams that we’ve been seeing lately?
Wang: Well, lately, ’cause, you know, online romance scam in general, you know, the scammers are trying to use fake identities to persuade the victims into giving up their monies by building a trusted relationships in the firsthand. So that is a very common online romance scam that we have been knowing in the societies. But however, in recent years, I wanna say online romance scam has been industrialized in a more Bitcoin or investment-based trusted scams that [are] happening online. Specifically, when the scammers are building trust with you first, and then the scammers are enticing you or luring you to go on fraudulent investment platforms where the scammers will tell the victims that, “oh, we need to build a wonderful future together. And in order to do so, we need to do the investment, or we need to invest on these platforms and accumulate our assets all together.” But in return, the victims will find out the scammers are actually building up the fake platforms by themselves to lure the victims to invest on. So in the end of the day, the victims are actually just investing their own money by putting the money just directly into the scammers’ pockets. So that is how the romance scam are gradually developing from simply just using persuasive cues into the scammers are industrialized their operations by building, like, an entrepreneur around their operations by, you know, luring the victims into the investment apps before, you know, they actually exploiting them voluntarily in some ways.
Feltman: So we’re not talking about, you know, somebody messaging you online and talking you into sending them some amount of money. We’re talking about, you know, big operations where they’re forming, in some cases, really, like, long-term online relationships with you. You know, there’s an entire operation then funneling you into giving them money in what seems like a business decision.
Wang: Exactly. I wanna more emphasize the online romance scam nowadays is developing more like an organized crime or more likely to be a white-collar crime, if you wanna say it more generally. So instead of just a petty crimes that impacting only a smaller portion of the victims, but, you know, the victims around the globe are impacted by this kind of scam. And we do not know exactly where majority of the scammers are coming from, but we just know they stay anonymized, they stay organized, they stay in a group and trying to get into as many victims’ mind as they can or even their bank account.
Feltman: So how do you go about studying romance scams?
Wang: So one area of my work actually examine how romance scam operates, so that is going to be the one central things I’m currently studying on. So I have been studying, you know, scam communications and offender strategies to understand how scammers actually use staged processes to construct identities, initiate, you know, relationships, build trust, and eventually, you know, transition into what I called a financial request or financial crisis. So this, kind of, help us to think about, you know, romance scam as a staged processes instead of just like one single deceptive messages, and then the victims just give out money. So the basic idea is very similar to a vaccine, if I use this example. So instead of, you know, simply telling people how scam actually exist, so we expose potential users or potential victims to weakened example of the persuasive strategies of the scammers that they could potentially be using during the scamming process and explain how those strategies actually work. So the goal is, of course, to cut the connection or cut the persuasion cues in the first place before the victims fall into the bigger traps. So the goal is, of course, to help people to recognize that or resist to those techniques when they encounter in a real relationships.
Some of my recent works also examine, you know, the role of AI in those scams, especially generative AIs. So they can potentially make it easier for the scammers to produce, you know, convincing messages—because nowadays, if we get a chance to interview an offenders in cyberspace, they’d probably be like, “We won’t be [writing] those prescam scripts by ourselves. We use generative AI to generate realistic images to target more people in the societies.” So, and they also use AI to generate those images and identities.
And of course, at the same time, our research also [asks] whether people can be trained or recognize manipulation regardless of whether deceptive content was created by [a] human or AI and which type of cue is more persuasive to the potential victims or the general crowd.

Wang: Well, I wanna say, all of my research that I just described in the previous questions, they are all in progress. But what is actually surprising me is, you know, how difficult it can be to translate, you know, general scam awareness into actual resistance. Because people, when they hear about online scam or romance scam, they may even be able to list, right, those clear and obvious warning signs. But recognizing a red flag in those [in the] abstract is very different than actually being able to tell them in the actual conversations when they are having [them] with the scammers. So this is one reasons that, you know, a lot of scam awareness, so-called trainings, can be less effective than they actually think they can [be]. Because a lot of time, you know, the scammers, they will read our papers as well. So they will adapt their strategies as well, simultaneously, when our researchers and our societies begin to progressing against those scams. So that is one central findings of my research.
And another interesting one, from my prevention research, is that, you know, simply creating a sense of threat or fear does not necessarily appear to be the most important mechanism for protecting people—because we do not want to, you know, entice a fear from the victims without actually telling them what the scam is actually about. [This] does not reduce their online activities or sometimes may have more adverse effects on how they actually talk to people online. So what seems especially important for me is that developing people’s motivation and ability to resist the persuasion is more important than enticing just, you know, the simple fear—because that kind of mentality suggests prevention messages should go beyond just saying, “Romance scam are dangerous,” right? So they should teach people what manipulation and persuasion looks like in the actual conversations and what to do when they actually encounter those red flags.
Feltman: And what are some of the red flags that people should be looking out for?
Wang: From a researcher’s standpoint, I think, the first one is not going to be the broken grammar again—because, a lot of [the] time, when people are saying, “Oh, the scammers are using a broken English, or they are using a fragmented sentencing when they are chatting with you, it’s the sign of a scammer,” [but] nowadays scammers are now, they are using AI to generate, you know, sentences. So of course, the grammar is gonna be great. It’s awesome. It’s just like a native, speakers when talking to the victims.
But I wanna say the most important sign I want everyone to notice [is the] use of images and the videos—because you want the person talking to you online [to] show their behavior is consistent, meaning that the images and the videos needs to be always consistent, telling the stories. But, however, it’s very hard in today’s world as well because the deepfakes can always help the scammers to create whatever images and videos they want to create, even in a consistent ways. So although I wanna say it is a red flag, but in some other ways it’s, you know, the scammers, if they really invest into the scam, they probably can overcome this challenge as well.
And the third red flag I wanna mention is whether they will have a video chat or voice chat with you in a live settings. So I wanna say, overall, in general, it’s just very hard to actually, like, completely eliminate the opportunities to encounter scams online, especially on the dating apps.

Tell them what is going on in these conversations, what’s actually raising your suspicions, and they might be the perfect individual that can help you to tell if it is a scam or give you more advice on how to talk to strangers on the platforms. So that’s my suggestions.
Feltman: Yeah. Europe’s carmakers face growing competition from AI for vital supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:39:56 UTC
19:39:56 KST

Europe's car industry is most at risk from its reliance on a handful of countries for chips and critical materials, according to a new report which warns that going electric is pitting carmakers against AI and data centres for the same supplies.
Europe's carmakers rely on a narrow group of countries, suppliers and processing hubs for the chips, magnets and metals their vehicles need, and that dependence is the biggest supply-chain risk facing automotive manufacturing in the bloc, a new study found.
The analysis, carried out by the Czech and German arms of consultancy EY at the request of the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) and published on Tuesday, scored ten critical materials and components against six factors that could constrain supply.
Concentration of supply scored highest, at 4.6 on a five-point scale.
Five inputs stood out as the most vulnerable: semiconductors, silicon, tungsten, neodymium-iron-boron magnets used in electric motors and wiring harnesses, the cable bundles that connect a car's electrical systems.
The industry has felt the risk before.
Chinese curbs on rare-earth exports shut several European production lines last year, according to suppliers' association CLEPA, while a supply crisis at chipmaker Nexperia prompted ACEA to warn of potential "significant disruption to European vehicle manufacturing" last October.
For six of the ten inputs, the riskiest stage is refining and processing the minerals rather than extraction.
China dominates rare-earth refining and magnet production as well as gallium and germanium processing, while Taiwan and South Korea are major chipmaking hubs.
"Europe's main challenge is not only access to raw materials. More critical are the shortages of processing capacity, qualified suppliers and specialised expertise," said Zdeněk Dušek, automotive consulting partner at EY Czech Republic.
"These capabilities cannot be built within one or two years," Dušek added.
Competing with AI
Electrification sharpens the problem.
Electric cars need fewer conventional parts but more semiconductors, power electronics and critical materials, putting carmakers in competition with AI, data centres, defence and clean energy for the same supplies.
The shift to electric vehicles increases competition with other industries for the same critical materials and components by about 15%, the study estimates.
Carmakers are often small customers in these markets, accounting for 17% of end demand for semiconductors and just 3% for gallium, a metal used in power electronics and radar.
Increased competition and concentrated supply chains are pushing prices higher. Gallium, for instance, has risen more than elevenfold in price since 2016, from about $197 to around $2,269 per kilogram, amid growing demand fuelled in part by AI development.
"Carmakers are increasingly competing for these supplies with other industries, such as manufacturers of chips for artificial intelligence," said Martina Nimčová, a manager in business consulting at EY Czech Republic.
Self-driving ambitions add to the pressure, as autonomous functions increase reliance on chips, sensors, gallium and germanium, the study notes.
For instance, Volkswagen partnered with Uber to deploy a fleet of autonomous, all-electric "ID. Buzz AD" microvans, with rides on the Uber platform planned to begin in Los Angeles in late 2026 before scaling to thousands of vehicles.
Meanwhile, Stellantis aims to start producing robotaxis for Uber in 2028 using Nvidia's self-driving technology.
No quick fix
The study outlines four scenarios in which disruptions around the world could leave European carmakers short of vital supplies: disruption to electronics supplies from Taiwan, resource nationalism in Asia, strained trade corridors in the Americas and instability along Africa's mineral export routes.
Logistics is the common thread, and even a short interruption can halt just-in-time production lines, as the 2021-2022 chip shortage showed.
"Expanding capacity for the most critical inputs often takes more than five years," Dušek explained, adding that the advantage goes "not to those with the best strategy on paper, but to those who act earlier and can scale capacity more quickly."
Full self-sufficiency is not realistic, the study concludes.
Instead, it urges Europe to speed up permitting and qualification, target investment at the tightest bottlenecks, diversify suppliers and logistics routes, monitor supply chains more closely and give private investors long-term demand certainty.
"This isn't just risk management. It's about safeguarding Europe's industrial strength," said Sigrid de Vries, ACEA's director general.
With new capacity measured in years, the study's message is that the time to act is before the next shortage, not during it.

How IVF ‘add-on’ treatments put patients in an impossible position
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:39:52 UTC
19:39:52 KST

Alessandra Dowling always wanted a big family. As one of four siblings, she hoped for three little ones of her own. When she found out she was pregnant in December 2022, after months of struggling with fertility, she was thrilled—she pictured sharing the news with family, meeting her baby and bringing her newborn home.
Then, in January 2023, she miscarried. “I was devastated,” Dowling, now age 33, recalls. “I told myself it was probably just bad luck because miscarriages are unfortunately common.” Indeed, around one in five pregnancies end in miscarriage. She still wanted a big family.
After a second miscarriage, “everything changed,” Dowling says. She stopped trusting her body. Every subsequent pregnancy test became associated with fear, not excitement. “I wasn’t just worried about getting pregnant anymore. I was terrified of losing another pregnancy,” she says.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Shortly after, she and her husband decided to turn to in vitro fertilization (IVF), a technique in which eggs are fertilized by sperm in a lab and then transferred to the uterus.
Dowling’s first egg retrieval was in March 2023; it was the beginning of what would be a long—and expensive—process. Insurance generally doesn’t cover IVF. Dowling and her husband paid out-of-pocket for most of their IVF procedures, as well as several “add-on” treatments that would supposedly boost her chances of delivering a baby. These included preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A) to detect any abnormalities in the embryos’ chromosomes; injections of human growth hormone to stimulate the ovaries; ozone therapy, an experimental treatment advertised as improving the odds of pregnancy; and medications to prevent blood clots and regulate her immune system. Dowling also received—and paid for—acupuncture before and throughout her IVF experience.
In all, she estimates she has spent close to $200,000 on fertility-related treatments.
Dowling’s experience isn’t unusual. In the U.S., IVF often costs individuals tens of thousands of dollars. And add-ons like the ones Dowling used are common; surveys conducted in the U.K. and Australia indicate that at least three quarters of IVF patients have tried them at one point or another in the course of their treatment. Yet in many cases, these treatments just aren’t backed by science.
A recent meta-analysis of 10 popular add-on treatments found that three treatments—endometrial receptivity testing (basically, testing of the uterine lining), corticosteroids (a category of immune system drugs) and PGT-A—had little to no impact on the odds of a live birth. Four add-ons—acupuncture, intralipid infusion (fat injections intended to regulate the immune system) and platelet-rich-plasma (PRP), or blood injections, in the uterus and ovaries—had either mixed evidence or low quality data backing them up.
Just three procedures had any evidence of a possible benefit, according to the review: endometrial scratching, a procedure similar to a biopsy, physiological intracytoplasmic sperm injection (PICSI), a method of selecting sperm, and EmbryoGlue, a type of treatment to help embryos attach to the uterus.
While the results don’t prove the treatments are ineffective, they reveal how many products are on the market with little to no evidence of helping people actually give birth to a baby. “Most add-ons are not proven to benefit patients going through IVF,” the study authors concluded.
That conclusion is no surprise to Dowling. She knew that many of the add-ons she used weren’t guaranteed to improve her chances of pregnancy or birth. Both she, a lawyer, and her husband, a physician, are data-oriented individuals, she says. They sifted through research repositories such as PubMed looking for clinical trials, consulted fertility experts and talked to other people who’d gone through the IVF process. Her doctors were transparent that some add-ons might help some people, while others, inexplicably, might see no benefit.
But as she struggled with her fertility, Dowling’s logic shifted. Turning down something that might help, even if the odds were low or unknowable, felt “impossible,” she says.
The add-ons helped her feel that she had “left no stone unturned,” she recalls. “By that point, I was very desperate to have a baby. We were willing to do anything and everything that might improve our chances.”
The reason why so many unproven treatments are available in the U.S. to begin with is murky. For one thing, the U.S. National Institutes of Health has historically restricted studies on IVF, particularly anything to do with the embryo, says Marcelle Cedars, director of the Center for Reproductive Health at the University of California, San Francisco. As a result, research is being done outside of academia—where investigators rely on federal funding—and in an environment “much more driven by market forces,” she says.
That means IVF treatment may be motivated by profit, with clinics being forced to compete over their fertility offerings. And because IVF is generally not covered by insurance, patients aren’t necessarily eager to spend time signing up for clinical trials to test new treatments. Instead they want to pursue the “best” course of action, even if doctors aren’t sure what that looks like, Cedars says.
Dowling had her first child, her son Joey, in August 2024 via IVF.
Before that fateful round, she had consulted a reproductive immunologist and discovered that she had lupus anticoagulant, an antibody associated with abnormal blood clotting and recurrent pregnancy loss. Thinking this may be related to her fertility struggles, Dowling opted to add three medications to her IVF protocol: Lovenox to help reduce abnormal blood clotting; prednisone, a corticosteroid to suppress a negative immune response to an embryo; and an immune regulation medication called Neupogen. Doctors also discovered, and removed, excess tissue in her uterus called a uterine septum.
The round of IVF worked—although Dowling isn’t entirely sure why. Less than a year after her son’s birth, Dowling tried to get pregnant again, opting for the same add-ons as before—with no luck. “Maybe it was the embryo itself,” she says, referring to her successful pregnancy. “Maybe it was simply chance. There’s just no way to know.”
After that unsuccessful round, Dowling found herself considering new add-ons, including platelet-rich plasma and EmbryoGlue, for the next time. Then she got pregnant, conceiving spontaneously without IVF. Her daughter, Gemma, was born in April 2026.
Being a mom is better than Dowling hoped it would be. “It’s exhausting, but it is something that gives me so much happiness,” she says. “It was worth everything and then some.”
Dowling still dreams about having a third baby. For now, she plans to try to get pregnant without assistance. If she returns to IVF, she has two embryos left. If those don’t work, she says, she’s prepared to put IVF behind her. The process has been financially, physically and emotionally draining, she says. “It’s been years of this.”
She also doesn’t regret her add-on treatments. On one level, it didn’t matter whether they’d been vetted or not. At the time, they offered something she needed: peace of mind.
“You’re not necessarily paying for certainty,” she says. “You’re paying for hope. And when you’ve spent years trying to have a child, hope can be incredibly powerful and moving.”

‘Iran determined to strengthen ties with China to contribute to peace, progress in region, world’
TEHRAN- The Embassy of China in Iran held a ceremony on the evening of September 29 at the embassy on the occasion of the 77th anniversary of the National Day of the People’s Republic of China, which was attended by Iranian officials and diplomats from the embassies of different foreign countries.
Iran’s Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, Seyyed Ali Madanizadeh, delivered a speech at the ceremony, the text of which follows below.
In the Name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful
His Excellency Mr. Cong Peiwu, Honorable Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to the Islamic Republic of Iran
Distinguished Guests; Ladies and Gentlemen,
I am sincerely pleased to be present at the ceremony commemorating the seventy-seventh anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China, and I extend my heartfelt congratulations on this great occasion to the people and government of the People’s Republic of China.
I begin my remarks by commemorating and honoring the names of the proud martyrs of the war of aggression against the Iranian people.
China’s National Day is more than an official symbol; it is an opportunity to honor the collective will of a nation that, over the course of decades, through perseverance and civilizational and historical awareness, has created new foundations for progress and prosperity. China’s progress in sustained economic transformation, technological leaps, and its movement toward building a shared future for humanity are manifestations of collective determination, continuous effort, and wise governance.
Distinguished Guests,
Relations between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the People’s Republic of China have ancient, historical-civilizational roots as well as contemporary ties. This year, we commemorate the fifty-fifth anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Iran and China and the tenth anniversary of the declaration of a comprehensive strategic partnership in bilateral relations. The achievements of the past remind us that bonds between nations can be passed from one generation to another and, within a framework of mutual respect, can endure and deepen.
China has adopted an effective and fair economic approach toward the “countries of the Global South” through balanced operational initiatives and multilateral economic institutions. The five initiatives introduced by His Excellency Xi Jinping, the esteemed President of China—namely, the “Belt and Road Initiative,” the “Global Development Initiative,” the “Global Security Initiative,” the “Global Civilization Initiative,” and the “Global Governance Initiative”—have introduced fair frameworks, from both economic and political perspectives, for global cooperation.
Fortunately, the People’s Republic of China is a global leader in the fields of industrial investment, new technologies, mining, clean energy, and the digital economy, and the Islamic Republic of Iran recognizes and appreciates Beijing’s leadership in these emerging areas of the economy.
We believe that, given China’s capacities in emerging sectors, the necessary foundations are in place for the two countries to participate in industrial projects, develop new business models for commercial resilience under conditions of global tension, pursue logistical cooperation, and undertake investment aimed at advancing the understandings reached by the Joint Commission for Economic Cooperation between the two countries.
Distinguished Guests,
Today’s world is facing, more than ever before, serious dangers to the ability of independent countries to determine their own course. The world’s need today is for synergy and cooperation in shaping an order based on justice and equality. Iran and China, as two countries of the Global South, have a decisive role in correcting unilateralist trends in the world. The constructive positions of the People’s Republic of China in support of Iran’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national dignity throughout the recent illegal aggression against Iran represent a turning point in respect for international law and opposition to hegemonic ambitions.
I express my appreciation for the humanitarian assistance provided by the government and people of the People’s Republic of China during the recent war, which has contributed to strengthening people-to-people ties between the two countries. The shared view of Tehran and Beijing on the necessity of respecting the sovereignty of states, reducing tensions, and safeguarding regional peace and stability provides an important foundation for constructive cooperation.
The Islamic Republic of Iran values China’s approach to the formation of an indigenous regional security order, as well as the initiatives of the esteemed President of China, and hopes that the future outlook will be shaped around productive cooperation, expanded intra-regional exchanges, and collective efforts to ensure security and development in the region. China’s practical economic measures to counter sanctions—including the action by China’s Ministry of Commerce prohibiting five Chinese companies from complying with sanctions; multilateral cooperation within the framework of BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, and other financial institutions centered around China—constitute key steps and demonstrate goodwill toward expanding economic cooperation.
Now, amid geopolitical tensions, the restrictive and unfair economic policies of the United States of America against the “economic security” of countries around the world, disruptions to global value chains, the creation of an insecure economic environment, and gaps in technological and mining investment, it is essential to make use of the economic capacities between the two countries through alliances and bilateral cooperation.
Ladies and Gentlemen,
The Islamic Republic of Iran is determined to strengthen comprehensive relations with its civilizational neighbor, the People’s Republic of China, so that, through synergy, it may contribute to peace and progress in the region and the world. Iran and China are moving toward a new chapter of strategic partnership and strong ties in order to implement the 25-year Comprehensive Cooperation Program.
In conclusion, I would like to take this opportunity, as the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance and the head of the Iranian side of the Joint Committee for Economic Cooperation between the two countries, to once again extend, on behalf of the people and government of the Islamic Republic of Iran, my congratulations on the seventy-seventh anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China.
As the renowned Chinese philosopher Mencius said, “Friendship is one soul in two bodies,” I believe that the horizon of Iran-China relations has been shaped on the basis of cooperation and consultation, and I hereby declare our readiness to employ our capacities toward further elevating relations between the two countries.
I wish the two great nations of Iran and China continued dignity, prosperity, and lasting well-being.
Thank you.

In her address, Undersecretary Lind stressed that the international community must respond to Russia’s unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children in a united and decisive manner. “Children are often the unseen victims of aggression,” Lind said. “The deportation and forced Russification of Ukrainian children is a deliberate and systematic activity that is an integral part of Russia’s war machine. The Kremlin’s aim is to sever children’s ties with their homeland, culture and identity and subject them to Russian propaganda, thereby influencing Ukraine’s future.”
“Since the beginning of the full-scale aggression, more than 20,500 Ukrainian children have been taken to Russia. This constitutes a grave violation of international law and human rights, and Russia must be held accountable for all the crimes it has committed,” she added.
According to the Undersecretary, Estonia will continue working with international partners to ensure that every deported child can return home. “Every child has the right to grow up in a safe environment surrounded by their family and loved ones. We must do everything in our power to bring every Ukrainian child home,” said Lind.
Supporting Ukrainian children is an important part of Estonia’s development cooperation with Ukraine. With the support of the Estonian Centre for International Development (ESTDEV), family homes, a kindergarten, a hobby school and a human rights centre have been established in Zhytomyr Oblast to support the education of Ukrainian children and strengthen their sense of security. Supporting the people of Ukraine is also one of the focuses of the human-centred dimension of the Ukraine Recovery Conference, which will take place in Tallinn in January 2027.
On the sidelines of the conference, Undersecretary Lind met with Andorran Foreign Minister Imma Tor Faus, Honduran Foreign Minister Mireya Agüero, Canadian Associate Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs David Angell, Ukrainian Deputy Foreign Minister Mariana Betsa, State Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of North Macedonia Jovica Palashevski, and UK Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State Lord Wood of Anfield.
During her visit, the Undersecretary also learned about the progress of the KESKUS Estonian cultural centre, met with representatives of the Estonian Central Council in Canada and visited the editorial office of Eesti Elu.

Ukraine’s New Electromagnetic System Makes Mines Detonate Before Armored Vehicles Reach Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:36:22 UTC
19:36:22 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s New Electromagnetic System Makes Mines Detonate Before Armored Vehicles Reach Them
Ukraine has developed and begun deploying an electromagnetic mine-clearing system designed to trigger mines with magnetic fuzes before armored vehicles reach them.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on September 29, the Ukrainian-made system, called PIDRYV, generates a controlled magnetic field ahead of a vehicle and can activate magnetically triggered mines from a distance of up to seven meters.
The system has been tested on armored vehicles, unmanned ground vehicles, and mine-clearing platforms. Militarnyi reported that PIDRYV systems have already been supplied to three brigades of the Armed Forces of Ukraine for combat use and have been codified within the NATO system.
Unlike conventional pressure mines, magnetic mines do not require a wheel or track to physically pass over them. Their fuzes can detect changes in the surrounding magnetic field caused by an approaching vehicle.
PIDRYV is intended to reproduce that magnetic signature ahead of the vehicle. If the system activates a mine, the detonation is expected to occur several meters in front of the platform rather than directly beneath it.
According to the Ukrainian manufacturer cited by Militarnyi, approximately 30% to 40% of mines used in remote mining operations are equipped with magnetic initiators.
The system operates while the vehicle is moving, meaning crews do not need to stop while attempting to activate magnetic fuzes along their route.
Images published by Militarnyi show PIDRYV installed on a Ukrainian-operated International MaxxPro armored vehicle and an unmanned ground vehicle. The system has also undergone testing on a dedicated mine-clearing vehicle.
Electromagnetic mine-clearing technology predates Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Soviet Union began developing a comparable system, known as Paishchik, in the early 1970s and adopted it in 1985.
That system used two electromagnets mounted on a mine-clearing frame to generate a magnetic field capable of activating mines roughly four to six meters ahead of a tank. Rather than functioning as an independent mine plow, it supplemented existing mechanical mine-clearing equipment with protection against magnetically triggered mines.
Earlier, Ukraine approved the domestically developed NEO-1 ground robot for deployment, a remote-controlled system designed to detect mines and unexploded ordnance while also carrying supplies for frontline units.

Iraq says US-led coalition mission has ended
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:36:18 UTC
19:36:18 KST

Iraq has announced the end of the US-led international coalition’s mission, marking a transition to bilateral relations with coalition member states, the prime minister’s security adviser said.
In a statement carried by the official Iraqi News Agency on Wednesday, Qasim al Araji called the move an “important milestone,” saying it followed negotiations and understandings that began in July 2021.
US forces completed their withdrawal from their remaining positions in Iraq at the end of this month.
He said the new phase would involve “bilateral relations with its countries” aimed at consolidating Iraq’s sovereignty.
Araji credited the victory over the Daesh terrorist group to “the sacrifices of Iraqis and the valour of our armed forces in their various branches and formations,” as well as support from the international coalition and brotherly and friendly countries.
He stressed that ending the coalition’s mission “does not mean the end of the partnership,” but rather a shift towards bilateral relations with its member states.
Security and intelligence cooperation, along with the exchange of information and expertise and capacity-building efforts, will continue “on the basis of mutual respect and shared interests,” he said.
Bilateral security relationship
The US Department of War said on Wednesday that the US and its coalition partners “formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq,” while the “orderly departure” of coalition forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base marked the conclusion of the military mission.
Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell said the milestone “marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.”
He said the 12-year campaign “defeated Daesh as an organised military threat in Iraq and across the region.”
Parnell said that the US expects the Iraqi Security Forces to “lead the continuing effort to secure Iraq and keep Daesh remnants suppressed,” noting that the US Department of Defense will continue to provide “targeted training and intelligence support” to its Iraqi partners.
“The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq’s remaining security challenges, including Daesh remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the Government of Iraq,” Parnell said.
Separately, US Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed on Wednesday that US forces and equipment had completed their “orderly departure” from Erbil Air Base in northern Iraq, marking the end of the Operation Inherent Resolve mission in Iraq.
CENTCOM said the move was “part of a planned transition to a US-Iraq bilateral defence relationship.”
The Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve “remains operational” and is now headquartered in Jordan, while US forces “continue the counter-Daesh mission in Syria alongside Coalition partners and the Syrian government,” CENTCOM said.
Baghdad and Washington agreed in September 2024 to end the coalition’s military mission in Iraq under a timetable extending through the end of September 2026, with a transition to bilateral security relations between Iraq and member states.
The coalition was formed under US leadership in 2014 after Daesh seized large areas of Iraq and Syria, providing Iraqi forces with air, intelligence and training support during operations against the terror group.
Iraq announced in December 2017 that it had regained full control of territory seized by Daesh.

KAZAN, September 30. /TASS/. Representatives from more than 40 countries have registered for the international Kazan Digital Week forum, which will take place on October 29-31, 2026, the forum’s organizers told TASS.
"Representatives from 47 countries have registered to participate in the forum. <...> The business program is 95% complete. The forum’s events will take place in 21 halls and three exhibition spaces. The plenary session will focus on ‘Trusted Digital Ecosystem: Artificial Intelligence, Data and Technological Sovereignty,’" the organizers said following a meeting of the organizing committee for the forum, chaired by Russian Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadaev.

The traditional exhibition held during the forum will be expanded this year. "It will occupy three pavilions with a total area of 20,000 square meters, one-third larger than last year. So far, 86% of the exhibition space has already been booked. Most of the solutions on display are related to artificial intelligence technologies," the statement said.
According to the organizers, participants will for the first time have access to an expanded startup alley and a pitch session area featuring 60 IT projects: 30 Russian, 20 foreign and 10 teams that won hackathons. The semifinals and final of the fourth season of the International Robot Battle Championship will also take place in Kazan during the forum. Ukraine Identifies 23 Companies Making Missiles for Russia’s Pantsir—One-Third Remain Unsanctioned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:36:00 UTC
19:36:00 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Identifies 23 Companies Making Missiles for Russia’s Pantsir—One-Third Remain Unsanctioned
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) has identified 23 Russian companies involved in producing 95Ya6 guided missiles for Russia’s Pantsir air defense systems, the agency said on September 30.
The information was published on HUR’s War&Sanctions portal and details companies participating in the production chain for the 95Ya6, the primary medium-range missile used by various modifications of the Pantsir system.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Pantsir is a family of Russian short-range self-propelled surface-to-air missile and gun systems designed to protect military, industrial, and other strategic facilities. Russia also uses the systems to strengthen air defenses at low and extremely low altitudes and counter large-scale aerial attacks.
According to HUR, the Shipunov Instrument Design Bureau plays a central role in the production chain as the primary developer and manufacturer of the 95Ya6 missile. The company is also involved in producing weapons for Russia’s Orion unmanned systems, Krasnopol guided artillery shells, and cannons for Sukhoi fighter jets.
Among the newly identified companies are the Komponent plant, which produces proximity target sensors for the missiles; the Sergo Ordzhonikidze Saratov Electrical Instrument-Making Plant, which supplies radiation and power units; and the Tambov Elektropribor plant, which manufactures control equipment for the 95Ya6.
HUR said approximately one-third of the 23 companies disclosed in the latest update are not currently sanctioned by any country participating in the international sanctions coalition.
The latest disclosure follows HUR’s earlier publication of information on more than 50 companies involved in manufacturing the 72V6 combat vehicle used in the Pantsir-S1 system.
Russia has deployed Pantsir systems to protect strategically important sites, including placing them on rooftops in Moscow since 2023. According to HUR, a newer Pantsir-SMD-E variant has also been observed in the Russian capital this year. Unlike previous versions, the system uses small TKB-1055 Gvozd missiles instead of automatic cannons.
“Air defense systems, including Pantsir systems, provide protection for Russian facilities producing cruise and ballistic missiles, while also shielding Russian military formations during offensive and defensive operations in Ukraine, as well as other strategically important sites in Russia,” the agency added.
The disclosure comes after Ukrainian forces destroyed two Russian Pantsir-S1 systems in separate strikes in temporarily occupied Crimea and Russia’s Krasnodar region in late August.
One system was destroyed near occupied Kerch on August 29, while another was struck near a military airfield in Yeysk, Krasnodar region, the following day, according to the open-source channel Dossier Shpiona, which published images of the destroyed systems.

“If People Are in a Bunker, Business Stops”: Missile Alerts Cost Ukraine $45 Million an Hour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:35:54 UTC
19:35:54 KST

- Category
- Life in Ukraine
“If People Are in a Bunker, Business Stops”: Missile Alerts Cost Ukraine $45 Million an Hour
Ukraine is losing an estimated $45 million for every hour that missile alerts force businesses to suspend operations, as intensified Russian aerial attacks increasingly disrupt economic activity across the country, The Guardian reported on September 30.
Ukraine’s Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said Russian forces have increasingly targeted infrastructure critical to the economy, including industrial facilities, warehouses, logistics hubs, and data centers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Kravchenko, the expanding use of jet-powered drones has added to the pressure on businesses, with Russian forces deploying the weapons against a growing range of targets.
“What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything,” Kravchenko told The Guardian.
The attacks have repeatedly brought economic activity to a halt as employees are required to move to shelters during air raid alerts, which can last for up to 10 hours a day.
“If people are in a bunker, business stops,” Kravchenko said.
In an effort to limit the economic impact of prolonged alerts, the Ukrainian government recently introduced a two-tier warning system intended to allow businesses to continue operating when the threat level permits.
Under the system, a “red” alert signals a missile threat and requires people to seek shelter, while a “yellow” warning indicates a drone threat and allows many businesses to remain open.
According to the outlet, Kravchenko said more than half of businesses continue operating during yellow alerts, allowing economic activity to continue despite the ongoing threat of Russian aerial attacks.
The economic disruption comes as Russia continues to target Ukraine’s commercial and logistics infrastructure. Russian attacks have damaged around 500,000 square meters of warehouse space, while Ukraine could lose more than $2 billion in export revenue in the second half of 2026.
The ministry said Russian forces carried out more than 25 strikes on warehouse facilities during the first half of the year alone. Russia has also targeted Ukraine’s broader logistics network, launching more than 1,000 attacks on railway infrastructure and repeatedly striking ports in the Greater Odesa area.
Overall, Russia launched 3,177 jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles against Ukraine in September, up from 2,850 recorded in August.

Russia posts highest crude export earnings since 2022 – Bloomberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
10:35:25 UTC
19:35:25 KST

Russia posts highest crude export earnings since 2022 – Bloomberg
Russia’s earnings from seaborne crude exports have surged to their highest weekly level since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, Bloomberg has reported. Rising oil prices and stronger shipment volumes have boosted Moscow’s revenues despite Western sanctions.
The gross value of Russian crude exports reached $2.75 billion in the week through September 27, the outlet reported on Tuesday. On a four-week basis, shipments averaged 3.71 million barrels per day, their highest since early August, while their value climbed to $2.39 billion a week.
According to the outlet, the increase has been driven by both higher crude prices and growing export volumes. Global oil prices have risen sharply during the US-Israeli war on Iran amid the disruption of shipping via the Strait of Hormuz, boosting earnings for major producers outside the Persian Gulf, including Russia.
The surge comes despite Western efforts to curb Moscow’s energy earnings. The G7, EU and Australia introduced a $60-per-barrel price cap on Russian crude in December 2022 alongside an EU embargo on seaborne imports, followed by restrictions on Russian petroleum products in February 2023.
The measures were designed to reduce Russia’s revenues while keeping its crude flowing to global markets and avoiding a supply shock. Moscow responded by redirecting much of its oil trade away from Europe toward China, India and other markets, which now account for the bulk of Russian seaborne crude purchases. According to Bloomberg, shipments to Asian customers, including cargoes whose final destination was not yet known, rose to 3.61 million barrels per day in the four weeks through September 27.
Russia’s latest crude windfall has, however, been partly offset by falling exports of refined fuels. Moscow has restricted diesel shipments to protect domestic supplies after an unprecedented wave of Ukrainian drone strikes damaged refineries across the country, while lower processing rates have left more crude available for export.
Russia has consequently raised its crude-export forecast for 2026 by about 150,000 barrels per day while cutting its forecast for refined-product shipments by roughly 500,000 barrels per day, according to Bloomberg.
Western governments are meanwhile continuing to pressure European states that still rely on Russian energy. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul urged Slovakia on Tuesday to phase out Russian oil and gas and increase pressure on Moscow, days after meeting Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in New York.
Slovakia has resisted a rapid cutoff, with Russian supplies accounting for more than 80% of its oil and over half of its gas imports in 2025, according to the European Commission. Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanar said the country had built its energy infrastructure around Russian supplies and warned that abandoning them immediately would create “enormous problems,” arguing that alternative routes currently lack sufficient capacity.

Erdoğan speaks at a meeting with provincial leaders in Ankara. (AA Photo)

“The AKP is a party that is pure, as its name suggests. It truly embodies the meaning of its name. No one can tarnish this party’s purity or cast a stain upon it,” Erdoğan said at a meeting with provincial leaders in Ankara.
Without naming specific individuals, Erdoğan noted that certain figures have tried to undermine the party.

Welcoming the decision to pursue the issue, Bahçeli expressed support for the announced measures. He cited financial-market stability, holding those engaging in market-distorting transactions responsible and protecting small investors from such situations as key priorities.
The MHP leader also warned against turning the scandal into what he described as an attack or slander against Erdoğan and the ruling alliance.

19:24:32 KST

At least 115,593 people, or 7.42% of Latvia’s 1,557,615 eligible voters, have cast their ballots so far ahead of the Saeima election, according to data compiled by the Central Election Commission (CVK).
In Riga, at least 47,843 people, or 7.98% of eligible voters, have cast their ballots. This figure also includes 4,907 people abroad who registered to vote by post.
For postal voting, the number of voters considered to have voted includes those who were sent voting materials and who have not voted or deposited a ballot for safekeeping in person at a polling station, the CVK explained.
Among the regions, the highest turnout over the four days has been recorded in Vidzeme, where at least 33,134 voters, or 8.26%, have deposited their ballots for safekeeping.
In Zemgale, turnout has reached 6.53%, with 13,019 citizens having visited polling stations so far.
 In Kurzeme, at least 11,568 people, or 6.64%, have deposited their ballots, while in Latgale 10,029 voters have cast their ballots so far, representing 5.46% of eligible voters.
As of Thursday, the highest turnout has been recorded in Ādaži Municipality, where 12.19% of registered eligible voters have cast their ballots. The lowest turnout has been recorded in Augšdaugava Municipality, at 4%.
Data from some polling stations are still being awaited.
Throughout the working days of this week, voters can deposit their ballots for safekeeping at any of the 933 polling stations across Latvia.
The CVK explains that this form of voting is conceptually similar to advance voting, although there are some procedural differences that allow voters to change their minds during the week leading up to election day and replace the ballot they have already deposited.
The official Saeima election day is Saturday.

====================================================================================================

Surviving the execution chamber: Five US cases before Christa Pike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:33:11 UTC
19:33:11 KST

Christa Pike, the only woman on Tennessee’s death row, has survived an execution attempt after receiving two injections of a lethal drug.
Her lawyers said on Thursday that she was being treated in hospital, while Governor Bill Lee suspended executions for the rest of the year and ordered an independent review.
Pike’s case is not the first in which a prisoner has left the execution chamber alive in the United States. Previous failed attempts have ended with prisoners later executed, sometimes using a different method, or dying in custody before another attempt.
Surviving an execution attempt does not automatically overturn a death sentence. US courts have permitted authorities to try again, including in a 2016 Ohio Supreme Court ruling that a second attempt was not inherently barred by the constitutional ban on cruel and unusual punishment.
Here are five earlier cases and what followed.
Tony Carruthers: Two failed executions, one doctor
Tennessee halted its attempt to execute Tony Carruthers on May 21 2026, after staff were unable to establish the intravenous access required by the state’s lethal injection protocol.
The physician involved was Dr Mark Fowler, who was later selected to oversee Pike’s execution and administer her lethal injection, according to NPR. Tennessee-based broadcaster WVLT subsequently reported that the same doctor administered the injection that Pike survived.
In Carruthers’ case, officials said medical personnel secured a primary IV line but could not establish a backup. An attempt to insert a central line also failed.
Carruthers, sentenced to death for the kidnapping and murder of three people in 1994, was returned to his cell after officials spent more than an hour attempting the procedure, according to Reuters report.
Governor Bill Lee then granted him a one-year reprieve, postponing his execution without commuting his death sentence.
Kenneth Eugene Smith: Executed with nitrogen after surviving lethal injection
Alabama’s first attempt to execute Kenneth Eugene Smith in 2022 was abandoned after officials were unable to access a vein to administer the lethal drugs.
Smith spent about four hours strapped to a gurney as legal challenges played out and staff repeatedly tried to access his veins, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
His lawyers later argued that a second execution attempt would violate the constitutional ban on cruel and unusual punishment, but the US Supreme Court declined to stop it.
On January 25 2024, Alabama executed Smith, this time using nitrogen gas. Smith, 58, became the first person executed using the method, breathing pure nitrogen through a mask that deprived him of oxygen.
The execution lasted about 22 minutes, and Smith appeared to remain conscious for several minutes.
Alan Eugene Miller: A second attempt using a different method
Alabama’s attempt to execute Alan Eugene Miller by lethal injection in September 2022 failed after difficulties accessing his veins. A federal judge subsequently ordered the state to preserve evidence relating to the aborted procedure.
On September 26 2024, Alabama executed him using nitrogen gas, making him the second person put to death by that method.
Witnesses reported that he shook, pulled against his restraints and gasped for several minutes. Alabama’s corrections commissioner said the movements were involuntary and that the execution had proceeded as planned.
Miller had been sentenced to death for killing three men in workplace shootings in 1999.
Doyle Lee Hamm: A bloodied execution chamber and a deal preventing another attempt
Alabama abandoned its attempt to execute Doyle Lee Hamm in February 2018, after about two and a half hours of unsuccessful efforts to access a vein to administer the lethal drugs.
The procedure left Hamm, then 61, with at least 12 puncture wounds and the execution chamber bloodied, his lawyer, Columbia Law School professor Bernard Harcourt, said, according to a 2018 Reuters report. Medical personnel had tried to access veins in his groin and lower legs.
His lawyers had warned that terminal cancer and a history of intravenous drug use had severely compromised his veins. Alabama maintained that it could carry out the procedure, but stopped when officials determined the difficulties could not be resolved before the death warrant expired at midnight.
A federal judge subsequently ordered the state to preserve evidence, including Hamm’s clothing.
In March 2018, Hamm and Alabama reached a confidential settlement preventing further execution attempts, according to Harcourt.
Hamm remained on death row and died in November 2021 after suffering from cancer. It was the agreement, rather than an automatic legal exemption for surviving the first attempt, that prevented another execution attempt.
Romell Broom: Courts allowed another attempt, but he died before it could take place
Ohio stopped Romell Broom’s execution on September 15 2009, after staff spent about two hours trying unsuccessfully to access a vein to administer the lethal drugs.
Broom challenged the state’s right to try again, arguing that another attempt would violate constitutional protections against being punished twice for the same crime and against cruel and unusual punishment.
In 2016, the Ohio Supreme Court rejected his challenge in a 4–3 decision, noting that no lethal drugs had been administered during the first attempt.
His execution was eventually rescheduled for March 2022 after a shortage of execution drugs forced another postponement.
But Broom died in custody on December 28 2020, aged 64, before another attempt could take place. Prison authorities said he was suspected to have died from complications of COVID-19, pending confirmation.

Modern cars’ smart features could be used to spy on you, drivers warned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:25:02 UTC
19:25:02 KST

Drivers have been warned that the smart features built into modern cars such as microphones, cameras and GPS trackers could be used by hostile states to spy on them.
The Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) called for “awareness of espionage risks around modern vehicles”, including microphones that can by switched on remotely to listen to conversations.
It did not mention an individual country, but the warning will add to concerns around a recent boom in Chinese car imports into the UK.
In a translated document released on Wednesday, the agency said cars are becoming “increasingly smart” with digital systems that collect data and connect to the internet.
“On the one hand this offers practical benefits, but on the other hand these systems collect a great deal of data about occupants, the vehicle itself, and about objects and people in the vicinity. Various parties, including state actors, can gain access to this data,” it added.
The warning follows reports last year that British defence firms working for the UK government had warned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices.
Chinese-owned brands now account for 15% of all new cars registered in the UK, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, almost 175,000 vehicles in the first half of 2026 and more than double the same period last year.
Models by MG, BYD and Jaecoo, whose parent company Chery is part-owned by the Chinese state, have led the surge, popular for their low price and in-car technology. The Jaecoo 7 was the UK’s bestselling car in March.
MPs have raised concerns that China’s national intelligence law requires its companies to assist the state’s intelligence services when requested.
The UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) has said it is working with other government departments “to understand and mitigate any potential threats to national security” from vehicles.
This year the MoD reportedly banned cars with Chinese parts from sensitive military sites, including RAF Wyton, a site in Cambridgeshire, and the Dorset headquarters of the Special Boat Service, a UK special operations unit.
The AIVD said it is “technically possible to activate” microphones and cameras remotely in some cars, allowing malicious actors to “eavesdrop on conversations” and “make recordings in and around the vehicle”.
The service warned drivers “do not hold confidential conversations in or around the vehicle”, and “do not use a vehicle with an external camera when travelling to a sensitive location”.
It also said connecting phones and other devices, either via Bluetooth, wifi or charging systems could allow malicious actors to “extract data from connected devices via the vehicle”. It suggested systems such as GPS navigation systems, telematics modules and charging stations could all be used to gather and send data about the car and drivers’ whereabouts elsewhere.
Earlier this week MI5 issued a rare public warning to UK universities to stop working with the China General Technology Research Institute, which it said was being used as a front by Beijing’s intelligence service to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.
The Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”.

Russian troop losses rose 46% since January, hit 2026 high in September, Ukraine says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:33:04 UTC
19:33:04 KST

Russian troop losses rose 46% since January, hit 2026 high in September, Ukraine says
Russian forces suffered an estimated 46,230 personnel losses in September, the highest monthly figure recorded by Ukraine so far in 2026, Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 1.
The September figure surpassed previous summer highs of 42,860 in July and 42,020 in August. According to the General Staff, Russian personnel losses have risen from 31,710 in January to 46,230 in September — an increase of nearly 46%.
"This dynamic demonstrates the complete inability of the occupying forces' military leadership to achieve its objectives, as well as the growing accuracy and effectiveness of Ukrainian units' strikes," the General Staff said on Telegram.
Inflicting heavy personnel losses has become a stated strategic objective of Ukraine. In January, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Ukraine aimed to "kill 50,000 Russians per month," arguing that losses on that scale could undermine Moscow's ability to sustain the war.
The September figure brings Russia's estimated monthly losses closer to that target than at any previous point this year.
The increase also comes as Russia faces growing pressure to replace troops while sustaining offensive operations along the front.
December 2025 marked the first month in which Russian personnel losses exceeded the number of troops Moscow managed to recruit, according to the General Staff. Since then, the manpower balance has remained an increasingly important issue as the Kremlin seeks to sustain the war without announcing a new wave of mobilization.
Russia continues to rely heavily on contract recruitment and financial incentives, but recruitment has slowed.
Janis Kluge, a research fellow at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, said, citing regional budget data, that 234,000 new military contracts were signed in the first eight months of this year, compared with 260,000 in the same period in 2025.
Ukrainian intelligence has also said Russia's General Staff is prepared to mobilize around 300,000 people in 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027 if needed.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in July that Russia has lost more than 1.5 million troops killed or wounded since the beginning of the full-scale invasion. The figures cannot be independently verified, and Moscow does not publish comprehensive casualty data.
